\part{About LAMMPS and this manual}
\label{\detokenize{Manual:about-lammps-and-this-manual}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS stands for \sphinxstylestrong{L}arge\sphinxhyphen{}scale \sphinxstylestrong{A}tomic/\sphinxstylestrong{M}olecular
\sphinxstylestrong{M}assively \sphinxstylestrong{P}arallel \sphinxstylestrong{S}imulator.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is a classical molecular dynamics simulation code focusing on
materials modeling.  It was designed to run efficiently on parallel
computers and to be easy to extend and modify.  Originally developed at
Sandia National Laboratories, a US Department of Energy facility, LAMMPS
now includes contributions from many research groups and individuals
from many institutions.  Most of the funding for LAMMPS has come from
the US Department of Energy (DOE).  LAMMPS is open\sphinxhyphen{}source software
distributed under the terms of the GNU Public License Version 2 (GPLv2).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org}{LAMMPS website} has a variety of information about the
code.  It includes links to an online version of this manual, an
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/forum.html}{online forum} where users can post
questions and discuss LAMMPS, and a \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps}{GitHub site} where all LAMMPS development is
coordinated.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The content for this manual is part of the LAMMPS distribution in its
doc directory.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The version of the manual on the LAMMPS website corresponds to the
latest LAMMPS feature release.  It is available at:
\sphinxurl{https://docs.lammps.org/}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A version of the manual corresponding to the latest LAMMPS stable
release (state of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} branch on GitHub) is available online
at: \sphinxurl{https://docs.lammps.org/stable/}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A version of the manual with the features most recently added to
LAMMPS (state of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch on GitHub) is available at:
\sphinxurl{https://docs.lammps.org/latest/}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If needed, you can build a copy on your local machine of the manual
(HTML pages or PDF file) for the version of LAMMPS you have
downloaded.  Follow the steps on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_manual::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build the LAMMPS documentation}}}} page.

\section{Overview of LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_overview:overview-of-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Intro_overview::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is a classical molecular dynamics (MD) code that models ensembles
of particles in a liquid, solid, or gaseous state.  It can model atomic,
polymeric, biological, solid\sphinxhyphen{}state (metals, ceramics, oxides), granular,
coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained, or macroscopic systems using a variety of interatomic
potentials (force fields) and boundary conditions.  It can model 2d or
3d systems with sizes ranging from only a few particles up to billions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can be built and run on single laptop or desktop machines, but is
designed for parallel computers.  It will run in serial and on any
parallel machine that supports the \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message\_Passing\_Interface}{MPI} message\sphinxhyphen{}passing
library.  This includes shared\sphinxhyphen{}memory multicore, multi\sphinxhyphen{}CPU servers and
distributed\sphinxhyphen{}memory clusters and supercomputers. Parts of LAMMPS also
support \sphinxhref{https://www.openmp.org}{OpenMP multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading}, vectorization, and GPU
acceleration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is written in C++ and requires a compiler that is at least
compatible with the C++\sphinxhyphen{}11 standard.  Earlier versions were written in
F77, F90, and C++\sphinxhyphen{}98.  See the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/history.html}{History page} of the website for details.  All
versions can be downloaded as source code from the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org}{LAMMPS website}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed to be easy to modify or extend with new capabilities,
such as new force fields, atom types, boundary conditions, or
diagnostics.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modifying \& extending LAMMPS}}}} section of for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the most general sense, LAMMPS integrates Newton’s equations of
motion for a collection of interacting particles.  A single particle can
be an atom or molecule or electron, a coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained cluster of atoms,
or a mesoscopic or macroscopic clump of material.  The interaction
models that LAMMPS includes are mostly short\sphinxhyphen{}ranged in nature; some
long\sphinxhyphen{}range models are included as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS uses neighbor lists to keep track of nearby particles.  The lists
are optimized for systems with particles that are repulsive at short
distances, so that the local density of particles never becomes too
large.  This is in contrast to methods used for modeling plasma or
gravitational bodies (like galaxy formation).

\sphinxAtStartPar
On parallel machines, LAMMPS uses spatial\sphinxhyphen{}decomposition techniques with
MPI parallelization to partition the simulation domain into subdomains
of equal computational cost, one of which is assigned to each processor.
Processors communicate and store “ghost” atom information for atoms that
border their subdomain.  Multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading parallelization and GPU
acceleration with particle\sphinxhyphen{}decomposition can be used in addition.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{What does a LAMMPS version mean}
\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:what-does-a-lammps-version-mean}}\label{\detokenize{Manual_version::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS “version” is the date when it was released, such as 1 May
2014.  LAMMPS is updated continuously, and we aim to keep it working
correctly and reliably at all times.  Also, several variants of static
code analysis are run regularly to maintain or improve the overall code
quality, consistency, and compliance with programming standards, best
practices and style conventions.  You can follow its development in a
public \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps}{git repository on GitHub}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each version of LAMMPS contains all the documented \sphinxstyleemphasis{features} up to and
including its version date.  For recently added features, we add markers
to the documentation at which specific LAMMPS version a feature or
keyword was added or significantly changed.


\subsection{Identifying the Version}
\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:identifying-the-version}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The version date is printed to the screen and log file every time you
run LAMMPS.  There also is an indication, if a LAMMPS binary was
compiled from version with modifications \sphinxstylestrong{after} a release.
It is also visible in the file src/version.h and in the LAMMPS directory
name created when you unpack a downloaded tarball.  And it is on the
first page of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Manual::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{manual}}}}.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you browse the HTML pages of the online version of the LAMMPS
manual, they will by default describe the most current feature release
version of LAMMPS.  In the navigation bar on the bottom left, there is
the option to view instead the documentation for the most recent
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} version or the documentation corresponding to the state of
the development branch.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you browse the HTML pages included in your downloaded tarball, they
describe the version you have, which may be older than the online
version.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{LAMMPS releases, branches, and tags}
\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:lammps-releases-branches-and-tags}}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{lammps-releases}.png}
\caption{Relations between releases, main branches, and tags in the LAMMPS git repository}\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:id1}}\end{figure}


\subsubsection{Development}
\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:development}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modifications of the LAMMPS source code (like bug fixes, code
refactoring, updates to existing features, or addition of new features)
are organized into pull requests.  Pull requests will be merged into the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch of the git repository after they pass automated testing
and code review by the LAMMPS developers.


\subsubsection{Feature Releases}
\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:feature-releases}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When a sufficient number of new features and updates have accumulated
\sphinxstyleemphasis{and} the LAMMPS version on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch passes an extended set
of automated tests, we release it as a \sphinxstyleemphasis{feature release}, which are
currently made every 4 to 8 weeks.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{release} branch of the git
repository is updated with every such \sphinxstyleemphasis{feature release} and a tag in the
format \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{patch\_1May2014}} is added.  A summary of the most important
changes of these releases for the current year are posted on \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bug.html}{this
website page}.  More detailed release
notes are \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/releases/}{available on GitHub}.


\subsubsection{Stable Releases}
\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:stable-releases}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
About once a year, we release a \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable release} version of LAMMPS.
This is done after a “stabilization period” where we apply only bug
fixes and small, non\sphinxhyphen{}intrusive changes to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch but no
new features.  At the same time, the code is subjected to more detailed
and thorough manual testing than the default automated testing.
After such a \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable release}, both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{release} and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable}
branches are updated and two tags are applied, a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{patch\_1May2014}} format
and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stable\_1May2014}} format tag.


\subsubsection{Stable Release Updates}
\label{\detokenize{Manual_version:stable-release-updates}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Between \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable releases}, we collect bug fixes and updates back\sphinxhyphen{}ported
from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch in a branch called \sphinxstyleemphasis{maintenance}.  From the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{maintenance} branch we make occasional \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable update releases} and
update the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} branch accordingly.  The first update to the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stable\_1May2014}} release would be tagged as
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stable\_1May2014\_update1}}.  These updates contain no new features.

\sphinxstepscope

\subsection{General features}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_features:general-features}}\label{\detokenize{Intro_features:general}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
runs on a single processor or in parallel

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
distributed memory message\sphinxhyphen{}passing parallelism (MPI)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
shared memory multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading parallelism (OpenMP)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
spatial decomposition of simulation domain for MPI parallelism

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
particle decomposition inside spatial decomposition for OpenMP and GPU parallelism

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GPLv2 licensed open\sphinxhyphen{}source distribution

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
highly portable C++\sphinxhyphen{}11 (optional packages may require C++17)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
modular code with most functionality in optional packages

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
only depends on MPI library for basic parallel functionality, MPI stub for serial compilation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
other libraries are optional and only required for specific packages

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GPU (CUDA, OpenCL, HIP, SYCL), Intel Xeon Phi, and OpenMP support for many code features

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
easy to extend with new features and functionality

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
runs from an input script

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
syntax for defining and using variables and formulas

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
syntax for looping over runs and breaking out of loops

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
run one or multiple simulations simultaneously (in parallel) from one script

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
build as library, invoke LAMMPS through library interface (from C, C++, Fortran) or provided Python wrapper or SWIG based wrappers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
couple with other codes: LAMMPS calls other code, other code calls LAMMPS, umbrella code calls both, MDI coupling interface

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
call out to Python for computing forces, time integration, or other tasks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
plugin interface for loading external features at runtime

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
large integrated collection of tests

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Interatomic potentials (force fields)}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_features:interatomic-potentials-force-fields}}\label{\detokenize{Intro_features:ff}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(See {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace style}}}}
commands)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pairwise potentials: Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones, Buckingham, Morse, Born\sphinxhyphen{}Mayer\sphinxhyphen{}Huggins, Yukawa, soft, Class II (COMPASS), hydrogen bond, harmonic, gaussian, tabulated, scripted

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
charged pairwise potentials: Coulombic, point\sphinxhyphen{}dipole

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials: EAM, Finnis/Sinclair, MEAM, MEAM+SW, EIM, EDIP, ADP, Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber, Tersoff, REBO, AIREBO, ReaxFF, COMB, Streitz\sphinxhyphen{}Mintmire, 3\sphinxhyphen{}body polymorphic, BOP, Vashishta

long\sphinxhyphen{}range interactions for charge, point\sphinxhyphen{}dipoles, and LJ dispersion:  Ewald, Wolf, PPPM (similar to particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh Ewald), MSM, ScaFaCoS

electron force field (eFF, AWPMD)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bond potentials: harmonic, FENE, Morse, nonlinear, Class II (COMPASS), quartic (breakable), tabulated, scripted

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dihedral potentials: harmonic, CHARMM, multi\sphinxhyphen{}harmonic, helix, Class II (COMPASS), OPLS, tabulated, scripted

\item {}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
polymer potentials: all\sphinxhyphen{}atom, united\sphinxhyphen{}atom, bead\sphinxhyphen{}spring, breakable

\item {}

water potentials: TIP3P, TIP4P, SPC, SPC/E and variants

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
interlayer potentials for graphene and analogues, hetero\sphinxhyphen{}junctions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
metal\sphinxhyphen{}organic framework potentials (QuickFF, MO\sphinxhyphen{}FF)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
implicit solvent potentials: hydrodynamic lubrication, Debye

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
force\sphinxhyphen{}field compatibility with CHARMM, AMBER, DREIDING, OPLS, GROMACS, Class II (COMPASS), UFF, ClayFF, DREIDING, AMOEBA, INTERFACE

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
access to the \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{OpenKIM Repository} of potentials via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
hybrid potentials: multiple pair, bond, angle, dihedral, improper potentials can be used in one simulation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
overlaid potentials: superposition of multiple pair potentials (including many\sphinxhyphen{}body) with optional scale factor

\end{itemize}

\section{LAMMPS non\sphinxhyphen{}features}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_nonfeatures:lammps-non-features}}\label{\detokenize{Intro_nonfeatures::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed to be a fast, parallel engine for molecular
dynamics (MD) simulations.  It provides only a modest amount of
functionality for setting up simulations and analyzing their output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Originally, LAMMPS was not conceived and designed for:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
being run through a GUI

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
building molecular systems, or building molecular topologies

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
assign force\sphinxhyphen{}field coefficients automagically

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
perform sophisticated analysis of your MD simulation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
visualize your MD simulation interactively

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
plot your output data

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Over the years many of these limitations have been reduced or
removed. In part through features added to LAMMPS and in part
through external tools that either closely interface with LAMMPS
or extend LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are suggestions on how to perform these tasks:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{GUI:} LAMMPS can be built as a library and a Python module that
wraps the library interface is provided.  Thus, GUI interfaces can be
written in Python or C/C++ that run LAMMPS and visualize or plot its
output.  Examples of this are provided in the python directory and
described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since version 2 August 2023 {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{a LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI tool}}}} is
included in LAMMPS.  Also, there are several external wrappers or GUI
front ends that are mentioned on the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/prepost.html}{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}/post\sphinxhyphen{}processing tools page} of the LAMMPS homepage.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Builder:} Several pre\sphinxhyphen{}processing tools are packaged with LAMMPS.
Some of them convert input files in formats produced by other MD codes
such as CHARMM, AMBER, or Insight into LAMMPS input formats.  Some of
them are simple programs that will build simple molecular systems,
such as linear bead\sphinxhyphen{}spring polymer chains.  The moltemplate program is
a true molecular builder that will generate complex molecular models.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tools}}}} page for details on tools packaged with
LAMMPS.  The \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/prepost.html}{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}/post\sphinxhyphen{}processing tools page} of the LAMMPS homepage
describes a variety of third party tools for this task.  Furthermore,
some internal LAMMPS commands allow reconstructing, or selectively adding
topology information, as well as provide the option to insert molecule
templates instead of atoms for building bulk molecular systems.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Force\sphinxhyphen{}field assignment:} The conversion tools described in the previous
bullet for CHARMM, AMBER, and Insight will also assign force field
coefficients in the LAMMPS format, assuming you provide CHARMM, AMBER,
or BIOVIA (formerly Accelrys) force field files. The tools
\sphinxhref{https://parmed.github.io/ParmEd/html/index.html}{ParmEd} and
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/shirtsgroup/InterMol}{InterMol} are particularly
powerful and flexible in converting force field and topology data
between various MD simulation programs.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Simulation analysis:} If you want to perform analysis on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly as
your simulation runs, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} doc pages, which list commands that can be used in a LAMMPS
input script.  Also see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}} page for info on
how to add your own analysis code or algorithms to LAMMPS.  For
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing, LAMMPS output such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump file snapshots}}}} can be converted into formats used by other MD or
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing codes.  To some degree, that conversion can be done
directly inside LAMMPS by interfacing to the VMD molfile plugins.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command also allows post\sphinxhyphen{}processing of existing
trajectories, and through being able to read a variety of file
formats, this can also be used for analyzing trajectories from other
MD codes.  Some post\sphinxhyphen{}processing tools packaged with LAMMPS will do
these conversions.  Scripts provided in the tools/python directory can
extract and massage data in dump files to make it easier to import
into other programs.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tools}}}} page for details on
these various options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/prepost.html}{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}/post\sphinxhyphen{}processing page}
on the LAMMPS homepage lists some external packages for analysis of MD
simulation data, including data produced by LAMMPS.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Visualization:} LAMMPS can produce NETPBM, JPG, or PNG format
snapshot images on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly via its {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}}
command and pass them to an external program, \sphinxhref{https://ffmpeg.org/}{FFmpeg}, to generate movies from them.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI tool}}}} has an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Snapshot Image Viewer}
which uses {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} and allows to modify the
visualization settings interactively.  It also has a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Slide Show}
feature where images created by {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} are
collected during a simulation and can be animated interactively or
exported to a movie with FFmpeg.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For high\sphinxhyphen{}quality, interactive visualization, there are many excellent
and free tools available.  See the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/viz.html}{Visualization Tools} page of the LAMMPS website for
visualization packages that can process LAMMPS output data.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Plotting:} See the next bullet about Pizza.py as well as the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python}}}} page for examples of plotting LAMMPS
output.  Scripts provided with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} tool in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools}}
directory will extract and process data in log and dump files to make
it easier to analyze and plot.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tools}}}} doc page
for more discussion of the various tools.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI tool}}}} has an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Chart Viewer} where
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic data}}}} computed by LAMMPS is
collected during the simulation and plotted immediately.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pizza.py:} Our group has also written a separate toolkit called
\sphinxhref{https://lammps.github.io/pizza}{Pizza.py} which can do certain kinds of
setup, analysis, plotting, and visualization (via OpenGL) for LAMMPS
simulations.  It thus provides some functionality for several of the
above bullets.  Pizza.py is written in \sphinxhref{https://www.python.org}{Python}
and is available for download from \sphinxhref{https://sjplimp.github.io/download.html}{this page}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{LAMMPS portability and compatibility}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability:lammps-portability-and-compatibility}}\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The primary form of distributing LAMMPS is through highly portable
source code.  But also several ways of obtaining LAMMPS as {\hyperref[\detokenize{Install::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{precompiled
packages or through automated build mechanisms}}}} exist.  Most
of LAMMPS is written in C++, some support tools are written in Fortran
or Python or MATLAB.


\subsection{Programming language standards}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability:programming-language-standards}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Most of the C++ code currently requires a compiler compatible with the
C++11 standard, the KOKKOS package currently requires C++17.  Most of
the Python code is written to be compatible with Python 3.5 or later or
Python 2.7.  Some Python scripts \sphinxstyleemphasis{require} Python 3 and a few others
still need to be ported from Python 2 to Python 3.


\subsection{Build systems}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability:build-systems}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can be compiled from source code using a (traditional) build
system based on shell scripts, a few shell utilities (grep, sed, cat,
tr) and the GNU make program. This requires running within a Bourne
shell (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/bin/sh}}).  Alternatively, a build system with different back ends
can be created using CMake.  CMake must be at least version 3.16.


\subsection{Operating systems}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability:operating-systems}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The primary development platform for LAMMPS is Linux.  Thus, the chances
for LAMMPS to compile without problems on Linux machines are the best.
Also, compilation and correct execution on macOS and Windows (using
Microsoft Visual C++) is checked automatically for largest part of the
source code.  Some (optional) features are not compatible with all
operating systems, either through limitations of the corresponding
LAMMPS source code or through source code or build system
incompatibilities of required libraries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Executables for Windows may be created natively using either Cygwin or
Visual Studio or with a Linux to Windows MinGW cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiler.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additionally, FreeBSD and Solaris have been tested successfully.


\subsection{Compilers}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability:compilers}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The most commonly used compilers are the GNU compilers, but also Clang
and the Intel compilers have been successfully used on Linux, macOS, and
Windows.  Also, the Nvidia HPC SDK (formerly PGI compilers) will compile
LAMMPS (tested on Linux).


\subsection{CPU architectures}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability:cpu-architectures}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The primary CPU architecture for running LAMMPS is 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit x86, but also
32\sphinxhyphen{}bit x86, and 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit ARM and PowerPC (64\sphinxhyphen{}bit, Little Endian) are
regularly tested.


\subsection{Portability compliance}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_portability:portability-compliance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a subset of the LAMMPS source code is \sphinxstyleemphasis{fully} compliant to \sphinxstyleemphasis{all}
of the above mentioned standards.  This is rather typical for projects
like LAMMPS that largely depend on contributions from the user community.
Not all contributors are trained as programmers and not all of them have
access to multiple platforms for testing.  As part of the continuous
integration process, however, all contributions are automatically tested
to compile, link, and pass some runtime tests on a selection of Linux
flavors, macOS, and Windows, and on Linux with different compilers.
Thus portability issues are often found before a pull request is merged.
Other platforms may be checked occasionally or when portability bugs are
reported.

\subsection{GPL version of LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_opensource:gpl-version-of-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is an open\sphinxhyphen{}source code, available free\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}charge, and distributed
under the terms of the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/LICENSE}{GNU Public License Version 2} (GPLv2),
which means you can use or modify the code however you wish for your own
purposes, but have to adhere to certain rules when redistributing it \sphinxhyphen{}
specifically in binary form \sphinxhyphen{} or are distributing software derived
from it or that includes parts of it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS comes with no warranty of any kind.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As each source file states in its header, it is a copyrighted code, and
thus not in the public domain. For more information about open\sphinxhyphen{}source
software and open\sphinxhyphen{}source distribution, see \sphinxhref{https://www.gnu.org}{www.gnu.org}
or \sphinxhref{https://www.opensource.org}{www.opensource.org}.  The legal text of the GPL as it
applies to LAMMPS is in the LICENSE file included in the LAMMPS distribution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a more specific summary of what the GPL means for LAMMPS users:

\sphinxAtStartPar
(1) Anyone is free to use, copy, modify, or extend LAMMPS in any way they
choose, including for commercial purposes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
(2) If you \sphinxstylestrong{distribute} a modified version of LAMMPS, it must remain
open\sphinxhyphen{}source, meaning you are required to distribute \sphinxstylestrong{all} of it under
the terms of the GPLv2.  You should \sphinxstylestrong{clearly} annotate such a modified
code as a derivative version of LAMMPS.  This is best done by changing
the name (example: LIGGGHTS is such a modified and extended version of
LAMMPS).

\sphinxAtStartPar
(3) If you release any code that includes or uses LAMMPS source code,
then it must also be open\sphinxhyphen{}sourced, meaning you distribute it under the
terms of the GPLv2.  You may write code that interfaces LAMMPS to a
differently licensed library.  In that case the code that provides the
interface must be licensed GPLv2, but not necessarily that library
unless you are distributing binaries that require the library to run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
(4) If you give LAMMPS files to someone else, the GPLv2 LICENSE file and
source file headers (including the copyright and GPLv2 notices) should
remain part of the code.


\subsection{LGPL version of LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_opensource:lgpl-version-of-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We occasionally make stable LAMMPS releases available under the \sphinxhref{https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/lgpl-2.1.html}{GNU
Lesser Public License v2.1}.  This is on request only and with
non\sphinxhyphen{}LGPL compliant files removed.  This allows uses linking non\sphinxhyphen{}GPL
compatible software with the (otherwise unmodified) LAMMPS library
or loading it dynamically at runtime.  Any \sphinxstylestrong{modifications} to
the LAMMPS code however, even with the LGPL licensed version, must still
be made available under the same open source terms as LAMMPS itself.

\section{Citing LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_citing:citing-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Intro_citing::doc}}

\subsection{Core Algorithms}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_citing:core-algorithms}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The paper mentioned below is the best overview of LAMMPS, but there are
also publications describing particular models or algorithms implemented
in LAMMPS or complementary software that is has interfaces to.  Please
see below for how to cite contributions to LAMMPS.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Intro_citing:lammps-paper}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The latest canonical publication that describes the basic features, the
source code design, the program structure, the spatial decomposition
approach, the neighbor finding, basic communications algorithms, and how
users and developers have contributed to LAMMPS is:
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2021.108171}{LAMMPS \sphinxhyphen{} A flexible simulation tool for particle\sphinxhyphen{}based materials modeling at the atomic, meso, and continuum scales, Comp. Phys. Comm. 271, 108171 (2022)}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
So a project using LAMMPS or a derivative application that uses LAMMPS
as a simulation engine should cite this paper.  The paper is expected to
be published in its final form under the same DOI in the first half
of 2022.  Please also give the URL of the LAMMPS website in your paper,
namely \sphinxurl{https://www.lammps.org}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original publication describing the parallel algorithms used in the
initial versions of LAMMPS is:
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://doi.org/10.1006/jcph.1995.1039}{S. Plimpton, Fast Parallel Algorithms for Short\sphinxhyphen{}Range Molecular Dynamics, J Comp Phys, 117, 1\sphinxhyphen{}19 (1995).}
\end{quote}


\subsection{DOI for the LAMMPS source code}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_citing:doi-for-the-lammps-source-code}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS developers use the \sphinxhref{https://zenodo.org/}{Zenodo service at CERN}
to create digital object identifiers (DOI) for stable releases of the
LAMMPS source code.  There are two types of DOIs for the LAMMPS source code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The canonical DOI for \sphinxstylestrong{all} versions of LAMMPS, which will always
point to the \sphinxstylestrong{latest} stable release version, is:

DOI: \sphinxhref{https://dx.doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3726416}{10.5281/zenodo.3726416}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition there are DOIs generated for individual stable releases:

\subsection{Home page}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_citing:home-page}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS website at \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org}{https://www.lammps.org/} is the canonical location for information
about LAMMPS and its features.


\subsection{Citing contributions}
\label{\detokenize{Intro_citing:citing-contributions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS has many features that use either previously published methods
and algorithms or novel features.  It also includes potential parameter
files for specific models.  Where available, a reminder about references
for optional features used in a specific run is printed to the screen
and log file.  Style and output location can be selected with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:cite}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}cite command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  Additional references are
given in the documentation of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_all::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{corresponding commands}}}} or in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto tutorials}}}}.  Please make
certain, that you provide the proper acknowledgments and citations in
any published works using LAMMPS.

\chapter{Install LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Install:install-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Install::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can download LAMMPS as an executable or as source code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When downloading the LAMMPS source code, you also have to {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{build
LAMMPS}}}}.  But you have more flexibility as to what features to
include or exclude in the build.  When you download and install
pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled LAMMPS executables, you are limited to install which
version of LAMMPS is available and which features are included of these
builds.  If you plan to {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{modify or extend LAMMPS}}}}, then
you \sphinxstylestrong{must} build LAMMPS from the source code.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have questions about the pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled LAMMPS executables, you
need to contact the people preparing those executables.  The LAMMPS
developers have no control over their choices of how they configure
and build their packages and when they update them.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxstepscope

\subsection{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built static Linux x86\_64 executables}
\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:pre-built-static-linux-x86-64-executables}}\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:static}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built LAMMPS executables for Linux, that are statically linked and
compiled for 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit x86 CPUs (x86\_64 or AMD64) are available for download
at \sphinxurl{https://download.lammps.org/static/}.
Because of that static linkage (and unlike the Linux distribution specific
packages listed below), they do not depend on any installed software and
thus should run on \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit x86 machine with \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} Linux version.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These executable include most of the available packages and multi\sphinxhyphen{}thread
parallelization (via INTEL, KOKKOS, or OPENMP package).  They are
\sphinxstylestrong{not} compatible with MPI.  Several of the LAMMPS tools executables
(e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{msi2lmp}}) are included as well.  Because of the static linkage,
there is no \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}} library file and thus also the LAMMPS
python module, which depends on it, is not included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compressed tar archives available for download have names following
the pattern \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}linux\sphinxhyphen{}x86\_64\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.tar.gz}} and will all unpack
into a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}static}} folder.  The executables are then in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}static/bin/}} folder.  Since they do not depend on any other
software, they may be freely moved or copied around.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built Ubuntu and Debian Linux executables}
\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:pre-built-ubuntu-and-debian-linux-executables}}\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:ubuntu}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A pre\sphinxhyphen{}built LAMMPS executable, suitable for running on the latest Ubuntu
and Debian Linux versions, can be downloaded as a Debian package.  This
allows you to install LAMMPS with a single command, and stay (mostly)
up\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}date with the current stable version of LAMMPS by simply updating
your operating system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To install LAMMPS do the following once:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYGZhy{}get\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This downloads an executable named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} to your box and multiple
packages with supporting data, examples and libraries as well as any
missing dependencies.  For example, the LAMMPS binary in this package is
built with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KIM package}}}} enabled, which results in the
above command also installing the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kim\sphinxhyphen{}api}} binaries when LAMMPS is
installed, unless they were installed already.  In order to use
potentials from \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{openkim.org}, you can also install the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{openkim\sphinxhyphen{}models}} package:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYGZhy{}get\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }openkim\PYGZhy{}models
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Or use the \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/doc/usage/obtaining-models/\#installing\_api}{KIM\sphinxhyphen{}API commands}
to download and install individual models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This LAMMPS executable can then be used in the usual way to run input
scripts:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To update LAMMPS to the latest packaged version, do the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYGZhy{}get\PYG{+w}{ }update
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will also update other packages on your system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To uninstall LAMMPS, do the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYGZhy{}get\PYG{+w}{ }remove\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp \sphinxhyphen{}help}} to see which compilation options, packages,
and styles are included in the binary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thanks to Anton Gladky (gladky.anton at gmail.com) for setting up this
Ubuntu package capability.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built Fedora Linux executables}
\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:pre-built-fedora-linux-executables}}\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:fedora}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built \sphinxhref{https://packages.fedoraproject.org/pkgs/lammps/}{LAMMPS packages for stable releases} are available in the
Fedora Linux distribution since Fedora version 28. The packages can be
installed via the dnf package manager. There are 3 basic varieties
(lammps = no MPI, lammps\sphinxhyphen{}mpich = MPICH MPI library, lammps\sphinxhyphen{}openmpi =
OpenMPI MPI library) and for each support for linking to the C library
interface (lammps\sphinxhyphen{}devel, lammps\sphinxhyphen{}mpich\sphinxhyphen{}devel, lammps\sphinxhyphen{}openmpi\sphinxhyphen{}devel), the
header for compiling programs using the C library interface
(lammps\sphinxhyphen{}headers), and the LAMMPS python module for Python 3. All
packages can be installed at the same time and the name of the LAMMPS
executable is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_openmpi}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_mpich}} respectively.
By default, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} will refer to the serial executable, unless one of
the MPI environment modules is loaded (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{module load mpi/mpich\sphinxhyphen{}x86\_64}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{module load mpi/openmpi\sphinxhyphen{}x86\_64}}).  Then the corresponding parallel
LAMMPS executable can be used.  The same mechanism applies when loading
the LAMMPS python module.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To install LAMMPS with OpenMPI and run an input \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in.lj}} with 2 CPUs do:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
dnf\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }lammps\PYGZhy{}openmpi
module\PYG{+w}{ }load\PYG{+w}{ }mpi/openmpi\PYGZhy{}x86\PYGZus{}64
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dnf install}} command is needed only once.  In case of a new LAMMPS
stable release, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dnf update}} will automatically update to the newer
version as soon as the RPM files are built and uploaded to the download
mirrors. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{module load}} command is needed once per (shell) session
or shell terminal instance, unless it is automatically loaded from the
shell profile.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS binary is built with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KIM package}}}} which
results in the above command also installing the \sphinxtitleref{kim\sphinxhyphen{}api} binaries when LAMMPS
is installed.  In order to use potentials from \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{openkim.org}, you
can install the \sphinxtitleref{openkim\sphinxhyphen{}models} package

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
dnf\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }openkim\PYGZhy{}models
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp \sphinxhyphen{}help}} to see which compilation options, packages,
and styles are included in the binary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thanks to Christoph Junghans (LANL) for making LAMMPS available in Fedora.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built EPEL Linux executable}
\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:pre-built-epel-linux-executable}}\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:epel}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built LAMMPS (and KIM) packages for stable releases are available
in the \sphinxhref{https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/epel/}{Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux (EPEL) repository}
for use with Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) or CentOS version 7.x
and compatible Linux distributions. Names of packages, executable,
and content are the same as described above for Fedora Linux.
But RHEL/CentOS 7.x uses the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{yum}} package manager instead of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dnf}}
in Fedora 28.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp \sphinxhyphen{}help}} to see which compilation options, packages,
and styles are included in the binary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thanks to Christoph Junghans (LANL) for making LAMMPS available in EPEL.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}built OpenSuse Linux executable}
\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:pre-built-opensuse-linux-executable}}\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:opensuse}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A pre\sphinxhyphen{}built LAMMPS package for stable releases is available
in OpenSuse as of Leap 15.0. You can install the package with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
zypper\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This includes support for OpenMPI. The name of the LAMMPS executable
is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}}. To run an input in parallel on 2 CPUs you would do:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp \sphinxhyphen{}help}} to see which compilation options, packages,
and styles are included in the binary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS binary is built with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KIM package}}}} which
results in the above command also installing the \sphinxtitleref{kim\sphinxhyphen{}api} binaries when LAMMPS
is installed.  In order to use potentials from \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{openkim.org}, you
can install the \sphinxtitleref{openkim\sphinxhyphen{}models} package

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
zypper\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }openkim\PYGZhy{}models
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thanks to Christoph Junghans (LANL) for making LAMMPS available in OpenSuse.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Gentoo Linux executable}
\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:gentoo-linux-executable}}\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:gentoo}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is part of \sphinxhref{https://packages.gentoo.org/packages/sci-physics/lammps}{Gentoo’s main package tree} and can be
installed by typing:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
emerge\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}ask\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that in Gentoo the LAMMPS source code is downloaded and the package is
then compiled and installed on your machine.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Certain LAMMPS packages can be enabled via USE flags, type

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
equery\PYG{+w}{ }uses\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thanks to Nicolas Bock and Christoph Junghans (LANL) for setting up
this Gentoo capability.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Archlinux build\sphinxhyphen{}script}
\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:archlinux-build-script}}\label{\detokenize{Install_linux:arch}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is available via Arch’s unofficial Arch User repository (AUR).
There are three scripts available, named \sphinxhref{https://aur.archlinux.org/packages/lammps}{lammps}, \sphinxhref{https://aur.archlinux.org/packages/lammps}{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}beta} and \sphinxhref{https://aur.archlinux.org/packages/lammps}{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}git}.  They respectively
package the stable, feature, and git releases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To install, you will need to have the git package installed. You may use
any of the above names in\sphinxhyphen{}place of lammps.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://aur.archlinux.org/lammps.git
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
makepkg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}s
makepkg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}i
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To update LAMMPS, you may repeat the above, or change into the cloned
directory, and execute the following, after which, if there are any
changes, you may use makepkg as above.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively, you may use an AUR helper to install these packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the AUR provides build\sphinxhyphen{}scripts that download the source code
and then build and install the package on your machine.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Download an executable for macOS}
\label{\detokenize{Install_mac:download-an-executable-for-macos}}\label{\detokenize{Install_mac::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can be downloaded, built, and configured for macOS with \sphinxhref{https://brew.sh}{Homebrew}.  (Alternatively, see the installation instructions for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Install_conda::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{downloading an executable via Conda}}}}.)  The
following LAMMPS packages are unavailable at this time because of
additional requirements not yet met: GPU, KOKKOS, MSCG, POEMS,
VORONOI.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After installing Homebrew, you can install LAMMPS on your system with
the following commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
brew\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will install the executables “lammps\_serial” and “lammps\_mpi”, as
well as the LAMMPS “doc”, “potentials”, “tools”, “bench”, and “examples”
directories.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once LAMMPS is installed, you can test the installation with the
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones benchmark file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
brew\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{test}\PYG{+w}{ }lammps\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS binary is built with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KIM package}}}}, which
results in Homebrew also installing the \sphinxtitleref{kim\sphinxhyphen{}api} binaries when LAMMPS
is installed.  In order to use potentials from \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{openkim.org}, you can install the \sphinxtitleref{openkim\sphinxhyphen{}models} package

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
brew\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }openkim\PYGZhy{}models
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have problems with the installation, you can post issues to
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/issues}{this link}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thanks to Derek Thomas (derekt at cello.t.u\sphinxhyphen{}tokyo.ac.jp) for setting
up the Homebrew capability.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Download an executable for Windows}
\label{\detokenize{Install_windows:download-an-executable-for-windows}}\label{\detokenize{Install_windows::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled Windows installers which install LAMMPS executables on a
Windows system can be downloaded from this site:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxurl{https://packages.lammps.org/windows.html}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that each installer package has a date in its name, which
corresponds to the LAMMPS version of the same date.  Installers for
current and older versions of LAMMPS are available.  32\sphinxhyphen{}bit and 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit
installers are available, and each installer contains both a serial
and parallel executable.  The installer website also explains how to
install the Windows MPI package (MPICH2 from Argonne National Labs),
needed to run in parallel with MPI.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS binaries contain \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{optional packages}}}}
included in the source distribution except: ADIOS, H5MD, KIM, ML\sphinxhyphen{}PACE,
ML\sphinxhyphen{}QUIP, MSCG, NETCDF, QMMM, SCAFACOS, and VTK.  The serial version also
does not include the LATBOLTZ package.  The PYTHON package is only
available in the Python installers that bundle a Python runtime.  The
GPU package is compiled for OpenCL with mixed precision kernels.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS library is compiled as a shared library and the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS Python module}}}} is installed, so that
it is possible to load LAMMPS into a Python interpreter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The installer site also has instructions on how to run LAMMPS under
Windows, once it is installed, in both serial and parallel.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When you download the installer package, you run it on your Windows
machine.  It will then prompt you with a dialog, where you can choose
the installation directory, unpack and copy several executables,
potential files, documentation PDFs, selected example files, etc.  It
will then update a few system settings (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_POTENTIALS}})
and add an entry into the Start Menu (with references to the
documentation, LAMMPS homepage and more).  From that menu, there is
also a link to an uninstaller that removes the files and undoes the
environment manipulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that to update to a newer version of LAMMPS, you should typically
uninstall the version you currently have, download a new installer, and
go through the installation procedure described above.  I.e. the same
procedure for installing/updating most Windows programs.  You can
install multiple versions of LAMMPS (in different directories), but only
the executable for the last\sphinxhyphen{}installed package will be found
automatically, so this should only be done for debugging purposes.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Download an executable for Linux or macOS via Conda}
\label{\detokenize{Install_conda:download-an-executable-for-linux-or-macos-via-conda}}\label{\detokenize{Install_conda::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled LAMMPS binaries are available for macOS and Linux via the
\sphinxhref{https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/index.html}{Conda} package management system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First, one must set up the Conda package manager on your system.  Follow
the instructions to install \sphinxhref{https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html}{Miniconda}, then
create a conda environment (named \sphinxtitleref{my\sphinxhyphen{}lammps\sphinxhyphen{}env} or whatever you
prefer) for your LAMMPS install:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
conda\PYG{+w}{ }config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}add\PYG{+w}{ }channels\PYG{+w}{ }conda\PYGZhy{}forge
conda\PYG{+w}{ }create\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }my\PYGZhy{}lammps\PYGZhy{}env
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Then, you can install LAMMPS on your system with the following command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
conda\PYG{+w}{ }activate\PYG{+w}{ }my\PYGZhy{}lammps\PYGZhy{}env
conda\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS binary is built with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KIM package}}}}, which
results in Conda also installing the \sphinxtitleref{kim\sphinxhyphen{}api} binaries when LAMMPS is
installed.  In order to use potentials from \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{openkim.org},
you can install the \sphinxtitleref{openkim\sphinxhyphen{}models} package

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
conda\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }openkim\PYGZhy{}models
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have problems with the installation, you can post issues to \sphinxhref{https://github.com/conda-forge/lammps-feedstock/issues}{this
link}.  Thanks to Jan Janssen
(Max\sphinxhyphen{}Planck\sphinxhyphen{}Institut fuer Eisenforschung) for setting up the Conda
capability.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have questions about these pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled LAMMPS executables,
you need to contact the people preparing those packages.  The LAMMPS
developers have no control over their choices of how they configure
and build their packages and when they update them.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Download source and documentation as a tarball}
\label{\detokenize{Install_tarball:download-source-and-documentation-as-a-tarball}}\label{\detokenize{Install_tarball::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can download a current LAMMPS tarball from the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/download.html}{download page}
of the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org}{LAMMPS website} or from GitHub (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
You have two choices of tarballs, either the most recent stable release
or the most recent feature release.  Stable releases occur a few times
per year, and undergo more testing before release.  Also, between stable
releases bug fixes from the feature releases are back\sphinxhyphen{}ported and the
tarball occasionally updated.  Feature releases occur every 4 to 8
weeks.  The new contents in all feature releases are listed on the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bug.html}{bug
and feature page} of the LAMMPS homepage.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tarballs of older LAMMPS versions can also be downloaded from \sphinxhref{https://download.lammps.org/tars/}{this page}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tarballs downloaded from the LAMMPS homepage include the pre\sphinxhyphen{}translated
LAMMPS documentation (HTML and PDF files) corresponding to that version.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once you have a tarball, uncompress and untar it with the following
command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
tar\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xzvf\PYG{+w}{ }lammps*.tar.gz
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will create a LAMMPS directory with the version date in its name,
e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}28Mar23}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also download a compressed tar or zip archives from the
“Assets” sections of the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/releases}{LAMMPS GitHub releases site}.
The file name will be lammps\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.zip which can be unzipped
with the following command, to create a lammps\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{} directory:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
unzip\PYG{+w}{ }lammps*.zip
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This version corresponds to the selected LAMMPS feature or stable
release (as indicated by the matching git tag) and will only contain the
source code and no pre\sphinxhyphen{}built documentation.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Download the LAMMPS source with git}
\label{\detokenize{Install_git:download-the-lammps-source-with-git}}\label{\detokenize{Install_git::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS development is coordinated through the “LAMMPS GitHub site”.
If you clone the LAMMPS repository onto your local machine, it has
several advantages:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can stay current with changes to LAMMPS with a single git
command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can create your own development branches to add code to LAMMPS.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can submit your new features back to GitHub for inclusion in
LAMMPS.  For that, you should first create your own {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_github::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fork on
GitHub}}}}, though.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You must have \sphinxhref{https://git-scm.com}{git} installed on your system to use the
commands explained below to communicate with the git servers on
GitHub.  For people still using subversion (svn), GitHub also
provides \sphinxhref{https://help.github.com/en/github/importing-your-projects-to-github/working-with-subversion-on-github}{limited support for subversion clients}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As of October 2016, the official home of public LAMMPS development is
on GitHub.  The previously advertised LAMMPS git repositories on
git.lammps.org and bitbucket.org are now offline or deprecated.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can follow the LAMMPS development on 4 different git branches:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{develop} : this branch follows the ongoing development and is
updated with every merge commit of a pull request

\item {} \begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{\sphinxstylestrong{release}}{[}this branch is updated with every “feature release”;{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
updates are always “fast\sphinxhyphen{}forward” merges from \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop}

\end{description}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{maintenance} : this branch collects back\sphinxhyphen{}ported bug fixes from the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} branch.  It is used to update the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} branch for “stable update releases”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{stable} : this branch is updated from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{release} branch with
every “stable release” version and also has selected bug fixes with
every “update release” when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maintenance} branch is merged into it

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To access the git repositories on your box, use the clone command to
create a local copy of the LAMMPS repository with a command like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}b\PYG{+w}{ }release\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git\PYG{+w}{ }mylammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where “mylammps” is the name of the directory you wish to create on
your machine and “release” is one of the 3 branches listed above.
(Note that you actually download all 3 branches; you can switch
between them at any time using “git checkout \textless{}branch name\textgreater{}”.)

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Saving time and disk space when using \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{git clone}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The complete git history of the LAMMPS project is quite large because
it contains the entire commit history of the project since fall 2006,
which includes the time when LAMMPS was managed with subversion.
This includes a few commits that have added and removed some large
files (mostly by accident).  If you do not need access to the entire
commit history (most people don’t), you can speed up the “cloning”
process and reduce local disk space requirements by using the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}depth}} git command line flag.  That will create a “shallow clone”
of the repository, which contains only a subset of the git history.
Using a depth of 1000 is usually sufficient to include the head
commits of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop}, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{release}, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maintenance}
branches.  To include the head commit of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} branch you may
need a depth of up to 10000.  If you later need more of the git
history, you can always convert the shallow clone into a “full
clone”.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the command completes, your directory will contain the same files
as if you unpacked a current LAMMPS tarball, with the exception, that
the HTML documentation files are not included. They can be generated
from the content provided in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc/src}} by typing \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make html}} from
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc}} directory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After initial cloning, as bug fixes and new features are added to
LAMMPS you can stay up\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}date by typing the following git commands
from within the “mylammps” directory:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }release\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} not needed if you always stay in this branch}
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }stable\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} use one of these 4 checkout commands}
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }develop\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to choose the branch to follow}
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }maintenance
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Doing a “pull” will not change any files you have added to the LAMMPS
directory structure.  It will also not change any existing LAMMPS files
you have edited, unless those files have changed in the repository.  In
that case, git will attempt to merge the changes from the repository
file with your version of the file and tell you if there are any
conflicts.  See the git documentation for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to access a particular previous release version of LAMMPS,
you can instead “check out” any version with a published tag. See the
output of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git tag \sphinxhyphen{}l}} for the list of tags.  The git command to do
this is as follows.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }tagID
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Stable versions and what tagID to use for a particular stable version
are discussed on \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bug.html\#version}{this page}.
Note that this command will print some warnings, because in order to get
back to the latest revision and to be able to update with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git pull}}
again, you will need to do \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git checkout release}} (or
check out any other desired branch) first.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once you have updated your local files with a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git pull}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git
checkout}}), you still need to re\sphinxhyphen{}build LAMMPS if any source files have
changed.  How to do this depends on the build system you are using.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Change to your build folder and type:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}build\PYG{+w}{ }.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake should auto\sphinxhyphen{}detect whether it needs to re\sphinxhyphen{}run the CMake
configuration step and otherwise redo the build for all files
that have been changed or files that depend on changed files.
In case some build options have been changed or renamed, you
may have to update those by running:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and then rebuild.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Switch to the src directory and type:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }purge\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} remove any deprecated src files}
make\PYG{+w}{ }package\PYGZhy{}update\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} sync package files with src files}
make\PYG{+w}{ }foo\PYG{+w}{               }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} re\PYGZhy{}build for your machine (mpi, serial, etc)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
to enforce consistency of the source between the src folder
and package directories.  This is OK to do even if you don’t
use any packages. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make purge}} command removes any deprecated
src files if they were removed by the update from a package
subdirectory.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you wish to edit/change a src file that is from a package,
you should edit the version of the file inside the package
subdirectory with src, then re\sphinxhyphen{}install the package.  The
version in the source directory is merely a copy and will be
wiped out if you type “make package\sphinxhyphen{}update”.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Git protocols}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The servers at github.com support the “https” access protocol for
anonymous, read\sphinxhyphen{}only access.  If you have a suitably configured
GitHub account, you may also use SSH protocol with the URL
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git@github.com:lammps/lammps.git}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS GitHub project is currently overseen by Axel Kohlmeyer
(Temple U, akohlmey at gmail.com).
