\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Build LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Build:build-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Build::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is built as a library and an executable from source code using
either traditional makefiles for use with GNU make (which may require
manual editing), or using a build environment generated by CMake (Unix
Makefiles, Ninja, Xcode, Visual Studio, KDevelop, CodeBlocks and more).

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an alternative, you can download a package with pre\sphinxhyphen{}built executables
or automated build trees, as described in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Install::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Install}}}}
section of the manual.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Build LAMMPS with CMake}
\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:build-lammps-with-cmake}}\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This page describes how to use \sphinxhref{https://cmake.org}{CMake} in general
to build LAMMPS.  Details for specific compile time settings and options
to enable and configure add\sphinxhyphen{}on packages are discussed with those
packages.  Links to those pages on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build overview}}}}
page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following text assumes some familiarity with CMake and focuses on
using the command line tool \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake}} and what settings are supported
for building LAMMPS.  A more detailed tutorial on how to use CMake
itself, the text mode or graphical user interface, to change the
generated output files for different build tools and development
environments is on a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{separate page}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS currently requires that CMake version 3.16 or later is available.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You must not mix the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_make::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{traditional make based}}}}
LAMMPS build procedure with using CMake.  No packages may be
installed or a build been previously attempted in the LAMMPS source
directory by using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make \textless{}machine\textgreater{}}}.  CMake will detect if this is
the case and generate an error.  To remove conflicting files from the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} you can use the command \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make no\sphinxhyphen{}all purge}} which will
uninstall all packages and delete all auto\sphinxhyphen{}generated files.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Advantages of using CMake}
\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:advantages-of-using-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake is an alternative to compiling LAMMPS in the traditional way
through {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_make::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{(manually customized) makefiles}}}}.  Using
CMake has multiple advantages that are specifically helpful for
people with limited experience in compiling software or for people
that want to modify or extend LAMMPS.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake can detect available hardware, tools, features, and libraries
and adapt the LAMMPS default build configuration accordingly.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake can generate files for different build tools and integrated
development environments (IDE).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake supports customization of settings with a command line, text
mode, or graphical user interface.  No manual editing of files,
knowledge of file formats or complex command line syntax is required.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
All enabled components are compiled in a single build operation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Automated dependency tracking for all files and configuration options.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for true out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}source compilation. Multiple configurations
and settings with different choices of LAMMPS packages, settings, or
compilers can be configured and built concurrently from the same
source tree.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Simplified packaging of LAMMPS for Linux distributions, environment
modules, or automated build tools like \sphinxhref{https://brew.sh/}{Homebrew}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integration of automated unit and regression testing (the LAMMPS side
of this is still under active development).

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Getting started}
\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:getting-started}}\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:cmake-build}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Building LAMMPS with CMake is a two\sphinxhyphen{}step process.  In the first step,
you use CMake to generate a build environment in a new directory.  For
that purpose you can use either the command\sphinxhyphen{}line utility \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake}} (or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake3}}), the text\sphinxhyphen{}mode UI utility \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ccmake}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ccmake3}}) or the
graphical utility \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake\sphinxhyphen{}gui}}, or use them interchangeably.  The
second step is then the compilation and linking of all objects,
libraries, and executables using the selected build tool.  Here is a
minimal example using the command line version of CMake to build LAMMPS
with no add\sphinxhyphen{}on packages enabled and no customization:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }lammps\PYG{+w}{                }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} change to the LAMMPS distribution directory}
mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} create and use a build directory}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} configuration reading CMake scripts from ../cmake}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}build\PYG{+w}{ }.\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} compilation (or type \PYGZdq{}make\PYGZdq{})}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will create and change into a folder called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}}, then run the
configuration step to generate build files for the default build command
and then launch that build command to compile LAMMPS.  During the
configuration step CMake will try to detect whether support for MPI,
OpenMP, FFTW, gzip, JPEG, PNG, and ffmpeg are available and enable the
corresponding configuration settings.  The progress of this
configuration can be followed on the screen and a summary of selected
options and settings will be printed at the end.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build
.}} command will launch the compilation, which, if successful, will
ultimately produce a library \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.a}} and the LAMMPS executable
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} inside the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} folder.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compilation can take a long time, since LAMMPS is a large project with
many features. If your machine has multiple CPU cores (most do these
days), you can speed this up by compiling sources in parallel with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make \sphinxhyphen{}j N}} (with N being the maximum number of concurrently executed
tasks).  Installation of the \sphinxhref{https://ccache.dev/}{ccache} (= Compiler
Cache) software may speed up repeated compilation even more, e.g. during
code development, especially when repeatedly switching between branches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the initial build, whenever you edit LAMMPS source files, enable
or disable packages, change compiler flags or build options, you must
re\sphinxhyphen{}compile and relink the LAMMPS executable with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build .}} (or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}}).  If the compilation fails for some reason, try running
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake .}} and then compile again. The included dependency tracking
should make certain that only the necessary subset of files is
re\sphinxhyphen{}compiled.  You can also delete compiled objects, libraries, and
executables with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build . \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}target clean}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make clean}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
After compilation, you may optionally install the LAMMPS executable into
your system with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} optional, copy compiled files into installation location}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will install the LAMMPS executable and library, some tools (if
configured) and additional files like LAMMPS API headers, manpages,
potential and force field files.  The location of the installation tree
defaults to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$\{HOME\}/.local}}.


\subsection{Configuration and build options}
\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:configuration-and-build-options}}\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:cmake-options}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The CMake commands have one mandatory argument: a folder containing a
file called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeLists.txt}} (for LAMMPS it is located in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake}} folder) or a build folder containing a file called
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeCache.txt}}, which is generated at the end of the CMake
configuration step.  The cache file contains all current CMake settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To modify settings, enable or disable features, you need to set
\sphinxstyleemphasis{variables} with either the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D}} command line flag (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
VARIABLE1\_NAME=value}}) or change them in the text mode of the graphical
user interface.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D}} flag can be used several times in one command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For your convenience, we provide {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package:cmake-presets}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{CMake presets}}}}
that combine multiple settings to enable optional LAMMPS packages or use
a different compiler tool chain.  Those are loaded with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C}} flag
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C ../cmake/presets/basic.cmake}}).  This step would only be needed
once, as the settings from the preset files are stored in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeCache.txt}} file. It is also possible to customize the build
by adding one or more \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D}} flags to the CMake command line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Generating files for alternate build tools (e.g. Ninja) and project files
for IDEs like Eclipse, CodeBlocks, or Kate can be selected using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}G}}
command line flag.  A list of available generator settings for your
specific CMake version is given when running \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}help}}.


\subsection{Multi\sphinxhyphen{}configuration build systems}
\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:multi-configuration-build-systems}}\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:cmake-multiconfig}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Throughout this manual, it is mostly assumed that LAMMPS is being built
on a Unix\sphinxhyphen{}like operating system with “make” as the underlying “builder”,
since this is the most common case.  In this case the build
“configuration” is chose using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D CMAKE\_BUILD\_TYPE=\textless{}configuration\textgreater{}}}
with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}configuration\textgreater{}}} being one of “Release”, “Debug”,
“RelWithDebInfo”, or “MinSizeRel”.  Some build tools, however, can also
use or even require having a so\sphinxhyphen{}called multi\sphinxhyphen{}configuration build system
setup.  For a multi\sphinxhyphen{}configuration build, the built type (or
configuration) is selected at compile time using the same build
files. E.g.  with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}build\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYGZhy{}multi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }Release
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In that case the resulting binaries are not in the build folder directly
but in subdirectories corresponding to the build type (i.e. Release in
the example from above).  Similarly, for running unit tests the
configuration is selected with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C}} flag:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ctest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }Debug
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The CMake scripts in LAMMPS have basic support for being compiled using
a multi\sphinxhyphen{}config build system, but not all of it has been ported.  This is
in particular applicable to compiling packages that require additional
libraries that would be downloaded and compiled by CMake.  The
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{windows.cmake}} preset file tries to keep track of which packages can
be compiled natively with the MSVC compilers out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}the box.  Not all of
the external libraries are portable to Windows, either.


\subsection{Installing CMake}
\label{\detokenize{Build_cmake:installing-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check if your machine already has CMake installed:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
which\PYG{+w}{ }cmake\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} do you have it?}
which\PYG{+w}{ }cmake3\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} version 3 may have this name}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}version\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} what specific version you have}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
On clusters or supercomputers which use environment modules to manage
software packages, do this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
module\PYG{+w}{ }list\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} is a module for cmake already loaded?}
module\PYG{+w}{ }avail\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} is a module for cmake available?}
module\PYG{+w}{ }load\PYG{+w}{ }cmake\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} load cmake module with appropriate name}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most Linux distributions offer pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled cmake packages through their
package management system. If you do not have CMake or a recent enough
version (Note: for CentOS 7.x you need to enable the EPEL repository),
you can download the latest version from \sphinxurl{https://cmake.org/download/}.  Instructions on how to install it on
various platforms can be found \sphinxhref{https://cmake.org/install/}{on this page}.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Build LAMMPS with make}
\label{\detokenize{Build_make:build-lammps-with-make}}\label{\detokenize{Build_make::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Building LAMMPS with traditional makefiles requires that you have a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.\textless{}machine\textgreater{}}} file appropriate for your system in either the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/MACHINES}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/OPTIONS}}, or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/MINE}} directory (see below).  It can include various options
for customizing your LAMMPS build with a number of global compilation
options and features.


\subsection{Requirements}
\label{\detokenize{Build_make:requirements}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Those makefiles are written for and tested with GNU make and may not
be compatible with other make programs.  In most cases, if the “make”
program is not GNU make, then there will be a GNU make program
available under the name “gmake”.  If GNU make or a compatible make is
not available, you may have to first install it or switch to building
with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{CMake}}}}.  The makefiles of the traditional
make based build process and the scripts they are calling expect a few
additional tools to be available and functioning.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A working C/C++ compiler toolchain supporting the C++11 standard; on
Linux, these are often the GNU compilers. Some older compiler versions
require adding flags like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}std=c++11}} to enable the C++11 mode.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A Bourne shell compatible “Unix” shell program (frequently this is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bash}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A few shell utilities: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ls}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mv}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ln}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rm}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{grep}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sed}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tr}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cat}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{touch}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{diff}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dirname}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Python (optional, required for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make lib\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}pkg\textgreater{}}} in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}}
folder).  Python scripts are currently tested with python 2.7 and
3.6 to 3.11. The procedure for {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_manual::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{building the documentation}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{requires} Python 3.5 or later.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Getting started}
\label{\detokenize{Build_make:getting-started}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To include LAMMPS packages (i.e. optional commands and styles) you must
enable (or “install”) them first, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} page.  If a package requires (provided or
external) libraries, you must configure and build those libraries
\sphinxstylestrong{before} building LAMMPS itself and especially \sphinxstylestrong{before} enabling
such a package with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make yes\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}package\textgreater{}}}.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Building LAMMPS with
CMake}}}} can automate much of this for many types of
machines, especially workstations, desktops, and laptops, so we suggest
you try it first when building LAMMPS in those cases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The commands below perform a default LAMMPS build, producing the LAMMPS
executable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_serial}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_mpi}} in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps/src}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }lammps/src\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} change to main LAMMPS source folder}
make\PYG{+w}{ }serial\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build a serial LAMMPS executable using GNU g++}
make\PYG{+w}{ }mpi\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build a parallel LAMMPS executable with MPI}
make\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} see a variety of make options}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compilation can take a long time, since LAMMPS is a large project with
many features. If your machine has multiple CPU cores (most do these
days), you can speed this up by compiling sources in parallel with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make \sphinxhyphen{}j N}} (with N being the maximum number of concurrently executed
tasks).  Installation of the \sphinxhref{https://ccache.dev/}{ccache} (= Compiler
Cache) software may speed up repeated compilation even more, e.g. during
code development, especially when repeatedly switching between branches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the initial build, whenever you edit LAMMPS source files, or add
or remove new files to the source directory (e.g. by installing or
uninstalling packages), you must re\sphinxhyphen{}compile and relink the LAMMPS
executable with the same \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make \textless{}machine\textgreater{}}} command.  The makefile’s
dependency tracking should ensure that only the necessary subset of
files is re\sphinxhyphen{}compiled.  If you change settings in the makefile, you have
to recompile \sphinxstyleemphasis{everything}.  To delete all objects, you can use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make
clean\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}machine\textgreater{}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before the actual compilation starts, LAMMPS will perform several
steps to collect information from the configuration and setup that is
then embedded into the executable.  When you build LAMMPS for the
first time, it will also compile a tool to quickly determine a list
of dependencies.  Those are required for the make program to
correctly detect, which files need to be recompiled or relinked
after changes were made to the sources.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Customized builds and alternate makefiles}
\label{\detokenize{Build_make:customized-builds-and-alternate-makefiles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE}} directory tree contains the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.\textless{}machine\textgreater{}}}
files included in the LAMMPS distribution.  Typing \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make example}} uses
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.example}} from one of those folders, if available.  The
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make serial}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make mpi}} lines above, for example, use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/Makefile.serial}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/Makefile.mpi}},
respectively.  Other makefiles are in these directories:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
OPTIONS\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Makefiles which enable specific options}
MACHINES\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Makefiles for specific machines}
MINE\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} customized Makefiles you create (you may need to create this folder)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Simply typing \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} lists all the available \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.\textless{}machine\textgreater{}}}
files with a single line description toward the end of the output.  A
file with the same name can appear in multiple folders (not a good
idea).  The order the directories are searched is as follows:
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/MINE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/OPTIONS}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/MACHINES}}.  This gives preference to a customized file you
put in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/MINE}}.  If you create your own custom makefile under
a new name, please edit the first line with the description and machine
name, so you will not confuse yourself, when looking at the machine
summary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Makefiles you may wish to try out, include those listed below (some
require a package first be installed).  Many of these include specific
compiler flags for optimized performance.  Please note, however, that
some of these customized machine Makefile are contributed by users, and
thus may have modifications specific to the systems of those users.
Since compilers, OS configurations, and LAMMPS itself keep changing,
their settings may become outdated, too:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }mac\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build serial LAMMPS on macOS}
make\PYG{+w}{ }mac\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build parallel LAMMPS on macOS}
make\PYG{+w}{ }intel\PYGZus{}cpu\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build with the INTEL package optimized for CPUs}
make\PYG{+w}{ }knl\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build with the INTEL package optimized for KNLs}
make\PYG{+w}{ }opt\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build with the OPT package optimized for CPUs}
make\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build with the OPENMP package optimized for OpenMP}
make\PYG{+w}{ }kokkos\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build with the KOKKOS package for OpenMP}
make\PYG{+w}{ }kokkos\PYGZus{}cuda\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build with the KOKKOS package for GPUs}
make\PYG{+w}{ }kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build with the KOKKOS package for KNLs}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Link LAMMPS as a library to another code}
\label{\detokenize{Build_link:link-lammps-as-a-library-to-another-code}}\label{\detokenize{Build_link::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed as a library of C++ objects that can be integrated
into other applications, including Python scripts.  The files
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.h}} define a C\sphinxhyphen{}style API for using
LAMMPS as a library.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_library::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Library interface to LAMMPS}}}} page for a
description of the interface and how to use it for your needs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_basics::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Basic build options}}}} page explains how to build LAMMPS as either a
shared or static library.  This results in a file in the compilation
folder called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.a}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_\textless{}name\textgreater{}.a}} in case of
building a static library.  In case of a shared library, the name is the
same only that the suffix is going to be either \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.so}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.dylib}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.dll}} instead of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.a}} depending on the OS.  In some cases, the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.so}} file may be a symbolic link to a file with the suffix \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.so.0}}
(or some other number).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Care should be taken to use the same MPI library for the calling code
and the LAMMPS library, unless LAMMPS is to be compiled without (real)
MPI support using the included STUBS MPI library.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Link with LAMMPS as a static library}
\label{\detokenize{Build_link:link-with-lammps-as-a-static-library}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The calling application can link to LAMMPS as a static library with
compilation and link commands, as in the examples shown below.  These
are examples for a code written in C in the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{caller.c}}.
The benefit of linking to a static library is, that the resulting
executable is independent of that library since all required
executable code from the library is copied into the calling executable.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This assumes that LAMMPS has been configured without setting a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_MACHINE}} name, installed with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make install}}, and the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PKG\_CONFIG\_PATH}} environment variable has been updated to
include the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.pc}} file installed into the configured
destination folder.  The commands to compile and link a coupled
executable are then:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpicc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}pkg\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}cflags\PYG{+w}{ }liblammps\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }caller.c
mpicxx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{caller}\PYG{+w}{ }caller.o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}pkg\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}libs\PYG{+w}{ }liblammps\PYG{k}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This assumes that LAMMPS has been compiled in the folder
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$\{HOME\}/lammps/src}} with “make mpi”. The commands to compile
and link a coupled executable are then:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpicc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}I\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }caller.c
mpicxx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{caller}\PYG{+w}{ }caller.o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}llammps\PYGZus{}mpi
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}I}} argument is the path to the location of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{library.h}}
header file containing the interface to the LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}style library
interface.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}L}} argument is the path to where the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_mpi.a}} file is located.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}llammps\_mpi}} argument
is shorthand for telling the compiler to link the file
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_mpi.a}}.  If LAMMPS has been built as a shared
library, then the linker will use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_mpi.so}} instead.
If both files are available, the linker will usually prefer the
shared library.  In case of a shared library, you may need to
update the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH}} environment variable or running the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{caller}} executable will fail since it cannot find the shared
library at runtime.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, it is only as simple as shown above for the case of a plain
LAMMPS library without any optional packages that depend on libraries
(bundled or external) or when using a shared library.  Otherwise, you
need to include all flags, libraries, and paths for the coupled
executable, that are also required to link the LAMMPS executable.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using CMake, additional libraries with sources in the lib
folder are built, but not included in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.a}} and
(currently) not installed with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make install}} and not included
in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pkgconfig}} configuration file.  They can be found in the
top level build folder, but you have to determine the necessary
link flags manually.  It is therefore recommended to either use
the traditional make procedure to build and link with a static
library or build and link with a shared library instead.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After you have compiled a static LAMMPS library using the
conventional build system for example with “make mode=static
serial”. And you also have installed the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POEMS}} package after
building its bundled library in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib/poems}}. Then the commands
to build and link the coupled executable change to:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gcc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}I\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}caller.c
g++\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{caller}\PYG{+w}{ }caller.o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/lib/poems\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{             }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src/STUBS\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{             }\PYGZhy{}llammps\PYGZus{}serial\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}lpoems\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}lmpi\PYGZus{}stubs
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note, that you need to link with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{g++}} instead of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gcc}} even
if you have written your code in C, since LAMMPS itself is C++
code.  You can display the currently applied settings for building
LAMMPS for the “serial” machine target by using the command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{mode}\PYG{o}{=}print\PYG{+w}{ }serial
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Which should output something like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Compiler:}
\PYG{n+nv}{CXX}\PYG{o}{=}g++
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Linker:}
\PYG{n+nv}{LD}\PYG{o}{=}g++
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Compilation:}
\PYG{n+nv}{CXXFLAGS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O3\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DLAMMPS\PYGZus{}GZIP\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DLAMMPS\PYGZus{}MEMALIGN\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{64}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}I\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/compile/lammps/lib/poems\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}I\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/compile/lammps/src/STUBS
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Linking:}
\PYG{n+nv}{LDFLAGS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Libraries:}
\PYG{n+nv}{LDLIBS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/compile/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}llammps\PYGZus{}serial\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/compile/lammps/lib/poems\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/compile/lammps/src/STUBS\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}lpoems\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}lmpi\PYGZus{}stubs
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
From this you can gather the necessary paths and flags.  With
makefiles for other \sphinxstyleemphasis{machine} configurations you need to do the
equivalent and replace “serial” with the corresponding “machine”
name of the makefile.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\subsection{Link with LAMMPS as a shared library}
\label{\detokenize{Build_link:link-with-lammps-as-a-shared-library}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When linking to LAMMPS built as a shared library, the situation becomes
much simpler, as all dependent libraries and objects are either included
in the shared library or registered as a dependent library in the shared
library file.  Thus, those libraries need not be specified when linking
the calling executable.  Only the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}I}} flags are needed.  So the example
case from above of the serial version static LAMMPS library with the
POEMS package installed becomes:
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The commands with a shared LAMMPS library compiled with the CMake
build process are the same as for the static library.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpicc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}pkg\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}cflags\PYG{+w}{ }liblammps\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }caller.c
mpicxx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{caller}\PYG{+w}{ }caller.o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}pkg\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}libs\PYG{+w}{ }liblammps\PYG{k}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The commands with a shared LAMMPS library compiled with the
traditional make build using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make mode=shared serial}} becomes:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gcc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}I\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}caller.c
g++\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{caller}\PYG{+w}{ }caller.o\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}llammps\PYGZus{}serial
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\subsubsection{Locating liblammps.so at runtime}
\label{\detokenize{Build_link:locating-liblammps-so-at-runtime}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike with a static link, now the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}} file is required at
runtime and needs to be in a folder, where the shared linker program of
the operating system can find it.  This would be either a folder like
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/local/lib64}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$\{HOME\}/.local/lib64}} or a folder pointed to
by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH}} environment variable. You can type

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
printenv\PYG{+w}{ }LD\PYGZus{}LIBRARY\PYGZus{}PATH
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
to see what directories are in that list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Or you can add the LAMMPS src directory or the directory you performed a
CMake style build in to your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH}} environment variable,
so that the current version of the shared library is always available to
programs that use it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the Bourne or Korn shells (/bin/sh, /bin/ksh, /bin/bash etc.), you
would add something like this to your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$\{HOME\}/.profile}} file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
LD\PYGZus{}LIBRARY\PYGZus{}PATH\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{LD\PYGZus{}LIBRARY\PYGZus{}PATH}\PYG{p}{\PYGZhy{}/usr/lib64}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}:\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src
\PYG{n+nb}{export}\PYG{+w}{ }LD\PYGZus{}LIBRARY\PYGZus{}PATH
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the csh or tcsh shells, you would equivalently add something like this
to your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$\{HOME\}/.cshrc}} file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{setenv }LD\PYGZus{}LIBRARY\PYGZus{}PATH \PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{LD\PYGZus{}LIBRARY\PYGZus{}PATH}\PYG{k}{\PYGZcb{}}:\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{k}{\PYGZcb{}}/lammps/src
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can verify whether all required shared libraries are found with the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ldd}} tool.  Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{LD\PYGZus{}LIBRARY\PYGZus{}PATH}\PYG{o}{=}/home/user/lammps/src\PYG{+w}{ }ldd\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{caller}
\PYG{+w}{     }linux\PYGZhy{}vdso.so.1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007ffe729e0000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }liblammps.so\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/home/user/lammps/src/liblammps.so\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fc91bb9e000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }libstdc++.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/lib64/libstdc++.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fc91b984000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }libm.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/lib64/libm.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fc91b83e000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }libgcc\PYGZus{}s.so.1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/lib64/libgcc\PYGZus{}s.so.1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fc91b824000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }libc.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/lib64/libc.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fc91b65b000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }/lib64/ld\PYGZhy{}linux\PYGZhy{}x86\PYGZhy{}64.so.2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fc91c094000\PYG{o}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a required library is missing, you would get a ‘not found’ entry:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ldd\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{caller}
\PYG{+w}{     }linux\PYGZhy{}vdso.so.1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007ffd672fe000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }liblammps.so\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }not\PYG{+w}{ }found
\PYG{+w}{     }libstdc++.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/usr/lib64/libstdc++.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fb7c7e86000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }libm.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/usr/lib64/libm.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fb7c7d40000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }libgcc\PYGZus{}s.so.1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/usr/lib64/libgcc\PYGZus{}s.so.1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fb7c7d26000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }libc.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }/usr/lib64/libc.so.6\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fb7c7b5d000\PYG{o}{)}
\PYG{+w}{     }/lib64/ld\PYGZhy{}linux\PYGZhy{}x86\PYGZhy{}64.so.2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{(}0x00007fb7c80a2000\PYG{o}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Serial vs parallel build}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:serial-vs-parallel-build}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:serial}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is written to use the ubiquitous \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message\_Passing\_Interface}{MPI (Message Passing Interface)} library API
for distributed memory parallel computation.  You need to have such a
library installed for building and running LAMMPS in parallel using a
domain decomposition parallelization.  It is compatible with the MPI
standard version 2.x and later.  LAMMPS can also be built into a
“serial” executable for use with a single processor using the bundled
MPI STUBS library.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Independent of the distributed memory MPI parallelization, parts of
LAMMPS are also written with support for shared memory parallelization
using the \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenMP}{OpenMP} threading
standard. A more detailed discussion of that is below.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}MPI}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} yes or no, default is yes if CMake finds MPI}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}OMP}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} yes or no, default is yes if a compatible}
\PYG{+w}{                          }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} compiler is detected}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}MACHINE}\PYG{o}{=}name\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} name = mpi, serial, mybox, titan, laptop, etc}
\PYG{+w}{                          }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} no default value}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The executable created by CMake (after running make) is named
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} unless the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_MACHINE}} option is set.  When setting
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_MACHINE=name}}, the executable will be called
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_name}}.  Using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BUILD\_MPI=no}} will enforce building a
serial executable using the MPI STUBS library.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The build with traditional makefiles has to be done inside the source folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }mpi\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} parallel build, produces lmp\PYGZus{}mpi using Makefile.mpi}
make\PYG{+w}{ }serial\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} serial build, produces lmp\PYGZus{}serial using Makefile/serial}
make\PYG{+w}{ }mybox\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} uses Makefile.mybox to produce lmp\PYGZus{}mybox}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make machine}} command will look up the make settings from a
file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.machine}} in the folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE}} or one of its
subdirectories \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MINE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MACHINES}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OPTIONS}}, create a
folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Obj\_machine}} with all objects and generated files and an
executable called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_machine}}.  The standard parallel build
with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make mpi}} assumes a standard MPI installation with MPI
compiler wrappers where all necessary compiler and linker flags to
get access and link with the suitable MPI headers and libraries
are set by the wrapper programs.  For other cases or the serial
build, you have to adjust the make file variables \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_INC}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_PATH}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_LIB}} as well as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CC}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LINK}}.  To
enable OpenMP threading usually a compiler specific flag needs to
be added to the compile and link commands.  For the GNU compilers,
this is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}fopenmp}}, which can be added to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CC}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LINK}} makefile variables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the serial build the following make variables are set (see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/Makefile.serial}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{CC}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{       }g++
\PYG{n+nv}{LINK}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{     }g++
\PYG{n+nv}{MPI\PYGZus{}INC}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYGZhy{}I../STUBS
\PYG{n+nv}{MPI\PYGZus{}PATH}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L../STUBS
\PYG{n+nv}{MPI\PYGZus{}LIB}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYGZhy{}lmpi\PYGZus{}stubs
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You also need to build the STUBS library for your platform before
making LAMMPS itself.  A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make serial}} build does this for you
automatically, otherwise, type \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make mpi\sphinxhyphen{}stubs}} from the src
directory, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/STUBS}} dir.  If the build
fails, you may need to edit the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{STUBS/Makefile}} for your
platform.  The stubs library does not provide MPI/IO functions
required by some LAMMPS packages, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LATBOLTZ}},
and thus is not compatible with those packages.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/STUBS/mpi.cpp}} provides a CPU timer function
called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Wtime()}} that calls \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gettimeofday()}}.  If your
operating system does not support \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gettimeofday()}}, you will
need to insert code to call another timer.  Note that the
ANSI\sphinxhyphen{}standard function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clock()}} rolls over after an hour or
so, and is therefore insufficient for timing long LAMMPS
simulations.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\subsubsection{MPI and OpenMP support in LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:mpi-and-openmp-support-in-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are installing MPI yourself to build a parallel LAMMPS
executable, we recommend either MPICH or OpenMPI, which are regularly
used and tested with LAMMPS by the LAMMPS developers.  MPICH can be
downloaded from the \sphinxhref{https://www.mpich.org}{MPICH home page}, and
OpenMPI can be downloaded correspondingly from the \sphinxhref{https://www.open-mpi.org}{OpenMPI home page}.  Other MPI packages should also work.  No
specific vendor provided and standard compliant MPI library is currently
known to be incompatible with LAMMPS.  If you are running on a large
parallel machine, your system admins or the vendor should have already
installed a version of MPI, which is likely to be faster than a
self\sphinxhyphen{}installed MPICH or OpenMPI, so you should study the provided
documentation to find out how to build and link with it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The majority of OpenMP (threading) support in LAMMPS is provided by the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OPENMP}} package; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_omp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{OPENMP package}}}}
page for details. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{INTEL}} package also includes OpenMP
threading (it is compatible with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OPENMP}} and will usually fall
back on styles from that package, if a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{INTEL}} does not exist)
and adds vectorization support when compiled with compatible compilers,
in particular the Intel compilers on top of OpenMP. Also, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KOKKOS}}
package can be compiled to include OpenMP threading.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition, there are a few commands in LAMMPS that have native OpenMP
support included as well.  These are commands in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ML\sphinxhyphen{}SNAP}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DIFFRACTION}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DPD\sphinxhyphen{}REACT}} packages.  Furthermore, some packages
support OpenMP threading indirectly through the libraries they interface
to: e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KSPACE}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{COLVARS}}.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Packages details}}}} page for more info on these packages, and the pages
for their respective commands for OpenMP threading info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For CMake, if you use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BUILD\_OMP=yes}}, you can use these packages
and turn on their native OpenMP support and turn on their native OpenMP
support at run time, by setting the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS}} environment
variable before you launch LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For building via conventional make, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LINKFLAGS}}
variables in Makefile.machine need to include the compiler flag that
enables OpenMP. For the GNU compilers or Clang, it is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}fopenmp}}.
For (recent) Intel compilers, it is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}qopenmp}}.  If you are using a
different compiler, please refer to its documentation.


\subsubsection{OpenMP Compiler compatibility}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:openmp-compiler-compatibility}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:default-none-issues}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some compilers do not fully support the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{default(none)}} directive and
others (e.g. GCC version 9 and beyond, Clang version 10 and later) may
implement strict OpenMP 4.0 and later semantics, which are incompatible
with the OpenMP 3.1 semantics used in LAMMPS for maximal compatibility
with compiler versions in use.  If compilation with OpenMP enabled fails
because of your compiler requiring strict OpenMP 4.0 semantics, you can
change the behavior by adding \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D LAMMPS\_OMP\_COMPAT=4}} to the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LMP\_INC}} variable in your makefile, or add it to the command line
while configuring with CMake.  LAMMPS will auto\sphinxhyphen{}detect a suitable setting
for most GNU, Clang, and Intel compilers.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Choice of compiler and compile/link options}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:choice-of-compiler-and-compile-link-options}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:compile}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The choice of compiler and compiler flags can be important for maximum
performance.  Vendor provided compilers for a specific hardware can
produce faster code than open\sphinxhyphen{}source compilers like the GNU compilers.
On the most common x86 hardware, the most popular C++ compilers are
quite similar in their ability to optimize regular C/C++ source code at
high optimization levels.  When using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{INTEL}} package, there is a
distinct advantage in using the \sphinxhref{https://software.intel.com/en-us/intel-compilers}{Intel C++ compiler} due to
much improved vectorization through SSE and AVX instructions on
compatible hardware.  The source code in that package conditionally
includes compiler specific directives to enable these high degrees of
vectorization.  This may change over time as equivalent vectorization
directives are included into the OpenMP standard and other compilers
adopt them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On parallel clusters or supercomputers which use “environment modules”
for their compile/link environments, you can often access different
compilers by simply loading the appropriate module before building
LAMMPS.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default CMake will use the compiler it finds according to
internal preferences, and it will add optimization flags
appropriate to that compiler and any {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{accelerator packages}}}} you have included in the build.  CMake will
check if the detected or selected compiler is compatible with the
C++ support requirements of LAMMPS and stop with an error, if this
is not the case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can tell CMake to look for a specific compiler with setting
CMake variables (listed below) during configuration.  For a few
common choices, there are also presets in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/presets}}
folder.  For convenience, there is a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMAKE\_TUNE\_FLAGS}} variable
that can be set to apply global compiler options (applied to
compilation only), to be used for adding compiler or host specific
optimization flags in addition to the “flags” variables listed
below. You may also specify the corresponding \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMAKE\_*\_FLAGS}}
variables individually, if you want to experiment with alternate
optimization flags.  You should specify all 3 compilers, so that
the (few) LAMMPS source files written in C or Fortran are built
with a compiler consistent with the one used for the C++ files:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}COMPILER}\PYG{o}{=}name\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} name of C++ compiler}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}COMPILER}\PYG{o}{=}name\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} name of C compiler}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}COMPILER}\PYG{o}{=}name\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} name of Fortran compiler}

\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}FLAGS}\PYG{o}{=}string\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} flags to use with C++ compiler}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}FLAGS}\PYG{o}{=}string\PYG{+w}{               }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} flags to use with C compiler}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}FLAGS}\PYG{o}{=}string\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} flags to use with Fortran compiler}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A few example command lines are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Building with GNU Compilers:}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}gcc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}g++\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}gfortran\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Building with Intel Classic Compilers:}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}icc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}icpc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}ifort\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Building with Intel oneAPI Compilers:}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}icx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}icpx\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}ifx\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Building with LLVM/Clang Compilers:}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}clang\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}clang++\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}flang\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Building with PGI/Nvidia Compilers:}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}pgcc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}pgc++\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}pgfortran\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Building with the NVHPC Compilers:}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}C\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}nvc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}CXX\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}nvc++\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYGZhy{}DCMAKE\PYGZus{}Fortran\PYGZus{}COMPILER\PYG{o}{=}nvfortran\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For compiling with the Clang/LLVM compilers a CMake preset is
provided that can be loaded with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C ../cmake/presets/clang.cmake}}.  Similarly,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C ../cmake/presets/intel.cmake}} should switch the compiler
toolchain to the legacy Intel compilers, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C ../cmake/presets/oneapi.cmake}}
will switch to the LLVM based oneAPI Intel compilers,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C ../cmake/presets/pgi.cmake}} will switch the compiler to the PGI compilers,
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}C ../cmake/presets/nvhpc.cmake}} will switch to the NVHPC compilers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Furthermore, you can set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMAKE\_TUNE\_FLAGS}} to specifically add
compiler flags to tune for optimal performance on given hosts.
This variable is empty by default.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When the cmake command completes, it prints a summary to the
screen which compilers it is using and what flags and settings
will be used for the compilation.  Note that if the top\sphinxhyphen{}level
compiler is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpicxx}}, it is simply a wrapper on a real compiler.
The underlying compiler info is what CMake will try to
determine and report.  You should check to confirm you are
using the compiler and optimization flags you want.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Makefile.machine settings for traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “compiler/linker settings” section of a Makefile.machine lists
compiler and linker settings for your C++ compiler, including
optimization flags.  For a parallel build it is recommended to use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpicxx}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiCC}}, since these compiler wrappers will
include a variety of settings appropriate for your MPI
installation and thus avoiding the guesswork of finding the right
flags.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Parallel build (see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/Makefile.mpi}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{CC}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{        }mpicxx
\PYG{n+nv}{CCFLAGS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O3
\PYG{n+nv}{LINK}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{      }mpicxx
\PYG{n+nv}{LINKFLAGS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Serial build with GNU gcc (see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/Makefile.serial}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{CC}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{        }g++
\PYG{n+nv}{CCFLAGS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O3
\PYG{n+nv}{LINK}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{      }g++
\PYG{n+nv}{LINKFLAGS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}O
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If compilation stops with a message like the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+go}{g++ \PYGZhy{}g \PYGZhy{}O3  \PYGZhy{}DLAMMPS\PYGZus{}GZIP \PYGZhy{}DLAMMPS\PYGZus{}MEMALIGN=64    \PYGZhy{}I../STUBS     \PYGZhy{}c ../main.cpp}
\PYG{g+go}{In file included from ../pointers.h:24:0,}
\PYG{g+go}{           from ../input.h:17,}
\PYG{g+go}{           from ../main.cpp:16:}
\PYG{g+go}{../lmptype.h:34:2: error: \PYGZsh{}error LAMMPS requires a C++11 (or later) compliant compiler. Enable C++11 compatibility or upgrade the compiler.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
then you have either an unsupported (old) compiler or you have
to turn on C++11 mode.  The latter applies to GCC 4.8.x shipped
with RHEL 7.x and CentOS 7.x or GCC 5.4.x shipped with Ubuntu16.04.
For those compilers, you need to add the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}std=c++11}} flag.
If there is no compiler that supports this flag (or equivalent),
you would have to install a newer compiler that supports C++11;
either as a binary package or through compiling from source.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you build LAMMPS with any {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} included,
there may be specific compiler or linker flags that are either
required or recommended to enable required features and to
achieve optimal performance.  You need to include these in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LINKFLAGS}} settings above.  For details, see the
documentation for the individual packages listed on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page.  Or examine these files in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/OPTIONS}} directory.  They correspond to each of the 5
accelerator packages and their hardware variants:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Makefile.opt\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} OPT package}
Makefile.omp\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} OPENMP package}
Makefile.intel\PYGZus{}cpu\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} INTEL package for CPUs}
Makefile.intel\PYGZus{}coprocessor\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} INTEL package for KNLs}
Makefile.gpu\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} GPU package}
Makefile.kokkos\PYGZus{}cuda\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} KOKKOS package for GPUs}
Makefile.kokkos\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} KOKKOS package for CPUs (OpenMP)}
Makefile.kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} KOKKOS package for KNLs (OpenMP)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Build the LAMMPS executable and library}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:build-the-lammps-executable-and-library}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:library}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:exe}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is always built as a library of C++ classes plus an executable.
The executable is a simple \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main()}} function that sets up MPI and then
creates a LAMMPS class instance from the LAMMPS library, which
will then process commands provided via a file or from the console
input.  The LAMMPS library can also be called from another application
or a scripting language.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_couple::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto couple}}}} doc
page for more info on coupling LAMMPS to other codes.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python}}}} page for more info on wrapping and
running LAMMPS from Python via its library interface.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For CMake builds, you can select through setting CMake variables
between building a shared or a static LAMMPS library and what kind
of suffix is added to them (in case you want to concurrently
install multiple variants of binaries with different settings). If
none are set, defaults are applied.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SHARED\PYGZus{}LIBS}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} yes or no (default)}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}MACHINE}\PYG{o}{=}name\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} name = mpi, serial, mybox, titan, laptop, etc}
\PYG{+w}{                             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} no default value}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compilation will always produce a LAMMPS library and an
executable linked to it.  By default, this will be a static
library named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.a}} and an executable named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}}
Setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BUILD\_SHARED\_LIBS=yes}} will instead produce a shared
library called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.dylib}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.dll}} depending on the platform) If
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_MACHINE=name}} is set in addition, the name of the
generated libraries will be changed to either \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_name.a}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_name.so}}, respectively and the executable will
be called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_name}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the traditional makefile based build process, the choice of
the generated executable or library depends on the “mode” setting.
Several options are available and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mode=static}} is the default.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }machine\PYG{+w}{               }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build LAMMPS executable lmp\PYGZus{}machine}
make\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{mode}\PYG{o}{=}static\PYG{+w}{ }machine\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} same as \PYGZdq{}make machine\PYGZdq{}}
make\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{mode}\PYG{o}{=}shared\PYG{+w}{ }machine\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build LAMMPS shared lib liblammps\PYGZus{}machine.so}
\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} instead}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “static” build will generate a static library called
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_machine.a}} and an executable named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_machine}},
while the “shared” build will generate a shared library
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_machine.so}} instead and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_machine}} will be
linked to it.  The build step will also create generic soft links,
named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.a}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}}, which point to the
specific \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_machine.a/so}} files.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\subsubsection{Additional information}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:additional-information}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for creating a shared library, all the libraries it depends on
must be compiled to be compatible with shared libraries.  This should be
the case for libraries included with LAMMPS, such as the dummy MPI
library in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/STUBS}} or any package libraries in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib}}
directory, since they are always built in a shared library compatible
way using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}fPIC}} compiler switch.  However, if an auxiliary
library (like MPI or FFTW) does not exist as a compatible format, the
shared library linking step may generate an error.  This means you will
need to install a compatible version of the auxiliary library.  The
build instructions for that library should tell you how to do this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, here is how to build and install the \sphinxhref{https://www.mpich.org}{MPICH library}, a popular open\sphinxhyphen{}source version of MPI, as a shared library
in the default /usr/local/lib location:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}enable\PYGZhy{}shared
make
make\PYG{+w}{ }install
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You may need to use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sudo make install}} in place of the last line if
you do not have write privileges for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/local/lib}} or use the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}prefix}} configuration option to select an installation folder,
where you do have write access.  The end result should be the file
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/local/lib/libmpich.so}}.  On many Linux installations, the folder
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$\{HOME\}/.local}} is an alternative to using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/usr/local}} and does
not require superuser or sudo access.  In that case the configuration
step becomes:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./configure\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}enable\PYGZhy{}shared\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}prefix\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HOME}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}/.local
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Avoiding the use of “sudo” for custom software installation (i.e. from
source and not through a package manager tool provided by the OS) is
generally recommended to ensure the integrity of the system software
installation.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Including or removing debug support}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:including-or-removing-debug-support}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:debug}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default the compilation settings will include the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}g}} flag which
instructs the compiler to include debug information (e.g. which line of
source code a particular instruction correspond to).  This can be
extremely useful in case LAMMPS crashes and can help to provide crucial
information in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Errors_debug::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tracking down the origin of a crash}}}}
and help the LAMMPS developers fix bugs in the source code.  However,
this increases the storage requirements for object files, libraries, and
the executable 3\sphinxhyphen{}5 fold.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If this is a concern, you can change the compilation settings or remove
the debug information from the LAMMPS executable:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Traditional make}: edit your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.\textless{}machine\textgreater{}}} to remove the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}g}} flag from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LINKFLAGS}} definitions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{CMake}: use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D CMAKE\_BUILD\_TYPE=Release}} or explicitly reset
the applicable compiler flags (best done using the text mode or
graphical user interface).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remove debug info}: If you are only concerned about the executable
being too large, you can use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strip}} tool (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strip
lmp\_serial}}) to remove the debug information from the executable file.
Do not strip libraries or object files, as that will render them unusable.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Build LAMMPS tools}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:build-lammps-tools}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:tools}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some tools described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Auxiliary tools}}}} can be built directly
using CMake or Make.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}TOOLS}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} yes or no (default). Build binary2txt,}
\PYG{+w}{                             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} chain.x, micelle2d.x, msi2lmp, phana,}
\PYG{+w}{                             }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} stl\PYGZus{}bin2txt}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}LAMMPS\PYGZus{}GUI}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} yes or no (default). Build LAMMPS\PYGZhy{}GUI}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The generated binaries will also become part of the LAMMPS installation
(see below).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }lammps/tools
make\PYG{+w}{ }all\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build all binaries of tools}
make\PYG{+w}{ }binary2txt\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build only binary2txt tool}
make\PYG{+w}{ }chain\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build only chain tool}
make\PYG{+w}{ }micelle2d\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} build only micelle2d tool}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Building the LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI \sphinxstyleemphasis{requires} building LAMMPS with CMake.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Install LAMMPS after a build}
\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:install-lammps-after-a-build}}\label{\detokenize{Build_basics:install}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After building LAMMPS, you may wish to copy the LAMMPS executable or
library, along with other LAMMPS files (library header, doc files), to a
globally visible place on your system, for others to access.  Note that
you may need super\sphinxhyphen{}user privileges (e.g. sudo) if the directory you want
to copy files to is protected.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CMake build}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}INSTALL\PYGZus{}PREFIX}\PYG{o}{=}path\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{[}options\PYG{+w}{ }...\PYG{o}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
make\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} perform make after CMake command}
make\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{                }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} perform the installation into prefix}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
During the installation process CMake will by default remove any runtime
path settings for loading shared libraries.  Because of this you may
have to set or modify the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DYLD\_LIBRARY\_PATH}})
environment variable, if you are installing LAMMPS into a non\sphinxhyphen{}system
location and/or are linking to libraries in a non\sphinxhyphen{}system location that
depend on such runtime path settings.
As an alternative, you may set the CMake variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_INSTALL\_RPATH}}
to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{on}} and then the runtime paths for any linked shared libraries
and the library installation folder for the LAMMPS library will be
embedded and thus the requirement to set environment variables is avoided.
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{off}} setting is usually preferred for packaged binaries or when
setting up environment modules, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{on}} setting is more convenient
for installing software into a non\sphinxhyphen{}system or personal folder.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Traditional make}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is no “install” option in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/Makefile}} for LAMMPS.
If you wish to do this you will need to first build LAMMPS, then
manually copy the desired LAMMPS files to the appropriate system
directories.
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}

\sphinxstepscope

\clearpage


\section{Optional build settings}
\label{\detokenize{Build_settings:optional-build-settings}}\label{\detokenize{Build_settings::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can be built with several optional settings.  Each subsection
explains how to do this for building both with CMake and make.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:c-11-standard-compliance}]{\sphinxcrossref{C++11 standard compliance}}} when building all of LAMMPS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:fft-library}]{\sphinxcrossref{FFT library}}} for use with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:size-of-lammps-integer-types-and-size-limits}]{\sphinxcrossref{Size of LAMMPS integer types and size limits}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:read-or-write-compressed-files}]{\sphinxcrossref{Read or write compressed files}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:output-of-jpeg-png-and-movie-files}]{\sphinxcrossref{Output of JPEG, PNG, and movie files}}} via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump movie}}}} commands

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:support-for-downloading-files}]{\sphinxcrossref{Support for downloading files}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:memory-allocation-alignment}]{\sphinxcrossref{Memory allocation alignment}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:workaround-for-long-long-integers}]{\sphinxcrossref{Workaround for long long integers}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:exception-handling-when-using-lammps-as-a-library}]{\sphinxcrossref{Exception handling when using LAMMPS as a library}}} to capture errors

{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:trigger-selected-floating-point-exceptions}]{\sphinxcrossref{Trigger selected floating\sphinxhyphen{}point exceptions}}}
