\section{Notes for building LAMMPS on Windows}
\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:notes-for-building-lammps-on-windows}}\label{\detokenize{Build_windows::doc}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_windows:generic}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{General remarks}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_windows:linux}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Running Linux on Windows}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_windows:gnu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Using GNU GCC ported to Windows}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_windows:msvc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Using Visual Studio}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_windows:oneapi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Using Intel oneAPI compilers and libraries}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_windows:cross}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Using a cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiler}}}}

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{General remarks}
\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:general-remarks}}\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:generic}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is developed and tested primarily on Linux machines.  The vast
majority of HPC clusters and supercomputers today run on Linux as well.
While portability to other platforms is desired, it is not always
achieved.  That is sometimes due to non\sphinxhyphen{}portable code in LAMMPS itself,
but more often due to portability limitations of external libraries and
tools required to build a specific feature or package.  The LAMMPS
developers are dependent on LAMMPS users giving feedback and providing
assistance in resolving portability issues.  This is particularly true
for compiling LAMMPS on Windows, since this platform has significant
differences in some low\sphinxhyphen{}level functionality.  As of LAMMPS version 14
December 2021, large parts of LAMMPS can be compiled natively with the
Microsoft Visual C++ Compilers.  As of LAMMPS version 31 May 2022, also
the Intel oneAPI compilers can compile large parts of LAMMPS natively on
Windows.  This is mostly facilitated by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_platform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Platform abstraction functions}}}} in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{platform}} namespace and CMake.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Before trying to build LAMMPS on Windows yourself, please consider the
\sphinxhref{https://packages.lammps.org/windows.html}{pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled Windows installer packages}
and see if they are sufficient for your needs.


\subsection{Running Linux on Windows}
\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:running-linux-on-windows}}\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:linux}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If it is necessary for you to compile LAMMPS on a Windows machine
(e.g. because it is your main desktop), please also consider using a
virtual machine software and compile and run LAMMPS in a Linux virtual
machine, or \sphinxhyphen{} if you have a sufficiently up\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}date Windows 10 or
Windows 11 installation \sphinxhyphen{} consider using the Windows subsystem for
Linux.  This optional Windows feature allows you to run the bash shell
of a Linux system (Ubuntu by default) from within Windows and from there
on, you can pretty much use that shell like you are running on a regular
Ubuntu Linux machine (e.g. installing software via apt\sphinxhyphen{}get and more).
For more details on that, please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_wsl::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{this tutorial}}}}.


\subsection{Using a GNU GCC ported to Windows}
\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:using-a-gnu-gcc-ported-to-windows}}\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:gnu}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One option for compiling LAMMPS on Windows natively is to install a Bash
shell, Unix shell utilities, Perl, Python, GNU make, and a GNU compiler
ported to Windows.  The Cygwin package provides a unix/linux interface
to low\sphinxhyphen{}level Windows functions, so LAMMPS can be compiled on Windows.
The necessary (minor) modifications to LAMMPS are included, but may not
always up\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}date for recently added functionality and the corresponding
new code.  A machine makefile for using cygwin for the old build system
is provided.  Using CMake for this mode of compilation is untested and
not likely to work.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When compiling for Windows do \sphinxstylestrong{not} set the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLAMMPS\_MEMALIGN}}
define in the LMP\_INC makefile variable and add \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}lwsock32 \sphinxhyphen{}lpsapi}} to
the linker flags in LIB makefile variable. Try adding \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}static\sphinxhyphen{}libgcc}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}static}} or both to the linker flags when your resulting LAMMPS
Windows executable complains about missing .dll files. The CMake
configuration should set this up automatically, but is untested.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In case of problems, you are recommended to contact somebody with
experience in using Cygwin.  If you do come across portability problems
requiring changes to the LAMMPS source code, or figure out corrections
yourself, please report them on the
\sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/c/lammps/lammps-development/}{LAMMPS forum at MatSci},
or file them as an issue or pull request on the LAMMPS GitHub project.


\subsection{Using Microsoft Visual Studio}
\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:using-microsoft-visual-studio}}\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:msvc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the integration of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_platform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{platform namespace}}}} into the LAMMPS code base, portability of LAMMPS
for native compilation on Windows using Visual Studio has been
significantly improved.  This has been tested with Visual Studio 2019
(aka version 16) and Visual Studio 2022 (aka version 17).  We strongly
recommend using Visual Studio 2022 version 17.1 or later.  Not all
features and packages in LAMMPS are currently supported out of the box,
but a preset \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/presets/windows.cmake}} is provided that contains
the packages that have been compiled successfully so far.  You \sphinxstylestrong{must}
use the CMake based build procedure, since there is no support for GNU
make or the Unix shell utilities required for the GNU make build
procedure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is possible to use both the integrated CMake support of the Visual
Studio IDE or use an external CMake installation (e.g. downloaded from
cmake.org) to create build files and compile LAMMPS from the command line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compilation via command line and unit tests are checked automatically
for the LAMMPS development branch through
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/actions/workflows/compile-msvc.yml}{GitHub Actions}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Versions of Visual Studio before version 17.1 may scan the entire
LAMMPS source tree and likely miss the correct master
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeLists.txt}} and get confused since there are multiple files
of that name in different folders but none in top level folder.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please note, that for either approach CMake will create a so\sphinxhyphen{}called
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_cmake:cmake-multiconfig}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{“multi\sphinxhyphen{}configuration” build environment}}}}, and
the command lines for building and testing LAMMPS must be adjusted
accordingly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS cmake folder contains a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeSettings.json}} file with
build configurations for MSVC compilers and the MS provided Clang
compiler package in Debug and Release mode.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To support running in parallel you can compile with OpenMP enabled using
the OPENMP package or install Microsoft MPI (including the SDK) and compile
LAMMPS with MPI enabled.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is work in progress and you should contact the LAMMPS developers
via GitHub or the \sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/c/lammps/lammps-development/}{LAMMPS forum at MatSci},
if you have questions or LAMMPS specific problems.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Using Intel oneAPI Compilers and Libraries}
\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:using-intel-oneapi-compilers-and-libraries}}\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:oneapi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 31May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After installing the \sphinxhref{https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/tools/oneapi/toolkits.html}{Intel oneAPI}
base toolkit and the HPC toolkit, it is also possible to compile large
parts of LAMMPS natively on Windows using Intel compilers.  The HPC
toolkit provides two sets of C/C++ and Fortran compilers: the so\sphinxhyphen{}called
“classic” compilers (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{icl.exe}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ifort.exe}}) and newer, LLVM
based compilers (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{icx.exe}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ifx.exe}}).  In addition to the
compilers and their dependent modules, also the thread building blocks
(TBB) and the math kernel library (MKL) need to be installed.  Two
presets (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/presets/windows\sphinxhyphen{}intel\sphinxhyphen{}llvm.cmake}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/presets/windows\sphinxhyphen{}intel\sphinxhyphen{}classic.cmake}}) are provided for
selecting the LLVM based or classic compilers, respectively. The preset
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/presets/windows.cmake}} enables compatible packages that are not
dependent on additional features or libraries.  You \sphinxstylestrong{must} use the
CMake based build procedure and use Ninja as build tool.  For compiling
from the command prompt, thus both \sphinxhref{https://cmake.org}{CMake} and
\sphinxhref{https://ninja-build.org}{Ninja\sphinxhyphen{}build} binaries must be installed.  It
is also possible to use Visual Studio, if it is started (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{devenv.exe}})
from a command prompt that has the Intel oneAPI compilers enabled.  The
Visual Studio settings file in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake}} folder contains
configurations for both compiler variants in debug and release settings.
Those will use the CMake and Ninja binaries bundled with Visual Studio,
thus a separate installation is not required.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Known Limitations}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to portability issues with several packages and external
libraries, the classic Intel compilers are currently not able to
compile the googletest libraries and thus enabling the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DENABLE\_TESTING}}
option will result in compilation failure.  The LLVM based compilers
are compatible.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is work in progress and you should contact the LAMMPS developers
via GitHub or the \sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/c/lammps/lammps-development/}{LAMMPS forum at MatSci},
if you have questions or LAMMPS specific problems.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Using a cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiler}
\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:using-a-cross-compiler}}\label{\detokenize{Build_windows:cross}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you need to provide custom LAMMPS binaries for Windows, but do not
need to do the compilation on Windows, please consider using a Linux to
Windows cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiler.  This is how currently the Windows binary
packages are created by the LAMMPS developers.  Because of that, this is
probably the currently best tested and supported way to build LAMMPS
executables for Windows.  A CMake preset selecting all packages
compatible with this cross\sphinxhyphen{}compilation build is provided.  The GPU
package can only be compiled with OpenCL support.  To compile with MPI
support, a pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled library and the corresponding header files are
required.  When building with CMake the matching package will be
downloaded automatically, but MPI support has to be explicitly enabled
with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DBUILD\_MPI=on}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please keep in mind, though, that this only applies to \sphinxstylestrong{compiling} LAMMPS.
Whether the resulting binaries do work correctly is rarely tested by the
LAMMPS developers.  We instead rely on the feedback of the users
of these pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled LAMMPS packages for Windows.  We will try to resolve
issues to the best of our abilities if we become aware of them. However
this is subject to time constraints and focus on HPC platforms.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Notes for saving disk space when building LAMMPS from source}
\label{\detokenize{Build_diskspace:notes-for-saving-disk-space-when-building-lammps-from-source}}\label{\detokenize{Build_diskspace::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is a large software project with a large number of source files,
extensive documentation, and a large collection of example files.
When downloading LAMMPS by cloning the
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps}{git repository from GitHub} this
will by default also download the entire commit history since September 2006.
Compiling LAMMPS will add the storage requirements of the compiled object
files and libraries to the tally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a user account on an HPC cluster with filesystem quotas or in other
environments with restricted disk space capacity it may be needed to
reduce the storage requirements. Here are some suggestions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create a so\sphinxhyphen{}called shallow repository by cloning only the last commit
instead of the full project history by using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git clone git@github.com:lammps/lammps \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}depth=1 \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}branch=develop}}.
This reduces the downloaded size to about half.  With \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}depth=1}} it is not possible to check out different
versions/branches of LAMMPS, using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}depth=1000}} will make multiple recent versions available at little
extra storage needs (the entire git history had nearly 30,000 commits in fall 2021).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Download a tar archive from either the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/download.html}{download section on the LAMMPS homepage}
or from the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/releases}{LAMMPS releases page on GitHub} these will not
contain the git history at all.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Build LAMMPS without the debug flag (remove \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}g}} from the machine makefile or use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DCMAKE\_BUILD\_TYPE=Release}})
or use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strip}} command on the LAMMPS executable when no more debugging would be needed.  The strip command
may also be applied to the LAMMPS shared library. The static library may be deleted entirely.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Delete compiled object files and libraries after copying the LAMMPS executable to a permanent location.
When using the traditional build process, one may use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make clean\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}machine\textgreater{}}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make clean\sphinxhyphen{}all}}
to delete object files in the src folder.  For CMake based builds, one may use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make clean}} or just
delete the entire build folder.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The folders containing the documentation tree (doc), the examples (examples) are not needed to build and
run LAMMPS and can be safely deleted.  Some files in the potentials folder are large and may be deleted,
if not needed.  The largest of those files (occupying about 120 MBytes combined) will only be downloaded on
demand, when the corresponding package is installed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the CMake build procedure, the compilation can be done on a (local) scratch storage that will not
count toward the quota.  A local scratch file system may offer the additional benefit of speeding up creating
object files and linking with libraries compared to a networked file system.  Also with CMake (and unlike with
the traditional make) it is possible to compile LAMMPS executables with different settings and packages included
from the same source tree since all the configuration information is stored in the build folder.  So it is
not necessary to have multiple copies of LAMMPS.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Development build options}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:development-build-options}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The build procedures in LAMMPS offers a few extra options which are
useful during development, testing or debugging.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Monitor compilation flags (CMake only)}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:monitor-compilation-flags-cmake-only}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development:compilation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sometimes it is necessary to verify the complete sequence of compilation flags
generated by the CMake build. To enable a more verbose output during
compilation you can use the following option.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{CMAKE\PYGZus{}VERBOSE\PYGZus{}MAKEFILE}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} value = no (default) or yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another way of doing this without reconfiguration is calling make with
variable VERBOSE set to 1:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{VERBOSE}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Enable static code analysis with clang\sphinxhyphen{}tidy (CMake only)}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:enable-static-code-analysis-with-clang-tidy-cmake-only}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development:clang-tidy}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-tidy/}{clang\sphinxhyphen{}tidy tool} is a
static code analysis tool to diagnose (and potentially fix) typical
programming errors or coding style violations.  It has a modular framework
of tests that can be adjusted to help identifying problems before they
become bugs and also assist in modernizing large code bases (like LAMMPS).
It can be enabled for all C++ code with the following CMake flag

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}CLANG\PYGZus{}TIDY}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} value = no (default) or yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With this flag enabled all source files will be processed twice, first to
be compiled and then to be analyzed. Please note that the analysis can be
significantly more time\sphinxhyphen{}consuming than the compilation itself.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Report missing and unneeded ‘\#include’ statements (CMake only)}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:report-missing-and-unneeded-include-statements-cmake-only}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development:iwyu-processing}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The conventions for how and when to use and order include statements in
LAMMPS are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS programming style}}}}.  To assist with following
these conventions one can use the \sphinxhref{https://include-what-you-use.org/}{Include What You Use tool}.
This tool is still under development and for large and complex projects like LAMMPS
there are some false positives, so suggested changes need to be verified manually.
It is recommended to use at least version 0.16, which has much fewer incorrect
reports than earlier versions.  To install the IWYU toolkit, you need to have
the clang compiler \sphinxstylestrong{and} its development package installed.  Download the IWYU
version that matches the version of the clang compiler, configure, build, and
install it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The necessary steps to generate the report can be enabled via a CMake variable
during CMake configuration.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}IWYU}\PYG{o}{=}value\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} value = no (default) or yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will check if the required binary (include\sphinxhyphen{}what\sphinxhyphen{}you\sphinxhyphen{}use or iwyu)
and python script script (iwyu\sphinxhyphen{}tool or iwyu\_tool or iwyu\_tool.py) can
be found in the path.  The analysis can then be started with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }iwyu
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This may first run some compilation, as the analysis is dependent
on recording all commands required to do the compilation.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Address, Leak, Undefined Behavior, and Thread Sanitizer Support (CMake only)}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:address-leak-undefined-behavior-and-thread-sanitizer-support-cmake-only}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development:sanitizer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compilers such as GCC and Clang support generating instrumented binaries
which use different sanitizer libraries to detect problems in the code
during run\sphinxhyphen{}time. They can detect issues like:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html\#memory-leak-detection}{memory leaks}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html}{undefined behavior}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThreadSanitizer.html}{data races}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please note that this kind of instrumentation usually comes with a
performance hit (but much less than using tools like \sphinxhref{https://valgrind.org}{Valgrind} with a more low level approach).  To enable
these features, additional compiler flags need to be added to the
compilation and linking stages.  This is done through setting the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ENABLE\_SANITIZER}} variable during configuration. Examples:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}SANITIZER}\PYG{o}{=}none\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} no sanitizer active (default)}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}SANITIZER}\PYG{o}{=}address\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} enable address sanitizer / memory leak checker}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}SANITIZER}\PYG{o}{=}hwaddress\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} enable hardware assisted address sanitizer / memory leak checker}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}SANITIZER}\PYG{o}{=}leak\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} enable memory leak checker (only)}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}SANITIZER}\PYG{o}{=}undefined\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} enable undefined behavior sanitizer}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}SANITIZER}\PYG{o}{=}thread\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} enable thread sanitizer}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Code Coverage and Unit Testing (CMake only)}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:code-coverage-and-unit-testing-cmake-only}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development:testing}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS code is subject to multiple levels of automated testing
during development:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integration testing (i.e. whether the code compiles
on various platforms and with a variety of compilers and settings),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unit testing (i.e. whether certain functions or classes of the code
produce the expected results for given inputs),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run testing (i.e. whether selected input decks can run to completion
without crashing for multiple configurations),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Regression testing (i.e. whether selected input examples reproduce the
same results over a given number of steps and operations within a
given error margin).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The status of this automated testing can be viewed on \sphinxurl{https://ci.lammps.org}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scripts and inputs for integration, run, and regression testing
are maintained in a
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps-testing}{separate repository}
of the LAMMPS project on GitHub.  A few tests are also run as GitHub
Actions and their configuration files are in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.github/workflows/}}
folder of the LAMMPS git tree.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The unit testing facility is integrated into the CMake build process of
the LAMMPS source code distribution itself.  It can be enabled by
setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D ENABLE\_TESTING=on}} during the CMake configuration step.
It requires the \sphinxhref{https://pyyaml.org/}{YAML} library and matching
development headers to compile (if those are not found locally a recent
version of that library will be downloaded and compiled along with
LAMMPS and the test programs) and will download and compile a specific
version of the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/google/googletest/}{GoogleTest} C++
test framework that is used to implement the tests.  Those unit tests
may be combined with memory access and leak checking with valgrind
(see below for how to enable it).  In that case, running so\sphinxhyphen{}called
death tests will create a lot of false positives and thus they can be
disabled by configuring compilation with the additional setting
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D SKIP\_DEATH\_TESTS=on}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Software version and LAMMPS configuration requirements}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compiler and library version requirements for the testing
framework are more strict than for the main part of LAMMPS.  For
example the default GNU C++ and Fortran compilers of RHEL/CentOS 7.x
(version 4.8.x) are not sufficient.  The CMake configuration will try
to detect incompatible versions and either skip incompatible tests or
stop with an error.  Also the number of available tests will depend on
installed LAMMPS packages, development environment, operating system,
and configuration settings.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After compilation is complete, the unit testing is started in the build
folder using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}} command, which is part of the CMake software.
The output of this command will be looking something like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{   \PYGZdl{} }ctest
\PYG{g+go}{   Test project /home/akohlmey/compile/lammps/build\PYGZhy{}testing}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start   1: RunLammps}
\PYG{g+go}{  1/563 Test   \PYGZsh{}1: RunLammps ..................................   Passed    0.28 sec}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start   2: HelpMessage}
\PYG{g+go}{  2/563 Test   \PYGZsh{}2: HelpMessage ................................   Passed    0.06 sec}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start   3: InvalidFlag}
\PYG{g+go}{  3/563 Test   \PYGZsh{}3: InvalidFlag ................................   Passed    0.06 sec}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start   4: Tokenizer}
\PYG{g+go}{  4/563 Test   \PYGZsh{}4: Tokenizer ..................................   Passed    0.05 sec}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start   5: MemPool}
\PYG{g+go}{  5/563 Test   \PYGZsh{}5: MemPool ....................................   Passed    0.05 sec}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start   6: ArgUtils}
\PYG{g+go}{  6/563 Test   \PYGZsh{}6: ArgUtils ...................................   Passed    0.05 sec}
\PYG{g+go}{      [...]}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start 561: ImproperStyle:zero}
\PYG{g+go}{561/563 Test \PYGZsh{}561: ImproperStyle:zero .........................   Passed    0.07 sec}

\PYG{g+go}{562/563 Test \PYGZsh{}562: TestMliapPyUnified .........................   Passed    0.16 sec}
\PYG{g+go}{        Start 563: TestPairList}
\PYG{g+go}{563/563 Test \PYGZsh{}563: TestPairList ...............................   Passed    0.06 sec}

\PYG{g+go}{100\PYGZpc{} tests passed, 0 tests failed out of 563}

\PYG{g+go}{Label Time Summary:}
\PYG{g+go}{generated    =   0.85 sec*proc (3 tests)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}} command has many options, the most important ones are:

\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In its full implementation, the unit test framework will consist of multiple
kinds of tests implemented in different programming languages (C++, C, Python,
Fortran) and testing different aspects of the LAMMPS software and its features.
The tests will adapt to the compilation settings of LAMMPS, so that tests
will be skipped if prerequisite features are not available in LAMMPS.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Work in Progress}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The unit test framework was added in spring 2020 and is under active
development.  The coverage is not complete and will be expanded over
time.  Preference is given to parts of the code base that are easy to
test or commonly used.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tests as shown by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}} program are command lines defined in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeLists.txt}} files in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest}} directory tree.  A few
tests simply execute LAMMPS with specific command line flags and check
the output to the screen for expected content.  A large number of unit
tests are special tests programs using the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/google/googletest/}{GoogleTest framework} and linked to the LAMMPS
library that test individual functions or create a LAMMPS class
instance, execute one or more commands and check data inside the LAMMPS
class hierarchy.  There are also tests for the C\sphinxhyphen{}library, Fortran, and
Python module interfaces to LAMMPS.  The Python tests use the Python
“unittest” module in a similar fashion than the others use \sphinxtitleref{GoogleTest}.
These special test programs are structured to perform multiple
individual tests internally and each of those contains several checks
(aka assertions) for internal data being changed as expected.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tests for force computing or modifying styles (e.g. styles for non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded
and bonded interactions and selected fixes) are run by using a more generic
test program that reads its input from files in YAML format. The YAML file
provides the information on how to customized the test program to test
a specific style and \sphinxhyphen{} if needed \sphinxhyphen{} with specific settings.
To add a test for another, similar style (e.g. a new pair style) it is
usually sufficient to add a suitable YAML file.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_unittest::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Detailed
instructions for adding tests}}}} are provided in the
Programmer Guide part of the manual.  A description of what happens
during the tests is given below.


\subsubsection{Unit tests for force styles}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:unit-tests-for-force-styles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A large part of LAMMPS are different “styles” for computing non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded
and bonded interactions selected through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style command}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style command}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style command}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style command}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style command}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style command}}}}.  Since these all share
common interfaces, it is possible to write generic test programs that
will call those common interfaces for small test systems with less than
100 atoms and compare the results with pre\sphinxhyphen{}recorded reference results.
A test run is then a a collection multiple individual test runs each
with many comparisons to reference results based on template input
files, individual command settings, relative error margins, and
reference data stored in a YAML format file with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.yaml}}
suffix. Currently the programs \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_pair\_style}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_bond\_style}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_angle\_style}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_dihedral\_style}}, and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_improper\_style}} are implemented.  They will compare forces,
energies and (global) stress for all atoms after a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{run 0}} calculation
and after a few steps of MD with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}, each in
multiple variants with different settings and also for multiple
accelerated styles. If a prerequisite style or package is missing, the
individual tests are skipped.  All force style tests will be executed on
a single MPI process, so using the CMake option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D BUILD\_MPI=off}} can
significantly speed up testing, since this will skip the MPI
initialization for each test run.  Below is an example command and
output:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZdl{} }test\PYGZus{}pair\PYGZus{}style\PYG{+w}{ }mol\PYGZhy{}pair\PYGZhy{}lj\PYGZus{}cut.yaml
\PYG{g+go}{[==========] Running 6 tests from 1 test suite.}
\PYG{g+go}{[\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}] Global test environment set\PYGZhy{}up.}
\PYG{g+go}{[\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}] 6 tests from PairStyle}
\PYG{g+go}{[ RUN      ] PairStyle.plain}
\PYG{g+go}{[       OK ] PairStyle.plain (24 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{[ RUN      ] PairStyle.omp}
\PYG{g+go}{[       OK ] PairStyle.omp (18 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{[ RUN      ] PairStyle.intel}
\PYG{g+go}{[       OK ] PairStyle.intel (6 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{[ RUN      ] PairStyle.opt}
\PYG{g+go}{[  SKIPPED ] PairStyle.opt (0 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{[ RUN      ] PairStyle.single}
\PYG{g+go}{[       OK ] PairStyle.single (7 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{[ RUN      ] PairStyle.extract}
\PYG{g+go}{[       OK ] PairStyle.extract (6 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{[\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}] 6 tests from PairStyle (62 ms total)}

\PYG{g+go}{[\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}] Global test environment tear\PYGZhy{}down}
\PYG{g+go}{[==========] 6 tests from 1 test suite ran. (63 ms total)}
\PYG{g+go}{[  PASSED  ] 5 tests.}
\PYG{g+go}{[  SKIPPED ] 1 test, listed below:}
\PYG{g+go}{[  SKIPPED ] PairStyle.opt}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this particular case, 5 out of 6 sets of tests were conducted, the
tests for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lj/cut/opt}} pair style was skipped, since the tests
executable did not include it.  To learn what individual tests are performed,
you (currently) need to read the source code.  You can use code coverage
recording (see next section) to confirm how well the tests cover the code
paths in the individual source files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The force style test programs have a common set of options:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{\X{25}{100}\X{75}{100}}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
Option
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Function
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}g \textless{}newfile\textgreater{}}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
regenerate reference data in new YAML file
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}u}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
update reference data in the original YAML file
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}s}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
print error statistics for each group of comparisons
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}v}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
verbose output: also print the executed LAMMPS commands
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabular}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}} tool has no mechanism to directly pass flags to the individual
test programs, but a workaround has been implemented where these flags can be
set in an environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TEST\_ARGS}}. Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
env\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{TEST\PYGZus{}ARGS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZhy{}s\PYG{+w}{ }ctest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}V\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}R\PYG{+w}{ }BondStyle
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To add a test for a style that is not yet covered, it is usually best
to copy a YAML file for a similar style to a new file, edit the details
of the style (how to call it, how to set its coefficients) and then
run test command with either the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}g}} and the replace the initial
test file with the regenerated one or the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}u}} option.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}u}} option
will destroy the original file, if the generation run does not complete,
so using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}g}} is recommended unless the YAML file is fully tested
and working.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some of the force style tests are rather slow to run and some are very
sensitive to small differences like CPU architecture, compiler
toolchain, compiler optimization. Those tests are flagged with a “slow”
and/or “unstable” label, and thus those tests can be selectively
excluded with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}LE}} flag or selected with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}L}} flag.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Recommendations and notes for YAML files}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The reference results should be recorded without any code
optimization or related compiler flags enabled.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{epsilon}} parameter defines the relative precision with which
the reference results must be met.  The test geometries often have
high and low energy parts and thus a significant impact from
floating\sphinxhyphen{}point math truncation errors is to be expected. Some
functional forms and potentials are more noisy than others, so this
parameter needs to be adjusted. Typically a value around 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}13
can be used, but it may need to be as large as 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}8 in some
cases.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tests for pair styles from OPT, OPENMP and INTEL are
performed with automatically rescaled epsilon to account for
additional loss of precision from code optimizations and different
summation orders.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When compiling with (aggressive) compiler optimization, some tests
are likely to fail.  It is recommended to inspect the individual
tests in detail to decide, whether the specific error for a specific
property is acceptable (it often is), or this may be an indication
of mis\sphinxhyphen{}compiled code (or an undesired large loss of precision due
to significant reordering of operations and thus less error cancellation).

\end{itemize}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Unit tests for timestepping related fixes}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:unit-tests-for-timestepping-related-fixes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A substantial subset of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix styles}}}} are invoked regularly
during MD timestepping and manipulate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties like
positions, velocities, and forces.  For those fix styles, testing can be
done in a very similar fashion as for force fields and thus there is a
test program \sphinxtitleref{test\_fix\_timestep} that shares a lot of code, properties,
and command line flags with the force field style testers described in
the previous section.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tester will set up a small molecular system run with verlet run
style for 4 MD steps, then write a binary restart and continue for
another 4 MD steps. At this point coordinates and velocities are
recorded and compared to reference data. Then the system is cleared,
restarted and running the second 4 MD steps again and the data is
compared to the same reference. That is followed by another restart
after which per atom type masses are replaced with per\sphinxhyphen{}atom masses and
the second 4 MD steps are repeated again and compared to the same
reference.  Also global scalar and vector data of the fix is recorded
and compared.  If the fix is a thermostat and thus the internal property
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t\_target}} can be extracted, then this is compared to the reference
data.  The tests are repeated with the respa run style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the fix has a multi\sphinxhyphen{}threaded version in the OPENMP package, then
the entire set of tests is repeated for that version as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For this to work, some additional conditions have to be met by the
YAML format test inputs.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix to be tested (and only this fix), should be listed in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{prerequisites:}} section

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix to be tested must be specified in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{post\_commands:}}
section with the fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test}}.  This section may contain other
commands and other fixes (e.g. an instance of fix nve for testing
a thermostat or force manipulation fix)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For fixes that can tally contributions to the global virial, the
line \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix\_modify test virial yes}} should be included in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{post\_commands:}} section of the test input.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For thermostat fixes the target temperature should be ramped from
an arbitrary value (e.g. 50K) to a pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined target temperature
entered as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$\{t\_target\}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For fixes that have thermostatting support included, but do not
have it enabled in the input (e.g. fix rigid with default settings),
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{post\_commands:}} section should contain the line
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{variable t\_target delete}} to disable the target temperature ramp
check to avoid false positives.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Use custom linker for faster link times when ENABLE\_TESTING is active}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:use-custom-linker-for-faster-link-times-when-enable-testing-is-active}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When compiling LAMMPS with enabled tests, most test executables will
need to be linked against the LAMMPS library.  Since this can be a very
large library with many C++ objects when many packages are enabled, link
times can become very long on machines that use the GNU BFD linker (e.g.
Linux systems).  Alternatives like the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mold}} linker, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lld}}
linker of the LLVM project, or the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gold}} linker available with GNU
binutils can speed up this step substantially (in this order).  CMake
will by default test if any of the three can be enabled and use it when
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ENABLE\_TESTING}} is active.  It can also be selected manually through
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMAKE\_CUSTOM\_LINKER}} CMake variable.  Allowed values are
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mold}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lld}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gold}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bfd}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{default}}.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{default}}
option will use the system default linker otherwise, the linker is
chosen explicitly.  This option is only available for the GNU or Clang
C++ compilers.


\subsubsection{Tests for other components and utility functions}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:tests-for-other-components-and-utility-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional tests that validate utility functions or specific components
of LAMMPS are implemented as standalone executable which may, or may not
require creating a suitable LAMMPS instance.  These tests are more specific
and do not require YAML format input files.  To add a test, either an
existing source file needs to be extended or a new file added, which in turn
requires additions to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeLists.txt}} file in the source folder.


\subsubsection{Collect and visualize code coverage metrics}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:collect-and-visualize-code-coverage-metrics}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also collect code coverage metrics while running LAMMPS or the
tests by enabling code coverage support during the CMake configuration:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{ENABLE\PYGZus{}COVERAGE}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} enable coverage measurements (off by default)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will instrument all object files to write information about which
lines of code were accessed during execution in files next to the
corresponding object files.  These can be post\sphinxhyphen{}processed to visually
show the degree of coverage and which code paths are accessed and which
are not taken.  When working on unit tests (see above), this can be
extremely helpful to determine which parts of the code are not executed
and thus what kind of tests are still missing. The coverage data is
cumulative, i.e. new data is added with each new run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Enabling code coverage will also add the following build targets to
generate coverage reports after running the LAMMPS executable or the
unit tests:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }gen\PYGZus{}coverage\PYGZus{}html\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} generate coverage report in HTML format}
make\PYG{+w}{ }gen\PYGZus{}coverage\PYGZus{}xml\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} generate coverage report in XML format}
make\PYG{+w}{ }clean\PYGZus{}coverage\PYGZus{}html\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} delete folder with HTML format coverage report}
make\PYG{+w}{ }reset\PYGZus{}coverage\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} delete all collected coverage data and HTML output}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These reports require \sphinxhref{https://gcovr.com/}{GCOVR} to be installed. The easiest way
to do this to install it via pip:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }git+https://github.com/gcovr/gcovr.git
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After post\sphinxhyphen{}processing with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gen\_coverage\_html}} the results are in
a folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{coverage\_html}} and can be viewed with a web browser.
The images below illustrate how the data is presented.

\begin{figure}[htbp]

\subsection{Coding style utilities}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:coding-style-utilities}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To aid with enforcing some of the coding style conventions in LAMMPS
some additional build targets have been added. These require Python 3.5
or later and will only work properly on Unix\sphinxhyphen{}like operating and file systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following options are available.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }check\PYGZhy{}whitespace\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} search for files with whitespace issues}
make\PYG{+w}{ }fix\PYGZhy{}whitespace\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} correct whitespace issues in files}
make\PYG{+w}{ }check\PYGZhy{}homepage\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} search for files with old LAMMPS homepage URLs}
make\PYG{+w}{ }fix\PYGZhy{}homepage\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} correct LAMMPS homepage URLs in files}
make\PYG{+w}{ }check\PYGZhy{}errordocs\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} search for deprecated error docs in header files}
make\PYG{+w}{ }fix\PYGZhy{}errordocs\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} remove error docs in header files}
make\PYG{+w}{ }check\PYGZhy{}permissions\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} search for files with permissions issues}
make\PYG{+w}{ }fix\PYGZhy{}permissions\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} correct permissions issues in files}
make\PYG{+w}{ }check\PYGZhy{}docs\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} search for several issues in the manual}
make\PYG{+w}{ }check\PYGZhy{}version\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} list files with pending release version tags}
make\PYG{+w}{ }check\PYG{+w}{               }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} run all check targets from above}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These should help to make source and documentation files conforming
to some the coding style preferences of the LAMMPS developers.


\subsection{Clang\sphinxhyphen{}format support}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:clang-format-support}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development:clang-format}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the code in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} trees we are transitioning
to use the \sphinxtitleref{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format} tool to assist with having a consistent source
code formatting style.  The \sphinxtitleref{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format} command bundled with Clang
version 8.0 or later is required.  The configuration is in files called
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.clang\sphinxhyphen{}format}} in the respective folders.  Since the modifications
from \sphinxtitleref{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format} can be significant and \sphinxhyphen{} especially for “legacy
style code” \sphinxhyphen{} they are not always improving readability, a large number
of files currently have a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{// clang\sphinxhyphen{}format off}} at the top, which will
disable the processing.  As of fall 2021 all files have been either
“protected” this way or are enabled for full or partial \sphinxtitleref{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format}
processing.  Over time, the “protected” files will be refactored and
updated so that \sphinxtitleref{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format} may be applied to them as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is recommended for all newly contributed files to use the clang\sphinxhyphen{}format
processing while writing the code or do the coding style processing
(including the scripts mentioned in the previous paragraph)

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxtitleref{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format} is available, files can be updated individually with
commands like the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
clang\PYGZhy{}format\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}i\PYG{+w}{ }some\PYGZus{}file.cpp
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following target are available for both, GNU make and CMake:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }format\PYGZhy{}src\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} apply clang\PYGZhy{}format to all files in src and the package folders}
make\PYG{+w}{ }format\PYGZhy{}tests\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} apply clang\PYGZhy{}format to all files in the unittest tree}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{GitHub command line interface}
\label{\detokenize{Build_development:github-command-line-interface}}\label{\detokenize{Build_development:gh-cli}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
GitHub is developing a \sphinxhref{https://cli.github.com}{tool for the command line} that interacts with the GitHub website via a
command called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gh}}.  This can be extremely convenient when working
with a Git repository hosted on GitHub (like LAMMPS).  It is thus highly
recommended to install it when doing LAMMPS development.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The capabilities of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gh}} command is continually expanding, so
please see the documentation at \sphinxurl{https://cli.github.com/manual/}

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Run LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Run_head:run-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Run_head::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pages explain how to run LAMMPS once you have {\hyperref[\detokenize{Install::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{installed an executable}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{Install::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{downloaded the source code}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{built an executable}}}}.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands}}}}
doc page describes how input scripts are structured and the commands
they can contain.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Basics of running LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Run_basics:basics-of-running-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Run_basics::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is run from the command line, reading commands from a file via
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}in}} command line flag, or from standard input.  Using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}in
in.file}} variant is recommended (see note below).  The name of the
LAMMPS executable is either \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_\textless{}machine\textgreater{}}} with
\sphinxtitleref{\textless{}machine\textgreater{}} being the machine string used when compiling LAMMPS.  This
is required when compiling LAMMPS with the traditional build system
(e.g. with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make mpi}}), but optional when using CMake to configure and
build LAMMPS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
lmp\PYGZus{}serial\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
lmp\PYGZus{}serial\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZlt{}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZlt{}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
/path/to/lammps/src/lmp\PYGZus{}serial\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}i\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }/path/to/lammps/src/lmp\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}n\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }/usr/local/bin/lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.file
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You normally run the LAMMPS command in the directory where your input
script is located.  That is also where output files are produced by
default, unless you provide specific other paths in your input script or
on the command line.  As in some of the examples above, the LAMMPS
executable itself can be placed elsewhere.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The redirection operator “\textless{}” will not always work when running in
parallel with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}}; for those systems the \sphinxhyphen{}in
form is required.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As LAMMPS runs it prints info to the screen and a logfile named
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{log.lammps}}.  More info about output is given on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{screen and
logfile output}}}} page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If LAMMPS encounters errors in the input script or while running a
simulation it will print an ERROR message and stop or a WARNING
message and continue.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Errors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Common Problems}}}} page for a
discussion of the various kinds of errors LAMMPS can or can’t detect,
a list of all ERROR and WARNING messages, and what to do about them.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can run the same problem on any number of processors, including a
single processor.  In theory you should get identical answers on any
number of processors and on any machine.  In practice, numerical
round\sphinxhyphen{}off due to using floating\sphinxhyphen{}point math can cause slight differences
and an eventual divergence of molecular dynamics trajectories.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Errors_common::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Errors common}}}} page for discussion of this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can run as large a problem as will fit in the physical memory of
one or more processors.  If you run out of memory, you must run on more
processors or define a smaller problem.  The amount of memory needed and
how well it can be distributed across processors may vary based
on the models and settings and commands used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you run LAMMPS in parallel via mpirun, you should be aware of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}} command, which controls how MPI tasks are
mapped to the simulation box, as well as mpirun options that control how
MPI tasks are assigned to physical cores of the node(s) of the machine
you are running on.  These settings can improve performance, though the
defaults are often adequate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, it is often important to bind MPI tasks (processes) to
physical cores (processor affinity), so that the operating system does
not migrate them during a simulation.  If this is not the default
behavior on your machine, the mpirun option \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}bind\sphinxhyphen{}to core}} (OpenMPI)
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}bind\sphinxhyphen{}to core}} (MPICH) can be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the LAMMPS command(s) you are using support multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading, you
can set the number of threads per MPI task via the environment
variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS}}, before you launch LAMMPS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{export}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} bash}
setenv\PYG{+w}{ }OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} csh or tcsh}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can also be done via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} command or via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}pk command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} which invokes the
package command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} command or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Speed}}}} doc pages for more details about which accelerator
packages and which commands support multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
You can experiment with running LAMMPS using any of the input scripts
provided in the examples or bench directory.  Input scripts are named
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in.*}} and sample outputs are named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{log.*.P}} where P is the number of
processors it was run on.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some of the examples or benchmarks require LAMMPS to be built with
optional packages.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Command\sphinxhyphen{}line options}
\label{\detokenize{Run_options:command-line-options}}\label{\detokenize{Run_options::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At run time, LAMMPS recognizes several optional command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches
which may be used in any order.  Either the full word or a one or two
letter abbreviation can be used:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:echo}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}e or \sphinxhyphen{}echo}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:help}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}h or \sphinxhyphen{}help}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:file}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}i or \sphinxhyphen{}in}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:run-kokkos}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}k or \sphinxhyphen{}kokkos}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:log}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}l or \sphinxhyphen{}log}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:mdi-flags}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}mdi}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:mpicolor}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}m or \sphinxhyphen{}mpicolor}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:cite}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}c or \sphinxhyphen{}cite}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:nocite}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}nc or \sphinxhyphen{}nocite}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:nonbuf}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}nb or \sphinxhyphen{}nonbuf}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:package}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}pk or \sphinxhyphen{}package}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:partition}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}p or \sphinxhyphen{}partition}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:plog}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}pl or \sphinxhyphen{}plog}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:pscreen}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}ps or \sphinxhyphen{}pscreen}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:reorder}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}ro or \sphinxhyphen{}reorder}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:restart2data}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}r2data or \sphinxhyphen{}restart2data}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:restart2dump}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}r2dump or \sphinxhyphen{}restart2dump}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:restart2info}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}r2info or \sphinxhyphen{}restart2info}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:screen}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}sc or \sphinxhyphen{}screen}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:skiprun}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}sr or skiprun}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:suffix}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}sf or \sphinxhyphen{}suffix}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:var}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxhyphen{}v or \sphinxhyphen{}var}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the lmp\_mpi executable might be launched as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }f\PYG{+w}{ }tmp.out\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}l\PYG{+w}{ }my.log\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sc\PYG{+w}{ }none\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}i\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.alloy
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}var\PYG{+w}{ }f\PYG{+w}{ }tmp.out\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}log\PYG{+w}{ }my.log\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}screen\PYG{+w}{ }none\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.alloy
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:echo}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}echo style}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the style of command echoing.  The style can be \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{screen}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{log} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{both}.  Depending on the style, each command read from
the input script will be echoed to the screen and/or logfile.  This
can be useful to figure out which line of your script is causing an
input error.  The default value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{log}.  The echo style can also be
set by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{echo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{echo}}}} command in the input script itself.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:help}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}help}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Print a brief help summary and a list of options compiled into this
executable for each LAMMPS style (atom\_style, fix, compute,
pair\_style, bond\_style, etc).  This can tell you if the command you
want to use was included via the appropriate package at compile time.
LAMMPS will print the info and immediately exit if this switch is
used.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}in file}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify a file to use as an input script.  This is an optional but
recommended switch when running LAMMPS in one\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode.  If it
is not specified, LAMMPS reads its script from standard input, typically
from a script via I/O redirection; e.g. lmp\_linux \textless{} in.run.
With many MPI implementations I/O redirection also works in parallel,
but using the \sphinxhyphen{}in flag will always work.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this is a required switch when running LAMMPS in
multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode, since multiple processors cannot all read from
stdin concurrently.  The file name may be “none” for starting
multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition calculations without reading an initial input file
from the library interface.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:run-kokkos}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}kokkos on/off keyword/value …}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Explicitly enable or disable KOKKOS support, as provided by the KOKKOS
package.  Even if LAMMPS is built with this package, as described
in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_kokkos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{the KOKKOS package page}}}}, this switch must be set to enable
running with KOKKOS\sphinxhyphen{}enabled styles the package provides.  If the
switch is not set (the default), LAMMPS will operate as if the KOKKOS
package were not installed; i.e. you can run standard LAMMPS or with
the GPU or OPENMP packages, for testing or benchmarking purposes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional optional keyword/value pairs can be specified which determine
how Kokkos will use the underlying hardware on your platform.  These
settings apply to each MPI task you launch via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}} command.  You may choose to run one or more MPI tasks per
physical node.  Note that if you are running on a desktop machine, you
typically have one physical node.  On a cluster or supercomputer there
may be dozens or 1000s of physical nodes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Either the full word or an abbreviation can be used for the keywords.
Note that the keywords do not use a leading minus sign.  I.e. the
keyword is “t”, not “\sphinxhyphen{}t”.  Also note that each of the keywords has a
default setting.  Examples of when to use these options and what
settings to use on different platforms is given on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_kokkos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{KOKKOS
package}}}} doc page.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
d or device

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
g or gpus

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
t or threads

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
device Nd
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This option is only relevant if you built LAMMPS with CUDA=yes, you
have more than one GPU per node, and if you are running with only one
MPI task per node.  The Nd setting is the ID of the GPU on the node to
run on.  By default Nd = 0.  If you have multiple GPUs per node, they
have consecutive IDs numbered as 0,1,2,etc.  This setting allows you
to launch multiple independent jobs on the node, each with a single
MPI task per node, and assign each job to run on a different GPU.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gpus Ng Ns
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This option is only relevant if you built LAMMPS with CUDA=yes, you
have more than one GPU per node, and you are running with multiple MPI
tasks per node (up to one per GPU).  The Ng setting is how many GPUs
you will use.  The Ns setting is optional.  If set, it is the ID of a
GPU to skip when assigning MPI tasks to GPUs.  This may be useful if
your desktop system reserves one GPU to drive the screen and the rest
are intended for computational work like running LAMMPS.  By default
Ng = 1 and Ns is not set.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on which flavor of MPI you are running, LAMMPS will look for
one of these 4 environment variables

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
SLURM\PYGZus{}LOCALID (various MPI variants compiled with SLURM support)
MPT\PYGZus{}LRANK (HPE MPI)
MV2\PYGZus{}COMM\PYGZus{}WORLD\PYGZus{}LOCAL\PYGZus{}RANK (Mvapich)
OMPI\PYGZus{}COMM\PYGZus{}WORLD\PYGZus{}LOCAL\PYGZus{}RANK (OpenMPI)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which are initialized by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{srun}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}}
commands.  The environment variable setting for each MPI rank is used to
assign a unique GPU ID to the MPI task.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
threads Nt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This option assigns Nt number of threads to each MPI task for
performing work when Kokkos is executing in OpenMP or pthreads mode.
The default is Nt = 1, which essentially runs in MPI\sphinxhyphen{}only mode.  If
there are Np MPI tasks per physical node, you generally want Np*Nt =
the number of physical cores per node, to use your available hardware
optimally.  This also sets the number of threads used by the host when
LAMMPS is compiled with CUDA=yes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,deprecated}{Deprecated since version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for the “numa” or “n” option was removed as its functionality
was ignored in Kokkos for some time already.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:log}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}log file}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify a log file for LAMMPS to write status information to.  In
one\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode, if the switch is not used, LAMMPS writes to the
file log.lammps.  If this switch is used, LAMMPS writes to the
specified file.  In multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode, if the switch is not used, a
log.lammps file is created with high\sphinxhyphen{}level status information.  Each
partition also writes to a log.lammps.N file where N is the partition
ID.  If the switch is specified in multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode, the high\sphinxhyphen{}level
logfile is named “file” and each partition also logs information to a
file.N.  For both one\sphinxhyphen{}partition and multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode, if the
specified file is “none”, then no log files are created.  Using a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{log::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{log}}}} command in the input script will override this setting.
Option \sphinxhyphen{}plog will override the name of the partition log files file.N.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:mdi-flags}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}mdi ‘multiple flags’}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This flag is only recognized and used when LAMMPS has support for the MolSSI
Driver Interface (MDI) included as part of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-mdi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{MDI}}}}
package.  This flag is specific to the MDI library and controls how LAMMPS
interacts with MDI.  There are usually multiple flags that have to follow it
and those have to be placed in quotation marks.  For more information about
how to launch LAMMPS in MDI client/server mode please refer to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_mdi::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{MDI Howto}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:mpicolor}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}mpicolor color}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If used, this must be the first command\sphinxhyphen{}line argument after the LAMMPS
executable name.  It is only used when LAMMPS is launched by an mpirun
command which also launches another executable(s) at the same time.
(The other executable could be LAMMPS as well.)  The color is an
integer value which should be different for each executable (another
application may set this value in a different way).  LAMMPS and the
other executable(s) perform an MPI\_Comm\_split() with their own colors
to shrink the MPI\_COMM\_WORLD communication to be the subset of
processors they are actually running on.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:cite}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}cite style} or \sphinxstylestrong{file name}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Select how and where to output a reminder about citing contributions
to the LAMMPS code that were used during the run. Available keywords
for styles are “both”, “none”, “screen”, or “log”.  Any other keyword
will be considered a file name to write the detailed citation info to
instead of logfile or screen.  Default is the “log” style where there
is a short summary in the screen output and detailed citations
in BibTeX format in the logfile.  The option “both” selects the detailed
output for both, “none”, the short output for both, and “screen” will
write the detailed info to the screen and the short version to the log
file.  If a dedicated citation info file is requested, the screen and
log file output will be in the short format (same as with “none”).

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Intro_citing::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{citation page}}}} for more details on
how to correctly reference and cite LAMMPS.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:nocite}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}nocite}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Disable generating a citation reminder (see above) at all.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:nonbuf}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}nonbuf}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Sep2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Turn off buffering for screen and logfile output.  For performance
reasons, output to the screen and logfile is usually buffered, i.e.
output is only written to a file if its buffer \sphinxhyphen{} typically 4096 bytes \sphinxhyphen{}
has been filled.  When LAMMPS crashes for some reason, however, that can
mean that there is important output missing.  With this flag the
buffering can be turned off (only for screen and logfile output) and any
output will be committed immediately.  Note that when running in
parallel with MPI, the screen output may still be buffered by the MPI
library and this cannot be changed by LAMMPS.  This flag should only be
used for debugging and not for production simulations as the performance
impact can be significant, especially for large parallel runs.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}package style args ….}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Invoke the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} command with style and args.  The
syntax is the same as if the command appeared at the top of the input
script.  For example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}package gpu 2}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk gpu 2}} is the same as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package gpu 2}}}} in the input script.  The possible styles
and args are documented on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} doc page.  This
switch can be used multiple times, e.g. to set options for the
INTEL and OPENMP packages which can be used together.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Along with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix}} command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch, this is a convenient
mechanism for invoking accelerator packages and their options without
having to edit an input script.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:partition}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}partition 8x2 4 5 …}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Invoke LAMMPS in multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode.  When LAMMPS is run on P
processors and this switch is not used, LAMMPS runs in one partition,
i.e. all P processors run a single simulation.  If this switch is
used, the P processors are split into separate partitions and each
partition runs its own simulation.  The arguments to the switch
specify the number of processors in each partition.  Arguments of the
form MxN mean M partitions, each with N processors.  Arguments of the
form N mean a single partition with N processors.  The sum of
processors in all partitions must equal P.  Thus the command
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}partition 8x2 4 5}} has 10 partitions and runs on a total of 25
processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Running with multiple partitions can be useful for running
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_replica::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulations}}}}, where each replica
runs on one or a few processors.  Note that with MPI installed on a
machine (e.g. your desktop), you can run on more (virtual) processors
than you have physical processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To run multiple independent simulations from one input script, using
multiple partitions, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_multiple::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto multiple}}}}
page.  World\sphinxhyphen{} and universe\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} are useful
in this context.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:plog}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}plog file}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify the base name for the partition log files, so partition N
writes log information to file.N. If file is none, then no partition
log files are created.  This overrides the filename specified in the
\sphinxhyphen{}log command\sphinxhyphen{}line option.  This option is useful when working with
large numbers of partitions, allowing the partition log files to be
suppressed (\sphinxhyphen{}plog none) or placed in a subdirectory (\sphinxhyphen{}plog
replica\_files/log.lammps) If this option is not used the log file for
partition N is log.lammps.N or whatever is specified by the \sphinxhyphen{}log
command\sphinxhyphen{}line option.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Run_options:pscreen}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxhyphen{}pscreen file}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify the base name for the partition screen file, so partition N
writes screen information to file.N. If file is “none”, then no
partition screen files are created.  This overrides the filename
specified in the \sphinxhyphen{}screen command\sphinxhyphen{}line option.  This option is useful
when working with large numbers of partitions, allowing the partition
screen files to be suppressed (\sphinxhyphen{}pscreen none) or placed in a
subdirectory (\sphinxhyphen{}pscreen replica\_files/screen).  If this option is not
