\subsection{KIM package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:kim-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-kim}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package contains a command with a set of sub\sphinxhyphen{}commands that serve as a
wrapper on the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{Open Knowledgebase of Interatomic Models (OpenKIM)}
repository of interatomic models (IMs) enabling compatible ones to be used in
LAMMPS simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This includes {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim init}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim interactions}}}} commands to select, initialize and
instantiate the IM, a {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim query}}}} command to perform web
queries for material property predictions of OpenKIM IMs, a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim param}}}} command to access KIM Model Parameters from
LAMMPS, and a {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim property}}}} command to write material
properties computed in LAMMPS to standard KIM property instance format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for KIM IMs that conform to the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/kim-api/}{KIM Application Programming Interface (API)}
is provided by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_kim::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style kim}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The command \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style kim} is called by \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim interactions} and is not
recommended to be directly used in input scripts.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use this package you must have the KIM API library available on your
system. The KIM API is available for download on the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/kim-api/}{OpenKIM website}.
When installing LAMMPS from binary, the kim\sphinxhyphen{}api package
is a dependency that is automatically downloaded and installed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Information about the KIM project can be found at its website:
\sphinxurl{https://openkim.org}.
The KIM project is led by Ellad Tadmor and Ryan Elliott (U Minnesota)
and is funded by the \sphinxhref{https://www.nsf.gov/}{National Science Foundation}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Authors:} Ryan Elliott (U Minnesota) is the main developer for the KIM
API and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style kim} command. Yaser Afshar (U Minnesota),
Axel Kohlmeyer (Temple U), Ellad Tadmor (U Minnesota), and
Daniel Karls (U Minnesota) contributed to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim command}}}} interface in close collaboration with
Ryan Elliott.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{KOKKOS package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:kokkos-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-kokkos}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dozens of atom, pair, bond, angle, dihedral, improper, fix, compute
styles adapted to compile using the Kokkos library which can convert
them to OpenMP or CUDA code so that they run efficiently on multicore
CPUs, KNLs, or GPUs.  All the styles have a “kk” as a suffix in their
style name.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_kokkos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{KOKKOS package}}}} page gives details
of what hardware and software is required on your system, and how to
build and use this package.  Its styles can be invoked at run time via
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf kk}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix kk}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches}}}}.
Also see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-gpu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{GPU}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-opt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{OPT}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-intel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{INTEL}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-openmp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{OPENMP}}}} packages, which have styles
optimized for CPUs, KNLs, and GPUs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You must have a C++17 compatible compiler to use this package.
KOKKOS makes extensive use of advanced C++ features, which can
expose compiler bugs, especially when compiling for maximum
performance at high optimization levels. Please see the file
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib/kokkos/README}} for a list of compilers and their respective
platforms, that are known to work.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Authors:} The KOKKOS package was created primarily by Christian Trott
and Stan Moore (Sandia), with contributions from other folks as well.
It uses the open\sphinxhyphen{}source \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kokkos}{Kokkos library}
which was developed by Carter Edwards, Christian Trott, and others at
Sandia, and which is included in the LAMMPS distribution in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib/kokkos}}.

\subsection{KSPACE package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:kspace-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-kspace}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A variety of long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic solvers, as well as pair styles which
compute the corresponding short\sphinxhyphen{}range pairwise Coulombic interactions.
These include Ewald, particle\sphinxhyphen{}particle particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh (PPPM), and
multilevel summation method (MSM) solvers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Install:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Building with this package requires a 1d FFT library be present on your
system for use by the PPPM solvers.  This can be the KISS FFT library
provided with LAMMPS, third party libraries like FFTW, or a
vendor\sphinxhyphen{}supplied FFT library.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build settings}}}} page for details on how to select different FFT
options for your LAMMPS build.

\subsection{LEPTON package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:lepton-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-lepton}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles for pair, bond, and angle forces that evaluate the potential
function from a string using the \sphinxhref{https://simtk.org/projects/lepton}{Lepton mathematical expression parser}.  Lepton is a C++ library that is
bundled with \sphinxhref{https://openmm.org/}{OpenMM} and can be used for
parsing, evaluating, differentiating, and analyzing mathematical
expressions.  This is a more lightweight and efficient alternative for
evaluating custom potential function to an embedded Python interpreter
as used in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-python}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{PYTHON package}}}}.  On the other hand,
since the potentials are evaluated form analytical expressions, they are
more precise than what can be done with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:tabulate}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{tabulated potentials}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Authors:} Axel Kohlmeyer (Temple U).  Lepton itself is developed
by Peter Eastman at Stanford University.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 8Feb2023.}

\subsection{MACHDYN package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:machdyn-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-machdyn}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An atom style, fixes, computes, and several pair styles which
implements smoothed Mach dynamics (SMD) for solids, which is a model
related to smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) for liquids (see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-sph}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SPH package}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package solves solids mechanics problems via a state of the art
stabilized meshless method with hourglass control.  It can specify
hydrostatic interactions independently from material strength models,
i.e. pressure and deviatoric stresses are separated.  It provides many
material models (Johnson\sphinxhyphen{}Cook, plasticity with hardening,
Mie\sphinxhyphen{}Grueneisen, Polynomial EOS) and allows new material models to be
added.  It implements rigid boundary conditions (walls) which can be
specified as surface geometries from *.STL files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author:} Georg Ganzenmuller (Fraunhofer\sphinxhyphen{}Institute for High\sphinxhyphen{}Speed
Dynamics, Ernst Mach Institute, Germany).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Install:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package has {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:machdyn}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{specific installation instructions}}}} on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build extras}}}} page.

\subsection{MANIFOLD package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:manifold-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-manifold}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Several fixes and a “manifold” class which enable simulations of
particles constrained to a manifold (a 2D surface within the 3D
simulation box).  This is done by applying the RATTLE constraint
algorithm to formulate single\sphinxhyphen{}particle constraint functions
g(xi,yi,zi) = 0 and their derivative (i.e. the normal of the manifold)
n = grad(g).

Technology (TU/e), The Netherlands; since 2017: Brandeis University,
Waltham, MA, USA)

\subsection{MESONT package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:mesont-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-mesont}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
MESONT is a LAMMPS package for simulation of nanomechanics of nanotubes
(NTs).  The model is based on a coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained representation of NTs as
“flexible cylinders” consisting of a variable number of
segments. Internal interactions within a NT and the van der Waals
interaction between the tubes are described by a mesoscopic force field
designed and parameterized based on the results of atomic\sphinxhyphen{}level
molecular dynamics simulations. The description of the force field is
provided in the papers listed in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MESONT/README}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package used to have two independent implementations of this model:
the original implementation using a Fortran library written by the
developers of the model and a second implementation written in C++ by
Philipp Kloza (U Cambridge).  Since the C++ implementation offers the
same features as the original implementation with the addition of
friction, is typically faster, and easier to compile/install, the
Fortran library based implementation has since been obsoleted and
removed from the distribution. You have to download and compile
an older version of LAMMPS if you want to use those.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Download of potential files:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential files for these pair styles are \sphinxstyleemphasis{very} large and thus are
not included in the regular downloaded packages of LAMMPS or the git
repositories.  Instead, they will be automatically downloaded from a web
server when the package is installed for the first time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Authors of the obsoleted *mesont* styles:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Maxim V. Shugaev (University of Virginia), Alexey N. Volkov (University
of Alabama), Leonid V. Zhigilei (University of Virginia)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,deprecated}{Deprecated since version 8Feb2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author of the C++ styles:}
Philipp Kloza (U Cambridge)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2020.}

\subsection{MGPT package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:mgpt-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-mgpt}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A pair style which provides a fast implementation of the quantum\sphinxhyphen{}based
MGPT multi\sphinxhyphen{}ion potentials.  The MGPT or model GPT method derives from
first\sphinxhyphen{}principles DFT\sphinxhyphen{}based generalized pseudopotential theory (GPT)
through a series of systematic approximations valid for mid\sphinxhyphen{}period
transition metals with nearly half\sphinxhyphen{}filled d bands.  The MGPT method
was originally developed by John Moriarty at LLNL.  The pair style in
this package calculates forces and energies using an optimized
matrix\sphinxhyphen{}MGPT algorithm due to Tomas Oppelstrup at LLNL.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Authors:} Tomas Oppelstrup and John Moriarty (LLNL).

\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:misc-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-misc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
A variety of compute, fix, pair, bond styles with specialized
capabilities that don’t align with other packages.  Do a directory

\subsection{MOLFILE package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:molfile-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-molfile}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_molfile::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump molfile}}}} command which uses molfile plugins
that are bundled with the \sphinxhref{https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/vmd/}{VMD}
molecular visualization and analysis program, to enable LAMMPS to dump
snapshots in formats compatible with various molecular simulation
tools.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use this package you must have the desired VMD plugins available on
your system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this package only provides the interface code, not the
plugins themselves, which will be accessed when requesting a specific
plugin via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_molfile::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump molfile}}}} command.  Plugins can
be obtained from a VMD installation which has to match the platform
that you are using to compile LAMMPS for. By adding plugins to VMD,
support for new file formats can be added to LAMMPS (or VMD or other
programs that use them) without having to re\sphinxhyphen{}compile the application
itself.  More information about the VMD molfile plugins can be found
at
\sphinxurl{https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/vmd/plugins/molfile}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author:} Axel Kohlmeyer (Temple U).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dump styles for writing NetCDF formatted dump files.  NetCDF is a
portable, binary, self\sphinxhyphen{}describing file format developed on top of
HDF5. The file contents follow the AMBER NetCDF trajectory conventions
(\sphinxurl{https://ambermd.org/netcdf/nctraj.xhtml}), but include extensions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use this package you must have the NetCDF library available on your
system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that NetCDF files can be directly visualized with the following
tools:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://www.ovito.org}{Ovito} (Ovito supports the AMBER convention and the extensions mentioned above)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/vmd/}{VMD}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author:} Lars Pastewka (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Install:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package has {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:netcdf}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{specific installation instructions}}}} on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build extras}}}} page.

\subsection{OPENMP package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:openmp-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-openmp}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Hundreds of pair, fix, compute, bond, angle, dihedral, improper, and
kspace styles which are altered to enable threading on many\sphinxhyphen{}core CPUs
via OpenMP directives.  All of them have an “omp” in their style name.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_omp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{OPENMP package}}}} page gives details of what hardware
and compilers are required on your system, and how to build and use
this package.  Its styles can be invoked at run time via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf omp}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix omp}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches}}}}.  Also see
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-kokkos}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KOKKOS}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-opt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{OPT}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-intel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{INTEL}}}}
packages, which have styles optimized for CPUs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author:} Axel Kohlmeyer (Temple U).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To enable multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading support the compile flag \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}fopenmp}}
and the link flag \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}fopenmp}} (for GNU compilers, you have to look up
the equivalent flags for other compilers) must be used to build LAMMPS.
When using Intel compilers, also the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}restrict}} flag is required.
The OPENMP package can be compiled without enabling OpenMP; then
all code will be compiled as serial and the only improvement over the
regular styles are some data access optimization. These flags should
be added to the CCFLAGS and LINKFLAGS lines of your Makefile.machine.
See \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/OPTIONS/Makefile}}.omp for an example.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once you have an appropriate Makefile.machine, you can
install/uninstall the package and build LAMMPS in the usual manner:

having to recompile and relink LAMMPS.

When the environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_PLUGIN\_PATH}} is set, then LAMMPS
will search the directory (or directories) listed in this path for files
with names that end in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plugin.so}} (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{helloplugin.so}}) and will
try to load the contained plugins automatically at start\sphinxhyphen{}up.

\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:qmmm-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-qmmm}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_qmmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix qmmm}}}} command which allows LAMMPS to be used as
the MM code in a QM/MM simulation.  This is currently only available
in combination with the \sphinxhref{https://www.quantum-espresso.org}{Quantum ESPRESSO} package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use this package you must have Quantum ESPRESSO (QE) available on
your system and include its coupling library in the compilation and
then compile LAMMPS as a library.  For QM/MM calculations you then
build a custom binary with MPI support, that sets up 3 partitions with
MPI sub\sphinxhyphen{}communicators (for inter\sphinxhyphen{} and intra\sphinxhyphen{}partition communication)
and then calls the corresponding library interfaces on each partition
(2x LAMMPS and 1x QE).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The current implementation supports an ONIOM style mechanical coupling
and a multi\sphinxhyphen{}pole based electrostatic coupling to the Quantum ESPRESSO
plane wave DFT package.  The QM/MM interface has been written in a
manner that coupling to other QM codes should be possible without
changes to LAMMPS itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Authors:} Axel Kohlmeyer (Temple U). Mariella Ippolito and Carlo Cavazzoni (CINECA, Italy)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Install:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package has {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:qmmm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{specific installation instructions}}}}
on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build extras}}}} page.

\subsection{QTB package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:qtb-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-qtb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two fixes which provide a self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent quantum treatment of
vibrational modes in a classical molecular dynamics simulation.  By
coupling the MD simulation to a colored thermostat, it introduces zero
point energy into the system, altering the energy power spectrum and
the heat capacity to account for their quantum nature. This is useful
when modeling systems at temperatures lower than their classical
limits or when temperatures ramp across the classical limits in a
simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author:} Yuan Shen (Stanford U).

\subsection{REACTION package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:reaction-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-reaction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package implements the REACTER protocol, which allows for complex
bond topology changes (reactions) during a running MD simulation when
using classical force fields. Topology changes are defined in pre\sphinxhyphen{} and
post\sphinxhyphen{}reaction molecule templates and can include creation and deletion
of bonds, angles, dihedrals, impropers, atom types, bond types, angle
types, dihedral types, improper types, and/or atomic charges. Other
options currently available include reaction constraints (e.g., angle
and Arrhenius constraints), deletion of reaction byproducts or other
small molecules, creation of new atoms or molecules bonded to existing
atoms, and using LAMMPS variables for input parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author:} Jacob R. Gissinger (NASA Langley Research Center).

\subsection{SPH package}
\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:sph-package}}\label{\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-sph}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Contents:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An atom style, fixes, computes, and several pair styles which
implements smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) for liquids.  See the
related {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-machdyn}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{MACHDYN package}}}} package for smooth Mach dynamics
(SMD) for solids.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This package contains ideal gas, Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones equation of states,
Tait, and full support for complete (i.e. internal\sphinxhyphen{}energy dependent)
equations of state.  It allows for plain or Monaghans XSPH integration
of the equations of motion.  It has options for density continuity or
density summation to propagate the density field.  It has
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command options to set the internal energy and density
of particles from the input script and allows the same quantities to
be output with thermodynamic output or to dump files via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Author:} Georg Ganzenmuller (Fraunhofer\sphinxhyphen{}Institute for High\sphinxhyphen{}Speed
Dynamics, Ernst Mach Institute, Germany).

\chapter{Accelerate performance}
\label{\detokenize{Speed:accelerate-performance}}\label{\detokenize{Speed::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section describes various methods for improving LAMMPS
performance for different classes of problems running on different
kinds of machines.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two thrusts to the discussion that follows.  The first is
using code options that implement alternate algorithms that can
speed\sphinxhyphen{}up a simulation.  The second is to use one of the several
accelerator packages provided with LAMMPS that contain code optimized
for certain kinds of hardware, including multicore CPUs, GPUs, and
Intel Xeon Phi co\sphinxhyphen{}processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bench.html}{Benchmark page} of the LAMMPS
website gives performance results for the various accelerator
packages discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page, for several of the standard LAMMPS benchmark problems, as a
function of problem size and number of compute nodes, on different
hardware platforms.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Benchmarks}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_bench:benchmarks}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_bench::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Current LAMMPS performance is discussed on the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bench.html}{Benchmarks page} of the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org}{LAMMPS website}
where timings and parallel efficiency are listed.  The page has
several sections, which are briefly described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
CPU performance on 5 standard problems, strong and weak scaling

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GPU and Xeon Phi performance on same and related problems

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparison of cost of interatomic potentials

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Performance of huge, billion\sphinxhyphen{}atom problems

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 5 standard problems are as follow:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LJ = atomic fluid, Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential with 2.5 sigma cutoff (55
neighbors per atom), NVE integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Chain = bead\sphinxhyphen{}spring polymer melt of 100\sphinxhyphen{}mer chains, FENE bonds and LJ
pairwise interactions with a \(2^{\frac{1}{6}}\) sigma cutoff (5 neighbors per
atom), NVE integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
EAM = metallic solid, Cu EAM potential with 4.95 Angstrom cutoff (45
neighbors per atom), NVE integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Chute = granular chute flow, frictional history potential with 1.1
sigma cutoff (7 neighbors per atom), NVE integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rhodo = rhodopsin protein in solvated lipid bilayer, CHARMM force
field with a 10 Angstrom LJ cutoff (440 neighbors per atom),
particle\sphinxhyphen{}particle particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh (PPPM) for long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombics, NPT
integration

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Input files for these 5 problems are provided in the bench directory
of the LAMMPS distribution.  Each has 32,000 atoms and runs for 100
timesteps.  The size of the problem (number of atoms) can be varied
using command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches as described in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bench/README}} file.
This is an easy way to test performance and either strong or weak
scalability on your machine.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The bench directory includes a few \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{log.*}} files that show performance
of these 5 problems on 1 or 4 cores of Linux desktop.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bench/FERMI}}
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bench/KEPLER}} directories have input files and scripts and instructions
for running the same (or similar) problems using OpenMP or GPU or Xeon
Phi acceleration options.  See the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{README}} files in those directories and the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} pages for instructions on how
to build LAMMPS and run on that kind of hardware.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bench/POTENTIALS}} directory has input files which correspond to the
table of results on the
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bench.html\#potentials}{Potentials} section of
the Benchmarks web page.  So you can also run those test problems on
your machine.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bench.html\#billion}{billion\sphinxhyphen{}atom} section
of the Benchmarks web page has performance data for very large
benchmark runs of simple Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones (LJ) models, which use the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bench/in.lj}} input script.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For all the benchmarks, a useful metric is the CPU cost per atom per
timestep.  Since performance scales roughly linearly with problem size
and timesteps for all LAMMPS models (i.e. interatomic or coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained
potentials), the run time of any problem using the same model (atom
style, force field, cutoff, etc) can then be estimated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Performance on a parallel machine can also be predicted from one\sphinxhyphen{}core
or one\sphinxhyphen{}node timings if the parallel efficiency can be estimated.  The
communication bandwidth and latency of a particular parallel machine
affects the efficiency.  On most machines LAMMPS will give a parallel
efficiency on these benchmarks above 50\% so long as the number of
atoms/core is a few 100 or greater, and closer to 100\% for large
numbers of atoms/core.  This is for all\sphinxhyphen{}MPI mode with one MPI task per
core.  For nodes with accelerator options or hardware (OpenMP, GPU,
Phi), you should first measure single node performance.  Then you can
estimate parallel performance for multi\sphinxhyphen{}node runs using the same logic
as for all\sphinxhyphen{}MPI mode, except that now you will typically need many more
atoms/node to achieve good scalability.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Measuring performance}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_measure:measuring-performance}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_measure::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before trying to make your simulation run faster, you should
understand how it currently performs and where the bottlenecks are.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The best way to do this is run the your system (actual number of
atoms) for a modest number of timesteps (say 100 steps) on several
different processor counts, including a single processor if possible.
Do this for an equilibrium version of your system, so that the
100\sphinxhyphen{}step timings are representative of a much longer run.  There is
typically no need to run for 1000s of timesteps to get accurate
timings; you can simply extrapolate from short runs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the set of runs, look at the timing data printed to the screen and
log file at the end of each LAMMPS run.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{screen and logfile output}}}} page gives an overview.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Running on one (or a few processors) should give a good estimate of
the serial performance and what portions of the timestep are taking
the most time.  Running the same problem on a few different processor
counts should give an estimate of parallel scalability.  I.e. if the
simulation runs 16x faster on 16 processors, its 100\% parallel
efficient; if it runs 8x faster on 16 processors, it’s 50\% efficient.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The most important data to look at in the timing info is the timing
breakdown and relative percentages.  For example, trying different
options for speeding up the long\sphinxhyphen{}range solvers will have little impact
if they only consume 10\% of the run time.  If the pairwise time is
dominating, you may want to look at GPU or OMP versions of the pair
style, as discussed below.  Comparing how the percentages change as
you increase the processor count gives you a sense of how different
operations within the timestep are scaling.  Note that if you are
running with a Kspace solver, there is additional output on the
breakdown of the Kspace time.  For PPPM, this includes the fraction
spent on FFTs, which can be communication intensive.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another important detail in the timing info are the histograms of
atoms counts and neighbor counts.  If these vary widely across
processors, you have a load\sphinxhyphen{}imbalance issue.  This often results in
inaccurate relative timing data, because processors have to wait when
communication occurs for other processors to catch up.  Thus the
reported times for “Communication” or “Other” may be higher than they
really are, due to load\sphinxhyphen{}imbalance.  If this is an issue, you can
use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timer sync}}}} command to obtain synchronized timings.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{General tips}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_tips:general-tips}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_tips::doc}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
this page is still a work in progress
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a list of general ideas for improving simulation performance.
Most of them are only applicable to certain models and certain
bottlenecks in the current performance, so let the timing data you
generate be your guide.  It is hard, if not impossible, to predict how
much difference these options will make, since it is a function of
problem size, number of processors used, and your machine.  There is
no substitute for identifying performance bottlenecks, and trying out
various options.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rRESPA

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Two\sphinxhyphen{}FFT PPPM

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Staggered PPPM

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
single vs double PPPM

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
partial charge PPPM

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
verlet/split run style

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
processor command for proc layout and numa layout

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing: balance and fix balance

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two\sphinxhyphen{}FFT PPPM, also called \sphinxstyleemphasis{analytic differentiation} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ad} PPPM,
uses 2 FFTs instead of the 4 FFTs used by the default \sphinxstyleemphasis{ik
differentiation} PPPM. However, 2\sphinxhyphen{}FFT PPPM also requires a slightly
larger mesh size to achieve the same accuracy as 4\sphinxhyphen{}FFT PPPM. For
problems where the FFT cost is the performance bottleneck (typically
large problems running on many processors), 2\sphinxhyphen{}FFT PPPM may be faster
than 4\sphinxhyphen{}FFT PPPM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Staggered PPPM performs calculations using two different meshes, one
shifted slightly with respect to the other.  This can reduce force
aliasing errors and increase the accuracy of the method, but also
doubles the amount of work required. For high relative accuracy, using
staggered PPPM allows one to half the mesh size in each dimension as
compared to regular PPPM, which can give around a 4x speedup in the
kspace time. However, for low relative accuracy, using staggered PPPM
gives little benefit and can be up to 2x slower in the kspace
time. For example, the rhodopsin benchmark was run on a single
processor, and results for kspace time vs. relative accuracy for the
different methods are shown in the figure below.  For this system,
staggered PPPM (using ik differentiation) becomes useful when using a
relative accuracy of slightly greater than 1e\sphinxhyphen{}5 and above.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{rhodo_staggered}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using staggered PPPM may not give the same increase in accuracy
of energy and pressure as it does in forces, so some caution must be
used if energy and/or pressure are quantities of interest, such as
when using a barostat.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Accelerator packages}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_packages:accelerator-packages}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerated versions of various {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}, and other commands have
been added to LAMMPS, which will typically run faster than the
standard non\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated versions.  Some require appropriate hardware
to be present on your system, e.g. GPUs or Intel Xeon Phi
co\sphinxhyphen{}processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar

overview of packages is give on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Packages}}}} doc
pages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the accelerator packages currently in LAMMPS:
