\subsection{GPU package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_gpu:gpu-package}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_gpu::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package was developed by Mike Brown while at SNL and ORNL (now
at Intel Corp.) and his collaborators, particularly Trung Nguyen (now at
Northwestern).  Support for AMD GPUs via HIP was added by Vsevolod Nikolskiy
and coworkers at HSE University.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package provides GPU versions of many pair styles and for
parts of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}} for long\sphinxhyphen{}range
Coulombics.  It has the following general features:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is designed to exploit common GPU hardware configurations where one
or more GPUs are coupled to many cores of one or more multicore CPUs,
e.g. within a node of a parallel machine.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom\sphinxhyphen{}based data (e.g. coordinates, forces) are moved back\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}forth
between the CPU(s) and GPU every timestep.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Neighbor lists can be built on the CPU or on the GPU

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The charge assignment and force interpolation portions of PPPM can be
run on the GPU.  The FFT portion, which requires MPI communication
between processors, runs on the CPU.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Force computations of different style (pair vs. bond/angle/dihedral/improper)
can be performed concurrently on the GPU and CPU(s), respectively.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It allows for GPU computations to be performed in single or double
precision, or in mixed\sphinxhyphen{}mode precision, where pairwise forces are
computed in single precision, but accumulated into double\sphinxhyphen{}precision
force vectors.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}specific code is in the GPU package.  It makes calls to a
generic GPU library in the lib/gpu directory.  This library provides
either Nvidia support, AMD support, or more general OpenCL support
(for Nvidia GPUs, AMD GPUs, Intel GPUs, and multicore CPUs).
so that the same functionality is supported on a variety of hardware.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Required hardware/software:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To compile and use this package in CUDA mode, you currently need
to have an NVIDIA GPU and install the corresponding NVIDIA CUDA
toolkit software on your system (this is only tested on Linux
and unsupported on Windows):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check if you have an NVIDIA GPU: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cat /proc/driver/nvidia/gpus/\textbackslash{}*/information}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Go to \sphinxurl{https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Install a driver and toolkit appropriate for your system (SDK is not necessary)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps/lib/gpu/nvc\_get\_devices}} (after building the GPU library, see below) to
list supported devices and properties

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To compile and use this package in OpenCL mode, you currently need
to have the OpenCL headers and the (vendor neutral) OpenCL library installed.
In OpenCL mode, the acceleration depends on having an \sphinxhref{https://www.khronos.org/news/permalink/opencl-installable-client-driver-icd-loader}{OpenCL Installable Client Driver (ICD)}
installed. There can be multiple of them for the same or different hardware
(GPUs, CPUs, Accelerators) installed at the same time. OpenCL refers to those
as ‘platforms’.  The GPU library will try to auto\sphinxhyphen{}select the best suitable platform,
but this can be overridden using the platform option of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}}
command. run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps/lib/gpu/ocl\_get\_devices}} to get a list of available
platforms and devices with a suitable ICD available.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To compile and use this package for Intel GPUs, OpenCL or the Intel oneAPI
HPC Toolkit can be installed using linux package managers. The latter also
provides optimized C++, MPI, and many other libraries and tools. See:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxurl{https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/tools/oneapi/hpc-toolkit/download.html}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you do not have a discrete GPU card installed, this package can still provide
significant speedups on some CPUs that include integrated GPUs. Additionally, for
many macs, OpenCL is already included with the OS and Makefiles are available
in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib/gpu}} directory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To compile and use this package in HIP mode, you have to have the AMD ROCm
software installed. Versions of ROCm older than 3.5 are currently deprecated
by AMD.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Building LAMMPS with the GPU package:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:gpu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Build extras}}}} page for
instructions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Run with the GPU package from the command line:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}} command sets the total number of MPI tasks
used by LAMMPS (one or multiple per compute node) and the number of MPI
tasks used per node.  E.g. the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} command in MPICH does this via
its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}ppn}} switches.  Ditto for OpenMPI via \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}npernode}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the GPU package, you cannot assign more than one GPU to a
single MPI task.  However multiple MPI tasks can share the same GPU,
and in many cases it will be more efficient to run this way.  Likewise
it may be more efficient to use less MPI tasks/node than the available
\# of CPU cores.  Assignment of multiple MPI tasks to a GPU will happen
automatically if you create more MPI tasks/node than there are
GPUs/mode.  E.g. with 8 MPI tasks/node and 2 GPUs, each GPU will be
shared by 4 MPI tasks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package also has limited support for OpenMP for both
multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading and vectorization of routines that are run on the CPUs.
This requires that the GPU library and LAMMPS are built with flags to
enable OpenMP support (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}fopenmp}}). Some styles for time integration
are also available in the GPU package. These run completely on the CPUs
in full double precision, but exploit multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading and vectorization
for faster performance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf gpu}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}, which will
automatically append “gpu” to styles that support it.  Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk
gpu Ng}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Ng}} = \# of
GPUs/node to use. If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Ng}} is 0, the number is selected automatically as
the number of matching GPUs that have the highest number of compute
cores.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 MPI task uses 1 GPU}
lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 12 MPI tasks share 2 GPUs on a single 16\PYGZhy{}core (or whatever) node}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} ditto on 4 16\PYGZhy{}core nodes}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{48}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf gpu}} switch is used, it also issues a default
{\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package gpu 0}}}} command, which will result in
automatic selection of the number of GPUs to use.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk}} switch explicitly allows for setting of the number of
GPUs/node to use and additional options.  Its syntax is the same as
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{package gpu}} command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}}
command page for details, including the default values used for
all its options if it is not specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the default for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package gpu}}}} command is to
set the Newton flag to “off” pairwise interactions.  It does not
affect the setting for bonded interactions (LAMMPS default is “on”).
The “off” setting for pairwise interaction is currently required for
GPU package pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Or run with the GPU package by editing an input script:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The discussion above for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}} command, MPI
tasks/node, and use of multiple MPI tasks/GPU is the same.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix gpu}}}} command, or you can explicitly add an
“gpu” suffix to individual styles in your input script, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{gpu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You must also use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package gpu}}}} command to enable the
GPU package, unless the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf gpu}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk gpu}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches}}}} were used.  It specifies the number of
GPUs/node to use, as well as other options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Speed\sphinxhyphen{}ups to expect:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The performance of a GPU versus a multicore CPU is a function of your
hardware, which pair style is used, the number of atoms/GPU, and the
precision used on the GPU (double, single, mixed). Using the GPU package
in OpenCL mode on CPUs (which uses vectorization and multithreading) is
usually resulting in inferior performance compared to using LAMMPS’ native
threading and vectorization support in the OPENMP and INTEL packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bench.html}{Benchmark page} of the
LAMMPS website for performance of the GPU package on various
hardware, including the Titan HPC platform at ORNL.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You should also experiment with how many MPI tasks per GPU to use to
give the best performance for your problem and machine.  This is also
a function of the problem size and the pair style being using.
Likewise, you should experiment with the precision setting for the GPU
library to see if single or mixed precision will give accurate
results, since they will typically be faster.

\sphinxAtStartPar
MPI parallelism typically outperforms OpenMP parallelism, but in some
cases using fewer MPI tasks and multiple OpenMP threads with the GPU
package can give better performance. 3\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials can often perform
better with multiple OMP threads because the inter\sphinxhyphen{}process communication
is higher for these styles with the GPU package in order to allow
deterministic results.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Guidelines for best performance:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using multiple MPI tasks per GPU will often give the best performance,
as allowed my most multicore CPU/GPU configurations.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the number of particles per MPI task is small (e.g. 100s of
particles), it can be more efficient to run with fewer MPI tasks per
GPU, even if you do not use all the cores on the compute node.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package gpu}}}} command has several options for tuning
performance.  Neighbor lists can be built on the GPU or CPU.  Force
calculations can be dynamically balanced across the CPU cores and
GPUs.  GPU\sphinxhyphen{}specific settings can be made which can be optimized
for different hardware.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} command
page for details.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As described by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package gpu}}}} command, GPU
accelerated pair styles can perform computations asynchronously with
CPU computations. The “Pair” time reported by LAMMPS will be the
maximum of the time required to complete the CPU pair style
computations and the time required to complete the GPU pair style
computations. Any time spent for GPU\sphinxhyphen{}enabled pair styles for
computations that run simultaneously with {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{long\sphinxhyphen{}range}}}}
calculations will not be included in the “Pair” time.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since only part of the pppm kspace style is GPU accelerated, it
may be faster to only use GPU acceleration for Pair styles with
long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatics.  See the “pair/only” keyword of the
package command for a shortcut to do that.  The work between kspace
on the CPU and non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions on the GPU can be balanced
through adjusting the coulomb cutoff without loss of accuracy.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting for the package gpu command is force/neigh,
the time for neighbor list calculations on the GPU will be added into
the “Pair” time, not the “Neigh” time.  An additional breakdown of the
times required for various tasks on the GPU (data copy, neighbor
calculations, force computations, etc) are output only with the LAMMPS
screen output (not in the log file) at the end of each run.  These
timings represent total time spent on the GPU for each routine,
regardless of asynchronous CPU calculations.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The output section “GPU Time Info (average)” reports “Max Mem / Proc”.
This is the maximum memory used at one time on the GPU for data
storage by a single MPI process.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_gpu:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{INTEL package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:intel-package}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The INTEL package is maintained by Mike Brown at Intel
Corporation.  It provides two methods for accelerating simulations,
depending on the hardware you have.  The first is acceleration on
Intel CPUs by running in single, mixed, or double precision with
vectorization.  The second is acceleration on Intel Xeon Phi
co\sphinxhyphen{}processors via offloading neighbor list and non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded force
calculations to the Phi.  The same C++ code is used in both cases.
When offloading to a co\sphinxhyphen{}processor from a CPU, the same routine is run
twice, once on the CPU and once with an offload flag. This allows
LAMMPS to run on the CPU cores and co\sphinxhyphen{}processor cores simultaneously.


\subsubsection{Currently Available INTEL Styles}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:currently-available-intel-styles}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Angle Styles: charmm, harmonic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bond Styles: fene, fourier, harmonic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dihedral Styles: charmm, fourier, harmonic, opls

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes: nve, npt, nvt, nvt/sllod, nve/asphere

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Improper Styles: cvff, harmonic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair Styles: airebo, airebo/morse, buck/coul/cut, buck/coul/long,
buck, dpd, eam, eam/alloy, eam/fs, gayberne, lj/charmm/coul/charmm,
lj/charmm/coul/long, lj/cut, lj/cut/coul/long, lj/long/coul/long,
rebo, sw, tersoff

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
K\sphinxhyphen{}Space Styles: pppm, pppm/disp

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the styles in the INTEL package currently
support computing per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress.  If any compute or fix in your
input requires it, LAMMPS will abort with an error message.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Speed\sphinxhyphen{}up to expect}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:speed-up-to-expect}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The speedup will depend on your simulation, the hardware, which
styles are used, the number of atoms, and the floating\sphinxhyphen{}point
precision mode. Performance improvements are shown compared to
LAMMPS \sphinxstyleemphasis{without using other acceleration packages} as these are
under active development (and subject to performance changes). The
measurements were performed using the input files available in
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/INTEL/TEST}} directory with the provided run script.
These are scalable in size; the results given are with 512K
particles (524K for Liquid Crystal). Most of the simulations are
standard LAMMPS benchmarks (indicated by the filename extension in
parenthesis) with modifications to the run length and to add a
warm\sphinxhyphen{}up run (for use with offload benchmarks).

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{user_intel}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Results are speedups obtained on Intel Xeon E5\sphinxhyphen{}2697v4 processors
(code\sphinxhyphen{}named Broadwell), Intel Xeon Phi 7250 processors (code\sphinxhyphen{}named
Knights Landing), and Intel Xeon Gold 6148 processors (code\sphinxhyphen{}named
Skylake) with “June 2017” LAMMPS built with Intel Parallel Studio
2017 update 2. Results are with 1 MPI task per physical core. See
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/INTEL/TEST/README}} for the raw simulation rates and
instructions to reproduce.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Accuracy and order of operations}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:accuracy-and-order-of-operations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In most molecular dynamics software, parallelization parameters
(\# of MPI, OpenMP, and vectorization) can change the results due
to changing the order of operations with finite\sphinxhyphen{}precision
calculations. The INTEL package is deterministic. This means
that the results should be reproducible from run to run with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{same} parallel configurations and when using deterministic
libraries or library settings (MPI, OpenMP, FFT). However, there
are differences in the INTEL package that can change the
order of operations compared to LAMMPS without acceleration:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Neighbor lists can be created in a different order

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bins used for sorting atoms can be oriented differently

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default stencil order for PPPM is 7. By default, LAMMPS will
calculate other PPPM parameters to fit the desired accuracy with
this order

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} setting applies to all atoms, not just atoms shared
between MPI tasks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Vectorization can change the order for adding pairwise forces

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_USE\_MKL\_RNG}} define (all included intel optimized
makefiles do) at build time, the random number generator for
dissipative particle dynamics (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair style dpd/intel}}) uses the Mersenne
Twister generator included in the Intel MKL library (that should be
more robust than the default Masaglia random number generator)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The precision mode (described below) used with the INTEL
package can change the \sphinxstyleemphasis{accuracy} of the calculations. For the
default \sphinxstyleemphasis{mixed} precision option, calculations between pairs or
triplets of atoms are performed in single precision, intended to
be within the inherent error of MD simulations. All accumulation
is performed in double precision to prevent the error from growing
with the number of atoms in the simulation. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Single} precision
mode should not be used without appropriate validation.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Quick Start for Experienced Users}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:quick-start-for-experienced-users}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS should be built with the INTEL package installed.
Simulations should be run with 1 MPI task per physical \sphinxstyleemphasis{core},
not \sphinxstyleemphasis{hardware thread}.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Edit \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/OPTIONS/Makefile.intel\_cpu\_intelmpi}} as necessary.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KMP\_BLOCKTIME=0}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel 0 omp \$t \sphinxhyphen{}sf intel}} added to LAMMPS command\sphinxhyphen{}line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$t}} should be 2 for Intel Xeon CPUs and 2 or 4 for Intel Xeon Phi

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For some of the simple 2\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials without long\sphinxhyphen{}range
electrostatics, performance and scalability can be better with
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{newton off}} setting added to the input script

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For simulations on higher node counts, add \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{processors * * * grid
numa}} to the beginning of the input script for better scalability

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kspace\_style pppm}} in the input script, add
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kspace\_modify diff ad}} for better performance

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For Intel Xeon Phi CPUs:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Runs should be performed using MCDRAM.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For simulations using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kspace\_style pppm}} on Intel CPUs supporting
AVX\sphinxhyphen{}512:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kspace\_modify diff ad}} to the input script

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The command\sphinxhyphen{}line option should be changed to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel 0 omp \$r lrt yes \sphinxhyphen{}sf intel}} where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$r}} is the number of
threads minus 1.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not use thread affinity (set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KMP\_AFFINITY=none}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{newton off}} setting may provide better scalability

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For Intel Xeon Phi co\sphinxhyphen{}processors (Offload):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Edit \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/OPTIONS/Makefile.intel\_co\sphinxhyphen{}processor}} as necessary

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel N omp 1}} added to command\sphinxhyphen{}line where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{N}} is the number of
co\sphinxhyphen{}processors per node.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Required hardware/software}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:required-hardware-software}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using Intel compilers version 16.0 or later is required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to use offload to co\sphinxhyphen{}processors, an Intel Xeon Phi
co\sphinxhyphen{}processor and an Intel compiler are required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Although any compiler can be used with the INTEL package,
currently, vectorization directives are disabled by default when
not using Intel compilers due to lack of standard support and
observations of decreased performance. The OpenMP standard now
supports directives for vectorization and we plan to transition the
code to this standard once it is available in most compilers. We
expect this to allow improved performance and support with other
compilers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For Intel Xeon Phi x200 series processors (code\sphinxhyphen{}named Knights
Landing), there are multiple configuration options for the hardware.
For best performance, we recommend that the MCDRAM is configured in
“Flat” mode and with the cluster mode set to “Quadrant” or “SNC4”.
“Cache” mode can also be used, although the performance might be
slightly lower.


\subsubsection{Notes about Simultaneous Multithreading}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:notes-about-simultaneous-multithreading}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modern CPUs often support Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT). On
Intel processors, this is called Hyper\sphinxhyphen{}Threading (HT) technology.
SMT is hardware support for running multiple threads efficiently on
a single core. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Hardware threads} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{logical cores} are often used
to refer to the number of threads that are supported in hardware.
For example, the Intel Xeon E5\sphinxhyphen{}2697v4 processor is described
as having 36 cores and 72 threads. This means that 36 MPI processes
or OpenMP threads can run simultaneously on separate cores, but that
up to 72 MPI processes or OpenMP threads can be running on the CPU
without costly operating system context switches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Molecular dynamics simulations will often run faster when making use
of SMT. If a thread becomes stalled, for example because it is
waiting on data that has not yet arrived from memory, another thread
can start running so that the CPU pipeline is still being used
efficiently. Although benefits can be seen by launching a MPI task
for every hardware thread, for multinode simulations, we recommend
that OpenMP threads are used for SMT instead, either with the
INTEL package, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_omp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{OPENMP package}}}}, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_kokkos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{KOKKOS package}}}}. In the example above, up
to 36X speedups can be observed by using all 36 physical cores with
LAMMPS. By using all 72 hardware threads, an additional 10\sphinxhyphen{}30\%
performance gain can be achieved.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The BIOS on many platforms allows SMT to be disabled, however, we do
not recommend this on modern processors as there is little to no
benefit for any software package in most cases. The operating system
will report every hardware thread as a separate core allowing one to
determine the number of hardware threads available. On Linux systems,
this information can normally be obtained with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cat\PYG{+w}{ }/proc/cpuinfo
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Building LAMMPS with the INTEL package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:building-lammps-with-the-intel-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:intel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Build extras}}}} page for
instructions.  Some additional details are covered here.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For building with make, several example Makefiles for building with
the Intel compiler are included with LAMMPS in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE/OPTIONS/}}
directory:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Makefile.intel\PYGZus{}cpu\PYGZus{}intelmpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Intel Compiler, Intel MPI, No Offload}
Makefile.knl\PYG{+w}{                }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Intel Compiler, Intel MPI, No Offload}
Makefile.intel\PYGZus{}cpu\PYGZus{}mpich\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Intel Compiler, MPICH, No Offload}
Makefile.intel\PYGZus{}cpu\PYGZus{}openpmi\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Intel Compiler, OpenMPI, No Offload}
Makefile.intel\PYGZus{}co\PYGZhy{}processor\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Intel Compiler, Intel MPI, Offload}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Makefile.knl is identical to Makefile.intel\_cpu\_intelmpi except that
it explicitly specifies that vectorization should be for Intel Xeon
Phi x200 processors making it easier to cross\sphinxhyphen{}compile. For users with
recent installations of Intel Parallel Studio, the process can be as
simple as:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }yes\PYGZhy{}intel
\PYG{n+nb}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }/opt/intel/parallel\PYGZus{}studio\PYGZus{}xe\PYGZus{}2016.3.067/psxevars.sh
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} or psxevars.csh for C\PYGZhy{}shell}
make\PYG{+w}{ }intel\PYGZus{}cpu\PYGZus{}intelmpi
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if you build with support for a Phi co\sphinxhyphen{}processor, the same
binary can be used on nodes with or without co\sphinxhyphen{}processors installed.
However, if you do not have co\sphinxhyphen{}processors on your system, building
without offload support will produce a smaller binary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The general requirements for Makefiles with the INTEL package
are as follows. When using Intel compilers, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}restrict}} is required
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}qopenmp}} is highly recommended for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LINKFLAGS}}.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}} should include \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_INTEL\_USELRT}} (unless POSIX Threads
are not supported in the build environment) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_USE\_MKL\_RNG}}
(unless Intel Math Kernel Library (MKL) is not available in the build
environment). For Intel compilers, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LIB}} should include \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}ltbbmalloc}}
or if the library is not available, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_INTEL\_NO\_TBB}} can be added
to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}}. For builds supporting offload, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_INTEL\_OFFLOAD}} is
required for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}qoffload}} is required for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LINKFLAGS}}. Other
recommended \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAG}} options for best performance are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}O2 \sphinxhyphen{}fno\sphinxhyphen{}alias
\sphinxhyphen{}ansi\sphinxhyphen{}alias \sphinxhyphen{}qoverride\sphinxhyphen{}limits fp\sphinxhyphen{}model fast=2 \sphinxhyphen{}no\sphinxhyphen{}prec\sphinxhyphen{}div}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/INTEL/README}} file for additional flags that
might be needed for best performance on Intel server processors
code\sphinxhyphen{}named “Skylake”.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The vectorization and math capabilities can differ depending on
the CPU. For Intel compilers, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}x}} flag specifies the type of
processor for which to optimize. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}xHost}} specifies that the compiler
should build for the processor used for compiling. For Intel Xeon Phi
x200 series processors, this option is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}xMIC\sphinxhyphen{}AVX512}}. For fourth
generation Intel Xeon (v4/Broadwell) processors, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}xCORE\sphinxhyphen{}AVX2}} should
be used. For older Intel Xeon processors, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}xAVX}} will perform best
in general for the different simulations in LAMMPS. The default
in most of the example Makefiles is to use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}xHost}}, however this
should not be used when cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiling.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Running LAMMPS with the INTEL package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:running-lammps-with-the-intel-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Running LAMMPS with the INTEL package is similar to normal use
with the exceptions that one should 1) specify that LAMMPS should use
the INTEL package, 2) specify the number of OpenMP threads, and
3) optionally specify the specific LAMMPS styles that should use the
INTEL package. 1) and 2) can be performed from the command\sphinxhyphen{}line
or by editing the input script. 3) requires editing the input script.
Advanced performance tuning options are also described below to get
the best performance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on a single node (including runs using offload to a
co\sphinxhyphen{}processor), best performance is normally obtained by using 1 MPI
task per physical core and additional OpenMP threads with SMT. For
Intel Xeon processors, 2 OpenMP threads should be used for SMT.
For Intel Xeon Phi CPUs, 2 or 4 OpenMP threads should be used
(best choice depends on the simulation). In cases where the user
specifies that LRT mode is used (described below), 1 or 3 OpenMP
threads should be used. For multi\sphinxhyphen{}node runs, using 1 MPI task per
physical core will often perform best, however, depending on the
machine and scale, users might get better performance by decreasing
the number of MPI tasks and using more OpenMP threads. For
performance, the product of the number of MPI tasks and OpenMP
threads should not exceed the number of available hardware threads in
almost all cases.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Setting core affinity is often used to pin MPI tasks and OpenMP
threads to a core or group of cores so that memory access can be
uniform. Unless disabled at build time, affinity for MPI tasks and
OpenMP threads on the host (CPU) will be set by default on the host
\sphinxstyleemphasis{when using offload to a co\sphinxhyphen{}processor}. In this case, it is unnecessary
to use other methods to control affinity (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{taskset}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{numactl}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{I\_MPI\_PIN\_DOMAIN}}, etc.). This can be disabled with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{no\_affinity}
option to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command or by disabling the
option at build time (by adding \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DINTEL\_OFFLOAD\_NOAFFINITY}} to the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}} line of your Makefile). Disabling this option is not
recommended, especially when running on a machine with Intel
Hyper\sphinxhyphen{}Threading technology disabled.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Run with the INTEL package from the command line}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:run-with-the-intel-package-from-the-command-line}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To enable INTEL optimizations for all available styles used in
the input script, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf intel}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} can be used without any requirement for
editing the input script. This switch will automatically append
“intel” to styles that support it. It also invokes a default command:
{\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel 1}}}}. This package command is used to set
options for the INTEL package.  The default package command will
specify that INTEL calculations are performed in mixed precision,
that the number of OpenMP threads is specified by the OMP\_NUM\_THREADS
environment variable, and that if co\sphinxhyphen{}processors are present and the
binary was built with offload support, that 1 co\sphinxhyphen{}processor per node
will be used with automatic balancing of work between the CPU and the
co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify different options for the INTEL package by using
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel Nphi}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} with
keyword/value pairs as specified in the documentation. Here, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Nphi}} = \#
of Xeon Phi co\sphinxhyphen{}processors/node (ignored without offload
support). Common options to the INTEL package include \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} to
override any \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS}} setting and specify the number of OpenMP
threads, \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} to set the floating\sphinxhyphen{}point precision mode, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{lrt} to
enable Long\sphinxhyphen{}Range Thread mode as described below. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command for details, including the default values
used for all its options if not specified, and how to set the number
of OpenMP threads via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS}} environment variable if
desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples (see documentation for your MPI/Machine for differences in
launching MPI applications):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 2 nodes, 36 MPI tasks/node, \PYGZdl{}OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS OpenMP Threads}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{72}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{36}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }intel\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Don\PYGZsq{}t use any co\PYGZhy{}processors that might be available,}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} use 2 OpenMP threads for each task, use double precision}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{72}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{36}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }intel\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{       }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }intel\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }mode\PYG{+w}{ }double
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Or run with the INTEL package by editing an input script}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:or-run-with-the-intel-package-by-editing-an-input-script}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As an alternative to adding command\sphinxhyphen{}line arguments, the input script
can be edited to enable the INTEL package. This requires adding
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command to the top of the input
script. For the second example above, this would be:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{package}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{intel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{omp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{double}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To enable the INTEL package only for individual styles, you can
add an “intel” suffix to the individual style, e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{intel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix intel}}}} command can be added to
the input script to enable INTEL styles for the commands that
follow in the input script.


\subsubsection{Tuning for Performance}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:tuning-for-performance}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The INTEL package will perform better with modifications
to the input script when {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{PPPM}}}} is used:
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify diff ad}}}} should be added to the
input script.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Long\sphinxhyphen{}Range Thread (LRT) mode is an option to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command that can improve performance when using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{PPPM}}}} for long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatics on processors
with SMT. It generates an extra pthread for each MPI task. The thread
is dedicated to performing some of the PPPM calculations and MPI
communications. This feature requires setting the pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor flag
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_INTEL\_USELRT}} in the makefile when compiling LAMMPS. It is unset
in the default makefiles (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.mpi}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.serial}}) but
it is set in all makefiles tuned for the INTEL package.  On Intel
Xeon Phi x200 series CPUs, the LRT feature will likely improve
performance, even on a single node. On Intel Xeon processors, using
this mode might result in better performance when using multiple nodes,
depending on the specific machine configuration. To enable LRT mode,
specify that the number of OpenMP threads is one less than would
normally be used for the run and add the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lrt yes}} option to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk}}
command\sphinxhyphen{}line suffix or “package intel” command. For example, if a run
would normally perform best with “\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel 0 omp 4”, instead use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel 0 omp 3 lrt yes}}. When using LRT, you should set the
environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KMP\_AFFINITY=none}}. LRT mode is not supported
when using offload.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Changing the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to off can improve
performance and/or scalability for simple 2\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials such as
lj/cut or when using LRT mode on processors supporting AVX\sphinxhyphen{}512.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Not all styles are supported in the INTEL package. You can mix
the INTEL package with styles from the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_opt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{OPT}}}}
package or the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_omp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{OPENMP package}}}}. Of course, this
requires that these packages were installed at build time. This can
performed automatically by using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf hybrid intel opt}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf hybrid
intel omp}} command\sphinxhyphen{}line options. Alternatively, the “opt” and “omp”
suffixes can be appended manually in the input script. For the latter,
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package omp}}}} command must be in the input script or
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk omp Nt}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} must be used
where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Nt}} is the number of OpenMP threads. The number of OpenMP threads
should not be set differently for the different packages. Note that
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix hybrid intel omp}}}} command can also be used
within the input script to automatically append the “omp” suffix to
styles when INTEL styles are not available.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For simulations on higher node counts, add {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors * * * grid numa}}}} to the beginning of the input script for
better scalability.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on many nodes, performance might be better when using
fewer OpenMP threads and more MPI tasks. This will depend on the
simulation and the machine. Using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{verlet/split}}}}
run style might also give better performance for simulations with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{PPPM}}}} electrostatics. Note that this is an
alternative to LRT mode and the two cannot be used together.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, when using Intel MPI with Intel Xeon Phi x200 series
CPUs, better performance might be obtained by setting the
environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{I\_MPI\_SHM\_LMT=shm}} for Linux kernels that do
not yet have full support for AVX\sphinxhyphen{}512. Runs on Intel Xeon Phi x200
series processors will always perform better using MCDRAM. Please
consult your system documentation for the best approach to specify
that MPI runs are performed in MCDRAM.


\subsubsection{Tuning for Offload Performance}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:tuning-for-offload-performance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default settings for offload should give good performance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using LAMMPS with offload to Intel co\sphinxhyphen{}processors, best performance
will typically be achieved with concurrent calculations performed on
both the CPU and the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor. This is achieved by offloading only
a fraction of the neighbor and pair computations to the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor or
using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid}}}} pair styles where only one style uses
the “intel” suffix. For simulations with long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatics or
bond, angle, dihedral, improper calculations, computation and data
transfer to the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor will run concurrently with computations
and MPI communications for these calculations on the host CPU. This
is illustrated in the figure below for the rhodopsin protein benchmark
running on E5\sphinxhyphen{}2697v2 processors with a Intel Xeon Phi 7120p
co\sphinxhyphen{}processor. In this plot, the vertical access is time and routines
running at the same time are running concurrently on both the host and
the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{offload_knc}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fraction of the offloaded work is controlled by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{balance}
keyword in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command. A balance of 0
runs all calculations on the CPU.  A balance of 1 runs all
supported calculations on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.  A balance of 0.5 runs half
of the calculations on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.  Setting the balance to \sphinxhyphen{}1
(the default) will enable dynamic load balancing that continuously
adjusts the fraction of offloaded work throughout the simulation.
Because data transfer cannot be timed, this option typically produces
results within 5 to 10 percent of the optimal fixed balance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If running short benchmark runs with dynamic load balancing, adding a
short warm\sphinxhyphen{}up run (10\sphinxhyphen{}20 steps) will allow the load\sphinxhyphen{}balancer to find a
near\sphinxhyphen{}optimal setting that will carry over to additional runs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command is to have
all the MPI tasks on a given compute node use a single Xeon Phi
co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.  In general, running with a large number of MPI tasks on
each node will perform best with offload.  Each MPI task will
automatically get affinity to a subset of the hardware threads
available on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.  For example, if your card has 61 cores,
with 60 cores available for offload and 4 hardware threads per core
(240 total threads), running with 24 MPI tasks per node will cause
each MPI task to use a subset of 10 threads on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.  Fine
tuning of the number of threads to use per MPI task or the number of
threads to use per core can be accomplished with keyword settings of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The INTEL package has two modes for deciding which atoms will be
handled by the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.  This choice is controlled with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost}
keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package intel}}}} command.  When set to 0,
ghost atoms (atoms at the borders between MPI tasks) are not offloaded
to the card.  This allows for overlap of MPI communication of forces
with computation on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor when the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}}
setting is “on”.  The default is dependent on the style being used,
however, better performance may be achieved by setting this option
explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using offload with CPU Hyper\sphinxhyphen{}Threading disabled, it may help
performance to use fewer MPI tasks and OpenMP threads than available
cores.  This is due to the fact that additional threads are generated
internally to handle the asynchronous offload tasks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If pair computations are being offloaded to an Intel Xeon Phi
co\sphinxhyphen{}processor, a diagnostic line is printed to the screen (not to the
log file), during the setup phase of a run, indicating that offload
mode is being used and indicating the number of co\sphinxhyphen{}processor threads
per MPI task.  Additionally, an offload timing summary is printed at
the end of each run.  When offloading, the frequency for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom sorting}}}} is changed to 1 so that the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data is
effectively sorted at every rebuild of the neighbor lists. All the
available co\sphinxhyphen{}processor threads on each Phi will be divided among MPI
tasks, unless the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tptask}} option of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} is used to limit the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor threads per
MPI task.


\subsubsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_intel:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When offloading to a co\sphinxhyphen{}processor, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid}}}} styles
that require skip lists for neighbor builds cannot be offloaded.
Using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid/overlay}}}} is allowed.  Only one intel
accelerated style may be used with hybrid styles when offloading.
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Special\_bonds}}}} exclusion lists are not currently
supported with offload, however, the same effect can often be
accomplished by setting cutoffs for excluded atom types to 0.  None of
the pair styles in the INTEL package currently support the
“inner”, “middle”, “outer” options for rRESPA integration via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command; only the “pair” option is
supported.
