\subsection{KOKKOS package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:kokkos-package}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Kokkos is a templated C++ library that provides abstractions to allow
a single implementation of an application kernel (e.g. a pair style)
to run efficiently on different kinds of hardware, such as GPUs, Intel
Xeon Phis, or many\sphinxhyphen{}core CPUs. Kokkos maps the C++ kernel onto
different back end languages such as CUDA, OpenMP, or Pthreads.  The
Kokkos library also provides data abstractions to adjust (at compile
time) the memory layout of data structures like 2d and 3d arrays to
optimize performance on different hardware. For more information on
Kokkos, see \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kokkos/kokkos}{the Kokkos GitHub page}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS KOKKOS package contains versions of pair, fix, and atom
styles that use data structures and macros provided by the Kokkos
library, which is included with LAMMPS in /lib/kokkos. The KOKKOS
package was developed primarily by Christian Trott (Sandia) and Stan
Moore (Sandia) with contributions of various styles by others,
including Sikandar Mashayak (UIUC), Ray Shan (Sandia), and Dan Ibanez
(Sandia). For more information on developing using Kokkos abstractions
see the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/kokkos/kokkos/wiki}{Kokkos Wiki}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Kokkos library is under active development and tracking the
availability of accelerator hardware, so is the KOKKOS package in
LAMMPS.  This means that only a certain range of versions of the
Kokkos library are compatible with the KOKKOS package of a certain
range of LAMMPS versions.  For that reason LAMMPS comes with a
bundled version of the Kokkos library that has been validated on
multiple platforms and may contain selected back\sphinxhyphen{}ported bug fixes
from upstream Kokkos versions.  While it is possible to build LAMMPS
with an external version of Kokkos, it is untested and may result in
incorrect execution or crashes.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Kokkos currently provides full support for 4 modes of execution (per MPI
task). These are Serial (MPI\sphinxhyphen{}only for CPUs and Intel Phi), OpenMP
(threading for many\sphinxhyphen{}core CPUs and Intel Phi), CUDA (for NVIDIA GPUs) and
HIP (for AMD GPUs).  Additional modes (e.g. OpenMP target, Intel data
center GPUs) are under development.  You choose the mode at build time
to produce an executable compatible with a specific hardware.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following compatibility notes have been last updated for LAMMPS
version 23 November 2023 and Kokkos version 4.2.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{C++17 support}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Kokkos requires using a compiler that supports the c++17 standard. For
some compilers, it may be necessary to add a flag to enable c++17 support.
For example, the GNU compiler uses the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}std=c++17}} flag. For a list of
compilers that have been tested with the Kokkos library, see the
\sphinxhref{https://kokkos.github.io/kokkos-core-wiki/requirements.html}{requirements document of the Kokkos Wiki}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{NVIDIA CUDA support}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To build with Kokkos support for NVIDIA GPUs, the NVIDIA CUDA toolkit
software version 11.0 or later must be installed on your system. See
the discussion for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_gpu::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{GPU package}}}} for details of
how to check and do this.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{AMD ROCm (HIP) support}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To build with Kokkos support for AMD GPUs, the AMD ROCm toolkit
software version 5.2.0 or later must be installed on your system.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{CUDA and MPI library compatibility}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Kokkos with CUDA currently implicitly assumes that the MPI library is
GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware.  This is not always the case, especially when using
pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled MPI libraries provided by a Linux distribution. This is
not a problem when using only a single GPU with a single MPI
rank.  When running with multiple MPI ranks, you may see segmentation
faults without GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI support. These can be avoided by adding
the flags {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}pk kokkos gpu/aware off}}}} to the
LAMMPS command line or by using the command {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos
gpu/aware off}}}} in the input file.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Intel Data Center GPU support}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for Kokkos with Intel Data Center GPU accelerators (formerly
known under the code name “Ponte Vecchio”) in LAMMPS is still a work
in progress.  Only a subset of the functionality works correctly.
Please contact the LAMMPS developers if you run into problems.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Building LAMMPS with the KOKKOS package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:building-lammps-with-the-kokkos-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kokkos}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Build extras}}}} page for instructions.


\subsubsection{Running LAMMPS with the KOKKOS package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:running-lammps-with-the-kokkos-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All Kokkos operations occur within the context of an individual MPI task
running on a single node of the machine. The total number of MPI tasks
used by LAMMPS (one or multiple per compute node) is set in the usual
manner via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}} commands, and is independent of
Kokkos. E.g. the mpirun command in OpenMPI does this via its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}npernode}} switches. Ditto for MPICH via \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}ppn}}.


\paragraph{Running on a multicore CPU}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:running-on-a-multicore-cpu}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a quick overview of how to use the KOKKOS package
for CPU acceleration, assuming one or more 16\sphinxhyphen{}core nodes.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 node, 16 MPI tasks/node, no multi\PYGZhy{}threading}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}only\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 2 nodes, 1 MPI task/node, 16 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 node,  2 MPI tasks/node, 8 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 8 nodes, 4 MPI tasks/node, 4 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{32}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To run using the KOKKOS package, use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}k on}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf kk}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk
kokkos}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches}}}} in your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}}
command.  You must use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}k on}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to enable the KOKKOS package. It takes
additional arguments for hardware settings appropriate to your system.
For OpenMP use:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}k on t Nt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t Nt}} option specifies how many OpenMP threads per MPI task to
use with a node. The default is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Nt}} = 1, which is MPI\sphinxhyphen{}only mode.  Note
that the product of MPI tasks * OpenMP threads/task should not exceed
the physical number of cores (on a node), otherwise performance will
suffer. If Hyper\sphinxhyphen{}Threading (HT) is enabled, then the product of MPI
tasks * OpenMP threads/task should not exceed the physical number of
cores * hardware threads.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}k on}} switch also issues a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{package kokkos}} command (with no additional arguments) which sets
various KOKKOS options to default values, as discussed on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} command doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf kk}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} will automatically
append the “/kk” suffix to styles that support it.  In this manner no
modification to the input script is needed. Alternatively, one can run
with the KOKKOS package by editing the input script as described
below.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using a single OpenMP thread, the Kokkos Serial back end (i.e.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.kokkos\_mpi\_only}}) will give better performance than the OpenMP
back end (i.e. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Makefile.kokkos\_omp}}) because some of the overhead to make
the code thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe is removed.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk kokkos}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to
change the default {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos}}}} options. See its doc
page for details and default settings. Experimenting with its options
can provide a speed\sphinxhyphen{}up for specific calculations. For example:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Newton on, Half neighbor list, non\PYGZhy{}threaded comm}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}only\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{       }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }kokkos\PYG{+w}{ }newton\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }neigh\PYG{+w}{ }half\PYG{+w}{ }comm\PYG{+w}{ }no\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} command is used in the input
script, it can also override the Newton flag defaults.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For half neighbor lists and OpenMP, the KOKKOS package uses data
duplication (i.e. thread\sphinxhyphen{}private arrays) by default to avoid
thread\sphinxhyphen{}level write conflicts in the force arrays (and other data
structures as necessary). Data duplication is typically fastest for
small numbers of threads (i.e. 8 or less) but does increase memory
footprint and is not scalable to large numbers of threads. An
alternative to data duplication is to use thread\sphinxhyphen{}level atomic operations
which do not require data duplication. The use of atomic operations can
be enforced by compiling LAMMPS with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_KOKKOS\_USE\_ATOMICS}}
pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor flag. Most but not all Kokkos\sphinxhyphen{}enabled pair\_styles support
data duplication. Alternatively, full neighbor lists avoid the need for
duplication or atomic operations but require more compute operations per
atom.  When using the Kokkos Serial back end or the OpenMP back end with
a single thread, no duplication or atomic operations are used. For CUDA
and half neighbor lists, the KOKKOS package always uses atomic operations.


\paragraph{CPU Cores, Sockets and Thread Affinity}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:cpu-cores-sockets-and-thread-affinity}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading, it is important for performance to bind
both MPI tasks to physical cores, and threads to physical cores, so
they do not migrate during a simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are not certain MPI tasks are being bound (check the defaults
for your MPI installation), binding can be forced with these flags:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} OpenMPI 1.8}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}bind\PYGZhy{}to\PYG{+w}{ }socket\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}map\PYGZhy{}by\PYG{+w}{ }socket\PYG{+w}{ }./lmp\PYGZus{}openmpi\PYG{+w}{ }...

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Mvapich2 2.0}
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}bind\PYGZhy{}to\PYG{+w}{ }socket\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}map\PYGZhy{}by\PYG{+w}{ }socket\PYG{+w}{ }./lmp\PYGZus{}mvapich\PYG{+w}{ }...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For binding threads with KOKKOS OpenMP, use thread affinity environment
variables to force binding. With OpenMP 3.1 (gcc 4.7 or later, intel 12
or later) setting the environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_PROC\_BIND=true}} should
be sufficient. In general, for best performance with OpenMP 4.0 or later
set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_PROC\_BIND=spread}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_PLACES=threads}}.  For binding
threads with the KOKKOS pthreads option, compile LAMMPS with the hwloc
or libnuma support enabled as described in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kokkos}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{extra build options page}}}}.


\paragraph{Running on Knight’s Landing (KNL) Intel Xeon Phi}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:running-on-knight-s-landing-knl-intel-xeon-phi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a quick overview of how to use the KOKKOS package for the
Intel Knight’s Landing (KNL) Xeon Phi:

\sphinxAtStartPar
KNL Intel Phi chips have 68 physical cores. Typically 1 to 4 cores are
reserved for the OS, and only 64 or 66 cores are used. Each core has 4
Hyper\sphinxhyphen{}Threads,so there are effectively N = 256 (4*64) or N = 264 (4*66)
cores to run on. The product of MPI tasks * OpenMP threads/task should
not exceed this limit, otherwise performance will suffer. Note that
with the KOKKOS package you do not need to specify how many KNLs there
are per node; each KNL is simply treated as running some number of MPI
tasks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples of mpirun commands that follow these rules are shown below.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Running on an Intel KNL node with 68 cores}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} (272 threads/node via 4x hardware threading):}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 node, 64 MPI tasks/node, 4 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{64}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 node, 66 MPI tasks/node, 4 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{66}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 node, 32 MPI tasks/node, 8 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{32}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 8 nodes, 64 MPI tasks/node, 4 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{512}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{64}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} setting of the mpirun command sets the number of MPI
tasks/node. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}k on t Nt}} command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch sets the number of
threads/task as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Nt}}. The product of these two values should be N, i.e.
256 or 264.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos}}}} command when
running on KNL is to use “half” neighbor lists and set the Newton
flag to “on” for both pairwise and bonded interactions. This will
typically be best for many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials. For simpler pairwise
potentials, it may be faster to use a “full” neighbor list with
Newton flag to “off”.  Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk kokkos}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to change the default {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos}}}}
options. See its documentation page for details and default
settings. Experimenting with its options can provide a speed\sphinxhyphen{}up for
specific calculations. For example:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  Newton on, half neighbor list, threaded comm}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{64}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }kokkos\PYG{+w}{ }comm\PYG{+w}{ }host\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.reax

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Newton off, full neighbor list, non\PYGZhy{}threaded comm}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{64}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}phi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{       }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }kokkos\PYG{+w}{ }newton\PYG{+w}{ }off\PYG{+w}{ }neigh\PYG{+w}{ }full\PYG{+w}{ }comm\PYG{+w}{ }no\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
MPI tasks and threads should be bound to cores as described
above for CPUs.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To build with Kokkos support for Intel Xeon Phi co\sphinxhyphen{}processors
such as Knight’s Corner (KNC), your system must be configured to use
them in “native” mode, not “offload” mode like the INTEL package
supports.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\paragraph{Running on GPUs}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:running-on-gpus}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}k}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to specify the
number of GPUs per node. Typically the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} setting of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} command
should set the number of MPI tasks/node to be equal to the number of
physical GPUs on the node. You can assign multiple MPI tasks to the same
GPU with the KOKKOS package, but this is usually only faster if some
portions of the input script have not been ported to use Kokkos. In this
case, also packing/unpacking communication buffers on the host may give
speedup (see the KOKKOS {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} command). Using CUDA MPS
is recommended in this scenario.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI library is highly recommended. GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI use can be
avoided by using {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}pk kokkos gpu/aware off}}}}. As above for
multicore CPUs (and no GPU), if N is the number of physical cores/node,
then the number of MPI tasks/node should not exceed N.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}k on g Ng
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are examples of how to use the KOKKOS package for GPUs, assuming
one or more nodes, each with two GPUs:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 node,   2 MPI tasks/node, 2 GPUs/node}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}cuda\PYGZus{}openmpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 16 nodes, 2 MPI tasks/node, 2 GPUs/node (32 GPUs total)}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{32}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}cuda\PYGZus{}openmpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos}}}} command when
running on GPUs is to use “full” neighbor lists and set the Newton
flag to “off” for both pairwise and bonded interactions, along with
threaded communication. When running on Maxwell or Kepler GPUs, this
will typically be best. For Pascal GPUs and beyond, using “half”
neighbor lists and setting the Newton flag to “on” may be faster. For
many pair styles, setting the neighbor binsize equal to twice the CPU
default value will give speedup, which is the default when running on
GPUs. Use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk kokkos}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}
to change the default {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos}}}} options. See
its documentation page for details and default
settings. Experimenting with its options can provide a speed\sphinxhyphen{}up for
specific calculations. For example:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Newton on, half neighbor list, set binsize = neighbor ghost cutoff}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}cuda\PYGZus{}openmpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{       }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }kokkos\PYG{+w}{ }newton\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }neigh\PYG{+w}{ }half\PYG{+w}{ }binsize\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}.8\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default binsize for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom sorting}}}} on GPUs
is equal to the default CPU neighbor binsize (i.e. 2x smaller than the
default GPU neighbor binsize). When running simple pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise
potentials like Lennard Jones on GPUs, using a 2x larger binsize for
atom sorting (equal to the default GPU neighbor binsize) and a more
frequent sorting than default (e.g. sorting every 100 time steps
instead of 1000) may improve performance.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on GPUs with many MPI ranks (tens of thousands and
more), the creation of the atom map (required for molecular systems)
on the GPU can slow down significantly or run out of GPU memory and
thus slow down the whole calculation or cause a crash.  You can use
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk kokkos atom/map no}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}
of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos atom/map no}}}} command to create
the atom map on the CPU instead.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using a GPU, you will achieve the best performance if your
input script does not use fix or compute styles which are not yet
Kokkos\sphinxhyphen{}enabled. This allows data to stay on the GPU for multiple
timesteps, without being copied back to the host CPU. Invoking a
non\sphinxhyphen{}Kokkos fix or compute, or performing I/O for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} output will cause data
to be copied back to the CPU incurring a performance penalty.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To get an accurate timing breakdown between time spend in pair,
kspace, etc., you must set the environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CUDA\_LAUNCH\_BLOCKING=1}}.
However, this will reduce performance and is not recommended for production runs.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\paragraph{Run with the KOKKOS package by editing an input script}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:run-with-the-kokkos-package-by-editing-an-input-script}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively the effect of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk}} switches can be
duplicated by adding the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix kk}}}} commands to your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The discussion above for building LAMMPS with the KOKKOS package, the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}} command, and setting appropriate thread
properties are the same.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You must still use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}k on}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}
to enable the KOKKOS package, and specify its additional arguments for
hardware options appropriate to your system, as documented above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix kk}}}} command, or you can explicitly add a
“kk” suffix to individual styles in your input script, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{kk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You only need to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package kokkos}}}} command if you
wish to change any of its option defaults, as set by the “\sphinxhyphen{}k on”
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Using OpenMP threading and CUDA together:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the KOKKOS package, both OpenMP multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading and GPUs can be
compiled and used together in a few special cases. In the makefile for
the conventional build, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KOKKOS\_DEVICES}} variable must include both,
“Cuda” and “OpenMP”, as is the case for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/src/MAKE/OPTIONS/Makefile.kokkos\_cuda\_mpi}}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{KOKKOS\PYGZus{}DEVICES}\PYG{o}{=}Cuda,OpenMP
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When building with CMake you need to enable both features as it is done
in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kokkos\sphinxhyphen{}cuda.cmake}} CMake preset file.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DKokkos\PYGZus{}ENABLE\PYGZus{}CUDA\PYG{o}{=}yes\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DKokkos\PYGZus{}ENABLE\PYGZus{}OPENMP\PYG{o}{=}yes\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The suffix “/kk” is equivalent to “/kk/device”, and for Kokkos CUDA,
using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf kk}} in the command line gives the default CUDA version
everywhere.  However, if the “/kk/host” suffix is added to a specific
style in the input script, the Kokkos OpenMP (CPU) version of that
specific style will be used instead.  Set the number of OpenMP threads
as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{t Nt}} and the number of GPUs as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{g Ng}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}k on t Nt g Ng
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the command to run with 1 GPU and 8 OpenMP threads is then:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpiexec\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}kokkos\PYGZus{}cuda\PYGZus{}openmpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.lj\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}k\PYG{+w}{ }on\PYG{+w}{ }g\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }t\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }kk
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Conversely, if the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf kk/host}} is used in the command line and then
the “/kk” or “/kk/device” suffix is added to a specific style in your
input script, then only that specific style will run on the GPU while
everything else will run on the CPU in OpenMP mode. Note that the
execution of the CPU and GPU styles will NOT overlap, except for a
special case:

\sphinxAtStartPar
A kspace style and/or molecular topology (bonds, angles, etc.) running
on the host CPU can overlap with a pair style running on the
GPU. First compile with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}default\sphinxhyphen{}stream per\sphinxhyphen{}thread}} added to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CCFLAGS}}
in the Kokkos CUDA Makefile.  Then explicitly use the “/kk/host”
suffix for kspace and bonds, angles, etc.  in the input file and the
“kk” suffix (equal to “kk/device”) on the command line.  Also make
sure the environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CUDA\_LAUNCH\_BLOCKING}} is not set to “1”
so CPU/GPU overlap can occur.


\subsubsection{Performance to expect}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:performance-to-expect}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The performance of KOKKOS running in different modes is a function of
your hardware, which KOKKOS\sphinxhyphen{}enable styles are used, and the problem
size.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Generally speaking, the following rules of thumb apply:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on CPUs only, with a single thread per MPI task,
performance of a KOKKOS style is somewhere between the standard
(un\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated) styles (MPI\sphinxhyphen{}only mode), and those provided by the
OPENMP package. However the difference between all 3 is small (less
than 20\%).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on CPUs only, with multiple threads per MPI task,
performance of a KOKKOS style is a bit slower than the OPENMP
package.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When running large number of atoms per GPU, KOKKOS is typically faster
than the GPU package when compiled for double precision.  The benefit
of using single or mixed precision with the GPU package depends
significantly on the hardware in use and the simulated system and pair
style.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on Intel Phi hardware, KOKKOS is not as fast as
the INTEL package, which is optimized for x86 hardware (not just
from Intel) and compilation with the Intel compilers.  The INTEL
package also can increase the vector length of vector instructions
by switching to single or mixed precision mode.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The KOKKOS package by default assumes that you are using exactly one
MPI rank per GPU. When trying to use multiple MPI ranks per GPU it is
mandatory to enable \sphinxhref{https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/mps/index.html}{CUDA Multi\sphinxhyphen{}Process Service (MPS)} to get good
performance.  In this case it is better to not use all available
MPI ranks in order to avoid competing with the MPS daemon for
CPU resources.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bench.html}{Benchmark page} of the
LAMMPS website for performance of the KOKKOS package on different
hardware.


\subsubsection{Advanced Kokkos options}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:advanced-kokkos-options}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are other allowed options when building with the KOKKOS package
that can improve performance or assist in debugging or profiling.
They are explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:kokkos}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KOKKOS section of the build extras}}}} doc page,


\subsubsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_kokkos:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, there are no precision options with the KOKKOS package. All
compilation and computation is performed in double precision.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{OPENMP package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:openmp-package}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The OPENMP package was developed by Axel Kohlmeyer at Temple
University.  It provides optimized and multi\sphinxhyphen{}threaded versions
of many pair styles, nearly all bonded styles (bond, angle, dihedral,
improper), several Kspace styles, and a few fix styles.  It uses
the OpenMP interface for multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading, but can also be compiled
without OpenMP support, providing optimized serial styles in that case.


\subsubsection{Required hardware/software}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:required-hardware-software}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To enable multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading, your compiler must support the OpenMP interface.
You should have one or more multicore CPUs, as multiple threads can only be
launched by each MPI task on the local node (using shared memory).


\subsubsection{Building LAMMPS with the OPENMP package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:building-lammps-with-the-openmp-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:openmp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Build extras}}}} page for
instructions.


\subsubsection{Run with the OPENMP package from the command line}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:run-with-the-openmp-package-from-the-command-line}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These examples assume one or more 16\sphinxhyphen{}core nodes.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 MPI task, 16 threads according to OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS}
env\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 1 MPI task, no threads, optimized kernels}
lmp\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 4 MPI tasks, 4 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 8 nodes, 4 MPI tasks/node, 4 threads/task}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{32}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}ppn\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pk\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}} command sets the total number of MPI tasks
used by LAMMPS (one or multiple per compute node) and the number of MPI
tasks used per node.  E.g. the mpirun command in MPICH does this via
its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}ppn}} switches.  Ditto for OpenMPI via \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}np}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}npernode}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You need to choose how many OpenMP threads per MPI task will be used
by the OPENMP package.  Note that the product of MPI tasks *
threads/task should not exceed the physical number of cores (on a
node), otherwise performance will suffer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As in the lines above, use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf omp}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}, which will automatically append “omp” to
styles that support it.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}sf omp}} switch also issues a default
{\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package omp 0}}}} command, which will set the number of
threads per MPI task via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS}} environment variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}pk omp Nt}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}, to explicitly set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Nt}} = \# of OpenMP threads
per MPI task to use, as well as additional options.  Its syntax is the
same as the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package omp}}}} command whose page gives
details, including the default values used if it is not specified.  It
also gives more details on how to set the number of threads via the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS}} environment variable.


\subsubsection{Or run with the OPENMP package by editing an input script}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:or-run-with-the-openmp-package-by-editing-an-input-script}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The discussion above for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpirun}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mpiexec}} command, MPI
tasks/node, and threads/MPI task is the same.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix omp}}}} command, or you can explicitly add an
“omp” suffix to individual styles in your input script, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{omp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You must also use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package omp}}}} command to enable the
OPENMP package.  When you do this you also specify how many threads
per MPI task to use.  The command page explains other options and
how to set the number of threads via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS}} environment
variable.


\subsubsection{Speed\sphinxhyphen{}up to expect}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:speed-up-to-expect}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on which styles are accelerated, you should look for a
reduction in the “Pair time”, “Bond time”, “KSpace time”, and “Loop
time” values printed at the end of a run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You may see a small performance advantage (5 to 20\%) when running a
OPENMP style (in serial or parallel) with a single thread per MPI
task, versus running standard LAMMPS with its standard un\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated
styles (in serial or all\sphinxhyphen{}MPI parallelization with 1 task/core).  This
is because many of the OPENMP styles contain similar optimizations
to those used in the OPT package, described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_opt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{the OPT package}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With multiple threads/task, the optimal choice of number of MPI
tasks/node and OpenMP threads/task can vary a lot and should always be
tested via benchmark runs for a specific simulation running on a
specific machine, paying attention to guidelines discussed in the next
subsection.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A description of the multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading strategy used in the OPENMP
package and some performance examples are
\sphinxhref{https://drive.google.com/file/d/1d1gLK6Ru6aPYB50Ld2tO10Li8zgPVNB8/view?usp=sharing}{presented here}.


\subsubsection{Guidelines for best performance}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:guidelines-for-best-performance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For many problems on current generation CPUs, running the OPENMP
package with a single thread/task is faster than running with multiple
threads/task.  This is because the MPI parallelization in LAMMPS is
often more efficient than multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading as implemented in the
OPENMP package.  The parallel efficiency (in a threaded sense) also
varies for different OPENMP styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using multiple threads/task can be more effective under the following
circumstances:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Individual compute nodes have a significant number of CPU cores but
the CPU itself has limited memory bandwidth, e.g. for Intel Xeon 53xx
(Clovertown) and 54xx (Harpertown) quad\sphinxhyphen{}core processors.  Running one
MPI task per CPU core will result in significant performance
degradation, so that running with 4 or even only 2 MPI tasks per node
is faster.  Running in hybrid MPI+OpenMP mode will reduce the
inter\sphinxhyphen{}node communication bandwidth contention in the same way, but
offers an additional speedup by utilizing the otherwise idle CPU
cores.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The interconnect used for MPI communication does not provide
sufficient bandwidth for a large number of MPI tasks per node.  For
example, this applies to running over gigabit ethernet or on Cray XT4
or XT5 series supercomputers.  As in the aforementioned case, this
effect worsens when using an increasing number of nodes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The system has a spatially inhomogeneous particle density which does
not map well to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{domain decomposition scheme}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing}}}} options that LAMMPS provides.  This is
because multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading achieves parallelism over the number of
particles, not via their distribution in space.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A machine is being used in “capability mode”, i.e. near the point
where MPI parallelism is maxed out.  For example, this can happen when
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{PPPM solver}}}} for long\sphinxhyphen{}range
electrostatics on large numbers of nodes.  The scaling of the KSpace
calculation (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command) becomes
the performance\sphinxhyphen{}limiting factor.  Using multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading allows less
MPI tasks to be invoked and can speed\sphinxhyphen{}up the long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver, while
increasing overall performance by parallelizing the pairwise and
bonded calculations via OpenMP.  Likewise additional speedup can be
sometimes be achieved by increasing the length of the Coulombic cutoff
and thus reducing the work done by the long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver.  Using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style verlet/split}}}} command, which is compatible
with the OPENMP package, is an alternative way to reduce the number
of MPI tasks assigned to the KSpace calculation.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional performance tips are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The best parallel efficiency from \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} styles is typically achieved
when there is at least one MPI task per physical CPU chip, i.e. socket
or die.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is usually most efficient to restrict threading to a single
socket, i.e. use one or more MPI task per socket.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTE: By default, several current MPI implementations use a processor
affinity setting that restricts each MPI task to a single CPU core.
Using multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading in this mode will force all threads to share the
one core and thus is likely to be counterproductive.  Instead, binding
MPI tasks to a (multicore) socket, should solve this issue.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_omp:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{OPT package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:opt-package}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The OPT package was developed by James Fischer (High Performance
Technologies), David Richie, and Vincent Natoli (Stone Ridge
Technologies).  It contains a handful of pair styles whose compute()
methods were rewritten in C++ templated form to reduce the overhead
due to if tests and other conditional code.


\subsubsection{Required hardware/software}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:required-hardware-software}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Any hardware. Any compiler.


\subsubsection{Building LAMMPS with the OPT package}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:building-lammps-with-the-opt-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:opt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Build extras}}}} page for instructions.


\subsubsection{Run with the OPT package from the command line}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:run-with-the-opt-package-from-the-command-line}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
lmp\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }opt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script\PYG{+w}{                }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} run in serial}
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }opt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} run in parallel}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the “\sphinxhyphen{}sf opt” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}, which will
automatically append “opt” to styles that support it.


\subsubsection{Or run with the OPT package by editing an input script}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:or-run-with-the-opt-package-by-editing-an-input-script}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix opt}}}} command, or you can explicitly add an
“opt” suffix to individual styles in your input script, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{opt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Speed\sphinxhyphen{}up to expect}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:speed-up-to-expect}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You should see a reduction in the “Pair time” value printed at the end
of a run.  On most machines for reasonable problem sizes, it will be a
5 to 20\% savings.


\subsubsection{Guidelines for best performance}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:guidelines-for-best-performance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Just try out an OPT pair style to see how it performs.


\subsubsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_opt:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None.

\sphinxAtStartPar

three kinds of hardware, via the listed packages:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Which package is fastest for your hardware may depend on the size
problem you are running and what commands (accelerated and
non\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated) are invoked by your input script.  While these doc
pages include performance guidelines, there is no substitute for
trying out the different packages appropriate to your hardware.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any accelerated style has the same name as the corresponding standard
style, except that a suffix is appended.  Otherwise, the syntax for
the command that uses the style is identical, their functionality is
the same, and the numerical results it produces should also be the
same, except for precision and round\sphinxhyphen{}off effects.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, all of these styles are accelerated variants of the
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut}}}}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/gpu}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/intel}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/kk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/omp}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/opt}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To see what accelerate styles are currently available for a particular
style, find the style name in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_all::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands}}}}
style pages (fix,compute,pair,etc) and see what suffixes are listed
(g,i,k,o,t) with it.  The doc pages for individual commands
(e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair lj/cut}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}) also list
any accelerated variants available for that style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use an accelerator package in LAMMPS, and one or more of the styles
it provides, follow these general steps.  Details vary from package to
package and are explained in the individual accelerator doc pages,
listed above:

Note that the first 4 steps can be done as a single command with
suitable make command invocations. This is discussed on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Packages}}}} doc pages, and its use is illustrated in the
individual accelerator sections.  Typically these steps only need to
be done once, to create an executable that uses one or more
accelerator packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last 4 steps can all be done from the command\sphinxhyphen{}line when LAMMPS is
launched, without changing your input script, as illustrated in the
individual accelerator sections.  Or you can add
{\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} commands to your input
script.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With a few exceptions, you can build a single LAMMPS executable
with all its accelerator packages installed.  Note however that the
INTEL and KOKKOS packages require you to choose one of their
hardware options when building for a specific platform.  I.e. CPU or
Phi option for the INTEL package.  Or the OpenMP, CUDA, HIP, SYCL,
or Phi option for the KOKKOS package.  Or the OpenCL, HIP, or CUDA
option for the GPU package.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the exceptions.  You cannot build a single executable with:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
both the INTEL Phi and KOKKOS Phi options

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the INTEL Phi or Kokkos Phi option, and the GPU package

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As mentioned above, the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bench.html}{Benchmark page} of the LAMMPS website gives
performance results for the various accelerator packages for several
of the standard LAMMPS benchmark problems, as a function of problem
size and number of compute nodes, on different hardware platforms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a brief summary of what the various packages provide.  Details
are in the individual accelerator sections.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a “gpu” suffix are part of the GPU package and can be run
on Intel, NVIDIA, or AMD GPUs.  The speed\sphinxhyphen{}up on a GPU depends on a
variety of factors, discussed in the accelerator sections.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with an “intel” suffix are part of the INTEL
package. These styles support vectorized single and mixed precision
calculations, in addition to full double precision.  In extreme cases,
this can provide speedups over 3.5x on CPUs.  The package also
supports acceleration in “offload” mode to Intel(R) Xeon Phi(TM)
co\sphinxhyphen{}processors.  This can result in additional speedup over 2x depending
on the hardware configuration.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a “kk” suffix are part of the KOKKOS package, and can be
run using OpenMP on multicore CPUs, on an NVIDIA or AMD GPU, or on an
Intel Xeon Phi in “native” mode.  The speed\sphinxhyphen{}up depends on a variety of
factors, as discussed on the KOKKOS accelerator page.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with an “omp” suffix are part of the OPENMP package and allow
a pair\sphinxhyphen{}style to be run in multi\sphinxhyphen{}threaded mode using OpenMP.  This can
be useful on nodes with high\sphinxhyphen{}core counts when using less MPI processes
than cores is advantageous, e.g. when running with PPPM so that FFTs
are run on fewer MPI processors or when the many MPI tasks would
overload the available bandwidth for communication.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with an “opt” suffix are part of the OPT package and typically
speed\sphinxhyphen{}up the pairwise calculations of your simulation by 5\sphinxhyphen{}25\% on a
CPU.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The individual accelerator package doc pages explain:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
what hardware and software the accelerated package requires

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
how to build LAMMPS with the accelerated package

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
how to run with the accelerated package either via command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches or modifying the input script

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
speed\sphinxhyphen{}ups to expect

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
guidelines for best performance

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
restrictions

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Comparison of various accelerator packages}
\label{\detokenize{Speed_compare:comparison-of-various-accelerator-packages}}\label{\detokenize{Speed_compare::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The next section compares and contrasts the various accelerator
options, since there are multiple ways to perform OpenMP threading,
run on GPUs, optimize for vector units on CPUs and run on Intel
Xeon Phi (co\sphinxhyphen{})processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of these packages can accelerate a LAMMPS calculation taking
advantage of hardware features, but they do it in different ways
and acceleration is not always guaranteed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a consequence, for a particular simulation on specific hardware,
one package may be faster than the other.  We give some guidelines
below, but the best way to determine which package is faster for your
input script is to try multiple of them on your machine and experiment
with available performance tuning settings.  See the benchmarking
section below for examples where this has been done.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Guidelines for using each package optimally:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Both, the GPU and the KOKKOS package allows you to assign multiple
MPI ranks (= CPU cores) to the same GPU. For the GPU package, this
can lead to a speedup through better utilization of the GPU (by
overlapping computation and data transfer) and more efficient
computation of the non\sphinxhyphen{}GPU accelerated parts of LAMMPS through MPI
parallelization, as all system data is maintained and updated on
the host. For KOKKOS, there is less to no benefit from this, due
to its different memory management model, which tries to retain
data on the GPU.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package moves per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data (coordinates, forces, and
(optionally) neighbor list data, if not computed on the GPU) between
the CPU and GPU at every timestep.  The KOKKOS/CUDA package only does
this on timesteps when a CPU calculation is required (e.g. to invoke
a fix or compute that is non\sphinxhyphen{}GPU\sphinxhyphen{}ized). Hence, if you can formulate
your input script to only use GPU\sphinxhyphen{}ized fixes and computes, and avoid
doing I/O too often (thermo output, dump file snapshots, restart files),
then the data transfer cost of the KOKKOS/CUDA package can be very low,
causing it to run faster than the GPU package.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package is often faster than the KOKKOS/CUDA package, when the
number of atoms per GPU is on the smaller side.  The crossover point,
in terms of atoms/GPU at which the KOKKOS/CUDA package becomes faster
depends strongly on the pair style.  For example, for a simple Lennard Jones
system the crossover (in single precision) is often about 50K\sphinxhyphen{}100K
atoms per GPU.  When performing double precision calculations the
crossover point can be significantly smaller.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Both KOKKOS and GPU package compute bonded interactions (bonds, angles,
etc) on the CPU.  If the GPU package is running with several MPI processes
assigned to one GPU, the cost of computing the bonded interactions is
spread across more CPUs and hence the GPU package can run faster in these
cases.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using LAMMPS with multiple MPI ranks assigned to the same GPU, its
performance depends to some extent on the available bandwidth between
the CPUs and the GPU. This can differ significantly based on the
available bus technology, capability of the host CPU and mainboard,
the wiring of the buses and whether switches are used to increase the
number of available bus slots, or if GPUs are housed in an external
enclosure.  This can become quite complex.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
To achieve significant acceleration through GPUs, both KOKKOS and GPU
package require capable GPUs with fast on\sphinxhyphen{}device memory and efficient
data transfer rates. This requests capable upper mid\sphinxhyphen{}level to high\sphinxhyphen{}end
(desktop) GPUs. Using lower performance GPUs (e.g. on laptops) may
result in a slowdown instead.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the GPU package, specifically when running in parallel with MPI,
if it often more efficient to exclude the PPPM kspace style from GPU
acceleration and instead run it \sphinxhyphen{} concurrently with a GPU accelerated
pair style \sphinxhyphen{} on the CPU. This can often be easily achieved with placing
a \sphinxstyleemphasis{suffix off} command before and a \sphinxstyleemphasis{suffix on} command after the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_style pppm} command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The KOKKOS/OpenMP and OPENMP package have different thread management
strategies, which should result in OPENMP being more efficient for a
small number of threads with increasing overhead as the number of threads
per MPI rank grows. The KOKKOS/OpenMP kernels have less overhead in that
case, but have lower performance with few threads.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The INTEL package contains many options and settings for achieving
additional performance on Intel hardware (CPU and accelerator cards), but
to unlock this potential, an Intel compiler is required. The package code
will compile with GNU gcc, but it will not be as efficient.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Differences between the GPU and KOKKOS packages:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package accelerates only pair force, neighbor list, and (parts
of) PPPM calculations. The KOKKOS package attempts to run most of the
calculation on the GPU, but can transparently support non\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated
code (with a performance penalty due to having data transfers between
host and GPU).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package requires neighbor lists to be built on the CPU when using
exclusion lists, or a triclinic simulation box.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU package can be compiled for CUDA or OpenCL and thus supports
both, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs well. On NVIDIA hardware, using CUDA is typically
resulting in equal or better performance over OpenCL.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
OpenCL in the GPU package does theoretically also support Intel CPUs or
Intel Xeon Phi, but the native support for those in KOKKOS (or INTEL)
is superior.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Howto discussions}
\label{\detokenize{Howto:howto-discussions}}\label{\detokenize{Howto::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These doc pages describe how to perform various tasks with LAMMPS,
both for users and developers.  The
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/glossary.html}{glossary} website page also lists MD
terminology, with links to corresponding LAMMPS manual pages.  The
example input scripts included in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples}} directory of the LAMMPS
source code distribution and highlighted on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Example scripts}}}} page
also show how to set up and run various kinds of simulations.


\section{General howto}
\label{\detokenize{Howto:general-howto}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Restart a simulation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_restart:restart-a-simulation}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_restart::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are 3 ways to continue a long LAMMPS simulation.  Multiple
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} commands can be used in the same input script.  Each
run will continue from where the previous run left off.  Or binary
restart files can be saved to disk using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}}
command.  At a later time, these binary files can be read via a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command in a new script.  Or they can
be converted to text data files using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}r command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} and read by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command in a
new script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here we give examples of 2 scripts that read either a binary restart
file or a converted data file and then issue a new run command to
continue where the previous run left off.  They illustrate what
settings must be made in the new script.  Details are discussed in the
documentation for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Look at the \sphinxstyleemphasis{in.chain} input script provided in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bench} directory
of the LAMMPS distribution to see the original script that these 2
scripts are based on.  If that script had the line

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.restart}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
added to it, it would produce two binary restart files (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tmp.restart.50}}
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tmp.restart.100}}) as it ran.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This script could be used to read the first restart file and re\sphinxhyphen{}run the
last 50 timesteps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}restart}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{tmp.restart.50}

\PYG{k}{neighbor}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}

\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{langevin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{904297}

\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+m}{0.012}

\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{l+m}{50}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the following commands do not need to be repeated because
their settings are included in the restart file: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{units}%
}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}%
}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}%
}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}%
}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}%
}}.  However, these commands do
need to be used, since their settings are not in the restart file:
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{neighbor}%
}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{fix}%
}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{timestep}%
}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you actually use this script to perform a restarted run, you will
notice that the thermodynamic data match at step 50 (if you also put a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{thermo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}%
}} command in the original script), but do not match at step
100.  This is because the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} command
uses random numbers in a way that does not allow for perfect restarts.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an alternate approach, the restart file could be converted to a data
file as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
lmp\PYGZus{}g++\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}r\PYG{+w}{ }tmp.restart.50\PYG{+w}{ }tmp.restart.data
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Then, this script could be used to re\sphinxhyphen{}run the last 50 steps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{n}{lj}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{bond}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.12}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{fene}
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}

\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{tmp.restart.data}

\PYG{k}{neighbor}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}

\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{langevin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{904297}

\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+m}{0.012}

\PYG{k}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{50}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{l+m}{50}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that nearly all the settings specified in the original \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in.chain}}
script must be repeated, except the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}%
}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}%
}}
commands, since the new data file lists the force field coefficients.
Also, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{reset_timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{reset\_timestep}}}} command is used to tell
LAMMPS the current timestep.  This value is stored in restart files, but
not in data files.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Visualize LAMMPS snapshots}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_viz:visualize-lammps-snapshots}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_viz::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Snapshots from LAMMPS simulations can be viewed, visualized, and
analyzed in a variety of ways.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS snapshots are created by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} command, which
can create files in several formats. The native LAMMPS dump format is a
text file (see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{atom}%
}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{custom}%
}}) which can be visualized by
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/viz.html}{several visualization tools} for MD
simulation trajectories.  \sphinxhref{https://www.ovito.org}{OVITO} and \sphinxhref{https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/vmd}{VMD} seem to be the most popular
choices among them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump movie}}}}
styles can output internally rendered images or convert them to a movie
during the MD run.  It is also possible to create visualizations from
LAMMPS inputs or restart file with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI}}}}, which uses the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}}
command internally.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Snapshot Image Viewer}} can be used to
adjust the visualization of the system interactively and then export
the corresponding LAMMPS commands to the clipboard to be inserted
into input files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Programs included with LAMMPS as auxiliary tools can convert
between LAMMPS format files and other formats.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tools}}}} page for details.  These are rarely needed these days.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Run multiple simulations from one input script}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_multiple:run-multiple-simulations-from-one-input-script}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_multiple::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be done in several ways.  See the documentation for
individual commands for more details on how these examples work.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If “multiple simulations” means to continue a previous simulation for
more timesteps, then you simply use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command
multiple times.  For example, this script

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atomic}
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.lj}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
would run 5 successive simulations of the same system for a total of
50,000 timesteps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you wish to run totally different simulations, one after the other,
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{clear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{clear}}}} command can be used in between them to
re\sphinxhyphen{}initialize LAMMPS.  For example, this script

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atomic}
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.lj}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{clear}
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atomic}
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.lj.new}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
would run 2 independent simulations, one after the other.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For large numbers of independent simulations, you can use
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} commands to loop over the same input script
multiple times with different settings.  For example, this
script, named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in.polymer}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{d}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run8}
\PYG{k}{shell}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}d}
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.polymer}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{shell}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}
\PYG{k}{clear}
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{d}
\PYG{k}{jump }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.polymer}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
would run 8 simulations in different directories, using a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data.polymer}}
file in each directory.  The same concept could be used to run the
same system at 8 different temperatures, using a temperature variable
and storing the output in different log and dump files, for example

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.85}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.95}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.05}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.15}
\PYG{k}{log}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{log.}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}a}
\PYG{n}{read}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.polymer}
\PYG{k}{velocity }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{352839}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dump.}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}a}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100000}
\PYG{k}{clear}
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{t}
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}
\PYG{k}{jump }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.polymer}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the above examples work whether you are running on 1 or
multiple processors, but assumed you are running LAMMPS on a single
partition of processors.  LAMMPS can be run on multiple partitions via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the last 2 examples, if LAMMPS were run on 3 partitions, the same
scripts could be used if the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{index}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{loop}} variables were
replaced with \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, as described in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command.  Also, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{t}%
}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}%
}}
commands would need to be replaced with a single \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{%
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t}%
}} command.
With these modifications, the 8 simulations of each script would run
on the 3 partitions one after the other until all were finished.
Initially, 3 simulations would be started simultaneously, one on each
partition.  When one finished, that partition would then start
the fourth simulation, and so forth, until all 8 were completed.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulations}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_replica:multi-replica-simulations}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_replica::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Several commands in LAMMPS run multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulations, meaning
that multiple instances (replicas) of your simulation are run
simultaneously, with small amounts of data exchanged between replicas
periodically.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the relevant commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{hyper::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hyper}}}} for bond boost hyperdynamics (HD)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neb}}}} for nudged elastic band calculations (NEB)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neb\_spin}}}} for magnetic nudged elastic band calculations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{prd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{prd}}}} for parallel replica dynamics (PRD)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{tad::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tad}}}} for temperature accelerated dynamics (TAD)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{temper::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temper}}}} for parallel tempering with fixed volume

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{temper_npt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temper/npt}}}} for parallel tempering extended for NPT

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{temper_grem::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temper/grem}}}} for parallel tempering with generalized replica exchange (gREM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pimd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pimd}}}} for path\sphinxhyphen{}integral molecular dynamics (PIMD)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
NEB is a method for finding transition states and barrier potential energies.
HD, PRD, and TAD are methods for performing accelerated dynamics to find and
perform infrequent events.  Parallel tempering or replica exchange runs
different replicas at a series of temperature to facilitate rare\sphinxhyphen{}event
sampling.  PIMD runs different replicas whose individual particles in different
replicas are coupled together by springs to model a system of ring\sphinxhyphen{}polymers which
can represent the quantum nature of atom cores.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the REPLICA
package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more
info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In all these cases, you must run with one or more processors per
replica.  The processors assigned to each replica are determined at
run\sphinxhyphen{}time by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to launch LAMMPS on multiple partitions, which in this
context are the same as replicas.  E.g.  these commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}linux\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}partition\PYG{+w}{ }8x2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.temper
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}linux\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}partition\PYG{+w}{ }8x1\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.neb
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
would each run 8 replicas, on either 16 or 8 processors.  Note the use
of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}in command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to specify the input
script which is required when running in multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica mode.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that with MPI installed on a machine (e.g. your desktop), you
can run on more (virtual) processors than you have physical processors.
Thus, the above commands could be run on a single\sphinxhyphen{}processor (or
