few\sphinxhyphen{}processor) desktop so that you can run a multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulation on
more replicas than you have physical processors. This is useful for
testing and debugging, since with most modern processors and MPI
libraries, the efficiency of a calculation can severely diminish when
oversubscribing processors.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Library interface to LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_library:library-interface-to-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_library::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_basics::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build basics}}}} doc page, LAMMPS
can be built as a static or shared library, so that it can be called by
another code, used in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_couple::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{coupled manner}}}} with other
codes, or driven through a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python interface}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the core of LAMMPS is the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS}} class, which encapsulates the
state of the simulation program through the state of the various class
instances that it is composed of.  So a calculation using LAMMPS
requires creating an instance of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS}} class and then send it
(text) commands, either individually or from a file, or perform other
operations that modify the state stored inside that instance or drive
simulations.  This is essentially what the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/main.cpp}} file does as
well for the standalone LAMMPS executable, reading commands either from
an input file or the standard input.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Creating a LAMMPS instance can be done by using C++ code directly or
through a C\sphinxhyphen{}style interface library to LAMMPS that is provided in the
files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.h}}.  This {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{C language
API}}}}, can be used from C and C++, and is also the basis
for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Fortran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fortran}}}}
interfaces or the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:swig}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWIG based wrappers}}}} included in the
LAMMPS source code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/COUPLE}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python/examples}} directories contain some
example programs written in C++, C, Fortran, and Python, which show how
a driver code can link to LAMMPS as a library, run LAMMPS on a subset of
processors (so the others are available to run some other code
concurrently), grab data from LAMMPS, change it, and send it back into
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A detailed documentation of the available APIs and examples of how to
use them can be found in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Manual:programmer-documentation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Programmer Guide}}}}
section of this manual.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Coupling LAMMPS to other codes}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_couple:coupling-lammps-to-other-codes}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_couple::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed to support being coupled to other codes.  For
example, a quantum mechanics code might compute forces on a subset of
atoms and pass those forces to LAMMPS.  Or a continuum finite element
(FE) simulation might use atom positions as boundary conditions on FE
nodal points, compute a FE solution, and return interpolated forces on
MD atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can be coupled to other codes in at least 4 different ways.  Each
has advantages and disadvantages, which you will have to think about in
the context of your application.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a new {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command
that calls the other code.  In this scenario, LAMMPS is the driver
code.  During timestepping, the fix or compute is invoked, and can
make library calls to the other code, which has been linked to LAMMPS
as a library.  This is the way the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-voronoi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{VORONOI}}}}
package, which computes Voronoi tesselations using the \sphinxhref{http://math.lbl.gov/voro++}{Voro++
library}, is interfaced to LAMMPS.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute voronoi}}}} command for more
details.  Also see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}} pages for information
on how to add a new fix or compute to LAMMPS.

\end{enumerate}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a new LAMMPS command that calls the other code.  This is
conceptually similar to method (1), but in this case LAMMPS and the
other code are on a more equal footing.  Note that now the other code
is not called during the timestepping of a LAMMPS run, but between
runs.  The LAMMPS input script can be used to alternate LAMMPS runs
with calls to the other code, invoked via the new command.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command facilitates this with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} option,
which makes it easy to run a few steps, invoke the command, run a few
steps, invoke the command, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this scenario, the other code can be called as a library, as in
1., or it could be a stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone code, invoked by a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{system()}} call
made by the command (assuming your parallel machine allows one or
more processors to start up another program).  In the latter case the
stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone code could communicate with LAMMPS through files that the
command writes and reads.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_command::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify command}}}} page for information
on how to add a new command to LAMMPS.

\end{enumerate}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use LAMMPS as a library called by another code.  In this case, the
other code is the driver and calls LAMMPS as needed.  Alternately, a
wrapper code could link and call both LAMMPS and another code as
libraries.  Again, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command has options that
allow it to be invoked with minimal overhead (no setup or clean\sphinxhyphen{}up)
if you wish to do multiple short runs, driven by another program.
Details about using the library interface are given in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Library::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{library API}}}} documentation.

\end{enumerate}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Couple LAMMPS with another code in a client/server fashion, using the
\sphinxhref{https://molssi-mdi.github.io/MDI\_Library/html/index.html}{MDI Library}
developed by the \sphinxhref{https://molssi.org}{Molecular Sciences Software Institute (MolSSI)} to run LAMMPS as either an MDI driver (client)
or an MDI engine (server).  The MDI driver issues commands to the MDI
server to exchange data between them.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_mdi::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Using LAMMPS with the MDI library for code coupling}}}} page for
more information about how LAMMPS can operate in either of these modes.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Using LAMMPS with the MDI library for code coupling}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_mdi:using-lammps-with-the-mdi-library-for-code-coupling}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_mdi::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Client/server coupling of two (or more) codes is where one code is the
“client” and sends request messages (data) to one (or more) “server”
code(s).  A server responds to each request with a reply message
(data).  This enables two (or more) codes to work in tandem to perform
a simulation.  In this context, LAMMPS can act as either a client or
server code.  It does this by using the \sphinxhref{https://molssi-mdi.github.io/MDI\_Library/html/index.html}{MolSSI Driver Interface (MDI)
library},
developed by the \sphinxhref{https://molssi.org}{Molecular Sciences Software Institute (MolSSI)}, which is supported by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-mdi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{MDI}}}}
package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternate methods for coupling codes with LAMMPS are described on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_couple::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Coupling LAMMPS to other codes}}}} page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some advantages of client/server coupling are that the codes can run
as stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone executables; they need not be linked together.  Thus,
neither code needs to have a library interface.  This also makes it
easy to run the two codes on different numbers of processors.  If a
message protocol (format and content) is defined for a particular kind
of simulation, then in principle any code which implements the
client\sphinxhyphen{}side protocol can be used in tandem with any code which
implements the server\sphinxhyphen{}side protocol.  Neither code needs to know what
specific other code it is working with.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In MDI nomenclature, a client code is the “driver”, and a server code is
an “engine”.  One driver code can communicate with one or more instances
of one or more engine codes.  Driver and engine codes can be written in
any language: C, C++, Fortran, Python, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to allowing driver and engine(s) to run as stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone
executables, MDI also enables an engine to be a \sphinxstyleemphasis{plugin} to the client
code.  In this scenario, server code(s) are compiled as shared
libraries, and one (or more) instances of the server are instantiated
by the driver code.  If the driver code runs in parallel, it can split
its MPI communicator into multiple sub\sphinxhyphen{}communicators, and launch each
plugin engine instance on a sub\sphinxhyphen{}communicator.  Driver processors
within that sub\sphinxhyphen{}communicator exchange messages with the corresponding
engine instance, and can also send MPI messages to other processors in
the driver.  The driver code can also destroy engine instances and
re\sphinxhyphen{}instantiate them.  LAMMPS can operate as either a stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone or
plugin MDI engine.  When it operates as a driver, it can use either
stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone or plugin MDI engines.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The way in which an MDI driver communicates with an MDI engine is by
making MDI\_Send() and MDI\_Recv() calls, which are conceptually similar
to MPI\_Send() and MPI\_Recv() calls.  Each send or receive operation
uses a string to identify the command name, and optionally some data,
which can be a single value or vector of values of any data type.
Inside the MDI library, data is exchanged between the driver and
engine via MPI calls or sockets.  This is a run\sphinxhyphen{}time choice by the user.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-mdi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{MDI}}}} package provides a {\hyperref[\detokenize{mdi::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mdi engine}}}}
command, which enables LAMMPS to operate as an MDI engine.  Its doc
page explains the variety of standard and custom MDI commands which
the LAMMPS engine recognizes and can respond to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The package also provides a {\hyperref[\detokenize{mdi::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mdi plugin}}}} command, which
enables LAMMPS to operate as an MDI driver and load an MDI engine as a
plugin library.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The package furthermore includes a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_mdi_qm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix mdi/qm}}}}
command, in which LAMMPS operates as an MDI driver in conjunction with a
quantum mechanics code as an MDI engine.  The post\_force() method of the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix\_mdi\_qm.cpp}} file shows how a driver issues MDI commands to
another code.  This command can be used to couple to an MDI engine,
which is either a stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone code or a plugin library.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_mdi_qm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix mdi/qm}}}} command
documentation, it can be used to perform \sphinxstyleemphasis{ab initio} MD simulations or
energy minimizations, or to evaluate the quantum energy and forces for a
series of independent systems.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/mdi}} directory has
example input scripts for all of these use cases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The package also has a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_mdi_qmmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix mdi/qmmm}}}} command in
which LAMMPS operates as an MDI driver in conjunction with a quantum
mechanics code as an MDI engine to perform QM/MM simulations.  The
LAMMPS input script partitions the system into QM and MM (molecular
mechanics) atoms.  As described below the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/QUANTUM}} directory
has examples for coupling to 3 different quantum codes in this manner.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/mdi}} directory contains Python scripts and LAMMPS input
script which use LAMMPS as either an MDI driver or engine, or both.
Currently, 5 example use cases are provided:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run ab initio MD (AIMD) using 2 instances of LAMMPS.  As a driver,
LAMMPS performs the timestepping in either NVE or NPT mode.  As an
engine, LAMMPS computes forces and is a surrogate for a quantum
code.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS runs an MD simulation as a driver.  Every N steps it passes the
current snapshot to an MDI engine to evaluate the energy, virial, and
peratom forces.  As the engine, LAMMPS is a surrogate for a quantum
code.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS loops over a series of data files and passes the configuration
to an MDI engine to evaluate the energy, virial, and peratom forces
and thus acts as a simulation driver.  As the engine, LAMMPS is used
as a surrogate for a quantum code.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A Python script driver invokes a sequence of unrelated LAMMPS
calculations.  Calculations can be single\sphinxhyphen{}point energy/force
evaluations, MD runs, or energy minimizations.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run AIMD with a Python driver code and 2 LAMMPS instances as engines.
The first LAMMPS instance performs MD timestepping.  The second LAMMPS
instance acts as a surrogate QM code to compute forces.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In any of these examples where LAMMPS is used as an engine, an actual
QM code (provided it has support for MDI) could be used in its place,
without modifying the input scripts or launch commands, except to
specify the name of the QM code.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/mdi/Run.sh}} file illustrates how to launch both driver
and engine codes so that they communicate using the MDI library via
either MPI or sockets, or using the engine as a stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone code, or
as a plugin library.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
As of March 2023, these are quantum codes with MDI support provided via
Python wrapper scripts included in the LAMMPS distribution.  These can
be used with the fix mdi/qm and fix mdi/qmmm commands to perform QM
calculations of an entire system (e.g. AIMD) or QM/MM simulations.  See
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/QUANTUM}} sub\sphinxhyphen{}directories for more details:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LATTE \sphinxhyphen{} AIMD only

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
PySCF \sphinxhyphen{} QM/MM only

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
NWChem \sphinxhyphen{} AIMD or QM/MM

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are also at least two quantum codes which have direct MDI
support, \sphinxhref{https://www.quantum-espresso.org/}{Quantum ESPRESSO (QE)}
and \sphinxhref{https://qsg.llnl.gov/node/101.html}{INQ}.  There are also
several QM codes which have indirect support through QCEngine or i\sphinxhyphen{}PI.
The former means they require a wrapper program (QCEngine) with MDI
support which writes/read files to pass data to the quantum code
itself.  The list of QCEngine\sphinxhyphen{}supported and i\sphinxhyphen{}PI\sphinxhyphen{}supported quantum
codes is on the \sphinxhref{https://molssi-mdi.github.io/MDI\_Library/html/index.html}{MDI webpage}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These direct\sphinxhyphen{} and indirect\sphinxhyphen{}support codes should be usable for full
system calculations (e.g. AIMD).  Whether they support QM/MM models
depends on the individual QM code.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Broken Bonds}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_broken_bonds:broken-bonds}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_broken_bonds::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically, molecular bond interactions persist for the duration of a
simulation in LAMMPS.  However, some commands break bonds dynamically,
including the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_break::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/break}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{BPM package}}}} bond styles

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A bond can break if it is stretched beyond a user\sphinxhyphen{}defined threshold or
more generally if other criteria are met.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the quartic bond style, when a bond is broken its bond type is set
to 0 to effectively break it and pairwise forces between the two atoms
in the broken bond are “turned on”.  Angles, dihedrals, etc cannot be
defined for a system when {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}} is
used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, bond styles in the BPM package are also incompatible with
angles, dihedrals, etc. and when a bond breaks its type is set to zero.
However, in the BPM package one can either turn off all pair interactions
between bonded particles or leave them on, overlaying pair forces on
top of bond forces. To remove pair forces, the special bond list is
dynamically updated.  More details can be found on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto BPM}}}} page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_break::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/break}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}} commands allow breaking of bonds within a molecular
topology with may also define angles, dihedrals, etc.  These commands
update internal topology data structures to remove broken bonds, as
well as the appropriate angle, dihedral, etc interactions which
include the bond.  They also trigger a rebuild of the neighbor list
when this occurs, to turn on the appropriate pairwise forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that when bonds are dumped to a file via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}} command, bonds with type 0 are not included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}} command can be used to query
the status of broken bonds with type = 0 or permanently delete them,
e.g.:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stats}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{remove}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_count_type::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{count/type}}}} command tallies the
current number of bonds (or angles, etc) for each bond (angle, etc)
type.  It also tallies broken bonds with type = 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_nbond_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{nbond/atom}}}} command tallies the
current number of bonds each atom is part of, excluding broken bonds
with type = 0.


\section{Settings howto}
\label{\detokenize{Howto:settings-howto}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{2d simulations}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_2d:d-simulations}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_2d::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You must use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dimension}}}} command to specify a 2d
simulation.  The default is 3d.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A 2d simulation box must be periodic in z as set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.  This is the default.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Simulation boxes in LAMMPS can be either orthogonal or triclinic in
shape.  Orthogonal boxes in 2d are a rectangle with 4 edges that are
each perpendicular to either the x or y coordinate axes.  Triclinic
boxes in 2d are a parallelogram with opposite pairs of faces parallel
to each other.  LAMMPS supports two forms of triclinic boxes,
restricted and general, which for 2d differ in how the box is oriented
with respect to the xy coordinate axes.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} for a detailed description of all 3 kinds of
simulation boxes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are examples of using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command
to define the simulation box for a 2d system.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 2d orthogonal box using a block\PYGZhy{}style region}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mybox}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{block}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mybox}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 2d restricted triclinic box using a prism\PYGZhy{}style region with only xy tilt}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mybox}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{prism}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mybox}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 2d general triclinic box using a primitive cell for a 2d hex lattice}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.86602540378}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{n}{a3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{triclinic}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{general}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for 2d orthogonal or restricted triclinic boxes, the box has
a 3rd dimension which must straddle z = 0.0 in the z dimension.
Typically the width of box in the z dimension should be narrow,
e.g. \sphinxhyphen{}0.5 to 0.5, but that is not required.  For a 2d general
triclinic box, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} vector defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}
command must be (0.0,0.0,1.0), which is its default value.  Also the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{clo} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{chi} arguments of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}
command must be \sphinxhyphen{}0.5 and 0.5.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are examples of using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command
to define the simulation box for a 2d system via keywords in the
header section of the data file.  These are the same boxes as the examples
for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 2d orthogonal box}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{xlo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xhi}
\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{ylo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yhi}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zlo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zhi}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} this is the default, so no need to specify}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 2d restricted triclinic box with only xy tilt}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{xlo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xhi}
\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{ylo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yhi}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zlo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zhi}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} this is the default, so no need to specify}
\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yz}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 3d general triclinic box using a primitive cell for a 2d hex lattice}
\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{n}{avec}
\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.3301270189}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bvec}
\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{n}{cvec}\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} this is the default, so no need to specify}
\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{n}{abc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{origin}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} this is the default for 2d, so no need to specify}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for 2d orthogonal or restricted triclinic boxes, the box has
a 3rd dimension specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{zlo zhi} values, which must straddle
z = 0.0.  Typically the width of box in the z dimension should be
narrow, e.g. \sphinxhyphen{}0.5 to 0.5, but that is not required.  For a 2d general
triclinic box, the z component of \sphinxstyleemphasis{avec} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{bvec} must be zero, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cvec} must be (0,0,1), which is the default.  The z component of \sphinxstyleemphasis{abc
origin} must also be \sphinxhyphen{}0.5, which is the default.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command to create
atoms in the 2d simulation box, all the z coordinates of created atoms
will be zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command to read in a data
file of atom coordinates for a 2d system, the z coordinates of all
atoms should be zero.  A value within epsilon of zero is also allowed
in case the data file was generated by another program with finite
numeric precision, in which case the z coord for the atom will be set
to zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_enforce2d::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix enforce2d}}}} command as the last fix
defined in the input script.  It ensures that the z\sphinxhyphen{}components of
velocities and forces are zeroed out every timestep.  The reason to
make it the last fix is so that any forces added by other fixes will
also be zeroed out.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many of the example input scripts included in the examples directory
are for 2d models.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some models in LAMMPS treat particles as finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spheres, as
opposed to point particles.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/sphere}}}} commands
for details.  By default, for 2d simulations, such particles will
still be modeled as 3d spheres, not 2d discs (circles), meaning
their moment of inertia will be that of a sphere.  If you wish to
model them as 2d discs, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set density/disc}}}}
command and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{disc} option for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/sphere}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sphere}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nph_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph/sphere}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt/sphere}}}} commands.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Type labels}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_type_labels:type-labels}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_type_labels::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Sep2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each atom in LAMMPS has an associated numeric atom type. Similarly,
each bond, angle, dihedral, and improper is assigned a bond type,
angle type, and so on.  The primary use of these types is to map
potential (force field) parameters to the interactions of the atom,
bond, angle, dihedral, and improper.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, type values are entered as integers from 1 to Ntypes
wherever they appear in LAMMPS input or output files.  The total number
Ntypes for each interaction is “locked in” when the simulation box
is created.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A recent addition to LAMMPS is the option to use strings \sphinxhyphen{} referred to
as type labels \sphinxhyphen{} as an alternative.  Using type labels instead of
numeric types can be advantageous in various scenarios.  For example,
type labels can make inputs more readable and generic (i.e. usable
through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{include::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{include command}}}} for different systems with
different numerical values assigned to types.  This generality also
applies to other inputs like data files read by {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or molecule template files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} command.  A discussion of the current type label support can
be found in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_type_labels:typelabel24}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Gissinger)}}}}.  See below for a list of
other commands that can use type labels in different ways.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS will \sphinxstyleemphasis{internally} continue to use numeric types, which means
that many previous restrictions still apply.  For example, the total
number of types is locked in when creating the simulation box, and
potential parameters for each type must be provided even if not used
by any interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A collection of type labels for all type\sphinxhyphen{}kinds (atom types, bond types,
etc.) is stored as a “label map” which is simply a list of numeric types
and their associated type labels.  Within a type\sphinxhyphen{}kind, each type label
must be unique.  It can be assigned to only one numeric type.  To read
and write type labels to data files for a given type\sphinxhyphen{}kind, \sphinxstyleemphasis{all}
associated numeric types need have a type label assigned.  Partial
maps can be saved with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap write}}}} command
and read back with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{include::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{include}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Valid type labels can contain most ASCII characters, but cannot start
with a number, a ‘\#’, or a ‘*’.  Also, labels must not contain whitespace
characters.  When using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap command}}}} in the
LAMMPS input, if certain characters appear in the type label, such as
the single (’) or double (”) quote or the ‘\#’ character, the label
must be put in either double, single, or triple (“””) quotes.  Triple
quotes allow for the most generic type label strings, but they require
to have a leading and trailing blank space.  When defining type labels
the blanks will be ignored. Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{angle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{ C1\PYGZsq{}\PYGZhy{}C2}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{C3}\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} \PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command will map the string \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textasciigrave{}C1\textquotesingle{}\sphinxhyphen{}C2"\sphinxhyphen{}C3\#\textasciigrave{}}} to the angle type 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two ways to define label maps.  One is via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} command.  The other is via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
command.  A data file can have sections such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{Atom Type Labels}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bond
Type Labels}, etc., which assign type labels to numeric types.  The
label map can be written out to data files by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{write_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_data}}}} command.  This map is also written to and read from
restart files, by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{write_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_restart}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Use of type labels in LAMMPS input or output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_type_labels:use-of-type-labels-in-lammps-input-or-output}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Many LAMMPS input script commands that take a numeric type as an
argument can use the associated type label instead.  If a type label
is not defined for a particular numeric type, only its numeric type
can be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This example assigns labels to the atom types, and then uses the type
labels to redefine the pair coefficients.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} numeric types}
\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} type labels}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding support for type labels to various commands is an ongoing
project.  If an input script command (or a section in a file read by a
command) allows substituting a type label for a numeric type argument,
it will be explicitly mentioned in that command’s documentation page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a temporary measure, input script commands can take advantage of
variables and how they can be expanded during processing of the input.
The variables can use functions that will translate type label strings
to their respective number as defined in the current label map.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, here is how the pair\_coeff command could be used with
type labels if it did not yet support them, either with an explicit
variable command or an implicit variable used in the pair\_coeff
command.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{atom1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{label2type}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{atom,C}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{atom2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{label2type}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{atom,H}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{atom1}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{atom2}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{label2type}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{atom,C}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{label2type}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{atom,H}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Commands that can use label types}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_type_labels:commands-that-can-use-label-types}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Any workflow that involves reading multiple data files, molecule
templates or a combination of the two can be streamlined by using type
labels instead of numeric types, because types are automatically synced
between the files.  The creation of simulation\sphinxhyphen{}ready reaction templates
for {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}} is much simpler when using
type labels, and results in templates that can be used without
modification in multiple simulations or different systems.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_type_labels:typelabel24}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Gissinger)} J. R. Gissinger, I. Nikiforov, Y. Afshar, B. Waters, M. Choi, D. S. Karls, A. Stukowski, W. Im, H. Heinz, A. Kohlmeyer, and E. B. Tadmor, J Phys Chem B, 128, 3282\sphinxhyphen{}3297 (2024).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Triclinic (non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal) simulation boxes}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic:triclinic-non-orthogonal-simulation-boxes}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, LAMMPS uses an orthogonal simulation box to encompass the
particles.  The orthogonal box has its “origin” at (xlo,ylo,zlo) and
extends to (xhi,yhi,zhi).  Conceptually it is defined by 3 edge
vectors starting from the origin given by \sphinxstylestrong{A} = (xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo,0,0); \sphinxstylestrong{B}
= (0,yhi\sphinxhyphen{}ylo,0); \sphinxstylestrong{C} = (0,0,zhi\sphinxhyphen{}zlo).  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command sets the boundary conditions for the 6 faces of
the box (periodic, non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic, etc).  The 6 parameters
(xlo,xhi,ylo,yhi,zlo,zhi) are defined at the time the simulation box
is created by one of these commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Internally, LAMMPS defines box size parameters lx,ly,lz where lx =
xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo, and similarly in the y and z dimensions.  The 6 parameters, as
well as lx,ly,lz, can be output via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_2d::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto 2d}}}} doc page
for info on how zlo and zhi are defined for 2d simulations.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Triclinic simulation boxes}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic:triclinic-simulation-boxes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS also allows simulations to be performed using triclinic
(non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal) simulation boxes shaped as a 3d parallelepiped with
triclinic symmetry.  For 2d simulations a triclinic simulation box is
effectively a parallelogram; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_2d::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto 2d}}}} doc
page for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One use of triclinic simulation boxes is to model solid\sphinxhyphen{}state crystals
with triclinic symmetry.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command can be
used with non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal basis vectors to define a lattice that will
tile a triclinic simulation box via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A second use is to run Parrinello\sphinxhyphen{}Rahman dynamics via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
npt}}}} command, which will adjust the xy, xz, yz tilt factors
to compensate for off\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal components of the pressure tensor.  The
analog for an {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}} is the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_box_relax::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
box/relax}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A third use is to shear a bulk solid to study the response of the
material.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command can be used for
this purpose.  It allows dynamic control of the xy, xz, yz tilt
factors as a simulation runs.  This is discussed in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_nemd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto
NEMD}}}} doc page on non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (NEMD) simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Conceptually, a triclinic parallelepiped is defined with an “origin”
at (xlo,ylo,zhi) and 3 edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A} = (ax,ay,az), \sphinxstylestrong{B} =
(bx,by,bz), \sphinxstylestrong{C} = (cx,cy,cz) which can be arbitrary vectors, so long
as they are non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, distinct, and not co\sphinxhyphen{}planar.  In addition, they
must define a right\sphinxhyphen{}handed system, such that (\sphinxstylestrong{A} cross \sphinxstylestrong{B})
points in the direction of \sphinxstylestrong{C}.  Note that a left\sphinxhyphen{}handed system can
be converted to a right\sphinxhyphen{}handed system by simply swapping the order of
any pair of the \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} vectors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 4 commands listed above for defining orthogonal simulation boxes
have triclinic options which allow for specification of the origin and
edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C}.  For each command, this can be done
in one of two ways, for what LAMMPS calls a \sphinxstyleemphasis{general} triclinic box or
a \sphinxstyleemphasis{restricted} triclinic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{general} triclinic box is specified by an origin (xlo, ylo, zlo)
and arbitrary edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A} = (ax,ay,az), \sphinxstylestrong{B} = (bx,by,bz), and
\sphinxstylestrong{C} = (cx,cy,cz).  So there are 12 parameters in total.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{restricted} triclinic box also has an origin (xlo,ylo,zlo), but its
edge vectors are of the following restricted form: \sphinxstylestrong{A} =
(xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo,0,0), \sphinxstylestrong{B} = (xy,yhi\sphinxhyphen{}ylo,0), \sphinxstylestrong{C} = (xz,yz,zhi\sphinxhyphen{}zlo).  So
there are 9 parameters in total.  Note that the restricted form
requires \sphinxstylestrong{A} to be along the x\sphinxhyphen{}axis, \sphinxstylestrong{B} to be in the xy plane
with a y\sphinxhyphen{}component in the +y direction, and \sphinxstylestrong{C} to have its
z\sphinxhyphen{}component in the +z direction.  Note that a restricted triclinic box
is \sphinxstyleemphasis{right\sphinxhyphen{}handed} by construction since (\sphinxstylestrong{A} cross \sphinxstylestrong{B}) points in
the direction of \sphinxstylestrong{C}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy,xz,yz} values can be zero or positive or negative.  They are
called “tilt factors” because they are the amount of displacement
applied to edges of faces of an orthogonal box to change it into a
restricted triclinic parallelepiped.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Any right\sphinxhyphen{}handed general triclinic box (i.e. solid\sphinxhyphen{}state crystal
basis vectors) can be rotated in 3d around its origin in order to
conform to the LAMMPS definition of a restricted triclinic box.
See the discussion in the next sub\sphinxhyphen{}section about general triclinic
simulation boxes in LAMMPS.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command has
keywords for outputting the various parameters that define the size
and shape of orthogonal, restricted triclinic, and general triclinic
simulation boxes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For orthogonal boxes there 6 thermo keywords (xlo,ylo,zlo) and
(xhi,yhi,zhi).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For restricted triclinic boxes there are 9 thermo keywords for
(xlo,ylo,zlo), (xhi,yhi,zhi), and the (xy,xz,yz) tilt factors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For general triclinic boxes there are 12 thermo keywords for
(xlo,ylo,zhi) and the components of the \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} edge
vectors, namely (avecx,avecy,avecz), (bvecx,bvecy,bvecz), and
(cvecx,cvecy,cvecz),

\sphinxAtStartPar
The remainder of this doc page explains (a) how LAMMPS operates with
general triclinic simulation boxes, (b) mathematical transformations
between general and restricted triclinic boxes which may be useful
when creating LAMMPS inputs or interpreting outputs for triclinic
simulations, and (c) how LAMMPS uses tilt factors for restricted
triclinic simulation boxes.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{General triclinic simulation boxes in LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic:general-triclinic-simulation-boxes-in-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS allows specification of general triclinic simulation boxes with
their atoms as a convenience for users who may be converting data from
solid\sphinxhyphen{}state crystallographic representations or from DFT codes for
input to LAMMPS.  Likewise it allows output of dump files, data files,
and thermodynamic data (e.g. pressure tensor) in a general triclinic
format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However internally, LAMMPS only uses restricted triclinic simulation
boxes.  This is for parallel efficiency and to formulate partitioning
of the simulation box across processors, neighbor list building, and
inter\sphinxhyphen{}processor communication of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data with methods similar to
those used for orthogonal boxes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means 4 things which are important to understand:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Input of a general triclinic system is immediately converted to a
restricted triclinic system.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If output of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data for a general triclinic system is
requested (e.g. for atom coordinates in a dump file),
conversion from a restricted to general triclinic system is done at
the time of output.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The conversion of the simulation box and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data from general
triclinic to restricted triclinic (and vice versa) is a 3d rotation
operation around an origin, which is the lower left corner of the
simulation box.  This means an input data file for a general
triclinic system should specify all per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities consistent
with the general triclinic box and its orientation relative to the
standard x,y,z coordinate axes.  For example, atom coordinates
should be inside the general triclinic simulation box defined by the
edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} and its origin.  Likewise per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
velocities should be in directions consistent with the general
triclinic box orientation.  E.g. a velocity vector which will be in
the +x direction once LAMMPS converts from a general to restricted
triclinic box, should be specified in the data file in the direction
of the \sphinxstylestrong{A} edge vector.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} doc
page for info on all the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector quantities to which this
rule applies when a data file for a general triclinic box is input.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If commands such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{write_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump
custom}}}} are used to output general triclinic information, it
is effectively the inverse of the operation described in the
preceding bullet.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Other LAMMPS commands such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}}, operate on a
restricted triclinic system even if a general triclinic system was
defined initially.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is the list of commands which have general triclinic options:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} define a general triclinic box

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} add atoms to a general triclinic box

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} define a custom lattice consistent with the \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} edge vectors of a general triclinic box

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} read a data file for a general triclinic system

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{write_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_data}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} write a data file for a general triclinic system

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump atom, dump custom}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} output dump snapshots in general triclinic format

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify triclinic/general}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} select general triclinic format for dump output

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} output the pressure tensor in
general triclinic format

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify triclinic/general}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} select general triclinic format for thermo output

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} read a restart file for a general triclinic system

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_restart}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} write a restart file for a general triclinic system

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Transformation from general to restricted triclinic boxes}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic:transformation-from-general-to-restricted-triclinic-boxes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \sphinxstylestrong{A},\sphinxstylestrong{B},\sphinxstylestrong{C} be the right\sphinxhyphen{}handed edge vectors of a
general triclinic simulation box.  The equivalent LAMMPS \sphinxstylestrong{a},\sphinxstylestrong{b},\sphinxstylestrong{c} for a restricted triclinic box are a 3d rotation of
\sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, and \sphinxstylestrong{C} and can be computed as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{a}  & \mathbf{b}  & \mathbf{c} \end{pmatrix} = &
\begin{pmatrix}
  a_x & b_x & c_x \\
  0   & b_y & c_y \\
  0   & 0   & c_z \\
\end{pmatrix} \\
a_x = & A \\
b_x = & \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{\hat{A}} \quad = \quad B \cos{\gamma} \\
b_y = & |\mathbf{\hat{A}} \times \mathbf{B}| \quad = \quad B \sin{\gamma} \quad =  \quad  \sqrt{B^2 - {b_x}^2} \\
c_x = & \mathbf{C} \cdot \mathbf{\hat{A}} \quad = \quad C \cos{\beta} \\
c_y = & \mathbf{C} \cdot \widehat{(\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B})} \times \mathbf{\hat{A}} \quad = \quad \frac{\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{C} - b_x c_x}{b_y} \\
c_z = & |\mathbf{C} \cdot \widehat{(\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B})}|\quad = \quad \sqrt{C^2 - {c_x}^2 - {c_y}^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where A = | \sphinxstylestrong{A} | indicates the scalar length of \sphinxstylestrong{A}. The hat
symbol (\textasciicircum{}) indicates the corresponding unit vector. \(\beta\) and
\(\gamma\) are angles between the \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} vectors
as described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For consistency, the same rotation applied to the triclinic box edge
vectors can also be applied to atom positions, velocities, and other
vector quantities.  This can be conveniently achieved by first
converting to fractional coordinates in the general triclinic
coordinates and then converting to coordinates in the restricted
triclinic basis.  The transformation is given by the following equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{x} = & \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{a}  & \mathbf{b}  & \mathbf{c} \end{pmatrix} \cdot \frac{1}{V}
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \mathbf{B \times C}  \\
    \mathbf{C \times A}  \\
    \mathbf{A \times B}
  \end{pmatrix} \cdot \mathbf{X}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \sphinxstyleemphasis{V} is the volume of the box (same in either basis), \sphinxstylestrong{X} is
the fractional vector in the general triclinic basis and \sphinxstylestrong{x} is the
resulting vector in the restricted triclinic basis.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Crystallographic general triclinic representation of a simulation box}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic:crystallographic-general-triclinic-representation-of-a-simulation-box}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
General triclinic crystal structures are often defined using three
lattice constants \sphinxstyleemphasis{a}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{b}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{c}, and three angles \(\alpha\),
\(\beta\), and \(\gamma\). Note that in this nomenclature, the
a, b, and c lattice constants are the scalar lengths of the edge
vectors \sphinxstylestrong{a}, \sphinxstylestrong{b}, and \sphinxstylestrong{c} defined above.  The relationship
between these 6 quantities (a, b, c, \(\alpha\), \(\beta\),
\(\gamma\)) and the LAMMPS restricted triclinic box sizes
(lx,ly,lz) = (xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo,yhi\sphinxhyphen{}ylo,zhi\sphinxhyphen{}zlo) and tilt factors (xy,xz,yz) is
as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a   = & {\rm lx} \\
b^2 = &  {\rm ly}^2 +  {\rm xy}^2 \\
c^2 = &  {\rm lz}^2 +  {\rm xz}^2 +  {\rm yz}^2 \\
\cos{\alpha} = & \frac{{\rm xy}*{\rm xz} + {\rm ly}*{\rm yz}}{b*c} \\
\cos{\beta}  = & \frac{\rm xz}{c} \\
\cos{\gamma} = & \frac{\rm xy}{b} \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The inverse relationship can be written as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{\rm lx}   = & a \\
{\rm xy}   = & b \cos{\gamma}  \\
{\rm xz}   = & c \cos{\beta}\\
{\rm ly}^2 = & b^2 - {\rm xy}^2 \\
{\rm yz}   = & \frac{b*c \cos{\alpha} - {\rm xy}*{\rm xz}}{\rm ly} \\
{\rm lz}^2 = & c^2 - {\rm xz}^2 - {\rm yz}^2 \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The values of \sphinxstyleemphasis{a}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{b}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{c}, \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\), and
\(\gamma\) can be printed out or accessed by computes using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{cella}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellb},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cellc}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellalpha}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellbeta}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellgamma}, respectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Output of restricted and general triclinic boxes in a dump file}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic:output-of-restricted-and-general-triclinic-boxes-in-a-dump-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} command doc page, when the BOX
BOUNDS for a snapshot is written to a dump file for a restricted
triclinic box, an orthogonal bounding box which encloses the triclinic
simulation box is output, along with the 3 tilt factors (xy, xz, yz) of
the restricted triclinic box, formatted as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ITEM: BOX BOUNDS xy xz yz
xlo\PYGZus{}bound xhi\PYGZus{}bound xy
ylo\PYGZus{}bound yhi\PYGZus{}bound xz
zlo\PYGZus{}bound zhi\PYGZus{}bound yz
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This bounding box is convenient for many visualization programs and is
calculated from the 9 restricted triclinic box parameters
(xlo,xhi,ylo,yhi,zlo,zhi,xy,xz,yz) as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
xlo\PYGZus{}bound = xlo + MIN(0.0,xy,xz,xy+xz)
xhi\PYGZus{}bound = xhi + MAX(0.0,xy,xz,xy+xz)
ylo\PYGZus{}bound = ylo + MIN(0.0,yz)
yhi\PYGZus{}bound = yhi + MAX(0.0,yz)
zlo\PYGZus{}bound = zlo
zhi\PYGZus{}bound = zhi
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These formulas can be inverted if you need to convert the bounding box
back into the restricted triclinic box parameters, e.g. xlo =
xlo\_bound \sphinxhyphen{} MIN(0.0,xy,xz,xy+xz).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Periodicity and tilt factors for triclinic simulation boxes}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_triclinic:periodicity-and-tilt-factors-for-triclinic-simulation-boxes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There is no requirement that a triclinic box be periodic in any
dimension, though it typically should be in y or z if you wish to
enforce a shift in coordinates due to periodic boundary conditions
across the y or z boundaries.  See the doc page for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command for an explanation of shifted coordinates for
restricted triclinic boxes which are periodic.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some commands that work with triclinic boxes, e.g. the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
deform}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} commands, require
periodicity or non\sphinxhyphen{}shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap boundary conditions in specific
dimensions.  See the command doc pages for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A restricted triclinic box can be defined with all 3 tilt factors =
0.0, so that it is initially orthogonal.  This is necessary if the box
will become non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal, e.g. due to use of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} commands.  Alternatively,
you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change\_box}}}} command to convert a
simulation box from orthogonal to restricted triclinic and vice versa.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Highly tilted restricted triclinic simulation boxes can be
computationally inefficient.  This is due to the large volume of
communication needed to acquire ghost atoms around a processor’s
irregular\sphinxhyphen{}shaped subdomain.  For extreme values of tilt, LAMMPS may
also lose atoms and generate an error.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS will issue a warning if you define a restricted triclinic box
with a tilt factor which skews the box more than half the distance of
the parallel box length, which is the first dimension in the tilt
factor (e.g. x for xz).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, if xlo = 2 and xhi = 12, then the x box length is 10 and
the xy tilt factor should be between \sphinxhyphen{}5 and 5 to avoid the warning.
Similarly, both xz and yz should be between \sphinxhyphen{}(xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo)/2 and
+(yhi\sphinxhyphen{}ylo)/2.  Note that these are not limitations, since if the
maximum tilt factor is 5 (as in this example), then simulations boxes
and atom configurations with tilt = …, \sphinxhyphen{}15, \sphinxhyphen{}5, 5, 15, 25, … are
all geometrically equivalent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the box tilt exceeds this limit during a dynamics run (e.g. due to
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command), then by default the box
is “flipped” to an equivalent shape with a tilt factor within the
warning bounds, and the run continues.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} page for further details.  Box flips that would normally
occur using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} commands can be suppressed using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{flip no} option with
either of the commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One exception to box flipping is if the first dimension in the tilt
factor (e.g. x for xy) is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic.  In that case, the limits on
the tilt factor are not enforced, since flipping the box in that
dimension would not change the atom positions due to non\sphinxhyphen{}periodicity.
In this mode, if the system tilts to large angles, the simulation will
simply become inefficient, due to the highly skewed simulation box.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Thermostats}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_thermostat:thermostats}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermostatting means controlling the temperature of particles in an MD
simulation.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_barostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Barostatting}}}} means controlling
the pressure.  Since the pressure includes a kinetic component due to
particle velocities, both these operations require calculation of the
temperature.  Typically a target temperature (T) and/or pressure (P)
is specified by the user, and the thermostat or barostat attempts to
equilibrate the system to the requested T and/or P.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermostatting in LAMMPS is performed by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}, or in one
case by a pair style.  Several thermostatting fixes are available:
Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover (nvt), Berendsen, CSVR, Langevin, and direct rescaling
(temp/rescale).  Dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) thermostatting
can be invoked via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/tstat} pair style:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/asphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sllod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sllod}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/berendsen}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_csvr::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/csvr}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_dpd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style dpd/tstat}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix nvt}}}} only thermostats the translational velocity of
particles.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sllod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix nvt/sllod}}}} also does this,
except that it subtracts out a velocity bias due to a deforming box
and integrates the SLLOD equations of motion.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_nemd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto
nemd}}}} page for further details.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix nvt/sphere}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/asphere}}}}
thermostat not only translation velocities but also rotational
velocities for spherical and aspherical particles.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A recent (2017) book by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat:daivis-thermostat}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Daivis and Todd)}}}}
discusses use of the SLLOD method and non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (NEMD)
thermostatting generally, for both simple and complex fluids,
e.g. molecular systems.  The latter can be tricky to do correctly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
DPD thermostatting alters pairwise interactions in a manner analogous
to the per\sphinxhyphen{}particle thermostatting of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any of the thermostatting fixes can be instructed to use custom
temperature computes that remove bias which has two effects: first,
the current calculated temperature, which is compared to the requested
target temperature, is calculated with the velocity bias removed;
second, the thermostat adjusts only the thermal temperature component
of the particle’s velocities, which are the velocities with the bias
removed.  The removed bias is then added back to the adjusted
velocities.  See the doc pages for the individual fixes and for the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} command for instructions on how to
assign a temperature compute to a thermostatting fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, you can apply a thermostat only to atoms in a spatial
region by using it in conjunction with {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/region}}}}.  Or you can apply a thermostat to only the x
and z components of velocity by using it with {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_partial::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
temp/partial}}}}.  Of you could thermostat only
the thermal temperature of a streaming flow of particles without
affecting the streaming velocity, by using {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_profile::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/profile}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is a list of custom temperature computes that can be used like
that:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/asphere command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/body command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/chunk command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_com::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/com command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/deform command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_partial::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/partial command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_profile::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/profile command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_ramp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/ramp command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/region command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_rotate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/rotate command}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/sphere command}}}}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Only the nvt fixes perform time integration, meaning they update
the velocities and positions of particles due to forces and velocities
respectively.  The other thermostat fixes only adjust velocities; they
do NOT perform time integration updates.  Thus they should be used in
conjunction with a constant NVE integration fix such as these:
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/asphere}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermodynamic output, which can be setup via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command, often includes temperature values.  As
explained on the page for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}
command, the default temperature is setup by the thermo command
itself.  It is NOT the temperature associated with any thermostatting
fix you have defined or with any compute you have defined that
calculates a temperature.  The doc pages for the thermostatting fixes
explain the ID of the temperature compute they create.  Thus if you
want to view these temperatures, you need to specify them explicitly
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command.  Or you can
use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command to re\sphinxhyphen{}define what
temperature compute is used for default thermodynamic output.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_thermostat:daivis-thermostat}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Daivis and Todd)} Daivis and Todd, Nonequilibrium Molecular Dynamics (book),
Cambridge University Press, \sphinxurl{https://doi.org/10.1017/9781139017848}, (2017).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Barostats}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_barostat:barostats}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_barostat::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Barostatting means controlling the pressure in an MD simulation.
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Thermostatting}}}} means controlling the
temperature of the particles.  Since the pressure includes a kinetic
component due to particle velocities, both these operations require
calculation of the temperature.  Typically a target temperature (T)
and/or pressure (P) is specified by the user, and the thermostat or
barostat attempts to equilibrate the system to the requested T and/or
P.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Barostatting in LAMMPS is performed by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}.  Two
barostatting methods are currently available: Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover (npt and
nph) and Berendsen:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt/asphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_press_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix press/berendsen}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} commands include a Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat
and barostat.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix nph}}}} is just a Nose/Hoover barostat;
it does no thermostatting.  Both {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_press_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix press/berendsen}}}} can be used in conjunction
with any of the thermostatting fixes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermostats}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph}}}} only use translational motion of the
particles in computing T and P and performing thermo/barostatting.
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix npt/sphere}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt/asphere}}}} thermo/barostat using not only
translation velocities but also rotational velocities for spherical
and aspherical particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the barostatting fixes use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} compute to calculate a current
pressure.  By default, this compute is created with a simple {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}} (see the last argument of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} command), which is used to calculated
the kinetic component of the pressure.  The barostatting fixes can
also use temperature computes that remove bias for the purpose of
computing the kinetic component which contributes to the current
pressure.  See the doc pages for the individual fixes and for the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} command for instructions on how to assign
a temperature or pressure compute to a barostatting fix.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As with the thermostats, the Nose/Hoover methods ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph}}}}) perform time integration.
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_press_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix press/berendsen}}}} does NOT, so it should
be used with one of the constant NVE fixes or with one of the NVT
fixes.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermodynamic output, which can be setup via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command, often includes pressure
values.  As explained on the page for the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command, the default pressure is
setup by the thermo command itself.  It is NOT the pressure associated
with any barostatting fix you have defined or with any compute you
have defined that calculates a pressure.  The doc pages for the
barostatting fixes explain the ID of the pressure compute they create.
Thus if you want to view these pressures, you need to specify them
explicitly via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command.
Or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command to
re\sphinxhyphen{}define what pressure compute is used for default thermodynamic
output.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Walls}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_walls:walls}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_walls::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Walls in an MD simulation are typically used to bound particle motion,
i.e. to serve as a boundary condition.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Walls in LAMMPS can be of rough (made of particles) or idealized
surfaces.  Ideal walls can be smooth, generating forces only in the
normal direction, or frictional, generating forces also in the
tangential direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rough walls, built of particles, can be created in various ways.  The
particles themselves can be generated like any other particle, via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} commands,
or read in via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Their motion can be constrained by many different commands, so that
they do not move at all, move together as a group at constant velocity
or in response to a net force acting on them, move in a prescribed
fashion (e.g. rotate around a point), etc.  Note that if a time
integration fix like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}
is not used with the group that contains wall particles, their
positions and velocities will not be updated.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_aveforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix aveforce}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} set force on particles to average value, so they move together

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} set force on particles to a value, e.g. 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_freeze::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix freeze}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} freeze particles for use as granular walls

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_noforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/noforce}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} advect particles by their velocity, but without force

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_move::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix move}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} prescribe motion of particles by a linear velocity, oscillation, rotation, variable

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_move::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix move}}}} command offers the most generality, since
the motion of individual particles can be specified with
