{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} formula which depends on time and/or the
particle position.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For rough walls, it may be useful to turn off pairwise interactions
between wall particles via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rough walls can also be created by specifying frozen particles that do
not move and do not interact with mobile particles, and then tethering
other particles to the fixed particles, via a {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond}}}}.
The bonded particles do interact with other mobile particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Idealized walls can be specified via several fix commands.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix wall/gran}}}} creates frictional walls for use with
granular particles; all the other commands create smooth walls.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_reflect::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/reflect}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} reflective flat walls

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/lj93}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} flat walls, with Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones 9/3 potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/lj126}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} flat walls, with Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones 12/6 potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/colloid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} flat walls, with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_colloid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style colloid}}}} potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/harmonic}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} flat walls, with repulsive harmonic spring potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/morse}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} flat walls, with Morse potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/region}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} use region surface as wall

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/gran}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} flat or curved walls with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style granular}}}} potential

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj93}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj126}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{colloid}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse} styles all
allow the flat walls to move with a constant velocity, or oscillate in
time.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/region}}}} command offers the
most generality, since the region surface is treated as a wall, and
the geometry of the region can be a simple primitive volume (e.g. a
sphere, or cube, or plane), or a complex volume made from the union
and intersection of primitive volumes.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Regions}}}} can also
specify a volume “interior” or “exterior” to the specified primitive
shape or \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersection}.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Regions}}}} can also be
“dynamic” meaning they move with constant velocity, oscillate, or
rotate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The only frictional idealized walls currently in LAMMPS are flat or
curved surfaces specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/gran}}}}
command.  At some point we plan to allow region surfaces to be used as
frictional walls, as well as triangulated surfaces.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{NEMD simulations}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_nemd:nemd-simulations}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_nemd::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium molecular dynamics or NEMD simulations are typically
used to measure a fluid’s rheological properties such as viscosity.
In LAMMPS, such simulations can be performed by first setting up a
non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal simulation box (see the preceding Howto section).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A shear strain can be applied to the simulation box at a desired
strain rate by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sllod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sllod}}}} command can be used to thermostat
the sheared fluid and integrate the SLLOD equations of motion for the
system.  Fix nvt/sllod uses {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/deform}}}} to compute a thermal temperature
by subtracting out the streaming velocity of the shearing atoms.  The
velocity profile or other properties of the fluid can be monitored via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A recent (2017) book by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_nemd:daivis-nemd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Daivis and Todd)}}}}
discusses use of the SLLOD method and non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (NEMD)
thermostatting generally, for both simple and complex fluids,
e.g. molecular systems.  The latter can be tricky to do correctly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed in the previous section on non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal simulation
boxes, the amount of tilt or skew that can be applied is limited by
LAMMPS for computational efficiency to be 1/2 of the parallel box
length.  However, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} can continuously strain
a box by an arbitrary amount.  As discussed in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command, when the tilt value reaches a limit,
the box is flipped to the opposite limit which is an equivalent tiling
of periodic space.  The strain rate can then continue to change as
before.  In a long NEMD simulation these box re\sphinxhyphen{}shaping events may
occur many times.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a NEMD simulation, the “remap” option of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} should be set to “remap v”, since that is what
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sllod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sllod}}}} assumes to generate a velocity
profile consistent with the applied shear strain rate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An alternative method for calculating viscosities is provided via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscosity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscosity}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NEMD simulations can also be used to measure transport properties of a fluid
through a pore or channel. Simulations of steady\sphinxhyphen{}state flow can be performed
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_flow_gauss::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix flow/gauss}}}} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_nemd:daivis-nemd}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Daivis and Todd)} Daivis and Todd, Nonequilibrium Molecular Dynamics (book),
Cambridge University Press, \sphinxurl{https://doi.org/10.1017/9781139017848}, (2017).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion settings}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_dispersion:long-range-dispersion-settings}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_dispersion::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The PPPM method computes interactions by splitting the pair potential
into two parts, one of which is computed in a normal pairwise fashion,
the so\sphinxhyphen{}called real\sphinxhyphen{}space part, and one of which is computed using the
Fourier transform, the so called reciprocal\sphinxhyphen{}space or kspace part.  For
both parts, the potential is not computed exactly but is approximated.
Thus, there is an error in both parts of the computation, the
real\sphinxhyphen{}space and the kspace error. The just mentioned facts are true
both for the PPPM for Coulomb as well as dispersion interactions. The
deciding difference \sphinxhyphen{} and also the reason why the parameters for
pppm/disp have to be selected with more care \sphinxhyphen{} is the impact of the
errors on the results: The kspace error of the PPPM for Coulomb and
dispersion interaction and the real\sphinxhyphen{}space error of the PPPM for
Coulomb interaction have the character of noise. In contrast, the
real\sphinxhyphen{}space error of the PPPM for dispersion has a clear physical
interpretation: the underprediction of cohesion. As a consequence, the
real\sphinxhyphen{}space error has a much stronger effect than the kspace error on
simulation results for pppm/disp.  Parameters must thus be chosen in a
way that this error is much smaller than the kspace error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using pppm/disp and not making any specifications on the PPPM
parameters via the kspace modify command, parameters will be tuned
such that the real\sphinxhyphen{}space error and the kspace error are equal.  This
will result in simulations that are either inaccurate or slow, both of
which is not desirable. For selecting parameters for the pppm/disp
that provide fast and accurate simulations, there are two approaches,
which both have their up\sphinxhyphen{} and downsides.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first approach is to set desired real\sphinxhyphen{}space an kspace accuracies
via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify force/disp/real} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify
force/disp/kspace} commands. Note that the accuracies have to be
specified in force units and are thus dependent on the chosen unit
settings. For real units, 0.0001 and 0.002 seem to provide reasonable
accurate and efficient computations for the real\sphinxhyphen{}space and kspace
accuracies.  0.002 and 0.05 work well for most systems using lj
units. PPPM parameters will be generated based on the desired
accuracies. The upside of this approach is that it usually provides a
good set of parameters and will work for both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify diff
ad} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify diff ik} options.  The downside of the method
is that setting the PPPM parameters will take some time during the
initialization of the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second approach is to set the parameters for the pppm/disp
explicitly using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify mesh/disp}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify
order/disp}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify gewald/disp} commands. This approach
requires a more experienced user who understands well the impact of
the choice of parameters on the simulation accuracy and
performance. This approach provides a fast initialization of the
simulation. However, it is sensitive to errors: A combination of
parameters that will perform well for one system might result in
far\sphinxhyphen{}from\sphinxhyphen{}optimal conditions for other simulations. For example,
parameters that provide accurate and fast computations for
all\sphinxhyphen{}atomistic force fields can provide insufficient accuracy or
united\sphinxhyphen{}atomistic force fields (which is related to that the latter
typically have larger dispersion coefficients).

\sphinxAtStartPar
To avoid inaccurate or inefficient simulations, the pppm/disp stops
simulations with an error message if no action is taken to control the
PPPM parameters. If the automatic parameter generation is desired and
real\sphinxhyphen{}space and kspace accuracies are desired to be equal, this error
message can be suppressed using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify disp/auto yes}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A reasonable approach that combines the upsides of both methods is to
make the first run using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify force/disp/real} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify force/disp/kspace} commands, write down the PPPM
parameters from the output, and specify these parameters using the
second approach in subsequent runs (which have the same composition,
force field, and approximately the same volume).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Concerning the performance of the pppm/disp there are two more things
to consider. The first is that when using the pppm/disp, the cutoff
parameter does no longer affect the accuracy of the simulation
(subject to that gewald/disp is adjusted when changing the cutoff).
The performance can thus be increased by examining different values
for the cutoff parameter. A lower bound for the cutoff is only set by
the truncation error of the repulsive term of pair potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second is that the mixing rule of the pair style has an impact on
the computation time when using the pppm/disp. Fastest computations
are achieved when using the geometric mixing rule. Using the
arithmetic mixing rule substantially increases the computational cost.
The computational overhead can be reduced using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify
mix/disp geom} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify splittol} commands. The first
command simply enforces geometric mixing of the dispersion
coefficients in kspace computations.  This introduces some error in
the computations but will also significantly speed\sphinxhyphen{}up the
simulations. The second keyword sets the accuracy with which the
dispersion coefficients are approximated using a matrix factorization
approach.  This may result in better accuracy then using the first
command, but will usually also not provide an equally good increase of
efficiency.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, pppm/disp can also be used when no mixing rules apply.
This can be achieved using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_modify mix/disp none} command.
Note that the code does not check automatically whether any mixing
rule is fulfilled. If mixing rules do not apply, the user will have
to specify this command explicitly.


\section{Analysis howto}
\label{\detokenize{Howto:analysis-howto}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Output from LAMMPS (thermo, dumps, computes, fixes, variables)}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:output-from-lammps-thermo-dumps-computes-fixes-variables}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are four basic forms of LAMMPS output:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Thermodynamic output}}}}, which is a list of
quantities printed every few timesteps to the screen and logfile.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Dump files}}}}, which contain snapshots of atoms and various
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values and are written at a specified frequency.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Certain fixes can output user\sphinxhyphen{}specified quantities to files:
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} for time averaging,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} for spatial or other averaging, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} for single\sphinxhyphen{}line output of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}}.  Fix print can also output to the screen.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Restart files}}}}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A simulation prints one set of thermodynamic output and (optionally)
restart files.  It can generate any number of dump files and fix
output files, depending on what {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}
commands you specify.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed below, LAMMPS gives you a variety of ways to determine
what quantities are calculated and printed when the thermodynamics,
dump, or fix commands listed above perform output.  Throughout this
discussion, note that users can also {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add their own computes and
fixes to LAMMPS}}}} which can generate values that can then be
output with these commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following subsections discuss different LAMMPS commands related
to output and the kind of data they operate on and produce:
\begin{itemize}
\item {}

\subsubsection{Global/per\sphinxhyphen{}atom/local/per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:global-per-atom-local-per-grid-data}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:global}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Various output\sphinxhyphen{}related commands work with four different “styles” of
data: global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid.  A global datum is one or
more system\sphinxhyphen{}wide values, e.g. the temperature of the system.  A
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom datum is one or more values per atom, e.g. the kinetic energy
of each atom.  Local datums are calculated by each processor based on
the atoms it owns, and there may be zero or more per atom, e.g. a list
of bond distances.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A per\sphinxhyphen{}grid datum is one or more values per grid cell, for a grid which
overlays the simulation domain.  Similar to atoms and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data,
the grid cells and the data they store are distributed across
processors; each processor owns the grid cells whose center points
fall within its subdomain.


\subsubsection{Scalar/vector/array data}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:scalar-vector-array-data}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:scalar}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid datums can come in three
“kinds”: a single scalar value, a vector of values, or a 2d array of
values.  More specifically these are the valid kinds for each style:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
global scalar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
global vector

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
global array

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
local vector

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
local array

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
per\sphinxhyphen{}grid vector

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
per\sphinxhyphen{}grid array

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector means a single value per atom; the “vector” is the
length of the number of atoms.  A per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array means multiple values
per atom.  Similarly a local vector or array means one or multiple
values per entity (e.g. per bond in the system).  And a per\sphinxhyphen{}grid
vector or array means one or multiple values per grid cell.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The doc page for a compute or fix or variable that generates data will
specify both the styles and kinds of data it produces, e.g. a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
vector.  Note that a compute or fix may generate multiple styles and
kinds of output.  However, for per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data only a vector or array is
output, never both.  Likewise for per\sphinxhyphen{}local and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data.  An
example of a fix which generates multiple styles and kinds of data is
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_mdi_qm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix mdi/qm}}}} command.  It outputs a global
scalar, global vector, and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array for the quantum mechanical
energy and virial of the system and forces on each atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By contrast, different variable styles generate only a single kind of
data: a global scalar for an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, global vector for a
vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, and a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector for an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When data is accessed by another command, as in many of the output
commands discussed below, it can be referenced via the following
bracket notation, where ID in this case is the ID of a compute.  The
leading “c\_” would be replaced by “f\_” for a fix, or “v\_” for a
variable (and ID would be the name of the variable):


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
entire scalar, vector, or array
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID{[}I{]}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
one element of vector, one column of array
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID{[}I{]}{[}J{]}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
one element of array
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that using one bracket reduces the dimension of the data once
(vector \sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{} scalar, array \sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{} vector).  Using two brackets reduces the
dimension twice (array \sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{} scalar).  Thus a command that uses scalar
values as input can also conceptually operate on an element of a
vector or array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Per\sphinxhyphen{}grid vectors or arrays are accessed similarly, except that the ID
for the compute or fix includes a grid name and a data name.  This is
because a fix or compute can create multiple grids (of different
sizes) and multiple sets of data (for each grid).  The fix or compute
defines names for each grid and for each data set, so that all of them
can be accessed by other commands.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto grid}}}} doc page for more details.


\subsubsection{Disambiguation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:disambiguation}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When a compute or fix produces data in multiple styles, e.g. global
and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, a reference to the data can sometimes be ambiguous.
Usually the context in which the input script references the data
determines which style is meant.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, if a compute outputs a global vector and a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
array, an element of the global vector will be accessed by using
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{c\_ID{[}I{]}}} in {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}}, while a
column of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array will be accessed by using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{c\_ID{[}I{]}}} in
a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, if a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} references
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{c\_ID{[}I{]}}}, then it could be intended to refer to a single element of
the global vector or a column of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array.  The doc page for
any command that has a potential ambiguity (variables are the most
common) will explain how to resolve the ambiguity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables references per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data if it
exists.  If access to an element of a global vector is needed (as in
this example), an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable which references the value can
be defined and used in the atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable formula instead.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}} can only
reference global data from a compute or fix.  But you can indirectly
access per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data as follows.  The reference \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{c\_ID{[}245{]}{[}2{]}}} for
the ID of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_displace_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute displace/atom}}}}
command, refers to the y\sphinxhyphen{}component of displacement for the atom with
ID 245.  While you cannot use that reference directly in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command, you can use it an
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable formula, and then reference the variable in
thermodynamic output.


\subsubsection{Thermodynamic output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:thermodynamic-output}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:thermo}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The frequency and format of thermodynamic output is set by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} commands.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command also specifies what values are calculated and
written out.  Pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined keywords can be specified (e.g. press, etotal,
etc).  Three additional kinds of keywords can also be specified (c\_ID,
f\_ID, v\_name), where a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} provides the value to be output.  In each
case, the compute, fix, or variable must generate global values for
input to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that thermodynamic output values can be “extensive” or
“intensive”.  The former scale with the number of atoms in the system
(e.g. total energy), the latter do not (e.g. temperature).  The
setting for {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify norm}}}} determines whether
extensive quantities are normalized or not.  Computes and fixes
produce either extensive or intensive values; see their individual doc
pages for details.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}} produce only
intensive values; you can include a division by “natoms” in the
formula if desired, to make an extensive calculation produce an
intensive result.


\subsubsection{Dump file output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:dump-file-output}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:dump}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dump file output is specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify}}}} commands.  There are several
pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined formats (dump atom, dump xtc, etc).

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is also a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} format where the user
specifies what values are output with each atom.  Pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined atom
attributes can be specified (id, x, fx, etc).  Three additional kinds
of keywords can also be specified (c\_ID, f\_ID, v\_name), where a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} provides the values to be output.  In each case, the
compute, fix, or variable must generate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values for input to
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is also a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}} format where the user specifies
what local values to output.  A pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined index keyword can be
specified to enumerate the local values.  Two additional kinds of
keywords can also be specified (c\_ID, f\_ID), where a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}
provides the values to be output.  In each case, the compute or fix
must generate local values for input to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is also a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid}}}} format where the user
specifies what per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values to output from computes or fixes that
generate per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data.


\subsubsection{Fixes that write output files}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:fixes-that-write-output-files}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:fixoutput}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Several fixes take various quantities as input and can write output
files: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_histo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/histo}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_correlate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
ave/correlate}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} command enables direct output
to a file and/or time\sphinxhyphen{}averaging of global scalars or vectors.  The
user specifies one or more quantities as input.  These can be global
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} values, global {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} values, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} of any style except the atom style which
produces per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values.  Since a variable can refer to keywords used
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command (like temp or
press) and individual per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values, a wide variety of quantities
can be time averaged and/or output in this way.  If the inputs are one
or more scalar values, then the fix generate a global scalar or vector
of output.  If the inputs are one or more vector values, then the fix
generates a global vector or array of output.  The time\sphinxhyphen{}averaged
output of this fix can also be used as input to other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command enables direct output
to a file of chunk\sphinxhyphen{}averaged per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities like those output in
dump files.  Chunks can represent spatial bins or other collections of
atoms, e.g. individual molecules.  The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities can be atom
density (mass or number) or atom attributes such as position,
velocity, force.  They can also be per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities calculated by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}, by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}, or by an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  The chunk\sphinxhyphen{}averaged output of this fix is
global and can also be used as input to other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/grid}}}} command can also
average the same per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities within spatial bins, but it does
this for a distributed grid whose grid cells are owned by different
processors.  It outputs per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data, not global data, so it is more
efficient for large numbers of averaging bins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_histo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/histo}}}} command enables direct output
to a file of histogrammed quantities, which can be global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
or local quantities.  The histogram output of this fix can also be
used as input to other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_correlate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/correlate}}}} command enables direct
output to a file of time\sphinxhyphen{}correlated quantities, which can be global
values.  The correlation matrix output of this fix can also be used as
input to other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} command can generate a line of output
written to the screen and log file or to a separate file, periodically
during a running simulation.  The line can contain one or more
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} values for any style variable except the
vector or atom styles).  As explained above, variables themselves can
contain references to global values generated by {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic
keywords}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}, or other {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}}, or to per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values
for a specific atom.  Thus the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} command is
a means to output a wide variety of quantities separate from normal
thermodynamic or dump file output.


\subsubsection{Computes that process output quantities}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:computes-that-process-output-quantities}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:computeoutput}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
reduce/region}}}} commands take one or more per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or
local vector quantities as inputs and “reduce” them (sum, min, max,
ave) to scalar quantities.  These are produced as output values which
can be used as input to other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_slice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute slice}}}} command take one or more
global vector or array quantities as inputs and extracts a subset of
their values to create a new vector or array.  These are produced as
output values which can be used as input to other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}} command takes
a list of one or more pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined atom attributes (id, x, fx, etc) and
stores the values in a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array.  These are produced
as output values which can be used as input to other output commands.
The list of atom attributes is the same as for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/local}}}} command
takes a list of one or more pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined local attributes (bond info,
angle info, etc) and stores the values in a local vector or array.
These are produced as output values which can be used as input to
other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/grid}}}} command takes
a list of one or more pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined per\sphinxhyphen{}grid attributes (id, grid cell
coords, etc) and stores the values in a per\sphinxhyphen{}grid vector or array.
These are produced as output values which can be used as input to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/chunk}}}} command
takes a list of one or more pre\sphinxhyphen{}defined chunk attributes (id, count,
coords for spatial bins) and stores the values in a global vector or
array.  These are produced as output values which can be used as input
to other output commands.


\subsubsection{Fixes that process output quantities}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:fixes-that-process-output-quantities}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:fixprocoutput}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_vector::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix vector}}}} command can create global vectors as
output from global scalars as input, accumulating them one element at
a time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/atom}}}} command performs time\sphinxhyphen{}averaging
of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors.  The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities can be atom attributes
such as position, velocity, force.  They can also be per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities calculated by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}, by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}, or by an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  The
time\sphinxhyphen{}averaged per\sphinxhyphen{}atom output of this fix can be used as input to
other output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_store_state::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix store/state}}}} command can archive one
or more per\sphinxhyphen{}atom attributes at a particular time, so that the old
values can be used in a future calculation or output.  The list of
atom attributes is the same as for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}}
command, including per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities calculated by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}, by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}, or by an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  The output of this fix can be used as input to other
output commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/grid}}}} command performs time\sphinxhyphen{}averaging
of either per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data it performs averaging for the atoms within each grid
cell, similar to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command when
its chunks are defined as regular 2d or 3d bins.  The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities can be atom density (mass or number) or atom attributes
such as position, velocity, force.  They can also be per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities calculated by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}, by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}, or by an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The chief difference between the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/grid}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} commands when used in this
context is that the former uses a distributed grid, while the latter
uses a global grid.  Distributed means that each processor owns the
subset of grid cells within its subdomain.  Global means that each
processor owns a copy of the entire grid.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/grid}}}} command is thus more efficient for large grids.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/grid}}}} command
takes inputs for grid data produced by other computes or fixes and
averages the values for each grid point over time.


\subsubsection{Computes that generate values to output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:computes-that-generate-values-to-output}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:compute}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Every {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} in LAMMPS produces either global or
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values.  The values can be scalars or
vectors or arrays of data.  These values can be output using the other
commands described in this section.  The page for each compute command
describes what it produces.  Computes that produce per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local
or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values have the word “atom” or “local” or “grid as the
last word in their style name.  Computes without the word “atom” or
“local” or “grid” produce global values.


\subsubsection{Fixes that generate values to output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:fixes-that-generate-values-to-output}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:fix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}} in LAMMPS produces either global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
or local or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values which can be accessed by other commands.
The values can be scalars or vectors or arrays of data.  These values
can be output using the other commands described in this section.  The
page for each fix command tells whether it produces any output
quantities and describes them.


\subsubsection{Variables that generate values to output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:variables-that-generate-values-to-output}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:variable}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Variables}}}} defined in an input script can store one or
more strings.  But equal\sphinxhyphen{}style, vector\sphinxhyphen{}style, and atom\sphinxhyphen{}style or
atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables generate a global scalar value, global vector
or values, or a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, respectively, when accessed.  The
formulas used to define these variables can contain references to the
thermodynamic keywords and to global and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data generated by
computes, fixes, and other variables.  The values generated by
variables can be used as input to and thus output by the other
commands described in this section.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Per\sphinxhyphen{}grid variables have not (yet) been implemented.


\subsubsection{Summary table of output options and data flow between commands}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:summary-table-of-output-options-and-data-flow-between-commands}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_output:table}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This table summarizes the various commands that can be used for
generating output from LAMMPS.  Each command produces output data of
some kind and/or writes data to a file.  Most of the commands can take
data from other commands as input.  Thus you can link many of these
commands together in pipeline form, where data produced by one command
is used as input to another command and eventually written to the
screen or to a file.  Note that to hook two commands together the
output and input data types must match, e.g. global/per\sphinxhyphen{}atom/local
data and scalar/vector/array data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that, as described above, when a command takes a scalar as
input, that could also be an element of a vector or array.  Likewise a
vector input could be a column of an array.

\subsection{Use chunks to calculate system properties}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_chunk:use-chunks-to-calculate-system-properties}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, “chunks” are collections of atoms, as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns
each atom to a chunk ID (or to no chunk at all).  The number of chunks
and the assignment of chunk IDs to atoms can be static or change over
time.  Examples of “chunks” are molecules or spatial bins or atoms
with similar values (e.g. coordination number or potential energy).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom chunk IDs can be used as input to two other kinds of
commands, to calculate various properties of a system:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
any of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute */chunk}}}} commands

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here a brief overview for each of the 4 kinds of chunk\sphinxhyphen{}related commands
is provided.  Then some examples are given of how to compute different
properties with chunk commands.


\subsubsection{Compute chunk/atom command:}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_chunk:compute-chunk-atom-command}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute can assign atoms to chunks of various styles.  Only atoms
in the specified group and optional specified region are assigned to a
chunk.  Here are some possible chunk definitions:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms in same molecule
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = molecule ID
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms of same atom type
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = atom type
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
all atoms with same atom property (charge, radius, etc)
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = output of compute property/atom
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms in same cluster
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = output of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute cluster/atom}}}} command
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms in same spatial bin
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = bin ID
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms in same rigid body
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = molecule ID used to define rigid bodies
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms with similar potential energy
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = output of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe/atom}}}}
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms with same local defect structure
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk ID = output of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_centro_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centro/atom}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_coord_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute coord/atom}}}} command
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that chunk IDs are integer values, so for atom properties or
computes that produce a floating point value, they will be truncated
to an integer.  You could also use the compute in a variable that
scales the floating point value to spread it across multiple integers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Spatial bins can be of various kinds, e.g. 1d bins = slabs, 2d bins =
pencils, 3d bins = boxes, spherical bins, cylindrical bins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute also calculates the number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk}, which is
used by other commands to tally per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk data.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} can be a
static value or change over time (e.g. the number of clusters).  The
chunk ID for an individual atom can also be static (e.g. a molecule
ID), or dynamic (e.g. what spatial bin an atom is in as it moves).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this compute allows the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom output of other
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} to be used to define chunk IDs for each
atom.  This means you can write your own compute or fix to output a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantity to use as chunk ID.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}}
doc pages for info on how to do this.  You can also define a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{per\sphinxhyphen{}atom variable}}}} in the input script that uses a formula to
generate a chunk ID for each atom.


\subsubsection{Fix ave/chunk command:}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_chunk:fix-ave-chunk-command}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix takes the ID of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command as input.  For each chunk,
it then sums one or more specified per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values over the atoms in
each chunk.  The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can be any atom property, such as
velocity, force, charge, potential energy, kinetic energy, stress,
etc.  Additional keywords are defined for per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk properties like
density and temperature.  More generally any per\sphinxhyphen{}atom value generated
by other {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{per\sphinxhyphen{}atom variables}}}}, can be summed over atoms in each chunk.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to other averaging fixes, this fix allows the summed per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk
values to be time\sphinxhyphen{}averaged in various ways, and output to a file.  The
fix produces a global array as output with one row of values per
chunk.


\subsubsection{Compute */chunk commands:}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_chunk:compute-chunk-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following computes operate on chunks of atoms to produce per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk
values.  Any compute whose style name ends in “/chunk” is in this
category:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_com_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute com/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_gyration_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute gyration/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute inertia/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_vcm_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute torque/chunk}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_vcm_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute vcm/chunk}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
They each take the ID of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command as input.  As their names
indicate, they calculate the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass, radius of gyration,
moments of inertia, mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement, temperature, torque,
and velocity of center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass for each chunk of atoms.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/chunk}}}} command can tally the
count of atoms in each chunk and extract other per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk properties.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The reason these various calculations are not part of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk command}}}}, is that each requires a more
complicated operation than simply summing and averaging over per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
values in each chunk.  For example, many of them require calculation
of a center of mass, which requires summing mass*position over the
atoms and then dividing by summed mass.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of these computes produce a global vector or global array as
output, with one or more values per chunk.  The output can be used in
various ways:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As input to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} command, which can
write the values to a file and optionally time average them.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As input to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_histo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/histo}}}} command to
histogram values across chunks.  E.g. a histogram of cluster sizes or
molecule diffusion rates.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As input to special functions of {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}}, like sum() and max() and ave().  E.g. to
find the largest cluster or fastest diffusing molecule or average
radius\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}gyration of a set of molecules (chunks).

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Other chunk commands:}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_chunk:other-chunk-commands}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/spread/atom}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce/chunk}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/spread/atom}}}} command
spreads per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values to each atom in the chunk, producing per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
values as its output.  This can be useful for outputting per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk
values to a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump file}}}}.  Or for using an atom’s
associated chunk value in an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.  Or
as input to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command to
spatially average per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values calculated by a per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce/chunk}}}} command reduces a
peratom value across the atoms in each chunk to produce a value per
chunk.  When used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/spread/atom}}}} command it can
create peratom values that induce a new set of chunks with a second
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.


\subsubsection{Example calculations with chunks}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_chunk:example-calculations-with-chunks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are examples using chunk commands to calculate various
properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average velocity in each of 1000 2d spatial bins:

\end{enumerate}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduced}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
2. Temperature in each spatial bin, after subtracting a flow
velocity:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
