\subsection{Using distributed grids}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_grid:using-distributed-grids}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_grid::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS has internal capabilities to create uniformly spaced grids
which overlay the simulation domain.  For 2d and 3d simulations these
are 2d and 3d grids respectively.  Conceptually a grid can be thought
of as a collection of grid cells.  Each grid cell can store one or
more values (data).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The grid cells and data they store are distributed across processors.
Each processor owns the grid cells (and data) whose center points lie
within the spatial subdomain of the processor.  If needed for its
computations, a processor may also store ghost grid cells with their
data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Distributed grids can overlay orthogonal or triclinic simulation
boxes; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} doc page for
an explanation of the latter.  For a triclinic box, the grid cell
shape conforms to the shape of the simulation domain,
e.g. parallelograms instead of rectangles in 2d.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the box size or shape changes during a simulation, the grid changes
with it, so that it always overlays the entire simulation domain.  For
non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic dimensions, the grid size in that dimension matches the
box size, as set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command for fixed
or shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing is invoked by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}} commands, then the subdomain owned
by a processor can change which may also change which grid cells they
own.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Post\sphinxhyphen{}processing and visualization of grid cell data can be enabled by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid/vtk}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} commands.  The latter has an optional
\sphinxstyleemphasis{grid} keyword.  The \sphinxhref{https://www.ovito.org}{OVITO visualization tool} also plans (as of Nov 2022) to add support
for visualizing grid cell data (along with atoms) using {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump
grid}}}} output files as input.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For developers, distributed grids are implemented within the code via
two classes: Grid2d and Grid3d.  These partition the grid across
processors and have methods which allow forward and reverse
communication of ghost grid data as well as load balancing.  If you
write a new compute or fix which needs a distributed grid, these are
the classes to look at.  A new pair style could use a distributed
grid by having a fix define it.  Please see the section on
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{using distributed grids within style classes}}}}
for a detailed description.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the commands which currently define or use distributed
grids:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ttm/grid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} store electron temperature on grid

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/grid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} time average per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/grid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} generate grid IDs and coords

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} output per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values in LAMMPS format

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid/vtk}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} output per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values in VTK format

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image grid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} include colored grid in output images

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style amoeba}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} FFT grids

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}} (and variants) \sphinxhyphen{} FFT grids

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style msm}}}} (and variants) \sphinxhyphen{} MSM grids

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The grids used by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} can not be
referenced by an input script.  However the grids and data created and
used by the other commands can be.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A compute or fix command may create one or more grids (of different
sizes).  Each grid can store one or more data fields.  A data field
can be a single value per grid point (per\sphinxhyphen{}grid vector) or multiple
values per grid point (per\sphinxhyphen{}grid array).  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page for an explanation of how per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data can
be generated by some commands and used by other commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A command accesses grid data from a compute or fix using a \sphinxstyleemphasis{grid
reference} with the following syntax:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID:gname:dname

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID:gname:dname{[}I{]}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
f\_ID:gname:dname

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
f\_ID:gname:dname{[}I{]}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The prefix “c\_” or “f\_” refers to the ID of the compute or fix; gname is
the name of the grid, which is assigned by the compute or fix; dname is
the name of the data field, which is also assigned by the compute or
fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the data field is a per\sphinxhyphen{}grid vector (one value per grid point),
then no brackets are used to access the values.  If the data field is
a per\sphinxhyphen{}grid array (multiple values per grid point), then brackets are
used to specify the column I of the array.  I ranges from 1 to Ncol
inclusive, where Ncol is the number of columns in the array and is
defined by the compute or fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, there are no per\sphinxhyphen{}grid variables implemented in LAMMPS.  We
may add this feature at some point.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Calculate temperature}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_temperature:calculate-temperature}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_temperature::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Temperature is computed as kinetic energy divided by some number of
degrees of freedom (and the Boltzmann constant).  Since kinetic energy
is a function of particle velocity, there is often a need to
distinguish between a particle’s advection velocity (due to some
aggregate motion of particles) and its thermal velocity.  The sum of
the two is the particle’s total velocity, but the latter is often what
is wanted to compute a temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS has several options for computing temperatures, any of which
can be used in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermostatting}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_barostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{barostatting}}}}.  These {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute commands}}}} calculate temperature:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/asphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_com::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/com}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/deform}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_partial::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/partial}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_profile::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/profile}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_ramp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/ramp}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/region}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All but the first 3 calculate velocity biases directly (e.g. advection
velocities) that are removed when computing the thermal temperature.
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Compute temp/sphere}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/asphere}}}} compute kinetic energy for
finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles that includes rotational degrees of freedom.
They both allow for velocity biases indirectly, via an optional extra
argument which is another temperature compute that subtracts a
velocity bias.  This allows the translational velocity of spherical or
aspherical particles to be adjusted in prescribed ways.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Calculate elastic constants}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_elastic:calculate-elastic-constants}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_elastic::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Elastic constants characterize the stiffness of a material. The formal
definition is provided by the linear relation that holds between the
stress and strain tensors in the limit of infinitesimal deformation.
In tensor notation, this is expressed as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_{ij} = C_{ijkl} e_{kl}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where
the repeated indices imply summation. \(s_{ij}\) are the elements of the
symmetric stress tensor. \(e_{kl}\) are the elements of the symmetric strain
tensor. \(C_{ijkl}\) are the elements of the fourth rank tensor of elastic
constants. In three dimensions, this tensor has \(3^4=81\) elements. Using
Voigt notation, the tensor can be written as a 6x6 matrix, where \(C_{ij}\)
is now the derivative of \(s_i\) w.r.t. \(e_j\). Because \(s_i\) is itself a
derivative w.r.t. \(e_i\), it follows that \(C_{ij}\) is also symmetric, with at
most \(\frac{7 \times 6}{2}\) = 21 distinct elements.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At zero temperature, it is easy to estimate these derivatives by
deforming the simulation box in one of the six directions using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change\_box}}}} command and measuring the change in the
stress tensor. A general\sphinxhyphen{}purpose script that does this is given in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/ELASTIC}} directory described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Examples}}}}
doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculating elastic constants at finite temperature is more
challenging, because it is necessary to run a simulation that performs
time averages of differential properties. There are at least
3 ways to do this in LAMMPS. The most reliable way to do this is
by exploiting the relationship between elastic constants, stress
fluctuations, and the Born matrix, the second derivatives of energy
w.r.t. strain {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_elastic:ray}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ray)}}}}.
The Born matrix calculation has been enabled by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_born_matrix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute born/matrix}}}} command,
which works for any bonded or non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded potential in LAMMPS.
The most expensive part of the calculation is the sampling of
the stress fluctuations. Several examples of this method are
provided in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/ELASTIC\_T/BORN\_MATRIX}} directory
described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Examples}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A second way is to measure
the change in average stress tensor in an NVT simulations when
the cell volume undergoes a finite deformation. In order to balance
the systematic and statistical errors in this method, the magnitude of
the deformation must be chosen judiciously, and care must be taken to
fully equilibrate the deformed cell before sampling the stress
tensor. An example of this method is provided in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/ELASTIC\_T/DEFORMATION}} directory
described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Examples}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another approach is to sample the triclinic cell fluctuations
that occur in an NPT simulation. This method can also be slow to
converge and requires careful post\sphinxhyphen{}processing {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_elastic:shinoda1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Shinoda)}}}}.
We do not provide an example of this method.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A nice review of the advantages and disadvantages of all of these methods
is provided in the paper by Clavier et al. {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_elastic:clavier}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Clavier)}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_elastic:ray}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Ray)} J. R. Ray and A. Rahman, J Chem Phys, 80, 4423 (1984).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_elastic:shinoda1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Shinoda)} Shinoda, Shiga, and Mikami, Phys Rev B, 69, 134103 (2004).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_elastic:clavier}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Clavier)} G. Clavier, N. Desbiens, E. Bourasseau, V. Lachet, N. Brusselle\sphinxhyphen{}Dupend and B. Rousseau, Mol Sim, 43, 1413 (2017).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Calculate thermal conductivity}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_kappa:calculate-thermal-conductivity}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_kappa::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermal conductivity \(\kappa\) of a material can be measured in at
least 4 ways using various options in LAMMPS.  See the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/KAPPA}}
directory for scripts that implement the 4 methods discussed here for
a simple Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones fluid model.  Also, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_viscosity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto viscosity}}}} page for an analogous discussion
for viscosity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermal conductivity tensor \(\mathbf{\kappa}\) is a measure of the propensity
of a material to transmit heat energy in a diffusive manner as given
by Fourier’s law
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}J = -\kappa \cdot \text{grad}(T)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(J\) is the heat flux in units of energy per area per time and
\(\text{grad}(T)\) is the spatial gradient of temperature.  The thermal
conductivity thus has units of energy per distance per time per degree
K and is often approximated as an isotropic quantity, i.e. as a
scalar.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first method is to setup two thermostatted regions at opposite
ends of a simulation box, or one in the middle and one at the end of a
periodic box.  By holding the two regions at different temperatures
with a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermostatting fix}}}}, the energy added to
the hot region should equal the energy subtracted from the cold region
and be proportional to the heat flux moving between the regions.  See
the papers by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_kappa:howto-ikeshoji}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Ikeshoji and Hafskjold}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_kappa:howto-wirnsberger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wirnsberger et al}}}} for details of this idea.  Note
that thermostatting fixes such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}} store the cumulative energy they
add/subtract.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively, as a second method, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_heat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix heat}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ehex::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ehex}}}} commands can be used in place of thermostats
on each of two regions to add/subtract specified amounts of energy to
both regions.  In both cases, the resulting temperatures of the two
regions can be monitored with the “compute temp/region” command and
the temperature profile of the intermediate region can be monitored
with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_ke_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute ke/atom}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The third method is to perform a reverse non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD simulation
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix thermal/conductivity}}}}
command which implements the rNEMD algorithm of Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe.
Kinetic energy is swapped between atoms in two different layers of the
simulation box.  This induces a temperature gradient between the two
layers which can be monitored with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_ke_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute ke/atom}}}} commands.  The fix tallies the
cumulative energy transfer that it performs.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix thermal/conductivity}}}} command for
details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fourth method is based on the Green\sphinxhyphen{}Kubo (GK) formula which
relates the ensemble average of the auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation of the heat flux
to \(\kappa\).  The heat flux can be calculated from the fluctuations of
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential and kinetic energies and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress tensor in
a steady\sphinxhyphen{}state equilibrated simulation.  This is in contrast to the
two preceding non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium methods, where energy flows continuously
between hot and cold regions of the simulation box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute heat/flux}}}} command can calculate
the needed heat flux and describes how to implement the Green\_Kubo
formalism using additional LAMMPS commands, such as the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_correlate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/correlate}}}} command to calculate the needed
auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation.  See the page for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute heat/flux}}}} command for an example input script
that calculates the thermal conductivity of solid Ar via the GK
formalism.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_kappa:howto-ikeshoji}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Ikeshoji)} Ikeshoji and Hafskjold, Molecular Physics, 81, 251\sphinxhyphen{}261
(1994).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_kappa:howto-wirnsberger}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Wirnsberger)} Wirnsberger, Frenkel, and Dellago, J Chem Phys, 143, 124104
(2015).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Calculate viscosity}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_viscosity:calculate-viscosity}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_viscosity::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The shear viscosity \(\eta\) of a fluid can be measured in at least 6 ways
using various options in LAMMPS.  See the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/VISCOSITY}} directory
for scripts that implement the 5 methods discussed here for a simple
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones fluid model and 1 method for SPC/E water model.
Also, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_kappa::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{page on calculating thermal conductivity}}}}
for an analogous discussion for thermal conductivity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\eta\) is a measure of the propensity of a fluid to transmit momentum in
a direction perpendicular to the direction of velocity or momentum
flow.  Alternatively it is the resistance the fluid has to being
sheared.  It is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}J = -\eta \cdot \text{grad}(V_{\text{stream}})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(J\) is the momentum flux in units of momentum per area per time.
and \(\text{grad}(V_{\text{stream}})\) is the spatial gradient of the velocity of the fluid
moving in another direction, normal to the area through which the
momentum flows.  Viscosity thus has units of pressure\sphinxhyphen{}time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first method is to perform a non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (NEMD) simulation
by shearing the simulation box via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}}
command, and using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sllod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sllod}}}} command to
thermostat the fluid via the SLLOD equations of motion.
Alternatively, as a second method, one or more moving walls can be
used to shear the fluid in between them, again with some kind of
thermostat that modifies only the thermal (non\sphinxhyphen{}shearing) components of
velocity to prevent the fluid from heating up.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A recent (2017) book by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_viscosity:daivis-viscosity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Daivis and Todd)}}}}
discusses use of the SLLOD method and non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (NEMD)
thermostatting generally, for both simple and complex fluids,
e.g. molecular systems.  The latter can be tricky to do correctly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In both cases, the velocity profile setup in the fluid by this
procedure can be monitored by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}
command, which determines \(\text{grad}(V_{\text{stream}})\) in the equation above.
E.g. the derivative in the y\sphinxhyphen{}direction of the \(V_x\) component of fluid
motion or \(\text{grad}(V_{\text{stream}}) = \frac{\text{d} V_x}{\text{d} y}\).  The \(P_{xy}\) off\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal component of
the pressure or stress tensor, as calculated by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} command, can also be monitored, which
is the \(J\) term in the equation above.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_nemd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto nemd}}}} page for details on NEMD simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The third method is to perform a reverse non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD simulation
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscosity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscosity}}}} command which implements
the rNEMD algorithm of Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe.  Momentum in one dimension is
swapped between atoms in two different layers of the simulation box in
a different dimension.  This induces a velocity gradient which can be
monitored with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command.
The fix tallies the cumulative momentum transfer that it performs.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscosity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscosity}}}} command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fourth method is based on the Green\sphinxhyphen{}Kubo (GK) formula which
relates the ensemble average of the auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation of the
stress/pressure tensor to \(\eta\).  This can be done in a fully
equilibrated simulation which is in contrast to the two preceding
non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium methods, where momentum flows continuously through the
simulation box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example input script that calculates the viscosity of
liquid Ar via the GK formalism:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k}{variable     }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ndens}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{all}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{vol}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{average viscosity: \PYGZdl{}v [Pa.s] @ \PYGZdl{}T K, \PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}ndens\PYGZcb{} atoms/A\PYGZca{}3}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fifth method is related to the above Green\sphinxhyphen{}Kubo method,
but uses the Einstein formulation, analogous to the Einstein
mean\sphinxhyphen{}square\sphinxhyphen{}displacement formulation for self\sphinxhyphen{}diffusivity. The
time\sphinxhyphen{}integrated momentum fluxes play the role of Cartesian
coordinates, whose mean\sphinxhyphen{}square displacement increases linearly
with time at sufficiently long times.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sixth is the periodic perturbation method, which is also a non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD method.
However, instead of measuring the momentum flux in response to an applied velocity gradient,
it measures the velocity profile in response to applied stress.
A cosine\sphinxhyphen{}shaped periodic acceleration is added to the system via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_accelerate_cos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix accelerate/cos}}}} command,
and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute viscosity/cos}}}} command is used to monitor the
generated velocity profile and remove the velocity bias before thermostatting.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An article by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_viscosity:hess3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hess)}}}} discussed the accuracy and efficiency of these methods.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\subsection{Calculate diffusion coefficients}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_diffusion:calculate-diffusion-coefficients}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_diffusion::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The diffusion coefficient \(D\) of a material can be measured in at least
2 ways using various options in LAMMPS.  See the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/DIFFUSE}}
directory for scripts that implement the 2 methods discussed here for
a simple Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones fluid model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first method is to measure the mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement (MSD) of
the system, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd}}}} command.  The slope
of the MSD versus time is proportional to the diffusion coefficient.
The instantaneous MSD values can be accumulated in a vector via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_vector::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix vector}}}} command, and a line fit to the vector to
compute its slope via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable slope}}}} function, and
thus extract \(D\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second method is to measure the velocity auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation function
(VACF) of the system, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_vacf::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute vacf}}}}
command.  The time\sphinxhyphen{}integral of the VACF is proportional to the
diffusion coefficient.  The instantaneous VACF values can be
accumulated in a vector via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_vector::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix vector}}}} command,
and time integrated via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable trap}}}} function,
and thus extract \(D\).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Output structured data from LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:output-structured-data-from-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can output structured data with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{print}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
print}}}} command.  This gives you flexibility since you can build
custom data formats that contain system properties, thermo data, and variables
values. This output can be directed to the screen and/or to a file for post
processing.


\subsubsection{Writing the current system state, thermo data, variable values}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:writing-the-current-system-state-thermo-data-variable-values}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{print}}}} command to output the current system state, which
can include system properties, thermo data and variable values.


\paragraph{YAML}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:yaml}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}}
\PYG{l+s}{timestep: \PYGZdl{}(step)}
\PYG{l+s}{pe: \PYGZdl{}(pe)}
\PYG{l+s}{ke: \PYGZdl{}(ke)}
\PYG{l+s}{...}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{current\PYGZus{}state.yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{screen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\sphinxSetupCaptionForVerbatim{current\_state.yaml}
\def\sphinxLiteralBlockLabel{\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:id2}}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nn}{\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}}
\PYG{n+nt}{timestep}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{250}
\PYG{n+nt}{pe}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{\PYGZhy{}4.7774327356321810711}
\PYG{n+nt}{ke}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{2.4962152903997174569}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{JSON}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:json}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{l+s}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n}{timestep}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{: \PYGZdl{}(step),}
\PYG{l+s}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{: \PYGZdl{}(pe),}
\PYG{l+s}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{: \PYGZdl{}(ke)}
\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{current\PYGZus{}state.json}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{screen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\sphinxSetupCaptionForVerbatim{current\_state.json}
\def\sphinxLiteralBlockLabel{\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:id3}}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}timestep\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{250}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}pe\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{\PYGZhy{}4.7774327356321810711}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{\PYGZdq{}ke\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.4962152903997174569}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\subsubsection{YAML format thermo\_style or dump\_style output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:yaml-format-thermo-style-or-dump-style-output}}

\paragraph{Extracting data from log file}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:extracting-data-from-log-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 24Mar2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS supports the thermo style “yaml” and for “custom” style
thermodynamic output the format can be changed to YAML with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify line yaml}}}}.  This will produce a
block of output in a compact YAML format \sphinxhyphen{} one “document” per run \sphinxhyphen{} of
the following style:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nn}{\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}}
\PYG{n+nt}{keywords}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Step}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Temp}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{E\PYGZus{}pair}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{E\PYGZus{}mol}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{TotEng}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Press}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{]}
\PYG{n+nt}{data}\PYG{p}{:}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{100}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.757453103239935}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}5.7585054860159}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}4.62236133677021}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.207261053624721}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{]}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{110}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.759322359337036}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}5.7614668389562}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}4.62251889318624}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.194314975399602}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{]}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{120}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.759372342462676}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}5.76149365656489}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}4.62247073844943}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.191600048851267}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{]}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{130}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.756833027516501}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}5.75777334823494}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZhy{}4.62255928350835}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{0.208792327853067}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{]}
\PYG{n+nn}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This data can be extracted and parsed from a log file using python with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{re}\PYG{o}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}
\PYG{k}{try}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{CSafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{Loader}
\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n+ne}{ImportError}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{SafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{Loader}

\PYG{n}{docs} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n+nb}{open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{log.lammps}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{line} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{m} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{re}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{search}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{r}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZca{}(keywords:.*\PYGZdl{}|data:\PYGZdl{}|\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZdl{}|}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.\PYGZdl{}|  \PYGZhy{} }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{[.*}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{]\PYGZdl{})}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{line}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{n}{docs} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}

\PYG{n}{thermo} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{yaml}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}all}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{docs}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{Loader}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{Loader}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Number of runs: }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{len}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{keywords}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{4}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{ = }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{data}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{4}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After loading the YAML data, \sphinxtitleref{thermo} is a list containing a dictionary
for each “run” where the tag “keywords” maps to the list of thermo
header strings and the tag “data” has a list of lists where the outer
list represents the lines of output and the inner list the values of the
columns matching the header keywords for that step.  The second print()
command for example will print the header string for the fifth keyword
of the second run and the corresponding value for the third output line
of that run:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Number of runs:  2
TotEng  =  \PYGZhy{}4.62140097780047
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Extracting data from dump file}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:extracting-data-from-dump-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 4May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
YAML format output has been added to multiple commands in LAMMPS,
for example {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump yaml}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
Depending on the kind of data being written, organization of the data
or the specific syntax used may change, but the principles are very
similar and all files should be readable with a suitable YAML parser.
A simple example for this is given below:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}
\PYG{k}{try}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{CSafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{YamlLoader}
\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n+ne}{ImportError}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{SafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{YamlLoader}

\PYG{n}{timesteps} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n+nb}{open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{dump.yaml}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{r}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{yaml}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}all}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{Loader}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{YamlLoader}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{d} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Processing timestep }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}d}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}} \PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}} \PYG{n}{d}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{timestep}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Read }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}d}\PYG{l+s+s1}{ timesteps from yaml dump}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}} \PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}} \PYG{n+nb}{len}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Second timestep: }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{timestep}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Box info: x: }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}} \PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{box}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{ y:}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{box}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{ z:}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{box}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{First 5 per\PYGZhy{}atom columns: }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{keywords}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Corresponding 10th atom data: }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{data}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{9}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The corresponding output for a YAML dump command added to the “melt” example is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Processing timestep 0
Processing timestep 50
Processing timestep 100
Processing timestep 150
Processing timestep 200
Processing timestep 250

Second timestep:  50
Box info: x:  [0, 16.795961913825074]  y: [0, 16.795961913825074]  z: [0, 16.795961913825074]
First 5 per\PYGZhy{}atom columns:  [\PYGZsq{}id\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}type\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}x\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}y\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}z\PYGZsq{}]
Corresponding 10th atom data:  [10, 1, 4.43828, 0.968481, 0.108555]

\paragraph{Processing scalar data with Python}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:processing-scalar-data-with-python}}

\begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.330\linewidth}
\centering
\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{thermo_bondeng}.png}
\end{wrapfigure}

\mbox{}\par\vskip-\dimexpr\baselineskip+\parskip\relax

\sphinxAtStartPar
After reading and parsing the YAML format data, it can be easily
imported for further processing and visualization with the \sphinxhref{https://pandas.pydata.org/}{pandas} and \sphinxhref{https://matplotlib.org/}{matplotlib} Python modules.  Because of the organization
of the data in the YAML format thermo output, it needs to be told to
process only the ‘data’ part of the imported data to create a pandas
data frame, and one needs to set the column names from the ‘keywords’
entry.  The following Python script code example demonstrates this, and
creates the image shown on the right of a simple plot of various bonded
energy contributions versus the timestep from a run of the ‘peptide’
example input after changing the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo style}}}} to
‘yaml’.  The properties to be used for x and y values can be
conveniently selected through the keywords.  Please note that those
keywords can be changed to custom strings with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify
colname}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{re}\PYG{o}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{pandas}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{pd}
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{matplotlib}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{pyplot}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{plt}

\PYG{k}{try}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{CSafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{Loader}
\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n+ne}{ImportError}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{SafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{Loader}

\PYG{n}{docs} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n+nb}{open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{log.lammps}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{line} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{m} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{re}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{search}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{r}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZca{}(keywords:.*\PYGZdl{}|data:\PYGZdl{}|\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZdl{}|}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.\PYGZdl{}|  \PYGZhy{} }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{[.*}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZbs{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{]\PYGZdl{})}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{line}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{n}{docs} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{m}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}

\PYG{n}{thermo} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{yaml}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}all}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{docs}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{Loader}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{Loader}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{df} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{pd}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{data}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{columns}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{keywords}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{fig} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{df}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{plot}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Step}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E\PYGZus{}bond}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E\PYGZus{}angle}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E\PYGZus{}dihed}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{E\PYGZus{}impro}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ylabel}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Energy in kcal/mol}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{plt}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{savefig}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{thermo\PYGZus{}bondeng.png}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Processing vector data with Python}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:processing-vector-data-with-python}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Global \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} data as produced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
uses a slightly different organization of the data. You still have the
dictionary keys ‘keywords’ and ‘data’ for the column headers and the
data.  But the data is a dictionary indexed by the time step and for
each step there are multiple rows of values each with a list of the
averaged properties.  This requires a slightly different processing,
since the entire data cannot be directly imported into a single pandas
DataFrame class instance.  The following Python script example
demonstrates how to read such data.  The result will combine the data
for the different steps into one large “multi\sphinxhyphen{}index” table.  The pandas
IndexSlice class can then be used to select data from this combined data
frame.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{pandas}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{pd}

\PYG{k}{try}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{CSafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{Loader}
\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n+ne}{ImportError}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{SafeLoader} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{Loader}

\PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n+nb}{open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ave.yaml}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{ave} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{yaml}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{Loader}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{Loader}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{keys} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{keywords}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{n}{df} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{k} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{data}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{keys}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{k}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{pd}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{data}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{k}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{columns}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{keys}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} create multi\PYGZhy{}index data frame}
\PYG{n}{df} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{pd}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{concat}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} output only the first 3 value for steps 200 to 300 of the column Pressure}
\PYG{n}{idx} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{pd}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{IndexSlice}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Pressure}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{loc}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{200}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{l+m+mi}{300}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Processing scalar data with Perl}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:processing-scalar-data-with-perl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ease of processing YAML data is not limited to Python. Here is an
example for extracting and processing a LAMMPS log file with Perl instead.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{use}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{YAML::XS}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{n+nb}{open}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LOG}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}log.lammps\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o+ow}{or}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{die}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}could not open log.lammps: \PYGZdl{}!\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{my}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{while}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{my}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{line}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+sr}{\PYGZlt{}LOG\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{line}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=\PYGZti{}}\PYG{l+s+sr}{ /\PYGZca{}(keywords:.*\PYGZdl{}|data:\PYGZdl{}|\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZdl{}|\PYGZbs{}.\PYGZbs{}.\PYGZbs{}.\PYGZdl{}|  \PYGZhy{} \PYGZbs{}[.*\PYGZbs{}]\PYGZdl{})/}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{line}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{n+nb}{close}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LOG}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} convert YAML to perl as nested hash and array references}
\PYG{k}{my}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{thermo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Load}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{file}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} convert references to real arrays}
\PYG{k}{my}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{@}\PYG{n+nv}{keywords}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{@}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{thermo}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}keywords\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{my}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{@}\PYG{n+nv}{data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{@}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}}\PYG{n+nv}{thermo}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}data\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} print first two columns}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdl{}keywords[0] \PYGZdl{}keywords[1]\PYGZbs{}n\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{foreach}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{@}\PYG{n+nv}{data}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}\PYGZdl{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZcb{}[0]  \PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}\PYGZdl{}\PYGZus{}\PYGZcb{}[1]\PYGZbs{}n\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Writing continuous data during a simulation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:writing-continuous-data-during-a-simulation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} command allows you to output an arbitrary string at defined times during a simulation run.


\paragraph{YAML}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:id1}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{extra}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZhy{} timestep: \PYGZdl{}(step)}
\PYG{l+s}{  pe: \PYGZdl{}(pe)}
\PYG{l+s}{  ke: \PYGZdl{}(ke)}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{output.yaml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{screen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\sphinxSetupCaptionForVerbatim{output.yaml}
\def\sphinxLiteralBlockLabel{\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:id4}}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nt}{timestep}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{0}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{pe}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{\PYGZhy{}6.77336805325924729}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{ke}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{4.4988750000000026219}

\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nt}{timestep}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{50}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{pe}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{\PYGZhy{}4.8082494418323200591}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{ke}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{2.5257981827119797558}

\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nt}{timestep}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{100}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{pe}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{\PYGZhy{}4.7875608875581505686}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{ke}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{2.5062598821985102582}

\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nt}{timestep}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{150}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{pe}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{\PYGZhy{}4.7471033686005483787}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{ke}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{2.466095925545450207}

\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nt}{timestep}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{200}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{pe}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{\PYGZhy{}4.7509052858544134068}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{ke}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{2.4701136792591693592}

\PYG{p+pIndicator}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nt}{timestep}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{250}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{pe}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{\PYGZhy{}4.7774327356321810711}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{ke}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{2.4962152903997174569}

Post\sphinxhyphen{}processing of YAML files can be easily be done with Python and other
scripting languages. In case of Python the \sphinxtitleref{yaml} package allows you to load the

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

 \PYGZob{}\PYGZsq{}timestep\PYGZsq{}: 200, \PYGZsq{}pe\PYGZsq{}: \PYGZhy{}4.750905285854413, \PYGZsq{}ke\PYGZsq{}: 2.4701136792591694\PYGZcb{},
 \PYGZob{}\PYGZsq{}timestep\PYGZsq{}: 250, \PYGZsq{}pe\PYGZsq{}: \PYGZhy{}4.777432735632181, \PYGZsq{}ke\PYGZsq{}: 2.4962152903997175\PYGZcb{}]

\paragraph{Line Delimited JSON (LD\sphinxhyphen{}JSON)}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_structured_data:line-delimited-json-ld-json}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The JSON format itself is very strict when it comes to delimiters. For continuous
output/streaming data it is beneficial use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{line delimited JSON} format.
Each line represents one JSON object.

\section{Force fields howto}
\label{\detokenize{Howto:force-fields-howto}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{CHARMM, AMBER, COMPASS, and DREIDING force fields}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:charmm-amber-compass-and-dreiding-force-fields}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_bioFF::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A compact summary of the concepts, definitions, and properties of
force fields with explicit bonded interactions (like the ones discussed
in this HowTo) is given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:typelabel2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Gissinger)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A force field has 2 parts: the formulas that define it and the
coefficients used for a particular system.  Here we only discuss
formulas implemented in LAMMPS that correspond to formulas commonly used
in the CHARMM, AMBER, COMPASS, and DREIDING force fields.  Setting
coefficients is done either from special sections in an input data file
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command or in the input script with
commands like {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}} and so on.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tools}}}} doc page for
additional tools that can use CHARMM, AMBER, or Materials Studio
generated files to assign force field coefficients and convert their
output into LAMMPS input. LAMMPS input scripts can also be generated by
\sphinxhref{https://charmm-gui.org/}{charmm\sphinxhyphen{}gui.org}.


\subsubsection{CHARMM and AMBER}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:charmm-and-amber}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://mackerell.umaryland.edu/charmm\_ff.shtml}{CHARMM force field} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-mackerell}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(MacKerell)}}}} and \sphinxhref{https://ambermd.org/AmberModels.php}{AMBER force field} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-cornell}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Cornell)}}}}
have potential energy function of the form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V & = \sum_{bonds} E_b + \sum_{angles} \!E_a + \!\overbrace{\sum_{dihedral} \!\!E_d}^{\substack{
       \text{charmm} \\
      \text{charmmfsw}
    }} +\!\!\! \sum_{impropers} \!\!\!E_i \\[.6em]
    & \quad + \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\underbrace{~\sum_{pairs} \left(E_{LJ}+E_{coul}\right)}_{\substack{
       \text{lj/charmm/coul/charmm} \\
      \text{lj/charmm/coul/charmm/implicit} \\
      \text{lj/charmm/coul/long} \\
      \text{lj/charmm/coul/msm} \\
       \text{lj/charmmfsw/coul/charmmfsh} \\
      \text{lj/charmmfsw/coul/long}
    }} \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!+ \!\!\sum_{special}\! E_s + \!\!\!\!\sum_{residues} \!\!\!{\scriptstyle\mathrm{CMAP}(\phi,\psi)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The terms are computed by bond styles (relationship between two atoms),
angle styles (between 3 atoms) , dihedral/improper styles (between 4
atoms), pair styles (non\sphinxhyphen{}covalently bonded pair interactions) and
special bonds. The CMAP term (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_cmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix cmap}}}} command for
details) corrects for pairs of dihedral angles (“Correction MAP”) to
significantly improve the structural and dynamic properties of proteins
in crystalline and solution environments {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-brooks}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Brooks)}}}}. The AMBER force field does not include the CMAP term.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interaction styles listed below compute force field formulas that
are consistent with common options in CHARMM or AMBER.  See each
command’s documentation for the formula it computes.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}} harmonic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style}}}} charmm

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}} charmmfsh

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}} charmm

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/charmmfsw/coul/charmmfsh

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/charmmfsw/coul/long

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/charmm/coul/charmm

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/charmm/coul/charmm/implicit

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/charmm/coul/long

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} charmm

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} amber

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair styles compute Lennard Jones (LJ) and Coulombic interactions
with additional switching or shifting functions that ramp the energy
and/or force smoothly to zero between an inner \((a)\) and outer
\((b)\) cutoff. The older styles with \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} (not \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsh}) in their name compute the LJ and Coulombic interactions
with an energy switching function (esw) \(S(r)\) which ramps the energy
smoothly to zero between the inner and outer cutoff. This can cause
irregularities in pairwise forces (due to the discontinuous second
derivative of energy at the boundaries of the switching region), which
in some cases can result in complications in energy minimization and
detectable artifacts in MD simulations.

\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-container-fluid}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-sphinx-override}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-mb-4}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-1}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-xs-1}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-sm-1}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-md-2}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-lg-2}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-col}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-d-flex-column}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}LJ(r) &= 4 \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
         \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]\\[.6em]
C(r) &= \frac{C q_i q_j}{ \epsilon r}\\[.6em]
S(r) &=  \frac{ \left(b^2 - r^2\right)^2 \left(b^2 + 2r^2 - 3{a^2}\right)}
        { \left(b^2 - a^2\right)^3 }\\[.6em]
E_{LJ}(r) &=  \begin{cases}
  LJ(r), & r \leq a \\
  LJ(r) S(r), & a < r \leq b \\
  0, &r > b
\end{cases} \\[.6em]
E_{coul}(r) &=  \begin{cases}
  C(r), & r \leq a \\
  C(r) S(r), & a < r \leq b \\
  0, & r > b
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-col}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-d-flex-column}
\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{howto_charmm_ELJ}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The newer styles with \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsh} in their name replace
energy switching with force switching (fsw) for LJ interactions and
force shifting (fsh) functions for Coulombic interactions
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-steinbach}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Steinbach)}}}}

\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-container-fluid}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-sphinx-override}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-mb-4}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-1}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-xs-1}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-sm-1}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-md-2}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-row-cols-lg-2}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-col}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-d-flex-column}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}    E_{LJ}(r) = & \begin{cases}
4  \epsilon \sigma^6  \left(\frac{\displaystyle\sigma
  ^6-r^6}{\displaystyle r^{12}}-\frac{\displaystyle\sigma ^6}{\displaystyle a^6
  b^6}+\frac{\displaystyle 1}{\displaystyle a^3 b^3}\right) & r\leq a \\
\frac{\displaystyle 4 \epsilon \sigma^6   \left(\sigma ^6
  \left(b^6-r^6\right)^2-b^3 r^6 \left(a^3+b^3\right)
  \left(b^3-r^3\right)^2\right)}{\displaystyle b^6 r^{12}
  \left(b^6-a^6\right)} & a<r \leq b\\
  0, & r>b
 \end{cases}\\[.6em]
  E_{coul}(r) & =  \begin{cases}
       C(r) \frac{\displaystyle (b-r)^2}{\displaystyle r b^2}, &  r \leq b \\
       0, & r > b
     \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-col}
\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-d-flex-column}
\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{howto_charmmfsw_ELJ}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These styles are used by LAMMPS input scripts generated by
\sphinxurl{https://charmm-gui.org/} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-brooks}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Brooks)}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For CHARMM, newer \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsh} styles were released in
March 2017.  We recommend they be used instead of the older \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm}
styles.  See discussion of the differences on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair charmm}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral charmm}}}} doc
pages.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The TIP3P water model is strongly recommended for use with the CHARMM
force field. In fact, \sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/t/using-spc-water-with-charmm-ff/24715}{“using the SPC model with CHARMM parameters is
a bad idea”} and \sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/t/hybrid-pair-styles-for-charmm-and-tip4p-ew/32609}{“to
enable TIP4P style water in CHARMM, you would have to write a new pair
style”}
. LAMMPS input scripts generated by Solution Builder on \sphinxurl{https://charmm-gui.org}
use TIP3P molecules for solvation.  Any other water model can and
probably will lead to false conclusions.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{COMPASS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:compass}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
COMPASS is a general force field for atomistic simulation of common
organic molecules, inorganic small molecules, and polymers which was
developed using ab initio and empirical parameterization techniques
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-sun}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sun)}}}}.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tools}}}} page for the
msi2lmp tool for creating LAMMPS template input and data files from
BIOVIA’s Materials Studio files.  Please note that the msi2lmp tool is
very old and largely unmaintained, so it does not support all features
of Materials Studio provided force field files, especially additions
during the last decade.  You should watch the output carefully and
compare results, where possible.  See {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-sun}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sun)}}}} for a
description of the COMPASS force field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These interaction styles listed below compute force field formulas that
are consistent with the COMPASS force field.  See each command’s
documentation for the formula it computes.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}} class2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style}}}} class2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}} class2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style}}}} class2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/class2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/class2/coul/cut

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} lj/class2/coul/long

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} lj/coul 0 0 1

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{DREIDING}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:dreiding}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
DREIDING is a generic force field developed by the \sphinxhref{http://www.wag.caltech.edu}{Goddard group} at Caltech and is useful for predicting
structures and dynamics of organic, biological and main\sphinxhyphen{}group inorganic
molecules.  The philosophy in DREIDING is to use general force constants
and geometry parameters based on simple hybridization considerations,
rather than individual force constants and geometric parameters that
depend on the particular combinations of atoms involved in the bond,
angle, or torsion terms.  DREIDING has an {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hbond_dreiding::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{explicit hydrogen bond
term}}}} to describe interactions involving a
hydrogen atom on very electronegative atoms (N, O, F).  Unlike CHARMM
or AMBER, the DREIDING force field has not been parameterized for
considering solvents (like water).

\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF:howto-mayo}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mayo)}}}} for a description of the DREIDING force field

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interaction styles listed below compute force field formulas that
are consistent with the DREIDING force field.  See each command’s
documentation for the formula it computes.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}} harmonic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_morse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}} morse

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_cosine_squared::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style}}}} cosine/squared

\subsection{AMOEBA and HIPPO force fields}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_amoeba:amoeba-and-hippo-force-fields}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_amoeba::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The AMOEBA and HIPPO polarizable force fields were developed by Jay
Ponder’s group at the U Washington at St Louis.  The LAMMPS
implementation is based on Fortran 90 code provided by the Ponder
group in their \sphinxhref{https://dasher.wustl.edu/tinker/}{Tinker MD software}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The current implementation (July 2022) of AMOEBA in LAMMPS matches the
version discussed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-ponder}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ponder)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-ren}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ren)}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-shi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Shi)}}}}.  Likewise the current
implementation of HIPPO in LAMMPS matches the version discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-rackers}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rackers)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These force fields can be used when polarization effects are desired
in simulations of water, organic molecules, and biomolecules including
proteins, provided that parameterizations (Tinker PRM force field
files) are available for the systems you are interested in.  Files in
the LAMMPS potentials directory with a “amoeba” or “hippo” suffix can
be used.  The Tinker distribution and website have additional force
field files as well:
\sphinxurl{https://github.com/TinkerTools/tinker/tree/release/params}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that currently, HIPPO can only be used for water systems, but
HIPPO files for a variety of small organic and biomolecules are in
preparation by the Ponder group.  Those force field files will be
included in the LAMMPS distribution when available.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use the AMOEBA or HIPPO force fields, a simulation must be 3d, and
fully periodic or fully non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic, and use an orthogonal (not
triclinic) simulation box.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The AMOEBA and HIPPO force fields contain the following terms in their
energy (U) computation.  Further details for AMOEBA equations are in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-ponder}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ponder)}}}}, further details for the HIPPO
equations are in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-rackers}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rackers)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U & = U_{intermolecular} + U_{intramolecular} \\
U_{intermolecular} & = U_{hal} + U_{repulsion} + U_{dispersion} + U_{multipole} + U_{polar} + U_{qxfer} \\
U_{intramolecular} & = U_{bond} + U_{angle} + U_{torsion} + U_{oop} + U_{b\theta} + U_{UB} + U_{pitorsion} + U_{bitorsion}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For intermolecular terms, the AMOEBA force field includes only the
\(U_{hal}\), \(U_{multipole}\), \(U_{polar}\) terms.  The
HIPPO force field includes all but the \(U_{hal}\) term.  In
LAMMPS, these are all computed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style amoeba or hippo}}}} command.  Note that the \(U_{multipole}\) and
\(U_{polar}\) terms in this formula are not the same for the
AMOEBA and HIPPO force fields.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For intramolecular terms, the \(U_{bond}\), \(U_{angle}\),
\(U_{torsion}\), \(U_{oop}\) terms are computed by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style class2}}}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style amoeba}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_fourier::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style fourier}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style amoeba}}}} commands respectively.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style amoeba}}}} command includes the
\(U_{b\theta}\) bond\sphinxhyphen{}angle cross term, and the \(U_{UB}\) term
for a Urey\sphinxhyphen{}Bradley bond contribution between the I,K atoms in the IJK
angle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(U_{pitorsion}\) term is computed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_pitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
amoeba/pitorsion}}}} command.  It computes 6\sphinxhyphen{}body
interaction between a pair of bonded atoms which each have 2
additional bond partners.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(U_{bitorsion}\) term is computed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_bitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
amoeba/bitorsion}}}} command.  It computes 5\sphinxhyphen{}body
interaction between two 4\sphinxhyphen{}body torsions (dihedrals) which overlap,
having 3 atoms in common.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These command doc pages have additional details on the terms they
compute:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style amoeba or hippo}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style class2}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style amoeba}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_fourier::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style fourier}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style amoeba}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_pitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix amoeba/pitorsion}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_bitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix amoeba/bitorsion}}}}
