\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
To use the AMOEBA or HIPPO force fields in LAMMPS, use commands like
the following appropriately in your input script.  The only change
needed for AMOEBA vs HIPPO simulation is for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} commands, as shown
below.  See examples/amoeba for example input scripts for both AMOEBA
and HIPPO.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{n}{real}\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} required}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n}{amoeba}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n}{class2}\PYG{+w}{                         }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} CLASS2 package}
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{amoeba}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{fourier}\PYG{+w}{                        }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} EXTRA\PYGZhy{}MOLECULE package}
\PYG{k}{improper\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{amoeba}
\PYG{+w}{                                                  }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} required per\PYGZhy{}atom data}
\PYG{k}{fix                }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{amtype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}amtype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ghost}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{fix                }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{extra}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}amgroup}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}ired}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}xaxis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}yaxis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}zaxis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{d\PYGZus{}pval}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ghost}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{fix                }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{polaxe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}polaxe}

\PYG{k}{fix                }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amoeba}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{pitorsion}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} PiTorsion terms in FF}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{energy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{+w}{                                                  }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Bitorsion terms in FF}
\PYG{k}{fix                }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{bit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amoeba}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{bitorsion}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bitorsion.ubiquitin.data}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{bit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{energy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}

\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{n}{data.ubiquitin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{amtype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Tinker Types}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{pitorsion types}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{PiTorsion Coeffs}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pitorsions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{PiTorsions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{bit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{bitorsions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{BiTorsions}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n}{amoeba}\PYG{+w}{                          }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} AMOEBA FF}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amoeba\PYGZus{}ubiquitin.prm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amoeba\PYGZus{}ubiquitin.key}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n}{hippo}\PYG{+w}{                           }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} HIPPO FF}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hippo\PYGZus{}water.prm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hippo\PYGZus{}water.key}

\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{one}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{five}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 1\PYGZhy{}5 neighbors}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command should
be created by the tools/tinker/tinker2lmp.py conversion program
described below.  It will create a section in the data file with the
header “Tinker Types”.  A {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}}
command for the data must be specified before the read\_data command.
In the example above the fix ID is \sphinxstyleemphasis{amtype}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, if the system you are simulating defines AMOEBA/HIPPO
pitorsion or bitorsion interactions, there will be entries in the data
file for those interactions.  They require a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_pitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
amoeba/pitortion}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_bitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
amoeba/bitorsion}}}} command be defined.  In the
example above, the IDs for these two fixes are \sphinxstyleemphasis{pit} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{bit}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Of course, if the system being modeled does not have one or more of
the following \textendash{} bond, angle, dihedral, improper, pitorsion,
bitorsion interactions \textendash{} then the corresponding style and fix
commands above do not need to be used.  See the example scripts in
examples/amoeba for water systems as examples; they are simpler than
what is listed above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} commands with IDs
(in the example above) \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{polaxe} are also needed to define
internal per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities used by the AMOEBA and HIPPO force
fields.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command used for either the AMOEBA
or HIPPO force field takes two arguments for Tinker force field files,
namely a PRM and KEY file.  The keyfile can be specified as NULL and
default values for a various settings will be used.  Note that these 2
files are meant to allow use of native Tinker files as\sphinxhyphen{}is.  However
LAMMPS does not support all the options which can be included
in a Tinker PRM or KEY file.  See specifics below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{one/five}
option is required, since the AMOEBA/HIPPO force fields define
weighting factors for not only 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 interactions, but also
1\sphinxhyphen{}5 interactions.  This command will trigger a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom list of 1\sphinxhyphen{}5
neighbors to be generated.  The AMOEBA and HIPPO force fields define
their own custom weighting factors for all the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4, 1\sphinxhyphen{}5
terms which in the Tinker PRM and KEY files; they can be different for
different terms in the force field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to the list above, these command doc pages have additional
details:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style amoeba}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Tinker PRM and KEY files

\sphinxAtStartPar
A Tinker PRM file is composed of sections, each of which has multiple
lines.  This is the list of PRM sections LAMMPS knows how to parse and
use.  Any other sections are skipped:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Angle Bending Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom Type Definitions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Atomic Multipole Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bond Stretching Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Charge Penetration Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Charge Transfer Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dipole Polarizability Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dispersion Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Force Field Definition

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Literature References

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}Plane Bend Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pauli Repulsion Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pi\sphinxhyphen{}Torsion Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Stretch\sphinxhyphen{}Bend Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Torsion\sphinxhyphen{}Torsion Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Torsional Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Urey\sphinxhyphen{}Bradley Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Van der Waals Pair Parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Van der Waals Parameters

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A Tinker KEY file is composed of lines, each of which has a keyword
followed by zero or more parameters.  This is the list of keywords
LAMMPS knows how to parse and use in the same manner Tinker does.  Any
other keywords are skipped.  The value in parenthesis is the default
value for the keyword if it is not specified, or if the keyfile in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command is specified as NULL:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a\sphinxhyphen{}axis (0.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
b\sphinxhyphen{}axis (0.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\sphinxhyphen{}axis (0.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ctrn\sphinxhyphen{}cutoff (6.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ctrn\sphinxhyphen{}taper (0.9 * ctrn\sphinxhyphen{}cutoff)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
delta\sphinxhyphen{}halgren (0.07)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dewald (no long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion unless specified)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dewald\sphinxhyphen{}alpha (0.4)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dewald\sphinxhyphen{}cutoff (7.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dispersion\sphinxhyphen{}cutoff (9.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dispersion\sphinxhyphen{}taper (9.0 * dispersion\sphinxhyphen{}cutoff)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dpme\sphinxhyphen{}grid

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dpme\sphinxhyphen{}order (4)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ewald (no long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatics unless specified)

\item {}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tinker2lmp.py tool

\sphinxAtStartPar
This conversion tool is found in the tools/tinker directory.
As shown in examples/amoeba/README, these commands produce
the data files found in examples/amoeba, and also illustrate
all the options available to use with the tinker2lmp.py script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }tinker2lmp.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xyz\PYG{+w}{ }water\PYGZus{}dimer.xyz\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}amoeba\PYG{+w}{ }amoeba\PYGZus{}water.prm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}data\PYG{+w}{ }data.water\PYGZus{}dimer.amoeba\PYG{+w}{                }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} AMOEBA non\PYGZhy{}periodic system}
python\PYG{+w}{ }tinker2lmp.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xyz\PYG{+w}{ }water\PYGZus{}dimer.xyz\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}hippo\PYG{+w}{ }hippo\PYGZus{}water.prm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}data\PYG{+w}{ }data.water\PYGZus{}dimer.hippo\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} HIPPO non\PYGZhy{}periodic system}
python\PYG{+w}{ }tinker2lmp.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xyz\PYG{+w}{ }water\PYGZus{}box.xyz\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}amoeba\PYG{+w}{ }amoeba\PYGZus{}water.prm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}data\PYG{+w}{ }data.water\PYGZus{}box.amoeba\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pbc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}.643\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}.643\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}.643\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} AMOEBA periodic system}
python\PYG{+w}{ }tinker2lmp.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xyz\PYG{+w}{ }water\PYGZus{}box.xyz\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}hippo\PYG{+w}{ }hippo\PYGZus{}water.prm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}data\PYG{+w}{ }data.water\PYGZus{}box.hippo\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pbc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}.643\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}.643\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}.643\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} HIPPO periodic system}
python\PYG{+w}{ }tinker2lmp.py\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}xyz\PYG{+w}{ }ubiquitin.xyz\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}amoeba\PYG{+w}{ }amoeba\PYGZus{}ubiquitin.prm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}data\PYG{+w}{ }data.ubiquitin.new\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}pbc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{54}.99\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{41}.91\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{41}.91\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}bitorsion\PYG{+w}{ }bitorsion.ubiquitin.data.new\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} system with bitorsions}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Switches and their arguments may be specified in any order.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhyphen{}xyz switch is required and specifies an input XYZ file as an
argument.  The format of this file is an extended XYZ format defined
and used by Tinker for its input.  Example *.xyz files are in the
examples/amoeba directory.  The file lists the atoms in the system.
Each atom has the following information: Tinker species name (ignored
by LAMMPS), xyz coordinates, Tinker numeric type, and a list of atom
IDs the atom is bonded to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is more information about the extended XYZ format defined and
used by Tinker, and links to programs that convert standard PDB files
to the extended XYZ format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxurl{https://openbabel.org/docs/current/FileFormats/Tinker\_XYZ\_format.html}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxurl{https://github.com/emleddin/pdbxyz-xyzpdb}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxurl{https://github.com/TinkerTools/tinker/blob/release/source/pdbxyz.f}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhyphen{}amoeba or \sphinxhyphen{}hippo switch is required.  It specifies an input
AMOEBA or HIPPO PRM force field file as an argument.  This should be
the same file used by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command in
the input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhyphen{}data switch is required.  It specifies an output file name for
the LAMMPS data file that will be produced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For periodic systems, the \sphinxhyphen{}pbc switch is required.  It specifies the
periodic box size for each dimension (x,y,z).  For a Tinker simulation
these are specified in the KEY file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhyphen{}bitorsion switch is only needed if the system contains Tinker
bitorsion interactions.  The data for each type of bitorsion
interaction will be written to the specified file, and read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_bitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix amoeba/bitorsion}}}} command.  The data
includes 2d arrays of values to which splines are fit, and thus is not
compatible with the LAMMPS data file format.

\subsection{TIP3P water model}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_tip3p:tip3p-water-model}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_tip3p::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The TIP3P water model as implemented in CHARMM {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip3p:howto-tip3p}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(MacKerell)}}}} specifies a 3\sphinxhyphen{}site rigid water molecule with charges and
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones parameters assigned to each of the three atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A suitable pair style with cutoff Coulomb would be:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/cut}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or these commands for a long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulomb model:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/long}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_fep_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/long/soft}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm/disp}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake or fix rattle}}}} command can be
used to hold the two O\sphinxhyphen{}H bonds and the H\sphinxhyphen{}O\sphinxhyphen{}H angle rigid.  A bond style
of {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{harmonic}}}} and an angle style of {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{harmonic}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{charmm}}}} should also be used.
In case of rigid bonds also bond style {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_zero::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{zero}}}} and angle
style {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_zero::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{zero}}}} can be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The table below lists the force field parameters (in real {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}) to for the water molecule atoms to run a rigid or flexible
TIP3P\sphinxhyphen{}CHARMM model with a cutoff, the original 1983 TIP3P model
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip3p:jorgensen1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Jorgensen)}}}}, or a TIP3P model with parameters
optimized for a long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulomb solver (e.g. Ewald or PPPM in LAMMPS)
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip3p:price1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Price)}}}}.   The K values can be used if a flexible TIP3P
model (without fix shake) is desired, for rigid bonds/angles they are
ignored.

\subsection{TIP4P water model}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_tip4p:tip4p-water-model}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_tip4p::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The four\sphinxhyphen{}point TIP4P rigid water model extends the traditional
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip3p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{three\sphinxhyphen{}point TIP3P}}}} model by adding an additional
site M, usually massless, where the charge associated with the oxygen
atom is placed.  This site M is located at a fixed distance away from
the oxygen along the bisector of the HOH bond angle.  A bond style of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{harmonic}}}} and an angle style of {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{harmonic}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{charmm}}}} should also be used.
In case of rigid bonds also bond style {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_zero::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{zero}}}} and angle
style {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_zero::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{zero}}}} can be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two ways to implement TIP4P water in LAMMPS:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use a specially written pair style that uses the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip3p:tip3p-molecule}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{TIP3P geometry}}}} without the point M. The point M location is then
implicitly derived from the other atoms or each water molecule and
used during the force computation.  The forces on M are then
projected on the oxygen and the two hydrogen atoms.  This is
computationally very efficient, but the charge distribution in space
is only correct within the tip4p labeled styles.  So all other
computations using charges will “see” the negative charge incorrectly
on the oxygen atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be done with the following pair styles for Coulomb with a cutoff:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style tip4p/cut}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_tip4p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/tip4p/cut}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or these commands for a long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulomb treatment:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style tip4p/long}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_tip4p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/tip4p/long}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_long::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/long/tip4p/long}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_fep_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style tip4p/long/soft}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_fep_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/tip4p/long/soft}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm/tip4p}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm/disp/tip4p}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The bond lengths and bond angles should be held fixed using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rattle}}}} command,
unless a parameterization for a flexible TIP4P model is used.  The
parameter sets listed below are all for rigid TIP4P model variants and
thus the bond and angle force constants are not used and can be set to
any legal value; only equilibrium length and angle are used.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use an {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip4p:tip4p-molecule}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{explicit 4 point TIP4P geometry}}}} where
the oxygen atom carries no charge and the M point no Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
interactions.  Since {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rattle}}}} may not be applied to this kind of geometry, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
rigid or fix rigid/small}}}} or its thermostatted variants
are required to maintain a rigid geometry.  This avoids some of the
issues with respect to analysis and non\sphinxhyphen{}tip4p styles, but it is a
more costly force computation (more atoms in the same volume and thus
more neighbors in the neighbor lists) and requires a much shorter
timestep for stable integration of the rigid body motion.  Since no
bonds or angles are required, they do not need to be defined and atom
style charge would be sufficient for a bulk TIP4P water system.  In
order to avoid that LAMMPS produces an error due to the massless M
site a tiny non\sphinxhyphen{}zero mass needs to be assigned.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The table below lists the force field parameters (in real {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}) to for a selection of popular variants of the TIP4P model.
There is the rigid TIP4P model with a cutoff {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip4p:jorgensen5}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Jorgensen)}}}}, the TIP4/Ice model {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip4p:abascal1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Abascal1)}}}}, the
TIP4P/2005 model {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip4p:abascal2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Abascal2)}}}} and a version of TIP4P
parameters adjusted for use with a long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic solver
(e.g. Ewald or PPPM in LAMMPS).  Note that for implicit TIP4P models the
OM distance is specified in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command,
not as part of the pair coefficients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the when using the TIP4P pair style, the neighbor list cutoff
for Coulomb interactions is effectively extended by a distance 2 * (OM
distance), to account for the offset distance of the fictitious charges
on O atoms in water molecules.  Thus it is typically best in an
efficiency sense to use a LJ cutoff \textgreater{}= Coulomb cutoff + 2*(OM
distance), to shrink the size of the neighbor list.  This leads to
slightly larger cost for the long\sphinxhyphen{}range calculation, so you can test the
trade\sphinxhyphen{}off for your model.  The OM distance and the LJ and Coulombic
cutoffs are set in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_tip4p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/tip4p/long}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar

the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip3p:tip3p-molecule}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{TIP3P molecule file}}}}.  Because the TIP4P
charges are different from TIP3P they need to be reset (or the molecule
file changed):

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is the code for a LAMMPS input file using the explicit method and
a TIP4P molecule file.  Because of using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} no bonds need to be defined and thus no extra storage needs
to be reserved for them, but we need to either switch to atom style full
or use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom mol}}}} so that fix
rigid/small can identify rigid bodies by their molecule ID.  Also a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}} command is added to exclude
computing intramolecular non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions, since those are
removed by the rigid fix anyway:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{real}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{charge}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{map}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{array}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{box}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{block}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{box}

\PYG{k}{mass}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{15.9994}
\PYG{k}{mass}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.008}
\PYG{k}{mass}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}100}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1550}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.1536}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}

\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ghost}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{water}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tip4p.mol}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{33}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{34564}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{water}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{25367}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{overlap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.33}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exclude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{intra}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}

\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}

\subsection{TIP5P water model}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_tip5p:tip5p-water-model}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_tip5p::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The five\sphinxhyphen{}point TIP5P rigid water model extends the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip3p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{three\sphinxhyphen{}point
TIP3P model}}}} by adding two additional sites L, usually
massless, where the charge associated with the oxygen atom is placed.
These sites L are located at a fixed distance away from the oxygen atom,
forming a tetrahedral angle that is rotated by 90 degrees from the HOH
plane.  Those sites thus somewhat approximate lone pairs of the oxygen
and consequently improve the water structure to become even more
“tetrahedral” in comparison to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip4p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{four\sphinxhyphen{}point TIP4P model}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A suitable pair style with cutoff Coulomb would be:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/cut}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or these commands for a long\sphinxhyphen{}range model:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/long}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_fep_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/long/soft}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm/disp}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A TIP5P model \sphinxstyleemphasis{must} be run using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rigid fix}}}} since
there is no other option to keep this kind of structure rigid in LAMMPS.
In order to avoid that LAMMPS produces an error due to the massless L
sites, those need to be assigned a tiny non\sphinxhyphen{}zero mass.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The table below lists the force field parameters (in real {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}) to for a the TIP5P model with a cutoff {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip5p:mahoney}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mahoney)}}}} and the TIP5P\sphinxhyphen{}E model {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip5p:rick}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rick)}}}} for use with a
long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic solver (e.g. Ewald or PPPM in LAMMPS).

Below is the code for a LAMMPS input file for setting up a simulation of
TIP5P water with a molecule file.  Because of using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
rigid/small}}}} no bonds need to be defined and thus no extra
storage needs to be reserved for them, but we need to either switch to
atom style full or use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom mol}}}}
so that fix rigid/small can identify rigid bodies by their molecule ID.
Also a {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}} command is added to
exclude computing intramolecular non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions, since those
are removed by the rigid fix anyway:

\subsection{SPC water model}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spc:spc-water-model}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_spc::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The SPC water model specifies a 3\sphinxhyphen{}site rigid water molecule with
charges and Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones parameters assigned to each of the three atoms.
In LAMMPS the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command can be used to hold
the two O\sphinxhyphen{}H bonds and the H\sphinxhyphen{}O\sphinxhyphen{}H angle rigid.  A bond style of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} and an angle style of \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} should also be
used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the additional parameters (in real units) to set for O and H
atoms and the water molecule to run a rigid SPC model.

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] O mass = 15.9994
\item[] H mass = 1.008
\item[] O charge = \sphinxhyphen{}0.820
\item[] H charge = 0.410
\item[] LJ \(\epsilon\) of OO = 0.1553
\item[] LJ \(\sigma\) of OO = 3.166
\item[] LJ \(\epsilon\), \(\sigma\) of OH, HH = 0.0
\item[] \(r_0\) of OH bond = 1.0
\item[] \(\theta_0\) of HOH angle = 109.47\(^{\circ}\)
\end{DUlineblock}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that as originally proposed, the SPC model was run with a 9
Angstrom cutoff for both LJ and Coulomb terms.  It can also be used
with long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatic solvers (e.g. Ewald or PPPM in LAMMPS)
without changing any of the parameters above, although it becomes
a different model in that mode of usage.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The SPC/E (extended) water model is the same, except
the partial charge assignments change:

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] O charge = \sphinxhyphen{}0.8476
\item[] H charge = 0.4238
\end{DUlineblock}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_spc:howto-berendsen}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Berendsen2)}}}} reference for more details on both
the SPC and SPC/E models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is the code for a LAMMPS input file and a molecule file
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{spce.mol}}) of SPC/E water for use with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule command}}}} demonstrating how to set up a small bulk water system for
SPC/E with rigid bonds.

\PYG{k}{minimize}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{velocity }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5463576}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{integrate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}

\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{density}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}
\PYG{k}{thermo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{upto}
\PYG{k}{write\PYGZus{}data }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{spce.data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nocoeff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{Finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical and aspherical particles}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spherical:finite-size-spherical-and-aspherical-particles}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_spherical::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Typical MD models treat atoms or particles as point masses.  Sometimes
it is desirable to have a model with finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles such as
spheroids or ellipsoids or generalized aspherical bodies.  The
difference is that such particles have a moment of inertia, rotational
energy, and angular momentum.  Rotation is induced by torque coming
from interactions with other particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS has several options for running simulations with these kinds of
particles.  The following aspects are discussed in turn:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
atom styles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pair potentials

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
time integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
computes, thermodynamics, and dump output

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rigid bodies composed of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example input scripts for these kinds of models are in the body,
colloid, dipole, ellipse, line, peri, pour, and tri directories of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{examples directory}}}} in the LAMMPS distribution.


\subsubsection{Atom styles}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spherical:atom-styles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom styles}}}} that allow for
definition of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles: sphere, dipole, ellipsoid, line,
tri, peri, and body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sphere style defines particles that are spheroids and each
particle can have a unique diameter and mass (or density).  These
particles store an angular velocity (omega) and can be acted upon by
torque.  The “set” command can be used to modify the diameter and mass
of individual particles, after then are created.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The dipole style does not actually define finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles, but
is often used in conjunction with spherical particles, via a command
like

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is because when dipoles interact with each other, they induce
torques, and a particle must be finite\sphinxhyphen{}size (i.e. have a moment of
inertia) in order to respond and rotate.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style dipole}}}} command for details.  The “set” command can be
used to modify the orientation and length of the dipole moment of
individual particles, after then are created.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ellipsoid style defines particles that are ellipsoids and thus can
be aspherical.  Each particle has a shape, specified by 3 diameters,
and mass (or density).  These particles store an angular momentum and
their orientation (quaternion), and can be acted upon by torque.  They
do not store an angular velocity (omega), which can be in a different
direction than angular momentum, rather they compute it as needed.
The “set” command can be used to modify the diameter, orientation, and
mass of individual particles, after then are created.  It also has a
brief explanation of what quaternions are.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The line style defines line segment particles with two end points and
a mass (or density).  They can be used in 2d simulations, and they can
be joined together to form rigid bodies which represent arbitrary
polygons.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tri style defines triangular particles with three corner points
and a mass (or density).  They can be used in 3d simulations, and they
can be joined together to form rigid bodies which represent arbitrary
particles with a triangulated surface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The peri style is used with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Peridynamic models}}}} and
defines particles as having a volume, that is used internally in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style peri}}}} potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The body style allows for definition of particles which can represent
complex entities, such as surface meshes of discrete points,
collections of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles, deformable objects, etc.  The body style
is discussed in more detail on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} doc
page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if one of these atom styles is used (or multiple styles via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style hybrid}}}} command), not all particles in
the system are required to be finite\sphinxhyphen{}size or aspherical.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, in the ellipsoid style, if the 3 shape parameters are set
to the same value, the particle will be a sphere rather than an
ellipsoid.  If the 3 shape parameters are all set to 0.0 or if the
diameter is set to 0.0, it will be a point particle.  In the line or
tri style, if the lineflag or triflag is specified as 0, then it
will be a point particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some of the pair styles used to compute pairwise interactions between
finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles also compute the correct interaction with point
particles as well, e.g. the interaction between a point particle and a
finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particle or between two point particles.  If necessary,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}} can be used to ensure the correct
interactions are computed for the appropriate style of interactions.
Likewise, using groups to partition particles (ellipsoids versus
spheres versus point particles) will allow you to use the appropriate
time integrators and temperature computations for each class of
particles.  See the doc pages for various commands for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that for {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{2d simulations}}}}, atom styles sphere
and ellipsoid still use 3d particles, rather than as circular disks or
ellipses.  This means they have the same moment of inertia as the 3d
object.  When temperature is computed, the correct degrees of freedom
are used for rotation in a 2d versus 3d system.


\subsubsection{Pair potentials}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spherical:pair-potentials}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When a system with finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles is defined, the particles
will only rotate and experience torque if the force field computes
such interactions.  These are the various {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair styles}}}} that generate torque:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style gran/history}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style gran/hertz}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style gran/no\_history}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_dipole::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style dipole/cut}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gayberne::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style gayberne}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_resquared::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style resquared}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_brownian::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style brownian}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lubricate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lubricate}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_line_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style line/lj}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tri_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style tri/lj}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style body/nparticle}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The granular pair styles are used with spherical particles.  The
dipole pair style is used with the dipole atom style, which could be
applied to spherical or ellipsoidal particles.  The GayBerne and
REsquared potentials require ellipsoidal particles, though they will
also work if the 3 shape parameters are the same (a sphere).  The
Brownian and lubrication potentials are used with spherical particles.
The line, tri, and body potentials are used with line segment,
triangular, and body particles respectively.


\subsubsection{Time integration}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spherical:time-integration}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several fixes that perform time integration on finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
spherical particles, meaning the integrators update the rotational
orientation and angular velocity or angular momentum of the particles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt/sphere}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Likewise, there are 3 fixes that perform time integration on
ellipsoidal particles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/asphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/asphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt/asphere}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The advantage of these fixes is that those which thermostat the
particles include the rotational degrees of freedom in the temperature
calculation and thermostatting.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}
command can also be used with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{omgea} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angmom} options to
thermostat the rotational degrees of freedom for spherical or
ellipsoidal particles.  Other thermostatting fixes only operate on the
translational kinetic energy of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes perform constant NVE time integration on line segment,
triangular, and body particles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_line::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/line}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_tri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/tri}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/body}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for mixtures of point and finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles, these
integration fixes can only be used with {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{groups}}}} which
contain finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles.


\subsubsection{Computes, thermodynamics, and dump output}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spherical:computes-thermodynamics-and-dump-output}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several computes that calculate the temperature or
rotational energy of spherical or ellipsoidal particles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/asphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute erotate/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute erotate/asphere}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These include rotational degrees of freedom in their computation.  If
you wish the thermodynamic output of temperature or pressure to use
one of these computes (e.g. for a system entirely composed of
finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles), then the compute can be defined and the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command used.  Note that by default
thermodynamic quantities will be calculated with a temperature that
only includes translational degrees of freedom.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands can be used to output various attributes of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
particles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_body_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute body/local}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Attributes include the dipole moment, the angular velocity, the
angular momentum, the quaternion, the torque, the end\sphinxhyphen{}point and
corner\sphinxhyphen{}point coordinates (for line and tri particles), and
sub\sphinxhyphen{}particle attributes of body particles.


\subsubsection{Rigid bodies composed of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spherical:rigid-bodies-composed-of-finite-size-particles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command treats a collection of
particles as a rigid body, computes its inertia tensor, sums the total
force and torque on the rigid body each timestep due to forces on its
constituent particles, and integrates the motion of the rigid body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If any of the constituent particles of a rigid body are finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
particles (spheres or ellipsoids or line segments or triangles), then
their contribution to the inertia tensor of the body is different than
if they were point particles.  This means the rotational dynamics of
the rigid body will be different.  Thus a model of a dimer is
different if the dimer consists of two point masses versus two
spheroids, even if the two particles have the same mass.  Finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
particles that experience torque due to their interaction with other
particles will also impart that torque to a rigid body they are part
of.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the “fix rigid” command for example of complex rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body models
it is possible to define in LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command can also be used to
treat 2, 3, or 4 particles as a rigid body, but it always assumes the
particles are point masses.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that body particles cannot be modeled with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command.  Body particles are treated by LAMMPS
as single particles, though they can store internal state, such as a
list of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles.  Individual body particles are typically treated
as rigid bodies, and their motion integrated with a command like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/body}}}}.  Interactions between pairs of body
particles are computed via a command like {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style body/nparticle}}}}.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Granular models}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_granular:granular-models}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_granular::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Granular system are composed of spherical particles with a diameter,
as opposed to point particles.  This means they have an angular
velocity and torque can be imparted to them to cause them to rotate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To run a simulation of a granular model, you will want to use
the following commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/sphere}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gravity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gravity}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute erotate/sphere}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
calculates rotational kinetic energy which can be {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output with thermodynamic info}}}}.
The compute
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fabric::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fabric}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
calculates various versions of the fabric tensor for granular and non\sphinxhyphen{}granular pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use one of these 4 pair potentials, which compute forces and torques
between interacting pairs of particles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style gran/history}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style gran/no\_history}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style gran/hertzian}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style granular}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands implement fix options specific to granular systems:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_freeze::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix freeze}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscous::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscous}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/gran}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_gran_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/gran/region}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix style \sphinxstyleemphasis{freeze} zeroes both the force and torque of frozen
atoms, and should be used for granular system instead of the fix style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{setforce}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To model heat conduction, one must add the temperature and heatflow
atom variables with:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
a temperature integration fix
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_heat_flow::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix heat/flow}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and a heat conduction option defined in both
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style granular}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/gran}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For computational efficiency, you can eliminate needless pairwise
computations between frozen atoms by using this command:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} exclude

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, for 2d systems, granular particles are still modeled
as 3d spheres, not 2d discs (circles), meaning their moment of inertia
will be the same as in 3d.  If you wish to model granular particles in
2d as 2d discs, see the note on this topic on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_2d::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto 2d}}}}
doc page, where 2d simulations are discussed.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To add custom granular contact models, see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_gran_sub_mod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{modifying granular sub\sphinxhyphen{}models page}}}}.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Body particles}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_body:body-particles}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Overview:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, body particles are generalized finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles.
Individual body particles can represent complex entities, such as
surface meshes of discrete points, collections of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles,
deformable objects, etc.  Note that other kinds of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
spherical and aspherical particles are also supported by LAMMPS, such
as spheres, ellipsoids, line segments, and triangles, but they are
simpler entities than body particles.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_spherical::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto spherical}}}} page for a general overview of all these
particle types.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Body particles are used via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style body}}}}
command.  It takes a body style as an argument.  The current body
styles supported by LAMMPS are as follows.  The name in the first
column is used as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bstyle} argument for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style body}}}} command.


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nparticle}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
rigid body with N sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
2d polygons with N vertices
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar

&
\sphinxAtStartPar
3d polyhedra with N vertices, E edges and F faces
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The body style determines what attributes are stored for each body and
thus how they can be used to compute pairwise body/body or
bond/non\sphinxhyphen{}body (point particle) interactions.  More details of each
style are described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More styles may be added in the future.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{page on creating new body styles}}}} for details on
how to add a new body style to the code.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{When to use body particles:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You should not use body particles to model a rigid body made of
simpler particles (e.g. point, sphere, ellipsoid, line segment,
triangular particles), if the interaction between pairs of rigid
bodies is just the summation of pairwise interactions between the
simpler particles.  LAMMPS already supports this kind of model via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command.  Any of the numerous pair styles
that compute interactions between simpler particles can be used.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command time integrates the motion of the
rigid bodies.  All of the standard LAMMPS commands for thermostatting,
adding constraints, performing output, etc will operate as expected on
the simple particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By contrast, when body particles are used, LAMMPS treats an entire
body as a single particle for purposes of computing pairwise
interactions, building neighbor lists, migrating particles between
processors, output of particles to a dump file, etc.  This means that
interactions between pairs of bodies or between a body and non\sphinxhyphen{}body
(point) particle need to be encoded in an appropriate pair style.  If
such a pair style were to mimic the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}
model, it would need to loop over the entire collection of
interactions between pairs of simple particles within the two bodies,
each time a single body/body interaction was computed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus it only makes sense to use body particles and develop such a pair
style, when particle/particle interactions are more complex than what
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command can already calculate.  For
example, consider particles with one or more of the following
attributes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
represented by a surface mesh

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
represented by a collection of geometric entities (e.g. planes + spheres)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
deformable

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
internal stress that induces fragmentation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For these models, the interaction between pairs of particles is likely
to be more complex than the summation of simple pairwise interactions.
An example is contact or frictional forces between particles with
planar surfaces that inter\sphinxhyphen{}penetrate.  Likewise, the body particle may
store internal state, such as a stress tensor used to compute a
fracture criterion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are additional LAMMPS commands that can be used with body
particles of different styles

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair styles currently defined for use with specific body styles
are listed in the sections below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for all the body styles, if the data file defines a general
triclinic box, then the orientation of the body particle and its
corresponding 6 moments of inertia and other orientation\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
values should reflect the fact the body is defined withing a general
triclinic box with edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A},**B**,**C**.  LAMMPS will rotate
the box to convert it to a restricted triclinic box.  This operation
will also rotate the orientation of the body particles.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} doc page for more details.
The sections below highlight the orientation\sphinxhyphen{}dependent values specific
to each body style.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Specifics of body style nparticle:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nparticle} body style represents body particles as a rigid body
with a variable number N of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles.  It is provided as a
vanilla, prototypical example of a body particle, although as
mentioned above, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command already
duplicates its functionality.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom\_style body command for this body style takes two additional
arguments:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom\PYGZus{}style body nparticle Nmin Nmax
Nmin = minimum \PYGZsh{} of sub\PYGZhy{}particles in any body in the system
Nmax = maximum \PYGZsh{} of sub\PYGZhy{}particles in any body in the system
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Nmin and Nmax arguments are used to bound the size of data
structures used internally by each particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command reads a data file for this
body style, the following information must be provided for each entry
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bodies} section of the data file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom\PYGZhy{}ID 1 M
N
ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz
x1 y1 z1
...
xN yN zN
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where M = 6 + 3*N, and N is the number of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles in the body
particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The integer line has a single value N.  The floating point line(s)
list 6 moments of inertia followed by the coordinates of the N
sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles (x1 to zN) as 3N values.  These values can be listed on
as many lines as you wish; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command
for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 6 moments of inertia (ixx,iyy,izz,ixy,ixz,iyz) should be the
values consistent with the current orientation of the rigid body
around its center of mass.  The values are with respect to the
simulation box XYZ axes, not with respect to the principal axes of the
rigid body itself.  LAMMPS performs the latter calculation internally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of each sub\sphinxhyphen{}particle are specified as its x,y,z
displacement from the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the body particle.  The
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position of the particle is specified by the x,y,z
values in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Atoms} section of the data file, as is the total mass
of the body particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if the data file defines a general triclinic simulation box,
these sub\sphinxhyphen{}particle displacements are orientation\sphinxhyphen{}dependent and, as
mentioned above, should reflect the body particle’s orientation within
the general triclinic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style body/nparticle}}}} command can be used
with this body style to compute body/body and body/non\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Specifics of body style rounded/polygon:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon} body style represents body particles as a 2d
polygon with a variable number of N vertices.  This style can only be
used for 2d models; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style body/rounded/polygon}}}} page for
a diagram of two squares with rounded circles at the vertices.  Special cases
for N = 1 (circle) and N = 2 (rod with rounded ends) can also be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One use of this body style is for 2d discrete element models, as
described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body:body-fraige}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Fraige}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to body style \sphinxstyleemphasis{nparticle}, the atom\_style body command for
this body style takes two additional arguments:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom\PYGZus{}style body rounded/polygon Nmin Nmax
Nmin = minimum \PYGZsh{} of vertices in any body in the system
Nmax = maximum \PYGZsh{} of vertices in any body in the system
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Nmin and Nmax arguments are used to bound the size of data
structures used internally by each particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command reads a data file for this
body style, the following information must be provided for each body
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bodies} section of the data file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom\PYGZhy{}ID 1 M
N
ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz
x1 y1 z1
...
xN yN zN
diameter
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where M = 6 + 3*N + 1, and N is the number of vertices in the body
particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The integer line has a single value N.  The floating point line(s)
list 6 moments of inertia, followed by the coordinates of the N
vertices (x1 to zN) as 3N values (with z = 0.0 for each), followed by
a diameter value = the rounded diameter of the circle that surrounds
each vertex. The diameter value can be different for each body
particle. These floating\sphinxhyphen{}point values can be listed on as many lines
as you wish; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for more
details.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is important that the vertices for each polygonal body particle be
listed in order around its perimeter, so that edges can be inferred.
LAMMPS does not check that this is the case.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 6 moments of inertia (ixx,iyy,izz,ixy,ixz,iyz) should be the
values consistent with the current orientation of the rigid body
around its center of mass.  The values are with respect to the
simulation box XYZ axes, not with respect to the principal axes of the
rigid body itself.  LAMMPS performs the latter calculation internally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of each vertex are specified as its x,y,z displacement
from the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the body particle.  The center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
position of the particle is specified by the x,y,z values in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Atoms} section of the data file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the following information would specify a square particle
whose edge length is sqrt(2) and rounded diameter is 1.0.  The
orientation of the square is aligned with the xy coordinate axes which
is consistent with the 6 moments of inertia: ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz =
1 1 4 0 0 0. Note that only Izz matters in 2D simulations.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
3 1 19
4
1 1 4 0 0 0
\PYGZhy{}0.7071 \PYGZhy{}0.7071 0
\PYGZhy{}0.7071 0.7071 0
0.7071 0.7071 0
0.7071 \PYGZhy{}0.7071 0
1.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A rod in 2D, whose length is 4.0, mass 1.0, rounded at two ends
by circles of diameter 0.5, is specified as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1 1 13
2
1 1 1.33333 0 0 0
\PYGZhy{}2 0 0
2 0 0
0.5
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A disk, whose diameter is 3.0, mass 1.0, is specified as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1 1 10
1
1 1 4.5 0 0 0
0 0 0
3.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if the data file defines a general triclinic simulation box,
these polygon vertex displacements are orientation\sphinxhyphen{}dependent and, as
mentioned above, should reflect the body particle’s orientation within
the general triclinic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style body/rounded/polygon}}}}
command can be used with this body style to compute body/body
interactions.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_body_polygon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/body/polygon}}}}
command can be used with this body style to compute the interaction of
body particles with a wall.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Specifics of body style rounded/polyhedron:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polyhedron} body style represents body particles as a 3d
polyhedron with a variable number of N vertices, E edges and F faces.
This style can only be used for 3d models; see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.  See the “pair\_style
body/rounded/polygon” page for a diagram of a two 2d squares with
rounded circles at the vertices.  A 3d cube with rounded spheres at
the 8 vertices and 12 rounded edges would be similar.  Special cases
for N = 1 (sphere) and N = 2 (rod with rounded ends) can also be
specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This body style is for 3d discrete element models, as described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body:body-wang}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wang}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to body style \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon}, the atom\_style body command
for this body style takes two additional arguments:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom\PYGZus{}style body rounded/polyhedron Nmin Nmax
Nmin = minimum \PYGZsh{} of vertices in any body in the system
Nmax = maximum \PYGZsh{} of vertices in any body in the system
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Nmin and Nmax arguments are used to bound the size of data
structures used internally by each particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command reads a data file for this
body style, the following information must be provided for each entry
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bodies} section of the data file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom\PYGZhy{}ID 3 M
N E F
ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz
x1 y1 z1
...
xN yN zN
0 1
1 2
2 3
...
0 1 2 \PYGZhy{}1
0 2 3 \PYGZhy{}1
...
1 2 3 4
diameter
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where M = 6 + 3*N + 2*E + 4*F + 1, and N is the number of vertices
in the body particle, E = number of edges, F = number of faces.  For N
= 1 or 2, the format is simpler.  E and F are ignored and no edges or
faces are listed, so that M = 6 + 3*N + 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The integer line has three values: number of vertices (N), number of
edges (E) and number of faces (F). The floating point line(s) list 6
moments of inertia followed by the coordinates of the N vertices (x1
to zN) as 3N values, followed by 2E vertex indices corresponding to
the end points of the E edges, then 4*F vertex indices defining F
faces.  The last value is the diameter value = the rounded diameter of
the sphere that surrounds each vertex. The diameter value can be
different for each body particle. These floating\sphinxhyphen{}point values can be
listed on as many lines as you wish; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that vertices are numbered from 0 to N\sphinxhyphen{}1 inclusive.  The order of
the 2 vertices in each edge does not matter.  Faces can be triangles
or quadrilaterals.  In both cases 4 vertices must be specified.  For a
triangle the 4th vertex is \sphinxhyphen{}1.  The 4 vertices within each triangle or
quadrilateral face should be ordered by the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand rule so that
the normal vector of the face points outwards from the center of mass.
For polyhedron with faces with more than 4 vertices, you should split
the complex face into multiple simple faces, each of which is a
triangle or quadrilateral.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If a face is a quadrilateral then its 4 vertices must be co\sphinxhyphen{}planar.
LAMMPS does not check that this is the case.  If you have a quad\sphinxhyphen{}face
of a polyhedron that is not planar (e.g. a cube whose vertices have
been randomly displaced), then you should represent the single quad
face as two triangle faces instead.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 6 moments of inertia (ixx,iyy,izz,ixy,ixz,iyz) should be the
values consistent with the current orientation of the rigid body
around its center of mass.  The values are with respect to the
simulation box XYZ axes, not with respect to the principal axes of the
rigid body itself.  LAMMPS performs the latter calculation internally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of each vertex are specified as its x,y,z displacement
from the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the body particle.  The center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
position of the particle is specified by the x,y,z values in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Atoms} section of the data file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the following information would specify a cubic particle
whose edge length is 2.0 and rounded diameter is 0.5.
The orientation of the cube is aligned with the xyz coordinate axes
which is consistent with the 6 moments of inertia: ixx iyy izz ixy ixz
iyz = 0.667 0.667 0.667 0 0 0.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1 3 79
8 12 6
0.667 0.667 0.667 0 0 0
1 1 1
1 \PYGZhy{}1 1
\PYGZhy{}1 \PYGZhy{}1 1
\PYGZhy{}1 1 1
1 1 \PYGZhy{}1
1 \PYGZhy{}1 \PYGZhy{}1
\PYGZhy{}1 \PYGZhy{}1 \PYGZhy{}1
\PYGZhy{}1 1 \PYGZhy{}1
0 1
1 2
2 3
3 0
4 5
5 6
6 7
7 4
0 4
1 5
2 6
3 7
0 1 2 3
4 5 6 7
0 1 5 4
1 2 6 5
2 3 7 6
3 0 4 7
0.5
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A rod in 3D, whose length is 4.0, mass 1.0 and rounded at two ends
by circles of diameter 0.5, is specified as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1 3 13
2 1 1
0 1.33333 1.33333 0 0 0
\PYGZhy{}2 0 0
2 0 0
0.5
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A sphere whose diameter is 3.0 and mass 1.0, is specified as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1 3 10
1 1 1
0.9 0.9 0.9 0 0 0
0 0 0
3.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of edges and faces for a rod or sphere must be listed,
but is ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if the data file defines a general triclinic simulation box,
these polyhedron vertex displacements are orientation\sphinxhyphen{}dependent and,
as mentioned above, should reflect the body particle’s orientation
within the general triclinic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polyhedron::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style body/rounded/polhedron}}}} command can be used with this body
style to compute body/body interactions.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_body_polygon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
wall/body/polyhedron}}}} command can be used with
this body style to compute the interaction of body particles with a
wall.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Output specifics for all body styles:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_body_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute body/local}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump
local}}}} commands, all 3 of the body styles described on his page
produces one datum for each of the N vertices (of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles) in a
body particle.  The datum has 3 values:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1 = x position of vertex (or sub\PYGZhy{}particle)
2 = y position of vertex
3 = z position of vertex
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values are the current position of the vertex within the
simulation domain, not a displacement from the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass (COM) of
the body particle itself.  These values are calculated using the
current COM and orientation of the body particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} command and its \sphinxstyleemphasis{body} keyword can
be used to render body particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nparticle} body style, each body is drawn as a
collection of spheres, one for each sub\sphinxhyphen{}particle.  The size of each
sphere is determined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bflag1} parameter for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{body} keyword.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{bflag2} argument is ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon} body style, each body is drawn as a polygon
with N line segments.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polyhedron} body style, each
face of each body is drawn as a polygon with N line segments.  The
drawn diameter of each line segment is determined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bflag1}
parameter for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{body} keyword.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{bflag2} argument is ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polyhedron}
styles, line segments are drawn between the pairs of vertices.
Depending on the diameters of the line segments this may be slightly
different than the physical extent of the body as calculated by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style rounded/polygon}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polyhedron::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style rounded/polyhedron}}}}
commands.  Conceptually, the pair styles define the surface of a 2d or
3d body by lines or planes that are tangent to the finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spheres
of specified diameter which are placed on each vertex position.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip
