\subsection{Bonded particle models}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_bpm:bonded-particle-models}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The BPM package implements bonded particle models which can be used to
simulate mesoscale solids.  Solids are constructed as a collection of
particles, which each represent a coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained region of space much
larger than the atomistic scale.  Particles within a solid region are
then connected by a network of bonds to provide solid elasticity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike traditional bonds in molecular dynamics, the equilibrium bond
length can vary between bonds. Bonds store the reference state.  This
includes setting the equilibrium length equal to the initial distance
between the two particles, but can also include data on the bond
orientation for rotational models. This produces a stress\sphinxhyphen{}free initial
state. Furthermore, bonds are allowed to break under large strains,
producing fracture. The examples/bpm directory has sample input scripts
for simulations of the fragmentation of an impacted plate and the
pouring of extended, elastic bodies. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm:howto-clemmer}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Clemmer)}}}}
for more general information on the approach and the LAMMPS implementation.
Example movies illustrating some of these capabilities are found at
\sphinxurl{https://www.lammps.org/movies.html\#bpmpackage}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Bonds can be created using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create bonds}}}} command. Alternatively, a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} template with bonds can be used with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}} to create
solid grains.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this implementation, bonds store their reference state when they are
first computed in the setup of the first simulation run. Data is then
preserved across run commands and is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart
files}}}} such that restarting the system will not reset the
reference state of a bond. Bonds that are created midway into a run,
such as those created by pouring grains using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}, are initialized on that timestep.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, there are two types of bonds included in the BPM package. The
first bond style, {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_bpm_spring::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond bpm/spring}}}}, only applies
pairwise, central body forces. Point particles must have {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond atom
style}}}} and may be thought of as nodes in a spring
network. Alternatively, the second bond style, {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_bpm_rotational::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond bpm/rotational}}}}, resolves tangential forces and torques arising
with the shearing, bending, and twisting of the bond due to rotation or
displacement of particles.  Particles are similar to those used in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_granular::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{granular package}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style sphere}}}}. However, they must also track the current orientation of
particles and store bonds, and therefore use a {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bpm/sphere atom
style}}}}.  This also requires a unique integrator {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_bpm_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
nve/bpm/sphere}}}} which numerically integrates
orientation similar to {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/asphere}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to bond styles, a new pair style {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_bpm_spring::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair bpm/spring}}}} was added to accompany the bpm/spring bond
style. This pair style is simply a hookean repulsion with similar
velocity damping as its sister bond style.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Bond data can be output using a combination of standard LAMMPS commands.
A list of IDs for bonded atoms can be generated using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/local}}}} command.
Various properties of bonds can be computed using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_bond_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute bond/local}}}} command. This
command allows one to access data saved to the bond’s history,
such as the reference length of the bond. More information on
bond history data can be found on the documentation pages for the specific
BPM bond styles. Finally, this data can be output using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}
command. As one may output many columns from the same compute, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{colname} option may be used to provide
more helpful column names. An example of this procedure is found in
/examples/bpm/pour/. External software, such as OVITO, can read these dump
files to render bond data.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
As bonds can be broken between neighbor list builds, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command works differently for BPM
bond styles. There are two possible settings which determine how pair
interactions work between bonded particles.  First, one can overlay
pair forces with bond forces such that all bonded particles also
feel pair interactions. This can be accomplished by setting the \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlay/pair}
keyword present in all bpm bond styles to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} and requires using the
following special bond settings
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively, one can turn off all pair interactions between bonded
particles. Unlike {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond quartic}}}}, this is not done
by subtracting pair forces during the bond computation, but rather by
dynamically updating the special bond list. This is the default behavior
of BPM bond styles and is done by updating the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 special bond list as
bonds break.  To do this, LAMMPS requires {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} bond off
such that all processors containing an atom know when a bond breaks.
Additionally, one must use the following special bond settings
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These settings accomplish two goals. First, they turn off 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 and 1\sphinxhyphen{}4
special bond lists, which are not currently supported for BPMs. As
BPMs often have dense bond networks, generating 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 and 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 special
bond lists is expensive.  By setting the lj weight for 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 bonds to
zero, this turns off pairwise interactions.  Even though there are no
charges in BPM models, setting a nonzero coul weight for 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 bonds
ensures all bonded neighbors are still included in the neighbor list
in case bonds break between neighbor list builds. If bond breakage is
disabled during a simulation run by setting the \sphinxstyleemphasis{break} keyword to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no},
a zero coul weight for 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 bonds can be used to exclude bonded atoms
from the neighbor list builds
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be useful for post\sphinxhyphen{}processing, or to determine pair interaction
properties between distinct bonded particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To monitor the fracture of bonds in the system, all BPM bond styles
have the ability to record instances of bond breakage to output using
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}} command. Since one may frequently output
a list of broken bonds and the time they broke, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump modify}}}} option \sphinxstyleemphasis{header no} may be useful to
avoid repeatedly printing the header of the dump file. An example of
this procedure is found in /examples/bpm/impact/. Additionally,
one can use {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_nbond_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute nbond/atom}}}} to tally the
current number of bonds per atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_broken_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto}}}} page on broken bonds for
more information.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
While LAMMPS has many utilities to create and delete bonds, \sphinxstyleemphasis{only}
the following are currently compatible with BPM bond styles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_bonds}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_create::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/create}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_break::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/break}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_swap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/swap}}}}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_bonds}}}} command requires certain
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} settings.  To subtract pair
interactions, one will need to switch between different \sphinxstyleemphasis{special\_bonds}
settings in the input script. An example is found in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/bpm/impact}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_bpm:howto-clemmer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Clemmer)} Clemmer, Monti, Lechman, Soft Matter, 20, 1702 (2024).

\subsection{Polarizable models}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_polarizable:polarizable-models}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_polarizable::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In polarizable force fields the charge distributions in molecules and
materials respond to their electrostatic environments. Polarizable
systems can be simulated in LAMMPS using three methods:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the fluctuating charge method, implemented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_qeq::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{QEQ}}}}
package,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the adiabatic core\sphinxhyphen{}shell method, implemented in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_coreshell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{CORESHELL}}}} package,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the thermalized Drude dipole method, implemented in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{DRUDE}}}} package.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fluctuating charge method calculates instantaneous charges on
interacting atoms based on the electronegativity equalization
principle. It is implemented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_qeq::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix qeq}}}} which is
available in several variants. It is a relatively efficient technique
since no additional particles are introduced. This method allows for
charge transfer between molecules or atom groups. However, because the
charges are located at the interaction sites, off\sphinxhyphen{}plane components of
polarization cannot be represented in planar molecules or atom groups.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two other methods share the same basic idea: polarizable atoms are
split into one core atom and one satellite particle (called shell or
Drude particle) attached to it by a harmonic spring.  Both atoms bear
a charge and they represent collectively an induced electric dipole.
These techniques are computationally more expensive than the QEq
method because of additional particles and bonds. These two
charge\sphinxhyphen{}on\sphinxhyphen{}spring methods differ in certain features, with the
core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model being normally used for ionic/crystalline materials,
whereas the so\sphinxhyphen{}called Drude model is normally used for molecular
systems and fluid states.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model is applicable to crystalline materials where the
high symmetry around each site leads to stable trajectories of the
core\sphinxhyphen{}shell pairs. However, bonded atoms in molecules can be so close
that a core would interact too strongly or even capture the Drude
particle of a neighbor. The Drude dipole model is relatively more
complex in order to remedy this and other issues. Specifically, the
Drude model includes specific thermostatting of the core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs
and short\sphinxhyphen{}range damping of the induced dipoles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The three polarization methods can be implemented through a
self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent calculation of charges or induced dipoles at each
timestep. In the fluctuating charge scheme this is done by the matrix
inversion method in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_qeq::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix qeq/point}}}}, but for core\sphinxhyphen{}shell
or Drude\sphinxhyphen{}dipoles the relaxed\sphinxhyphen{}dipoles technique would require an slow
iterative procedure. These self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent solutions yield accurate
trajectories since the additional degrees of freedom representing
polarization are massless.  An alternative is to attribute a mass to
the additional degrees of freedom and perform time integration using
an extended Lagrangian technique. For the fluctuating charge scheme
this is done by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_qeq::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix qeq/dynamic}}}}, and for the
charge\sphinxhyphen{}on\sphinxhyphen{}spring models by the methods outlined in the next two
sections. The assignment of masses to the additional degrees of
freedom can lead to unphysical trajectories if care is not exerted in
choosing the parameters of the polarizable models and the simulation
conditions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model the vibration of the shells is kept faster
than the ionic vibrations to mimic the fast response of the
polarizable electrons.  But in molecular systems thermalizing the
core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs at temperatures comparable to the rest of the
simulation leads to several problems (kinetic energy transfer, too
short a timestep, etc.) In order to avoid these problems the relative
motion of the Drude particles with respect to their cores is kept
“cold” so the vibration of the core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs is very slow,
approaching the self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent regime.  In both models the
temperature is regulated using the velocities of the center of mass of
core+shell (or Drude) pairs, but in the Drude model the actual
relative core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude particle motion is thermostatted separately as
well.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Adiabatic core/shell model}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_coreshell:adiabatic-core-shell-model}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_coreshell::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The adiabatic core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_coreshell:mitchellfincham}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Mitchell and Fincham}}}} is a simple method for adding polarizability
to a system.  In order to mimic the electron shell of an ion, a
satellite particle is attached to it. This way the ions are split into
a core and a shell where the latter is meant to react to the
electrostatic environment inducing polarizability.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_polarizable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto polarizable}}}} page for a discussion of all
the polarizable models available in LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Technically, shells are attached to the cores by a spring force f =
k*r where k is a parameterized spring constant and r is the distance
between the core and the shell. The charges of the core and the shell
add up to the ion charge, thus q(ion) = q(core) + q(shell). This
setup introduces the ion polarizability (alpha) given by
alpha = q(shell)\textasciicircum{}2 / k. In a
similar fashion the mass of the ion is distributed on the core and the
shell with the core having the larger mass.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To run this model in LAMMPS, {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} can
be used since atom charge and bonds are needed.  Each kind of
core/shell pair requires two atom types and a bond type.  The core and
shell of a core/shell pair should be bonded to each other with a
harmonic bond that provides the spring force. For example, a data file
for NaCl, as found in examples/coreshell, has this format:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
432   atoms  \PYGZsh{} core and shell atoms
216   bonds  \PYGZsh{} number of core/shell springs

4     atom types  \PYGZsh{} 2 cores and 2 shells for Na and Cl
2     bond types

0.0 24.09597 xlo xhi
0.0 24.09597 ylo yhi
0.0 24.09597 zlo zhi

Masses       \PYGZsh{} core/shell mass ratio = 0.1

1 20.690784  \PYGZsh{} Na core
2 31.90500   \PYGZsh{} Cl core
3 2.298976   \PYGZsh{} Na shell
4 3.54500    \PYGZsh{} Cl shell

Atoms

1    1    2   1.5005    0.00000000   0.00000000   0.00000000 \PYGZsh{} core of core/shell pair 1
2    1    4  \PYGZhy{}2.5005    0.00000000   0.00000000   0.00000000 \PYGZsh{} shell of core/shell pair 1
3    2    1   1.5056    4.01599500   4.01599500   4.01599500 \PYGZsh{} core of core/shell pair 2
4    2    3  \PYGZhy{}0.5056    4.01599500   4.01599500   4.01599500 \PYGZsh{} shell of core/shell pair 2
(...)

Bonds   \PYGZsh{} Bond topology for spring forces

1     2     1     2   \PYGZsh{} spring for core/shell pair 1
2     2     3     4   \PYGZsh{} spring for core/shell pair 2
(...)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Non\sphinxhyphen{}Coulombic (e.g. Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones) pairwise interactions are only
defined between the shells.  Coulombic interactions are defined
between all cores and shells.  If desired, additional bonds can be
specified between cores.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command should be used to
turn\sphinxhyphen{}off the Coulombic interaction within core/shell pairs, since that
interaction is set by the bond spring.  This is done using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command with a 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 weight = 0.0,
which is the default value.  It needs to be considered whether one has
to adjust the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} weighting according
to the molecular topology since the interactions of the shells are
bypassed over an extra bond.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this core/shell implementation does not require all ions to
be polarized.  One can mix core/shell pairs and ions without a
satellite particle if desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since the core/shell model permits distances of r = 0.0 between the
core and shell, a pair style with a “cs” suffix needs to be used to
implement a valid long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic correction.  Several such pair
styles are provided in the CORESHELL package.  See {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_cs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{this page}}}} for details.  All of the core/shell enabled pair
styles require the use of a long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic solver, as specified
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command.  Either the PPPM or
Ewald solvers can be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the NaCL example problem, these pair style and bond style settings
are used:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{born}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.000}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{487.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.23768}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1.05}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}Na\PYGZhy{}Na}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{145134.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.23768}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{6.99}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{8.70}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}Na\PYGZhy{}Cl}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{405774.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.23768}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{72.40}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{145.40}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}Cl\PYGZhy{}Cl}

\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{harmonic}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{63.014}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{25.724}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running dynamics with the adiabatic core/shell model, the
following issues should be considered.  The relative motion of
the core and shell particles corresponds to the polarization,
hereby an instantaneous relaxation of the shells is approximated
and a fast core/shell spring frequency ensures a nearly constant
internal kinetic energy during the simulation.
Thermostats can alter this polarization behavior, by scaling the
internal kinetic energy, meaning the shell will not react freely to
its electrostatic environment.
Therefore it is typically desirable to decouple the relative motion of
the core/shell pair, which is an imaginary degree of freedom, from the
real physical system.  To do that, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_cs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/cs}}}} command can be used, in conjunction with
any of the thermostat fixes, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}.  This compute uses the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity
of the core/shell pairs to calculate a temperature, and ensures that
velocity is what is rescaled for thermostatting purposes.  This
compute also works for a system with both core/shell pairs and
non\sphinxhyphen{}polarized ions (ions without an attached satellite particle).  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_cs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/cs}}}} command requires input of two
groups, one for the core atoms, another for the shell atoms.
Non\sphinxhyphen{}polarized ions which might also be included in the treated system
should not be included into either of these groups, they are taken
into account by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} (second argument) of the compute.  The
groups can be defined using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group *type*}}}} command.
Note that to perform thermostatting using this definition of
temperature, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix modify temp}}}} command should be
used to assign the compute to the thermostat fix.  Likewise the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify temp}}}} command can be used to make
this temperature be output for the overall system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the NaCl example, this can be done as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cores}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{shells}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{CSequ}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cores}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shells}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermoberendsen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{berendsen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1427}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1427}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} thermostat for the true physical system}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermostatequ}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}\PYG{+w}{                               }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} integrator as needed for the berendsen thermostat}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermoberendsen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CSequ}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CSequ}\PYG{+w}{                                }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} output of center\PYGZhy{}of\PYGZhy{}mass derived temperature}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pressure for the core/shell system is computed via the regular
LAMMPS convention by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_coreshell:mitchellfincham2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{treating the cores and shells as individual particles}}}}. For the thermo output of the pressure
as well as for the application of a barostat, it is necessary to
use an additional {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pressure}}}} compute based on
the default {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temperature}}}} and specifying it as a
second argument in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix modify}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} resulting in:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{...}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{CSequ}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cores}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shells}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}press\PYGZus{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pressure}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}temp}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} pressure for individual particles}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CSequ}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}press\PYGZus{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} modify thermo to regular pressure}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{press\PYGZus{}bar}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{npt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.04}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{press\PYGZus{}bar}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CSequ}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}press\PYGZus{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} pressure modification for correct kinetic scalar}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_cs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/cs}}}} is used, the decoupled
relative motion of the core and the shell should in theory be
stable.  However numerical fluctuation can introduce a small
momentum to the system, which is noticeable over long trajectories.
Therefore it is recommendable to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_momentum::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix momentum}}}} command in combination with {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_cs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/cs}}}} when equilibrating the system to
prevent any drift.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When initializing the velocities of a system with core/shell pairs, it
is also desirable to not introduce energy into the relative motion of
the core/shell particles, but only assign a center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity to
the pairs.  This can be done by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity create}}}} command and assigning the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_cs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/cs}}}} command to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} command, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{velocity }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1427}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{134}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bias}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CSequ}
\PYG{k}{velocity }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1427}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CSequ}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To maintain the correct polarizability of the core/shell pairs, the
kinetic energy of the internal motion shall remain nearly constant.
Therefore the choice of spring force and mass ratio need to ensure
much faster relative motion of the two atoms within the core/shell pair
than their center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity. This allows the shells to
effectively react instantaneously to the electrostatic environment and
limits energy transfer to or from the core/shell oscillators.
This fast movement also dictates the timestep that can be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The primary literature of the adiabatic core/shell model suggests that
the fast relative motion of the core/shell pairs only allows negligible
energy transfer to the environment.
The mentioned energy transfer will typically lead to a small drift
in total energy over time.  This internal energy can be monitored
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/chunk}}}} commands.  The internal kinetic
energies of each core/shell pair can then be summed using the sum()
special function of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command.  Or they can
be time/averaged and output using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command.  To use these commands, each core/shell pair must be defined
as a “chunk”.  If each core/shell pair is defined as its own molecule,
the molecule ID can be used to define the chunks.  If cores are bonded
to each other to form larger molecules, the chunks can be identified
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} via assigning a
core/shell ID to each atom using a special field in the data file read
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.  This field can then be
accessed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}}
command, to use as input to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command to define the core/shell
pairs as chunks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example if core/shell pairs are the only molecules:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NaCl\PYGZus{}CS\PYGZus{}x0.1\PYGZus{}prop.data}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cs\PYGZus{}chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cstherm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cs\PYGZus{}chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{internal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cdof}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} note the chosen degrees of freedom for the core/shell pairs}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ave\PYGZus{}chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cstherm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example if core/shell pairs and other molecules are present:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{csinfo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}CSID}\PYG{+w}{                       }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} property/atom command}
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NaCl\PYGZus{}CS\PYGZus{}x0.1\PYGZus{}prop.data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{csinfo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CS}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{Info}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} atom property added in the data\PYGZhy{}file}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}CSID}
\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{...}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The additional section in the date file would be formatted like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
CS\PYGZhy{}Info         \PYGZsh{} header of additional section

1   1           \PYGZsh{} column 1 = atom ID, column 2 = core/shell ID
2   1
3   2
4   2
5   3
6   3
7   4
8   4
(...)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Mitchell and Fincham)} Mitchell, Fincham, J Phys Condensed Matter,
5, 1031\sphinxhyphen{}1038 (1993).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_coreshell:mitchellfincham2}}

\subsection{Drude induced dipoles}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_drude:drude-induced-dipoles}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_drude::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermalized Drude model represents induced dipoles by a pair of
charges (the core atom and the Drude particle) connected by a harmonic
spring.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_polarizable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto polarizable}}}} doc page
for a discussion of all the polarizable models available in LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Drude model has a number of features aimed at its use in
molecular systems ({\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude:howto-lamoureux}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Lamoureux and Roux}}}}):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermostatting of the additional degrees of freedom associated with the
induced dipoles at very low temperature, in terms of the reduced
coordinates of the Drude particles with respect to their cores. This
makes the trajectory close to that of relaxed induced dipoles.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consistent definition of 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 to 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors. A core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude particle
pair represents a single (polarizable) atom, so the special screening
factors in a covalent structure should be the same for the core and
the Drude particle.  Drude particles have to inherit the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4
special neighbor relations from their respective cores.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Stabilization of the interactions between induced dipoles. Drude
dipoles on covalently bonded atoms interact too strongly due to the
short distances, so an atom may capture the Drude particle of a
neighbor, or the induced dipoles within the same molecule may align
too much. To avoid this, damping at short range can be done by Thole
functions (for which there are physical grounds). This Thole damping
is applied to the point charges composing the induced dipole (the
charge of the Drude particle and the opposite charge on the core, not
to the total charge of the core atom).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A detailed tutorial covering the usage of Drude induced dipoles in
LAMMPS is on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{here}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As with the core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model, the cores and Drude particles should
appear in the data file as standard atoms. The same holds for the
springs between them, which are described by standard harmonic bonds.
The nature of the atoms (core, Drude particle or non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable) is
specified via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix drude}}}} command.  The special
list of neighbors is automatically refactored to account for the
equivalence of core and Drude particles as regards special 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 to 1\sphinxhyphen{}4
screening. It may be necessary to use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/special/per/atom}
keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command. If using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}, make sure no Drude particle is in this fix
group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are three ways to thermostat the Drude particles at a low
temperature: use either {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin/drude}}}}
for a Langevin thermostat, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_drude_transform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix drude/transform/*}}}} for a Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover
thermostat, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix tgnvt/drude}}}} for a temperature\sphinxhyphen{}grouped Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat.
The first and third require use of the command {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel yes}}}}. The second requires two separate integration
fixes like \sphinxstyleemphasis{nvt} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{npt}. The correct temperatures of the reduced
degrees of freedom can be calculated using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/drude}}}}. This requires also to use the
command \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_modify vel yes}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Short\sphinxhyphen{}range damping of the induced dipole interactions can be achieved
using Thole functions through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_thole::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style thole}}}} in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid/overlay}}}}
with a Coulomb pair style. It may be useful to use \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long/cs} or
similar from the CORESHELL package if the core and Drude particle come
too close, which can cause numerical issues.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_drude:howto-lamoureux}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Lamoureux and Roux)} G. Lamoureux, B. Roux, J. Chem. Phys 119, 3025 (2003)

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Tutorial for Thermalized Drude oscillators in LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_drude2:tutorial-for-thermalized-drude-oscillators-in-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_drude2::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This tutorial explains how to use Drude oscillators in LAMMPS to
simulate polarizable systems using the DRUDE package. As an
illustration, the input files for a simulation of 250 phenol molecules
are documented. First of all, LAMMPS has to be compiled with the
DRUDE package activated. Then, the data file and input scripts
have to be modified to include the Drude dipoles and how to handle
them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example input scripts available: examples/PACKAGES/drude


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Overview of Drude induced dipoles}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Polarizable atoms acquire an induced electric dipole moment under the
action of an external electric field, for example the electric field
created by the surrounding particles.  Drude oscillators represent
these dipoles by two fixed charges: the core (DC) and the Drude
particle (DP) bound by a harmonic potential. The Drude particle can be
thought of as the electron cloud whose center can be displaced from
the position of the corresponding nucleus.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum of the masses of a core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pair should be the mass of the
initial (unsplit) atom, \(m_C + m_D = m\).  The sum of their charges
should be the charge of the initial (unsplit) atom, \(q_C + q_D = q\).
A harmonic potential between the core and Drude partners should be
present, with force constant \(k_D\) and an equilibrium distance of
zero. The (half\sphinxhyphen{})stiffness of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{harmonic bond}}}}
\(K_D = k_D/2\) and the Drude charge \(q_D\) are related to the atom
polarizability \(\alpha\) by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}K_D = \frac 1 2\, \frac {q_D^2} \alpha\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ideally, the mass of the Drude particle should be small, and the
stiffness of the harmonic bond should be large, so that the Drude
particle remains close to the core. The values of Drude mass, Drude
charge, and force constant can be chosen following different
strategies, as in the following examples of polarizable force
fields:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:lamoureux2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Lamoureux and Roux}}}} suggest adopting a global half\sphinxhyphen{}stiffness, \(K_D\) = 500 kcal/(mol Ang \({}^2\)) \sphinxhyphen{} which corresponds to a force constant \(k_D\) = 4184 kJ/(mol Ang \({}^2\)) \sphinxhyphen{} for all types of core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude bond, a global mass \(m_D\) = 0.4 g/mol (or u) for all types of Drude particles, and to calculate the Drude charges for individual atom types from the atom polarizabilities using equation (1). This choice is followed in the polarizable CHARMM force field.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternately {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:schroeder}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Schroeder and Steinhauser}}}} suggest adopting a global charge \(q_D\) = \sphinxhyphen{}1.0e and a global mass \(m_D\) = 0.1 g/mol (or u) for all Drude particles, and to calculate the force constant for each type of core\sphinxhyphen{}Drude bond from equation (1). The timesteps used by these authors are between 0.5 and 2 fs, with the degrees of freedom of the Drude oscillators kept cold at 1 K.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In both these force fields hydrogen atoms are treated as non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The motion of of the Drude particles can be calculated by minimizing
the energy of the induced dipoles at each timestep, by an iterative,
self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent procedure. The Drude particles can be massless and
therefore do not contribute to the kinetic energy. However, the
relaxed method is computational slow. An extended\sphinxhyphen{}lagrangian method
can be used to calculate the positions of the Drude particles, but
this requires them to have mass. It is important in this case to
decouple the degrees of freedom associated with the Drude oscillators
from those of the normal atoms. Thermalizing the Drude dipoles at
temperatures comparable to the rest of the simulation leads to several
problems (kinetic energy transfer, very short timestep, etc.), which
can be remedied by the “cold Drude” technique ({\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:lamoureux2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Lamoureux and Roux}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two closely related models are used to represent polarization through
“charges on a spring”: the core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model and the Drude
model. Although the basic idea is the same, the core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model is
normally used for ionic/crystalline materials, whereas the Drude model
is normally used for molecular systems and fluid states. In ionic
crystals the symmetry around each ion and the distance between them
are such that the core\sphinxhyphen{}shell model is sufficiently stable. But to be
applicable to molecular/covalent systems the Drude model includes two
important features:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The possibility to thermostat the additional degrees of freedom associated with the induced dipoles at very low temperature, in terms of the reduced coordinates of the Drude particles with respect to their cores. This makes the trajectory close to that of relaxed induced dipoles.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Drude dipoles on covalently bonded atoms interact too strongly due to the short distances, so an atom may capture the Drude particle (shell) of a neighbor, or the induced dipoles within the same molecule may align too much.  To avoid this, damping at short of the interactions between the point charges composing the induced dipole can be done by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:thole2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Thole}}}} functions.

\end{enumerate}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Preparation of the data file}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The data file is similar to a standard LAMMPS data file for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atom\_style full}.  The DPs and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic bonds} connecting them
to their DC should appear in the data file as normal atoms and bonds.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{polarizer} tool (Python script distributed with the
DRUDE package) to convert a non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable data file (here
\sphinxstyleemphasis{data.102494.lmp}) to a polarizable data file (\sphinxstyleemphasis{data\sphinxhyphen{}p.lmp})

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
polarizer\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}q\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }phenol.dff\PYG{+w}{ }data.102494.lmp\PYG{+w}{ }data\PYGZhy{}p.lmp
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will automatically insert the new atoms and bonds.
The masses and charges of DCs and DPs are computed
from \sphinxstyleemphasis{phenol.dff}, as well as the DC\sphinxhyphen{}DP bond constants.  The file
\sphinxstyleemphasis{phenol.dff} contains the polarizabilities of the atom types
and the mass of the Drude particles, for instance:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\# units: kJ/mol, A, deg
\# kforce is in the form k/2 r\_D\textasciicircum{}2
\# type  m\_D/u   q\_D/e    k\_D   alpha/A3  thole
OH      0.4    \sphinxhyphen{}1.0    4184.0   0.63     0.67
CA      0.4    \sphinxhyphen{}1.0    4184.0   1.36     2.51
CAI     0.4    \sphinxhyphen{}1.0    4184.0   1.09     2.51
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The hydrogen atoms are absent from this file, so they will be treated
as non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atoms.  In the non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable data file
\sphinxstyleemphasis{data.102494.lmp}, atom names corresponding to the atom type numbers
have to be specified as comments at the end of lines of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Masses}
section.  You probably need to edit it to add these names. It should
look like

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Masses

1 12.011 \PYGZsh{} CAI
2 12.011 \PYGZsh{} CA
3 15.999 \PYGZsh{} OH
4 1.008  \PYGZsh{} HA
5 1.008  \PYGZsh{} HO
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Basic input file}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom style should be set to (or derive from) \sphinxstyleemphasis{full}, so that you
can define atomic charges and molecular bonds, angles, dihedrals…

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{polarizer} tool also outputs certain lines related to the input
script (the use of these lines will be explained below).  In order for
LAMMPS to recognize that you are using Drude oscillators, you should
use the fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{drude}. The command is

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{D}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{D}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{D}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The N, C, D following the \sphinxstyleemphasis{drude} keyword have the following meaning:
There is one tag for each atom type. This tag is C for DCs, D for DPs
and N for non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atoms.  Here the atom types 1 to 3 (C and O
atoms) are DC, atom types 4 and 5 (H atoms) are non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable and
the atom types 6 to 8 are the newly created DPs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By recognizing the fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{drude}, LAMMPS will find and store matching
DC\sphinxhyphen{}DP pairs and will treat DP as equivalent to their DC in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{special bonds} relations.  It may be necessary to extend the space
for storing such special relations.  In this case extra space should
be reserved by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/special/per/atom} keyword of either
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}
command.  With our phenol, there is 1 more special neighbor for which
space is required.  Otherwise LAMMPS crashes and gives the required
value.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{p.lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{extra}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{per}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let us assume we want to run a simple NVT simulation at 300 K.  Note
that Drude oscillators need to be thermalized at a low temperature in
order to approximate a self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent field (SCF), therefore it is not
possible to simulate an NVE ensemble with this package.  Since dipoles
are approximated by a charged DC\sphinxhyphen{}DP pair, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style} must
include Coulomb interactions, for instance \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long} with
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_style pppm}. For example, with a cutoff of 10. and a precision
1.e\sphinxhyphen{}4:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{kspace\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pppm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}4}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As compared to the non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable input file, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} lines need
to be added for the DPs.  Since the DPs have no Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
interactions, their \(\epsilon\) is 0. so the only \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} line
that needs to be added is

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} All\PYGZhy{}DPs}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now for the thermalization, the simplest choice is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin/drude}}}}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LANG}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{langevin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12435}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{13977}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This applies a Langevin thermostat at temperature 300. to the centers
of mass of the DC\sphinxhyphen{}DP pairs, with relaxation time 100 and with random
seed 12345.  This fix applies also a Langevin thermostat at temperature
1. to the relative motion of the DPs around their DCs, with relaxation
time 20 and random seed 13977.  Only the DCs and non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable
atoms need to be in this fix’s group.  LAMMPS will thermostat the DPs
together with their DC.  For this, ghost atoms need to know their
velocities. Thus you need to add the following command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to avoid that the center of mass of the whole system
drifts due to the random forces of the Langevin thermostat on DCs, you
can add the \sphinxstyleemphasis{zero yes} option at the end of the fix line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{shake} is used to constrain the C\sphinxhyphen{}H bonds, it should be
invoked after the fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{langevin/drude} for more accuracy.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{SHAKE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shake}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The group of the fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{shake} must not include the DPs.  If the
group \sphinxstyleemphasis{ATOMS} is defined by non\sphinxhyphen{}DPs atom types, you could use
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since the fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{langevin/drude} does not perform time integration (just
modification of forces but no position/velocity updates), the fix
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nve} should be used in conjunction.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To avoid the flying ice cube artifact, where the atoms progressively freeze and the
center of mass of the whole system drifts faster and faster, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix momentum}
can be used. For instance:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{MOMENTUM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{momentum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, do not forget to update the atom type elements if you use
them in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump\_modify … element …} command, by adding the element
type of the DPs. Here for instance

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DUMP}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dump.lammpstrj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{element}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ix}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iz}
\PYG{k}{dump\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DUMP}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{element}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{D}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{D}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{D}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The input file should now be ready for use!

\sphinxAtStartPar
You will notice that the global temperature \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_temp} computed by
LAMMPS is not 300. K as wanted.  This is because LAMMPS treats DPs as
standard atoms in his default compute.  If you want to output the
temperatures of the DC\sphinxhyphen{}DP pair centers of mass and of the DPs relative
to their DCs, you should use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp\_drude}}}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{TDRUDE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{drude}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
And then output the correct temperatures of the Drude oscillators
using \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_style custom} with respectively \sphinxstyleemphasis{c\_TDRUDE{[}1{]}} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{c\_TDRUDE{[}2{]}}. These should be close to 300.0 and 1.0 on average.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}TDRUDE[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}TDRUDE[2]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Thole screening}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dipolar interactions represented by point charges on springs may not
be stable, for example if the atomic polarizability is too high for
instance, a DP can escape from its DC and be captured by another DC,
which makes the force and energy diverge and the simulation
crash. Even without reaching this extreme case, the correlation
between nearby dipoles on the same molecule may be exaggerated.  Often,
special bond relations prevent bonded neighboring atoms to see the
charge of each other’s DP, so that the problem does not always appear.
It is possible to use screened dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_thole::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{*pair\_style thole*}}}}.  This is implemented as a
correction to the Coulomb pair\_styles, which dampens at short distance
the interactions between the charges representing the induced dipoles.
It is to be used as \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} with any standard \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul} pair
style.  In our example, we would use

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tells LAMMPS that we are using two pair\_styles.  The first one is
as above (\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long 10.0}).  The second one is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{thole}
pair\_style with default screening factor 2.6 ({\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:noskov2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Noskov}}}}) and
cutoff 10.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} does not support mixing rules, the interaction
coefficients of all the pairs of atom types with i \textless{} j should be
explicitly defined.  The output of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{polarizer} script can be used
to complete the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} section of the input file.  In our
example, this will look like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0700}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{3.550}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0700}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{3.550}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.1091}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{3.310}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0458}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.985}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0700}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{3.550}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.1091}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{3.310}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0458}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.985}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.1700}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{3.070}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0714}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.745}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0300}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.420}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0000}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.000}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0.0000}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.000}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.090}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.218}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.829}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.590}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.090}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.218}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.829}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.590}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.360}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.218}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.360}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.926}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.590}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.630}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.670}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.630}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.670}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.090}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{7}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.360}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2.510}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{7}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.926}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1.590}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thole}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.630}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0.670}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{thole} pair style the coefficients are
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the atom polarizability in units of cubic length

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the screening factor of the Thole function (optional, default value
specified by the pair\_style command)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the cutoff (optional, default value defined by the pair\_style command)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The special neighbors have charge\sphinxhyphen{}charge and charge\sphinxhyphen{}dipole
interactions screened by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul} factors of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{special\_bonds}
command (0.0, 0.0, and 0.5 in the example above).  Without using the
pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{thole}, dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions are screened by the
same factor.  By using the pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{thole}, dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole
interactions are screened by Thole’s function, whatever their special
relationship (except within each DC\sphinxhyphen{}DP pair of course).  Consider for
example 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 neighbors: using the pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{thole}, their dipoles
will see each other (despite the \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul} factor being 0.) and the
interactions between these dipoles will be damped by Thole’s function.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Thermostats and barostats}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover barostat with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{langevin/drude} thermostat is
straightforward using fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{nph} instead of \sphinxstyleemphasis{nve}.  For example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NPH}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nph}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible to use a Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover instead of a Langevin
thermostat.  This requires to use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_drude_transform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{*fix drude/transform*}}}} just before and after the
time integration fixes.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix drude/transform/direct} converts the
atomic masses, positions, velocities and forces into a reduced
representation, where the DCs transform into the centers of mass of
the DC\sphinxhyphen{}DP pairs and the DPs transform into their relative position
with respect to their DC. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix drude/transform/inverse} performs
the reverse transformation.  For a NVT simulation, with the DCs and
atoms at 300 K and the DPs at 1 K relative to their DC one would use

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DIRECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{direct}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVT1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVT2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{INVERSE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{inverse}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For our phenol example, the groups would be defined as

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} DCs and non\PYGZhy{}polarizable atoms}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{CORES}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} DCs}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} DPs}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that with the fixes \sphinxstyleemphasis{drude/transform}, it is not required to
specify \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_modify vel yes} because the fixes do it anyway (several
times and for the forces also).

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is a bit more tricky to run a NPT simulation with Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover
barostat and thermostat.  First, the volume should be integrated only
once. So the fix for DCs and atoms should be \sphinxstyleemphasis{npt} while the fix for
DPs should be \sphinxstyleemphasis{nvt} (or vice versa).  Second, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix npt} computes a
global pressure and thus a global temperature whatever the fix group.
We do want the pressure to correspond to the whole system, but we want
the temperature to correspond to the fix group only.  We must then use
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\_modify} command for this.  In the end, the block of
instructions for thermostatting and barostatting will look like

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{TATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DIRECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{direct}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NPT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{npt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NPT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{TATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}press}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{INVERSE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{inverse}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another option for thermalizing the Drude model is to use the
temperature\sphinxhyphen{}grouped Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover (TGNH) thermostat proposed by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:tgnh-son}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Son)}}}}.
This is implemented as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix tgnvt/drude}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix tgnpt/drude}}}}.
It separates the kinetic energy into three contributions:
the molecular center of mass (COM) motion, the motion of atoms or atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs relative to molecular COMs,
and the relative motion of atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs.
An independent Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover chain is applied to each type of motion.
When TGNH is used, the temperatures of molecular, atomic and Drude motion can be printed out with {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style command}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NVT simulation with TGNH thermostat

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{TGNVT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tgnvt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}TGNVT[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}TGNVT[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}TGNVT[3]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
NPT simulation with TGNH thermostat

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{TGNPT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tgnpt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}TGNPT[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}TGNPT[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}TGNPT[3]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Rigid bodies}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You may want to simulate molecules as rigid bodies (but polarizable).
Common cases are water models such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:swm4-ndp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SWM4\sphinxhyphen{}NDP}}}}, which is a
kind of polarizable TIP4P water.  The rigid bodies and the DPs should
be integrated separately, even with the Langevin thermostat.  Let us
review the different thermostats and ensemble combinations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NVT ensemble using Langevin thermostat:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LANG}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{langevin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12435}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{13977}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RIGID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nve}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{small}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
NVT ensemble using Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DIRECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{direct}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RIGID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{small}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{INVERSE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{inverse}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
NPT ensemble with Langevin thermostat:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LANG}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{langevin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12435}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{13977}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RIGID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nph}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{small}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
NPT ensemble using Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{TATOM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DIRECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{direct}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RIGID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ATOMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{npt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{small}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RIGID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{TATOM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}press}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NVT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{INVERSE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{inverse}
