\subsection{Peridynamics with LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridynamics-with-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This Howto is based on the Sandia report 2010\sphinxhyphen{}5549 by Michael L. Parks,
Pablo Seleson, Steven J. Plimpton, Richard B. Lehoucq, and
Stewart A. Silling.


\subsubsection{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Peridynamics is a nonlocal extension of classical continuum mechanics.
The discrete peridynamic model has the same computational structure as a
molecular dynamics model.  This Howto provides a brief overview of the
peridynamic model of a continuum, then discusses how the peridynamic
model is discretized within LAMMPS as described in the original article
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:parks2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Parks)}}}}.  An example problem with comments is also
included.


\subsubsection{Quick Start}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:quick-start}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The peridynamics styles are included in the optional {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-peri}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{PERI package}}}}.  If your LAMMPS executable does not already include the
PERI package, you can see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{build instructions for packages}}}} for how to enable the package when compiling a custom
version of LAMMPS from source.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a minimal example for setting up a peridynamics simulation.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n}{si}
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{sc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0005}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{peri}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{map}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{array}
\PYG{k}{neighbor}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{0.0010}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}
\PYG{k}{region        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{target}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cylinder}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0050}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.0050}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{target}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{target}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{peri}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{pmb}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.6863e22}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0015001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0005}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}
\PYG{k}{set}\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{density}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2200}
\PYG{k}{set}\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.25e\PYGZhy{}10}
\PYG{k}{velocity      }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{k}{fix           }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\PYG{k}{compute       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{damage}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}7}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some notes on this input example:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
peridynamics simulations typically use SI {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
particles must be created on a {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{simple cubic lattice}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style peri}}}} is required

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
an {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom map}}}} is required for indexing particles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{skin distance}}}} used when computing neighbor lists
should be defined appropriately for your choice of simulation
parameters. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{skin} should be set to a value such that the
peridynamic horizon plus the skin distance is larger than the maximum
possible distance between two bonded particles (before their bond
breaks). Here it is set to 0.001 meters.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{peridynamics pair style}}}} is required.  Available
choices are currently: \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/eps}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/lps}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/pmb}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/ves}.  The model parameters are set with a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the mass density and volume fraction for each particle must be
defined.  This is done with the two {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} commands for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{density} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume}.  For a simple cubic lattice, the volume of a
particle should be equal to the cube of the lattice constant, here
\(V_i = \Delta x ^3\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} command all particles are initially at rest

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a plain {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet time integrator}}}} is used,
which is algebraically equivalent to a centered difference in time,
but numerically more stable

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you can compute the damage at the location of each particle with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_damage_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute damage/atom}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
finally, the timestep is set to 0.1 microseconds with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} command.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Peridynamic Model of a Continuum}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridynamic-model-of-a-continuum}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following is not a complete overview of peridynamics, but a
discussion of only those details specific to the model we have
implemented within LAMMPS. For more on the peridynamic theory, the
reader is referred to {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}. To begin,
we define the notation we will use.


\paragraph{Basic Notation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:basic-notation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Within the peridynamic literature, the following notational conventions
are generally used. The position of a given point in the reference
configuration is \(\textbf{x}\). Let
\(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t)\) and \(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x},t)\)
denote the displacement and position, respectively, of the point
\(\mathbf{x}\) at time \(t\). Define the relative position and
displacement vectors of two bonded points \(\textbf{x}\) and
\(\textbf{x}^\prime\) as \(\mathbf{\xi} = \textbf{x}^\prime -
\textbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{\eta} = \textbf{u}(\textbf{x}^\prime,t) -
\textbf{u}(\textbf{x},t)\), respectively. We note here that
\(\mathbf{\eta}\) is time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent, and that \(\mathbf{\xi}\)
is not. It follows that the relative position of the two bonded points
in the current configuration can be written as \(\boldsymbol{\xi} +
\boldsymbol{\eta} =
\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime},t)-\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x},t)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Peridynamic models are frequently written using \sphinxstyleemphasis{states}, which we
briefly describe here. For the purposes of our discussion, all states
are operators that act on vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). For a more
complete discussion of states, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}. A \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector state} is an operator whose image is a
vector, and may be viewed as a generalization of a second\sphinxhyphen{}rank
tensor. Similarly, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalar state} is an operator whose image is a
scalar. Of particular interest is the vector force state
\(\underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[ \mathbf{x},t \right]\left<
\mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x} \right>\), which is a mapping, having
units of force per volume squared, of the vector
\(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x}\) to the force vector state
field. The vector state operator \(\underline{\mathbf{T}}\) may
itself be a function of \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(t\). The
constitutive model is completely contained within
\(\underline{\mathbf{T}}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the peridynamic theory, the deformation at a point depends
collectively on all points interacting with that point. Using the
notation of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}, we write the
peridynamic equation of motion as

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:perinewtonii}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho(\mathbf{x}) \ddot{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{x},t) =
\int_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{x}}} \left\{
\underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[\mathbf{x},t
\right]\left<\mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x} \right> -
\underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[\mathbf{x}^{\prime},t
\right]\left<\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime} \right> \right\}
{d}V_{\mathbf{x}^\prime} + \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x},t), \qquad\qquad\textrm{(1)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\rho\) represents the mass density,
\(\underline{\mathbf{T}}\) the force vector state, and
\(\mathbf{b}\) an external body force density. A point
\(\mathbf{x}\) interacts with all the points
\(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\) within the neighborhood
\(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{x}}\), assumed to be a spherical region of
radius \(\delta>0\) centered at \(\mathbf{x}\). \(\delta\)
is called the \sphinxstyleemphasis{horizon}, and is analogous to the cutoff radius used in
molecular dynamics. Conditions on \(\underline{\mathbf{T}}\) for
which {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:perinewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(1)}}}} satisfies the balance of linear and angular
momentum are given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We consider only force vector states that can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underline{\mathbf{T}} = \underline{t}\,\underline{\mathbf{M}},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\underline{t}\) a \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalar force state} and
\(\underline{\mathbf{M}}\) the \sphinxstyleemphasis{deformed direction vector
state}, defined by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underline{\mathbf{M}}\left< \boldsymbol{\xi} \right> =
\left\{ \begin{array}{cl}
\frac{\boldsymbol{\xi} + \boldsymbol{\eta}}{
\left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi} + \boldsymbol{\eta} \right\Vert
} & \left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi} + \boldsymbol{\eta} \right\Vert \neq 0 \\
\boldsymbol{0}  & \textrm{otherwise}
\end{array}
\right. . \qquad\qquad\textrm{(2)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Such force states correspond to so\sphinxhyphen{}called \sphinxstyleemphasis{ordinary} materials
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}. These are the materials for which
the force between any two interacting points \(\textbf{x}\) and
\(\textbf{x}^\prime\) acts along the line between the points.


\paragraph{Linear Peridynamic Solid (LPS) Model}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:linear-peridynamic-solid-lps-model}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We summarize the linear peridynamic solid (LPS) material model. For more
on this model, the reader is referred to {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}.  This model is a nonlocal analogue to a classical
linear elastic isotropic material. The elastic properties of a a
classical linear elastic isotropic material are determined by (for
example) the bulk and shear moduli. For the LPS model, the elastic
properties are analogously determined by the bulk and shear moduli,
along with the horizon \(\delta\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LPS model has a force scalar state
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underline{t} = \frac{3K\theta}{m}\underline{\omega}\,\underline{x} +
\alpha \underline{\omega}\,\underline{e}^{\rm d}, \qquad\qquad\textrm{(3)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(K\) the bulk modulus and \(\alpha\) related to the shear
modulus \(G\) as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\alpha = \frac{15 G}{m}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The remaining components of the model are described as follows. Define
the reference position scalar state \(\underline{x}\) so that
\(\underline{x}\left<\boldsymbol{\xi} \right> = \left\Vert
\boldsymbol{\xi} \right\Vert\). Then, the weighted volume \(m\) is
defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}m\left[ \mathbf{x} \right] = \int_{\mathcal{H}_\mathbf{x}}
\underline{\omega} \left<\boldsymbol{\xi}\right>
\underline{x}\left<\boldsymbol{\xi} \right>
\underline{x}\left<\boldsymbol{\xi} \right>{d}V_{\boldsymbol{\xi} }.  \qquad\qquad\textrm{(4)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underline{e}\left[ \mathbf{x},t \right] \left<\boldsymbol{\xi}
\right> = \left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi} + \boldsymbol{\eta}
\right\Vert - \left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi} \right\Vert\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
be the extension scalar state, and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\theta\left[ \mathbf{x}, t \right] = \frac{3}{m\left[ \mathbf{x}
\right]}\int_{\mathcal{H}_\mathbf{x}} \underline{\omega}
\left<\boldsymbol{\xi}\right> \underline{x}\left<\boldsymbol{\xi}
\right> \underline{e}\left[ \mathbf{x},t
\right]\left<\boldsymbol{\xi} \right>{d}V_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
be the dilatation. The isotropic and deviatoric parts of the extension
scalar state are defined, respectively, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underline{e}^{\rm i}=\frac{\theta \underline{x}}{3}, \qquad
\underline{e}^{\rm d} = \underline{e}- \underline{e}^{\rm i},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the arguments of the state functions and the vectors on which they
operate are omitted for simplicity. We note that the LPS model is linear
in the dilatation \(\theta\), and in the deviatoric part of the
extension \(\underline{e}^{\rm d}\).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The weighted volume \(m\) is time\sphinxhyphen{}independent, and does
not change as bonds break. It is computed with respect to the bond
family defined at the reference (initial) configuration.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The non\sphinxhyphen{}negative scalar state \(\underline{\omega}\) is an
\sphinxstyleemphasis{influence function} {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}. For more on
influence functions, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:seleson2010}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Seleson 2010)}}}}. If an
influence function \(\underline{\omega}\) depends only upon the
scalar \(\left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi} \right\Vert\), (i.e.,
\(\underline{\omega}\left<\boldsymbol{\xi}\right> =
\underline{\omega}\left<\left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi} \right\Vert\right>\)), then \(\underline{\omega}\) is a spherical influence function.
For a spherical influence function, the LPS model is isotropic
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the LAMMPS implementation of the LPS model, the influence function
\(\underline{\omega}\left<\left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi}
\right\Vert\right> = 1 / \left\Vert \boldsymbol{\xi} \right\Vert\) is
used. However, the user can define their own influence function by
altering the method “influence\_function” in the file
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_peri\_lps.cpp}}. The LAMMPS peridynamics code permits both
spherical and non\sphinxhyphen{}spherical influence functions (e.g., isotropic and
non\sphinxhyphen{}isotropic materials).
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\paragraph{Prototype Microelastic Brittle (PMB) Model}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:prototype-microelastic-brittle-pmb-model}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We summarize the prototype microelastic brittle (PMB) material
model. For more on this model, the reader is referred to
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2000-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2000)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2005)}}}}.  This model is a special case of the LPS model; see
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:seleson2010}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Seleson 2010)}}}} for the derivation. The elastic
properties of the PMB model are determined by the bulk modulus \(K\)
and the horizon \(\delta\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The PMB model is expressed using the scalar force state field

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peripmbstate}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underline{t}\left[ \mathbf{x},t \right]\left< \boldsymbol{\xi} \right> = \frac{1}{2} f\left( \boldsymbol{\eta} ,\boldsymbol{\xi} \right), \qquad\qquad\textrm{(5)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(f\) a scalar\sphinxhyphen{}valued function. We assume that \(f\) takes
the form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f = c s,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peric}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c = \frac{18K}{\pi \delta^4}, \qquad\qquad\textrm{(6)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(K\) the bulk modulus and \(\delta\) the horizon, and
\(s\) the bond stretch, defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi}) = \frac{ \left\Vert {\mathbf{\eta}+\mathbf{\xi}} \right\Vert - \left\Vert {\mathbf{\xi}} \right\Vert }{\left\Vert {\mathbf{\xi}} \right\Vert}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bond stretch is a unitless quantity, and identical to a one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional
definition of strain. As such, we see that a bond at its equilibrium
length has stretch \(s=0\), and a bond at twice its equilibrium
length has stretch \(s=1\).  The constant \(c\) given above is
appropriate for 3D models only. For more on the origins of the constant
\(c\), see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2005)}}}}. For the derivation
of \(c\) for 1D and 2D models, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:emmrich2007}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Emmrich)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peripmbstate}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(5)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:perinewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(1)}}}} reduces to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho(\mathbf{x}) \ddot{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \int_{\mathcal{H}_\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{f} \left( \boldsymbol{\eta},\boldsymbol{\xi} \right){d}V_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} + \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x},t), \qquad\qquad\textrm{(7)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{f} \left( \boldsymbol{\eta},  \boldsymbol{\xi}\right) =f \left( \boldsymbol{\eta},  \boldsymbol{\xi}\right)  \frac{\boldsymbol{\xi}+ \boldsymbol{\eta}}{ \left\Vert {\boldsymbol{\xi} + \boldsymbol{\eta}} \right\Vert}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike the LPS model, the PMB model has a Poisson ratio of
\(\nu=1/4\) in 3D, and \(\nu=1/3\) in 2D. This is reflected in
the input for the PMB model, which requires only the bulk modulus of the
material, whereas the LPS model requires both the bulk and shear moduli.


\paragraph{Damage}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:damage}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridamage}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bonds are made to break when they are stretched beyond a given
limit. Once a bond fails, it is failed forever {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling)}}}}. Further, new bonds are never created during the course
of a simulation. We discuss only one criterion for bond breaking, called
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{critical stretch} criterion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define \(\mu\) to be the history\sphinxhyphen{}dependent scalar
boolean function

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:perimu}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mu(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi}) = \left\{
\begin{array}{cl}
1 & \mbox{if $s(t^\prime,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi})< \min \left(s_0(t^\prime,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi}) , s_0(t^\prime,\mathbf{\eta}^\prime,\mathbf{\xi}^\prime) \right)$ for all $0 \leq t^\prime \leq t$} \\
0 & \mbox{otherwise}
\end{array}\right\}.  \qquad\qquad\textrm{(8)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\mathbf{\eta}^\prime = \textbf{u}(\textbf{x}^{\prime
\prime},t) - \textbf{u}(\textbf{x}^\prime,t)\) and
\(\mathbf{\xi}^\prime = \textbf{x}^{\prime \prime} -
\textbf{x}^\prime\). Here, \(s_0(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi})\) is a
critical stretch defined as

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peris0}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_0(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi}) = s_{00} - \alpha s_{\min}(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi}), \qquad s_{\min}(t) = \min_{\mathbf{\xi}} s(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi}), \qquad\qquad\textrm{(9)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(s_{00}\) and \(\alpha\) are material\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
constants. The history function \(\mu\) breaks bonds when the
stretch \(s\) exceeds the critical stretch \(s_0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Although \(s_0(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi})\) is expressed as a
property of a particle, bond breaking must be a symmetric operation for
all particle pairs sharing a bond. That is, particles \(\textbf{x}\)
and \(\textbf{x}^\prime\) must utilize the same test when deciding
to break their common bond. This can be done by any method that treats
the particles symmetrically. In the definition of \(\mu\) above, we
have chosen to take the minimum of the two \(s_0\) values for
particles \(\textbf{x}\) and \(\textbf{x}^\prime\) when
determining if the \(\textbf{x}\)\textendash{}\(\textbf{x}^\prime\) bond
should be broken.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling)}}}}, we can define the damage at a
point \(\textbf{x}\) as

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridamageeq}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(\textbf{x}, t) = 1 - \frac{\int_{\mathcal{H}_{\textbf{x}}} \mu(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi}) dV_{\textbf{x}^\prime}
}{ \int_{\mathcal{H}_{\textbf{x}}} dV_{\textbf{x}^\prime} }.  \qquad\qquad\textrm{(10)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Discrete Peridynamic Model and LAMMPS Implementation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:discrete-peridynamic-model-and-lammps-implementation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, instead of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:perinewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(1)}}}}, we model this equation of
motion:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho(\mathbf{x}) \ddot{\textbf{y}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \int_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{x}}}
\left\{ \underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[ \mathbf{x},t \right]\left<\mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x} \right>
- \underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[\mathbf{x}^{\prime},t \right]\left<\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime} \right> \right\}
  {d}V_{\mathbf{x}^\prime} + \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x},t),\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where we explicitly track and store at each timestep the positions and
not the displacements of the particles. We observe that
\(\ddot{\textbf{y}}(\textbf{x}, t) = \ddot{\textbf{x}} +
\ddot{\textbf{u}}(\textbf{x}, t) = \ddot{\textbf{u}}(\textbf{x}, t)\), so
that this is equivalent to {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:perinewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(1)}}}}.


\paragraph{Spatial Discretization}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:spatial-discretization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The region defining a peridynamic material is discretized into particles
forming a simple cubic lattice with lattice constant \(\Delta x\),
where each particle \(i\) is associated with some volume fraction
\(V_i\). For any particle \(i\), let \(\mathcal{F}_i\)
denote the family of particles for which particle \(i\) shares a
bond in the reference configuration.  That is,

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peribondfamily}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{F}_i = \{ p ~ | ~ \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert \leq \delta \}. \qquad\qquad\textrm{(11)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The discretized equation of motion replaces {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:perinewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(1)}}}} with

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridiscretenewtonii}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho \ddot{\textbf{y}}_i^n =
\sum_{p \in \mathcal{F}_i}
\left\{ \underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[ \textbf{x}_i,t \right]\left<\textbf{x}_p^{\prime}-\textbf{x}_i \right>
- \underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[\textbf{x}_p,t \right]\left<\textbf{x}_i-\textbf{x}_p \right> \right\}
  V_{p} + \textbf{b}_i^n, \qquad\qquad\textrm{(12)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(n\) is the timestep number and subscripts denote the particle number.


\paragraph{Short\sphinxhyphen{}Range Forces}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:short-range-forces}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the model discussed so far, particles interact only through their
bond forces. A particle with no bonds becomes a free non\sphinxhyphen{}interacting
particle. To account for contact forces, short\sphinxhyphen{}range forces are
introduced {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}. We add to the force in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridiscretenewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(12)}}}} the following force
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\textbf{f}_S(\textbf{y}_p,\textbf{y}_i) = \min \left\{ 0, \frac{c_S}{\delta}(\left\Vert {\textbf{y}_p-\textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert - d_{pi}) \right\}
\frac{\textbf{y}_p-\textbf{y}_i}{\left\Vert {\textbf{y}_p-\textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert}, \qquad\qquad\textrm{(13)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(d_{pi}\) is the short\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction distance between
particles \(p\) and \(i\), and \(c_S\) is a multiple of the
constant \(c\) from {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peric}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(6)}}}}. Note that the short\sphinxhyphen{}range force
is always repulsive, never attractive. In practice, we choose

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:perics}}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_S = 15 \frac{18K}{\pi \delta^4}. \qquad\qquad\textrm{(14)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the short\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction distance, we choose {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2007-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}d_{pi} = \min \left\{ 0.9 \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert, 1.35 (r_p + r_i) \right\}, \qquad\qquad\textrm{(15)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(r_i\) is called the \sphinxstyleemphasis{node radius} of particle
\(i\). Given a discrete lattice, we choose \(r_i\) to be half
the lattice constant.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a simple cubic lattice, \(\Delta x = \Delta y = \Delta z\).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given this definition of \(d_{pi}\), contact forces appear only when
particles are under compression.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When accounting for short\sphinxhyphen{}range forces, it is convenient to define the
short\sphinxhyphen{}range family of particles
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{F}^S_i = \{ p ~ | ~ \left\Vert {\textbf{y}_p - \textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert \leq d_{pi} \}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{Modification to the Particle Volume}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:modification-to-the-particle-volume}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The right\sphinxhyphen{}hand side of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridiscretenewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(12)}}}} may be thought of as
a midpoint quadrature of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:perinewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(1)}}}}. To slightly improve the
accuracy of this quadrature, we discuss a modification to the particle
volume used in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridiscretenewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(12)}}}}. In a situation where two
particles share a bond with \(\left\Vert { \textbf{x}_p -
\textbf{x}_i }\right\Vert = \delta\), for example, we suppose that only
approximately half the volume of each particle is “seen” by the other
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri:silling2007}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2007)}}}}. When computing the force of each
particle on the other we use \(V_p / 2\) rather than \(V_p\) in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridiscretenewtonii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(12)}}}}. As such, we introduce a nodal volume
scaling function for all bonded particles where \(\delta - r_i \leq
\left\Vert { \textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i } \right\Vert \leq \delta\) (see
the Figure below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
We choose to use a linear unitless nodal volume scaling function
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nu(\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i) = \left\{
\begin{array}{cl}
-\frac{1}{2 r_i} \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert + \left( \frac{\delta}{2 r_i} + \frac{1}{2} \right) & \mbox{if }
\delta - r_i \leq \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i } \right\Vert \leq \delta \\
1 & \mbox{if } \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i } \right\Vert \leq \delta - r_i \\
0 & \mbox{otherwise}
\end{array}
\right\}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(\left\Vert {\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert = \delta\), \(\nu = 0.5\), and if
\(\left\Vert {\textbf{x}_p - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert = \delta - r_i\), \(\nu = 1.0\), for
example.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{pdlammps_fig1}.png}
\caption{Diagram showing horizon of a particular particle, demonstrating that
the volume associated with particles near the boundary of the horizon is
not completely contained within the horizon.}\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:id2}}\end{figure}


\paragraph{Temporal Discretization}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:temporal-discretization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When discretizing time in LAMMPS, we use a velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet scheme, where
both the position and velocity of the particle are stored
explicitly. The velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet scheme is generally expressed in three
steps. In {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 1}}}}, \(\rho_i\) denotes the
mass density of a particle and \(\widetilde{\textbf{f}}_i^n\)
denotes the the net force density on particle \(i\) at timestep
\(n\). The LAMMPS command {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} performs a
velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet integration.
\begin{quote}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Algorithm 1: Velocity Verlet}

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] 1: \(\textbf{v}_i^{n + 1/2} = \textbf{v}_i^n + \frac{\Delta t}{2 \rho_i} \widetilde{\textbf{f}}_i^n\)
\item[] 2: \(\textbf{y}_i^{n+1}     = \textbf{y}_i^n + \Delta t \textbf{v}_i^{n + 1/2}\)
\item[] 3: \(\textbf{v}_i^{n+1} = \textbf{v}_i^{n+1/2} + \frac{\Delta t}{2 \rho_i} \widetilde{\textbf{f}}_i^{n+1}\)
\end{DUlineblock}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\paragraph{Breaking Bonds}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:breaking-bonds}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
During the course of simulation, it may be necessary to break bonds, as
described in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridamage}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Damage section}}}}. Bonds are recorded
as broken in a simulation by removing them from the bond family
\(\mathcal{F}_i\) (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peribondfamily}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(11)}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A naive implementation would have us first loop over all bonds and
compute \(s_{min}\) in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peris0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(9)}}}}, then loop over all bonds
again and break bonds with a stretch \(s > s0\) as in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:perimu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(8)}}}}, and finally loop over all particles and compute forces
for the next step of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 1}}}}. For reasons of
computational efficiency, we will utilize the values of \(s_0\) from
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{previous} timestep when deciding to break a bond.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the first timestep, \(s_0\) is initialized to
\(\mathbf{\infty}\) for all nodes. This means that no bonds may
be broken until the second timestep. As such, it is recommended that
the first few timesteps of the peridynamic simulation not involve any
actions that might result in the breaking of bonds. As a practical
example, the projectile in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:periexample}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{commented example below}}}} is placed such that it does not impact the target
brittle plate until several timesteps into the simulation.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\paragraph{LPS Pseudocode}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:lps-pseudocode}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A sketch of the LPS model implementation in the PERI package appears in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 2}}}}. This algorithm makes use of the
routines in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilpsm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 3}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilpstheta}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 4}}}}.
\begin{quote}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilps}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Algorithm 2: LPS Peridynamic Model Pseudocode}

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] Fix \(s_{00}\), \(\alpha\), horizon \(\delta\), bulk modulus \(K\), shear modulus \(G\), timestep \(\Delta t\), and generate initial lattice of particles with lattice constant \(\Delta x\). Let there be \(N\) particles. Define constant \(c_S\) for repulsive short\sphinxhyphen{}range forces.
\item[] Initialize bonds between all particles \(i \neq j\) where \(\left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert \leq \delta\)
\item[] Initialize weighted volume \(m\) for all particles using {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilpsm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 3}}}}
\item[] Initialize \(s_0 = \mathbf{\infty}\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Initialize each entry to MAX\_DOUBLE}\}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{while} not done \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] Perform step 1 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 1}}}}, updating velocities of all particles
\item[] Perform step 2 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 1}}}}, updating positions of all particles
\item[] \(\tilde{s}_0 = \mathbf{\infty}\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Initialize each entry to MAX\_DOUBLE}\}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for} \(i=1\) to \(N\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \{Compute short\sphinxhyphen{}range forces\}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for all} particles \(j \in \mathcal{F}^S_i\) (the short\sphinxhyphen{}range family of nodes for particle \(i\)) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(r = \left\Vert {\textbf{y}_j - \textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert\)
\item[] \(dr = \min \{ 0, r - d \}\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Short\sphinxhyphen{}range forces are only repulsive, never attractive}\}
\item[] \(k = \frac{c_S}{\delta} V_k dr\) \{\(c_S\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{defined in :ref:\textasciigrave{}(14) \textless{}pericS\textgreater{}\textasciigrave{}}\}
\item[] \(\textbf{f} = \textbf{f} + k \frac{\textbf{y}_j-\textbf{y}_i}{\left\Vert {\textbf{y}_j-\textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert}\)
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\item[] Compute the dilatation for each particle using {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilpstheta}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 4}}}}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for} \(i=1\) to \(N\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \{Compute bond forces\}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for all} particles \(j\) sharing an unbroken bond with particle \(i\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(e = \left\Vert {\textbf{y}_j - \textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert - \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert\)
\item[] \(\omega_+ = \underline{\omega}\left<\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i\right>\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Influence function evaluation}\}
\item[] \(\omega_- = \underline{\omega}\left<\textbf{x}_i - \textbf{x}_j\right>\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Influence function evaluation}\}
\item[] \(\hat{f} = \left[ (3K-5G)\left( \frac{\theta(i)}{m(i)}\omega_+ + \frac{\theta(j)}{m(j)}\omega_- \right) \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert + 15G \left( \frac{\omega_+}{m(i)} + \frac{\omega_-}{m(j)} \right) e \right] \nu(\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i) V_j\)
\item[] \(\textbf{f} = \textbf{f} + \hat{f} \frac{\textbf{y}_j-\textbf{y}_i}{\left\Vert {\textbf{y}_j-\textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert}\)
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{if} \((dr / \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert) > \min(s_0(i), s_0(j))\) \sphinxstylestrong{then}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] Break \(i\)’s bond with \(j\) \{\(j\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{‘s bond with} \(i\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{will be broken when this loop iterates on} \(j\)\}
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end if}
\item[] \(\tilde{s}_0(i) = \min (\tilde{s}_0(i),s_{00}-\alpha(dr / \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert))\)
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\item[] \(s_0 = \tilde{s}_0\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Store for use in next timestep}\}
\item[] Perform step 3 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 1}}}}, updating velocities of all particles
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end while}
\end{DUlineblock}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilpsm}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Algorithm 3: Computation of Weighted Volume \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}}

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for} \(i=1\) to \(N\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(m(i) = 0.0\)
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for all} particles \(j\) sharing a bond with particle \(i\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(m(i) = m(i) + \underline{\omega}\left<\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i\right> \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert^2 \nu(\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i) V_j\)
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\end{DUlineblock}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilpstheta}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Algorithm 4: Computation of Dilatation \protect\(\theta\protect\)}

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for} \(i=1\) to \(N\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(\theta(i) = 0.0\)
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for all} particles \(j\) sharing an unbroken bond with particle \(i\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(e = \left\Vert {\textbf{y}_i - \textbf{y}_j} \right\Vert - \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_i - \textbf{x}_j} \right\Vert\)
\item[] \(\theta(i) = \theta(i) + \underline{\omega}\left<\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i\right> \left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert e  \nu(\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i) V_j\)
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\item[] \(\theta(i) = \frac{3}{m(i)}\theta(i)\)
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\end{DUlineblock}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}


\paragraph{PMB Pseudocode}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:pmb-pseudocode}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A sketch of the PMB model implementation in the PERI package appears in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperipmb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 5}}}}.
\begin{quote}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperipmb}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Algorithm 5: PMB Peridynamic Model Pseudocode}

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] Fix \(s_{00}\), \(\alpha\), horizon \(\delta\), spring constant \(c\), timestep \(\Delta t\), and generate initial lattice of particles with lattice constant \(\Delta x\). Let there be \(N\) particles.
\item[] Initialize bonds between all particles \(i \neq j\) where \(\left\Vert {\textbf{x}_j - \textbf{x}_i} \right\Vert \leq \delta\)
\item[] Initialize \(s_0 = \mathbf{\infty}\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Initialize each entry to MAX\_DOUBLE}\}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{while} not done \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] Perform step 1 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 1}}}}, updating velocities of all particles
\item[] Perform step 2 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algvelverlet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 1}}}}, updating positions of all particles
\item[] \(\tilde{s}_0 = \mathbf{\infty}\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Initialize each entry to MAX\_DOUBLE}\}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for} \(i=1\) to \(N\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \{Compute short\sphinxhyphen{}range forces\}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for all} particles \(j \in \mathcal{F}^S_i\) (the short\sphinxhyphen{}range family of nodes for particle \(i\)) \sphinxstylestrong{do}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(r = \left\Vert {\textbf{y}_j - \textbf{y}_i} \right\Vert\)
\item[] \(dr = \min \{ 0, r - d \}\) \{\sphinxstyleemphasis{Short\sphinxhyphen{}range forces are only repulsive, never attractive}\}
\item[] \(k = \frac{c_S}{\delta} V_k dr\) \{\(c_S\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{defined in :ref:\textasciigrave{}(14) \textless{}pericS\textgreater{}\textasciigrave{}}\}

\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end for}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{for} \(i=1\) to \(N\) \sphinxstylestrong{do}

\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}

\paragraph{Damage}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The damage associated with every particle (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peridamageeq}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(10)}}}}) can
optionally be computed and output with a LAMMPS data dump. To do this,
your input script must contain the command {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_damage_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute damage/atom}}}} This enables a LAMMPS per\sphinxhyphen{}atom compute to
calculate the damage associated with each particle every time a LAMMPS
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data dump}}}} frame is written.


\paragraph{Visualizing Simulation Results}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:visualizing-simulation-results}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are multiple ways to visualize the simulation results. Typically,
you want to display the particles and color code them by the value
computed with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_damage_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute damage/atom}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be done, for example, by using the built\sphinxhyphen{}in visualizer of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image or dump movie}}}} command to create snapshot
images or a movie. Below are example command lines for using dump image
with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:periexample}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{example listed below}}}} and a set of images
created for steps 300, 600, and 2000 this way.

\PYG{k}{dump\PYGZus{}modify     }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{D2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pad}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adiam}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ca}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{blue}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yellow}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{max}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{red}

\paragraph{Pitfalls}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:pitfalls}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Parallel Scalability}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS operates in parallel in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_part::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{spatial\sphinxhyphen{}decomposition mode}}}}, where each processor owns a spatial subdomain of
the overall simulation domain and communicates with its neighboring
processors via distributed\sphinxhyphen{}memory message passing (MPI) to acquire ghost
atom information to allow forces on the atoms it owns to be
computed. LAMMPS also uses Verlet neighbor lists which are recomputed
every few timesteps as particles move. On these timesteps, particles
also migrate to new processors as needed. LAMMPS decomposes the overall
simulation domain so that spatial subdomains of nearly equal volume are
assigned to each processor. When each subdomain contains nearly the
same number of particles, this results in a reasonable load balance
among all processors. As is more typical with some peridynamic
simulations, some subdomains may contain many particles while other
subdomains contain few particles, resulting in a load imbalance that
impacts parallel scalability.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Setting the “skin” distance}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} command with LAMMPS is used to set the
so\sphinxhyphen{}called “skin” distance used when building neighbor lists. All atom
pairs within a cutoff distance equal to the horizon \(\delta\) plus
the skin distance are stored in the list. Unexpected crashes in LAMMPS
may be due to too small a skin distance. The skin should be set to a
value such that \(\delta\) plus the skin distance is larger than the
maximum possible distance between two bonded particles. For example, if
\(s_{00}\) is increased, the skin distance may also need to be
increased.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{“Lost” particles}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All particles are contained within the “simulation box” of LAMMPS. The
boundaries of this box may change with time, or not, depending on how
the LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command has been set. If a
particle drifts outside the simulation box during the course of a
simulation, it is called \sphinxstyleemphasis{lost}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an option of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{themo\_modify}}}} command of
LAMMPS, the lost keyword determines whether LAMMPS checks for lost atoms
each time it computes thermodynamics and what it does if atoms are
lost. If the value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{ignore}, LAMMPS does not check for lost atoms. If
the value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{error} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{warn}, LAMMPS checks and either issues an error
or warning. The code will exit with an error and continue with a
warning. This can be a useful debugging option. The default behavior of
LAMMPS is to exit with an error if a particle is lost.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The peridynamic module within LAMMPS does not check for lost atoms. If a
particle with unbroken bonds is lost, those bonds are marked as broken
by the remaining particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Defining the peridynamic horizon} \(\mathbf{\delta}\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command, the user must specify the
horizon \(\delta\). This argument determines which particles are
bonded when the simulation is initialized. It is recommended that
\(\delta\) be set to a small fraction of a lattice constant larger than
desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, if the lattice constant is 0.0005 and you wish to set the
horizon to three times the lattice constant, then set \(\delta\) to
be 0.0015001, a value slightly larger than three times the lattice
constant. This guarantees that particles three lattice constants away
from each other are still bonded. If \(\delta\) is set to 0.0015,
for example, floating point error may result in some pairs of particles
three lattice constants apart not being bonded.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Breaking bonds too early}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For technical reasons, the bonds in the simulation are not created until
the end of the first timestep of the simulation. Therefore, one should
not attempt to break bonds until at least the second step of the
simulation.


\paragraph{Bugs}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:bugs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The user is cautioned that this code is a beta release. If you are
confident that you have found a bug in the peridynamic module, please
report it in a \sphinxtitleref{GitHub Issue \textless{}https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues\textgreater{}}
or send an email to the LAMMPS developers. First, check the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bug.html}{New
features and bug fixes} section of
the LAMMPS website site to see if the bug has already been reported or
fixed. If not, the most useful thing you can do for us is to isolate the
problem. Run it on the smallest number of atoms and fewest number of
processors and with the simplest input script that reproduces the
bug. In your message, describe the problem and any ideas you have as to
what is causing it or where in the code the problem might be.  We’ll
request your input script and data files if necessary.


\paragraph{Modifying and Extending the Peridynamic Module}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:modifying-and-extending-the-peridynamic-module}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To add new features or peridynamic potentials to the peridynamic module,
the user is referred to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modifying \& extending LAMMPS}}}}
section. To develop a new bond\sphinxhyphen{}based material, start with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/pmb}
pair style as a template. To develop a new state\sphinxhyphen{}based material, start
with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/lps} pair style as a template.


\subsubsection{A Numerical Example}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:a-numerical-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To introduce the peridynamic implementation within LAMMPS, we replicate
a numerical experiment taken from section 6 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2005)}}}}.


\paragraph{Problem Description and Setup}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:problem-description-and-setup}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We consider the impact of a rigid sphere on a homogeneous disk of
brittle material. The sphere has diameter \(0.01\) m and velocity
100 m/s directed normal to the surface of the target. The target
material has density \(\rho = 2200\) kg/m:math:\sphinxtitleref{\textasciicircum{}3}. A PMB material
model is used with \(K = 14.9\) GPa and critical bond stretch
parameters given by \(s_{00} = 0.0005\) and \(\alpha = 0.25\). A
three\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional simple cubic lattice is constructed with lattice
constant \(0.0005\) m and horizon \(0.0015\) m. (The horizon is
three times the lattice constant.) The target is a cylinder of diameter
\(0.074\) m and thickness \(0.0025\) m, and the associated
lattice contains 103,110 particles. Each particle \(i\) has volume
fraction \(V_i = 1.25 \times 10^{-10} \textrm{m}^3\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The spring constant in the PMB material model is (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peric}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(6)}}}})
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c = \frac{18k}{\pi \delta^4} = \frac{18 (14.9 \times 10^9)}{ \pi (1.5 \times 10^{-3})^4} \approx 1.6863 \times 10^{22}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The CFL analysis from {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling2005)}}}} shows that a
timestep of \(1.0 \times 10^{-7}\) is safe.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We observe here that in IEEE double\sphinxhyphen{}precision floating point arithmetic
when computing the bond stretch \(s(t,\mathbf{\eta},\mathbf{\xi})\)
at each iteration where \(\left\Vert {\mathbf{\eta}+\mathbf{\xi}}
\right\Vert\) is computed during the iteration and \(\left\Vert
{\mathbf{\xi}} \right\Vert\) was computed and stored for the initial
lattice, it may be that \(fl(s) = \varepsilon\) with \(\left|
\varepsilon \right| \leq \varepsilon_{machine}\) for an unstretched
bond. Taking \(\varepsilon = 2.220446049250313 \times 10^{-16}\), we
see that the value \(c s V_i \approx 4.68 \times 10^{-4}\), computed
when determining \(f\), is perhaps larger than we would like,
especially when the true force should be zero. One simple way to avoid
this issue is to insert the following instructions in Algorithm
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperipmb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 5}}}} after instruction 21 (and similarly for
Algorithm {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:algperilps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Algorithm 2}}}}):
\begin{quote}

\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{if} \(\left| dr \right| < \varepsilon_{machine}\) \sphinxstylestrong{then}
\item[]
\begin{DUlineblock}{\DUlineblockindent}
\item[] \(dr = 0\)
\end{DUlineblock}
\item[] \sphinxstylestrong{end if}
\end{DUlineblock}
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Qualitatively, this says that displacements from equilibrium on the
order of \(10^{-16}\)m are taken to be exactly zero, a seemingly
reasonable assumption.


\paragraph{The Projectile}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:the-projectile}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The projectile used in the following experiments is not the one used in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:silling2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silling 2005)}}}}. The projectile used here exerts a
force
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F(r) = - k_s (r - R)^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
on each atom where \(k_s\) is a specified force constant, \(r\) is
the distance from the atom to the center of the indenter, and \(R\)
is the radius of the projectile. The force is repulsive and \(F(r) =
0\) for \(r > R\). For our problem, the projectile radius \(R =
0.05\) m, and we have chosen \(k_s = 1.0 \times 10^{17}\) (compare
with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:peric}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(6)}}}} above).


\paragraph{Writing the LAMMPS Input File}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:writing-the-lammps-input-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We discuss the example input script {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:periexample}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{listed below}}}}.
In line 2 we specify that SI units are to be used. We specify the
dimension (3) and boundary conditions (“shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped”) for the
computational domain in lines 3 and 4. In line 5 we specify that
peridynamic particles are to be used for this simulation. In line 7, we
set the “skin” distance used in building the LAMMPS neighbor list. In
line 8 we set the lattice constant (in meters) and in line 10 we define
the spatial region where the target will be placed. In line 12 we
specify a rectangular box enclosing the target region that defines the
simulation domain. Line 14 fills the target region with atoms. Lines 15
and 17 define the peridynamic material model, and lines 19 and 21 set
the particle density and particle volume, respectively. The particle
volume should be set to the cube of the lattice constant for a simple
cubic lattice. Line 23 sets the initial velocity of all particles to
zero. Line 25 instructs LAMMPS to integrate time with velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet,
and lines 27\sphinxhyphen{}30 create the spherical projectile, sending it with a
velocity of 100 m/s towards the target. Line 32 declares a compute style
for the damage (percentage of broken bonds) associated with each
particle.  Line 33 sets the timestep, line 34 instructs LAMMPS to
provide a screen dump of thermodynamic quantities every 200 timesteps,
and line 35 instructs LAMMPS to create a data file (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dump.peri}}) with
a complete snapshot of the system every 100 timesteps. This file can be
used to create still images or movies. Finally, line 36 instructs LAMMPS
to run for 2000 timesteps.

\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}

\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{y0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00510}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{vy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{v\PYGZus{}y0 + step*dt*v\PYGZus{}vy}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{F2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{indent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e17}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0050}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Compute damage for each particle}
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{C1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{damage}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}7}
\PYG{k}{thermo}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{200}
\PYG{k}{dump            }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{D1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dump.peri}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}C1}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{l+m}{2000}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\paragraph{Numerical Results and Discussion}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_peri:numerical-results-and-discussion}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We ran the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri:periexample}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{input script from above}}}}. Images of the
disk (projectile not shown) appear in Figure below.  The plot of damage
on the top monolayer was created by coloring each particle according to
its damage.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The symmetry in the computed solution arises because a “perfect” lattice
was used, and a because a perfectly spherical projectile impacted the
lattice at its geometric center. To break the symmetry in the solution,
the nodes in the peridynamic body may be perturbed slightly from the
lattice sites. To do this, the lattice of points can be slightly
perturbed using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{displace_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{displace\_atoms}}}} command.

\subsection{Manifolds (surfaces)}

\sphinxstylestrong{Overview:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This page is not about a LAMMPS input script command, but about
manifolds, which are generalized surfaces, as defined and used by the
MANIFOLD package, to track particle motion on the manifolds.  See
the src/MANIFOLD/README file for more details about the package
and its commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is a list of currently supported manifolds by the MANIFOLD
package, their parameters and a short description of them.  The
parameters listed here are in the same order as they should be passed
to the relevant fixes.

\subsection{Reproducing hydrodynamics and elastic objects (RHEO)}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_rheo:reproducing-hydrodynamics-and-elastic-objects-rheo}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_rheo::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The RHEO package is a hybrid implementation of smoothed particle
hydrodynamics (SPH) for fluid flow, which can couple to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{BPM package}}}} to model solid elements. RHEO combines these methods to enable
mesh\sphinxhyphen{}free modeling of multi\sphinxhyphen{}phase material systems. Its SPH solver supports
many advanced options including reproducing kernels, particle shifting, free
surface identification, and solid surface reconstruction. To model fluid\sphinxhyphen{}solid
systems, the status of particles can dynamically change between a fluid and
solid state, e.g. during melting/solidification, which determines how they
interact and their physical behavior. The package is designed with modularity
in mind, so one can easily turn various features on/off, adjust physical
details of the system, or develop new capabilities. For instance, the numerics
associated with calculating gradients, reproducing kernels, etc. are separated
into distinct classes to simplify the development of new integration schemes
which can call these calculations. Additional numerical details can be found in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_rheo:howto-rheo-clemmer}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Clemmer)}}}}. Example movies illustrating some of these
capabilities are found at \sphinxurl{https://www.lammps.org/movies.html\#rheopackage}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note, if you simply want to run a traditional SPH simulation, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-sph}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SPH package}}}} package is likely better suited for your application. It has fewer advanced
features and therefore benefits from improved performance. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-machdyn}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{MACHDYN}}}} package for solids may also be relevant for fluid\sphinxhyphen{}solid problems.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
At the core of the package is {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo}}}} which integrates
particle trajectories and controls many optional features (e.g. the use
of reproducing kernels). In conjunction to fix rheo, one must specify an
instance of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo/pressure}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo_viscosity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo/viscosity}}}} to define a pressure equation
of state and viscosity model, respectively. Optionally, one can model
a heat equation with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo_thermal::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo/thermal}}}}, which also
allows the user to specify equations for a particle’s thermal conductivity,
specific heat, latent heat, and melting temperature. The ordering of these
fixes in an an input script matters. Fix rheo must be defined prior to all
other RHEO fixes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically, RHEO requires atom style rheo. In addition to typical atom
properties like positions and forces, particles store a local density,
viscosity, pressure, and status. If thermal evolution is modeled, one must
use atom style rheo/thermal which also includes a local energy, temperature, and
conductivity. Note that the temperature is always derived from the energy.
This implies the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temperature} attribute of {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{the set command}}}} does not
affect particles. Instead, one should use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sph/e} attribute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The status variable uses bit\sphinxhyphen{}masking to track various properties of a particle
such as its current state of matter (fluid or solid) and its location relative
to a surface. Some of these properties (and others) can be accessed using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute rheo/property/atom}}}}. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{status}
attribute in {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{the set command}}}} only allows control over the first bit
which sets the state of matter, 0 is fluid and 1 is solid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fluid interactions, including pressure forces, viscous forces, and heat exchange,
are calculated using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rheo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair rheo}}}}. Unlike typical pair styles,
pair rheo ignores the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special bond}}}} settings. Instead,
it determines whether to calculate forces based on the status of particles: e.g.,
hydrodynamic forces are only calculated if a fluid particle is involved.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
To model elastic objects, there are currently two mechanisms in RHEO, one designed
for bulk solid bodies and the other for thin shells. Both mechanisms rely on
introducing bonded forces between particles and therefore require a hybrid of atom
style bond and rheo (or rheo/thermal).

\sphinxAtStartPar
To create an elastic solid body, one has to (a) change the status of constituent
particles to solid (e.g. with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command), (b) create bpm
bonds between the particles (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bpm howto}}}} page for
more details), and (c) use {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rheo_solid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair rheo/solid}}}} to
apply repulsive contact forces between distinct solid bodies. Akin to pair rheo,
pair rheo/solid considers a particles fluid/solid phase to determine whether to
apply forces. However, unlike pair rheo, pair rheo/solid does obey special bond
settings such that contact forces do not have to be calculated between two bonded
solid particles in the same elastic body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In systems with thermal evolution, fix rheo/thermal can optionally set a
melting/solidification temperature allowing particles to dynamically swap their
state between fluid and solid when the temperature exceeds or drops below the
critical temperature, respectively. Using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{react} option, one can specify a maximum
bond length and a bond type. Then, when solidifying, particles will search their
local neighbors and automatically create bonds with any neighboring solid particles
in range. For BPM bond styles, bonds will then use the immediate position of the two
particles to calculate a reference state. When melting, particles will delete any
bonds of the specified type when reverting to a fluid state. Special bonds are updated
as bonds are created/broken.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The other option for elastic objects is an elastic shell that is nominally much
thinner than a particle diameter, e.g. a oxide skin which gradually forms over time
on the surface of a fluid. Currently, this is implemented using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo_oxidation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo/oxidation}}}} and bond style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_rheo_shell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rheo/shell}}}}. Essentially, fix rheo/oxidation creates candidate
bonds of a specified type between surface fluid particles within a specified distance.
a newly created rheo/shell bond will then start a timer. While the timer is counting
down, the bond will delete itself if particles move too far apart or move away from the
surface. However, if the timer reaches a user\sphinxhyphen{}defined threshold, then the bond will
activate and apply additional forces to the fluid particles. Bond style rheo/shell
then operates very similarly to a BPM bond style, storing a reference length and
breaking if stretched too far. Unlike the above method, this option does not remove
the underlying fluid interactions (although particle shifting is turned off) and does
not modify special bond settings of particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
While these two options are not expected to be appropriate for every system,
either framework can be modified to create more suitable models (e.g. by changing the
criteria for creating/deleting a bond or altering force calculations).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_rheo:howto-rheo-clemmer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Clemmer)} Clemmer, Pierce, O’Connor, Nevins, Jones, Lechman, Tencer, Appl. Math. Model., 130, 310\sphinxhyphen{}326 (2024).
