\subsection{Magnetic spins}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_spins:magnetic-spins}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_spins::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The magnetic spin simulations are enabled by the SPIN package, whose
implementation is detailed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_spins:tranchida}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Tranchida}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The model represents the simulation of atomic magnetic spins coupled
to lattice vibrations. The dynamics of those magnetic spins can be used
to simulate a broad range a phenomena related to magneto\sphinxhyphen{}elasticity, or
or to study the influence of defects on the magnetic properties of
materials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The magnetic spins are interacting with each others and with the
lattice via pair interactions. Typically, the magnetic exchange
interaction can be defined using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spin_exchange::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair/spin/exchange}}}} command. This exchange
applies a magnetic torque to a given spin, considering the orientation
of its neighboring spins and their relative distances.
It also applies a force on the atoms as a function of the spin
orientations and their associated inter\sphinxhyphen{}atomic distances.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The command {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_precession_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix precession/spin}}}} allows to
apply a constant magnetic torque on all the spins in the system. This
torque can be an external magnetic field (Zeeman interaction), and an
uniaxial or cubic magnetic anisotropy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A Langevin thermostat can be applied to those magnetic spins using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin/spin}}}}. Typically, this thermostat
can be coupled to another Langevin thermostat applied to the atoms
using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} in order to simulate
thermostatted spin\sphinxhyphen{}lattice systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The magnetic damping can also be applied
using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin/spin}}}}.
It allows to either dissipate the thermal energy of the Langevin
thermostat, or to perform a relaxation of the magnetic configuration
toward an equilibrium state.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The command {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce/spin}}}} allows to set the
components of the magnetic precession vectors (while erasing and
replacing the previously computed magnetic precession vectors on
the atom).
This command can be used to freeze the magnetic moment of certain
atoms in the simulation by zeroing their precession vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The command {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/spin}}}} can be used to
perform a symplectic integration of the combined dynamics of spins
and atomic motions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimization style {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min/spin}}}} can be applied
to the spins to perform a minimization of the spin configuration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All the computed magnetic properties can be output by two main
commands. The first one is {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute spin}}}}, that
enables to evaluate magnetic averaged quantities, such as the total
magnetization of the system along x, y, or z, the spin temperature, or
the magnetic energy. The second command
is {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}}.
It enables to output all the per atom magnetic quantities. Typically,
the orientation of a given magnetic spin, or the magnetic force
acting on this spin.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Howto_spins:tranchida}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Tranchida)} Tranchida, Plimpton, Thibaudeau and Thompson,
Journal of Computational Physics, 372, 406\sphinxhyphen{}425, (2018).


\section{Tutorials howto}
\label{\detokenize{Howto:tutorials-howto}}
\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Using CMake with LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:using-cmake-with-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The support for building LAMMPS with CMake is a recent addition to
LAMMPS thanks to the efforts of Christoph Junghans (LANL) and Richard
Berger (LANL).  One of the key strengths of CMake is that it is not
tied to a specific platform or build system. Instead it generates the
files necessary to build and develop for different build systems and on
different platforms.  Note, that this applies to the build system itself
not the LAMMPS code. In other words, without additional porting effort,
it is not possible \sphinxhyphen{} for example \sphinxhyphen{} to compile LAMMPS with Visual C++ on
Windows.  The build system output can also include support files
necessary to program LAMMPS as a project in integrated development
environments (IDE) like Eclipse, Visual Studio, QtCreator, Xcode,
CodeBlocks, Kate and others.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A second important feature of CMake is that it can detect and validate
available libraries, optimal settings, available support tools and so
on, so that by default LAMMPS will take advantage of available tools
without requiring to provide the details about how to enable/integrate
them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The downside of this approach is, that there is some complexity
associated with running CMake itself and how to customize the building
of LAMMPS.  This tutorial will show how to manage this through some
selected examples.  Please see the chapter about {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{building LAMMPS}}}} for descriptions of specific flags and options for LAMMPS in
general and for specific packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake can be used through either the command\sphinxhyphen{}line interface (CLI)
program \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake3}}), a text mode interactive user
interface (TUI) program \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ccmake}} (or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ccmake3}}), or a graphical user
interface (GUI) program \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake\sphinxhyphen{}gui}}.  All of them are portable
software available on all supported platforms and can be used
interchangeably.  As of LAMMPS version 2 August 2023, the minimum
required CMake version is 3.16.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All details about features and settings for CMake are in the \sphinxhref{https://cmake.org/documentation/}{CMake
online documentation}. We focus
below on the most important aspects with respect to compiling LAMMPS.


\subsubsection{Prerequisites}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:prerequisites}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This tutorial assumes that you are operating in a command\sphinxhyphen{}line environment
using a shell like Bash or Zsh.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Linux: any Terminal window will work or text console

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
macOS: launch the Terminal application

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows 10 or 11: install and run the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_wsl::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Windows Subsystem for Linux}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
other Unix\sphinxhyphen{}like operating systems like FreeBSD

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible to use CMake on Windows 10 or 11 through either the Microsoft
Visual Studio IDE with the bundled CMake or from the Windows command prompt using
a separately installed CMake package, both using the native Microsoft Visual C++
compilers and (optionally) the Microsoft MPI SDK.  This tutorial, however, only
covers unix\sphinxhyphen{}like command line interfaces.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We also assume that you have downloaded and unpacked a recent LAMMPS source code package
or used Git to create a clone of the LAMMPS sources on your compilation machine.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You should change into the top level directory of the LAMMPS source tree all
paths mentioned in the tutorial are relative to that.  Immediately after downloading
it should look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZdl{} }ls
\PYG{g+go}{bench  doc       lib      potentials  README  tools}
\PYG{g+go}{cmake  examples  LICENSE  python      src}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Build versus source directory}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:build-versus-source-directory}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using CMake the build procedure is separated into multiple distinct phases:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Configuration:} detect or define which features and settings
should be enable and used and how LAMMPS should be compiled

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compilation:} generate and compile all necessary source files
and build libraries and executables.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Installation:} copy selected files from the compilation into
your file system, so they can be used without having to keep the
source and build tree around.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The configuration and compilation of LAMMPS has to happen in a dedicated
\sphinxstyleemphasis{build directory} which must be different from the source directory.
Also the source directory (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}}) must remain pristine, so it is not
allowed to “install” packages using the traditional make process and
after an compilation attempt all created source files must be removed.
This can be achieved with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make no\sphinxhyphen{}all purge}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can pick \sphinxstylestrong{any} folder outside the source tree. We recommend to
create a folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} in the top\sphinxhyphen{}level directory, or multiple
folders in case you want to have separate builds of LAMMPS with
different options (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build\sphinxhyphen{}parallel}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build\sphinxhyphen{}serial}}) or with
different compilers (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build\sphinxhyphen{}gnu}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build\sphinxhyphen{}clang}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build\sphinxhyphen{}intel}})
and so on.  All the auxiliary files created by one build process
(executable, object files, log files, etc) are stored in this directory
or subdirectories within it that CMake creates.


\subsubsection{Running CMake}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:running-cmake}}

\paragraph{CLI version}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:cli-version}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the (empty) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} directory, we now run the command \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake
../cmake}}, which will start the configuration phase and you will see
the progress of the configuration printed to the screen followed by a
summary of the enabled features, options and compiler settings. A typical
summary screen will look like this:

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake}} command has one mandatory argument, and that is a folder
with either the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeLists.txt}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeCache.txt}}. The
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeCache.txt}} file is created during the CMake configuration run
and contains all active settings, thus after a first run of CMake
all future runs in the build folder can use the folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.}} and CMake
will know where to find the CMake scripts and reload the settings
from the previous step.  This means, that one can modify an existing
configuration by re\sphinxhyphen{}running CMake, but only needs to provide flags
indicating the desired change, everything else will be retained. One
can also mix compilation and configuration, i.e. start with a minimal
configuration and then, if needed, enable additional features and
recompile.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The steps above \sphinxstylestrong{will NOT compile the code}. The compilation can be
started in a portable fashion with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build .}}, or you use the
selected built tool, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}}.


\paragraph{TUI version}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:tui-version}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the text mode UI CMake program the basic principle is the same.
You start the command \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ccmake ../cmake}} in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} folder.

\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will show you the initial screen (left image) with the empty
configuration cache. Now you type the ‘c’ key to run the configuration
step. That will do a first configuration run and show the summary
(center image). You exit the summary screen with ‘e’ and see now the
main screen with detected options and settings. You can now make changes
by moving and down with the arrow keys of the keyboard and modify
entries. For on/off settings, the enter key will toggle the state.
For others, hitting enter will allow you to modify the value and
you commit the change by hitting the enter key again or cancel using
the escape key.  All “new” settings will be marked with a star ‘*’
and for as long as one setting is marked like this, you have to
re\sphinxhyphen{}run the configuration by hitting the ‘c’ key again, sometimes
multiple times unless the TUI shows the word “generate” next to the
letter ‘g’ and by hitting the ‘g’ key the build files will be written
to the folder and the TUI exits.  You can quit without generating
build files by hitting ‘q’.


\paragraph{GUI version}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:gui-version}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the graphical CMake program the steps are similar to the TUI
version.  You can type the command \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake\sphinxhyphen{}gui ../cmake}} in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} folder.  In this case the path to the CMake script folder is
not required, it can also be entered from the GUI.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Again, you start with an empty configuration cache (left image) and need
to start the configuration step.  For the very first configuration in a
folder, you will have a pop\sphinxhyphen{}up dialog (center image) asking to select
the desired build tool and some configuration settings (stick with the
default) and then you get the option screen with all new settings
highlighted in red.  You can modify them (or not) and click on the
“configure” button again until satisfied and click on the “generate”
button to write out the build files. You can exit the GUI from the
“File” menu or hit “ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}q”.


\subsubsection{Setting options}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:setting-options}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Options that enable, disable or modify settings are modified by setting
the value of CMake variables. This is done on the command line with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{\sphinxhyphen{}D} flag in the format \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D VARIABLE=value}}, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
CMAKE\_BUILD\_TYPE=Release}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D BUILD\_MPI=on}}.  There is one quirk:
when used before the CMake directory, there may be a space between the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{\sphinxhyphen{}D} flag and the variable, after it must not be. Such CMake variables
can have boolean values (on/off, yes/no, or 1/0 are all valid) or are
strings representing a choice, or a path, or are free format. If the
string would contain whitespace, it must be put in quotes, for example
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D CMAKE\_TUNE\_FLAGS="\sphinxhyphen{}ftree\sphinxhyphen{}vectorize \sphinxhyphen{}ffast\sphinxhyphen{}math"}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
CMake variables fall into two categories: 1) common CMake variables that
are used by default for any CMake configuration setup and 2) project
specific variables, i.e. settings that are specific for LAMMPS.
Also CMake variables can be flagged as \sphinxstyleemphasis{advanced}, which means they are
not shown in the text mode or graphical CMake program in the overview
of all settings by default, but only when explicitly requested (by hitting
the ‘t’ key or clicking on the ‘Advanced’ check\sphinxhyphen{}box).

\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:some-common-cmake-variables}}

\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BUILD\_DOC}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
include building the HTML format documentation for packaging/installing (default: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{off}})
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMAKE\_TUNE\_FLAGS}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
common compiler flags, for optimization or instrumentation (default:)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_MACHINE}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
when set to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{name}} the LAMMPS executable and library will be called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp\_name}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_name.a}}
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FFT}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
select which FFT library to use: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FFTW3}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MKL}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KISS}} (default, unless FFTW3 is found)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FFT\_KOKKOS}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
select which FFT library to use in Kokkos\sphinxhyphen{}enabled styles: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FFTW3}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MKL}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{HIPFFT}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CUFFT}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KISS}} (default)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FFT\_SINGLE}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
select whether to use single precision FFTs (default: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{off}})
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WITH\_JPEG}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
whether to support JPEG format in {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} (default: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{on}} if found)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WITH\_PNG}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
whether to support PNG format in  {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} (default: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{on}} if found)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WITH\_GZIP}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
whether to support reading and writing compressed files (default: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{on}} if found)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WITH\_FFMPEG}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
whether to support generating movies with {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump movie}}}} (default: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{on}} if found)
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}


\paragraph{Enabling or disabling LAMMPS packages}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:enabling-or-disabling-lammps-packages}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS software is organized into a common core that is always
included and a large number of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add\sphinxhyphen{}on packages}}}} that
have to be enabled to be included into a LAMMPS executable.  Packages
are enabled through setting variables of the kind \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PKG\_\textless{}NAME\textgreater{}}} to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{on}} and disabled by setting them to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{off}} (or using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{yes}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{no}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}} correspondingly).  \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}NAME\textgreater{}}} has to be replaced by
the name of the package, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MOLECULE}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR}}.


\subsubsection{Using presets}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:using-presets}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since LAMMPS has a lot of optional features and packages, specifying
them all on the command line can be tedious. Or when selecting a
different compiler toolchain, multiple options have to be changed
consistently and that is rather error prone. Or when enabling certain
packages, they require consistent settings to be operated in a
particular mode.  For this purpose, we are providing a selection of
“preset files” for CMake in the folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/presets}}.  They
represent a way to pre\sphinxhyphen{}load or override the CMake configuration cache by
setting or changing CMake variables.  Preset files are loaded using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{\sphinxhyphen{}C} command line flag. You can combine loading multiple preset files or
change some variables later with additional \sphinxstyleemphasis{\sphinxhyphen{}D} flags.  A few examples:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/basic.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PKG\PYGZus{}MISC}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/clang.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/most.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/basic.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}MPI}\PYG{o}{=}off\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first command will install the packages \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{KSPACE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MANYBODY}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MOLECULE}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RIGID}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MISC}}; the first four from the preset
file and the fifth from the explicit variable definition.  The second
command will first switch the compiler toolchain to use the Clang
compilers and install a large number of packages that are not depending
on any special external libraries or tools and are not very unusual.
The third command will enable the first four packages like above and
then enforce compiling LAMMPS as a serial program (using the MPI STUBS
library).

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible to do this incrementally.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/basic.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PKG\PYGZus{}MISC}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{ }.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
will achieve the same final configuration as in the first example above.
In this scenario it is particularly convenient to do the second
configuration step using either the text mode or graphical user
interface (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ccmake}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake\sphinxhyphen{}gui}}).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a preset to select a compiler package (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clang.cmake}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gcc.cmake}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{intel.cmake}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{oneapi.cmake}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pgi.cmake}})
are an exception to the mechanism of updating the configuration
incrementally, as they will trigger a reset of cached internal CMake
settings and thus reset settings to their default values.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Compilation and build targets}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:compilation-and-build-targets}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The actual compilation will be started by running the selected build
command (on Linux this is by default \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}}, see below how to select
alternatives).  You can also use the portable command \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build .}}
which will adapt to whatever the selected build command is.
This is particularly convenient, if you have set a custom build command
via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMAKE\_MAKE\_PROGRAM}} variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When calling the build program, you can also select which “target” is to
be build through appending the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}target}} flag and the name of the target
to the build command.  When using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} as build tool, you can just append
the target name to the command. Example: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build . \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}target all}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make all}}.  The following abstract targets are available:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxstyletheadfamily 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Target
&\sphinxstyletheadfamily 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Description
\\
\sphinxmidrule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{all}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
build “everything” (default)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
build the LAMMPS library and executable
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
build the HTML documentation (if configured)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{install}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
install all target files into folders in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMAKE\_INSTALL\_PREFIX}}
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
run some tests (if configured with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D ENABLE\_TESTING=on}})
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{clean}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
remove all generated files
\\
\sphinxbottomrule

\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}


\subsubsection{Choosing generators}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_cmake:choosing-generators}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
While CMake usually defaults to creating makefiles to compile software
with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} program, it supports multiple alternate build tools
(e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ninja\sphinxhyphen{}build}} which tends to be faster and more efficient in
parallelizing builds than \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}}) and can generate project files for
integrated development environments (IDEs) like VisualStudio, Eclipse or
CodeBlocks.  This is specific to how the local CMake version was
configured and compiled. The list of available options can be seen at
the end of the output of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}help}}. Example on Fedora 31 this is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Generators

The following generators are available on this platform (* marks default):
* Unix Makefiles               = Generates standard UNIX makefiles.
  Green Hills MULTI            = Generates Green Hills MULTI files
                                 (experimental, work\PYGZhy{}in\PYGZhy{}progress).
  Ninja                        = Generates build.ninja files.
  Ninja Multi\PYGZhy{}Config           = Generates build\PYGZhy{}\PYGZlt{}Config\PYGZgt{}.ninja files.
  Watcom WMake                 = Generates Watcom WMake makefiles.
  CodeBlocks \PYGZhy{} Ninja           = Generates CodeBlocks project files.
  CodeBlocks \PYGZhy{} Unix Makefiles  = Generates CodeBlocks project files.
  CodeLite \PYGZhy{} Ninja             = Generates CodeLite project files.
  CodeLite \PYGZhy{} Unix Makefiles    = Generates CodeLite project files.
  Sublime Text 2 \PYGZhy{} Ninja       = Generates Sublime Text 2 project files.
  Sublime Text 2 \PYGZhy{} Unix Makefiles
                               = Generates Sublime Text 2 project files.
  Kate \PYGZhy{} Ninja                 = Generates Kate project files.
  Kate \PYGZhy{} Unix Makefiles        = Generates Kate project files.
  Eclipse CDT4 \PYGZhy{} Ninja         = Generates Eclipse CDT 4.0 project files.
  Eclipse CDT4 \PYGZhy{} Unix Makefiles= Generates Eclipse CDT 4.0 project files.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is a screenshot of using the CodeBlocks IDE with the ninja build tool
after running CMake as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}G\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}CodeBlocks \PYGZhy{} Ninja\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/most.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{cmake-codeblocks}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{LAMMPS GitHub tutorial}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_github:lammps-github-tutorial}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_github::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{written by Stefan Paquay}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This document describes the process of how to use GitHub to integrate
changes or additions you have made to LAMMPS into the official LAMMPS
distribution.  It uses the process of updating this very tutorial as an
example to describe the individual steps and options.  You need to be
familiar with git and you may want to have a look at the \sphinxhref{https://git-scm.com/book/}{git book} to familiarize yourself with some of the
more advanced git features used below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As of fall 2016, submitting contributions to LAMMPS via pull requests
on GitHub is the preferred option for integrating contributed features
or improvements to LAMMPS, as it significantly reduces the amount of
work required by the LAMMPS developers. Consequently, creating a pull
request will increase your chances to have your contribution included
and will reduce the time until the integration is complete. For more
information on the requirements to have your code included into LAMMPS
please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_contribute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{this page}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Making an account}

\sphinxAtStartPar
First of all, you need a GitHub account. This is fairly simple, just
go to \sphinxhref{https://github.com}{GitHub} and create an account by clicking
the “Sign up for GitHub” button. Once your account is created, you
can sign in by clicking the button in the top left and filling in your
username or e\sphinxhyphen{}mail address and password.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Forking the repository}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To get changes into LAMMPS, you need to first fork the \sphinxtitleref{lammps/lammps}
repository on GitHub. At the time of writing, \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} is the preferred
target branch. Thus go to \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps}{LAMMPS on GitHub}
and make sure branch is set to “develop”, as shown in the figure below.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_branch}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If it is not, use the button to change it to \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop}. Once it is, use
the fork button to create a fork.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_fork}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will create a fork (which is essentially a copy, but uses less
resources) of the LAMMPS repository under your own GitHub account. You
can make changes in this fork and later file \sphinxstyleemphasis{pull requests} to allow
the upstream repository to merge changes from your own fork into the one
we just forked from (or others that were forked from the same repository).
At the same time, you can set things up, so you can include changes from
upstream into your repository and thus keep it in sync with the ongoing
LAMMPS development.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adding changes to your own fork}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additions to the upstream version of LAMMPS are handled using \sphinxstyleemphasis{feature
branches}.  For every new feature, a so\sphinxhyphen{}called feature branch is
created, which contains only those modification relevant to one specific
feature. For example, adding a single fix would consist of creating a
branch with only the fix header and source file and nothing else.  It is
explained in more detail here: \sphinxhref{https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/comparing-workflows/feature-branch-workflow}{feature branch workflow}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Feature branches}

\sphinxAtStartPar
First of all, create a clone of your version on GitHub on your local
machine via HTTPS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/\PYGZlt{}your\PYG{+w}{ }user\PYG{+w}{ }name\PYGZgt{}/lammps.git\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZlt{}some\PYG{+w}{ }name\PYGZgt{}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or, if you have set up your GitHub account for using SSH keys, via SSH:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }git@github.com:\PYGZlt{}your\PYG{+w}{ }user\PYG{+w}{ }name\PYGZgt{}/lammps.git
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can find the proper URL by clicking the “Clone or download”\sphinxhyphen{}button:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_https_block}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The above command copies (“clones”) the git repository to your local
machine to a directory with the name you chose. If none is given, it will
default to “lammps”. Typical names are “mylammps” or something similar.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use this local clone to make changes and test them without
interfering with the repository on GitHub.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To pull changes from upstream into this copy, you can go to the directory
and use git pull:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }mylammps
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }develop
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/lammps/lammps\PYG{+w}{ }develop
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also add this URL as a remote:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }remote\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }upstream\PYG{+w}{ }https://www.github.com/lammps/lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
From then on you can update your upstream branches with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }fetch\PYG{+w}{ }upstream
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and then refer to the upstream repository branches with
\sphinxtitleref{upstream/develop} or \sphinxtitleref{upstream/release} and so on.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At this point, you typically make a feature branch from the updated
branch for the feature you want to work on. This tutorial contains the
workflow that updated this tutorial, and hence we will call the branch
“github\sphinxhyphen{}tutorial\sphinxhyphen{}update”:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }fetch\PYG{+w}{ }upstream
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}b\PYG{+w}{ }github\PYGZhy{}tutorial\PYGZhy{}update\PYG{+w}{ }upstream/develop
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now that we have changed branches, we can make our changes to our local
repository. Just remember that if you want to start working on another,
unrelated feature, you should switch branches!

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Committing changes to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{release}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} branches
is strongly discouraged.  While it may be convenient initially, it
will create more work in the long run.  Various texts and tutorials
on using git effectively discuss the motivation for using feature
branches instead.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{After changes are made}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After everything is done, add the files to the branch and commit them:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }doc/src/Howto\PYGZus{}github.txt
git\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }doc/src/JPG/tutorial*.png
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not use \sphinxstyleemphasis{git commit \sphinxhyphen{}a} (or \sphinxstyleemphasis{git add \sphinxhyphen{}A}).  The \sphinxhyphen{}a flag (or \sphinxhyphen{}A
flag) will automatically include \sphinxstylestrong{all} modified \sphinxstylestrong{and} new files
and that is rarely the behavior you want.  It can easily lead to
accidentally adding unrelated and unwanted changes into the
repository.  Instead it is preferable to explicitly use \sphinxstyleemphasis{git add},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{git rm}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{git mv} for adding, removing, renaming individual files,
respectively, and then \sphinxstyleemphasis{git commit} to finalize the commit.
Carefully check all pending changes with \sphinxstyleemphasis{git status} before
committing them.  If you find doing this on the command line too
tedious, consider using a GUI, for example the one included in git
distributions written in Tk, i.e. use \sphinxstyleemphasis{git gui} (on some Linux
distributions it may be required to install an additional package to
use it).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After adding all files, the change set can be committed with some
useful message that explains the change.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }commit\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}Finally updated the GitHub tutorial\PYGZsq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the commit, the changes can be pushed to the same branch on GitHub:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }push
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Git will ask you for your user name and password on GitHub if you have
not configured anything. If your local branch is not present on GitHub yet,
it will ask you to add it by running

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }push\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}set\PYGZhy{}upstream\PYG{+w}{ }origin\PYG{+w}{ }github\PYGZhy{}tutorial\PYGZhy{}update
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you correctly type your user name and
password, the feature branch should be added to your fork on GitHub.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to make really sure you push to the right repository
(which is good practice), you can provide it explicitly:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }push\PYG{+w}{ }origin
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or using an explicit URL:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }push\PYG{+w}{ }git@github.com:Pakketeretet2/lammps.git
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Filing a pull request}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Up to this point in the tutorial, all changes were to \sphinxstyleemphasis{your} clones of
LAMMPS.  Eventually, however, you want this feature to be included into
the official LAMMPS version.  To do this, you will want to file a pull
request by clicking on the “New pull request” button:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_new_pull_request}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Make sure that the current branch is set to the correct one, which, in
this case, is “github\sphinxhyphen{}tutorial\sphinxhyphen{}update”. If done correctly, the only
changes you will see are those that were made on this branch.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will open up a new window that lists changes made to the
repository. If you are just adding new files, there is not much to do,
but I suppose merge conflicts are to be resolved here if there are
changes in existing files. If all changes can automatically be merged,
green text at the top will say so and you can click the “Create pull
request” button, see image.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_create_new_pull_request1}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Before creating the pull request, make sure the short title is accurate
and add a comment with details about your pull request.  Here you write
what your modifications do and why they should be incorporated upstream.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note the checkbox that says “Allow edits from maintainers”.
This is checked by default checkbox (although in my version of Firefox, only the checkmark is visible):

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_edits_maintainers}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If it is checked, maintainers can immediately add their own edits to the
pull request.  This helps the inclusion of your branch significantly, as
simple/trivial changes can be added directly to your pull request branch
by the LAMMPS maintainers.  The alternative would be that they make
changes on their own version of the branch and file a reverse pull
request to you.  Just leave this box checked unless you have a very good
reason not to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now just write some nice comments and click on “Create pull request”.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_create_new_pull_request2}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{After filing a pull request}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you submit a pull request (or ask for a pull request) for the
first time, you will receive an invitation to become a LAMMPS project
collaborator. Please accept this invite as being a collaborator will
simplify certain administrative tasks and will probably speed up the
merging of your feature, too.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You will notice that after filing the pull request, some checks are
performed automatically:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_automated_checks}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If all is fine, you will see this:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_automated_checks_passed}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If any of the checks are failing, your pull request will not be
processed, as your changes may break compilation for certain
configurations or may not merge cleanly. It is your responsibility
to remove the reason(s) for the failed test(s). If you need help
with this, please contact the LAMMPS developers by adding a comment
explaining your problems with resolving the failed tests.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A few further interesting things (can) happen to pull requests before
they are included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Additional changes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
First of all, any additional changes you push into your branch in your
repository will automatically become part of the pull request:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_additional_changes}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means you can add changes that should be part of the feature after
filing the pull request, which is useful in case you have forgotten
them, or if a developer has requested that something needs to be changed
before the feature can be accepted into the official LAMMPS version.
After each push, the automated checks are run again.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Labels}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS developers may add labels to your pull request to assign it to
categories (mostly for bookkeeping purposes), but a few of them are
important: \sphinxstyleemphasis{needs\_work}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{work\_in\_progress}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{run\_tests},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{test\_for\_regression}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ready\_for\_merge}.  The first two indicate,
that your pull request is not considered to be complete. With
“needs\_work” the burden is on exclusively on you; while
“work\_in\_progress” can also mean, that a LAMMPS developer may want to
add changes. Please watch the comments to the pull requests. The two
“test” labels are used to trigger extended tests before the code is
merged. This is sometimes done by LAMMPS developers, if they suspect
that there may be some subtle side effects from your changes. It is not
done by default, because those tests are very time\sphinxhyphen{}consuming.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ready\_for\_merge} label is usually attached when the LAMMPS developer
assigned to the pull request considers this request complete and to
trigger a final full test evaluation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reviews}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As of Fall 2021, a pull request needs to pass all automatic tests and at
least 1 approving review from a LAMMPS developer with write access to
the repository before it is eligible for merging.  In case your changes
touch code that certain developers are associated with, they are
auto\sphinxhyphen{}requested by the GitHub software.  Those associations are set in
the file \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/.github/CODEOWNERS}{.github/CODEOWNERS} Thus
if you want to be automatically notified to review when anybody changes
files or packages, that \sphinxstylestrong{you} have contributed to LAMMPS, you can add
suitable patterns to that file, or a LAMMPS developer may add you.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Otherwise, you can also manually request reviews from specific developers,
or LAMMPS developers \sphinxhyphen{} in their assessment of your pull request \sphinxhyphen{} may
determine who else should be reviewing your contribution and add that person.
Through reviews, LAMMPS developers also may request specific changes from you.
If those are not addressed, your pull requests cannot be merged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Assignees}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is an assignee property for pull requests. If the request has not
been reviewed by any developer yet, it is not assigned to anyone. After
revision, a developer can choose to assign it to either a) you, b) a
LAMMPS developer (including him/herself) or c) Axel Kohlmeyer (akohlmey).
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Case a) happens if changes are required on your part

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Case b) means that at the moment, it is being tested and reviewed by a
LAMMPS developer with the expectation that some changes would be required.
After the review, the developer can choose to implement changes directly
or suggest them to you.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Case c) means that the pull request has been assigned to the developer
overseeing the merging of pull requests into the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, Axel assigned the tutorial to Steve:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_steve_assignee}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Edits from LAMMPS maintainers}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you allowed edits from maintainers (the default), any LAMMPS
maintainer can add changes to your pull request.  In this case, both
Axel and Richard made changes to the tutorial:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_changes_others}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Reverse pull requests}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Sometimes, however, you might not feel comfortable having other people
push changes into your own branch, or maybe the maintainers are not sure
their idea was the right one.  In such a case, they can make changes,
reassign you as the assignee, and file a “reverse pull request”, i.e.
file a pull request in \sphinxstylestrong{your} forked GitHub repository to include
changes in the branch, that you have submitted as a pull request
yourself.  In that case, you can choose to merge their changes back into
your branch, possibly make additional changes or corrections and proceed
from there.  It looks something like this:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_reverse_pull_request}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For some reason, the highlighted button did not work in my case, but I
can go to my own repository and merge the pull request from there:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_reverse_pull_request2}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Be sure to check the changes to see if you agree with them by clicking
on the tab button:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_reverse_pull_request3}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, most of it is changes in the markup and a short rewrite of
Axel’s explanation of the “git gui” and “git add” commands.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_reverse_pull_request4}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Because the changes are OK with us, we are going to merge by clicking on
“Merge pull request”.  After a merge it looks like this:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_reverse_pull_request5}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, since in the meantime our local text for the tutorial also changed,
we need to pull Axel’s change back into our branch, and merge them:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }Howto\PYGZus{}github.txt
git\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }JPG/tutorial\PYGZus{}reverse\PYGZus{}pull\PYGZus{}request*.png
git\PYG{+w}{ }commit\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}Updated text and images on reverse pull requests\PYGZdq{}}
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, the merge was painless because git could auto\sphinxhyphen{}merge:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_reverse_pull_request6}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With Axel’s changes merged in and some final text updates, our feature
branch is now perfect as far as we are concerned, so we are going to
commit and push again:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }Howto\PYGZus{}github.txt
git\PYG{+w}{ }add\PYG{+w}{ }JPG/tutorial\PYGZus{}reverse\PYGZus{}pull\PYGZus{}request6.png
git\PYG{+w}{ }commit\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}Merged Axel\PYGZsq{}s suggestions and updated text\PYGZdq{}}
git\PYG{+w}{ }push\PYG{+w}{ }git@github.com:Pakketeretet2/lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This merge also shows up on the lammps GitHub page:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_reverse_pull_request7}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{After a merge}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When everything is fine, the feature branch is merged into the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{tutorial_merged}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now one question remains: What to do with the feature branch that got
merged into upstream?

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is in principle safe to delete them from your own fork. This helps
keep it a bit more tidy. Note that you first have to switch to another
branch!

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }checkout\PYG{+w}{ }develop
git\PYG{+w}{ }pull\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/lammps/lammps\PYG{+w}{ }develop
git\PYG{+w}{ }branch\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}d\PYG{+w}{ }github\PYGZhy{}tutorial\PYGZhy{}update
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you do not pull first, it is not really a problem but git will warn
you at the next statement that you are deleting a local branch that
was not yet fully merged into HEAD. This is because git does not yet
know your branch just got merged into LAMMPS upstream. If you
first delete and then pull, everything should still be fine.
You can display all branches that are fully merged by:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, if you delete the branch locally, you might want to push this
to your remote(s) as well:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }push\PYG{+w}{ }origin\PYG{+w}{ }:github\PYGZhy{}tutorial\PYGZhy{}update
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Recent changes in the workflow}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some recent changes to the workflow are not captured in this tutorial.
For example, in addition to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch, to which all new
features should be submitted, there is also a \sphinxstyleemphasis{release}, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable}, and
a \sphinxstyleemphasis{maintenance} branch; the \sphinxstyleemphasis{release} branch is updated from the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch as part of a “feature release”, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} (together
with \sphinxstyleemphasis{release}) are updated from \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} when a “stable release” is
made. In between stable releases, selected bug fixes and infrastructure
updates are back\sphinxhyphen{}ported from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{develop} branch to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maintenance}
branch and occasionally merged to \sphinxstyleemphasis{stable} as an update release.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Furthermore, the naming of the release tags now follow the pattern
“patch\_\textless{}Day\textgreater{}\textless{}Month\textgreater{}\textless{}Year\textgreater{}” to simplify comparisons between releases.
For stable releases additional “stable\_\textless{}Day\textgreater{}\textless{}Month\textgreater{}\textless{}Year\textgreater{}” tags are
applied and update releases are tagged with
“stable\_\textless{}Day\textgreater{}\textless{}Month\textgreater{}\textless{}Year\textgreater{}\_update\textless{}Number\textgreater{}”, Finally, all releases and
submissions are subject to automatic testing and code checks to make
sure they compile with a variety of compilers and popular operating
systems.  Some unit and regression testing is applied as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A detailed discussion of the LAMMPS developer GitHub workflow can be
found in the file \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/doc/github-development-workflow.md}{doc/github\sphinxhyphen{}development\sphinxhyphen{}workflow.md}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Using LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:using-lammps-gui}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This document describes \sphinxstylestrong{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI version 1.6}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI is a graphical text editor customized for editing LAMMPS
input files that is linked to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS library}}}}
and thus can run LAMMPS directly using the contents of the editor’s text
buffer as input.  It can retrieve and display information from LAMMPS
while it is running, display visualizations created with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump
image command}}}}, and is adapted specifically for editing
LAMMPS input files through text completion and reformatting, and linking
to the online LAMMPS documentation for known LAMMPS commands and styles.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled, ready\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}use LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI executables for Linux x86\_64
(Ubuntu 20.04LTS or later and compatible), macOS (version 11 aka Big
Sur or later), and Windows (version 10 or later) {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui-install}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{are available}}}} for download.  Non\sphinxhyphen{}MPI LAMMPS executables (as
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}}) for running LAMMPS from the command line and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{some
LAMMPS tools}}}} compiled executables are also included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The source code for LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI is included in the LAMMPS source code
distribution and can be found in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools/lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui}} folder.  It
can be compiled alongside LAMMPS when {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compiling with CMake}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI tries to provide an experience similar to what people
traditionally would have running LAMMPS using a command line window and
the console LAMMPS executable but just rolled into a single executable:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
writing \& editing LAMMPS input files with a text editor

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
run LAMMPS on those input file with selected command line flags

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
extract data from the created files and visualize it with and
external software

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
That procedure is quite effective for people proficient in using the
command line, as that allows them to use tools for the individual steps
that they are most comfortable with.  In fact, it is often \sphinxstyleemphasis{required} to
adopt this workflow when running LAMMPS simulations on high\sphinxhyphen{}performance
computing facilities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The main benefit of using LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI is that many basic tasks can be
done directly from the GUI \sphinxstylestrong{without} switching to a text console
window or using external programs, let alone writing scripts to extract
data from the generated output.  It also integrates well with graphical
desktop environments where the \sphinxtitleref{.lmp} filename extension can be
registered with LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI as the executable to launch when double
clicking on such files.  Also, LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI has support for drag\sphinxhyphen{}n\sphinxhyphen{}drop,
i.e.  an input file can be selected and then moved and dropped on the
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI executable, and LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI will launch and read the file into
its buffer.  In many cases LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI will be integrated into the
graphical desktop environment and can be launched like other
applications.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI thus makes it easier for beginners to get started running
simple LAMMPS simulations.  It is very suitable for tutorials on LAMMPS
since you only need to learn how to use a single program for most tasks
and thus time can be saved and people can focus on learning LAMMPS.
The tutorials at \sphinxurl{https://lammpstutorials.github.io/} are specifically
updated for use with LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another design goal is to keep the barrier low when replacing part of
the functionality of LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI with external tools.  That said, LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI
has some unique functionality that is not found elsewhere:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
auto\sphinxhyphen{}adapting to features available in the integrated LAMMPS library

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
interactive visualization using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}}
command with the option to copy\sphinxhyphen{}paste the resulting settings

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
automatic slide show generation from dump image out at runtime

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
automatic plotting of thermodynamics data at runtime

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
inspection of binary restart files

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following text provides a detailed tour of the features and
functionality of LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI.  Suggestions for new features and
reports of bugs are always welcome.  You can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Errors_bugs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{the same
channels as for LAMMPS itself}}}} for that purpose.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Installing Pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI Packages}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:installing-pre-compiled-lammps-gui-packages}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI is available as pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled binary packages for Linux
x86\_64, macOS 11 and later, and Windows 10 and later.  Alternately, it
can be compiled from source.


\paragraph{Windows 10 and later}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:windows-10-and-later}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After downloading the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}Win10\sphinxhyphen{}64bit\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.exe}} installer
package, you need to execute it, and start the installation process.
Since those packages are currently unsigned, you have to enable “Developer Mode”
in the Windows System Settings to run the installer.


\paragraph{MacOS 11 and later}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:macos-11-and-later}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After downloading the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}macOS\sphinxhyphen{}multiarch\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.dmg}}
installer package, you need to double\sphinxhyphen{}click it and then, in the window
that opens, drag the app bundle as indicated into the “Applications”
folder.  The follow the instructions in the “README.txt” file to
get access to the other included executables.


\paragraph{Linux on x86\_64}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:linux-on-x86-64}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For Linux with x86\_64 CPU there are currently two variants. The first
is compiled on Ubuntu 20.04LTS, is using some wrapper scripts, and
should be compatible with more recent Linux distributions.  After
downloading and unpacking the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}Linux\sphinxhyphen{}x86\_64\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.tar.gz}} package.  You can switch
into the “LAMMPS\_GUI” folder and execute “./lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui” directly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second variant uses \sphinxhref{https://www.flatpak.org}{flatpak} and
requires the flatpak management and runtime software to be installed.
After downloading the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}Linux\sphinxhyphen{}x86\_64\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.tar.gz}}
flatpak bundle, you can install it with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flatpak install \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}user
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}Linux\sphinxhyphen{}x86\_64\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.tar.gz}}.  After installation,
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI should be integrated into your desktop environment under
“Applications \textgreater{} Science” but also can be launched from the console with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flatpak run org.lammps.lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui}}.  The flatpak bundle also includes
the console LAMMPS executable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} which can be launched to run
simulations with, for example: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flatpak run \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}command=lmp
org.lammps.lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui \sphinxhyphen{}in in.melt}}.


\paragraph{Compiling from Source}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:compiling-from-source}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There also are instructions for {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui-compilation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{compiling LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI from source
code}}}} available elsewhere in the manual.
Compilation from source \sphinxstyleemphasis{requires} using CMake.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Starting LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:starting-lammps-gui}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI starts, it shows the main window, labeled \sphinxstyleemphasis{Editor}, with
either an empty buffer or the contents of the file used as argument. In
the latter case it may look like the following:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.480\linewidth]{{lammps-gui-main}.png}  \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.480\linewidth]{{lammps-gui-dark}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is the typical menu bar at the top, then the main editor buffer,
and a status bar at the bottom.  The input file contents are shown
with line numbers on the left and the input is colored according to
the LAMMPS input file syntax.  The status bar shows the status of
LAMMPS execution on the left (e.g. “Ready.” when idle) and the current
working directory on the right.  The name of the current file in the
buffer is shown in the window title; the word \sphinxtitleref{*modified*} is added if
the buffer edits have not yet saved to a file.  The geometry of the main
window is stored when exiting and restored when starting again.


\paragraph{Opening Files}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:opening-files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI application can be launched without command line arguments
and then starts with an empty buffer in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Editor} window.  If arguments
are given LAMMPS will use first command line argument as the file name for
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Editor} buffer and reads its contents into the buffer, if the file
exists.  All further arguments are ignored.  Files can also be opened via
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{File} menu, the \sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}O} (\sphinxtitleref{Command\sphinxhyphen{}O} on macOS) keyboard shortcut
or by drag\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}drop of a file from a graphical file manager into the editor
window.  If a file extension (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.lmp}}) has been registered with the
graphical environment to launch LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI, an existing input file can
be launched with LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI through double clicking.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only one file can be edited at a time, so opening a new file with a
filled buffer closes that buffer.  If the buffer has unsaved
modifications, you are asked to either cancel the operation, discard the
changes, or save them.  A buffer with modifications can be saved any
time from the “File” menu, by the keyboard shortcut \sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}S}
(\sphinxtitleref{Command\sphinxhyphen{}S} on macOS), or by clicking on the “Save” button at the very
left in the status bar.


\paragraph{Running LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:running-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
From within the LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI main window LAMMPS can be started either from
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Run} menu using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Run LAMMPS from Editor Buffer} entry, by
the keyboard shortcut \sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}Enter} (\sphinxtitleref{Command\sphinxhyphen{}Enter} on macOS), or by
clicking on the green “Run” button in the status bar.  All of these
operations causes LAMMPS to process the entire input script in the
editor buffer, which may contain multiple {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS runs in a separate thread, so the GUI stays responsive and is
able to interact with the running calculation and access data it
produces.  It is important to note that running LAMMPS this way is
using the contents of the input buffer for the run (via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_execute:_CPPv422lammps_commands_stringPvPKc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_commands\_string()}}}}} function of the LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}library
interface), and \sphinxstylestrong{not} the original file it was read from.  Thus, if
there are unsaved changes in the buffer, they \sphinxstyleemphasis{will} be used.  As an
alternative, it is also possible to run LAMMPS by reading the contents
of a file from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Run LAMMPS from File} menu entry or with
\sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}Shift\sphinxhyphen{}Enter}.  This option may be required in some rare cases
where the input uses some functionality that is not compatible with
running LAMMPS from a string buffer.  For consistency, any unsaved
changes in the buffer must be either saved to the file or undone
before LAMMPS can be run from a file.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.75]{{lammps-gui-running}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
While LAMMPS is running, the contents of the status bar change.  On
the left side there is a text indicating that LAMMPS is running, which
also indicates the number of active threads, when thread\sphinxhyphen{}parallel
acceleration was selected in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Preferences} dialog.  On the right
side, a progress bar is shown that displays the estimated progress for
the current {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also, the line number of the currently executed command is highlighted
in green.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If an error occurs (in the example below the command {\hyperref[\detokenize{label::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{label}}}} was incorrectly capitalized as “Label”), an error message
dialog is shown and the line of the input which triggered the error is
highlighted.  The state of LAMMPS in the status bar is set to “Failed.”
instead of “Ready.”

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.75]{{lammps-gui-run-error}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Up to three additional windows may open during a run:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window with the captured screen output from LAMMPS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Charts} window with a line graph created from thermodynamic output of the run

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Slide Show} window with images created by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image command}}}}
in the input

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
More information on those windows and how to adjust their behavior and
contents is given below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An active LAMMPS run can be stopped cleanly by using either the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Stop
LAMMPS} entry in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Run} menu, the keyboard shortcut \sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}/}
(\sphinxtitleref{Command\sphinxhyphen{}/} on macOS), or by clicking on the red button in the status
bar.  This will cause the running LAMMPS process to complete the current
timestep (or iteration for energy minimization) and then complete the
processing of the buffer while skipping all run or minimize commands.
This is equivalent to the input script command {\hyperref[\detokenize{timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timer timeout 0}}}} and is implemented by calling the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_utility:_CPPv420lammps_force_timeoutPv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_force\_timeout()}}}}} function of the LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}library
interface.  Please see the corresponding documentation pages to
understand the implications of this operation.


\subsubsection{Output Window}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:output-window}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, when starting a run, an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window opens that displays
the screen output of the running LAMMPS calculation, as shown below.
This text would normally be seen in the command line window.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{lammps-gui-log}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI captures the screen output from LAMMPS as it is generated and
updates the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window regularly during a run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window is replaced each time a run is started.
The runs are counted and the run number for the current run is displayed
in the window title.  It is possible to change the behavior of
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI in the preferences dialog to create a \sphinxstyleemphasis{new} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window
for every run or to not show the current \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window.  It is also
possible to show or hide the \sphinxstyleemphasis{current} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{View}
menu.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The text in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window is read\sphinxhyphen{}only and cannot be modified, but
keyboard shortcuts to select and copy all or parts of the text can be
used to transfer text to another program. Also, the keyboard shortcut
\sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}S} (\sphinxtitleref{Command\sphinxhyphen{}S} on macOS) is available to save the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} buffer to a
file.  The “Select All” and “Copy” functions, as well as a “Save Log to
File” option are also available from a context menu by clicking with the
right mouse button into the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window text area.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{lammps-gui-yaml}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Should the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window contain embedded YAML format text (see above for a
demonstration), for example from using {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style yaml}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify line yaml}}}}, the
keyboard shortcut \sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}Y} (\sphinxtitleref{Command\sphinxhyphen{}Y} on macOS) is available to save
only the YAML parts to a file.  This option is also available from a
context menu by clicking with the right mouse button into the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window
text area.


\subsubsection{Charts Window}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:charts-window}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, when starting a run, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Charts} window opens that displays a
plot of thermodynamic output of the LAMMPS calculation as shown below.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.33]{{lammps-gui-chart}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The drop down menu on the top right allows selection of different
properties that are computed and written to thermo output.  Only one
property can be shown at a time.  The plots are updated regularly with
new data as the run progresses, so they can be used to visually monitor
the evolution of available properties.  The update interval can be set
in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Preferences} dialog.  By default, the raw data for the selected
property is plotted as a blue graph. As soon as there are a sufficient
number of data points, there will be a second graph shown in red with a
smoothed version of the data.  From the drop down menu on the top left,
you can select whether to plot only the raw data, only the smoothed
data or both.  The smoothing uses a \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savitzky\%E2\%80\%93Golay\_filter}{Savitzky\sphinxhyphen{}Golay convolution filter} The
window width (left) and order (right) parameters can be set in the boxes
next to the drop down menu.  Default settings are 10 and 4 which means
that the smoothing window includes 10 points each to the left and the
right of the current data point and a fourth order polynomial is fit to
the data in the window.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use the mouse to zoom into the graph (hold the left button and
drag to mark an area) or zoom out (right click) and you can reset the
view with a click to the “lens” button next to the data drop down menu.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The window title shows the current run number that this chart window
corresponds to.  Same as for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window, the chart window is
replaced on each new run, but the behavior can be changed in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Preferences} dialog.

\sphinxAtStartPar
From the \sphinxstyleemphasis{File} menu on the top left, it is possible to save an image
of the currently displayed plot or export the data in either plain text
columns (for use by plotting tools like \sphinxhref{http://www.gnuplot.info/}{gnuplot} or \sphinxhref{https://plasma-gate.weizmann.ac.il/Grace/}{grace}), as CSV data which can be
imported for further processing with Microsoft Excel \sphinxhref{https://www.libreoffice.org/}{LibreOffice Calc} or with Python via \sphinxhref{https://pandas.pydata.org/}{pandas}, or as YAML which can be imported into
Python with \sphinxhref{https://pyyaml.org/}{PyYAML} or pandas.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermo output data from successive run commands in the input script is
combined into a single data set unless the format, number, or names of
output columns are changed with a {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} or
a {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command, or the current time step
is reset with {\hyperref[\detokenize{reset_timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{reset\_timestep}}}}, or if a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{clear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{clear}}}} command is issued.  This is where the YAML export
from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Charts} window differs from that of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} window:
here you get the compounded data set starting with the last change of
output fields or timestep setting, while the export from the log will
contain \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} YAML output but \sphinxstyleemphasis{segmented} into individual runs.


\subsubsection{Image Slide Show}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:image-slide-show}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, if the LAMMPS input contains a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} command, a “Slide Show” window opens which loads and
displays the images created by LAMMPS as they are written.  This is a
convenient way to visually monitor the progress of the simulation.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{lammps-gui-slideshow}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The various buttons at the bottom right of the window allow single
stepping through the sequence of images or playing an animation (as a
continuous loop or once from first to last).  It is also possible to
zoom in or zoom out of the displayed images. The button on the very
left triggers an export of the slide show animation to a movie file,
provided the \sphinxhref{https://ffmpeg.org/}{FFmpeg program} is installed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When clicking on the “garbage can” icon, all image files of the slide
show will be deleted.  Since their number can be large for long
simulations, this option enables to safely and quickly clean up the
clutter caused in the working directory by those image files without
risk of deleting other files by accident when using wildcards.


\subsubsection{Variable Info}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:variable-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
During a run, it may be of interest to monitor the value of input script
variables, for example to monitor the progress of loops.  This can be
done by enabling the “Variables Window” in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{View} menu or by using
the \sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}Shift\sphinxhyphen{}W} keyboard shortcut.  This shows info similar to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{info::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{info variables}}}} command in a separate window as shown
below.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{lammps-gui-variable-info}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Like for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Charts} windows, its content is continuously
updated during a run.  It will show “(none)” if there are no variables
defined.  Note that it is also possible to \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{index style
variables}}}}, that would normally be set via command line
flags, via the “Set Variables…” dialog from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Run} menu.
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI automatically defines the variable “gui\_run” to the current
value of the run counter.  That way it is possible to automatically
record a separate log for each run attempt by using the command

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{log}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{logfile}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{gui\PYGZus{}run}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{n}{.txt}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
at the beginning of an input file. That would record logs to files
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{logfile\sphinxhyphen{}1.txt}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{logfile\sphinxhyphen{}2.txt}}, and so on for successive runs.


\subsubsection{Snapshot Image Viewer}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:snapshot-image-viewer}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui:snapshot-viewer}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By selecting the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Create Image} entry in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Run} menu, or by
hitting the \sphinxtitleref{Ctrl\sphinxhyphen{}I} (\sphinxtitleref{Command\sphinxhyphen{}I} on macOS) keyboard shortcut, or by
