\subsubsection{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} is a Python wrapper class for
LAMMPS which can be created on its own or use an existing
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps Python}}}}} object.  It creates a simpler,
more “pythonic” interface to common LAMMPS functionality, in contrast to
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} wrapper for the LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{C
language library interface API}}}} which is written using
\sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html}{Python ctypes}.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}}
wrapper is discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Use Python with LAMMPS}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike the flat \sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html}{ctypes} interface, PyLammps exposes a
discoverable API.  It no longer requires knowledge of the underlying C++
code implementation.  Finally, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.IPyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{IPyLammps}}}}} wrapper builds on top of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} and adds some additional features for \sphinxhref{https://ipython.org/}{IPython
integration} into \sphinxhref{https://jupyter.org/}{Jupyter notebooks}, e.g. for
embedded visualization output from {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump style image}}}}.


\paragraph{Comparison of lammps and PyLammps interfaces}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:comparison-of-lammps-and-pylammps-interfaces}}

\subparagraph{lammps.lammps}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:lammps-lammps}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
uses \sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html}{ctypes}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
direct memory access to native C++ data with optional support for NumPy arrays

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
provides functions to send and receive data to LAMMPS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
interface modeled after the LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{C language library interface API}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
requires knowledge of how LAMMPS internally works (C pointers, etc)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
full support for running Python with MPI using \sphinxhref{https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io}{mpi4py}

\end{itemize}


\subparagraph{lammps.PyLammps}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:lammps-pylammps}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
higher\sphinxhyphen{}level abstraction built on \sphinxstyleemphasis{top} of original {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctypes based interface}}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
manipulation of Python objects

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
communication with LAMMPS is hidden from API user

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
shorter, more concise Python

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
better IPython integration, designed for quick prototyping

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
designed for serial execution

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Quick Start}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:quick-start}}

\paragraph{System\sphinxhyphen{}wide Installation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:system-wide-installation}}

\subparagraph{Step 1: Building LAMMPS as a shared library}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:step-1-building-lammps-as-a-shared-library}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To use LAMMPS inside of Python it has to be compiled as shared
library. This library is then loaded by the Python interface. In this
example we enable the MOLECULE package and compile LAMMPS with PNG, JPEG
and FFMPEG output support enabled.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Step 1a: For the CMake based build system, the steps are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}LAMMPS\PYGZus{}DIR}/build\PYGZhy{}shared
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}LAMMPS\PYGZus{}DIR}/build\PYGZhy{}shared

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} MPI, PNG, Jpeg, FFMPEG are auto\PYGZhy{}detected}
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DPKG\PYGZus{}MOLECULE\PYG{o}{=}yes\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DBUILD\PYGZus{}LIB\PYG{o}{=}yes\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DBUILD\PYGZus{}SHARED\PYGZus{}LIBS\PYG{o}{=}yes
make
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Step 1b: For the legacy, make based build system, the steps are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}LAMMPS\PYGZus{}DIR}/src

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} add packages if necessary}
make\PYG{+w}{ }yes\PYGZhy{}MOLECULE

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} compile shared library using Makefile}
make\PYG{+w}{ }mpi\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{mode}\PYG{o}{=}shlib\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{LMP\PYGZus{}INC}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZhy{}DLAMMPS\PYGZus{}PNG \PYGZhy{}DLAMMPS\PYGZus{}JPEG \PYGZhy{}DLAMMPS\PYGZus{}FFMPEG\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{JPG\PYGZus{}LIB}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZhy{}lpng \PYGZhy{}ljpeg\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subparagraph{Step 2: Installing the LAMMPS Python package}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:step-2-installing-the-lammps-python-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
PyLammps is part of the lammps Python package. To install it simply install
that package into your current Python installation with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYGZhy{}python
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Recompiling the shared library requires re\sphinxhyphen{}installing the Python package
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\paragraph{Installation inside of a virtualenv}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:installation-inside-of-a-virtualenv}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use virtualenv to create a custom Python environment specifically tuned
for your workflow.


\subparagraph{Benefits of using a virtualenv}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:benefits-of-using-a-virtualenv}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
isolation of your system Python installation from your development installation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
installation can happen in your user directory without root access (useful for HPC clusters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
installing packages through pip allows you to get newer versions of packages than e.g., through apt\sphinxhyphen{}get or yum package managers (and without root access)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you can even install specific old versions of a package if necessary

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Prerequisite (e.g. on Ubuntu)}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
apt\PYGZhy{}get\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYGZhy{}virtualenv
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subparagraph{Creating a virtualenv with lammps installed}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:creating-a-virtualenv-with-lammps-installed}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} create virtualenv named \PYGZsq{}testing\PYGZsq{}}
virtualenv\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}HOME}/python/testing

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} activate \PYGZsq{}testing\PYGZsq{} environment}
\PYG{n+nb}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}HOME}/python/testing/bin/activate
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now configure and compile the LAMMPS shared library as outlined above.
When using CMake and the shared library has already been build, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}run CMake to update the location of the python executable
to the location in the virtual environment with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }.\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}DPython\PYGZus{}EXECUTABLE\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}which\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{k}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} install LAMMPS package in virtualenv}
\PYG{o}{(}testing\PYG{o}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }make\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYGZhy{}python

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} install other useful packages}
\PYG{o}{(}testing\PYG{o}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }matplotlib\PYG{+w}{ }jupyter\PYG{+w}{ }mpi4py

...

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} return to original shell}
\PYG{o}{(}testing\PYG{o}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }deactivate
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Creating a new instance of PyLammps}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:creating-a-new-instance-of-pylammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To create a PyLammps object you need to first import the class from the lammps
module. By using the default constructor, a new \sphinxstyleemphasis{lammps} instance is created.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{PyLammps}
\PYG{n}{L} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{PyLammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also initialize PyLammps on top of this existing \sphinxstyleemphasis{lammps} object:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{PyLammps}
\PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{L} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{PyLammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Commands}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sending a LAMMPS command with the existing library interfaces is done using
the command method of the lammps object instance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For instance, let’s take the following LAMMPS command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{box}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{block}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the original interface this command can be executed with the following
Python code if \sphinxstyleemphasis{L} was a lammps instance:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{region box block 0 10 0 5 \PYGZhy{}0.5 0.5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the PyLammps interface, any command can be split up into arbitrary parts
separated by white\sphinxhyphen{}space, passed as individual arguments to a region method.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{region}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{box block}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.5}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.5}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that each parameter is set as Python literal floating\sphinxhyphen{}point number. In the
PyLammps interface, each command takes an arbitrary parameter list and transparently
merges it to a single command string, separating individual parameters by white\sphinxhyphen{}space.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The benefit of this approach is avoiding redundant command calls and easier
parameterization. In the original interface parameterization needed to be done
manually by creating formatted strings.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{region box block }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}} \PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{xlo}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{xhi}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ylo}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{yhi}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{zlo}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{zhi}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In contrast, methods of PyLammps accept parameters directly and will convert
them automatically to a final command string.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{region}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{box block}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{xlo}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{xhi}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ylo}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{yhi}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{zlo}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{zhi}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{System state}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:system-state}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to dispatching commands directly through the PyLammps object, it
also provides several properties which allow you to query the system state.
\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{L.system}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Is a dictionary describing the system such as the bounding box or number of atoms

\sphinxlineitem{L.system.xlo, L.system.xhi}
\sphinxAtStartPar
bounding box limits along x\sphinxhyphen{}axis

\sphinxlineitem{L.system.ylo, L.system.yhi}
\sphinxAtStartPar
bounding box limits along y\sphinxhyphen{}axis

\sphinxlineitem{L.system.zlo, L.system.zhi}
\sphinxAtStartPar
bounding box limits along z\sphinxhyphen{}axis

\sphinxlineitem{L.communication}
\sphinxAtStartPar
configuration of communication subsystem, such as the number of threads or processors

\sphinxlineitem{L.communication.nthreads}
\sphinxAtStartPar
number of threads used by each LAMMPS process

\sphinxlineitem{L.communication.nprocs}
\sphinxAtStartPar
number of MPI processes used by LAMMPS

\sphinxlineitem{L.fixes}
\sphinxAtStartPar
List of fixes in the current system

\sphinxlineitem{L.computes}
\sphinxAtStartPar
List of active computes in the current system

\sphinxlineitem{L.dump}
\sphinxAtStartPar
List of active dumps in the current system

\sphinxlineitem{L.groups}
\sphinxAtStartPar
List of groups present in the current system

\end{description}


\subsubsection{Working with LAMMPS variables}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:working-with-lammps-variables}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS variables can be both defined and accessed via the PyLammps interface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To define a variable you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{variable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{a index 2}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A dictionary of all variables is returned by L.variables

\sphinxAtStartPar
you can access an individual variable by retrieving a variable object from the
L.variables dictionary by name

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{a} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{variables}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{a}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The variable value can then be easily read and written by accessing the value
property of this object.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{value} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{4}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Retrieving the value of an arbitrary LAMMPS expressions}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:retrieving-the-value-of-an-arbitrary-lammps-expressions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS expressions can be immediately evaluated by using the eval method. The
passed string parameter can be any expression containing global thermo values,
variables, compute or fix data.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eval}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ke}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} kinetic energy}
\PYG{n}{result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eval}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pe}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} potential energy}

\PYG{n}{result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eval}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{v\PYGZus{}t/2.0}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Accessing atom data}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:accessing-atom-data}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All atoms in the current simulation can be accessed by using the L.atoms list.
Each element of this list is an object which exposes its properties (id, type,
position, velocity, force, etc.).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} access first atom}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{id}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{type}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} access second atom}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{velocity}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{force}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some properties can also be used to set:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set position in 2D simulation}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set position in 3D simulation}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Evaluating thermo data}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:evaluating-thermo-data}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Each simulation run usually produces thermo output based on system state,
computes, fixes or variables. The trajectories of these values can be queried
after a run via the L.runs list. This list contains a growing list of run data.
The first element is the output of the first run, the second element that of
the second run.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1000}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{runs}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} data of first 1000 time steps}

\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1000}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{runs}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} data of second 1000 time steps}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each run contains a dictionary of all trajectories. Each trajectory is
accessible through its thermo name:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{runs}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Step} \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} list of time steps in first run}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{runs}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Ke}   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} list of kinetic energy values in first run}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Together with matplotlib plotting data out of LAMMPS becomes simple:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{matplotlib}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{plot}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{plt}
\PYG{n}{steps} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{runs}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Step}
\PYG{n}{ke}    \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{runs}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Ke}
\PYG{n}{plt}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{plot}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{steps}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Error handling with PyLammps}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:error-handling-with-pylammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using C++ exceptions in LAMMPS for errors allows capturing them on the
C++ side and rethrowing them on the Python side.  This way you can handle
LAMMPS errors through the Python exception handling mechanism.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Capturing a LAMMPS exception in Python can still mean that the
current LAMMPS process is in an illegal state and must be
terminated. It is advised to save your data and terminate the Python
instance as quickly as possible.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Using PyLammps in IPython notebooks and Jupyter}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:using-pylammps-in-ipython-notebooks-and-jupyter}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the LAMMPS Python package is installed for the same Python interpreter as
IPython, you can use PyLammps directly inside of an IPython notebook inside of
Jupyter. Jupyter is a powerful integrated development environment (IDE) for
many dynamic languages like Python, Julia and others, which operates inside of
any web browser. Besides auto\sphinxhyphen{}completion and syntax highlighting it allows you
to create formatted documents using Markup, mathematical formulas, graphics and
animations intermixed with executable Python code. It is a great format for
tutorials and showcasing your latest research.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To launch an instance of Jupyter simply run the following command inside your
Python environment (this assumes you followed the Quick Start instructions):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
jupyter\PYG{+w}{ }notebook
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{IPyLammps Examples}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:ipylammps-examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples of IPython notebooks can be found in the python/examples/pylammps
subdirectory. To open these notebooks launch \sphinxstyleemphasis{jupyter notebook} inside this
directory and navigate to one of them. If you compiled and installed
a LAMMPS shared library with exceptions, PNG, JPEG and FFMPEG support
you should be able to rerun all of these notebooks.


\paragraph{Validating a dihedral potential}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:validating-a-dihedral-potential}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This example showcases how an IPython Notebook can be used to compare a simple
LAMMPS simulation of a harmonic dihedral potential to its analytical solution.
Four atoms are placed in the simulation and the dihedral potential is applied on
them using a datafile. Then one of the atoms is rotated along the central axis by
setting its position from Python, which changes the dihedral angle.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{phi} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{d} \PYGZbs{}\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pi} \PYG{o}{/} \PYG{l+m+mi}{180} \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{d} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{360}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}

\PYG{n}{pos} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{cos}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{sin}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{p} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{phi}\PYG{p}{]}

\PYG{n}{pe} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{p} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{pos}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{p}
    \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eval}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pe}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
By evaluating the potential energy for each position we can verify that
trajectory with the analytical formula.  To compare both solutions, we plot
both trajectories over each other using matplotlib, which embeds the generated
plot inside the IPython notebook.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{pylammps_dihedral}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}


\paragraph{Running a Monte Carlo relaxation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:running-a-monte-carlo-relaxation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This second example shows how to use PyLammps to create a 2D Monte Carlo Relaxation
simulation, computing and plotting energy terms and even embedding video output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Initially, a 2D system is created in a state with minimal energy.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{pylammps_mc_minimum}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is then disordered by moving each atom by a random delta.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{seed}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{27848}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{deltaperturb} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.2}

\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{system}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{natoms}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position}
    \PYG{n}{dx} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{deltaperturb} \PYGZbs{}\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{uniform}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{dy} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{deltaperturb} \PYGZbs{}\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{uniform}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{dx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{dy}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{pylammps_mc_disordered}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, the Monte Carlo algorithm is implemented in Python. It continuously
moves random atoms by a random delta and only accepts certain moves.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{estart} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eval}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pe}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{elast} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{estart}

\PYG{n}{naccept} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}
\PYG{n}{energies} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{estart}\PYG{p}{]}

\PYG{n}{niterations} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3000}
\PYG{n}{deltamove} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.1}
\PYG{n}{kT} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.05}

\PYG{n}{natoms} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{system}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{natoms}

\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{niterations}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{iatom} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{randrange}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{natoms}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{current\PYGZus{}atom} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{iatom}\PYG{p}{]}

    \PYG{n}{x0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y0} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{current\PYGZus{}atom}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position}

    \PYG{n}{dx} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{deltamove} \PYGZbs{}\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{uniform}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{dy} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{deltamove} \PYGZbs{}\PYG{o}{*} \PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{uniform}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{n}{current\PYGZus{}atom}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{x0}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{dx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y0}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{dy}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pre no post no}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{n}{e} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eval}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pe}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{energies}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{e}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{e} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{elast}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{naccept} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
        \PYG{n}{elast} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{e}
    \PYG{k}{elif} \PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{exp}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{natoms}\PYGZbs{}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{elast}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{e}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{kT}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{naccept} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
        \PYG{n}{elast} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{e}
    \PYG{k}{else}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{current\PYGZus{}atom}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{x0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{y0}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energies of each iteration are collected in a Python list and finally plotted using matplotlib.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{pylammps_mc_energies_plot}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The IPython notebook also shows how to use dump commands and embed video files
inside of the IPython notebook.


\subsubsection{Using PyLammps and mpi4py (Experimental)}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_pylammps:using-pylammps-and-mpi4py-experimental}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
PyLammps can be run in parallel using \sphinxhref{https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io}{mpi4py}. This python package can be installed
using

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }mpi4py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually, any {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} command must be
executed by \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} MPI processes. However, evaluations and querying
the system state is only available on MPI rank 0.  Using these
functions from other MPI ranks will raise an exception.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following is a short example which reads in an existing LAMMPS input
file and executes it in parallel.  You can find in.melt in the
examples/melt folder.  Please take note that the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps.eval}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps.eval()}}}}} is called only from
MPI rank 0.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{mpi4py}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{MPI}
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{PyLammps}

\PYG{n}{L} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{PyLammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{in.melt}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{MPI}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{COMM\PYGZus{}WORLD}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{rank} \PYG{o}{==} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Potential energy: }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eval}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pe}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{MPI}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Finalize}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To run this script (melt.py) in parallel using 4 MPI processes we invoke the
following mpirun command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }python\PYG{+w}{ }melt.py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{Using LAMMPS on Windows 10 with WSL}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:using-lammps-on-windows-10-with-wsl}}\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{written by Richard Berger}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
It’s always been tricky for us to have LAMMPS users and developers work on
Windows. We primarily develop LAMMPS to run on Linux clusters. To teach
LAMMPS in workshop settings, we had to redirect Windows users to
Linux Virtual Machines such as VirtualBox or Unix\sphinxhyphen{}like compilation with
Cygwin.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the latest updates in Windows 10 (Version 2004, Build 19041 or
higher), Microsoft has added a new way to work on Linux\sphinxhyphen{}based code. The
\sphinxhref{https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/}{Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)}.  With WSL Version 2,
you now get a Linux Virtual Machine that transparently integrates into
Windows.  All you need is to ensure you have the latest Windows updates
installed and enable this new feature.  Linux VMs are then easily
installed using the Microsoft Store.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this tutorial, I’ll show you how to set up and compile LAMMPS for both serial
and MPI usage in WSL2.


\subsubsection{Installation}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:installation}}

\paragraph{Upgrade to the latest Windows 10}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:upgrade-to-the-latest-windows-10}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Type “Updates” in Windows Start and select “Check for Updates”.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{updates}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Install all pending updates and reboot your system as many times as
necessary. Continue until your Windows installation is updated.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{windows_update}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Verify your system has at least \sphinxstylestrong{version 2004 and build 19041 or later}. You
can find this information by clicking on “OS build info”.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{osinfo}.png}


\paragraph{Enable WSL}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:enable-wsl}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Next, we must install two additional Windows features to enable WSL support.
Open a PowerShell window as an administrator. Type “PowerShell” in Windows
Start and select “Run as Administrator”.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{powershell}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows will ask you for administrator access. After you accept a new command
line window will appear. Type in the following command to install WSL:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
dism.exe /online /enable\PYGZhy{}feature /featurename:Microsoft\PYGZhy{}Windows\PYGZhy{}Subsystem\PYGZhy{}Linux /all /norestart
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{wsl_install1}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Next, enable the VirtualMachinePlatform feature using the following command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
dism.exe /online /enable\PYGZhy{}feature /featurename:VirtualMachinePlatform /all /norestart
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{wsl_install2}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, reboot your system.


\paragraph{Update WSL kernel component}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:update-wsl-kernel-component}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Download and install the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WSL Kernel Component Update}}.
Afterwards, reboot your system.


\paragraph{Set WSL2 as default}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:set-wsl2-as-default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Again, open PowerShell as administrator and run the following command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{wsl} \PYG{p}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{\PYGZhy{}set}\PYG{n}{\PYGZhy{}default}\PYG{n}{\PYGZhy{}version} \PYG{n}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command ensures that all future Linux installations will use WSL version 2.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{wsl_install3}.png}


\paragraph{Install a Linux Distribution}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:install-a-linux-distribution}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Next, we need to install a Linux distribution via the Microsoft Store.
Install \sphinxhref{ms-windows-store://pdp/?ProductId=9n6svws3rx71}{Ubuntu 20.04 LTS}.
Once installed, you can launch it like any other application from the Start
Menu.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{ubuntu_in_store}.png}


\subparagraph{Initial Setup}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:initial-setup}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first time you launch the Ubuntu Linux console, it will prompt you for a
UNIX username and password. You will need this password to perform \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sudo}}
commands later. Once completed, your Linux shell is ready for use. All your
actions and commands will run as the Linux user you specified.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{first_login}.png}


\subsubsection{Windows Explorer / WSL integration}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:windows-explorer-wsl-integration}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Your Linux installation will have its own Linux filesystem, which contains
the Ubuntu files. Your Linux user will have a regular Linux home directory in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/home/\textless{}USERNAME\textgreater{}}}. This directory is different from your Windows User
directory. Windows and Linux filesystems are connected through WSL.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All hard drives in Windows are accessible in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/mnt}} directory in Linux.
E.g., WSL maps the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}} hard drive to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/mnt/c}} directory. That means you
can access your Windows User directory in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/mnt/c/Users/\textless{}WINDOWS\_USERNAME\textgreater{}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Windows Explorer can also access the Linux filesystem. To illustrate this
integration, open an Ubuntu console and navigate to a directory of your
choice. To view this location in Windows Explorer, use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{explorer.exe .}}
command (do not forget the final dot!).

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{wsl_integration}.png}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Compiling LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:compiling-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You now have a fully functioning Ubuntu installation and can follow most
guides to install LAMMPS on a Linux system. Here are some of the essential
steps to follow:


\paragraph{Install prerequisite packages}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:install-prerequisite-packages}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before we can begin, we need to download the necessary compiler toolchain and
libraries to compile LAMMPS. In our Ubuntu\sphinxhyphen{}based Linux installation, we will
use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{apt}} package manager to install additional packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First, upgrade all existing packages using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{apt update}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{apt upgrade}}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYG{+w}{ }update
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYG{+w}{ }upgrade\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}y
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Next, install the following packages with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{apt install}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
sudo\PYG{+w}{ }apt\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}y\PYG{+w}{ }cmake\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYGZhy{}essential\PYG{+w}{ }ccache\PYG{+w}{ }gfortran\PYG{+w}{ }openmpi\PYGZhy{}bin\PYG{+w}{ }libopenmpi\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{                    }libfftw3\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }libjpeg\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }libpng\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }python3\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }python3\PYGZhy{}pip\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{                    }python3\PYGZhy{}virtualenv\PYG{+w}{ }libblas\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }liblapack\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }libhdf5\PYGZhy{}serial\PYGZhy{}dev\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{                    }hdf5\PYGZhy{}tools
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Download LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:download-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Obtain a copy of the LAMMPS source code and go into it using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cd}} command.


\subparagraph{Option 1: Download a LAMMPS tarball using wget}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:option-1-download-a-lammps-tarball-using-wget}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
wget\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/lammps/lammps/archive/stable\PYGZus{}3Mar2020.tar.gz
tar\PYG{+w}{ }xvzf\PYG{+w}{ }stable\PYGZus{}3Mar2020.tar.gz
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subparagraph{Option 2: Download a LAMMPS development version from GitHub}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:option-2-download-a-lammps-development-version-from-github}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}depth\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }lammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Configure and Compile LAMMPS with CMake}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:configure-and-compile-lammps-with-cmake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A beginner\sphinxhyphen{}friendly way to compile LAMMPS is to use CMake. Create a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}}
directory to compile LAMMPS and move into it. This directory will store the
build configuration and any binaries generated during compilation.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }build
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }build
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are countless ways to compile LAMMPS. It is beyond the scope of this
tutorial. If you want to find out more about what can be enabled, please
consult the extensive \sphinxhref{https://docs.lammps.org/Build\_cmake.html}{documentation}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To compile a minimal version of LAMMPS, we’re going to use a preset.
Presets are a way to specify a collection of CMake options using a file.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/basic.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command configures the build and generates the necessary Makefiles. To compile the binary, run the make command.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}j\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}j}} option specifies how many parallel processes will perform the
compilation. This option can significantly speed up compilation times. Use a
number that corresponds to the number of processors in your system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the compilation completes successfully, you will have an executable
called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} directory.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.5]{{compilation_result}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please take note of the absolute path of your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} directory. You will
need to know the location to execute the LAMMPS binary later.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One way of getting the absolute path of the current directory is through the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$PWD}} variable:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} prints out the current value of the PWD variable}
\PYG{n+nb}{echo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let us save this value in a temporary variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_BUILD\_DIR}} for future use:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nv}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}BUILD\PYGZus{}DIR}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PWD}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The full path of the LAMMPS binary then is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$LAMMPS\_BUILD\_DIR/lmp}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Running an example script}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:running-an-example-script}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now that we have a LAMMPS binary, we will run a script from the examples folder.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Switch into the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/melt}} folder:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
cd ../examples/melt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To run this example in serial, use the following command line:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZdl{}LAMMPS\PYGZus{}BUILD\PYGZus{}DIR/lmp \PYGZhy{}in in.melt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To run the same script in parallel using MPI with 4 processes, do the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}LAMMPS\PYGZus{}BUILD\PYGZus{}DIR}/lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.melt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you run LAMMPS for the first time, the Windows Firewall might prompt you
to confirm access. LAMMPS is accessing the network stack to enable parallel
computation. Allow the access.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.75]{{windows_firewall}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In either serial or MPI case, LAMMPS executes and will output something similar to this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
LAMMPS (30 Jun 2020)
...
...
...
Total \PYGZsh{} of neighbors = 151513
Ave neighs/atom = 37.878250
Neighbor list builds = 12
Dangerous builds not checked
Total wall time: 0:00:00
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Congratulations! You’ve successfully compiled and executed LAMMPS on WSL!}


\subsubsection{Final steps}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:final-steps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is cumbersome to always specify the path of your LAMMPS binary. You can
avoid this by adding the absolute path of your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} directory to your PATH
environment variable.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{export}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PATH}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}LAMMPS\PYGZus{}BUILD\PYGZus{}DIR}:\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PATH}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can then run LAMMPS input scripts like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.melt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.melt
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of this \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}} variable will disappear once you close your
console window. To persist this setting edit the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$HOME/.bashrc}} file using your
favorite text editor and add this line:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{export}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PATH}\PYG{o}{=}/full/path/to/your/lammps/build:\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PATH}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example:}
If the LAMMPS executable \sphinxtitleref{lmp} has the following absolute path:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
/home/\PYGZlt{}USERNAME\PYGZgt{}/lammps/build/lmp
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}} variable should be:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{export}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PATH}\PYG{o}{=}/home/\PYGZlt{}USERNAME\PYGZgt{}/lammps/build:\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}PATH}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once set up, all your Ubuntu consoles will always have access to your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}}
binary without having to specify its location.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Conclusion}
\label{\detokenize{Howto_wsl:conclusion}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
I hope this gives you good overview on how to start compiling and running LAMMPS on
Windows. WSL makes preparing and running scripts on Windows a much better
experience.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are completely new to Linux, I highly recommend investing some time in
studying Linux online tutorials. E.g., tutorials about Bash Shell and Basic
Unix commands (e.g., \sphinxhref{https://linuxjourney.com/}{Linux Journey}). Acquiring
these skills will make you much more productive in this environment.


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/}{Windows Subsystem for Linux Documentation}

\end{itemize}


\end{sphinxseealso}


\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Example scripts}
\label{\detokenize{Examples:example-scripts}}\label{\detokenize{Examples::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS distribution includes an examples subdirectory with many
sample problems.  Many are 2d models that run quickly and are
straightforward to visualize, requiring at most a couple of minutes to
run on a desktop machine.  Each problem has an input script (in.*) and
produces a log file (log.*) when it runs.  Some use a data file
(data.*) of initial coordinates as additional input.  A few sample log
file run on different machines and different numbers of processors are
included in the directories to compare your answers to.  E.g. a log
file like log.date.crack.foo.P means the “crack” example was run on P
processors of machine “foo” on that date (i.e. with that version of
LAMMPS).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many of the input files have commented\sphinxhyphen{}out lines for creating dump
files and image files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you uncomment the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} command in the input script, a
text dump file will be produced, which can be animated by various
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/viz.html}{visualization programs}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you uncomment the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} command in the input
script, and assuming you have built LAMMPS with a JPG library, JPG
snapshot images will be produced when the simulation runs.  They can
be quickly post\sphinxhyphen{}processed into a movie using commands described on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Animations of many of the examples can be viewed on the Movies section
of the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/movies.html}{LAMMPS website}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two kinds of subdirectories in the examples folder.  Lower
case named directories contain one or a few simple, quick\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}run
problems.  Upper case named directories contain up to several complex
scripts that illustrate a particular kind of simulation method or
model.  Some of these run for longer times, e.g. to measure a
particular quantity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lists of both kinds of directories are given below.

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Running the simulation produces the files \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump.indent} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{log.lammps}.  You can visualize the dump file of snapshots with a
variety of third\sphinxhyphen{}party tools highlighted on the
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/viz.html}{Visualization} page of the LAMMPS
website.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you uncomment the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} line(s) in the input
script a series of JPG images will be produced by the run (assuming
you built LAMMPS with JPG support; see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build\_settings}}}} page for details).  These can
be viewed individually or turned into a movie or animated by tools
like ImageMagick or QuickTime or various Windows\sphinxhyphen{}based tools.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} page for more details.  E.g. this
Imagemagick command would create a GIF file suitable for viewing in a
browser.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZpc{}\PYG{+w}{ }convert\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}loop\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }*.jpg\PYG{+w}{ }foo.gif
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\chapter{Auxiliary tools}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:auxiliary-tools}}\label{\detokenize{Tools::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed to be a computational kernel for performing
molecular dynamics computations.  Additional pre\sphinxhyphen{} and post\sphinxhyphen{}processing
steps are often necessary to setup and analyze a simulation.  A list
of such tools can be found on the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org}{LAMMPS webpage} at these links:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/prepost.html}{Pre/Post processing}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/external.html}{External LAMMPS packages \& tools}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxhref{https://lammps.github.io/pizza}{Pizza.py toolkit}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last link for \sphinxhref{https://lammps.github.io/pizza}{Pizza.py} is a Python\sphinxhyphen{}based tool developed at
Sandia which provides tools for doing setup, analysis, plotting, and
visualization for LAMMPS simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional tools included in the LAMMPS distribution are described on
this page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that many users write their own setup or analysis tools or use
other existing codes and convert their output to a LAMMPS input format
or vice versa.  The tools listed here are included in the LAMMPS
distribution as examples of auxiliary tools.  Some of them are not
actively supported by the LAMMPS developers, as they were contributed
by LAMMPS users.  If you have problems using them, we can direct you
to the authors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The source code for each of these codes is in the tools subdirectory
of the LAMMPS distribution.  There is a Makefile (which you may need
to edit for your platform) which will build several of the tools which
reside in that directory.  Most of them are larger packages in their
own subdirectories with their own Makefiles and/or README files.
