\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\section{Tool descriptions}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:tool-descriptions}}

\subsection{amber2lmp tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:amber2lmp-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:amber}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The amber2lmp subdirectory contains three Python scripts for converting
files back\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}forth between the AMBER MD code and LAMMPS.  See the
README file in amber2lmp for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These tools were written by Keir Novik while he was at Queen Mary
University of London.  Keir is no longer there and cannot support
these tools which are out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}date with respect to the current LAMMPS
version (and maybe with respect to AMBER as well).  Since we don’t use
these tools at Sandia, you will need to experiment with them and make
necessary modifications yourself.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{binary2txt tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:binary2txt-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:binary}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file binary2txt.cpp converts one or more binary LAMMPS dump file
into ASCII text files.  The syntax for running the tool is

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
binary2txt\PYG{+w}{ }file1\PYG{+w}{ }file2\PYG{+w}{ }...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which creates file1.txt, file2.txt, etc.  This tool must be compiled
on a platform that can read the binary file created by a LAMMPS run,
since binary files are not compatible across all platforms.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{ch2lmp tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:ch2lmp-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:charmm}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ch2lmp subdirectory contains tools for converting files
back\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}forth between the CHARMM MD code and LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
They are intended to make it easy to use CHARMM as a builder and as a
post\sphinxhyphen{}processor for LAMMPS. Using charmm2lammps.pl, you can convert a
PDB file with associated CHARMM info, including CHARMM force field
data, into its LAMMPS equivalent. Support for the CMAP correction of
CHARMM22 and later is available as an option. This tool can also add
solvent water molecules and Na+ or Cl\sphinxhyphen{} ions to the system.
Using lammps2pdb.pl you can convert LAMMPS atom dumps into PDB files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the README file in the ch2lmp subdirectory for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These tools were created by Pieter in’t Veld (pjintve at sandia.gov)
and Paul Crozier (pscrozi at sandia.gov) at Sandia.

\sphinxAtStartPar
CMAP support added and tested by Xiaohu Hu (hux2 at ornl.gov) and
Robert A. Latour (latourr at clemson.edu), David Hyde\sphinxhyphen{}Volpe, and
Tigran Abramyan, (Clemson University) and
Chris Lorenz (chris.lorenz at kcl.ac.uk), King’s College London.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{chain tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:chain-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:chain}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file chain.f90 creates a LAMMPS data file containing bead\sphinxhyphen{}spring
polymer chains and/or monomer solvent atoms.  It uses a text file
containing chain definition parameters as an input.  The created
chains and solvent atoms can strongly overlap, so LAMMPS needs to run
the system initially with a “soft” pair potential to un\sphinxhyphen{}overlap it.
The syntax for running the tool is

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
chain\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZlt{}\PYG{+w}{ }def.chain\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }data.file
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the def.chain or def.chain.ab files in the tools directory for
examples of definition files.  This tool was used to create the system
for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_bench::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{chain benchmark}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{LAMMPS coding standard}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:lammps-coding-standard}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:coding-standard}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{coding\_standard}} folder contains multiple python scripts to
check for and apply some LAMMPS coding conventions.  The following
scripts are available:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
permissions.py   \PYGZsh{} detects if sources have executable permissions and scripts have not
whitespace.py    \PYGZsh{} detects TAB characters and trailing whitespace
homepage.py      \PYGZsh{} detects outdated LAMMPS homepage URLs (pointing to sandia.gov instead of lammps.org)
errordocs.py     \PYGZsh{} detects deprecated error docs in header files
versiontags.py   \PYGZsh{} detects .. versionadded:: or .. versionchanged:: with pending version date
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools need to be given the main folder of the LAMMPS distribution
or individual file names as argument and will by default check them
and report any non\sphinxhyphen{}compliance.  With the optional \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}f}} argument the
corresponding script will try to change the non\sphinxhyphen{}compliant file(s) to
match the conventions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For convenience this scripts can also be invoked by the make file in
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} folder with, \sphinxtitleref{make check\sphinxhyphen{}whitespace} or \sphinxtitleref{make fix\sphinxhyphen{}whitespace}
to either detect or edit the files.  Correspondingly for the other python
scripts. \sphinxtitleref{make check} will run all checks.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{colvars tools}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:colvars-tools}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The colvars directory contains a collection of tools for post\sphinxhyphen{}processing
data produced by the colvars collective variable library.
To compile the tools, edit the makefile for your system and run “make”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please report problems and issues the colvars library and its tools
at: \sphinxurl{https://github.com/colvars/colvars/issues}

\sphinxAtStartPar
abf\_integrate:

\sphinxAtStartPar
MC\sphinxhyphen{}based integration of multidimensional free energy gradient
Version 20110511
\begin{sphinxalltt}
./abf\_integrate \textless{} filename \textgreater{} {[}\sphinxhyphen{}n \textless{} nsteps \textgreater{}{]} {[}\sphinxhyphen{}t \textless{} temp \textgreater{}{]} {[}\sphinxhyphen{}m {[}0|1{]} (metadynamics){]} {[}\sphinxhyphen{}h \textless{} hill\_height \textgreater{}{]} {[}\sphinxhyphen{}f \textless{} variable\_hill\_factor \textgreater{}{]}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS interface to the colvars collective variable library, as
well as these tools, were created by Axel Kohlmeyer (akohlmey at
gmail.com) while at ICTP, Italy.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{createatoms tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:createatoms-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:createatoms}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/createatoms directory contains a Fortran program called
createAtoms.f which can generate a variety of interesting crystal
structures and geometries and output the resulting list of atom
coordinates in LAMMPS or other formats.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the included Manual.pdf for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tool is authored by Xiaowang Zhou (Sandia), xzhou at sandia.gov.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{drude tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:drude-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:drude}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/drude directory contains a Python script called
polarizer.py which can add Drude oscillators to a LAMMPS
data file in the required format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the header of the polarizer.py file for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tool is authored by Agilio Padua and Alain Dequidt: agilio.padua
at ens\sphinxhyphen{}lyon.fr, alain.dequidt at uca.fr


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{eam database tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:eam-database-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:eamdb}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/eam\_database directory contains a Fortran and a Python program
that will generate EAM alloy setfl potential files for any combination
of the 17 elements: Cu, Ag, Au, Ni, Pd, Pt, Al, Pb, Fe, Mo, Ta, W, Mg,
Co, Ti, Zr, Cr.  The files can then be used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style
eam/alloy}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Fortran version of the tool was authored by Xiaowang Zhou (Sandia),
xzhou at sandia.gov, with updates from Lucas Hale (NIST) lucas.hale at
nist.gov and is based on his paper:

\sphinxAtStartPar
X. W. Zhou, R. A. Johnson, and H. N. G. Wadley, Phys. Rev. B, 69,
144113 (2004).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters for Cr were taken from:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lin Z B, Johnson R A and Zhigilei L V, Phys. Rev. B 77 214108 (2008).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Python version of the tool was authored  by Germain Clavier
(Unicaen) germain.clavier at unicaen.fr

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters in the database are only optimized for individual
elements. The mixed parameters for interactions between different
elements generated by this tool are derived from simple mixing rules
and are thus inferior to parameterizations that are specifically
optimized for specific mixtures and combinations of elements.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{eam generate tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:eam-generate-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:eamgn}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/eam\_generate directory contains several one\sphinxhyphen{}file C programs
that convert an analytic formula into a tabulated {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{embedded atom
method (EAM)}}}} setfl potential file.  The potentials they
produce are in the potentials directory, and can be used with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style eam/alloy}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The source files and potentials were provided by Gerolf Ziegenhain
(gerolf at ziegenhain.com).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{eff tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:eff-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:eff}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/eff directory contains various scripts for generating
structures and post\sphinxhyphen{}processing output for simulations using the
electron force field (eFF).

\sphinxAtStartPar
These tools were provided by Andres Jaramillo\sphinxhyphen{}Botero at CalTech
(ajaramil at wag.caltech.edu).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{emacs tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:emacs-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:emacs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/emacs directory contains an Emacs Lisp add\sphinxhyphen{}on file for GNU Emacs
that enables a lammps\sphinxhyphen{}mode for editing input scripts when using GNU Emacs,
with various highlighting options set up.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These tools were provided by Aidan Thompson at Sandia
(athomps at sandia.gov).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{fep tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:fep-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:fep}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/fep directory contains Python scripts useful for
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing results from performing free\sphinxhyphen{}energy perturbation
simulations using the FEP package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scripts were contributed by Agilio Padua (ENS de Lyon), agilio.padua at ens\sphinxhyphen{}lyon.fr.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See README file in the tools/fep directory.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{i\sphinxhyphen{}PI tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:i-pi-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:ipi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 27June2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/i\sphinxhyphen{}pi directory used to contain a bundled version of the i\sphinxhyphen{}PI
software package for use with LAMMPS.  This version, however, was
removed in 06/2024.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The i\sphinxhyphen{}PI package was created and is maintained by Michele Ceriotti,
michele.ceriotti at gmail.com, to interface to a variety of molecular
dynamics codes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
i\sphinxhyphen{}PI is now available via PyPI using the pip package manager at:
\sphinxurl{https://pypi.org/project/ipi/}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are the commands to set up a virtual environment and install
i\sphinxhyphen{}PI into it with all its dependencies.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
python\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }venv\PYG{+w}{ }ipienv
\PYG{n+nb}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }ipienv/bin/activate
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}upgrade\PYG{+w}{ }pip
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }ipi
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To install the development version from GitHub, please use:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }git+https://github.com/i\PYGZhy{}pi/i\PYGZhy{}pi.git
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For further information, please consult the {[}i\sphinxhyphen{}PI home
page{]}(\sphinxurl{https://ipi-code.org}).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{ipp tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:ipp-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:ipp}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/ipp directory contains a Perl script ipp which can be used
to facilitate the creation of a complicated file (say, a LAMMPS input
script or tools/createatoms input file) using a template file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
ipp was created and is maintained by Reese Jones (Sandia), rjones at
sandia.gov.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See two examples in the tools/ipp directory.  One of them is for the
tools/createatoms tool’s input file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{kate tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:kate-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:kate}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file in the tools/kate directory is an add\sphinxhyphen{}on to the Kate editor
in the KDE suite that allow syntax highlighting of LAMMPS input
scripts.  See the README.txt file for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file was provided by Alessandro Luigi Sellerio
(alessandro.sellerio at ieni.cnr.it).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:id2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 2Aug2023.}


\subsubsection{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI is a graphical text editor customized for editing LAMMPS
input files that is linked to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}library}}}}
and thus can run LAMMPS directly using the contents of the editor’s text
buffer as input.  It can retrieve and display information from LAMMPS
while it is running, display visualizations created with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump
image command}}}}, and is adapted specifically for editing
LAMMPS input files through syntax highlighting, text completion, and
reformatting, and linking to the online LAMMPS documentation for known
LAMMPS commands and styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is similar to what people traditionally would do to run LAMMPS but
all rolled into a single application: that is, using a text editor,
plotting program, and a visualization program to edit the input, run
LAMMPS, process the output into graphs and visualizations from a command
line window.  This similarity is a design goal. While making it easy for
beginners to start with LAMMPS, it is also the expectation that
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI users will eventually transition to workflows that most
experienced LAMMPS users employ.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All features have been extensively exposed to keyboard shortcuts, so
that there is also appeal for experienced LAMMPS users for prototyping
and testing simulation setups.


\subsubsection{Features}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:features}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A detailed discussion and explanation of all features and functionality
are in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_lammps_gui::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Using LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI}}}} tutorial Howto page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are a few highlights of LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Text editor with line numbers and syntax highlighting customized for LAMMPS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Text editor features command completion and auto\sphinxhyphen{}indentation for known commands and styles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Text editor will switch its working directory to folder of file in buffer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Many adjustable settings and preferences that are persistent including the 5 most recent files

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Context specific LAMMPS command help via online documentation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is running in a concurrent thread, so the GUI remains responsive

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Progress bar indicates how far a run command is completed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can be started and stopped with a mouse click or a hotkey

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Screen output is captured in an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Output} Window

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermodynamic output is captured and displayed as line graph in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Chart} Window

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Indicator for currently executed command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Indicator for line that caused an error

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Visualization of current state in Image Viewer (via calling {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_dump image}}}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Capture of images created via {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_image::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump image}}}} in Slide show window

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dialog to set variables, similar to the LAMMPS command line flag ‘\sphinxhyphen{}v’ / ‘\sphinxhyphen{}var’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS/OpenMP, OPENMAP, and OPT and accelerator packages

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Parallelization}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:parallelization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Due to its nature as a graphical application, it is not possible to use
the LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI in parallel with MPI, but OpenMP multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading and GPU
acceleration is available and enabled by default.


\subsubsection{Prerequisites and portability}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:prerequisites-and-portability}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI is programmed in C++ based on the C++11 standard and using
the \sphinxhref{https://www.qt.io/product/framework}{Qt GUI framework}.
Currently, Qt version 5.12 or later is required; Qt 5.15LTS is
recommended; support for Qt version 6.x is available.  Building LAMMPS
with CMake is required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI has been successfully compiled and tested on:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ubuntu Linux 20.04LTS x86\_64 using GCC 9, Qt version 5.12

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fedora Linux 40 x86\_64 using GCC 14 and Clang 17, Qt version 5.15LTS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fedora Linux 40 x86\_64 using GCC 14, Qt version 6.7

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Apple macOS 12 (Monterey) and macOS 13 (Ventura) with Xcode on arm64 and x86\_64, Qt version 5.15LTS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows 10 and 11 x86\_64 with Visual Studio 2022 and Visual C++ 14.36, Qt version 5.15LTS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows 10 and 11 x86\_64 with Visual Studio 2022 and Visual C++ 14.40, Qt version 6.7

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows 10 and 11 x86\_64 with MinGW / GCC 10.0 cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiler on Fedora 38, Qt version 5.15LTS

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled executables}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:pre-compiled-executables}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui-install}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled LAMMPS executable packages that include the GUI are
currently available from \sphinxurl{https://download.lammps.org/static} or
\sphinxurl{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/releases}.  For Windows, you need to
download and then run the application installer.  For macOS you download
and mount the disk image and then drag the application bundle to the
Applications folder.  For Linux (x86\_64) you currently have two
options: 1) you can download the tar.gz archive, unpack it and run the
GUI directly in place.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_GUI}} folder may also be moved
around and added to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}} environment variable so the executables
will be found automatically.  2) you can download the \sphinxhref{https://www.flatpak.org/}{Flatpak file} and then install it locally with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flatpak} command: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flatpak install \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}user
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}Linux\sphinxhyphen{}x86\_64\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}version\textgreater{}.flatpak}} and run it with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flatpak
run org.lammps.lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui}}.  The flatpak bundle also includes the
command line version of LAMMPS and some LAMMPS tools like msi2lmp.  The
can be launched by using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}command}} flag. For example to run
LAMMPS directly on the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in.lj}} benchmark input you would type in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bench}} folder: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{flatpak run \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}command=lmp \sphinxhyphen{}in in.lj}} The flatpak
version should also appear in the applications menu of standard desktop
environments.  The LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI executable is called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui}} and
either takes no arguments or attempts to load the first argument as
LAMMPS input file.


\subsubsection{Compilation}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:compilation}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:lammps-gui-compilation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The source for the LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI is included with the LAMMPS source code
distribution in the folder \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools/lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui}} and thus it can be can
be built as part of a regular LAMMPS compilation.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Using CMake}}}} is required.  To enable its compilation, the CMake
variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D BUILD\_LAMMPS\_GUI=on}} must be set when creating the CMake
configuration.  All other settings (compiler, flags, compile type) for
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI are then inherited from the regular LAMMPS build.  If the Qt
library is packaged for Linux distributions, then its location is
typically auto\sphinxhyphen{}detected since the required CMake configuration files are
stored in a location where CMake can find them without additional help.
Otherwise, the location of the Qt library installation must be indicated
by setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D Qt5\_DIR=/path/to/qt5/lib/cmake/Qt5}}, which is a path to
a folder inside the Qt installation that contains the file
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Qt5Config.cmake}}. Similarly, for Qt6 the location of the Qt library
installation can be indicated by setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
Qt6\_DIR=/path/to/qt6/lib/cmake/Qt6}}, if necessary.  When both, Qt5 and
Qt6 are available, Qt6 will be preferred unless \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
LAMMPS\_GUI\_USE\_QT5=yes}} is set.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is possible to build the LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI as a standalone compilation
(e.g. when LAMMPS has been compiled with traditional make).  Then the
CMake configuration needs to be told where to find the LAMMPS headers
and the LAMMPS library, via \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D LAMMPS\_SOURCE\_DIR=/path/to/lammps/src}}.
CMake will try to guess a build folder with the LAMMPS library from that
path, but it can also be set with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D LAMMPS\_LIB\_DIR=/path/to/lammps/lib}}.


\paragraph{Plugin version}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:plugin-version}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rather than linking to the LAMMPS library during compilation, it is also
possible to compile the GUI with a plugin loader that will load the
LAMMPS library dynamically at runtime during the start of the GUI from a
shared library; e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.dylib}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.dll}} (depending on the operating system).  This has the
advantage that the LAMMPS library can be built from updated or modified
LAMMPS source without having to recompile the GUI.  The ABI of the
LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}library interface is very stable and generally backward
compatible.  This feature is enabled by setting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
LAMMPS\_GUI\_USE\_PLUGIN=on}} and then \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
LAMMPS\_PLUGINLIB\_DIR=/path/to/lammps/plugin/loader}}. Typically, this
would be the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/COUPLE/plugin}} folder of the LAMMPS
distribution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When compiling LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI with plugin support, there is an additional
command line flag (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}p \textless{}path\textgreater{}}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}pluginpath \textless{}path\textgreater{}}}) which
allows to override the path to LAMMPS shared library used by the GUI.
This is usually auto\sphinxhyphen{}detected on the first run and can be changed in the
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI \sphinxstyleemphasis{Preferences} dialog.  The command line flag allows to reset
this path to a valid value in case the original setting has become
invalid.  An empty path (“”) as argument restores the default setting.


\subsubsection{Platform notes}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:platform-notes}}

\paragraph{macOS}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:macos}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When building on macOS, the build procedure will try to manufacture a
drag\sphinxhyphen{}n\sphinxhyphen{}drop installer, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}macOS\sphinxhyphen{}multiarch.dmg}}, when using the
‘dmg’ target (i.e. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build \textless{}build dir\textgreater{} \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}target dmg}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make dmg}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To build multi\sphinxhyphen{}arch executables that will run on both, arm64 and x86\_64
architectures natively, it is necessary to set the CMake variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
CMAKE\_OSX\_ARCHITECTURES=arm64;x86\_64}}.  To achieve wide compatibility
with different macOS versions, you can also set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
CMAKE\_OSX\_DEPLOYMENT\_TARGET=11.0}} which will set compatibility to macOS
11 (Big Sur) and later, even if you are compiling on a more recent macOS
version.


\paragraph{Windows}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:windows}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
On Windows either native compilation from within Visual Studio 2022 with
Visual C++ is supported and tested, or compilation with the MinGW / GCC
cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiler environment on Fedora Linux.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Visual Studio}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using CMake and Ninja as build system are required.  Qt needs to be
installed, tested was a binary package downloaded from
\sphinxurl{https://www.qt.io}, which installs into the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C:\textbackslash{}\textbackslash{}Qt}} folder by default.
There is a custom \sphinxtitleref{x64\sphinxhyphen{}GUI\sphinxhyphen{}MSVC} build configuration provided in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeSettings.json}} file that Visual Studio uses to store different
compilation settings for project.  Choosing this configuration will
activate building the \sphinxtitleref{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui.exe} executable in addition to LAMMPS
through importing package selection from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{windows.cmake}} preset
file and enabling building the LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI and disabling building with MPI.
When requesting an installation from the \sphinxtitleref{Build} menu in Visual Studio,
it will create a compressed \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}Win10\sphinxhyphen{}amd64.zip}} zip file with the
executables and required dependent .dll files.  This zip file can be
uncompressed and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui.exe}} run directly from there.  The
uncompressed folder can be added to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}} environment and LAMMPS
and LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI can be launched from anywhere from the command line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{MinGW64 Cross\sphinxhyphen{}compiler}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The standard CMake build procedure can be applied and the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mingw\sphinxhyphen{}cross.cmake}} preset used. By using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mingw64\sphinxhyphen{}cmake}} the CMake
command will automatically include a suitable CMake toolchain file (the
regular cmake command can be used after that to modify the configuration
settings, if needed).  After building the libraries and executables,
you can build the target ‘zip’ (i.e. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build \textless{}build dir\textgreater{} \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}target zip}}
or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make zip}} to stage all installed files into a LAMMPS\_GUI folder
and then run a script to copy all required dependencies, some other files,
and create a zip file from it.


\paragraph{Linux}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:linux}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Version 5.12 or later of the Qt library is required. Those are provided
by, e.g., Ubuntu 20.04LTS.  Thus older Linux distributions are not
likely to be supported, while more recent ones will work, even for
pre\sphinxhyphen{}compiled executables (see above).  After compiling with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build \textless{}build folder\textgreater{}}}, use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build \textless{}build
folder\textgreater{} \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}target tgz}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make tgz}} to build a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}Linux\sphinxhyphen{}amd64.tar.gz}} file with the executables and their
support libraries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible to build a \sphinxhref{https://docs.flatpak.org/en/latest/single-file-bundles.html}{flatpak bundle} which is
a way to distribute applications in a way that is compatible with most
Linux distributions.  Use the “flatpak” target to trigger a compile
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}build \textless{}build folder\textgreater{} \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}target flatpak}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make flatpak}}).
Please note that this will not build from the local sources but from the
repository and branch listed in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{org.lammps.lammps\sphinxhyphen{}gui.yml}}
LAMMPS\sphinxhyphen{}GUI source folder.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{lmp2arc tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:lmp2arc-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:arc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The lmp2arc subdirectory contains a tool for converting LAMMPS output
files to the format for Accelrys’ Insight MD code (formerly
MSI/Biosym and its Discover MD code).  See the README file for more
information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by John Carpenter (Cray), Michael Peachey
(Cray), and Steve Lustig (Dupont).  John is now at the Mayo Clinic
(jec at mayo.edu), but still fields questions about the tool.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was updated for the current LAMMPS C++ version by Jeff
Greathouse at Sandia (jagreat at sandia.gov).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{lmp2cfg tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:lmp2cfg-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:cfg}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The lmp2cfg subdirectory contains a tool for converting LAMMPS output
files into a series of *.cfg files which can be read into the
\sphinxhref{http://li.mit.edu/Archive/Graphics/A/}{AtomEye} visualizer.  See
the README file for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by Ara Kooser at Sandia (askoose at sandia.gov).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Magic patterns for the “file” command}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:magic-patterns-for-the-file-command}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:magic}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 10Mar2021.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{magic}} contains patterns that are used by the
\sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File\_(command)}{file program}
available on most Unix\sphinxhyphen{}like operating systems which enables it
to detect various LAMMPS files and print some useful information
about them.  To enable these patterns, append or copy the contents
of the file to either the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.magic}} in your home directory
or (as administrator) to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/etc/magic}} (for a system\sphinxhyphen{}wide
installation).  Afterwards the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{file}} command should be able to
detect most LAMMPS restarts, dump, data and log files. Examples:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZdl{} }file\PYG{+w}{ }*.*
\PYG{g+go}{dihedral\PYGZhy{}quadratic.restart:   LAMMPS binary restart file (rev 2), Version 10 Mar 2021, Little Endian}
\PYG{g+go}{mol\PYGZhy{}pair\PYGZhy{}wf\PYGZus{}cut.restart:      LAMMPS binary restart file (rev 2), Version 24 Dec 2020, Little Endian}
\PYG{g+go}{atom.bin:                     LAMMPS atom style binary dump (rev 2), Little Endian, First time step: 445570}
\PYG{g+go}{custom.bin:                   LAMMPS custom style binary dump (rev 2), Little Endian, First time step: 100}
\PYG{g+go}{bn1.lammpstrj:                LAMMPS text mode dump, First time step: 5000}
\PYG{g+go}{data.fourmol:                 LAMMPS data file written by LAMMPS}
\PYG{g+go}{pnc.data:                     LAMMPS data file written by msi2lmp}
\PYG{g+go}{data.spce:                    LAMMPS data file written by TopoTools}
\PYG{g+go}{B.data:                       LAMMPS data file written by OVITO}
\PYG{g+go}{log.lammps:                   LAMMPS log file written by version 10 Feb 2021}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{matlab tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:matlab-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:matlab}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The matlab subdirectory contains several \sphinxhref{https://www.mathworks.com}{MATLAB} scripts for
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing LAMMPS output.  The scripts include readers for log
and dump files, a reader for EAM potential files, and a converter that
reads LAMMPS dump files and produces CFG files that can be visualized
with the \sphinxhref{http://li.mit.edu/Archive/Graphics/A/}{AtomEye}
visualizer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the README.pdf file for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These scripts were written by Arun Subramaniyan at Purdue Univ
(asubrama at purdue.edu).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{micelle2d tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:micelle2d-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:micelle}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file micelle2d.f creates a LAMMPS data file containing short lipid
chains in a monomer solution.  It uses a text file containing lipid
definition parameters as an input.  The created molecules and solvent
atoms can strongly overlap, so LAMMPS needs to run the system
initially with a “soft” pair potential to un\sphinxhyphen{}overlap it.  The syntax
for running the tool is

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
micelle2d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZlt{}\PYG{+w}{ }def.micelle2d\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }data.file
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the def.micelle2d file in the tools directory for an example of a
definition file.  This tool was used to create the system for the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{micelle example}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{moltemplate tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:moltemplate-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:moltemplate}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The moltemplate subdirectory contains instructions for installing
moltemplate, a Python\sphinxhyphen{}based tool for building molecular systems based
on a text\sphinxhyphen{}file description, and creating LAMMPS data files that encode
their molecular topology as lists of bonds, angles, dihedrals, etc.
See the README.txt file for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by Andrew Jewett (jewett.aij at gmail.com), who
supports it.  It has its own WWW page at
\sphinxurl{https://moltemplate.org}.
The latest sources can be found \sphinxhref{https://github.com/jewettaij/moltemplate/releases}{on its GitHub page}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{msi2lmp tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:msi2lmp-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:msi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The msi2lmp subdirectory contains a tool for creating LAMMPS template
input and data files from BIOVIA’s Materias Studio files (formerly
Accelrys’ Insight MD code, formerly MSI/Biosym and its Discover MD code).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by John Carpenter (Cray), Michael Peachey
(Cray), and Steve Lustig (Dupont). Several people contributed changes
to remove bugs and adapt its output to changes in LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool has several known limitations and is no longer under active
development, so there are no changes except for the occasional bug fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the README file in the tools/msi2lmp folder for more information.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Scripts for building LAMMPS when offline}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:scripts-for-building-lammps-when-offline}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:offline}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In some situations it might be necessary to build LAMMPS on a system
without direct internet access. The scripts in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools/offline}} folder
allow you to pre\sphinxhyphen{}load external dependencies for both the documentation
build and for building LAMMPS with CMake.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It does so by
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
downloading necessary \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}} packages,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cloning \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git}} repositories

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
downloading tarballs

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
to a designated cache folder.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As of April 2021, all of these downloads make up around 600MB. By
default, the offline scripts will download everything into the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\$HOME/.cache/lammps}} folder, but this can be changed by setting the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_CACHING\_DIR}} environment variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the caches have been initialized, they can be used for building the
LAMMPS documentation or compiling LAMMPS using CMake on an offline
system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{use\_caches.sh}} script must be sourced into the current shell
to initialize the offline build environment. Note that it must use
the same \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_CACHING\_DIR}}. This script does the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set up environment variables that modify the behavior of both,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Start a simple local HTTP server using Python to host files for CMake

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Afterwards, it will print out instruction on how to modify the CMake
command line to make sure it uses the local HTTP server.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To undo the environment changes and shutdown the local HTTP server,
run the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{deactivate\_caches}} command.


\subsubsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For all of the examples below, you first need to create the cache, which
requires an internet connection.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
./tools/offline/init\PYGZus{}caches.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Afterwards, you can disconnect or copy the contents of the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_CACHING\_DIR}} folder to an offline system.


\subsubsection{Documentation Build}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:documentation-build}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The documentation build will create a new virtual environment that
typically first installs dependencies from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}}. With the offline
environment loaded, these installations will instead grab the necessary
packages from your local cache.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} if LAMMPS\PYGZus{}CACHING\PYGZus{}DIR is different from default, make sure to set it first}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} export LAMMPS\PYGZus{}CACHING\PYGZus{}DIR=path/to/folder}
\PYG{n+nb}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }tools/offline/use\PYGZus{}caches.sh
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }doc/
make\PYG{+w}{ }html

deactivate\PYGZus{}caches
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{CMake Build}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:cmake-build}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When compiling certain packages with external dependencies, the CMake
build system will download necessary files or sources from the web. For
more flexibility the CMake configuration allows users to specify the URL
of each of these dependencies.  What the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_caches.sh}} script does
is create a CMake “preset” file, which sets the URLs for all of the known
dependencies and redirects the download to the local cache.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} if LAMMPS\PYGZus{}CACHING\PYGZus{}DIR is different from default, make sure to set it first}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} export LAMMPS\PYGZus{}CACHING\PYGZus{}DIR=path/to/folder}
\PYG{n+nb}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }tools/offline/use\PYGZus{}caches.sh

mkdir\PYG{+w}{ }build
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }build
cmake\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}DOWNLOADS\PYGZus{}URL}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{HTTP\PYGZus{}CACHE\PYGZus{}URL}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}HTTP\PYGZus{}CACHE\PYGZus{}CONFIG}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}C\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake/presets/most.cmake\PYG{+w}{ }../cmake
make\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}j\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}

deactivate\PYGZus{}caches
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{phonon tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:phonon-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:phonon}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The phonon subdirectory contains a post\sphinxhyphen{}processing tool, \sphinxstyleemphasis{phana}, useful
for analyzing the output of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_phonon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix phonon}}}} command
in the PHONON package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the README file for instruction on building the tool and what
library it needs.  And see the examples/PACKAGES/phonon directory
for example problems that can be post\sphinxhyphen{}processed with this tool.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by Ling\sphinxhyphen{}Ti Kong at Shanghai Jiao Tong
University.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{polybond tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:polybond-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:polybond}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The polybond subdirectory contains a Python\sphinxhyphen{}based tool useful for
performing “programmable polymer bonding”.  The Python file
lmpsdata.py provides a “Lmpsdata” class with various methods which can
be invoked by a user\sphinxhyphen{}written Python script to create data files with
complex bonding topologies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the Manual.pdf for details and example scripts.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by Zachary Kraus at Georgia Tech.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{pymol\_asphere tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:pymol-asphere-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:pymol}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The pymol\_asphere subdirectory contains a tool for converting a
LAMMPS dump file that contains orientation info for ellipsoidal
particles into an input file for the \sphinxhref{https://www.pymol.org}{PyMol visualization package} or its \sphinxhref{https://github.com/schrodinger/pymol-open-source}{open source variant}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specifically, the tool triangulates the ellipsoids so they can be
viewed as true ellipsoidal particles within PyMol.  See the README and
examples directory within pymol\_asphere for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by Mike Brown at Sandia.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{python tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:python-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:pythontools}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The python subdirectory contains several Python scripts
that perform common LAMMPS post\sphinxhyphen{}processing tasks, such as:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
extract thermodynamic info from a log file as columns of numbers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
plot two columns of thermodynamic info from a log file using GnuPlot

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
sort the snapshots in a dump file by atom ID

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
convert multiple {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{NEB}}}} dump files into one dump file for viz

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
convert dump files into XYZ, CFG, or PDB format for viz by other packages

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are simple scripts built on \sphinxhref{https://lammps.github.io/pizza}{Pizza.py} modules.  See the
README for more info on Pizza.py and how to use these scripts.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Regression tester tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:regression-tester-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:regression}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The regression\sphinxhyphen{}tests subdirectory contains a tool for performing
regression tests with a given LAMMPS binary.  The tool launches the
LAMMPS binary with any given input script under one of the \sphinxtitleref{examples}
subdirectories, and compares the thermo output in the generated log file
with those in the provided log file with the same number of processors
ub the same subdirectory. If the differences between the actual and
reference values are within specified tolerances, the test is considered
passed.  For each test batch, that is, a set of example input scripts,
the mpirun command, the LAMMPS command line arguments, and the
tolerances for individual thermo quantities can be specified in a
configuration file in YAML format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tool also reports if and how the run fails, and if a reference log file
is missing.  See the README file for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by Trung Nguyen at U of Chicago (ndactrung at gmail.com).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{replica tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:replica-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:replica}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tools/replica directory contains the reorder\_remd\_traj python script which
can be used to reorder the replica trajectories (resulting from the use of the
temper command) according to temperature. This will produce discontinuous
trajectories with all frames at the same temperature in each trajectory.
Additional options can be used to calculate the canonical configurational
log\sphinxhyphen{}weight for each frame at each temperature using the pymbar package. See
the README.md file for further details. Try out the peptide example provided.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by (and is maintained by) Tanmoy Sanyal,
while at the Shell lab at UC Santa Barbara. (tanmoy dot 7989 at gmail.com)


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{smd tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:smd-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:smd}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The smd subdirectory contains a C++ file dump2vtk\_tris.cpp and
Makefile which can be compiled and used to convert triangle output
files created by the Smooth\sphinxhyphen{}Mach Dynamics (MACHDYN) package into a
VTK\sphinxhyphen{}compatible unstructured grid file.  It could then be read in and
visualized by VTK.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the header of dump2vtk.cpp for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by the MACHDYN package author, Georg
Ganzenmuller at the Fraunhofer\sphinxhyphen{}Institute for High\sphinxhyphen{}Speed Dynamics,
Ernst Mach Institute in Germany (georg.ganzenmueller at emi.fhg.de).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{spin tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:spin-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:spin}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The spin subdirectory contains a C file interpolate.c which can
be compiled and used to perform a cubic polynomial interpolation of
the MEP following a GNEB calculation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the README file in tools/spin/interpolate\_gneb for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tool was written by the SPIN package author, Julien
Tranchida at Sandia National Labs (jtranch at sandia.gov, and by Aleksei
Ivanov, at University of Iceland (ali5 at hi.is).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{singularity/apptainer tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:singularity-apptainer-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:singularity-tool}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The singularity subdirectory contains container definitions files that
can be used to build container images for building and testing LAMMPS on
specific OS variants using the \sphinxhref{https://apptainer.org}{Apptainer} or
\sphinxhref{https://sylabs.io}{Singularity} container software. Contributions for
additional variants are welcome.  For more details please see the
README.md file in that folder.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{stl\_bin2txt tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:stl-bin2txt-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:stlconvert}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file stl\_bin2txt.cpp converts binary STL files \sphinxhyphen{} like they are
frequently offered for download on the web \sphinxhyphen{} into ASCII format STL files
that LAMMPS can read with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms mesh}}}} or
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_smd_wall_surface::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix smd/wall\_surface}}}} commands.  The syntax
for running the tool is

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
stl\PYGZus{}bin2txt\PYG{+w}{ }infile.stl\PYG{+w}{ }outfile.stl
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which creates outfile.stl from infile.stl.  This tool must be compiled
on a platform compatible with the byte\sphinxhyphen{}ordering that was used to create
the binary file.  This usually is a so\sphinxhyphen{}called little endian hardware
(like x86).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{SWIG interface}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:swig-interface}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:swig}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://swig.org}{SWIG tool} offers a mostly automated way to
incorporate compiled code modules into scripting languages.  It
processes the function prototypes in C and generates wrappers for a wide
variety of scripting languages from it.  Thus it can also be applied to
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{C language library interface}}}} of LAMMPS so that
build a wrapper that allows to call LAMMPS from programming languages
like: C\#/Mono, Lua, Java, JavaScript, Perl, Python, R, Ruby, Tcl, and
more.


\subsubsection{What is included}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:what-is-included}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We provide here an “interface file”, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.i}}, that has the content
of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{library.h}} file adapted so SWIG can process it.  That will
create wrappers for all the functions that are present in the LAMMPS C
library interface.  Please note that not all kinds of C functions can be
automatically translated, so you would have to add custom functions to
be able to utilize those where the automatic translation does not work.
A few functions for converting pointers and accessing arrays are
predefined.  We provide the file here on an “as is” basis to help people
getting started, but not as a fully tested and supported feature of the
LAMMPS distribution.  Any contributions to complete this are, of course,
welcome.  Please also note, that for the case of creating a Python wrapper,
a fully supported {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Ctypes based lammps module}}}}
already exists.  That module is designed to be object\sphinxhyphen{}oriented while
SWIG will generate a 1:1 translation of the functions in the interface file.


\subsubsection{Building the wrapper}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:building-the-wrapper}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using CMake, the build steps for building a wrapper
module are integrated for the languages: Java, Lua,
Perl5, Python, Ruby, and Tcl.  These require that the
LAMMPS library is build as a shared library and all
necessary development headers and libraries are present.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{WITH\PYGZus{}SWIG}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to enable building any SWIG wrapper}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SWIG\PYGZus{}JAVA}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to enable building the Java wrapper}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SWIG\PYGZus{}LUA}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to enable building the Lua wrapper}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SWIG\PYGZus{}PERL5}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to enable building the Perl 5.x wrapper}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SWIG\PYGZus{}PYTHON}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to enable building the Python wrapper}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SWIG\PYGZus{}RUBY}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to enable building the Ruby wrapper}
\PYGZhy{}D\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{BUILD\PYGZus{}SWIG\PYGZus{}TCL}\PYG{o}{=}on\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} to enable building the Tcl wrapper}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Manual building allows a little more flexibility. E.g. one can choose
the name of the module and build and use a dynamically loaded object
for Tcl with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
swig\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}tcl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}module\PYG{+w}{ }tcllammps\PYG{+w}{ }lammps.i
gcc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}fPIC\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}shared\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}pkg\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }tcl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}cflags\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }tcllammps.so\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{            }lammps\PYGZus{}wrap.c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{+w}{ }../src/\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}llammps
tclsh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Or one can build an extended Tcl shell command with the wrapped
functions included with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
swig\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}tcl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}module\PYG{+w}{ }tcllmps\PYG{+w}{ }lammps\PYGZus{}shell.i
gcc\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}o\PYG{+w}{ }tcllmpsh\PYG{+w}{ }lammps\PYGZus{}wrap.c\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}Xlinker\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}export\PYGZhy{}dynamic\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{         }\PYGZhy{}DHAVE\PYGZus{}CONFIG\PYGZus{}H\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}pkg\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }tcl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}cflags\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}}
\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}pkg\PYGZhy{}config\PYG{+w}{ }tcl\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}libs\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}L\PYG{+w}{ }../src\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}llammps
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In both cases it is assumed that the LAMMPS library was compiled
as a shared library in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} folder. Otherwise the last
part of the commands needs to be adjusted.


\subsubsection{Utility functions}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:utility-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Definitions for several utility functions required to manage and access
data passed or returned as pointers are included in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.i}}
file.  So most of the functionality of the library interface should be
accessible.  What works and what does not depends a bit on the
individual language for which the wrappers are built and how well SWIG
supports those.  The \sphinxhref{https://swig.org/doc.html}{SWIG documentation}
has very detailed instructions and recommendations.


\subsubsection{Usage examples}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:usage-examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools/swig}} folder has multiple shell scripts, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{run\_\textless{}name\textgreater{}\_example.sh}}
that will create a small example script and demonstrate how to load
the wrapper and run LAMMPS through it in the corresponding programming
language.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For illustration purposes below is a part of the Tcl example script.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{load}\PYG{+w}{ }.\PYG{o}{/}tcllammps.so
\PYG{k}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{lammps\PYGZus{}open\PYGZus{}no\PYGZus{}mpi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }NULL\PYG{+w}{ }NULL\PYG{k}{]}
\PYG{n+nv}{lammps\PYGZus{}command}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{u}\PYG{l+s+s2}{n}\PYG{l+s+s2}{i}\PYG{l+s+s2}{t}\PYG{l+s+s2}{s}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{r}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e}\PYG{l+s+s2}{a}\PYG{l+s+s2}{l}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{lammps\PYGZus{}command}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{l}\PYG{l+s+s2}{a}\PYG{l+s+s2}{t}\PYG{l+s+s2}{t}\PYG{l+s+s2}{i}\PYG{l+s+s2}{c}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{c}\PYG{l+s+s2}{c}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{2}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.}\PYG{l+s+s2}{5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{lammps\PYGZus{}command}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{r}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e}\PYG{l+s+s2}{g}\PYG{l+s+s2}{i}\PYG{l+s+s2}{o}\PYG{l+s+s2}{n}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{b}\PYG{l+s+s2}{o}\PYG{l+s+s2}{x}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{b}\PYG{l+s+s2}{l}\PYG{l+s+s2}{o}\PYG{l+s+s2}{c}\PYG{l+s+s2}{k}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{5}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{lammps\PYGZus{}command}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{c}\PYG{l+s+s2}{r}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e}\PYG{l+s+s2}{a}\PYG{l+s+s2}{t}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZus{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{b}\PYG{l+s+s2}{o}\PYG{l+s+s2}{x}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{1}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{b}\PYG{l+s+s2}{o}\PYG{l+s+s2}{x}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nv}{lammps\PYGZus{}command}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{c}\PYG{l+s+s2}{r}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e}\PYG{l+s+s2}{a}\PYG{l+s+s2}{t}\PYG{l+s+s2}{e}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZus{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{a}\PYG{l+s+s2}{t}\PYG{l+s+s2}{o}\PYG{l+s+s2}{m}\PYG{l+s+s2}{s}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{1}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{b}\PYG{l+s+s2}{o}\PYG{l+s+s2}{x}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{k}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }dt\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{doublep\PYGZus{}value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{voidp\PYGZus{}to\PYGZus{}doublep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{lammps\PYGZus{}extract\PYGZus{}global}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}lmp}\PYG{+w}{ }dt\PYG{k}{]}\PYG{k}{]}\PYG{k}{]}

\subsection{tabulate tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:tabulate-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:tabulate}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tabulate}} folder contains Python scripts scripts to generate tabulated
potential files for LAMMPS.  The bulk of the code is in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tabulate}} module
in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tabulate.py}} file.  Some example files demonstrating its use are
included.  See the README file for more information.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{tinker tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:tinker-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:tinker}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tinker}} folder contains Python scripts scripts to convert Tinker input
files to LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the README file for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Those scripts were written by Steve Plimpton sjplimp at gmail.com


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{valgrind tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:valgrind-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:valgrind}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{valgrind}} folder contains additional suppressions fur LAMMPS when using
valgrind’s memcheck tool to search for memory access violation and memory
leaks. These suppressions are automatically invoked when running tests through
CMake “ctest \sphinxhyphen{}T memcheck”. See the provided README file to add these
suppressions when running LAMMPS.

that allow easier editing of LAMMPS input scripts.  See the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{README.txt}}
file for details.

\subsection{xmgrace tool}
\label{\detokenize{Tools:xmgrace-tool}}\label{\detokenize{Tools:xmgrace}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The files in the tools/xmgrace directory can be used to plot the
thermodynamic data in LAMMPS log files via the xmgrace plotting
package.  There are several tools in the directory that can be used in
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing mode.  The lammpsplot.cpp file can be compiled and
used to create plots from the current state of a running LAMMPS
simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the README file for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These files were provided by Vikas Varshney (vv0210 at gmail.com)

\chapter{Errors}
\label{\detokenize{Errors:errors}}\label{\detokenize{Errors::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These doc pages describe many of the error and warning message you can
encounter when using LAMMPS.  The common problems include conceptual
issues.  The messages and warnings doc pages give complete lists of all
the messages the code may generate, with additional details for many of
them.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Common problems}
\label{\detokenize{Errors_common:common-problems}}\label{\detokenize{Errors_common::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If two LAMMPS runs do not produce the exact same answer on different
machines or different numbers of processors, this is typically not a
bug.  In theory you should get identical answers on any number of
processors and on any machine.  In practice, numerical round\sphinxhyphen{}off can
cause slight differences and eventual divergence of molecular dynamics
phase space trajectories within a few 100s or few 1000s of timesteps.
However, the statistical properties of the two runs (e.g. average
energy or temperature) should still be the same.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} command is used to set initial atom
velocities, a particular atom can be assigned a different velocity
when the problem is run on a different number of processors or on
different machines.  If this happens, the phase space trajectories of
the two simulations will rapidly diverge.  See the discussion of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} option in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} command for details and
options that avoid this issue.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command generates a
lattice of atoms.  For the same physical system, the ordering and
numbering of atoms by atom ID may be different depending on the number
of processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some commands use random number generators which may be setup to
produce different random number streams on each processor and hence
will produce different effects when run on different numbers of
processors.  A commonly\sphinxhyphen{}used example is the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} command for thermostatting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A LAMMPS simulation typically has two stages, setup and run.  Most
LAMMPS errors are detected at setup time; others like a bond
stretching too far may not occur until the middle of a run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS tries to flag errors and print informative error messages so
you can fix the problem.  For most errors it will also print the last
input script command that it was processing.  Of course, LAMMPS cannot
figure out your physics or numerical mistakes, like choosing too big a
timestep, specifying erroneous force field coefficients, or putting 2
atoms on top of each other!  If you run into errors that LAMMPS
does not catch that you think it should flag, please send an email to
the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/authors.html}{developers} or create an new
topic on the dedicated \sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/lammps/}{MatSci forum section}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you get an error message about an invalid command in your input
script, you can determine what command is causing the problem by
looking in the log.lammps file or using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{echo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{echo command}}}}
to see it on the screen.  If you get an error like “Invalid …
style”, with … being fix, compute, pair, etc, it means that you
mistyped the style name or that the command is part of an optional
package which was not compiled into your executable.  The list of
available styles in your executable can be listed by using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{the \sphinxhyphen{}h command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  The installation and
compilation of optional packages is explained on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build packages}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a given command, LAMMPS expects certain arguments in a specified
order.  If you mess this up, LAMMPS will often flag the error, but it
may also simply read a bogus argument and assign a value that is
valid, but not what you wanted.  E.g. trying to read the string “abc”
as an integer value of 0.  Careful reading of the associated doc page
for the command should allow you to fix these problems. In most cases,
where LAMMPS expects to read a number, either integer or floating point,
it performs a stringent test on whether the provided input actually
is an integer or floating\sphinxhyphen{}point number, respectively, and reject the
input with an error message (for instance, when an integer is required,
but a floating\sphinxhyphen{}point number 1.0 is provided):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ERROR: Expected integer parameter instead of \PYGZsq{}1.0\PYGZsq{} in input script or data file
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some commands allow for using variable references in place of numeric
constants so that the value can be evaluated and may change over the
course of a run.  This is typically done with the syntax \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name} for a
parameter, where name is the name of the variable. On the other hand,
immediate variable expansion with the syntax \$\{name\} is performed while
reading the input and before parsing commands,

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a variable reference (i.e. \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name}) is only allowed if
the documentation of the corresponding command explicitly says it is.
Otherwise, you will receive an error message of this kind:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ERROR: Expected floating point parameter instead of \PYGZsq{}v\PYGZus{}name\PYGZsq{} in input script or data file
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Generally, LAMMPS will print a message to the screen and logfile and
exit gracefully when it encounters a fatal error.  Sometimes it will
print a WARNING to the screen and logfile and continue on; you can
decide if the WARNING is important or not.  A WARNING message that is
generated in the middle of a run is only printed to the screen, not to
the logfile, to avoid cluttering up thermodynamic output.  If LAMMPS
crashes or hangs without spitting out an error message first then it
could be a bug (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Errors_bugs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{this section}}}}) or one of the following
cases:

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS runs in the available memory a processor allows to be
allocated.  Most reasonable MD runs are compute limited, not memory
limited, so this should not be a bottleneck on most platforms.  Almost
all large memory allocations in the code are done via C\sphinxhyphen{}style malloc’s
which will generate an error message if you run out of memory.
Smaller chunks of memory are allocated via C++ “new” statements.  If
you are unlucky you could run out of memory just when one of these
small requests is made, in which case the code will crash or hang (in
parallel), since LAMMPS does not trap on those errors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Illegal arithmetic can cause LAMMPS to run slow or crash.  This is
typically due to invalid physics and numerics that your simulation is
computing.  If you see wild thermodynamic values or NaN values in your
LAMMPS output, something is wrong with your simulation.  If you
suspect this is happening, it is a good idea to print out
thermodynamic info frequently (e.g. every timestep) via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo}}}} so you can monitor what is happening.
Visualizing the atom movement is also a good idea to ensure your model
is behaving as you expect.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In parallel, one way LAMMPS can hang is due to how different MPI
implementations handle buffering of messages.  If the code hangs
without an error message, it may be that you need to specify an MPI
setting or two (usually via an environment variable) to enable
buffering or boost the sizes of messages that can be buffered.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Error and warning details}
\label{\detokenize{Errors_details:error-and-warning-details}}\label{\detokenize{Errors_details::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Many errors or warnings are self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory and thus straightforward to
resolve.  However, there are also cases, where there is no single cause
and explanation, where LAMMPS can only detect symptoms of an error but
not the exact cause, or where the explanation needs to be more detailed than
what can be fit into a message printed by the program.  The following are
discussions of such cases.


\subsection{Unknown identifier in data file}
\label{\detokenize{Errors_details:unknown-identifier-in-data-file}}\label{\detokenize{Errors_details:err0001}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This error happens when LAMMPS encounters a line of text with an
unexpected keyword while {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{reading a data file}}}}.  This
would be either header keywords or section header keywords.  This is
most commonly due to a mistyped keyword or due to a keyword that is
inconsistent with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style}}}} used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The header section informs LAMMPS how many entries or lines are expected
in the various sections (like Atoms, Masses, Pair Coeffs, \sphinxstyleemphasis{etc.}) of
the data file.  If there is a mismatch, LAMMPS will either keep reading
beyond the end of a section or stop reading before the section has
ended.  In that case the next line will not contain a recognized keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Such a mismatch can also happen when the first line of the data
is \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} a comment as required by the format, but a line with a valid
header keyword.  That would result in LAMMPS expecting, for instance,
0 atoms because the “atoms” header line is the first line and thus
treated as a comment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another possibility to trigger this error is to have a keyword in the
data file that corresponds to a fix (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_cmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix cmap}}}})
but the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command is missing the (optional)
arguments that identify the fix and the header keyword and section
keyword or those arguments are inconsistent with the keywords in the
data file.


\subsection{Incorrect format in … section of data file}
\label{\detokenize{Errors_details:incorrect-format-in-section-of-data-file}}\label{\detokenize{Errors_details:err0002}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This error happens when LAMMPS reads the contents of a section of a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data file}}}} and the number of parameters in the line
differs from what is expected.  This most commonly happens, when the
atom style is different from what is expected for a specific data file
since changing the atom style usually changes the format of the line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This error can also happen when the number of entries indicated in the
header of a data file (e.g. the number of atoms) is larger than the
number of lines provided (e.g. in the corresponding Atoms section)
and then LAMMPS will continue reading into the next section and that
would have a completely different format.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Reporting bugs}
\label{\detokenize{Errors_bugs:reporting-bugs}}\label{\detokenize{Errors_bugs::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are confident that you have found a bug in LAMMPS, please follow
the steps outlined below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/bug.html}{New features and bug fixes} section of the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org}{LAMMPS WWW site} or the
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/releases}{GitHub Releases page} to
see if the bug has already been addressed in a patch release.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check that your issue can be reproduced with the latest development
version of LAMMPS.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the manual carefully to verify that the unexpected behavior you
are observing is indeed in conflict with the documentation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues}{GitHub Issue page}
if your issue has already been reported and if it is still open.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/pulls}{GitHub Pull Requests page}
to see if there is already a fix for your bug pending.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check the \sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/lammps/}{LAMMPS forum at MatSci}
to see if the issue has been discussed before.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If none of these steps yields any useful information, please file a new
bug report on the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues}{GitHub Issue page}.
The website will offer you to select a suitable template with explanations
and then you should replace those explanations with the information that
you can provide to reproduce your issue.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The most useful thing you can do to help us verify and fix a bug is to
isolate the problem.  Run it on the smallest number of atoms and fewest
number of processors with the simplest input script that reproduces the
bug.  Try to identify what command or combination of commands is causing
the problem and upload the complete input deck as a tar or zip archive.
Please avoid using binary restart files unless the issue requires it.
In the latter case you should also include an input deck to quickly
generate this restart from a data file or a simple additional input.
This input deck can be used with tools like a debugger or \sphinxhref{https://valgrind.org}{valgrind} to further {\hyperref[\detokenize{Errors_debug::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{debug the crash}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You may also post a message in the \sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/c/lammps/lammps-development/}{development category of the LAMMPS
forum at MatSci}
describing the problem with the same kind of information.  The forum can
provide a faster response, especially if the bug reported is actually
expected behavior or other LAMMPS users have come across it before.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Debugging crashes}
\label{\detokenize{Errors_debug:debugging-crashes}}\label{\detokenize{Errors_debug::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If LAMMPS crashes with a “segmentation fault” or a “bus error” or
similar message, then you can use the following two methods to further
narrow down the origin of the issue.  This will help the LAMMPS
developers (or yourself) to understand the reason for the crash and
apply a fix (either to the input script or the source code).
This requires that your LAMMPS executable includes the required
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_basics:debug}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{debug information}}}}. Otherwise it is not possible to
look up the names of functions or variables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following patch will introduce a bug into the code for pair style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lj/cut}}}} when using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/melt/in.melt}} input.
We use it to show how to identify the origin of a segmentation fault.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gd}{\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} a/src/pair\PYGZus{}lj\PYGZus{}cut.cpp}
\PYG{g+gi}{+++ b/src/pair\PYGZus{}lj\PYGZus{}cut.cpp}
\PYG{g+gu}{@@ \PYGZhy{}81,6 +81,7 @@ void PairLJCut::compute(int eflag, int vflag)}
\PYG{+w}{ }  int nlocal = atom\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}nlocal;
\PYG{+w}{ }  double *special\PYGZus{}lj = force\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}special\PYGZus{}lj;
\PYG{+w}{ }  int newton\PYGZus{}pair = force\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}newton\PYGZus{}pair;
\PYG{g+gi}{+  double comx = 0.0;}

\PYG{+w}{ }  inum = list\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}inum;
\PYG{+w}{ }  ilist = list\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}ilist;
\PYG{g+gu}{@@ \PYGZhy{}134,8 +135,10 @@ void PairLJCut::compute(int eflag, int vflag)}
\PYG{+w}{ }                             evdwl,0.0,fpair,delx,dely,delz);
\PYG{+w}{ }      \PYGZcb{}
\PYG{+w}{ }    \PYGZcb{}
\PYG{g+gd}{\PYGZhy{}  \PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{g+gi}{+    comx += atom\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{}rmass[i]*x[i][0]; /* BUG */}
\PYG{g+gi}{+  \PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{g+gi}{+  printf(\PYGZdq{}comx = \PYGZpc{}g\PYGZbs{}n\PYGZdq{},comx);}
\PYG{+w}{ }  if (vflag\PYGZus{}fdotr) virial\PYGZus{}fdotr\PYGZus{}compute();
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZcb{}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After recompiling LAMMPS and running the input you should get something like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZdl{} }./lmp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.melt
\PYG{g+go}{LAMMPS (19 Mar 2020)}
\PYG{g+go}{  using 1 OpenMP thread(s) per MPI task}
\PYG{g+go}{Lattice spacing in x,y,z = 1.6796 1.6796 1.6796}
\PYG{g+go}{Created orthogonal box = (0 0 0) to (16.796 16.796 16.796)}
\PYG{g+go}{  1 by 1 by 1 MPI processor grid}
\PYG{g+go}{Created 4000 atoms}
\PYG{g+go}{  create\PYGZus{}atoms CPU = 0.000432253 secs}
\PYG{g+go}{Neighbor list info ...}
