\subsection{Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties}
\label{\detokenize{Python_atoms:per-atom-properties}}\label{\detokenize{Python_atoms::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to what is described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties}}}}, the instances of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}}, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.IPyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{IPyLammps}}}}} can be used to extract atom quantities
and modify some of them. The main difference between the interfaces is how the information
is exposed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
While the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} is just a thin layer that wraps C API calls,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.IPyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{IPyLammps}}}}} expose
information as objects and properties.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In some cases the data returned is a direct reference to the original data
inside LAMMPS cast to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctypes}} pointers. Where possible, the wrappers will
determine the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctypes}} data type and cast pointers accordingly. If
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{numpy}} is installed arrays can also be extracted as numpy arrays, which
will access the C arrays directly and have the correct dimensions to protect
against invalid accesses.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When accessing per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data,
please note that this data is the per\sphinxhyphen{}processor local data and indexed
accordingly. These arrays can change sizes and order at every neighbor list
rebuild and atom sort event as atoms are migrating between subdomains.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{lammps API}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}

\PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{in.sysinit}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{nlocal} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}global}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{nlocal}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}atom}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{x}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nlocal}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
   \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{(x,y,z) = (}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{)}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{close}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Methods}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_atom}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extract\_atom()}}}}}: extract a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantity

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Numpy Methods}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.numpy_wrapper.numpy_wrapper.extract_atom}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{numpy.extract\_atom()}}}}}: extract a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantity as numpy array

\end{itemize}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{PyLammps/IPyLammps API}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All atoms in the current simulation can be accessed by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps.atoms}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps.atoms}}}}} property.
Each element of this list is a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.Atom}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Atom}}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.Atom2D}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Atom2D}}}}} object. The attributes of
these objects provide access to their data (id, type, position, velocity, force, etc.):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} access first atom}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{id}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{type}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} access second atom}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{velocity}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{force}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some attributes can be changed:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set position in 2D simulation}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set position in 3D simulation}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{position} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Compute, fixes, variables}
\label{\detokenize{Python_objects:compute-fixes-variables}}\label{\detokenize{Python_objects::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section documents accessing or modifying data from objects like
computes, fixes, or variables in LAMMPS using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} module.
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{lammps API}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_compute}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.extract\_compute()}}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_fix}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.extract\_fix()}}}}}, the global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom,
or local data calculated by the compute or fix can be accessed. What is returned
depends on whether the compute or fix calculates a scalar or vector or array.
For a scalar, a single double value is returned.  If the compute or fix calculates
a vector or array, a pointer to the internal LAMMPS data is returned, which you can
use via normal Python subscripting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The one exception is that for a fix that calculates a
global vector or array, a single double value from the vector or array
is returned, indexed by I (vector) or I and J (array).  I,J are
zero\sphinxhyphen{}based indices.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for a discussion of
global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, and local data, and of scalar, vector, and array
data types.  See the doc pages for individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}} for a description of what they calculate and
store.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_variable}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.extract\_variable()}}}}},
an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style or atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} is evaluated and
its result returned.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables a single \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{c\_double}} value is returned and the
group argument is ignored.  For atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, a vector of
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{c\_double}} is returned, one value per atom, which you can use via normal
Python subscripting. The values will be zero for atoms not in the
specified group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.numpy_wrapper.numpy_wrapper.extract_compute}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.numpy.extract\_compute()}}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.numpy_wrapper.numpy_wrapper.extract_fix}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.numpy.extract\_fix()}}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.numpy_wrapper.numpy_wrapper.extract_variable}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.numpy.extract\_variable()}}}}} are
equivalent NumPy implementations that return NumPy arrays instead of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctypes}} pointers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.set_variable}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.set\_variable()}}}}} method sets an
existing string\sphinxhyphen{}style variable to a new string value, so that subsequent LAMMPS
commands can access the variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Methods}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_compute}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.extract\_compute()}}}}}: extract value(s) from a compute

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_fix}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.extract\_fix()}}}}}: extract value(s) from a fix

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_variable}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.extract\_variable()}}}}}: extract value(s) from a variable

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.set_variable}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.set\_variable()}}}}}: set existing named string\sphinxhyphen{}style variable to value

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NumPy Methods}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.numpy_wrapper.numpy_wrapper.extract_compute}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.numpy.extract\_compute()}}}}}: extract value(s) from a compute, return arrays as numpy arrays

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.numpy_wrapper.numpy_wrapper.extract_fix}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.numpy.extract\_fix()}}}}}: extract value(s) from a fix, return arrays as numpy arrays

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.numpy_wrapper.numpy_wrapper.extract_variable}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.numpy.extract\_variable()}}}}}: extract value(s) from a variable, return arrays as numpy arrays

\end{itemize}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{PyLammps/IPyLammps API}

\sphinxAtStartPar
PyLammps and IPyLammps classes currently do not add any additional ways of
retrieving information out of computes and fixes. This information can still be accessed by using the lammps API:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}fix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} OR}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{numpy}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{numpy}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}fix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS variables can be both defined and accessed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} interface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To define a variable you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{variable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{a index 2}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A dictionary of all variables is returned by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps.variables}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps.variables}}}}} property:

\sphinxAtStartPar
you can access an individual variable by retrieving a variable object from the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{L.variables}} dictionary by name

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{a} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{L}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{variables}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{a}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The variable value can then be easily read and written by accessing the value
property of this object.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{value} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{4}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\end{quote}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Scatter/gather operations}
\label{\detokenize{Python_scatter:scatter-gather-operations}}\label{\detokenize{Python_scatter::doc}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{gather\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} return per\PYGZhy{}atom property of all atoms gathered into data, ordered by atom ID}
                                          \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} name = \PYGZdq{}x\PYGZdq{}, \PYGZdq{}charge\PYGZdq{}, \PYGZdq{}type\PYGZdq{}, etc}
\PYG{n}{data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{gather\PYGZus{}atoms\PYGZus{}concat}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} ditto, but concatenated atom values from each proc (unordered)}
\PYG{n}{data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{gather\PYGZus{}atoms\PYGZus{}subset}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{ndata}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{ids}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} ditto, but for subset of Ndata atoms with IDs}

\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{scatter\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{)}   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} scatter per\PYGZhy{}atom property to all atoms from data, ordered by atom ID}
                                          \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} name = \PYGZdq{}x\PYGZdq{}, \PYGZdq{}charge\PYGZdq{}, \PYGZdq{}type\PYGZdq{}, etc}
                                          \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} count = \PYGZsh{} of per\PYGZhy{}atom values, 1 or 3, etc}

\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{scatter\PYGZus{}atoms\PYGZus{}subset}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{ndata}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{ids}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{data}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} ditto, but for subset of Ndata atoms with IDs}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The gather methods collect peratom info of the requested type (atom
coords, atom types, forces, etc) from all processors, and returns the
same vector of values to each calling processor.  The scatter
functions do the inverse.  They distribute a vector of peratom values,
passed by all calling processors, to individual atoms, which may be
owned by different processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the data returned by the gather methods,
e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gather\_atoms("x")}}, is
different from the data structure returned by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.extract_atom}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extract\_atom("x")}}}}} in four ways.
(1) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gather\_atoms()}} returns a vector which you index as x{[}i{]};
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extract\_atom()}} returns an array which you index as x{[}i{]}{[}j{]}.
(2) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gather\_atoms()}} orders the atoms by atom ID while
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extract\_atom()}} does not.  (3) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gather\_atoms()}} returns
a list of all atoms in the simulation; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extract\_atoms()}} returns just
the atoms local to each processor.  (4) Finally, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gather\_atoms()}}
data structure is a copy of the atom coords stored internally in
LAMMPS, whereas \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extract\_atom()}} returns an array that effectively
points directly to the internal data.  This means you can change
values inside LAMMPS from Python by assigning a new values to the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{extract\_atom()}} array.  To do this with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gather\_atoms()}} vector, you
need to change values in the vector, then invoke the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scatter\_atoms("x")}} method.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the scatter methods, the array of coordinates passed to must be a
ctypes vector of ints or doubles, allocated and initialized something
like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{ctypes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}double}
\PYG{n}{natoms} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}natoms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{n3} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{natoms}
\PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{n3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}double}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{x} \PYG{n}{coord} \PYG{n}{of} \PYG{n}{atom} \PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n}{ID} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{y} \PYG{n}{coord} \PYG{n}{of} \PYG{n}{atom} \PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n}{ID} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{z} \PYG{n}{coord} \PYG{n}{of} \PYG{n}{atom} \PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n}{ID} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{x} \PYG{n}{coord} \PYG{n}{of} \PYG{n}{atom} \PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n}{ID} \PYG{l+m+mi}{2}
\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{n3}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{z} \PYG{n}{coord} \PYG{n}{of} \PYG{n}{atom} \PYG{k}{with} \PYG{n}{ID} \PYG{n}{natoms}
\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{scatter\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{x}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates can also be provided as arguments to the initializer of x:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{ctypes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}double}
\PYG{n}{natoms} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{2}
\PYG{n}{n3} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{natoms}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} init in constructor}
\PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{n3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}double}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{scatter\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{x}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} or using a list}
\PYG{n}{coords} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{3.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{3.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{n}{x} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}double}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nb}{len}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{coords}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternatively, you can just change values in the vector returned by
the gather methods, since they are also ctypes vectors.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Neighbor list access}
\label{\detokenize{Python_neighbor:neighbor-list-access}}\label{\detokenize{Python_neighbor::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Access to neighbor lists is handled through a couple of wrapper classes
that allows one to treat it like either a python list or a NumPy array.  The
access procedure is similar to that of the C\sphinxhyphen{}library interface: use one
of the “find” functions to look up the index of the neighbor list in the
global table of neighbor lists and then get access to the neighbor list
data. The code sample below demonstrates reading the neighbor list data
using the NumPy access method.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{numpy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{np}

\PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{commands\PYGZus{}string}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{region box block \PYGZhy{}2 2 \PYGZhy{}2 2 \PYGZhy{}2 2}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{lattice fcc 1.0}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{create\PYGZus{}box 1 box}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{create\PYGZus{}atoms 1 box}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{mass 1 1.0}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{pair\PYGZus{}style lj/cut 2.5}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff 1 1 1.0 1.0}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{run 0 post no}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} look up the neighbor list}
\PYG{n}{nlidx} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{find\PYGZus{}pair\PYGZus{}neighlist}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{lj/cut}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{nl} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{numpy}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}neighlist}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nlidx}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{tags} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}atom}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{id}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{half neighbor list with }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ entries}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nl}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} print neighbor list contents}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{nl}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{nlist}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nl}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s+s2}{atom }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ with ID }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ has }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ neighbors:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{tags}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{nlist}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{nlist}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size} \PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{n} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{np}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nditer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nlist}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{  atom }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ with ID }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{tags}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another example for extracting a full neighbor list without evaluating a
potential is shown below.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{numpy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{np}

\PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{commands\PYGZus{}string}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{newton off}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{region box block \PYGZhy{}2 2 \PYGZhy{}2 2 \PYGZhy{}2 2}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{lattice fcc 1.0}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{create\PYGZus{}box 1 box}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{create\PYGZus{}atoms 1 box}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{mass 1 1.0}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{pair\PYGZus{}style zero 1.0 full}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff * *}
\PYG{l+s+s2}{run 0 post no}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} look up the neighbor list}
\PYG{n}{nlidx} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{find\PYGZus{}pair\PYGZus{}neighlist}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{zero}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{nl} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{numpy}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}neighlist}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nlidx}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{tags} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}atom}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{id}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{full neighbor list with }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ entries}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nl}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} print neighbor list contents}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{nl}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{nlist}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nl}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s+s2}{atom }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ with ID }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ has }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ neighbors:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{tags}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{nlist}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{nlist}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{size} \PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}

            \PYG{k}{pass}
            \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{  atom }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ with ID }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{tags}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\subsection{Configuration information}
\label{\detokenize{Python_config:configuration-information}}\label{\detokenize{Python_config::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following methods can be used to query the LAMMPS library
about compile time settings and included packages and styles.
\sphinxSetupCaptionForVerbatim{Example for using configuration settings functions}
\def\sphinxLiteralBlockLabel{\label{\detokenize{Python_config:id1}}}

\section{The \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{lammps}} Python module}
\label{\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Python_module:the-lammps-python-module}}\label{\detokenize{Python_module::doc}}\index{module@\spxentry{module}!lammps@\spxentry{lammps}}\index{lammps@\spxentry{lammps}!module@\spxentry{module}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS Python interface is implemented as a module called {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}}
which is defined in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}} package in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python}} folder of the
LAMMPS source code distribution.  After compilation of LAMMPS, the module can
be installed into a Python system folder or a user folder with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make
install\sphinxhyphen{}python}}.  Components of the module can then loaded into a Python
session with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{import}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are multiple Python interface classes in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} module:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} class. This is a wrapper around
the C\sphinxhyphen{}library interface and its member functions try to replicate the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{C\sphinxhyphen{}library API}}}} closely.  This is the most
feature\sphinxhyphen{}complete Python API.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} class. This is a more high\sphinxhyphen{}level
and more Python style class implemented on top of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} class.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.IPyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{IPyLammps}}}}} class is derived from
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} and adds embedded graphics
features to conveniently include LAMMPS into \sphinxhref{https://jupyter.org/}{Jupyter} notebooks.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Version check}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} module stores the version number of the LAMMPS
version it is installed from.  When initializing the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} class, this version is checked to
be the same as the result from {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.version}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.version()}}}}}, the version
of the LAMMPS shared library that the module interfaces to.  If the
they are not the same an AttributeError exception is raised since a
mismatch of versions (e.g.  due to incorrect use of the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LD\_LIBRARY\_PATH}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PYTHONPATH}} environment variables can lead
to crashes or data corruption and otherwise incorrect behavior.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{The \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{lammps}} class API}
\label{\detokenize{Python_module:the-lammps-class-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} class is the core of the LAMMPS
Python interfaces.  It is a wrapper around the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS C library
API}}}} using the \sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html}{Python ctypes module} and a shared library
compiled from the LAMMPS sources code.  The individual methods in this
class try to closely follow the corresponding C functions.  The handle
argument that needs to be passed to the C functions is stored internally
in the class and automatically added when calling the C library
functions. Below is a detailed documentation of the API.
\index{lammps (class in lammps)@\spxentry{lammps}\spxextra{class in lammps}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{class\DUrole{w}{ }}}\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{name}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{cmdargs}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{ptr}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{comm}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}}{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create an instance of the LAMMPS Python class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a Python wrapper class that exposes the LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}library
interface to Python.  It either requires that LAMMPS has been compiled
as shared library which is then dynamically loaded via the ctypes
Python module or that this module called from a Python function that
is called from a Python interpreter embedded into a LAMMPS executable,
for example through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python invoke}}}} command.
When the class is instantiated it calls the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_create:_CPPv411lammps_openiPPc8MPI_CommPPv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_open()}}}}}
function of the LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}library interface, which in
turn will create an instance of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS6LAMMPSE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS}}}}}
C++ class.  The handle to this C++ class is stored internally
and automatically passed to the calls to the C library interface.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{name}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{string}}) \textendash{} “machine” name of the shared LAMMPS library (“mpi” loads \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_mpi.so}}, “” loads \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{cmdargs}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}) \textendash{} list of command line arguments to be passed to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_create:_CPPv411lammps_openiPPc8MPI_CommPPv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_open()}}}}} function.  The executable name is automatically added.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ptr}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{pointer}}) \textendash{} pointer to a LAMMPS C++ class instance when called from an embedded Python interpreter.  None means load symbols from shared library.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{comm}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Comm}}) \textendash{} MPI communicator (as provided by \sphinxhref{https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io/}{mpi4py}). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{None}} means use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_COMM\_WORLD}} implicitly.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

variable or an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable. The variable type can be

constants: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LMP\_VAR\_EQUAL}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LMP\_VAR\_ATOM}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LMP\_VAR\_VECTOR}},

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is a wrapper around the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_scatter:_CPPv419lammps_create_atomsPviPKiPKiPKdPKdPKii}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_create\_atoms()}}}}}
function of the C\sphinxhyphen{}library interface, and the behavior is similar except
that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{v}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{image}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{shrinkexceed} arguments are optional and
default to \sphinxstyleemphasis{None}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{None}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{False}, respectively. With \sphinxstyleemphasis{None} being
equivalent to a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} pointer in C.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The lists of coordinates, types, atom IDs, velocities, image flags can
be provided in any format that may be converted into the required
internal data types.  Also the list may contain more than \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} entries,
but not fewer.  In the latter case, the function will return without
attempting to create atoms.  You may use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps.encode_image_flags}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{encode\_image\_flags}}}}} method to properly combine three integers
with image flags into a single integer.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{id}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{ of }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{lammps.tagint}}) \textendash{} list of atom IDs with at least n elements or None

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{type}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{ of }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} list of atom types

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{x}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{ of }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}) \textendash{} list of coordinates for x\sphinxhyphen{}, y\sphinxhyphen{}, and z (flat list of 3n entries)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{v}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{ of }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}) \textendash{} list of velocities for x\sphinxhyphen{}, y\sphinxhyphen{}, and z (flat list of 3n entries) or None (optional)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{image}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{ of }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{lammps.imageint}}) \textendash{} list of encoded image flags (optional)

Find neighbor list index of pair style neighbor list

\sphinxAtStartPar
Search for a neighbor list requested by a pair style instance that
matches “style”.  If exact is True, the pair style name must match
exactly. If exact is False, the pair style name is matched against
“style” as regular expression or sub\sphinxhyphen{}string. If the pair style is a
hybrid pair style, the style is instead matched against the hybrid
sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles. If the same pair style is used as sub\sphinxhyphen{}style multiple
types, you must set nsub to a value n \textgreater{} 0 which indicates the nth
instance of that sub\sphinxhyphen{}style to be used (same as for the pair\_coeff
command). The default value of 0 will fail to match in that case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the pair style instance has been identified, it may have
requested multiple neighbor lists. Those are uniquely identified by
a request ID \textgreater{} 0 as set by the pair style. Otherwise the request
ID is 0.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{style}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{string}}) \textendash{} name of pair style that should be searched for

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{exact}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{bool}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} controls whether style should match exactly or only must be contained in pair style name, defaults to True

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{nsub}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} match nsub\sphinxhyphen{}th hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}style, defaults to 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{reqid}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} list request id, \textgreater{} 0 in case there are more than one, defaults to 0

\end{itemize}

It behaves the same as the original method, but returns NumPy arrays
instead of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctypes}} pointers.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The returned arrays of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data are by default dimensioned
for the range {[}0:nlocal{]} since that data is \sphinxstyleemphasis{always} valid.  The
underlying storage for the data, however, is typically allocated
for the range of {[}0:nmax{]}. Whether there is valid data in the range
{[}nlocal:nlocal+nghost{]} depends on whether the property of interest
is also updated for ghost atoms.  This is not often the case.  In
some cases, it depends on a LAMMPS setting, see for example
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel yes}}}}.  By using the optional
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nelem} parameter the size of the returned NumPy can be overridden.

\subsection{The \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}} class API}
\label{\detokenize{Python_module:the-pylammps-class-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}} class is a wrapper that creates a
simpler, more “Pythonic” interface to common LAMMPS functionality. LAMMPS
data structures are exposed through objects and properties. This makes Python
scripts shorter and more concise. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_pylammps::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{PyLammps Tutorial}}}} for an introduction on how to use this interface.
\index{PyLammps (class in lammps)@\spxentry{PyLammps}\spxextra{class in lammps}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{class\DUrole{w}{ }}}\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{name}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{cmdargs}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{ptr}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{comm}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{verbose}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{False}}}{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a Python wrapper class around the lower\sphinxhyphen{}level
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} class, exposing a more Python\sphinxhyphen{}like,
object\sphinxhyphen{}oriented interface for prototyping systems inside of IPython and
Jupyter notebooks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It either creates its own instance of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} or can be
initialized with an existing instance. The arguments are the same of the
lower\sphinxhyphen{}level interface. The original interface can still be accessed via
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps.lmp}}.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{name}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{string}}) \textendash{} “machine” name of the shared LAMMPS library (“mpi” loads \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_mpi.so}}, “” loads \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{cmdargs}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}) \textendash{} list of command line arguments to be passed to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_create:_CPPv411lammps_openiPPc8MPI_CommPPv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_open()}}}}} function.  The executable name is automatically added.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ptr}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{pointer}}) \textendash{} pointer to a LAMMPS C++ class instance when called from an embedded Python interpreter.  None means load symbols from shared library.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{comm}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Comm}}) \textendash{} MPI communicator (as provided by \sphinxhref{https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io/}{mpi4py}). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{None}} means use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_COMM\_WORLD}} implicitly.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{verbose}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{bool}}) \textendash{} print all LAMMPS output to stdout

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Variables}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} ({\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}}) \textendash{} instance of original LAMMPS Python interface

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{runs}} \textendash{} list of completed runs, each storing the thermo output

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

needs to be enabled in LAMMPS. Otherwise, it will only capture the final
timestep.

\subsection{The \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{IPyLammps}} class API}
\label{\detokenize{Python_module:the-ipylammps-class-api}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{IPyLammps}}}}} class is an extension of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.PyLammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps}}}}}, adding additional functions to
quickly display visualizations such as images and videos inside of IPython.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_pylammps::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{PyLammps Tutorial}}}} for examples.
\index{IPyLammps (class in lammps)@\spxentry{IPyLammps}\spxextra{class in lammps}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.IPyLammps}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret{\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{class\DUrole{w}{ }}}\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{IPyLammps}}}{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{name}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{cmdargs}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{ptr}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{comm}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}}{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
IPython wrapper for LAMMPS which adds embedded graphics capabilities to PyLammps interface

\sphinxAtStartPar
It either creates its own instance of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:module-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}} or can be
initialized with an existing instance. The arguments are the same of the
lower\sphinxhyphen{}level interface. The original interface can still be accessed via
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PyLammps.lmp}}.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{name}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{string}}) \textendash{} “machine” name of the shared LAMMPS library (“mpi” loads \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_mpi.so}}, “” loads \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps.so}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{cmdargs}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{list}}) \textendash{} list of command line arguments to be passed to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_create:_CPPv411lammps_openiPPc8MPI_CommPPv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_open()}}}}} function.  The executable name is automatically added.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ptr}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{pointer}}) \textendash{} pointer to a LAMMPS C++ class instance when called from an embedded Python interpreter.  None means load symbols from shared library.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{comm}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Comm}}) \textendash{} MPI communicator (as provided by \sphinxhref{https://mpi4py.readthedocs.io/}{mpi4py}). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{None}} means use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_COMM\_WORLD}} implicitly.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\section{Extending the Python interface}
\label{\detokenize{Python_ext:extending-the-python-interface}}\label{\detokenize{Python_ext::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As noted previously, most of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}}}}}
Python class methods correspond one\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}one with the functions in the
LAMMPS library interface in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{library.h}}.
This means you can extend the Python wrapper by following these steps:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add a new interface function to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.cpp}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.h}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rebuild LAMMPS as a shared library.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add a wrapper method to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python/lammps/core.py}} for this interface
function.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define the corresponding \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{argtypes}} list and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{restype}}
in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.\_\_init\_\_()}} function.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Re\sphinxhyphen{}install the shared library and the python module, if needed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
You should now be able to invoke the new interface function from a
Python script.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Calling Python from LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Python_call:calling-python-from-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Python_call::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS has several commands which can be used to invoke Python
code directly from an input script:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable python}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_python_invoke::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix python/invoke}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style python}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python}}}} command which can be used to define and
execute a Python function that you write the code for.  The Python
function can also be assigned to a LAMMPS python\sphinxhyphen{}style variable via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command.  Each time the variable is
evaluated, either in the LAMMPS input script itself, or by another
LAMMPS command that uses the variable, this will trigger the Python
function to be invoked.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Python code for the function can be included directly in the input
script or in an auxiliary file.  The function can have arguments which
are mapped to LAMMPS variables (also defined in the input script) and
it can return a value to a LAMMPS variable.  This is thus a mechanism
for your input script to pass information to a piece of Python code,
ask Python to execute the code, and return information to your input
script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a Python function can be arbitrarily complex.  It can import
other Python modules, instantiate Python classes, call other Python
functions, etc.  The Python code that you provide can contain more
code than the single function.  It can contain other functions or
Python classes, as well as global variables or other mechanisms for
storing state between calls from LAMMPS to the function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Python function you provide can consist of “pure” Python code that
only performs operations provided by standard Python.  However, the
Python function can also “call back” to LAMMPS through its
Python\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped library interface, in the manner described in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python run}}}} doc page.  This means it can issue LAMMPS
input script commands or query and set internal LAMMPS state.  As an
example, this can be useful in an input script to create a more
complex loop with branching logic, than can be created using the
simple looping and branching logic enabled by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{if::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{if}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python}}}} page and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}
doc page for its python\sphinxhyphen{}style variables for more info, including
examples of Python code you can write for both pure Python operations
and callbacks to LAMMPS.

\sphinxstepscope

scripts that specifies the path and name of the executable.  See the
AtomEye web pages for more details:

needed by these Python scripts.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for PyMol, you need to have built and installed the
open\sphinxhyphen{}source version of PyMol in your Python, so that you can import it

The latter link is to the open\sphinxhyphen{}source version.

variables that have to match the VMD installation on your system.

\section{Handling LAMMPS errors}
\label{\detokenize{Python_error:handling-lammps-errors}}\label{\detokenize{Python_error::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS and the LAMMPS library are compiled with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:exceptions}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{C++ exception support}}}} to provide a better error handling experience.  LAMMPS errors
trigger throwing a C++ exception. These exceptions allow capturing errors on
the C++ side and rethrowing them on the Python side.  This way LAMMPS errors
can be handled through the Python exception handling mechanism.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{MPIAbortException}

\PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{k}{try}\PYG{p}{:}
   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} LAMMPS will normally terminate itself and the running process if an error}
   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} occurs. This would kill the Python interpreter.  The library wrapper will}
   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} detect that an error has occurred and throw a Python exception}

   \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{unknown}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n}{MPIAbortException} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{ae}\PYG{p}{:}
   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Single MPI process got killed. This would normally be handled by an MPI abort}
   \PYG{k}{pass}
\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n+ne}{Exception} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{e}\PYG{p}{:}
   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} All (MPI) processes have reached this error}
   \PYG{k}{pass}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Capturing a LAMMPS exception in Python can still mean that the
current LAMMPS process is in an illegal state and must be
terminated. It is advised to save your data and terminate the Python
instance as quickly as possible when running in parallel with MPI.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Troubleshooting}
\label{\detokenize{Python_trouble:troubleshooting}}\label{\detokenize{Python_trouble::doc}}

\subsection{Testing if Python can launch LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Python_trouble:testing-if-python-can-launch-lammps}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To test if LAMMPS is callable from Python, launch Python interactively
and type:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you get no errors, you’re ready to use LAMMPS from Python.  If the
second command fails, the most common error to see is

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
OSError:\PYG{+w}{ }Could\PYG{+w}{ }not\PYG{+w}{ }load\PYG{+w}{ }LAMMPS\PYG{+w}{ }dynamic\PYG{+w}{ }library
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which means Python was unable to load the LAMMPS shared library.  This
typically occurs if the system can’t find the LAMMPS shared library or
one of the auxiliary shared libraries it depends on, or if something
about the library is incompatible with your Python.  The error message
should give you an indication of what went wrong.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If your shared library uses a suffix, such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{liblammps\_mpi.so}}, change
the constructor call as follows (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_create:python-create-lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Creating or deleting a LAMMPS object}}}} for more details):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{mpi}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also test the load directly in Python as follows, without
first importing from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps}} module:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{ctypes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{CDLL}
\PYG{g+gp}{\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{}\PYGZgt{} }\PYG{n}{CDLL}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{liblammps.so}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If an error occurs, carefully go through the steps in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_install:python-install-guides}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Installing the LAMMPS Python Module and Shared Library}}}} and on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_basics::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build\_basics}}}} page about building a shared library.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are not familiar with \sphinxhref{https://www.python.org}{Python}, it is a
powerful scripting and programming language which can do almost
everything that compiled languages like C, C++, or Fortran can do in
fewer lines of code. It also comes with a large collection of add\sphinxhyphen{}on
modules for many purposes (either bundled or easily installed from
Python code repositories).  The major drawback is slower execution speed
of the script code compared to compiled programming languages.  But when
the script code is interfaced to optimized compiled code, performance
can be on par with a standalone executable, for as long as the scripting
is restricted to high\sphinxhyphen{}level operations.  Thus Python is also convenient
to use as a “glue” language to “drive” a program through its library
interface, or to hook multiple pieces of software together, such as a
simulation code and a visualization tool, or to run a coupled
multi\sphinxhyphen{}scale or multi\sphinxhyphen{}physics model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_couple::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Coupling LAMMPS to other codes}}}} page for more ideas about coupling LAMMPS
to other codes.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS Library Interfaces}}}} page for a description of the
LAMMPS library interfaces.  That interface is exposed to Python either
when calling LAMMPS from Python or when calling Python from a LAMMPS
input script and then calling back to LAMMPS from Python code.  The
C\sphinxhyphen{}library interface is designed to be easy to add functionality to,
thus the Python interface to LAMMPS is easy to extend as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you create interesting Python scripts that run LAMMPS or
interesting Python functions that can be called from a LAMMPS input
script, that you think would be generally useful, please post them as
a pull request to our \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps}{GitHub site},
and they can be added to the LAMMPS distribution or web page.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Modifying \& extending LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Modify:modifying-extending-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Modify::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS has a modular design, so that it is easy to modify or extend with
new functionality.  In fact, about 95\% of its source code is optional.
The following pages give basic instructions on adding new features to
LAMMPS.  More in\sphinxhyphen{}depth explanations and documentation of individual
functions and classes are given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Information for Developers}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you add a new feature to LAMMPS and think it will be of general
interest to other users, we encourage you to submit it for inclusion in
LAMMPS. This process is explained in the following three pages:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_contribute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{how to prepare and submit your code}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_requirements::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{requirements for submissions}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{style guidelines}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A summary description of various types of styles in LAMMPS follows.
A discussion of implementing specific styles from scratch is given
in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{writing new styles}}}}.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_overview:overview}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_overview::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The best way to add a new feature to LAMMPS is to find a similar
feature and look at the corresponding source and header files to
figure out what it does.  You will need some knowledge of C++ to
understand the high\sphinxhyphen{}level structure of LAMMPS and its class
organization.  Functions (class methods) that do actual computations
are mostly written in C\sphinxhyphen{}style code and operate on simple C\sphinxhyphen{}style data
structures (vectors and arrays).  A high\sphinxhyphen{}level overview of the
programming style choices in LAMMPS is {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_code_design::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{given elsewhere}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most of the new features described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}} doc
page require you to write a new C++ derived class (excluding exceptions
described below, this can often be done by making small edits to existing
files).  Creating a new class requires 2 files, a source code file
(*.cpp) and a header file (*.h).  The derived class must provide
certain methods to work as a new option.  Depending on how different
your new feature is compared to existing features, you can either
derive from the base class itself, or from a derived class that
already exists.  Enabling LAMMPS to invoke the new class is as simple
as putting the two source files in the src directory and re\sphinxhyphen{}building
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The advantage of C++ and its object\sphinxhyphen{}orientation is that all the code
and variables needed to define the new feature are in the 2 files you
write.  Thus, it should not make the rest of LAMMPS more complex or
cause bugs through unwanted side effects.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a concrete example.  Suppose you write 2 files
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_foo.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_foo.h}} that define a new class
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairFoo}} which computes pairwise potentials described in the
classic 1997 {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_overview:foo}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{paper}}}} by Foo, \sphinxstyleemphasis{et al.} If you wish to invoke
those potentials in a LAMMPS input script with a command like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{foo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
then your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_foo.h}} file should be structured as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{ifdef PAIR\PYGZus{}CLASS}
\PYG{c+c1}{// clang\PYGZhy{}format off}
\PYG{n}{PairStyle}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{foo}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{PairFoo}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{else}
\PYG{c+c1}{// clang\PYGZhy{}format on}
\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{definition}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{PairFoo}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{p}{.}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{endif}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where “foo” is the style keyword in the pair\_style command, and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairFoo}} is the class name defined in your \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_foo.cpp}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_foo.h}} files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When you re\sphinxhyphen{}build LAMMPS, your new pairwise potential becomes part of
the executable and can be invoked with a pair\_style command like the
example above.  Arguments like 0.1 and 3.5 can be defined and
processed by your new class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As illustrated by this example, many features referred to in the
LAMMPS documentation are called a “style” of a particular command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify page}}}} lists all the common styles in LAMMPS,
and discusses the header file for the base class that these styles
derive from.  Public variables in that file can be used and set by the
derived classes, and may also be used by the base class.  Sometimes
they are also accessed by the rest of LAMMPS.  Pure functions, which
means functions declared as virtual in the base class header file and
which are also set to 0, are functions you \sphinxstylestrong{must} implement in your
new derived class to give it the functionality LAMMPS expects. Virtual
functions that are not set to 0 are functions you may override or not.
Those are usually defined with an empty function body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additionally, new output options can be added directly to the
thermo.cpp, dump\_custom.cpp, and variable.cpp files.  These are also
listed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify page}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are additional guidelines for modifying LAMMPS and adding new
functionality:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Think about whether what you want to do would be better as a pre\sphinxhyphen{} or
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing step.  Many computations are more easily and more
quickly done that way.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not try to do anything within the timestepping of a run that is not
parallel.  For example, do not accumulate a bunch of data on a single
processor and analyze it.  That would run the risk of seriously degrading
the parallel efficiency.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your new feature reads arguments or writes output, make sure you
follow the unit conventions discussed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}
command.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Modify_overview:foo}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Foo)} Foo, Morefoo, and Maxfoo, J of Classic Potentials, 75, 345 (1997).

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Submitting new features for inclusion in LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute:submitting-new-features-for-inclusion-in-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We encourage LAMMPS users to submit new features they write for LAMMPS
to be included in the LAMMPS distribution and thus become easily
accessible to all LAMMPS users.  The LAMMPS source code is managed
with git and public development is hosted on \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps}{GitHub}.  You can monitor the repository
to be notified of releases, follow the ongoing development, and
comment on topics of interest to you.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section contains general information regarding the preparation
and submission of new features to LAMMPS. If you are new to
development in LAMMPS, we recommend you read one of the tutorials on
developing a new {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
style}}}} which provide a friendly introduction to
what LAMMPS development entails and common vocabulary used on this
section.


\subsection{Communication with the LAMMPS developers}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute:communication-with-the-lammps-developers}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For any larger modifications or programming project, you are
encouraged to contact the LAMMPS developers ahead of time to discuss
implementation strategies. That will make it easier to integrate your
contribution and typically results in less work for everyone involved.
You are also encouraged to search through the list of \sphinxhref{https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues}{open issues on
GitHub} and submit a new
issue for a planned feature, to avoid duplicating work (and possibly
being scooped).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For informal communication with the LAMMPS developers, you may ask to
join the \sphinxhref{https://lammps.slack.com}{LAMMPS developers on Slack}.
This slack work space is by invitation only.  For access, please send
an e\sphinxhyphen{}mail to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{slack@lammps.org}} explaining what part of LAMMPS you
are working on.  Only discussions related to LAMMPS development are
tolerated in that work space, so this is \sphinxstylestrong{NOT} for people looking
for help with compiling, installing, or using LAMMPS.  Please post a
message to the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/forum.html}{LAMMPS forum} for
those purposes.


\subsection{Time and effort required}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute:time-and-effort-required}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
How quickly your contribution will be integrated can vary widely.  It
depends largely on how much effort is required by the LAMMPS
developers to integrate and test it, if any and what kind of changes
to the core code are required, how quickly you can address them, and
how much interest the contribution is to the larger LAMMPS
community. This process can be streamlined by following the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_requirements::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{requirements}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{style
guidelines}}}}.  A small, modular, well written
contribution may be integrated within hours, but a complex change that
requires a re\sphinxhyphen{}design of a core functionality in LAMMPS can take months
before inclusion (though this is rare).


\subsection{Submission procedure}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute:submission-procedure}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All changes to LAMMPS (including those from LAMMPS developers) are
integrated via pull requests on GitHub and cannot be merged without
passing the automated testing and an approving review by a LAMMPS core
developer.  Before submitting your contribution, you should therefore
first ensure that your added or modified code compiles and works
correctly with the latest development version of LAMMPS and contains
all bug fixes from it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once you have prepared everything, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_github::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS GitHub
Tutorial}}}} page for instructions on how to submit your
changes or new files through a GitHub pull request.  If you are unable
or unwilling to submit via GitHub yourself, you may also send patch
files or full files to the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/authors.html}{LAMMPS developers} and ask them to submit a pull
request on GitHub on your behalf.  If this is the case, create a
gzipped tar file of all new or changed files or a corresponding patch
file using ‘diff \sphinxhyphen{}u’ or ‘diff \sphinxhyphen{}c’ format and compress it with gzip.
Please only use gzip compression, as this works well and is available
on all platforms.  This mode of submission may delay the integration
as it depends more on the LAMMPS developers.


\subsection{External contributions}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute:external-contributions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you prefer to do so, you can also develop and support your add\sphinxhyphen{}on
feature \sphinxstylestrong{without} having it included in the LAMMPS distribution, for
example as a download from a website of your own.  See the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/external.html}{External
LAMMPS packages and tools}
page of the LAMMPS website for examples of groups that do this.  We
are happy to advertise your package and website from that page.
Simply email the \sphinxhref{https://www.lammps.org/authors.html}{developers}
with info about your package, and we will post it there.  We recommend
naming external packages USER\sphinxhyphen{}\textless{}name\textgreater{} so they can be easily
distinguished from packages in the LAMMPS distribution which do not
have the USER\sphinxhyphen{} prefix.


\subsection{Location of files: individual files and packages}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute:location-of-files-individual-files-and-packages}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We rarely accept new styles in the core src folder.  Thus, please
review the list of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{available Packages}}}} to see
if your contribution should be added to one of them.  It should fit
into the general purpose of that package.  If it does not fit well, it
may be added to one of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{} packages or the MISC package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, if your project includes many related features that are not
covered by one of the existing packages or is dependent on a library
(bundled or external), it is best to create a new package with its own
directory (with a name like FOO).  In addition to your new files, the
directory should contain a README text file containing your name and
contact information and a brief description of what your new package
does.


\subsection{Changes to core LAMMPS files}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_contribute:changes-to-core-lammps-files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If designed correctly, most additions do not require any changes to
the core code of LAMMPS; they are simply add\sphinxhyphen{}on files that are
compiled with the rest of LAMMPS.  To make those styles work, you may
need some trivial changes to the core code.  An example of a trivial
change is making a parent\sphinxhyphen{}class method “virtual” when you derive a new
child class from it.  If your features involve more substantive
changes to the core LAMMPS files, it is particularly encouraged that
you communicate with the LAMMPS developers early in development.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Requirements for contributions to LAMMPS}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:requirements-for-contributions-to-lammps}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following is a summary of the current requirements and
recommendations for including contributed source code or documentation
into the LAMMPS software distribution.


\subsection{Motivation}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:motivation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS developers are committed to provide a software package that
is versatile, reliable, high\sphinxhyphen{}quality, efficient, portable, and easy to
maintain and modify.  Achieving all of these goals is challenging
since a large part of LAMMPS consists of contributed code from many
different authors who may not be professionally trained programmers or
familiar with the idiosyncrasies of maintaining a large software
package.  In addition, changes that interfere with the parallel
efficiency of the core code must be avoided.  As LAMMPS continues to
grow and more features and functionality are added, it is necessary to
follow established guidelines when accepting new contributions while
also working at the same time to improve the existing code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following requirements and recommendations are provided as a
guide.  They indicate which individual requirements are strict, and
which represent a preference and thus are negotiable or optional.
Please feel free to contact the LAMMPS core developers in case you
need additional explanations or clarifications, or you need assistance
in implementing the (strict) requirements for your contributions.
Requirements include:
