\subsection{Licensing requirements (strict)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:licensing-requirements-strict}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqlicense}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Contributing authors agree when submitting a pull request that their
contributions can be distributed under the LAMMPS license conditions.
This is the GNU public license in version 2 (not 3 or later) for the
publicly distributed versions, e.g. on the LAMMPS homepage or on
GitHub.  We also have a version of LAMMPS under LGPL 2.1 terms which
is available on request; this will usually be the latest available or
a previous stable version with a few LGPL 2.1 incompatible files
removed.  More details are found on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Intro_opensource::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS open\sphinxhyphen{}source
license page}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Your new source files should have the LAMMPS copyright and GPL notice,
followed by your name and email address at the top, like other
user\sphinxhyphen{}contributed LAMMPS source files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Contributions may be under a different license as long as that license
does not conflict with the aforementioned terms.  Contributions that
use code with a conflicting license can be split into two parts:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the core parts (i.e. parts that must be in the \sphinxtitleref{src} tree) that are
licensed under compatible terms and bundled with the LAMMPS sources

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
an external library that must be downloaded and compiled (either
separately or as part of the LAMMPS compilation)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please note, that this split licensing mode may complicate including
the contribution in binary packages.


\subsection{Integration testing (strict)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:integration-testing-strict}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqintegrationtesting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where possible we use available continuous integration tools to search
for common programming mistakes, portability limitations, incompatible
formatting, and undesired side effects. Contributed code must pass the
automated tests on GitHub before it can be merged with the LAMMPS
distribution. These tests compile LAMMPS in a variety of environments
and settings and run the bundled unit tests.  At the discretion of the
LAMMPS developer managing the pull request, additional tests may be
activated that test for “side effects” on running a collection of
input decks and create consistent results.  The translation of the
documentation to HTML and PDF is also tested.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means that contributed source code \sphinxstylestrong{must} compile with the most
current version of LAMMPS with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLAMMPS\_BIGBIG}} in addition to the
default setting of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLAMMPS\_SMALLBIG}}.  The code needs to work
correctly in both cases, and also in serial and parallel using MPI.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some “disruptive” changes may break tests and require updates to the
testing tools or scripts or tests themselves.  This is rare.  If in
doubt, contact the LAMMPS developer that is assigned to the pull
request.


\subsection{Documentation (strict)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:documentation-strict}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqdocumentation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Contributions that add new styles or commands or augment existing ones
must include the corresponding new or modified documentation in
\sphinxhref{https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/restructuredtext/index.html}{ReStructuredText format} (.rst files in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc/src/}}
folder). The documentation should be written in American English and the
.rst file must only use ASCII characters, so it can be cleanly
translated to PDF files (via \sphinxhref{https://www.sphinx-doc.org}{sphinx} and
PDFLaTeX).  Special characters may be included via embedded math
expression typeset in a LaTeX subset.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When adding new commands, they need to be integrated into the sphinx
documentation system, and the corresponding command tables and lists
updated. When translating the documentation into html files there
should be no warnings. When adding a new package, some lists
describing packages must also be updated as well as a package specific
description added.  Likewise, if necessary, some package specific
build instructions should be included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As appropriate, the text files with the documentation can include
inline mathematical expressions or figures (see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc/JPG}} for
examples).  Additional PDF files with further details may also be
included; see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc/PDF}} for examples.  The page should also include
literature citations as appropriate; see the bottom of
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc/fix\_nh.rst}} for examples and the earlier part of the same file
for how to format the cite itself.  Citation labels must be unique
across \sphinxstylestrong{all} .rst files.  The “Restrictions” section of the page
should indicate if your command is only available if LAMMPS is built
with the appropriate package.  See other command doc files for
examples of how to do this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please run at least “make html” and “make spelling” from within the
doc/src directory, and carefully inspect and proofread the resulting
HTML format doc page before submitting your code.  Upon submission of
a pull request, checks for error free completion of the HTML and PDF
build will be performed and also a spell check, a check for correct
anchors and labels, and a check for completeness of references to all
styles in their corresponding tables and lists is run.  In case the
spell check reports false positives, they can be added to the file
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{doc/utils/sphinx\sphinxhyphen{}config/false\_positives.txt}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Contributions that add or modify the library interface or “public”
APIs from the C++ code or the Fortran module must include suitable
doxygen comments in the source and corresponding changes to the
documentation sources for the “Programmer Guide” guide section of the
LAMMPS manual.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If your feature requires some more complex steps and explanations to
be used correctly or some external or bundled tools or scripts, we
recommend that you also contribute a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto document}}}}
providing some more background information and some tutorial material.
This can also be used to provide more in\sphinxhyphen{}depth explanations of models
that require use of multiple commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a rule\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}thumb, the more clear and self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory you make your
documentation, README files and examples, and the easier you make it
for people to get started, the more likely it is that users will try
out your new feature.


\subsubsection{Programming language standards (strict)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:programming-language-standards-strict}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqprogrammingstandards}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The core of LAMMPS is written in C++11 in a style that can be mostly
described as “C with classes”.  Advanced C++ features like operator
overloading or excessive use of templates are avoided with the intent to
keep the code readable to programmers that have limited C++ programming
experience.  C++ constructs are acceptable when they help improve the
readability and reliability of the code, e.g. when using the
\sphinxtitleref{std::string} class instead of manipulating pointers and calling the
string functions of the C library.  In addition, a collection of
convenient {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{utility functions and classes}}}} for
recurring tasks and a collection of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_platform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{platform neutral functions}}}} for improved portability are provided.
Contributions with code requiring more recent C++ standards are only
accepted as packages with the post C++11 standard code confined to the
package so that it is optional.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Included Fortran code has to be compatible with the Fortran 2003
standard.  Since not all platforms supported by LAMMPS provide good
support for compiling Fortran files, it should be considered to rewrite
these parts as C++ code, if possible, and thus allow for a wider adoption
of the contribution.  As of January 2023, all previously included
Fortran code for the LAMMPS executable has been replaced by equivalent
C++ code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Python code must be compatible with Python 3.5 and later.  Large parts
of LAMMPS (including the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-python}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{PYTHON package}}}}) are also
compatible with Python 2.7.  Compatibility with Python 2.7 is desirable,
but compatibility with Python 3.5 is \sphinxstylestrong{required}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compatibility with older programming language standards is very
important to maintain portability and availability of LAMMPS on many
platforms.  This applies especially to HPC cluster environments, which
tend to be running older software stacks and where LAMMPS users may be
required to use those older tools for access to advanced hardware
features or not have the option to install newer compilers or libraries.


\subsection{Build system (strict)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:build-system-strict}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqbuildsystem}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS currently supports two build systems: one that is based on
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_make::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{traditional Makefiles}}}} and one that is based on
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{CMake}}}}.  Therefore, your contribution must be
compatible with and support both build systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a single pair of header and implementation files that are an
independent feature, it is usually only required to add them to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/.gitignore}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For traditional make, if your contributed files or package depend on
other LAMMPS style files or packages also being installed
(e.g. because your file is a derived class from the other LAMMPS
class), then an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Install.sh}} file is also needed to check for those
dependencies and modifications to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/Depend.sh}} to trigger the checks.
See other README and Install.sh files in other directories as
examples.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, for CMake support, changes may need to be made to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/CMakeLists.txt}}, some of the files in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/presets}}, and
possibly a file with specific instructions needs to be added to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/Modules/Packages/}}.  Please check out how this is handled for
existing packages and ask the LAMMPS developers if you need assistance.


\subsection{Command or style names, file names, and keywords (strict)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:command-or-style-names-file-names-and-keywords-strict}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqnaming}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All user\sphinxhyphen{}visible command or style names should be all lower case and
should only use letters, numbers, or forward slashes.  They should be
descriptive and initialisms should be avoided unless they are well
established (e.g. lj for Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones).  For a compute style
“some/name” the source files must be called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compute\_some\_name.h}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compute\_some\_name.cpp}}. The “include guard” in the header file would
then be \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LMP\_COMPUTE\_SOME\_NAME\_H}} and the class name
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ComputeSomeName}}.


\subsection{Programming style requirements (varied)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:programming-style-requirements-varied}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqprogrammingstyle}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To maintain source code consistency across contributions from many
people, there are various programming style requirements for
contributions to LAMMPS.  Some of these requirements are strict and
must be followed, while others are only preferred and thus may be
skipped.  An in\sphinxhyphen{}depth discussion of the style guidelines is provided
in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{programming style doc page}}}}.


\subsection{Examples (preferred)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:examples-preferred}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqexamples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For many new features, it is preferred that example scripts (simple,
small, fast to complete on 1 CPU) are included that demonstrate the
use of new or extended functionality. These are typically include
under the examples or examples/PACKAGES directory and are further
described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Examples::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{examples page}}}}.  Guidelines for
input scripts include:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
commands that generate output should be commented out (except when the
output is the sole purpose or the feature, e.g. for a new compute)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
commands like {\hyperref[\detokenize{log::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{log}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{echo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{echo}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} may
\sphinxstylestrong{not} be used in the input file (exception: “processors * * 1” or
similar is acceptable when used to avoid unwanted domain decomposition
of empty volumes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
outside of the log files, no generated output should be included

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
custom thermo\_style settings may not include output measuring CPU or other
time as it complicates comparisons between different runs

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
input files should be named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in.name}}, data files should be named
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data.name}} and log files should be named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{log.version.name.\textless{}compiler\textgreater{}.\textless{}ncpu\textgreater{}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the total file size of all the inputs and outputs should be small

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
where possible, potential files from the “potentials” folder or data
file from other folders should be re\sphinxhyphen{}used through symbolic links

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Error or warning messages and explanations (preferred)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:error-or-warning-messages-and-explanations-preferred}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqerrormessages}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 4May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Starting with LAMMPS version 4 May 2022, the LAMMPS developers have
agreed on a new policy for error and warning messages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Previously, all error and warning strings were supposed to be listed in
the class header files with an explanation.  Those would then be
regularly “harvested” and transferred to alphabetically sorted lists in
the manual.  To avoid excessively long lists and to reduce effort, this
came with a requirement to have rather generic error messages (e.g.
“Illegal … command”).  To identify the specific cause, the name of the
source file and the line number of the error location would be printed,
so that one could look up the cause by reading the source code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The new policy encourages more specific error messages that ideally
indicate the cause directly, and requiring no further lookup. This is
aided by the \sphinxhref{https://fmt.dev}{\{fmt\} library} enabling Error class
methods that take a variable number of arguments and an error text that
will be treated like a \{fmt\} syntax format string. Error messages should
still preferably be kept to a single line or two lines at most.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For more complex explanations or errors that have multiple possible
reasons, a paragraph should be added to the \sphinxtitleref{Error\_details} page with an
error code reference (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.. \_err0001:}}) then the utility function
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils8errorurlEi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::errorurl()}}}}} can be used
to generate a URL that will directly lead to that paragraph.  An error
for missing arguments can be easily generated using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils16missing_cmd_argsERKNSt6stringEiRKNSt6stringEP5Error}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::missing\_cmd\_args()}}}}} convenience function.
An example for this approach would be the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/read\_data.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/atom.cpp}} files that implement the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify}}}}
commands and that may create {\hyperref[\detokenize{Errors_details:err0001}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{“Unknown identifier in data file”}}}}
errors that may have multiple possible reasons which complicates debugging,
and thus require some additional explanation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The transformation of existing LAMMPS code to this new scheme is
ongoing.  Given the size of the LAMMPS code base, it will take a
significant amount of time to complete.  For new code, however,
following the new approach is strongly preferred.  The expectation is
that the new scheme will make understanding errors easier for LAMMPS
users, developers, and maintainers.


\subsection{Citation reminder (optional)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:citation-reminder-optional}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:reqcitation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If there is a paper of yours describing your feature (either the
algorithm/science behind the feature itself, or its initial usage, or
its implementation in LAMMPS), you can add the citation to the *.cpp
source file.  See \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/DIFFRACTION/compute\_saed.cpp}} for an example.
A BibTeX format citation is stored in a string variable at the top of
the file, and a single line of code registering this variable is added
to the constructor of the class.  When your feature is used, then
LAMMPS (by default) will print the brief info and the DOI in the first
line to the screen and the full citation to the log file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If there is additional functionality (which may have been added later)
described in a different publication, additional citation descriptions
may be added so long as they are only registered when the
corresponding keyword activating this functionality is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With these options, it is possible to have LAMMPS output a specific
citation reminder whenever a user invokes your feature from their
input script.  Please note that you should \sphinxstyleemphasis{only} use this for the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{most} relevant paper for a feature and a publication that you or your
group authored.  E.g. adding a citation in the source code for a paper
by Nose and Hoover if you write a fix that implements their integrator
is not the intended usage.  That kind of citation should just be
included in the documentation page you provide describing your
contribution.  If you are not sure what the best option would be,
please contact the LAMMPS developers for advice.


\subsection{Testing (optional)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:testing-optional}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_requirements:requnittesting}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your contribution contains new utility functions or a supporting
class (i.e. anything that does not depend on a LAMMPS object), new
unit tests should be added to a suitable folder in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest}}
tree.  When adding a new LAMMPS style computing forces or selected
fixes, a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.yaml}} file with a test configuration and reference data
should be added for the styles where a suitable tester program already
exists (e.g. pair styles, bond styles, etc.). Please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_development:testing}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{this
section in the manual}}}} for more information on how to
enable, run, and expand testing.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{LAMMPS programming style}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_style:lammps-programming-style}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The aim of the LAMMPS developers is to use a consistent programming
style and naming conventions across the entire code base, as this
helps with maintenance, debugging, and understanding the code, both
for developers and users.  This page provides a list of standard style
choices used in LAMMPS.  Some of these standards are required, while
others are just preferred.  Following these conventions will make it
much easier to integrate your contribution.  If you are uncertain,
please ask.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The files \sphinxtitleref{pair\_lj\_cut.h}, \sphinxtitleref{pair\_lj\_cut.cpp}, \sphinxtitleref{utils.h}, and
\sphinxtitleref{utils.cpp} may serve as representative examples.


\subsection{Include files (varied)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_style:include-files-varied}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Header files that define a new LAMMPS style (i.e. that have a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SomeStyle(some/name,SomeName);}} macro in them) should only use
the include file for the base class and otherwise use forward
declarations and pointers; when interfacing to a library use the
PIMPL (pointer to implementation) approach where you have a pointer
to a struct that contains all library specific data (and thus
requires the library header) but use a forward declaration and
define the struct only in the implementation file. This is a
\sphinxstylestrong{strict} requirement since this is where type clashes between
packages and hard\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}find bugs have regularly manifested in the
past.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Header files, especially those defining a “style”, should only use the
absolute minimum number of include files and \sphinxstylestrong{must not} contain any
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{using}} statements. Typically, that would only be the header for the
base class.  Instead, any include statements should be put in the
corresponding implementation files and forward declarations be used.
For implementation files, the “include what you use” principle should
be employed.  However, there is the notable exception that when the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pointers.h}} header is included (or the header of one of the classes
derived from it), certain headers will \sphinxstyleemphasis{always} be included and thus
do not need to be explicitly specified.  These are: \sphinxtitleref{mpi.h},
\sphinxtitleref{cstddef}, \sphinxtitleref{cstdio}, \sphinxtitleref{cstdlib}, \sphinxtitleref{string}, \sphinxtitleref{utils.h}, \sphinxtitleref{vector},
\sphinxtitleref{fmt/format.h}, \sphinxtitleref{climits}, \sphinxtitleref{cinttypes}.  This also means any such file
can assume that \sphinxtitleref{FILE}, \sphinxtitleref{NULL}, and \sphinxtitleref{INT\_MAX} are defined.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Class members variables should not be initialized in the header file,
but instead should be initialized either in the initializer list of
the constructor or explicitly assigned in the body of the constructor.
If the member variable is relevant to the functionality of a class
(for example when it stores a value from a command line argument), the
member variable declaration is followed by a brief comment explaining
its purpose and what its values can be.  Class members that are
pointers should always be initialized to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nullptr}} in the
initializer list of the constructor.  This reduces clutter in the
header and avoids accessing uninitialized pointers, which leads to
hard to debug issues, class members are often implicitly initialized
to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NULL}} on the first use (but \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} after a {\hyperref[\detokenize{clear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{clear command}}}}).  Please see the files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reset\_atoms\_mol.h}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reset\_atoms\_mol.cpp}} as an example.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
System headers or headers from installed libraries are included with
angular brackets (example: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include \textless{}vector\textgreater{}}}), while local
include files use double quotes (example: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include "atom.h"}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When including system header files from the C library use the
C++\sphinxhyphen{}style names (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}cstdlib\textgreater{}}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}cstring\textgreater{}}}) instead of the
C\sphinxhyphen{}style names (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}stdlib.h\textgreater{}}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}string.h\textgreater{}}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The order of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include}} statements in a file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{some\_name.cpp}}
that implements a class \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SomeName}} defined in a header file
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{some\_name.h}} should be as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include "some\_name.h"}} followed by an empty line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS include files e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include "comm.h"}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include
"modify.h"}} in alphabetical order followed by an empty line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
System header files from the C++ or C standard library followed by
an empty line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{using namespace LAMMPS\_NS}} or other namespace imports.

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Whitespace (preferred)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_style:whitespace-preferred}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Source files should not contain TAB characters unless required by the
syntax (e.g. in makefiles) and no trailing whitespace.  Text files
should have Unix\sphinxhyphen{}style line endings (LF\sphinxhyphen{}only). Git will automatically
convert those in both directions when running on Windows; use dos2unix
on Linux machines to convert files to Unix\sphinxhyphen{}style line endings.  The
last line of text files include a line ending.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can check for these issues with the python scripts in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:coding-standard}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{“tools/coding\_standard”}}}} folder.  When run
normally with a source file or a source folder as argument, they will
list all non\sphinxhyphen{}conforming lines.  By adding the \sphinxtitleref{\sphinxhyphen{}f} flag to the command
line, they will modify the flagged files to try to remove the detected
issues.


\subsection{Constants (strongly preferred)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_style:constants-strongly-preferred}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Global or per\sphinxhyphen{}file constants should be declared as \sphinxtitleref{static constexpr}
variables rather than via the pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor with \sphinxtitleref{\#define}.  The name of
constants should be all uppercase.  This has multiple advantages:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
constants are easily identified as such by their all upper case name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rather than a pure text substitution during pre\sphinxhyphen{}processing, \sphinxtitleref{constexpr
variables} have a type associated with them and are processed later in
the parsing process where the syntax checks and type specific
processing (e.g. via overloads) can be applied to them.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compilers can emit a warning if the constant is not used and thus can
be removed (we regularly check for and remove dead code like this)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
there are no unexpected substitutions and thus confusing syntax errors
when compiling leading to, for instance, conflicts so that LAMMPS
cannot be compiled with certain combinations of packages (this \sphinxstyleemphasis{has}
happened multiple times in the past).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor defines should be limited to macros (but consider C++
templates) and conditional compilation.  If a per\sphinxhyphen{}processor define must
be used, it should be defined at the top of the .cpp file after the
include statements and at all cost it should be avoided to put them into
header files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some sets of commonly used constants are provided in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MathConst}}
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{EwaldConst}} namespaces and implemented in the files
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{math\_const.h}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ewald\_const.h}}, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are always exceptions, special cases, and legacy code in LAMMPS,
so please contact the LAMMPS developers if you are not sure.


\subsection{Placement of braces (strongly preferred)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_style:placement-of-braces-strongly-preferred}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For new files added to the “src” tree, a \sphinxhref{https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormat.html}{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format} configuration file is
provided under the name \sphinxtitleref{.clang\sphinxhyphen{}format}.  This file is compatible with
clang\sphinxhyphen{}format version 8 and later. With that file present, files can be
reformatted according to the configuration with a command like:
\sphinxtitleref{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format \sphinxhyphen{}i new\sphinxhyphen{}file.cpp}.  Ideally, this is done while writing
the code or before a pull request is submitted.  Blocks of code where
the reformatting from clang\sphinxhyphen{}format yields hard\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}read or otherwise
undesirable output may be protected with placing a pair \sphinxtitleref{//
clang\sphinxhyphen{}format off} and \sphinxtitleref{// clang\sphinxhyphen{}format on} comments around that block.


\subsection{Miscellaneous standards (varied)}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_style:miscellaneous-standards-varied}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
I/O is done via the C\sphinxhyphen{}style stdio library and \sphinxstylestrong{not} iostreams.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not use so\sphinxhyphen{}called “alternative tokens” like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{and}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{or}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{not}} and similar, but rather use the corresponding operators
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\&\&}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{||}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{!}}.  The alternative tokens are not available
by default on all compilers.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Output to the screen and the logfile should use the corresponding
FILE pointers and only be done on MPI rank 0.  Use the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::logmesg()}} convenience function where possible.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usage of C++11 \sphinxtitleref{virtual}, \sphinxtitleref{override}, \sphinxtitleref{final} keywords: Please
follow the \sphinxhref{https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines\#Rh-override}{C++ Core Guideline C.128}.
That means, you should only use \sphinxtitleref{virtual} to declare a new virtual
function, \sphinxtitleref{override} to indicate you are overriding an existing
virtual function, and \sphinxtitleref{final} to prevent any further overriding.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Trivial destructors: Do not write destructors when they are empty
and \sphinxtitleref{default}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{protected}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pointers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}
\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{o}{\PYGZti{}}\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{B}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{protected}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pointers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}
\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{B}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{o}{\PYGZti{}}\PYG{n}{B}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{default}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// instead, let the compiler create the implicit default destructor by not writing it}

\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{protected}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pointers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}
\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{B}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{protected}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pointers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}
\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{B}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Please use clang\sphinxhyphen{}format only to reformat files that you have
contributed.  For header files containing a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SomeStyle(keyword,
ClassName)}} macros it is required to have this macro embedded with
a pair of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{// clang\sphinxhyphen{}format off}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{// clang\sphinxhyphen{}format on}} comments

\section{Atom styles}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_atom:atom-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_atom::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Classes that define an {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style}}}} are derived from
the AtomVec class and managed by the Atom class.  The atom style
determines what attributes are associated with an atom and
communicated when it is a ghost atom or migrates to a new processor.
A new atom style can be created if one of the existing atom styles
does not define all the attributes you need to store and communicate
with atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atom\_vec\_atomic.cpp}} is the simplest example of an atom style.
Examining the code for others will make these instructions more clear.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style hybrid}}}} command can be used
to define atoms or particles which have the union of properties of
individual styles.  Also the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command can be used to add a single property
(e.g. charge or a molecule ID) to a style that does not have it.  It can
also be used to add custom properties to an atom, with options to
communicate them with ghost atoms or read them from a data file.  Other
LAMMPS commands can access these custom properties, as can new pair,
fix, compute styles that are written to work with these properties.  For
example, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command can be used to set the values of
custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties from an input script.  All of these methods
are less work than writing and testing(!) code for a new atom style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you follow these directions your new style will automatically work
in tandem with others via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style hybrid}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first step is to define a set of string lists in the constructor of
the new derived class.  Each list will have zero or more comma\sphinxhyphen{}separated
strings that correspond to the variable names used in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atom.h}}
header file for per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties.  Note that some represent per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
vectors (q, molecule) while other are per\sphinxhyphen{}atom arrays (x,v).  For all
but the last two lists you do not need to specify any of
(id,type,x,v,f).  Those are included automatically as needed in the
other lists.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In these lists you can list variable names which LAMMPS already defines
(in some other atom style), or you can create new variable names.  You
should not re\sphinxhyphen{}use a LAMMPS variable in your atom style that is used for
something with a different meaning in another atom style.  If the
meaning is related, but interpreted differently by your atom style, then
using the same variable name means a user must not use your style and
the other style together in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style hybrid}}}}
command.  Because there will only be one value of the variable and
different parts of LAMMPS will then likely use it differently.  LAMMPS
has no way of checking for this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are defining new variable names then make them descriptive and
unique to your new atom style.  For example choosing “e” for energy is
a bad choice; it is too generic.  A better choice would be “e\_foo”,
where “foo” is specific to your style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If any of the variable names in your new atom style do not exist in
LAMMPS, you need to add them to the src/atom.h and atom.cpp files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Search for the word “customize” or “customization” in these 2 files to
see where to add your variable.  Adding a flag to the 2nd customization
section in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atom.h}} is only necessary if your code (e.g. a pair style)
needs to check that a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom property is defined.  These flags should
also be set in the constructor of the atom style child class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atom.cpp}}, aside from the constructor and destructor, there are 3
methods that a new variable name or flag needs to be added to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Atom::peratom\_create()}} when using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Atom::add\_peratom()}}
method, a cols argument of 0 is for per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors, a length \textgreater{}
1 is for per\sphinxhyphen{}atom arrays.  Note the use of the extra per\sphinxhyphen{}thread flag and
the add\_peratom\_vary() method when the last dimension of the array is
variable\sphinxhyphen{}length.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding the variable name to Atom::extract() enables the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data
to be accessed through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_library::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS library interface}}}} by a calling code, including from {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The constructor of the new atom style will also typically set a few
flags which are defined at the top of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atom\_vec.h}}.  If these are
unclear, see how other atom styles use them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The grow\_pointers() method is also required to make a copy of peratom
data pointers, as explained in the code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are a number of other optional methods which your atom style can
implement.  These are only needed if you need to do something
out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}ordinary which the default operation of the AtomVec parent
class does not take care of.  The best way to figure out why they are
sometimes useful is to look at how other atom styles use them.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
process\_args = use if the atom style has arguments

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
init = called before each run

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Pair styles}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_pair:pair-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_pair::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Classes that compute pairwise non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions are derived from
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}} class.  In LAMMPS, pairwise force calculations include
many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials such as EAM, Tersoff, or ReaxFF where particles
interact without an explicit bond topology but include interactions
beyond pairwise non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded contributions.  New styles can be created to
add support for additional pair potentials to LAMMPS.  When the
modifications are small, sometimes it is more effective to derive from
an existing pair style class.  This latter approach is also used by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} where the accelerated style
names differ from their base classes by an appended suffix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/pair\_lj\_cut.cpp}} is an example of a Pair class with a
very simple potential function.  It includes several optional methods to
enable its use with {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_group_group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
group/group}}}}.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Writing new pair styles}}}} contains
a detailed discussion of writing new pair styles from scratch, and how
simple and more complex pair styles can be implemented with examples
from existing pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a brief list of some the class methods in the Pair class that
\sphinxstyleemphasis{must} be or \sphinxstyleemphasis{may} be overridden in a derived class for a new pair style.

\section{Bond, angle, dihedral, improper styles}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_bond:bond-angle-dihedral-improper-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_bond::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Classes that compute molecular interactions are derived from the Bond,
Angle, Dihedral, and Improper classes.  New styles can be created to
add new potentials to LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Bond\_harmonic.cpp is the simplest example of a bond style.  Ditto for
the harmonic forms of the angle, dihedral, and improper style
commands.

\section{Compute styles}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_compute:compute-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_compute::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Classes that compute scalar and vector quantities like temperature
and the pressure tensor, as well as classes that compute per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities like kinetic energy and the centro\sphinxhyphen{}symmetry parameter
are derived from the Compute class.  New styles can be created
to add new calculations to LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute\_temp.cpp is a simple example of computing a scalar
temperature.  Compute\_ke\_atom.cpp is a simple example of computing
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom kinetic energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tally\sphinxhyphen{}style computes are a special case, as their computation is done
in two stages: the callback function is registered with the pair style
and then called from the Pair::ev\_tally() function, which is called for
each pair after force and energy has been computed for this pair. Then
the tallied values are retrieved with the standard compute\_scalar or
compute\_vector or compute\_peratom methods. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_tally::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute styles in the TALLY package}}}}
provide \sphinxstyleemphasis{examples} for utilizing this mechanism.

\section{Fix styles}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_fix:fix-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_fix::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, a “fix” is any operation that is computed during
timestepping that alters some property of the system.  Essentially
everything that happens during a simulation besides force computation,
neighbor list construction, and output, is a “fix”.  This includes
time integration (update of coordinates and velocities), force
constraints or boundary conditions (SHAKE or walls), and diagnostics
(compute a diffusion coefficient).  New styles can be created to add
new options to LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix\_setforce.cpp is a simple example of setting forces on atoms to
prescribed values.  There are dozens of fix options already in LAMMPS;
choose one as a template that is similar to what you want to
implement.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a brief description of methods you can define in your new
derived class.  See fix.h for details.

\end{longtable}
\sphinxtableafterendhook
\sphinxatlongtableend
\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically, only a small fraction of these methods are defined for a
particular fix.  Setmask is mandatory, as it determines when the fix
will be invoked during the timestep.  Fixes that perform time
integration (\sphinxstyleemphasis{nve}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{nvt}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{npt}) implement initial\_integrate() and
final\_integrate() to perform velocity Verlet updates.  Fixes that
constrain forces implement post\_force().

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes that perform diagnostics typically implement end\_of\_step().  For
an end\_of\_step fix, one of your fix arguments must be the variable
“nevery” which is used to determine when to call the fix and you must
set this variable in the constructor of your fix.  By convention, this
is the first argument the fix defines (after the ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID, style).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the fix needs to store information for each atom that persists from
timestep to timestep, it can manage that memory and migrate the info
with the atoms as they move from processors to processor by
implementing the grow\_arrays, copy\_arrays, pack\_exchange, and
unpack\_exchange methods.  Similarly, the pack\_restart and
unpack\_restart methods can be implemented to store information about
the fix in restart files.  If you wish an integrator or force
constraint fix to work with rRESPA (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}}
command), the initial\_integrate, post\_force\_integrate, and
final\_integrate\_respa methods can be implemented.  The thermo method
enables a fix to contribute values to thermodynamic output, as printed
quantities and/or to be summed to the potential energy of the system.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Input script command style}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_command:input-script-command-style}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_command::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
New commands can be added to LAMMPS input scripts by adding new classes
that are derived from the Command class and thus must have a “command”
method.  For example, the create\_atoms, read\_data, velocity, and run
commands are all implemented in this fashion.  When such a command is
encountered in the LAMMPS input script, LAMMPS simply creates a class
instance with the corresponding name, invokes the “command” method of
the class, and passes it the arguments from the input script.  The
command method can perform whatever operations it wishes on LAMMPS data
structures.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The single method your new class must define is as follows:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
command
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
operations performed by the new command
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Of course, the new class can define other methods and variables as
needed.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Dump styles}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_dump:dump-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_dump::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Classes that dump per\sphinxhyphen{}atom info to files are derived from the Dump
class.  To dump new quantities or in a new format, a new derived dump
class can be added, but it is typically simpler to modify the
DumpCustom class contained in the dump\_custom.cpp file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dump\_atom.cpp is a simple example of a derived dump class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is a brief description of methods you define in your new derived
class.  See dump.h for details.


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
write\_header
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
write the header section of a snapshot of atoms
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
count
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
count the number of lines a processor will output
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
pack
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
pack a proc’s output data into a buffer
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
write\_data
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
write a proc’s data to a file
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} command and its \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} style for a list of
keywords for atom information that can already be dumped by
DumpCustom.  It includes options to dump per\sphinxhyphen{}atom info from Compute
classes, so adding a new derived Compute class is one way to calculate
new quantities to dump.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that new keywords for atom properties are not typically
added to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command.  Instead they are added
to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}} command.

\section{Granular Sub\sphinxhyphen{}Model styles}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_gran_sub_mod:granular-sub-model-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_gran_sub_mod::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In granular models, particles are spheres with a finite radius and rotational
degrees of freedom as further described in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_granular::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto granular page}}}}. Interactions between pair of
particles or particles and walls may therefore depend on many different modes
of motion as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair granular}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/gran}}}}. In both cases, the exchange of forces,
torques, and heat flow between two types of bodies is defined using a
GranularModel class. The GranularModel class organizes the details of an
interaction using a series of granular sub\sphinxhyphen{}models each of which describe a
particular interaction mode (e.g. normal forces or rolling friction). From a
parent GranSubMod class, several types of sub\sphinxhyphen{}model classes are derived:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GranSubModNormal: normal force sub\sphinxhyphen{}model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GranSubModDamping: normal damping sub\sphinxhyphen{}model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GranSubModTangential: tangential forces and sliding friction sub\sphinxhyphen{}model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GranSubModRolling: rolling friction sub\sphinxhyphen{}model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GranSubModTwisting: twisting friction sub\sphinxhyphen{}model

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
GranSubModHeat: heat conduction sub\sphinxhyphen{}model

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For each type of sub\sphinxhyphen{}model, more classes are further derived, each describing a
specific implementation. For instance, from the GranSubModNormal class the
GranSubModNormalHooke, GranSubModNormalHertz, and GranSubModNormalJKR classes
are derived which calculate Hookean, Hertzian, or JKR normal forces,
respectively.  This modular structure simplifies the addition of new granular
contact models as one only needs to create a new GranSubMod class without
having to modify the more complex PairGranular, FixGranWall, and GranularModel
classes. Most GranSubMod methods are also already defined by the parent classes
so new contact models typically only require edits to a few relevant methods
(e.g. methods that define coefficients and calculate forces).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each GranSubMod class has a pointer to both the LAMMPS class and the GranularModel
class which owns it, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gm}}, respectively. The GranularModel class
includes several public variables that describe the geometry/dynamics of the
contact such as


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{\X{25}{100}\X{75}{100}}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xi}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xj}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Positions of the two contacting bodies
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vi}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vj}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Velocities of the two contacting bodies
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omegai}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omegaj}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Angular velocities of the two contacting bodies
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dx}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nx}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
The displacement and normalized displacement vectors
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{r}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rsq}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rinv}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
The distance, distance squared, and inverse distance
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{radsum}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum of particle radii
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vr}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vn}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{vt}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
The relative velocity vector and its normal and tangential components
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{wr}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
The relative rotational velocity
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabular}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These quantities, among others, are calculated in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GranularModel\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}check\_contact()}}
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GranularModel\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}calculate\_forces()}} methods which can be referred to for more
details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To create a new GranSubMod class, it is recommended that one first looks at similar
GranSubMod classes. All GranSubMod classes share several general methods which may
need to be defined


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{\X{25}{100}\X{75}{100}}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mix\_coeff()}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional method to define how coefficients are mixed for different atom types. By default, coefficients are mixed using a geometric mean.
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{coeffs\_to\_local()}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Parses coefficients to define local variables. Run once at model construction.
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init()}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional method to define local variables after other GranSubMod types were created. For instance, this method may be used by a tangential model that derives parameters from the normal model.
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabular}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Normal, Damping, Tangential, Twisting, and Rolling sub\sphinxhyphen{}models also have a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_forces()}} method which calculate the respective forces/torques.
Correspondingly, the Heat sub\sphinxhyphen{}model has a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_heat()}} method. Lastly,
the Normal sub\sphinxhyphen{}model has a few extra optional methods:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{\X{25}{100}\X{75}{100}}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{touch()}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tests whether particles are in contact. By default, when particles overlap.
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pulloff\_distance()}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Returns the distance at which particles stop interacting. By default, when particles no longer overlap.
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_radius()}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Returns the radius of the contact. By default, the radius of the geometric cross section.
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{set\_fncrit()}}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Defines the critical force to break the contact used by some tangential, rolling, and twisting sub\sphinxhyphen{}models. By default, the current total normal force including damping.
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabular}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, say one wanted to create a new normal force option that consisted
of a Hookean force with a piecewise stiffness. This could be done by adding a new
set of files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gran\_sub\_mod\_custom.h}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{ifdef GranSubMod\PYGZus{}CLASS}
\PYG{c+c1}{// clang\PYGZhy{}format off}
\PYG{n}{GranSubModStyle}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{hooke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{piecewise}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{GranSubModNormalHookePiecewise}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{NORMAL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{c+c1}{// clang\PYGZhy{}format on}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{else}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{ifndef GRAN\PYGZus{}SUB\PYGZus{}MOD\PYGZus{}CUSTOM\PYGZus{}H\PYGZus{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{define GRAN\PYGZus{}SUB\PYGZus{}MOD\PYGZus{}CUSTOM\PYGZus{}H\PYGZus{}}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZdq{}gran\PYGZus{}sub\PYGZus{}mod.h\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZdq{}gran\PYGZus{}sub\PYGZus{}mod\PYGZus{}normal.h\PYGZdq{}}

\section{Thermodynamic output options}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_thermo:thermodynamic-output-options}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_thermo::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thermo}} class computes and prints thermodynamic information to
the screen and log file; see the files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thermo.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thermo.h}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are four styles defined in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thermo.cpp}}: “one”, “multi”, “yaml”,
and “custom”.  The “custom” style allows the user to explicitly list
keywords for individual quantities to print when thermodynamic output is
generated.  The others have a fixed list of keywords.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command for a list of available
quantities.  The formatting of the “custom” style defaults to the “one”
style, but can be adapted using {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify line}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermo styles (one, multi, etc) are defined by lists of keywords
with associated formats for integer and floating point numbers and
identified by an enumerator constant.  Adding a new style thus mostly
requires defining a new list of keywords and the associated formats and
then inserting the required output processing where the enumerators are
identified.  Search for the word “CUSTOMIZATION” with references to
“thermo style” in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thermo.cpp}} file to see the locations where
code will need to be added.  The member function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thermo::header()}}
prints output at the very beginning of a thermodynamic output block and
can be used to print column headers or other front matter.  The member
function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thermo::footer()}} prints output at the end of a
thermodynamic output block.  The formatting of the output is done by
assembling a “line” (which may span multiple lines if the style inserts
newline characters (”n” as in the “multi” style).

\sphinxAtStartPar
New thermodynamic keywords can also be added to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thermo.cpp}} to
compute new quantities for output.  Search for the word “CUSTOMIZATION”
with references to “keyword” in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thermo.cpp}} to see the several
locations where code will need to be added.  Effectively, you need to
define a member function that computes the property, add an if statement
in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thermo::parse\_fields()}} where the corresponding header string for
the keyword and the function pointer is registered by calling the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thermo::addfield()}} method, and add an if statement in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thermo::evaluate\_keyword()}} which is called from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Variable}}
class when a thermo keyword is encountered.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The third argument to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thermo::addfield()}} is a flag indicating
whether the function for the keyword computes a floating point
(FLOAT), regular integer (INT), or big integer (BIGINT) value.  This
information is used for formatting the thermodynamic output.  Inside
the function the result must then be stored either in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dvalue}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ivalue}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bivalue}} member variable, respectively.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command allows to
use output of quantities calculated by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}}, it may often
be simpler to compute what you wish via one of those constructs, rather
than by adding a new keyword to the thermo\_style command.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Variable options}
\label{\detokenize{Modify_variable:variable-options}}\label{\detokenize{Modify_variable::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Variable}} class computes and stores {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}
information in LAMMPS; see the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{variable.cpp}}.  The value
associated with a variable can be periodically printed to the screen
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{print}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}}, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} commands.  Variables of style
“equal” can compute complex equations that involve the following types
of arguments:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
thermo keywords = ke, vol, atoms, ...
other variables = v\PYGZus{}a, v\PYGZus{}myvar, ...
math functions = div(x,y), mult(x,y), add(x,y), ...
group functions = mass(group), xcm(group,x), ...
atom values = x[123], y[3], vx[34], ...
compute values = c\PYGZus{}mytemp[0], c\PYGZus{}thermo\PYGZus{}press[3], ...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding keywords for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}}
command (which can then be accessed by variables) is discussed in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_thermo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify thermo}}}} documentation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding a new math function of one or two arguments can be done by
editing one section of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Variable::evaluate()}} method.  Search for
the word “customize” to find the appropriate location.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding a new group function can be done by editing one section of the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Variable::evaluate()}} method.  Search for the word “customize” to
find the appropriate location.  You may need to add a new method to the
Group class as well (see the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{group.cpp}} file).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Accessing a new atom\sphinxhyphen{}based vector can be done by editing one section
of the Variable::evaluate() method.  Search for the word “customize”
to find the appropriate location.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding new {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute styles}}}} (whose calculated values can
then be accessed by variables) is discussed in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify compute}}}} documentation.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Information for Developers}
\label{\detokenize{Developer:information-for-developers}}\label{\detokenize{Developer::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section describes the internal structure and basic algorithms
of the LAMMPS code. This is a work in progress and additional
information will be added incrementally depending on availability
of time and requests from the LAMMPS user community.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Source files}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_org:source-files}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_org::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The source files of the LAMMPS code are found in two directories of the
distribution: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib}}.  Most of the code is written in C++
but there are small a number of files in several other languages like C,
Fortran, Shell script, or Python.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The core of the code is located in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} folder and its
subdirectories.  A sizable number of these files are in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}}
directory itself, but there are plenty of {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{packages}}}},
which can be included or excluded when LAMMPS is built.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Include packages in build}}}} section of the manual
for more information about that part of the build process.  LAMMPS
currently supports building with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_make::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{conventional makefiles}}}} and through {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{CMake}}}}.  Those procedures
differ in how packages are enabled or disabled for inclusion into a
LAMMPS binary, so they cannot be mixed.  The source files for each
package are in all\sphinxhyphen{}uppercase subdirectories of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} folder, for
example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MOLECULE}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}MOLECULE}}.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/STUBS}}
subdirectory is not a package but contains a dummy MPI library, that is
used when building a serial version of the code. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/MAKE}}
directory and its subdirectories contain makefiles with settings and
flags for a variety of configuration and machines for the build process
with traditional makefiles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib}} directory contains the source code for several supporting
libraries or files with configuration settings to use globally installed
libraries, that are required by some optional packages.  They may
include python scripts that can transparently download additional source
code on request.  Each subdirectory, like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib/poems}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib/gpu}},
contains the source files, some of which are in different languages such
as Fortran or CUDA. These libraries included in the LAMMPS build, if the
corresponding package is installed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS C++ source files almost always come in pairs, such as
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/run.cpp}} (implementation file) and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/run.h}} (header file).
Each pair of files defines a C++ class, for example the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Run}} class, which contains the code invoked by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command in a LAMMPS input script.  As this example
illustrates, source file and class names often have a one\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}one
correspondence with a command used in a LAMMPS input script.  Some
source files and classes do not have a corresponding input script
command, for example \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/force.cpp}} and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Force}}
class.  They are discussed in the next section.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The names of all source files are in lower case and may use the
underscore character ‘\_’ to separate words. Apart from bundled,
externally maintained libraries, which may have different conventions,
all C and C++ header files have a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.h}} extension, all C++ files have a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.cpp}} extension, and C files a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.c}} extension.  A few C++ classes
and utility functions are implemented with only a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.h}} file. Examples
are the Pointers and Commands classes or the MathVec functions.


\section{Class topology}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_org:class-topology}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Though LAMMPS has a lot of source files and classes, its class topology
is not very deep, which can be seen from the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_org:id1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS class topology}}}}
figure.  In that figure, each name refers to a class and has a pair of
associated source files in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} folder, for example the class
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Memory}} corresponds to the files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{memory.cpp}}
and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{memory.h}}, or the class \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::AtomVec}}
corresponds to the files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atom\_vec.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atom\_vec.h}}.  Full
lines in the figure represent compositing: that is, the class at the
base of the arrow holds a pointer to an instance of the class at the
tip.  Dashed lines instead represent inheritance: the class at the tip
of the arrow is derived from the class at the base.  Classes with a red
boundary are not instantiated directly, but they represent the base
classes for “styles”.  Those “styles” make up the bulk of the LAMMPS
code and only a few representative examples are included in the figure,
so it remains readable.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{lammps-classes}.png}
\caption{LAMMPS class topology}\label{\detokenize{Developer_org:id2}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_org:id1}}
\begin{sphinxlegend}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This figure shows relations of base classes of the LAMMPS
simulation package.  Full lines indicate that a class holds an
instance of the class it is pointing to; dashed lines point to
derived classes that are given as examples of what classes may be
instantiated during a LAMMPS run based on the input commands and
accessed through the API define by their respective base classes.
At the core is the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS6LAMMPSE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS}}}}} class,
which holds pointers to class instances with specific purposes.
Those may hold instances of other classes, sometimes directly, or
only temporarily, sometimes as derived classes or derived classes
of derived classes, which may also hold instances of other
classes.
\end{quote}
\end{sphinxlegend}
\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS6LAMMPSE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::LAMMPS}}}}} class is the topmost class and
represents what is generally referred to as an “instance of LAMMPS”.  It
is a composite holding pointers to instances of other core classes
providing the core functionality of the MD engine in LAMMPS and through
them abstractions of the required operations.  The constructor of the
LAMMPS class will instantiate those instances, process the command line
flags, initialize MPI (if not already done) and set up file pointers for
input and output.  The destructor will shut everything down and free all
associated memory.  Thus code for the standalone LAMMPS executable in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main.cpp}} simply initializes MPI, instantiates a single instance of
LAMMPS while passing it the command line flags and input script. It
deletes the LAMMPS instance after the method reading the input returns
and shuts down the MPI environment before it exits the executable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS8PointersE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Pointers}}}}} class is not shown in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_org:id1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS class topology}}}} figure for clarity.  It holds references to many
of the members of the \sphinxtitleref{LAMMPS\_NS::LAMMPS}, so that all classes derived
from {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS8PointersE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Pointers}}}}} have direct access to those
references.  From the class topology all classes with blue boundary are
referenced in the Pointers class and all classes in the second and third
columns, that are not listed as derived classes, are instead derived
from {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS8PointersE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Pointers}}}}}.  To initialize the pointer
references in Pointers, a pointer to the LAMMPS class instance needs to
be passed to the constructor. All constructors for classes derived from
it, must do so and thus pass that pointer to the constructor for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS8PointersE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Pointers}}}}}.  The default constructor for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS8PointersE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Pointers}}}}} is disabled to enforce this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since all storage is supposed to be encapsulated (there are a few
exceptions), the LAMMPS class can also be instantiated multiple times by
a calling code.  Outside the aforementioned exceptions, those LAMMPS
instances can be used alternately.  As of the time of this writing
(early 2023) LAMMPS is not yet sufficiently thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe for concurrent
execution.  When running in parallel with MPI, care has to be taken,
that suitable copies of communicators are used to not create conflicts
between different instances.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS class currently holds instances of 19 classes representing
the core functionality.  There are a handful of virtual parent classes
in LAMMPS that define what LAMMPS calls \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{styles}}.  These are shaded
red in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_org:id1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS class topology}}}} figure.  Each of these are parents of a
number of child classes that implement the interface defined by the
parent class.  There are two main categories of these \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{styles}}: some
may only have one instance active at a time (e.g. atom, pair, bond,
angle, dihedral, improper, kspace, comm) and there is a dedicated
pointer variable for each of them in the corresponding composite class.
Setups that require a mix of different such styles have to use a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} class instance that acts as a proxy, and manages and forwards
calls to the corresponding sub\sphinxhyphen{}style class instances for the designated
subset of atoms or data.  The composite class may also have lists of
class instances, e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Modify}} handles lists of compute and fix
styles, while \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Output}} handles a list of dump class instances.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The exception to this scheme are the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{command}} style classes.  These
implement specific commands that can be invoked before, after, or in
between runs.  For these an instance of the class is created, its
command() method called and then, after completion, the class instance
deleted.  Examples for this are the create\_box, create\_atoms, minimize,
run, set, or velocity command styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all those \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{styles}}, certain naming conventions are employed: for
the fix nve command the class is called FixNVE and the source files are
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix\_nve.h}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix\_nve.cpp}}. Similarly, for fix ave/time we have
FixAveTime and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix\_ave\_time.h}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix\_ave\_time.cpp}}.  Style names
are lower case and without spaces or special characters. A suffix or
words are appended with a forward slash ‘/’ which denotes a variant of
the corresponding class without the suffix.  To connect the style name
and the class name, LAMMPS uses macros like: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{AtomStyle()}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairStyle()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BondStyle()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{RegionStyle()}}, and so on in the
corresponding header file.  During configuration or compilation, files
with the pattern \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{style\_\textless{}name\textgreater{}.h}} are created that consist of a list
of include statements including all headers of all styles of a given
type that are currently enabled (or “installed”).

\sphinxAtStartPar
More details on individual classes in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_org:id1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS class topology}}}} are as
follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Memory class handles allocation of all large vectors and arrays.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Error class prints all (terminal) error and warning messages.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Universe class sets up one or more partitions of processors so
that one or multiple simulations can be run, on the processors
allocated for a run, e.g. by the mpirun command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Input class reads and processes input (strings and files), stores
variables, and invokes {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_all::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{commands}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Command style classes are derived from the Command class. They provide
input script commands that perform one\sphinxhyphen{}time operations
before/after/between simulations or which invoke a simulation.  They
are usually instantiated from within the Input class, its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{command}}
method invoked, and then immediately destructed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Finish class is instantiated to print statistics to the screen
after a simulation is performed, by commands like run and minimize.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Special class walks the bond topology of a molecular system to
find first, second, third neighbors of each atom.  It is invoked by
several commands, like {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{replicate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{replicate}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Atom class stores per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties associated with atom styles.
More precisely, they are allocated and managed by a class derived from
the AtomVec class, and the Atom class simply stores pointers to them.
