The classes derived from AtomVec represent the different atom styles,
and they are instantiated through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}}
command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Update class holds instances of an integrator and a minimizer
class.  The Integrate class is a parent style for the Verlet and
r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA time integrators, as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}} command.  The Min class is a parent style for various
energy minimizers.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Neighbor class builds and stores neighbor lists.  The NeighList
class stores a single list (for all atoms).  A NeighRequest class
instance is created by pair, fix, or compute styles when they need a
particular kind of neighbor list and use the NeighRequest properties
to select the neighbor list settings for the given request.  There can
be multiple instances of the NeighRequest class. The Neighbor class
will try to optimize how the requests are processed.  Depending on the
NeighRequest properties, neighbor lists are constructed from scratch,
aliased, or constructed by post\sphinxhyphen{}processing an existing list into
sub\sphinxhyphen{}lists.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Comm class performs inter\sphinxhyphen{}processor communication, typically of
ghost atom information.  This usually involves MPI message exchanges
with 6 neighboring processors in the 3d logical grid of processors
mapped to the simulation box. There are two {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{communication styles}}}}, enabling different ways to perform the domain
decomposition.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Irregular class is used, when atoms may migrate to arbitrary
processors.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Domain class stores the simulation box geometry, as well as
geometric Regions and any user definition of a Lattice.  The latter
are defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}
commands in an input script.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Force class computes various forces between atoms.  The Pair
parent class is for non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded or pairwise forces, which in LAMMPS
also includes many\sphinxhyphen{}body forces such as the Tersoff 3\sphinxhyphen{}body potential if
those are computed by walking pairwise neighbor lists.  The Bond,
Angle, Dihedral, Improper parent classes are styles for bonded
interactions within a static molecular topology.  The KSpace parent
class is for computing long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interactions.  One of its
child classes, PPPM, uses the FFT3D and Remap classes to redistribute
and communicate grid\sphinxhyphen{}based information across the parallel processors.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Modify class stores lists of class instances derived from the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Compute}}}} base classes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Group class manipulates groups that atoms are assigned to via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}} command.  It also has functions to compute
various attributes of groups of atoms.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Output class is used to generate 3 kinds of output from a LAMMPS
simulation: thermodynamic information printed to the screen and log
file, dump file snapshots, and restart files.  These correspond to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Thermo}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Dump}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{write_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{WriteRestart}}}} classes respectively.  The Dump
class is a base class, with several derived classes implementing
various dump style variants.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Timer class logs timing information, output at the end
of a run.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Code design}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:code-design}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section explains some code design choices in LAMMPS with the goal
of helping developers write new code similar to the existing code.
Please see the section on {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Requirements for contributed code}}}} for more specific recommendations and guidelines.  While
that section is organized more in the form of a checklist for code
contributors, the focus here is on overall code design strategy, choices
made between possible alternatives, and discussing some relevant C++
programming language constructs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Historically, the basic design philosophy of the LAMMPS C++ code was a
“C with classes” style.  The motivation was to make it easy to modify
LAMMPS for people without significant training in C++ programming.  Data
structures and code constructs were used that resemble the previous
implementation(s) in Fortran.  A contributing factor to this choice was
that at the time, C++ compilers were often not mature and some advanced
features contained bugs or did not function as the standard required.
There were also disagreements between compiler vendors as to how to
interpret the C++ standard documents.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, C++ compilers and the C++ programming language have advanced
significantly.  In 2020, the LAMMPS developers decided to require the
C++11 standard as the minimum C++ language standard for LAMMPS.  Since
then, we have begun to replace C\sphinxhyphen{}style constructs with equivalent C++
functionality.  This was taken either from the C++ standard library or
implemented as custom classes or functions.  The goal is to improve
readability of the code and to increase code reuse through abstraction
of commonly used functionality.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Please note that as of spring 2023 there is still a sizable chunk of
legacy code in LAMMPS that has not yet been refactored to reflect
these style conventions in full.  LAMMPS has a large code base and
many contributors.  There is also a hierarchy of precedence in which
the code is adapted.  Highest priority has been the code in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src}} folder, followed by code in packages in order of their
popularity and complexity (simpler code gets adapted sooner), followed
by code in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib}} folder.  Source code that is downloaded from
external packages or libraries during compilation is not subject to
the conventions discussed here.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Object\sphinxhyphen{}oriented code}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:object-oriented-code}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed to be an object\sphinxhyphen{}oriented code.  Each simulation is
represented by an instance of the LAMMPS class.  When running in
parallel, each MPI process creates such an instance.  This can be seen
in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main.cpp}} file where the core steps of running a LAMMPS
simulation are the following 3 lines of code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{LAMMPS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{new}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LAMMPS}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{argc}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{argv}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lammps\PYGZus{}comm}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{input}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{delete}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first line creates a LAMMPS class instance and passes the command
line arguments and the global communicator to its constructor.  The
second line triggers the LAMMPS instance to process the input (either
from standard input or a provided input file) until the simulation
ends.  The third line deletes the LAMMPS instance.  The remainder of
the main.cpp file has code for error handling, MPI configuration, and
other special features.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The basic LAMMPS class hierarchy which is created by the LAMMPS class
constructor is shown in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_org:id1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{LAMMPS class topology}}}}.  When input commands
are processed, additional class instances are created, or deleted, or
replaced.  Likewise, specific member functions of specific classes are
called to trigger actions such as creating atoms, computing forces,
computing properties, time\sphinxhyphen{}propagating the system, or writing output.


\subsubsection{Compositing and Inheritance}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:compositing-and-inheritance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS makes extensive use of the object\sphinxhyphen{}oriented programming (OOP)
principles of \sphinxstyleemphasis{compositing} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{inheritance}. Classes like the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS}} class are a \sphinxstylestrong{composite} containing pointers to instances
of other classes like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Atom}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Comm}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Force}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Neighbor}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Modify}}, and so on.  Each of these classes implements certain
functionality by storing and manipulating data related to the
simulation and providing member functions that trigger certain
actions.  Some of those classes like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Force}} are themselves
composites, containing instances of classes describing different force
interactions.  Similarly, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Modify}} class contains a list of
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Fix}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Compute}} classes.  If the input commands that
correspond to these classes include the word \sphinxstyleemphasis{style}, then LAMMPS
stores only a single instance of that class.  E.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom\_style},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_style}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond\_style}.  If the input command does
\sphinxstylestrong{not} include the word \sphinxstyleemphasis{style}, then there may be many instances of
that class defined, for example \sphinxstyleemphasis{region}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inheritance} enables creation of \sphinxstyleemphasis{derived} classes that can share
common functionality in their base class while providing a consistent
interface.  The derived classes replace (dummy or pure) functions in
the base class.  The higher level classes can then call those methods
of the instantiated classes without having to know which specific
derived class variant was instantiated.  In LAMMPS these derived
classes are often referred to as “styles”, e.g.  pair styles, fix
styles, atom styles and so on.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is the origin of the flexibility of LAMMPS.  For example, pair
styles implement a variety of different non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interatomic
potentials functions.  All details for the implementation of a
potential are stored and executed in a single class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As mentioned above, there can be multiple instances of classes derived
from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Fix}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Compute}} base classes.  They represent a
different facet of LAMMPS’ flexibility, as they provide methods which
can be called at different points within a timestep, as explained in
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_flow::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{How a timestep works}}}} doc page.  This allows
the input script to tailor how a specific simulation is run, what
diagnostic computations are performed, and how the output of those
computations is further processed or output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional code sharing is possible by creating derived classes from the
derived classes (e.g., to implement an accelerated version of a pair
style) where only a subset of the derived class methods are replaced
with accelerated versions.


\subsubsection{Polymorphism}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:polymorphism}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Polymorphism and dynamic dispatch are another OOP feature that play an
important role in how LAMMPS selects what code to execute.  In a
nutshell, this is a mechanism where the decision of which member
function to call from a class is determined at runtime and not when
the code is compiled.  To enable it, the function has to be declared
as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{virtual}} and all corresponding functions in derived classes
should use the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{override}} property. Below is a brief example.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{Base}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{virtual}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZti{}}\PYG{n}{Base}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{default}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{call}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{normal}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{virtual}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{poly}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{Base::call}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{normal}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{poly}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{Derived}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Base}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZti{}}\PYG{n}{Derived}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{default}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{normal}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{poly}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// [....]}

\PYG{n}{Base}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{base1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{new}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Base}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{Base}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{base2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{new}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Derived}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{n}{base1}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{call}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{base2}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{call}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The difference in behavior of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{normal()}} and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{poly()}} member
functions is which of the two member functions is called when executing
\sphinxtitleref{base1\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}call()} versus \sphinxtitleref{base2\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}call()}.  Without polymorphism, a
function within the base class can only call member functions within the
same scope: that is, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Base::call()}} will always call
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Base::normal()}}.  But for the \sphinxtitleref{base2\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}call()} case, the call of the
virtual member function will be dispatched to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Derived::poly()}}
instead.  This mechanism results in calling functions that are within
the scope of the class that was used to \sphinxstyleemphasis{create} the instance, even if
they are assigned to a pointer for their base class.  This is the
desired behavior, and this way LAMMPS can even use styles that are loaded
at runtime from a shared object file with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{plugin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{plugin command}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A special case of virtual functions are so\sphinxhyphen{}called pure functions.  These
are virtual functions that are initialized to 0 in the class declaration
(see example below).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{Base}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}
\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{virtual}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pure}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This has the effect that an instance of the base class cannot be
created and that derived classes \sphinxstylestrong{must} implement these functions.
Many of the functions listed with the various class styles in the
section {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modifying \& extending LAMMPS}}}} are pure functions.  The motivation for this is
to define the interface or API of the functions, but defer their
implementation to the derived classes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, there are downsides to this. For example, calls to virtual
functions from within a constructor, will \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} be in the scope of the
derived class, and thus it is good practice to either avoid calling them
or to provide an explicit scope such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Base::poly()}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Derived::poly()}}.  Furthermore, any destructors in classes containing
virtual functions should be declared virtual too, so they will be
processed in the expected order before types are removed from dynamic
dispatch.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Important Notes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to be able to detect incompatibilities at compile time and
to avoid unexpected behavior, it is crucial that all member functions
that are intended to replace a virtual or pure function use the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{override}} property keyword.  For the same reason, the use of
overloads or default arguments for virtual functions should be
avoided, as they lead to confusion over which function is supposed to
override which, and which arguments need to be declared.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Style Factories}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:style-factories}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to create class instances for different styles, LAMMPS often
uses a programming pattern called \sphinxtitleref{Factory}.  Those are functions that
create an instance of a specific derived class, say \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairLJCut}} and
return a pointer to the type of the common base class of that style,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}} in this case.  To associate the factory function with the
style keyword, a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{std::map}} class is used with function pointers
indexed by their keyword (for example “lj/cut” for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairLJCut}} and
“morse” for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairMorse}}).  A couple of typedefs help keep the code
readable, and a template function is used to implement the actual
factory functions for the individual classes.  Below is an example
of such a factory function from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Force}} class as declared in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force.h}} and implemented in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force.cpp}}.  The file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{style\_pair.h}}
is generated during compilation and includes all main header files
(i.e. those starting with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_}}) of pair styles and then the
macro \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairStyle()}} will associate the style name “lj/cut”
with a factory function creating an instance of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairLJCut}}
class.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{// from force.h}
\PYG{k}{typedef}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{PairCreator}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LAMMPS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{typedef}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{map}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{string}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{PairCreator}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{PairCreatorMap}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{PairCreatorMap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{pair\PYGZus{}map}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+c1}{// from force.cpp}
\PYG{k}{template}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{k}{typename}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{S}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{typename}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{T}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{static}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{style\PYGZus{}creator}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LAMMPS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{new}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{T}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{c+c1}{// [...]}

\PYG{n}{pair\PYGZus{}map}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{new}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{PairCreatorMap}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{define PAIR\PYGZus{}CLASS}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{define PairStyle(key, Class) (*pair\PYGZus{}map)[\PYGZsh{}key] = \PYGZam{}style\PYGZus{}creator\PYGZlt{}Pair, Class\PYGZgt{};}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZdq{}style\PYGZus{}pair.h\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{undef PairStyle}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{undef PAIR\PYGZus{}CLASS}

\PYG{c+c1}{// from pair\PYGZus{}lj\PYGZus{}cut.h}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{ifdef PAIR\PYGZus{}CLASS}
\PYG{n}{PairStyle}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{PairLJCut}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{else}
\PYG{c+c1}{// [...]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar code constructs are present in other files like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{modify.cpp}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{modify.h}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{neighbor.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{neighbor.h}}.  Those contain
similar macros and include \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{style\_*.h}} files for creating class instances
of styles they manage.


\subsection{I/O and output formatting}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:i-o-and-output-formatting}}

\subsubsection{C\sphinxhyphen{}style stdio versus C++ style iostreams}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:c-style-stdio-versus-c-style-iostreams}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS uses the “stdio” library of the standard C library for reading
from and writing to files and console instead of C++ “iostreams”.
This is mainly motivated by better performance, better control over
formatting, and less effort to achieve specific formatting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since mixing “stdio” and “iostreams” can lead to unexpected behavior,
use of the latter is strongly discouraged.  Output to the screen should
\sphinxstyleemphasis{not} use the predefined \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stdout}} FILE pointer, but rather the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{screen}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{logfile}} FILE pointers managed by the LAMMPS class.
Furthermore, output should generally only be done by MPI rank 0
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{comm\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}me == 0}}).  Output that is sent to both \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{screen}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{logfile}} should use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4IDpEN9LAMMPS_NS5utils7logmesgEvP6LAMMPSRKNSt6stringEDpRR4Args}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::logmesg() convenience
function}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We discourage the use of stringstreams because the bundled \{fmt\} library
and the customized tokenizer classes provide the same functionality in a
cleaner way with better performance.  This also helps maintain a
consistent programming syntax with code from many different
contributors.


\subsubsection{Formatting with the \{fmt\} library}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:formatting-with-the-fmt-library}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS source code includes a copy of the \sphinxhref{https://fmt.dev}{\{fmt\} library}, which is preferred over formatting with the
“printf()” family of functions.  The primary reason is that it allows
a typesafe default format for any type of supported data.  This is
particularly useful for formatting integers of a given size (32\sphinxhyphen{}bit or
64\sphinxhyphen{}bit) which may require different format strings depending on
compile time settings or compilers/operating systems.  Furthermore,
\{fmt\} gives better performance, has more functionality, a familiar
formatting syntax that has similarities to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{format()}} in Python, and
provides a facility that can be used to integrate format strings and a
variable number of arguments into custom functions in a much simpler
way than the varargs mechanism of the C library.  Finally, \{fmt\} has
been included into the C++20 language standard, so changes to adopt it
are future\sphinxhyphen{}proof.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Formatted strings are frequently created by calling the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fmt::format()}} function, which will return a string as a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{std::string}} class instance.  In contrast to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\%}} placeholder in
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{printf()}}, the \{fmt\} library uses \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{\}}} to embed format descriptors.
In the simplest case, no additional characters are needed, as \{fmt\} will
choose the default format based on the data type of the argument.
Otherwise, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fmt::print()}} function may be used instead of
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{printf()}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fprintf()}}.  In addition, several LAMMPS output
functions, that originally accepted a single string as argument have
been overloaded to accept a format string with optional arguments as
well (e.g., \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Error::all()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Error::one()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::logmesg()}}).


\subsubsection{Summary of the \{fmt\} format syntax}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:summary-of-the-fmt-format-syntax}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The syntax of the format string is “\{{[}\textless{}argument id\textgreater{}{]}{[}:\textless{}format spec\textgreater{}{]}\}”,
where either the argument id or the format spec (separated by a colon
‘:’) is optional.  The argument id is usually a number starting from 0
that is the index to the arguments following the format string.  By
default, these are assigned in order (i.e. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 etc.).  The
most common case for using argument id would be to use the same argument
in multiple places in the format string without having to provide it as
an argument multiple times. The argument id is rarely used in the LAMMPS
source code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More common is the use of a format specifier, which starts with a colon.
This may optionally be followed by a fill character (default is ‘ ‘). If
provided, the fill character \sphinxstylestrong{must} be followed by an alignment
character (‘\textless{}’, ‘\textasciicircum{}’, ‘\textgreater{}’ for left, centered, or right alignment
(default)).  The alignment character may be used without a fill
character.  The next important format parameter would be the minimum
width, which may be followed by a dot ‘.’ and a precision for floating
point numbers.  The final character in the format string would be an
indicator for the “presentation”, i.e. ‘d’ for decimal presentation of
integers, ‘x’ for hexadecimal, ‘o’ for octal, ‘c’ for character etc.
This mostly follows the “printf()” scheme, but without requiring an
additional length parameter to distinguish between different integer
widths.  The \{fmt\} library will detect those and adapt the formatting
accordingly.  For floating point numbers there are correspondingly, ‘g’
for generic presentation, ‘e’ for exponential presentation, and ‘f’ for
fixed point presentation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The format string “\{:8\}” would thus represent \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} type argument and be
replaced by at least 8 characters; “\{:\textless{}8\}” would do this as left
aligned, “\{:\textasciicircum{}8\}” as centered, “\{:\textgreater{}8\}” as right aligned.  If a specific
presentation is selected, the argument type must be compatible or else
the \{fmt\} formatting code will throw an exception.  Some format string
examples are given below:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mesg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fmt}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{  CPU time: \PYGZob{}:4d\PYGZcb{}:\PYGZob{}:02d\PYGZcb{}:\PYGZob{}:02d\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cpuh}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cpum}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cpus}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{mesg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fmt}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZob{}:\PYGZlt{}8s\PYGZcb{}| \PYGZob{}:\PYGZlt{}10.5g\PYGZcb{} | \PYGZob{}:\PYGZlt{}10.5g\PYGZcb{} | \PYGZob{}:\PYGZlt{}10.5g\PYGZcb{} |\PYGZob{}:6.1f\PYGZcb{} |\PYGZob{}:6.2f\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{                   }\PYG{n}{label}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{time\PYGZus{}min}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{time\PYGZus{}max}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{time\PYGZus{}sq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{logmesg}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZob{}:\PYGZgt{}6\PYGZcb{} = max \PYGZsh{} of 1\PYGZhy{}2 neighbors}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{maxall}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{logmesg}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Lattice spacing in x,y,z = \PYGZob{}:.8\PYGZcb{} \PYGZob{}:.8\PYGZcb{} \PYGZob{}:.8\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{               }\PYG{n}{xlattice}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{ylattice}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{zlattice}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which will create the following output lines:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
CPU time:    0:02:16
Pair    | 2.0133     | 2.0133     | 2.0133     |   0.0 | 84.21
     4 = max \PYGZsh{} of 1\PYGZhy{}2 neighbors
Lattice spacing in x,y,z = 1.6795962 1.6795962 1.6795962
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, a special feature of the \{fmt\} library is that format
parameters like the width or the precision may be also provided as
arguments. In that case a nested format is used where a pair of curly
braces (with an optional argument id) “\{\}” are used instead of the
value, for example “\{:\{\}d\}” will consume two integer arguments, the
first will be the value shown and the second the minimum width.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For more details and examples, please consult the \sphinxhref{https://fmt.dev/latest/syntax.html}{\{fmt\} syntax
documentation} website.


\subsection{Memory management}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_code_design:memory-management}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dynamical allocation of small data and objects can be done with the C++
commands “new” and “delete/delete{[}{]}”.  Large data should use the member
functions of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory}} class, most commonly, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory::create()}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory::grow()}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory::destroy()}}, which provide variants
for vectors, 2d arrays, 3d arrays, etc.  These can also be used for
small data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The use of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{malloc()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{calloc()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{realloc()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{free()}}
directly is strongly discouraged.  To simplify adapting legacy code
into the LAMMPS code base the member functions \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory::smalloc()}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory::srealloc()}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory::sfree()}} are available, which
perform additional error checks for safety.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use of these custom memory allocation functions is motivated by the
following considerations:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Memory allocation failures on \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} MPI rank during a parallel run
will trigger an immediate abort of the entire parallel calculation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A failing “new” will trigger an exception, which is also captured by
LAMMPS and triggers a global abort.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Allocation of multidimensional arrays will be done in a C compatible
fashion, but such that the storage of the actual data is stored in one
large contiguous block.  Thus, when MPI communication is needed,
the data can be communicated directly (similar to Fortran arrays).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “destroy()” and “sfree()” functions may safely be called on NULL
pointers.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “destroy()” functions will nullify the pointer variables, thus
making “use after free” errors easy to detect.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is possible to use a larger than default memory alignment (not on
all operating systems, since the allocated storage pointers must be
compatible with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{free()}} for technical reasons).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the practical implementation of code this means, that any pointer
variables, that are class members should be initialized to a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nullptr}}
value in their respective constructors.  That way, it is safe to call
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Memory::destroy()}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{delete{[}{]}}} on them before \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} allocation
outside the constructor.  This helps prevent memory leaks.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Parallel algorithms}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_parallel:parallel-algorithms}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_parallel::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed to enable running simulations in parallel using the
MPI parallel communication standard with distributed data via domain
decomposition.  The parallelization aims to be efficient, and resulting
in good strong scaling (= good speedup for the same system) and good
weak scaling (= the computational cost of enlarging the system is
proportional to the system size).  Additional parallelization using GPUs
or OpenMP can also be applied within the subdomain assigned to an MPI
process.  For clarity, most of the following illustrations show the 2d
simulation case. The underlying algorithms in those cases, however,
apply to both 2d and 3d cases equally well.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The text and most of the figures in this chapter were adapted
for the manual from the section on parallel algorithms in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Intro_citing:lammps-paper}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{new LAMMPS paper}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Partitioning}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_part:partitioning}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_part::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The underlying spatial decomposition strategy used by LAMMPS for
distributed\sphinxhyphen{}memory parallelism is set with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style command}}}} and can be either “brick” (a regular grid) or “tiled”.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{domain-decomp}.png}
\caption{Domain decomposition schemes}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_part:id1}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_part:domain-decomposition}}
\begin{sphinxlegend}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This figure shows the different kinds of domain decomposition used
for MPI parallelization: “brick” on the left with an orthogonal
(left) and a triclinic (middle) simulation domain, and a “tiled”
decomposition (right).  The black lines show the division into
subdomains, and the contained atoms are “owned” by the
corresponding MPI process. The green dashed lines indicate how
subdomains are extended with “ghost” atoms up to the communication
cutoff distance.
\end{quote}
\end{sphinxlegend}
\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS simulation box is a 3d or 2d volume, which can be of
orthogonal or triclinic shape, as illustrated in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_part:domain-decomposition}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Domain decomposition schemes}}}} figure for the 2d case.  Orthogonal means
the box edges are aligned with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} Cartesian axes, and the
box faces are thus all rectangular.  Triclinic allows for a more general
parallelepiped shape in which edges are aligned with three arbitrary
vectors and the box faces are parallelograms.  In each dimension, box
faces can be periodic, or non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic with fixed or shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped
boundaries.  In the fixed case, atoms which move outside the face are
deleted; shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped means the position of the box face adjusts
continuously to enclose all the atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For distributed\sphinxhyphen{}memory MPI parallelism, the simulation box is spatially
decomposed (partitioned) into non\sphinxhyphen{}overlapping subdomains which fill the
box. The default partitioning, “brick”, is most suitable when atom
density is roughly uniform, as shown in the left\sphinxhyphen{}side images of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_part:domain-decomposition}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Domain decomposition schemes}}}} figure.  The subdomains comprise a regular
grid, and all subdomains are identical in size and shape.  Both the
orthogonal and triclinic boxes can deform continuously during a
simulation, e.g. to compress a solid or shear a liquid, in which case
the processor subdomains likewise deform.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For models with non\sphinxhyphen{}uniform density, the number of particles per
processor can be load\sphinxhyphen{}imbalanced with the default partitioning.  This
reduces parallel efficiency, as the overall simulation rate is limited
by the slowest processor, i.e. the one with the largest computational
load.  For such models, LAMMPS supports multiple strategies to reduce
the load imbalance:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The processor grid decomposition is by default based on the simulation
cell volume and tries to optimize the volume to surface ratio for the subdomains.
This can be changed with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors command}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The parallel planes defining the size of the subdomains can be shifted
with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance command}}}}. Which can be done in addition
to choosing a more optimal processor grid.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The recursive bisectioning algorithm in combination with the “tiled”
communication style can produce a partitioning with equal numbers of
particles in each subdomain.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.240\linewidth]{{decomp-regular}.png}  \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.240\linewidth]{{decomp-processors}.png}  \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.240\linewidth]{{decomp-balance}.png}  \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.240\linewidth]{{decomp-rcb}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pictures above demonstrate different decompositions for a 2d system
with 12 MPI ranks.  The atom colors indicate the load imbalance of each
subdomain, with green being optimal and red the least optimal.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Due to the vacuum in the system, the default decomposition is
unbalanced, with several MPI ranks without atoms (left). By forcing a
1x12x1 processor grid, every MPI rank does computations now, but the
number of atoms per subdomain is still uneven, and the thin slice shape
increases the amount of communication between subdomains (center
left). With a 2x6x1 processor grid and shifting the subdomain divisions,
the load imbalance is further reduced and the amount of communication
required between subdomains is less (center right).  And using the
recursive bisectioning leads to further improved decomposition (right).

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Communication}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_comm:communication}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_comm::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the selected partitioning scheme, all per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data is
distributed across the MPI processes, which allows LAMMPS to handle very
large systems provided it uses a correspondingly large number of MPI
processes.  To be able to compute the short\sphinxhyphen{}range interactions, MPI
processes need not only access to the data of atoms they “own” but also
information about atoms from neighboring subdomains, in LAMMPS referred
to as “ghost” atoms.  These are copies of atoms storing required
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data for up to the communication cutoff distance. The green
dashed\sphinxhyphen{}line boxes in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_part:domain-decomposition}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Domain decomposition schemes}}}} figure illustrate
the extended ghost\sphinxhyphen{}atom subdomain for one processor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This approach is also used to implement periodic boundary
conditions: atoms that lie within the cutoff distance across a periodic
boundary are also stored as ghost atoms and taken from the periodic
replication of the subdomain, which may be the same subdomain, e.g. if
running in serial.  As a consequence of this, force computation in
LAMMPS is not subject to minimum image conventions and thus cutoffs may
be larger than half the simulation domain.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{ghost-comm}.png}
\caption{ghost atom communication}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_comm:id1}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_comm:ghost-atom-comm}}
\begin{sphinxlegend}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This figure shows the ghost atom communication patterns between
subdomains for “brick” (left) and “tiled” communication styles for
2d simulations.  The numbers indicate MPI process ranks.  Here the
subdomains are drawn spatially separated for clarity.  The
dashed\sphinxhyphen{}line box is the extended subdomain of processor 0 which
includes its ghost atoms.  The red\sphinxhyphen{} and blue\sphinxhyphen{}shaded boxes are the
regions of communicated ghost atoms.
\end{sphinxlegend}
\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Efficient communication patterns are needed to update the “ghost” atom
data, since that needs to be done at every MD time step or minimization
step.  The diagrams of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_comm:ghost-atom-comm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{ghost atom communication}}}} figure illustrate how ghost
atom communication is performed in two stages for a 2d simulation (three
in 3d) for both a regular and irregular partitioning of the simulation
box.  For the regular case (left) atoms are exchanged first in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{x}\sphinxhyphen{}direction, then in \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, with four neighbors in the grid of processor
subdomains.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} stage, processor ranks 1 and 2 send owned atoms in their
red\sphinxhyphen{}shaded regions to rank 0 (and vice versa).  Then in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} stage,
ranks 3 and 4 send atoms in their blue\sphinxhyphen{}shaded regions to rank 0, which
includes ghost atoms they received in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} stage.  Rank 0 thus
acquires all its ghost atoms; atoms in the solid blue corner regions
are communicated twice before rank 0 receives them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the irregular case (right) the two stages are similar, but a
processor can have more than one neighbor in each direction.  In the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{x} stage, MPI ranks 1,2,3 send owned atoms in their red\sphinxhyphen{}shaded regions to
rank 0 (and vice versa).  These include only atoms between the lower
and upper \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}\sphinxhyphen{}boundary of rank 0’s subdomain.  In the \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} stage, ranks
4,5,6 send atoms in their blue\sphinxhyphen{}shaded regions to rank 0.  This may
include ghost atoms they received in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} stage, but only if they
are needed by rank 0 to fill its extended ghost atom regions in the
+/\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{y} directions (blue rectangles).  Thus, in this case, ranks 5 and
6 do not include ghost atoms they received from each other (in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}
stage) in the atoms they send to rank 0.  The key point is that while
the pattern of communication is more complex in the irregular
partitioning case, it can still proceed in two stages (three in 3d)
via atom exchanges with only neighboring processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When attributes of owned atoms are sent to neighboring processors to
become attributes of their ghost atoms, LAMMPS calls this a “forward”
communication.  On timesteps when atoms migrate to new owning processors
and neighbor lists are rebuilt, each processor creates a list of its
owned atoms which are ghost atoms in each of its neighbor processors.
These lists are used to pack per\sphinxhyphen{}atom coordinates (for example) into
message buffers in subsequent steps until the next reneighboring.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A “reverse” communication is when computed ghost atom attributes are
sent back to the processor who owns the atom.  This is used (for
example) to sum partial forces on ghost atoms to the complete force on
owned atoms.  The order of the two stages described in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_comm:ghost-atom-comm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{ghost atom communication}}}} figure is inverted, and the same lists of atoms
are used to pack and unpack message buffers with per\sphinxhyphen{}atom forces.  When
a received buffer is unpacked, the ghost forces are summed to owned atom
forces.  As in forward communication, forces on atoms in the four blue
corners of the diagrams are sent, received, and summed twice (once at
each stage) before owning processors have the full force.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These two operations are used in many places within LAMMPS aside from
exchange of coordinates and forces, for example by manybody potentials
to share intermediate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values, or by rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body integrators to
enable each atom in a body to access body properties.  Here are
additional details about how these communication operations are
performed in LAMMPS:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When exchanging data with different processors, forward and reverse
communication is done using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Send()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_IRecv()}} calls.
If a processor is “exchanging” atoms with itself, only the pack and
unpack operations are performed, e.g. to create ghost atoms across
periodic boundaries when running on a single processor.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For forward communication of owned atom coordinates, periodic box
lengths are added and subtracted when the receiving processor is
across a periodic boundary from the sender.  There is then no need to
apply a minimum image convention when calculating distances between
atom pairs when building neighbor lists or computing forces.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The cutoff distance for exchanging ghost atoms is typically equal to
the neighbor cutoff.  But it can also set to a larger value if needed,
e.g. half the diameter of a rigid body composed of multiple atoms or
over 3x the length of a stretched bond for dihedral interactions.  It
can also exceed the periodic box size.  For the regular communication
pattern (left), if the cutoff distance extends beyond a neighbor
processor’s subdomain, then multiple exchanges are performed in the
same direction.  Each exchange is with the same neighbor processor,
but buffers are packed/unpacked using a different list of atoms. For
forward communication, in the first exchange, a processor sends only
owned atoms.  In subsequent exchanges, it sends ghost atoms received
in previous exchanges.  For the irregular pattern (right) overlaps of
a processor’s extended ghost\sphinxhyphen{}atom subdomain with all other processors
in each dimension are detected.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Neighbor lists}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_neigh:neighbor-lists}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_neigh::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To compute forces efficiently, each processor creates a Verlet\sphinxhyphen{}style
neighbor list which enumerates all pairs of atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i,j} (\sphinxstyleemphasis{i} = owned,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{j} = owned or ghost) with separation less than the applicable neighbor
list cutoff distance.  In LAMMPS, the neighbor lists are stored in a
multiple\sphinxhyphen{}page data structure; each page is a contiguous chunk of memory
which stores vectors of neighbor atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} for many \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} atoms.  This
allows pages to be incrementally allocated or deallocated in blocks as
needed.  Neighbor lists typically consume the most memory of any data
structure in LAMMPS.  The neighbor list is rebuilt (from scratch) once
every few timesteps, then used repeatedly each step for force or other
computations.  The neighbor cutoff distance is \(R_n = R_f +
\Delta_s\), where \(R_f\) is the (largest) force cutoff defined by
the interatomic potential for computing short\sphinxhyphen{}range pairwise or manybody
forces and \(\Delta_s\) is a “skin” distance that allows the list to
be used for multiple steps assuming that atoms do not move very far
between consecutive time steps.  Typically, the code triggers
reneighboring when any atom has moved half the skin distance since the
last reneighboring; this and other options of the neighbor list rebuild
can be adjusted with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On steps when reneighboring is performed, atoms which have moved outside
their owning processor’s subdomain are first migrated to new processors
via communication.  Periodic boundary conditions are also (only)
enforced on these steps to ensure each atom is re\sphinxhyphen{}assigned to the
correct processor.  After migration, the atoms owned by each processor
are stored in a contiguous vector.  Periodically, each processor
spatially sorts owned atoms within its vector to reorder it for improved
cache efficiency in force computations and neighbor list building.  For
that, atoms are spatially binned and then reordered so that atoms in the
same bin are adjacent in the vector.  Atom sorting can be disabled or
its settings modified with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify}}}} command.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{neigh-stencil}.png}
\caption{neighbor list stencils}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_neigh:id1}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_neigh:neighbor-stencil}}
\begin{sphinxlegend}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A 2d simulation subdomain (thick black line) and the corresponding
ghost atom cutoff region (dashed blue line) for both orthogonal
(left) and triclinic (right) domains.  A regular grid of neighbor
bins (thin lines) overlays the entire simulation domain and need not
align with subdomain boundaries; only the portion overlapping the
augmented subdomain is shown.  In the triclinic case, it overlaps the
bounding box of the tilted rectangle.  The blue\sphinxhyphen{} and red\sphinxhyphen{}shaded bins
represent a stencil of bins searched to find neighbors of a particular
atom (black dot).
\end{sphinxlegend}
\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To build a local neighbor list in linear time, the simulation domain is
overlaid (conceptually) with a regular 3d (or 2d) grid of neighbor bins,
as shown in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_neigh:neighbor-stencil}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{neighbor list stencils}}}} figure for 2d models and a
single MPI processor’s subdomain.  Each processor stores a set of
neighbor bins which overlap its subdomain, extended by the neighbor
cutoff distance \(R_n\).  As illustrated, the bins need not align
with processor boundaries; an integer number in each dimension is fit to
the size of the entire simulation box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most often, LAMMPS builds what is called a “half” neighbor list where
each \sphinxstyleemphasis{i,j} neighbor pair is stored only once, with either atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{j} as the central atom.  The build can be done efficiently by using a
pre\sphinxhyphen{}computed “stencil” of bins around a central origin bin which
contains the atom whose neighbors are being searched for.  A stencil
is simply a list of integer offsets in \sphinxstyleemphasis{x,y,z} of nearby bins
surrounding the origin bin which are close enough to contain any
neighbor atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} within a distance \(R_n\) from any atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} in the
origin bin.  Note that for a half neighbor list, the stencil can be
asymmetric, since each atom only need store half its nearby neighbors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These stencils are illustrated in the figure for a half list and a bin
size of \(\frac{1}{2} R_n\).  There are 13 red+blue stencil bins in
2d (for the orthogonal case, 15 for triclinic).  In 3d there would be
63, 13 in the plane of bins that contain the origin bin and 25 in each
of the two planes above it in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} direction (75 for triclinic).  The
triclinic stencil has extra bins because the bins tile the bounding box
of the entire triclinic domain, and thus are not periodic with respect
to the simulation box itself.  The stencil and logic for determining
which \sphinxstyleemphasis{i,j} pairs to include in the neighbor list are altered slightly
to account for this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To build a neighbor list, a processor first loops over its “owned” plus
“ghost” atoms and assigns each to a neighbor bin.  This uses an integer
vector to create a linked list of atom indices within each bin.  It then
performs a triply\sphinxhyphen{}nested loop over its owned atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}, the stencil of
bins surrounding atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}’s bin, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} atoms in each stencil bin
(including ghost atoms).  If the distance \(r_{ij} < R_n\), then
atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} is added to the vector of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}’s neighbors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are additional details about neighbor list build options LAMMPS
supports:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The choice of bin size is an option; a size half of \(R_n\) has
been found to be optimal for many typical cases.  Smaller bins incur
additional overhead to loop over; larger bins require more distance
calculations.  Note that for smaller bin sizes, the 2d stencil in the
figure would be of a more semicircular shape (hemispherical in 3d),
with bins near the corners of the square eliminated due to their
distance from the origin bin.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on the interatomic potential(s) and other commands used in
an input script, multiple neighbor lists and stencils with different
attributes may be needed.  This includes lists with different cutoff
distances, e.g. for force computation versus occasional diagnostic
computations such as a radial distribution function, or for the
r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA time integrator which can partition pairwise forces by
distance into subsets computed at different time intervals.  It
includes “full” lists (as opposed to half lists) where each \sphinxstyleemphasis{i,j} pair
appears twice, stored once with \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}, and which use a larger
symmetric stencil.  It also includes lists with partial enumeration of
ghost atom neighbors.  The full and ghost\sphinxhyphen{}atom lists are used by
various manybody interatomic potentials.  Lists may also use different
criteria for inclusion of a pairwise interaction.  Typically, this
simply depends only on the distance between two atoms and the cutoff
distance.  But for finite\sphinxhyphen{}size coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained particles with
individual diameters (e.g. polydisperse granular particles), it can
also depend on the diameters of the two particles.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style hybrid}}}} multiple sub\sphinxhyphen{}lists
of the master neighbor list for the full system need to be generated,
one for each sub\sphinxhyphen{}style, which contains only the \sphinxstyleemphasis{i,j} pairs needed to
compute interactions between subsets of atoms for the corresponding
potential.  This means, not all \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} atoms owned by a processor
are included in a particular sub\sphinxhyphen{}list.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some models use different cutoff lengths for pairwise interactions
between different kinds of particles, which are stored in a single
neighbor list.  One example is a solvated colloidal system with large
colloidal particles where colloid/colloid, colloid/solvent, and
solvent/solvent interaction cutoffs can be dramatically different.
Another is a model of polydisperse finite\sphinxhyphen{}size granular particles;
pairs of particles interact only when they are in contact with each
other.  Mixtures with particle size ratios as high as 10\sphinxhyphen{}100x may be
used to model realistic systems.  Efficient neighbor list building
algorithms for these kinds of systems are available in LAMMPS.  They
include a method which uses different stencils for different cutoff
lengths and trims the stencil to only include bins that straddle the
cutoff sphere surface.  More recently a method which uses both
multiple stencils and multiple bin sizes was developed; it builds
neighbor lists efficiently for systems with particles of any size
ratio, though other considerations (timestep size, force computations)
may limit the ability to model systems with huge polydispersity.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For small and sparse systems and as a fallback method, LAMMPS also
supports neighbor list construction without binning by using a full
\(O(N^2)\) loop over all \sphinxstyleemphasis{i,j} atom pairs in a subdomain when
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor nsq}}}} command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dependent on the “pair” setting of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} command,
the “half” neighbor lists may contain \sphinxstylestrong{all} pairs of atoms where
atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} is a ghost atom (i.e. when the newton pair setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}).
For the newton pair \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} setting the atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} is only added to the
list if its \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} coordinate is larger, or if equal the \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} coordinate
is larger, and that is equal, too, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} coordinate is larger.  For
homogeneously dense systems, that will result in picking neighbors from
a same size sector in always the same direction relative to the
“owned” atom, and thus it should lead to similar length neighbor lists
and reduce the chance of a load imbalance.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Long\sphinxhyphen{}range interactions}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_long:long-range-interactions}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_long::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For charged systems, LAMMPS can compute long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic
interactions via the FFT\sphinxhyphen{}based particle\sphinxhyphen{}particle/particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh (PPPM)
method implemented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace style pppm and its variants}}}}.  For that Coulombic interactions are partitioned into
short\sphinxhyphen{} and long\sphinxhyphen{}range components.  The short\sphinxhyphen{}ranged portion is computed
in real space as a loop over pairs of charges within a cutoff distance,
using neighbor lists.  The long\sphinxhyphen{}range portion is computed in reciprocal
space using a kspace style.  For the PPPM implementation the simulation
cell is overlaid with a regular FFT grid in 3d. It proceeds in several stages:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\alph}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
each atom’s point charge is interpolated to nearby FFT grid points,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a forward 3d FFT is performed,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a convolution operation is performed in reciprocal space,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more inverse 3d FFTs are performed, and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
electric field values from grid points near each atom are interpolated to compute
its forces.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For any of the spatial\sphinxhyphen{}decomposition partitioning schemes each processor
owns the brick\sphinxhyphen{}shaped portion of FFT grid points contained within its
subdomain.  The two interpolation operations use a stencil of grid
points surrounding each atom.  To accommodate the stencil size, each
processor also stores a few layers of ghost grid points surrounding its
brick.  Forward and reverse communication of grid point values is
performed similar to the corresponding {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_comm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom data communication}}}}.  In this case, electric field values on owned
grid points are sent to neighboring processors to become ghost point
values.  Likewise charge values on ghost points are sent and summed to
values on owned points.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For triclinic simulation boxes, the FFT grid planes are parallel to
the box faces, but the mapping of charge and electric field values
to/from grid points is done in reduced coordinates where the tilted
box is conceptually a unit cube, so that the stencil and FFT
operations are unchanged.  However the FFT grid size required for a
given accuracy is larger for triclinic domains than it is for
orthogonal boxes.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{fft-decomp-parallel}.png}
\caption{Parallel FFT in PPPM}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_long:id1}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_long:fft-parallel}}
\begin{sphinxlegend}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Stages of a parallel FFT for a simulation domain overlaid with an
8x8x8 3d FFT grid, partitioned across 64 processors.  Within each
of the 4 diagrams, grid cells of the same color are owned by a
single processor; for simplicity, only cells owned by 4 or 8 of
the 64 processors are colored.  The two images on the left
illustrate brick\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil communication.  The two images on the
right illustrate pencil\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil communication, which in this
case transposes the \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} dimensions of the grid.
\end{quote}
\end{sphinxlegend}
\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Parallel 3d FFTs require substantial communication relative to their
computational cost.  A 3d FFT is implemented by a series of 1d FFTs
along the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x\sphinxhyphen{}}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y\sphinxhyphen{}}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z\sphinxhyphen{}}direction of the FFT grid.  Thus, the
FFT grid cannot be decomposed like atoms into 3 dimensions for parallel
processing of the FFTs but only in 1 (as planes) or 2 (as pencils)
dimensions and in between the steps the grid needs to be transposed to
have the FFT grid portion “owned” by each MPI process complete in the
direction of the 1d FFTs it has to perform. LAMMPS uses the
pencil\sphinxhyphen{}decomposition algorithm as shown in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_long:fft-parallel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Parallel FFT in PPPM}}}}
figure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Initially (far left), each processor owns a brick of same\sphinxhyphen{}color grid
cells (actually grid points) contained within in its subdomain.  A
brick\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil communication operation converts this layout to 1d
pencils in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}\sphinxhyphen{}dimension (center left).  Again, cells of the same
color are owned by the same processor.  Each processor can then compute
a 1d FFT on each pencil of data it wholly owns using a call to the
configured FFT library.  A pencil\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil communication then converts
this layout to pencils in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} dimension (center right) which
effectively transposes the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} dimensions of the grid, followed
by 1d FFTs in \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}.  A final transpose of pencils from \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} (far
right) followed by 1d FFTs in \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} completes the forward FFT.  The data
is left in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}\sphinxhyphen{}pencil layout for the convolution operation.  One or
more inverse FFTs then perform the sequence of 1d FFTs and communication
steps in reverse order; the final layout of resulting grid values is the
same as the initial brick layout.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each communication operation within the FFT (brick\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil or
pencil\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil or pencil\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}brick) converts one tiling of the 3d grid
to another, where a tiling in this context means an assignment of a
small brick\sphinxhyphen{}shaped subset of grid points to each processor, the union of
which comprise the entire grid.  The parallel \sphinxhref{https://lammps.github.io/fftmpi/}{fftMPI library} written for LAMMPS allows arbitrary
definitions of the tiling so that an irregular partitioning of the
simulation domain can use it directly.  Transforming data from one
tiling to another is implemented in \sphinxtitleref{fftMPI} using point\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}point
communication, where each processor sends data to a few other
processors, since each tile in the initial tiling overlaps with a
handful of tiles in the final tiling.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The transformations could also be done using collective communication
across all \(P\) processors with a single call to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Alltoall()}}, but
this is typically much slower.  However, for the specialized brick and
pencil tiling illustrated in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_long:fft-parallel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Parallel FFT in PPPM}}}} figure, collective
communication across the entire MPI communicator is not required.  In
the example, an \(8^3\) grid with 512 grid cells is partitioned
across 64 processors; each processor owns a 2x2x2 3d brick of grid
cells.  The initial brick\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil communication (upper left to upper
right) only requires collective communication within subgroups of 4
processors, as illustrated by the 4 colors.  More generally, a
brick\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil communication can be performed by partitioning \sphinxstyleemphasis{P}
processors into \(P^{\frac{2}{3}}\) subgroups of
\(P^{\frac{1}{3}}\) processors each.  Each subgroup performs
collective communication only within its subgroup.  Similarly,
pencil\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}pencil communication can be performed by partitioning \sphinxstyleemphasis{P}
processors into \(P^{\frac{1}{2}}\) subgroups of
\(P^{\frac{1}{2}}\) processors each.  This is illustrated in the
figure for the \(y \Rightarrow z\) communication (center).  An
eight\sphinxhyphen{}processor subgroup owns the front \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} plane of data and performs
collective communication within the subgroup to transpose from a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{y}\sphinxhyphen{}pencil to \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}\sphinxhyphen{}pencil layout.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS invokes point\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}point communication by default, but also
provides the option of partitioned collective communication when using a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify collective yes}}}} command to switch to
that mode.  In the latter case, the code detects the size of the
disjoint subgroups and partitions the single \sphinxstyleemphasis{P}\sphinxhyphen{}size communicator into
multiple smaller communicators, each of which invokes collective
communication.  Testing on a large IBM Blue Gene/Q machine at Argonne
National Labs showed a significant improvement in FFT performance for
large processor counts; partitioned collective communication was faster
than point\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}point communication or global collective communication
involving all \sphinxstyleemphasis{P} processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are some additional details about FFTs for long\sphinxhyphen{}range and related
grid/particle operations that LAMMPS supports:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The fftMPI library allows each grid dimension to be a multiple of
small prime factors (2,3,5), and allows any number of processors to
perform the FFT.  The resulting brick and pencil decompositions are
thus not always as well\sphinxhyphen{}aligned, but the size of subgroups of
processors for the two modes of communication (brick/pencil and
pencil/pencil) still scale as \(O(P^{\frac{1}{3}})\) and
\(O(P^{\frac{1}{2}})\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For efficiency in performing 1d FFTs, the grid transpose
operations illustrated in Figure {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_long:fft-parallel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Parallel FFT in PPPM}}}} also involve
reordering the 3d data so that a different dimension is contiguous
in memory.  This reordering can be done during the packing or
unpacking of buffers for MPI communication.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For large systems and particularly many MPI processes, the dominant
cost for parallel FFTs is often the communication, not the computation
of 1d FFTs, even though the latter scales as \(N \log(N)\) in the
number of grid points \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} per grid direction.  This is due to the fact
that only a 2d decomposition into pencils is possible while atom data
(and their corresponding short\sphinxhyphen{}range force and energy computations)
can be decomposed efficiently in 3d.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reducing the number of MPI processes involved in the MPI communication
will reduce this kind of overhead.  By using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_omp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid MPI +
OpenMP parallelization}}}} it is still possible to use all
processes for parallel computation.  It will use OpenMP
parallelization inside the MPI domains. While that may have a lower
parallel efficiency for some part of the computation, that can be less
than the communication overhead in the 3d FFTs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an alternative, it is also possible to start a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options:partition}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition}}}} calculation and then use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{verlet/split
integrator}}}} to perform the PPPM computation on a
dedicated, separate partition of MPI processes.  This uses an integer
“1:\sphinxstyleemphasis{p}” mapping of \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} subdomains of the atom decomposition to one
subdomain of the FFT grid decomposition and where pairwise non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded
and bonded forces and energies are computed on the larger partition
and the PPPM kspace computation concurrently on the smaller partition.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS also implements PPPM\sphinxhyphen{}based solvers for other long\sphinxhyphen{}range
interactions, dipole and dispersion (Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones), which can be used
in conjunction with long\sphinxhyphen{}range  Coulombics for point charges.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS implements a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GridComm}} class which overlays the simulation
domain with a regular grid, partitions it across processors in a
manner consistent with processor subdomains, and provides methods for
forward and reverse communication of owned and ghost grid point
values.  It is used for PPPM as an FFT grid (as outlined above) and
also for the MSM algorithm, which uses a cascade of grid sizes from
fine to coarse to compute long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic forces.  The GridComm
class is also useful for models where continuum fields interact with
particles.  For example, the two\sphinxhyphen{}temperature model (TTM) defines heat
transfer between atoms (particles) and electrons (continuum gas) where
spatial variations in the electron temperature are computed by finite
differences of a discretized heat equation on a regular grid.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ttm/grid}}}} command uses the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GridComm}} class
internally to perform its grid operations on a distributed grid
instead of the original {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ttm}}}} which uses a
replicated grid.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{OpenMP Parallelism}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_openmp:openmp-parallelism}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_openmp::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The styles in the INTEL, KOKKOS, and OPENMP packages offer to use OpenMP
thread parallelism to predominantly distribute loops over local data
and thus follow an orthogonal parallelization strategy to the
decomposition into spatial domains used by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_part::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{MPI partitioning}}}}.  For clarity, this section discusses only the
implementation in the OPENMP package, as it is the simplest. The INTEL
and KOKKOS packages offer additional options and are more complex since
they support more features and different hardware like co\sphinxhyphen{}processors
or GPUs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One of the key decisions when implementing the OPENMP package was to
keep the changes to the source code small, so that it would be easier to
maintain the code and keep it in sync with the non\sphinxhyphen{}threaded standard
implementation.  This is achieved by a) making the OPENMP version a
derived class from the regular version (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairLJCutOMP}} from
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairLJCut}}) and only overriding methods that are multi\sphinxhyphen{}threaded or
need to be modified to support multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading (similar to what was done
in the OPT package), b) keeping the structure in the modified code very
similar so that side\sphinxhyphen{}by\sphinxhyphen{}side comparisons are still useful, and c)
offloading additional functionality and multi\sphinxhyphen{}thread support functions
into three separate classes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ThrOMP}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ThrData}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FixOMP}}.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ThrOMP}} provides additional, multi\sphinxhyphen{}thread aware functionality not
available in the corresponding base class (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}} for
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairLJCutOMP}}) like multi\sphinxhyphen{}thread aware variants of the “tally”
functions. Those functions are made available through multiple
inheritance, so those new functions have to have unique names to avoid
ambiguities; typically \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_thr}} is appended to the name of the function.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ThrData}} is a class that manages per\sphinxhyphen{}thread data structures.  It is
used instead of extending the corresponding storage to per\sphinxhyphen{}thread arrays
to avoid slowdowns due to “false sharing” when multiple threads update
adjacent elements in an array and thus force the CPU cache lines to be
reset and re\sphinxhyphen{}fetched.  \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FixOMP}} finally manages the “multi\sphinxhyphen{}thread
state” like settings and access to per\sphinxhyphen{}thread storage, it is activated
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package omp}}}} command.


\subsubsection{Avoiding data races}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_openmp:avoiding-data-races}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A key problem when implementing thread parallelism in an MD code is
to avoid data races when updating accumulated properties like forces,
energies, and stresses.  When interactions are computed, they always
involve multiple atoms and thus there are race conditions when multiple
threads want to update per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data of the same atoms.  Five possible
strategies have been considered to avoid this:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Restructure the code so that there is no overlapping access possible
when computing in parallel, e.g. by breaking lists into multiple
parts and synchronizing threads in between.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Have each thread be “responsible” for a specific group of atoms and
compute these interactions multiple times, once on each thread that
is responsible for a given atom, and then have each thread only update
the properties of this atom.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use mutexes around functions and regions of code where the data race
could happen.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use atomic operations when updating per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use replicated per\sphinxhyphen{}thread data structures to accumulate data without
conflicts and then use a reduction to combine those results into the
data structures used by the regular style.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Option 5 was chosen for the OPENMP package because it would retain the
performance for the case of a single thread and the code would be more
maintainable.  Option 1 would require extensive code changes,
particularly to the neighbor list code; option 2 would have incurred a
2x or more performance penalty for the serial case; option 3 causes
significant overhead and would enforce serialization of operations in
inner loops and thus defeat the purpose of multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading; option 4
slows down the serial case although not quite as bad as option 2.  The
downside of option 5 is that the overhead of the reduction operations
grows with the number of threads used, so there would be a crossover
point where options 2 or 4 would result in faster executing.  That is
why option 2 for example is used in the GPU package because a GPU is a
processor with a massive number of threads.  However, since the MPI
parallelization is generally more effective for typical MD systems, the
expectation is that thread parallelism is only used for a smaller number
of threads (2\sphinxhyphen{}8).  At the time of its implementation, that number was
equivalent to the number of CPU cores per CPU socket on high\sphinxhyphen{}end
supercomputers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus arrays like the force array are dimensioned to the number of atoms
times the number of threads when enabling OpenMP support, and inside the
compute functions a pointer to a different chunk is obtained by each thread.
Similarly, accumulators like potential energy or virial are kept in
per\sphinxhyphen{}thread instances of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ThrData}} class and then only reduced and
stored in their global counterparts at the end of the force computation.


\subsubsection{Loop scheduling}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_openmp:loop-scheduling}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Multi\sphinxhyphen{}thread parallelization is applied by distributing (outer) loops
statically across threads.  Typically, this would be the loop over local
atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} when processing \sphinxstyleemphasis{i,j} pairs of atoms from a neighbor list.
