The design of the neighbor list code results in atoms having a similar
number of neighbors for homogeneous systems and thus load imbalances
across threads are not common and typically happen for systems where
also the MPI parallelization would be unbalanced, which would typically
have a more pronounced impact on the performance.  This same loop
scheduling scheme can also be applied to the reduction operations on
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data to try and reduce the overhead of the reduction operation.


\subsubsection{Neighbor list parallelization}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_par_openmp:neighbor-list-parallelization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition to the parallelization of force computations, also the
generation of the neighbor lists is parallelized.  As explained
previously, neighbor lists are built by looping over “owned” atoms and
storing the neighbors in “pages”.  In the OPENMP variants of the
neighbor list code, each thread operates on a different chunk of “owned”
atoms and allocates and fills its own set of pages with neighbor list
data.  This is achieved by each thread keeping its own instance of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4I0EN9LAMMPS_NS6MyPageE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MyPage}}}}} page allocator class.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Accessing per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_atom:accessing-per-atom-data}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_atom::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This page discusses how per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data is managed in LAMMPS, how it can
be accessed, what communication patterns apply, and some of the utility
functions that exist for a variety of purposes.


\subsection{Owned and ghost atoms}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_atom:owned-and-ghost-atoms}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_part::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{parallel partitioning algorithms}}}} page, LAMMPS uses a domain decomposition of the
simulation domain, either in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled} manner.  Each MPI
process \sphinxstyleemphasis{owns} exactly one subdomain and the atoms within it. To compute
forces for tuples of atoms that are spread across sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain boundaries,
also a “halo” of \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost} atoms are maintained within the communication
cutoff distance of its subdomain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The total number of atoms is stored in \sphinxtitleref{Atom::natoms} (within any
typical class this can be referred to at \sphinxtitleref{atom\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}natoms}). The number of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{owned} (or “local” atoms) are stored in \sphinxtitleref{Atom::nlocal}; the number of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost} atoms is stored in \sphinxtitleref{Atom::nghost}.  The sum of \sphinxtitleref{Atom::nlocal}
over all MPI processes should be \sphinxtitleref{Atom::natoms}. This is by default
regularly checked by the Thermo class, and if the sum does not match,
LAMMPS stops with a “lost atoms” error.  For convenience also the
property \sphinxtitleref{Atom::nmax} is available, this is the maximum of
\sphinxtitleref{Atom::nlocal + Atom::nghost} across all MPI processes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties are either managed by the atom style, individual
classes,  or as custom arrays by the individual classes. If only access
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{owned} atoms is needed, they are usually allocated to be of size
\sphinxtitleref{Atom::nlocal}, otherwise of size \sphinxtitleref{Atom::nmax}. Please note that not all
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties are available or updated on \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost} atoms. For
example, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom velocities are only updated with {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel
yes}}}}.


\subsection{Atom indexing}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_atom:atom-indexing}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When referring to individual atoms, they may be indexed by their local
\sphinxstyleemphasis{index}, their index in their \sphinxtitleref{Atom::x} array. This is densely populated
containing first all \sphinxstyleemphasis{owned} atoms (index \textless{} \sphinxtitleref{Atom::nlocal}) and then all
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost} atoms.  The order of atoms in these arrays can change due to
atoms migrating between between subdomains, atoms being added or
deleted, or atoms being sorted for better cache efficiency.  Atoms are
globally uniquely identified by their \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom ID}. There may be multiple
atoms with the same atom ID present, but only one of them may be an
\sphinxstyleemphasis{owned} atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To find the local \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} of an atom, when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom ID} is known, the
\sphinxtitleref{Atom::map()} function may be used. It will return the local atom index
or \sphinxhyphen{}1. If the returned value is between 0 (inclusive) and \sphinxtitleref{Atom::nlocal}
(exclusive) it is an \sphinxstyleemphasis{owned} or “local” atom; for larger values the atom
is present as a ghost atom; for a value of \sphinxhyphen{}1, the atom is not present
on the current subdomain at all.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If multiple atoms with the same tag exist in the same subdomain, they
can be found via the \sphinxtitleref{Atom::sametag} array. It points to the next atom
index with the same tag or \sphinxhyphen{}1 if there are no more atoms with the same
tag.  The list will be exhaustive when starting with an index of an
\sphinxstyleemphasis{owned} atom, since the atom IDs are unique, so there can only be one
such atom.  Example code to count atoms with same atom ID in a subdomain:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{nlocal}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{while}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sametag}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sametag}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{printf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Atom ID: \PYGZpc{}ld is present \PYGZpc{}d times}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{tag}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Atom class versus AtomVec classes}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_atom:atom-class-versus-atomvec-classes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{Atom} class contains all kinds of flags and counters about atoms in
the system and that includes pointers to \sphinxstylestrong{all} per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties
available for atoms.  However, only a subset of these pointers are
non\sphinxhyphen{}NULL and which those are depends on the atom style.  For each atom
style there is a corresponding \sphinxtitleref{AtomVecXXX} class derived from the
\sphinxtitleref{AtomVec} base class, where the XXX indicates the atom style.  This
\sphinxtitleref{AtomVecXXX} class will update the counters and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom pointers if
atoms are added or removed to the system or migrate between subdomains.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Communication patterns}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:communication-patterns}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This page describes various inter\sphinxhyphen{}processor communication operations
provided by LAMMPS, mostly in the core \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm} class.  These are operations
for common tasks implemented using MPI library calls.  They are used by
other classes to perform communication of different kinds.  These
operations are useful to know about when writing new code for LAMMPS
that needs to communicate data between processors.


\subsection{Owned and ghost atoms}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:owned-and-ghost-atoms}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_part::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{parallel partitioning algorithms}}}} page, LAMMPS spatially decomposes the simulation
domain, either in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled} manner.  Each processor (MPI
task) owns atoms within its subdomain and additionally stores ghost
atoms within a cutoff distance of its subdomain.


\subsubsection{Forward and reverse communication}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:forward-and-reverse-communication}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_comm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{parallel communication algorithms}}}} page, the most common communication operations are
first, \sphinxstyleemphasis{forward communication} which sends owned atom information from
each processor to nearby processors to store with their ghost atoms.
The need to do this communication arises when data from the owned atoms
is updated (e.g. their positions) and this updated information needs to
be \sphinxstylestrong{copied} to the corresponding ghost atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
And second, \sphinxstyleemphasis{reverse communication}, which sends ghost atom information
from each processor to the owning processor to \sphinxstylestrong{accumulate} (sum)
the values with the corresponding owned atoms.  The need for this
arises when data is computed and also stored with ghost atoms
(e.g. forces when using a “half” neighbor list) and thus those terms
need to be added to their corresponding atoms on the process where
they are “owned” atoms.  Please note, that with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton off}}}} setting this does not happen and the neighbor lists are
constructed so that these interactions are computed on both MPI
processes containing one of the atoms and only the data pertaining to
the local atom is stored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The time\sphinxhyphen{}integration classes in LAMMPS invoke these operations each
timestep via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{forward\_comm()} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{reverse\_comm()} methods in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm} class.  Which per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data is communicated depends on the
currently used {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style}}}} and whether
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel}}}} setting is “no” (default) or
“yes”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pair} style classes can invoke the \sphinxstyleemphasis{forward\_comm(this)}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{reverse\_comm(this)} methods in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm} class to perform the
same operations on per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data that is generated and stored within
the pair style class. Note that this function requires passing the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{this}} pointer as the first argument to enable the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm} class to
call the “pack” and “unpack” functions discussed below.  An example of
the use of these functions are many\sphinxhyphen{}body pair styles like the
embedded\sphinxhyphen{}atom method (EAM) which compute intermediate values in the
first part of the compute() function that need to be stored by both
owned and ghost atoms for the second part of the force computation.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm} class methods perform the MPI communication for buffers of
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data.  They “call back” to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pair} class, so it can \sphinxstyleemphasis{pack}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{unpack} the buffer with data the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pair} class owns.  There are 4
such methods that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pair} class must define, assuming it uses both
forward and reverse communication:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pack\_forward\_comm()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
unpack\_forward\_comm()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pack\_reverse\_comm()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
unpack\_reverse\_comm()

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The arguments to these methods include the buffer and a list of atoms
to pack or unpack.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pair} class also must set the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_forward}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_reverse} variables, which store the number of values stored
in the communication buffers for each operation.  This means, if
desired, it can choose to store multiple per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values in the
buffer, and they will be communicated together to minimize
communication overhead.  The communication buffers are defined vectors
containing \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{double}} values.  To correctly store integers that may be
64\sphinxhyphen{}bit (bigint, tagint, imageint) in the buffer, you need to use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:communication-buffer-coding-with-ubuf}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{ubuf union}}}} construct.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Fix}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Compute}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Dump} classes can also invoke the same kind
of forward and reverse communication operations using the same \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm}
class methods.  Likewise, the same pack/unpack methods and
comm\_forward/comm\_reverse variables must be defined by the calling
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Fix}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Compute}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Dump} class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{Fix} classes, there is an optional second argument to the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{forward\_comm()} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{reverse\_comm()} call which can be used when the
fix performs multiple modes of communication, with different numbers
of values per atom.  The fix should set the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_forward} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_reverse} variables to the maximum value, but can invoke the
communication for a particular mode with a smaller value.  For this
to work, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pack\_forward\_comm()}, etc methods typically use a class
member variable to choose which values to pack/unpack into/from the
buffer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, for reverse communications in \sphinxstyleemphasis{Fix} classes there is also the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{reverse\_comm\_variable()} method that allows the communication to have
a different amount of data per\sphinxhyphen{}atom.  It invokes these corresponding
callback methods:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pack\_reverse\_comm\_size()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
unpack\_reverse\_comm\_size()

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which have extra arguments to specify the amount of data stored
in the buffer for each atom.


\subsection{Higher level communication}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:higher-level-communication}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are also several higher\sphinxhyphen{}level communication operations provided
in LAMMPS which work for either \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled} decompositions.
They may be useful for a new class to invoke if it requires more
sophisticated communication than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{forward} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{reverse} methods
provide.  The 3 communication operations described here are
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ring

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
irregular

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rendezvous

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can invoke these \sphinxstyleemphasis{grep} command in the LAMMPS src directory, to
see a list of classes that invoke the 3 operations.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{grep "\textbackslash{}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}ring" *.cpp */*.cpp}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{grep "irregular\textbackslash{}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}" *.cpp}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{grep "\textbackslash{}\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}rendezvous" *.cpp */*.cpp}}

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Ring operation}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:ring-operation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring} operation is invoked via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring()} method in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm}
class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each processor first creates a buffer with a list of values, typically
associated with a subset of the atoms it owns.  Now think of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{P}
processors as connected to each other in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring}.  Each processor \sphinxstyleemphasis{M}
sends data to the next \sphinxstyleemphasis{M+1} processor.  It receives data from the
preceding \sphinxstyleemphasis{M\sphinxhyphen{}1} processor.  The ring is periodic so that the last
processor sends to the first processor, and the first processor
receives from the last processor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Invoking the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring()} method passes each processor’s buffer in \sphinxstyleemphasis{P}
steps around the ring.  At each step a \sphinxstyleemphasis{callback} method, provided as
an argument to ring(), in the caller is invoked.  This allows each
processor to examine the data buffer provided by every other
processor.  It may extract values needed by its atoms from the
buffers, or it may alter placeholder values in the buffer.  In the
latter case, when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring} operation is complete, each processor can
examine its original buffer to extract modified values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring} operation is similar to an MPI\_Alltoall()
operation, where every processor effectively sends and receives data to
every other processor.  The difference is that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring} operation
does it one step at a time, so the total volume of data does not need
to be stored by every processor.  However, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring} operation is
also less efficient than MPI\_Alltoall() because of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{P} stages
required.  So it is typically only suitable for small data buffers and
occasional operations that are not time\sphinxhyphen{}critical.


\subsubsection{Irregular operation}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:irregular-operation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{irregular} operation is provided by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Irregular} class.  What
LAMMPS terms irregular communication is when each processor knows what
data it needs to send to what processor, but does not know what
processors are sending it data.  An example is when load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing is
performed and each processor needs to send some of its atoms to new
processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Irregular} class provides 5 high\sphinxhyphen{}level methods useful in this
context:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
create\_data()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
exchange\_data()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
create\_atom()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
exchange\_atom()

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
migrate\_atoms()

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{create\_data()} method, each processor specifies a list of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
datums to send, each to a specified processor.  Internally, the method
creates efficient data structures for performing the communication.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{exchange\_data()} method triggers the communication to be
performed.  Each processor provides the vector of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} datums to send,
and the size of each datum.  All datums must be the same size.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{create\_atom()} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{exchange\_atom()} methods are similar, except
that the size of each datum can be different.  Typically, this is used
to communicate atoms, each with a variable amount of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data, to
other processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{migrate\_atoms()} method is a convenience wrapper on the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{create\_atom()} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{exchange\_atom()} methods to simplify
communication of all the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data associated with an atom so that
the atom can effectively migrate to a new owning processor.  It is
similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{exchange()} method in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm} class invoked when
atoms move to neighboring processors (in the regular or tiled
decomposition) during timestepping, except that it allows atoms to
have moved arbitrarily long distances and still be properly
communicated to a new owning processor.


\subsubsection{Rendezvous operation}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:rendezvous-operation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rendezvous} operation is invoked via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rendezvous()}
method in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Comm} class.  Depending on how much communication is
needed and how many processors a LAMMPS simulation is running on, it
can be a much more efficient choice than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ring()} method.  It uses
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{irregular} operation internally once or twice to do its
communication.  The rendezvous algorithm is described in detail in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:plimpton}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Plimpton)}}}}, including some LAMMPS use cases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rendezvous()} method, each processor specifies a list of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
datums to send and which processor to send each of them to.
Internally, this communication is performed as an irregular operation.
The received datums are returned to the caller via invocation of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{callback} function, provided as an argument to \sphinxstyleemphasis{rendezvous()}.  The
caller can then process the received datums and (optionally) assemble
a new list of datums to communicate to a new list of specific
processors.  When the callback function exits, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rendezvous()}
method performs a second irregular communication on the new list of
datums.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples in LAMMPS of use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rendezvous} operation are the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} commands (for one\sphinxhyphen{}time identification of the rigid body
atom clusters) and the identification of special\_bond 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 and 1\sphinxhyphen{}4
neighbors within molecules.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command for context.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops:plimpton}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Plimpton)} Plimpton and Knight, JPDC, 147, 184\sphinxhyphen{}195 (2021).

\sphinxstepscope


\section{How a timestep works}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_flow:how-a-timestep-works}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_flow::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first and most fundamental operation within LAMMPS to understand is
how a timestep is structured.  Timestepping is performed by calling
methods of the Integrate class instance within the Update class.  Since
Integrate is a base class, it will point to an instance of a derived
class corresponding to what is selected by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}} input script command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this section, the timestep implemented by the Verlet class is
described.  A similar timestep protocol is implemented by the Respa
class, for the r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA hierarchical timestepping method.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Min base class performs energy minimization, so does not perform a
literal timestep.  But it has logic similar to what is described here,
to compute forces and invoke fixes at each iteration of a minimization.
Differences between time integration and minimization are highlighted at
the end of this section.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Verlet class is encoded in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/verlet.cpp}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{verlet.h}}
files.  It implements the velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet timestepping algorithm.  The
workhorse method is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Verlet::run()}}, but first we highlight several
other methods in the class.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init()}} method is called at the beginning of each dynamics
run.  It simply sets some internal flags, based on user settings in
other parts of the code.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup()}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup\_minimal()}} methods are also called before
each run.  The velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet method requires current forces be
calculated before the first timestep, so these routines compute
forces due to all atomic interactions, using the same logic that
appears in the timestepping described next.  A few fixes are also
invoked, using the mechanism described in the next section.  Various
counters are also initialized before the run begins.  The
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup\_minimal()}} method is a variant that has a flag for performing
less setup.  This is used when runs are continued and information
from the previous run is still valid.  For example, if repeated
short LAMMPS runs are being invoked, interleaved by other commands,
via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pre no} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} options of the run command, the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup\_minimal()}} method is used.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force\_clear()}} method initializes force and other arrays to
zero before each timestep, so that forces (torques, etc) can be
accumulated.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Verlet::run()}} method.  Its basic structure in hi\sphinxhyphen{}level
pseudocode is shown below.  In the actual code in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/verlet.cpp}}
some of these operations are conditionally invoked.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{loop} \PYG{n}{over} \PYG{n}{N} \PYG{n}{timesteps}\PYG{p}{:}
  \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{timeout} \PYG{n}{condition}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{k}{break}
  \PYG{n}{ev\PYGZus{}set}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{initial\PYGZus{}integrate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{post\PYGZus{}integrate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{n}{nflag} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{decide}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{nflag}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{pre\PYGZus{}exchange}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{domain}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{pbc}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{domain}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{reset\PYGZus{}box}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{setup}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{setup\PYGZus{}bins}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{exchange}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{borders}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{pre\PYGZus{}neighbor}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{build}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{post\PYGZus{}neighbor}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{k}{else}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{forward\PYGZus{}comm}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{n}{force\PYGZus{}clear}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{pre\PYGZus{}force}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{angle}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{improper}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{pre\PYGZus{}reverse}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{reverse\PYGZus{}comm}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{post\PYGZus{}force}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{final\PYGZus{}integrate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{end\PYGZus{}of\PYGZus{}step}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n+nb}{any} \PYG{n}{output} \PYG{n}{on} \PYG{n}{this} \PYG{n}{step}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{output}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{write}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} after loop}
\PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{post\PYGZus{}run}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ev\_set()}} method (in the parent Integrate class), sets two flags
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{eflag} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vflag}) for energy and virial computation.  Each flag
encodes whether global and/or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy and virial should be
calculated on this timestep, because some fix or variable or output will
need it.  These flags are passed to the various methods that compute
particle interactions, so that they either compute and tally the
corresponding data or can skip the extra calculations if the energy and
virial are not needed.  See the comments for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Integrate::ev\_set()}}
method, which document the flag values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At various points of the timestep, fixes are invoked,
e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}initial\_integrate()}}.  In the code, this is actually done
via the Modify class, which stores all the Fix objects and lists of which
should be invoked at what point in the timestep.  Fixes are the LAMMPS
mechanism for tailoring the operations of a timestep for a particular
simulation.  As described elsewhere, each fix has one or more methods,
each of which is invoked at a specific stage of the timestep, as show in
the timestep pseudocode.  All the active fixes defined in an input
script, that are flagged to have an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{initial\_integrate()}} method, are
invoked at the beginning of each timestep.  Examples are {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt or fix npt}}}} which perform the
start\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}timestep velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet integration operations to update
velocities by a half\sphinxhyphen{}step, and coordinates by a full step.  The
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{post\_integrate()}} method is next for operations that need to happen
immediately after those updates.  Only a few fixes use this, e.g. to
reflect particles off box boundaries in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_reflect::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{FixWallReflect class}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{decide()}} method in the Neighbor class determines whether
neighbor lists need to be rebuilt on the current timestep (conditions
can be changed using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify every/delay/check}}}} command).  If not, coordinates of ghost atoms are
acquired by each processor via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{forward\_comm()}} method of the Comm
class.  If neighbor lists need to be built, several operations within
the inner if clause of the pseudocode are first invoked.  The
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pre\_exchange()}} method of any defined fixes is invoked first.
Typically, this inserts or deletes particles from the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Periodic boundary conditions are then applied by the Domain class via
its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pbc()}} method to remap particles that have moved outside the
simulation box back into the box.  Note that this is not done every
timestep, but only when neighbor lists are rebuilt.  This is so that
each processor’s subdomain will have consistent (nearby) atom
coordinates for its owned and ghost atoms.  It is also why dumped atom
coordinates may be slightly outside the simulation box if not dumped
on a step where the neighbor lists are rebuilt.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The box boundaries are then reset (if needed) via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reset\_box()}}
method of the Domain class, e.g. if box boundaries are shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped to
current particle coordinates.  A change in the box size or shape
requires internal information for communicating ghost atoms (Comm class)
and neighbor list bins (Neighbor class) to be updated.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup()}}
method of the Comm class and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup\_bins()}} method of the Neighbor
class perform the update.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The code is now ready to migrate atoms that have left a processor’s
geometric subdomain to new processors.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{exchange()}} method of
the Comm class performs this operation.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{borders()}} method of the
Comm class then identifies ghost atoms surrounding each processor’s
subdomain and communicates ghost atom information to neighboring
processors.  It does this by looping over all the atoms owned by a
processor to make lists of those to send to each neighbor processor.  On
subsequent timesteps, the lists are used by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Comm::forward\_comm()}}
method.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes with a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pre\_neighbor()}} method are then called.  These typically
re\sphinxhyphen{}build some data structure stored by the fix that depends on the
current atoms owned by each processor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now that each processor has a current list of its owned and ghost
atoms, LAMMPS is ready to rebuild neighbor lists via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build()}}
method of the Neighbor class.  This is typically done by binning all
owned and ghost atoms, and scanning a stencil of bins around each
owned atom’s bin to make a Verlet list of neighboring atoms within the
force cutoff plus neighbor skin distance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the next portion of the timestep, all interaction forces between
particles are computed, after zeroing the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom force vector via the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force\_clear()}} method.  If the newton flag is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} by the
newton command, forces are added to both owned and ghost atoms, otherwise
only to owned (aka local) atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pairwise forces are calculated first, which enables the global virial
(if requested) to be calculated cheaply (at O(N) cost instead of O(N**2)
at the end of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::compute()}} method), by a dot product of atom
coordinates and forces.  By including owned and ghost atoms in the dot
product, the effect of periodic boundary conditions is correctly
accounted for.  Molecular topology interactions (bonds, angles,
dihedrals, impropers) are calculated next (if supported by the current
atom style).  The final contribution is from long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic
interactions, invoked by the KSpace class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pre\_reverse()}} method in fixes is used for operations that have to
be done \sphinxstyleemphasis{before} the upcoming reverse communication (e.g. to perform
additional data transfers or reductions for data computed during the
force computation and stored with ghost atoms).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the newton flag is on, forces on ghost atoms are communicated and
summed back to their corresponding owned atoms.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reverse\_comm()}}
method of the Comm class performs this operation, which is essentially
the inverse operation of sending copies of owned atom coordinates to
other processor’s ghost atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At this point in the timestep, the total force on each (local) atom is
known.  Additional force constraints (external forces, SHAKE, etc) are
applied by Fixes that have a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{post\_force()}} method.  The second half
of the velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet integration, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{final\_integrate()}} is then
performed (another half\sphinxhyphen{}step update of the velocities) via fixes like
nve, nvt, npt.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the end of the timestep, fixes that contain an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{end\_of\_step()}}
method are invoked.  These typically perform a diagnostic calculation,
e.g. the ave/time and ave/spatial fixes.  The final operation of the
timestep is to perform any requested output, via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{write()}} method
of the Output class.  There are 3 kinds of LAMMPS output: thermodynamic
output to the screen and log file, snapshots of atom data to a dump
file, and restart files.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} commands for more
details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The flow of control during energy minimization iterations is similar to
that of a molecular dynamics timestep.  Forces are computed, neighbor
lists are built as needed, atoms migrate to new processors, and atom
coordinates and forces are communicated to neighboring processors.  The
only difference is what Fix class operations are invoked when.  Only a
subset of LAMMPS fixes are useful during energy minimization, as
explained in their individual doc pages.  The relevant Fix class methods
are \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{min\_pre\_exchange()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{min\_pre\_force()}}, and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{min\_post\_force()}}.  Each fix is invoked at the appropriate place
within the minimization iteration.  For example, the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{min\_post\_force()}} method is analogous to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{post\_force()}} method
for dynamics; it is used to alter or constrain forces on each atom,
which affects the minimization procedure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After all iterations are completed, there is a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cleanup}} step which
calls the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{post\_run()}} method of fixes to perform operations only required
at the end of a calculation (like freeing temporary storage or creating
final outputs).

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Writing new styles}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write:writing-new-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_write::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modifying \& extending LAMMPS}}}} section of the manual gives an overview of how LAMMPS can
be extended by writing new classes that derive from existing
parent classes in LAMMPS.  Here, some specific coding
details are provided for writing code for LAMMPS.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Writing new pair styles}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:writing-new-pair-styles}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair styles are at the core of most simulations with LAMMPS, since they
are used to compute the forces (plus energy and virial contributions, if
needed) on atoms for pairs or small clusters of atoms within a given
cutoff.  This is often the dominant computation in LAMMPS, and sometimes
even the only one.  Pair styles can be grouped into multiple categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
simple pairwise additive interactions of point particles
(e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_morse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Morse}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_buck::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Buckingham}}}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pairwise additive interactions of point particles with added
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Coulomb}}}} interactions or \sphinxstyleemphasis{only} the Coulomb interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
manybody interactions of point particles (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{EAM}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tersoff}}}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
complex interactions that include additional per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties
(e.g. Discrete Element Models (DEM), Peridynamics, Ellipsoids)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
special purpose pair styles that may not even compute forces like
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_zero::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style zero}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tracker::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style tracker}}}}, or are a wrapper for multiple kinds of interactions
like {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_list::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style list}}}},
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_kim::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style kim}}}}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the text below, we will discuss aspects of implementing pair styles
in LAMMPS by looking at representative case studies.  The design of
LAMMPS allows developers to focus on the essentials, which is to compute
the forces (and energies or virial contributions), enter and manage the
global settings as well as the potential parameters, and the pair style
specific parts of reading and writing restart and data files.  Most of
the complex tasks like management of the atom positions, domain
decomposition and boundaries, or neighbor list creation are handled
transparently by other parts of the LAMMPS code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As shown on the page for {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{writing or extending pair styles}}}}, in order to implement a new pair style, a new class must
be written that is either directly or indirectly derived from the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}} class.  If that class is directly derived from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}}, there
are three methods that \sphinxstyleemphasis{must} be re\sphinxhyphen{}implemented, since they are “pure”
in the base class: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::compute()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::settings()}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::coeff()}}.  In addition, a custom constructor is needed.  All
other methods are optional and have default implementations in the base
class (most of which do nothing), but they may need to be overridden
depending on the requirements of the model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We are looking at the following cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:case-1-a-pairwise-additive-model}]{\sphinxcrossref{Case 1: a pairwise additive model}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:case-2-a-many-body-potential}]{\sphinxcrossref{Case 2: a many\sphinxhyphen{}body potential}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:case-3-a-potential-requiring-communication}]{\sphinxcrossref{Case 3: a potential requiring communication}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:case-4-potentials-without-a-compute-function}]{\sphinxcrossref{Case 4: potentials without a compute() function}}}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Package and build system considerations}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:package-and-build-system-considerations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In general, new pair styles should be added to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-extra-pair}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR
package}}}} unless they are an accelerated pair style and
then they should be added to the corresponding accelerator package
({\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-gpu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{GPU}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-intel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{INTEL}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-kokkos}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{KOKKOS}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-openmp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{OPENMP}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-opt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{OPT}}}}).  If
you feel that your contribution should be added to a different package,
please consult with the LAMMPS developers first.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The contributed code needs to support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_make::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{traditional GNU make
build process}}}} \sphinxstylestrong{and} the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_cmake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{CMake build process}}}}.  For the GNU make process and if the package has an
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Install.sh}} file, most likely that file needs to be updated to
correctly copy the sources when installing the package and properly
delete them when uninstalling.  This is particularly important when
added a new pair style that is a derived class from an existing pair
style in a package, so that its installation depends on the the
installation status of the package of the derived class.  For the CMake
process, it is sometimes necessary to make changes to the package
specific CMake scripting in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmake/Modules/Packages}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Case 1: a pairwise additive model}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:case-1-a-pairwise-additive-model}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In this section, we will describe the procedure of adding a simple pair
style to LAMMPS: an empirical model that can be used to model liquid
mercury.  The pair style shall be called {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_born_gauss::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond/gauss}}}} and the complete implementation can be found in the
files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR/pair\_born\_gauss.cpp}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR/pair\_born\_gauss.h}} of the LAMMPS source code.


\subsubsection{Model and general considerations}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:model-and-general-considerations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The functional form of the model according to {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:bomont2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bomont)}}}}
consists of a repulsive Born\sphinxhyphen{}Mayer exponential term and a temperature
dependent, attractive Gaussian term.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = A_0 \exp \left( -\alpha r \right) - A_1 \exp\left[ -\beta \left(r - r_0 \right)^2 \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the application to mercury, the following parameters are listed:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_0 = 8.2464 \times 10^{13} \; \textrm{eV}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\alpha = 12.48 \; \AA^{-1}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\beta = 0.44 \; \AA^{-2}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_0 = 3.56 \; \AA\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_1\) is temperature dependent and can be determined from
\(A_1 = a_0 + a_1 T + a_2 T^2\) with:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a_0 = 1.97475 \times 10^{-2} \; \textrm{eV}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a_1 = 8.40841 \times 10^{-5} \; \textrm{eV/K}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a_2 = -2.58717 \times 10^{-8} \; \textrm{eV/K}^{-2}\)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the optional cutoff, this means we have a total of 5 or 6
parameters for each pair of atom types. Additionally, we need to input a
default cutoff value as a global setting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Because of the combination of Born\sphinxhyphen{}Mayer with a Gaussian, the pair style
shall be named “born/gauss” and thus the class name would be
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairBornGauss}} and the source files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_born\_gauss.h}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_born\_gauss.cpp}}.  Since this is a rather uncommon potential, it
shall be added to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-extra-pair}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR}}}} package.


\subsubsection{Header file}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:header-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first segment of any LAMMPS source should be the copyright and
license statement.  Note the marker in the first line to indicate to
editors like emacs that this file is a C++ source, even though the .h
extension suggests a C source (this is a convention inherited from the
very beginning of the C++ version of LAMMPS).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/* \PYGZhy{}*\PYGZhy{} c++ \PYGZhy{}*\PYGZhy{} \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}}

\PYG{c+cm}{   certain rights in this software.  This software is distributed under}

\PYG{c+cm}{\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} */}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Every pair style must be registered in LAMMPS by including the following
lines of code in the second part of the header after the copyright
message and before the include guards for the class definition:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{ifdef PAIR\PYGZus{}CLASS}
\PYG{c+c1}{// clang\PYGZhy{}format off}
\PYG{n}{PairStyle}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{born}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{gauss}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{PairBornGauss}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{c+c1}{// clang\PYGZhy{}format on}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{else}

\PYG{c+cm}{/* the definition of the PairBornGauss class (see below) is inserted here */}

\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{endif}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This block of between \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#ifdef PAIR\_CLASS}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#else}} will be
included by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Force}} class in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force.cpp}} to build a map of
“factory functions” that will create an instance of these classes and
return a pointer to it.  The map connects the name of the pair style,
“born/gauss”, to the name of the class, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairBornGauss}}.  During
compilation, LAMMPS constructs a file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{style\_pair.h}} that contains
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#include}} statements for all “installed” pair styles.  Before
including \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{style\_pair.h}} into \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force.cpp}}, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PAIR\_CLASS}} define
is set and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairStyle(name,class)}} macro defined.  The code of the
macro adds the installed pair styles to the “factory map” which enables
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style command}}}} to create the pair style
instance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The list of header files to include is automatically updated by the
build system if there are new files, so the presence of the new header
file in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR}} folder and the enabling of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR
package will trigger LAMMPS to include the new pair style when it is
(re\sphinxhyphen{})compiled.  The “// clang\sphinxhyphen{}format” format comments are needed so that
running {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_development:clang-format}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{clang\sphinxhyphen{}format}}}} on the file will not insert
unwanted blanks between “born”, “/”, and “gauss” which would break the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairStyle}} macro.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The third part of the header file is the actual class definition of the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairBornGauss}} class.  This has the prototypes for all member
functions that will be implemented by this pair style.  This includes
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{a few required and a number of optional functions}}}}.
All functions that were labeled in the base class as “virtual” must be
given the “override” property, as it is done in the code shown below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “override” property helps to detect unexpected mismatches because
compilation will stop with an error in case the signature of a function
is changed in the base class without also changing it in all derived
classes.  For example, if this change added an optional argument with a
default value, then all existing source code \sphinxstyleemphasis{calling} the function
would not need changes and still compile, but the function in the
derived class would no longer override the one in the base class due to
the different number of arguments and the behavior of the pair style is
thus changed in an unintended way.  Using the “override” keyword
prevents such issues.

\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{public}\PYG{o}{:}

\subsubsection{Implementation file}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:implementation-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We move on to the implementation of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairBornGauss}} class in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_born\_gauss.cpp}} file.  This file also starts with a LAMMPS
copyright and license header.  Below that notice is typically the space
where comments may be added with additional information about this
specific file, the author(s), affiliation(s), and email address(es).
This way the contributing author(s) can be easily contacted, when
there are questions about the implementation later.  Since the file(s)
may be around for a long time, it is beneficial to use some kind of
“permanent” email address, if possible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second section of the implementation file has various include
statements.  The include file for the class header has to come first,
then a block of LAMMPS classes (sorted alphabetically) followed by a
block of system headers and others, if needed.  Note the standardized
C++ notation for headers of C\sphinxhyphen{}library functions (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cmath}} instead of
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{math.h}}).  The final statement of this segment imports the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::}} namespace globally for this file.  This way, all LAMMPS
specific functions and classes do not have to be prefixed with
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::}}.


\subsubsection{Constructor and destructor (required)}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:constructor-and-destructor-required}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first two functions in the implementation source file are typically
the constructor and the destructor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair styles are different from most classes in LAMMPS that define a
“style”, as their constructor only uses the LAMMPS class instance
pointer as an argument, but \sphinxstylestrong{not} the command line arguments of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style command}}}}.  Instead, those arguments are
processed in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::settings()}} function (or rather the version in
the derived class).  The constructor is the place where global defaults
are set and specifically flags are set indicating which optional
features of a pair style are available.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cm}{/* \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} */}

\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{writedata}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxtitleref{writedata = 1;} statement indicates that the pair style is capable
of writing the current pair coefficient parameters to data files.  That
is, the class implements specific versions for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::data()}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::data\_all()}}.  Other statements that could be added here would
be \sphinxtitleref{single\_enable = 1;} or \sphinxtitleref{respa\_enable = 0;} to indicate that the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::single()}} function is present and the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::compute\_(inner|middle|outer)}} functions are not, but those are
also the default settings and already set in the base class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the destructor, we need to delete all memory that was allocated by the
pair style, usually to hold force field parameters that were entered
with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff command}}}}.  Most of those array
pointers will need to be declared in the derived class header, but some
(e.g. setflag, cutsq) are already declared in the base class.

\subsubsection{Settings and coefficients (required)}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:settings-and-coefficients-required}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To enter the global pair style settings and the pair style parameters,
the functions \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::settings()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::coeff()}} need to be
re\sphinxhyphen{}implemented.  The arguments to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{settings()}} function are the
arguments given to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style command}}}}.
Normally, those would already be processed as part of the constructor,
but moving this to a separate function allows users to change global
settings like the default cutoff without having to reissue all
pair\_coeff commands or re\sphinxhyphen{}read the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair Coeffs}} sections from the
data file.  In the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{settings()}} function, also the arrays for storing
parameters, to define cutoffs, track which pairs of parameters have been
explicitly set and allocated and, if needed, initialized.  In this case,
the memory allocation and initialization are moved to a function
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{allocate()}}.

The arguments to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{coeff()}} function are the arguments to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff command}}}}.  The function is also called
when processing the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair Coeffs}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairIJ Coeffs}} sections of
data files.  In the case of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair Coeffs}} section, there is only
one atom type per line and thus the first argument is duplicated.  Since
the atom type arguments of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff command}}}}
may be a range (e.g. *3 for atom types 1, 2, and 3), the
corresponding arguments are passed to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4I0EN9LAMMPS_NS5utils6boundsEvPKciRKNSt6stringE6bigint6bigintR4TYPER4TYPEP5Error}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::bounds()}}}}} function which will then return the low
and high end of the range.  Note that the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setflag}} array is set to 1
for all pairs of atom types processed by this call.  This information is
later used in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_one()}} function to determine if any coefficients
are missing and, if supported by the potential, generate those missing
coefficients from the selected mixing rule.

\subsubsection{Initialization}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:initialization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_one()}} function is called during the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_flow::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{“init” phase}}}} of a simulation.  This is where potential parameters
are checked for completeness, derived parameters computed (e.g. the
“offset” of the potential energy at the cutoff distance for use with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify shift yes}}}} command).  If a pair style
supports generating “mixed” parameters (i.e. where both atoms of a pair
have a different atom type) using a “mixing rule” from the parameters of
the type with itself, this is the place to compute and store those mixed
values.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{born/gauss} pair style does not support mixing, so we only
check for completeness.  Another purpose of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_one()}} function
is to symmetrize the potential parameter arrays.  The return value of
the function is the cutoff for the given pair of atom types.  This
information is used by the neighbor list code to determine the largest
cutoff and then build the neighbor lists accordingly.

\subsubsection{Computing forces from the neighbor list (required)}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:computing-forces-from-the-neighbor-list-required}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compute()}} function is the “workhorse” of a pair style.  This is
where we have the nested loops over all pairs of particles from the
neighbor list to compute forces and \sphinxhyphen{} if needed \sphinxhyphen{} energies and virials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first part is to define some variables for later use and store
cached copies of data or pointers that we need to access frequently.  Also,
this is a good place to call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::ev\_init()}}, which initializes
several flags derived from the \sphinxtitleref{eflag} and \sphinxtitleref{vflag} parameters signaling
whether the energy and virial need to be tallied and whether only globally
or also per\sphinxhyphen{}atom.

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{inum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{inum}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{firstneigh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{firstneigh}\PYG{p}{;}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The outer loop (index \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}) is over local atoms of our sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain.
Typically, the value of \sphinxtitleref{inum} (the number of neighbor lists) is the
same as the number of local atoms (= atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{owned} by this sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain).
But when the pair style is used as a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid pair
style}}}} or neighbor list entries are removed with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}}, this number may be
smaller. The array \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}ilist}} has the (local) indices of the atoms
for which neighbor lists have been created. Then \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}numneigh}} is
an \sphinxtitleref{inum} sized array with the number of entries of each list of
neighbors, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{list\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}firstneigh}} is a list of pointers to those lists.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For efficiency reasons, cached copies of some properties of the outer
loop atoms are also initialized.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{// loop over neighbors of my atoms}

\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{ii}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ii}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inum}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ii}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ilist}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{ii}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{xtmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{ytmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{jnum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{numneigh}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The inner loop (index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}) processes the neighbor lists.  The neighbor
list code encodes extra information using the upper 3 bits. The 2
highest bits encode whether a pair is a regular pair of neighbor (= 0)
or a pair of 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 (= 1), 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 (= 2), or 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 (= 3) {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{“special” neighbor}}}}.  The next highest bit encodes whether the pair stores
data in a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fix neigh/history}} instance (an undocumented internal fix
style).  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sbmask()}} inline function extracts those bits and
converts them into a number.  This number is used to look up the
corresponding scaling factor for the non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interaction from the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}special\_lj}} array and stores it in the \sphinxtitleref{factor\_lj} variable.
Due to the additional bits, the value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} would be out of range when
accessing data from per\sphinxhyphen{}atom arrays, so we apply the NEIGHMASK constant
with a bit\sphinxhyphen{}wise and operation to mask them out.  This step \sphinxstyleemphasis{must} be
done, even if a pair style does not use special bond scaling of forces
and energies to avoid segmentation faults.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the corrected \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} index, it is now possible to compute the distance
of the pair.  For efficiency reasons, the square root is only taken
\sphinxstyleemphasis{after} the check for the cutoff (which has been stored as squared
cutoff by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}} base class).  For some pair styles, like the 12\sphinxhyphen{}6
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential, computing the square root can be avoided
entirely.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{jlist}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jj}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{dely}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ytmp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following block of code is the actual application of the model
potential to compute the force.  Note, that \sphinxstyleemphasis{fpair} is the pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise
force divided by the distance, as this simplifies the projection of the
x\sphinxhyphen{}, y\sphinxhyphen{}, and z\sphinxhyphen{}components of the force vector by simply multiplying with
the respective distances in those directions.

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{bexp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{biga1}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{beta}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dr}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dr}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the next block, the force is added to the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom force arrays.  This
pair style uses a “half” neighbor list (each pair is listed only once)
so we take advantage of the fact that \(\vec{F}_{ij} =
-\vec{F}_{ji}\), i.e.  apply Newton’s third law.  The force is \sphinxstyleemphasis{always}
stored when the atom is a “local” atom. Index \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} atoms are always “local”
(i.e. \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} \textless{} nlocal); index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} atoms may be “ghost” atoms (\sphinxstyleemphasis{j} \textgreater{}= nlocal).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on the settings used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton command}}}},
those pairs are only listed once globally (newton\_pair == 1), then
forces must be stored even with ghost atoms and after all forces are
computed a “reverse communication” is performed to add those ghost atom
forces to their corresponding local atoms.  If the setting is disabled,
then the extra communication is skipped, since for pairs straddling
sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain boundaries, the forces are computed twice and only stored
with the local atoms in the domain that \sphinxstyleemphasis{owns} it.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fpair}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dely}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fpair}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fpair}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{newton\PYGZus{}pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nlocal}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fpair}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dely}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fpair}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fpair}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ev\_tally()}} function tallies global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy and
virial.  For typical MD simulations, the potential energy is merely a
diagnostic and only needed on output.  Similarly, the pressure may only
be computed for (infrequent) thermodynamic output.  For all timesteps
where this information is not needed either, \sphinxtitleref{eflag} or \sphinxtitleref{evflag} are
zero and the computation and call to the tally function skipped.  Note
that evdwl is initialized to zero at the beginning of the function, so
that it still is valid to access it, even if the energy is not computed
(e.g. when only the virial is needed).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{eflag}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{evdwl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{factor\PYGZus{}lj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{aexp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bexp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{offset}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{evflag}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ev\PYGZus{}tally}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nlocal}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{newton\PYGZus{}pair}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{evdwl}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fpair}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delx}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dely}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delz}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If only the global virial is needed and no energy, then calls to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ev\_tally()}} can be avoided altogether, and the global virial can be
computed more efficiently from the dot product of the total per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
force vector and the position vector of the corresponding atom,
\(\vec{F}\cdot\vec{r}\).  This has to be done \sphinxstyleemphasis{after} all pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise
forces are computed and \sphinxstyleemphasis{before} the reverse communication to collect
data from ghost atoms, since the position has to be the position that was
used to compute the force, i.e. \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} the “local” position if that ghost
atom is a periodic copy.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{vflag\PYGZus{}fdotr}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{virial\PYGZus{}fdotr\PYGZus{}compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Computing force and energy for a single pair}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:computing-force-and-energy-for-a-single-pair}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Certain features in LAMMPS only require computing interactions between
individual pairs of atoms and the (optional) \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{single()}} function is
needed to support those features (e.g. for tabulation of force and
energy with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}}).  This is a repetition of
the force kernel in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compute()}} function, but only for a single
pair of atoms, where the (squared) distance is provided as a parameter
(so it may not even be an existing distance between two specific atoms).
The energy is returned as the return value of the function and the force
as the \sphinxtitleref{fforce} reference.  Note, that this is, similar to how \sphinxstyleemphasis{fpair}
is used in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compute()}} function, the magnitude of the force along
the vector between the two atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{divided} by the distance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{single()}} function is optional, but it is expected to be
implemented for any true pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise additive potential. Many\sphinxhyphen{}body
potentials and special case potentials do not implement it. In a few
special cases (EAM, long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulomb), the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{single()}} function
implements the pairwise additive part of the complete force interaction
and depends on either pre\sphinxhyphen{}computed properties (derivative of embedding
term for EAM) or post\sphinxhyphen{}computed non\sphinxhyphen{}pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise force contributions (KSpace
style in case of long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulomb).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The member variable \sphinxtitleref{single\_enable} should be set to 0 in the
constructor, if it is not implemented (its default value is 1).

\subsubsection{Reading and writing of restart files}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_write_pair:reading-and-writing-of-restart-files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for writing and reading binary restart files is provided by the
following four functions.  Writing is only done by MPI processor rank 0.
The output of global (not related to atom types) settings is usually
delegated to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{write\_restart\_settings()}} function.  This restart
facility is commonly only used, if there are small number of per\sphinxhyphen{}type
parameters.  For potentials that use per\sphinxhyphen{}element parameters or tabulated
data and read these from files, those parameters and the name of the
potential file are not written to restart files and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff
command}}}} has to re\sphinxhyphen{}issued when restarting.  For pair styles
like “born/gauss” that do support writing to restart files, this is not
required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Implementing the functions to read and write binary restart files is
optional.  The member variable \sphinxtitleref{restartinfo} should be set to 0 in the
constructor, if they are not implemented (its default value is 1).

\PYG{c+cm}{   proc 0 writes to restart file}
\PYG{c+cm}{\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} */}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, on reading, only MPI processor rank 0 has opened the restart
file and will read the data.  The data is then distributed across all
parallel processes using calls to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Bcast()}}.  Before reading atom
type specific data, the corresponding storage needs to be allocated.
Order and number or storage size of items read must be exactly the same
as when writing, or else the data will be read incorrectly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reading uses the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils6sfreadEPKciPv6size_t6size_tP4FILEPKcP5Error}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::sfread}}}}}
utility function to detect read errors and short reads, so that LAMMPS
can abort if that happens, e.g. when the restart file is corrupted.
