\subsection{Reading and parsing of text and text files}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_notes:reading-and-parsing-of-text-and-text-files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Classes in LAMMPS frequently need to read in additional
data from a file, e.g. potential parameters from a potential file for
manybody potentials.  LAMMPS provides several custom classes and
convenience functions to simplify the process.  They offer the
following benefits:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
better code reuse and fewer lines of code needed to implement reading
and parsing data from a file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
better detection of format errors, incompatible data, and better error messages

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
exit with an error message instead of silently converting only part of the
text to a number or returning a 0 on unrecognized text and thus reading incorrect values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
re\sphinxhyphen{}entrant code through avoiding global static variables (as used by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strtok()}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
transparent support for translating unsupported UTF\sphinxhyphen{}8 characters to their ASCII equivalents
(the text\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}value conversion functions \sphinxstylestrong{only} accept ASCII characters)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In most cases (e.g. potential files) the same data is needed on all MPI
ranks.  Then it is best to do the reading and parsing only on MPI rank
0, and communicate the data later with one or more \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MPI\_Bcast()}}
calls.  For reading generic text and potential parameter files the
custom classes {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS14TextFileReaderE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TextFileReader}}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS19PotentialFileReaderE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PotentialFileReader}}}}}
are available. They allow reading the file as individual lines for which
they can return a tokenizer class (see below) for parsing the line.  Or
they can return blocks of numbers as a vector directly.  The
documentation on {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:file-reader-classes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{File reader classes}}}}
contains an example for a typical case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When reading per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data, the data on each line of the file usually
needs to include an atom ID so it can be associated with a particular
atom.  In that case the data can be read in multi\sphinxhyphen{}line chunks and
broadcast to all MPI ranks with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils20read_lines_from_fileEP4FILEiiPci8MPI_Comm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::read\_lines\_from\_file()}}}}}.  Those chunks are then
split into lines, parsed, and applied only to atoms the MPI rank
“owns”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For splitting a string (incrementally) into words and optionally
converting those to numbers, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS9TokenizerE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Tokenizer}}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS14ValueTokenizerE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ValueTokenizer}}}}} can be used.  Those provide a superset of
the functionality of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strtok()}} from the C\sphinxhyphen{}library and the latter
also includes conversion to different types.  Any errors while
processing the string in those classes will result in an exception,
which can be caught and the error processed as needed.  Unlike the
C\sphinxhyphen{}library functions \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atoi()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atof()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strtol()}}, or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strtod()}} the conversion will check if the converted text is a
valid integer or floating point number and will not silently return an
unexpected or incorrect value.  For example, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atoi()}} will return 12
when converting “12.5”, while the ValueTokenizer class will throw an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS23InvalidIntegerExceptionE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{InvalidIntegerException}}}}} if
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS14ValueTokenizer8next_intEv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ValueTokenizer::next\_int()}}}}} is called on the same string.


\subsection{Requesting and accessing neighbor lists}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_notes:requesting-and-accessing-neighbor-lists}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_notes:request-neighbor-list}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS uses Verlet\sphinxhyphen{}style neighbor lists to avoid having to loop over
\sphinxstyleemphasis{all} pairs of \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} atoms when computing pairwise properties with a
cutoff (e.g. pairwise forces or radial distribution functions).  There
are three main algorithms that can be selected by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor
command}}}}: \sphinxtitleref{bin} (the default, uses binning to achieve linear
scaling with system size), \sphinxtitleref{nsq} (without binning, quadratic scaling),
\sphinxtitleref{multi} (with binning, optimized for varying cutoffs or polydisperse
granular particles).  In addition to how the neighbor lists are
constructed a number of different variants of neighbor lists need to be
created (e.g. “full” or “half”) for different purposes and styles and
those may be required in every time step (“perpetual”) or on some steps
(“occasional”).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list creation is managed by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Neighbor}} class.
Individual classes can obtain a neighbor list by creating an instance of
a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NeighRequest}} class which is stored in a list inside the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Neighbor}} class.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Neighbor}} class will then analyze the
various requests and apply optimizations where neighbor lists that have
the same settings will be created only once and then copied, or a list
may be constructed by processing a neighbor list from a different
request that is a superset of the requested list.  The neighbor list
build is then {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_par_neigh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processed in parallel}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The most commonly required neighbor list is a so\sphinxhyphen{}called “half” neighbor
list, where each pair of atoms is listed only once (except when the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton command setting}}}} for pair is off; in that case
pairs straddling subdomains or periodic boundaries will be listed twice).
Thus these are the default settings when a neighbor list request is created in:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{Pair::init\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{Pair::init\PYGZus{}list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cm}{/*id*/}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighList}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{list}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{this}} pointer argument is required so the neighbor list code can
access the requesting class instance to store the assembled neighbor
list with that instance by calling its \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_list()}} member function.
The optional second argument (omitted here) contains a bitmask of flags
that determines the kind of neighbor list requested.  The default value
used here asks for a perpetual “half” neighbor list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Non\sphinxhyphen{}default values of the second argument need to be used to adjust a
neighbor list request to the specific needs of a style.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tersoff}}}} pair style, for example, needs a “full” neighbor list:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{PairTersoff::init\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{// [...]}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}FULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a pair style supports r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA time integration with different cutoff regions,
the request flag may depend on the corresponding r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA settings. Here is an
example from pair style lj/cut:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{PairLJCut::init\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}DEFAULT}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{update}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{whichflag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{strmatch}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{update}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{integrate\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZca{}respa}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{Respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{update}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{integrate}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{level\PYGZus{}inner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}RESPA\PYGZus{}INOUT}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{level\PYGZus{}middle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}RESPA\PYGZus{}ALL}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{// [...]}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Granular pair styles need neighbor lists based on particle sizes and not cutoff
and also may need to store data across timesteps (“history”).
For example with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{use\PYGZus{}history}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}SIZE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}HISTORY}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{else}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}SIZE}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In case a class would need to make multiple neighbor list requests with different
settings, each request can set an id which is then used in the corresponding
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{init\_list()}} function to assign it to the suitable pointer variable. This is
done for example by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_meam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style meam}}}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{PairMEAM::init\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{c+c1}{// [...]}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}FULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{PairMEAM::init\PYGZus{}list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighList}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{listfull}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{else}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{listhalf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes may require a neighbor list that is only build occasionally (or
just once) and this can also be indicated by a flag.  As an example here
is the request from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FixPeriNeigh}} class which is created
internally by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Peridynamics pair styles}}}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}FULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}OCCASIONAL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible to request a neighbor list that uses a different cutoff
than what is usually inferred from the pair style settings (largest cutoff of
all pair styles plus neighbor list skin).  The following is used in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_rdf::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute rdf}}}} command implementation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{cutflag}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}OCCASIONAL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}cutoff}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{mycutneigh}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{else}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}OCCASIONAL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list request function has a slightly different set of arguments
when created by a command style.  In this case the neighbor list is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{always} an occasional neighbor list, so that flag is not needed. However
for printing the neighbor list summary the name of the requesting command
should be set.  Below is the request from the {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete atoms}}}}
command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{neighbor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}request}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NeighConst}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{REQ\PYGZus{}FULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Choosing between a custom atom style, fix property/atom, and fix STORE/ATOM}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_notes:choosing-between-a-custom-atom-style-fix-property-atom-and-fix-store-atom}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are multiple ways to manage per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data within LAMMPS.  Often
the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom storage is only used locally and managed by the class that
uses it.  If the data has to persist between multiple time steps and
migrate with atoms when they move from sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain to sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain or
across periodic boundaries, then using a custom atom style, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
property/atom}}}}, or the internal fix STORE/ATOM are
possible options.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the atom style is usually the most programming effort and mostly
needed when the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data is an integral part of the model like a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom charge or diameter and thus should be part of the Atoms
section of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data file}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix property/atom is useful if the data is optional or should be
entered by the user, or accessed as a (named) custom property. In this
case the fix should be entered as part of the input (and not
internally) which allows to enter and store its content with data files.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix STORE/ATOM should be used when the data should be accessed internally
only and thus the fix can be created internally.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Fix contributions to instantaneous energy, virial, and cumulative energy}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_notes:fix-contributions-to-instantaneous-energy-virial-and-cumulative-energy}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes can calculate contributions to the instantaneous energy and/or
virial of the system, both in a global and peratom sense.  Fixes that
perform thermostatting or barostatting can calculate the cumulative
energy they add to or subtract from the system, which is accessed by
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve} thermodynamic keywords.  This subsection
explains how both work and what flags to set in a new fix to enable
this functionality.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s start with thermostatting and barostatting fixes.  Examples are
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}
commands.  Here is what the fix needs to do:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple\_flag} = 1 in the constructor.  Also set
\sphinxstyleemphasis{scalar\_flag} = 1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{extscalar} = 1, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{global\_freq} to a timestep
increment which matches how often the fix is invoked.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Implement a compute\_scalar() method that returns the cumulative
energy added or subtracted by the fix, e.g. by rescaling the
velocity of atoms.  The sign convention is that subtracted energy is
positive, added energy is negative.  This must be the total energy
added to the entire system, i.e. an “extensive” quantity, not a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy.  Cumulative means the summed energy since the fix
was instantiated, even across multiple runs.  This is because the
energy is used by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve} thermodynamic keyword to check
that the fix is conserving the total energy of the system,
i.e. potential energy + kinetic energy + coupling energy = a
constant.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
And here is how the code operates:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Modify class makes a list of all fixes that set \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple\_flag} = 1.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command defines
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve} keywords.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
These keywords sum the energy contributions from all the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple\_flag} = 1 fixes by invoking the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy\_couple()} method in
the Modify class, which calls the \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute\_scalar()} method of each
fix in the list.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Next, here is how a fix contributes to the instantaneous energy and
virial of the system.  First, it sets any or all of these flags to a
value of 1 in their constructor:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{energy\_global\_flag} to contribute to global energy, example: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_indent::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix indent}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{energy\_peratom\_flag} to contribute to peratom energy, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_cmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix cmap}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{virial\_global\_flag} to contribute to global virial, example: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{virial\_peratom\_flag} to contribute to peratom virial, example: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix must also do the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For global energy, implement a compute\_scalar() method that returns
the energy added or subtracted on this timestep.  Here the sign
convention is that added energy is positive, subtracted energy is
negative.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For peratom energy, invoke the ev\_init(eflag,vflag) function each
time the fix is invoked, which initializes per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy storage.
The value of eflag may need to be stored from an earlier call to the
fix during the same timestep.  See how the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_cmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix cmap}}}} command does this in src/MOLECULE/fix\_cmap.cpp.  When an
energy for one or more atoms is calculated, invoke the ev\_tally()
function to tally the contribution to each atom.  Both the ev\_init()
and ev\_tally() methods are in the parent Fix class.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For global and/or peratom virial, invoke the v\_init(vflag) function
each time the fix is invoked, which initializes virial storage.
When forces on one or more atoms are calculated, invoke the
v\_tally() function to tally the contribution.  Both the v\_init() and
v\_tally() methods are in the parent Fix class.  Note that there are
several variants of v\_tally(); choose the one appropriate to your
fix.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The ev\_init() and ev\_tally() methods also account for global and
peratom virial contributions.  Thus you do not need to invoke the
v\_init() and v\_tally() methods if the fix also calculates peratom
energies.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix must also specify whether (by default) to include or exclude
these contributions to the global/peratom energy/virial of the system.
For the fix to include the contributions, set either or both of these
variables in the constructor:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_energy} = 1, for global and peratom energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_virial} = 1, for global and peratom virial

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that these variables are zeroed in fix.cpp.  Thus if you don’t
set the variables, the contributions will be excluded (by default).

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, the user has ultimate control over whether to include or
exclude the contributions of the fix via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix modify}}}} command:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fix modify \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy yes} to include global and peratom energy contributions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fix modify \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial yes} to include global and peratom virial contributions

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the fix contributes to any of the global/peratom energy/virial
values for the system, it should be explained on the fix doc page,
along with the default values for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy yes/no} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial
yes/no} settings of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, these 4 contributions are included in the output of 4
computes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
global energy in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
peratom energy in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe/atom}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
global virial in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
peratom virial in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes invoke a method of the Modify class to include
contributions from fixes that have the corresponding flags set,
e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy\_peratom\_flag} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_energy} for {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
pe/atom}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that each compute has an optional keyword to either include or
exclude all contributions from fixes.  Also note that {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} are what
is used (by default) by {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}} to
calculate values for its \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{press} keywords.


\subsection{KSpace PPPM FFT grids}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_notes:kspace-pppm-fft-grids}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The various {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{KSpace PPPM}}}} styles in LAMMPS use
FFTs to solve Poisson’s equation.  This subsection describes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
how FFT grids are defined

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
how they are decomposed across processors

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
how they are indexed by each processor

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
how particle charge and electric field values are mapped to/from
the grid

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An FFT grid cell is a 3d volume; grid points are corners of a grid
cell and the code stores values assigned to grid points in vectors or
3d arrays.  A global 3d FFT grid has points indexed 0 to N\sphinxhyphen{}1 inclusive
in each dimension.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each processor owns two subsets of the grid, each subset is
brick\sphinxhyphen{}shaped.  Depending on how it is used, these subsets are
allocated as a 1d vector or 3d array.  Either way, the ordering of
values within contiguous memory x fastest, then y, z slowest.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3d decomposition}} of the grid, the global grid is
partitioned into bricks that correspond to the subdomains of the
simulation box that each processor owns.  Often, this is a regular 3d
array (Px by Py by Pz) of bricks, where P = number of processors =
Px * Py * Pz.  More generally it can be a tiled decomposition, where
each processor owns a brick and the union of all the bricks is the
global grid.  Tiled decompositions are produced by load balancing with
the RCB algorithm; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance rcb}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FFT decompostion}} of the grid, each processor owns a brick
that spans the entire x dimension of the grid while the y and z
dimensions are partitioned as a regular 2d array (P1 by P2), where P =
P1 * P2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following indices store the inclusive bounds of the brick a
processor owns, within the global grid:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
nFOO\PYGZus{}in = 3d decomposition brick
nFOO\PYGZus{}fft = FFT decomposition brick
nFOO\PYGZus{}out = 3d decomposition brick + ghost cells
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FOO}} corresponds to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{xlo, xhi, ylo, yhi, zlo,}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{zhi}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fft}} indices are from 0 to N\sphinxhyphen{}1 inclusive in each
dimension, where N is the grid size.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{out}} indices index an array which stores the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in}} subset of
the grid plus ghost cells that surround it.  These indices can thus be
\textless{} 0 or \textgreater{}= N.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of ghost cells a processor owns in each of the 6 directions
is a function of:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
neighbor skin distance (since atoms can move outside a proc subdomain)
qdist = offset or charge from atom due to TIP4P fictitious charge
order = mapping stencil size
shift = factor used when order is an even number (see below)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an explanation of how the PPPM variables \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{order}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nlower}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nupper}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{shift}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OFFSET}} work. They are the
relevant variables that determine how atom charge is mapped to grid
points and how field values are mapped from grid points to atoms:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
order = \PYGZsh{} of nearby grid points in each dim that atom charge/field are mapped to/from
nlower,nupper = extent of stencil around the grid point an atom is assigned to
OFFSET = large integer added/subtracted when mapping to avoid int(\PYGZhy{}0.75) = 0 when \PYGZhy{}1 is the desired result
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The particle\_map() method assigns each atom to a grid point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If order is even, say 4:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom is assigned to grid point to its left (in each dim)
shift = OFFSET
nlower = \PYGZhy{}1, nupper = 2, which are offsets from assigned grid point
window of mapping grid pts is thus 2 grid points to left of atom, 2 to right
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If order is odd, say 5:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atom is assigned to left/right grid pt it is closest to (in each dim)
shift = OFFSET + 0.5
nlower = 2, nupper = 2
if point is in left half of cell, then window of affected grid pts is 3 grid points to left of atom, 2 to right
if point is in right half of cell, then window of affected grid pts is 2 grid points to left of atom, 3 to right
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These settings apply to each dimension, so that if order = 5, an
atom’s charge is mapped to 125 grid points that surround the atom.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Notes for updating code written for older LAMMPS versions}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:notes-for-updating-code-written-for-older-lammps-versions}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section documents how C++ source files that are available \sphinxstyleemphasis{outside
of the LAMMPS source distribution} (e.g. in external USER packages or as
source files provided as a supplement to a publication) that are written
for an older version of LAMMPS and thus need to be updated to be
compatible with the current version of LAMMPS.  Due to the active
development of LAMMPS it is likely to always be incomplete.  Please
contact \sphinxhref{mailto:developers@lammps.org}{developers@lammps.org} in case you run across an issue that is not
(yet) listed here.  Please also review the latest information about the
LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{programming style conventions}}}}, especially
if you are considering to submit the updated version for inclusion into
the LAMMPS distribution.

\subsection{Setting flags in the constructor}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:setting-flags-in-the-constructor}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As LAMMPS gains additional functionality, new flags may need to be set
in the constructor or a class to signal compatibility with such features.
Most of the time the defaults are chosen conservatively, but sometimes
the conservative choice is the uncommon choice, and then those settings
need to be made when updating code.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair styles:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{manybody\_flag}}: set to 1 if your pair style is not pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise additive

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{restartinfo}}: set to 0 if your pair style does not store data in restart files

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Rename of pack/unpack\_comm() to pack/unpack\_forward\_comm()}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:rename-of-pack-unpack-comm-to-pack-unpack-forward-comm}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 8Aug2014.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this change set, the functions to pack/unpack data into communication buffers
for {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_comm_ops::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{forward communications}}}} were renamed from
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pack\_comm()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unpack\_comm()}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pack\_forward\_comm()}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unpack\_forward\_comm()}}, respectively.  Also the meaning of the return
value of these functions was changed: rather than returning the number
of items per atom stored in the buffer, now the total number of items
added (or unpacked) needs to be returned.  Here is an example from the
\sphinxtitleref{PairEAM} class.  Of course the member function declaration in corresponding
header file needs to be updated accordingly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{PairEAM::pack\PYGZus{}comm}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{list}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{double}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pbc\PYGZus{}flag}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{pbc}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{m}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{m}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fp}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{PairEAM::pack\PYGZus{}forward\PYGZus{}comm}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{list}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{double}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pbc\PYGZus{}flag}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{pbc}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{m}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{m}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fp}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{m}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Because the various “pack” and “unpack” functions are defined in the
respective base classes as dummy functions doing nothing, and because
of the the name mismatch the custom versions in the derived class
will no longer be called, there will be no compilation error when
this change is not applied.  Only calculations will suddenly produce
incorrect results because the required forward communication calls
will cease to function correctly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Use ev\_init() to initialize variables derived from eflag and vflag}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:use-ev-init-to-initialize-variables-derived-from-eflag-and-vflag}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 29Mar2019.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several variables that need to be initialized based on
the values of the “eflag” and “vflag” variables and since sometimes
there are new bits added and new variables need to be set to 1 or 0.
To make this consistent across all styles, there is now an inline
function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ev\_init(eflag, vflag)}} that makes those settings
consistently and calls either \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ev\_setup()}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ev\_unset()}}.
Example from a pair style:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{eflag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{o}{|}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vflag}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ev\PYGZus{}setup}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{eflag}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vflag}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{else}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{evflag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vflag\PYGZus{}fdotr}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eflag\PYGZus{}global}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eflag\PYGZus{}atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{ev\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{eflag}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vflag}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Not applying this change will not cause a compilation error, but
can lead to inconsistent behavior and incorrect tallying of
energy or virial.


\subsection{Use utils::count\_words() functions instead of atom\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}count\_words()}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:use-utils-count-words-functions-instead-of-atom-count-words}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 2Jun2020.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “count\_words()” functions for parsing text have been moved from the
Atom class to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{utils namespace}}}}.  The
“count\_words()” function in “utils” uses the Tokenizer class internally
to split a line into words and count them, thus it will not modify the
argument string as the function in the Atoms class did and thus had a
variant using a copy buffer.  Unlike the old version, the new version
does not remove comments. For that you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils12trim_commentERKNSt6stringE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::trim\_comment() function}}}}} as shown in the example below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{nwords}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{count\PYGZus{}words}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{line}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nwords}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{count\PYGZus{}words}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{nwords}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{count\PYGZus{}words}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{line}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nwords}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{count\PYGZus{}words}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{trim\PYGZus{}comment}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils11count_wordsERKNSt6stringERKNSt6stringE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::count\_words()}}}}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::trim\_comments()}}


\end{sphinxseealso}



\subsection{Use utils::numeric() functions instead of force\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}numeric()}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:use-utils-numeric-functions-instead-of-force-numeric}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 18Sep2020.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “numeric()” conversion functions (including “inumeric()”,
“bnumeric()”, and “tnumeric()”) have been moved from the Force class to
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{utils namespace}}}}.  Also they take an
additional argument that selects whether the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Error::all()}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Error::one()}} function should be called in case of an error.  The
former should be used when \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} MPI processes call the conversion
function and the latter \sphinxstyleemphasis{must} be used when they are called from only
one or a subset of the MPI processes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{val}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{numeric}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{FLERR}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{num}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{inumeric}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{FLERR}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{val}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{numeric}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{FLERR}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{num}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{inumeric}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{FLERR}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{false}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\begin{sphinxseealso}{See also:}

\subsection{Use utils::open\_potential() function to open potential files}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:use-utils-open-potential-function-to-open-potential-files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 18Sep2020.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils14open_potentialERKNSt6stringEP6LAMMPSPi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::open\_potential()}}}}} function must be used to replace
calls to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{force\sphinxhyphen{}\textgreater{}open\_potential()}} and should be used to replace
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fopen()}} for opening potential files for reading.  The custom
function does three additional steps compared to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fopen()}}: 1) it will
try to parse the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UNITS:}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DATE:}} metadata and will stop with an
error on a units mismatch and will print the date info, if present, in
the log file; 2) for pair styles that support it, it will set up
possible automatic unit conversions based on the embedded unit
information and LAMMPS’ current units setting; 3) it will not only try
to open a potential file at the given path, but will also search in the
folders listed in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_POTENTIALS}} environment variable.  This
allows potential files to reside in a common location instead of having to
copy them around for simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{fp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{open\PYGZus{}potential}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{filename}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{fp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fopen}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{filename}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{r}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Simplify customized error messages}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:simplify-customized-error-messages}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 14May2021.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Aided by features of the bundled \{fmt\} library, error messages now
can have a variable number of arguments and the string will be interpreted
as a \{fmt\} style format string so that error messages can be
easily customized without having to use temporary buffers and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sprintf()}}.
Example:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fptr}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{NULL}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{str}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{128}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{sprintf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{str}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Cannot open AEAM potential file \PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{filename}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{error}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{one}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{FLERR}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{str}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fptr}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{nullptr}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{error}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{one}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{FLERR}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Cannot open AEAM potential file \PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}: \PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{filename}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{utils}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{getsyserror}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\subsection{Use of “override” instead of “virtual”}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:use-of-override-instead-of-virtual}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 17Feb2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since LAMMPS requires C++11, we switched to use the “override” keyword
instead of “virtual” to indicate polymorphism in derived classes.  This
allows the C++ compiler to better detect inconsistencies when an
override is intended or not.  Please note that “override” has to be
added to \sphinxstylestrong{all} polymorph functions in derived classes and “virtual”
\sphinxstyleemphasis{only} to the function in the base class (or the destructor).  Here is
an example from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FixWallReflect}} class:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{FixWallReflect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{LAMMPS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{virtual}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZti{}}\PYG{n}{FixWallReflect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{setmask}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{post\PYGZus{}integrate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{FixWallReflect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{LAMMPS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{char}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{o}{\PYGZti{}}\PYG{n}{FixWallReflect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{setmask}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{post\PYGZus{}integrate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{override}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This change set will neither cause a compilation failure, nor will it
change functionality, but if you plan to submit the updated code for
inclusion into the LAMMPS distribution, it will be requested for achieve
a consistent {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{programming style}}}}.

\PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{reverse\PYGZus{}comm\PYGZus{}fix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{reverse\PYGZus{}comm\PYGZus{}compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{reverse\PYGZus{}comm\PYGZus{}dump}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{forward\PYGZus{}comm}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{comm}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{reverse\PYGZus{}comm}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{this}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\subsection{Split of fix STORE into fix STORE/GLOBAL and fix STORE/PERATOM}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:split-of-fix-store-into-fix-store-global-and-fix-store-peratom}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 15Sep2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This change splits the GLOBAL and PERATOM modes of fix STORE into two
separate fixes STORE/GLOBAL and STORE/PERATOM.  There was very little
shared code between the two fix STORE modes and the two different code
paths had to be prefixed with if statements.  Furthermore, some flags
were used differently in the two modes leading to confusion.  Splitting
the code into two fix styles, makes it more easily maintainable.  Since
these are internal fixes, there is no user visible change.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZdq{}fix\PYGZus{}store.h\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{n}{FixStore}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{dynamic\PYGZus{}cast}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{FixStore}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{(}
\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}fix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{fmt}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{} \PYGZob{}\PYGZcb{} STORE peratom 1 13}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{id\PYGZus{}pole}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{names}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{n}{FixStore}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{dynamic\PYGZus{}cast}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{FixStore}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}fix\PYGZus{}by\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{id\PYGZus{}pole}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\subsection{Rename of fix STORE/PERATOM to fix STORE/ATOM and change of arguments}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:rename-of-fix-store-peratom-to-fix-store-atom-and-change-of-arguments}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 28Mar2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The available functionality of the internal fix to store per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
properties was expanded to enable storing data with ghost atoms and to
support binary restart files.  With those changes, the fix was renamed
to fix STORE/ATOM and the number and order of (required) arguments has
changed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Old syntax: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ID group\sphinxhyphen{}ID STORE/PERATOM rflag n1 n2 {[}n3{]}}}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rflag} = 0/1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} store per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values in restart file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n1 = 1, n2 = 1, \mathrm{no}\;n3 \to\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, single value per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n1 = 1, n2 > 1, \mathrm{no}\;n3 \to\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array, \sphinxstyleemphasis{n2} values per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n1 = 1, n2 > 0, n3 > 0 \to\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom tensor, \sphinxstyleemphasis{n2} x \sphinxstyleemphasis{n3} values per atom

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
New syntax:  \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ID group\sphinxhyphen{}ID STORE/ATOM n1 n2 gflag rflag}}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n1 = 1, n2 = 0 \to\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, single value per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n1 > 1, n2 = 0 \to\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array, \sphinxstyleemphasis{n1} values per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n1 > 0, n2 > 0 \to\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom tensor, \sphinxstyleemphasis{n1} x \sphinxstyleemphasis{n2} values per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{gflag} = 0/1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} communicate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values with ghost atoms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rflag} = 0/1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} store per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values in restart file

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since this is an internal fix, there is no user visible change.

\subsection{Refactored grid communication using Grid3d/Grid2d classes instead of GridComm}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_updating:refactored-grid-communication-using-grid3d-grid2d-classes-instead-of-gridcomm}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GridComm}} class was for creating and communicating distributed
grids was replaced by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid3d}} class with added functionality.
A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid2d}} class was also added for additional flexibility.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The new functionality and commands using the two grid classes are
discussed on the following documentation pages:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Using distributed grids}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Use of distributed grids within style classes}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have custom LAMMPS code, which uses the GridComm class, here are some notes
on how to adapt it for using the Grid3d class.
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{(}{)}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The constructor has changed to allow the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid3d}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid2d}}
classes to partition the global grid across processors, both for
owned and ghost grid cells.  Previously any class which called
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GridComm}} performed the partitioning itself and that information
was passed in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GridComm::GridComm()}} constructor.  There are
several “set” functions which can be called to alter how \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid3d}}
/ \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid2d}} perform the partitioning.  They should be sufficient
for most use cases of the grid classes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The partitioning is triggered by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup\_grid()}} method.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup()}} method of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GridComm}} class has been replaced
by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{setup\_comm()}} method in the new grid classes.  The syntax
for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{forward\_comm()}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reverse\_comm()}} methods is
slightly altered as is the syntax of the associated pack/unpack
callback methods.  But the functionality of these operations is the
same as before.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The new \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid3d}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Grid2d}} classes have additional
functionality for dynamic load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing of grids and their
associated data across processors.  This did not exist in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GridComm}} class.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This and more is explained in detail on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Use of distributed grids within style classes}}}} page.
The following LAMMPS source files can be used as illustrative examples
for how the new grid classes are used by computes, fixes, and various
KSpace solvers which use distributed FFT grids:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/fix\_ave\_grid.cpp}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/compute\_property\_grid.cpp}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}FIX/fix\_ttm\_grid.cpp}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/KSPACE/pppm.cpp}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This change is \sphinxstylestrong{required} or else the code will not compile.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Writing plugins}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_plugins:writing-plugins}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_plugins::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Plugins provide a mechanism to add functionality to a LAMMPS executable
without recompiling LAMMPS.  The functionality for this and the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{plugin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{plugin command}}}} are implemented in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details:pkg-plugin}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{PLUGIN package}}}} which must be installed to use plugins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Plugins use the operating system’s capability to load dynamic shared
object (DSO) files in a way similar shared libraries and then reference
specific functions in those DSOs.  Any DSO file with plugins has to
include an initialization function with a specific name,
“lammpsplugin\_init”, that has to follow specific rules described below.
When loading the DSO with the “plugin” command, this function is looked
up and called and will then register the contained plugin(s) with
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_PLUGIN\_PATH}} is set, then LAMMPS
will search the directory (or directories) listed in this path for files
with names that end in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plugin.so}} (e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{helloplugin.so}}) and will
try to load the contained plugins automatically at start\sphinxhyphen{}up.  For
plugins that are loaded this way, the behavior of LAMMPS should be
identical to a binary where the corresponding code was compiled in
statically as a package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
From the programmer perspective this can work because of the object
oriented design of LAMMPS where all pair style commands are derived from
the class Pair, all fix style commands from the class Fix and so on and
usually only functions present in those base classes are called
directly.  When a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style command}}}} command or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix command}}}} command is
issued a new instance of such a derived class is created.  This is done
by a so\sphinxhyphen{}called factory function which is mapped to the style name.  Thus
when, for example, the LAMMPS processes the command \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_style lj/cut
2.5}}, LAMMPS will look up the factory function for creating the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairLJCut}} class and then execute it.  The return value of that
function is a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair *}} pointer and the pointer will be assigned to the
location for the currently active pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A DSO file with a plugin thus has to implement such a factory function
and register it with LAMMPS so that it gets added to the map of available
styles of the given category.  To register a plugin with LAMMPS an
initialization function has to be present in the DSO file called
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_init}} which is called with three \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{void *}} arguments:
a pointer to the current LAMMPS instance, a pointer to the opened DSO
handle, and a pointer to the registration function.  The registration
function takes two arguments: a pointer to a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_t}} struct
with information about the plugin and a pointer to the current LAMMPS
instance.  Please see below for an example of how the registration is
done.


\subsection{Members of \sphinxstyleliteralintitle{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_t}}}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_plugins:members-of-lammpsplugin-t}}

\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only one of the two alternate creator entries can be used at a time and
which of those is determined by the style of plugin. The “creator.v1”
element is for factory functions of supported styles computing forces
(i.e. pair, bond, angle, dihedral, or improper styles) or command styles
and the function takes as single argument the pointer to the LAMMPS
instance. The factory function is cast to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_factory1}}
type before assignment.  The “creator.v2” element is for factory
functions creating an instance of a fix, compute, or region style and
takes three arguments: a pointer to the LAMMPS instance, an integer with
the length of the argument list and a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{char **}} pointer to the list of
arguments. The factory function pointer needs to be cast to the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_factory2}} type before assignment.


\subsection{Pair style example}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_plugins:pair-style-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, a hypothetical pair style plugin “morse2” implemented in
a class \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairMorse2}} in the files \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_morse2.h}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pair\_morse2.cpp}} with the factory function and initialization
function would look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZdq{}lammpsplugin.h\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZdq{}version.h\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{c+cp}{\PYGZsh{}}\PYG{c+cp}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+cpf}{\PYGZdq{}pair\PYGZus{}morse2.h\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{k}{using}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{namespace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}NS}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{static}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nf}{morse2creator}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LAMMPS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{new}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{PairMorse2}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k}{extern}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{C}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lammpsplugin\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{handle}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{regfunc}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{lammpsplugin\PYGZus{}regfunc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{register\PYGZus{}plugin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lammpsplugin\PYGZus{}regfunc}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{regfunc}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{lammpsplugin\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{version}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}VERSION}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{pair}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{morse2}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{info}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Morse2 variant pair style v1.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{author}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Axel Kohlmeyer (akohlmey@gmail.com)}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{creator}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{v1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lammpsplugin\PYGZus{}factory1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{morse2creator}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{handle}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{handle}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{register\PYGZus{}plugin}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The factory function in this example is called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{morse2creator()}}.  It
receives a pointer to the LAMMPS class as only argument and thus has to
be assigned to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{creator.v1} member of the plugin struct and cast to
the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_factory1}} function pointer type.  It returns a
pointer to the allocated class instance derived from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}} class.
This function may be declared static to avoid clashes with other
plugins.  The name of the derived class, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairMorse2}}, however must be
unique inside the entire LAMMPS executable.


\subsection{Fix style example}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_plugins:fix-style-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the factory function is for a fix or compute, which take three
arguments (a pointer to the LAMMPS class, the number of arguments and the
list of argument strings), then the pointer type is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_factory2}}
and it must be assigned to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{creator.v2} member of the plugin struct.
Below is an example for that:

\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{new}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{FixNVE2}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{argc}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{argv}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k}{extern}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{C}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lammpsplugin\PYGZus{}init}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{handle}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{void}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{regfunc}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{plugin}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{author}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Axel Kohlmeyer (akohlmey@gmail.com)}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\subsection{Command style example}

Command styles also use the first variant of factory function as
demonstrated in the following example, which also shows that the

\subsection{Additional Details}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_plugins:additional-details}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The initialization function \sphinxstylestrong{must} be called \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_init}}, it
\sphinxstylestrong{must} have C bindings and it takes three void pointers as arguments.
The first is a pointer to the LAMMPS class that calls it and it needs to
be passed to the registration function.  The second argument is a
pointer to the internal handle of the DSO file, this needs to be added
to the plugin info struct, so that the DSO can be closed and unloaded
when all its contained plugins are unloaded.  The third argument is a
function pointer to the registration function and needs to be stored
in a variable of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_regfunc}} type and then called with a
pointer to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_t}} struct and the pointer to the LAMMPS
instance as arguments to register a single plugin.  There may be multiple
calls to multiple plugins in the same initialization function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To register a plugin a struct of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_t}} needs to be filled
with relevant info: current LAMMPS version string, kind of style, name of
style, info string, author string, pointer to factory function, and the
DSO handle.  The registration function is called with a pointer to the address
of this struct and the pointer of the LAMMPS class.  The registration function
will then add the factory function of the plugin style to the respective
style map under the provided name.  It will also make a copy of the struct
in a list of all loaded plugins and update the reference counter for loaded
plugins from this specific DSO file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair style itself (i.e. the PairMorse2 class in this example) can be
written just like any other pair style that is included in LAMMPS.  For
a plugin, the use of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PairStyle}} macro in the section encapsulated
by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\#ifdef PAIR\_CLASS}} is not needed, since the mapping of the class
name to the style name is done by the plugin registration function with
the information from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammpsplugin\_t}} struct.  It may be included
in case the new code is intended to be later included in LAMMPS directly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A plugin may be registered under an existing style name.  In that case
the plugin will override the existing code.  This can be used to modify
the behavior of existing styles or to debug new versions of them without
having to re\sphinxhyphen{}compile or re\sphinxhyphen{}install all of LAMMPS.


\subsection{Compiling plugins}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_plugins:compiling-plugins}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Plugins need to be compiled with the same compilers and libraries
(e.g. MPI) and compilation settings (MPI on/off, OpenMP, integer sizes)
as the LAMMPS executable and library.  Otherwise the plugin will likely
not load due to mismatches in the function signatures (LAMMPS is C++ so
scope, type, and number of arguments are encoded into the symbol names
and thus differences in them will lead to failed plugin load commands).
Compilation of the plugin can be managed via both, CMake or traditional
GNU makefiles.  Some examples that can be used as a template are in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/plugins}} folder.  The CMake script code has some small
adjustments to allow building the plugins for running unit tests with
them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another example that converts the KIM package into a plugin can be found
in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/kim/plugin}} folder.  No changes to the sources of the
KIM package themselves are needed; only the plugin interface and loader
code needs to be added.  This example only supports building with CMake,
but is probably a more typical example. To compile you need to run CMake
with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}DLAMMPS\_SOURCE\_DIR=\textless{}path/to/lammps/src/folder\textgreater{}}}.  Other
configuration setting are identical to those for compiling LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A second example for a plugin from a package is in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/PACKAGES/pace/plugin}} folder that will create a plugin from
the ML\sphinxhyphen{}PACE package.  In this case the bulk of the code is in a static
external library that is being downloaded and compiled first and then
combined with the pair style wrapper and the plugin loader.  This
example also contains a NSIS script that can be used to create an
Installer package for Windows (the mutual licensing terms of the
external library and LAMMPS conflict when distributing binaries, so the
ML\sphinxhyphen{}PACE package cannot be linked statically, but the LAMMPS headers
required to build the plugin are also available under a less restrictive
license).  This will automatically set the required environment variable
and launching a (compatible) LAMMPS binary will load and register the
plugin and the ML\sphinxhyphen{}PACE package can then be used as it was linked into
LAMMPS.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{Adding tests for unit testing}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:adding-tests-for-unit-testing}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This section discusses adding or expanding tests for the unit test
infrastructure included into the LAMMPS source code distribution.
Unlike example inputs, unit tests focus on testing the “local” behavior
of individual features, tend to run fast, and should be set up to cover
as much of the added code as possible.  When contributing code to the
distribution, the LAMMPS developers will appreciate if additions to the
integrated unit test facility are included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given the complex nature of MD simulations where many operations can
only be performed when suitable “real” simulation environment has been
set up, not all tests will be unit tests in the strict definition of
the term.  They are rather executed on a more abstract level by issuing
LAMMPS script commands and then inspecting the changes to the internal
data.  For some classes of tests, generic test programs have been
written that can be applied to parts of LAMMPS that use the same
interface (via polymorphism) and those are driven by input files, so
tests can be added by simply adding more of those input files.  Those
tests should be seen more as a hybrid between unit and regression tests.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When adding tests it is recommended to also {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_development:testing}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{enable support for
code coverage reporting}}}}, and study the coverage reports
so that it is possible to monitor which parts of the code of a given
file are executed during the tests and which tests would need to be
added to increase the coverage.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tests are grouped into categories and corresponding folders.
The following sections describe how the tests are implemented and
executed in those categories with increasing complexity of tests
and implementation.


\subsection{Tests for utility functions}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-utility-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These tests are driven by programs in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/utils}} folder
and most closely resemble conventional unit tests. There is one test
program for each namespace or group of classes or file. The naming
convention for the sources and executables is that they start with
with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_}}.  The following sources and groups of tests are currently
available:
