\sphinxAtStartPar
To add tests either an existing source file needs to be modified or a
new source file needs to be added to the distribution and enabled for
testing.  To add a new file suitable CMake script code needs to be added
to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CMakeLists.txt}} file in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/utils}} folder.  Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{add\PYGZus{}executable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}tokenizer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}tokenizer.cpp}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{target\PYGZus{}link\PYGZus{}libraries}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}tokenizer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{PRIVATE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{GTest::GMockMain}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{GTest::GMock}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{GTest::GTest}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{add\PYGZus{}test}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{Tokenizer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}tokenizer}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This adds instructions to build the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_tokenizer}} executable from
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_tokenizer.cpp}} and links it with the GoogleTest libraries and the
LAMMPS library as well as it uses the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{main()}} function from the
GoogleMock library of GoogleTest.  The third line registers the executable
as a test program to be run from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}} under the name \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Tokenizer}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The test executable itself will execute multiple individual tests
through the GoogleTest framework. In this case each test consists of
creating a tokenizer class instance with a given string and explicit or
default separator choice, and then executing member functions of the
class and comparing their results with expected values. A few examples:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{TEST}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{Tokenizer}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{empty\PYGZus{}string}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{Tokenizer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}EQ}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{n}{TEST}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{Tokenizer}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{two\PYGZus{}words}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{Tokenizer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{test word}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}EQ}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{n}{TEST}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{Tokenizer}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{default\PYGZus{}separators}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{Tokenizer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{ }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}r}\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s}{ test }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}t}\PYG{l+s}{ word }\PYG{l+s+se}{\PYGZbs{}f}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}THAT}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{next}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Eq}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{test}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}THAT}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{next}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Eq}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{word}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}EQ}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each of these TEST functions will become an individual
test run by the test program. When using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}}
command as a front end to run the tests, their output
will be suppressed and only a summary printed, but adding
the ‘\sphinxhyphen{}V’ option will then produce output from the tests
above like the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+go}{[...]}
\PYG{g+go}{1: [ RUN      ] Tokenizer.empty\PYGZus{}string}
\PYG{g+go}{1: [       OK ] Tokenizer.empty\PYGZus{}string (0 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{1: [ RUN      ] Tokenizer.two\PYGZus{}words}
\PYG{g+go}{1: [       OK ] Tokenizer.two\PYGZus{}words (0 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{1: [ RUN      ] Tokenizer.default\PYGZus{}separators}
\PYG{g+go}{1: [       OK ] Tokenizer.default\PYGZus{}separators (0 ms)}
\PYG{g+go}{[...]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The MathEigen test collection has been adapted from a standalone test
and does not use the GoogleTest framework and thus not representative.
The other test sources, however, can serve as guiding examples for
additional tests.


\subsection{Tests for individual LAMMPS commands}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-individual-lammps-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tests \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/commands}} are a bit more complex as they require
to first create a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_lammps:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS6LAMMPSE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS}}}}} class instance
and then use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Cplusplus::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{C++ API}}}} to pass individual commands
to that LAMMPS instance.  For that reason these tests use a GoogleTest
“test fixture”, i.e. a class derived from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{testing::Test}} that will
create (and delete) the required LAMMPS class instance for each set of
tests in a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TEST\_F()}} function.  Please see the individual source files
for different examples of setting up suitable test fixtures.  Here is an
example for implementing a test using a fixture by first checking the
default value and then issuing LAMMPS commands and checking whether they
have the desired effect:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{TEST\PYGZus{}F}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{SimpleCommandsTest}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ResetTimestep}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}EQ}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{update}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{ntimestep}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{BEGIN\PYGZus{}HIDE\PYGZus{}OUTPUT}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep 10}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{END\PYGZus{}HIDE\PYGZus{}OUTPUT}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}EQ}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{update}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{ntimestep}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{BEGIN\PYGZus{}HIDE\PYGZus{}OUTPUT}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{END\PYGZus{}HIDE\PYGZus{}OUTPUT}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{ASSERT\PYGZus{}EQ}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{update}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{ntimestep}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{TEST\PYGZus{}FAILURE}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{.*ERROR: Timestep must be \PYGZgt{}= 0.*}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep \PYGZhy{}10}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{TEST\PYGZus{}FAILURE}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{.*ERROR: Illegal reset\PYGZus{}timestep .*}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{TEST\PYGZus{}FAILURE}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{.*ERROR: Illegal reset\PYGZus{}timestep .*}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep 10 10}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{TEST\PYGZus{}FAILURE}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{.*ERROR: Expected integer .*}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep xxx}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please note the use of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BEGIN\_HIDE\_OUTPUT}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{END\_HIDE\_OUTPUT}}
functions that will capture output from running LAMMPS.  This is normally
discarded but by setting the verbose flag (via setting the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TEST\_ARGS}}
environment variable, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TEST\_ARGS=\sphinxhyphen{}v}}) it can be printed and used to
understand why tests fail unexpectedly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The specifics of so\sphinxhyphen{}called “death tests”, i.e. conditions where LAMMPS
should fail and throw an exception, are implemented in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TEST\_FAILURE()}} macro. These tests operate by capturing the screen
output when executing the failing command and then comparing that with a
provided regular expression string pattern.  Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{TEST\PYGZus{}F}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{SimpleCommandsTest}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{UnknownCommand}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{TEST\PYGZus{}FAILURE}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{.*ERROR: Unknown command.*}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{input}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{n}{one}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{XXX one two}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Tests for the C\sphinxhyphen{}style library interface}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-the-c-style-library-interface}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tests for validating the LAMMPS C\sphinxhyphen{}style library interface are in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/c\sphinxhyphen{}library}} folder.  They are implemented either to be used
for utility functions or for LAMMPS commands, but use the functions
implemented in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/library.cpp}} file as much as possible.  There
may be some overlap with other tests, but only in as much as is required
to test the C\sphinxhyphen{}style library API.  The tests are distributed over
multiple test programs which try to match the grouping of the
functions in the source code and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:lammps-c-api}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{in the manual}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This group of tests also includes tests invoking LAMMPS in parallel
through the library interface, provided that LAMMPS was compiled with
MPI support.  These include tests where LAMMPS is run in multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition
mode or only on a subset of the MPI world communicator.  The CMake
script code for adding this kind of test looks like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{BUILD\PYGZus{}MPI}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nb}{add\PYGZus{}executable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}library\PYGZus{}mpi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}library\PYGZus{}mpi.cpp}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nb}{target\PYGZus{}link\PYGZus{}libraries}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}library\PYGZus{}mpi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{PRIVATE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{GTest::GTest}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{GTest::GMock}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nb}{target\PYGZus{}compile\PYGZus{}definitions}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{test\PYGZus{}library\PYGZus{}mpi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{PRIVATE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{TEST\PYGZus{}CONFIG\PYGZus{}DEFS}\PYG{o}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nb}{add\PYGZus{}mpi\PYGZus{}test}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{NAME}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{LibraryMPI}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{NUM\PYGZus{}PROCS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{COMMAND}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n+nv}{TARGET\PYGZus{}FILE:test\PYGZus{}library\PYGZus{}mpi}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{endif}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note the custom function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{add\_mpi\_test()}} which adapts how \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}}
will execute the test so it is launched in parallel (with 4 MPI ranks).


\subsection{Tests for the Python module and package}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-the-python-module-and-package}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/python}} folder contains primarily tests for classes and
functions in the LAMMPS python module but also for commands in the
PYTHON package.  These tests are only enabled if the necessary
prerequisites are detected or enabled during configuration and
compilation of LAMMPS (shared library build enabled, Python interpreter
found, Python development files found).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Python tests are implemented using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest}} standard Python
module and split into multiple files with similar categories as the
tests for the C\sphinxhyphen{}style library interface.


\subsection{Tests for the Fortran interface}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-the-fortran-interface}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tests for using the Fortran module are in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/fortran}}
folder.  Since they are also using the GoogleTest library, they require
implementing test wrappers in C++ that will call fortran functions
which provide a C function interface through ISO\_C\_BINDINGS that will in
turn call the functions in the LAMMPS Fortran module.


\subsection{Tests for the C++\sphinxhyphen{}style library interface}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tests in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/cplusplus}} folder are somewhat similar to
the tests for the C\sphinxhyphen{}style library interface, but do not need to test the
several convenience and utility functions that are only available through
the C\sphinxhyphen{}style interface.  Instead it can focus on the more generic features
that are used internally.  This part of the unit tests is currently still
mostly in the planning stage.


\subsection{Tests for reading and writing file formats}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-reading-and-writing-file-formats}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/formats}} folder contains test programs for reading and
writing files like data files, restart files, potential files or dump files.
This covers simple things like the file i/o convenience functions in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::}} namespace to complex tests of atom styles where creating and
deleting atoms with different properties is tested in different ways
and through script commands or reading and writing of data or restart files.


\subsection{Tests for styles computing or modifying forces}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-styles-computing-or-modifying-forces}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These are tests common configurations for pair styles, bond styles,
angle styles, kspace styles and certain fix styles.  Those are tests
driven by some test executables build from sources in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/force\sphinxhyphen{}styles}} folder and use LAMMPS input template and data
files as well as input files in YAML format from the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/force\sphinxhyphen{}styles/tests}} folder. The YAML file names have to
follow some naming conventions so they get associated with the test
programs and categorized and listed with canonical names in the list
of tests as displayed by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest \sphinxhyphen{}N}}.  If you add a new YAML file,
you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}run CMake to update the corresponding list of tests.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A minimal YAML file for a (molecular) pair style test will looks
something like the following (see \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mol\sphinxhyphen{}pair\sphinxhyphen{}zero.yaml}}):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nn}{\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}}
\PYG{n+nt}{lammps\PYGZus{}version}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{24}\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{Aug}\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{2020}
\PYG{n+nt}{date\PYGZus{}generated}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{Tue}\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{Sep}\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{15}\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{09:44:21}\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{202}
\PYG{n+nt}{epsilon}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{1e\PYGZhy{}14}
\PYG{n+nt}{prerequisites}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{!}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{|}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{atom full}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{pair zero}
\PYG{n+nt}{pre\PYGZus{}commands}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{!}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nt}{post\PYGZus{}commands}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{!}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nt}{input\PYGZus{}file}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{in.fourmol}
\PYG{n+nt}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{zero}\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{8.0}
\PYG{n+nt}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{!}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{|}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{* *}
\PYG{n+nt}{extract}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{!}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n+nt}{natoms}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{29}
\PYG{n+nt}{init\PYGZus{}vdwl}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{0}
\PYG{n+nt}{init\PYGZus{}coul}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{0}

\PYG{p+pIndicator}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{...}\PYG{p+pIndicator}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following table describes the available keys and their purpose for
testing pair styles:

\sphinxAtStartPar
The test program will read all this data from the YAML file and then
create a LAMMPS instance, apply the settings/commands from the YAML file
as needed and then issue a “run 0” command, write out a restart file, a
data file and a coeff file. The actual test will then compare computed
energies, stresses, and forces with the reference data, issue a “run 4”
command and compare to the second set of reference data.  This will be
run with both the newton\_pair setting enabled and disabled and is
expected to generate the same results (allowing for some numerical
noise). Then it will restart from the previously generated restart and
compare with the reference and also start from the data file.  A final
check will use multi\sphinxhyphen{}cutoff r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA (if supported by the pair style) at
a 1:1 split and compare to the Verlet results.  These sets of tests are
run with multiple test fixtures for accelerated styles (OPT, OPENMP,
INTEL, KOKKOS (OpenMP only)) and for the latter three with 4 OpenMP
threads enabled.  For these tests the relative error (epsilon) is lowered
by a common factor due to the additional numerical noise, but the tests
are still comparing to the same reference data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional tests will check whether all listed extract keywords are
supported and have the correct dimensionality and the final set of tests
will set up a few pairs of atoms explicitly and in such a fashion that
the forces on the atoms computed from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::compute()}} will match
individually with the results from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::single()}}, if the pair style
does support that functionality.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With this scheme a large fraction of the code of any tested pair style
will be executed and consistent results are required for different
settings and between different accelerated pair style variants and the
base class, as well as for computing individual pairs through the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::single()}} method where supported.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_pair\_style}} tester is used with 4 categories of test inputs:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pair styles compatible with molecular systems using bonded
interactions and exclusions.  For pair styles requiring a KSpace style
the KSpace computations are disabled.  The YAML files match the
pattern “mol\sphinxhyphen{}pair\sphinxhyphen{}*.yaml” and the tests are correspondingly labeled
with “MolPairStyle:*”

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pair styles not compatible with the previous input template.
The YAML files match the pattern “atomic\sphinxhyphen{}pair\sphinxhyphen{}*.yaml” and the tests are
correspondingly labeled with “AtomicPairStyle:*”

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
manybody pair styles.
The YAML files match the pattern “atomic\sphinxhyphen{}pair\sphinxhyphen{}*.yaml” and the tests are
correspondingly labeled with “AtomicPairStyle:*”

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
kspace styles.
The YAML files match the pattern “kspace\sphinxhyphen{}*.yaml” and the tests are
correspondingly labeled with “KSpaceStyle:*”. In these cases a compatible
pair style is defined, but the computation of the pair style contributions
is disabled.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_bond\_style}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_angle\_style}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_dihedral\_style}}, and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_improper\_style}} tester programs are set up in a similar fashion and
share support functions with the pair style tester.  The final group of
tests in this section is for fix styles that add/manipulate forces and
velocities, e.g. for time integration, thermostats and more.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding a new test is easiest done by copying and modifying an existing YAML
file for a style that is similar to one to be tested.  The file name should
follow the naming conventions described above and after copying the file,
the first step is to replace the style names where needed.  The coefficient
values do not have to be meaningful, just in a reasonable range for the
given system.  It does not matter if some forces are large, as long as
they do not diverge.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The template input files define a large number of index variables at the top
that can be modified inside the YAML file to control the behavior.  For example,
if a pair style requires a “newton on” setting, the following can be used in
as the “pre\_commands” section:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nt}{pre\PYGZus{}commands}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{!}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{|}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{variable newton\PYGZus{}pair delete}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{variable newton\PYGZus{}pair index on}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
And for a pair style requiring a kspace solver the following would be used as
the “post\_commands” section:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nt}{post\PYGZus{}commands}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kt}{!}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p+pIndicator}{|}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{pair\PYGZus{}modify table 0}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{kspace\PYGZus{}style pppm/tip4p 1.0e\PYGZhy{}6}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{kspace\PYGZus{}modify gewald 0.3}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+no}{kspace\PYGZus{}modify compute no}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this disables computing the kspace contribution, but still will run
the setup.  The “gewald” parameter should be set explicitly to speed up the run.
For styles with long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatics, typically two tests are added one using
the (slower) analytic approximation of the erfc() function and the other using
the tabulated coulomb, to test both code paths.  The reference results in the YAML
files then should be compared manually, if they agree well enough within the limits
of those two approximations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_pair\_style}} and equivalent programs have special command line options
to update the YAML files. Running a command like

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
test\PYGZus{}pair\PYGZus{}style\PYG{+w}{ }mol\PYGZhy{}pair\PYGZhy{}lennard\PYGZus{}mdf.yaml\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{+w}{ }new.yaml
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
will read the settings from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mol\sphinxhyphen{}pair\sphinxhyphen{}lennard\_mdf.yaml}} file and then compute
the reference data and write a new file with to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{new.yaml}}.  If this step fails,
there are likely some (LAMMPS or YAML) syntax issues in the YAML file that need to
be resolved and then one can compare the two files to see if the output is as expected.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible to do an update in place with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
test\PYGZus{}pair\PYGZus{}style\PYG{+w}{ }mol\PYGZhy{}pair\PYGZhy{}lennard\PYGZus{}mdf.yaml\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
And one can finally run the full set of tests with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
test\PYGZus{}pair\PYGZus{}style\PYG{+w}{ }mol\PYGZhy{}pair\PYGZhy{}lennard\PYGZus{}mdf.yaml
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will just print a summary of the groups of tests.  When using the “\sphinxhyphen{}v” flag
the test will also keep any LAMMPS output and when using the “\sphinxhyphen{}s” flag, there
will be some statistics reported on the relative errors for the individual checks
which can help to figure out what would be a good choice of the epsilon parameter.
It should be as small as possible to catch any unintended side effects from changes
elsewhere, but large enough to accommodate the numerical noise due to the implementation
of the potentials and differences in compilers.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These kinds of tests can be very sensitive to compiler optimization and
thus the expectation is that they pass with compiler optimization turned
off. When compiler optimization is enabled, there may be some failures, but
one has to carefully check whether those are acceptable due to the enhanced
numerical noise from reordering floating\sphinxhyphen{}point math operations or due to
the compiler mis\sphinxhyphen{}compiling the code. That is not always obvious.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Tests for programs in the tools folder}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:tests-for-programs-in-the-tools-folder}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest/tools}} folder contains tests for programs in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools}} folder.  This currently only contains tests for the LAMMPS
shell, which are implemented as a python scripts using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unittest}}
Python module and launching the tool commands through the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{subprocess}}
Python module.


\subsection{Troubleshooting failed unit tests}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_unittest:troubleshooting-failed-unit-tests}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The are by default no unit tests for newly added features (e.g. pair, fix,
or compute styles) unless your pull request also includes tests for the
added features.  If you are modifying some features, you may see failures
for existing tests, if your modifications have some unexpected side effects
or your changes render the existing test invalid.  If you are adding an
accelerated version of an existing style, then only tests for INTEL,
KOKKOS (with OpenMP only), OPENMP, and OPT will be run automatically.
Tests for the GPU package are time consuming and thus are only run
\sphinxstyleemphasis{after} a merge, or when a special label, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gpu\_unit\_tests}} is added
to the pull request.  After the test has started, it is often best to
remove the label since every PR activity will re\sphinxhyphen{}trigger the test (that
is a limitation of triggering a test with a label).  Support for unit
tests when using KOKKOS with GPU acceleration is currently not supported.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When you see a failed build on GitHub, click on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Details}} to be taken
to the corresponding LAMMPS Jenkins CI web page.  Click on the “Exit”
symbol near the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Logout}} button on the top right of that page to go to
the “classic view”.  In the classic view, there is a list of the
individual runs that make up this test run (they are shown but cannot be
inspected in the default view).  You can click on any of those.
Clicking on \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Test Result}} will display the list of failed tests. Click
on the “Status” column to sort the tests based on their Failed or Passed
status.  Then click on the failed test to expand its output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the following output snippet shows the failed unit test

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+go}{[ RUN      ] PairStyle.gpu}
\PYG{g+go}{/home/builder/workspace/dev/pull\PYGZus{}requests/ubuntu\PYGZus{}gpu/unit\PYGZus{}tests/cmake\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}opencl\PYGZus{}mixed\PYGZus{}smallbig\PYGZus{}clang\PYGZus{}static/unittest/force\PYGZhy{}styles/test\PYGZus{}main.cpp:63: Failure}
\PYG{g+go}{Expected: (err) \PYGZlt{}= (epsilon)}
\PYG{g+go}{Actual: 0.00018957912910606503 vs 0.0001}
\PYG{g+go}{Google Test trace:}
\PYG{g+go}{/home/builder/workspace/dev/pull\PYGZus{}requests/ubuntu\PYGZus{}gpu/unit\PYGZus{}tests/cmake\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}opencl\PYGZus{}mixed\PYGZus{}smallbig\PYGZus{}clang\PYGZus{}static/unittest/force\PYGZhy{}styles/test\PYGZus{}main.cpp:56: EXPECT\PYGZus{}FORCES: init\PYGZus{}forces (newton off)}
\PYG{g+go}{/home/builder/workspace/dev/pull\PYGZus{}requests/ubuntu\PYGZus{}gpu/unit\PYGZus{}tests/cmake\PYGZus{}gpu\PYGZus{}opencl\PYGZus{}mixed\PYGZus{}smallbig\PYGZus{}clang\PYGZus{}static/unittest/force\PYGZhy{}styles/test\PYGZus{}main.cpp:64: Failure}
\PYG{g+go}{Expected: (err) \PYGZlt{}= (epsilon)}
\PYG{g+go}{Actual: 0.00022892713393549854 vs 0.0001}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The failed assertions provide line numbers in the test source
(e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{test\_main.cpp:56}}), from which one can understand what
specific assertion failed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the force style engine runs one of a small number of systems
in a rather off\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium configuration with a few atoms for a few
steps, writes data and restart files, uses {\hyperref[\detokenize{clear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{the clear command}}}} to reset LAMMPS, and then runs from those files with different
settings (e.g. newton on/off) and integrators (e.g. verlet vs. respa).
Beyond potential issues/bugs in the source code, the mismatch between
the expected and actual values could be that force arrays are not
properly cleared between multiple run commands or that class members are
not correctly initialized or written to or read from a data or restart
file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
While the epsilon (relative precision) for a single, \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE\_754}{IEEE 754 compliant}, double precision floating
point operation is at about 2.2e\sphinxhyphen{}16, the achievable precision for the
tests is lower due to most numbers being sums over intermediate results
and the non\sphinxhyphen{}associativity of floating point math leading to larger
errors.  As a rule of thumb, the test epsilon can often be in the range
5.0e\sphinxhyphen{}14 to 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}13.  But for “noisy” force kernels, e.g. those a larger
amount of arithmetic operations involving \sphinxtitleref{exp()}, \sphinxtitleref{log()} or \sphinxtitleref{sin()}
functions, and also due to the effect of compiler optimization or differences
between compilers or platforms, epsilon may need to be further relaxed,
sometimes epsilon can be relaxed to 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}12. If interpolation or lookup
tables are used, epsilon may need to be set to 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}10 or even higher.
For tests of accelerated styles, the per\sphinxhyphen{}test epsilon is multiplied
by empirical factors that take into account the differences in the order
of floating point operations or that some or most intermediate operations
may be done using approximations or with single precision floating point
math.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To rerun the failed unit test individually, change to the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build}} directory
and run the test with verbose output. For example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
env\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{TEST\PYGZus{}ARGS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }ctest\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}R\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZca{}MolPairStyle:lj\PYGZus{}cut\PYGZus{}coul\PYGZus{}long\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}V
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ctest}} with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}V}} flag also shows the exact command line
of the test. One can then use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gdb \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}args}} to further debug and
catch exceptions with the test command, for example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
gdb\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}args\PYG{+w}{ }/path/to/lammps/build/test\PYGZus{}pair\PYGZus{}style\PYG{+w}{ }/path/to/lammps/unittest/force\PYGZhy{}styles/tests/mol\PYGZhy{}pair\PYGZhy{}lj\PYGZus{}cut\PYGZus{}coul\PYGZus{}long.yaml
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is recommended to configure the build with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}D
BUILD\_SHARED\_LIBS=on}} and use a custom linker to shorten the build time
during recompilation.  Installing \sphinxtitleref{ccache} in your development
environment helps speed up recompilation by caching previous
compilations and detecting when the same compilation is being done
again.  Please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_development::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Development build options}}}} for further details.

\sphinxstepscope


\section{C++ base classes}
\label{\detokenize{Classes:c-base-classes}}\label{\detokenize{Classes::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS is designed to be used as a C++ class library where one can set
up and drive a simulation through creating a class instance and then
calling some abstract operations or commands on that class or its member
class instances.  These are interfaced to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{C library API}}}}, which providing an additional level of abstraction
simplification for common operations. The C API is also the basis for
calling LAMMPS from Python or Fortran.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When used from a C++ program, most of the symbols and functions in
LAMMPS are wrapped into the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS}} namespace so they will not
collide with your own classes or other libraries. This, however, does
not extend to the additional libraries bundled with LAMMPS in the lib
folder and some of the low\sphinxhyphen{}level code of some packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Behind the scenes this is implemented through inheritance and
polymorphism where base classes define the abstract interface and
derived classes provide the specialized implementation for specific
models or optimizations or ports to accelerator platforms.  This
document will provide an outline of the fundamental class hierarchy and
some selected examples for derived classes of specific models.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Please see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library:thread-safety}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{note about thread\sphinxhyphen{}safety}}}}
in the library Howto doc page.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{LAMMPS Class}
\label{\detokenize{Classes_lammps:lammps-class}}\label{\detokenize{Classes_lammps::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS class is encapsulating an MD simulation state and thus it is
the class that needs to be created when starting a new simulation system
state.  The LAMMPS executable essentially creates one instance of this
class and passes the command line flags and tells it to process the
provided input (a file or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stdin}}).  It shuts the class down when
control is returned to it and then exits.  When using LAMMPS as a
library from another code it is required to create an instance of this
class, either directly from C++ with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{new LAMMPS()}} or through one
of the library interface functions like {\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_create:_CPPv411lammps_openiPPc8MPI_CommPPv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_open()}}}}} of the
C\sphinxhyphen{}library interface, or the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module:lammps.lammps}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps.lammps}}}}} class constructor
of the Python module, or the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps()}} constructor of the Fortran
module.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to avoid clashes of function names, all of the core code in
LAMMPS is placed into the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS}} namespace.  Functions or variables
outside of that namespace must be “static”, i.e.  visible only to the
scope of the file/object they are defined in.  Code in packages or the
libraries in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lib}} folder may not adhere to this as some of them
are adapted from legacy code or consist of external libraries with their
own requirements and policies.

\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Class to provide access to atom data. 

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Atom class provides access to atom style related global settings and
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data that is stored with atoms and migrates with them from
sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain to sub\sphinxhyphen{}domain as atoms move around.  This includes topology
data, which is stored with either one specific atom or all atoms involved
depending on the settings of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton command}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The actual per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data is allocated and managed by one of the various
classes derived from the AtomVec class as determined by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style command}}}}.  The pointers in the Atom class
are updated by the AtomVec class as needed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function returns the list index of a custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom property
with the name “name”, also returning by reference its data type,
number of values per atom, and if it is communicated to ghost particles.
Classes rarely need to check on ghost communication and so \sphinxtitleref{find\_custom}
is typically preferred to this function. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair amoeba}}}}
for an example where checking ghost communication is necessary.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{\&flag}} \textendash{} Returns data type of property: 0 for int, 1 for double 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{\&cols}} \textendash{} Returns number of values: 0 for a single value, 1 or more for a vector of values 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is a way to access internal per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data.  This data is
distributed across MPI ranks and thus only the data for “local” atoms
are expected to be available.  Whether also data for “ghost” atoms is
stored and up\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}date depends on various simulation settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This table lists a large part of the supported names, their data types,
length of the data area, and a short description.

Class for processing commands and input files. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Input class contains methods for reading, pre\sphinxhyphen{}processing and
parsing LAMMPS commands and input files and will dispatch commands
to the respective class instances or contain the code to execute
the commands directly.  It also contains the instance of the
Variable class which performs computations and text substitutions.

Return the wall clock state for the current process in seconds

\sphinxAtStartPar
This clock is counting continuous time and is initialized during load of the executable/library. Its absolute value must be considered arbitrary and thus elapsed wall times are measured in taking differences. It is therefore to be used in a similar fashion as MPI\_Wtime() but has a different offset, usually leading to better resolution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Try to detect pathname from FILE pointer

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently only supported on Linux, MacOS, and Windows. Otherwise will report “(unknown)”.

\sphinxAtStartPar

On Linux the folder /proc/self/fd holds symbolic links to the actual pathnames associated with each open file descriptor of the current process. On MacOS the same kind of information can be obtained using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fcntl(fd,F\_GETPATH,buf)}}. On Windows we use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GetFinalPathNameByHandleA()}} which is available with Windows Vista and later. If the buffer is too small (\textless{} 16 bytes) a null pointer is returned.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function is used to provide a filename with error messages in functions where the filename is not passed as an argument, but the FILE * pointer. 
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{fp}} \textendash{} FILE pointer struct from STDIO library for which we want to detect the name 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{buf}} \textendash{} storage buffer for pathname. output will be truncated if not large enough 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{len}} \textendash{} size of storage buffer. output will be truncated to this length \sphinxhyphen{} 1 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
pointer to the storage buffer with path or a NULL pointer if buf is invalid or the buffer size is too small

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

Find pathname of an executable in the standard search path

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function will traverse the list of directories in the PATH environment variable and look for the executable \sphinxstyleemphasis{cmd}. If the file exists and is executable the full path is returned as string, otherwise an empty string is returned.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On Windows the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cmd} string must not include an extension as this function will automatically append the extensions “.exe”, “.com” and “.bat” and look for those paths. On Windows also the current directory is checked (and first), but otherwise is not checked unless “.” exists in the PATH environment variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Because of the nature of the check, this will not detect shell functions built\sphinxhyphen{}in command or aliases.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Utility functions}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:utility-functions}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils}} sub\sphinxhyphen{}namespace inside the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS}} namespace provides
a collection of convenience functions and utilities that perform common
tasks that are required repeatedly throughout the LAMMPS code like
reading or writing to files with error checking or translation of
strings into specific types of numbers with checking for validity.  This
reduces redundant implementations and encourages consistent behavior and
thus has some overlap with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_platform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{“platform” sub\sphinxhyphen{}namespace}}}}.


\subsection{I/O with status check and similar functions}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:i-o-with-status-check-and-similar-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The the first two functions are wrappers around the corresponding C
library calls \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fgets()}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fread()}}.  They will check if there
were errors on reading or an unexpected end\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}file state was reached.
In that case, the functions will stop with an error message, indicating
the name of the problematic file, if possible unless the \sphinxstyleemphasis{error} argument
is a NULL pointer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils11fgets_truncEPciP4FILE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::fgets\_trunc()}}}}}
function will work similar for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fgets()}} but it will read in a whole
line (i.e. until the end of line or end of file), but store only as many
characters as will fit into the buffer including a final newline
character and the terminating NULL byte.  If the line in the file is
longer it will thus be truncated in the buffer.  This function is used
by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils20read_lines_from_fileEP4FILEiiPci8MPI_Comm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::read\_lines\_from\_file()}}}}} to read individual lines but
make certain they follow the size constraints.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils20read_lines_from_fileEP4FILEiiPci8MPI_Comm}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::read\_lines\_from\_file()}}}}} function will read the
requested number of lines of a maximum length into a buffer and will
return 0 if successful or 1 if not. It also guarantees that all lines
are terminated with a newline character and the entire buffer with a
NULL character.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Read N lines of text from file into buffer and broadcast them

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function uses repeated calls to fread() to fill a buffer with newline terminated text. If a line does not end in a newline (e.g. at the end of a file), it is added. The caller has to allocate an nlines by nmax sized buffer for storing the text data. Reading is done by MPI rank 0 of the given communicator only, and thus only MPI rank 0 needs to provide a valid file pointer.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{fp}} \textendash{} file pointer used by fread 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{nlines}} \textendash{} number of lines to be read 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{nmax}} \textendash{} maximum length of a single line 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{buffer}} \textendash{} buffer for storing the data. 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{me}} \textendash{} MPI rank of calling process in MPI communicator 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{comm}} \textendash{} MPI communicator for broadcast 

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
1 if the read was short, 0 if read was successful 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\subsection{String to number conversions with validity check}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:string-to-number-conversions-with-validity-check}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These functions should be used to convert strings to numbers. They are
are strongly preferred over C library calls like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atoi()}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{atof()}} since they check if the \sphinxstylestrong{entire} string is a valid
(floating\sphinxhyphen{}point or integer) number, and will error out instead of
silently returning the result of a partial conversion or zero in cases
where the string is not a valid number.  This behavior improves
detecting typos or issues when processing input files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils7logicalEPKciPKcbP6LAMMPS}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::logical()}}}}} function
will convert a string into a boolean and will only accept certain words.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{do\_abort} flag should be set to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}} in case  this function
is called only on a single MPI rank, as that will then trigger the
a call to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Error::one()}} for errors instead of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Error::all()}}
and avoids a “hanging” calculation when run in parallel.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please also see {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils10is_integerERKNSt6stringE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::is\_integer()}}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils9is_doubleERKNSt6stringE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::is\_double()}}}}} for testing
strings for compliance without conversion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Check if a string will likely have UTF\sphinxhyphen{}8 encoded characters

\sphinxAtStartPar
UTF\sphinxhyphen{}8 uses the 7\sphinxhyphen{}bit standard ASCII table for the first 127 characters and all other characters are encoded as multiple bytes. For the multi\sphinxhyphen{}byte characters the first byte has either the highest two, three, or four bits set followed by a zero bit and followed by one, two, or three more bytes, respectively, where the highest bit is set and the second highest bit set to 0. The remaining bits combined are the character code, which is thus limited to 21\sphinxhyphen{}bits.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the sake of efficiency this test only checks if a character in the string has the highest bit set and thus is very likely an UTF\sphinxhyphen{}8 character. It will not be able to tell this this is a valid UTF\sphinxhyphen{}8 character or whether it is a 2\sphinxhyphen{}byte, 3\sphinxhyphen{}byte, or 4\sphinxhyphen{}byte character.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Match text against a simplified regex pattern

\sphinxAtStartPar

More flexible and specific matching of a string against a pattern. This function is supposed to be a more safe, more specific and simple to use API to find pattern matches. The purpose is to replace uses of either strncmp() or strstr() in the code base to find sub\sphinxhyphen{}strings safely. With strncmp() finding prefixes, the number of characters to match must be counted, which can lead to errors, while using “\textasciicircum{}pattern” will do the same with less problems. Matching for suffixes using strstr() is not as specific as ‘pattern\$’, and complex matches, e.g. “\textasciicircum{}rigid.*\textbackslash{}/small.*”, to match all small body optimized rigid fixes require only one test.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The use of std::string arguments allows for simple concatenation even with char * type variables. Example: utils::strmatch(text, std::string(“\textasciicircum{}”) + charptr)

Check if string is a valid type label, or numeric type, or numeric type range. Numeric type or type range may only contain digits or the ‘*’ character. Type label strings may not contain a digit, or a ‘*’, or a ‘\#’ character as the first character to distinguish them from comments and numeric types or type ranges. They also may not contain any whitespace. If the string is a valid numeric type or type range the function returns 0, if it is a valid type label the function returns 1, otherwise it returns \sphinxhyphen{}1.

Compute index bounds derived from a string with a possible wildcard

\sphinxAtStartPar
This functions processes the string in \sphinxstyleemphasis{str} and set the values of \sphinxstyleemphasis{nlo} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{nhi} according to the following five cases:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a single number, i: nlo = i; nhi = i;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a single asterisk, *: nlo = nmin; nhi = nmax;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a single number followed by an asterisk, i*: nlo = i; nhi = nmax;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a single asterisk followed by a number, *i: nlo = nmin; nhi = i;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
two numbers with an asterisk in between. i*j: nlo = i; nhi = j;

\end{itemize}

Expand list of arguments when containing fix/compute wildcards

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function searches the list of arguments in \sphinxstyleemphasis{arg} for strings of the kind c\_ID{[}*{]}, f\_ID{[}*{]}, v\_ID{[}*{]}, i2\_ID{[}*{]}, d2\_ID{[}*{]}, or c\_ID:gname:dname{[}*{]} referring to computes, fixes, vector style variables, custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom arrays, or grids, respectively. Any such strings are replaced by one or more strings with the ‘*’ character replaced by the corresponding possible numbers as determined from the fix, compute, variable, property, or grid instance. Unrecognized strings are just copied. If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} parameter is set to 0, expand global vectors, but not global arrays; if it is set to 1, expand global arrays (by column) but not global vectors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If any expansion happens, the earg list and all its strings are new allocations and must be freed explicitly by the caller. Otherwise arg and earg will point to the same address and no explicit de\sphinxhyphen{}allocation is needed by the caller.

This function implements an optimized version of pow(2.0, x) that does not check for valid arguments and thus may only be used where arguments are well behaved. The implementation makes assumptions about the layout of double precision floating point numbers in memory and thus will only work on little endian CPUs. If little endian cannot be safely detected, the result of calling pow(2.0, x) will be returned. This function also is the basis for the fast exponential fm\_exp(x).

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}

value of 2\textasciicircum{}x as double precision number 

\end{description}\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function implements an optimized version of exp(x) for little endian CPUs. It calls the exp2\_x86(x) function with a suitable prefactor to x to return exp(x). The implementation makes assumptions about the layout of double precision floating point numbers in memory and thus will only work on little endian CPUs. If little endian cannot be safely detected, the result of calling the exp(x) implementation in the standard math library will be returned.

Fast scaled error function complement exp(x*x)*erfc(x) for coul/long styles

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a portable fast implementation of exp(x*x)*erfc(x) that can be used in coul/long pair styles as a replacement for the polynomial expansion that is/was widely used. Unlike the polynomial expansion, that is only accurate at the level of single precision floating point it provides full double precision accuracy, but at comparable speed (unlike the erfc() implementation shipped with GNU standard math library).

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\section{Tokenizer classes}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:tokenizer-classes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The purpose of the tokenizer classes is to simplify the recurring task
of breaking lines of text down into words and/or numbers.
Traditionally, LAMMPS code would be using the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{strtok()}} function from
the C library for that purpose, but that function has two significant
disadvantages: 1) it cannot be used concurrently from different LAMMPS
instances since it stores its status in a global variable and 2) it
modifies the string that it is processing.  These classes were
implemented to avoid both of these issues and also to reduce the amount
of code that needs to be written.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The basic procedure is to create an instance of the tokenizer class with
the string to be processed as an argument and then do a loop until all
available tokens are read.  The constructor has a default set of
separator characters, but that can be overridden. The default separators
are all “whitespace” characters, i.e. the space character, the tabulator
character, the carriage return character, the linefeed character, and
the form feed character.

Most tokenizer operations cannot fail except for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS9Tokenizer4nextEv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Tokenizer::next()}}}}} (when used without first
checking with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4NK9LAMMPS_NS9Tokenizer8has_nextEv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Tokenizer::has\_next()}}}}}) and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS9Tokenizer4skipEi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Tokenizer::skip()}}}}}.  In case of failure, the class
will throw an exception, so you may need to wrap the code using the
tokenizer into a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{try}} / \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{catch}} block to handle errors.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS14ValueTokenizerE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::ValueTokenizer}}}}} class may also throw an exception
when a (type of) number is requested as next token that is not
compatible with the string representing the next word.

Class for splitting text into words

\sphinxAtStartPar
This tokenizer will break down a string into sub\sphinxhyphen{}strings (i.e words) separated by the given separator characters. If the string contains certain known UTF\sphinxhyphen{}8 characters they will be replaced by their ASCII equivalents processing the string.

\section{Argument parsing classes}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:argument-parsing-classes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The purpose of argument parsing classes it to simplify and unify how
arguments of commands in LAMMPS are parsed and to make abstractions of
repetitive tasks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS7ArgInfoE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::ArgInfo}}}}} class provides an abstraction
for parsing references to compute or fix styles, variables or custom
integer or double properties handled by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}}.
These would start with a “c\_”, “f\_”, “v\_”, “d\_”, “d2\_”, “i\_”, or “i2\_”
followed by the ID or name of than instance and may be postfixed with
one or two array indices “{[}\textless{}number\textgreater{}{]}” with numbers \textgreater{} 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Class for processing references to fixes, computes and variables

\sphinxAtStartPar
This class provides an abstraction for the repetitive task of parsing arguments that may contain references to fixes, computes, variables, or custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties. It will identify the name and the index value in the first and second dimension, if present.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{arg}} \textendash{} string with possible reference 

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{allowed}} \textendash{} integer with bitmap of allowed types of references 

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

make copy of the ID of the reference as C\sphinxhyphen{}style string

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID is copied into a buffer allocated with “new” and thus must be later deleted with “delete {[}{]}” to avoid a memory leak. Because it is a full copy in a newly allocated buffer, the lifetime of this string extends beyond the the time the ArgInfo class is in scope.

\section{File reader classes}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:file-reader-classes}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The purpose of the file reader classes is to simplify the recurring task
of reading and parsing files. They can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS14ValueTokenizerE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ValueTokenizer}}}}} class to process
the read in text.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS14TextFileReaderE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TextFileReader}}}}} is a more general version while
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS19PotentialFileReaderE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PotentialFileReader}}}}} is
specialized to implement the behavior expected for looking up and
reading/parsing files with potential parameters in LAMMPS.  The
potential file reader class requires a LAMMPS instance, requires to be
run on MPI rank 0 only, will use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils23get_potential_file_pathERKNSt6stringE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::get\_potential\_file\_path}}}}} function to look up and
open the file, and will call the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS::Error}} class in
case of failures to read or to convert numbers, so that LAMMPS will be
aborted.
\sphinxSetupCaptionForVerbatim{Use of PotentialFileReader class in pair style coul/streitz}

Read the next line(s) until \sphinxstyleemphasis{nparams} words have been read.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This reads a line and counts the words in it, if the number is less than the requested number, it will read the next line, as well. Output will be a string with all read lines combined. The purpose is to somewhat replicate the reading behavior of formatted files in Fortran.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ignore\_comments} class member has the value \sphinxstyleemphasis{true}, then any text read in is truncated at the first ‘\#’ character.

\section{Memory pool classes}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:memory-pool-classes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The memory pool classes are used for cases where otherwise many
small memory allocations would be needed and where the data would
be either all used or all freed.  One example for that is the
storage of neighbor lists.  The memory management strategy is
based on the assumption that allocations will be in chunks of similar
sizes.  The allocation is then not done per individual call for a
reserved chunk of memory, but for a “page” that can hold multiple
chunks of data.  A parameter for the maximum chunk size must be
provided, as that is used to determine whether a new page of memory
must be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4I0EN9LAMMPS_NS6MyPageE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MyPage}}}}} class offers two ways to
reserve a chunk: 1) with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS6MyPage3getEi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MyPage::get()}}}}} the
chunk size needs to be known in advance, 2) with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS6MyPage4vgetEv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MyPage::vget()}}}}} a pointer to the next chunk is returned, but
its size is registered later with {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS6MyPage4vgotEi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MyPage::vgot()}}}}}.

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4I0EN9LAMMPS_NS6MyPageE}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv3I0EN9LAMMPS_NS6MyPageE}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv2I0EN9LAMMPS_NS6MyPageE}}

\pysigline{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:classLAMMPS__NS_1_1MyPage}}\DUrole{k}{class}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{MyPage}}}}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Templated class for storing chunks of datums in pages. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The size of the chunk may vary from call to call, but must be less or equal than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxchunk} setting. The chunks are not returnable like with malloc() (i.e. you cannot call free() on them individually). One can only reset and start over. The purpose of this class is to replace many small memory allocations via malloc() with a few large ones. Since the pages are never freed until the class is re\sphinxhyphen{}initialized, they can be re\sphinxhyphen{}used without having to re\sphinxhyphen{}allocate them by calling the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:classLAMMPS__NS_1_1MyPage_1ad20897c5c8bd47f5d4005989bead0e55}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{reset()}}}} method.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The settings \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxchunk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pagesize}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pagedelta} control the memory allocation strategy. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxchunk} value represents the expected largest number of items per chunk. If there is less space left on the current page, a new page is allocated for the next chunk. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pagesize} value represents how many items can fit on a single page. It should have space for multiple chunks of size \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxchunk}. The combination of these two parameters determines how much memory is wasted by either switching to the next page too soon or allocating too large pages that never get properly used. An error is issued if a requested chunk is larger than \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxchunk}. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pagedelta} parameter determines how many pages are allocated in one go. In combination with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pagesize} setting, this determines how often blocks of memory get allocated (fewer allocations will result in faster execution).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a template class with explicit instantiation. If the class is used with a new data type, a new explicit instantiation may need to be added at the end of the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/my\_page.cpp}} to avoid symbol lookup errors. 
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Templated class for storing chunks of datums in pages. 

\sphinxAtStartPar
The size of the chunk may vary from call to call between the \sphinxstyleemphasis{minchunk} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxchunk} setting. Chunks may be returned to the pool for re\sphinxhyphen{}use. Chunks can be reserved in \sphinxstyleemphasis{nbin} different sizes between \sphinxstyleemphasis{minchunk} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxchunk}. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksperpage} setting specifies how many chunks are stored on any page and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pagedelta} setting determines how many pages are allocated in one go. Pages are never freed, so they can be re\sphinxhyphen{}used without re\sphinxhyphen{}allocation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a template class with explicit instantiation. If the class is used with a new data type, a new explicit instantiation may need to be added at the end of the file \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{src/my\_pool\_chunk.cpp}} to avoid symbol lookup errors. 
\end{sphinxadmonition}

The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MathEigen}} sub\sphinxhyphen{}namespace of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_NS}} namespace contains
functions and classes for eigensolvers. Currently only the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9MathEigen7jacobi3EAL3E_AL3E_KdPdAL3E_AL3E_di}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{jacobi3 function}}}}} is used in various
places in LAMMPS.  That function is built on top of a group of more
generic eigensolvers that are maintained in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{math\_eigen\_impl.h}}
header file.  This header contains the implementation of three template
classes:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
“Jacobi” calculates all of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors
of a dense, symmetric, real matrix.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “PEigenDense” class only calculates the principal eigenvalue
(i.e. the largest or smallest eigenvalue), and its corresponding
eigenvector.  However it is much more efficient than “Jacobi” when
applied to large matrices (larger than 13x13).  PEigenDense also can
understand complex\sphinxhyphen{}valued Hermitian matrices.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “LambdaLanczos” class is a generalization of “PEigenDense” which can be
applied to arbitrary sparse matrices.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “math\_eigen\_impl.h” code is an amalgamation of \sphinxhref{https://github.com/jewettaij/jacobi\_pd}{jacobi\_pd} by Andrew Jewett at Scripps
Research (under CC0\sphinxhyphen{}1.0 license) and \sphinxhref{https://github.com/mrcdr/lambda-lanczos}{Lambda Lanczos} by Yuya Kurebayashi at
Tohoku University (under MIT license)

\section{Communication buffer coding with \sphinxstyleemphasis{ubuf}}
\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:communication-buffer-coding-with-ubuf}}\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:id2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS uses communication buffers where it collects data from various
class instances and then exchanges the data with neighboring subdomains.
For simplicity those buffers are defined as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{double}} buffers and
used for doubles and integer numbers. This presents a unique problem
when 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit integers are used.  While the storage needed for a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{double}}
is also 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit, it cannot be used by a simple assignment.  To get around
that limitation, LAMMPS uses the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS4ubufE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ubuf}}}}}
union.  It is used in the various “pack” and “unpack” functions in the
LAMMPS classes to store and retrieve integers that may be 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit from
the communication buffers.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\index{ubuf (C++ union)@\spxentry{ubuf}\spxextra{C++ union}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS4ubufE}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv3N9LAMMPS_NS4ubufE}}\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv2N9LAMMPS_NS4ubufE}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysigstartmultiline
\pysigline{\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{Developer_utils:unionLAMMPS__NS_1_1ubuf}}\DUrole{k}{union}\DUrole{w}{ }\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{\DUrole{n}{ubuf}}}}
\pysigstopmultiline
\pysigstopsignatures\sphinxstyleemphasis{\#include \textless{}lmptype.h\textgreater{}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Data structure for packing 32\sphinxhyphen{}bit and 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit integers into double (communication) buffers

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using this union avoids aliasing issues by having member types (double, int) referencing the same buffer memory location.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The explicit constructor for 32\sphinxhyphen{}bit integers prevents compilers from (incorrectly) calling the double constructor when storing an int into a double buffer. 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Usage:}
\sphinxSetupCaptionForVerbatim{To copy an integer into a double buffer:}

\PYG{k+kt}{int}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{foo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{tagint}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bar}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{40}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ubuf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{foo}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{buf}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ubuf}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{bar}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
