\index{atom\_modify@\spxentry{atom\_modify}}\ignorespaces 

\section{atom\_modify command}
\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:atom-modify-command}}\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{id} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{map} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{array} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hash}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{first} value = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = group whose atoms will appear first in internal atom lists
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} values = Nfreq binsize
  Nfreq = sort atoms spatially every this many time steps
  binsize = bin size for spatial sorting (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{map}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{map}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hash}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sort}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{first}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{colloid}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modify certain attributes of atoms defined and stored within LAMMPS,
in addition to what is specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}}
command.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} keywords must be specified before a
simulation box is defined; other keywords can be specified any time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} keyword determines whether non\sphinxhyphen{}zero atom IDs can be assigned
to each atom.  If the value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, which is the default, IDs are
assigned, whether you use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create atoms}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands to initialize atoms.  If the value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} the IDs for all
atoms are assumed to be 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If atom IDs are used, they must all be positive integers.  They should
also be unique, though LAMMPS does not check for this.  Typically they
should also be consecutively numbered (from 1 to Natoms), though this
is not required.  Molecular {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom styles}}}} are those
that store bond topology information (styles bond, angle, molecular,
full).  These styles require atom IDs since the IDs are used to encode
the topology.  Some other LAMMPS commands also require the use of atom
IDs.  E.g. some many\sphinxhyphen{}body pair styles use them to avoid double
computation of the I\sphinxhyphen{}J interaction between two atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The only reason not to use atom IDs is if you are running an atomic
simulation so large that IDs cannot be uniquely assigned.  For a
default LAMMPS build this limit is 2\textasciicircum{}31 or about 2 billion atoms.
However, even in this case, you can use 64\sphinxhyphen{}bit atom IDs, allowing 2\textasciicircum{}63
or about 9e18 atoms, if you build LAMMPS with the \sphinxhyphen{} DLAMMPS\_BIGBIG
switch.  This is described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build\_settings}}}}
doc page.  If atom IDs are not used, they must be specified as 0 for
all atoms, e.g. in a data or restart file.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{triclinic simulation box}}}} is used,
atom IDs are required, due to how neighbor lists are built.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} keyword determines how atoms with specific IDs are found
when required.  For example, the bond (angle, etc) methods need to
find the local index of an atom with a specific global ID which is a
bond (angle, etc) partner.  LAMMPS performs this operation efficiently
by creating a “map”, which is either an \sphinxstyleemphasis{array} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hash} table, as
described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} keyword is not specified in your input script, LAMMPS
only creates a map for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_styles}}}} for molecular
systems which have permanent bonds (angles, etc).  No map is created
for atomic systems, since it is normally not needed.  However some
LAMMPS commands require a map, even for atomic systems, and will
generate an error if one does not exist.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} keyword thus
allows you to force the creation of a map.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specifying a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} will create either an array\sphinxhyphen{}style or
hash\sphinxhyphen{}style map, depending on the size of the system.  If no atom ID is
larger than 1 million, then an array\sphinxhyphen{}style map is used, otherwise a
hash\sphinxhyphen{}style map is used.  Specifying a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{array} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hash}
creates an array\sphinxhyphen{}style or hash\sphinxhyphen{}style map respectively, regardless of
the size of the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For an array\sphinxhyphen{}style map, each processor stores a lookup table of length
N, where N is the largest atom ID in the system.  This is a fast,
simple method for many simulations, but requires too much memory for
large simulations.  For a hash\sphinxhyphen{}style map, a hash table is created on
each processor, which finds an atom ID in constant time (independent
of the global number of atom IDs).  It can be slightly slower than the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{array} map, but its memory cost is proportional to the number of
atoms owned by a processor, i.e. N/P when N is the total number of
atoms in the system and P is the number of processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} keyword allows a {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}} to be specified
whose atoms will be maintained as the first atoms in each processor’s
list of owned atoms.  This in only useful when the specified group is
a small fraction of all the atoms, and there are other operations
LAMMPS is performing that will be sped\sphinxhyphen{}up significantly by being able
to loop over the smaller set of atoms.  Otherwise the reordering
required by this option will be a net slow\sphinxhyphen{}down.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify include}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify group}}}} commands are two examples of commands that require this
setting to work efficiently.  Several {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}, most notably
time integration fixes like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}, also take
advantage of this setting if the group they operate on is the group
specified by this command.  Note that specifying “all” as the group\sphinxhyphen{}ID
effectively turns off the \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is OK to use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} keyword with a group that has not yet been
defined, e.g. to use the atom\_modify first command at the beginning of
your input script.  LAMMPS does not use the group until a simulation
is run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} keyword turns on a spatial sorting or reordering of atoms
within each processor’s subdomain every \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfreq} timesteps.  If
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfreq} is set to 0, then sorting is turned off.  Sorting can improve
cache performance and thus speed\sphinxhyphen{}up a LAMMPS simulation, as discussed
in a paper by {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify:meloni}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Meloni)}}}}.  Its efficacy depends on the problem
size (atoms/processor), how quickly the system becomes disordered, and
various other factors.  As a general rule, sorting is typically more
effective at speeding up simulations of liquids as opposed to solids.
In tests we have done, the speed\sphinxhyphen{}up can range from zero to 3\sphinxhyphen{}4x.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reordering is performed every \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfreq} timesteps during a dynamics run
or iterations during a minimization.  More precisely, reordering
occurs at the first reneighboring that occurs after the target
timestep.  The reordering is performed locally by each processor,
using bins of the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize}.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} is set to 0.0,
then a binsize equal to half the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} cutoff
distance (force cutoff plus skin distance) is used, which is a
reasonable value.  After the atoms have been binned, they are
reordered so that atoms in the same bin are adjacent to each other in
the processor’s 1d list of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The goal of this procedure is for atoms to put atoms close to each
other in the processor’s one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional list of atoms that are also
near to each other spatially.  This can improve cache performance when
pairwise interactions and neighbor lists are computed.  Note that if
bins are too small, there will be few atoms/bin.  Likewise if bins are
too large, there will be many atoms/bin.  In both cases, the goal of
cache locality will be undermined.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Running a simulation with sorting on versus off should not change
the simulation results in a statistical sense.  However, a
different ordering will induce round\sphinxhyphen{}off differences, which will
lead to diverging trajectories over time when comparing two
simulations.  Various commands, particularly those which use random
numbers (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity create}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
langevin}}}}), may generate (statistically identical)
results which depend on the order in which atoms are processed.
The order of atoms in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} file will also typically
change if sorting is enabled.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When running simple pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise potentials like Lennard Jones on GPUs
with the KOKKOS package, using a larger binsize (e.g. 2x larger than
default) and a more frequent reordering than default (e.g. every 100
time steps) may improve performance.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} options cannot be used together.  Since sorting
is on by default, it will be turned off if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} keyword is
used with a group\sphinxhyphen{}ID that is not “all”.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} is yes.  By default, atomic systems (no bond topology
info) do not use a map.  For molecular systems (with bond topology
info), the default is to use a map of either \sphinxstyleemphasis{array} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hash} style
depending on the size of the system, as explained above for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{map
yes} keyword/value option.  By default, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} group is not
defined.  By default, sorting is enabled with a frequency of 1000 and
a binsize of 0.0, which means the neighbor cutoff will be used to set
the bin size. If no neighbor cutoff is defined, sorting will be turned
off.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{atom_modify:meloni}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Meloni)} Meloni, Rosati and Colombo, J Chem Phys, 126, 121102 (2007).

\sphinxstepscope

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{atom_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom\_style} command selects which per\sphinxhyphen{}atom attributes are
associated with atoms in a LAMMPS simulation and thus stored and
communicated with those atoms as well as read from and stored in data
and restart files.  Different models (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair styles}}}}) require access to specific per\sphinxhyphen{}atom attributes and thus
require a specific atom style.  For example, to compute Coulomb
interactions, the atom must have a “charge” (aka “q”) attribute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A number of distinct atom styles exist that combine attributes.  Some
atom styles are a superset of other atom styles.  Further attributes
may be added to atoms either via using a hybrid style which provides a
union of the attributes of the sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles, or via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
property/atom}}}} command.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom\_style} command
must be used before a simulation is setup via a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Many of the atom styles discussed here are only enabled if LAMMPS was
built with a specific package, as listed below in the Restrictions
section.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once a style is selected and the simulation box defined, it cannot be
changed but only augmented with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command.  So one should select an atom style
general enough to encompass all attributes required.  E.g. with atom
style \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}, it is not possible to define angles and use angle styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is OK to use a style more general than needed, though it may be
slightly inefficient because it will allocate and communicate
additional unused data.


\subsection{Atom style attributes}
\label{\detokenize{atom_style:atom-style-attributes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom style \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomic} has the minimum subset of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom attributes
and is also the default setting.  It encompasses the following per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
attributes (name of the vector or array in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Classes_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Atom class}}}} is given in parenthesis): atom\sphinxhyphen{}ID (tag), type (type),
position (x), velocities (v), forces (f), image flags (image), group
membership (mask).  Since all atom styles are a superset of atom style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atomic}, they all include these attributes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This table lists all the available atom styles, which attributes they
provide, which {\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{package}}}} is required to use them, and
what the typical applications are that use them.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} commands for details on how to set these various
quantities.  More information about many of the styles is provided in
the Additional Information section below.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is possible to add some attributes, such as a molecule ID and
charge, to atom styles that do not have them built in using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command.  This command
also allows new custom\sphinxhyphen{}named attributes consisting of extra integer
or floating\sphinxhyphen{}point values or vectors to be added to atoms.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} page for examples of
cases where this is useful and details on how to initialize,
access, and output these custom values.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Particle size and mass}
\label{\detokenize{atom_style:particle-size-and-mass}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the atom styles define point particles unless they (1) define
finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical particles via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} attribute, or (2)
define finite\sphinxhyphen{}size aspherical particles (e.g. the \sphinxstyleemphasis{body}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ellipsoid},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{line}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tri} styles).  Most of these styles can also be used with
mixtures of point and finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} property may need to be provided as a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{diameter} (e.g. in {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule files}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data
files}}}}).  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_spherical::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto spherical}}}}
page for an overview of using finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical and aspherical
particle models with LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unless an atom style defines the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmass} attribute, particle
masses are defined on a per\sphinxhyphen{}type basis, using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{mass::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mass}}}}
command.  This means each particle’s mass is indexed by its atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A few styles define the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmass} attribute which can also be
added using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command.
In this case each particle stores its own mass.  Atom styles that have
a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom rmass may define it indirectly through setting particle
diameter and density on a per\sphinxhyphen{}particle basis.  If both per\sphinxhyphen{}type mass
and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmass} are defined (e.g. in a hybrid style), the
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom mass will take precedence in any operation which which works
with both flavors of mass.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Additional information about specific atom styles}
\label{\detokenize{atom_style:additional-information-about-specific-atom-styles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{body} style, the particles are arbitrary bodies with internal
attributes defined by the “style” of the bodies, which is specified by
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bstyle} argument.  Body particles can represent complex entities,
such as surface meshes of discrete points, collections of
sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles, deformable objects, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} page describes the body styles
LAMMPS currently supports, and provides more details as to the kind of
body particles they represent.  For all styles, each body particle
stores moments of inertia and a quaternion 4\sphinxhyphen{}vector, so that its
orientation and position can be time integrated due to forces and
torques.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that there may be additional arguments required along with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bstyle} specification, in the atom\_style body command.  These
arguments are described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dielectric} style, each particle can be either a physical
particle (e.g. an ion), or an interface particle representing a
boundary element between two regions of different dielectric
constant. For interface particles, in addition to the properties
associated with atom\_style full, each particle also should be assigned
a unit dipole vector (mu) representing the direction of the induced
dipole moment at each interface particle, an area (area/patch), the
difference and mean of the dielectric constants of two sides of the
interface along the direction of the normal vector (ed and em), the
local dielectric constant at the boundary element (epsilon), and a
mean local curvature (curv).  Physical particles must be assigned
these values, as well, but only their local dielectric constants will
be used; see documentation for associated {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_dielectric::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair styles}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_polarize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}.  The distinction
between the physical and interface particles is only meaningful when
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_polarize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix polarize}}}} commands are applied to the
interface particles. This style is part of the DIELECTRIC package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole} style, a point dipole vector mu is defined for each
point particle.  Note that if you wish the particles to be finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
spheres as in a Stockmayer potential for a dipolar fluid, so that the
particles can rotate due to dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions, then you need
to use the command \sphinxtitleref{atom\_style hybrid sphere dipole}, which will
assign both a diameter and dipole moment to each particle.  This also
requires using an integrator with a “/sphere” suffix like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
nve/sphere}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sphere}}}}
and the “update dipole” or “update dlm” parameters to the fix
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd} style is for reactive dissipative particle dynamics (DPD)
particles.  Note that it is part of the DPD\sphinxhyphen{}REACT package, and is not
required for use with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_dpd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style dpd or dpd/stat}}}}
commands, which only require the attributes from atom\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomic}.
Atom\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd} extends DPD particle properties with internal
temperature (dpdTheta), internal conductive energy (uCond), internal
mechanical energy (uMech), and internal chemical energy (uChem).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{edpd} style is for energy\sphinxhyphen{}conserving dissipative particle
dynamics (eDPD) particles which store a temperature (edpd\_temp), and
heat capacity (edpd\_cv).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{electron} style, the particles representing electrons are 3d
Gaussians with a specified position and bandwidth or uncertainty in
position, which is represented by the eradius = electron size.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ellipsoid} style, particles can be ellipsoids which each
stores a shape vector with the 3 diameters of the ellipsoid and a
quaternion 4\sphinxhyphen{}vector with its orientation.  Each particle stores a flag
in the ellipsoid vector which indicates whether it is an ellipsoid (1)
or a point particle (0).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{line} style, particles can be are idealized line segments
which store a per\sphinxhyphen{}particle mass and length and orientation (i.e. the
end points of the line segment).  Each particle stores a flag in the
line vector which indicates whether it is a line segment (1) or a
point particle (0).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mdpd} style is for many\sphinxhyphen{}body dissipative particle dynamics (mDPD)
particles which store a density (rho) for considering density\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{oxdna} style is for coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained nucleotides and stores the
3’\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}5’ polarity of the nucleotide strand, which is set through
the bond topology in the data file. The first (second) atom in a
bond definition is understood to point towards the 3’\sphinxhyphen{}end (5’\sphinxhyphen{}end)
of the strand.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri} style, the particles are spherical and each stores a
per\sphinxhyphen{}particle mass and volume.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{smd} style is for Smooth Particle Mach dynamics.  Both fluids and
solids can be modeled.  Particles store the mass and volume of an
integration point, a kernel diameter used for calculating the field
variables (e.g. stress and deformation) and a contact radius for
calculating repulsive forces which prevent individual physical bodies
from penetrating each other.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sph} style is for smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) particles
which store a density (rho), energy (esph), and heat capacity (cv).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin} style, a magnetic spin is associated with each atom.
Those spins have a norm (their magnetic moment) and a direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tdpd} style is for transport dissipative particle dynamics (tDPD)
particles which store a set of chemical concentration. An integer
“cc\_species” is required to specify the number of chemical species
involved in a tDPD system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{wavepacket} style is similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{electron} style, but the
electrons may consist of several Gaussian wave packets, summed up with
coefficients cs= (cs\_re,cs\_im).  Each of the wave packets is treated
as a separate particle in LAMMPS, wave packets belonging to the same
electron must have identical \sphinxstyleemphasis{etag} values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{bpm/sphere} styles allow particles to be either point
particles or finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} attribute is \textgreater{}
0.0, the particle is a finite\sphinxhyphen{}size sphere.  If the diameter = 0.0, it
is a point particle.  Note that by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{disc} keyword with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/sphere}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nvt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt/sphere}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nph_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph/sphere}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_npt_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
npt/sphere}}}} commands for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere} style, spheres
can be effectively treated as 2d discs for a 2d simulation if desired.
See also the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set density/disc}}}} command.  These styles also
take an optional 0 or 1 argument.  A value of 0 means the radius of
each sphere is constant for the duration of the simulation (this is
the default).  A value of 1 means the radii may vary dynamically
during the simulation, e.g. due to use of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{template} style allows molecular topology (bonds,angles,etc) to be
defined via a molecule template using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}}
command.  The template stores one or more molecules with a single copy
of the topology info (bonds,angles,etc) of each.  Individual atoms only
store a template index and template atom to identify which molecule and
which atom\sphinxhyphen{}within\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}molecule they represent.  Using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{template}
style instead of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecular} styles can save memory
for systems comprised of a large number of small molecules, all of a
single type (or small number of types).  See the paper by Grime and
Voth, in {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style:grime}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Grime)}}}}, for examples of how this can be
advantageous for large\sphinxhyphen{}scale coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained systems.  The
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/template}} directory has a few demo inputs and examples
showing the use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{template} atom style versus \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecular}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{template} style with a {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule template}}}} that contains multiple molecules, you should ensure the
atom types, bond types, angle\_types, etc in all the molecules are
consistent.  E.g. if one molecule represents H2O and another CO2,
then you probably do not want each molecule file to define two atom
types and a single bond type, because they will conflict with each
other when a mixture system of H2O and CO2 molecules is defined,
e.g. by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.  Rather the H2O
molecule should define atom types 1 and 2, and bond type 1.  And
the CO2 molecule should define atom types 3 and 4 (or atom types 3
and 2 if a single oxygen type is desired), and bond type 2.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tri} style, particles can be planar triangles which each
stores a per\sphinxhyphen{}particle mass and size and orientation (i.e. the corner
points of the triangle).  Each particle stores a flag in the tri
vector which indicates whether it is a triangle (1) or a point
particle (0).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically, simulations require only a single (non\sphinxhyphen{}hybrid) atom style.
If some atoms in the simulation do not have all the properties defined
by a particular style, use the simplest style that defines all the
needed properties by any atom.  For example, if some atoms in a
simulation are charged, but others are not, use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{charge} style.
If some atoms have bonds, but others do not, use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The only scenario where the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} style is needed is if there is no
single style which defines all needed properties of all atoms.  For
example, as mentioned above, if you want dipolar particles which will
rotate due to torque, you need to use “atom\_style hybrid sphere
dipole”.  When a hybrid style is used, atoms store and communicate the
union of all quantities implied by the individual styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} style, you cannot combine the \sphinxstyleemphasis{template} style
with another molecular style that stores bond, angle, etc info on a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom basis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can be extended with new atom styles as well as new body styles;
see the corresponding manual page on {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{modifying \& extending LAMMPS}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\section{balance command}
\label{\detokenize{balance:balance-command}}\label{\detokenize{balance:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{balance::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{balance:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thresh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
thresh = imbalance threshold that must be exceeded to perform a re\sphinxhyphen{}balance

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one style/arg pair can be used (or multiple for \sphinxstyleemphasis{x},\sphinxstyleemphasis{y},\sphinxstyleemphasis{z})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcb}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{x} args = \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} or Px\sphinxhyphen{}1 numbers between 0 and 1
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} = evenly spaced cuts between processors in x dimension
  numbers = Px\sphinxhyphen{}1 ascending values between 0 and 1, Px \sphinxhyphen{} \# of processors in x dimension
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} can be specified together with \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{y} args = \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} or Py\sphinxhyphen{}1 numbers between 0 and 1
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} = evenly spaced cuts between processors in y dimension
  numbers = Py\sphinxhyphen{}1 ascending values between 0 and 1, Py \sphinxhyphen{} \# of processors in y dimension
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} can be specified together with \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{z} args = \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} or Pz\sphinxhyphen{}1 numbers between 0 and 1
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} = evenly spaced cuts between processors in z dimension
  numbers = Pz\sphinxhyphen{}1 ascending values between 0 and 1, Pz \sphinxhyphen{} \# of processors in z dimension
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} can be specified together with \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} args = dimstr Niter stopthresh
  dimstr = sequence of letters containing "x" or "y" or "z", each not more than once
  Niter = \# of times to iterate within each dimension of dimstr sequence
  stopthresh = stop balancing when this imbalance threshold is reached
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rcb} args = none
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/arg pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{out}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} style args = use weighted particle counts for the balancing
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{style} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{store}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} args = Ngroup group1 weight1 group2 weight2 ...
      Ngroup = number of groups with assigned weights
      group1, group2, ... = group IDs
      weight1, weight2, ...   = corresponding weight factors
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} factor = compute weight based on number of neighbors
      factor = scaling factor (\textgreater{} 0)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} factor = compute weight based on time spend computing
      factor = scaling factor (\textgreater{} 0)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} name = take weight from atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable
      name = name of the atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{store} name = store weight in custom atom property defined by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command
      name = atom property name (without d\_ prefix)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{out} arg = filename
  filename = write each processor\textquotesingle{}s subdomain to a file
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
