\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{uniform}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.6}
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rcb}
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{weight}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fast}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{slow}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{weight}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{weight}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{neigh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{weight}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{store}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{balance}
\PYG{k}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.balance}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{balance:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command adjusts the size and shape of processor subdomains
within the simulation box, to attempt to balance the number of atoms
or particles and thus indirectly the computational cost (load) more
evenly across processors.  The load balancing is “static” in the sense
that this command performs the balancing once, before or between
simulations.  The processor subdomains will then remain static during
the subsequent run.  To perform “dynamic” balancing, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
balance}}}} command, which can adjust processor subdomain
sizes and shapes on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly during a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing is typically most useful if the particles in the
simulation box have a spatially\sphinxhyphen{}varying density distribution or when
the computational cost varies significantly between different
particles.  E.g. a model of a vapor/liquid interface, or a solid with
an irregular\sphinxhyphen{}shaped geometry containing void regions, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid
pair style simulations}}}} which combine pair styles with
different computational cost.  In these cases, the LAMMPS default of
dividing the simulation box volume into a regular\sphinxhyphen{}spaced grid of 3d
bricks, with one equal\sphinxhyphen{}volume subdomain per processor, may assign
numbers of particles per processor in a way that the computational
effort varies significantly.  This can lead to poor performance when
the simulation is run in parallel.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The balancing can be performed with or without per\sphinxhyphen{}particle weighting.
With no weighting, the balancing attempts to assign an equal number of
particles to each processor.  With weighting, the balancing attempts
to assign an equal aggregate computational weight to each processor,
which typically induces a different number of atoms assigned to each
processor.  Details on the various weighting options and examples for
how they can be used are {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance:weighted-balance}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{given below}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}} command allows some
control over how the box volume is split across processors.
Specifically, for a Px by Py by Pz grid of processors, it allows
choice of Px, Py, and Pz, subject to the constraint that Px * Py *
Pz = P, the total number of processors.  This is sufficient to achieve
good load\sphinxhyphen{}balance for some problems on some processor counts.
However, all the processor subdomains will still have the same shape
and same volume.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The requested load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing operation is only performed if the
current “imbalance factor” in particles owned by each processor
exceeds the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{thresh} parameter.  The imbalance factor is
defined as the maximum number of particles (or weight) owned by any
processor, divided by the average number of particles (or weight) per
processor.  Thus an imbalance factor of 1.0 is perfect balance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, for 10000 particles running on 10 processors, if the
most heavily loaded processor has 1200 particles, then the factor is
1.2, meaning there is a 20\% imbalance.  Note that a re\sphinxhyphen{}balance can be
forced even if the current balance is perfect (1.0) be specifying a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{thresh} \textless{} 1.0.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Balancing is performed even if the imbalance factor does not
exceed the \sphinxstyleemphasis{thresh} parameter if a “grid” style is specified when the
current partitioning is “tiled”.  The meaning of “grid” vs “tiled” is
explained below.  This is to allow forcing of the partitioning to
“grid” so that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style brick}}}} command can then
be used to replace a current {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style tiled}}}}
setting.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the balance command completes, it prints statistics about the
result, including the change in the imbalance factor and the change in
the maximum number of particles on any processor.  For “grid” methods
(defined below) that create a logical 3d grid of processors, the
positions of all cutting planes in each of the 3 dimensions (as
fractions of the box length) are also printed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command attempts to minimize the imbalance factor, as
defined above.  But depending on the method a perfect balance (1.0)
may not be achieved.  For example, “grid” methods (defined below) that
create a logical 3d grid cannot achieve perfect balance for many
irregular distributions of particles.  Likewise, if a portion of the
system is a perfect lattice, e.g. the initial system is generated by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command, then “grid” methods may
be unable to achieve exact balance.  This is because entire lattice
planes will be owned or not owned by a single processor.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The imbalance factor is also an estimate of the maximum speed\sphinxhyphen{}up
you can hope to achieve by running a perfectly balanced simulation
versus an imbalanced one.  In the example above, the 10000 particle
simulation could run up to 20\% faster if it were perfectly balanced,
versus when imbalanced.  However, computational cost is not strictly
proportional to particle count, and changing the relative size and
shape of processor subdomains may lead to additional computational
and communication overheads, e.g. in the PPPM solver used via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command.  Thus you should benchmark
the run times of a simulation before and after balancing.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The method used to perform a load balance is specified by one of the
listed styles (or more in the case of \sphinxstyleemphasis{x},\sphinxstyleemphasis{y},\sphinxstyleemphasis{z}), which are
described in detail below.  There are 2 kinds of styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} styles are “grid” methods which
produce a logical 3d grid of processors.  They operate by changing the
cutting planes (or lines) between processors in 3d (or 2d), to adjust
the volume (area in 2d) assigned to each processor, as in the
following 2d diagram where processor subdomains are shown and
particles are colored by the processor that owns them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.320\linewidth]{{balance_uniform}.jpg}  \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.320\linewidth]{{balance_nonuniform}.jpg}  \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.320\linewidth]{{balance_rcb}.jpg}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The leftmost diagram is the default partitioning of the simulation box
across processors (one sub\sphinxhyphen{}box for each of 16 processors); the middle
diagram is after a “grid” method has been applied.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcb} style is
a “tiling” method which does not produce a logical 3d grid of
processors.  Rather it tiles the simulation domain with rectangular
sub\sphinxhyphen{}boxes of varying size and shape in an irregular fashion so as to
have equal numbers of particles (or weight) in each sub\sphinxhyphen{}box, as in the
rightmost diagram above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “grid” methods can be used with either of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style}}}} command options, \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled}.  The “tiling”
methods can only be used with {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style tiled}}}}.
Note that it can be useful to use a “grid” method with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style tiled}}}} to return the domain partitioning
to a logical 3d grid of processors so that “comm\_style brick” can
afterwords be specified for subsequent {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a “grid” method is specified, the current domain partitioning can
be either a logical 3d grid or a tiled partitioning.  In the former
case, the current logical 3d grid is used as a starting point and
changes are made to improve the imbalance factor.  In the latter case,
the tiled partitioning is discarded and a logical 3d grid is created
with uniform spacing in all dimensions.  This becomes the starting
point for the balancing operation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a “tiling” method is specified, the current domain partitioning
(“grid” or “tiled”) is ignored, and a new partitioning is computed
from scratch.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} styles invoke a “grid” method for balancing, as
described above.  Note that any or all of these 3 styles can be
specified together, one after the other, but they cannot be used with
any other style.  This style adjusts the position of cutting planes
between processor subdomains in specific dimensions.  Only the
specified dimensions are altered.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} argument spaces the planes evenly, as in the left
diagrams above.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{numeric} argument requires listing Ps\sphinxhyphen{}1 numbers
that specify the position of the cutting planes.  This requires
knowing Ps = Px or Py or Pz = the number of processors assigned by
LAMMPS to the relevant dimension.  This assignment is made (and the
Px, Py, Pz values printed out) when the simulation box is created by
the “create\_box” or “read\_data” or “read\_restart” command and is
influenced by the settings of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each of the numeric values must be between 0 and 1, and they must be
listed in ascending order.  They represent the fractional position of
the cutting place.  The left (or lower) edge of the box is 0.0, and
the right (or upper) edge is 1.0.  Neither of these values is
specified.  Only the interior Ps\sphinxhyphen{}1 positions are specified.  Thus is
there are 2 processors in the x dimension, you specify a single value
such as 0.75, which would make the left processor’s subdomain 3x
larger than the right processor’s subdomain.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} style invokes a “grid” method for balancing, as
described above.  It changes the positions of cutting planes between
processors in an iterative fashion, seeking to reduce the imbalance
factor, similar to how the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance shift}}}}
command operates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dimstr} argument is a string of characters, each of which must be
an “x” or “y” or “z”. Each character can appear zero or one time,
since there is no advantage to balancing on a dimension more than
once.  You should normally only list dimensions where you expect there
to be a density variation in the particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Balancing proceeds by adjusting the cutting planes in each of the
dimensions listed in \sphinxstyleemphasis{dimstr}, one dimension at a time.  For a single
dimension, the balancing operation (described below) is iterated on up
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Niter} times.  After each dimension finishes, the imbalance factor
is re\sphinxhyphen{}computed, and the balancing operation halts if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stopthresh}
criterion is met.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A re\sphinxhyphen{}balance operation in a single dimension is performed using a
recursive multisectioning algorithm, where the position of each
cutting plane (line in 2d) in the dimension is adjusted independently.
This is similar to a recursive bisectioning for a single value, except
that the bounds used for each bisectioning take advantage of
information from neighboring cuts if possible.  At each iteration, the
count of particles on either side of each plane is tallied.  If the
counts do not match the target value for the plane, the position of
the cut is adjusted to be halfway between a low and high bound.  The
low and high bounds are adjusted on each iteration, using new count
information, so that they become closer together over time.  Thus as
the recursion progresses, the count of particles on either side of the
plane gets closer to the target value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the balanced plane positions are determined, if any pair of
adjacent planes are closer together than the neighbor skin distance
(as specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} command), then
the plane positions are shifted to separate them by at least this
amount.  This is to prevent particles being lost when dynamics are run
with processor subdomains that are too narrow in one or more
dimensions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the re\sphinxhyphen{}balancing is complete and final processor subdomains
assigned, particles are migrated to their new owning processor, and
the balance procedure ends.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At each re\sphinxhyphen{}balance operation, the bisectioning for each cutting
plane (line in 2d) typically starts with low and high bounds separated
by the extent of a processor’s subdomain in one dimension.  The size
of this bracketing region shrinks by 1/2 every iteration.  Thus if
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Niter} is specified as 10, the cutting plane will typically be
positioned to 1 part in 1000 accuracy (relative to the perfect target
position).  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{Niter} = 20, it will be accurate to 1 part in a
million.  Thus there is no need to set \sphinxstyleemphasis{Niter} to a large value.
LAMMPS will check if the threshold accuracy is reached (in a
dimension) is less iterations than \sphinxstyleemphasis{Niter} and exit early.  However,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Niter} should also not be set too small, since it will take roughly
the same number of iterations to converge even if the cutting plane is
initially close to the target value.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcb} style invokes a “tiled” method for balancing, as described
above.  It performs a recursive coordinate bisectioning (RCB) of the
simulation domain. The basic idea is as follows.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simulation domain is cut into 2 boxes by an axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned cut in
one of the dimensions, leaving one new sub\sphinxhyphen{}box on either side of the
cut.  Which dimension is chosen for the cut depends on the particle
(weight) distribution within the parent box.  Normally the longest
dimension of the box is cut, but if all (or most) of the particles are
at one end of the box, a cut may be performed in another dimension to
induce sub\sphinxhyphen{}boxes that are more cube\sphinxhyphen{}ish (3d) or square\sphinxhyphen{}ish (2d) in
shape.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the cut is made, all the processors are also partitioned into 2
groups, half assigned to the box on the lower side of the cut, and
half to the box on the upper side.  (If the processor count is odd,
one side gets an extra processor.)  The cut is positioned so that the
number of (weighted) particles in the lower box is exactly the number
that the processors assigned to that box should own for load balance
to be perfect.  This also makes load balance for the upper box
perfect.  The positioning of the cut is done iteratively, by a
bisectioning method (median search).  Note that counting particles on
either side of the cut requires communication between all processors
at each iteration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
That is the procedure for the first cut.  Subsequent cuts are made
recursively, in exactly the same manner.  The subset of processors
assigned to each box make a new cut in one dimension of that box,
splitting the box, the subset of processors, and the particles in the
box in two.  The recursion continues until every processor is assigned
a sub\sphinxhyphen{}box of the entire simulation domain, and owns the (weighted)
particles in that sub\sphinxhyphen{}box.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{balance:weighted-balance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This subsection describes how to perform weighted load balancing
using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, all particles have a weight of 1.0, which means each
particle is assumed to require the same amount of computation during a
timestep.  There are, however, scenarios where this is not a good
assumption.  Measuring the computational cost for each particle
accurately would be impractical and slow down the computation.
Instead the \sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} keyword implements several ways to influence the
per\sphinxhyphen{}particle weights empirically by properties readily available or
using the user’s knowledge of the system.  Note that the absolute
value of the weights are not important; only their relative ratios
affect which particle is assigned to which processor.  A particle with
a weight of 2.5 is assumed to require 5x more computational than a
particle with a weight of 0.5.  For all the options below the weight
assigned to a particle must be a positive value; an error will be be
generated if a weight is \textless{}= 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is a list of possible weight options with a short description of
their usage and some example scenarios where they might be applicable.
It is possible to apply multiple weight flags and the weightings they
induce will be combined through multiplication.  Most of the time,
however, it is sufficient to use just one method.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} weight style assigns weight factors to specified
{\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{groups}}}} of particles.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} style keyword is
followed by the number of groups, then pairs of group IDs and the
corresponding weight factor.  If a particle belongs to none of the
specified groups, its weight is not changed.  If it belongs to
multiple groups, its weight is the product of the weight factors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This weight style is useful in combination with pair style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid}}}}, e.g. when combining a more costly many\sphinxhyphen{}body
potential with a fast pairwise potential.  It is also useful when
using {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} where some portions of the
system have many bonded interactions and others none.  It assumes that
the computational cost for each group remains constant over time.
This is a purely empirical weighting, so a series test runs to tune
the assigned weight factors for optimal performance is recommended.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} weight style assigns the same weight to each particle
owned by a processor based on the total count of neighbors in the
neighbor list owned by that processor.  The motivation is that more
neighbors means a higher computational cost.  The style does not use
neighbors per atom to assign a unique weight to each atom, because
that value can vary depending on how the neighbor list is built.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor} setting is applied as an overall scale factor to the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} weights which allows adjustment of their impact on the
balancing operation.  The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor} value must be positive.
A value \textgreater{} 1.0 will increase the weights so that the ratio of max
weight to min weight increases by \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor}.  A value \textless{} 1.0 will
decrease the weights so that the ratio of max weight to min weight
decreases by \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor}.  In both cases the intermediate weight values
increase/decrease proportionally as well.  A value = 1.0 has no effect
on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} weights.  As a rule of thumb, we have found a \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor}
of about 0.8 often results in the best performance, since the number
of neighbors is likely to overestimate the ideal weight.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This weight style is useful for systems where there are different
cutoffs used for different pairs of interactions, or the density
fluctuates, or a large number of particles are in the vicinity of a
wall, or a combination of these effects.  If a simulation uses
multiple neighbor lists, this weight style will use the first suitable
neighbor list it finds.  It will not request or compute a new list.  A
warning will be issued if there is no suitable neighbor list available
or if it is not current, e.g. if the balance command is used before a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command is used, in which
case the neighbor list may not yet have been built.  In this case no
weights are computed.  Inserting a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run 0 post no}}}} command
before issuing the \sphinxstyleemphasis{balance} command, may be a workaround for this
case, as it will induce the neighbor list to be built.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} weight style uses {\hyperref[\detokenize{timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timer data}}}} to estimate
weights.  It assigns the same weight to each particle owned by a
processor based on the total computational time spent by that
processor.  See details below on what time window is used.  It uses
the same timing information as is used for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{MPI task timing
breakdown}}}}, namely, for sections \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pair}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Bond},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Kspace}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Neigh}.  The time spent in those portions of the
timestep are measured for each MPI rank, summed, then divided by the
number of particles owned by that processor.  I.e. the weight is an
effective CPU time/particle averaged over the particles on that
processor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor} setting is applied as an overall scale factor to the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{time} weights which allows adjustment of their impact on the
balancing operation.  The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor} value must be positive.
A value \textgreater{} 1.0 will increase the weights so that the ratio of max
weight to min weight increases by \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor}.  A value \textless{} 1.0 will
decrease the weights so that the ratio of max weight to min weight
decreases by \sphinxstyleemphasis{factor}.  In both cases the intermediate weight values
increase/decrease proportionally as well.  A value = 1.0 has no effect
on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} weights.  As a rule of thumb, effective values to use
are typically between 0.5 and 1.2.  Note that the timer quantities
mentioned above can be affected by communication which occurs in the
middle of the operations, e.g. pair styles with intermediate exchange
of data witin the force computation, and likewise for KSpace solves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} weight style with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{balance} command, the
timing data is taken from the preceding run command, i.e. the timings
are for the entire previous run.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix balance} command the
timing data is for only the timesteps since the last balancing
operation was performed.  If timing information for the required
sections is not available, e.g. at the beginning of a run, or when the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timer}}}} command is set to either \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}, a warning
is issued.  In this case no weights are computed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} weight style is the most generic option, and should
be tried first, unless the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} style is easily applicable.
However, since the computed cost function is averaged over all
particles on a processor, the weights may not be highly accurate.
This style can also be effective as a secondary weight in combination
with either \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} to offset some of inaccuracies in
either of those heuristics.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} weight style assigns per\sphinxhyphen{}particle weights by evaluating an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} specified by \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}.  This is
provided as a more flexible alternative to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} weight style,
allowing definition of a more complex heuristics based on information
(global and per atom) available inside of LAMMPS.  For example,
atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can reference the position of a particle, its
velocity, the volume of its Voronoi cell, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{store} weight style does not compute a weight factor.  Instead it
stores the current accumulated weights in a custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector
specified by \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}.  This must be a vector defined as \sphinxstyleemphasis{d\_name} via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command.  This means
the values in the vector can be read as part of a data file with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command or specified with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command.  These weights can also be output in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} file, so this is a way to examine, debug, or visualize the
per\sphinxhyphen{}particle weights used during the load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing operation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the name of the custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector is specified just
as \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}, not as \sphinxstyleemphasis{d\_name} as it is for other commands that use
different kinds of custom atom vectors or arrays as arguments.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} keyword determines whether the communication of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
data to other processors during load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing will be random or
deterministic.  Random is generally faster; deterministic will ensure
the new ordering of atoms on each processor is the same each time the
same simulation is run.  This can be useful for debugging purposes.
Since the balance command is a one\sphinxhyphen{}time operation, the default is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} to perform sorting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{out} keyword writes a text file to the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{filename} with
the results of the balancing operation.  The file contains the bounds
of the subdomain for each processor after the balancing operation
completes.  The format of the file is compatible with the
\sphinxhref{https://lammps.github.io/pizza}{Pizza.py} \sphinxstyleemphasis{mdump} tool which has support for manipulating and
visualizing mesh files.  An example is shown here for a balancing by 4
processors for a 2d problem:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ITEM: TIMESTEP
0
ITEM: NUMBER OF NODES
16
ITEM: BOX BOUNDS
0 10
0 10
0 10
ITEM: NODES
1 1 0 0 0
2 1 5 0 0
3 1 5 5 0
4 1 0 5 0
5 1 5 0 0
6 1 10 0 0
7 1 10 5 0
8 1 5 5 0
9 1 0 5 0
10 1 5 5 0
11 1 5 10 0
12 1 10 5 0
13 1 5 5 0
14 1 10 5 0
15 1 10 10 0
16 1 5 10 0
ITEM: TIMESTEP
0
ITEM: NUMBER OF SQUARES
4
ITEM: SQUARES
1 1 1 2 3 4
2 1 5 6 7 8
3 1 9 10 11 12
4 1 13 14 15 16
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of all the vertices are listed in the NODES section, 5
per processor.  Note that the 4 subdomains share vertices, so there
will be duplicate nodes in the list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “SQUARES” section lists the node IDs of the 4 vertices in a
rectangle for each processor (1 to 4).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a 3d problem, the syntax is similar with 8 vertices listed for
each processor, instead of 4, and “SQUARES” replaced by “CUBES”.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{balance:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For 2d simulations, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} style cannot be used.  Nor can a “z”
appear in \sphinxstyleemphasis{dimstr} for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Balancing through recursive bisectioning (\sphinxstyleemphasis{rcb} style) requires
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style tiled}}}}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{balance:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{balance:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default setting is sort = yes.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{bond\_coeff@\spxentry{bond\_coeff}}\ignorespaces 

\section{bond\_coeff command}
\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:bond-coeff-command}}\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = numeric bond type (see asterisk form below), or type label

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = coefficients for one or more bond types

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{30.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{30.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} (for bond\PYGZus{}style hybrid)}

\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{carbonyl}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{carbonyl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify the bond force field coefficients for one or more bond types.
The number and meaning of the coefficients depends on the bond style.
Bond coefficients can also be set in the data file read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command or in a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N\) can be specified in one of several ways.  An explicit numeric
value can be used, as in the first example above.  Or \(N\) can be a
type label, which is an alphanumeric string defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} command or in a section of a data file read
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For numeric values only, a wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can be used to set the
coefficients for multiple bond types.  This takes the form “*” or “*n”
or “n*” or “m*n”.  If \(N\) is the number of bond types, then an
asterisk with no numeric values means all types from 1 to \(N\).  A
leading asterisk means all types from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all types from n to \(N\) (inclusive).  A middle
asterisk means all types from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that using a bond\_coeff command can override a previous setting
for the same bond type.  For example, these commands set the coeffs
for all bond types, then overwrite the coeffs for just bond type 2:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A line in a data file that specifies bond coefficients uses the exact
same format as the arguments of the bond\_coeff command in an input
script, except that wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisks should not be used since
coefficients for all \(N\) types must be listed in the file.  For
example, under the “Bond Coeffs” section of a data file, the line that
corresponds to the first example above would be listed as

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
5 80.0 1.2
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The list of all bond styles defined in LAMMPS is given on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}} doc page.  They are also listed in more
compact form on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_bond::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands bond}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On either of those pages, click on the style to display the formula it
computes and its coefficients as specified by the associated
bond\_coeff command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command must come after the simulation box is defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A bond style must be defined before any bond coefficients are set,
either in the input script or in a data file.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{bond_coeff:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{bond\_style@\spxentry{bond\_style}}\ignorespaces 

\section{bond\_style command}
\label{\detokenize{bond_style:bond-style-command}}\label{\detokenize{bond_style:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{bond_style::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{bond_style:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{zero} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bpm/rotational} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bpm/spring} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fene} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fene/expand} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fene/nm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gaussian} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gromos} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/restrain} \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/shift} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/shift/cut} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lepton} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nonlinear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{oxdna/fene} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{oxdena2/fene} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{oxrna2/fene} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{quartic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{table}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = none for any style except \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} args = list of one or more styles

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{bond_style:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fene}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fene}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{bond_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the formula(s) LAMMPS uses to compute bond interactions between
pairs of atoms.  In LAMMPS, a bond differs from a pairwise
interaction, which are set via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}}
command.  Bonds are defined between specified pairs of atoms and
remain in force for the duration of the simulation (unless new bonds
are created or existing bonds break, which is possible in some fixes
and bond potentials).  The list of bonded atoms is read in by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
command from a data or restart file.  By contrast, pair potentials are
typically defined between all pairs of atoms within a cutoff distance
and the set of active interactions changes over time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Hybrid models where bonds are computed using different bond potentials
can be setup using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} bond style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficients associated with a bond style can be specified in a
data or restart file or via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All bond potentials store their coefficient data in binary restart
files which means bond\_style and {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}} commands
do not need to be re\sphinxhyphen{}specified in an input script that restarts a
simulation.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for
details on how to do this.  The one exception is that bond\_style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} only stores the list of sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles in the restart file; bond
coefficients need to be re\sphinxhyphen{}specified.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When both a bond and pair style is defined, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command often needs to be used to
turn off (or weight) the pairwise interaction that would otherwise
exist between two bonded atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the formulas listed for each bond style, \sphinxstyleemphasis{r} is the distance
between the two atoms in the bond.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an alphabetic list of bond styles defined in LAMMPS.  Click on
the style to display the formula it computes and coefficients
specified by the associated {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Click on the style to display the formula it computes, any additional
arguments specified in the bond\_style command, and coefficients
specified by the associated {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are also additional accelerated pair styles included in the
LAMMPS distribution for faster performance on CPUs, GPUs, and KNLs.
The individual style names on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_bond::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands bond}}}}
doc page are followed by one or more of (g,i,k,o,t) to indicate which
accelerated styles exist.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_none::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{none}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} turn off bonded interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_zero::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{zero}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} topology but no interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} define multiple styles of bond interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_bpm_rotational::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bpm/rotational}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} breakable bond with forces and torques based on deviation from reference state

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_bpm_spring::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bpm/spring}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} breakable bond with forces based on deviation from reference length

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{class2}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} COMPASS (class 2) bond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_fene::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fene}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} FENE (finite\sphinxhyphen{}extensible non\sphinxhyphen{}linear elastic) bond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_fene_expand::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fene/expand}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} FENE bonds with variable size particles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_fene::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fene/nm}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} FENE bonds with a generalized Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_gaussian::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{gaussian}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} multicentered Gaussian\sphinxhyphen{}based bond potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_gromos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{gromos}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} GROMOS force field bond

\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{bond_style:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bond styles can only be set for atom styles that allow bonds to be
defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most bond styles are part of the MOLECULE package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.  The doc pages for
individual bond potentials tell if it is part of a package.
