\index{bond\_write@\spxentry{bond\_write}}\ignorespaces 

\section{bond\_write command}
\label{\detokenize{bond_write:bond-write-command}}\label{\detokenize{bond_write:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{bond_write::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{bond_write:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{btype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{outer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{jtype}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
btype = bond type

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = \# of values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
inner,outer = inner and outer bond length (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file = name of file to write values to

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = section name in file for this set of tabulated values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
itype,jtype = two atom types (optional)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{bond_write:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Harmonic\PYGZus{}1}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Morse}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{bond_write:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write energy and force values to a file as a function of distance for
the currently defined {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond style}}}} for a selected bond
type.  This is useful for plotting the potential function or otherwise
debugging its values.  The resulting file can also be used as input for
use with {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond style table}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the file already exists, the table of values is appended to the end
of the file to allow multiple tables of energy and force to be included
in one file.  The individual sections may be identified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{keyword}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy and force values are computed at distances from \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner} to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} for two interacting atoms forming a bond of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{btype}, using
the appropriate {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}} coefficients. N evenly
spaced distances are used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, for N = 7, inner = 1.0, and outer = 4.0,
values are computed at r = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file is written in the format used as input for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style
table}}}} option with \sphinxstyleemphasis{keyword} as the section name.  Each
line written to the file lists an index number (1\sphinxhyphen{}N), a distance (in
distance units), an energy (in energy units), and a force (in force
units).  In case a new file is created, the first line will be a comment
with a “DATE:” and “UNITS:” tag with the current date and {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} settings.  For subsequent invocations of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond\_write}
command for the same file, data will be appended and the current units
settings will be compared to the data from the header, if present.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond\_write} command will refuse to add a table to an existing file if
the units are not the same.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{bond_write:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All force field coefficients for bond and other kinds of interactions
must be set before this command can be invoked.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Due to how the bond force is computed, an inner value \textgreater{} 0.0 must
be specified even if the potential has a finite value at r = 0.0.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{bond_write:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style table}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_write}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{bond_write:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{boundary@\spxentry{boundary}}\ignorespaces 

\section{boundary command}
\label{\detokenize{boundary:boundary-command}}\label{\detokenize{boundary:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{boundary::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{boundary:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
x,y,z = \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{s} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{f} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}, one or two letters
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p} is periodic
\sphinxstyleemphasis{f} is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and fixed
\sphinxstyleemphasis{s} is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped
\sphinxstyleemphasis{m} is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped with a minimum value
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{boundary:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f}
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fm}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{boundary:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the style of boundaries for the global simulation box in each
dimension.  A single letter assigns the same style to both the lower
and upper face of the box.  Two letters assigns the first style to the
lower face and the second style to the upper face.  The initial size
of the simulation box is set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The style \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} means the box is periodic, so that particles interact
across the boundary, and they can exit one end of the box and re\sphinxhyphen{}enter
the other end.  A periodic dimension can change in size due to
constant pressure boundary conditions or box deformation (see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} commands).
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} style must be applied to both faces of a dimension.  For 2d
simulations the z dimension must be periodic (which is the default).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{f}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{s}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} mean the box is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic, so that
particles do not interact across the boundary and do not move from one
side of the box to the other.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{f}, the position of the face is fixed.  If an atom moves
outside the face it will be deleted on the next timestep that
reneighboring occurs.  This will typically generate an error unless
you have set the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify lost}}}} option to
allow for lost atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{s}, the position of the face is set so as to encompass the
atoms in that dimension (shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapping), no matter how far they
move. Note that when the difference between the current box dimensions
and the shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap box dimensions is large, this can lead to lost
atoms at the beginning of a run when running in parallel. This is due
to the large change in the (global) box dimensions also causing
significant changes in the individual subdomain sizes. If these
changes are farther than the communication cutoff, atoms will be lost.
This is best addressed by setting initial box dimensions to match the
shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped dimensions more closely, by using \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} style boundaries
(see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}, shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapping occurs, but is bounded by the value
specified in the data or restart file or set by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.  For example, if the upper z
face has a value of 50.0 in the data file, the face will always be
positioned at 50.0 or above, even if the maximum z\sphinxhyphen{}extent of all the
atoms becomes less than 50.0.  This can be useful if you start a
simulation with an empty box or if you wish to leave room on one side
of the box, e.g. for atoms to evaporate from a surface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS also allows use of triclinic (non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal) simulation boxes.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} page for a
description of both general and restricted triclinic boxes and how to
define them.  General triclinic boxes (arbitrary edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A},
\sphinxstylestrong{B}, and \sphinxstylestrong{C}) are converted internally to restricted triclinic
boxes with tilt factors (xy,xz,yz) which skew an otherwise orthogonal
box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The boundary \textless{}boundary\textgreater{} command settings explained above for the 6
faces of an orthogonal box also apply in similar manner to the 6 faces
of a restricted triclinic box (and thus to the corresponding 6 faces
of a general triclinic box), with the following context.

\sphinxAtStartPar
if the second dimension of a tilt factor (e.g. y for xy) is periodic,
then the periodicity is enforced with the tilt factor offset.  This
means that for y periodicity a particle which exits the lower y
boundary is displaced in the x\sphinxhyphen{}direction by xy before it re\sphinxhyphen{}enters the
upper y boundary.  And vice versa if a particle exits the upper y
boundary.  Likewise the ghost atoms surrounding a particle near the
lower y boundary include images of particles near the upper y\sphinxhyphen{}boundary
which are displaced in the x\sphinxhyphen{}direction by xy.  Similar rules apply for
z\sphinxhyphen{}periodicity and the xz and/or yz tilt factors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the first dimension of a tilt factor is shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped, then the
shrink wrapping is applied to the tilted box face, to encompass the
atoms.  E.g. for a positive xy tilt, the xlo and xhi faces of the box
are planes tilting in the +y direction as y increases.  The position
of these tilted planes are adjusted dynamically to shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap around
the atoms to determine the xlo and xhi extents of the box.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{boundary:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command cannot be used after the simulation box is defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change\_box}}}} command for how to change the
simulation box boundaries after it has been defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For 2d simulations, the z dimension must be periodic.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{boundary:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command for a discussion
of lost atoms.


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{boundary:default}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope

\index{change\_box@\spxentry{change\_box}}\ignorespaces 

\section{change\_box command}
\label{\detokenize{change_box:change-box-command}}\label{\detokenize{change_box:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{change_box::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{change_box:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{parameter}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of group of atoms to (optionally) displace

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more parameter/arg pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
parameter = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ortho} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} args = style value(s)
    style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{final} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{final} values = lo hi
        lo hi = box boundaries after displacement (distance units)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta} values = dlo dhi
        dlo dhi = change in box boundaries after displacement (distance units)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} values = factor
        factor = multiplicative factor for change in box length after displacement
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} value = none = adjust this dim to preserve volume of system
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} args = style value
    style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{final} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{final} value = tilt
        tilt = tilt factor after displacement (distance units)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta} value = dtilt
        dtilt = change in tilt factor after displacement (distance units)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary} args = x y z
    x,y,z = \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{s} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{f} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}, one or two letters
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} is periodic
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{f} is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and fixed
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{s} is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped with a minimum value
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{ortho} args = none = change box to orthogonal
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic} args = none = change box to triclinic
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} args = none = store state of current box
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} args = none = remap atom coords from last saved state to current box
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{units}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{units} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{box}
  lattice = distances are defined in lattice units
  box = distances are defined in simulation box units
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{change_box:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{final}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{final}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{remap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{remap}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{change_box:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Change the volume and/or shape and/or boundary conditions for the
simulation box.  Orthogonal simulation boxes have 3 adjustable size
parameters (x,y,z).  Triclinic (non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal) simulation boxes have
6 adjustable size/shape parameters (x,y,z,xy,xz,yz).  Any or all of
them can be adjusted independently by this command.  Thus it can be
used to expand or contract a box, or to apply a shear strain to a
non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal box.  It can also be used to change the boundary
conditions for the simulation box, similar to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The size and shape of the initial simulation box are specified by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command used to setup the simulation.
The size and shape may be altered by subsequent runs, e.g. by use of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} commands.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read data}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands also determine whether the
simulation box is orthogonal or triclinic and their doc pages explain
the meaning of the xy,xz,yz tilt factors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} page for a
geometric description of triclinic boxes, as defined by LAMMPS, and
how to transform these parameters to and from other commonly used
triclinic representations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keywords used in this command are applied sequentially to the
simulation box and the atoms in it, in the order specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Before the sequence of keywords are invoked, the current box
size/shape is stored, in case a \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} keyword is used to map the
atom coordinates from a previously stored box size/shape to the
current one.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After all the keywords have been processed, any shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap boundary
conditions are invoked (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command)
which may change simulation box boundaries, and atoms are migrated to
new owning processors.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This means that you cannot use the change\_box command to enlarge
a shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped box, e.g. to make room to insert more atoms via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command, because the simulation box
will be re\sphinxhyphen{}shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped before the change\_box command completes.
Instead you could do something like this, assuming the simulation box
is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and atoms extend from 0 to 20 in all dimensions:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{final}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} this will fail to insert an atom}

\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{final}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{s}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} this will work}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike the earlier “displace\_box” version of this command, atom
remapping is NOT performed by default.  This command allows remapping
to be done in a more general way, exactly when you specify it (zero or
more times) in the sequence of transformations.  Thus if you do not
use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} keyword, atom coordinates will not be changed even if
the box size/shape changes.  If a uniformly strained state is desired,
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} keyword should be specified.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is possible to lose atoms with this command.  E.g. by
changing the box without remapping the atoms, and having atoms end up
outside of non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic boundaries.  It is also possible to alter
bonds between atoms straddling a boundary in bad ways.  E.g. by
converting a boundary from periodic to non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic.  It is also
possible when remapping atoms to put them (nearly) on top of each
other.  E.g. by converting a boundary from non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic to periodic.
All of these will typically lead to bad dynamics and/or generate error
messages.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The simulation box size/shape can be changed by arbitrarily large
amounts by this command.  This is not a problem, except that the
mapping of processors to the simulation box is not changed from its
initial 3d configuration; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}}
command.  Thus, if the box size/shape changes dramatically, the
mapping of processors to the simulation box may not end up as
optimal as the initial mapping attempted to be.  You may wish to
re\sphinxhyphen{}balance the atoms by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}} command
if that is the case.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You cannot use this command after reading a restart file (and
before a run is performed) if the restart file stored per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
information from a fix and any of the specified keywords change the
box size or shape or boundary conditions.  This is because atoms
may be moved to new processors and the restart info will not
migrate with them.  LAMMPS will generate an error if this could
happen.  Only the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ortho} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic} keywords do not trigger
this error.  One solution is to perform a “run 0” command before
using the change\_box command.  This clears the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom restart
data, whether it has been re\sphinxhyphen{}assigned to a new fix or not.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Because the keywords used in this command are applied one at a time
to the simulation box and the atoms in it, care must be taken with
triclinic cells to avoid exceeding the limits on skew after each
transformation in the sequence.  If skew is exceeded before the
final transformation this can be avoided by changing the order of
the sequence, or breaking the transformation into two or more
smaller transformations.  For more information on the allowed
limits for box skew see the discussion on triclinic boxes on
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} doc page.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} parameters, this is the meaning of their
styles and values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{final}, the final lo and hi box boundaries of a dimension
are specified.  The values can be in lattice or box distance units.
See the discussion of the units keyword below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta}, plus or minus changes in the lo/hi box boundaries
of a dimension are specified.  The values can be in lattice or box
distance units.  See the discussion of the units keyword below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale}, a multiplicative factor to apply to the box length
of a dimension is specified.  For example, if the initial box length
is 10, and the factor is 1.1, then the final box length will be 11.  A
factor less than 1.0 means compression.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} style changes the specified dimension in such a way that
the overall box volume remains constant with respect to the operation
performed by the preceding keyword.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} style can only be
used following a keyword that changed the volume, which is any of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} keywords.  If the preceding keyword “key” had a \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume}
style, then both it and the current keyword apply to the keyword
preceding “key”.  I.e. this sequence of keywords is allowed:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} style changes the associated dimension so that the
overall box volume is unchanged relative to its value before the
preceding keyword was invoked.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the following command is used, then the z box length will shrink by
the same 1.1 factor the x box length was increased by:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the following command is used, then the y,z box lengths will each
shrink by sqrt(1.1) to keep the volume constant.  In this case, the
y,z box lengths shrink so as to keep their relative aspect ratio
constant:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the following command is used, then the final box will be a factor
of 10\% larger in x and y, and a factor of 21\% smaller in z, so as to
keep the volume constant:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{change\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{volume}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For solids or liquids, when one dimension of the box is
expanded, it may be physically undesirable to hold the other 2 box
lengths constant since that implies a density change.  For solids,
adjusting the other dimensions via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} style may make
physical sense (just as for a liquid), but may not be correct for
materials and potentials whose Poisson ratio is not 0.5.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} styles, the box length is expanded or
compressed around its mid point.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} parameters, this is the meaning of their
styles and values.  Note that changing the tilt factors of a triclinic
box does not change its volume.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{final}, the final tilt factor is specified.  The value
can be in lattice or box distance units.  See the discussion of the
units keyword below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta}, a plus or minus change in the tilt factor is
specified.  The value can be in lattice or box distance units.  See
the discussion of the units keyword below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of these styles change the xy, xz, yz tilt factors.  In LAMMPS,
tilt factors (xy,xz,yz) for triclinic boxes are required to be no more
than half the distance of the parallel box length.  For example, if
xlo = 2 and xhi = 12, then the x box length is 10 and the xy tilt
factor must be between \sphinxhyphen{}5 and 5.  Similarly, both xz and yz must be
between \sphinxhyphen{}(xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo)/2 and +(yhi\sphinxhyphen{}ylo)/2.  Note that this is not a
limitation, since if the maximum tilt factor is 5 (as in this
example), then configurations with tilt = …, \sphinxhyphen{}15, \sphinxhyphen{}5, 5, 15, 25,
… are all equivalent.  Any tilt factor specified by this command
must be within these limits.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary} keyword takes arguments that have exactly the same
meaning as they do for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.  In each
dimension, a single letter assigns the same style to both the lower
and upper face of the box.  Two letters assigns the first style to the
lower face and the second style to the upper face.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The style \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} means the box is periodic; the other styles mean
non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic. For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{f}, the position of the face is fixed.  For
style \sphinxstyleemphasis{s}, the position of the face is set so as to encompass the
atoms in that dimension (shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapping), no matter how far they
move.  For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}, shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapping occurs, but is bounded by the
current box edge in that dimension, so that the box will become no
smaller.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command for more
explanation of these style options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the “boundary” command itself can only be used before the
simulation box is defined via a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
command.  This command allows the boundary conditions to be changed
later in your input script.  Also note that the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} will change boundary conditions to
match what is stored in the restart file.  So if you wish to change
them, you should use the change\_box command after the read\_restart
command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Changing a periodic boundary to a non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic one will also cause
the image flag for that dimension of all atoms to be reset to 0.
LAMMPS will print a warning message, if that happens.
Please note that this reset can lead to undesired changes when
atoms are involved in bonded interactions that straddle periodic
boundaries and thus the values of the image flag differs for those
atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ortho} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic} keywords convert the simulation box to be
orthogonal or triclinic (non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simulation box is defined as either orthogonal or triclinic when
it is created via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These keywords allow you to toggle the existing simulation box from
orthogonal to triclinic and vice versa.  For example, an initial
equilibration simulation can be run in an orthogonal box, the box can
be toggled to triclinic, and then a {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_nemd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (NEMD) simulation}}}} can be run with deformation via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the simulation box is currently triclinic and has non\sphinxhyphen{}zero tilt in
xy, yz, or xz, then it cannot be converted to an orthogonal box.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keyword saves the current box size/shape.  This can be
useful if you wish to use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} keyword more than once or if you
wish it to be applied to an intermediate box size/shape in a sequence
of keyword operations.  Note that the box size/shape is saved before
any of the keywords are processed, i.e. the box size/shape at the time
the create\_box command is encountered in the input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} keyword remaps atom coordinates from the last saved box
size/shape to the current box state.  For example, if you stretch the
box in the x dimension or tilt it in the xy plane via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}
keywords, then the \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} command will dilate or tilt the atoms to
conform to the new box size/shape, as if the atoms moved with the box
as it deformed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this operation is performed without regard to periodic
boundaries.  Also, any shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapping of non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic boundaries (see
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command) occurs after all keywords,
including this one, have been processed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only atoms in the specified group are remapped.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{units} keyword determines the meaning of the distance units used
to define various arguments.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} value selects standard distance
units as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command, e.g. Angstroms for
units = real or metal.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} value means the distance units are
in lattice spacings.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command must have
been previously used to define the lattice spacing.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{change_box:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ortho} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic} keywords, then at the point in
the input script when this command is issued, no {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dumps}}}} can
be active, nor can a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} be active.  This is
because these commands test whether the simulation box is orthogonal
when they are first issued.  Note that these commands can be used in
your script before a change\_box command is issued, so long as an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{undump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{undump}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{unfix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{unfix}}}} command is also used to
turn them off.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{change_box:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{change_box:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option default is units = lattice.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{clear@\spxentry{clear}}\ignorespaces 

\section{clear command}
\label{\detokenize{clear:clear-command}}\label{\detokenize{clear:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{clear::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{clear:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{clear}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{clear:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} (commands for 1st simulation)}
\PYG{k}{clear}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} (commands for 2nd simulation)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{clear:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command deletes all atoms, restores all settings to their default
values, and frees all memory allocated by LAMMPS.  Once a clear command
has been executed, it is almost as if LAMMPS were starting over, with
only the exceptions noted below.  This command enables multiple jobs to
be run sequentially from one input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These settings are not affected by a clear command: the working
directory ({\hyperref[\detokenize{shell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{shell}}}} command), log file status ({\hyperref[\detokenize{log::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{log}}}} command), echo status ({\hyperref[\detokenize{echo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{echo}}}} command), and input
script variables except for \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile} style variables ({\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{clear:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{clear:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{clear:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{comm\_modify@\spxentry{comm\_modify}}\ignorespaces 

\section{comm\_modify command}
\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:comm-modify-command}}\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/multi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{reduce/multi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vel}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{single}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/old} = communicate atoms within a single or multiple distances
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} value = Rcut (distance units) = communicate atoms from this far away
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/multi} collection value
   collection = atom collection or collection range (supports asterisk notation)
   value = Rcut (distance units) = communicate atoms for selected types from this far away
\sphinxstyleemphasis{reduce/multi} arg = none = reduce number of communicated ghost atoms for multi style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/multi/old} type value
   type = atom type or type range (supports asterisk notation)
   value = Rcut (distance units) = communicate atoms for selected types from this far away
\sphinxstyleemphasis{group} value = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = only communicate atoms in the group
\sphinxstyleemphasis{vel} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = do or do not communicate velocity info with ghost atoms
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{multi}
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{solvent}
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{15.0}
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command sets parameters that affect the inter\sphinxhyphen{}processor
communication of atom information that occurs each timestep as
coordinates and other properties are exchanged between neighboring
processors and stored as properties of ghost atoms.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These options apply to the currently defined comm style.  When
you specify a {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command, all communication settings
are restored to their default or stored values, including those
previously reset by a comm\_modify command.  Thus if your input script
specifies a comm\_style or read\_restart command, you should use the
comm\_modify command after it.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} keyword determines whether a single or multiple cutoff
distances are used to determine which atoms to communicate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default mode is \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} which means each processor acquires
information for ghost atoms that are within a single distance from its
subdomain.  The distance is by default the maximum of the neighbor
cutoff across all atom type pairs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For many systems this is an efficient algorithm, but for systems with
widely varying cutoffs for different type pairs, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/old} mode can
be faster.  In \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi}, each atom is assigned to a collection which should
correspond to a set of atoms with similar interaction cutoffs.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} command for a detailed description of collections.
In this case, each atom collection is assigned its own distance
cutoff for communication purposes, and fewer atoms will be
communicated. in \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/old}, a similar technique is used but atoms
are grouped by atom type. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor multi}}}}  and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor multi/old}}}} commands for
neighbor list construction options that may also be beneficial for
simulations of this kind. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} communication mode is only compatible
with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} neighbor style. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/old} communication mode is comparable
with both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/old} neighbor styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword allows you to extend the ghost cutoff distance
for communication mode \sphinxstyleemphasis{single}, which is the distance from the borders
of a processor’s subdomain at which ghost atoms are acquired from other
processors.  By default the ghost cutoff = neighbor cutoff = pairwise
force cutoff + neighbor skin.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} command
for more information about the skin distance.  If the specified Rcut is
greater than the neighbor cutoff, then extra ghost atoms will be acquired.
If the provided cutoff is smaller, the provided value will be ignored,
the ghost cutoff is set to the neighbor cutoff and a warning will be
printed. Specifying a cutoff value of 0.0 will reset any previous value
to the default. If bonded interactions exist and equilibrium bond length
information is available, then also a heuristic based on that bond length
is computed. It is used as communication cutoff, if there is no pair
style present and no \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_modify cutoff} command used. Otherwise a
warning is printed, if this bond based estimate is larger than the
communication cutoff used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/multi} option is equivalent to \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}, but applies to
communication mode \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} instead. Since the communication cutoffs are
determined per atom collections, a collection specifier is needed and
cutoff for one or multiple collections can be extended. Also ranges of
collections using the usual asterisk notation can be given.  Collections
are indexed from 1 to N where N is the total number of collections.
Note that the arguments for \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/multi} are parsed right before each
simulation to account for potential changes in the number of
collections.  Custom cutoffs are preserved between runs but if
collections are redefined, one may want to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the communication
cutoffs.  For granular pair styles,the default cutoff is set to the sum
of the current maximum atomic radii for each collection.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/multi/old} option is similar to \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/multi} except it
operates on atom types as opposed to collections.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{reduce/multi} option applies to \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} and sets the communication
cutoff for a particle equal to the maximum interaction distance between particles
in the same collection. This reduces the number of
ghost atoms that need to be communicated. This method is only compatible with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} neighbor style and requires a half neighbor list and Newton on.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor multi}}}} command for more information.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are simulation scenarios in which it may be useful or even
necessary to set a ghost cutoff \textgreater{} neighbor cutoff:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a single polymer chain with bond interactions, but no pairwise interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bonded interactions (e.g. dihedrals) extend further than the pairwise cutoff

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ghost atoms beyond the pairwise cutoff are needed for some computation

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the first scenario, a pairwise potential is not defined.  Thus the
pairwise neighbor cutoff will be 0.0.  But ghost atoms are still
needed for computing bond, angle, etc interactions between atoms on
different processors, or when the interaction straddles a periodic
boundary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The appropriate ghost cutoff depends on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton bond}}}}
setting.  For newton bond \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}, the distance needs to be the furthest
distance between any two atoms in the bond, angle, etc.  E.g. the
distance between 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 atoms in a dihedral.  For newton bond \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}, the
distance between the central atom in the bond, angle, etc and any
other atom is sufficient.  E.g. the distance between 2\sphinxhyphen{}4 atoms in a
dihedral.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the second scenario, a pairwise potential is defined, but its
neighbor cutoff is not sufficiently long enough to enable bond, angle,
etc terms to be computed.  As in the previous scenario, an appropriate
ghost cutoff should be set.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the last scenario, a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pairwise potential}}}} needs to calculate with ghost
atoms beyond the normal pairwise cutoff for some computation it
performs (e.g. locate neighbors of ghost atoms in a manybody pair
potential).  Setting the ghost cutoff appropriately can ensure it will
find the needed atoms.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In these scenarios, if you do not set the ghost cutoff long
enough, and if there is only one processor in a periodic dimension
(e.g. you are running in serial), then LAMMPS may “find” the atom it
is looking for (e.g. the partner atom in a bond), that is on the far
side of the simulation box, across a periodic boundary.  This will
typically lead to bad dynamics (i.e. the bond length is now the
simulation box length).  To detect if this is happening, see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify cluster}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} keyword will limit communication to atoms in the specified
group.  This can be useful for models where no ghost atoms are needed
for some kinds of particles.  All atoms (not just those in the
specified group) will still migrate to new processors as they move.
The group specified with this option must also be specified via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify first}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{vel} keyword enables velocity information to be communicated with
ghost particles.  Depending on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}},
velocity info includes the translational velocity, angular velocity,
and angular momentum of a particle.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{vel} option is set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then ghost atoms store these quantities; if \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} then they do
not.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} setting is needed by some pair styles which require
the velocity state of both the I and J particles to compute a pairwise
I,J interaction, as well as by some compute and fix commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command is being used
with its “remap v” option enabled, then the velocities for ghost atoms
(in the fix deform group) mirrored across a periodic boundary will
also include components due to any velocity shift that occurs across
that boundary (e.g. due to dilation or shear).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Communication mode \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} is currently only available for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick}.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{comm_modify:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are mode = single, group = all, cutoff = 0.0, vel =
no.  The cutoff default of 0.0 means that ghost cutoff = neighbor
cutoff = pairwise force cutoff + neighbor skin.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{comm\_style@\spxentry{comm\_style}}\ignorespaces 

\section{comm\_style command}
\label{\detokenize{comm_style:comm-style-command}}\label{\detokenize{comm_style:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{comm_style::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{comm_style:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{comm_style:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{brick}
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tiled}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{comm_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command sets the style of inter\sphinxhyphen{}processor communication of atom
information that occurs each timestep as coordinates and other
properties are exchanged between neighboring processors and stored as
properties of ghost atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the default \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} style, the domain decomposition used by LAMMPS
to partition the simulation box must be a regular 3d grid of bricks,
one per processor.  Each processor communicates with its 6 Cartesian
neighbors in the grid to acquire information for nearby atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled} style, a more general domain decomposition can be
used, as triggered by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}} commands.  The simulation box can be
partitioned into non\sphinxhyphen{}overlapping rectangular\sphinxhyphen{}shaped “tiles” or varying
sizes and shapes.  Again there is one tile per processor.  To acquire
information for nearby atoms, communication must now be done with a
more complex pattern of neighboring processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this command does not actually define a partitioning of the
simulation box (a domain decomposition), rather it determines what
kinds of decompositions are allowed and the pattern of communication
used to enable the decomposition.  A decomposition is created when the
simulation box is first created, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands.  For both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled} styles, the initial
decomposition will be the same, as described by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}}
commands.  The decomposition can be changed via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}} commands.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{comm_style:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{comm_style:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{comm_style:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default style is brick.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute@\spxentry{compute}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute command}
\label{\detokenize{compute:compute-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID = user\sphinxhyphen{}assigned name for the computation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of the group of atoms to perform the computation on

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = one of a list of possible style names (see below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = arguments used by a particular style

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{newtemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{flow}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{partial}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a diagnostic computation that will be performed on a group of
atoms.  Quantities calculated by a compute are instantaneous values,
meaning they are calculated from information about atoms on the
current timestep or iteration, though internally a compute may store
some information about a previous state of the system.  Defining a
compute does not perform the computation.  Instead computes are
invoked by other LAMMPS commands as needed (e.g., to calculate a
temperature needed for a thermostat fix or to generate thermodynamic
or dump file output).  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page
for a summary of various LAMMPS output options, many of which involve
computes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID of a compute can only contain alphanumeric characters and
underscores.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Computes calculate and store any of four \sphinxstyleemphasis{styles} of quantities:
global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A global quantity is one or more system\sphinxhyphen{}wide values, e.g. the
temperature of the system.  A per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantity is one or more values
per atom, e.g. the kinetic energy of each atom.  Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values are
set to 0.0 for atoms not in the specified compute group.  Local
quantities are calculated by each processor based on the atoms it
owns, but there may be zero or more per atom, e.g. a list of bond
distances.  Per\sphinxhyphen{}grid quantities are calculated on a regular 2d or 3d
grid which overlays a 2d or 3d simulation domain.  The grid points and
the data they store are distributed across processors; each processor
owns the grid points which fall within its subdomain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a general rule of thumb, computes that produce per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities
have the word “atom” at the end of their style, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke/atom}.
Computes that produce local quantities have the word “local” at the
end of their style, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/local}.  Computes that produce
per\sphinxhyphen{}grid quantities have the word “grid” at the end of their style,
e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{property/grid}.  And styles with neither “atom” or “local” or
“grid” at the end of their style name produce global quantities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid quantities can also be of three
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kinds}: a single scalar value (global only), a vector of values, or a
2d array of values.  For per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid quantities, a
“vector” means a single value for each atom, each local entity
(e.g. bond), or grid cell.  Likewise an “array”, means multiple values
for each atom, each local entity, or each grid cell.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a single compute can produce any combination of global,
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values.  Likewise it can produce any
combination of scalar, vector, or array output for each style.  The
exception is that for per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid output, either a
vector or array can be produced, but not both.  The doc page for each
compute explains the values it produces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a compute output is accessed by another input script command it
is referenced via the following bracket notation, where ID is the ID
of the compute:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
entire scalar, vector, or array
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID{[}I{]}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
one element of vector, one column of array
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
c\_ID{[}I{]}{[}J{]}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
one element of array
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In other words, using one bracket reduces the dimension of the
quantity once (vector \(\to\) scalar, array \(\to\) vector).
Using two brackets reduces the dimension twice (array \(\to\)
scalar).  Thus, for example, a command that uses global scalar compute
values as input can also process elements of a vector or array.
Depending on the command, this can either be done directly using the
syntax in the table, or by first defining a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}
of the appropriate style to store the quantity, then using the
variable as an input to the command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that commands and {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} which take compute
outputs as input typically do not allow for all styles and kinds of
data (e.g., a command may require global but not per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values, or
it may require a vector of values, not a scalar).  This means there is
typically no ambiguity about referring to a compute output as c\_ID
even if it produces, for example, both a scalar and vector.  The doc
pages for various commands explain the details, including how any
ambiguities are resolved.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, the values generated by a compute can be used in several
ways:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The results of computes that calculate a global temperature or
pressure can be used by fixes that do thermostatting or barostatting
or when atom velocities are created.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Global values can be output via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} command.
Or the values can be referenced in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable equal}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable atom}}}} command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can be output via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command.
Or they can be time\sphinxhyphen{}averaged via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/atom}}}}
command or reduced by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}}
command.  Or the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can be referenced in an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Local values can be reduced by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} command, or histogrammed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_histo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/histo}}}} command, or output by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}} command.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The results of computes that calculate global quantities can be either
“intensive” or “extensive” values.  Intensive means the value is
independent of the number of atoms in the simulation
(e.g., temperature).  Extensive means the value scales with the number of
atoms in the simulation (e.g., total rotational kinetic energy).
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Thermodynamic output}}}} will normalize extensive
values by the number of atoms in the system, depending on the
“thermo\_modify norm” setting.  It will not normalize intensive values.
If a compute value is accessed in another way (e.g., by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}), you may want to know whether it is an
intensive or extensive value.  See the page for individual
computes for further info.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS creates its own computes internally for thermodynamic output.
Three computes are always created, named “thermo\_temp”,
“thermo\_press”, and “thermo\_pe”, as if these commands had been invoked
in the input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pressure}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}temp}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional computes for other quantities are created if the thermo
style requires it.  See the documentation for the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes that calculate temperature or pressure, i.e. for thermostatting
or barostatting, may also create computes.  These are discussed in the
documentation for specific {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In all these cases, the default computes LAMMPS creates can be
replaced by computes defined by the user in the input script, as
described by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix modify}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Properties of either a default or user\sphinxhyphen{}defined compute can be modified
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Computes can be deleted with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{uncompute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{uncompute}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Code for new computes can be added to LAMMPS; see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}} page for details.  The results of their
calculations accessed in the various ways described above.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Each compute style has its own page which describes its arguments
and what it does.  Here is an alphabetic list of compute styles
available in LAMMPS.  They are also listed in more compact form on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands compute}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are also additional accelerated compute styles included in the
LAMMPS distribution for faster performance on CPUs, GPUs, and KNLs.
The individual style names on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands compute}}}} page are followed by one or more of
(g,i,k,o,t) to indicate which accelerated styles exist.

\index{compute\_modify@\spxentry{compute\_modify}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute\_modify command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:compute-modify-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{compute\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of the compute to modify

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dof} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dof} value = N
  N = \# of extra degrees of freedom to subtract
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
  yes/no = do or do not re\sphinxhyphen{}compute the number of degrees of freedom (DOF) contributing to the temperature
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{extra}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dof}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{compute\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{newtemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dynamic}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dof}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{extra}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dof}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{600}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modify one or more parameters of a previously defined compute.  Not
all compute styles support all parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dof} keyword refers to how many degrees of freedom are
subtracted (typically from \(3N\)) as a normalizing factor in a
temperature computation.  Only computes that compute a temperature use
this option.  The default is 2 or 3 for {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{2d or 3d systems}}}} which is a correction factor for an ensemble of velocities
with zero total linear momentum. For compute temp/partial, if one or
more velocity components are excluded, the value used for \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dof} is
scaled accordingly. You can use a negative number for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dof}
parameter if you need to add degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
temp/asphere}}}} command for an example.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof} keyword determines whether the number
of atoms \(N\) in the compute group and their associated degrees
of freedom (DOF) are re\sphinxhyphen{}computed each time a temperature is computed.
Only compute styles that calculate a temperature use this option.  By
default, \(N\) and their DOF are assumed to be constant.  If you
are adding atoms or molecules to the system (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gcmc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gcmc}}}} commands) or expect atoms or molecules to be lost
(e.g. due to exiting the simulation box or via {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_evaporate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix evaporate}}}}), then this option should be used to ensure the
temperature is correctly normalized.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_modify:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are extra/dof = 2 or 3 for 2d or 3d systems,
respectively, and dynamic/dof = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{create\_atoms@\spxentry{create\_atoms}}\ignorespaces 

\section{create\_atoms command}
\label{\detokenize{create_atoms:create-atoms-command}}\label{\detokenize{create_atoms:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{create_atoms:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type = atom type (1\sphinxhyphen{}Ntypes or type label) of atoms to create (offset for molecule creation)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{random}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{box} args = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{region} args = region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = particles will only be created if contained in the region
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single} args = x y z
  x,y,z = coordinates of a single particle (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} args = STL\sphinxhyphen{}file
  STL\sphinxhyphen{}file = file with triangle mesh in STL format
\sphinxstyleemphasis{random} args = N seed region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  N = number of particles to create
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
  region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = create atoms within this region, use NULL for entire simulation box
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{basis} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ratio} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{subset} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{radscale} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{meshmode} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxtry} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{units}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} values = template\sphinxhyphen{}ID seed
  template\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of molecule template specified in a separate {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} command
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{basis} values = M itype
  M = which basis atom
  itype = atom type (1\sphinxhyphen{}Ntypes or type label) to assign to this basis atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ratio} values = frac seed
  frac = fraction of lattice sites (0 to 1) to populate randomly
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{subset} values = Nsubset seed
  Nsubset = \# of lattice sites to populate randomly
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{var} value = name = variable name to evaluate for test of atom creation
\sphinxstyleemphasis{set} values = dim name
  dim = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
  name = name of variable to set with x, y, or z atom position
\sphinxstyleemphasis{radscale} value = factor
  factor = scale factor for setting atom radius
\sphinxstyleemphasis{meshmode} values = mode arg
  mode = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{qrand}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect} arg = radthresh
    radthresh = threshold value for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} to determine when to split triangles (distance units)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{qrand} arg = density
    density = minimum number density for atoms place on \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} triangles (inverse distance squared units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} values = theta Rx Ry Rz
  theta = rotation angle for single molecule (degrees)
  Rx,Ry,Rz = rotation vector for single molecule
\sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} value = Doverlap
  Doverlap = only insert if at least this distance from all existing atoms
\sphinxstyleemphasis{maxtry} value = Ntry
  Ntry = number of attempts to insert a particle before failure
\sphinxstyleemphasis{units} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{box}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} = the geometry is defined in lattice units
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} = the geometry is defined in simulation box units
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{regsphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ratio}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{74637}
