\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12345}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{overlap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{maxtry}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mesh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{open\PYGZus{}box.stl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{meshmode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{qrand}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mesh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{funnel.stl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{meshmode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bisect}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{radscale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{create_atoms:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command creates atoms (or molecules) within the simulation box,
either on a lattice, or at random points, or on a surface defined by a
triangulated mesh.  Or it creates a single atom (or molecule) at a
specified point.  It is an alternative to reading in atom coordinates
explicitly via a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use this command a simulation box must already exist, which is
typically created via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.
Before using this command, a lattice must typically also be defined
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command, unless you specify the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style with units = box or the \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style.  To
create atoms on a lattice for general triclinic boxes, see the
discussion below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the remainder of this doc page, a created atom or molecule is
referred to as a “particle”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If created particles are individual atoms, they are assigned the
specified atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{type}, though this can be altered via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{basis}
keyword as discussed below.  If molecules are being created, the type
of each atom in the created molecule is specified in a specified file
read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} command, and those values are
added to the specified atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} (e.g., if \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} = 2 and the file
specifies atom types 1, 2, and 3, then each created molecule will have
atom types 3, 4, and 5).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You cannot use this command to create atoms that are outside the
simulation box; they will just be ignored by LAMMPS.  This is true
even if you are using shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped box boundaries, as specified
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.  However, you can first
use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change\_box}}}} command to temporarily
expand the box, then add atoms via create\_atoms, then finally use
change\_box command again if needed to re\sphinxhyphen{}shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap the new atoms.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change\_box}}}} doc page for an example of
how to do this, using the create\_atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} style to insert a
new atom outside the current simulation box.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} style, the create\_atoms command fills the entire
simulation box with particles on the lattice.  If your simulation box
is periodic, you should ensure its size is a multiple of the lattice
spacings, to avoid unwanted atom overlaps at the box boundaries.  If
your box is periodic and a multiple of the lattice spacing in a
particular dimension, LAMMPS is careful to put exactly one particle at
the boundary (on either side of the box), not zero or two.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} style, a geometric volume is filled with particles on
the lattice.  This volume is what is both inside the simulation box
and also consistent with the region volume.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} command for details.  Note that a region can be specified so
that its “volume” is either inside or outside its geometric boundary.
Also note that if a region is the same size as a periodic simulation
box (in some dimension), LAMMPS does NOT implement the same logic
described above for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} style, to ensure exactly one particle at
periodic boundaries.  If this is desired, you should either use the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{box} style, or tweak the region size to get precisely the particles
you want.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If the simulation box is formulated as a general triclinic box defined
by arbitrary edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C}, then the \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{region} styles will create atoms on a lattice commensurate with those
edge vectors.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc
page for a detailed explanation of orthogonal, restricted triclinic,
and general triclinic simulation boxes.  As with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command used by
this command must be of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} and use its \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general}
option.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1, *a2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} settings of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}
command define the edge vectors of a unit cell of the general
triclinic lattice. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command creates
a simulation box which replicates that unit cell along each of the
\sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} edge vectors.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS allows specification of general triclinic simulation boxes
as a convenience for users who may be converting data from
solid\sphinxhyphen{}state crystallographic representations or from DFT codes for
input to LAMMPS.  However, as explained on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc page, internally,
LAMMPS only uses restricted triclinic simulation boxes.  This means
the box created by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command as
well as the atoms created by this command with their per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
information (e.g. coordinates, velocities) are converted (rotated)
from general to restricted triclinic form when the two commands are
invoked.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc page also
discusses other LAMMPS commands which can input/output general
triclinic representations of the simulation box and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} style will fill the entire general triclinic box with
particles on the lattice, as explained above.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} style also operates as explained above, but the check
for particles inside the region is performed \sphinxstyleemphasis{after} the particle
coordinates have been converted to the restricted triclinic box.
This means the region must also be defined with respect to the
restricted triclinic box, not the general triclinic box.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the simulation box is general triclinic, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{random},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} styles described next operate on the box \sphinxstyleemphasis{after} it has
been converted to restricted triclinic.  So all the settings for those
styles should be made in that context.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} style, a single particle is added to the system at
the specified coordinates.  This can be useful for debugging purposes
or to create a tiny system with a handful of particles at specified
positions.  For a 2d simulation the specified z coordinate must be
0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 2Jun2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{porosity} style has been renamed to \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} with added functionality.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style, \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} particles are added to the system at
randomly generated coordinates, which can be useful for generating an
amorphous system.  For 2d simulations, the z coordinates of all added
atoms will be 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The particles are created one by one using the specified random number
\sphinxstyleemphasis{seed}, resulting in the same set of particle coordinates, independent
of how many processors are being used in the simulation.  Unless the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword is specified, particles created by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{random}
style will typically be highly overlapped.  Various additional
criteria can be used to accept or reject a random particle insertion;
see the keyword discussion below.  Multiple attempts per particle are
made (see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxtry} keyword) until the insertion is either
successful or fails.  If this command fails to add all requested \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
particles, a warning will be output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region\sphinxhyphen{}ID} argument is specified as NULL, then the randomly
created particles will be anywhere in the simulation box.  If a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{region\sphinxhyphen{}ID} is specified, a geometric volume is filled that is both
inside the simulation box and is also consistent with the region
volume.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} command for details.  Note
that a region can be specified so that its “volume” is either inside
or outside its geometric boundary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the create\_atoms command adds particles to those that
already exist.  This means it can be used to add particles to a system
previously read in from a data or restart file.  Or the create\_atoms
command can be used multiple times, to add multiple sets of particles
to the simulation.  For example, grain boundaries can be created, by
interleaving the create\_atoms command with {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}
commands specifying different orientations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When this command is used, care should be taken to ensure the
resulting system does not contain particles that are highly
overlapped.  Such overlaps will cause many interatomic potentials to
compute huge energies and forces, leading to bad dynamics.  There are
several strategies to avoid this problem:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_atoms overlap}}}} command after
create\_atoms.  For example, this strategy can be used to overlay and
surround a large protein molecule with a volume of water molecules,
then delete water molecules that overlap with the protein atoms.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style, use the optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword to avoid
overlaps when each new particle is created.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before running dynamics on an overlapped system, perform an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.  Or run initial dynamics with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style soft}}}} or with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_limit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/limit}}}} to un\sphinxhyphen{}overlap the particles, before running normal
dynamics.

\end{itemize}


\begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.330\linewidth}
\centering
\sphinxhref{\_images/marble\_race.jpg}{\sphinxincludegraphics{{marble_race}.jpg}}
\end{wrapfigure}

\mbox{}\par\vskip-\dimexpr\baselineskip+\parskip\relax

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 2Jun2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style, a file with a triangle mesh in \sphinxhref{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STL\_(file\_format)}{STL format} is read and one or
more particles are placed into the area of each triangle.  The reader
supports both ASCII and binary files conforming to the format on the
Wikipedia page.  Binary STL files (e.g. as frequently offered for
3d\sphinxhyphen{}printing) can also be first converted to ASCII for editing with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:stlconvert}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{stl\_bin2txt tool}}}}.  The use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{units box} option
is required. There are two algorithms available for placing atoms:
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{qrand}. They can be selected via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{meshmode} option;
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect} is the default.  If the atom style allows it, the radius will
be set to a value depending on the algorithm and the value of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{radscale} parameter (see below), and the atoms created from the mesh
are assigned a new molecule ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect} mode a particle is created at the center of each triangle
unless the average distance of the triangle vertices from its center is
larger than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{radthresh} value (default is lattice spacing in
x\sphinxhyphen{}direction).  In case the average distance is over the threshold, the
triangle is recursively split into two halves along the the longest side
until the threshold is reached. There will be at least one sphere per
triangle. The value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{radthresh} is set as an argument to \sphinxstyleemphasis{meshmode
bisect}.  The average distance of the vertices from the center is also
used to set the radius.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxstyleemphasis{qrand} mode a quasi\sphinxhyphen{}random sequence is used to distribute particles
on mesh triangles using an approach by {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms:roberts2019}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Roberts)}}}}.
Particles are added to the triangle until the minimum number density is
met or exceeded such that every triangle will have at least one
particle.  The minimum number density is set as an argument to the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{qrand} option.  The radius will be set so that the sum of the area of
the radius of the particles created in place of a triangle will be equal
to the area of that triangle.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom placement algorithms in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style benefit from meshes
where triangles are close to equilateral.  It is therefore
recommended to pre\sphinxhyphen{}process STL files to optimize the mesh
accordingly.  There are multiple open source and commercial software
tools available with the capability to generate optimized meshes.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In most cases the atoms created in \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style will become an
immobile or rigid object that would not be time integrated or moved
by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_move::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix move}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  For
computational efficiency \sphinxstyleemphasis{and} to avoid undesired contributions to
pressure and potential energy due to close contacts, it is usually
beneficial to exclude computing interactions between the created
particles using {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Individual atoms are inserted by this command, unless the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}
keyword is used.  It specifies a \sphinxstyleemphasis{template\sphinxhyphen{}ID} previously defined
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} command, which reads a file that
defines the molecule.  The coordinates, atom types, charges, etc, as
well as any bond/angle/etc and special neighbor information for the
molecule can be specified in the molecule file.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} command for details.  The only settings
required to be in this file are the coordinates and types of atoms in
the molecule.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keyword in combination with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style template}}}} command, they must use
the same molecule template\sphinxhyphen{}ID.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a lattice to add molecules, e.g. via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single} styles, is exactly the same as adding atoms on lattice
points, except that entire molecules are added at each point, i.e. on
the point defined by each basis atom in the unit cell as it tiles the
simulation box or region.  This is done by placing the geometric
center of the molecule at the lattice point, and (by default) giving
the molecule a random orientation about the point.  The random \sphinxstyleemphasis{seed}
specified with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keyword is used for this operation, and the
random numbers generated by each processor are different.  This means
the coordinates of individual atoms (in the molecules) will be
different when running on different numbers of processors, unlike when
atoms are being created in parallel.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that with random rotations, it may be important to use a lattice
with a large enough spacing that adjacent molecules will not overlap,
regardless of their relative orientations.  See the description of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keyword below, which overrides the default random orientation
and inserts all molecules at a specified orientation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command is used to create
the simulation box, followed by the create\_atoms command with its
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} option for adding molecules, then you typically need to use the
optional keywords allowed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command
for extra bonds (angles,etc) or extra special neighbors.  This is
because by default, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command sets up a
non\sphinxhyphen{}molecular system that does not allow molecules to be added.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This is the meaning of the other optional keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{basis} keyword is only used when atoms (not molecules) are being
created.  It specifies an atom type that will be assigned to specific
basis atoms as they are created.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}
command for specifics on how basis atoms are defined for the unit cell
of the lattice.  By default, all created atoms are assigned the
argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} as their atom type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ratio} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{subset} keywords can be used in conjunction with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{box} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} styles to limit the total number of particles
inserted.  The lattice defines a set of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nlatt} eligible sites for
inserting particles, which may be limited by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} style or the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{var} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keywords.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ratio} keyword, only the specified
fraction of them (\(0 \le f \le 1\)) will be assigned particles.
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{subset} keyword only the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nsubset} of them will be
assigned particles.  In both cases the assigned lattice sites are
chosen randomly.  An iterative algorithm is used that ensures the
correct number of particles are inserted, in a perfectly random
fashion.  Which lattice sites are selected will change with the number
of processors used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} keyword only applies to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} style.  If it is set
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then if the specified position is outside the simulation
box, it will mapped back into the box, assuming the relevant
dimensions are periodic.  If it is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, no remapping is done
and no particle is created if its position is outside the box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keywords can be used together to provide a
criterion for accepting or rejecting the addition of an individual
atom, based on its coordinates.  They apply to all styles except
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{name} specified for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} keyword is the name of
an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} that should evaluate to a
zero or non\sphinxhyphen{}zero value based on one or two or three variables that
will store the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} coordinates of an atom (one variable per
coordinate).  If used, these other variables must be
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{internal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}} defined in the input
script; their initial numeric value can be anything.  They must be
internal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, because this command resets their values
directly.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keyword is used to identify the names of these
other variables, one variable for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate of a created atom,
one for \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and one for \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}.


\begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.500\linewidth}
\centering
\sphinxhref{\_images/sinusoid.jpg}{\sphinxincludegraphics{{sinusoid}.jpg}}
\end{wrapfigure}

\mbox{}\par\vskip-\dimexpr\baselineskip+\parskip\relax

\sphinxAtStartPar
When an atom is created, its \((x,y,z)\) coordinates become the values for
any \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} variable that is defined.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} variable is then
evaluated.  If the returned value is 0.0, the atom is not created.  If
it is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, the atom is created.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, these commands can be used in a 2d simulation, to
create a sinusoidal surface.  Note that the surface is “rough” due to
individual lattice points being “above” or “below” the mathematical
expression for the sinusoidal curve.  If a finer lattice were used,
the sinusoid would appear to be “smoother”.  Also note the use of the
“xlat” and “ylat” {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} keywords, which
converts lattice spacings to distance.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dimension}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{25}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{hex}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8442}
\PYG{k}{region      }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{box}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{block}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box  }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{box}

\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{xx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{internal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{yy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{internal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{v}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{(0.2*v\PYGZus{}y*ylat * cos(v\PYGZus{}xx/xlat * 2.0*PI*4.0/v\PYGZus{}x) + 0.5*v\PYGZus{}y*ylat \PYGZhy{} v\PYGZus{}yy) \PYGZgt{} 0.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{var}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yy}
\PYG{k}{write\PYGZus{}dump  }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sinusoid.lammpstrj}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keyword allows specification of the orientation
at which molecules are inserted.  The axis of rotation is
determined by the rotation vector \((R_x,R_y,R_z)\) that goes through the
insertion point.  The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{theta} determines the angle of
rotation around that axis.  Note that the direction of rotation for
the atoms around the rotation axis is consistent with the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand
rule: if your right\sphinxhyphen{}hand’s thumb points along \sphinxstyleemphasis{R}, then your fingers
wrap around the axis in the direction of rotation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{radscale} keyword only applies to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style and adjusts the
radius of created particles (see above), provided this is supported by
the atom style.  Its value is a prefactor (must be \(>\) 0.0, default is
1.0) that is applied to the atom radius inferred from the size of the
individual triangles in the triangle mesh that the particle corresponds
to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 2Jun2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword only applies to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style.  It prevents
newly created particles from being created closer than the specified
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Doverlap} distance from any other particle.  If particles have finite
size (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}} for example) \sphinxstyleemphasis{Doverlap}
should be specified large enough to include the particle size in the
non\sphinxhyphen{}overlapping criterion.  If molecules are being randomly inserted, then
an insertion is only accepted if each particle in the molecule meets the
overlap criterion with respect to other particles (not including particles
in the molecule itself).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Checking for overlaps is a costly \(\mathcal{O}(N(N+M))\) operation for
inserting \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} new particles into a system with \sphinxstyleemphasis{M} existing particles.
This is because distances to all \sphinxstyleemphasis{M} existing particles are computed for
each new particle that is added.  Thus the intended use of this
keyword is to add relatively small numbers of particles to systems
that remain at a relatively low density even after the new
particles are created.  Careful use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxtry} keyword in
combination with \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} is recommended.  See the discussion
above about systems with overlapped particles for alternate
strategies that allow for overlapped insertions.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 2Jun2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxtry} keyword only applies to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style.  It limits
the number of attempts to generate valid coordinates for a single new
particle that satisfy all requirements imposed by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{var},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keywords.  The default is 10 attempts per particle
before the loop over the requested \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} particles advances to the next
particle.  Note that if insertion success is unlikely (e.g., inserting
new particles into a dense system using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword),
setting the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxtry} keyword to a large value may result in this
command running for a long time.


\begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.300\linewidth}
\centering
\sphinxhref{\_images/overlap.png}{\sphinxincludegraphics{{overlap}.png}}
\end{wrapfigure}

\mbox{}\par\vskip-\dimexpr\baselineskip+\parskip\relax

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style using these commands

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n}{lj}
\PYG{k}{dimension}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{region        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{box}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{block}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{box}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{13487}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{overlap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{maxtry}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
to produce a system as shown in the image with 1520 particles (out of
2000 requested) that are moderately dense and which have no overlaps
sufficient to prevent the LJ pair\_style from running properly (because
the overlap criterion is 1.0).  The create\_atoms command ran for 0.3 s
on a single CPU core.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{units} keyword determines the meaning of the distance units used
by parameters for various styles.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} value selects standard
distance units as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command (e.g.,
\(\AA\) for units = \sphinxstyleemphasis{real} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal}.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} value means
the distance units are in lattice spacings.  These are affected settings:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} style: coordinates of the particle created

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style: overlap distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{Doverlap} by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style: \sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect} threshold value for \sphinxstyleemphasis{meshmode} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style: \sphinxstyleemphasis{radthresh} value for \sphinxstyleemphasis{meshmode} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bisect}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style: \sphinxstyleemphasis{density} value for \sphinxstyleemphasis{meshmode} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{qrand}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since \sphinxstyleemphasis{density} represents an area (distance \textasciicircum{}2), the lattice spacing
factor is also squared.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom IDs are assigned to created atoms in the following way.  The
collection of created atoms are assigned consecutive IDs that start
immediately following the largest atom ID existing before the
create\_atoms command was invoked.  This is done by the processor’s
communicating the number of atoms they each own, the first processor
numbering its atoms from \(1\) to \(N_1\), the second processor from
\(N_1+1\) to \(N_2\), and so on, where \(N_1\) is the number of
atoms owned by the first processor, \(N_2\) is the number owned by the
second processor, and so forth.  Thus, when the same simulation is performed on
different numbers of processors, there is no guarantee a particular created
atom will be assigned the same ID in both simulations.  If molecules are being
created, molecule IDs are assigned to created molecules in a similar fashion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Aside from their ID, atom type, and \(xyz\) position, other properties of
created atoms are set to default values, depending on which quantities
are defined by the chosen {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style}}}}.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style}}}} command for more details.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} commands for info on
how to change these values.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
charge = 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dipole moment magnitude = 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
diameter = 1.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
shape = 0.0 0.0 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density = 1.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
volume = 1.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
velocity = 0.0 0.0 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
angular velocity = 0.0 0.0 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
angular momentum = 0.0 0.0 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
quaternion = (1,0,0,0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bonds, angles, dihedrals, impropers = none

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If molecules are being created, these defaults can be overridden by
values specified in the file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}}
command. That is, the file typically defines bonds (angles, etc.) between
atoms in the molecule, and can optionally define charges on each atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere} atom style sets the default particle diameter to
1.0 as well as the density.  This means the mass for the particle is not
1.0, but is \(\frac{\pi}{6} d^3 = 0.5236\), where \(d\) is the
diameter.  When using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} style, the particle diameter is adjusted from
the size of the individual triangles in the triangle mesh.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ellipsoid} atom style sets the default particle shape
to (0.0 0.0 0.0) and the density to 1.0, which means it is a point
particle, not an ellipsoid, and has a mass of 1.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri} style sets the default volume and density to 1.0
and thus also set the mass for the particle to 1.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command can be used to override many of these
default settings.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{create_atoms:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
An {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} must be previously defined to use this
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A rotation vector specified for a single molecule must be in
the z\sphinxhyphen{}direction for a 2d model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule templates}}}} that are created from multiple
files, i.e. contain multiple molecule \sphinxstyleemphasis{sets}, only the first set is
used.  To create multiple molecules the files currently need to be
merged and different molecule IDs assigned with a Molecules section.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{create_atoms:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{create_atoms:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{basis} keyword is that all created atoms are
assigned the argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} as their atom type (when single atoms are
being created).  The other defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap} = no, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} = random,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{radscale} = 1.0, \sphinxstyleemphasis{radthresh} = x\sphinxhyphen{}lattice spacing, \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} not
checked, \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxtry} = 10, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{units} = lattice.

\section{create\_bonds command}
\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:create-bonds-command}}\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{create_bonds::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{many} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/improper}

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{many} args = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID btype rmin rmax
  group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of first group
  group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of second group, bonds will be between atoms in the 2 groups
  btype = bond type of created bonds
  rmin = minimum distance between pair of atoms to bond together
  rmax = maximum distance between pair of atoms to bond together
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single/bond} args = btype batom1 batom2
  btype = bond type of new bond
  batom1,batom2 = atom IDs for two atoms in bond
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single/angle} args = atype aatom1 aatom2 aatom3
  atype = angle type of new angle
  aatom1,aatom2,aatom3 = atom IDs for three atoms in angle
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single/dihedral} args = dtype datom1 datom2 datom3 datom4
  dtype = dihedral type of new dihedral
  datom1,datom2,datom3,datom4 = atom IDs for four atoms in dihedral
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single/improper} args = itype iatom1 iatom2 iatom3 iatom4
  itype = improper type of new improper
  iatom1,iatom2,iatom3,iatom4 = atom IDs for four atoms in improper
\end{sphinxalltt}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{special}

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{special} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{many}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{many}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{surf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{solvent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.4}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{angle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{52}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{98}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{107}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{19}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{27}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{101}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{improper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{23}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{26}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{31}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{57}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create bonds between pairs of atoms that meet a specified distance
criteria.  Or create a single bond, angle, dihedral or improper between 2, 3,
or 4 specified atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The new bond (angle, dihedral, improper) interactions will then be computed
during a simulation by the bond (angle, dihedral, improper) potential defined by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_coeff}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_coeff}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_coeff}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{many} style is useful for adding bonds to a system (e.g., between
nearest neighbors in a lattice of atoms) without having to enumerate
all the bonds in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} styles are useful for adding bonds, angles, dihedrals, and
impropers to a system incrementally, then continuing a simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this command does not auto\sphinxhyphen{}create any angle, dihedral, or improper
interactions when a bond is added, nor does it auto\sphinxhyphen{}create any bonds
when an angle, dihedral, or improper is added.  It also will not auto\sphinxhyphen{}create
any angles when a dihedral or improper is added.  Thus, the flexibility of this
command is limited.  It can be used several times to create different types of
bond at different distances, but it cannot typically auto\sphinxhyphen{}create all the
bonds or angles or dihedrals or impropers that would normally be defined in a
data file for a complex system of molecules.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the system has no bonds (angles, dihedrals, impropers) to begin
with, or if more bonds per atom are being added than currently exist,
then you must ensure that the number of bond types and the maximum
number of bonds per atom are set to large enough values, and
similarly for angles, dihedrals, impropers, and special neighbors,
otherwise an error may occur when too many bonds (angles, dihedrals,
impropers) are added to an atom.  If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
command is used to define the system, these parameters can be set via
its optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/bond/types}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/bond/per/atom}, and similar
keywords to the command.  If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}
command is used to define the system, these two parameters can be set
via its optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/types} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/bond/per/atom} arguments,
and similarly for angles, dihedrals, and impropers.  See the
corresponding documentation pages for these two commands for details.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{many} style will create bonds between pairs of atoms \(I,J\),
where \(I\) is in one of the two specified groups and \(J\) is in the
other.  The two groups can be the same (e.g., group “all”).  The created bonds
will be of bond type \sphinxstyleemphasis{btype}, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{btype} must be a value between 1 and the
number of bond types defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a bond to be created, an \(I,J\) pair of atoms must be a distance
\(D\) apart such that \(r_\text{min} \le D \le r_\text{max}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following settings must have been made in an input script before
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{many} style is used:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
special\_bonds weight for 1\textendash{}2 interactions must be 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} must be defined

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
no {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} defined

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
minimum {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} cutoff + {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}}
skin \(\ge r_\text{max}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These settings are required so that a neighbor list can be created to
search for nearby atoms.  Pairs of atoms that are already bonded cannot
appear in the neighbor list, to avoid creation of duplicate bonds.  The
neighbor list for all atom type pairs must also extend to a distance
that encompasses the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmax} for new bonds to create.  When using
periodic boundary conditions, the box length in each periodic dimension
must be larger than \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmax}, so that no bonds are created between the
system and its own periodic image.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to create bonds between pairs of 1\textendash{}3 or 1\textendash{}4 atoms in
the current bond topology, then you need to use {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds
lj 0 1 1}}}} to ensure those pairs appear in the
neighbor list.  They will not appear with the default special\_bonds
settings, which are zero for 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, and 1\textendash{}4 atoms.  1\textendash{}3 or 1\textendash{}4
atoms are those which are two hops or three hops apart in the bond
topology.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An additional requirement for this style is that your system must be
ready to perform a simulation.  This means, for example, that all
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} coefficients be set via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.  A {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}}
command and all bond coefficients must also be set, even if no bonds
exist before this command is invoked.  This is because the building of
neighbor list requires initialization and setup of a simulation,
similar to what a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command would require.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that you can change any of these settings after this command
executes (e.g., if you wish to use long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interactions)
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command for your subsequent
simulation.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/bond} style creates a single bond of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{btype} between
two atoms with IDs \sphinxstyleemphasis{batom1} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{batom2}.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Btype} must be a value
between 1 and the number of bond types defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/angle} style creates a single angle of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{atype}
between three atoms with IDs \sphinxstyleemphasis{aatom1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{aatom2}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{aatom3}.  The
ordering of the atoms is the same as in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Angles} section of a data
file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command (i.e., the three atoms
are ordered linearly within the angle; the central atom is \sphinxstyleemphasis{aatom2}).
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Atype} must be a value between 1 and the number of angle types
defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/dihedral} style creates a single dihedral of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{dtype}
between four atoms with IDs \sphinxstyleemphasis{datom1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{datom2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{datom3}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{datom4}.  The
ordering of the atoms is the same as in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Dihedrals} section of a data file
read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.  I.e. the 4 atoms are ordered
linearly within the dihedral.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{dtype} must be a value between 1 and
the number of dihedral types defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{single/improper} style creates a single improper of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{itype}
between four atoms with IDs \sphinxstyleemphasis{iatom1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{iatom2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{iatom3}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{iatom4}.  The
ordering of the atoms is the same as in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Impropers} section of a data file
read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.  I.e. the 4 atoms are ordered
linearly within the improper.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{itype} must be a value between 1 and
the number of improper types defined.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} controls whether an internal list of special
bonds is created after one or more bonds, or a single angle, dihedral, or
improper is added to the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}.  A value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} cannot be used
with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{many} style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is an expensive operation since the bond topology for the system
must be walked to find all 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, and 1\textendash{}4 interactions to store in an
internal list, which is used when pairwise interactions are weighted;
see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus if you are adding a few bonds or a large list of angles all at
the same time, by using this command repeatedly, it is more efficient
to only trigger the internal list to be created once, after the last
bond (or angle, or dihedral, or improper) is added:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{52}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{98}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{73}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{74}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{17}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{386}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{112}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{183}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that you \sphinxstylestrong{must} ensure the internal list is rebuilt after the last
bond (angle, dihedral, improper) is added, \sphinxstyleemphasis{before} performing a simulation.
Otherwise, pairwise interactions will not be properly excluded or
weighted.  LAMMPS does \sphinxstylestrong{not} check that you have done this correctly.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command cannot be used with molecular systems defined using
molecule template files via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style template}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{many}, no {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace style}}}} must be
defined. Also, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmax} value must be smaller than any periodic box
length and the neighbor list cutoff (largest pair cutoff plus neighbor
skin).


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{create_bonds:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword default is special = yes.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{create\_box@\spxentry{create\_box}}\ignorespaces 

\section{create\_box command}
\label{\detokenize{create_box:create-box-command}}\label{\detokenize{create_box:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{create_box::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{create_box:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{region\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{alo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ahi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{blo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bhi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{clo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = \# of atom types to use in this simulation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of region to use as simulation domain or NULL for general triclinic box

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
alo,ahi,blo,bhi,clo,chi = multipliers on a1,a2,a3 vectors defined by {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command (only when region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = NULL)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/types} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle/types} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral/types} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper/types} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/bond/per/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/angle/per/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dihedral/per/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/improper/per/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/special/per/atom}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/types} value = \# of bond types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{angle/types} value = \# of angle types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral/types} value = \# of dihedral types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{improper/types} value = \# of improper types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/bond/per/atom} value = \# of bonds per atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/angle/per/atom} value = \# of angles per atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dihedral/per/atom} value = \# of dihedrals per atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/improper/per/atom} value = \# of impropers per atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/special/per/atom} value = \# of special neighbors per atom
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{create_box:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} orthogonal or restricted triclinic box using regionID = mybox}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mybox}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mybox}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{types}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{extra}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{per}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 2d general triclinic box using primitive cell for 2d hex lattice}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.86602540378}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{n}{a3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{triclinic}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{general}
\PYG{k}{create\PYGZus{}box    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 3d general triclinic box using primitive cell for 3d fcc lattice}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{triclinic}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{general}
\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{create_box:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command creates a simulation box. It also partitions the box into
a regular 3d grid of smaller sub\sphinxhyphen{}boxes, one per processor (MPI task).
The geometry of the partitioning is based on the size and shape of the
simulation box, the number of processors being used and the settings
of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}} command.  The partitioning can
later be changed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Simulation boxes in LAMMPS can be either orthogonal or triclinic in
shape.  Orthogonal boxes are a brick in 3d (rectangle in 2d) with 6
faces that are each perpendicular to one of the standard xyz
coordinate axes.  Triclinic boxes are a parallelepiped in 3d
(parallelogram in 2d) with opposite pairs of faces parallel to each
other.  LAMMPS supports two forms of triclinic boxes, restricted and
general, which differ in how the box is oriented with respect to the
xyz coordinate axes.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}}
for a detailed description of all 3 kinds of simulation boxes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} is the number of atom types that will be used in the
simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Orthogonal and restricted triclinic boxes are created by specifying a
region ID previously defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} command.
General triclinic boxes are discussed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the region is not of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism}, then LAMMPS encloses the region
(block, sphere, etc.) with an axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned orthogonal bounding box
which becomes the simulation domain.  For a 2d simulation, the zlo and
zhi values of the simulation box must straddle zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the region is of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism}, LAMMPS creates a non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal
simulation domain shaped as a parallelepiped with triclinic symmetry.
As defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region prism}}}} command, the
parallelepiped has an “origin” at (xlo,ylo,zlo) and three edge vectors
starting from the origin given by \(\vec a =
(x_\text{hi}-x_\text{lo},0,0)\); \(\vec b =
(xy,y_\text{hi}-y_\text{lo},0)\); and \(\vec c =
(xz,yz,z_\text{hi}-z_\text{lo})\).  In LAMMPS lingo, this is a
restricted triclinic box because the three edge vectors cannot be
defined in arbitrary (general) directions.  The parameters \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} can be 0.0 or positive or negative values and are
called “tilt factors” because they are the amount of displacement
applied to faces of an originally orthogonal box to transform it into
the parallelepiped.  For a 2d simulation, the zlo and zhi values of
the simulation box must straddle zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically a \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism} region used with the create\_box command should
have tilt factors \((xy,xz,yz)\) that do not skew the box more
than half the distance of the parallel box length.  For example, if
\(x_\text{lo} = 2\) and \(x_\text{hi} = 12\), then the
\(x\) box length is 10 and the \(xy\) tilt factor must be
between \(-5\) and \(5\).  Similarly, both \(xz\) and
\(yz\) must be between \(-(x_\text{hi}-x_\text{lo})/2\) and
\(+(y_\text{hi}-y_\text{lo})/2\).  Note that this is not a
limitation, since if the maximum tilt factor is 5 (as in this
example), then configurations with tilt \(= \dots, -15\),
\(-5\), \(5\), \(15\), \(25, \dots\) are all
geometrically equivalent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS will issue a warning if the tilt factors of the created box do
not meet this criterion.  This is because simulations with large tilt
factors may run inefficiently, since they require more ghost atoms and
thus more communication.  With very large tilt factors, LAMMPS may
eventually produce incorrect trajectories and stop with errors due to
lost atoms or similar issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} page for geometric
descriptions of triclinic boxes and tilt factors, as well as how to
transform the restricted triclinic parameters to and from other
commonly used triclinic representations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a prism region is used, the simulation domain should normally be
periodic in the dimension that the tilt is applied to, which is given
by the second dimension of the tilt factor (e.g., \(y\) for
\(xy\) tilt).  This is so that pairs of atoms interacting across
that boundary will have one of them shifted by the tilt factor.
Periodicity is set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.  For
example, if the \(xy\) tilt factor is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, then the \(y\)
dimension should be periodic.  Similarly, the \(z\) dimension
should be periodic if \(xz\) or \(yz\) is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero.  LAMMPS
does not require this periodicity, but you may lose atoms if this is
not the case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if your simulation will tilt the box (e.g., via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command), the simulation box must be
created as triclinic, even if the tilt factors are initially 0.0.  You
can also change an orthogonal box to a triclinic box or vice versa by
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change box}}}} command with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{ortho} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic} options.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the system is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic (in a dimension), then you should not
make the lo/hi box dimensions (as defined in your {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} command) radically smaller/larger than the extent of the
atoms you eventually plan to create (e.g., via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command).  For example, if your
atoms extend from 0 to 50, you should not specify the box bounds as
\(-10000\) and \(10000\). This is because as described
above, LAMMPS uses the specified box size to lay out the 3d grid of
processors.  A huge (mostly empty) box will be sub\sphinxhyphen{}optimal for
performance when using “fixed” boundary conditions (see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command).  When using “shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap”
boundary conditions (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command), a
huge (mostly empty) box may cause a parallel simulation to lose
atoms the first time that LAMMPS shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wraps the box around the
atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
As noted above, general triclinic boxes in LAMMPS allow the box to
have arbitrary edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C}.  The only
restrictions are that the three vectors be distinct, non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, and not
co\sphinxhyphen{}planar.  They must also define a right\sphinxhyphen{}handed system such that
(\sphinxstylestrong{A} x \sphinxstylestrong{B}) points in the direction of \sphinxstylestrong{C}.  Note that a
left\sphinxhyphen{}handed system can be converted to a right\sphinxhyphen{}handed system by simply
swapping the order of any pair of the \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} vectors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To create a general triclinic boxes, the region is specified as NULL
and the next 6 parameters (alo,ahi,blo,bhi,clo,chi) define the three
edge vectors \sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} using additional information
previously defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The lattice must be of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} and use its \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general}
option.  This insures the lattice satisfies the restrictions listed
above.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1, *a2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} settings of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}
command define the edge vectors of a unit cell of the general
triclinic lattice.  This command uses them to define the three edge
vectors and origin of the general triclinic box as:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{A} = (ahi\sphinxhyphen{}alo) * \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{B} = (bhi\sphinxhyphen{}blo) * \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{C} = (chi\sphinxhyphen{}clo) * \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
origin = (alo*a1 + blo*a2 + clo*a3)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For 2d general triclinic boxes, clo = \sphinxhyphen{}0.5 and chi = 0.5 is required.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS allows specification of general triclinic simulation boxes
as a convenience for users who may be converting data from
solid\sphinxhyphen{}state crystallographic representations or from DFT codes for
input to LAMMPS.  However, as explained on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc page, internally,
LAMMPS only uses restricted triclinic simulation boxes.  This means
the box defined by this command and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom information
(e.g. coordinates, velocities) defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command are converted (rotated) from general to
restricted triclinic form when the two commands are invoked.  The
\textless{}Howto\_triclinic\textgreater{}\textasciigrave{} doc page also discusses other LAMMPS commands
which can input/output general triclinic representations of the
simulation box and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keywords can be used to create a system that allows for
bond (angle, dihedral, improper) interactions, or for molecules with
special 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, or 1\textendash{}4 neighbors to be added later.  These
optional keywords serve the same purpose as the analogous keywords
that can be used in a data file which are recognized by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command when it sets up a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if these keywords are not used, then the create\_box command
creates an atomic (non\sphinxhyphen{}molecular) simulation that does not allow bonds
between pairs of atoms to be defined, or a {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond potential}}}} to be specified, or for molecules with special neighbors
to be added to the system by commands such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms mol}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, see the examples/deposit/in.deposit.molecule script,
which deposits molecules onto a substrate.  Initially there are no
molecules in the system, but they are added later by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
deposit}}}} command.  The create\_box command in the script
uses the bond/types and extra/bond/per/atom keywords to allow this.
If the added molecule contained more than one special bond (allowed by
default), an extra/special/per/atom keyword would also need to be
specified.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
An {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} must have
been previously defined to use this command.
