\section{delete\_atoms command}
\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:delete-atoms-command}}\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{group} args = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID
\sphinxstyleemphasis{region} args = region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
\sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} args = cutoff group1\sphinxhyphen{}ID group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  cutoff = delete one atom from pairs of atoms within the cutoff (distance units)
  group1\sphinxhyphen{}ID = one atom in pair must be in this group
  group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID = other atom in pair must be in this group
\sphinxstyleemphasis{random} args = ranstyle value eflag group\sphinxhyphen{}ID region\sphinxhyphen{}ID seed
  ranstyle = \sphinxstyleemphasis{fraction} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{count}
    for \sphinxstyleemphasis{fraction}:
      value = fraction (0.0 to 1.0) of eligible atoms to delete
      eflag =  \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} for fast approximate deletion, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} for exact deletion
    for \sphinxstyleemphasis{count}:
      value = number of atoms to delete
      eflag = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} for warning if count \textgreater{} eligible atoms, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} for error
  group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = group within which to perform deletions
  region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = region within which to perform deletions
              or NULL to only impose the group criterion
  seed = random number seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{variable} args = variable\sphinxhyphen{}name
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{compress} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compress} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{edge}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{sphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{compress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{overlap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{overlap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{solvent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{colloid}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fraction}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cube}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{482793}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fraction}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{polymer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{482793}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{random}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{482793}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{checkers}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Delete the specified atoms.  This command can be used, for example, to
carve out voids from a block of material or to delete created atoms
that are too close to each other (e.g., at a grain boundary).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{group}, all atoms belonging to the group are deleted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{region}, all atoms in the region volume are deleted.
Additional atoms can be deleted if they are in a molecule for which
one or more atoms were deleted within the region; see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}
keyword discussion below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} pairs of atoms whose distance of separation is
within the specified cutoff distance are searched for, and one of the
two atoms is deleted.  Only pairs where one of the two atoms is in the
first group specified and the other atom is in the second group are
considered.  The atom that is in the first group is the one that is
deleted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that it is OK for the two group IDs to be the same (e.g., group
\sphinxstyleemphasis{all}), or for some atoms to be members of both groups.  In these
cases, either atom in the pair may be deleted.  Also note that if
there are atoms which are members of both groups, the only guarantee
is that at the end of the deletion operation, enough deletions will
have occurred that no atom pairs within the cutoff will remain
(subject to the group restriction).  There is no guarantee that the
minimum number of atoms will be deleted, or that the same atoms will
be deleted when running on different numbers of processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} a subset of eligible atoms are deleted.  Which
atoms to delete are chosen randomly using the specified random number
\sphinxstyleemphasis{seed}.  Which atoms are deleted may vary when running on different
numbers of processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{ranstyle} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{fraction}, the specified fractional \sphinxstyleemphasis{value} (0.0 to
1.0) of eligible atoms are deleted.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{eflag} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, then
the number of deleted atoms will be approximate, but the operation
will be fast.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{eflag} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then the number deleted
will match the requested fraction, but for large systems the selection
of deleted atoms may take additional time to determine.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{ranstyle} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{count}, the specified integer \sphinxstyleemphasis{value} is the number
of eligible atoms are deleted.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{eflag} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, then if the
requested number is larger then the number of eligible atoms, a
warning is issued and only the eligible atoms are deleted instead of
the requested \sphinxstyleemphasis{value}.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{eflag} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, an error is
triggered instead and LAMMPS will exit.  For large systems the
selection of atoms to delete may take additional time to determine,
the same as for requesting an exact fraction with \sphinxstyleemphasis{pstyle} =
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fraction}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Which atoms are eligible for deletion for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} is determined
by the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{region\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.  To be eligible, an atom
must be in both the specified group and region.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} = all,
there is effectively no group criterion.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{region\sphinxhyphen{}ID} is specified
as NULL, no region criterion is imposed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 4May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable}, all atoms for which the atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable with
the given name evaluates to non\sphinxhyphen{}zero will be deleted. Additional atoms
can be deleted if they are in a molecule for which one or more atoms
were deleted within the region; see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keyword discussion below.
This option allows complex selections of atoms not covered by the
other options listed above.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is the meaning of the optional keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{compress} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then after atoms are
deleted, then atom IDs are re\sphinxhyphen{}assigned so that they run from 1 to the
number of atoms in the system.  Note that this is not done for
molecular systems (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} command),
regardless of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{compress} setting, since it would foul up the bond
connectivity that has already been assigned.  However, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{reset_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{reset\_atoms id}}}} command can be used after this
command to accomplish the same thing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the re\sphinxhyphen{}assignment of IDs is not really a compression, where
gaps in atom IDs are removed by decrementing atom IDs that are larger.
Instead the IDs for all atoms are erased, and new IDs are assigned so
that the atoms owned by individual processors have consecutive IDs, as
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command explains.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A molecular system with fixed bonds, angles, dihedrals, or improper
interactions, is one where the topology of the interactions is
typically defined in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command, and where the interactions themselves are
defined with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style}}}}, etc. commands.  If you delete atoms from such a system,
you must be careful not to end up with bonded interactions that are
stored by remaining atoms but which include deleted atoms.  This will
cause LAMMPS to generate a “missing atoms” error when the bonded
interaction is computed.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keywords offer two ways
to do that.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} then any bond or angle or
dihedral or improper interaction that includes a deleted atom is also
removed from the lists of such interactions stored by non\sphinxhyphen{}deleted
atoms.  Note that simply deleting interactions due to dangling bonds
(e.g., at a surface) may result in a inaccurate or invalid model for
the remaining atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then for every atom that is
deleted, all other atoms in the same molecule (with the same molecule
ID) will also be deleted.  This is not done for atoms with molecule ID
= 0, since such an ID is assumed to flag isolated atoms that are not
part of molecules.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The molecule deletion operation is invoked after all individual
atoms have been deleted using the rules described above for each
style.  This means additional atoms may be deleted that are not in the
group or region, that are not required by the overlap cutoff
criterion, or that will create a higher fraction of porosity than was
requested.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} styles requires inter\sphinxhyphen{}processor communication to acquire
ghost atoms and build a neighbor list.  This means that your system
must be ready to perform a simulation before using this command (force
fields setup, atom masses set, etc.).  Since a neighbor list is used to
find overlapping atom pairs, it also means that you must define a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}} with the minimum force cutoff distance
between any pair of atoms types (plus the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}}
skin) \(\ge\) the specified overlap cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command is used with a
setting of 0, then a pair of bonded atoms (1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, or 1\textendash{}4) will not
appear in the neighbor list, and thus will not be considered for
deletion by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} styles.  You probably do not want to
delete one atom in a bonded pair anyway.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond yes} option cannot be used with molecular systems defined
using molecule template files via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style template}}}} commands.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{reset_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{reset\_atoms id}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{delete_atoms:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are compress = yes, bond = no, mol = no.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{delete\_bonds@\spxentry{delete\_bonds}}\ignorespaces 

\section{delete\_bonds command}
\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:delete-bonds-command}}\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = group ID

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{stats}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} arg = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} arg = an atom type or range of types (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} arg = a bond type or range of types (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} arg = an angle type or range of types (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} arg = a dihedral type or range of types (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} arg = an improper type or range of types (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stats} arg = none
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{undo} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{remove} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{special}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{any} arg = none = turn off interactions if any atoms are in the group (or on if \sphinxstyleemphasis{undo} is also used)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{undo} arg = none = turn specified bonds on instead of off
\sphinxstyleemphasis{remove} arg = permanently remove bonds that have been turned off
\sphinxstyleemphasis{special} arg = recompute pairwise 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, and 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 lists
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{frozen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{remove}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stats}

\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hc}
\PYG{k}{delete\PYGZus{}bonds }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Turn off (or on) molecular topology interactions (i.e., bonds, angles,
dihedrals, and/or impropers).  This command is useful for deleting
interactions that have been previously turned off by bond\sphinxhyphen{}breaking
potentials.  It is also useful for turning off topology interactions
between frozen or rigid atoms.  Pairwise interactions can be turned
off via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}} command.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command also effectively turns off certain
bond and angle interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all styles, by default, an interaction is only turned off (or on)
if all the atoms involved are in the specified group.  See the \sphinxstyleemphasis{any}
keyword to change the behavior.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Several of the styles (\sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper})
take a \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} as an argument.  The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} can be a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_type_labels::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{type label}}}}.  Otherwise, the type should be an
integer from 0 to \(N\), where \(N\) is the number of relevant
types (atom types, bond types, etc.).  A value of 0 is only relevant for
style \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}; see details below.  For numeric types, a wildcard asterisk
can be used in place of or in conjunction with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} argument to
specify a range of types.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or “m*” or
“m*n”.  If \(N\) is the number of types, then an asterisk with no
numeric values means all types from 0 to \(N\).  A leading asterisk
means all types from 0 to n (inclusive).  A trailing asterisk means all
types from m to N (inclusive).  A middle asterisk means all types from m to
n (inclusive).  Note that it is fine to include a type of 0 for non\sphinxhyphen{}bond
styles; it will simply be ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} all bond, angle, dihedral, and improper interactions
of any type, involving atoms in the group, are turned off.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} is the same as style \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} except that in addition, one
or more of the atoms involved in the bond, angle, dihedral, or
improper interaction must also be of the specified atom type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}, only bonds are candidates for turn\sphinxhyphen{}off, and the bond
must also be of the specified type.  Styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} are treated similarly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}, you can set the type to 0 to delete bonds that have
been previously broken by a bond\sphinxhyphen{}breaking potential (which sets the
bond type to 0 when a bond is broken); for example, see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{stats} no interactions are turned off (or on); the status
of all interactions in the specified group is simply reported.  This
is useful for diagnostic purposes if bonds have been turned off by a
bond\sphinxhyphen{}breaking potential during a previous run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default behavior of the delete\_bonds command is to turn off
interactions by toggling their type to a negative value, but not to
permanently remove the interaction.  For example, a bond\_type of 2 is set to
\(-2.\)  The neighbor list creation routines will not include such an
interaction in their interaction lists.  The default is also to not
alter the list of 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, or 1\textendash{}4 neighbors computed by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command and used to weight pairwise
force and energy calculations.  This means that pairwise computations
will proceed as if the bond (or angle, etc.) were still turned on.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Several keywords can be appended to the argument list to alter the
default behaviors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} keyword changes the requirement that all atoms in the bond
(angle, etc.) must be in the specified group in order to turn off the
interaction.  Instead, if any of the atoms in the interaction are in
the specified group, it will be turned off (or on if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{undo}
keyword is used).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{undo} keyword inverts the delete\_bonds command so that the
specified bonds, angles, etc. are turned on if they are currently
turned off.  This means a negative value is toggled to positive.  For
example, for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle}, if \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} is specified as 2, then all
angles with current type = \(-2\) are reset to type = \(2\).
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command also sets bond and angle
types negative, so this option should not be used on those interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{remove} keyword is invoked at the end of the delete\_bonds
operation.  It causes turned\sphinxhyphen{}off bonds (angles, etc.) to be removed
from each atom’s data structure and then adjusts the global bond
(angle, etc.) counts accordingly.  Removal is a permanent change;
removed bonds cannot be turned back on via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{undo} keyword.
Removal does not alter the pairwise 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, or 1\textendash{}4 weighting list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} keyword is invoked at the end of the delete\_bonds
operation, after (optional) removal.  It re\sphinxhyphen{}computes the pairwise 1\textendash{}2,
1\textendash{}3, 1\textendash{}4 weighting list.  The weighting list computation treats
turned\sphinxhyphen{}off bonds the same as turned\sphinxhyphen{}on.  Thus, turned\sphinxhyphen{}off bonds must
be removed if you wish to change the weighting list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the choice of \sphinxstyleemphasis{remove} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} options affects how
1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, 1\textendash{}4 pairwise interactions will be computed across bonds that
have been modified by the delete\_bonds command.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command requires inter\sphinxhyphen{}processor communication to acquire ghost
atoms, to coordinate the deleting of bonds, angles, etc. between atoms
shared by multiple processors.  This means that your system must be
ready to perform a simulation before using this command (force fields
setup, atom masses set, etc.).  Just as would be needed to run
dynamics, the force field you define should define a cutoff
(e.g., through a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command) which is long
enough for a processor to acquire the ghost atoms its needs to compute
bond, angle, etc. interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If deleted bonds (or angles, etc.) are removed but the 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, and 1\textendash{}4
weighting list is not recomputed, this can cause a later
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command to fail due to an atom’s bonds being
inconsistent with the weighting list.  This should only happen if the
group used in the fix command includes both atoms in the bond, in
which case you probably should be recomputing the weighting list.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} exclude,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{delete_bonds:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\section{dielectric command}
\label{\detokenize{dielectric:dielectric-command}}\label{\detokenize{dielectric:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dielectric::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dielectric:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dielectric}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
value = dielectric constant

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dielectric:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dielectric}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dielectric:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the dielectric constant for Coulombic interactions (pairwise and
long\sphinxhyphen{}range) to this value.  The constant is unitless, since it is used
to reduce the strength of the interactions.  The value is used in the
denominator of the formulas for Coulombic interactions (e.g., a value
of 4.0 reduces the Coulombic interactions to 25\% of their default
strength).  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command for more
details.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dielectric:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{dielectric:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}}

\label{\detokenize{dielectric:default}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dielectric}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\index{dihedral\_coeff@\spxentry{dihedral\_coeff}}\ignorespaces 

\section{dihedral\_coeff command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:dihedral-coeff-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = numeric dihedral type (see asterisk form below) or alphanumeric type label

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = coefficients for one or more dihedral types

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}

\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{backbone}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{backbone}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify the dihedral force field coefficients for one or more dihedral
types.  The number and meaning of the coefficients depends on the
dihedral style.  Dihedral coefficients can also be set in the data file
read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command or in a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N\) can be specified in one of two ways.  An explicit numeric
value can be used, as in the first example above.  Or \(N\) can be
an alphanumeric type label, which is a string defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} command or in a corresponding section of a
data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For numeric values only, a wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can be used to set the
coefficients for multiple dihedral types.  This takes the form “*” or
“*n” or “n*” or “m*n”.  If \(N\) is the number of dihedral types,
then an asterisk with no numeric values means all types from 1 to
\(N\).  A leading asterisk means all types from 1 to n (inclusive).
A trailing asterisk means all types from n to \(N\) (inclusive).  A
middle asterisk means all types from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that using a dihedral\_coeff command can override a previous setting
for the same dihedral type.  For example, these commands set the coeffs
for all dihedral types, then overwrite the coeffs for just dihedral type
2:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A line in a data file that specifies dihedral coefficients uses the exact
same format as the arguments of the dihedral\_coeff command in an input
script, except that wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisks should not be used since
coefficients for all \(N\) types must be listed in the file.  For example,
under the “Dihedral Coeffs” section of a data file, the line that
corresponds to the first example above would be listed as

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1 80.0 1 3
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style class2}}}} is an exception to
this rule, in that an additional argument is used in the input script
to allow specification of the cross\sphinxhyphen{}term coefficients.  See its doc
page for details.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When comparing the formulas and coefficients for various LAMMPS
dihedral styles with dihedral equations defined by other force fields,
note that some force field implementations divide/multiply the energy
prefactor \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} by the multiple number of torsions that contain the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{J}\textendash{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{K} bond in an \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{J}\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{L} torsion.  LAMMPS does
not do this (i.e., the listed dihedral equation applies to each individual
dihedral).  Thus, you need to define \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} appropriately to account for this
difference, if necessary.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The list of all dihedral styles defined in LAMMPS is given on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}} doc page.  They are also listed
in more compact form on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_bond:dihedral}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Commands dihedral}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On either of those pages, click on the style to display the formula it
computes and its coefficients as specified by the associated
dihedral\_coeff command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command must come after the simulation box is defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A dihedral style must be defined before any dihedral coefficients are
set, either in the input script or in a data file.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_coeff:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{dihedral\_style@\spxentry{dihedral\_style}}\ignorespaces 

\section{dihedral\_style command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_style:dihedral-style-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_style:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_style:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{zero} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cosine/shift/exp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cosine/squared/restricted} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fourier} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{helix} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lepton} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/harmonic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nharmonic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opls} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spherical} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/cut}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_style:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{multi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{harmonic}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{charmm}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the formula(s) LAMMPS uses to compute dihedral interactions
between quadruplets of atoms, which remain in force for the duration
of the simulation.  The list of dihedral quadruplets is read in by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command
from a data or restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Hybrid models where dihedrals are computed using different dihedral
potentials can be setup using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} dihedral style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficients associated with a dihedral style can be specified in
a data or restart file or via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All dihedral potentials store their coefficient data in binary restart
files which means dihedral\_style and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} commands do not need to be
re\sphinxhyphen{}specified in an input script that restarts a simulation.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for details on how to do
this.  The one exception is that dihedral\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} only stores
the list of sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles in the restart file; dihedral coefficients need
to be re\sphinxhyphen{}specified.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When both a dihedral and pair style is defined, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command often needs to be used to
turn off (or weight) the pairwise interaction that would otherwise
exist between four bonded atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the formulas listed for each dihedral style, \sphinxstyleemphasis{phi} is the torsional
angle defined by the quadruplet of atoms.  This angle has a sign
convention as shown in this diagram:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{dihedral_sign}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where the \(I,J,K,L\) ordering of the four atoms that define the dihedral
is from left to right.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This sign convention effects several of the dihedral styles listed
below (e.g., charmm, helix) in the sense that the energy formula
depends on the sign of phi, which may be reflected in the value of the
coefficients you specify.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When comparing the formulas and coefficients for various LAMMPS
dihedral styles with dihedral equations defined by other force fields,
note that some force field implementations divide/multiply the energy
prefactor \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} by the multiple number of torsions that contain the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{J}\textendash{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{K} bond in an \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}\textendash{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{J}\textendash{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\textendash{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{L} torsion.  LAMMPS does
not do this (i.e., the listed dihedral equation applies to each individual
dihedral).  Thus, you need to define \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} appropriately via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command to account for this
difference if necessary.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an alphabetic list of dihedral styles defined in LAMMPS.  Click on
the style to display the formula it computes and coefficients
specified by the associated {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Click on the style to display the formula it computes, any additional
arguments specified in the dihedral\_style command, and coefficients
specified by the associated {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are also additional accelerated pair styles included in the
LAMMPS distribution for faster performance on CPUs, GPUs, and KNLs.
The individual style names on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_bond:dihedral}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Commands dihedral}}}} page are
followed by one or more of (g,i,k,o,t) to indicate which accelerated styles
exist.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_none::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{none}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} turn off dihedral interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} define multiple styles of dihedral interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{charmm}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} CHARMM dihedral

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{charmmfsw}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} CHARMM dihedral with force switching

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{class2}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} COMPASS (class 2) dihedral

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_cosine_shift_exp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{cosine/shift/exp}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} dihedral with exponential in spring constant

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_cosine_squared_restricted::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{cosine/squared/restricted}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} squared cosine dihedral with restricted term

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_fourier::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fourier}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} dihedral with multiple cosine terms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{harmonic}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} harmonic dihedral

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_helix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{helix}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} helix dihedral

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_lepton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lepton}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} dihedral potential from evaluating a string

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_multi_harmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{multi/harmonic}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} dihedral with 5 harmonic terms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_nharmonic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{nharmonic}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} same as multi\sphinxhyphen{}harmonic with N terms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_opls::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{opls}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} OPLS dihedral

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{quadratic}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} dihedral with quadratic term in angle

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_spherical::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{spherical}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} dihedral which includes angle terms to avoid singularities

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{table}}}} \sphinxhyphen{} tabulated dihedral

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_style:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dihedral styles can only be set for atom styles that allow dihedrals

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most dihedral styles are part of the MOLECULE package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.  The doc pages for
individual dihedral potentials tell if it is part of a package.

\index{dihedral\_write@\spxentry{dihedral\_write}}\ignorespaces 

\section{dihedral\_write command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:dihedral-write-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dtype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dtype = dihedral type

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = \# of values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file = name of file to write values to

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = section name in file for this set of tabulated values

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Harmonic\PYGZus{}1}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Harmonic\PYGZus{}3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 8Feb2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Write energy and force values to a file as a function of the dihedral
angle for the currently defined dihedral potential.  Force in this
context means the force with respect to the dihedral angle, not the
force on individual atoms.  This is useful for plotting the potential
function or otherwise debugging its values.  The resulting file can also
be used as input for use with {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral style table}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the file already exists, the table of values is appended to the end
of the file to allow multiple tables of energy and force to be included
in one file.  The individual sections may be identified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{keyword}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy and force values are computed for dihedrals ranging from 0
degrees to 360 degrees for 4 interacting atoms forming an dihedral type
dtype, using the appropriate {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}
coefficients. N evenly spaced dihedrals are used.  Since 0 and 360
degrees are the same dihedral angle, the latter entry is skipped.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, for N = 6, values would be computed at
\(\phi = 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file is written in the format used as input for the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style table}}}} option with \sphinxstyleemphasis{keyword} as
the section name.  Each line written to the file lists an index number
(1\sphinxhyphen{}N), an dihedral angle (in degrees), an energy (in energy units), and
a force (in force units per radians\textasciicircum{}2).  In case a new file is created,
the first line will be a comment with a “DATE:” and “UNITS:” tag with
the current date and {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} settings.  For subsequent
invocations of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral\_write} command for the same file, data will
be appended and the current units settings will be compared to the data
from the header, if present. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral\_write} will refuse to add a
table to an existing file if the units are not the same.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All force field coefficients for dihedrals and other kinds of interactions
must be set before this command can be invoked.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The table of the dihedral energy and force data data is created by using a
separate, internally created, new LAMMPS instance with a dummy system of
4 atoms for which the dihedral potential energy is computed after
transferring the dihedral style and coefficients and arranging the 4 atoms
into the corresponding geometries.  The dihedral force is then determined
from the potential energies through numerical differentiation.  As a
consequence of this approach, not all dihedral styles are compatible. The
following conditions must be met:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The dihedral style must be able to write its coefficients to a data file.
This condition excludes for example {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral style hybrid}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral style table}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential function must not have any terms that depend on geometry
properties other than the dihedral.  This condition excludes for
example {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral style class2}}}}.  Please note
that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{write\_dihedral} command has no way of checking for this
condition.  It will check the style name against an internal list of
known to be incompatible styles.  The resulting tables may be bogus
for unlisted dihedral styles if the requirement is not met.  It is
thus recommended to make careful tests for any created tables.

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style table}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_write}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_write}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_write:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{dimension@\spxentry{dimension}}\ignorespaces 

\section{dimension command}
\label{\detokenize{dimension:dimension-command}}\label{\detokenize{dimension:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dimension::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dimension:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dimension}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = 2 or 3

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dimension:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dimension}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dimension:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the dimensionality of the simulation.  By default LAMMPS runs 3d
simulations.  To run a 2d simulation, this command should be used
prior to setting up a simulation box via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} commands.
Restart files also store this setting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the discussion on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_2d::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto 2d}}}} page for
additional instructions on how to run 2d simulations.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some models in LAMMPS treat particles as finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spheres or
ellipsoids, as opposed to point particles.  In 2d, the particles will
still be spheres or ellipsoids, not circular disks or ellipses,
meaning their moment of inertia will be the same as in 3d.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dimension:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command must be used before the simulation box is defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{dimension:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_enforce2d::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix enforce2d}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{dimension:default}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dimension}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope

\index{displace\_atoms@\spxentry{displace\_atoms}}\ignorespaces 

\section{displace\_atoms command}
\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:displace-atoms-command}}\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{displace\PYGZus{}atoms }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of group of atoms to displace

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{move} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ramp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{move} args = delx dely delz
  delx,dely,delz = distance to displace in each dimension (distance units)
  any of delx,dely,delz can be a variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ramp} args = ddim dlo dhi dim clo chi
  ddim = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
  dlo,dhi = displacement distance between dlo and dhi (distance units)
  dim = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
  clo,chi = lower and upper bound of domain to displace (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{random} args = dx dy dz seed
  dx,dy,dz = random displacement magnitude in each dimension (distance units)
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} args = Px Py Pz Rx Ry Rz theta
  Px,Py,Pz = origin point of axis of rotation (distance units)
  Rx,Ry,Rz = axis of rotation vector
  theta = angle of rotation (degrees)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{units}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{units} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{displace\PYGZus{}atoms }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{top}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{move}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{k}{displace\PYGZus{}atoms }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{flow}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ramp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Displace a group of atoms.  This can be used to move atoms a large
distance before beginning a simulation or to randomize atoms initially
on a lattice.  For example, in a shear simulation, an initial strain
can be imposed on the system.  Or two groups of atoms can be brought
into closer proximity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{move} style displaces the group of atoms by the specified 3d
displacement vector.  Any of the three quantities defining the vector
components can be specified as an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style or atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  If the value is a variable, it should be
specified as v\_name, where name is the variable name.  In this case,
the variable will be evaluated, and its value(s) used for the
displacement(s).  The scale factor implied by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{units} keyword will
also be applied to the variable result.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can specify formulas with various mathematical
functions, and include {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command
keywords for the simulation box parameters and timestep and elapsed
time.  Atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can specify the same formulas as
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables but can also include per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values, such as
atom coordinates or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values read from a file.  Note that if
the variable references other {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}
commands, those values must be up\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}date for the current timestep.
See the “Variable Accuracy” section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}
doc page for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ramp} style displaces atoms a variable amount in one dimension
depending on the atom’s coordinate in a (possibly) different
dimension.  For example, the second example command displaces atoms in
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}\sphinxhyphen{}direction an amount between 0.0 and 5.0 distance units.  Each
atom’s displacement depends on the fractional distance its \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}
coordinate is between 2.0 and 20.5.  Atoms with \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}\sphinxhyphen{}coordinates outside
those bounds will be moved the minimum (0.0) or maximum (5.0) amount.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{random} style independently moves each atom in the group by a
random displacement, uniformly sampled from a value between \(-dx\) and
\(+dx\) in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} dimension, and similarly for \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}.
Random numbers are used in such a way that the displacement of a particular
atom is the same, regardless of how many processors are being used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} style rotates each atom in the group by the angle \sphinxstyleemphasis{theta}
around a rotation axis \(R = (R_x,R_y,R_z)\) that goes through a point
\(P = (P_x,P_y,P_z)\).  The direction of rotation for the atoms around the
rotation axis is consistent with the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand rule: if your
right\sphinxhyphen{}hand thumb points along \sphinxstyleemphasis{R}, then your fingers wrap around the
axis in the direction of positive theta.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the defined {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} assigns an orientation to
each atom ({\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom styles}}}} ellipsoid, line, tri, body),
then that property is also updated appropriately to correspond to the
atom’s rotation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Distance units for displacements and the origin point of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate}
style are determined by the setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} for the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{units} keyword.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Box} means distance units as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command (e.g., \(\AA\) for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{real} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units). \sphinxstyleemphasis{Lattice} means distance units are in lattice
spacings.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command must have been previously used
to define the lattice spacing.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Care should be taken not to move atoms on top of other atoms.
After the move, atoms are remapped into the periodic simulation box if
needed, and any shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap boundary conditions (see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command) are enforced which may change the
box size.  Other than this effect, this command does not change the
size or shape of the simulation box.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change\_box}}}} command if that effect is desired.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Atoms can be moved arbitrarily long distances by this command.
If the simulation box is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic and shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped (see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command), this can change its size or shape.
This is not a problem, except that the mapping of processors to the
simulation box is not changed by this command from its initial 3d
configuration; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}} command.  Thus, if
the box size/shape changes dramatically, the mapping of processors to
the simulation box may not end up as optimal as the initial mapping
attempted to be.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a 2d simulation, only rotations around the a vector parallel to
the \(z\)\sphinxhyphen{}axis are allowed.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{change_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{change\_box}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_move::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix move}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{displace_atoms:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are units = lattice.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{dynamical\_matrix@\spxentry{dynamical\_matrix}}\ignorespaces 
\index{dynamical\_matrix/kk@\spxentry{dynamical\_matrix/kk}}\ignorespaces 

\section{dynamical\_matrix command}
\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:dynamical-matrix-command}}\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variant: dynamical\_matrix/kk


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dynamical\PYGZus{}matrix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of group of atoms to displace

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{regular} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eskm}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gamma = finite different displacement length (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/arg pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{binary}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} name = name of output file for the dynamical matrix
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{binary} arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gzip}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dynamical\PYGZus{}matrix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{regular}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.000001}
\PYG{k}{dynamical\PYGZus{}matrix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eskm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.000001}
\PYG{k}{dynamical\PYGZus{}matrix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{regular}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00004}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dynmat.dat}
\PYG{k}{dynamical\PYGZus{}matrix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eskm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00000001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dynamical.dat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{binary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the dynamical matrix by finite difference of the selected group,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D = \frac{\Phi_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}}{\sqrt{M_i M_j}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where D is the dynamical matrix and \(\Phi\) is the force constant
matrix defined by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Phi_{ij}^{\alpha\beta} = \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial x_{i,\alpha} \partial x_{j,\beta}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The output for the dynamical matrix is printed three elements at a time.
The three elements are the three \(\beta\) elements for a respective
i/\(\alpha\)/j combination.  Each line is printed in order of j
increasing first, \(\alpha\) second, and i last.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the style eskm is selected, the dynamical matrix will be in units of
inverse squared femtoseconds. These units will then conveniently leave
frequencies in THz.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The command collects an array of nine times the number of atoms in a group
on every single MPI rank, so the memory requirements can be very significant
for large systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command is part of the PHONON package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_phonon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix phonon}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_numdiff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix numdiff}}}},

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_hma::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute hma}}}} uses an analytic formulation of the
Hessian provided by a pair\_style’s Pair::single\_hessian() function,
if implemented.


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{dynamical_matrix:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default settings are file = “dynmat.dyn”, binary = no

\sphinxstepscope

\index{echo@\spxentry{echo}}\ignorespaces 

\section{echo command}
\label{\detokenize{echo:echo-command}}\label{\detokenize{echo:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{echo::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{echo:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{echo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{screen} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{log} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{both}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{echo:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{echo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{both}
\PYG{k}{echo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{log}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{echo:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command determines whether LAMMPS echoes each input script
command to the screen and/or log file as it is read and processed.  If
an input script has errors, it can be useful to look at echoed output
to see the last command processed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}echo can be used in place
of this command.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{echo:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{echo:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{echo:default}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{echo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{log}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\index{fix@\spxentry{fix}}\ignorespaces 

\section{fix command}
\label{\detokenize{fix:fix-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID = user\sphinxhyphen{}assigned name for the fix

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of the group of atoms to apply the fix to

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = one of a long list of possible style names (see below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = arguments used by a particular style

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.01}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mine}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{top}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{setforce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set a fix that will be applied to a group of atoms.  In LAMMPS, a
“fix” is any operation that is applied to the system during
timestepping or minimization.  Examples include updating of atom
positions and velocities due to time integration, controlling
temperature, applying constraint forces to atoms, enforcing boundary
conditions, computing diagnostics, etc.  There are hundreds of fixes
defined in LAMMPS and new ones can be added; see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}} page for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes perform their operations at different stages of the timestep.
If two or more fixes operate at the same stage of the timestep, they are
invoked in the order they were specified in the input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID of a fix can only contain alphanumeric characters and
underscores.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes can be deleted with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{unfix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{unfix}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{unfix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{unfix}}}} command is the only way to turn off a
fix; simply specifying a new fix with a similar style will not turn
off the first one.  This is especially important to realize for
integration fixes.  For example, using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}
command for a second run after using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} command
for the first run will not cancel out the NVT time integration
invoked by the “fix nvt” command.  Thus, two time integrators would be
in place!
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you specify a new fix with the same ID and style as an existing
fix, the old fix is deleted and the new one is created (presumably
with new settings).  This is the same as if an “unfix” command were
first performed on the old fix, except that the new fix is kept in the
same order relative to the existing fixes as the old one originally
was.  Note that this operation also wipes out any additional changes
made to the old fix via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix modify}}}} command allows settings for some
fixes to be reset.  See the page for individual fixes for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some fixes store an internal “state” which is written to binary
restart files via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{write_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_restart}}}} commands.  This allows the fix to
continue on with its calculations in a restarted simulation.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for info on how to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify
a fix in an input script that reads a restart file.  See the doc pages
for individual fixes for info on which ones can be restarted.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Some fixes calculate and store any of four \sphinxstyleemphasis{styles} of quantities:
global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A global quantity is one or more system\sphinxhyphen{}wide values, e.g. the energy
of a wall interacting with particles.  A per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantity is one or
more values per atom, e.g. the original coordinates of each atom at
time 0.  Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values are set to 0.0 for atoms not in the specified
fix group.  Local quantities are calculated by each processor based on
the atoms it owns, but there may be zero or more per atom, e.g. values
for each bond.  Per\sphinxhyphen{}grid quantities are calculated on a regular 2d or
3d grid which overlays a 2d or 3d simulation domain.  The grid points
and the data they store are distributed across processors; each
processor owns the grid points which fall within its subdomain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a general rule of thumb, fixes that produce per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities
have the word “atom” at the end of their style, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{ave/atom}.
Fixes that produce local quantities have the word “local” at the end
of their style, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{store/local}.  Fixes that produce per\sphinxhyphen{}grid
quantities have the word “grid” at the end of their style,
e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{ave/grid}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid quantities can also be of three
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kinds}: a single scalar value (global only), a vector of values, or a
2d array of values.  For per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid quantities, a
“vector” means a single value for each atom, each local entity
(e.g. bond), or grid cell.  Likewise an “array”, means multiple values
for each atom, each local entity, or each grid cell.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a single fix can produce any combination of global,
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, or per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values.  Likewise it can produce any
combination of scalar, vector, or array output for each style.  The
exception is that for per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid output, either a
vector or array can be produced, but not both.  The doc page for each
fix explains the values it produces, if any.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a fix output is accessed by another input script command it is
referenced via the following bracket notation, where ID is the ID of
the fix:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
f\_ID
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
entire scalar, vector, or array
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
f\_ID{[}I{]}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
one element of vector, one column of array
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
f\_ID{[}I{]}{[}J{]}
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
one element of array
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In other words, using one bracket reduces the dimension of the
quantity once (vector \(\to\) scalar, array \(\to\) vector).
Using two brackets reduces the dimension twice (array \(\to\)
scalar).  Thus, for example, a command that uses global scalar fix
values as input can also process elements of a vector or array.
Depending on the command, this can either be done directly using the
syntax in the table, or by first defining a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}
of the appropriate style to store the quantity, then using the
variable as an input to the command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that commands and {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} which take fix
outputs as input typically do not allow for all styles and kinds of
data (e.g., a command may require global but not per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values, or
it may require a vector of values, not a scalar).  This means there is
typically no ambiguity about referring to a fix output as c\_ID even if
it produces, for example, both a scalar and vector.  The doc pages for
various commands explain the details, including how any ambiguities
are resolved.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, the values generated by a fix can be used in several ways:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Global values can be output via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} command.
Alternatively, the values can be referenced in an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can be output via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command,
or they can be time\sphinxhyphen{}averaged via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/atom}}}}
command or reduced by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}}
command.  Alternatively, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can be referenced in an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Local values can be reduced by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}}
command or histogrammed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_histo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/histo}}}} command.
They can also be output by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}} command.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for a summary of
various LAMMPS output options, many of which involve fixes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The results of fixes that calculate global quantities can be either
“intensive” or “extensive” values.  Intensive means the value is
independent of the number of atoms in the simulation
(e.g., temperature).  Extensive means the value scales with the number of
atoms in the simulation (e.g., total rotational kinetic energy).
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Thermodynamic output}}}} will normalize extensive
values by the number of atoms in the system, depending on the
“thermo\_modify norm” setting.  It will not normalize intensive values.
If a fix value is accessed in another way (e.g., by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}), you may want to know whether it is an
intensive or extensive value.  See the page for individual fix styles
for further info.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Each fix style has its own page that describes its arguments and
what it does, as listed below.  Here is an alphabetical list of fix
