on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands fix}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are also additional accelerated fix styles included in the
LAMMPS distribution for faster performance on CPUs, GPUs, and KNLs.
The individual style names on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands fix}}}} doc
page are followed by one or more of (g,i,k,o,t) to indicate which
accelerated styles exist.

\subsection{Restrictions}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some fix styles are part of specific packages.  They are only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.  The doc pages for
individual fixes tell if it is part of a package.

\section{fix\_modify command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_modify:fix-modify-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_modify:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_modify:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fix\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of the fix to modify

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bodyforces} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{colname} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{press} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bodyforces} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{early} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{late}
  early/late = compute rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body forces/torques early or late in the timestep
\sphinxstyleemphasis{colname} values =  ID string
  string = new column header name
  ID = integer from 1 to N, or integer from \sphinxhyphen{}1 to \sphinxhyphen{}N, where N = \# of quantities being output
       \sphinxstyleemphasis{or} a fix output property keyword or reference to compute, fix, property or variable.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
  yes/no = do or do not re\sphinxhyphen{}compute the number of degrees of freedom (DOF) contributing to the temperature
\sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{press} value = compute ID that calculates a pressure
\sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{max respa level} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} (for outermost level)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} value = compute ID that calculates a temperature
\sphinxstyleemphasis{virial} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_modify:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myPress}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{energy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{tether}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ave}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{colname}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}thermo\PYGZus{}press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pressure}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{colname}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Temperature}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_modify:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modify one or more parameters of a previously defined fix.  Only
specific fix styles support specific parameters.  See the doc pages
for individual fix commands for info on which ones support which
fix\_modify parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword is used to determine how a fix computes
temperature.  The specified compute ID must have been previously
defined by the user via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command and it must
be a style of compute that calculates a temperature.  All fixes that
compute temperatures define their own compute by default, as described
in their documentation.  Thus this option allows the user to override
the default method for computing T.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{press} keyword is used to determine how a fix computes pressure.
The specified compute ID must have been previously defined by the user
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command and it must be a style of
compute that calculates a pressure.  All fixes that compute pressures
define their own compute by default, as described in their
documentation.  Thus this option allows the user to override the
default method for computing P.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword can be used with fixes that support it, which is
explained at the bottom of their doc page.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Energy yes} will add a
contribution to the potential energy of the system.  More
specifically, the fix’s global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy is included in the
calculation performed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe/atom}}}} commands.  The former is what
is used the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command for output of
any quantity that includes the global potential energy of the system.
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe/atom}}}} commands also have an option to include or exclude
the contribution from fixes.  For fixes that tally a global energy, it
can also be printed with thermodynamic output by using the keyword
f\_ID in the thermo\_style custom command, where ID is the fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID of the
appropriate fix.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are performing an {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}} with
one of these fixes and want the energy and forces it produces to be
part of the optimization criteria, you must specify the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy
yes} setting.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For most fixes that support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword, the default
setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.  For a few it is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, when a user would expect
that to be the case.  The page of each fix gives the default.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial} keyword can be used with fixes that support it, which is
explained at the bottom of their doc page.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Virial yes} will add a
contribution to the virial of the system.  More specifically, the
fix’s global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom virial is included in the calculation
performed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}} commands.  The former
is what is used the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command for
output of any quantity that includes the global pressure of the
system.  Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}} commands also have an
option to include or exclude the contribution from fixes.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you are performing an {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}} with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_box_relax::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{box relaxation}}}} and one of these fixes and
want the virial contribution of the fix to be part of the
optimization criteria, you must specify the \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial yes} setting.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For most fixes that support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial} keyword, the default
setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.  For a few it is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, when a user would expect
that to be the case.  The page of each fix gives the default.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For fixes that set or modify forces, it may be possible to select at
which {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA}}}} level the fix operates via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa}
keyword. The RESPA level at which the fix is active can be selected.
This is a number ranging from 1 to the number of levels. If the RESPA
level is larger than the current maximum, the outermost level will be
used, which is also the default setting. This default can be restored
using a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} for the RESPA level. The affected fix has to be
enabled to support this feature; if not, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\_modify} will report an
error. Active fixes with a custom RESPA level setting are reported
with their specified level at the beginning of a r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof} keyword determines whether the number of atoms N in
the fix group and their associated degrees of freedom are re\sphinxhyphen{}computed
each time a temperature is computed.  Only fix styles that calculate
their own internal temperature use this option.  Currently this is only
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/nvt/small}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/npt/small}}}} commands for the purpose of thermostatting rigid body
translation and rotation.  By default, N and their DOF are assumed to be
constant.  If you are adding atoms or molecules to the system (see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gcmc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gcmc}}}} commands) or expect atoms or molecules to be
lost (e.g. due to exiting the simulation box or via {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_evaporate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix evaporate}}}}), then this option should be used to ensure the
temperature is correctly normalized.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Other thermostatting fixes, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}, do not
use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof} keyword because they use a temperature compute
to calculate temperature.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify dynamic/dof}}}} command for a similar way to ensure correct
temperature normalization for those thermostats.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{bodyforces} keyword determines whether the forces and torques
acting on rigid bodies are computed \sphinxstyleemphasis{early} at the post\sphinxhyphen{}force stage of
each timestep (right after per\sphinxhyphen{}atom forces have been computed and
communicated among processors), or \sphinxstyleemphasis{late} at the final\sphinxhyphen{}integrate stage
of each timestep (after any other fixes have finished their post\sphinxhyphen{}force
tasks).  Only the rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body integration fixes use this option, which
includes {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}}, and their variants, and also {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_poems::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix poems}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default is \sphinxstyleemphasis{late}.  If there are other fixes that add forces to
individual atoms, then the rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body constraints will include these
forces when time\sphinxhyphen{}integrating the rigid bodies.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{early} is
specified, then new fixes can be written that use or modify the
per\sphinxhyphen{}body force and torque, before time\sphinxhyphen{}integration of the rigid bodies
occurs.  Note however this has the side effect, that fixes such as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_addforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix addforce}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_spring::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix spring}}}}, which add forces to individual atoms
will have no effect on the motion of the rigid bodies if they are
specified in the input script after the fix rigid command.  LAMMPS
will give a warning if that is the case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{colname} keyword can be used to change the default header keywords
in output files of fix styles that support it: currently only {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
ave/time}}}} is supported.  The setting for \sphinxstyleemphasis{ID string}
replaces the default text with the provided string.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{ID} can be a
positive integer when it represents the column number counting from the
left, a negative integer when it represents the column number from the
right (i.e. \sphinxhyphen{}1 is the last column/keyword), or a custom fix output
keyword (or compute, fix, property, or variable reference) and then it
replaces the string for that specific keyword. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{colname} keyword can
be used multiple times. If multiple \sphinxstyleemphasis{colname} settings refer to the same
keyword, the last setting has precedence.


\subsection{Restrictions}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Related commands}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_modify:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are temp = ID defined by fix, press = ID defined
by fix, energy = no, virial = different for each fix style, respa = 0,
bodyforce = late.

\index{fitpod@\spxentry{fitpod}}\ignorespaces 

\section{fitpod command}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:fitpod-command}}\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fitpod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}data.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}coefficients.pod}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fitpod = style name of this command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ta\_param.pod = an input file that describes proper orthogonal descriptors (PODs)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ta\_data.pod = an input file that specifies DFT data used to fit a POD potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ta\_coefficients.pod (optional) = an input file that specifies trainable coefficients of a POD potential

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fitpod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}data.pod}
\PYG{k}{fitpod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}data.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}coefficients.pod}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fit a machine\sphinxhyphen{}learning interatomic potential (ML\sphinxhyphen{}IAP) based on proper
orthogonal descriptors (POD); please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command:nguyen20222a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen and Rohskopf)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command:nguyen20232a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen2023)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command:nguyen20242a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen2024)}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command:nguyen20243a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen and Sema)}}}} for details.
The fitted POD potential can be used to run MD simulations via
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style pod}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two input files are required for this command. The first input file
describes a POD potential parameter settings, while the second input
file specifies the DFT data used for the fitting procedure. All keywords
except \sphinxstyleemphasis{species} have default values. If a keyword is not set in the
input file, its default value is used. The table below has one\sphinxhyphen{}line
descriptions of all the keywords that can be used in the first input

\sphinxAtStartPar
All keywords except \sphinxstyleemphasis{path\_to\_training\_data\_set} have default values. If
a keyword is not set in the input file, its default value is used.  After
successful training, a number of output files are produced, if enabled:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}basename\textgreater{}\_training\_errors.pod}}  reports the errors in energy and forces for the training data set

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}basename\textgreater{}\_training\_analysis.pod}} reports detailed errors for all training configurations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}basename\textgreater{}\_test\_errors.pod}} reports errors for the test data set

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}basename\textgreater{}\_test\_analysis.pod}} reports detailed errors for all test configurations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}basename\textgreater{}\_coefficients.pod}} contains the coefficients of the POD potential

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After training the POD potential, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Ta\_param.pod}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}basename\textgreater{}\_coefficients.pod}} are the two files needed to use the POD
potential in LAMMPS.  See {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style pod}}}} for using the
POD potential. Examples about training and using POD potentials are
found in the directory lammps/examples/PACKAGES/pod and the Github repo
\sphinxurl{https://github.com/cesmix-mit/pod-examples}.


\subsubsection{Loss Function Group Weights}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:loss-function-group-weights}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\_weights} keyword in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data.pod}} file is responsible for
weighting certain groups of configurations in the loss function. For
example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{group\PYGZus{}weights}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This will apply an energy weight of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{100.0}} and a force weight of
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1.0}} for all groups in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Ta}} example. The groups are named by
their respective filename. If certain groups are left out of this table,
then the globally defined weights from the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fitting\_weight\_energy}} and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fitting\_weight\_force}} keywords will be used.


\subsection{POD Potential}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:pod-potential}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We consider a multi\sphinxhyphen{}element system of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} atoms with \(N_{\rm e}\)
unique elements.  We denote by \(\boldsymbol r_n\) and \(Z_n\)
position vector and type of an atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} in the system,
respectively. Note that we have \(Z_n \in \{1, \ldots, N_{\rm e}
\}\), \(\boldsymbol R = (\boldsymbol r_1, \boldsymbol r_2, \ldots,
\boldsymbol r_N) \in \mathbb{R}^{3N}\), and \(\boldsymbol Z = (Z_1,
Z_2, \ldots, Z_N) \in \mathbb{N}^{N}\). The total energy of the
POD potential is expressed as \(E(\boldsymbol R, \boldsymbol Z) =
\sum_{i=1}^N E_i(\boldsymbol R_i, \boldsymbol Z_i)\), where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_i(\boldsymbol R_i, \boldsymbol Z_i) \ = \ \sum_{m=1}^M c_m \mathcal{D}_{im}(\boldsymbol R_i, \boldsymbol Z_i)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \(c_m\) are trainable coefficients and
\(\mathcal{D}_{im}(\boldsymbol R_i, \boldsymbol Z_i)\) are per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
POD descriptors. Summing the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom descriptors over \(i\) yields
the global descriptors \(d_m(\boldsymbol R, \boldsymbol Z) =
\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{D}_{im}(\boldsymbol R_i, \boldsymbol Z_i)\).  It
thus follows that \(E(\boldsymbol R, \boldsymbol Z) = \sum_{m=1}^M
c_m d_m(\boldsymbol R, \boldsymbol Z)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom POD descriptors include one, two, three, four, five, six,
and seven\sphinxhyphen{}body descriptors, which can be specified in the first input
file. Furthermore, the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom POD descriptors also depend on the
number of environment clusters specified in the first input file.
Please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command:nguyen20242a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen2024)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command:nguyen20243a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen and Sema)}}}} for the detailed description of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom POD
descriptors.


\subsection{Training}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:training}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A POD potential is trained using the least\sphinxhyphen{}squares regression against
density functional theory (DFT) data.  Let \(J\) be the number of
training configurations, with \(N_j\) being the number of atoms in
the j\sphinxhyphen{}th configuration. The training configurations are extracted from
the extended XYZ files located in a directory (i.e.,
path\_to\_training\_data\_set in the second input file).  Let
\(\{E^{\star}_j\}_{j=1}^{J}\) and \(\{\boldsymbol
F^{\star}_j\}_{j=1}^{J}\) be the DFT energies and forces for \(J\)
configurations. Next, we calculate the global descriptors and their
derivatives for all training configurations. Let \(d_{jm}, 1 \le m
\le M\), be the global descriptors associated with the j\sphinxhyphen{}th
configuration, where \(M\) is the number of global descriptors. We
then form a matrix \(\boldsymbol A \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times M}\)
with entries \(A_{jm} = d_{jm}/ N_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,J\) and
\(m=1,\ldots,M\).  Moreover, we form a matrix \(\boldsymbol B
\in \mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{N} \times M}\) by stacking the derivatives of
the global descriptors for all training configurations from top to
bottom, where \(\mathcal{N} = 3\sum_{j=1}^{J} N_j\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol c\) of the POD potential is
found by solving the following least\sphinxhyphen{}squares problem
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{\min}_{\boldsymbol c \in \mathbb{R}^{M}} \ w_E \|\boldsymbol A \boldsymbol c - \bar{\boldsymbol E}^{\star} \|^2 + w_F \|\boldsymbol B \boldsymbol c + \boldsymbol F^{\star} \|^2 + w_R \|\boldsymbol c \|^2,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(w_E\) and \(w_F\) are weights for the energy
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{fitting\_weight\_energy}) and force (\sphinxstyleemphasis{fitting\_weight\_force}),
respectively; and \(w_R\) is the regularization parameter
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{fitting\_regularization\_parameter}).  Here \(\bar{\boldsymbol
E}^{\star} \in \mathbb{R}^{J}\) is a vector of with entries
\(\bar{E}^{\star}_j = E^{\star}_j/N_j\) and \(\boldsymbol
F^{\star}\) is a vector of \(\mathcal{N}\) entries obtained by
stacking \(\{\boldsymbol F^{\star}_j\}_{j=1}^{J}\) from top to
bottom.


\subsection{Validation}
\label{\detokenize{fitpod_command:validation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
POD potential can be validated on a test dataset in a directory
specified by setting path\_to\_test\_data\_set in the second input file.  It
is possible to validate the POD potential after the training is
complete.  This is done by providing the coefficient file as an input to
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fitpod}}}}, for example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fitpod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}data.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}coefficients.pod}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pod_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pod/atom}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pod_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute podd/atom}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pod_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pod/local}}}},

\section{geturl command}
\label{\detokenize{geturl:geturl-command}}\label{\detokenize{geturl:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{geturl::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{geturl:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{geturl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{url}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
url = URL of the file to download

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword argument pairs may be provided

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{output} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{verify} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{overwrite} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{output} filename = write to \sphinxstyleemphasis{filename} instead of inferring the name from the URL
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verify} yes/no = verify SSL certificate and hostname if \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, do not if \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{overwrite} yes/no = if \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} overwrite the output file in case it exists, do not if \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} yes/no = if \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} write verbose debug output from libcurl to screen, do not if \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{geturl:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{geturl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{https}://www.ctcms.nist.gov/potentials/Download/1990\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}Ackland\PYGZhy{}G\PYGZhy{}J\PYGZhy{}Vitek\PYGZhy{}V\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}Cu/2/Cu2.eam.fs
\PYG{k}{geturl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{https}://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/bench/in.lj\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{output}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{in.bench}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{lj}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{geturl:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 29Aug2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Download a file from an URL to the local disk. This is implemented with
the \sphinxhref{https:://curl.se/libcurl/}{libcurl library} which supports a
large variety of protocols including “http”, “https”, “ftp”, “scp”,
“sftp”, “file”.  The transfer will only be performed on MPI rank 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{output} keyword can be used to set the filename. By default, the last part
of the URL is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{verify} keyword determines whether \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{libcurl}} will validate the
SSL certificate and hostname for encrypted connections.  Turning this
off may be required when using a proxy or connecting to a server with a
self\sphinxhyphen{}signed SSL certificate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{overwrite} keyword determines whether a file should be overwritten if it
already exists.  If the argument is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, then the download will be skipped
if the file exists.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} keyword determines whether a detailed protocol of the steps
performed by libcurl is written to the screen.  Using the argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
can be used to debug connection issues when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{geturl} command does not
behave as expected.  If the argument is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, geturl will operate silently
and only report the error status number provided by libcurl, in case of a
failure.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{geturl:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMMAND package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.  It also requires that LAMMPS was
built with support for \sphinxhref{https://curl.se/libcurl/}{the libcurl library}.  See the page about {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings:libcurl}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Compiling LAMMPS
with libcurl support}}}} for further info.  If support for
libcurl is not included, using \sphinxstyleemphasis{geturl} will trigger an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{shell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{shell}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{geturl:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{group command}
\label{\detokenize{group:group-command}}\label{\detokenize{group:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{group::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{group:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID = user\sphinxhyphen{}defined name of the group

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{clear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{empty} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{include} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{subtract} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{static}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} = no args
\sphinxstyleemphasis{clear} = no args
\sphinxstyleemphasis{empty} = no args
\sphinxstyleemphasis{region} args = region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule}
  args = list of one or more atom types (1\sphinxhyphen{}Ntypes or type label), atom IDs, or molecule IDs
    any numeric entry in list can be a sequence formatted as A:B or A:B:C where
    A = starting index, B = ending index,
    C = increment between indices, 1 if not specified
  args = logical value
    logical = "\textless{}" or "\textless{}=" or "\textgreater{}" or "\textgreater{}=" or "==" or "!="
    value = an atom type (1\sphinxhyphen{}Ntypes or type label) or atom ID or molecule ID (depending on \sphinxstyleemphasis{style})
  args = logical value1 value2
    logical = "\textless{}\textgreater{}"
    value1,value2 = atom types or atom IDs or molecule IDs (depending on \sphinxstyleemphasis{style})
\sphinxstyleemphasis{variable} args = variable\sphinxhyphen{}name
\sphinxstyleemphasis{include} args = molecule
  molecule = add atoms to group with same molecule ID as atoms already in group
\sphinxstyleemphasis{subtract} args = two or more group IDs
\sphinxstyleemphasis{union} args = one or more group IDs
\sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} args = two or more group IDs
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic} args = parent\sphinxhyphen{}ID keyword value ...
  one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
  keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{property} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{every}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} value = region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} value = name of variable
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{property} value = name of custom integer or floating point vector
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} value = N = update group every this many timesteps
\sphinxstyleemphasis{static} = no args
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{group:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{edge}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{regstrip}

\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{sub}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{25}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500:1000}

\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{polyA}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{250}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hienergy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{eng}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hienergy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{subtract}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a3}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{union}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{upper}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{intersect}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{upper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flow}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delete}
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mine}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dynamic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myRegion}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{group:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identify a collection of atoms as belonging to a group.  The group ID
can then be used in other commands such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}}
to act on those atoms together.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the group ID already exists, the group command adds the specified
atoms to the group.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default groups are static, meaning the atoms are permanently
assigned to the group.  For example, if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} style is used to
assign atoms to a group, the atoms will remain in the group even if
they later move out of the region.  As explained below, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic}
style can be used to make a group dynamic so that a periodic
determination is made as to which atoms are in the group.  Since many
LAMMPS commands operate on groups of atoms, you should think carefully
about whether making a group dynamic makes sense for your model.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A group with the ID \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} is predefined.  All atoms belong to this group.
This group cannot be deleted, or made dynamic.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} style removes the named group and un\sphinxhyphen{}assigns all atoms
that were assigned to that group.  Since there is a restriction (see
below) that no more than 32 groups can be defined at any time, the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} style allows you to remove groups that are no longer needed,
so that more can be specified.  You cannot delete a group if it has
been used to define a current {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{clear} style un\sphinxhyphen{}assigns all atoms that were assigned to that
group.  This may be dangerous to do during a simulation run
(e.g., using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run every}}}} command if a fix or compute or
other operation expects the atoms in the group to remain constant), but
LAMMPS does not check for this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{empty} style creates an empty group, which is useful for commands
like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gcmc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gcmc}}}} or with complex scripts that add atoms
to a group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} style puts all atoms in the region volume into the group.
Note that this is a static one\sphinxhyphen{}time assignment.  The atoms remain
assigned (or not assigned) to the group even in they later move out of
the region volume.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{type}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{id}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} styles put all atoms with the
specified atom types, atom IDs, or molecule IDs into the group.  These
three styles can use arguments specified in one of two formats.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first format is a list of values (types or IDs).  For example, the
second command in the examples above puts all atoms of type 3 or 4 into
the group named \sphinxstyleemphasis{water}.  Each numeric entry in the list can be a
colon\sphinxhyphen{}separated sequence \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{A:B}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{A:B:C}}, as in two of the examples
above.  A “sequence” generates a sequence of values (types or IDs),
with an optional increment.  The first example with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{500:1000}} has the
default increment of 1 and would add all atom IDs from 500 to 1000
(inclusive) to the group sub, along with 10, 25, and 50 since they also
appear in the list of values.  The second example with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{100:10000:10}}
uses an increment of 10 and would thus would add atoms IDs
\(100, 110, 120, \dots, 9990, 10000\) to the group sub.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second format is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{logical} followed by one or two values (type
or ID).  The 7 valid logicals are listed above.  All the logicals
except \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}\textgreater{}}} take a single argument.  The third example above adds all
atoms with IDs from 1 to 150 to the group named \sphinxstyleemphasis{sub}.  The logical \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\textless{}\textgreater{}}}
means “between” and takes 2 arguments.  The fourth example above adds all
atoms belonging to molecules with IDs from 50 to 250 (inclusive) to
the group named polyA.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} style, type labels are converted into
numeric types before being evaluated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable} style evaluates a variable to determine which atoms to
add to the group.  It must be an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}
previously defined in the input script.  If the variable evaluates
to a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero value for a particular atom, then that atom is added
to the specified group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can specify formulas that include thermodynamic
quantities, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values such as atom coordinates, or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities calculated by computes, fixes, or other variables.  They
can also include Boolean logic where two numeric values are compared to
yield a 1 or 0 (effectively a true or false).  Thus, using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{variable} style is a general way to flag specific atoms to include
or exclude from a group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, these lines define a variable “eatom” that calculates the
potential energy of each atom and includes it in the group if its
potential energy is above the threshold value \(-3.0\).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{l+m}{0}

\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{eatom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{c\PYGZus{}1 \PYGZgt{} \PYGZhy{}3.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{group           }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hienergy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{eatom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that these lines

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
are necessary to ensure that the “eatom” variable is current when the
group command invokes it.  Because the eatom variable computes the
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy via the pe/atom compute, it will only be current if a
run has been performed which evaluated pairwise energies, and the
pe/atom compute was actually invoked during the run.  Printing the
thermodynamic info for compute 2 ensures that this is the case, since
it sums the pe/atom compute values (in the reduce compute) to output
them to the screen.  See the “Variable Accuracy” section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} page for more details on ensuring that
variables are current when they are evaluated between runs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{include} style with its arg \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} adds atoms to a group that
have the same molecule ID as atoms already in the group.  The molecule
ID = 0 is ignored in this operation, since it is assumed to flag
isolated atoms that are not part of molecules.  An example of where
this operation is useful is if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} style has been used
previously to add atoms to a group that are within a geometric region.
If molecules straddle the region boundary, then atoms outside the
region that are part of molecules with atoms inside the region will
not be in the group.  Using the group command a second time with \sphinxstyleemphasis{include
molecule} will add those atoms that are outside the region to the
group.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{include molecule} operation is relatively expensive in a
parallel sense.  This is because it requires communication of relevant
molecule IDs between all the processors and each processor to loop
over its atoms once per processor, to compare its atoms to the list of
molecule IDs from every other processor.  Hence it scales as N, rather
than N/P as most of the group operations do, where N is the number of
atoms, and P is the number of processors.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{subtract} style takes a list of two or more existing group names
as arguments.  All atoms that belong to the first group, but not to any
of the other groups are added to the specified group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} style takes a list of one or more existing group names as
arguments.  All atoms that belong to any of the listed groups are
added to the specified group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} style takes a list of two or more existing group names
as arguments.  Atoms that belong to every one of the listed groups are
added to the specified group.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic} style flags an existing or new group as dynamic.  This
means atoms will be (re)assigned to the group periodically as a
simulation runs.  This is in contrast to static groups where atoms are
permanently assigned to the group.  The way the assignment occurs is
as follows.  Only atoms in the group specified as the parent group via
the parent\sphinxhyphen{}ID are assigned to the dynamic group before the following
conditions are applied.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} keyword is used, atoms not in the specified region are
removed from the dynamic group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{var} keyword is used, the variable name must be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.  The variable is evaluated and atoms whose
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values are 0.0, are removed from the dynamic group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{property} keyword is used, the name refers to a custom integer
or floating point per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector defined via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
property/atom}}}} command.  This means the values in
the vector can be read as part of a data file with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command or specified with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command.
Or accessed and changed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_library::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{library interface to LAMMPS}}}}, or by styles you add to LAMMPS (pair, fix, compute,
etc) which access the custom vector and modify its values.  Which
means the values can be modified between or during simulations.  Atoms
whose values in the custom vector are zero are removed from the
dynamic group.  Note that the name of the custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector is
specified just as \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}, not as \sphinxstyleemphasis{i\_name} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{d\_name} as it is for
other commands that use different kinds of custom atom vectors or
arrays as arguments.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The assignment of atoms to a dynamic group is done at the beginning of
each run and on every timestep that is a multiple of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}, which is
the argument for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword (\(N = 1\) is the default).  For an
energy minimization, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command, an
assignment is made at the beginning of the minimization, but not
during the iterations of the minimizer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The point in the timestep at which atoms are assigned to a dynamic
group is after interatomic forces have been computed, but before any
fixes which alter forces or otherwise update the system have been
invoked.  This means that atom positions have been updated, neighbor
lists and ghost atoms are current, and both intermolecular and
intramolecular forces have been calculated based on the new
coordinates.  Thus the region criterion, if applied, should be
accurate.  Also, any computes invoked by an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable should
use updated information for that timestep (e.g., potential energy/atom
or coordination number/atom).  Similarly, fixes or computes which are
invoked after that point in the timestep, should operate on the new
group of atoms.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} keyword is used to determine what atoms are in
the dynamic group, atoms can move outside of the simulation box
between reneighboring events.  Thus if you want to include all atoms
on the left side of the simulation box, you probably want to set the
left boundary of the region to be outside the simulation box by some
reasonable amount (e.g., up to the cutoff of the potential), else they
may be excluded from the dynamic region.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of using a dynamic group to shrink the set of atoms
being integrated by using a spherical region with a variable radius
(shrinking from 18 to 5 over the course of the run).  This could be
used to model a quench of the system, freezing atoms outside the
shrinking sphere, then converting the remaining atoms to a static
group and running further.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{nsteps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5000}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{rad}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{step/v\PYGZus{}nsteps}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{18\PYGZhy{}5}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{region          }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ss}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}rad}
\PYG{k}{group           }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dynamic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ss}
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{nsteps}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{k}{group           }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{static}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{nsteps}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All fixes and computes take a group ID as an argument, but they do
not all allow for use of a dynamic group.  If you get an error
message that this is not allowed, but feel that it should be for the
fix or compute in question, then please post your reasoning to the
\sphinxhref{https://matsci.org/c/lammps-development/42}{LAMMPS forum at MatSci}
and we can look into changing it.  The same applies if you come
across inconsistent behavior when dynamic groups are allowed.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{static} style removes the setting for a dynamic group, converting
it to a static group (the default).  The atoms in the static group are
those currently in the dynamic group.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{group:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There can be no more than 32 groups defined at one time, including
“all”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parent group of a dynamic group cannot itself be a dynamic group.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{group:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{group:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All atoms belong to the “all” group.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{group2ndx@\spxentry{group2ndx}}\ignorespaces 
\index{ndx2group@\spxentry{ndx2group}}\ignorespaces 

\section{group2ndx command}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:group2ndx-command}}\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{group2ndx::doc}}

\section{ndx2group command}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:ndx2group-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{group2ndx }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\PYG{k}{ndx2group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file = name of index file to write out or read in

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = zero or more group IDs may be appended

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{group2ndx }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{allindex.ndx}
\PYG{k}{group2ndx }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{someindex.ndx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{upper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mobile}
\PYG{k}{ndx2group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{someindex.ndx}
\PYG{k}{ndx2group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{someindex.ndx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mobile}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write or read a Gromacs style index file in text format that associates
atom IDs with the corresponding group definitions. This index file can be
used with in combination with Gromacs analysis tools or to import group
definitions into the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_colvars::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix colvars}}}} input file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It can also be used to save and restore group definitions for static groups
using the individual atom IDs. This may be important if the original
group definition depends on a region or otherwise on the geometry and thus
cannot be easily recreated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another application would be to import atom groups defined for Gromacs
simulation into LAMMPS.  When translating Gromacs topology and geometry
data to LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{group2ndx} command will write group definitions to an index file.
Without specifying any group IDs, all groups will be written to the
index file.  When specifying group IDs, only those groups will be
written to the index file.  In order to follow the Gromacs conventions,
the group \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} will be renamed to \sphinxstyleemphasis{System} in the index file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ndx2group} command will create of update group definitions from
those stored in an index file.  Without specifying any group IDs, all
groups except \sphinxstyleemphasis{System} will be read from the index file and the
corresponding groups recreated.  If a group of the same name already
exists, it will be completely reset.  When specifying group IDs, those
groups, if present, will be read from the index file and restored.


\subsection{File Format}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:file-format}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The file format is equivalent and compatible with what is produced by
the \sphinxhref{https://manual.gromacs.org/current/onlinehelp/gmx-make\_ndx.html}{Gromacs make\_ndx command}.
and follows the \sphinxhref{https://manual.gromacs.org/current/reference-manual/file-formats.html\#ndx}{Gromacs definition of an ndx file}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each group definition begins with the group name in square brackets with
blanks, e.g. {[} water {]} and is then followed by the list of atom
indices, which may be spread over multiple lines.  Here is a small
example file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{[ Oxygen ]}
\PYG{n+na}{1  4  7}
\PYG{k}{[ Hydrogen ]}
\PYG{n+na}{2  3  5  6}
\PYG{n+na}{8  9}
\PYG{k}{[ Water ]}
\PYG{n+na}{1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The index file defines 3 groups: Oxygen, Hydrogen, and Water and the
latter happens to be the union of the first two.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands require that atoms have atom IDs, since this is the
information that is written to the index file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands are part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMMAND package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_colvars::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix colvars}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{group2ndx:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\section{hyper command}
\label{\detokenize{hyper:hyper-command}}\label{\detokenize{hyper:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{hyper::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{hyper:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{hyper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nevent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = \# of timesteps to run

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nevent = check for events every this many steps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of a fix that applies a global or local bias potential, can be NULL

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of a compute that identifies when an event has occurred

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{min} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rebond}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{min} values = etol ftol maxiter maxeval
  etol = stopping tolerance for energy, used in quenching
  ftol = stopping tolerance for force, used in quenching
  maxiter = max iterations of minimize, used in quenching
  maxeval = max number of force/energy evaluations, used in quenching
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} value = dump\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  dump\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of dump to trigger whenever an event takes place
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rebond} value = Nrebond
  Nrebond = frequency at which to reset bonds, even if no event has occurred
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{hyper:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{event}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{event}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{displace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{HG}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hyper}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{global}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{800.0}
\PYG{k}{hyper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{HG}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{event}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{hyper:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run a bond\sphinxhyphen{}boost hyperdynamics (HD) simulation where time is
accelerated by application of a bias potential to one or more pairs of
nearby atoms in the system.  This command can be used to run both
global and local hyperdynamics.  In global HD a single bond within the
system is biased on each timestep.  In local HD multiple bonds
(separated by a sufficient distance) can be biased simultaneously at
each timestep.  In the bond\sphinxhyphen{}boost hyperdynamics context, a “bond” is
not a covalent bond between a pair of atoms in a molecule.  Rather it
is simply a pair of nearby atoms as discussed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both global and local HD are described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{hyper:voter2013}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Voter2013)}}}} by Art Voter and collaborators.  Similar to parallel
replica dynamics (PRD), global and local HD are methods for performing
accelerated dynamics that are suitable for infrequent\sphinxhyphen{}event systems
that obey first\sphinxhyphen{}order kinetics.  A good overview of accelerated
dynamics methods (AMD) for such systems in given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{hyper:voter2002hd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Voter2002)}}}} from the same group.  To quote from the review paper:
“The dynamical evolution is characterized by vibrational excursions
within a potential basin, punctuated by occasional transitions between
basins.  The transition probability is characterized by p(t) =
k*exp(\sphinxhyphen{}kt) where k is the rate constant.”

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both HD and PRD produce a time\sphinxhyphen{}accurate trajectory that effectively
extends the timescale over which a system can be simulated, but they
do it differently.  HD uses a single replica of the system and
accelerates time by biasing the interaction potential in a manner such
that each timestep is effectively longer.  PRD creates Nr replicas of
the system and runs dynamics on each independently with a normal
unbiased potential until an event occurs in one of the replicas.  The
time between events is reduced by a factor of Nr replicas.  For both
methods, per CPU second, more physical time elapses and more events
occur.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{prd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{prd}}}} page for more info about PRD.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An HD run has several stages, which are repeated each time an event
occurs, as explained below.  The logic for an HD run is as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
quench
create initial list of bonds

while (time remains):
  run dynamics for Nevent steps
  quench
  check for an event
  if event occurred: reset list of bonds
  restore pre\PYGZhy{}quench state
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The list of bonds is the list of atom pairs of atoms that are within a
short cutoff distance of each other after the system energy is
minimized (quenched).  This list is created and reset by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_hyper_global::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix hyper/global}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_hyper_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix hyper/local}}}} command specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.  At
every dynamics timestep, the same fix selects one of more bonds to
apply a bias potential to.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The style of fix associated with the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID}
determines whether you are running the global versus local
hyperdynamics algorithm.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dynamics (with the bias potential) is run continuously, stopping every
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevent} steps to check if a transition event has occurred.  The
specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} for total steps must be a multiple of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevent}.  check
is performed by quenching the system and comparing the resulting atom
coordinates to the coordinates from the previous basin.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A quench is an energy minimization and is performed by whichever
algorithm has been defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}} command.
Minimization parameters may be set via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_modify}}}} command and by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{min} keyword of the
hyper command.  The latter are the settings that would be used with
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.  Note that typically, you do not
need to perform a highly\sphinxhyphen{}converged minimization to detect a transition
event, though you may need to in order to prevent a set of atoms in
the system from relaxing to a saddle point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The event check is performed by a compute with the specified
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.  Currently there is only one compute that works with the
hyper command, which is the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_event_displace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute event/displace}}}} command.  Other
event\sphinxhyphen{}checking computes may be added.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_event_displace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Compute event/displace}}}} checks whether any atom in
the compute group has moved further than a specified threshold
distance.  If so, an event has occurred.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If this happens, the list of bonds is reset, since some bond pairs
are likely now too far apart, and new pairs are likely close enough
to be considered a bond.  The pre\sphinxhyphen{}quenched state of the
system (coordinates and velocities) is restored, and dynamics continue.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the end of the hyper run, a variety of statistics are output to the
screen and logfile.  These include info relevant to both global and
local hyperdynamics, such as the number of events and the elapsed
hyper time (accelerated time), And it includes info specific to one or
the other, depending on which style of fix was specified by \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keywords operate as follows.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained above, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{min} keyword can be used to specify
parameters for the quench.  Their meaning is the same
as for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} keyword can be used to trigger a specific dump command with
the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump\sphinxhyphen{}ID} to output a snapshot each time an event is
detected.  It can be specified multiple times with different \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump\sphinxhyphen{}ID}
values, as in the example above.  These snapshots will be for the
quenched state of the system on a timestep that is a multiple of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevent}, i.e. a timestep after the event has occurred.  Note that any
dump command in the input script will also output snapshots at
whatever timestep interval it defines via its \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} argument; see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} command for details.  This means if you only want a
particular dump to output snapshots when events are detected, you
should specify its \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} as a value larger than the length of the
hyperdynamics run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As in the code logic above, the bond list is normally only reset when
an event occurs.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rebond} keyword will force a reset of the bond
list every \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nrebond} steps, even if an event has not occurred.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nrebond} must be a multiple of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevent}.  This can be useful to check
if more frequent resets alter event statistics, perhaps because the
parameters chosen for defining what is a bond and what is an event are
producing bad dynamics in the presence of the bias potential.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{hyper:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the REPLICA
package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc
page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{hyper:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_hyper_global::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix hyper/global}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_hyper_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix hyper/local}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_event_displace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute event/displace}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{prd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{prd}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{hyper:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are min = 0.1 0.1 40 50 and time = steps.
