\sphinxAtStartPar
In \sphinxstyleemphasis{unit\_conversion\_mode} the results obtained from a \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim query} would need
to be converted to the appropriate units system.  For example, in the above
script, the lattice command would need to be changed to:
“lattice fcc \$(v\_a0*v\_\_u\_distance)”.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Define an equilibrium hcp crystal}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{EAM\PYGZus{}Dynamo\PYGZus{}MendelevAckland\PYGZus{}2007v3\PYGZus{}Zr\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}004835508849\PYGZus{}000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{query}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{latconst}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{split}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}lattice\PYGZus{}constant\PYGZus{}hexagonal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{crystal}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[hcp]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[Zr]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[angstrom]}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{latconst\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.866025}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.866025}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{latconst\PYGZus{}2/latconst\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.333333}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.666666}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.666666}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.333333}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.75}
\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim query} returns two arguments (since the hexagonal close
packed (hcp) structure has two independent lattice constants).  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg}
keyword “split” places the two values into the variables \sphinxstyleemphasis{latconst\_1} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{latconst\_2}.  (These variables are created if they do not already exist.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Define a crystal at finite temperature accounting for thermal expansion}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{EAM\PYGZus{}Dynamo\PYGZus{}ErcolessiAdams\PYGZus{}1994\PYGZus{}Al\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}123629422045\PYGZus{}005}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{k}{boundary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{query}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}lattice\PYGZus{}constant\PYGZus{}cubic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{crystal}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[fcc]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[Al]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[angstrom]}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{query}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{alpha}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}linear\PYGZus{}thermal\PYGZus{}expansion\PYGZus{}coefficient\PYGZus{}cubic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{crystal}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[fcc]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[Al]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[1}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{K]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temperature}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[293.15]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temperature\PYGZus{}units}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[K]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{DeltaT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{fcc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{v\PYGZus{}a0*v\PYGZus{}alpha*v\PYGZus{}DeltaT}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As in the previous example, the equilibrium lattice constant is obtained for the
Ercolessi and Adams (1994) potential.  However, in this case the crystal is
scaled to the appropriate lattice constant at room temperature (293.15 K) by
using the linear thermal expansion constant predicted by the potential.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When passing numerical values as arguments (as in the case of the temperature
in the above example) it is also possible to pass a tolerance indicating how
close to the value is considered a match.  If no tolerance is passed a default
value is used.  If multiple results are returned (indicating that the
tolerance is too large), \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim query} will return an error.  See the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/doc/usage/kim-query}{query documentation} to see which
numerical arguments and tolerances are available for a given
\sphinxstyleemphasis{query\_function}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compute defect formation energy}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{EAM\PYGZus{}Dynamo\PYGZus{}ErcolessiAdams\PYGZus{}1994\PYGZus{}Al\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}123629422045\PYGZus{}005}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Build}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fcc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{crystal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{containing}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{some}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{defect}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{and}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{the}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{total}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{energy}
\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{which}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{is}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stored}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{in}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{the}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{Etot}\PYG{o}{*}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{query}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ec}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}cohesive\PYGZus{}energy\PYGZus{}cubic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{crystal}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[fcc]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[Al]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[eV]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Eform}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{Etot}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{all}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{Ec}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The defect formation energy \sphinxstyleemphasis{Eform} is computed by subtracting the ideal fcc
cohesive energy of the atoms in the system from \sphinxstyleemphasis{Etot}.  The ideal fcc
cohesive energy of the atoms is obtained from
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{OpenKIM} for the Ercolessi and Adams (1994) potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Retrieve equilibrium fcc crystal of all EAM potentials that support a specific species}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim   }\PYG{l+s+s1}{query}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}available\PYGZus{}models}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[Al]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{potential\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[eam]}
\PYG{k}{label }\PYG{l+s+sc}{model\PYGZus{}loop}
\PYG{k}{kim   }\PYG{l+s+s1}{query}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{latconst}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}lattice\PYGZus{}constant\PYGZus{}cubic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{crystal}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[fcc]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[Al]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[angstrom]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{[}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{model}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{FCC lattice constant (\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}model\PYGZcb{} potential) = \PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}latconst\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{do}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{something}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{with}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{current}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{of}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{latconst}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{next  }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{model}
\PYG{k}{jump  }\PYG{l+s+sc}{SELF}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{model\PYGZus{}loop}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this example, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} mode of \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} is used.  The first \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim query}
returns the list of all available EAM potentials that support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Al} species
and archived in \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{OpenKIM}.  The result of the query
operation is stored in the LAMMPS variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{model} as an index \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable}.
This variable is used later to access the values one at a time within a loop as
shown in the example.  The second \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim query} command retrieves from
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{OpenKIM} the equilibrium lattice constant predicted by
each potential for the fcc structure and places it in variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{latconst}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim query} commands return results archived in
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{OpenKIM}.  These results are obtained using programs
for computing material properties (KIM Tests and KIM Test Drivers) that were
contributed to OpenKIM.  In order to give credit to Test developers, the
number of times results from these programs are queried is tracked.  No other
information about the nature of the query or its source is recorded.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Accessing KIM Model Parameters from LAMMPS (\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param})}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:accessing-kim-model-parameters-from-lammps-kim-param}}\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:param}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All IMs are functional forms containing a set of parameters.  These parameters’
values are typically selected to best reproduce a training set of quantum
mechanical calculations or available experimental data.  For example, a
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential intended to model argon might have the values of its two
parameters, epsilon, and sigma, fit to the dimer dissociation energy or
thermodynamic properties at a critical point of the phase diagram.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Normally a user employing an IM should not modify its parameters since, as noted
above, these are selected to reproduce material properties.  However, there are
cases where accessing and modifying IM parameters is desired, such as for
assessing uncertainty, fitting an IM, or working with an ensemble of IMs.  As
explained {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands:im-types}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{above}}}}, IMs archived in OpenKIM are either Portable
Models (PMs) or Simulator Models (SMs).  KIM PMs are complete independent
implementations of an IM, whereas KIM SMs are wrappers to an IM implemented
within LAMMPS.  Two different mechanisms are provided for accessing IM
parameters in these two cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a KIM PM, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param} command can be used to \sphinxstyleemphasis{get} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} the
values of the PM’s parameters as explained below.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a KIM SM, the user should consult the documentation page for the specific
IM and follow instructions there for how to modify its parameters (if
possible).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param get} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param set} commands provide an interface to access
and change the parameters of a KIM PM that “publishes” its parameters and makes
them publicly available (see the
\sphinxhref{https://kim-api.readthedocs.io/en/devel/features.html}{KIM API documentation}
for details).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param set/get} command must be preceded by a \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim interactions}
command (or alternatively by a \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style kim} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} commands).
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param set} command may be used wherever a \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command may
occur.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:id13}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{param\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index\PYGZus{}range}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{formatarg}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{param\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index\PYGZus{}range}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:formatarg-options}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
param\_name = name of a KIM portable model parameter (which is published by the
PM and available for access). The specific string used to identify a parameter
is defined by the PM.  For example, for the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/id/SW\_StillingerWeber\_1985\_Si\_\_MO\_405512056662\_005}{Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber (SW) potential in OpenKIM},
the parameter names are \sphinxstyleemphasis{A, B, p, q, sigma, gamma, cutoff, lambda, costheta0}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
index\_range = KIM portable model parameter index range (an integer for a
single element, or pair of integers separated by a colon for a range of
elements)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
variable(s) = single name or list of names of (string style) LAMMPS
variable(s) where a query result or parameter get result is stored.  Variables
that do not exist will be created by the command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
formatarg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{list} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{explicit} (optional)
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{list} = returns a single string with a list of space separated values
       (e.g. "1.0 2.0 3.0"), which is placed in a LAMMPS variable as
       defined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable} argument
\sphinxstyleemphasis{split} = returns the values separately in new variables with names based
       on the prefix specified in \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable} and a number appended to
       indicate which element in the list of values is in the variable
\sphinxstyleemphasis{explicit} = returns the values separately in one more more variable names
       provided as arguments that precede \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} (default)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
values = new value(s) to replace the current value(s) of a KIM portable model
parameter

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The list of all the parameters that a PM exposes for access/mutation are
automatically written to the lammps log file when \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim init} is called.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each published parameter of a KIM PM takes the form of an array of numerical
values.  The array can contain one element for a single\sphinxhyphen{}valued parameter, or a
set of values.  For example, the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/id/SW\_ZhouWardMartin\_2013\_CdTeZnSeHgS\_\_MO\_503261197030\_002}{multispecies SW potential for the Zn\sphinxhyphen{}Cd\sphinxhyphen{}Hg\sphinxhyphen{}S\sphinxhyphen{}Se\sphinxhyphen{}Te system}
has the same parameter names as the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/id/SW\_StillingerWeber\_1985\_Si\_\_MO\_405512056662\_005}{single\sphinxhyphen{}species SW potential},
but each parameter array contains 21 entries that correspond to the parameter
values used for each pairwise combination of the model’s six supported species
(this model does not have parameters specific to individual ternary combinations
of its supported species).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{index\_range} argument may either be an integer referring to a specific
element within the array associated with the parameter specified by
\sphinxstyleemphasis{param\_name}, or a pair of integers separated by a colon that refer to a slice
of this array.  In both cases, one\sphinxhyphen{}based indexing is used to refer to the
entries of the array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The result of a \sphinxstyleemphasis{get} operation for a specific \sphinxstyleemphasis{index\_range} is stored in
one or more {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS string style variables}}}} as determined by the
optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} argument {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands:formatarg-options}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{documented above.}}}} If
not specified, the default for \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} is “explicit” for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the case where the result is an array with multiple values (i.e.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{index\_range} contains a range), the optional “split” or “explicit” \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg}
keywords can be used to separate the results into multiple variables; see the
examples below.  Multiple parameters can be retrieved with a single call to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param get} by repeating the argument list following \sphinxstyleemphasis{get}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} operation, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{values} argument contains the new value(s) for the
element(s) of the parameter specified by \sphinxstyleemphasis{index\_range}.  For the case where
multiple values are being set, \sphinxstyleemphasis{values} contains a set of values separated by
spaces.  Multiple parameters can be set with a single call to \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param set} by
repeating the argument list following \sphinxstyleemphasis{set}.


\subsubsection{\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim param} Usage Examples and Further Clarifications}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:kim-param-usage-examples-and-further-clarifications}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples of getting and setting KIM PM parameters with further clarifications
are provided below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Getting a scalar parameter}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SW\PYGZus{}StillingerWeber\PYGZus{}1985\PYGZus{}Si\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}405512056662\PYGZus{}005}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{VARA}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{SW\PYGZus{}StillingerWeber\PYGZus{}1985\PYGZus{}Si\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}405512056662\PYGZus{}005}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{VARA}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In these cases, the value of the SW \sphinxstyleemphasis{A} parameter is retrieved and placed in the
LAMMPS variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{VARA}.  The variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{VARA} can be used in the remainder of
the input script in the same manner as any other LAMMPS variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Getting multiple scalar parameters with a single call}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{VARA}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{B}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{VARB}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this example, it is shown how to retrieve the \sphinxstyleemphasis{A} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{B} parameters of the
SW potential and store them in the LAMMPS variables \sphinxstyleemphasis{VARA} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{VARB}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Getting a range of values from a parameter}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several options when getting a range of values from a parameter
determined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} argument.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SW\PYGZus{}ZhouWardMartin\PYGZus{}2013\PYGZus{}CdTeZnSeHgS\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}503261197030\PYGZus{}002}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Te}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Zn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Se}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lambda}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7:9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LAM\PYGZus{}TeTe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LAM\PYGZus{}TeZn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LAM\PYGZus{}TeSe}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} is not specified and therefore the default
“explicit” mode is used. (The behavior would be the same if the word
\sphinxstyleemphasis{explicit} were added after \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_TeSe}.) Elements 7, 8 and 9 of parameter
lambda retrieved by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{get} operation are placed in the LAMMPS variables
\sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_TeTe}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_TeZn} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_TeSe}, respectively.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the above example, elements 7\sphinxhyphen{}9 of the lambda parameter correspond to
Te\sphinxhyphen{}Te, Te\sphinxhyphen{}Zm and Te\sphinxhyphen{}Se interactions.  This can be determined by visiting the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/id/SW\_ZhouWardMartin\_2013\_CdTeZnSeHgS\_\_MO\_503261197030\_002}{model page for the specified potential}
and looking at its parameter file linked to at the bottom of the page (file
with .param ending) and consulting the README documentation provided with the
driver for the PM being used.  A link to the driver is provided at the top of
the model page.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Te}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Zn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Se}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lambda}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{15:17}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LAMS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LAM\PYGZus{}VALUE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{LAMS}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{k}{label    }\PYG{l+s+sc}{loop\PYGZus{}on\PYGZus{}lambda}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{do}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{something}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{with}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{the}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{current}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{of}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lambda}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{next     }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LAM\PYGZus{}VALUE}
\PYG{k}{jump     }\PYG{l+s+sc}{SELF}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop\PYGZus{}on\PYGZus{}lambda}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, the “list” mode of \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} is used.  The result of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{get}
operation is stored in the LAMMPS variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAMS} as a string containing the
three retrieved values separated by spaces, e.g “1.0 2.0 3.0”.  This can be used
in LAMMPS with an \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} variable to access the values one at a time within a
loop as shown in the example.  At each iteration of the loop \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_VALUE}
contains the current value of lambda.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Te}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Zn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Se}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lambda}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{15:17}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LAM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{split}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, the “split” mode of \sphinxstyleemphasis{formatarg} is used.  The three values
retrieved by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{get} operation are stored in the three LAMMPS variables
\sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_15}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_16} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAM\_17}.  The provided name “LAM” is used as prefix
and the location in the lambda array is appended to create the variable names.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Setting a scalar parameter}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SW\PYGZus{}StillingerWeber\PYGZus{}1985\PYGZus{}Si\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}405512056662\PYGZus{}005}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.6}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, the SW potential’s gamma parameter is set to 2.6.  Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{get}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} commands work together, so that a \sphinxstyleemphasis{get} following a \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} operation
will return the new value that was set.  For example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ORIG\PYGZus{}GAMMA}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.6}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{get}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NEW\PYGZus{}GAMMA}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{original gamma = \PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}ORIG\PYGZus{}GAMMA\PYGZcb{}, new gamma = \PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}NEW\PYGZus{}GAMMA\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ORIG\_GAMMA} will contain the original gamma value for the SW potential,
while \sphinxstyleemphasis{NEW\_GAMMA} will contain the value 2.6.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Setting multiple scalar parameters with a single call}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SW\PYGZus{}ZhouWardMartin\PYGZus{}2013\PYGZus{}CdTeZnSeHgS\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}503261197030\PYGZus{}002}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Te}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{VARG}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.6}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{VARS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0951}
\PYG{k}{kim      }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{VARG}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{VARS}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, the first element of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gamma} parameter and third element of
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sigma} parameter are set to 2.6 and 2.0951, respectively.  This example
also shows how LAMMPS variables can be used when setting parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Setting a range of values of a parameter}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{init}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SW\PYGZus{}ZhouWardMartin\PYGZus{}2013\PYGZus{}CdTeZnSeHgS\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}MO\PYGZus{}503261197030\PYGZus{}002}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{interactions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Te}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Zn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Se}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Hg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{S}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{param}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2:6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.35214}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.23869}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.04516}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.43269}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.80415}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, elements 2 through 6 of the parameter \sphinxstyleemphasis{sigma} are set to the
values 2.35214, 2.23869, 2.04516, 2.43269 and 1.80415 in order.


\subsection{Writing material properties in standard KIM Property Instance format (\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property})}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:writing-material-properties-in-standard-kim-property-instance-format-kim-property}}\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:property}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The OpenKIM system includes a
collection of Tests (material property calculation codes), Models (interatomic
potentials), Predictions, and Reference Data (DFT or experiments).
Specifically, a KIM Test is a computation that when coupled with a KIM Model
generates the prediction of that model for a specific material property
rigorously defined by a KIM Property Definition (see the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/doc/schema/properties-framework/}{KIM Properties Framework}
for further details).  A prediction of a material property for a given model is
a specific numerical realization of a property definition, referred to as a
“Property Instance.” The objective of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property} command is to make it
easy to output material properties in a standardized, machine readable, format
that can be easily ingested by other programs.  Additionally, it aims to make it
as easy as possible to convert a LAMMPS script that computes a material property
into a KIM Test that can then be uploaded to
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{openkim.org}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A developer interested in creating a KIM Test using a LAMMPS script should first
determine whether a property definition that applies to their calculation
already exists in OpenKIM by searching the \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/properties}{properties page}.  If none exists, it is possible to use a
locally defined property definition contained in a file until it can be
uploaded to the official repository (see below).  Once one or more applicable
property definitions have been identified, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property create},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property modify}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property remove}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property destroy},
commands provide an interface to create, set, modify, remove, and destroy
instances of them within a LAMMPS script.


\subsubsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:id14}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{instance\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property\PYGZus{}id}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{instance\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}name\PYGZus{}key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}name\PYGZus{}value}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{remove}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{instance\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}name}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{destroy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{instance\PYGZus{}id}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{dump    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{file}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
instance\_id = a positive integer identifying the KIM property instance;
(note that the results file can contain multiple property instances)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
property\_id = identifier of a
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/properties}{KIM Property Definition}, which can be (1)
a property short name, (2) the full unique ID of the property (including the
contributor and date), (3) a file name corresponding to a local property
definition file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
key\_name = one of the keys belonging to the specified KIM property definition

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
key\_name\_key = a key belonging to a key\sphinxhyphen{}value pair (standardized in the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/doc/schema/properties-framework}{KIM Properties Framework})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
key\_name\_value = value to be associated with a key\_name\_key in a key\sphinxhyphen{}value
pair

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file = name of a file to write the currently defined set of KIM property
instances to

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples of each of the three \sphinxstyleemphasis{property\_id} cases are shown below,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atomic}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{mass}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cohesive}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{energy}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{relation}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{cubic}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{crystal}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tag}:brunnels@noreply.openkim.org,2016\PYGZhy{}05\PYGZhy{}11:property/atomic\PYGZhy{}mass
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tag}:staff@noreply.openkim.org,2014\PYGZhy{}04\PYGZhy{}15:property/cohesive\PYGZhy{}energy\PYGZhy{}relation\PYGZhy{}cubic\PYGZhy{}crystal
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{new}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{property.edn}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{home}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{mary}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{marys}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{kim}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{properties}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dissociation}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{energy.edn}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the last example, “new\sphinxhyphen{}property.edn” and
“/home/mary/marys\sphinxhyphen{}kim\sphinxhyphen{}properties/dissociation\sphinxhyphen{}energy.edn” are the names of files
that contain user\sphinxhyphen{}defined (local) property definitions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A KIM property instance takes the form of a “map”, i.e. a set of key\sphinxhyphen{}value
pairs akin to Perl’s hash, Python’s dictionary, or Java’s Hashtable.  It
consists of a set of property key names, each of which is referred to here by
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name} argument, that are defined as part of the relevant KIM Property
Definition and include only lowercase alphanumeric characters and dashes.  The
value paired with each property key is itself a map whose possible keys are
defined as part of the \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/doc/schema/properties-framework}{KIM Properties Framework}; these keys are
referred to by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name\_key} argument and their associated values by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name\_value} argument.  These values may either be scalars or arrays,
as stipulated in the property definition.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Each map assigned to a \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name} must contain the \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name\_key}
“source\sphinxhyphen{}value” and an associated \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name\_value} of the appropriate
type (as defined in the relevant KIM Property Definition).  For keys that
are defined as having physical units, the “source\sphinxhyphen{}unit” \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name\_key} must
also be given a string value recognized by
\sphinxhref{https://www.gnu.org/software/units/}{GNU units}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once a \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property create} command has been given to instantiate a property
instance, maps associated with the property’s keys can be edited using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property modify} command.  In using this command, the special keyword
“key” should be given, followed by the property key name and the key\sphinxhyphen{}value pair
in the map associated with the key that is to be set.  For example, the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/properties/show/2016-05-11/brunnels@noreply.openkim.org/atomic-mass}{atomic\sphinxhyphen{}mass}
property definition consists of two property keys named “mass” and “species.”
An instance of this property could be created like so:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atomic}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{mass}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{26.98154}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{unit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amu}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or, equivalently,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atomic}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{mass}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                      }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{26.98154}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                                  }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{unit}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{amu}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property} Usage Examples and Further Clarifications}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:kim-property-usage-examples-and-further-clarifications}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Create}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{instance\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property\PYGZus{}id}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property create} command takes as input a property instance ID and the
property definition name, and creates an initial empty property instance data
structure.  For example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atomic}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{mass}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cohesive}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{energy}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{relation}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{cubic}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{crystal}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
creates an empty property instance of the “atomic\sphinxhyphen{}mass” property definition
with instance ID 1 and an empty instance of the
“cohesive\sphinxhyphen{}energy\sphinxhyphen{}relation\sphinxhyphen{}cubic\sphinxhyphen{}crystal” property with ID 2.  A list of
published property definitions in OpenKIM can be found on the \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/properties}{properties page}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One can also provide the name of a file in the current working directory or the
path of a file containing a valid property definition.  For example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{new}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{property.edn}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where “new\sphinxhyphen{}property.edn” refers to a file name containing a new property
definition that does not exist in OpenKIM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{property\_id} given cannot be found in OpenKIM and no file of this name
containing a valid property definition can be found, this command will produce
an error with an appropriate message.  Calling \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property create} with the
same instance ID multiple times will also produce an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Modify}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{instance\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}name\PYGZus{}key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key\PYGZus{}name\PYGZus{}value}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property modify} command incrementally builds the property instance
by receiving property definition keys along with associated arguments.  Each
\sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name} is associated with a map containing one or more key\sphinxhyphen{}value pairs (in
the form of \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name\_key}\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name\_value} pairs).  For example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{26.98154}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{unit}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{amu}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where the special keyword “key” is followed by a \sphinxstyleemphasis{key\_name} (“species” or
“mass” in the above) and one or more key\sphinxhyphen{}value pairs.  These key\sphinxhyphen{}value pairs
may continue until either another “key” keyword is given or the end of the
command line is reached.  Thus, the above could equivalently be written as

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                      }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{26.98154}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                      }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{unit}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{amu}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example of modifying multiple key\sphinxhyphen{}value pairs belonging to the map of a
single property key, the following command modifies the map of the
“cohesive\sphinxhyphen{}potential\sphinxhyphen{}energy” property key to contain the key “source\sphinxhyphen{}unit” which
is assigned a value of “eV” and the key “digits” which is assigned a value of
5,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cohesive}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{potential}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{energy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{unit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eV}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{digits}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The relevant data types of the values in the map are handled automatically
based on the specification of the key in the KIM Property Definition.  In
the example above, this means that the value “eV” will automatically be
interpreted as a string while the value 5 will be interpreted as an integer.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values contained in maps can either be scalars, as in all of the examples
above, or arrays depending on which is stipulated in the corresponding Property
Definition.  For one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional arrays, a single one\sphinxhyphen{}based index must be
supplied that indicates which element of the array is to be modified.  For
multidimensional arrays, multiple indices must be given depending on the
dimensionality of the array.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All array indexing used by \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property modify} is one\sphinxhyphen{}based, i.e. the
indices are enumerated 1, 2, 3, …
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The dimensionality of arrays are defined in the the corresponding Property
Definition.  The extent of each dimension of an array can either be a
specific finite number or indefinite and determined at run time.  If
an array has a fixed extent, attempting to modify an out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}range index will
fail with an error message.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the “species” property key of the
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/properties/show/2014-04-15/staff@noreply.openkim.org/cohesive-energy-relation-cubic-crystal}{cohesive\sphinxhyphen{}energy\sphinxhyphen{}relation\sphinxhyphen{}cubic\sphinxhyphen{}crystal}
property is a one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional array that can contain any number of entries
based on the number of atoms in the unit cell of a given cubic crystal.  To
assign an array containing the string “Al” four times to the “source\sphinxhyphen{}value” key
of the “species” property key, we can do so by issuing:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No declaration of the number of elements in this array was given;
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property modify} will automatically handle memory management to allow
an arbitrary number of elements to be added to the array.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the event that \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim property modify} is used to set the value of an
array index without having set the values of all lesser indices, they will
be assigned default values based on the data type associated with the key in
the map:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
Data type
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
Default value
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
int
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
0
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
float
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
0.0
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
string
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
""
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
file
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
""
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, doing the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cohesive}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{energy}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{relation}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{cubic}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{crystal}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
will result in the “source\sphinxhyphen{}value” key in the map for the property key
“species” being assigned the array {[}“”, “”, “”, “Al”{]}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For convenience, the index argument provided may refer to an inclusive range of
indices by specifying two integers separated by a colon (the first integer must
be less than or equal to the second integer, and no whitespace should be
included).  Thus, the snippet above could equivalently be written:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{species}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Calling this command with a non\sphinxhyphen{}positive index, e.g.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kim property modify 2 key species source\sphinxhyphen{}value 0 Al}}, or an incorrect
number of input arguments, e.g.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{kim property modify 2 key species source\sphinxhyphen{}value 1:4 Al Al}}, will result in an
error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example of modifying multidimensional arrays, consider the “basis\sphinxhyphen{}atoms”
key in the \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/properties/show/2014-04-15/staff@noreply.openkim.org/cohesive-energy-relation-cubic-crystal}{cohesive\sphinxhyphen{}energy\sphinxhyphen{}relation\sphinxhyphen{}cubic\sphinxhyphen{}crystal}
property definition.  This is a two\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional array containing the fractional
coordinates of atoms in the unit cell of the cubic crystal.  In the case of,
e.g. a conventional fcc unit cell, the “source\sphinxhyphen{}value” key in the map associated
with this key should be assigned the following value:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
 [0.5, 0.5, 0.0],
 [0.5, 0.0, 0.5],
 [0.0, 0.5, 0.5]]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
While each of the twelve components could be set individually, we can instead
set each row at a time using colon notation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{coordinates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{coordinates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{coordinates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{coordinates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Where the first index given refers to a row and the second index refers to a
column.  We could, instead, choose to set each column at a time like so:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kim }\PYG{l+s+s1}{property}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{coordinates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                      }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{coordinates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                      }\PYG{n}{key}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{coordinates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1:4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{Citation of OpenKIM IMs}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:citation-of-openkim-ims}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When publishing results obtained using OpenKIM IMs researchers are
requested to cite the OpenKIM project {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands:kim-mainpaper}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tadmor)}}}},
KIM API {\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands:id18}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Elliott)}}}}, and the specific IM codes used in
the simulations, in addition to the relevant scientific references for
the IM. The citation format for an IM is displayed on its page on
\sphinxhref{https://openkim.org}{OpenKIM} along with the corresponding BibTex
file, and is automatically added to the LAMMPS citation reminder.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Citing the IM software (KIM infrastructure and specific PM or SM codes) used in
the simulation gives credit to the researchers who developed them and enables
open source efforts like OpenKIM to function.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{kim_commands:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim} command is part of the KIM package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS is built with that package.  A requirement for the KIM package,
is the KIM API library that must be downloaded from the \sphinxhref{https://openkim.org/kim-api/}{OpenKIM website} and installed before LAMMPS is
compiled.  When installing LAMMPS from binary, the kim\sphinxhyphen{}api package is a
dependency that is automatically downloaded and installed.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim
query} command requires the \sphinxstyleemphasis{libcurl} library to be installed.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim
property} command requires \sphinxstyleemphasis{Python} 3.6 or later and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim\sphinxhyphen{}property}
python package to be installed.  See the KIM section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Packages_details::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Packages details}}}} for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Furthermore, when using \sphinxstyleemphasis{kim} command to run KIM SMs, any packages required by
the native potential being used or other commands or fixes that it invokes must
be installed.

\section{kspace\_modify command}
\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify:kspace-modify-command}}\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kspace\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{collective} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/adjust} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{diff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{disp/auto} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fftbench} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/kspace} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/real} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald/disp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kmax/ewald} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mix/disp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{order/disp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{order} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{scafacos} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{slab} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{splittol} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wire}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{collective} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/adjust} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{diff} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{ad} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ik} = 2 or 4 FFTs for PPPM in smoothed or non\sphinxhyphen{}smoothed mode
\sphinxstyleemphasis{disp/auto} value = yes or no
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fftbench} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/real} value = accuracy (force units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/kspace} value = accuracy (force units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} value = accuracy (force units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald} value = rinv (1/distance units)
  rinv = G\sphinxhyphen{}ewald parameter for Coulombics
\sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald/disp} value = rinv (1/distance units)
  rinv = G\sphinxhyphen{}ewald parameter for dispersion
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kmax/ewald} value = kx ky kz
  kx,ky,kz = number of Ewald sum kspace vectors in each dimension
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} value = x y z
  x,y,z = grid size in each dimension for long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombics
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh/disp} value = x y z
  x,y,z = grid size in each dimension for 1/r\textasciicircum{}6 dispersion
\sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder} value = M
  M = min allowed extent of Gaussian when auto\sphinxhyphen{}adjusting to minimize grid communication
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mix/disp} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{geom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{order} value = N
  N = extent of Gaussian for PPPM or MSM mapping of charge to grid
\sphinxstyleemphasis{order/disp} value = N
  N = extent of Gaussian for PPPM mapping of dispersion term to grid
\sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = whether the grid stencil for PPPM is allowed to overlap into more than the nearest\sphinxhyphen{}neighbor processor
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure/scalar} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{scafacos} values = option value1 value2 ...
  option = \sphinxstyleemphasis{tolerance}
    value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy\_rel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{field} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{field\_rel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential\_rel}
  option = \sphinxstyleemphasis{fmm\_tuning}
    value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{1}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{slab} value = volfactor or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nozforce}
  volfactor = ratio of the total extended volume used in the
    2d approximation compared with the volume of the simulation domain
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{nozforce} turns off kspace forces in the z direction
\sphinxstyleemphasis{splittol} value = tol
  tol = relative size of two eigenvalues (see discussion below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{wire} value = volfactor (available with ELECTRODE package)
  volfactor = ratio of the total extended dimension used in the 1d
    approximation compared with the dimension of the simulation domain
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}
