\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set parameters used by the kspace solvers defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command.  Not all parameters are
relevant to all kspace styles.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{collective} keyword applies only to PPPM.  It is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} by
default, except on IBM BlueGene machines.  If this option is set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, LAMMPS will use MPI collective operations to remap data for
3d\sphinxhyphen{}FFT operations instead of the default point\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}point communication.
This is faster on IBM BlueGene machines, and may also be faster on
other machines if they have an efficient implementation of MPI
collective operations and adequate hardware.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute} keyword allows Kspace computations to be turned off,
even though a {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} is defined.  This is
not useful for running a real simulation, but can be useful for
debugging purposes or for computing only partial forces that do not
include the Kspace contribution.  You can also do this by simply not
defining a {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}}, but a Kspace\sphinxhyphen{}compatible
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} requires a kspace style to be defined.
This keyword gives you that option.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff/adjust} keyword applies only to MSM. If this option is
turned on, the Coulombic cutoff will be automatically adjusted at the
beginning of the run to give the desired estimated error. Other
cutoffs such as LJ will not be affected. If the grid is not set using
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} command, this command will also attempt to use the optimal
grid that minimizes cost using an estimate given by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:hardy1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hardy)}}}}. Note that this cost estimate is not exact, somewhat
experimental, and still may not yield the optimal parameters.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{diff} keyword specifies the differentiation scheme used by the
PPPM method to compute forces on particles given electrostatic
potentials on the PPPM mesh.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ik} approach is the default for
PPPM and is the original formulation used in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:hockney1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hockney)}}}}.  It
performs differentiation in Kspace, and uses 3 FFTs to transfer each
component of the computed fields back to real space for total of 4
FFTs per timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The analytic differentiation \sphinxstyleemphasis{ad} approach uses only 1 FFT to transfer
information back to real space for a total of 2 FFTs per timestep.  It
then performs analytic differentiation on the single quantity to
generate the 3 components of the electric field at each grid point.
This is sometimes referred to as “smoothed” PPPM.  This approach
requires a somewhat larger PPPM mesh to achieve the same accuracy as
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ik} method. Currently, only the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ik} method (default) can be
used for a triclinic simulation cell with PPPM. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ad} method is
always used for MSM.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, not all PPPM styles support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ad} option.  Support
for those PPPM variants will be added later.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{disp/auto} option controls whether the pppm/disp is allowed to
generate PPPM parameters automatically. If set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, parameters have
to be specified using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald/disp}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh/disp},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/real} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/kspace} keywords, or
the code will stop with an error message. When this option is set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, the error message will not appear and the simulation will start.
For a typical application, using the automatic parameter generation
will provide simulations that are either inaccurate or slow. Using this
option is thus not recommended. For guidelines on how to obtain good
parameters, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_dispersion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion howto}}}}
discussion.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fftbench} keyword applies only to PPPM. It is off by default. If
this option is turned on, LAMMPS will perform a short FFT benchmark
computation and report its timings, and will thus finish some seconds
later than it would if this option were off.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/real} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/kspace} keywords set the force
accuracy for the real and reciprocal space computations for the dispersion
part of pppm/disp. As shown in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:isele-holder1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Isele\sphinxhyphen{}Holder)}}}},
optimal performance and accuracy in the results is obtained when these
values are different.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} keyword overrides the relative accuracy parameter set by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command with an absolute
accuracy.  The accuracy determines the RMS error in per\sphinxhyphen{}atom forces
calculated by the long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver and is thus specified in force
units.  A negative value for the accuracy setting means to use the
relative accuracy parameter.  The accuracy setting is used in
conjunction with the pairwise cutoff to determine the number of
K\sphinxhyphen{}space vectors for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald}, the FFT grid size for style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm}, or the real space grid size for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald} keyword sets the value of the Ewald or PPPM G\sphinxhyphen{}ewald
parameter for charge as \sphinxstyleemphasis{rinv} in reciprocal distance units.  Without
this setting, LAMMPS chooses the parameter automatically as a function
of cutoff, precision, grid spacing, etc.  This means it can vary from
one simulation to the next which may not be desirable for matching a
KSpace solver to a pre\sphinxhyphen{}tabulated pairwise potential.  This setting can
also be useful if Ewald or PPPM fails to choose a good grid spacing
and G\sphinxhyphen{}ewald parameter automatically.  If the value is set to 0.0,
LAMMPS will choose the G\sphinxhyphen{}ewald parameter automatically.  MSM does not
use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald} parameter.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald/disp} keyword sets the value of the Ewald or PPPM G\sphinxhyphen{}ewald
parameter for dispersion as \sphinxstyleemphasis{rinv} in reciprocal distance units.  It
has the same meaning as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald} setting for Coulombics.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kmax/ewald} keyword sets the number of kspace vectors in each
dimension for kspace style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald}.  The three values must be positive
integers, or else (0,0,0), which unsets the option.  When this option
is not set, the Ewald sum scheme chooses its own kspace vectors,
consistent with the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified accuracy and pairwise cutoff. In
any case, if kspace style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} is invoked, the values used are
printed to the screen and the log file at the start of the run.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} keyword sets the grid size for kspace style \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{msm}.  In the case of PPPM, this is the FFT mesh, and each dimension
must be factorizable into powers of 2, 3, and 5.  In the case of MSM,
this is the finest scale real\sphinxhyphen{}space mesh, and each dimension must be
factorizable into powers of 2.  When this option is not set, the PPPM
or MSM solver chooses its own grid size, consistent with the
user\sphinxhyphen{}specified accuracy and pairwise cutoff.  Values for x,y,z of
0,0,0 unset the option.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh/disp} keyword sets the grid size for kspace style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/disp}.  This is the FFT mesh for long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion and ach
dimension must be factorizable into powers of 2, 3, and 5.  When this
option is not set, the PPPM solver chooses its own grid size,
consistent with the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified accuracy and pairwise cutoff.
Values for x,y,z of 0,0,0 unset the option.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder} keyword allows LAMMPS to reduce the \sphinxstyleemphasis{order} setting if
necessary to keep the communication of ghost grid point limited to
exchanges between nearest\sphinxhyphen{}neighbor processors.  See the discussion of
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword for details.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword is set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, which is the default, this is never needed.  If it set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
and overlap occurs, then LAMMPS will reduce the order setting, one
step at a time, until the ghost grid overlap only extends to nearest
neighbor processors.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder} keyword limits how small the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{order} setting can become.  The minimum allowed value for PPPM is 2,
which is the default.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder} is set to the same value as
\sphinxstyleemphasis{order} then no reduction is allowed, and LAMMPS will generate an
error if the grid communication is non\sphinxhyphen{}nearest\sphinxhyphen{}neighbor and \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap}
is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder} keyword is not currently supported in
MSM.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mix/disp} keyword selects the mixing rule for the dispersion
coefficients.  With \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair}, the dispersion coefficients of unlike
types are computed as indicated with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}.
With \sphinxstyleemphasis{geom}, geometric mixing is enforced on the dispersion
coefficients in the kspace coefficients. When using the arithmetic
mixing rule, this will speed\sphinxhyphen{}up the simulations but introduces some
error in the force computations, as shown in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:wennberg}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wennberg)}}}}.
With \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}, it is assumed that no mixing rule is
applicable. Splitting of the dispersion coefficients will be performed
as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:isele-holder1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Isele\sphinxhyphen{}Holder)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This splitting can be influenced with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{splittol} keywords.  Only
the eigenvalues that are larger than tol compared to the largest
eigenvalues are included. Using this keywords the original matrix of
dispersion coefficients is approximated. This leads to faster
computations, but the accuracy in the reciprocal space computations of
the dispersion part is decreased.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{order} keyword determines how many grid spacings an atom’s charge
extends when it is mapped to the grid in kspace style \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm}.
The default for this parameter is 5 for PPPM and 8 for MSM, which
means each charge spans 5 or 8 grid cells in each dimension,
respectively.  For the LAMMPS implementation of MSM, the order can
range from 4 to 10 and must be even. For PPPM, the minimum allowed
setting is 2 and the maximum allowed setting is 7.  The larger the
value of this parameter, the smaller that LAMMPS will set the grid
size, to achieve the requested accuracy.  Conversely, the smaller the
order value, the larger the grid size will be.  Note that there is an
inherent trade\sphinxhyphen{}off involved: a small grid will lower the cost of FFTs
or MSM direct sum, but a larger order parameter will increase the cost
of interpolating charge/fields to/from the grid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The PPPM order parameter may be reset by LAMMPS when it sets up the
FFT grid if the implied grid stencil extends beyond the grid cells
owned by neighboring processors.  Typically this will only occur when
small problems are run on large numbers of processors.  A warning will
be generated indicating the order parameter is being reduced to allow
LAMMPS to run the problem. Automatic adjustment of the order parameter
is not supported in MSM.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{order/disp} keyword determines how many grid spacings an atom’s
dispersion term extends when it is mapped to the grid in kspace style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/disp}.  It has the same meaning as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{order} setting for
Coulombics.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword can be used in conjunction with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder}
keyword with the PPPM styles to adjust the amount of communication
that occurs when values on the FFT grid are exchanged between
processors.  This communication is distinct from the communication
inherent in the parallel FFTs themselves, and is required because
processors interpolate charge and field values using grid point values
owned by neighboring processors (i.e. ghost point communication).  If
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} then this communication is
allowed to extend beyond nearest\sphinxhyphen{}neighbor processors, e.g. when using
lots of processors on a small problem.  If it is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} then the
communication will be limited to nearest\sphinxhyphen{}neighbor processors and the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{order} setting will be reduced if necessary, as explained by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{minorder} keyword discussion. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{overlap} keyword is always set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} in MSM.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure/scalar} keyword applies only to MSM. If this option is
turned on, only the scalar pressure (i.e. (Pxx + Pyy + Pzz)/3.0) will
be computed, which can be used, for example, to run an isotropic barostat.
Computing the full pressure tensor with MSM is expensive, and this option
provides a faster alternative. The scalar pressure is computed using a
relationship between the Coulombic energy and pressure {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:hummer}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hummer)}}}}
instead of using the virial equation. This option cannot be used to access
individual components of the pressure tensor, to compute per\sphinxhyphen{}atom virial,
or with suffix kspace/pair styles of MSM, like OMP or GPU.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{scafacos} keyword is used for settings that are passed to the
ScaFaCoS library when using {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style scafacos}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tolerance} option affects how the \sphinxstyleemphasis{accuracy} specified with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command is interpreted by ScaFaCoS.
The following values may be used:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
energy = absolute accuracy in total Coulombic energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
energy\_rel = relative accuracy in total Coulombic energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
potential = absolute accuracy in total Coulombic potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
potential\_rel = relative accuracy in total Coulombic potential

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
field = absolute accuracy in electric field

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
field\_rel = relative accuracy in electric field

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values with suffix \_rel indicate the tolerance is a relative
tolerance; the other values impose an absolute tolerance on the given
quantity. Absolute tolerance in this case means, that for a given
quantity q and a given absolute tolerance of t\_a the result should
be between q\sphinxhyphen{}t\_a and q+t\_a. For a relative tolerance t\_r the relative
error should not be greater than t\_r, i.e. abs(1 \sphinxhyphen{} (result/q)) \textless{} t\_r.
As a consequence of this, the tolerance type should be checked, when
performing computations with a high absolute field / energy. E.g.
if the total energy in the system is 1000000.0 an absolute tolerance
of 1e\sphinxhyphen{}3 would mean that the result has to be between 999999.999 and
1000000.001, which would be equivalent to a relative tolerance of
1e\sphinxhyphen{}9.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy and energy\_rel values, set a tolerance based on the total
Coulombic energy of the system.  The potential and potential\_rel set a
tolerance based on the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom Coulombic energy.  The field and
field\_rel tolerance types set a tolerance based on the electric field
values computed by ScaFaCoS.  Since per\sphinxhyphen{}atom forces are derived from
the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom electric field, this effectively sets a tolerance on the
forces, similar to other LAMMPS KSpace styles, as explained on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that not all ScaFaCoS solvers support all tolerance types.
These are the allowed values for each method:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fmm = energy and energy\_rel

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
p2nfft = field (1d\sphinxhyphen{},2d\sphinxhyphen{},3d\sphinxhyphen{}periodic systems) or potential (0d\sphinxhyphen{}periodic)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
p3m = field

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ewald = field

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
direct = has no tolerance tuning

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the tolerance type is not changed, the default values for the
tolerance type are the first values in the above list, e.g. energy
is the default tolerance type for the fmm solver.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fmm\_tuning} option is only relevant when using the FMM method.
It activates (value=1) or deactivates (value=0) an internal tuning
mechanism for the FMM solver.  The tuning operation runs sequentially
and can be very time\sphinxhyphen{}consuming.  Usually it is not needed for systems
with a homogeneous charge distribution. The default for this option is
therefore \sphinxstyleemphasis{0}. The FMM internal tuning is performed once, when the
solver is set up.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{slab} keyword allows an Ewald or PPPM solver to be used for a
systems that are periodic in x,y but non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic in z \sphinxhyphen{} a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} setting of “boundary p p f”.  This is done
by treating the system as if it were periodic in z, but inserting
empty volume between atom slabs and removing dipole inter\sphinxhyphen{}slab
interactions so that slab\sphinxhyphen{}slab interactions are effectively turned
off.  The volfactor value sets the ratio of the extended dimension in
z divided by the actual dimension in z.  It must be a value \textgreater{}= 1.0.  A
value of 1.0 (the default) means the slab approximation is not used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The recommended value for volfactor is 3.0.  A larger value is
inefficient; a smaller value introduces unwanted slab\sphinxhyphen{}slab
interactions.  The use of fixed boundaries in z means that the user
must prevent particle migration beyond the initial z\sphinxhyphen{}bounds, typically
by providing a wall\sphinxhyphen{}style fix.  The methodology behind the \sphinxstyleemphasis{slab}
option is explained in the paper by {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:yeh}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Yeh)}}}}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{slab}
option is also extended to non\sphinxhyphen{}neutral systems {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:ballenegger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ballenegger)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An alternative slab option can be invoked with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nozforce} keyword
in lieu of the volfactor.  This turns off all kspace forces in the z
direction.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nozforce} option is not supported by MSM. For MSM,
any combination of periodic, non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic, or shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped
boundaries can be set using {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} (the slab
approximation in not needed).  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{slab} keyword is not currently
supported by Ewald or PPPM when using a triclinic simulation cell. The
slab correction has also been extended to point dipole interactions
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:klapp}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Klapp)}}}} in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/disp}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/dipole}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/dipole}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you wish to apply an electric field in the Z\sphinxhyphen{}direction, in
conjunction with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{slab} keyword, you should do it by adding
explicit charged particles to the +/\sphinxhyphen{} Z surfaces.  If you do it via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_efield::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix efield}}}} command, it will not give the correct
dielectric constant due to the Yeh/Berkowitz {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:yeh}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Yeh)}}}} correction
not being compatible with how {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_efield::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix efield}}}} works.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/real} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/kspace} keywords set the force
accuracy for the real and reciprocal space computations for the dispersion
part of pppm/disp. As shown in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify:isele-holder1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Isele\sphinxhyphen{}Holder)}}}},
optimal performance and accuracy in the results is obtained when these
values are different.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{disp/auto} option controls whether the pppm/disp is allowed to
generate PPPM parameters automatically. If set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, parameters
have to be specified using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gewald/disp}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh/disp},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/real} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/disp/kspace} keywords, or the code will
stop with an error message. When this option is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, the
error message will not appear and the simulation will start.  For a
typical application, using the automatic parameter generation will
provide simulations that are either inaccurate or slow. Using this
option is thus not recommended.  For guidelines on how to obtain good
parameters, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_dispersion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto dispersion}}}} doc page.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{kspace_modify:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute = yes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff/adjust = yes (MSM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
diff = ik (PPPM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
disp/auto = no

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fftbench = no (PPPM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
force = \sphinxhyphen{}1.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
force/disp/kspace = \sphinxhyphen{}1.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
force/disp/real = \sphinxhyphen{}1.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gewald = gewald/disp = 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mesh = mesh/disp = 0 0 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
minorder = 2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mix/disp = pair

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
order = 10 (MSM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
order = order/disp = 5 (PPPM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
order = order/disp = 7 (PPPM/intel)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
overlap = yes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pressure/scalar = yes (MSM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
slab = 1.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
split = 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tol = 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}6

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For scafacos settings, the scafacos tolerance option depends on the
method chosen, as documented above.  The scafacos fmm\_tuning default
= 0.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{kspace_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver for LAMMPS to use each timestep to compute
long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interactions or long\sphinxhyphen{}range \(1/r^6\) interactions.
Most of the long\sphinxhyphen{}range solvers perform their computation in K\sphinxhyphen{}space,
hence the name of this command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When such a solver is used in conjunction with an appropriate pair
style, the cutoff for Coulombic or \(1/r^N\) interactions is effectively
infinite.  If the Coulombic case, this means each charge in the system
interacts with charges in an infinite array of periodic images of the
simulation domain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that using a long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver requires use of a matching {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}} to perform consistent short\sphinxhyphen{}range pairwise
calculations.  This means that the name of the pair style contains a
matching keyword to the name of the KSpace style, as in this table:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
KSpace style
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
coul/long
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
ewald or pppm
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
coul/msm
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
msm
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
lj/long or buck/long
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
disp (for dispersion)
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
tip4p/long
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
tip4p
\\
\sphinxhline
\sphinxAtStartPar
dipole/long
&
\sphinxAtStartPar
dipole
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} style performs a standard Ewald summation as described in
any solid\sphinxhyphen{}state physics text.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/disp} style adds a long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion sum option for
\(1/r^6\) potentials and is useful for simulation of interfaces
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:veld}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Veld)}}}}.  It also performs standard Coulombic Ewald summations,
but in a more efficient manner than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} style.  The \(1/r^6\)
capability means that Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones or Buckingham potentials can be
used without a cutoff, i.e. they become full long\sphinxhyphen{}range potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/disp/dipole} style can also be used with point\sphinxhyphen{}dipoles, see
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:toukmaji}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Toukmaji)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/dipole} style adds long\sphinxhyphen{}range standard Ewald summations
for dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:toukmaji}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Toukmaji)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/dipole/spin} style adds long\sphinxhyphen{}range standard Ewald
summations for magnetic dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions between
magnetic spins.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} style invokes a particle\sphinxhyphen{}particle particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh solver
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:hockney}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hockney)}}}} which maps atom charge to a 3d mesh, uses 3d FFTs
to solve Poisson’s equation on the mesh, then interpolates electric
fields on the mesh points back to the atoms.  It is closely related to
the particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh Ewald technique (PME) {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:darden}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Darden)}}}} used in
AMBER and CHARMM.  The cost of traditional Ewald summation scales as
\(N^{\frac{3}{2}}\) where \(N\) is the number of atoms in the system.  The PPPM solver
scales as \(N \log{N}\) due to the FFTs, so it is almost always a faster
choice {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:pollock}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Pollock)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/cg} style is identical to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} style except that it
has an optimization for systems where most particles are uncharged.
Similarly the \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm/cg} style implements the same optimization for \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm}.
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{smallq} argument defines the cutoff for the absolute
charge value which determines whether a particle is considered charged
or not.  Its default value is 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}5.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/dipole} style invokes a particle\sphinxhyphen{}particle particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh solver
for dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions, following the method of {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:cerda2008}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Cerda)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/dipole/spin} style invokes a particle\sphinxhyphen{}particle particle\sphinxhyphen{}mesh solver
for magnetic dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions between magnetic spins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/tip4p} style is identical to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} style except that it
adds a charge at the massless fourth site in each TIP4P water molecule.
It should be used with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair styles}}}} with a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tip4p/long} in their style name.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/stagger} style performs calculations using two different
meshes, one shifted slightly with respect to the other.  This can
reduce force aliasing errors and increase the accuracy of the method
for a given mesh size.  Or a coarser mesh can be used for the same
target accuracy, which saves CPU time.  However, there is a trade\sphinxhyphen{}off
since FFTs on two meshes are now performed which increases the
computation required.  See {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:cerutti}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Cerutti)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:neelov}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Neelov)}}}},
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:hockney}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hockney)}}}} for details of the method.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For high relative accuracy, using staggered PPPM allows the mesh size
to be reduced by a factor of 2 in each dimension as compared to
regular PPPM (for the same target accuracy).  This can give up to a 4x
speedup in the KSpace time (8x less mesh points, 2x more expensive).
However, for low relative accuracy, the staggered PPPM mesh size may
be essentially the same as for regular PPPM, which means the method
will be up to 2x slower in the KSpace time (simply 2x more expensive).
For more details and timings, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_tips::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Speed tips}}}} doc
page.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/stagger} may not give the same increase in the
accuracy of energy and pressure as it does in forces, so some caution
must be used if energy and/or pressure are quantities of interest,
such as when using a barostat.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/disp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/disp/tip4p} styles add a mesh\sphinxhyphen{}based long\sphinxhyphen{}range
dispersion sum option for 1/r\textasciicircum{}6 potentials {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:isele-holder2012}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Isele\sphinxhyphen{}Holder)}}}},
similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/disp} style. The 1/r\textasciicircum{}6 capability means
that Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones or Buckingham potentials can be used without a cutoff,
i.e. they become full long\sphinxhyphen{}range potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For these styles, you will possibly want to adjust the default choice
of parameters by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}} command.
This can be done by either choosing the Ewald and grid parameters, or
by specifying separate accuracies for the real and kspace
calculations. When not making any settings, the simulation will stop
with an error message. Further information on the influence of the
parameters and how to choose them is described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:isele-holder2012}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Isele\sphinxhyphen{}Holder)}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:isele-holder2013}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Isele\sphinxhyphen{}Holder2)}}}} and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_dispersion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto dispersion}}}} doc page.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the PPPM styles can be used with single\sphinxhyphen{}precision FFTs by
using the compiler switch \sphinxhyphen{}DFFT\_SINGLE for the FFT\_INC setting in your
low\sphinxhyphen{}level Makefile.  This setting also changes some of the PPPM
operations (e.g. mapping charge to mesh and interpolating electric
fields to particles) to be performed in single precision.  This option
can speed\sphinxhyphen{}up long\sphinxhyphen{}range calculations, particularly in parallel or on
GPUs.  The use of the \sphinxhyphen{}DFFT\_SINGLE flag is discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build settings}}}} doc page. MSM does not currently support
the \sphinxhyphen{}DFFT\_SINGLE compiler switch.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode} styles add methods that are required for the constant potential
method implemented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix electrode/*}}}}.  The styles
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/electrode}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/electrode} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/electrode/intel} are available.
These styles do not support the \sphinxtitleref{kspace\_modify slab nozforce} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm} style invokes a multi\sphinxhyphen{}level summation method MSM solver,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:hardy2006}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hardy)}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:hardy2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hardy2)}}}}, which maps atom charge
to a 3d mesh, and uses a multi\sphinxhyphen{}level hierarchy of coarser and coarser
meshes on which direct Coulomb solvers are done.  This method does not
use FFTs and scales as \(N\). It may therefore be faster than the other
K\sphinxhyphen{}space solvers for relatively large problems when running on large
core counts. MSM can also be used for non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic boundary conditions
and for mixed periodic and non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
MSM is most competitive versus Ewald and PPPM when only relatively
low accuracy forces, about 1e\sphinxhyphen{}4 relative error or less accurate,
are needed. Note that use of a larger Coulombic cutoff (i.e. 15
Angstroms instead of 10 Angstroms) provides better MSM accuracy for
both the real space and grid computed forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently calculation of the full pressure tensor in MSM is expensive.
Using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure/scalar yes}
command provides a less expensive way to compute the scalar pressure
(Pxx + Pyy + Pzz)/3.0. The scalar pressure can be used, for example,
to run an isotropic barostat. If the full pressure tensor is needed,
then calculating the pressure at every timestep or using a fixed
pressure simulation with MSM will cause the code to run slower.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{scafacos} style is a wrapper on the \sphinxhref{http://www.scafacos.de}{ScaFaCoS Coulomb solver
library} which provides a variety of solver
methods which can be used with LAMMPS.  The paper by {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:sutmann2014}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sutman)}}}} gives an overview of ScaFaCoS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
ScaFaCoS was developed by a consortium of German research facilities
with a BMBF (German Ministry of Science and Education) funded project
in 2009\sphinxhyphen{}2012. Participants of the consortium were the Universities of
Bonn, Chemnitz, Stuttgart, and Wuppertal as well as the
Forschungszentrum Juelich.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The library is available for download at “\sphinxurl{http://scafacos.de}” or can
be cloned from the git\sphinxhyphen{}repository
“\sphinxurl{https://github.com/scafacos/scafacos.git}”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to use this KSpace style, you must download and build the
ScaFaCoS library, then build LAMMPS with the SCAFACOS package
installed package which links LAMMPS to the ScaFaCoS library.
See details on {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:scafacos}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{this page}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike other KSpace solvers in LAMMPS, ScaFaCoS computes all
Coulombic interactions, both short\sphinxhyphen{} and long\sphinxhyphen{}range.  Thus you should
NOT use a Coulombic pair style when using kspace\_style scafacos.  This
also means the total Coulombic energy (short\sphinxhyphen{} and long\sphinxhyphen{}range) will be
tallied for {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}} command as part
of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{elong} keyword; the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul} keyword will be zero.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See the current restriction below about use of ScaFaCoS in
LAMMPS with molecular charged systems or the TIP4P water model.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{method} determines which ScaFaCoS algorithm is used.
These are the ScaFaCoS methods currently available from LAMMPS:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fmm} = Fast Multi\sphinxhyphen{}Pole method

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p2nfft} = FFT\sphinxhyphen{}based Coulomb solver

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} = Ewald summation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{direct} = direct O(N\textasciicircum{}2) summation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p3m} = PPPM

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
We plan to support additional ScaFaCoS solvers from LAMMPS in the
future.  For an overview of the included solvers, refer to
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:sutmann2013}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sutmann)}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{accuracy} is similar to the accuracy setting for other
LAMMPS KSpace styles, but is passed to ScaFaCoS, which can interpret
it in different ways for different methods it supports.  Within the
ScaFaCoS library the \sphinxstyleemphasis{accuracy} is treated as a tolerance level
(either absolute or relative) for the chosen quantity, where the
quantity can be either the Columic field values, the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom Columic
energy or the total Columic energy.  To select from these options, see
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify scafacos accuracy}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify scafacos}}}} command also explains
other ScaFaCoS options currently exposed to LAMMPS.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{accuracy} determines the relative RMS error in per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
forces calculated by the long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver.  It is set as a
dimensionless number, relative to the force that two unit point
charges (e.g. 2 monovalent ions) exert on each other at a distance of
1 Angstrom.  This reference value was chosen as representative of the
magnitude of electrostatic forces in atomic systems.  Thus an accuracy
value of 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}4 means that the RMS error will be a factor of 10000
smaller than the reference force.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The accuracy setting is used in conjunction with the pairwise cutoff
to determine the number of K\sphinxhyphen{}space vectors for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} or the
grid size for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that style \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} only computes the grid size at the beginning of
a simulation, so if the length or triclinic tilt of the simulation
cell increases dramatically during the course of the simulation, the
accuracy of the simulation may degrade.  Likewise, if the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify slab}}}} option is used with
shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrap boundaries in the z\sphinxhyphen{}dimension, and the box size changes
dramatically in z.  For example, for a triclinic system with all three
tilt factors set to the maximum limit, the PPPM grid should be
increased roughly by a factor of 1.5 in the y direction and 2.0 in the
z direction as compared to the same system using a cubic orthogonal
simulation cell.  One way to handle this issue if you have a long
simulation where the box size changes dramatically, is to break it
into shorter simulations (multiple {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} commands).  This
works because the grid size is re\sphinxhyphen{}computed at the beginning of each
run.  Another way to ensure the described accuracy requirement is met
is to run a short simulation at the maximum expected tilt or length,
note the required grid size, and then use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{mesh} command to manually set the
PPPM grid size to this value for the long run.  The simulation then
will be “too accurate” for some portion of the run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
RMS force errors in real space for \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} are estimated
using equation 18 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:kolafa}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kolafa)}}}}, which is also referenced as
equation 9 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:petersen}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Petersen)}}}}. RMS force errors in K\sphinxhyphen{}space for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} are estimated using equation 11 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:petersen}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Petersen)}}}},
which is similar to equation 32 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:kolafa}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kolafa)}}}}. RMS force
errors in K\sphinxhyphen{}space for \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} are estimated using equation 38 of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:deserno}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Deserno)}}}}. RMS force errors for \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm} are estimated
using ideas from chapter 3 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:hardy2006}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hardy)}}}}, with equation 3.197
of particular note. When using \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm} with non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic boundary
conditions, it is expected that the error estimation will be too
pessimistic. RMS force errors for dipoles when using \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/disp}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/dipole} are estimated using equations 33 and 46 of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:wang}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wang)}}}}. The RMS force errors for \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/dipole} are estimated
using the equations in {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style:cerda2008}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Cerda)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}} command for additional
options of the K\sphinxhyphen{}space solvers that can be set, including a \sphinxstyleemphasis{force}
option for setting an absolute RMS error in forces, as opposed to a
relative RMS error.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the GPU package, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/gpu} style performs charge assignment
and force interpolation calculations on the GPU.  These processes
are performed either in single or double precision, depending on
whether the \sphinxhyphen{}DFFT\_SINGLE setting was specified in your low\sphinxhyphen{}level
Makefile, as discussed above.  The FFTs themselves are still
calculated on the CPU.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/gpu} is used with a GPU\sphinxhyphen{}enabled
pair style, part of the PPPM calculation can be performed
concurrently on the GPU while other calculations for non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded and
bonded force calculation are performed on the CPU.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the KOKKOS package, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/kk} style performs charge
assignment and force interpolation calculations, along with the FFTs
themselves, on the GPU or (optionally) threaded on the CPU when
using OpenMP and FFTW3. The specific FFT library is selected using
the FFT\_KOKKOS CMake parameter. See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build settings}}}} doc page for how to select a
3rd\sphinxhyphen{}party FFT library.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{kspace_style:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatic solvers in LAMMPS assume conducting
metal (tinfoil) boundary conditions for both charge and dipole
interactions. Vacuum boundary conditions are not currently supported.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/disp}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm} styles support
non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal (triclinic symmetry) simulation boxes. However,
triclinic simulation cells may not yet be supported by all suffix
versions of these styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most of the base kspace styles are part of the KSPACE package.  They are
only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm/dielectric} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/dielectric} kspace styles are part of the
DIELECTRIC package. They are only enabled if LAMMPS was built with
that package \sphinxstylestrong{and} the KSPACE package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For MSM, a simulation must be 3d and one can use any combination of
periodic, non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic, but not shrink\sphinxhyphen{}wrapped boundaries (specified
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For Ewald and PPPM, a simulation must be 3d and periodic in all
dimensions.  The only exception is if the slab option is set with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}}, in which case the xy dimensions
must be periodic and the z dimension must be non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scafacos KSpace style will only be enabled if LAMMPS is built with
the SCAFACOS package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}}
doc page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The use of ScaFaCos in LAMMPS does not yet support molecular charged
systems where the short\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interactions between atoms in
the same bond/angle/dihedral are weighted by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command.  Likewise it does not
support the “TIP4P water style” where a fictitious charge site is
introduced in each water molecule.
Finally, the methods \sphinxstyleemphasis{p3m} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} do not support computing the
virial, so this contribution is not included.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{label:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Label this line of the input script with the chosen ID.  Unless a jump
command was used previously, this does nothing.  But if a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} command was used with a label argument to begin
invoking this script file, then all command lines in the script prior
to this line will be ignored.  I.e. execution of the script will begin
at this line.  This is useful for looping over a section of the input
script as discussed in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} command.

none
\end{quote}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{labelmap:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Sep2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define alphanumeric type labels to associate with one or more numeric
atom, bond, angle, dihedral or improper types.  A collection of type
labels for all atom types, bond types, etc. is stored as a label map.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The label map can also be defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
command when it reads these sections in a data file: Atom Type Labels,
Bond Type Labels, etc.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_type_labels::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto type labels}}}} doc page for a general discussion of how type
labels can be used.  See {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap:typelabel1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Gissinger)}}}} for a
discussion of the type label implementation in LAMMPS and its uses.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Valid type labels can contain any alphanumeric character, but must not
start with a number, a ‘\#’, or a ‘*’ character.  They can contain other
standard ASCII characters such as angular or square brackets ‘\textless{}’ and ‘\textgreater{}’
or ‘{[}’ and ‘{]}’, parenthesis ‘(’ and ‘)’, dash ‘\sphinxhyphen{}’, underscore ‘\_’, plus
‘+’ and equals ‘=’ signs and more.  They must not contain blanks or any
other whitespace.  Note that type labels must be put in single or double
quotation marks if they contain the ‘\#’ character or if they contain a
double (”) or single quotation mark (‘).  If the label contains both
a single and a double quotation mark, then triple quotation (“””) must
be used.  When enclosing a type label with quotation marks, the
LAMMPS input parser may require adding leading or trailing blanks
around the type label so it can identify the enclosing quotation
marks.  Those blanks will be removed when defining the label.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{labelmap} command can only modify the label map for one type\sphinxhyphen{}kind
(atom types, bond types, etc).  Any number of numeric\sphinxhyphen{}type/type\sphinxhyphen{}label
pairs may follow.  If a type label already exists for the same numeric
type, it will be overwritten.  Type labels must be unique; assigning the
same type label to multiple numeric types within the same type\sphinxhyphen{}kind is
not allowed.  When reading and writing data files, it is required that
there is a label defined for \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} numeric type within a given
type\sphinxhyphen{}kind in order to write out the type label section for that
type\sphinxhyphen{}kind.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{clear} option resets the label map and thus discards all previous
settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{write} option takes a filename as argument and writes the current
label mappings to a file as a sequence of \sphinxstyleemphasis{labelmap} commands, so the
file can be copied into a new LAMMPS input file or read in using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{include::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{include}}}} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{labelmap:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command must come after the simulation box is defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Label maps are currently not supported when using the KOKKOS package.

\section{lattice command}
\label{\detokenize{lattice:lattice-command}}\label{\detokenize{lattice:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{lattice::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{lattice:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bcc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fcc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hcp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{diamond} or         \sphinxstyleemphasis{sq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sq2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hex} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
scale = scale factor between lattice and simulation box
\begin{sphinxalltt}
scale = reduced density rho* (for LJ units)
scale = lattice constant in distance units (for all other units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{origin} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spacing} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{basis} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{origin} values = x y z
  x,y,z = fractions of a unit cell (0 \textless{}= x,y,z \textless{} 1)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} values = dim i j k
  dim = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
  i,j,k = integer lattice directions
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spacing} values = dx dy dz
  dx,dy,dz = lattice spacings in the x,y,z box directions
\sphinxstyleemphasis{a1},\sphinxstyleemphasis{a2},\sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} values = x y z
  x,y,z = primitive vector components that define unit cell
\sphinxstyleemphasis{basis} values = x y z
  x,y,z = fractional coords of a basis atom (0 \textless{}= x,y,z \textless{} 1)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general} values = no values
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hex}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.85}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{origin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orient}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orient}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.52}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                    }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{basis}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{triclinic}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{general}
\PYG{k}{lattice}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{none}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{lattice:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a lattice for use by other commands.  In LAMMPS, a lattice is
simply a set of points in space, determined by a unit cell with basis
atoms, that is replicated infinitely in all dimensions.  The arguments
of the lattice command can be used to define a wide variety of
crystallographic lattices.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A lattice is used by LAMMPS in two ways.  First, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command creates atoms on the lattice
points inside the simulation box.  Note that the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command allows different atom types
to be assigned to different basis atoms of the lattice.  Second, the
lattice spacing in the x,y,z dimensions implied by the lattice, can be
used by other commands as distance units
(e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}}), which are often convenient to use when the
underlying problem geometry is atoms on a lattice.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The lattice style must be consistent with the dimension of the
simulation \sphinxhyphen{} see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dimension}}}} command.  Styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{sc}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bcc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fcc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hcp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{diamond} are for 3d problems.  Styles
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sq2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hex} are for 2d problems.  Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} can be
used for either 2d or 3d problems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A lattice consists of a unit cell, a set of basis atoms within that
cell, and a set of transformation parameters (scale, origin, orient)
that map the unit cell into the simulation box.  The vectors a1,a2,a3
are the edge vectors of the unit cell.  This is the nomenclature for
“primitive” vectors in solid\sphinxhyphen{}state crystallography, but in LAMMPS the
unit cell they determine does not have to be a “primitive cell” of
minimum volume.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the lattice command can be used multiple times in an input
script.  Each time it is invoked, the lattice attributes are
re\sphinxhyphen{}defined and are used for all subsequent commands (that use lattice
attributes).  For example, a sequence of lattice,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} commands
can be repeated multiple times to build a poly\sphinxhyphen{}crystalline model with
different geometric regions populated with atoms in different lattice
orientations.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
A lattice of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} does not define a unit cell and basis set,
so it cannot be used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}}
command.  However it does define a lattice spacing via the specified
scale parameter.  As explained above the lattice spacings in x,y,z can
be used by other commands as distance units.  No additional
keyword/value pairs can be specified for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} style.  By
default, a “lattice none 1.0” is defined, which means the lattice
spacing is the same as one distance unit, as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lattices of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{sc}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fcc}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bcc}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{diamond} are 3d lattices
that define a cubic unit cell with edge length = 1.0.  This means a1 =
1 0 0, a2 = 0 1 0, and a3 = 0 0 1.  Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hcp} has a1 = 1 0 0, a2 = 0
sqrt(3) 0, and a3 = 0 0 sqrt(8/3).  The placement of the basis atoms
within the unit cell are described in any solid\sphinxhyphen{}state physics text.  A
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sc} lattice has 1 basis atom at the lower\sphinxhyphen{}left\sphinxhyphen{}bottom corner of the
cube.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{bcc} lattice has 2 basis atoms, one at the corner and one at
the center of the cube.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{fcc} lattice has 4 basis atoms, one at the
corner and 3 at the cube face centers.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{hcp} lattice has 4 basis
atoms, two in the z = 0 plane and 2 in the z = 0.5 plane.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{diamond}
lattice has 8 basis atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lattices of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{sq} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{sq2} are 2d lattices that define a square
unit cell with edge length = 1.0.  This means a1 = 1 0 0 and a2 = 0 1
0.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{sq} lattice has 1 basis atom at the lower\sphinxhyphen{}left corner of the
square.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{sq2} lattice has 2 basis atoms, one at the corner and one
at the center of the square.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{hex} style is also a 2d lattice, but
the unit cell is rectangular, with a1 = 1 0 0 and a2 = 0 sqrt(3) 0.
It has 2 basis atoms, one at the corner and one at the center of the
rectangle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A lattice of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} allows you to specify a1, a2, a3, and a
list of basis atoms to put in the unit cell.  By default, a1 and a2
and a3 are 3 orthogonal unit vectors (edges of a unit cube).  But you
can specify them to be of any length and non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal to each other,
so that they describe a tilted parallelepiped.  Via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{basis}
keyword you add atoms, one at a time, to the unit cell.  Its arguments
are fractional coordinates (0.0 \textless{}= x,y,z \textless{} 1.0).  For 2d simulations,
the fractional z coordinate for any basis atom must be 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The position vector x of a basis atom within the unit cell is a linear
combination of the unit cell’s 3 edge vectors, i.e. x = bx a1 + by
a2 + bz a3, where bx,by,bz are the 3 values specified for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{basis}
keyword.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This subsection discusses the arguments that determine how the
idealized unit cell is transformed into a lattice of points within the
simulation box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} argument determines how the size of the unit cell will be
scaled when mapping it into the simulation box.  I.e. it determines a
multiplicative factor to apply to the unit cell, to convert it to a
lattice of the desired size and distance units in the simulation box.
The meaning of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} argument depends on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}
being used in your simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all unit styles except \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj}, the scale argument is specified in
the distance units defined by the unit style.  For example, in \sphinxstyleemphasis{real}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units, if the unit cell is a unit cube with edge length
1.0, specifying scale = 3.52 would create a cubic lattice with a
spacing of 3.52 Angstroms.  In \sphinxstyleemphasis{cgs} units, the spacing would be 3.52
cm.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For unit style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj}, the scale argument is the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones reduced
density, typically written as rho*.  LAMMPS converts this value into
the multiplicative factor via the formula “factor\textasciicircum{}dim = rho/rho*”,
where rho = N/V with V = the volume of the lattice unit cell and N =
the number of basis atoms in the unit cell (described below), and dim
= 2 or 3 for the dimensionality of the simulation.  Effectively, this
means that if LJ particles of size sigma = 1.0 are used in the
simulation, the lattice of particles will be at the desired reduced
density.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{origin} option specifies how the unit cell will be shifted or
translated when mapping it into the simulation box.  The x,y,z values
are fractional values (0.0 \textless{}= x,y,z \textless{} 1.0) meaning shift the lattice
by a fraction of the lattice spacing in each dimension.  The meaning
of “lattice spacing” is discussed below.  For 2d simulations, the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{origin} z value must be 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} option specifies how the unit cell will be rotated when
mapping it into the simulation box.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dim} argument is one of the
3 coordinate axes in the simulation box.  The other 3 arguments are
the crystallographic direction in the lattice that you want to orient
along that axis, specified as integers.  E.g. “orient x 2 1 0” means
the x\sphinxhyphen{}axis in the simulation box will be the {[}210{]} lattice direction,
and similarly for y and z.  The 3 lattice directions you specify do
not have to be unit vectors, but they must be mutually orthogonal and
obey the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand rule, i.e. (X cross Y) points in the Z direction.
For 2d simulations, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} x and y vectors must define 0 for
their 3rd component.  Similarly the \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} z vector must define 0
for its 1st and 2nd components.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The preceding paragraph describing lattice directions is only
valid for orthogonal cubic unit cells (or square in 2d).  If you are
using a \sphinxstyleemphasis{hcp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hex} lattice or the more general lattice style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} with non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal a1,a2,a3 vectors, then you should think
of the 3 \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} vectors as creating a 3x3 rotation matrix which is
applied to a1,a2,a3 to rotate the original unit cell to a new
orientation in the simulation box.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general} option specifies that the defined lattice is
for use with a general triclinic simulation box, as opposed to an
orthogonal or restricted triclinic box.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} doc page explains all 3 kinds of simulation boxes
LAMMPS supports.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If this option is specified, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} lattice style must be used.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} vectors should define the edge vectors of a
single unit cell of the lattice with one or more basis atoms.  They
edge vectors can be arbitrary so long as they are non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, distinct,
and not co\sphinxhyphen{}planar.  In addition, they must define a right\sphinxhyphen{}handed
system, such that (\sphinxstyleemphasis{a1} cross \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2}) points in the direction of \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3}.
Note that a left\sphinxhyphen{}handed system can be converted to a right\sphinxhyphen{}handed
system by simply swapping the order of any pair of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} vectors.  For 2d simulations, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} vector must be specified
as (0.0,0.0,1.0), which is its default value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If this option is used, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{origin} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} settings must have
their default values.  Namely (0.0,0.0,0.0) for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{origin} and
(100), (010), (001) for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} vectors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command can be used to create a
general triclinic box that replicates the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} unit cell
vectors in each direction to create the 3 arbitrary edge vectors of
the overall simulation box.  It requires a lattice with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general} option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Likewise, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command can be used
to add atoms (or molecules) to a general triclinic box which lie on
the lattice points defined by \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} and the unit cell basis
atoms.  To do this, it also requires a lattice with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general} option.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS allows specification of general triclinic lattices and
simulation boxes as a convenience for users who may be converting
data from solid\sphinxhyphen{}state crystallographic representations or from DFT
codes for input to LAMMPS.  However, as explained on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc page, internally,
LAMMPS only uses restricted triclinic simulation boxes.  This means
the box and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom information (e.g. coordinates, velocities)
defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} commands are converted from
general to restricted triclinic form when the two commands are
invoked.  It also means that any other commands which use lattice
spacings from this command (e.g. the region command), will be
operating on a restricted triclinic simulation box, even if the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general} option was used to define the lattice.  See the
next section for details.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Several LAMMPS commands have the option to use distance units that are
inferred from “lattice spacings” in the x,y,z box directions.
E.g. the {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} command can create a block of size
10x20x20, where 10 means 10 lattice spacings in the x direction.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Though they are called lattice spacings, all the commands that
have a “units lattice” option, simply use the 3 values as scale
factors on the distance units defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}
command.  Thus if you do not like the lattice spacings computed by
LAMMPS (e.g. for a non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal or rotated unit cell), you can
define the 3 values to be whatever you wish, via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spacing} option.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spacing} option is not specified, the lattice spacings are
computed by LAMMPS in the following way.  A unit cell of the lattice
is mapped into the simulation box (scaled and rotated), so that it now
has (perhaps) a modified size and orientation.  The lattice spacing in
X is defined as the difference between the min/max extent of the x
coordinates of the 8 corner points of the modified unit cell (4 in
2d).  Similarly, the Y and Z lattice spacings are defined as the
difference in the min/max of the y and z coordinates.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general} option is specified, the unit cell
defined by \sphinxstyleemphasis{a1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a3} edge vectors is first converted to a
restricted triclinic orientation, which is a rotation operation.
The min/max extent of the 8 corner points is then determined, as
described in the preceding paragraph, to set the lattice
spacings. As explained for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{triclinic/general} option above,
this is because any use of the lattice spacings by other commands
will be for a restricted triclinic simulation box, not a general
triclinic box.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if the unit cell is orthogonal with axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned edges (no
rotation via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} keyword), then the lattice spacings in each
dimension are simply the scale factor (described above) multiplied by
the length of a1,a2,a3.  Thus a \sphinxstyleemphasis{hex} style lattice with a scale
factor of 3.0 Angstroms, would have a lattice spacing of 3.0 in x and
3*sqrt(3.0) in y.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal unit cells and/or when a rotation is applied
via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{orient} keyword, then the lattice spacings computed by LAMMPS
are typically less intuitive.  In particular, in these cases, there is
no guarantee that a particular lattice spacing is an integer multiple
of the periodicity of the lattice in that direction.  Thus, if you
create an orthogonal periodic simulation box whose size in a dimension
is a multiple of the lattice spacing, and then fill it with atoms via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command, you will NOT necessarily
create a periodic system.  I.e. atoms may overlap incorrectly at the
faces of the simulation box.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{spacing} option sets the 3 lattice spacings directly.  All must
be non\sphinxhyphen{}zero (use 1.0 for dz in a 2d simulation).  The specified values
are multiplied by the multiplicative factor described above that is
associated with the scale factor.  Thus a spacing of 1.0 means one
unit cell edge length independent of the scale factor.  As mentioned
above, this option can be useful if the spacings LAMMPS computes are
inconvenient to use in subsequent commands, which can be the case for
non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal or rotated lattices.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that whenever the lattice command is used, the values of the
lattice spacings LAMMPS calculates are printed out.  Thus their effect
in commands that use the spacings should be decipherable.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Example commands for generating a Wurtzite crystal.
The lattice constants approximate those of CdSe.
The \(\sqrt{3}\times 1\) orthorhombic supercell is used
with the x, y, and z directions oriented
along \([\bar{1}\bar{2}30]\),
\([10\bar{1}0]\), and \([0001]\), respectively.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{4.34}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}a}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{sqrt}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{3.0}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{c}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}a}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{sqrt}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{8.0/3.0}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
