\section{minimize command}
\label{\detokenize{minimize:minimize-command}}\label{\detokenize{minimize:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{minimize:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{minimize::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variant: minimize/kk


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{minimize:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{minimize}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ftol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{maxiter}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{maxeval}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
etol = stopping tolerance for energy (unitless)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ftol = stopping tolerance for force (force units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
maxiter = max iterations of minimizer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
maxeval = max number of force/energy evaluations

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{minimize:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{minimize}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{minimize}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100000}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{minimize:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform an energy minimization of the system, by iteratively adjusting
atom coordinates.  Iterations are terminated when one of the stopping
criteria is satisfied.  At that point the configuration will hopefully
be in a local potential energy minimum.  More precisely, the
configuration should approximate a critical point for the objective
function (see below), which may or may not be a local minimum.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimization algorithm used is set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}} command.  Other options are set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_modify}}}} command.  Minimize commands can be interspersed with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} commands to alternate between relaxation and dynamics.
The minimizers bound the distance atoms may move in one iteration, so
that you can relax systems with highly overlapped atoms (large energies
and forces) by pushing the atoms off of each other.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Neighbor list update settings}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The distance that atoms can move during individual minimization steps
can be quite large, especially at the beginning of a minimization.
Thus {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor list settings}}}} of \sphinxstyleemphasis{every = 1} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{delay = 0} are \sphinxstylestrong{required}.  This may be combined with either
\sphinxstyleemphasis{check = no} (always update the neighbor list) or \sphinxstyleemphasis{check = yes} (only
update the neighbor list if at least one atom has moved more than
half the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor list skin}}}} distance since the last
reneighboring).  Using \sphinxstyleemphasis{check = yes} is recommended since it avoids
unneeded reneighboring steps when the system is closer to the minimum
and thus atoms move only small distances.  Using \sphinxstyleemphasis{check = no} may be
required for debugging or when coupling LAMMPS with external codes
that require a predictable sequence of neighbor list updates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the settings are \sphinxstylestrong{not} \sphinxstyleemphasis{every = 1} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay = 0}, LAMMPS will
temporarily apply a {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify every 1 delay 0 check yes}}}} setting during the minimization and restore the
original setting at the end of the minimization.  A corresponding
message will be printed to the screen and log file, if this happens.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternate means of relaxing a system are to run dynamics with a small or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_limit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{limited timestep}}}}.  Or dynamics can be run using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscous::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscous}}}} to impose a damping force that slowly
drains all kinetic energy from the system.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style soft}}}} potential can be used to un\sphinxhyphen{}overlap atoms while running
dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that you can minimize some atoms in the system while holding the
coordinates of other atoms fixed by applying {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce 0.0 0.0
0.0}}}} to the other atoms.  See a more detailed discussion
of {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize:fix-minimize}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{using fixes while minimizing below}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimization styles}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{cg}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{sd}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hftn}
involves an outer iteration loop which sets the search direction along
which atom coordinates are changed.  An inner iteration is then
performed using a line search algorithm.  The line search typically
evaluates forces and energies several times to set new coordinates.
Currently, a backtracking algorithm is used which may not be optimal
in terms of the number of force evaluations performed, but appears to
be more robust than previous line searches we have tried.  The
backtracking method is described in Nocedal and Wright’s Numerical
Optimization (Procedure 3.1 on p 41).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimization styles}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{quickmin}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fire} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fire/old} perform damped dynamics using an Euler integration step.  Thus
they require a {\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} be defined.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The damped dynamic minimizer algorithms will use the timestep you
have defined via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} command or its
default value.  Often they will converge more quickly if you use a
timestep about 10x larger than you would normally use for regular
molecular dynamics simulations.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
In all cases, the objective function being minimized is the total
potential energy of the system as a function of the N atom
coordinates:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(r_1,r_2, \ldots ,r_N)  = & \sum_{i,j} E_{\it pair}(r_i,r_j) +
                             \sum_{ij} E_{\it bond}(r_i,r_j) +
                             \sum_{ijk} E_{\it angle}(r_i,r_j,r_k) + \\
                           & \sum_{ijkl} E_{\it dihedral}(r_i,r_j,r_k,r_l) +
                             \sum_{ijkl} E_{\it improper}(r_i,r_j,r_k,r_l) +
                             \sum_i E_{\it fix}(r_i)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the first term is the sum of all non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pairwise
interactions}}}} including {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic
interactions}}}}, the second through fifth terms are {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper}}}} interactions
respectively, and the last term is energy due to {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}
which can act as constraints or apply force to atoms, such as through
interaction with a wall.  See the discussion below about how fix
commands affect minimization.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The starting point for the minimization is the current configuration
of the atoms.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimization procedure stops if any of several criteria are met:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the change in energy between outer iterations is less than \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the 2\sphinxhyphen{}norm (length) of the global force vector is less than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the line search fails because the step distance backtracks to 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the number of outer iterations or timesteps exceeds \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxiter}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the number of total force evaluations exceeds \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxeval}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimization style}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/cg}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/lbfgs} replace
the force tolerance \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} by a torque tolerance.
The minimization procedure stops if the 2\sphinxhyphen{}norm (length) of the torque vector on atom
(defined as the cross product between the
atomic spin and its precession vectors omega) is less than \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol},
or if any of the other criteria are met. Torque have the same units as the energy.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_halt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix halt}}}} command to specify
a general criterion for exiting a minimization, that is a
calculation performed on the state of the current system, as
defined by an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the first criterion, the specified energy tolerance \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} is
unitless; it is met when the energy change between successive
iterations divided by the energy magnitude is less than or equal to
the tolerance.  For example, a setting of 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}4 for \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} means an
energy tolerance of one part in 10\textasciicircum{}4.  For the damped dynamics
minimizers this check is not performed for a few steps after
velocities are reset to 0, otherwise the minimizer would prematurely
converge.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the second criterion, the specified force tolerance \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} is in
force units, since it is the length of the global force vector for all
atoms, e.g. a vector of size 3N for N atoms.  Since many of the
components will be near zero after minimization, you can think of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} as an upper bound on the final force on any component of any
atom.  For example, a setting of 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}4 for \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} means no x, y, or z
component of force on any atom will be larger than 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}4 (in force
units) after minimization.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Either or both of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} values can be set to 0.0, in
which case some other criterion will terminate the minimization.

\sphinxAtStartPar
During a minimization, the outer iteration count is treated as a
timestep.  Output is triggered by this timestep, e.g. thermodynamic
output or dump and restart files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fmax} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fnorm} keywords can be useful for monitoring the progress
of the minimization.  Note that these outputs will be calculated only
from forces on the atoms, and will not include any extra degrees of
freedom, such as from the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_box_relax::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix box/relax}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following minimization, a statistical summary is printed that lists
which convergence criterion caused the minimizer to stop, as well as
information about the energy, force, final line search, and iteration
counts.  An example is as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Minimization stats:
  Stopping criterion = max iterations
  Energy initial, next\PYGZhy{}to\PYGZhy{}last, final =
       \PYGZhy{}0.626828169302     \PYGZhy{}2.82642039062     \PYGZhy{}2.82643549739
  Force two\PYGZhy{}norm initial, final = 2052.1 91.9642
  Force max component initial, final = 346.048 9.78056
  Final line search alpha, max atom move = 2.23899e\PYGZhy{}06 2.18986e\PYGZhy{}05
  Iterations, force evaluations = 2000 12724
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 3 energy values are for before and after the minimization and on
the next\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}last iteration.  This is what the \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} parameter checks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two\sphinxhyphen{}norm force values are the length of the global force vector
before and after minimization.  This is what the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} parameter
checks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The max\sphinxhyphen{}component force values are the absolute value of the largest
component (x,y,z) in the global force vector, i.e. the infinity\sphinxhyphen{}norm
of the force vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The alpha parameter for the line\sphinxhyphen{}search, when multiplied by the max
force component (on the last iteration), gives the max distance any
atom moved during the last iteration.  Alpha will be 0.0 if the line
search could not reduce the energy.  Even if alpha is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, if the
“max atom move” distance is tiny compared to typical atom coordinates,
then it is possible the last iteration effectively caused no atom
movement and thus the evaluated energy did not change and the
minimizer terminated.  Said another way, even with non\sphinxhyphen{}zero forces,
it’s possible the effect of those forces is to move atoms a distance
less than machine precision, so that the energy cannot be further
reduced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The iterations and force evaluation values are what is checked by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{maxiter} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxeval} parameters.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are several force fields in LAMMPS which have discontinuities
or other approximations which may prevent you from performing an
energy minimization to tight tolerances.  For example, you should use
a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}} that goes to 0.0 at the cutoff
distance when performing minimization (even if you later change it
when running dynamics).  If you do not do this, the total energy of
the system will have discontinuities when the relative distance
between any pair of atoms changes from cutoff \sphinxstyleemphasis{plus} epsilon to
cutoff \sphinxstyleemphasis{minus} epsilon and the minimizer may thus behave poorly.
Some of the many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials use splines and other internal
cutoffs that inherently have this problem.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{long\sphinxhyphen{}range
Coulombic styles}}}} (PPPM, Ewald) are approximate to
within the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified tolerance, which means their energy and
forces may not agree to a higher precision than the Kspace\sphinxhyphen{}specified
tolerance.  This agreement is further reduced when using tabulation
to speed up the computation of the real\sphinxhyphen{}space part of the Coulomb
interactions, which is enabled by default.  In all these cases, the
minimizer may give up and stop before finding a minimum to the
specified energy or force tolerance.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a cutoff Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential (and others) can be shifted
so that its energy is 0.0 at the cutoff via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command.  See the doc pages for individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair
styles}}}} for details.  Note that most Coulombic potentials
have a cutoff, unless versions with a long\sphinxhyphen{}range component are used
(e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/long}}}}) or some
other damping/smoothing schemes are used.  The CHARMM potentials go to
0.0 at the cutoff (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/charmm/coul/charmm}}}}), as do the GROMACS potentials (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gromacs::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style
lj/gromacs}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a soft potential ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style soft}}}}) is used the
Astop value is used for the prefactor (no time dependence).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{minimize:fix-minimize}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_box_relax::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix box/relax}}}} command can be used to apply an
external pressure to the simulation box and allow it to shrink/expand
during the minimization.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a few other fixes (typically those that add forces) are invoked
during minimization.  See the doc pages for individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}
commands to see which ones are relevant.  Current examples of fixes
that can be used include:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_addforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix addforce}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_addtorque::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix addtorque}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_efield::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix efield}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_enforce2d::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix enforce2d}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_indent::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix indent}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_lineforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix lineforce}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_planeforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix planeforce}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_spring::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix spring}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_spring_self::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix spring/self}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscous::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscous}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/region}}}}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some fixes which are invoked during minimization have an
associated potential energy.  For that energy to be included in the
total potential energy of the system (the quantity being minimized),
you MUST enable the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} option for
that fix.  The doc pages for individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} commands
specify if this should be done.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimizers in LAMMPS do not allow for bonds (or angles, etc)
to be held fixed while atom coordinates are being relaxed, e.g. via
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  See more
info in the Restrictions section below.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{minimize:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Features that are not yet implemented are listed here, in case someone
knows how they could be coded:

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is an error to use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} with minimization
because it turns off bonds that should be included in the potential
energy of the system.  The effect of a fix shake can be approximated
during a minimization by using stiff spring constants for the bonds
and/or angles that would normally be constrained by the SHAKE
algorithm.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Fix rigid}}}} is also not supported by minimization.  It
is not an error to have it defined, but the energy minimization will
not keep the defined body(s) rigid during the minimization.  Note that
if bonds, angles, etc internal to a rigid body have been turned off
(e.g. via {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}}), they will not
contribute to the potential energy which is probably not what is
desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair potentials that produce torque on a particle (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{granular potentials}}}} or the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gayberne::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{GayBerne potential}}}} for ellipsoidal particles) are not
relaxed by a minimization.  More specifically, radial relaxations are
induced, but no rotations are induced by a minimization, so such a
system will not fully relax.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{minimize:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_modify}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{minimize:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{molecule@\spxentry{molecule}}\ignorespaces 

\section{molecule command}
\label{\detokenize{molecule:molecule-command}}\label{\detokenize{molecule:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{molecule::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{molecule:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fileN}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID = user\sphinxhyphen{}assigned name for the molecule template

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file1,file2,… = names of files containing molecule descriptions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended after each file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{offset} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{toff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{boff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{aoff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{doff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ioff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{offset} values = Toff Boff Aoff Doff Ioff
  Toff = offset to add to atom types
  Boff = offset to add to bond types
  Aoff = offset to add to angle types
  Doff = offset to add to dihedral types
  Ioff = offset to add to improper types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{toff} value = Toff
  Toff = offset to add to atom types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{boff} value = Boff
  Boff = offset to add to bond types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{aoff} value = Aoff
  Aoff = offset to add to angle types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{doff} value = Doff
  Doff = offset to add to dihedral types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ioff} value = Ioff
  Ioff = offset to add to improper types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} value = sfactor
  sfactor = scale factor to apply to the size and mass of the molecule
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{molecule:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mymol.txt}
\PYG{k}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{co2.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{h2o.txt}
\PYG{k}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CO2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{co2.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{boff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{aoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mymol.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{offset}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{18}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{23}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{14}
\PYG{k}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{objects}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{molecule:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a molecule template that can be used as part of other LAMMPS
commands, typically to define a collection of particles as a bonded
molecule or a rigid body.  Commands that currently use molecule
templates include:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gcmc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gcmc}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style template}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID of a molecule template can only contain alphanumeric characters
and underscores.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A single template can contain multiple molecules, listed one per file.
Some of the commands listed above currently use only the first
molecule in the template, and will issue a warning if the template
contains multiple molecules.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style template}}}} command allows multiple\sphinxhyphen{}molecule templates to define a
system with more than one templated molecule.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each filename can be followed by optional keywords which are applied
only to the molecule in the file as used in this template.  This is to
make it easy to use the same molecule file in different molecule
templates or in different simulations.  You can specify the same file
multiple times with different optional keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{offset}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{toff}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{boff}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{aoff}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{doff}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ioff} keywords
add the specified offset values to the atom types, bond types, angle
types, dihedral types, and/or improper types as they are read from the
molecule file.  E.g. if \sphinxstyleemphasis{toff} = 2, and the file uses atom types
1,2,3, then each created molecule will have atom types 3,4,5.  For the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{offset} keyword, all five offset values must be specified, but
individual values will be ignored if the molecule template does not
use that attribute (e.g. no bonds).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Offsets are \sphinxstylestrong{ignored} on lines using type labels, as the type
labels will determine the actual types directly depending on the
current {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} settings.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} keyword scales the size of the molecule.  This can be
useful for modeling polydisperse granular rigid bodies.  The scale
factor is applied to each of these properties in the molecule file, if
they are defined: the individual particle coordinates (Coords
section), the individual mass of each particle (Masses section), the
individual diameters of each particle (Diameters section), the total
mass of the molecule (header keyword = mass), the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of
the molecule (header keyword = com), and the moments of inertia of the
molecule (header keyword = inertia).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The molecule command can be used to define molecules with bonds,
angles, dihedrals, impropers, or special bond lists of neighbors
within a molecular topology, so that you can later add the molecules
to your simulation, via one or more of the commands listed above.
Since this topology\sphinxhyphen{}related information requires that suitable storage
is reserved when LAMMPS creates the simulation box (e.g. when using
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command or the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command) suitable space has to be reserved
so you do not overflow those pre\sphinxhyphen{}allocated data structures when adding
molecules later.  Both the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command and
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command have “extra” options which
ensure space is allocated for storing topology info for molecules that
are added later.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Format of a molecule file}
\label{\detokenize{molecule:format-of-a-molecule-file}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of an individual molecule file looks similar but is
different than that of a data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
commands.  Here is a simple example for a TIP3P water molecule:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} Water molecule. TIP3P geometry
\PYGZsh{} header section:
3 atoms
2 bonds
1 angles

\PYGZsh{} body section:
Coords

1    0.00000  \PYGZhy{}0.06556   0.00000
2    0.75695   0.52032   0.00000
3   \PYGZhy{}0.75695   0.52032   0.00000

Types

1        1   \PYGZsh{} O
2        2   \PYGZsh{} H
3        2   \PYGZsh{} H

Charges

1       \PYGZhy{}0.834
2        0.417
3        0.417

Bonds

1   1      1      2
2   1      1      3

Angles

1   1      2      1      3
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A molecule file has a header and a body.  The header appears first.  The
first line of the header and thus of the molecule file is \sphinxstyleemphasis{always}
skipped; it typically contains a description of the file or a comment
from the software that created the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Then lines are read one line at a time.  Lines can have a trailing
comment starting with ‘\#’ that is ignored.  There \sphinxstyleemphasis{must} be at least one
blank between any valid content and the comment.  If the line is blank
(i.e. contains only white\sphinxhyphen{}space after comments are deleted), it is
skipped.  If the line contains a header keyword, the corresponding
value(s) is/are read from the line.  A line that is \sphinxstyleemphasis{not} blank and does
\sphinxstyleemphasis{not} contains a header keyword begins the body of the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The body of the file contains zero or more sections.  The first line
of a section has only a keyword.  The next line is skipped.  The
remaining lines of the section contain values.  The number of lines
depends on the section keyword as described below.  Zero or more blank
lines can be used between sections.  Sections can appear in any order,
with a few exceptions as noted below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the recognized header keywords.  Header lines can come in
any order.  The numeric value(s) are read from the beginning of the
line.  The keyword should appear at the end of the line.  All these
settings have default values, as explained below.  A line need only
appear if the value(s) are different than the default, except when
defining a \sphinxstyleemphasis{body} particle, which requires setting the number of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atoms} to 1, and setting the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inertia} in a specific section (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{mass}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{com}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{inertia}, the default is for LAMMPS to calculate
this quantity itself if needed, assuming the molecules consist of a set
of point particles or finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles (with a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero diameter)
that do \sphinxstylestrong{not} overlap.  If finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles in the molecule
\sphinxstylestrong{do} overlap, LAMMPS will not account for the overlap effects when
calculating any of these 3 quantities, so you should pre\sphinxhyphen{}compute them
yourself and list the values in the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The mass and center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass coordinates (Xc,Yc,Zc) are
self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory.  The 6 moments of inertia (ixx,iyy,izz,ixy,ixz,iyz)
should be the values consistent with the current orientation of the
rigid body around its center of mass.  The values are with respect to
the simulation box XYZ axes, not with respect to the principal axes of
the rigid body itself.  LAMMPS performs the latter calculation
internally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the allowed section keywords for the body of the file.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Coords, Types, Molecules, Fragments, Charges, Diameters, Dipoles, Masses} = atom\sphinxhyphen{}property sections

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Bonds, Angles, Dihedrals, Impropers} = molecular topology sections

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Special Bond Counts, Special Bonds} = special neighbor info

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Shake Flags, Shake Atoms, Shake Bond Types} = SHAKE info

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Body Integers, Body Doubles} = body\sphinxhyphen{}property sections

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the Types, Bonds, Angles, Dihedrals, and Impropers sections, each
atom/bond/angle/etc type can be specified either as a number (numeric
type) or as an alphanumeric type label.  The latter is only allowed if
type labels have been defined, either by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} command or in data files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command which have sections for Atom Type Labels, Bond
Type Labels, Angle Type Labels, etc.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_type_labels::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto type labels}}}} doc page for the allowed syntax of type labels
and a general discussion of how type labels can be used.
When using type labels, any values specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{offset} are ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a Bonds section is specified then the Special Bond Counts and
Special Bonds sections can also be used, if desired, to explicitly
list the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors within the molecule topology (see
details below).  This is optional since if these sections are not
included, LAMMPS will auto\sphinxhyphen{}generate this information.  Note that
LAMMPS uses this info to properly exclude or weight bonded pairwise
interactions between bonded atoms.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command for more details.  One reason to list the
special bond info explicitly is for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermalized Drude
oscillator model}}}} which treats the bonds between nuclear
cores and Drude electrons in a different manner.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Whether a section is required depends on how the molecule template
is used by other LAMMPS commands.  For example, to add a molecule
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}} command, the Coords and
Types sections are required.  To add a rigid body via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
pour}}}} command, the Bonds (Angles, etc) sections are not
required, since the molecule will be treated as a rigid body.  Some
sections are optional.  For example, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}
command can be used to add “molecules” which are clusters of
finite\sphinxhyphen{}size granular particles.  If the Diameters section is not
specified, each particle in the molecule will have a default
diameter of 1.0.  See the doc pages for LAMMPS commands that use
molecule templates for more details.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each section is listed below in alphabetic order.  The format of each
section is described including the number of lines it must contain and
rules (if any) for whether it can appear in the data file.  For per\sphinxhyphen{}
atom sections, entries should be numbered from 1 to Natoms (where
Natoms is the number of atoms in the template), indicating which atom
(or bond, etc) the entry applies to.  Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom sections need to
include a setting for every atom, but the atoms can be listed in any
order.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Coords} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID x y z

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
x,y,z = coordinate of atom

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Types} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID type

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type = atom type of atom (1\sphinxhyphen{}Natomtype, or type label)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Molecules} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID molecule\sphinxhyphen{}ID

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
molecule\sphinxhyphen{}ID = molecule ID of atom

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Fragments} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per fragment

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID a b c d …

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a,b,c,d,… = IDs of atoms in fragment

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID of a fragment can only contain alphanumeric characters and
underscores.  The atom IDs should be values from 1 to Natoms, where
Natoms = \# of atoms in the molecule.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Charges} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID q

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
q = charge on atom

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only allowed for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom styles}}}} that
support charge.  If this section is not included, the default charge
on each atom in the molecule is 0.0.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Diameters} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID diam

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
diam = diameter of atom

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only allowed for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom styles}}}} that
support finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical particles, e.g. atom\_style sphere.  If
not listed, the default diameter of each atom in the molecule is 1.0.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 7Feb2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Dipoles} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID mux muy muz

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mux,muy,muz = x\sphinxhyphen{}, y\sphinxhyphen{}, and z\sphinxhyphen{}component of point dipole vector of atom

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only allowed for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom styles}}}} that
support particles with point dipoles, e.g. atom\_style dipole.  If not
listed, the default dipole component of each atom in the molecule is set
to 0.0.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Masses} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID mass

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mass = mass of atom

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only allowed for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom styles}}}} that
support per\sphinxhyphen{}atom mass, as opposed to per\sphinxhyphen{}type mass.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{mass::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mass}}}} command for details.  If this section is not
included, the default mass for each atom is derived from its volume
(see Diameters section) and a default density of 1.0, in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} of mass/volume.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Bonds} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per bond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID type atom1 atom2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type = bond type (1\sphinxhyphen{}Nbondtype, or type label)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
atom1,atom2 = IDs of atoms in bond

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The IDs for the two atoms in each bond should be values
from 1 to Natoms, where Natoms = \# of atoms in the molecule.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Angles} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per angle

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID type atom1 atom2 atom3

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type = angle type (1\sphinxhyphen{}Nangletype, or type label)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
atom1,atom2,atom3 = IDs of atoms in angle

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The IDs for the three atoms in each angle should be values from 1 to
Natoms, where Natoms = \# of atoms in the molecule.  The three atoms are
ordered linearly within the angle.  Thus the central atom (around
which the angle is computed) is the atom2 in the list.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Dihedrals} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per dihedral

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID type atom1 atom2 atom3 atom4

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type = dihedral type (1\sphinxhyphen{}Ndihedraltype, or type label)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
atom1,atom2,atom3,atom4 = IDs of atoms in dihedral

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The IDs for the four atoms in each dihedral should be values from 1 to
Natoms, where Natoms = \# of atoms in the molecule.  The 4 atoms are
ordered linearly within the dihedral.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Impropers} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per improper

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID type atom1 atom2 atom3 atom4

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type = improper type (1\sphinxhyphen{}Nimpropertype, or type label)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
atom1,atom2,atom3,atom4 = IDs of atoms in improper

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The IDs for the four atoms in each improper should be values from 1 to
Natoms, where Natoms = \# of atoms in the molecule.  The ordering of
the 4 atoms determines the definition of the improper angle used in
the formula for the defined {\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper style}}}}.  See
the doc pages for individual styles for details.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Special Bond Counts} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID N1 N2 N3

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N1 = \# of 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 bonds

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N2 = \# of 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 bonds

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N3 = \# of 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 bonds

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
N1, N2, N3 are the number of 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors respectively of
this atom within the topology of the molecule.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} page for more discussion of
1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors.  If this section appears, the Special Bonds
section must also appear.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained above, LAMMPS will auto\sphinxhyphen{}generate this information if this
section is not specified.  If specified, this section will
override what would be auto\sphinxhyphen{}generated.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Special Bonds} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID a b c d …

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a,b,c,d,… = IDs of atoms in N1+N2+N3 special bonds

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A, b, c, d, etc are the IDs of the n1+n2+n3 atoms that are 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3,
1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors of this atom.  The IDs should be values from 1 to
Natoms, where Natoms = \# of atoms in the molecule.  The first N1
values should be the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 neighbors, the next N2 should be the 1\sphinxhyphen{}3
neighbors, the last N3 should be the 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors.  No atom ID should
appear more than once.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} doc
page for more discussion of 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors.  If this section
appears, the Special Bond Counts section must also appear.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained above, LAMMPS will auto\sphinxhyphen{}generate this information if this
section is not specified.  If specified, this section will override
what would be auto\sphinxhyphen{}generated.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Shake Flags} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID flag

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flag = 0,1,2,3,4

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only needed when molecules created using the template
will be constrained by SHAKE via the “fix shake” command.  The other
two Shake sections must also appear in the file, following this one.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The meaning of the flag for each atom is as follows.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} page for a further description of SHAKE
clusters.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
0 = not part of a SHAKE cluster

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1 = part of a SHAKE angle cluster (two bonds and the angle they form)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
2 = part of a 2\sphinxhyphen{}atom SHAKE cluster with a single bond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
3 = part of a 3\sphinxhyphen{}atom SHAKE cluster with two bonds

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
4 = part of a 4\sphinxhyphen{}atom SHAKE cluster with three bonds

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Shake Atoms} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID a b c d

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a,b,c,d = IDs of atoms in cluster

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only needed when molecules created using the template
will be constrained by SHAKE via the “fix shake” command.  The other
two Shake sections must also appear in the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The a,b,c,d values are atom IDs (from 1 to Natoms) for all the atoms
in the SHAKE cluster that this atom belongs to.  The number of values
that must appear is determined by the shake flag for the atom (see the
Shake Flags section above).  All atoms in a particular cluster should
list their a,b,c,d values identically.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 0, no a,b,c,d values are listed on the line, just the
(ignored) ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 1, a,b,c are listed, where a = ID of central atom in the
angle, and b,c the other two atoms in the angle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 2, a,b are listed, where a = ID of atom in bond with the
lowest ID, and b = ID of atom in bond with the highest ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 3, a,b,c are listed, where a = ID of central atom,
and b,c = IDs of other two atoms bonded to the central atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 4, a,b,c,d are listed, where a = ID of central atom,
and b,c,d = IDs of other three atoms bonded to the central atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} page for a further description
of SHAKE clusters.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Shake Bond Types} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: ID a b c

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a,b,c = bond types (or angle type) of bonds (or angle) in cluster

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only needed when molecules created using the template
will be constrained by SHAKE via the “fix shake” command.  The other
two Shake sections must also appear in the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The a,b,c values are bond types for all bonds in the SHAKE cluster that
this atom belongs to.  Bond types may be either numbers (from 1 to Nbondtypes)
or bond type labels as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} command
or a “Bond Type Labels” section of a data file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of values that must appear is determined by the shake flag
for the atom (see the Shake Flags section above).  All atoms in a
particular cluster should list their a,b,c values identically.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 0, no a,b,c values are listed on the line, just the
(ignored) ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 1, a,b,c are listed, where a = bondtype of the bond between
the central atom and the first non\sphinxhyphen{}central atom (value b in the Shake
Atoms section), b = bondtype of the bond between the central atom and
the second non\sphinxhyphen{}central atom (value c in the Shake Atoms section), and c
= the angle type (1 to Nangletypes, or angle type label) of the angle
between the three atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 2, only a is listed, where a = bondtype of the bond between
the two atoms in the cluster.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 3, a,b are listed, where a = bondtype of the bond between
the central atom and the first non\sphinxhyphen{}central atom (value b in the Shake
Atoms section), and b = bondtype of the bond between the central atom
and the second non\sphinxhyphen{}central atom (value c in the Shake Atoms section).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If flag = 4, a,b,c are listed, where a = bondtype of the bond between
the central atom and the first non\sphinxhyphen{}central atom (value b in the Shake
Atoms section), b = bondtype of the bond between the central atom and
the second non\sphinxhyphen{}central atom (value c in the Shake Atoms section), and c
= bondtype of the bond between the central atom and the third
non\sphinxhyphen{}central atom (value d in the Shake Atoms section).

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} page for a further description
of SHAKE clusters.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\sphinxstyleemphasis{Body Integers} section:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: N E F

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = number of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles or number or vertices

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
E,F = number of edges and faces

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only needed when the molecule is a body particle. the other
Body section must also appear in the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The total number of values that must appear is determined by the body style, and
must be equal to the Ninteger value given in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{body} header.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{nparticle} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon}, only the number of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles or
vertices N is required, and Ninteger should have a value of 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polyhedron}, the number of edges E and faces F is required, and
Ninteger should have a value of 3.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} page for a further description of
the file format.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Body Doubles} section:
\begin{itemize}

first line

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: Ixx Iyy Izz Ixy Ixz Iyz

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ixx Iyy Izz Ixy Ixz Iyz = 6 components of inertia tensor of body particle

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one line per sub\sphinxhyphen{}particle or vertex

\item {}

x, y, z = coordinates of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particle or vertex

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N1, N2, N3, N4 = vertex indices

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
line syntax: diam

diam = rounded diameter that surrounds each vertex

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section is only needed when the molecule is a body particle. the other
Body section must also appear in the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The total number of values that must appear is determined by the body style, and
must be equal to the Ndouble value given in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{body} header. The 6 moments of
inertia and the 3N coordinates of the sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles or vertices are required

For \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon}, the E = 6 + 3*N + 1 edges are automatically determined

\section{neb command}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{neb:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ftol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nevery}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
etol = stopping tolerance for energy (dimensionless)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ftol = stopping tolerance for force (force units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N1 = max \# of iterations (timesteps) to run initial NEB

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N2 = max \# of iterations (timesteps) to run barrier\sphinxhyphen{}climbing NEB

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nevery = print replica energies and reaction coordinates every this many timesteps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file\sphinxhyphen{}style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{final} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{each} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{final} arg = filename
  filename = file with initial coords for final replica
    coords for intermediate replicas are linearly interpolated
    between first and last replica
\sphinxstyleemphasis{each} arg = filename
  filename = unique filename for each replica (except first)
    with its initial coords
\sphinxstyleemphasis{none} arg = no argument all replicas assumed to already have
    their initial coords
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbosity}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verbosity} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{default} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{terse}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} = very detailed per\sphinxhyphen{}replica output
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{default} = some per\sphinxhyphen{}replica output
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{terse} = only global state output
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\PYG{k}{neb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{each}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coords.initial.}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}i}
\PYG{k}{neb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{none}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{verbose}
