\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{neb:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a nudged elastic band (NEB) calculation using multiple
replicas of a system.  Two or more replicas must be used; the first
and last are the end points of the transition path.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NEB is a method for finding both the atomic configurations and height of
the energy barrier associated with a transition state, e.g. for an atom
to perform a diffusive hop from one energy basin to another in a
coordinated fashion with its neighbors.  The implementation in LAMMPS
follows the discussion in these 4 papers: {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb:henkelmana}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(HenkelmanA)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb:henkelmanb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(HenkelmanB)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb:nakano3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nakano)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb:maras2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Maras)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each replica runs on a partition of one or more processors.  Processor
partitions are defined at run\sphinxhyphen{}time using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition
command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  Note that if you have MPI
installed, you can run a multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulation with more replicas
(partitions) than you have physical processors, e.g you can run a
10\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulation on just one or two processors.  You will simply
not get the performance speed\sphinxhyphen{}up you would see with one or more physical
processors per replica.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_replica::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto replica}}}}
doc page for further discussion.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained below, a NEB calculation performs a damped dynamics
minimization across all the replicas.  The minimizer uses whatever
timestep you have defined in your input script, via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} command.  Often NEB will converge more
quickly if you use a timestep about 10x larger than you would normally
use for dynamics simulations.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a NEB calculation is performed, it is assumed that each replica
is running the same system, though LAMMPS does not check for this.
I.e. the simulation domain, the number of atoms, the interaction
potentials, and the starting configuration when the neb command is
issued should be the same for every replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a NEB calculation each replica is connected to other replicas by
inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica nudging forces.  These forces are imposed by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix neb}}}} command, which must be used in conjunction
with the neb command.  The group used to define the fix neb command
defines the NEB atoms which are the only ones that inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica springs
are applied to.  If the group does not include all atoms, then non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB
atoms have no inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica springs and the forces they feel and their
motion is computed in the usual way due only to other atoms within
their replica.  Conceptually, the non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB atoms provide a background
force field for the NEB atoms.  They can be allowed to move during the
NEB minimization procedure (which will typically induce different
coordinates for non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB atoms in different replicas), or held fixed
using other LAMMPS commands such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}}.
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{partition::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{partition}}}} command can be used to invoke
a command on a subset of the replicas, e.g. if you wish to hold NEB or
non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB atoms fixed in only the end\sphinxhyphen{}point replicas.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The initial atomic configuration for each of the replicas can be
specified in different manners via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting, as
discussed below.  Only atoms whose initial coordinates should differ
from the current configuration need be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Conceptually, the initial and final configurations for the first
replica should be states on either side of an energy barrier.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained below, the initial configurations of intermediate
replicas can be atomic coordinates interpolated in a linear fashion
between the first and last replicas.  This is often adequate for
simple transitions.  For more complex transitions, it may lead to slow
convergence or even bad results if the minimum energy path (MEP, see
below) of states over the barrier cannot be correctly converged to
from such an initial path.  In this case, you will want to generate
initial states for the intermediate replicas that are geometrically
closer to the MEP and read them in.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{final}, a filename is specified which
contains atomic coordinates for zero or more atoms, in the format
described below.  For each atom that appears in the file, the new
coordinates are assigned to that atom in the final replica.  Each
intermediate replica also assigns a new position to that atom in an
interpolated manner.  This is done by using the current position of
the atom as the starting point and the read\sphinxhyphen{}in position as the final
point.  The distance between them is calculated, and the new position
is assigned to be a fraction of the distance.  E.g. if there are 10
replicas, the second replica will assign a position that is 10\% of the
distance along a line between the starting and final point, and the
9th replica will assign a position that is 90\% of the distance along
the line.  Note that for this procedure to produce consistent
coordinates across all the replicas, the current coordinates need to
be the same in all replicas.  LAMMPS does not check for this, but
invalid initial configurations will likely result if it is not the
case.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “distance” between the starting and final point is
calculated in a minimum\sphinxhyphen{}image sense for a periodic simulation box.
This means that if the two positions are on opposite sides of a box
(periodic in that dimension), the distance between them will be small,
because the periodic image of one of the atoms is close to the other.
Similarly, even if the assigned position resulting from the
interpolation is outside the periodic box, the atom will be wrapped
back into the box when the NEB calculation begins.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{each}, a filename is specified which is
assumed to be unique to each replica.  This can be done by using a
variable in the filename, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{part}
\PYG{k}{neb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{each}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coords.initial.}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}i}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which in this case will substitute the partition ID (0 to N\sphinxhyphen{}1) for the
variable I, which is also effectively the replica ID.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command for other options, such as using
world\sphinxhyphen{}, universe\sphinxhyphen{}, or uloop\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each replica (except the first replica) will read its file, formatted
as described below, and for any atom that appears in the file, assign
the specified coordinates to its atom.  The various files do not need
to contain the same set of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}, no filename is specified.  Each
replica is assumed to already be in its initial configuration at the
time the neb command is issued.  This allows each replica to define
its own configuration by reading a replica\sphinxhyphen{}specific data or restart or
dump file, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}}
commands.  The replica\sphinxhyphen{}specific names of these files can be specified
as in the discussion above for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{each} file\sphinxhyphen{}style.  Also see the
section below for how a NEB calculation can produce restart files, so
that a long calculation can be restarted if needed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} settings change the initial
configuration of any atom in the first replica.  The first replica
must thus be in the correct initial configuration at the time the neb
command is issued.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
A NEB calculation proceeds in two stages, each of which is a
minimization procedure, performed via damped dynamics.  To enable
this, you must first define a damped dynamics
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}}, such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{quickmin} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fire}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cg},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sd}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hftn} styles cannot be used, since they perform iterative
line searches in their inner loop, which cannot be easily synchronized
across multiple replicas.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimizer tolerances for energy and force are set by \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol}, the same as for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A non\sphinxhyphen{}zero \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} means that the NEB calculation will terminate if the
energy criterion is met by every replica.  The energies being compared
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} do not include any contribution from the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica
nudging forces, since these are non\sphinxhyphen{}conservative.  A non\sphinxhyphen{}zero \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol}
means that the NEB calculation will terminate if the force criterion
is met by every replica.  The forces being compared to \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} include
the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica nudging forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The maximum number of iterations in each stage is set by \sphinxstyleemphasis{N1} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N2}.  These are effectively timestep counts since each iteration of
damped dynamics is like a single timestep in a dynamics
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}.  During both stages, the potential energy of each
replica and its normalized distance along the reaction path (reaction
coordinate RD) will be printed to the screen and log file every
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} timesteps.  The RD is 0 and 1 for the first and last replica.
For intermediate replicas, it is the cumulative distance (normalized
by the total cumulative distance) between adjacent replicas, where
“distance” is defined as the length of the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}vector of differences in
atomic coordinates, where N is the number of NEB atoms involved in the
transition.  These outputs allow you to monitor NEB’s progress in
finding a good energy barrier.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{N1} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{N2} must both be multiples
of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the first stage of NEB, the set of replicas should converge toward
a minimum energy path (MEP) of conformational states that transition
over a barrier.  The MEP for a transition is defined as a sequence of
3N\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional states, each of which has a potential energy gradient
parallel to the MEP itself.  The configuration of highest energy along
a MEP corresponds to a saddle point.  The replica states will also be
roughly equally spaced along the MEP due to the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica nudging
force added by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix neb}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the second stage of NEB, the replica with the highest energy is
selected and the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica forces on it are converted to a force
that drives its atom coordinates to the top or saddle point of the
barrier, via the barrier\sphinxhyphen{}climbing calculation described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb:henkelmanb}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(HenkelmanB)}}}}.  As before, the other replicas rearrange
themselves along the MEP so as to be roughly equally spaced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When both stages are complete, if the NEB calculation was successful,
the configurations of the replicas should be along (close to) the MEP
and the replica with the highest energy should be an atomic
configuration at (close to) the saddle point of the transition. The
potential energies for the set of replicas represents the energy
profile of the transition along the MEP.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
A few other settings in your input script are required or advised to
perform a NEB calculation.  See the NOTE about the choice of timestep
at the beginning of this doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An atom map must be defined which it is not by default for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style atomic}}}} problems.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify map}}}} command can be used to do this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimizers in LAMMPS operate on all atoms in your system, even
non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB atoms, as defined above.  To prevent non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB atoms from moving
during the minimization, you should use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}} command to set the force on each of those
atoms to 0.0.  This is not required, and may not even be desired in
some cases, but if those atoms move too far (e.g. because the initial
state of your system was not well\sphinxhyphen{}minimized), it can cause problems
for the NEB procedure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The damped dynamics {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimizers}}}}, such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{quickmin}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fire}), adjust the position and velocity of the atoms via an
Euler integration step.  Thus you must define an appropriate
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} to use with NEB.  As mentioned above, NEB
will often converge more quickly if you use a timestep about 10x
larger than you would normally use for dynamics simulations.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Each file read by the neb command containing atomic coordinates used
to initialize one or more replicas must be formatted as follows.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file can be ASCII text or a gzipped text file (detected by a .gz
suffix).  The file can contain initial blank lines or comment lines
starting with “\#” which are ignored.  The first non\sphinxhyphen{}blank, non\sphinxhyphen{}comment
line should list N = the number of lines to follow.  The N successive
lines contain the following information:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ID1 x1 y1 z1
ID2 x2 y2 z2
...
IDN xN yN zN
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fields are the atom ID, followed by the x,y,z coordinates.  The
lines can be listed in any order.  Additional trailing information on
the line is OK, such as a comment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for a typical NEB calculation you do not need to specify
initial coordinates for very many atoms to produce differing starting
and final replicas whose intermediate replicas will converge to the
energy barrier.  Typically only new coordinates for atoms
geometrically near the barrier need be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note there is no requirement that the atoms in the file
correspond to the NEB atoms in the group defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix neb}}}} command.  Not every NEB atom need be in the file,
and non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB atoms can be listed in the file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Four kinds of output can be generated during a NEB calculation: energy
barrier statistics, thermodynamic output by each replica, dump files,
and restart files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running with multiple partitions (each of which is a replica in
this case), the print\sphinxhyphen{}out to the screen and master log.lammps file
contains a line of output, printed once every \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} timesteps.  The
amount of information printed in this line can be selected with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verbosity} keyword.  Available options are \sphinxstyleemphasis{terse}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{default}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{terse} setting, it contains the timestep, the maximum force of
a replica, the maximum force per atom (in any replica), potential
gradients in the initial, final, and climbing replicas, the forward and
backward energy barriers, the total reaction coordinate (RDT).

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{default} setting, additionally the normalized
reaction coordinate and potential energy of each replica are printed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} setting, additional per\sphinxhyphen{}replica properties are
printed: the “path angle” (pathangle), the angle between the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length
tangent vector and the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length force vector at image \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}
(angletangrad), the angle between the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length energy gradient vector
of replica \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and that of replica \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}+1 (anglegrad), the norm of the
energy gradient (gradV), the the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length force vector
(RepForce), and the maximum force component of any atom (MaxAtomForce).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “maximum force per replica” is the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length force
vector for the atoms in each replica, maximized across replicas, which
is what the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ftol} setting is checking against.  In this case, N is
all the atoms in each replica.  The “maximum force per atom” is the
maximum force component of any atom in any replica.  The potential
gradients are the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length force vector solely due to
the interaction potential i.e.  without adding in inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica
forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “reaction coordinate” (RD) for each replica is the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the
3N\sphinxhyphen{}length vector of distances between its atoms and the preceding
replica’s atoms, added to the RD of the preceding replica. The RD of
the first replica RD1 = 0.0; the RD of the final replica RDN = RDT,
the total reaction coordinate.  The normalized RDs are divided by RDT,
so that they form a monotonically increasing sequence from zero to
one. When computing RD, N only includes the atoms being operated on by
the fix neb command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forward (reverse) energy barrier is the potential energy of the
highest replica minus the energy of the first (last) replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “path angle” (pathangle) for the replica i which is the angle
between the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length vectors \((R_{i-1} - R_i)\) and
\((R_{i+1} - R_i)\) (where \(R_i\) is the atomic coordinates of
replica \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}). A “path angle” of 180 indicates that replicas \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}\sphinxhyphen{}1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}+1 are aligned.  “angletangrad” is the angle between the
3N\sphinxhyphen{}length tangent vector and the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length force vector at image
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i}. The tangent vector is calculated as in {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb:henkelmana}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(HenkelmanA)}}}} for all intermediate replicas and at R2 \sphinxhyphen{} R1 and RM \sphinxhyphen{} RM\sphinxhyphen{}1
for the first and last replica, respectively.  “anglegrad” is the angle
between the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length energy gradient vector of replica \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and that of
replica \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}+1. It is not defined for the final replica and reads nan.
gradV is the norm of the energy gradient of image \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} (\(\nabla
V\)).  ReplicaForce is the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length force vector
(including nudging forces) for replica \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}.  MaxAtomForce is the maximum
force component of any atom in replica \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a NEB calculation does not converge properly, the supplementary
information can help understanding what is going wrong. For instance
when the path angle becomes acute, the definition of tangent used in
the NEB calculation is questionable and the NEB cannot may diverge
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb:maras2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Maras)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on multiple partitions, LAMMPS produces additional log
files for each partition, e.g. log.lammps.0, log.lammps.1, etc.  For a
NEB calculation, these contain the thermodynamic output for each
replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} commands in the input script define a filename
that includes a \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}},
then one dump file (per dump command) will be created for each
replica.  At the end of the NEB calculation, the final snapshot in
each file will contain the sequence of snapshots that transition the
system over the energy barrier.  Earlier snapshots will show the
convergence of the replicas to the MEP.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Likewise, {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} filenames can be specified with a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}, to generate
restart files for each replica.  These may be useful if the NEB
calculation fails to converge properly to the MEP, and you wish to
restart the calculation from an intermediate point with altered
parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are 2 Python scripts provided in the tools/python directory,
neb\_combine.py and neb\_final.py, which are useful in analyzing output
from a NEB calculation.  Assume a NEB simulation with M replicas, and
the NEB atoms labeled with a specific atom type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neb\_combine.py script extracts atom coords for the NEB atoms from
all M dump files and creates a single dump file where each snapshot
contains the NEB atoms from all the replicas and one copy of non\sphinxhyphen{}NEB
atoms from the first replica (presumed to be identical in other
replicas).  This can be visualized/animated to see how the NEB atoms
relax as the NEB calculation proceeds.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neb\_final.py script extracts the final snapshot from each of the M
dump files to create a single dump file with M snapshots.  This can be
visualized to watch the system make its transition over the energy
barrier.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To illustrate, here are images from the final snapshot produced by the
neb\_combine.py script run on the dump files produced by the two
example input scripts in examples/neb.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.480\linewidth]{{hop1}.jpg}  \sphinxincludegraphics[width=0.480\linewidth]{{hop2}.jpg}

\index{neb/spin@\spxentry{neb/spin}}\ignorespaces 

\section{neb/spin command}
\label{\detokenize{neb_spin:neb-spin-command}}\label{\detokenize{neb_spin:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{neb_spin::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{neb_spin:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neb/spin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ttol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nevery}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
etol = stopping tolerance for energy (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ttol = stopping tolerance for torque ( units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N1 = max \# of iterations (timesteps) to run initial NEB

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N2 = max \# of iterations (timesteps) to run barrier\sphinxhyphen{}climbing NEB

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nevery = print replica energies and reaction coordinates every this many timesteps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file\sphinxhyphen{}style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{final} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{each} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{final} arg = filename
  filename = file with initial coords for final replica
    coords for intermediate replicas are linearly interpolated
    between first and last replica
\sphinxstyleemphasis{each} arg = filename
  filename = unique filename for each replica (except first)
    with its initial coords
\sphinxstyleemphasis{none} arg = no argument all replicas assumed to already have
    their initial coords
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} = print supplemental information
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{neb_spin:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neb/spin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{final}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coords.final}
\PYG{k}{neb/spin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{each}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coords.initial.}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}i}
\PYG{k}{neb/spin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{none}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{verbose}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{neb_spin:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a geodesic nudged elastic band (GNEB) calculation using multiple
replicas of a system.  Two or more replicas must be used; the first
and last are the end points of the transition path.

\sphinxAtStartPar
GNEB is a method for finding both the spin configurations and height
of the energy barrier associated with a transition state, e.g.
spins to perform a collective rotation from one energy basin to
another.
The implementation in LAMMPS follows the discussion in the
following paper: {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each replica runs on a partition of one or more processors.  Processor
partitions are defined at run\sphinxhyphen{}time using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  Note that if you have MPI installed, you
can run a multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulation with more replicas (partitions)
than you have physical processors, e.g you can run a 10\sphinxhyphen{}replica
simulation on just one or two processors.  You will simply not get the
performance speed\sphinxhyphen{}up you would see with one or more physical
processors per replica.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_replica::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto replica}}}}
doc page for further discussion.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained below, a GNEB calculation performs a
minimization across all the replicas. One of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{spin}}}}
style minimizers has to be defined in your input script.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a GNEB calculation is performed, it is assumed that each replica
is running the same system, though LAMMPS does not check for this.
I.e. the simulation domain, the number of magnetic atoms, the
interaction potentials, and the starting configuration when the neb
command is issued should be the same for every replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a GNEB calculation each replica is connected to other replicas by
inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica nudging forces.  These forces are imposed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_neb_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix neb/spin}}}} command, which must be used in conjunction
with the neb command.
The group used to define the fix neb/spin command defines the
GNEB magnetic atoms which are the only ones that inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica springs
are applied to.
If the group does not include all magnetic atoms, then non\sphinxhyphen{}GNEB
magnetic atoms have no inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica springs and the torques they feel
and their precession motion is computed in the usual way due only
to other magnetic atoms within their replica.
Conceptually, the non\sphinxhyphen{}GNEB atoms provide a background force field for
the GNEB atoms.
Their magnetic spins can be allowed to evolve during the GNEB
minimization procedure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The initial spin configuration for each of the replicas can be
specified in different manners via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting, as
discussed below.  Only atomic spins whose initial coordinates should
differ from the current configuration need to be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Conceptually, the initial and final configurations for the first
replica should be states on either side of an energy barrier.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained below, the initial configurations of intermediate
replicas can be spin coordinates interpolated in a linear fashion
between the first and last replicas.  This is often adequate for
simple transitions.  For more complex transitions, it may lead to slow
convergence or even bad results if the minimum energy path (MEP, see
below) of states over the barrier cannot be correctly converged to
from such an initial path.  In this case, you will want to generate
initial states for the intermediate replicas that are geometrically
closer to the MEP and read them in.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{final}, a filename is specified which
contains atomic and spin coordinates for zero or more atoms, in the
format described below.
For each atom that appears in the file, the new coordinates are
assigned to that atom in the final replica.  Each intermediate replica
also assigns a new spin to that atom in an interpolated manner.
This is done by using the current direction of the spin at the starting
point and the read\sphinxhyphen{}in direction as the final point.
The “angular distance” between them is calculated, and the new direction
is assigned to be a fraction of the angular distance.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “angular distance” between the starting and final point is
evaluated in the geodesic sense, as described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The angular interpolation between the starting and final point
is achieved using Rodrigues formula:
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{m}_i^{\nu} = \vec{m}_i^{I} \cos(\omega_i^{\nu})
+ (\vec{k}_i \times \vec{m}_i^{I}) \sin(\omega_i^{\nu})
+ (1.0-\cos(\omega_i^{\nu})) \vec{k}_i (\vec{k}_i\cdot
\vec{m}_i^{I})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\vec{m}_i^I\) is the initial spin configuration for
spin i, \(\omega_i^{\nu}\) is a rotation angle defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\omega_i^{\nu} = (\nu - 1) \Delta \omega_i {\rm ~~and~~} \Delta \omega_i = \frac{\omega_i}{Q-1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\nu\) the image number, Q the total number of images, and
\(\omega_i\) the total rotation between the initial and final spins.
\(\vec{k}_i\) defines a rotation axis such as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{k}_i =  \frac{\vec{m}_i^I \times \vec{m}_i^F}{\left|\vec{m}_i^I \times \vec{m}_i^F\right|}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
if the initial and final spins are not aligned.
If the initial and final spins are aligned, then their cross
product is null, and the expression above does not apply.
If they point toward the same direction, the intermediate images
conserve the same orientation.
If the initial and final spins are aligned, but point toward
opposite directions, an arbitrary rotation vector belonging to
the plane perpendicular to initial and final spins is chosen.
In this case, a warning message is displayed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{each}, a filename is specified which is
assumed to be unique to each replica.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neb}}}} documentation page for more information about this
option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}, no filename is specified.  Each
replica is assumed to already be in its initial configuration at the
time the neb command is issued.  This allows each replica to define
its own configuration by reading a replica\sphinxhyphen{}specific data or restart or
dump file, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}}
commands.  The replica\sphinxhyphen{}specific names of these files can be specified
as in the discussion above for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{each} file\sphinxhyphen{}style.  Also see the
section below for how a NEB calculation can produce restart files, so
that a long calculation can be restarted if needed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file\sphinxhyphen{}style} settings change the initial
configuration of any atom in the first replica.  The first replica
must thus be in the correct initial configuration at the time the neb
command is issued.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
A NEB calculation proceeds in two stages, each of which is a
minimization procedure.  To enable
this, you must first define a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}}, using either the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/cg}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/lbfgs} style (see
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_spin}}}} for more information).
The other styles cannot be used, since they relax the lattice
degrees of freedom instead of the spins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimizer tolerances for energy and force are set by \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ttol}, the same as for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A non\sphinxhyphen{}zero \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} means that the GNEB calculation will terminate if the
energy criterion is met by every replica.  The energies being compared
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{etol} do not include any contribution from the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica
nudging forces, since these are non\sphinxhyphen{}conservative.  A non\sphinxhyphen{}zero \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttol}
means that the GNEB calculation will terminate if the torque criterion
is met by every replica.  The torques being compared to \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttol} include
the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica nudging forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The maximum number of iterations in each stage is set by \sphinxstyleemphasis{N1} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N2}.  These are effectively timestep counts since each iteration of
damped dynamics is like a single timestep in a dynamics
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}.  During both stages, the potential energy of each
replica and its normalized distance along the reaction path (reaction
coordinate RD) will be printed to the screen and log file every
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} timesteps.  The RD is 0 and 1 for the first and last replica.
For intermediate replicas, it is the cumulative angular distance
(normalized by the total cumulative angular distance) between adjacent
replicas, where “distance” is defined as the length of the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}vector of
the geodesic distances in spin coordinates, with N the number of
GNEB spins involved (see equation (13) in {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}).
These outputs allow you to monitor NEB’s progress in
finding a good energy barrier.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{N1} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{N2} must both be multiples
of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the first stage of GNEB, the set of replicas should converge toward
a minimum energy path (MEP) of conformational states that transition
over a barrier.  The MEP for a transition is defined as a sequence of
3N\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional spin states, each of which has a potential energy
gradient parallel to the MEP itself.
The configuration of highest energy along a MEP corresponds to a saddle
point.  The replica states will also be roughly equally spaced along
the MEP due to the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica nudging force added by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix neb}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the second stage of GNEB, the replica with the highest energy is
selected and the inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica forces on it are converted to a force
that drives its spin coordinates to the top or saddle point of the
barrier, via the barrier\sphinxhyphen{}climbing calculation described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}.  As before, the other replicas rearrange
themselves along the MEP so as to be roughly equally spaced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When both stages are complete, if the GNEB calculation was successful,
the configurations of the replicas should be along (close to) the MEP
and the replica with the highest energy should be a spin
configuration at (close to) the saddle point of the transition. The
potential energies for the set of replicas represents the energy
profile of the transition along the MEP.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
An atom map must be defined which it is not by default for {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style atomic}}}} problems.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify map}}}} command can be used to do this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An initial value can be defined for the timestep. Although, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin}
minimization algorithm is an adaptive timestep methodology, so that
this timestep is likely to evolve during the calculation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The minimizers in LAMMPS operate on all spins in your system, even
non\sphinxhyphen{}GNEB atoms, as defined above.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Each file read by the neb/spin command containing spin coordinates used
to initialize one or more replicas must be formatted as follows.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file can be ASCII text or a gzipped text file (detected by a .gz
suffix).  The file can contain initial blank lines or comment lines
starting with “\#” which are ignored.  The first non\sphinxhyphen{}blank, non\sphinxhyphen{}comment
line should list N = the number of lines to follow.  The N successive
lines contain the following information:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ID1 g1 x1 y1 z1 sx1 sy1 sz1
ID2 g2 x2 y2 z2 sx2 sy2 sz2
...
IDN gN yN zN sxN syN szN
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fields are the atom ID, the norm of the associated magnetic spin,
followed by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x,y,z} coordinates and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sx,sy,sz} spin coordinates.
The lines can be listed in any order.  Additional trailing information on
the line is OK, such as a comment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for a typical GNEB calculation you do not need to specify
initial spin coordinates for very many atoms to produce differing starting
and final replicas whose intermediate replicas will converge to the
energy barrier.  Typically only new spin coordinates for atoms
geometrically near the barrier need be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note there is no requirement that the atoms in the file
correspond to the GNEB atoms in the group defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix neb}}}} command.  Not every GNEB atom need be in the file,
and non\sphinxhyphen{}GNEB atoms can be listed in the file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Four kinds of output can be generated during a GNEB calculation: energy
barrier statistics, thermodynamic output by each replica, dump files,
and restart files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running with multiple partitions (each of which is a replica in
this case), the print\sphinxhyphen{}out to the screen and master log.lammps file
contains a line of output, printed once every \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} timesteps.  It
contains the timestep, the maximum torque per replica, the maximum
torque per atom (in any replica), potential gradients in the initial,
final, and climbing replicas, the forward and backward energy
barriers, the total reaction coordinate (RDT), and the normalized
reaction coordinate and potential energy of each replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “maximum torque per replica” is the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the
3N\sphinxhyphen{}length vector given by the cross product of a spin by its
precession vector omega, in each replica, maximized across replicas,
which is what the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttol} setting is checking against.  In this case, N is
all the atoms in each replica.  The “maximum torque per atom” is the
maximum torque component of any atom in any replica.  The potential
gradients are the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the 3N\sphinxhyphen{}length magnetic precession vector
solely due to the interaction potential i.e. without adding in
inter\sphinxhyphen{}replica forces, and projected along the path tangent (as detailed
in Appendix D of {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “reaction coordinate” (RD) for each replica is the two\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the
3N\sphinxhyphen{}length vector of geodesic distances between its spins and the preceding
replica’s spins (see equation (13) of {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}), added to
the RD of the preceding replica. The RD of the first replica RD1 = 0.0;
the RD of the final replica RDN = RDT, the total reaction coordinate.
The normalized RDs are divided by RDT, so that they form a monotonically
increasing sequence from zero to one. When computing RD, N only includes
the spins being operated on by the fix neb/spin command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forward (reverse) energy barrier is the potential energy of the
highest replica minus the energy of the first (last) replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Supplementary information for all replicas can be printed out to the
screen and master log.lammps file by adding the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} keyword. This
information include the following.
The “GradVidottan” are the projections of the potential gradient for
the replica i on its tangent vector (as detailed in Appendix D of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}).
The “DNi” are the non normalized geodesic distances (see equation (13)
of {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}), between a replica i and the next replica
i+1. For the last replica, this distance is not defined and a “NAN”
value is the corresponding output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a NEB calculation does not converge properly, the supplementary
information can help understanding what is going wrong.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on multiple partitions, LAMMPS produces additional log
files for each partition, e.g. log.lammps.0, log.lammps.1, etc.  For a
GNEB calculation, these contain the thermodynamic output for each
replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} commands in the input script define a filename
that includes a \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}},
then one dump file (per dump command) will be created for each
replica.  At the end of the GNEB calculation, the final snapshot in
each file will contain the sequence of snapshots that transition the
system over the energy barrier.  Earlier snapshots will show the
convergence of the replicas to the MEP.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Likewise, {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} filenames can be specified with a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}, to generate
restart files for each replica.  These may be useful if the GNEB
calculation fails to converge properly to the MEP, and you wish to
restart the calculation from an intermediate point with altered
parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A c file script in provided in the tool/spin/interpolate\_gneb
directory, that interpolates the MEP given the information provided
by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verbose} output option (as detailed in Appendix D of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neb_spin:bessaraba}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bessarab)}}}}).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{neb_spin:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the SPIN
package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc
page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For magnetic GNEB calculations, only the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin\_none} value for the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{line} keyword can be used when minimization styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/cg} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/lbfgs} are employed.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{neb_spin:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min/spin}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_neb_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix neb/spin}}}}


\subsection{Default}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
