\index{neigh\_modify@\spxentry{neigh\_modify}}\ignorespaces 

\section{neigh\_modify command}
\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:neigh-modify-command}}\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be listed
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{check} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{once} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cluster} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{include} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{page} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{collection/type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{collection/interval}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} value = N
    N = delay building neighbor lists until this many steps since last build
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} value = M
    M = consider building neighbor lists every this many steps
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{check} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = only build if at least one atom has moved half the skin distance or more
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = always build on 1st step where \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} are conditions are satisfied
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{once} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = only build neighbor list once at start of run and never rebuild
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = rebuild neighbor list according to other settings
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{cluster} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = check bond,angle,etc neighbor list for nearby clusters
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = do not check bond,angle,etc neighbor list for nearby clusters
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{include} value = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID
    group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = only build pair neighbor lists for atoms in this group
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude} values:
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} M N
      M,N = exclude if one atom in pair is type M, other is type N (M and N may be type labels)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} group1\sphinxhyphen{}ID group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID
      group1\sphinxhyphen{}ID,group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID = exclude if one atom is in 1st group, other in 2nd
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule/intra} group\sphinxhyphen{}ID
      group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = exclude if both atoms are in the same molecule and in group
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule/inter} group\sphinxhyphen{}ID
      group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = exclude if both atoms are in different molecules and in group
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}
      delete all exclude settings
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{page} value = N
    N = number of pairs stored in a single neighbor page
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} value = N
    N = max number of neighbors of one atom
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} value = size
    size = bin size for neighbor list construction (distance units)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{collection/type} values = N arg1 ... argN
    N = number of custom collections
    arg = N separate lists of types (see below)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{collection/interval} values = N arg1 ... argN
    N = number of custom collections
    arg = N separate cutoffs for intervals (see below)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{check}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{page}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100000}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exclude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exclude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{frozen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{frozen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{check}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exclude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{residue1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chain3}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exclude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{intra}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{collection}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{2},5\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{collection}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{interval}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command sets parameters that affect the building and use of
pairwise neighbor lists.  Depending on what pair interactions and other
commands are defined, a simulation may require one or more neighbor
lists.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{every}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{check}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{once} options affect how often lists
are built as a simulation runs.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} setting means never build
new lists until at least N steps after the previous build.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{every}
setting means attempt to build lists every M steps (after the delay has
passed).  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{check} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, the lists are built on the
first step that satisfies the \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} settings.  If the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{check} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then the \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} settings
determine when a build may possibly be performed, but an actual build
only occurs if at least one atom has moved more than half the neighbor
skin distance (specified in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} command)
since the last neighbor list build.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Impact of neighbor list settings}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The choice of neighbor list settings can have a significant impact on
the (parallel) performance of LAMMPS and the correctness of the
simulation results.  Since building the neighbor lists is time
consuming, doing it less frequently can speed up a calculation.  If
the lists are rebuilt too infrequently, however, interacting pairs
may be missing and thus the resulting pairwise interactions
incorrect.  The optimal settings depend on many factors like the
properties of the simulated system (density, geometry, topology,
temperature, pressure), the force field parameters and settings, the
size of the timestep, neighbor list skin distance and more.  The
default settings are chosen to be very conservative to guarantee
correctness of the simulation.  They depend on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{check} flag
heuristics to reduce the number of neighbor list rebuilds at a minor
expense for executing the check.  Determining the correctness of a
specific choice of neighbor list settings is complicated by the fact
that a neighbor list rebuild changes the order in which pairwise
interactions are computed and thus
\sphinxhyphen{} due to the limitations of floating\sphinxhyphen{}point math \sphinxhyphen{} the trajectory.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{once} setting is yes, then the neighbor list is only built once
at the beginning of each run, and never rebuilt, except on steps when a
restart file is written, or steps when a fix forces a rebuild to occur
(e.g. fixes that create or delete atoms, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_evaporate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix evaporate}}}}).  This setting
should only be made if you are certain atoms will not move far enough
that the neighbor list should be rebuilt, e.g. running a simulation of a
cold crystal.  Note that it is not that expensive to check if neighbor
lists should be rebuilt.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the rRESPA integrator is used (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}}
command), the \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} parameters refer to the longest
(outermost) timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cluster} option does a sanity test every time neighbor lists are
built for bond, angle, dihedral, and improper interactions, to check
that each set of 2, 3, or 4 atoms is a cluster of nearby atoms.  It
does this by computing the distance between pairs of atoms in the
interaction and ensuring they are not further apart than half the
periodic box length.  If they are, an error is generated, since the
interaction would be computed between far\sphinxhyphen{}away atoms instead of their
nearby periodic images.  The only way this should happen is if the
pairwise cutoff is so short that atoms that are part of the same
interaction are not communicated as ghost atoms.  This is an unusual
model (e.g. no pair interactions at all) and the problem can be fixed
by use of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify cutoff}}}} command.  Note
that to save time, the default \sphinxstyleemphasis{cluster} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, so that this
check is not performed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{include} option limits the building of pairwise neighbor lists to
atoms in the specified group.  This can be useful for models where a
large portion of the simulation is particles that do not interact with
other particles or with each other via pairwise interactions.  The
group specified with this option must also be specified via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify first}}}} command.  Note that specifying
“all” as the group\sphinxhyphen{}ID effectively turns off the \sphinxstyleemphasis{include} option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude} option turns off pairwise interactions between certain
pairs of atoms, by not including them in the neighbor list.  These are
sample scenarios where this is useful:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
In crack simulations, pairwise interactions can be shut off between 2
slabs of atoms to effectively create a crack.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When a large collection of atoms is treated as frozen, interactions
between those atoms can be turned off to save needless
computation. E.g. Using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}} command
to freeze a wall or portion of a bio\sphinxhyphen{}molecule.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When one or more rigid bodies are specified, interactions within each
body can be turned off to save needless computation.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command for more details.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 29Aug2024: }Support for type labels was added.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude type} option turns off the pairwise interaction if one atom
is of type M and the other of type N.  M can equal N.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude
group} option turns off the interaction if one atom is in the first
group and the other is the second.  Group1\sphinxhyphen{}ID can equal group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude molecule/intra} option turns off the interaction if both atoms
are in the specified group and in the same molecule, as determined by
their molecule ID.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude molecule/inter} turns off the
interaction between pairs of atoms that have different molecule IDs and
are both in the specified group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each of the exclude options can be specified multiple times.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude type} option is the most efficient option to use; it requires
only a single check, no matter how many times it has been specified.
The other exclude options are more expensive if specified multiple
times; they require one check for each time they have been specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the exclude options only affect pairwise interactions; see
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}} command for information on
turning off bond interactions.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Excluding pairwise interactions will not work correctly when
also using a long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command.  LAMMPS will give a warning
to this effect.  This is because the short\sphinxhyphen{}range pairwise interaction
needs to subtract off a term from the total energy for pairs whose
short\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction is excluded, to compensate for how the
long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver treats the interaction.  This is done correctly for
pairwise interactions that are excluded (or weighted) via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command.  But it is not done for
interactions that are excluded via these neigh\_modify exclude options.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{page} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} options affect how memory is allocated for the
neighbor lists.  For most simulations the default settings for these
options are fine, but if a very large problem is being run or a very
long cutoff is being used, these parameters can be tuned.  The indices
of neighboring atoms are stored in “pages”, which are allocated one
after another as they fill up.  The size of each page is set by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{page} value.  A new page is allocated when the next atom’s neighbors
could potentially overflow the list.  This threshold is set by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{one} value which tells LAMMPS the maximum number of neighbor’s one
atom can have.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS can crash without an error message if the number of
neighbors for a single particle is larger than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{page} setting,
which means it is much, much larger than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} setting.  This is
because LAMMPS does not error check these limits for every pairwise
interaction (too costly), but only after all the particle’s neighbors
have been found.  This problem usually means something is very wrong
with the way you have setup your problem (particle spacing, cutoff
length, neighbor skin distance, etc).  If you really expect that many
neighbors per particle, then boost the \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{page} settings
accordingly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} option allows you to specify what size of bins will be
used in neighbor list construction to sort and find neighboring atoms.
By default, for {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor style bin}}}}, LAMMPS uses bins
that are 1/2 the size of the maximum pair cutoff.  For {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor
style multi}}}}, the bins are 1/2 the size of the collection
interaction cutoff.  Typically these are good values for minimizing the
time for neighbor list construction.  This setting overrides the
default.  If you make it too big, there is little overhead due to
looping over bins, but more atoms are checked.  If you make it too
small, the optimal number of atoms is checked, but bin overhead goes up.
If you set the binsize to 0.0, LAMMPS will use the default binsize of
1/2 the cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{collection/type} option allows you to define collections of atom
types, used by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} neighbor mode.  By grouping atom types with
similar physical size or interaction cutoff lengths, one may be able to
improve performance by reducing overhead.  You must first specify the
number of collections N to be defined followed by N lists of types.
Each list consists of a series of type ranges separated by commas. The
range can be specified as a single numeric value, or a wildcard asterisk
can be used to specify a range of values.  This takes the form “*” or
“*n” or “n*” or “m*n”.  For example, if M = the number of atom types,
then an asterisk with no numeric values means all types from 1 to M.  A
leading asterisk means all types from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all types from n to M (inclusive).  A middle asterisk
means all types from m to n (inclusive).  Note that all atom types must
be included in exactly one of the N collections.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{collection/interval} option provides a similar capability.  This
command allows a user to define collections by specifying a series of
cutoff intervals.  LAMMPS will automatically sort atoms into these
intervals based on their type\sphinxhyphen{}dependent cutoffs or their finite size.
You must first specify the number of collections N to be defined
followed by N values representing the upper cutoff of each interval.
This command is particularly useful for granular pair styles where the
interaction distance of particles depends on their radius and may not
depend on their atom type.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} setting is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, then it must be a multiple of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{every} setting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule/intra} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule/inter} exclusion options can only
be used with atom styles that define molecule IDs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{page} setting must be at least 10x larger than the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{one} setting.  This ensures neighbor pages are not mostly empty
space.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{exclude group} setting is currently not compatible with dynamic groups.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{neigh_modify:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are delay = 0, every = 1, check = yes, once = no,
cluster = no, include = all (same as no include option defined),
exclude = none, page = 100000, one = 2000, and binsize = 0.0.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{neighbor@\spxentry{neighbor}}\ignorespaces 

\section{neighbor command}
\label{\detokenize{neighbor:neighbor-command}}\label{\detokenize{neighbor:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{neighbor::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{neighbor:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neighbor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{skin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
skin = extra distance beyond force cutoff (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bin} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nsq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/old}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{neighbor:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neighbor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}
\PYG{k}{neighbor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nsq}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{neighbor:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command sets parameters that affect the building of pairwise
neighbor lists.  All atom pairs within a neighbor cutoff distance
equal to the their force cutoff plus the \sphinxstyleemphasis{skin} distance are stored in
the list.  Typically, the larger the skin distance, the less often
neighbor lists need to be built, but more pairs must be checked for
possible force interactions every timestep.  The default value for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{skin} depends on the choice of units for the simulation; see the
default values below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{skin} distance is also used to determine how often atoms migrate
to new processors if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{check} option of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} command is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}.  Atoms are
migrated (communicated) to new processors on the same timestep that
neighbor lists are re\sphinxhyphen{}built.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{style} value selects what algorithm is used to build the list.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{bin} style creates the list by binning which is an operation that
scales linearly with N/P, the number of atoms per processor where N =
total number of atoms and P = number of processors.  It is almost
always faster than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nsq} style which scales as (N/P)\textasciicircum{}2.  For
unsolvated small molecules in a non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic box, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nsq} choice can
sometimes be faster.  Either style should give the same answers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} style is a modified binning algorithm that is useful for
systems with a wide range of cutoff distances, e.g. due to different
size particles. For granular pair styles, cutoffs are set to the sum of
the maximum atomic radii for each atom type.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bin} style, the
bin size is set to 1/2 of the largest cutoff distance between any pair
of atom types and a single set of bins is defined to search over for all
atom types.  This can be inefficient if one pair of types has a very
long cutoff, but other type pairs have a much shorter cutoff. The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} style uses different sized bins for collections of different
sized particles, where “size” may mean the physical size of the particle
or its cutoff distance for interacting with other particles. Different
sets of bins are then used to construct the neighbor lists as as further
described by Shire, Hanley, and Stratford {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor:multi-shire}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Shire)}}}}
and Monti et al. {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor:multi-monti}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Monti)}}}}. This imposes some extra
setup overhead, but the searches themselves may be much faster.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For instance in a dense binary system in d\sphinxhyphen{}dimensions with a ratio of the size
of the largest to smallest collection bin \(\lambda\), the computational
costs of building a default neighbor list grows as \(\lambda^{2d}\) while
the costs for \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} grows as \(\lambda^d\), equivalent to the cost
of force evaluations, as argued in Monti et al. {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor:multi-monti}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Monti)}}}}.
In other words, the neighboring costs of \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} are expected to scale the
same as force calculations, such that its relative cost is independent of
the particle size ratio. This is not the case for the default style which
becomes substantially more expensive with increasing size ratios.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default in \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi}, each atom type defines a separate collection
of particles. For systems where two or more atom types have the same
size (either physical size or cutoff distance), the definition of
collections can be customized, which can result in less overhead and
faster performance. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} command
for how to define custom collections. Whether the collection definition
is customized or not, also see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify mode multi}}}} command for communication options that further improve
performance in a manner consistent with neighbor style multi.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An alternate style, \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/old}, sets the bin size to 1/2 of the shortest
cutoff distance and multiple sets of bins are defined to search over for
different atom types. This algorithm used to be the default \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi}
algorithm in LAMMPS but was found to be significantly slower than the new
approach. For the dense binary system, computational costs still grew as
\(\lambda^{2d}\) at large enough \(\lambda\). This is equivalent
to the default style, albeit with a smaller prefactor. For now we are
keeping the old option in case there are use cases where multi/old
outperforms the new multi style.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If there are multiple sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid/overlay pair style}}}} that cover the same atom types, but have significantly
different cutoffs, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} style does not apply.  Instead, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify neigh/trim}}}} setting applies (which is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} by default).  Please check the neighbor list summary printed at
the beginning of a calculation to verify that the desired set of
neighbor list builds is performed.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} command has additional options
that control how often neighbor lists are built and which pairs are
stored in the list.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a run is finished, counts of the number of neighbors stored in
the pairwise list and the number of times neighbor lists were built
are printed to the screen and log file.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Run output}}}} page for details.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{neighbor:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{neighbor:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{neighbor:default}}
\begin{DUlineblock}{0em}
\item[] 0.3 bin for units = lj, skin = 0.3 sigma
\item[] 2.0 bin for units = real or metal, skin = 2.0 Angstroms
\item[] 0.001 bin for units = si, skin = 0.001 meters = 1.0 mm
\item[] 0.1 bin for units = cgs, skin = 0.1 cm = 1.0 mm
\item[] 
\end{DUlineblock}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{neighbor:multi-shire}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Shire)} Shire, Hanley and Stratford, Comp. Part. Mech., (2020).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{neighbor:multi-monti}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Monti)} Monti, Clemmer, Srivastava, Silbert, Grest, and Lechman, Phys. Rev. E, (2022).

\sphinxstepscope

\index{newton@\spxentry{newton}}\ignorespaces 

\section{newton command}
\label{\detokenize{newton:newton-command}}\label{\detokenize{newton:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{newton::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{newton:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{newton}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flag}
\PYG{k}{newton}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flag1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flag2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flag = \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} for both pairwise and bonded interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flag1 = \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} for pairwise interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flag2 = \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} for bonded interactions

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{newton:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{newton}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}
\PYG{k}{newton}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{on}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{newton:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command turns Newton’s third law \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} for pairwise and
bonded interactions.  For most problems, setting Newton’s third law to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{on} means a modest savings in computation at the cost of two times
more communication.  Whether this is faster depends on problem size,
force cutoff lengths, a machine’s compute/communication ratio, and how
many processors are being used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Setting the pairwise newton flag to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} means that if two
interacting atoms are on different processors, both processors compute
their interaction and the resulting force information is not
communicated.  Similarly, for bonded interactions, newton \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} means
that if a bond, angle, dihedral, or improper interaction contains
atoms on 2 or more processors, the interaction is computed by each
processor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS should produce the same answers for any newton flag settings,
except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} and only bonded interactions
(bond, angle, etc) computed in the innermost timestep, it may be
faster to turn newton \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} for bonded interactions, to avoid extra
communication in the innermost loop.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{newton:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The newton bond setting cannot be changed after the simulation box is
defined by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{newton:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}} respa


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{newton:default}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{newton}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{on}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope

\index{next@\spxentry{next}}\ignorespaces 

\section{next command}
\label{\detokenize{next:next-command}}\label{\detokenize{next:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{next::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{next:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{variables}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
variables = one or more variable names

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{next:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{x}
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myTemp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{next:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command is used with variables defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command.  It assigns the next value to the
variable from the list of values defined for that variable by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command.  Thus when that variable is
subsequently substituted for in an input script command, the new value
is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command for info on how to define and
use different kinds of variables in LAMMPS input scripts.  If a
variable name is a single lower\sphinxhyphen{}case character from “a” to “z”, it can
be used in an input script command as \$a or \$z.  If it is multiple
letters, it can be used as \$\{myTemp\}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If multiple variables are used as arguments to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{next} command,
then all must be of the same variable style: \sphinxstyleemphasis{index}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{file},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop}.  An exception is that \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}\sphinxhyphen{} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can be mixed in the same \sphinxstyleemphasis{next} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All the variables specified with the next command are incremented by
one value from their respective list of values.  A \sphinxstyleemphasis{file}\sphinxhyphen{}style
variable reads the next line from its associated file.  An
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile}\sphinxhyphen{}style variable reads the next set of lines (one per atom)
from its associated file.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{String\sphinxhyphen{}} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}\sphinxhyphen{} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal}\sphinxhyphen{} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{world}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables cannot be used with the next command,
since they only store a single value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When any of the variables in the next command has no more values, a
flag is set that causes the input script to skip the next
{\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} command encountered.  This enables a loop containing
a next command to exit.  As explained in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}
command, the variable that has exhausted its values is also deleted.
This allows it to be used and re\sphinxhyphen{}defined later in the input script.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{File}\sphinxhyphen{}style and \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are exhausted when the
end\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}file is reached.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the next command is used with \sphinxstyleemphasis{index}\sphinxhyphen{} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables,
the next value is assigned to the variable for all processors.  When
the next command is used with \sphinxstyleemphasis{file}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, the next line is
read from its file and the string assigned to the variable.  When the
next command is used with \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, the next set of
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values is read from its file and assigned to the variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the next command is used with \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}\sphinxhyphen{} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop}\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables, all \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}\sphinxhyphen{} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables must be listed
in the next command.  This is because of the manner in which the
incrementing is done, using a single lock file for all variables.  The
next value (for each variable) is assigned to whichever processor
partition executes the command first.  All processors in the partition
are assigned the same value(s).  Running LAMMPS on multiple partitions
of processors via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Universe}\sphinxhyphen{} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are
incremented using the files “tmp.lammps.variable” and
“tmp.lammps.variable.lock” which you will see in your directory during
and after such a LAMMPS run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of running a series of simulations using the next
command with an \sphinxstyleemphasis{index}\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.  If this input script is named
in.polymer, 8 simulations would be run using data files from
directories run1 through run8.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{d}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{run8}
\PYG{k}{shell}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}d}
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.polymer}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{shell}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}
\PYG{k}{clear}
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{d}
\PYG{k}{jump }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.polymer}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the variable “d” were of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}, and the same in.polymer
input script were run on 3 partitions of processors, then the first 3
simulations would begin, one on each set of processors.  Whichever
partition finished first, it would assign variable “d” the fourth value
and run another simulation, and so forth until all 8 simulations were
finished.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Jump and next commands can also be nested to enable multi\sphinxhyphen{}level loops.
For example, this script will run 15 simulations in a double loop.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{j}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{clear}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.polymer.}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}i}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}j}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Running}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{simulation}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}i}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}j}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{j}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{jump }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.script}
\PYG{k}{next }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{i}
\PYG{k}{jump }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.script}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of a double loop which uses the {\hyperref[\detokenize{if::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{if}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} commands to break out of the inner loop when a
condition is met, then continues iterating through the outer loop.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{label       }\PYG{l+s+sc}{loopa}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{label     }\PYG{l+s+sc}{loopb}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{variable  }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{print}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{A,B = \PYGZdl{}a,\PYGZdl{}b}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{jump in.script break}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{next      }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{b}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{jump      }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.script}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loopb}
\PYG{k}{label       }\PYG{l+s+sc}{break}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delete}

\PYG{k}{next        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}
\PYG{k}{jump        }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.script}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loopa}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kokkos} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = arguments specific to the style
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu} args = Ngpu keyword value ...
  Ngpu = \# of GPUs per node
  zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
  keywords = \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpuID} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpa} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{blocksize} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{platform} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device\_type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ocl\_args}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = neighbor list build on GPU (default)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = neighbor list build on CPU
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = set Newton pairwise flag off (default and required)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} = set Newton pairwise flag on (currently not allowed)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = apply "gpu" suffix to all available styles in the GPU package (default)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} = apply "gpu" suffix only pair styles
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} value = size
      size = bin size for neighbor list construction (distance units)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} = fraction
      fraction = fraction of atoms assigned to GPU (default = 1.0)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpa} value = Nlanes
      Nlanes = \# of GPU vector lanes (CUDA threads) used per atom
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{blocksize} value = size
      size = thread block size for pair force computation
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} value = Nthreads
      Nthreads = number of OpenMP threads to use on CPU (default = 0)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{platform} value = id
      id = For OpenCL, platform ID for the GPU or accelerator
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpuID} values = id
      id = ID of first GPU to be used on each node
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{device\_type} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{intelgpu} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nvidiagpu} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{amdgpu} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{applegpu} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{generic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom},val1,val2,...
      val1,val2,... = custom OpenCL accelerator configuration parameters (see below for details)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{ocl\_args} value = args
      args = List of additional OpenCL compiler arguments delimited by colons
\sphinxstyleemphasis{intel} args = NPhi keyword value ...
  Nphi = \# of co\sphinxhyphen{}processors per node
  zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
  keywords = \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lrt} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{balance} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tptask} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm\_table} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no\_affinity}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mixed} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{double}
      single = perform force calculations in single precision
      mixed = perform force calculations in mixed precision
      double = perform force calculations in double precision
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} value = Nthreads
      Nthreads = number of OpenMP threads to use on CPU (default = 0)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{lrt} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = use additional thread dedicated for some PPPM calculations
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = do not dedicate an extra thread for some PPPM calculations
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{balance} value = split
      split = fraction of work to offload to co\sphinxhyphen{}processor, \sphinxhyphen{}1 for dynamic
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = include ghost atoms for offload
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = do not include ghost atoms for offload
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpc} value = Ntpc
      Ntpc = max number of co\sphinxhyphen{}processor threads per co\sphinxhyphen{}processor core (default = 4)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{tptask} value = Ntptask
      Ntptask = max number of co\sphinxhyphen{}processor threads per MPI task (default = 240)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm\_table} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = Precompute pppm values in table (doesn\textquotesingle{}t change accuracy)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = Compute pppm values on the fly
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{no\_affinity} values = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kokkos} args = keyword value ...
  zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
  keywords = \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/qeq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/thread} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/transpose} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/exchange} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/forward} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/forward} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/fix/forward} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/reverse} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/reverse} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom/map} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu/aware} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{half}
      full = full neighbor list
      half = half neighbor list built in thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe manner
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/qeq} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{half}
      full = full neighbor list
      half = half neighbor list built in thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe manner
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/thread} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = thread only over atoms
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} = thread over both atoms and neighbors
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/transpose} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = use same memory layout for GPU neigh list build as pair style
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} = use transposed memory layout for GPU neigh list build
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = set Newton pairwise and bonded flags off
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} = set Newton pairwise and bonded flags on
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} value = size
      size = bin size for neighbor list construction (distance units)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
      use value for comm/exchange and comm/forward and comm/pair/forward and comm/fix/forward and comm/reverse
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/exchange} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/forward} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/forward} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/fix/forward} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/reverse} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = perform communication pack/unpack in non\sphinxhyphen{}KOKKOS mode
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} = perform pack/unpack on host (e.g. with OpenMP threading)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} = perform pack/unpack on device (e.g. on GPU)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/reverse} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = perform communication pack/unpack in non\sphinxhyphen{}KOKKOS mode
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} = perform pack/unpack on device (e.g. on GPU)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = perform atom sorting in non\sphinxhyphen{}KOKKOS mode
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} = perform atom sorting on device (e.g. on GPU)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom/map} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = build atom map in non\sphinxhyphen{}KOKKOS mode
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} = build atom map on device (e.g. on GPU)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu/aware} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = do not use GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} = use GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI (default)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = use device acceleration (e.g. GPU) for all available styles in the KOKKOS package (default)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}  = use device acceleration only for pair styles (and host acceleration for others)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} args = Nthreads keyword value ...
  Nthreads = \# of OpenMP threads to associate with each MPI process
  zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
  keywords = \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = threaded neighbor list build (default)
      \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = non\sphinxhyphen{}threaded neighbor list build
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}
