\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{package:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command invokes package\sphinxhyphen{}specific settings for the various
accelerator packages available in LAMMPS.  Currently the following
packages use settings from this command: GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS, and
OPENMP.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If this command is specified in an input script, it must be near the
top of the script, before the simulation box has been defined.  This
is because it specifies settings that the accelerator packages use in
their initialization, before a simulation is defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can also be specified from the command\sphinxhyphen{}line when
launching LAMMPS, using the “\sphinxhyphen{}pk” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  The syntax is exactly the same as when used
in an input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that all of the accelerator packages require the package command
to be specified (except the OPT package), if the package is to be used
in a simulation (LAMMPS can be built with an accelerator package
without using it in a particular simulation).  However, in all cases,
a default version of the command is typically invoked by other
accelerator settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The KOKKOS package requires a “\sphinxhyphen{}k on” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} respectively, which invokes a “package
kokkos” command with default settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the GPU, INTEL, and OPENMP packages, if a “\sphinxhyphen{}sf gpu” or “\sphinxhyphen{}sf
intel” or “\sphinxhyphen{}sf omp” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} is used to
auto\sphinxhyphen{}append accelerator suffixes to various styles in the input
script, then those switches also invoke a “package gpu”, “package
intel”, or “package omp” command with default settings.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A package command for a particular style can be invoked multiple
times when a simulation is setup, e.g. by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}c on, \sphinxhyphen{}k on, \sphinxhyphen{}sf, and \sphinxhyphen{}pk command\sphinxhyphen{}line switches}}}}, and by using this command
in an input script.  Each time it is used all of the style options are
set, either to default values or to specified settings.  I.e. settings
from previous invocations do not persist across multiple invocations.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more details
about using the various accelerator packages for speeding up LAMMPS
simulations.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu} style invokes settings associated with the use of the GPU
package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ngpu} argument sets the number of GPUs per node. If \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ngpu} is 0
and no other keywords are specified, GPU or accelerator devices are
auto\sphinxhyphen{}selected. In this process, all platforms are searched for
accelerator devices and GPUs are chosen if available. The device with
the highest number of compute cores is selected. The number of devices
is increased to be the number of matching accelerators with the same
number of compute cores. If there are more devices than MPI tasks,
the additional devices will be unused. The auto\sphinxhyphen{}selection of GPUs/
accelerator devices and platforms can be restricted by specifying
a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero value for \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ngpu} and / or using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpuID}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{platform},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{device\_type} keywords as described below. If there are more MPI
tasks (per node) than GPUs, multiple MPI tasks will share each GPU.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional keyword/value pairs can also be specified.  Each has a
default value as listed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} keyword specifies where neighbor lists for pair style
computation will be built.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, which is the default,
neighbor list building is performed on the GPU.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no},
neighbor list building is performed on the CPU.  GPU neighbor list
building currently cannot be used with a triclinic box.  GPU neighbor
lists are not compatible with commands that are not GPU\sphinxhyphen{}enabled.  When
a non\sphinxhyphen{}GPU enabled command requires a neighbor list, it will also be
built on the CPU.  In these cases, it will typically be more efficient
to only use CPU neighbor list builds.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} keyword sets the Newton flags for pairwise (not bonded)
interactions to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}, the same as the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}}
command allows.  Currently, only an \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} value is allowed, since all
the GPU package pair styles require this setting.  This means more
computation is done, but less communication.  In the future a value of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{on} may be allowed, so the \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} keyword is included as an option
for compatibility with the package command for other accelerator
styles.  Note that the newton setting for bonded interactions is not
affected by this keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only} keyword can change how any “gpu” suffix is applied.
By default a suffix is applied to all styles for which an accelerated
variant is available.  However, that is not always the most effective
way to use an accelerator.  With \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only} set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} the suffix
will only by applied to supported pair styles, which tend to be the
most effective in using an accelerator and their operation can be
overlapped with all other computations on the CPU.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} keyword sets the size of bins used to bin atoms in
neighbor list builds performed on the GPU, if \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} is set.
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} is set to 0.0 (the default), then the binsize is set
automatically using heuristics in the GPU package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} keyword can be used for load balancing force calculations
between CPU and GPU cores in GPU\sphinxhyphen{}enabled pair styles. If 0 \textless{} \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} \textless{}
1.0, a fixed fraction of particles is offloaded to the GPU while force
calculation for the other particles occurs simultaneously on the CPU.
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} \textless{} 0.0, the optimal fraction (based on CPU and GPU timings)
is calculated every 25 timesteps, i.e. dynamic load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing across
the CPU and GPU is performed.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} = 1.0, all force
calculations for GPU accelerated pair styles are performed on the GPU.
In this case, other {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid}}}} pair interactions,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{long\sphinxhyphen{}range}}}} calculations can be performed on the
CPU while the GPU is performing force calculations for the GPU\sphinxhyphen{}enabled
pair style.  If all CPU force computations complete before the GPU
completes, LAMMPS will block until the GPU has finished before
continuing the timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, if you have two GPUs per node and 8 CPU cores per node,
and would like to run on 4 nodes (32 cores) with dynamic balancing of
force calculation across CPU and GPU cores, you could specify

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{32}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} launch command}
package\PYG{+w}{ }gpu\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }split\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}1\PYG{+w}{                 }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} input script command}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this case, all CPU cores and GPU devices on the nodes would be
utilized.  Each GPU device would be shared by 4 CPU cores. The CPU
cores would perform force calculations for some fraction of the
particles at the same time the GPUs performed force calculation for
the other particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpuID} keyword is used to specify the first ID for the GPU or
other accelerator that LAMMPS will use. For example, if the ID is
1 and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ngpu} is 3, GPUs 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 will be used. Device IDs should be
determined from the output of nvc\_get\_devices, ocl\_get\_devices,
or hip\_get\_devices
as provided in the lib/gpu directory. When using OpenCL with
accelerators that have main memory NUMA, the accelerators can be
split into smaller virtual accelerators for more efficient use
with MPI.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpa} keyword sets the number of GPU vector lanes per atom used to
perform force calculations.  With a default value of 1, the number of
lanes will be chosen based on the pair style, however, the value can
be set explicitly with this keyword to fine\sphinxhyphen{}tune performance.  For
large cutoffs or with a small number of particles per GPU, increasing
the value can improve performance. The number of lanes per atom must
be a power of 2 and currently cannot be greater than the SIMD width
for the GPU / accelerator. In the case it exceeds the SIMD width, it
will automatically be decreased to meet the restriction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{blocksize} keyword allows you to tweak the number of threads used
per thread block. This number should be a multiple of 32 (for GPUs)
and its maximum depends on the specific GPU hardware. Typical choices
are 64, 128, or 256. A larger block size increases occupancy of
individual GPU cores, but reduces the total number of thread blocks,
thus may lead to load imbalance. On modern hardware, the sensitivity
to the blocksize is typically low.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} value for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} keyword sets the number of OpenMP
threads allocated for each MPI task. This setting controls OpenMP
parallelism only for routines run on the CPUs. For more details on
setting the number of OpenMP threads, see the discussion of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} setting on this page for the “package omp” command.
The meaning of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} is exactly the same for the GPU, INTEL,
and GPU packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{platform} keyword is only used with OpenCL to specify the ID for
an OpenCL platform. See the output from ocl\_get\_devices in the lib/gpu
directory. In LAMMPS only one platform can be active at a time and by
default (id=\sphinxhyphen{}1) the platform is auto\sphinxhyphen{}selected to find the GPU with the
most compute cores. When \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ngpu} or other keywords are specified, the
auto\sphinxhyphen{}selection is appropriately restricted. For example, if \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ngpu} is
3, only platforms with at least 3 accelerators are considered. Similar
restrictions can be enforced by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpuID} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{device\_type} keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{device\_type} keyword can be used for OpenCL to specify the type of
GPU to use or specify a custom configuration for an accelerator. In most
cases this selection will be automatic and there is no need to use the
keyword. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{applegpu} type is not specific to a particular GPU vendor,
but is separate due to the more restrictive Apple OpenCL implementation.
For expert users, to specify a custom configuration, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} keyword
followed by the next parameters can be specified:

\sphinxAtStartPar
CONFIG\_ID, SIMD\_SIZE, MEM\_THREADS, SHUFFLE\_AVAIL, FAST\_MATH,
THREADS\_PER\_ATOM, THREADS\_PER\_CHARGE, THREADS\_PER\_THREE, BLOCK\_PAIR,
BLOCK\_BIO\_PAIR, BLOCK\_ELLIPSE, PPPM\_BLOCK\_1D, BLOCK\_NBOR\_BUILD,
BLOCK\_CELL\_2D, BLOCK\_CELL\_ID, MAX\_SHARED\_TYPES, MAX\_BIO\_SHARED\_TYPES,
PPPM\_MAX\_SPLINE, NBOR\_PREFETCH.

\sphinxAtStartPar
CONFIG\_ID can be 0. SHUFFLE\_AVAIL in \{0,1\} indicates that inline\sphinxhyphen{}PTX
(NVIDIA) or OpenCL extensions (Intel) should be used for horizontal
vector operations. FAST\_MATH in \{0,1\} indicates that OpenCL fast math
optimizations are used during the build and hardware\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated
transcendental functions are used when available. THREADS\_PER\_* give the
default \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpa} values for ellipsoidal models, styles using charge, and
any other styles. The BLOCK\_* parameters specify the block sizes for
various kernel calls and the MAX\_*SHARED*\_ parameters are used to
determine the amount of local shared memory to use for storing model
parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For OpenCL, the routines are compiled at runtime for the specified GPU
or accelerator architecture. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ocl\_args} keyword can be used to
specify additional flags for the runtime build.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel} style invokes settings associated with the use of the INTEL
package.  The keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{balance}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpc}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tptask} are
\sphinxstylestrong{only} applicable if LAMMPS was built with Xeon Phi co\sphinxhyphen{}processor
support and are otherwise ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nphi} argument sets the number of co\sphinxhyphen{}processors per node.
This can be set to any value, including 0, if LAMMPS was not
built with co\sphinxhyphen{}processor support.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional keyword/value pairs can also be specified.  Each has a
default value as listed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} value for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} keyword sets the number of OpenMP
threads allocated for each MPI task. This setting controls OpenMP
parallelism only for routines run on the CPUs. For more details on
setting the number of OpenMP threads, see the discussion of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} setting on this page for the “package omp” command.
The meaning of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} is exactly the same for the GPU, INTEL,
and GPU packages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} keyword determines the precision mode to use for
computing pair style forces, either on the CPU or on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor,
when using a INTEL supported {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}}.  It
can take a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{single}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{mixed} which is the default, or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{double}.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Single} means single precision is used for the entire
force calculation.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Mixed} means forces between a pair of atoms are
computed in single precision, but accumulated and stored in double
precision, including storage of forces, torques, energies, and virial
quantities.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Double} means double precision is used for the entire
force calculation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lrt} keyword can be used to enable “Long Range Thread (LRT)”
mode. It can take a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} to enable and \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} to disable.
LRT mode generates an extra thread (in addition to any OpenMP threads
specified with the OMP\_NUM\_THREADS environment variable or the \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}
keyword). The extra thread is dedicated for performing part of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{PPPM solver}}}} computations and communications. This
can improve parallel performance on processors supporting
Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT) such as Hyper\sphinxhyphen{}Threading (HT) on Intel
processors. In this mode, one additional thread is generated per MPI
process. LAMMPS will generate a warning in the case that more threads
are used than available in SMT hardware on a node. If the PPPM solver
from the INTEL package is not used, then the LRT setting is
ignored and no extra threads are generated. Enabling LRT will replace
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}} with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/lrt/intel} style that
is identical to the default \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet} style aside from supporting the
LRT feature. This feature requires setting the pre\sphinxhyphen{}processor flag
\sphinxhyphen{}DLMP\_INTEL\_USELRT in the makefile when compiling LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{balance} keyword sets the fraction of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}} work
offloaded to the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor for split values between 0.0 and 1.0 inclusive.
While this fraction of work is running on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor, other calculations
will run on the host, including neighbor and pair calculations that are not
offloaded, as well as angle, bond, dihedral, kspace, and some MPI
communications.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{split} is set to \sphinxhyphen{}1, the fraction of work is dynamically
adjusted automatically throughout the run.  This typically give performance
within 5 to 10 percent of the optimal fixed fraction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost} keyword determines whether or not ghost atoms, i.e. atoms
at the boundaries of processor subdomains, are offloaded for neighbor
and force calculations.  When the value = “no”, ghost atoms are not
offloaded.  This option can reduce the amount of data transfer with
the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor and can also overlap MPI communication of forces with
computation on the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor when the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton pair}}}}
setting is “on”.  When the value = “yes”, ghost atoms are offloaded.
In some cases this can provide better performance, especially if the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{balance} fraction is high.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpc} keyword sets the max \# of co\sphinxhyphen{}processor threads \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntpc} that
will run on each core of the co\sphinxhyphen{}processor.  The default value = 4,
which is the number of hardware threads per core supported by the
current generation Xeon Phi chips.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tptask} keyword sets the max \# of co\sphinxhyphen{}processor threads (Ntptask*
assigned to each MPI task.  The default value = 240, which is the
total \# of threads an entire current generation Xeon Phi chip can run
(240 = 60 cores * 4 threads/core).  This means each MPI task assigned
to the Phi will enough threads for the chip to run the max allowed,
even if only 1 MPI task is assigned.  If 8 MPI tasks are assigned to
the Phi, each will run with 30 threads.  If you wish to limit the
number of threads per MPI task, set \sphinxstyleemphasis{tptask} to a smaller value.
E.g. for \sphinxstyleemphasis{tptask} = 16, if 8 MPI tasks are assigned, each will run
with 16 threads, for a total of 128.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the default settings for \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpc} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tptask} are fine for
most problems, regardless of how many MPI tasks you assign to a Phi.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm\_table} keyword with the argument yes allows to use a
pre\sphinxhyphen{}computed table to efficiently spread the charge to the PPPM grid.
This feature is enabled by default but can be turned off using the
keyword with the argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{no\_affinity} keyword will turn off automatic setting of core
affinity for MPI tasks and OpenMP threads on the host when using
offload to a co\sphinxhyphen{}processor. Affinity settings are used when possible
to prevent MPI tasks and OpenMP threads from being on separate NUMA
domains and to prevent offload threads from interfering with other
processes/threads used for LAMMPS.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kokkos} style invokes settings associated with the use of the
KOKKOS package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the settings are optional keyword/value pairs. Each has a default
value as listed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} keyword determines how neighbor lists are built. A value of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{half} uses a thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe variant of half\sphinxhyphen{}neighbor lists, the same as
used by most pair styles in LAMMPS, which is the default when running on
CPUs (i.e. the Kokkos CUDA back end is not enabled).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} uses a full neighbor lists and is the default when
running on GPUs. This performs twice as much computation as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{half}
option, however that is often a win because it is thread\sphinxhyphen{}safe and
does not require atomic operations in the calculation of pair forces. For
that reason, \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} is the default setting for GPUs. However, when
running on CPUs, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{half} neighbor list is the default because it are
often faster, just as it is for non\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated pair styles. Similarly,
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/qeq} keyword determines how neighbor lists are built for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_qeq_reaxff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix qeq/reaxff/kk}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/thread} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}, then the KOKKOS package
threads only over atoms. However, for small systems, this may not expose
enough parallelism to keep a GPU busy. When this keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{on},
the KOKKOS package threads over both atoms and neighbors of atoms. When
using \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/thread} \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton pair}}}} setting must
be “off”. Using \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/thread} \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} may be slower for large systems, so
this this option is turned on by default only when running on one or
more GPUs and there are 16k atoms or less owned by an MPI rank. Not all
KOKKOS\sphinxhyphen{}enabled potentials support this keyword yet, and only thread over
atoms. Many simple pairwise potentials such as Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones do support
threading over both atoms and neighbors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/transpose} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}, then the KOKKOS
package will use the same memory layout for building the neighbor list on
GPUs as used for the pair style. When this keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} it
will use a different (transposed) memory layout to build the neighbor
list on GPUs. This can be faster in some cases (e.g. ReaxFF HNS
benchmark) but slower in others (e.g. Lennard Jones benchmark). The
copy between different memory layouts is done out of place and
therefore doubles the memory overhead of the neighbor list, which can
be significant.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} keyword sets the Newton flags for pairwise and bonded
interactions to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}, the same as the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}}
command allows. The default for GPUs is \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} because this will almost
always give better performance for the KOKKOS package. This means more
computation is done, but less communication. However, when running on
CPUs a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} is the default since it can often be faster, just
as it is for non\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated pair styles

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{binsize} keyword sets the size of bins used to bin atoms during
neighbor list builds. The same value can be set by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify binsize}}}} command. Making it an option
in the package kokkos command allows it to be set from the command line.
The default value for CPUs is 0.0, which means the LAMMPS default will be
used, which is bins = 1/2 the size of the pairwise cutoff + neighbor skin
distance. This is fine when neighbor lists are built on the CPU. For GPU
builds, a 2x larger binsize equal to the pairwise cutoff + neighbor skin
is often faster, which is the default. Note that if you use a
longer\sphinxhyphen{}than\sphinxhyphen{}usual pairwise cutoff, e.g. to allow for a smaller fraction
of KSpace work with a {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic solver}}}}
because the GPU is faster at performing pairwise interactions, then this
rule of thumb may give too large a binsize and the default should be
overridden with a smaller value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/exchange} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/forward} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/forward}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/fix/forward} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/reverse} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/reverse}
keywords determine whether the host or device performs the packing and
unpacking of data when communicating per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data between processors.
“Exchange” communication happens only on timesteps that neighbor lists
are rebuilt. The data is only for atoms that migrate to new processors.
“Forward” communication happens every timestep. “Reverse” communication
happens every timestep if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{newton} option is on. The data is for
atom coordinates and any other atom properties that needs to be updated
for ghost atoms owned by each processor. “Pair/comm” controls additional
communication in pair styles, such as pair\_style EAM. “Fix/comm” controls
additional communication in fixes, such as fix SHAKE.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm} keyword is simply a short\sphinxhyphen{}cut to set the same value for all
the comm keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value options for the keywords are \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}. A
value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} means to use the standard non\sphinxhyphen{}KOKKOS method of
packing/unpacking data for the communication. A value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} means to
use the host, typically a multicore CPU, and perform the
packing/unpacking in parallel with threads. A value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} means to
use the device, typically a GPU, to perform the packing/unpacking
operation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/forward} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/fix/forward} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/reverse}
keywords, if a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} is used it will be automatically
be changed to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} since these keywords don’t support \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} mode. The
value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} will also always be used when running on the CPU, i.e. setting
the value to \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} will have no effect if the pair/fix style is
running on the CPU. For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/fix/forward} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm/pair/reverse}
keywords, not all styles support \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} mode and in that case will run
in \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} mode instead.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optimal choice for these keywords depends on the input script and
the hardware used. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} value is useful for verifying that the
Kokkos\sphinxhyphen{}based \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} values are working correctly. It is the
default when running on CPUs since it is usually the fastest.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on CPUs or Xeon Phi, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} values work
identically. When using GPUs, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} value is the default since it
will typically be optimal if all of your styles used in your input
script are supported by the KOKKOS package. In this case data can stay
on the GPU for many timesteps without being moved between the host and
GPU, if you use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} value. If your script uses styles (e.g.
fixes) which are not yet supported by the KOKKOS package, then data has
to be moved between the host and device anyway, so it is typically faster
to let the host handle communication, by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} value. Using
\sphinxstyleemphasis{host} instead of \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} will enable use of multiple threads to
pack/unpack communicated data. When running small systems on a GPU,
performing the exchange pack/unpack on the host CPU can give speedup
since it reduces the number of CUDA kernel launches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} keyword determines whether the host or device performs atom
sorting, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify sort}}}} command.  The value
options for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} keyword are \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm}
keywords above. If a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} is used it will be automatically be
changed to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} since the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} keyword does not support \sphinxstyleemphasis{host} mode. Not
all fix styles with extra atom data support \sphinxstyleemphasis{device} mode and in that case
a warning will be given and atom sorting will run in \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} mode instead.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 17Apr2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom/map} keyword determines whether the host or device builds the
atom\_map, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_modify map}}}} command.  The
value options for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom/map} keyword are identical to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort}
keyword above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu/aware} keyword chooses whether GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI will be used. When
this keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}, buffers in GPU memory are passed directly
through MPI send/receive calls. This reduces overhead of first copying
the data to the host CPU. However GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI is not supported on all
systems, which can lead to segmentation faults and would require using a
value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}. If LAMMPS can safely detect that GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI is not
available (currently only possible with OpenMPI v2.0.0 or later), then
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu/aware} keyword is automatically set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} by default. When
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu/aware} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} while any of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm}
keywords are set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{device}, the value for these \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm} keywords will
be automatically changed to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}. This setting has no effect if not
running on GPUs or if using only one MPI rank. GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI is available
for OpenMPI 1.8 (or later versions), Mvapich2 1.9 (or later) when the
“MV2\_USE\_CUDA” environment variable is set to “1”, CrayMPI, and IBM
Spectrum MPI when the “\sphinxhyphen{}gpu” flag is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only} keyword can change how the KOKKOS suffix “kk” is applied
when using an accelerator device.  By default device acceleration is always
used for all available styles.  With \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair/only} set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} the suffix
setting will choose device acceleration only for pair styles and run all
other force computations on the host CPU.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm} flags, along with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom/map} keywords will also automatically be changed to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.
This can result in better performance for certain configurations and
system sizes.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} style invokes settings associated with the use of the
OPENMP package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} argument sets the number of OpenMP threads allocated for
each MPI task.  For example, if your system has nodes with dual
quad\sphinxhyphen{}core processors, it has a total of 8 cores per node.  You could
use two MPI tasks per node (e.g. using the \sphinxhyphen{}ppn option of the mpirun
command in MPICH or \sphinxhyphen{}npernode in OpenMPI), and set \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} = 4.
This would use all 8 cores on each node.  Note that the product of MPI
tasks * threads/task should not exceed the physical number of cores
(on a node), otherwise performance will suffer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Setting \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} = 0 instructs LAMMPS to use whatever value is the
default for the given OpenMP environment. This is usually determined
via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS} environment variable or the compiler
runtime.  Note that in most cases the default for OpenMP capable
compilers is to use one thread for each available CPU core when
\sphinxstyleemphasis{OMP\_NUM\_THREADS} is not explicitly set, which can lead to poor
performance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are examples of how to set the environment variable when
launching LAMMPS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
env\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script
env\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script
mpirun\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}x\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{OMP\PYGZus{}NUM\PYGZus{}THREADS}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}np\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }lmp\PYGZus{}machine\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}sf\PYG{+w}{ }omp\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}in\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{in}.script
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or you can set it permanently in your shell’s start\sphinxhyphen{}up script.
All three of these examples use a total of 4 CPU cores.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that different MPI implementations have different ways of passing
the OMP\_NUM\_THREADS environment variable to all MPI processes.  The
second example line above is for MPICH; the third example line with \sphinxhyphen{}x is
for OpenMPI.  Check your MPI documentation for additional details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
What combination of threads and MPI tasks gives the best performance
is difficult to predict and can depend on many components of your
input.  Not all features of LAMMPS support OpenMP threading via the
OPENMP package and the parallel efficiency can be very different,
too.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you build LAMMPS with the GPU, INTEL, and / or OPENMP
packages, be aware these packages all allow setting of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads}
value via their package commands, but there is only a single global
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} value used by OpenMP.  Thus if multiple package commands are
invoked, you should ensure the values are consistent.  If they are
not, the last one invoked will take precedence, for all packages.
Also note that if the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}sf hybrid intel omp command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} is used, it invokes a “package intel” command, followed by a
“package omp” command, both with a setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nthreads} = 0. Likewise
for a hybrid suffix for gpu and omp. Note that KOKKOS also supports
setting the number of OpenMP threads from the command line using the
“\sphinxhyphen{}k on” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}. The default for
KOKKOS is 1 thread per MPI task, so any other number of threads should
be explicitly set using the “\sphinxhyphen{}k on” command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch (and this
setting should be consistent with settings from any other packages
used).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional keyword/value pairs can also be specified.  Each has a
default value as listed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} keyword specifies whether neighbor list building will be
multi\sphinxhyphen{}threaded in addition to force calculations.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} is set
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} then neighbor list calculation is performed only by MPI tasks
with no OpenMP threading.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} (the default), a
multi\sphinxhyphen{}threaded neighbor list build is used.  Using \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} is
almost always faster and should produce identical neighbor lists at the
expense of using more memory.  Specifically, neighbor list pages are
allocated for all threads at the same time and each thread works
within its own pages.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{package:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command cannot be used after the simulation box is defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu} style of this command can only be invoked if LAMMPS was built
with the GPU package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc
page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel} style of this command can only be invoked if LAMMPS was
built with the INTEL package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kokkos} style of this command can only be invoked if LAMMPS was built
with the KOKKOS package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}}
doc page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} style of this command can only be invoked if LAMMPS was built
with the OPENMP package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}}
doc page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{package:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}pk command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}


\subsection{Defaults}
\label{\detokenize{package:defaults}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the GPU package, the default parameters and settings are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Ngpu = 0, neigh = yes, newton = off, binsize = 0.0, split = 1.0, gpuID = 0 to Ngpu\PYGZhy{}1, tpa = 1, omp = 0, platform=\PYGZhy{}1.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These settings are made automatically if the “\sphinxhyphen{}sf gpu”
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} is used.  If it is not used,
you must invoke the package gpu command in your input script or via the
“\sphinxhyphen{}pk gpu” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the INTEL package, the default parameters and settings are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Nphi = 1, omp = 0, mode = mixed, lrt = no, balance = \PYGZhy{}1, tpc = 4, tptask = 240, pppm\PYGZus{}table = yes
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default ghost option is determined by the pair style being used.
This value is output to the screen in the offload report at the end of each
run.  Note that all of these settings, except “omp” and “mode”, are ignored if
LAMMPS was not built with Xeon Phi co\sphinxhyphen{}processor support.  These settings are
made automatically if the “\sphinxhyphen{}sf intel” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}
is used.  If it is not used, you must invoke the package intel command in your
input script or via the “\sphinxhyphen{}pk intel” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the KOKKOS package when using GPUs, the option defaults are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
neigh = full, neigh/qeq = full, newton = off, binsize = 2x LAMMPS default value, comm = device, sort = device, atom/map = device, neigh/transpose = off, gpu/aware = on
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For GPUs, option neigh/thread = on when there are 16k atoms or less on
an MPI rank, otherwise it is “off”. When LAMMPS can safely detect that
GPU\sphinxhyphen{}aware MPI is not available, the default value of gpu/aware becomes
“off”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the KOKKOS package when using CPUs or Xeon Phis, the option defaults are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
neigh = half, neigh/qeq = half, newton = on, binsize = 0.0, comm = no, sort = no, atom/map = no
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These settings are made automatically by
the required “\sphinxhyphen{}k on” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  You can
change them by using the package kokkos command in your input script or
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}pk kokkos command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the OMP package, the defaults are

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Nthreads = 0, neigh = yes
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These settings are made automatically if the “\sphinxhyphen{}sf omp”
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} is used.  If it is not used,
you must invoke the package omp command in your input script or via the
“\sphinxhyphen{}pk omp” {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\index{pair\_coeff@\spxentry{pair\_coeff}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_coeff command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_coeff:pair-coeff-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_coeff:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_coeff:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{I}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{J}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
I,J = numeric atom types (see asterisk form below), or type labels

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = coefficients for one or more pairs of atom types

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_coeff:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nialhjea}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{morse.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ENTRY1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} (for pair\PYGZus{}style hybrid)}

\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_coeff:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify the pairwise force field coefficients for one or more pairs of
atom types.  The number and meaning of the coefficients depends on the
pair style.  Pair coefficients can also be set in the data file read
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command or in a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
I and J can be specified in one of several ways.  Explicit numeric
values can be used for each, as in the first example above.  Or, one
or both of the types in the I,J pair can be a type label, which is an
alphanumeric string defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} command
or in a section of a data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command, and which converts internally to a numeric type.
Internally, LAMMPS will set coefficients for the symmetric J,I
interaction to the same values as the I,J interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For numeric values only, a wildcard asterisk can be used in place of or
in conjunction with the I,J arguments to set the coefficients for
multiple pairs of atom types.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or
“n*” or “m*n”.  If \(N\) is the number of atom types, then an
asterisk with no numeric values means all types from 1 to \(N\).  A
leading asterisk means all types from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all types from n to \(N\) (inclusive).  A middle
asterisk means all types from m to n (inclusive).  For the asterisk
syntax, only type pairs with I \textless{}= J are considered; if asterisks imply
type pairs where J \textless{} I, they are ignored. Again internally, LAMMPS will
set the coefficients for the symmetric J,I interactions to the same
values as the I \textless{}= J interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a pair\_coeff command can override a previous setting for the
same I,J pair.  For example, these commands set the coeffs for all I,J
pairs, then overwrite the coeffs for just the I,J = 2,3 pair:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.12}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A line in a data file that specifies pair coefficients uses the exact
same format as the arguments of the pair\_coeff command in an input
script, with the exception of the I,J type arguments.  In each line of
the “Pair Coeffs” section of a data file, only a single type I is
specified, which sets the coefficients for type I interacting with
type I.  This is because the section has exactly \(N\) lines, where
\(N\) is the number of atom types.  For this reason, the wild\sphinxhyphen{}card
asterisk should also not be used as part of the I argument.  Thus in a
data file, the line corresponding to the first example above would be
listed as

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
2 1.0 1.0 2.5
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For many potentials, if coefficients for type pairs with I != J are
not set explicitly by a pair\_coeff command, the values are inferred
from the I,I and J,J settings by mixing rules; see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command for a discussion.  Details on
this option as it pertains to individual potentials are described on
the page for the potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many pair styles, typically for many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials, use tabulated
potential files as input, when specifying the pair\_coeff command.
Potential files provided with LAMMPS are in the potentials directory
of the distribution.  For some potentials, such as EAM, other archives
of suitable files can be found on the Web.  They can be used with
LAMMPS so long as they are in the format LAMMPS expects, as discussed
on the individual doc pages.  The first line of potential files may
contain metadata with upper case tags followed their value. These may
be parsed and used by LAMMPS.  Currently supported are the “DATE:”
tag and the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UNITS:}} tag.  For pair styles that have been programmed
to support the metadata, the value of the “DATE:” tag is printed to
the screen and logfile so that the version of a potential file can be
later identified.  The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UNITS:}} tag indicates the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}
setting required for this particular potential file.  If the potential
file was created for a different sets of units, LAMMPS will terminate
with an error.  If the potential file does not contain the tag, no
check will be made and it is the responsibility of the user to determine
that the unit style is correct.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In some select cases and for specific combinations of unit styles,
LAMMPS is capable of automatically converting potential parameters
from a file. In those cases, a warning message signaling that an
automatic conversion has happened is printed to the screen.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a pair\_coeff command using a potential file is specified, LAMMPS
looks for the potential file in 2 places.  First it looks in the
location specified.  E.g. if the file is specified as “niu3.eam”, it
is looked for in the current working directory.  If it is specified as
“../potentials/niu3.eam”, then it is looked for in the potentials
directory, assuming it is a sister directory of the current working
directory.  If the file is not found, it is then looked for in one of
the directories specified by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_POTENTIALS}} environment variable.
Thus if this is set to the potentials directory in the LAMMPS distribution,
then you can use those files from anywhere on your system, without
copying them into your working directory.  Environment variables are
set in different ways for different shells.  Here are example settings
for

\sphinxAtStartPar
csh, tcsh:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{setenv }LAMMPS\PYGZus{}POTENTIALS /path/to/lammps/potentials
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
bash:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nb}{export}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{LAMMPS\PYGZus{}POTENTIALS}\PYG{o}{=}/path/to/lammps/potentials
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Windows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{g+go}{set LAMMPS\PYGZus{}POTENTIALS=\PYGZdq{}C:\PYGZbs{}\PYGZbs{}Path to LAMMPS\PYGZbs{}\PYGZbs{}Potentials\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_POTENTIALS}} environment variable may contain paths
to multiple folders, if they are separated by “;” on Windows and
“:” on all other operating systems, just like the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PATH}} and
similar environment variables.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The alphabetic list of pair styles defined in LAMMPS is given on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} doc page.  They are also listed in more
compact form on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands pair}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Click on the style to display the formula it computes and its
coefficients as specified by the associated pair\_coeff command.

{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.


\subsection{Related commands}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}}

\index{pair\_modify@\spxentry{pair\_modify}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_modify command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:pair-modify-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mix} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/disp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tabinner}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tabinner/disp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nofdotr} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute/tally} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/trim}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} value = sub\sphinxhyphen{}style N
  sub\sphinxhyphen{}style = sub\sphinxhyphen{}style of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair hybrid}}}}
  N = which instance of sub\sphinxhyphen{}style (1 to M), only specify if sub\sphinxhyphen{}style is used multiple times
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mix} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{arithmetic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sixthpower}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{table} value = N
  2\textasciicircum{}N = \# of values in table
\sphinxstyleemphasis{table/disp} value = N
  2\textasciicircum{}N = \# of values in table
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tabinner} value = cutoff
  cutoff = inner cutoff at which to begin table (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tabinner/disp} value = cutoff
  cutoff = inner cutoff at which to begin table (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nofdotr} value = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{special} values = which wt1 wt2 wt3
   which = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/coul} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul}
   w1,w2,w3 = 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 weights from 0.0 to 1.0 inclusive
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute/tally} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/trim} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mix}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{geometric}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tail}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{no}
\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8333333}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Modify the parameters of the currently defined pair style.  If the
pair style is {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid or hybrid/overlay}}}}, then the
specified parameters are by default modified for all the hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The behavior for hybrid pair styles can be changed by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair}
keyword, which allows selection of a specific sub\sphinxhyphen{}style to apply all
remaining keywords to.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute/tally} keywords can \sphinxstylestrong{only} be
used in conjunction with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword.  See further details about
these 3 keywords below.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mix} keyword affects pair coefficients for interactions between
atoms of type I and J, when I != J and the coefficients are not
explicitly set in the input script.  Note that coefficients for I = J
must be set explicitly, either in the input script via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command or in the “Pair Coeffs” or “PairIJ Coeffs”
sections of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data file}}}}.  For some pair styles it is not
necessary to specify coefficients when I != J, since a “mixing” rule
will create them from the I,I and J,J settings.  The pair\_modify
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mix} value determines what formulas are used to compute the mixed
coefficients.  In each case, the cutoff distance is mixed the same way
as sigma.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that not all pair styles support mixing and some mix options are
not available for certain pair styles. Also, there are additional
restrictions when using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style hybrid or hybrid/overlay}}}}.  See the page for individual pair styles for those
restrictions.  Note also that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command
also can be used to directly set coefficients for a specific I != J
pairing, in which case no mixing is performed.  If possible, LAMMPS will
print an informational message about how many of the mixed pair
coefficients were generated and which mixing rule was applied.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mix \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\epsilon_{ij} = & \sqrt{\epsilon_i  \epsilon_j} \\
\sigma_{ij}   = & \sqrt{\sigma_i  \sigma_j}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mix \sphinxstyleemphasis{arithmetic}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\epsilon_{ij} = & \sqrt{\epsilon_i  \epsilon_j} \\
\sigma_{ij}   = & \frac{1}{2} (\sigma_i + \sigma_j)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mix \sphinxstyleemphasis{sixthpower}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\epsilon_{ij} = & \frac{2 \sqrt{\epsilon_i \epsilon_j} \sigma_i^3 \sigma_j^3}{\sigma_i^6 + \sigma_j^6} \\
\sigma_{ij} =   & \left(\frac{1}{2} (\sigma_i^6 + \sigma_j^6) \right)^{\frac{1}{6}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword determines whether a Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential is
shifted at its cutoff to 0.0.  If so, this adds an energy term to each
pairwise interaction which will be included in the thermodynamic
output, but does not affect pair forces or atom trajectories.  See the
doc page for individual pair styles to see which ones support this
option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/disp} keywords apply to pair styles with a
long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic term or long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion term respectively;
see the page for individual styles to see which potentials support
these options.  If N is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, a table of length 2\textasciicircum{}N is
pre\sphinxhyphen{}computed for forces and energies, which can shrink their
computational cost by up to a factor of 2.  The table is indexed via a
bit\sphinxhyphen{}mapping technique {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify:wolff1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wolff)}}}} and a linear
interpolation is performed between adjacent table values.  In our
experiments with different table styles (lookup, linear, spline), this
method typically gave the best performance in terms of speed and
accuracy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The choice of table length is a tradeoff in accuracy versus speed.  A
larger N yields more accurate force computations, but requires more
memory which can slow down the computation due to cache misses.  A
reasonable value of N is between 8 and 16.  The default value of 12
(table of length 4096) gives approximately the same accuracy as the
no\sphinxhyphen{}table (N = 0) option.  For N = 0, forces and energies are computed
directly, using a polynomial fit for the needed erfc() function
evaluation, which is what earlier versions of LAMMPS did.  Values
greater than 16 typically slow down the simulation and will not
improve accuracy; values from 1 to 8 give unreliable results.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tabinner} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tabinner/disp} keywords set an inner cutoff above
which the pairwise computation is done by table lookup (if tables are
invoked), for the corresponding Coulombic and dispersion tables
discussed with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/disp} keywords.  The smaller the
cutoff is set, the less accurate the table becomes (for a given number
of table values), which can require use of larger tables.  The default
cutoff value is sqrt(2.0) distance units which means nearly all
pairwise interactions are computed via table lookup for simulations
with “real” units, but some close pairs may be computed directly
(non\sphinxhyphen{}table) for simulations with “lj” units.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, certain pair styles will
add a long\sphinxhyphen{}range VanderWaals tail “correction” to the energy and
pressure.  These corrections are bookkeeping terms which do not affect
dynamics, unless a constant\sphinxhyphen{}pressure simulation is being performed.
See the page for individual styles to see which support this
option.  These corrections are included in the calculation and
printing of thermodynamic quantities (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command).  Their effect will also be included in
constant NPT or NPH simulations where the pressure influences the
simulation box dimensions (e.g. the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph}}}} commands).  The formulas used for the
long\sphinxhyphen{}range corrections come from equation 5 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify:sun}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sun)}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tail correction terms are computed at the beginning of each
run, using the current atom counts of each atom type.  If atoms are
deleted (or lost) or created during a simulation, e.g. via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gcmc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gcmc}}}} command, the correction factors are not
re\sphinxhyphen{}computed.  If you expect the counts to change dramatically, you
can break a run into a series of shorter runs so that the
correction factors are re\sphinxhyphen{}computed more frequently.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Several additional assumptions are inherent in using tail corrections,
including the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The simulated system is a 3d bulk homogeneous liquid. This option
should not be used for systems that are non\sphinxhyphen{}liquid, 2d, have a slab
geometry (only 2d periodic), or inhomogeneous.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
G(r), the radial distribution function (rdf), is unity beyond the
cutoff, so a fairly large cutoff should be used (i.e. 2.5 sigma for
an LJ fluid), and it is probably a good idea to verify this
assumption by checking the rdf.  The rdf is not exactly unity beyond
the cutoff for each pair of interaction types, so the tail
correction is necessarily an approximation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tail corrections are computed at the beginning of each
simulation run.  If the number of atoms changes during the run,
e.g. due to atoms leaving the simulation domain, or use of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gcmc::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gcmc}}}} command, then the corrections are not
updated to reflect the changed atom count.  If this is a large
effect in your simulation, you should break the long run into
several short runs, so that the correction factors are re\sphinxhyphen{}computed
multiple times.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thermophysical properties obtained from calculations with this
option enabled will not be thermodynamically consistent with the
truncated force\sphinxhyphen{}field that was used.  In other words, atoms do not
feel any LJ pair interactions beyond the cutoff, but the energy and
pressure reported by the simulation include an estimated
contribution from those interactions.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute} keyword allows pairwise computations to be turned off,
even though a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} is defined.  This is not
useful for running a real simulation, but can be useful for debugging
purposes or for performing a {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} simulation, when you
only wish to compute partial forces that do not include the pairwise
contribution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two examples are as follows.  First, this option allows you to perform
a simulation with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}} with only a
subset of the hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles enabled.  Second, this option allows
you to perform a simulation with only long\sphinxhyphen{}range interactions but no
short\sphinxhyphen{}range pairwise interactions.  Doing this by simply not defining
a pair style will not work, because the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command requires a Kspace\sphinxhyphen{}compatible pair style be
defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nofdotr} keyword allows to disable an optimization that computes
the global stress tensor from the total forces and atom positions
rather than from summing forces between individual pairs of atoms.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword can only be used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid and
hybrid/overlay}}}} pair styles.  If used, it must appear
first in the list of keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Its meaning is that all the following parameters will only be modified
for the specified sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.  If the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style is defined multiple
times, then an additional numeric argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} must also be specified,
which is a number from 1 to M where M is the number of times the
sub\sphinxhyphen{}style was listed in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}}
command.  The extra number indicates which instance of the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style
the remaining keywords will be applied to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute/tally} keywords can \sphinxstylestrong{only} be used in
conjunction with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword and they must directly follow it.
I.e. any other keyword, must appear after \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{special}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute/tally}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} keyword overrides the global {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 exclusion settings (weights) for the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style selected
by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command, it takes
4 arguments.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{which} argument can be \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj} to change only the
non\sphinxhyphen{}Coulomb weights (e.g. Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones or Buckingham), \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul} to change
only the Coulombic settings, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/coul} to change both to the same
values.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{wt1,wt2,wt3} values are numeric weights from 0.0 to 1.0
inclusive, for the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, and 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 bond topology neighbors, respectively.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} keyword can be used multiple times, e.g. to set the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul} settings to different values.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} keyword is not compatible with pair styles from the
GPU or the INTEL package and attempting to use it will cause
an error.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Weights of exactly 0.0 or 1.0 in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command have implications on the neighbor list construction, which
means that they cannot be overridden by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} keyword.
One workaround for this restriction is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command with weights like 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}10 or 0.999999999 instead of 0.0 or 1.0,
respectively, which enables to reset each them to any value between 0.0
and 1.0 inclusively.  Otherwise you can set \sphinxstylestrong{all} global weights to
an arbitrary number between 0.0 or 1.0, like 0.5, and then you have
to override \sphinxstylestrong{all} \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} settings for \sphinxstylestrong{all} sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles which use
the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, and 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 exclusion weights in their force/energy computation.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute/tally} keyword disables or enables registering {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_tally::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
*/tally}}}} computes for the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style specified by
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword.  Use \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} to disable, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} to enable.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “pair\_modify pair compute/tally” command must be issued
\sphinxstylestrong{before} the corresponding compute style is defined.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 3Aug2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh/trim} keyword controls whether an explicit cutoff is set for
each neighbor list request issued by individual pair sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles when
using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair hybrid/overlay}}}}.  When this keyword is
set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, then the cutoff of each pair sub\sphinxhyphen{}style neighbor list will
be set equal to the largest cutoff, even if a shorter cutoff is
specified for a particular sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.  If possible the neighbor list
will be copied directly from another list.  When this keyword is set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} then the cutoff of the neighbor list will be explicitly set to the
value requested by the pair sub\sphinxhyphen{}style, and if possible the list will be
created by trimming neighbors from another list with a longer cutoff,
otherwise a new neighbor list will be created with the specified cutoff.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} option can be faster when there are multiple pair styles with
different cutoffs since the number of pair\sphinxhyphen{}wise distance checks between
neighbors is reduced (but the time required to build the neighbor lists
is increased). The \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} option could be faster when two or more neighbor
lists have similar (but not exactly the same) cutoffs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “pair\_modify neigh/trim” command \sphinxstyleemphasis{only} applies when there are
multiple pair sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles for the same atoms with different cutoffs,
i.e. when using pair style hybrid/overlay.  If you have different
cutoffs for different pairs for atoms type, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor style
multi}}}} should be used to create optimized neighbor lists.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You cannot use \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} yes with \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} yes, since those are
conflicting options.  You cannot use \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} yes with 2d simulations.
You cannot use \sphinxstyleemphasis{special} with pair styles from the GPU or
INTEL package.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_tally::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute */tally}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor multi}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{pair_modify:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are mix = geometric, shift = no, table = 12,
tabinner = sqrt(2.0), tail = no, compute = yes, and neigh/trim yes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that some pair styles perform mixing, but only a certain style of
mixing.  See the doc pages for individual pair styles for details.
