\index{pair\_style@\spxentry{pair\_style}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_style:pair-style-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_style:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_style::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_style:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = one of the styles from the list below

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = arguments used by a particular style

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_style:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eam}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{alloy}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{charmm}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eam}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{none}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the formula(s) LAMMPS uses to compute pairwise interactions.  In
LAMMPS, pair potentials are defined between pairs of atoms that are
within a cutoff distance and the set of active interactions typically
changes over time.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style}}}} command to
define potentials between pairs of bonded atoms, which typically
remain in place for the duration of a simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, pairwise force fields encompass a variety of interactions,
some of which include many\sphinxhyphen{}body effects, e.g. EAM, Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber,
Tersoff, REBO potentials.  They are still classified as “pairwise”
potentials because the set of interacting atoms changes with time
(unlike molecular bonds) and thus a neighbor list is used to find
nearby interacting atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Hybrid models where specified pairs of atom types interact via
different pair potentials can be setup using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficients associated with a pair style are typically set for
each pair of atom types, and are specified by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command or read from a file by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command sets options for mixing of
type I\sphinxhyphen{}J interaction coefficients and adding energy offsets or tail
corrections to Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potentials.  Details on these options as
they pertain to individual potentials are described on the doc page
for the potential.  Likewise, info on whether the potential
information is stored in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{write_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart file}}}} is listed
on the potential doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the formulas listed for each pair style, \sphinxstyleemphasis{E} is the energy of a
pairwise interaction between two atoms separated by a distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{r}.
The force between the atoms is the negative derivative of this
expression.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the pair\_style command has a cutoff argument, it sets global
cutoffs for all pairs of atom types.  The distance(s) can be smaller
or larger than the dimensions of the simulation box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In many cases, the global cutoff value can be overridden for a
specific pair of atom types by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a new pair\_style command is specified with a new style, all
previous {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command settings are erased; those commands must be
re\sphinxhyphen{}specified if necessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a new pair\_style command is specified with the same style, then
only the global settings in that command are reset.  Any previous
doc:\sphinxtitleref{pair\_coeff \textless{}pair\_coeff\textgreater{}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
command settings are preserved.  The only exception is that if the
global cutoff in the pair\_style command is changed, it will override
the corresponding cutoff in any of the previous {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two pair styles which do not follow this rule are the pair\_style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{table} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} commands.  A new pair\_style command for these
styles will wipe out all previously specified {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} settings, including
for the sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

Click on the style to display the formula it computes, any additional
arguments specified in the pair\_style command, and coefficients
specified by the associated {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{pair\_write command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_write:pair-write-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_write:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_write::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_write:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{outer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Qi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Qj}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
itype,jtype = 2 atom types (numeric or type label)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = \# of values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{r} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rsq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
inner,outer = inner and outer cutoff (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file = name of file to write values to

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = section name in file for this set of tabulated values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Qi,Qj = 2 atom charges (charge units) (optional)

\end{itemize}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Yukawa\PYGZus{}1\PYGZus{}1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}

\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{r}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table.txt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LJ}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_write:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write energy and force values to a file as a function of distance for
the currently defined pair potential.  This is useful for plotting the
potential function or otherwise debugging its values.  If the file
already exists, the table of values is appended to the end of the file
to allow multiple tables of energy and force to be included in one
file.  In case a new file is created, the first line will be a comment
containing a “DATE:” and “UNITS:” tag with the current date and the
current {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} setting as argument.  For subsequent
invocations of the pair\_write command, the current units setting is
compared against the entry in the file, if present, and pair\_write
will refuse to add a table if the units are not the same.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy and force values are computed at distances from inner to
outer for 2 interacting atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{itype} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtype}, using the
appropriate {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} coefficients.  If the style
is \sphinxstyleemphasis{r}, then N distances are used, evenly spaced in r; if the style is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rsq}, N distances are used, evenly spaced in r\textasciicircum{}2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, for N = 7, style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{r}, inner = 1.0, and outer = 4.0,
values are computed at r = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the style is \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap}, then 2\textasciicircum{}N values are written to the file in a
format and order consistent with how they are read in by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command for pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table}.  For
reasonable accuracy in a bitmapped table, choose N \textgreater{}= 12, an \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}
value that is smaller than the distance of closest approach of 2
atoms, and an \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} value \textless{}= cutoff of the potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the pair potential is computed between charged atoms, the charges
of the pair of interacting atoms can optionally be specified.  If not
specified, values of Qi = Qj = 1.0 are used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file is written in the format used as input for the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} option with \sphinxstyleemphasis{keyword} as the
section name.  Each line written to the file lists an index number
(1\sphinxhyphen{}N), a distance (in distance units), an energy (in energy units),
and a force (in force units).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_write:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All force field coefficients for pair and other kinds of interactions
must be set before this command can be invoked.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Due to how the pairwise force is computed, an inner value \textgreater{} 0.0 must
be specified even if the potential has a finite value at r = 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_write} command can only be used for pairwise additive
interactions for which a \sphinxtitleref{Pair::single()} function can be and has
been implemented.  This excludes for example manybody potentials
or TIP4P coulomb styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{partition:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command invokes the specified command on a subset of the
partitions of processors you have defined via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Normally, every input script command in your script is invoked by
every partition.  This behavior can be modified by defining world\sphinxhyphen{} or
universe\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} that have different values
for each partition.  This mechanism can be used to cause your script
to jump to different input script files on different partitions, if
such a variable is used in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “partition” command is another mechanism for having as input
script operate differently on different partitions.  It is basically a
prefix on any LAMMPS command.  The command will only be invoked on
the partition(s) specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{style} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} arguments.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{style} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, the command will be invoked on any partition
which matches the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} argument.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{style} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} the command
will be invoked on all the partitions which do not match the Np
argument.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Partitions are numbered from 1 to Np, where Np is the number of
partitions specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} can be specified in one of two ways.  An explicit numeric value
can be used, as in the first example above.  Or a wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can
be used to span a range of partition numbers.  This takes the form “*”
or “*n” or “n*” or “m*n”.  An asterisk with no numeric values means
all partitions from 1 to Np.  A leading asterisk means all partitions
from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing asterisk means all partitions
from n to Np (inclusive).  A middle asterisk means all partitions from
m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can be useful for the “run\_style verlet/split” command
which imposed requirements on how the {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}}
command lays out a 3d grid of processors in each of 2 partitions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style verlet/split}}}}

\index{plugin@\spxentry{plugin}}\ignorespaces 

\section{plugin command}
\label{\detokenize{plugin:plugin-command}}\label{\detokenize{plugin:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{plugin::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{plugin:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{plugin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
command = \sphinxstyleemphasis{load} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{unload} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{list} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{clear}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = list of arguments for a particular plugin command
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{load} file = load plugin(s) from shared object in \sphinxstyleemphasis{file}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{unload} style name = unload plugin \sphinxstyleemphasis{name} of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{style}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{style} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{command}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{list} = print a list of currently loaded plugins
\sphinxstyleemphasis{clear} = unload all currently loaded plugins
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{plugin:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{plugin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{load}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{morse2plugin.so}
\PYG{k}{plugin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{unload}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{morse2}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{omp}
\PYG{k}{plugin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{unload}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hello}
\PYG{k}{plugin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{list}
\PYG{k}{plugin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{clear}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{plugin:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The plugin command allows to load (and unload) additional styles and
commands into a LAMMPS binary from so\sphinxhyphen{}called dynamic shared object (DSO)
files.  This enables to add new functionality to an existing LAMMPS
binary without having to recompile and link the entire executable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{load} command will load and initialize all plugins contained in the
plugin DSO with the given filename.  A message with information the
plugin style and name and more will be printed.  Individual DSO files
may contain multiple plugins.  More details about how to write and
compile the plugin DSO is given in programmer’s guide part of the manual
under {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_plugins::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Writing plugins}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{unload} command will remove the given style or the given name from
the list of available styles.  If the plugin style is currently in use,
that style instance will be deleted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{list} command will print a list of the loaded plugins and their
styles and names.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{clear} command will unload all currently loaded plugins.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Automatic loading of plugins}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 4May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the environment variable \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_PLUGIN\_PATH}} is set, then
LAMMPS will search the directory (or directories) listed in this path
for files with names that end in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{plugin.so}}
(e.g. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{helloplugin.so}}) and will try to load the contained plugins
automatically at start\sphinxhyphen{}up.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{plugin:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{plugin} command is part of the PLUGIN package.  It is
only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If plugins access functions or classes from a package,
LAMMPS must have been compiled with that package included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Plugins are dependent on the LAMMPS binary interface (ABI)
and particularly the MPI library used. So they are not guaranteed
to work when the plugin was compiled with a different MPI library
or different compilation settings or a different LAMMPS version.
There are no checks, so if there is a mismatch the plugin object
will either not load or data corruption and crashes may happen.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{plugin:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{plugin:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{prd@\spxentry{prd}}\ignorespaces 

\section{prd command}
\label{\detokenize{prd:prd-command}}\label{\detokenize{prd:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{prd::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{prd:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{prd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}event}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{n\PYGZus{}dephase}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}dephase}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}correlate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = \# of timesteps to run (not including dephasing/quenching)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
t\_event = timestep interval between event checks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
n\_dephase = number of velocity randomizations to perform in each dephase run

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
t\_dephase = number of timesteps to run dynamics after each velocity randomization during dephase

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
t\_correlate = number of timesteps within which 2 consecutive events are considered to be correlated

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of the compute used for event detection

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
random\_seed = random \# seed (positive integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{min} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{time}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{min} values = etol ftol maxiter maxeval
  etol = stopping tolerance for energy, used in quenching
  ftol = stopping tolerance for force, used in quenching
  maxiter = max iterations of minimize, used in quenching
  maxeval = max number of force/energy evaluations, used in quenching
\sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} value = Tdephase
  Tdephase = target temperature for velocity randomization, used in dephasing
\sphinxstyleemphasis{vel} values = loop dist
  loop = \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{local} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{geom}, used in dephasing
  dist = \sphinxstyleemphasis{uniform} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gaussian}, used in dephasing
\sphinxstyleemphasis{time} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{steps} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{clock}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{steps} = simulation runs for N timesteps on each replica (default)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{clock} = simulation runs for N timesteps across all replicas
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{prd:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{prd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{54982}
\PYG{k}{prd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{54982}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{prd:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run a parallel replica dynamics (PRD) simulation using multiple
replicas of a system.  One or more replicas can be used.  The total
number of steps \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} to run can be interpreted in one of two ways; see
discussion of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} keyword below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
PRD is described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{prd:voter1998}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Voter1998)}}}} by Art Voter.
Similar to global or local hyperdynamics (HD), PRD is a method for
performing accelerated dynamics that is suitable for infrequent\sphinxhyphen{}event
systems that obey first\sphinxhyphen{}order kinetics.  A good overview of
accelerated dynamics methods (AMD) for such systems in given in this
review paper {\hyperref[\detokenize{prd:voter2002prd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Voter2002)}}}} from Art’s group.  To
quote from the paper: “The dynamical evolution is characterized by
vibrational excursions within a potential basin, punctuated by
occasional transitions between basins.  The transition probability is
characterized by p(t) = k*exp(\sphinxhyphen{}kt) where k is the rate constant.”

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both PRD and HD produce a time\sphinxhyphen{}accurate trajectory that effectively
extends the timescale over which a system can be simulated, but they
do it differently.  PRD creates Nr replicas of the system and runs
dynamics on each independently with a normal unbiased potential until
an event occurs in one of the replicas.  The time between events is
reduced by a factor of Nr replicas.  HD uses a single replica of the
system and accelerates time by biasing the interaction potential in a
manner such that each timestep is effectively longer.  For both
methods, per CPU second, more physical time elapses and more events
occur.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{hyper::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hyper}}}} page for more info about HD.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In PRD, each replica runs on a partition of one or more processors.
Processor partitions are defined at run\sphinxhyphen{}time using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  Note that if you have MPI
installed, you can run a multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulation with more replicas
(partitions) than you have physical processors, e.g you can run a
10\sphinxhyphen{}replica simulation on one or two processors.  However for PRD, this
makes little sense, since running a replica on virtual instead of
physical processors,offers no effective parallel speed\sphinxhyphen{}up in searching
for infrequent events.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_replica::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto replica}}}} doc
page for further discussion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a PRD simulation is performed, it is assumed that each replica is
running the same model, though LAMMPS does not check for this.
I.e. the simulation domain, the number of atoms, the interaction
potentials, etc should be the same for every replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A PRD run has several stages, which are repeated each time an “event”
occurs in one of the replicas, as explained below.  The logic for a
PRD run is as follows:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
while (time remains):
  dephase for n\_dephase*t\_dephase steps
  until (event occurs on some replica):
    run dynamics for t\_event steps
    quench
    check for uncorrelated event on any replica
  until (no correlated event occurs):
    run dynamics for t\_correlate steps
    quench
    check for correlated event on this replica
  event replica shares state with all replicas
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Before this loop begins, the state of the system on replica 0 is
shared with all replicas, so that all replicas begin from the same
initial state. The first potential energy basin is identified by
quenching (an energy minimization, see below) the initial state and
storing the resulting coordinates for reference.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the first stage, dephasing is performed by each replica
independently to eliminate correlations between replicas.  This is
done by choosing a random set of velocities, based on the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{random\_seed} that is specified, and running \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_dephase} timesteps of
dynamics.  This is repeated \sphinxstyleemphasis{n\_dephase} times.  At each of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{n\_dephase} stages, if an event occurs during the \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_dephase} steps of
dynamics for a particular replica, the replica repeats the stage until
no event occurs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword is not specified, the target temperature for
velocity randomization for each replica is the current temperature of
that replica.  Otherwise, it is the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdephase} temperature.
The style of velocity randomization is controlled using the keyword
\sphinxstyleemphasis{vel} with arguments that have the same meaning as their counterparts
in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the second stage, each replica runs dynamics continuously, stopping
every \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_event} steps to check if a transition event has occurred.
This check is performed by quenching the system and comparing the
resulting atom coordinates to the coordinates from the previous basin.
The first time through the PRD loop, the “previous basin” is the set
of quenched coordinates from the initial state of the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A quench is an energy minimization and is performed by whichever
algorithm has been defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}} command.
Minimization parameters may be set via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_modify}}}} command and by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{min} keyword of the
PRD command.  The latter are the settings that would be used with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.  Note that typically, you do not
need to perform a highly\sphinxhyphen{}converged minimization to detect a transition
event, though you may need to in order to prevent a set of atoms in
the system from relaxing to a saddle point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The event check is performed by a compute with the specified
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.  Currently there is only one compute that works with the
PRD command, which is the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_event_displace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute event/displace}}}} command.  Other
event\sphinxhyphen{}checking computes may be added.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_event_displace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Compute event/displace}}}} checks whether any atom in
the compute group has moved further than a specified threshold
distance.  If so, an “event” has occurred.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the third stage, the replica on which the event occurred (event
replica) continues to run dynamics to search for correlated events.
This is done by running dynamics for \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_correlate} steps, quenching
every \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_event} steps, and checking if another event has occurred.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first time no correlated event occurs, the final state of the
event replica is shared with all replicas, the new basin reference
coordinates are updated with the quenched state, and the outer loop
begins again. While the replica event is searching for correlated
events, all the other replicas also run dynamics and event checking
with the same schedule, but the final states are always overwritten by
the state of the event replica.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The outer loop of the pseudocode above continues until \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} steps of
dynamics have been performed.  Note that \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} only includes the
dynamics of stages 2 and 3, not the steps taken during dephasing or
the minimization iterations of quenching.  The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} is
interpreted in one of two ways, depending on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} keyword.  If
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{steps}, which is the default, then each replica
runs for \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} timesteps.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{clock}, then the
simulation runs until \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} aggregate timesteps across all replicas have
elapsed.  This aggregate time is the “clock” time defined below, which
typically advances nearly M times faster than the timestepping on a
single replica, where M is the number of replicas.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Four kinds of output can be generated during a PRD run: event
statistics, thermodynamic output by each replica, dump files, and
restart files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running with multiple partitions (each of which is a replica in
this case), the print\sphinxhyphen{}out to the screen and master log.lammps file is
limited to event statistics.  Note that if a PRD run is performed on
only a single replica then the event statistics will be intermixed
with the usual thermodynamic output discussed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The quantities printed each time an event occurs are the timestep, CPU
time, clock, event number, a correlation flag, the number of
coincident events, and the replica number of the chosen event.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The timestep is the usual LAMMPS timestep, except that time does not
advance during dephasing or quenches, but only during dynamics.  Note
that are two kinds of dynamics in the PRD loop listed above that
contribute to this timestepping.  The first is when all replicas are
performing independent dynamics, waiting for an event to occur.  The
second is when correlated events are being searched for, but only one
replica is running dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The CPU time is the total elapsed time on each processor, since the
start of the PRD run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The clock is the same as the timestep except that it advances by M
steps per timestep during the first kind of dynamics when the M
replicas are running independently.  The clock advances by only 1 step
per timestep during the second kind of dynamics, when only a single
replica is checking for a correlated event.  Thus “clock” time
represents the aggregate time (in steps) that has effectively elapsed
during a PRD simulation on M replicas.  If most of the PRD run is
spent in the second stage of the loop above, searching for infrequent
events, then the clock will advance nearly M times faster than it
would if a single replica was running.  Note the clock time between
successive events should be drawn from p(t).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The event number is a counter that increments with each event, whether
it is uncorrelated or correlated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The correlation flag will be 0 when an uncorrelated event occurs
during the second stage of the loop listed above, i.e. when all
replicas are running independently.  The correlation flag will be 1
when a correlated event occurs during the third stage of the loop
listed above, i.e. when only one replica is running dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When more than one replica detects an event at the end of the same
event check (every \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_event} steps) during the second stage, then
one of them is chosen at random.  The number of coincident events is
the number of replicas that detected an event.  Normally, this value
should be 1.  If it is often greater than 1, then either the number of
replicas is too large, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_event} is too large.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The replica number is the ID of the replica (from 0 to M\sphinxhyphen{}1) in which
the event occurred.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
When running on multiple partitions, LAMMPS produces additional log
files for each partition, e.g. log.lammps.0, log.lammps.1, etc.  For
the PRD command, these contain the thermodynamic output for each
replica.  You will see short runs and minimizations corresponding to
the dynamics and quench operations of the loop listed above.  The
timestep will be reset appropriately depending on whether the
operation advances time or not.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the PRD command completes, timing statistics for the PRD run are
printed in each replica’s log file, giving a breakdown of how much CPU
time was spent in each stage (dephasing, dynamics, quenching, etc).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Any {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump files}}}} defined in the input script, will be
written to during a PRD run at timesteps corresponding to both
uncorrelated and correlated events.  This means the requested dump
frequency in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} command is ignored.  There will be
one dump file (per dump command) created for all partitions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom coordinates of the dump snapshot are those of the minimum
energy configuration resulting from quenching following a transition
event.  The timesteps written into the dump files correspond to the
timestep at which the event occurred and NOT the clock.  A dump
snapshot corresponding to the initial minimum state used for event
detection is written to the dump file at the beginning of each PRD
run.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} command is used, a single restart file
for all the partitions is generated, which allows a PRD run to be
continued by a new input script in the usual manner.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The restart file is generated at the end of the loop listed above.  If
no correlated events are found, this means it contains a snapshot of
the system at time T + \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_correlate}, where T is the time at which the
uncorrelated event occurred.  If correlated events were found, then it
contains a snapshot of the system at time T + \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_correlate}, where T
is the time of the last correlated event.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The restart frequency specified in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} command
is interpreted differently when performing a PRD run.  It does not
mean the timestep interval between restart files.  Instead it means an
event interval for uncorrelated events.  Thus a frequency of 1 means
write a restart file every time an uncorrelated event occurs.  A
frequency of 10 means write a restart file every 10th uncorrelated
event.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When an input script reads a restart file from a previous PRD run, the
new script can be run on a different number of replicas or processors.
However, it is assumed that \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_correlate} in the new PRD command is
the same as it was previously.  If not, the calculation of the “clock”
value for the first event in the new run will be slightly off.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{prd:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the REPLICA
package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc
page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_correlate} settings must be integer multiples of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_event}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Runs restarted from restart file written during a PRD run will not
produce identical results due to changes in the random numbers used
for dephasing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command cannot be used when any fixes are defined that keep track
of elapsed time to perform time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent operations.  Examples
include the “ave” fixes such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}.
Also {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}}.


\subsection{Related commands}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_event_displace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute event/displace}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{min_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_modify}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{temper::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temper}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neb::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neb}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{tad::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tad}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{hyper::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hyper}}}}


\subsection{Default}

\sphinxAtStartPar

geom gaussian, and time = steps.

\index{print@\spxentry{print}}\ignorespaces 

\section{print command}
\label{\detokenize{print:print-command}}\label{\detokenize{print:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{print::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{print:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{string}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
string = text string to print, which may contain variables

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{append} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{screen} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{file} value = filename
\sphinxstyleemphasis{append} value = filename
\sphinxstyleemphasis{screen} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{print:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Done with equilibration}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{info.dat}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Vol}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}v}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{append}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{info.dat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{screen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{The system volume is now \PYGZdl{}v}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{The system volume is now \PYGZdl{}v}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{NEB calculation 1 complete}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{screen}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{universe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{l+s}{System volume = \PYGZdl{}v}
\PYG{l+s}{System temperature = \PYGZdl{}t}
\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{print:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Print a text string to the screen and logfile.  The text string must
be a single argument, so if it is one line but more than one word, it
should be enclosed in single or double quotes.  To generate multiple
lines of output, the string can be enclosed in triple quotes, as in
the last example above.  If the text string contains variables, they
will be evaluated and their current values printed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023: }support for vector style variables

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command for a description of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} style variables which are typically the most
useful ones to use with the print command.  Equal\sphinxhyphen{} and vector\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables can calculate formulas involving mathematical operations,
atom properties, group properties, thermodynamic properties, global
values calculated by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}},
or references to other {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}}.  Vector\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables are printed in a bracketed, comma\sphinxhyphen{}separated format,
e.g. {[}1,2,3,4{]} or {[}12.5,2,4.6,10.1{]}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_parse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands parse}}}} doc
page, the text string can use “immediate” variables, specified as
\$(formula) with parenthesis, where the numeric formula has the same
syntax as equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} doc page.  This is a convenient way to evaluate a
formula immediately without using the variable command to define a
named variable and then use that variable in the text string.  The
formula can include a trailing colon and format string which
determines the precision with which the numeric value is output.
This is also explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_parse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands parse}}}} doc page.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the print command to be executed multiple times (with
changing variable values), there are 3 options.  First, consider using
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} command, which will print a string
periodically during a simulation.  Second, the print command can be
used as an argument to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} option of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}
command.  Third, the print command could appear in a section of the
input script that is looped over (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} commands).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{append} keyword is used, a filename is specified to
which the output will be written.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} is used, then the
filename is overwritten if it already exists.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{append} is used,
then the filename is appended to if it already exists, or created if
it does not exist.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{screen} keyword is used, output to the screen and logfile can
be turned on or off as desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} keyword is used, output to the global screen and
logfile can be turned on or off as desired. In multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition
calculations, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{screen} option and the corresponding output only
apply to the screen and logfile of the individual partition.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{print:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{print:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{print:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are no file output, screen = yes, and universe = no.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{processors@\spxentry{processors}}\ignorespaces 

\section{processors command}
\label{\detokenize{processors:processors-command}}\label{\detokenize{processors:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{processors::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{processors:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Px}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Py}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Pz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Px,Py,Pz = \# of processors in each dimension of 3d grid overlaying the simulation domain

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/arg pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{grid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{part} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{file}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{grid} arg = gstyle params ...
  gstyle = \sphinxstyleemphasis{onelevel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{onelevel} params = none
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} params = Nc Cx Cy Cz
      Nc = number of cores per node
      Cx,Cy,Cz = \# of cores in each dimension of 3d sub\sphinxhyphen{}grid assigned to each node
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa} params = none
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} params = infile
      infile = file containing grid layout
\sphinxstyleemphasis{numa\_nodes} arg = Nn
      Nn = number of numa domains per node
\sphinxstyleemphasis{map} arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart/reorder} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xyz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xzy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yxz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yzx} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{zxy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{zyx}
   cart = use MPI\_Cart() methods to map processors to 3d grid with reorder = 0
   cart/reorder = use MPI\_Cart() methods to map processors to 3d grid with reorder = 1
   xyz,xzy,yxz,yzx,zxy,zyx = map processors to 3d grid in IJK ordering
\sphinxstyleemphasis{part} args = Psend Precv cstyle
  Psend = partition \# (1 to Np) which will send its processor layout
  Precv = partition \# (1 to Np) which will recv the processor layout
  cstyle = \sphinxstyleemphasis{multiple}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{multiple} = Psend grid will be multiple of Precv grid in each dimension
\sphinxstyleemphasis{file} arg = outfile
  outfile = name of file to write 3d grid of processors to
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{processors:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{map}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xyz}
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{grid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{numa}
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{grid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{twolevel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{grid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myfile}
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{part}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{multiple}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{processors:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Specify how processors are mapped as a regular 3d grid to the global
simulation box.  The mapping involves 2 steps.  First if there are P
processors it means choosing a factorization P = Px by Py by Pz so
that there are Px processors in the x dimension, and similarly for the
y and z dimensions.  Second, the P processors are mapped to the
regular 3d grid.  The arguments to this command control each of these
2 steps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Px, Py, Pz parameters affect the factorization.  Any of the 3
parameters can be specified with an asterisk “*”, which means LAMMPS
will choose the number of processors in that dimension of the grid.
It will do this based on the size and shape of the global simulation
box so as to minimize the surface\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}volume ratio of each processor’s
subdomain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Choosing explicit values for Px or Py or Pz can be used to override
the default manner in which LAMMPS will create the regular 3d grid of
processors, if it is known to be sub\sphinxhyphen{}optimal for a particular problem.
E.g. a problem where the extent of atoms will change dramatically in a
particular dimension over the course of the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The product of Px, Py, Pz must equal P, the total \# of processors
LAMMPS is running on.  For a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{2d simulation}}}}, Pz must
equal 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if you run on a prime number of processors P, then a grid
such as 1 x P x 1 will be required, which may incur extra
communication costs due to the high surface area of each processor’s
subdomain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that if multiple partitions are being used then P is the
number of processors in this partition; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} page for details.  Also note
that you can prefix the processors command with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{partition::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{partition}}}} command to easily specify different
Px,Py,Pz values for different partitions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{partition::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{partition}}}} command to specify
different processor grids for different partitions, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{partition}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{partition}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command only affects the initial regular 3d grid created
when the simulation box is first specified via a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command.  Or if the simulation box is
re\sphinxhyphen{}created via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{replicate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{replicate}}}} command.  The same
regular grid is initially created, regardless of which
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style}}}} command is in effect.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing is never invoked via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}} commands, then the initial regular grid
will persist for all simulations.  If balancing is performed, some of
the methods invoked by those commands retain the logical topology of
the initial 3d grid, and the mapping of processors to the grid
specified by the processors command.  However the grid spacings in
different dimensions may change, so that processors own subdomains of
different sizes.  If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_style tiled}}}} command is
used, methods invoked by the balancing commands may discard the 3d
grid of processors and tile the simulation domain with subdomains of
different sizes and shapes which no longer have a logical 3d
connectivity.  If that occurs, all the information specified by the
processors command is ignored.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{grid} keyword affects the factorization of P into Px,Py,Pz and it
can also affect how the P processor IDs are mapped to the 3d grid of
processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{onelevel} style creates a 3d grid that is compatible with the
Px,Py,Pz settings, and which minimizes the surface\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}volume ratio of
each processor’s subdomain, as described above.  The mapping of
processors to the grid is determined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} keyword setting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} style can be used on machines with multicore nodes to
minimize off\sphinxhyphen{}node communication.  It ensures that contiguous
subsections of the 3d grid are assigned to all the cores of a node.
For example if \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nc} is 4, then 2x2x1 or 2x1x2 or 1x2x2 subsections of
the 3d grid will correspond to the cores of each node.  This affects
both the factorization and mapping steps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Cx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Cy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Cz} settings are similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Px}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Py}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pz}
settings, only their product should equal \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nc}.  Any of the 3
parameters can be specified with an asterisk “*”, which means LAMMPS
will choose the number of cores in that dimension of the node’s
sub\sphinxhyphen{}grid.  As with Px,Py,Pz, it will do this based on the size and
shape of the global simulation box so as to minimize the
surface\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}volume ratio of each processor’s subdomain.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} style to work correctly, it assumes the MPI
ranks of processors LAMMPS is running on are ordered by core and then
by node.  E.g. if you are running on 2 quad\sphinxhyphen{}core nodes, for a total of
8 processors, then it assumes processors 0,1,2,3 are on node 1, and
processors 4,5,6,7 are on node 2.  This is the default rank ordering
for most MPI implementations, but some MPIs provide options for this
ordering, e.g. via environment variable settings.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa} style operates similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} keyword except that
it auto\sphinxhyphen{}detects which cores are running on which nodes.  It will also
subdivide the cores into numa domains. Currently, the number of numa
domains is not auto\sphinxhyphen{}detected and must be specified using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{numa\_nodes} keyword; otherwise, the default value is used. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa}
style uses a different algorithm than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} keyword for doing
the two\sphinxhyphen{}level factorization of the simulation box into a 3d processor
grid to minimize off\sphinxhyphen{}node communication and communication across numa
domains. It does its own MPI\sphinxhyphen{}based mapping of nodes and cores to the
regular 3d grid.  Thus it may produce a different layout of the
processors than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa} style will give an error if the number of MPI processes is
not divisible by the number of cores used per node, or any of the Px
or Py or Pz values is greater than 1.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} style, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa} style does not require
any particular ordering of MPI ranks in order to work correctly. This
is because it auto\sphinxhyphen{}detects which processes are running on which nodes.
However, it assumes that the lowest ranks are in the first numa
domain, and so forth. MPI rank orderings that do not preserve this
property might result in more intra\sphinxhyphen{}node communication between CPUs.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} style uses the file \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} to define both the 3d
factorization and the mapping of processors to the grid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The file should have the following format.  Any number of initial
blank or comment lines (starting with a “\#” character) can be present.
The first non\sphinxhyphen{}blank, non\sphinxhyphen{}comment line should have
3 values:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Px Py Py
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These must be compatible with the total number of processors
and the Px, Py, Pz settings of the processors command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This line should be immediately followed by
P = Px*Py*Pz lines of the form:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ID I J K
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where ID is a processor ID (from 0 to P\sphinxhyphen{}1) and I,J,K are the
processors location in the 3d grid.  I must be a number from 1 to Px
(inclusive) and similarly for J and K.  The P lines can be listed in
any order, but no processor ID should appear more than once.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa\_nodes} keyword is used to specify the number of numa domains
per node. It is currently only used by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{numa} style for two\sphinxhyphen{}level
factorization to reduce the amount of MPI communications between CPUs.
A good setting for this will typically be equal to the number of CPU
sockets per node.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} keyword affects how the P processor IDs (from 0 to P\sphinxhyphen{}1) are
mapped to the 3d grid of processors.  It is only used by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{onelevel} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} grid settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart} style uses the family of MPI Cartesian functions to perform
the mapping, namely MPI\_Cart\_create(), MPI\_Cart\_get(),
MPI\_Cart\_shift(), and MPI\_Cart\_rank().  It invokes the
MPI\_Cart\_create() function with its reorder flag = 0, so that MPI is
not free to reorder the processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart/reorder} style does the same thing as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart} style
except it sets the reorder flag to 1, so that MPI can reorder
processors if it desires.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{xyz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xzy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yxz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yzx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zxy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{zyx} styles are all
similar.  If the style is IJK, then it maps the P processors to the
grid so that the processor ID in the I direction varies fastest, the
processor ID in the J direction varies next fastest, and the processor
ID in the K direction varies slowest.  For example, if you select
style \sphinxstyleemphasis{xyz} and you have a 2x2x2 grid of 8 processors, the assignments
of the 8 octants of the simulation domain will be:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
proc 0 = lo x, lo y, lo z octant
proc 1 = hi x, lo y, lo z octant
proc 2 = lo x, hi y, lo z octant
proc 3 = hi x, hi y, lo z octant
proc 4 = lo x, lo y, hi z octant
proc 5 = hi x, lo y, hi z octant
proc 6 = lo x, hi y, hi z octant
proc 7 = hi x, hi y, hi z octant
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that, in principle, an MPI implementation on a particular machine
should be aware of both the machine’s network topology and the
specific subset of processors and nodes that were assigned to your
simulation.  Thus its MPI\_Cart calls can optimize the assignment of
MPI processes to the 3d grid to minimize communication costs.  In
practice, however, few if any MPI implementations actually do this.
So it is likely that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart/reorder} styles simply give
the same result as one of the IJK styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note, that for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twolevel} grid style, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{map} setting is
used to first map the nodes to the 3d grid, then again to the cores
within each node.  For the latter step, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cart/reorder}
styles are not supported, so an \sphinxstyleemphasis{xyz} style is used in their place.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{part} keyword affects the factorization of P into Px,Py,Pz.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It can be useful when running in multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode, e.g. with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style verlet/split}}}} command.  It specifies a
dependency between a sending partition \sphinxstyleemphasis{Psend} and a receiving
partition \sphinxstyleemphasis{Precv} which is enforced when each is setting up their own
mapping of their processors to the simulation box.  Each of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Psend}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Precv} must be integers from 1 to Np, where Np is the number of
partitions you have defined via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A “dependency” means that the sending partition will create its
regular 3d grid as Px by Py by Pz and after it has done this, it will
send the Px,Py,Pz values to the receiving partition.  The receiving
partition will wait to receive these values before creating its own
regular 3d grid and will use the sender’s Px,Py,Pz values as a
constraint.  The nature of the constraint is determined by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cstyle} argument.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{cstyle} of \sphinxstyleemphasis{multiple}, each dimension of the sender’s processor
grid is required to be an integer multiple of the corresponding
dimension in the receiver’s processor grid.  This is a requirement of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style verlet/split}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, assume the sending partition creates a 4x6x10 grid = 240
processor grid.  If the receiving partition is running on 80
processors, it could create a 4x2x10 grid, but it will not create a
2x4x10 grid, since in the y\sphinxhyphen{}dimension, 6 is not an integer multiple of
4.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{partition::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{partition}}}} command to invoke
different “processors” commands on different partitions, and you also
use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{part} keyword, then you must ensure that both the sending and
receiving partitions invoke the “processors” command that connects the
2 partitions via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{part} keyword.  LAMMPS cannot easily check for
this, but your simulation will likely hang in its setup phase if this
error has been made.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} keyword writes the mapping of the factorization of P
processors and their mapping to the 3d grid to the specified file
\sphinxstyleemphasis{outfile}.  This is useful to check that you assigned physical
processors in the manner you desired, which can be tricky to figure
out, especially when running on multiple partitions or on, a multicore
machine or when the processor ranks were reordered by use of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}reorder command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} or due to use of
MPI\sphinxhyphen{}specific launch options such as a config file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have multiple partitions you should ensure that each one writes
to a different file, e.g. using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{world\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}
for the filename.  The file has a self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory header, followed by
one\sphinxhyphen{}line per processor in this format:

\sphinxAtStartPar
world\sphinxhyphen{}ID universe\sphinxhyphen{}ID original\sphinxhyphen{}ID: I J K: name

\sphinxAtStartPar
The IDs are the processor’s rank in this simulation (the world), the
universe (of multiple simulations), and the original MPI communicator
used to instantiate LAMMPS, respectively.  The world and universe IDs
will only be different if you are running on more than one partition;
see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  The
universe and original IDs will only be different if you used the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}reorder command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to reorder the
processors differently than their rank in the original communicator
LAMMPS was instantiated with.

\sphinxAtStartPar
I,J,K are the indices of the processor in the regular 3d grid, each
from 1 to Nd, where Nd is the number of processors in that dimension
of the grid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{name} is what is returned by a call to MPI\_Get\_processor\_name()
and should represent an identifier relevant to the physical processors
in your machine.  Note that depending on the MPI implementation,
multiple cores can have the same \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{processors:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command cannot be used after the simulation box is defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.
It can be used before a restart file is read to change the 3d
processor grid from what is specified in the restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{grid numa} keyword only currently works with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{map cart}
option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{part} keyword (for the receiving partition) only works with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{grid onelevel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{grid twolevel} options.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{processors:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{partition::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{partition}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}reorder command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{processors:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are Px Py Pz = * * *, grid = onelevel, map =
cart, and numa\_nodes = 2.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{python@\spxentry{python}}\ignorespaces 

\section{python command}
\label{\detokenize{python:python-command}}\label{\detokenize{python:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{python::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{python:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mode = \sphinxstyleemphasis{source} or name of Python function

\sphinxAtStartPar
if mode is \sphinxstyleemphasis{source}:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} or name of a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Python file}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} arg = inline
    inline = one or more lines of Python code which defines func
             must be a single argument, typically enclosed between triple quotes
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Python file} = name of a file with Python code which will be executed immediately
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} is the name of a Python function, one or more keywords with/without arguments must be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{invoke} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{return} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{length} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{exists}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{invoke} arg = none = invoke the previously defined Python function
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} args = N i1 i2 ... iN
    N = \# of inputs to function
    i1,...,iN = value, SELF, or LAMMPS variable name
      value = integer number, floating point number, or string
      SELF = reference to LAMMPS itself which can be accessed by Python function
      variable = v\_name, where name = name of LAMMPS variable, e.g. v\_abc
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{return} arg = varReturn
    varReturn = v\_name  = LAMMPS variable name which the return value of the Python function will be assigned to
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} arg = fstring with M characters
    M = N if no return value, where N = \# of inputs
    M = N+1 if there is a return value
    fstring = each character (i,f,s,p) corresponds in order to an input or return value
    \textquotesingle{}i\textquotesingle{} = integer, \textquotesingle{}f\textquotesingle{} = floating point, \textquotesingle{}s\textquotesingle{} = string, \textquotesingle{}p\textquotesingle{} = SELF
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{length} arg = Nlen
    Nlen = max length of string returned from Python function
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} arg = filename
    filename = file of Python code, which defines func
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} arg = inline
    inline = one or more lines of Python code which defines func
             must be a single argument, typically enclosed between triple quotes
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{exists} arg = none = Python code has been loaded by previous python command
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pForce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{invoke}

\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{factorial}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myN}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}fac}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ii}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{here}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SELF}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{here}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{l+s}{  \PYGZsh{} loop N times, increasing cutoff each time}

\PYG{l+s}{  for i in range(N):}
\PYG{l+s}{    cut = cut0 + i*0.1}
\PYG{l+s}{    lmp.set\PYGZus{}variable(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{,cut)               \PYGZsh{} set a variable in LAMMPS}
\PYG{l+s}{    lmp.command(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{cut}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{)   \PYGZsh{} LAMMPS commands}
\PYG{l+s}{    lmp.command(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{)}
\PYG{l+s}{    lmp.command(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{n}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{)}
\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{funcdef.py}

\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{here}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{from lammps import lammps}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
