\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{python:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} command allows interfacing LAMMPS with an embedded Python
interpreter and enables either executing arbitrary python code in that
interpreter, registering a Python function for future execution (as a
python style variable, from a fix interfaced with python, or for direct
invocation), or invoking such a previously registered function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Arguments, including LAMMPS variables, can be passed to the function
from the LAMMPS input script and a value returned by the Python function
assigned to a LAMMPS variable.  The Python code for the function can be included
directly in the input script or in a separate Python file.  The function
can be standard Python code or it can make “callbacks” to LAMMPS through
its library interface to query or set internal values within LAMMPS.
This is a powerful mechanism for performing complex operations in a
LAMMPS input script that are not possible with the simple input script
and variable syntax which LAMMPS defines.  Thus your input script can
operate more like a true programming language.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use of this command requires building LAMMPS with the PYTHON package
which links to the Python library so that the Python interpreter is
embedded in LAMMPS.  More details about this process are given below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two ways to invoke a Python function once it has been
registered.  One is using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{invoke} keyword.  The other is to assign
the function to a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} defined in
your input script.  Whenever the variable is evaluated, it will execute
the Python function to assign a value to the variable.  Note that
variables can be evaluated in many different ways within LAMMPS.  They
can be substituted with their result directly in an input script, or
they can be passed to various commands as arguments, so that the
variable is evaluated during a simulation run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A broader overview of how Python can be used with LAMMPS is given in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Use Python with LAMMPS}}}} section of the
documentation.  There also is an \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/python}} directory which
illustrates use of the python command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The first argument of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} command is either the \sphinxstyleemphasis{source}
keyword or the name of a Python function.  This defines the mode
of the python command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{source} keyword is used, it is followed by either a file name or
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} keyword.  No other keywords can be used.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} keyword
is followed by a string with python commands, either on a single line
enclosed in quotes, or as multiple lines enclosed in triple quotes.
These Python commands will be passed to the python interpreter and
executed immediately without registering a Python function for future
execution.  The code will be loaded into and run in the “main” module of
the Python interpreter.  This allows running arbitrary Python code at
any time while processing the LAMMPS input file.  This can be used to
pre\sphinxhyphen{}load Python modules, initialize global variables, define functions
or classes, or perform operations using the python programming language.
The Python code will be executed in parallel on all MPI processes.  No
arguments can be passed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In all other cases, the first argument is the name of a Python function
that will be registered with LAMMPS for future execution.  The function
may already be defined (see \sphinxstyleemphasis{exists} keyword) or must be defined using
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} keywords as explained below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{invoke} keyword is used, no other keywords can be used, and a
previous \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} command must have registered the Python function
referenced by this command.  This invokes the Python function with the
previously defined arguments and the return value is processed as
explained below.  You can invoke the function as many times as you wish
in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} keyword defines how many arguments \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} the Python function
expects.  If it takes no arguments, then the \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} keyword should not
be used.  Each argument can be specified directly as a value, e.g. ‘6’
or ‘3.14159’ or ‘abc’ (a string of characters).  The type of each
argument is specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} keyword as explained below, so
that Python will know how to interpret the value.  If the word SELF is
used for an argument it has a special meaning.  A pointer is passed to
the Python function which it can convert into a reference to LAMMPS
itself using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{LAMMPS Python module}}}}.  This
enables the function to call back to LAMMPS through its library
interface as explained below.  This allows the Python function to query
or set values internal to LAMMPS which can affect the subsequent
execution of the input script.  A LAMMPS variable can also be used as an
argument, specified as v\_name, where “name” is the name of the variable.
Any style of LAMMPS variable returning a scalar or a string can be used,
as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{format}
keyword must be used to set the type of data that is passed to Python.
Each time the Python function is invoked, the LAMMPS variable is
evaluated and its value is passed to the Python function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{return} keyword is only needed if the Python function returns a
value.  The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{varReturn} must be of the form v\_name, where
“name” is the name of a python\sphinxhyphen{}style LAMMPS variable, defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command.  The Python function can return a
numeric or string value, as specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} doc page, the definition
of a python\sphinxhyphen{}style variable associates a Python function name with the
variable.  This must match the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Python function name} first argument of
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} command.  For example these two commands would be
consistent:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{foo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myMultiply}
\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myMultiply}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}foo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{funcs.py}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two commands can appear in either order in the input script so
long as both are specified before the Python function is invoked for
the first time.  Afterwards, the variable ‘foo’ is associated with
the Python function ‘myMultiply’.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} keyword must be used if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{return} keywords
are used.  It defines an \sphinxstyleemphasis{fstring} with M characters, where M = sum of
number of inputs and outputs.  The order of characters corresponds to
the N inputs, followed by the return value (if it exists).  Each
character must be one of the following: “i” for integer, “f” for
floating point, “s” for string, or “p” for SELF.  Each character defines
the type of the corresponding input or output value of the Python
function and affects the type conversion that is performed internally as
data is passed back and forth between LAMMPS and Python.  Note that it
is permissible to use a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} in a
LAMMPS command that allows for an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable as an argument,
but only if the output of the Python function is flagged as a numeric
value (“i” or “f”) via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{return} keyword is used and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} keyword specifies the
output as a string, then the default maximum length of that string is
63 characters (64\sphinxhyphen{}1 for the string terminator).  If you want to return
a longer string, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{length} keyword can be specified with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nlen}
value set to a larger number (the code allocates space for Nlen+1 to
include the string terminator).  If the Python function generates a
string longer than the default 63 or the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nlen}, it will be
truncated.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Either the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{here}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{exists} keyword must be used, but only
one of them.  These keywords specify what Python code to load into the
Python interpreter.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} keyword gives the name of a file
containing Python code, which should end with a “.py” suffix.  The code
will be immediately loaded into and run in the “main” module of the
Python interpreter.  The Python code will be executed in parallel on all
MPI processes.  Note that Python code which contains a function
definition does not “execute” the function when it is run; it simply
defines the function so that it can be invoked later.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} keyword does the same thing, except that the Python code
follows as a single argument to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} keyword.  This can be done
using triple quotes as delimiters, as in the examples above.  This
allows Python code to be listed verbatim in your input script, with
proper indentation, blank lines, and comments, as desired.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_parse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands parse}}}} doc page, for an explanation of
how triple quotes can be used as part of input script syntax.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{exists} keyword takes no argument.  It means that Python code
containing the required Python function with the given name has already
been executed, for example by a \sphinxstyleemphasis{python source} command or in the same
file that was used previously with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the Python code that is loaded and run must contain a function
with the specified function name.  To operate properly when later
invoked, the function code must match the \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{return} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{format} keywords specified by the python command.  Otherwise Python
will generate an error.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This section describes how Python code can be written to work with
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Whether you load Python code from a file or directly from your input
script, via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{here} keywords, the code can be identical.
It must be indented properly as Python requires.  It can contain
comments or blank lines.  If the code is in your input script, it cannot
however contain triple\sphinxhyphen{}quoted Python strings, since that will conflict
with the triple\sphinxhyphen{}quote parsing that the LAMMPS input script performs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All the Python code you specify via one or more python commands is
loaded into the Python “main” module, i.e. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_\_name\_\_ == \textquotesingle{}\_\_main\_\_\textquotesingle{}}}.
The code can define global variables, define global functions, define
classes or execute statements that are outside of function definitions.
It can contain multiple functions, only one of which matches the \sphinxstyleemphasis{func}
setting in the python command.  This means you can use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file}
keyword once to load several functions, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{exists} keyword
thereafter in subsequent python commands to register the other functions
that were previously loaded with LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A Python function you define (or more generally, the code you load)
can import other Python modules or classes, it can make calls to other
system functions or functions you define, and it can access or modify
global variables (in the “main” module) which will persist between
successive function calls.  The latter can be useful, for example, to
prevent a function from being invoke multiple times per timestep by
different commands in a LAMMPS input script that access the returned
python\sphinxhyphen{}style variable associated with the function.  For example,
consider this function loaded with two global variables defined
outside the function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{nsteplast} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
\PYG{n}{nvaluelast} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}

\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{expensive}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nstep}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
  \PYG{k}{global} \PYG{n}{nsteplast}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{nvaluelast}
  \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{nstep} \PYG{o}{==} \PYG{n}{nsteplast}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{nvaluelast}
  \PYG{n}{nsteplast} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nstep}
  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} perform complicated calculation}
  \PYG{n}{nvalue} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
  \PYG{n}{nvaluelast} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nvalue}
  \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{nvalue}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The variable ‘nsteplast’ stores the previous timestep the function was
invoked (passed as an argument to the function).  The variable
‘nvaluelast’ stores the return value computed on the last function
invocation.  If the function is invoked again on the same timestep, the
previous value is simply returned, without re\sphinxhyphen{}computing it.  The
“global” statement inside the Python function allows it to overwrite the
global variables from within the local context of the function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if you load Python code multiple times (via multiple python
commands), you can overwrite previously loaded variables and functions
if you are not careful.  E.g. if the code above were loaded twice, the
global variables would be re\sphinxhyphen{}initialized, which might not be what you
want.  Likewise, if a function with the same name exists in two chunks
of Python code you load, the function loaded second will override the
function loaded first.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It’s important to realize that if you are running LAMMPS in parallel,
each MPI task will load the Python interpreter and execute a local
copy of the Python function(s) you define.  There is no connection
between the Python interpreters running on different processors.
This implies three important things.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First, if you put a print or other statement creating output to the
screen in your Python function, you will see P copies of the output,
when running on P processors.  If the prints occur at (nearly) the same
time, the P copies of the output may be mixed together.  When loading
the LAMMPS Python module into the embedded Python interpreter, it is
possible to pass the pointer to the current LAMMPS class instance and
via the Python interface to the LAMMPS library interface, it is possible
to determine the MPI rank of the current process and thus adapt the
Python code so that output will only appear on MPI rank 0.  The
following LAMMPS input demonstrates how this could be done. The text
‘Hello, LAMMPS!’ should be printed only once, even when running LAMMPS
in parallel.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python\PYGZus{}hello}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SELF}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{here}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{l+s}{def python\PYGZus{}hello(handle):}
\PYG{l+s}{    from lammps import lammps}
\PYG{l+s}{    lmp = lammps(ptr=handle)}
\PYG{l+s}{    me = lmp.extract\PYGZus{}setting(\PYGZsq{}world\PYGZus{}rank\PYGZsq{})}
\PYG{l+s}{    if me == 0:}
\PYG{l+s}{        print(\PYGZsq{}Hello, LAMMPS!\PYGZsq{})}
\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python\PYGZus{}hello}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{invoke}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If your Python code loads Python modules that are not pre\sphinxhyphen{}loaded by the
Python library, then it will load the module from disk.  This may be a
bottleneck if 1000s of processors try to load a module at the same time.
On some large supercomputers, loading of modules from disk by Python may
be disabled.  In this case you would need to pre\sphinxhyphen{}build a Python library
that has the required modules pre\sphinxhyphen{}loaded and link LAMMPS with that
library.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Third, if your Python code calls back to LAMMPS (discussed in the
next section) and causes LAMMPS to perform an MPI operation requires
global communication (e.g. via MPI\_Allreduce), such as computing the
global temperature of the system, then you must ensure all your Python
functions (running independently on different processors) call back to
LAMMPS.  Otherwise the code may hang.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Your Python function can “call back” to LAMMPS through its
library interface, if you use the SELF input to pass Python
a pointer to LAMMPS.  The mechanism for doing this in your
Python function is as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{foo}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{handle}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
  \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}
  \PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{handle}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{print }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Hello from inside Python}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The function definition must include a variable (‘handle’ in this case)
which corresponds to SELF in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} command.  The first line of
the function imports the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{“lammps” Python module}}}}.
The second line creates a Python object \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lmp}} which wraps the instance
of LAMMPS that called the function.  The ‘ptr=handle’ argument is what
makes that happen.  The third line invokes the command() function in the
LAMMPS library interface.  It takes a single string argument which is a
LAMMPS input script command for LAMMPS to execute, the same as if it
appeared in your input script.  In this case, LAMMPS should output

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Hello from inside Python
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
to the screen and log file.  Note that since the LAMMPS print command
itself takes a string in quotes as its argument, the Python string
must be delimited with a different style of quotes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Use Python with LAMMPS}}}} page describes the syntax
for how Python wraps the various functions included in the LAMMPS
library interface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A more interesting example is in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/python/in.python}} script
which loads and runs the following function from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/python/funcs.py}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{loop}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{cut0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{thresh}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{lmpptr}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
  \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{LOOP ARGS}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{N}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{cut0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{thresh}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{lmpptr}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{lammps}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lammps}
  \PYG{n}{lmp} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lammps}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{ptr}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{lmpptr}\PYG{p}{)}
  \PYG{n}{natoms} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}natoms}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

  \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{cut} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{cut0} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{n}{i}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.1}

    \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{set\PYGZus{}variable}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{cut}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{p}{)}                 \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set a variable in LAMMPS}
    \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pair\PYGZus{}style lj/cut \PYGZdl{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}cut\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}     \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} LAMMPS command}
    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}lmp.command(\PYGZdq{}pair\PYGZus{}style lj/cut \PYGZpc{}d\PYGZdq{} \PYGZpc{} cut)  \PYGZsh{} LAMMPS command option}

    \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff * * 1.0 1.0}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}       \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} ditto}
    \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{command}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{run 10}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}                       \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} ditto}
    \PYG{n}{pe} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lmp}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{thermo\PYGZus{}pe}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}   \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} extract total PE from LAMMPS}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{PE}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{natoms}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{thresh}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{natoms} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}} \PYG{n}{thresh}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{k}{return}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with these input script commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{4.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SELF}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iffp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{funcs.py}
\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{invoke}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This has the effect of looping over a series of 10 short runs (10
timesteps each) where the pair style cutoff is increased from a value
of 1.0 in distance units, in increments of 0.1.  The looping stops
when the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy falls below a threshold of \sphinxhyphen{}4.0 in
energy units.  More generally, Python can be used to implement a loop
with complex logic, much more so than can be created using the LAMMPS
{\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{if::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{if}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Several LAMMPS library functions are called from the loop function.
Get\_natoms() returns the number of atoms in the simulation, so that it
can be used to normalize the potential energy that is returned by
extract\_compute() for the “thermo\_pe” compute that is defined by
default for LAMMPS thermodynamic output.  Set\_variable() sets the
value of a string variable defined in LAMMPS.  This library function
is a useful way for a Python function to return multiple values to
LAMMPS, more than the single value that can be passed back via a
return statement.  This cutoff value in the “cut” variable is then
substituted (by LAMMPS) in the pair\_style command that is executed
next.  Alternatively, the “LAMMPS command option” line could be used
in place of the 2 preceding lines, to have Python insert the value
into the LAMMPS command string.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the callback mechanism just described, recognize that
there are some operations you should not attempt because LAMMPS cannot
execute them correctly.  If the Python function is invoked between
runs in the LAMMPS input script, then it should be OK to invoke any
LAMMPS input script command via the library interface command() or
file() functions, so long as the command would work if it were
executed in the LAMMPS input script directly at the same point.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, a Python function can also be invoked during a run, whenever
an associated LAMMPS variable it is assigned to is evaluated.  If the
variable is an input argument to another LAMMPS command (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}}), then the Python function will be invoked
inside the class for that command, in one of its methods that is
invoked in the middle of a timestep.  You cannot execute arbitrary
input script commands from the Python function (again, via the
command() or file() functions) at that point in the run and expect it
to work.  Other library functions such as those that invoke computes
or other variables may have hidden side effects as well.  In these
cases, LAMMPS has no simple way to check that something illogical is
being attempted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The same applies to Python functions called during a simulation run at
each time step using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_python_invoke::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix python/invoke}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If you run Python code directly on your workstation, either
interactively or by using Python to launch a Python script stored in a
file, and your code has an error, you will typically see informative
error messages.  That is not the case when you run Python code from
LAMMPS using an embedded Python interpreter.  The code will typically
fail silently.  LAMMPS will catch some errors but cannot tell you
where in the Python code the problem occurred.  For example, if the
Python code cannot be loaded and run because it has syntax or other
logic errors, you may get an error from Python pointing to the
offending line, or you may get one of these generic errors from
LAMMPS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Could not process Python file
Could not process Python string
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the Python function is invoked, if it does not return properly,
you will typically get this generic error from LAMMPS:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Python function evaluation failed
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are three suggestions for debugging your Python code while
running it under LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First, don’t run it under LAMMPS, at least to start with!  Debug it
using plain Python.  Load and invoke your function, pass it arguments,
check return values, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Second, add Python print statements to the function to check how far
it gets and intermediate values it calculates.  See the discussion
above about printing from Python when running in parallel.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Third, use Python exception handling.  For example, say this statement
in your Python function is failing, because you have not initialized the
variable foo:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{foo} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you put one (or more) statements inside a “try” statement,
like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{exceptions}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Inside simple function}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{k}{try}\PYG{p}{:}
  \PYG{n}{foo} \PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}      \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} one or more statements here}
\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n+ne}{Exception} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{e}\PYG{p}{:}
  \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{FOO error:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{e}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
then you will get this message printed to the screen:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
FOO error: local variable \PYGZsq{}foo\PYGZsq{} referenced before assignment
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If there is no error in the try statements, then nothing is printed.
Either way the function continues on (unless you put a return or
sys.exit() in the except clause).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{python:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command is part of the PYTHON package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Building LAMMPS with the PYTHON package will link LAMMPS with the Python
library on your system.  Settings to enable this are in the
lib/python/Makefile.lammps file.  See the lib/python/README file for
information on those settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use Python code which calls back to LAMMPS, via the SELF input
argument explained above, there is an extra step required when building
LAMMPS.  LAMMPS must also be built as a shared library and your Python
function must be able to load the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_module::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{“lammps” Python module}}}} that wraps the LAMMPS library interface.  These are the
same steps required to use Python by itself to wrap LAMMPS.  Details on
these steps are explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Python_head::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Python}}}} doc page.
Note that it is important that the stand\sphinxhyphen{}alone LAMMPS executable and the
LAMMPS shared library be consistent (built from the same source code
files) in order for this to work.  If the two have been built at
different times using different source files, problems may occur.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another limitation of calling back to Python from the LAMMPS module
using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} command in a LAMMPS input is that both, the Python
interpreter and LAMMPS, must be linked to the same Python runtime as a
shared library.  If the Python interpreter is linked to Python
statically (which seems to happen with Conda) then loading the shared
LAMMPS library will create a second python “main” module that hides the
one from the Python interpreter and all previous defined function and
global variables will become invisible.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{python:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{shell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{shell}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_python_invoke::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix python/invoke}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{python:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{quit@\spxentry{quit}}\ignorespaces 

\section{quit command}
\label{\detokenize{quit:quit-command}}\label{\detokenize{quit:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{quit::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{quit:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{quit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{status}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
status = numerical exit status (optional)


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{quit:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{quit}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdl{}n \PYGZgt{} 10000}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{quit 1}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{quit:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command causes LAMMPS to exit, after shutting down all output
cleanly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It can be used as a debug statement in an input script, to terminate
the script at some intermediate point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It can also be used as an invoked command inside the “then” or “else”
portion of an {\hyperref[\detokenize{if::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{if}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional status argument is an integer which signals the return
status to a program calling LAMMPS.  A return status of 0 usually
indicates success.  A status != 0 is failure, where the specified
value can be used to distinguish the kind of error, e.g. where in the
input script the quit was invoked.  If not specified, a status of 0 is
returned.
