\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{outside}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{union}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{side1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{side2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{side3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{side4}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{side}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{move}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}left}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}up}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{openbox}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{block}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{open}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{open}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{funnel}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cone}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{open}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{region:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command defines a geometric region of space.  Various other
commands use regions.  For example, the region can be filled with
atoms via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command.  Or a bounding
box around the region, can be used to define the simulation box via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} command.  Or the atoms in the region
can be identified as a group via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}} command, or
deleted via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_atoms}}}} command.  Or the
surface of the region can be used as a boundary wall via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall_region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/region}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Commands which use regions typically test whether an atom’s position
is contained in the region or not.  For this purpose, coordinates
exactly on the region boundary are considered to be interior to the
region.  This means, for example, for a spherical region, an atom on
the sphere surface would be part of the region if the sphere were
defined with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{side in} keyword, but would not be part of the
region if it were defined using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{side out} keyword.  See more
details on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{side} keyword below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Normally, regions in LAMMPS are “static”, meaning their geometric
extent does not change with time.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{move} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keyword
is used, as described below, the region becomes “dynamic”, meaning
it’s location or orientation changes with time.  This may be useful,
for example, when thermostatting a region, via the compute temp/region
command, or when the fix wall/region command uses a region surface as
a bounding wall on particle motion, i.e. a rotating container.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} style removes the named region.  Since there is little
overhead to defining extra regions, there is normally no need to do
this, unless you are defining and discarding large numbers of regions
in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The lo/hi values for \sphinxstyleemphasis{block} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism} styles
can be specified as EDGE or INF.  EDGE means they extend all the way
to the global simulation box boundary.  Note that this is the current
box boundary; if the box changes size during a simulation, the region
does not.  INF means a large negative or positive number (1.0e20), so
it should encompass the simulation box even if it changes size.  If a
region is defined before the simulation box has been created (via
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands), then an EDGE or INF
parameter cannot be used.  For a \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism} region, a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero tilt
factor in any pair of dimensions cannot be used if both the lo/hi
values in either of those dimensions are INF.  E.g. if the xy tilt is
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, then xlo and xhi cannot both be INF, nor can ylo and yhi.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Regions in LAMMPS do not get wrapped across periodic boundaries,
as specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}} command.  For example, a
spherical region that is defined so that it overlaps a periodic
boundary is not treated as 2 half\sphinxhyphen{}spheres, one on either side of the
simulation box.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Regions in LAMMPS are always 3d geometric objects, regardless of
whether the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dimension}}}} of a simulation is 2d or 3d.
Thus when using regions in a 2d simulation, you should be careful to
define the region so that its intersection with the 2d x\sphinxhyphen{}y plane of
the simulation has the 2d geometric extent you want.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone}, an axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned cone is defined which is like a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder} except that two different radii (one at each end) can be
defined.  Either of the radii (but not both) can be 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder}, the c1,c2 params are coordinates in
the 2 other dimensions besides the cylinder axis dimension.  For dim =
x, c1/c2 = y/z; for dim = y, c1/c2 = x/z; for dim = z, c1/c2 = x/y.
Thus the third example above specifies a cylinder with its axis in the
y\sphinxhyphen{}direction located at x = 2.0 and z = 3.0, with a radius of 5.0, and
extending in the y\sphinxhyphen{}direction from \sphinxhyphen{}5.0 to the upper box boundary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 4May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ellipsoid}, an axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned ellipsoid is defined. The
ellipsoid has its center at (x,y,z) and is defined by 3 axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned
vectors given by A = (a,0,0); B = (0,b,0); C = (0,0,c).  Note that
although the ellipsoid is specified as axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned it can be rotated
via the optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{plane}, a plane is defined which contain the point
(px,py,pz) and has a normal vector (nx,ny,nz).  The normal vector does
not have to be of unit length.  The “inside” of the plane is the
half\sphinxhyphen{}space in the direction of the normal vector; see the discussion
of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{side} option below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism}, a parallelepiped is defined (it’s too hard to spell
parallelepiped in an input script!).  The parallelepiped has its
“origin” at (xlo,ylo,zlo) and is defined by 3 edge vectors starting
from the origin given by A = (xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo,0,0); B = (xy,yhi\sphinxhyphen{}ylo,0); C =
(xz,yz,zhi\sphinxhyphen{}zlo).  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Xy,xz,yz} can be 0.0 or positive or negative values
and are called “tilt factors” because they are the amount of
displacement applied to faces of an originally orthogonal box to
transform it into the parallelepiped.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A prism region that will be used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}
command to define a triclinic simulation box must have tilt factors
(xy,xz,yz) that do not skew the box more than half the distance of
corresponding the parallel box length.  For example, if xlo = 2 and
xhi = 12, then the x box length is 10 and the xy tilt factor must be
between \sphinxhyphen{}5 and 5.  Similarly, both xz and yz must be between
\sphinxhyphen{}(xhi\sphinxhyphen{}xlo)/2 and +(yhi\sphinxhyphen{}ylo)/2.  Note that this is not a limitation,
since if the maximum tilt factor is 5 (as in this example), then
configurations with tilt = …, \sphinxhyphen{}15, \sphinxhyphen{}5, 5, 15, 25, … are all
geometrically equivalent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere}, a sphere is defined with its center at (x,y,z)
and with radius as its radius.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} value for styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder}, and the
parameters a,b,c for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ellipsoid}, can each be specified as an
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  Likewise, for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ellipsoid} the x\sphinxhyphen{}, y\sphinxhyphen{}, and z\sphinxhyphen{} coordinates of the center of the
sphere/ellipsoid can be specified as an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.  And for
style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder} the two center positions c1 and c2 for the location
of the cylinder axes can be specified as a equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable. For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone}
all properties can be defined via equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the value is a variable, it should be specified as v\_name, where
name is the variable name.  In this case, the variable will be
evaluated each timestep, and its value used to determine the radius of
the region.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can specify formulas with various mathematical
functions, and include {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command
keywords for the simulation box parameters and timestep and elapsed
time.  Thus it is easy to specify a time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent radius or have
a time dependent position of the sphere or cylinder region.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto tricilinc}}}} page for a
geometric description of triclinic boxes, as defined by LAMMPS, and
how to transform these parameters to and from other commonly used
triclinic representations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} style creates a region consisting of the volume of all the
listed regions combined.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} style creates a region
consisting of the volume that is common to all the listed regions.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} regions operate by invoking methods
from their list of sub\sphinxhyphen{}regions.  Thus you cannot delete the
sub\sphinxhyphen{}regions after defining a \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersection} region.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{side} keyword determines whether the region is considered to be
inside or outside of the specified geometry.  Using this keyword in
conjunction with \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} regions, complex geometries
can be built up.  For example, if the interior of two spheres were
each defined as regions, and a \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} style with \sphinxstyleemphasis{side} = out was
constructed listing the region\sphinxhyphen{}IDs of the 2 spheres, the resulting
region would be all the volume in the simulation box that was outside
both of the spheres.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{units} keyword determines the meaning of the distance units used
to define the region for any argument above listed as having distance
units.  It also affects the scaling of the velocity vector specified
with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{vel} keyword, the amplitude vector specified with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{wiggle} keyword, and the rotation point specified with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate}
keyword, since they each involve a distance metric.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} value selects standard distance units as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command, e.g. Angstroms for units = real or metal.
A \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} value means the distance units are in lattice spacings.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}} command must have been previously used to
define the lattice spacings which are used as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{block}, the lattice spacing in dimension x is applied to
xlo and xhi, similarly the spacings in dimensions y,z are applied to
ylo/yhi and zlo/zhi.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone}, the lattice spacing in argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{dim} is applied to
lo and hi.  The spacings in the two radial dimensions are applied to
c1 and c2.  The two cone radii are scaled by the lattice
spacing in the dimension corresponding to c1.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder}, the lattice spacing in argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{dim} is applied
to lo and hi.  The spacings in the two radial dimensions are applied
to c1 and c2.  The cylinder radius is scaled by the lattice
spacing in the dimension corresponding to c1.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ellipsoid}, the lattice spacing in dimensions x,y,z are
applied to the ellipsoid center x,y,z.  The spacing in dimensions
x,y,z are applied to the ellipsoid radii a,b,c respectively.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{plane}, the lattice spacing in dimension x is applied to
px and nx, similarly the spacings in dimensions y,z are applied to
py/ny and pz/nz.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism}, the lattice spacing in dimension x is applied to
xlo and xhi, similarly for ylo/yhi and zlo/zhi.  The lattice spacing
in dimension x is applied to xy and xz, and the spacing in dimension y
to yz.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere}, the lattice spacing in dimensions x,y,z are
applied to the sphere center x,y,z.  The spacing in dimension x is
applied to the sphere radius.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{move} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keywords are used, the region is “dynamic”,
meaning its location or orientation changes with time.  These keywords
cannot be used with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} style region.  Instead,
the keywords should be used to make the individual sub\sphinxhyphen{}regions of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{union} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} region dynamic.  Normally, each sub\sphinxhyphen{}region
should be “dynamic” in the same manner (e.g. rotate around the same
point), though this is not a requirement.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{move} keyword allows one or more {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}} to be used to specify the x,y,z displacement
of the region, typically as a function of time.  A variable is
specified as v\_name, where name is the variable name.  Any of the
three variables can be specified as NULL, in which case no
displacement is calculated in that dimension.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can specify formulas with various
mathematical functions, and include {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}
command keywords for the simulation box parameters and timestep and
elapsed time.  Thus it is easy to specify a region displacement that
change as a function of time or spans consecutive runs in a continuous
fashion.  For the latter, see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keywords of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{elaplong} keyword of {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, these commands would displace a region from its initial
position, in the positive x direction, effectively at a constant
velocity:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ramp}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{0,10}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{move}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the initial displacement is 0.0, though that is not required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Either of these variables would “wiggle” the region back and forth in
the y direction:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{swiggle}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{0,5,100}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dysame}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{sin}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{2*PI*elaplong*dt/100}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{move}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keyword rotates the region around a rotation axis \sphinxstyleemphasis{R} =
(Rx,Ry,Rz) that goes through a point \sphinxstyleemphasis{P} = (Px,Py,Pz).  The rotation
angle is calculated, presumably as a function of time, by a variable
specified as v\_theta, where theta is the variable name.  The variable
should generate its result in radians.  The direction of rotation for
the region around the rotation axis is consistent with the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand
rule: if your right\sphinxhyphen{}hand thumb points along \sphinxstyleemphasis{R}, then your fingers
wrap around the axis in the direction of rotation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{move} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keywords can be used together.  In this case,
the displacement specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{move} keyword is applied to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{P}
point of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} keyword.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} keyword can be used (multiple times) to indicate that one
or more faces of the region are ignored for purposes of particle/wall
interactions.  This keyword is only relevant for regions used by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fix wall/region} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix wall/gran/region} commands.  It can be used
to create “open” containers where only some of the region faces are
walls.  For example, a funnel can be created with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone} style
region that has an open face at the smaller radius for particles to
flow out, or at the larger radius for pouring particles into the cone,
or both.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} keyword partly overrides the \sphinxstyleemphasis{side}
keyword, since both exterior and interior surfaces of an open region
are tested for particle contacts.  The exception to this is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{union}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} region which includes an open sub\sphinxhyphen{}region.  In that case
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{side} keyword is still used to define the union/intersect region
volume, and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} settings are only applied to the individual
sub\sphinxhyphen{}regions that use them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The indices specified as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} keyword have the following
meanings:

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{block}, indices 1\sphinxhyphen{}6 correspond to the xlo, xhi, ylo, yhi,
zlo, zhi surfaces of the block.  I.e. 1 is the yz plane at x = xlo, 2
is the yz\sphinxhyphen{}plane at x = xhi, 3 is the xz plane at y = ylo, 4 is the xz
plane at y = yhi, 5 is the xy plane at z = zlo, 6 is the xy plane at z
= zhi).  In the second\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}last example above, the region is a box open
at both xy planes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism}, values 1\sphinxhyphen{}6 have the same mapping as for style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{block}.  I.e. in an untilted \sphinxstyleemphasis{prism}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} indices correspond to
the xlo, xhi, ylo, yhi, zlo, zhi surfaces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder}, index 1 corresponds to the flat end cap at the
low coordinate along the cylinder axis, index 2 corresponds to the
high\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate flat end cap along the cylinder axis, and index 3 is
the curved cylinder surface.  For example, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder} region with
\sphinxstyleemphasis{open 1 open 2} keywords will be open at both ends (e.g. a section of
pipe), regardless of the cylinder orientation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone}, the mapping is the same as for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cylinder}.
Index 1 is the low\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate flat end cap, index 2 is the
high\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate flat end cap, and index 3 is the curved cone surface.
In the last example above, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{cone} region is defined along the z\sphinxhyphen{}axis
that is open at the zlo value (e.g. for use as a funnel).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all other styles, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} keyword is ignored.  As indicated
above, this includes the \sphinxstyleemphasis{intersect} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{union} regions, though their
sub\sphinxhyphen{}regions can be defined with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{open} keyword.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, only \sphinxstyleemphasis{block} style regions are supported by Kokkos.  The
code using the region (such as a fix or compute) must also be
supported by Kokkos or no acceleration will occur.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{region:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A prism cannot be of 0.0 thickness in any dimension; use a small z
thickness for 2d simulations.  For 2d simulations, the xz and yz
parameters must be 0.0.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{region:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{lattice::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lattice}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_atoms}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{region:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are side = in, units = lattice, and no move or
rotation.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{replicate@\spxentry{replicate}}\ignorespaces 

\section{replicate command}
\label{\detokenize{replicate:replicate-command}}\label{\detokenize{replicate:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{replicate::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{replicate:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{replicate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ny}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
nx,ny,nz = replication factors in each dimension
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bbox} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bbox} = use a bounding\sphinxhyphen{}box algorithm which is faster for large proc counts
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic} = use an algorithm that correctly replicates periodic bond loops
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{replicate:examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For examples of replicating simple linear polymer chains (periodic or
non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic) or periodic carbon nanotubes, see examples/replicate.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{replicate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{replicate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bbox}
\PYG{k}{replicate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{periodic}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{replicate:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Replicate the current system one or more times in each dimension.  For
example, replication factors of 2,2,2 will create a simulation with 8x
as many atoms by doubling the size of the simulation box in each
dimension.  A replication factor of 1 leaves the simulation domain
unchanged in that dimension.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the new simulation box is created it is partitioned into a
regular 3d grid of rectangular bricks, one per processor, based on the
number of processors being used and the settings of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}} command.  The partitioning can be
changed by subsequent {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All properties of each atom are replicated (except per\sphinxhyphen{}atom fix data,
see the Restrictions section below).  This includes their velocities,
which may or may not be desirable.  New atom IDs are assigned to new
atoms, as are new molecule IDs.  Bonds and other topology interactions
are created between pairs of new atoms as well as between old and new
atoms.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The bond discussion which follows only refers to models with
permanent covalent bonds typically defined in LAMMPS via a data
file.  It is not relevant to systems modeled with many\sphinxhyphen{}body
potentials which can define bonds on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly, based on the current
positions of nearby atoms, e.g. models using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{AIREBO}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_reaxff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{ReaxFF}}}} potentials.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic} keyword is not specified, bond replication is
done by using the image flag for each atom to “unwrap” it out of the
periodic box before replicating it.  After replication is performed,
atoms outside the new periodic box are wrapped back into it.  This
assigns correct images flags to all atoms in the system.  For this to
work, all original atoms in the original simulation box must have
consistent image flags.  This means that if two atoms have a bond
between them which crosses a periodic boundary, their respective image
flags will differ by 1 in that dimension.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Image flag consistency is not possible if a system has a periodic bond
loop, meaning there is a chain of bonds which crosses an entire
dimension and re\sphinxhyphen{}connects to itself across a periodic boundary.  In
this case you MUST use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic} keyword to correctly
replicate the system.  This option zeroes the image flags for all
atoms and uses a different algorithm to find new (nearby) bond
neighbors in the replicated system.  In the final replicated system
all image flags are zero (in each dimension).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS does not check for image flag consistency before performing
the replication (it does issue a warning about this before a
simulation is run).  If the original image flags are inconsistent,
the replicated system will also have inconsistent image flags, but
will otherwise be correctly replicated.  This is NOT the case if
there is a periodic bond loop.  See the next note.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS does not check for periodic bond loops.  If you use the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic} keyword for a system without periodic bond loops,
the system will be correctly replicated, but image flag information
will be lost (which may or may not be important to your model).  If
you do not use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic} keyword for a system with
periodic bond loops, the replicated system will have invalid bonds
(typically very long), resulting in bad dynamics.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If possible, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bbox} keyword should be used when running on a large
number of processors, as it can result in a substantial speed\sphinxhyphen{}up for
the replication operation.  It uses a bounding box to only check atoms
in replicas that overlap with each processor’s new subdomain when
assigning atoms to processors.  It also preserves image flag
information.  The only drawback to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bbox} option is that it
requires a temporary use of more memory.  Each processor must be able
to store all atoms (and their per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data) in the original system,
before it is replicated.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The algorithm used by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic} keyword builds on the
algorithm used by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bbox} keyword and thus has the same memory
requirements.  If you specify only the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/peridoic} keyword it
will internally set the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bbox} keyword as well.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{replicate:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A 2d simulation cannot be replicated in the z dimension.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a simulation is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic in a dimension, care should be used
when replicating it in that dimension, as it may generate atoms nearly
on top of each other.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the current simulation was read in from a restart file (before a
run is performed), there must not be any fix information stored in the
file for individual atoms.  Similarly, no fixes can be defined at the
time the replicate command is used that require vectors of atom
information to be stored.  This is because the replicate command does
not know how to replicate that information for new atoms it creates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To work around this restriction two options are possible.  (1) Fixes
which use the stored data in the restart file can be defined before
replication and then deleted via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{unfix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{unfix}}}} command and
re\sphinxhyphen{}defined after it.  Or (2) the restart file can be converted to a
data file (which deletes the stored fix information) and fixes defined
after the replicate command.  In both these scenarios, the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
fix information in the restart file is lost.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{replicate:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{replicate:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No settings for using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bbox} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/periodic} algorithms.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{rerun@\spxentry{rerun}}\ignorespaces 

\section{rerun command}
\label{\detokenize{rerun:rerun-command}}\label{\detokenize{rerun:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{rerun::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{rerun:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{rerun}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file1,file2,… = dump file(s) to read

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keywords may be appended, keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} must appear and be last
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{last} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{skip} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{post} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump}
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} args = Nfirst
   Nfirst = dump timestep to start on
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{last} args = Nlast
   Nlast = dumptimestep to stop on
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} args = Nevery
   Nevery = read snapshots matching every this many timesteps
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{skip} args = Nskip
   Nskip = read one out of every Nskip snapshots
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} args = Nstart
   Nstart = timestep on which pseudo run will start
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} args = Nstop
   Nstop = timestep to which pseudo run will end
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{post} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
 \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} args = same as {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}} command starting with its field arguments
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{rerun:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{rerun}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dump.file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vz}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{rerun:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform a pseudo simulation run where atom information is read one
snapshot at a time from a dump file(s), and energies and forces are
computed on the shapshot to produce thermodynamic or other output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be useful in the following kinds of scenarios, after an
initial simulation produced the dump file:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the energy and forces of snapshots using a different potential.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate one or more diagnostic quantities on the snapshots that
were not computed in the initial run.  These can also be computed with
settings not used in the initial run, e.g. computing an RDF via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_rdf::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute rdf}}}} command with a longer cutoff than was
used initially.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the portion of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom forces resulting from a subset of
the potential.  E.g. compute only Coulombic forces.  This can be done
by only defining only a Coulombic pair style in the rerun script.
Doing this in the original script would result in different (bad)
dynamics.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Conceptually, using the rerun command is like running an input script
that has a loop in it (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}}
commands).  Each iteration of the loop reads one snapshot from the
dump file via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}} command, sets the
timestep to the appropriate value, and then invokes a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}
command for zero timesteps to simply compute energy and forces, and
any other {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}} or diagnostic info
you have defined.  This computation also invokes any fixes you have
defined that apply constraints to the system, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_indent::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix indent}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a simulation box must already be defined before using the
rerun command.  This can be done by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that reading per\sphinxhyphen{}atom information from dump snapshots is
limited to the atom coordinates, velocities and image flags as
explained in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}} command.  Other atom
properties, which may be necessary to compute energies and forces,
such as atom charge, or bond topology information for a molecular
system, are not read from (or even contained in) dump files.  Thus
this auxiliary information should be defined in the usual way, e.g. in
a data file read in by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command, before
using the rerun command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that the frequency of thermodynamic or dump output from the
rerun simulation will depend on settings made in the rerun script, the
same as for output from any LAMMPS simulation.  See further info below
as to what that means if the timesteps for snapshots read from dump
files do not match the specified output frequency.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If more than one dump file is specified, the dump files are read one
after the other in the order specified.  It is assumed that snapshot
timesteps will be in ascending order.  If a snapshot is encountered that
is not in ascending order, it will skip the snapshot until it reads one
that is.
This allows skipping of a duplicate snapshot (same timestep),
e.g. that appeared at the end of one file and beginning of the next.
However if you specify a series of dump files in an incorrect order
(with respect to the timesteps they contain), you may skip large
numbers of snapshots.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the dump files specified as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} keyword can be
parallel files, i.e. written as multiple files either per processor
and/or per snapshot.  If that is the case they will also be read in
parallel which can make the rerun command operate dramatically faster
for large systems.  See the page for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} commands which describe how to read
and write parallel dump files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{first}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{last}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{every}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{skip} keywords determine which
snapshots are read from the dump file(s).  Snapshots are skipped until
they have a timestep \textgreater{}= \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfirst}.  When a snapshot with a timestep \textgreater{}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nlast} is encountered, the rerun command finishes.  Note that
the defaults for \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{last} are to read all snapshots.  If the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword is set to a value \textgreater{} 0, then only snapshots with
timesteps that are a multiple of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} are read (the first
snapshot is always read).  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} = 0, then this criterion is
ignored, i.e. every snapshot is read that meets the other criteria.
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{skip} keyword is used, then after the first snapshot is read,
every Nth snapshot is read, where N = \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nskip}.  E.g. if \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nskip} = 3,
then only 1 out of every 3 snapshots is read, assuming the snapshot
timestep is also consistent with the other criteria.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Not all dump formats contain the timestep and not all dump readers
support reading it.  In that case individual snapshots are assigned
consecutive timestep numbers starting at 1.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keywords do not affect which snapshots are read
from the dump file(s).  Rather, they have the same meaning that they
do for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  They only need to be defined if
(a) you are using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command that changes some value
over time, and (b) you want the reference point for elapsed time (from
start to stop) to be different than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{first} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{last} settings.
See the page for individual fixes to see which ones can be used
with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords.  Note that if you define neither of
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{first}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{last} keywords, then LAMMPS treats the
pseudo run as going from 0 to a huge value (effectively infinity).
This means that any quantity that a fix scales as a fraction of
elapsed time in the run, will essentially remain at its initial value.
Also note that an error will occur if you read a snapshot from the
dump file with a timestep value larger than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} setting you
have specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{post} keyword can be used to minimize the output to the screen that
happens after a \sphinxstyleemphasis{rerun} command, similar to the post keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run command}}}}. It is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} by default.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} keyword is required and must be the last keyword specified.
Its arguments are passed internally to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}}
command.  The first argument following the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump} keyword should be
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{field1} argument of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}} command.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}} page for details on the various
options it allows for extracting information from the dump file
snapshots, and for using that information to alter the LAMMPS
simulation.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
In general, a LAMMPS input script that uses a rerun command can
include and perform all the usual operations of an input script that
uses the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  There are a few exceptions and
points to consider, as discussed here.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixes that perform time integration, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} are not invoked, since no time integration
is performed.  Fixes that perturb or constrain the forces on atoms
will be invoked, just as they would during a normal run.  Examples are
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_indent::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix indent}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}.
So you should think carefully as to whether that makes sense for the
manner in which you are reprocessing the dump snapshots.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you only want the rerun script to perform an analysis that does not
involve pair interactions, such as use compute msd to calculated
displacements over time, you do not need to define a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}}, which may also mean neighbor lists will not need to be
calculated which saves time.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify cutoff}}}} command can also be used to ensure ghost atoms are
acquired from far enough away for operations like bond and angle
evaluations, if no pair style is being used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Every time a snapshot is read, the timestep for the simulation is reset,
as if the {\hyperref[\detokenize{reset_timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{reset\_timestep}}}} command were used.
This command has some restrictions as to what fixes can be defined.  See
its documentation page for details.  For example, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}} fixes are in this
category.  They also make no sense to use with a rerun command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If time\sphinxhyphen{}averaging fixes like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} are
used, they are invoked on timesteps that are a function of their
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nrepeat}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfreq} settings.  As an example, see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} page for details.  You must
ensure those settings are consistent with the snapshot timestamps that
are read from the dump file(s).  If an averaging fix is not invoked on
a timestep it expects to be, LAMMPS will flag an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The various forms of LAMMPS output, as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} commands occur with
specified frequency, e.g. every N steps.  If the timestep for a dump
snapshot is not a multiple of N, then it will be read and processed,
but no output will be produced.  If you want output for every dump
snapshot, you can simply use N=1 for an output frequency, e.g. for
thermodynamic output or new dump file output.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{rerun:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rerun} command is subject to all restrictions of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}} command.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{rerun:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_dump}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{rerun:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are first = 0, last = a huge value (effectively
infinity), start = same as first, stop = same as last, every = 0, skip
= 1, post = no;

\PYG{k}{reset\PYGZus{}atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{solvent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{compress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{reset_atoms:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{reset\_atoms} command resets the values of a specified atom
property.  In contrast to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} command, it does this in a
collective manner which resets the values for many atoms in a
self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent way.  This command is often useful when the simulated
system has undergone significant modifications like adding or removing
atoms or molecules, joining data files, changing bonds, or large\sphinxhyphen{}scale
diffusion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The new values can be thought of as a \sphinxstyleemphasis{reset}, similar to values atoms
would have if a new data file were being read or a new simulation
performed.  Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} command also resets atom properties to
new values, but it treats each atom independently.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{property} setting can be \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{image} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}.  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{id}, the
IDs of all the atoms are reset to contiguous values.  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{image}, the
image flags of atoms in the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} are reset so that at
least one atom in each molecule is in the simulation box (image flag =
0).  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}, the molecule IDs of all atoms are reset to contiguous
values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More details on these operations and their arguments or optional
keyword/value settings are given below.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Property: \sphinxstyleemphasis{id}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reset atom IDs for the entire system, including all the global IDs
stored for bond, angle, dihedral, improper topology data.  This will
create a set of IDs that are numbered contiguously from 1 to N for a N
atoms system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be useful to do after performing a “delete\_atoms” command for
a molecular system.  The delete\_atoms compress yes option will not
perform this operation due to the existence of bond topology.  It can
also be useful to do after any simulation which has lost atoms,
e.g. due to atoms moving outside a simulation box with fixed
boundaries (see the “boundary command”), or due to evaporation (see
the “fix evaporate” command).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sort} keyword is used with a setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then the
assignment of new atom IDs will be the same no matter how many
processors LAMMPS is running on.  This is done by first doing a
spatial sort of all the atoms into bins and sorting them within each
bin.  Because the set of bins is independent of the number of
processors, this enables a consistent assignment of new IDs to each
atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be useful to do after using the “create\_atoms” command and/or
“replicate” command.  In general those commands do not guarantee
assignment of the same atom ID to the same physical atom when LAMMPS
is run on different numbers of processors.  Enforcing consistent IDs
can be useful for debugging or comparing output from two different
runs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the spatial sort requires communication of atom IDs and
coordinates between processors in an all\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}all manner.  This is done
efficiently in LAMMPS, but it is more expensive than how atom IDs are
reset without sorting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that whether sorting or not, the resetting of IDs is not a
compression, where gaps in atom IDs are removed by decrementing atom
IDs that are larger.  Instead the IDs for all atoms are erased, and
new IDs are assigned so that the atoms owned by an individual
processor have consecutive IDs, as the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command explains.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If this command is used before a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}} is
defined, an error about bond topology atom IDs not being found may
result.  This is because the cutoff distance for ghost atom
communication was not sufficient to find atoms in bonds, angles, etc
that are owned by other processors.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify cutoff}}}} command can be used to correct this issue.  Or you can
define a pair style before using this command.  If you do the former,
you should unset the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_modify cutoff} after using \sphinxstyleemphasis{reset
atoms id} so that subsequent communication is not inefficient.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Property: \sphinxstyleemphasis{image}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reset the image flags of atoms so that at least one atom in each
molecule has an image flag of 0.  Molecular topology is respected so
that if the molecule straddles a periodic simulation box boundary, the
images flags of all atoms in the molecule will be consistent.  This
avoids inconsistent image flags that could result from resetting all
image flags to zero with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the system has no bonds, there is no reason to use this command,
since image flags for different atoms do not need to be
consistent.  Use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{image}
keyword instead.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only image flags for atoms in the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} are reset; all
others remain unchanged.  No check is made for whether the group
covers complete molecule fragments and thus whether the command will
result in inconsistent image flags.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Molecular fragments are identified by the algorithm used by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fragment/atom}}}} command.  For each
fragment the average of the largest and the smallest image flag in
each direction across all atoms in the fragment is computed and
subtracted from the current image flag in the same direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be a useful operation to perform after running longer
equilibration runs of mobile systems where molecules would pass
through the system multiple times and thus produce non\sphinxhyphen{}zero image
flags.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Same as explained for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fragment/atom}}}} command, molecules are identified using the
current bond topology.  This will \sphinxstylestrong{not} account for bonds broken by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}} command, because this
bond style does not perform a full update of the bond topology data
structures within LAMMPS.  In that case, using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds
all bond 0 remove}}}} will permanently delete such
broken bonds and should thus be used first.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Property: \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Reset molecule IDs for a specified group of atoms based on current
bond connectivity.  This will typically create a new set of molecule
IDs for atoms in the group.  Only molecule IDs for atoms in the
specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} are reset; molecule IDs for atoms not in the
group are not changed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For purposes of this operation, molecules are identified by the current
bond connectivity in the system, which may or may not be consistent with
the current molecule IDs.  A molecule in this context is a set of atoms
connected to each other with explicit bonds.  The specific algorithm
used is the one of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fragment/atom}}}}.
Once the molecules are identified and a new molecule ID computed for
each, this command will update the current molecule ID for all atoms in
the group with the new molecule ID.  Note that if the group excludes
atoms within molecules, one (physical) molecule may become two or more
(logical) molecules.  For example if the group excludes atoms in the
middle of a linear chain, then each end of the chain is considered an
independent molecule and will be assigned a different molecule ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be a useful operation to perform after running reactive
molecular dynamics run with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_create::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/create}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_break::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/break}}}}, all of which can change molecule topologies. It can
also be useful after molecules have been deleted with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_atoms}}}} command or after a simulation which
has lost molecules, e.g. via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_evaporate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix evaporate}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{compress} keyword determines how new molecule IDs are computed.  If
the setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} (the default) and there are N molecules in the
group, the new molecule IDs will be a set of N contiguous values.  See
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{offset} keyword for details on selecting the range of these values.
If the setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, the molecule ID of every atom in the molecule
will be set to the smallest atom ID of any atom in the molecule.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} keyword determines whether single atoms (not bonded to
another atom) are treated as one\sphinxhyphen{}atom molecules or not, based on the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} setting.  If the setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} (the default), their
molecule IDs are set to 0.  This setting can be important if the new
molecule IDs will be used as input to other commands such as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom molecule}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
rigid molecule}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{offset} keyword is only used if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{compress} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}.
Its default value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{Noffset} = \sphinxhyphen{}1.  In that case, if the specified
group is \sphinxstyleemphasis{all}, then the new compressed molecule IDs will range from 1
to N.  If the specified group is not \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} and the largest molecule ID
of atoms outside that group is M, then the new compressed molecule IDs will
range from M+1 to M+N, to avoid collision with existing molecule
IDs.  If an \sphinxstyleemphasis{Noffset} \textgreater{}= 0 is specified, then the new compressed
molecule IDs will range from \sphinxstyleemphasis{Noffset}+1 to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Noffset}+N.  If the group
is not \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} there may be collisions with the molecule IDs of other atoms.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Same as explained for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fragment/atom}}}} command, molecules are identified using the
current bond topology.  This will \sphinxstylestrong{not} account for bonds broken by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}} command, because this
bond style does not perform a full update of the bond topology data
structures within LAMMPS.  In that case, using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds
all bond 0 remove}}}} will permanently delete such broken
bonds and should thus be used first.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{reset_atoms:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{image} property can only be used when the atom style supports bonds.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{reset_atoms:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fragment/atom}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_create::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/create}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_break::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/break}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_evaporate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix evaporate}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_atoms}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}}


\subsection{Defaults}
\label{\detokenize{reset_atoms:defaults}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For property \sphinxstyleemphasis{id}, the default keyword setting is sort = no.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For property \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}, the default keyword settings are compress = yes,
single = no, and offset = \sphinxhyphen{}1.
