\index{reset\_timestep@\spxentry{reset\_timestep}}\ignorespaces 

\section{reset\_timestep command}
\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:reset-timestep-command}}\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = timestep number

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{time}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{time} value = atime
   atime = accumulated simulation time
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4000000}
\PYG{k}{reset\PYGZus{}timestep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the timestep counter to the specified value.  This command
usually comes after the timestep has been set by reading a restart
file via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command, or a previous
simulation run or minimization advanced the timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} keyword allows to also set the accumulated
simulation time.  This is usually the number of timesteps times
the size of the timestep, but when using variable size timesteps
with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}} it can differ.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}}
commands set the timestep to 0; the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
command sets the timestep to the value it had when the restart file
was written.  The same applies to the accumulated simulation time.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command cannot be used when any fixes are defined that keep track
of elapsed time to perform certain kinds of time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent operations.
Examples are the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}} commands.  The former adds atoms on specific timesteps.
The latter keeps track of accumulated time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Various fixes use the current timestep to calculate related quantities.
If the timestep is reset, this may produce unexpected behavior, but
LAMMPS allows the fixes to be defined even if the timestep is reset.
For example, commands which thermostat the system, e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}, allow you to specify a target temperature which ramps from
Tstart to Tstop which may persist over several runs.  If you change the
timestep, you may induce an instantaneous change in the target
temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Resetting the timestep clears flags for {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}} that
may have calculated some quantity from a previous run.  This means these
quantity cannot be accessed by a variable in between runs until a new
run is performed.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command for more
details.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{reset_timestep:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{restart@\spxentry{restart}}\ignorespaces 

\section{restart command}
\label{\detokenize{restart:restart-command}}\label{\detokenize{restart:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{restart::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{restart:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{root}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = write a restart file on timesteps which are multiples of N

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N can be a variable (see below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
root = filename to which timestep \# is appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file1,file2 = two full filenames, toggle between them when writing file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{fileper} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nfile}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fileper} arg = Np
  Np = write one file for every this many processors
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nfile} arg = Nf
  Nf = write this many files, one from each of Nf processors
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{restart:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{poly.restart}
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{restart.}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{.equil}
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{poly.}\PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}}\PYG{n}{.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{poly.}\PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}}\PYG{n}{.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nfile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}mystep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{poly.restart}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{restart:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write out a binary restart file with the current state of the
simulation on timesteps which are a multiple of N.  A value of N = 0
means do not write out any restart files, which is the default.
Restart files are written in one (or both) of two modes as a run
proceeds.  If one filename is specified, a series of filenames will be
created which include the timestep in the filename.  If two filenames
are specified, only 2 restart files will be created, with those names.
LAMMPS will toggle between the 2 names as it writes successive restart
files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that you can specify the restart command twice, once with a
single filename and once with two filenames.  This would allow you,
for example, to write out archival restart files every 100000 steps
using a single filename, and more frequent temporary restart files
every 1000 steps, using two filenames.  Using restart 0 will turn off
both modes of output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} files, the restart filename(s) can contain
two wild\sphinxhyphen{}card characters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a “*” appears in the single filename, it is replaced with the
current timestep value.  This is only recognized when a single
filename is used (not when toggling back and forth).  Thus, the third
example above creates restart files as follows: restart.1000.equil,
restart.2000.equil, etc.  If a single filename is used with no “*”,
then the timestep value is appended.  E.g. the second example above
creates restart files as follows: poly.restart.1000,
poly.restart.2000, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a “\%” character appears in the restart filename(s), then one file
is written for each processor and the “\%” character is replaced with
the processor ID from 0 to P\sphinxhyphen{}1.  An additional file with the “\%”
replaced by “base” is also written, which contains global information.
For example, the files written on step 1000 for filename restart.\%
would be restart.base.1000, restart.0.1000, restart.1.1000, …,
restart.P\sphinxhyphen{}1.1000.  This creates smaller files and can be a fast mode
of output and subsequent input on parallel machines that support
parallel I/O.  The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{fileper} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{nfile} keywords discussed
below can alter the number of files written.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Restart files are written on timesteps that are a multiple of N but
not on the first timestep of a run or minimization.  You can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{write_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_restart}}}} command to write a restart file
before a run begins.  A restart file is not written on the last
timestep of a run unless it is a multiple of N.  A restart file is
written on the last timestep of a minimization if N \textgreater{} 0 and the
minimization converges.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Instead of a numeric value, N can be specified as an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style
variable}}}}, which should be specified as v\_name, where name is
the variable name.  In this case, the variable is evaluated at the
beginning of a run to determine the next timestep at which a restart
file will be written out.  On that timestep, the variable will be
evaluated again to determine the next timestep, etc.  Thus the variable
should return timestep values.  See the stagger() and logfreq() and
stride() math functions for {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}}, as
examples of useful functions to use in this context.  Other similar math
functions could easily be added as options for {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the following commands will write restart files
every step from 1100 to 1200, and could be useful for debugging
a simulation where something goes wrong at step 1163:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stride}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{1100,1200,1}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.restart}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for information about
what is stored in a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Restart files can be read by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
command to restart a simulation from a particular state.  Because the
file is binary (to enable exact restarts), it may not be readable on
another machine.  In this case, you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}r command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} to convert a restart file to a data file.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Although the purpose of restart files is to enable restarting a
simulation from where it left off, not all information about a
simulation is stored in the file.  For example, the list of fixes that
were specified during the initial run is not stored, which means the
new input script must specify any fixes you want to use.  Even when
restart information is stored in the file, as it is for some fixes,
commands may need to be re\sphinxhyphen{}specified in the new input script, in order
to re\sphinxhyphen{}use that information.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
command for information about what is stored in a restart file.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{nfile} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fileper} keywords can be used in conjunction
with the “\%” wildcard character in the specified restart file name(s).
As explained above, the “\%” character causes the restart file to be
written in pieces, one piece for each of P processors.  By default P =
the number of processors the simulation is running on.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nfile} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fileper} keyword can be used to set P to a smaller value, which can
be more efficient when running on a large number of processors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nfile} keyword sets P to the specified Nf value.  For example, if
Nf = 4, and the simulation is running on 100 processors, 4 files will
be written, by processors 0,25,50,75.  Each will collect information
from itself and the next 24 processors and write it to a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fileper} keyword, the specified value of Np means write one
file for every Np processors.  For example, if Np = 4, every fourth
processor (0,4,8,12,etc) will collect information from itself and the
next 3 processors and write it to a restart file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{restart:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{restart:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{write_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_restart}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{restart:default}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope

\index{run@\spxentry{run}}\ignorespaces 

\section{run command}
\label{\detokenize{run:run-command}}\label{\detokenize{run:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{run::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{run:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = \# of timesteps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{upto} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pre} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{post} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{every}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{upto} value = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{start} value = N1
  N1 = timestep at which 1st run started
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} value = N2
  N2 = timestep at which last run will end
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pre} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{post} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{every} values = M c1 c2 ...
  M = break the run into M\sphinxhyphen{}timestep segments and invoke one or more commands between each segment
  c1,c2,...,cN = one or more LAMMPS commands, each enclosed in quotes
  c1 = NULL means no command will be invoked
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{run:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{upto}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{start}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pre}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{post}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{start}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}Protein Rg = \PYGZdl{}r\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{run:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run or continue dynamics for a specified number of timesteps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run style}}}} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa}, N refers to outer
loop (largest) timesteps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A value of N = 0 is acceptable; only the thermodynamics of the system
are computed and printed without taking a timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{upto} keyword means to perform a run starting at the current
timestep up to the specified timestep.  E.g. if the current timestep
is 10,000 and “run 100000 upto” is used, then an additional 90,000
timesteps will be run.  This can be useful for very long runs on a
machine that allocates chunks of time and terminate your job when time
is exceeded.  If you need to restart your script multiple times
(reading in the last restart file), you can keep restarting your
script with the same run command until the simulation finally
completes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keywords can be used if multiple runs are being
performed and you want a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command that changes some
value over time (e.g. temperature) to make the change across the
entire set of runs and not just a single run.  See the page for
individual fixes to see which ones can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop}
keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, consider this fix followed by 10 run commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{start}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{start}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{start}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The NVT fix ramps the target temperature from 200.0 to 300.0 during a
run.  If the run commands did not have the start/stop keywords (just
“run 1000”), then the temperature would ramp from 200.0 to 300.0
during the 1000 steps of each run.  With the start/stop keywords, the
ramping takes place over the 10000 steps of all runs together.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pre} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{post} keywords can be used to streamline the setup,
clean\sphinxhyphen{}up, and associated output to the screen that happens before and
after a run.  This can be useful if you wish to do many short runs in
succession (e.g. LAMMPS is being called as a library which is doing
other computations between successive short LAMMPS runs).

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default (pre and post = yes), LAMMPS creates neighbor lists,
computes forces, and imposes fix constraints before every run.  And
after every run it gathers and prints timings statistics.  If a run is
just a continuation of a previous run (i.e. no settings are changed),
the initial computation is not necessary; the old neighbor list is
still valid as are the forces.  So if \sphinxstyleemphasis{pre} is specified as “no” then
the initial setup is skipped, except for printing thermodynamic info.
Note that if \sphinxstyleemphasis{pre} is set to “no” for the very first run LAMMPS
performs, then it is overridden, since the initial setup computations
must be done.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your input script changes the system between 2 runs, then the
initial setup must be performed to ensure the change is recognized by
all parts of the code that are affected.  Examples are adding a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}, changing
a {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} list parameter, or writing restart file
which can migrate atoms between processors.  LAMMPS has no easy way to
check if this has happened, but it is an error to use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pre no}
option in this case.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{post} is specified as “no”, the full timing summary is skipped;
only a one\sphinxhyphen{}line summary timing is printed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword provides a means of breaking a LAMMPS run into a
series of shorter runs.  Optionally, one or more LAMMPS commands (c1,
c2, …, cN) will be executed in between the short runs.  If used, the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword must be the last keyword, since it has a variable
number of arguments.  Each of the trailing arguments is a single
LAMMPS command, and each command should be enclosed in quotes, so that
the entire command will be treated as a single argument.  This will
also prevent any variables in the command from being evaluated until
it is executed multiple times during the run.  Note that if a command
itself needs one of its arguments quoted (e.g. the {\hyperref[\detokenize{print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{print}}}}
command), then you can use a combination of single and double quotes,
as in the example above or below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword is a means to avoid listing a long series of runs
and interleaving commands in your input script.  For example, a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{print}}}} command could be invoked or a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} could
be redefined, e.g. to reset a thermostat temperature.  Or this could
be useful for invoking a command you have added to LAMMPS that wraps
some other code (e.g. as a library) to perform a computation
periodically during a long LAMMPS run.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}}
doc page for info about how to add new commands to LAMMPS.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_couple::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto couple}}}} page for ideas about how to
couple LAMMPS to other codes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} option, N total steps are simulated, in shorter runs
of M steps each.  After each M\sphinxhyphen{}length run, the specified commands are
invoked.  If only a single command is specified as NULL, then no
command is invoked.  Thus these lines:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{q}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x[100]}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}Coord = \PYGZdl{}q\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
are the equivalent of:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{q}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x[100]}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Coord = \PYGZdl{}q}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Coord = \PYGZdl{}q}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Coord = \PYGZdl{}q}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which does 3 runs of 2000 steps and prints the x\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate of a
particular atom between runs.  Note that the variable “\$q” will
be evaluated afresh each time the print command is executed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that by using the line continuation character “\&”, the run every
command can be spread across many lines, though it is still a single
command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}Minimum value = \PYGZdl{}a\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}Maximum value = \PYGZdl{}b\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}Temp = \PYGZdl{}c\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}Press = \PYGZdl{}d\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pre} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{post} options are set to “no” when used with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword, then the first run will do the full setup and the last
run will print the full timing summary, but these operations will be
skipped for intermediate runs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You might wish to specify a command that exits the run by
jumping out of the loop, e.g.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{if \PYGZsq{}\PYGZdl{}t \PYGZlt{} 300.0\PYGZsq{} then \PYGZsq{}jump SELF afterrun\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, this will not work.  The run command simply executes each
command one at a time each time it pauses, then continues the run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Instead, you should use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_halt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix halt}}}} command, which
has additional options for how to exit the run.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{run:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When not using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{upto} keyword, the number of specified timesteps N
must fit in a signed 32\sphinxhyphen{}bit integer, so you are limited to slightly
more than 2 billion steps (2\textasciicircum{}31) in a single run.  When using \sphinxstyleemphasis{upto},
N can be larger than a signed 32\sphinxhyphen{}bit integer, however the difference
between N and the current timestep must still be no larger than
2\textasciicircum{}31 steps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, with or without the \sphinxstyleemphasis{upto} keyword, you can perform
successive runs to run a simulation for any number of steps (ok, up to
2\textasciicircum{}63 total steps).  I.e. the timestep counter within LAMMPS is a
64\sphinxhyphen{}bit signed integer.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{run:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{temper::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temper}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_halt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix halt}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{run:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are start = the current timestep, stop = current
timestep + N, pre = yes, and post = yes.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{run\_style@\spxentry{run\_style}}\ignorespaces 

\section{run\_style command}
\label{\detokenize{run_style:run-style-command}}\label{\detokenize{run_style:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{run_style::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{run_style:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa/omp}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet} args = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split} args = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} args = N n1 n2 ... keyword values ...
  N = \# of levels of rRESPA
  n1, n2, ... = loop factors between rRESPA levels (N\sphinxhyphen{}1 values)
  zero or more keyword/value pairings may be appended to the loop factors
  keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} or
            \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace}
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} value = M
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute bond forces in
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} value = M
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute angle forces in
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} value = M
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute dihedral forces in
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} value = M
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute improper forces in
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} value = M
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute pair forces in
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner} values = M cut1 cut2
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute pair inner forces in
      cut1 = inner cutoff between pair inner and
             pair middle or outer  (distance units)
      cut2 = outer cutoff between pair inner and
             pair middle or outer  (distance units)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle} values = M cut1 cut2
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute pair middle forces in
      cut1 = inner cutoff between pair middle and pair outer (distance units)
      cut2 = outer cutoff between pair middle and pair outer (distance units)
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} value = M
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute pair outer forces in
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} values = M1 M2 ... (as many values as there are hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles
      M1 = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute the first pair\_style hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}style in
      M2 = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute the second pair\_style hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}style in
      M3,etc
    \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} value = M
      M = which level (1\sphinxhyphen{}N) to compute kspace forces in
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{run_style:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{verlet}
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{outer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{run_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Choose the style of time integrator used for molecular dynamics
simulations performed by LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet} style is the velocity form of the
Stoermer\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet time integration algorithm (velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet)


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split} style is also a velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet integrator, but it
splits the force calculation within each timestep over 2 partitions of
processors.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}
for info on how to run LAMMPS with multiple partitions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specifically, this style performs all computation except the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} portion of the force field on the
first partition.  This include the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor list building}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}} including time integration, and output.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} portion of the calculation is
performed on the second partition.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can lead to a significant speedup, if the number of processors can
be easily increased and the fraction of time is spent in computing
Kspace interactions is significant, too.  The two partitions may have a
different number of processors.  This is most useful for the PPPM
kspace\_style when its performance on a large number of processors
degrades due to the cost of communication in its 3d FFTs.  In this
scenario, splitting your P total processors into 2 subsets of
processors, P1 in the first partition and P2 in the second partition,
can enable your simulation to run faster.  This is because the
long\sphinxhyphen{}range forces in PPPM can be calculated at the same time as pairwise
and bonded forces are being calculated \sphinxstyleemphasis{and} the parallel 3d FFTs can be
faster to compute when running on fewer processors.  Please note that
the scenario of using fewer MPI processes to reduce communication
overhead can also be implemented through using MPI with OpenMP threads
via the INTEL, KOKKOS, or OPENMP package.  This alternative option is
typically more effective in case of a fixed number of available
processors and less complex to execute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split} style, you must define 2 partitions with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}, where partition P1
is either the same size or an integer multiple of the size of the
partition P2.  Typically having P1 be 3x larger than P2 is a good
choice, since the (serial) performance of LAMMPS is often best if the
time spent in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair}} computation versus \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Kspace}} is a 3:1 split.
The 3d processor layouts in each partition must overlay in the following
sense.  If P1 is a Px1 by Py1 by Pz1 grid, and P2 = Px2 by Py2 by Pz2,
then Px1 must be an integer multiple of Px2, and similarly for Py1 a
multiple of Py2, and Pz1 a multiple of Pz2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically the best way to do this is to let the first partition choose
its own optimal layout, then require the second partition’s layout to
match the integer multiple constraint.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}} command with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{part} keyword for a way
to control this, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{part}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{multiple}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can also use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{partition::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{partition}}}} command to explicitly
specify the processor layout on each partition.  E.g. for 2 partitions
of 60 and 15 processors each:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{partition}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{k}{partition}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{processors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When you run in 2\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split} style, the
thermodynamic data for the entire simulation will be output to the log
and screen file of the first partition, which are log.lammps.0 and
screen.0 by default; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}plog and \sphinxhyphen{}pscreen command\sphinxhyphen{}line
switches}}}} to change this.  The log and screen file for the
second partition will not contain thermodynamic output beyond the first
timestep of the run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for
performance details of the speed\sphinxhyphen{}up offered by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split}
style.  One important performance consideration is the assignment of
logical processors in the 2 partitions to the physical cores of a
parallel machine.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{processors::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{processors}}}} command has
options to support this, and strategies are discussed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Section
5}}}} of the manual.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} style implements the rRESPA multi\sphinxhyphen{}timescale integrator
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style:tuckerman3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tuckerman)}}}} with N hierarchical levels, where level
1 is the innermost loop (shortest timestep) and level N is the outermost
loop (largest timestep).  The loop factor arguments specify what the
looping factor is between levels.  N1 specifies the number of iterations
of level 1 for a single iteration of level 2, N2 is the iterations of
level 2 per iteration of level 3, etc.  N\sphinxhyphen{}1 looping parameters must be
specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus with a 4\sphinxhyphen{}level respa setting of “2 2 2” for the 3 loop factors, you
could choose to have bond interactions computed 8x per large timestep,
angle interactions computed 4x, pair interactions computed 2x, and
long\sphinxhyphen{}range interactions once per large timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} command sets the large timestep for the
outermost rRESPA level.  Thus if the 3 loop factors are “2 2 2” for
4\sphinxhyphen{}level rRESPA, and the outer timestep is set to 4.0 fs, then the inner
timestep would be 8x smaller or 0.5 fs.  All other LAMMPS commands that
specify number of timesteps (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo}}}} for thermo
output every N steps, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify delay/every}}}}
parameters, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} every N steps, etc) refer to the
outermost timesteps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rRESPA keywords enable you to specify at what level of the hierarchy
various forces will be computed.  If not specified, the defaults are
that bond forces are computed at level 1 (innermost loop), angle forces
are computed where bond forces are, dihedral forces are computed where
angle forces are, improper forces are computed where dihedral forces
are, pair forces are computed at the outermost level, and kspace forces
are computed where pair forces are.  The inner, middle, outer forces
have no defaults.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For fixes that support it, the rRESPA level at which a given fix is
active, can be selected through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle} keywords take additional arguments for cutoffs
that are used by the pairwise force computations.  If the 2 cutoffs for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner} are 5.0 and 6.0, this means that all pairs up to 6.0 apart are
computed by the inner force.  Those between 5.0 and 6.0 have their force
go ramped to 0.0 so the overlap with the next regime (middle or outer)
is smooth.  The next regime (middle or outer) will compute forces for
all pairs from 5.0 outward, with those from 5.0 to 6.0 having their
value ramped in an inverse manner.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that you can use \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} without using \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle} to
split the pairwise computations into two portions instead of three.
Unless you are using a very long pairwise cutoff, a 2\sphinxhyphen{}way split is often
faster than a 3\sphinxhyphen{}way split, since it avoids too much duplicate
computation of pairwise interactions near the intermediate cutoffs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that only a few pair potentials support the use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.  If not, only the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword can
be used with that pair style, meaning all pairwise forces are computed
at the same rRESPA level.  See the doc pages for individual pair styles
for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another option for using pair potentials with rRESPA is with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} keyword, which requires the use of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid
or hybrid/overlay}}}} command.  In this scenario, different
sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles of the hybrid pair style are evaluated at different rRESPA
levels.  This can be useful, for example, to set different timesteps for
hybrid coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained/all\sphinxhyphen{}atom models.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} keyword requires as
many level assignments as there are hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles, which assigns
each sub\sphinxhyphen{}style to a rRESPA level, following their order of definition in
the pair\_style command. Since the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} keyword operates on pair
style computations, it is mutually exclusive with either the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using rRESPA (or for any MD simulation) care must be taken to
choose a timestep size(s) that ensures the Hamiltonian for the chosen
ensemble is conserved.  For the constant NVE ensemble, total energy
must be conserved.  Unfortunately, it is difficult to know \sphinxstyleemphasis{a priori}
how well energy will be conserved, and a fairly long test simulation
(\textasciitilde{}10 ps) is usually necessary in order to verify that no long\sphinxhyphen{}term
drift in energy occurs with the trial set of parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With that caveat, a few rules\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}thumb may be useful in selecting
\sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} settings.  The following applies mostly to biomolecular
simulations using the CHARMM or a similar all\sphinxhyphen{}atom force field, but
the concepts are adaptable to other problems.  Without SHAKE, bonds
involving hydrogen atoms exhibit high\sphinxhyphen{}frequency vibrations and require
a timestep on the order of 0.5 fs in order to conserve energy.  The
relatively inexpensive force computations for the bonds, angles,
impropers, and dihedrals can be computed on this innermost 0.5 fs
step.  The outermost timestep cannot be greater than 4.0 fs without
risking energy drift.  Smooth switching of forces between the levels
of the rRESPA hierarchy is also necessary to avoid drift, and a 1\sphinxhyphen{}2
Angstrom “healing distance” (the distance between the outer and inner
cutoffs) works reasonably well.  We thus recommend the following
settings for use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} style without SHAKE in biomolecular
simulations:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{middle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{outer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With these settings, users can expect good energy conservation and
roughly a 2.5 fold speedup over the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet} style with a 0.5 fs
timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If SHAKE is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} style, time reversibility is lost,
but substantially longer time steps can be achieved.  For biomolecular
simulations using the CHARMM or similar all\sphinxhyphen{}atom force field, bonds
involving hydrogen atoms exhibit high frequency vibrations and require
a time step on the order of 0.5 fs in order to conserve energy.
These high frequency modes also limit the outer time step sizes since
the modes are coupled.  It is therefore desirable to use SHAKE with
respa in order to freeze out these high frequency motions and increase
the size of the time steps in the respa hierarchy.  The following
settings can be used for biomolecular simulations with SHAKE and
rRESPA:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shake}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.000001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{m}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{outer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With these settings, users can expect good energy conservation and
roughly a 1.5 fold speedup over the \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet} style with SHAKE and a
2.0 fs timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For non\sphinxhyphen{}biomolecular simulations, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} style can be
advantageous if there is a clear separation of time scales \sphinxhyphen{} fast and
slow modes in the simulation.  For example, a system of slowly\sphinxhyphen{}moving
charged polymer chains could be setup as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is two\sphinxhyphen{}level rRESPA with an 8x difference between the short and
long timesteps.  The bonds, angles, dihedrals will be computed every
0.5 fs (assuming real units), while the pair and kspace interactions
will be computed once every 4 fs.  These are the default settings for
each kind of interaction, so no additional keywords are necessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Even a LJ system can benefit from rRESPA if the interactions are
divided by the inner, middle and outer keywords.  A 2\sphinxhyphen{}fold or more
speedup can be obtained while maintaining good energy conservation.
In real units, for a pure LJ fluid at liquid density, with a sigma of
3.0 Angstroms, and epsilon of 0.1 kcal/mol, the following settings
seem to work well:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{36.0}
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{respa}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{middle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{outer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa/omp} style is a variant of \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} adapted for use with
pair, bond, angle, dihedral, improper, or kspace styles with an \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}
suffix. It is functionally equivalent to \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} but performs
additional operations required for managing \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} styles.  For more on
\sphinxstyleemphasis{omp} styles see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_omp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Speed omp}}}} doc page.  Accelerated
styles take the same arguments and should produce the same results,
except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa/omp} explicitly in your input script, or you
can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you
invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in
your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{run_style:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split} style can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
REPLICA package.  Correspondingly the \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa/omp} style is available
only if the OPENMP package was included. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Run style \sphinxstyleemphasis{verlet/split} is not compatible with kspace styles from
the INTEL package and it is not compatible with any tip4p, dipole,
or spin kspace styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Whenever using rRESPA, the user should experiment with trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs in
speed and accuracy for their system, and verify that they are
conserving energy to adequate precision.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{run_style:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{run_style:default}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{run\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{verlet}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For run\_style respa, the default assignment of interactions
to rRESPA levels is as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bond forces = level 1 (innermost loop)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
angle forces = same level as bond forces

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dihedral forces = same level as angle forces

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
improper forces = same level as dihedral forces

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pair forces = level N (outermost level)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
kspace forces = same level as pair forces

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
inner, middle, outer forces = no default

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{run_style:tuckerman3}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Tuckerman)} Tuckerman, Berne and Martyna, J Chem Phys, 97, p 1990
(1992).

\sphinxstepscope

\index{set@\spxentry{set}}\ignorespaces 

\section{set command}
\label{\detokenize{set:set-command}}\label{\detokenize{set:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{set::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{set:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{region}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID = depends on style

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
for style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}, ID = a range of atom IDs
for style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{type}, ID = a range of numeric types or a single type label
for style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}, ID = a range of molecule IDs
for style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{group}, ID = a group ID
for style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{region}, ID = a region ID
\end{sphinxalltt}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{type/fraction} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{type/ratio} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{type/subset}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vx} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charge} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/random} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{quat} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/atom/random} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/electron} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius/electron} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{quat} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{quat/random} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{diameter} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{shape} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{length} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tri} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{theta} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{theta/random} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angmom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{omega} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mass} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{density} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{density/disc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{temperature} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{image} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sph/e} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sph/cv} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sph/rho} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{smd/contact/radius} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{smd/mass/density} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/theta} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{edpd/temp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{edpd/cv} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{epsilon} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i\_name} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{d\_name} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{i2\_name} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{d2\_name}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type} value = numeric atom type or type label
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type/fraction} values = type fraction seed
  type = numeric atom type or type label
  fraction = approximate fraction of selected atoms to set to new atom type
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type/ratio} values = type fraction seed
  type = numeric atom type or type label
  fraction = exact fraction of selected atoms to set to new atom type
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type/subset} values = type Nsubset seed
  type = numeric atom type or type label
  Nsubset = exact number of selected atoms to set to new atom type
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} value = molecule ID
value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{x},\sphinxstyleemphasis{y},\sphinxstyleemphasis{z} value = atom coordinate (distance units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{vx},\sphinxstyleemphasis{vy},\sphinxstyleemphasis{vz} value = atom velocity (velocity units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{charge} value = atomic charge (charge units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole} values = x y z
  x,y,z = orientation of dipole moment vector
  any of x,y,z can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/random} value = seed Dlen
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer) for dipole moment orientations
  Dlen = magnitude of dipole moment (dipole units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/atom} values = g x y z
  g = magnitude of magnetic spin vector (in Bohr magneton\textquotesingle{}s unit)
  x,y,z = orientation of magnetic spin vector
  any of x,y,z can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/atom/random} value = seed Dlen
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer) for magnetic spin orientations
  Dlen = magnitude of magnetic spin vector (in Bohr magneton\textquotesingle{}s unit)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{radius/electron} values = eradius
  eradius = electron radius (or fixed\sphinxhyphen{}core radius) (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/electron} value = espin
  espin = electron spin (+1/\sphinxhyphen{}1), 0 = nuclei, 2 = fixed\sphinxhyphen{}core, 3 = pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}cores (i.e. ECP)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{quat} values = a b c theta
  a,b,c = unit vector to rotate particle around via right\sphinxhyphen{}hand rule
  theta = rotation angle (degrees)
  any of a,b,c,theta can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{quat/random} value = seed
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer) for quaternion orientations
\sphinxstyleemphasis{diameter} value = diameter of spherical particle (distance units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{shape} value = Sx Sy Sz
  Sx,Sy,Sz = 3 diameters of ellipsoid (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{length} value = len
  len = length of line segment (distance units)
  len can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tri} value = side
  side = side length of equilateral triangle (distance units)
  side can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{theta} value = angle (degrees)
  angle = orientation of line segment with respect to x\sphinxhyphen{}axis
  angle can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{theta/random} value = seed
  seed = random \# seed (positive integer) for line segment orienations
\sphinxstyleemphasis{angmom} values = Lx Ly Lz
  Lx,Ly,Lz = components of angular momentum vector (distance\sphinxhyphen{}mass\sphinxhyphen{}velocity units)
  any of Lx,Ly,Lz can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{omega} values = Wx Wy Wz
  Wx,Wy,Wz = components of angular velocity vector (radians/time units)
  any of wx,wy,wz can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mass} value = per\sphinxhyphen{}atom mass (mass units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{density} value = particle density for a sphere or ellipsoid (mass/distance\textasciicircum{}3 units), or for a triangle (mass/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units) or line (mass/distance units) particle
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{density/disc} value = particle density for a 2d disc or ellipse (mass/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{temperature} value = temperature for finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles (temperature units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} value = particle volume for Peridynamic particle (distance\textasciicircum{}3 units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{image} nx ny nz
  nx,ny,nz = which periodic image of the simulation box the atom is in
  any of nx,ny,nz can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} value = numeric bond type or bond type label, for all bonds between selected atoms
\sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} value = numeric angle type or angle type label, for all angles between selected atoms
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} value = numeric dihedral type or dihedral type label, for all dihedrals between selected atoms
\sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} value = numeric improper type or improper type label, for all impropers between selected atoms
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rheo/rho} value = density of RHEO particles (mass/distance\textasciicircum{}3)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rheo/status} value = status or phase of RHEO particles (unitless)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sph/e} value = energy of SPH particles (need units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sph/cv} value = heat capacity of SPH particles (need units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sph/rho} value = density of SPH particles (need units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{smd/contact/radius} = radius for short range interactions, i.e. contact and friction
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{smd/mass/density} = set particle mass based on volume by providing a mass density
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/theta} value = internal temperature of DPD particles (temperature units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
  value can be NULL which sets internal temp of each particle to KE temp
\sphinxstyleemphasis{edpd/temp} value = temperature of eDPD particles (temperature units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{edpd/cv} value = volumetric heat capacity of eDPD particles (energy/temperature/volume units)
  value can be an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable (see below)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cc} values = index cc
  index = index of a chemical species (1 to Nspecies)
  cc = chemical concentration of tDPD particles for a species (mole/volume units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{epsilon} value = dielectric constant of the medium where the atoms reside
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i\_name} value = custom integer vector with name
\sphinxstyleemphasis{d\_name} value = custom floating\sphinxhyphen{}point vector with name
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i2\_name} value = column of a custom integer array with name
                  column specified as i2\_name{[}N{]} where N is 1 to Ncol
\sphinxstyleemphasis{d2\_name} value = column of a custom floating\sphinxhyphen{}point array with name
                  column specified as d2\_name{[}N{]} where N is 1 to Ncol
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}
