\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{thermo_style:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the style and content for printing thermodynamic data to the
screen and log files.  The units for each column of output
corresponding to the list of keywords is determined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command for the simulation.  E.g. energies will be in energy
units, temperature in temperature units, pressure in pressure units.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} prints a single line of thermodynamic info that is the
equivalent of “thermo\_style custom step temp epair emol etotal press”.
The line contains only numeric values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi} prints a multiple\sphinxhyphen{}line listing of thermodynamic info
that is the equivalent of “thermo\_style custom etotal ke temp pe ebond
eangle edihed eimp evdwl ecoul elong press”.  The listing contains
numeric values and a string ID for each quantity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 24Mar2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{yaml} is similar to style \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} but prints the output in \sphinxhref{https://yaml.org/}{YAML} format which can be easily read by a variety of
script languages and data handling packages.  Since LAMMPS may print
other output before, after, or in between thermodynamic output, the
YAML format content needs to be separated from the rest.  All YAML
format thermodynamic output can be matched with a regular expression
and can thus be extracted with commands like \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{egrep}} as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
egrep\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}\PYGZca{}(keywords:|data:\PYGZdl{}|\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZdl{}|\PYGZbs{}.\PYGZbs{}.\PYGZbs{}.\PYGZdl{}|  \PYGZhy{} \PYGZbs{}[)\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }log.lammps\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZgt{}\PYG{+w}{ }log.yaml
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Information about processing such YAML files is in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_structured_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{structured
data output howto}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} is the most general setting and allows you to specify
which of the keywords listed above you want printed on each
thermodynamic timestep.  Note that the keywords c\_ID, f\_ID, v\_name are
references to {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}}, and
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} that have been defined elsewhere
in the input script or can even be new styles which users have added
to LAMMPS.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Modify}}}} page for details on the
latter.  Thus the \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} style provides a flexible means of
outputting essentially any desired quantity as a simulation proceeds.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All styles except \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} have \sphinxstyleemphasis{vol} appended to their list of
outputs if the simulation box volume changes during the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values printed by the various keywords are instantaneous values,
calculated on the current timestep.  Time\sphinxhyphen{}averaged quantities, which
include values from previous timesteps, can be output by using the
f\_ID keyword and accessing a fix that does time\sphinxhyphen{}averaging such as the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Options invoked by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command can
be used to set the one\sphinxhyphen{} or multi\sphinxhyphen{}line format of the print\sphinxhyphen{}out, the
normalization of thermodynamic output (total values versus per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
values for extensive quantities (ones which scale with the number of
atoms in the system), and the numeric precision of each printed value.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you use a “thermo\_style” command, all thermodynamic
settings are restored to their default values, including those
previously set by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command.  Thus
if your input script specifies a thermo\_style command, you should use
the thermo\_modify command after it.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Several of the thermodynamic quantities require a temperature to be
computed: “temp”, “press”, “ke”, “etotal”, “enthalpy”, “pxx”, etc.  By
default this is done by using a \sphinxstyleemphasis{temperature} compute which is created
when LAMMPS starts up, as if this command had been issued:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}} command for details.  Note
that the ID of this compute is \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_temp} and the group is \sphinxstyleemphasis{all}.
You can change the attributes of this temperature (e.g. its
degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom) via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}}
command.  Alternatively, you can directly assign a new compute (that
calculates temperature) which you have defined, to be used for
calculating any thermodynamic quantity that requires a temperature.
This is done via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Several of the thermodynamic quantities require a pressure to be
computed: “press”, “enthalpy”, “pxx”, etc.  By default this is done by
using a \sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure} compute which is created when LAMMPS starts up, as
if this command had been issued:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pressure}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}temp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} command for details.
Note that the ID of this compute is \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_press} and the group is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{all}.  You can change the attributes of this pressure via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command.  Alternatively, you can
directly assign a new compute (that calculates pressure) which you
have defined, to be used for calculating any thermodynamic quantity
that requires a pressure.  This is done via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Several of the thermodynamic quantities require a potential energy to
be computed: “pe”, “etotal”, “ebond”, etc.  This is done by using a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pe} compute which is created when LAMMPS starts up, as if this
command had been issued:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}} command for details.  Note that
the ID of this compute is \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_pe} and the group is \sphinxstyleemphasis{all}.  You can
change the attributes of this potential energy via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The kinetic energy of the system \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} is inferred from the temperature
of the system with \(\frac{1}{2} k_B T\) of energy for each degree
of freedom.  Thus, using different {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute commands}}}}
for calculating temperature, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify temp}}}} command, may yield different kinetic energies, since
different computes that calculate temperature can subtract out
different non\sphinxhyphen{}thermal components of velocity and/or include different
degrees of freedom (translational, rotational, etc).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential energy of the system \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe} will include contributions
from fixes if the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify energy yes}}}} option is
set for a fix that calculates such a contribution.  For example, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/lj93}}}} fix calculates the energy of atoms
interacting with the wall.  See the doc pages for “individual fixes”
to see which ones contribute and whether their default
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify energy}}}} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail correction \sphinxstyleemphasis{etail} for the van der Waals pairwise
energy will be non\sphinxhyphen{}zero only if the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify tail}}}} option is turned on.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{etail} contribution is
included in \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{etotal}, and the
corresponding tail correction to the pressure is included in \sphinxstyleemphasis{press}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pxx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pyy}, etc.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is more information on other keywords whose meaning may not be
clear.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{step}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{elapsed}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{elaplong} keywords refer to timestep
count.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Step} is the current timestep, or iteration count when a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimization}}}} is being performed.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Elapsed} is the
number of timesteps elapsed since the beginning of this run.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Elaplong} is the number of timesteps elapsed since the beginning of
an initial run in a series of runs.  See the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop}
keywords for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} for info on how to invoke a series of
runs that keep track of an initial starting time.  If these keywords
are not used, then \sphinxstyleemphasis{elapsed} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{elaplong} are the same value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dt} keyword is the current timestep size in time {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{time} keyword is the current elapsed simulation time,
also in time {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, which is simply (step*dt) if the
timestep size has not changed and the timestep has not been reset.  If
the timestep has changed (e.g. via {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}})
or the timestep has been reset (e.g. via the “reset\_timestep”
command), then the simulation time is effectively a cumulative value
up to the current point.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cpu} keyword is elapsed CPU seconds since the beginning of this
run.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpcpu} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{spcpu} keywords are measures of how fast your
simulation is currently running.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpcpu} keyword is simulation
time per CPU second, where simulation time is in time
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  E.g. for metal units, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpcpu} value would be
picoseconds per CPU second.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{spcpu} keyword is the number of
timesteps per CPU second.  Both quantities are on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly metrics,
measured relative to the last time they were invoked.  Thus if you are
printing out thermodynamic output every 100 timesteps, the two keywords
will continually output the time and timestep rate for the last 100
steps.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tpcpu} keyword does not attempt to track any changes in
timestep size, e.g. due to using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cpuremain} keyword estimates the CPU time remaining in the
current run, based on the time elapsed thus far.  It will only be a
good estimate if the CPU time/timestep for the rest of the run is
similar to the preceding timesteps.  On the initial timestep the value
will be 0.0 since there is no history to estimate from.  For a
minimization run performed by the “minimize” command, the estimate is
based on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxiter} parameter, assuming the minimization will
proceed for the maximum number of allowed iterations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{part} keyword is useful for multi\sphinxhyphen{}replica or multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition
simulations to indicate which partition this output and this file
corresponds to, or for use in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} to append to
a filename for output specific to this partition.  See discussion of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} for details on
running in multi\sphinxhyphen{}partition mode.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{timeremain} keyword is the seconds remaining when a timeout has
been configured via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timer timeout}}}} command.  If the
timeout timer is inactive, the value of this keyword is 0.0 and if the
timer is expired, it is negative. This allows for example to exit
loops cleanly, if the timeout is expired with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdl{}(timeremain) \PYGZlt{} 0.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{quit 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple} keyword is cumulative energy change in the system due to
any thermostatting or barostatting fixes that are being used.  A
positive value means that energy has been subtracted from the system
(added to the coupling reservoir).  See the \sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve} keyword for an
explanation of why this sign choice makes sense.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve} keyword is the sum of the potential and kinetic energy
of the system as well as the energy that has been transferred by
thermostatting or barostatting to their coupling reservoirs \textendash{} that is,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe} + \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} + \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple}.  Ideally, for a simulation in
the NVT, NPH, or NPT ensembles, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve} quantity should remain
constant over time even though \sphinxstyleemphasis{etotal} may change.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, the simulation box can be defined as orthogonal or
triclinic (non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal).  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc page for a detailed explanation of orthogonal,
restricted triclinic, and general triclinic simulation boxes and how
LAMMPS rotates a general triclinic box to be restricted triclinic
internally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ly}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{lz} keywords are the extent of the simulation box in
each dimension.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{xlo}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xhi}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ylo}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yhi}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zlo}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zhi} keywords
are the lower and upper bounds of the simulation box in each dimension.
I.e. \sphinxstyleemphasis{lx} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{xhi} \sphinxhyphen{} \sphinxstyleemphasis{xlo}).  These 9 values are the same for all 3 kinds
of boxes.  I.e. for a restricted triclinic box, they are the values as
if the box were not tilted.  For a general triclinic box, they are the
values after it is internally rotated to be a restricted triclinic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} are the current tilt factors for a triclinic box.
They are the same for restricted and general triclinic boxes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{avecx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{avecy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{avecz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bvecx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bvecy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bvecz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cvecx},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cvecy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cvecz} are the components of the 3 edge vectors of the
current general simulation box.  If it is an orthogonal box the
vectors are along the x, y, z coordinate axes.  If it is a restricted
triclinic box, the \sphinxstylestrong{A} vector is along the x axis, the \sphinxstylestrong{B} vector
is in the xy plane with a +y coordinate, and the \sphinxstylestrong{C} vector has a +z
coordinate, as explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc page.  If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify
triclinic/general}}}} option is set then they are the
\sphinxstylestrong{A}, \sphinxstylestrong{B}, \sphinxstylestrong{C} vector which define the general triclinic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cella}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellb}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellc}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellalpha}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellbeta}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cellgamma}
keywords correspond to the usual crystallographic quantities that
define the periodic simulation box of a crystalline system.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto triclinic}}}} page for a precise definition
of these quantities in terms of the LAMMPS representation of a
restricted triclinic simulation box via \sphinxstyleemphasis{lx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ly}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{lz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pxx,pyy,pzz,pxy,pxz,pyz} keywords are the 6 components of the
symmetric pressure tensor for the system.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
pressure}}}} command doc page for details of how it is
calculated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify triclinic/general}}}} option
is set then the 6 components will be output as values consistent with
the orientation of the general triclinic box relative to the standard
xyz coordinate axes.  If this keyword is not used, the values will be
consistent with the orientation of the restricted triclinic box (which
aligns with the xyz coordinate axes).  As explained on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_triclinic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto\_triclinic}}}} doc page, even if the
simulation box is created as a general triclinic box, internally
LAMMPS uses a restricted triclinic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that because the pressure tensor components are computed using
force vectors and atom coordinates, both of which are rotated in the
general versus restricted triclinic representation, the values will
typically be different for the two cases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fmax} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fnorm} keywords are useful for monitoring the progress
of an {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fmax} keyword
calculates the maximum force in any dimension on any atom in the
system, or the infinity\sphinxhyphen{}norm of the force vector for the system.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fnorm} keyword calculates the 2\sphinxhyphen{}norm or length of the force vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nbuild} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ndanger} keywords are useful for monitoring neighbor
list builds during a run.  Note that both these values are also
printed with the end\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}run statistics.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nbuild} keyword is the
number of re\sphinxhyphen{}builds during the current run.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ndanger} keyword is
the number of re\sphinxhyphen{}builds that LAMMPS considered potentially
“dangerous”.  If atom movement triggered neighbor list rebuilding (see
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}} command), then dangerous
reneighborings are those that were triggered on the first timestep
atom movement was checked for.  If this count is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero you may wish
to reduce the delay factor to ensure no force interactions are missed
by atoms moving beyond the neighbor skin distance before a rebuild
takes place.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For output values from a compute or fix or variable, the bracketed
index I used to index a vector, as in \sphinxstyleemphasis{c\_ID{[}I{]}} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{f\_ID{[}I{]}} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name{[}I{]}}, can be specified using a wildcard asterisk with the index
to effectively specify multiple values.  This takes the form “*” or
“*n” or “n*” or “m*n”.  If N = the size of the vector, then an
asterisk with no numeric values means all indices from 1 to N.  A
leading asterisk means all indices from 1 to n (inclusive).  A
trailing asterisk means all indices from n to N (inclusive).  A middle
asterisk means all indices from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a wildcard is the same as if the individual elements of the
vector had been listed one by one.  E.g. these 2 thermo\_style commands
are equivalent, since the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}} command
creates a global vector with 6 values.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp[3]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{             }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp[4]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp[5]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp[6]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, only the wildcard forms “*n” or
“m*n” are allowed.  You must specify the upper bound, because
vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable lengths are not determined until the variable
is evaluated.  If n is specified larger than the vector length
turns out to be, zeroes are output for missing vector values.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{c\_ID} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{c\_ID{[}I{]}} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{c\_ID{[}I{]}{[}J{]}} keywords allow global values
calculated by a compute to be output.  As discussed on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} doc page, computes can calculate global,
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values.  Only global values can be
referenced by this command.  However, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom compute values for an
individual atom can be referenced in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} and the variable referenced by thermo\_style custom, as
discussed below.  See the discussion above for how the I in \sphinxstyleemphasis{c\_ID{[}I{]}}
can be specified with a wildcard asterisk to effectively specify
multiple values from a global compute vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID in the keyword should be replaced by the actual ID of a compute
that has been defined elsewhere in the input script.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command for details.  If the compute
calculates a global scalar, vector, or array, then the keyword formats
with 0, 1, or 2 brackets will reference a scalar value from the
compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that some computes calculate “intensive” global quantities like
temperature; others calculate “extensive” global quantities like
kinetic energy that are summed over all atoms in the compute group.
Intensive quantities are printed directly without normalization by
thermo\_style custom.  Extensive quantities may be normalized by the
total number of atoms in the simulation (NOT the number of atoms in
the compute group) when output, depending on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify
norm}}}} option being used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{f\_ID} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{f\_ID{[}I{]}} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{f\_ID{[}I{]}{[}J{]}} keywords allow global values
calculated by a fix to be output.  As discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} doc page, fixes can calculate global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and
per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values.  Only global values can be referenced by this
command.  However, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom fix values can be referenced for an
individual atom in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} and the
variable referenced by thermo\_style custom, as discussed below.  See
the discussion above for how the I in \sphinxstyleemphasis{f\_ID{[}I{]}} can be specified with
a wildcard asterisk to effectively specify multiple values from a
global fix vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID in the keyword should be replaced by the actual ID of a fix
that has been defined elsewhere in the input script.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command for details.  If the fix calculates a global
scalar, vector, or array, then the keyword formats with 0, 1, or 2
brackets will reference a scalar value from the fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that some fixes calculate “intensive” global quantities like
timestep size; others calculate “extensive” global quantities like
energy that are summed over all atoms in the fix group.  Intensive
quantities are printed directly without normalization by thermo\_style
custom.  Extensive quantities may be normalized by the total number of
atoms in the simulation (NOT the number of atoms in the fix group)
when output, depending on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify norm}}}} option being used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name} keyword allow the current value of a variable to be
output.  The name in the keyword should be replaced by the variable
name that has been defined elsewhere in the input script.  Only
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style and vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can be referenced; the latter
requires a bracketed term to specify the Ith element of the vector
calculated by the variable.  However, an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can use
an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable in its formula indexed by the ID of an
individual atom.  This is a way to output a specific atom’s per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
coordinates or other per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties in thermo output.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command for details.  Note that variables
of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} define a formula which can
reference per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties or thermodynamic keywords, or they can
invoke other computes, fixes, or variables when evaluated, so this is
a very general means of creating thermodynamic output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that equal\sphinxhyphen{}style and vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are assumed to
produce “intensive” global quantities, which are thus printed as\sphinxhyphen{}is,
without normalization by thermo\_style custom.  You can include a
division by “natoms” in the variable formula if this is not the case.

\index{third\_order@\spxentry{third\_order}}\ignorespaces 
\index{third\_order/kk@\spxentry{third\_order/kk}}\ignorespaces 

\section{third\_order command}
\label{\detokenize{third_order:third-order-command}}\label{\detokenize{third_order:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{third_order:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{third_order::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variant: third\_order/kk


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{third_order:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{third\PYGZus{}order}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delta}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of group of atoms to displace

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{regular} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eskm}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
delta = finite different displacement length (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/arg pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{binary}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} name = name of output file for the third order tensor
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{binary} arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gzip}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{third_order:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{third\PYGZus{}order}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{regular}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.000001}
\PYG{k}{third\PYGZus{}order}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eskm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.000001}
\PYG{k}{third\PYGZus{}order}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{regular}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00004}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{third\PYGZus{}order.dat}
\PYG{k}{third\PYGZus{}order}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eskm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00000001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{third\PYGZus{}order.dat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{binary}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{third_order:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the third order force constant tensor by finite difference of the selected group,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Phi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}_{ijk} = \frac{\partial^3 U}{\partial x_{i,\alpha} \partial x_{j,\beta} \partial x_{k, \gamma}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where Phi is the third order force constant tensor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output of the command is the tensor, three elements at a time. The
three elements correspond to the three gamma elements for a specific i/alpha/j/beta/k.
The initial five numbers are i, alpha, j, beta, and k respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the style eskm is selected, the tensor will be using energy units of 10 J/mol.
These units conform to eskm style from the dynamical\_matrix command, which
will simplify operations using dynamical matrices with third order tensors.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{third_order:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The command collects a 9 times the number of atoms in the group on every single MPI rank,
so the memory requirements can be very significant for large systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command is part of the PHONON package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{third_order:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_phonon::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix phonon}}}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{dynamical_matrix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dynamical\_matrix}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{third_order:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default settings are file = “third\_order.dat”, binary = no

\index{timer@\spxentry{timer}}\ignorespaces 

\section{timer command}
\label{\detokenize{timer:timer-command}}\label{\detokenize{timer:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{timer::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{timer:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{args} = one or more of \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{normal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sync} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nosync} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{timeout} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{every}

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{off} = do not collect or print any timing information
\sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} = collect only the total time for the simulation loop
\sphinxstyleemphasis{normal} = collect timer information broken down by sections (default)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{full} = like \sphinxstyleemphasis{normal} but also include CPU and thread utilization
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sync} = explicitly synchronize MPI tasks between sections
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nosync} = do not synchronize MPI tasks between sections (default)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{timeout} elapse = set wall time limit to \sphinxstyleemphasis{elapse}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{every} Ncheck = perform timeout check every \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ncheck} steps
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{timer:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{full}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sync}
\PYG{k}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{timeout}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2:00:00}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{timer:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Select the level of detail at which LAMMPS performs its CPU timings.
Multiple keywords can be specified with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{timer} command.  For
keywords that are mutually exclusive, the last one specified takes
precedence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
During a simulation run LAMMPS collects information about how much
time is spent in different sections of the code and thus can provide
information for determining performance and load imbalance problems.
This can be done at different levels of detail and accuracy.  For more
information about the timing output, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Run output}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} setting will turn all time measurements off. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop}
setting will only measure the total time for a run and not collect any
detailed per section information.  With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{normal} setting, timing
information for portions of the timestep (pairwise calculations,
neighbor list construction, output, etc) are collected as well as
information about load imbalances for those sections across
processors.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} setting adds information about CPU
utilization and thread utilization, when multi\sphinxhyphen{}threading is enabled.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sync} setting, all MPI tasks are synchronized at each timer
call which measures load imbalance for each section more accurately,
though it can also slow down the simulation by prohibiting overlapping
independent computations on different MPI ranks  Using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nosync}
setting (which is the default) turns this synchronization off.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{timeout} keyword a wall time limit can be imposed, that
affects the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} commands.
This can be convenient when calculations have to comply with execution
time limits, e.g. when running under a batch system when you want to
maximize the utilization of the batch time slot, especially for runs
where the time per timestep varies much and thus it becomes difficult
to predict how many steps a simulation can perform for a given wall time
limit. This also applies for difficult to converge minimizations.
The timeout \sphinxstyleemphasis{elapse} value should be somewhat smaller than the maximum
wall time requested from the batch system, as there is usually
some overhead to launch jobs, and it is advisable to write
out a restart after terminating a run due to a timeout.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The timeout timer starts when the command is issued. When the time
limit is reached, the run or energy minimization will exit on the
next step or iteration that is a multiple of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ncheck} value
which can be set with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword. Default is checking
every 10 steps. After the timer timeout has expired all subsequent
run or minimize commands in the input script will be skipped.
The remaining time or timer status can be accessed with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo}}}} variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{timeremain}, which will be
zero, if the timeout is inactive (default setting), it will be
negative, if the timeout time is expired and positive if there
is time remaining and in this case the value of the variable are
the number of seconds remaining.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{timeout} key word is used a second time, the timer is
restarted with a new time limit. The timeout \sphinxstyleemphasis{elapse} value can
be specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{unlimited} to impose a no timeout condition
(which is the default).  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{elapse} setting can be specified as
a single number for seconds, two numbers separated by a colon (MM:SS)
for minutes and seconds, or as three numbers separated by colons for
hours, minutes, and seconds (H:MM:SS).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{every} keyword sets how frequently during a run or energy
minimization the wall clock will be checked.  This check count applies
to the outer iterations or time steps during minimizations or {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA runs}}}}, respectively.  Checking for timeout too often,
can slow a calculation down.  Checking too infrequently can make the
timeout measurement less accurate, with the run being stopped later
than desired.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{sync} options provides the most detailed
and accurate timing information, but can also have a negative
performance impact due to the overhead of the many required system
calls. It is thus recommended to use these settings only when testing
tests to identify performance bottlenecks. For calculations with few
atoms or a very large number of processors, even the \sphinxstyleemphasis{normal} setting
can have a measurable negative performance impact. In those cases you
can just use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} setting.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{timer:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{timer:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run post no}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify fftbench}}}}

\label{\detokenize{timer:default}}

\PYG{k}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{timeout}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}
\PYG{k}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\index{units@\spxentry{units}}\ignorespaces 

\section{units command}
\label{\detokenize{units:units-command}}\label{\detokenize{units:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{units::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{units:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{real} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{si} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cgs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{electron} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{micro} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nano}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{units:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metal}
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{units:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command sets the style of units used for a simulation.  It
determines the units of all quantities specified in the input script
and data file, as well as quantities output to the screen, log file,
and dump files.  Typically, this command is used at the very beginning
of an input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all units except \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj}, LAMMPS uses physical constants from
www.physics.nist.gov.  For the definition of kcal in real units,
LAMMPS uses the thermochemical calorie = 4.184 J.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The choice you make for units simply sets some internal conversion
factors within LAMMPS.  This means that any simulation you perform for
one choice of units can be duplicated with any other unit setting
LAMMPS supports.  In this context “duplicate” means the particles will
have identical trajectories and all output generated by the simulation
will be identical.  This will be the case for some number of timesteps
until round\sphinxhyphen{}off effects accumulate, since the conversion factors for
two different unit systems are not identical to infinite precision.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To perform the same simulation in a different set of units you must
change all the unit\sphinxhyphen{}based input parameters in your input script and
other input files (data file, potential files, etc) correctly to the
new units.  And you must correctly convert all output from the new
units to the old units when comparing to the original results.  That
is often not simple to do.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Potential or table files may have a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UNITS:}} tag included in the
first line indicating the unit style those files were created for.
If the tag exists, its value will be compared to the chosen unit style
and LAMMPS will stop with an error message if there is a mismatch.
In some select cases and for specific combinations of unit styles,
LAMMPS is capable of automatically converting potential parameters
from a file. In those cases, a warning message signaling that an
automatic conversion has happened is printed to the screen.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj}, all quantities are unitless.  Without loss of
generality, LAMMPS sets the fundamental quantities mass, \(\sigma\),
\(\epsilon\), and the Boltzmann constant \(k_B = 1\).  The
masses, distances, energies you specify are multiples of these
fundamental values.  The formulas relating the reduced or unitless
quantity (with an asterisk) to the same quantity with units is also
given.  Thus you can use the mass, \(\sigma\), and \(\epsilon\)
values for a specific material and convert the results from a unitless
LJ simulation into physical quantities.  Please note that using
these three properties as base, your unit of time has to conform
to the relation \(\epsilon = \frac{m \sigma^2}{\tau^2}\) since
energy is a derived unit (in SI units you equivalently have the relation
\(1\mathsf{J} = 1\frac{\mathsf{kg}\cdot\mathsf{m}^2}{\mathsf{s}^2}\)).
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mass = mass or \(m\), where \(M^* = \frac{M}{m}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
distance = \(\sigma\), where \(x^* = \frac{x}{\sigma}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
time = \(\tau\), where \(\tau^* = \tau \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{m \sigma^2}}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
energy = \(\epsilon\), where \(E^* = \frac{E}{\epsilon}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
velocity = \(\frac{\sigma}{\tau}\), where \(v^* = v \frac{\tau}{\sigma}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
force = \(\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma}\), where \(f^* = f \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
torque = \(\epsilon\), where \(t^* = \frac{t}{\epsilon}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temperature = reduced LJ temperature, where \(T^* = \frac{T k_B}{\epsilon}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pressure = reduced LJ pressure, where \(p^* = p \frac{\sigma^3}{\epsilon}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dynamic viscosity = reduced LJ viscosity, where \(\eta^* = \eta \frac{\sigma^3}{\epsilon\tau}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
charge = reduced LJ charge, where \(q^* = q \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \sigma \epsilon}}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dipole = reduced LJ dipole, moment where \(\mu^* = \mu \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \sigma^3 \epsilon}}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
electric field = force/charge, where \(E^* = E \frac{\sqrt{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \sigma \epsilon} \sigma}{\epsilon}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density = mass/volume, where \(\rho^* = \rho \frac{\sigma^{dim}}{m}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for LJ units, the default mode of thermodynamic output via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command is to normalize all
extensive quantities by the number of atoms.  E.g. potential energy is
extensive because it is summed over atoms, so it is output as
energy/atom.  Temperature is intensive since it is already normalized
by the number of atoms, so it is output as\sphinxhyphen{}is.  This behavior can be
changed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify norm}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{real}, these are the units:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mass = grams/mole

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
distance = Angstroms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
time = femtoseconds

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
energy = kcal/mol

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
velocity = Angstroms/femtosecond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
force = (kcal/mol)/Angstrom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
torque = kcal/mol

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temperature = Kelvin

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pressure = atmospheres

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dynamic viscosity = Poise

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
charge = multiple of electron charge (1.0 is a proton)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dipole = charge*Angstroms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
electric field = volts/Angstrom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density = g/cm\textasciicircum{}dim

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal}, these are the units:

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{si}, these are the units:

\item {}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cgs}, these are the units:

\sphinxAtStartPar
The units command also sets the timestep size and neighbor skin
distance to default values for each style:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj} these are dt = 0.005 \(\tau\) and skin = 0.3 \(\sigma\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{real} these are dt = 1.0 femtoseconds and skin = 2.0 Angstroms.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} these are dt = 0.001 picoseconds and skin = 2.0 Angstroms.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{si} these are dt = 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}8 seconds and skin = 0.001 meters.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{cgs} these are dt = 1.0e\sphinxhyphen{}8 seconds and skin = 0.1 centimeters.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{electron} these are dt = 0.001 femtoseconds and skin = 2.0 Bohr.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{micro} these are dt = 2.0 microseconds and skin = 0.1 micrometers.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{nano} these are dt = 0.00045 nanoseconds and skin = 0.1 nanometers.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{getenv} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{string} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{timer} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{world} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} = no args
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile} arg = filename
\sphinxstyleemphasis{file} arg = filename
\sphinxstyleemphasis{format} args = vname fstr
  vname = name of equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable to evaluate
  fstr = C\sphinxhyphen{}style format string
\sphinxstyleemphasis{getenv} arg = one string
\sphinxstyleemphasis{index} args = one or more strings
\sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} arg = numeric value
\sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} args = N
  N = integer size of loop, loop from 1 to N inclusive
\sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} args = N pad
  N = integer size of loop, loop from 1 to N inclusive
  pad = all values will be same length, e.g. 001, 002, ..., 100
\sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} args = N1 N2
  N1,N2 = loop from N1 to N2 inclusive
\sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} args = N1 N2 pad
  N1,N2 = loop from N1 to N2 inclusive
  pad = all values will be same length, e.g. 050, 051, ..., 100
\sphinxstyleemphasis{python} arg = function
\sphinxstyleemphasis{string} arg = one string
\sphinxstyleemphasis{timer} arg = no arguments
\sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} args = N
  N = integer size of loop
\sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} args = N pad
  N = integer size of loop
  pad = all values will be same length, e.g. 001, 002, ..., 100
\sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} args = one or more strings
\sphinxstyleemphasis{world} args = one string for each partition of processors

\sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} args = one formula containing numbers, thermo keywords, math operations, built\sphinxhyphen{}in functions, atom values and vectors, compute/fix/variable references
  numbers = 0.0, 100, \sphinxhyphen{}5.4, 2.8e\sphinxhyphen{}4, etc
  constants = PI, version, on, off, true, false, yes, no
  thermo keywords = vol, ke, press, etc from {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}
  math operators = (), \sphinxhyphen{}x, x+y, x\sphinxhyphen{}y, x*y, x/y, x\textasciicircum{}y, x\%y,
                   x == y, x != y, x \textless{} y, x \textless{}= y, x \textgreater{} y, x \textgreater{}= y, x \&\& y, x || y, x |\textasciicircum{} y, !x
  math functions = sqrt(x), exp(x), ln(x), log(x), abs(x),
                   sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), asin(x), acos(x), atan(x), atan2(y,x),
                   random(x,y,z), normal(x,y,z), ceil(x), floor(x), round(x), ternary(x,y,z),

                    inertia(group,dimdim,region), omega(group,dim,region)
  special functions = sum(x), min(x), max(x), ave(x), trap(x), slope(x), sort(x), rsort(x), gmask(x), rmask(x), grmask(x,y), next(x), is\_file(name), is\_os(name), extract\_setting(name), label2type(kind,label), is\_typelabel(kind,label), is\_timeout()
  feature functions = is\_available(category,feature), is\_active(category,feature), is\_defined(category,id)
  atom value = id{[}i{]}, mass{[}i{]}, type{[}i{]}, mol{[}i{]}, x{[}i{]}, y{[}i{]}, z{[}i{]}, vx{[}i{]}, vy{[}i{]}, vz{[}i{]}, fx{[}i{]}, fy{[}i{]}, fz{[}i{]}, q{[}i{]}
  atom vector = id, mass, type, mol, radius, q, x, y, z, vx, vy, vz, fx, fy, fz
  custom atom property = i\_name, d\_name, i\_name{[}i{]}, d\_name{[}i{]}, i2\_name{[}i{]}, d2\_name{[}i{]}, i2\_name{[}i{]}{[}j{]}, d\_name{[}i{]}{[}j{]}
  compute references = c\_ID, c\_ID{[}i{]}, c\_ID{[}i{]}{[}j{]}, C\_ID, C\_ID{[}i{]}
  fix references = f\_ID, f\_ID{[}i{]}, f\_ID{[}i{]}{[}j{]}, F\_ID, F\_ID{[}i{]}
  variable references = v\_name, v\_name{[}i{]}
  vector initialization = {[}1,3,7,10{]} (for \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} variables only)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}
