\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{variable:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command assigns one or more strings to a variable name for
evaluation later in the input script or during a simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Variables can thus be useful in several contexts.  A variable can be
defined and then referenced elsewhere in an input script to become
part of a new input command.  For variable styles that store multiple
strings, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command can be used to increment which
string is assigned to the variable.  Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} store
a formula which when evaluated produces a single numeric value which
can be output either directly (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{print}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
print}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run every}}}} commands) or as part of
thermodynamic output (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}
command), or used as input to an averaging fix (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
ave/time}}}} command).  Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} store
a formula which produces a vector of such values which can be used as
input to various averaging fixes, or elements of which can be part of
thermodynamic output.  Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} store a formula which
when evaluated produces one numeric value per atom which can be output
to a dump file (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command) or used as
input to an averaging fix (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/atom}}}} commands).
Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile} can be used anywhere in an input script
that atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are used; they get their per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values
from a file rather than from a formula.  Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{python}
can be hooked to Python functions using code you provide, so that the
variable gets its value from the evaluation of the Python code.
Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} are used by a few commands which set
their value directly.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_parse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands parse}}}} doc
page, an input script can use “immediate” variables, specified as
\$(formula) with parenthesis, where the numeric formula has the same
syntax as equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables described on this page.  This is a
convenient way to evaluate a formula immediately without using the
variable command to define a named variable and then evaluate that
variable.  The formula can include a trailing colon and format
string which determines the precision with which the numeric value
is generated.  This is also explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_parse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands parse}}}} doc page.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the discussion that follows, the “name” of the variable is the
arbitrary string that is the first argument in the variable command.
This name can only contain alphanumeric characters and underscores.
The “string” is one or more of the subsequent arguments.  The “string”
can be simple text as in the first example above, it can contain other
variables as in the second example, or it can be a formula as in the third
example.  The “value” is the numeric quantity resulting from
evaluation of the string.  Note that the same string can generate
different values when it is evaluated at different times during a
simulation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When an input script line is encountered that defines a variable
of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} that contains a
formula or Python code, the formula is NOT immediately evaluated.  It
will be evaluated every time when the variable is \sphinxstylestrong{used} instead.  If
you simply want to evaluate a formula in place you can use as
so\sphinxhyphen{}called. See the section below about “Immediate Evaluation of
Variables” for more details on the topic.  This is also true of a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{format} style variable since it evaluates another variable when it is
invoked.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} can be used as
inputs to various other commands which evaluate their formulas as
needed, e.g. at different timesteps during a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}.  In
this context, variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{timer} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} can
be used in place of an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, with the following two
caveats.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First, internal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can be used except by commands that
set the value stored by the internal variable.  When the LAMMPS
command evaluates the internal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, it will use the value
set (internally) by another command.  Second, python\sphinxhyphen{}style variables
can be used so long as the associated Python function, as defined by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python}}}} command, returns a numeric value.  When the
LAMMPS command evaluates the python\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, the Python
function will be executed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When a variable command is encountered in the input script and
the variable name has already been specified, the command is ignored.
This means variables can NOT be re\sphinxhyphen{}defined in an input script (with
two exceptions, read further).  This is to allow an input script to be
processed multiple times without resetting the variables; see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{include::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{include}}}} commands.  It also means
that using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} \sphinxhyphen{}var will
override a corresponding index variable setting in the input script.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two exceptions to this rule.  First, variables of style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{string}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{getenv}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{python} ARE redefined each time the command is encountered.  This
allows these style of variables to be redefined multiple times in an
input script.  In a loop, this means the formula associated with an
\sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} style variable can change if it contains a
substitution for another variable, e.g. \$x or v\_x.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Second, as described below, if a variable is iterated on to the end of
its list of strings via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command, it is removed
from the list of active variables, and is thus available to be
re\sphinxhyphen{}defined in a subsequent variable command.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} style does
the same thing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Variables are \sphinxstylestrong{not} deleted by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{clear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{clear}}}} command with
the exception of atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_parse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands parse}}}} page explains how
occurrences of a variable name in an input script line are replaced by
the variable’s string.  The variable name can be referenced as \$x if
the name “x” is a single character, or as \$\{LoopVar\} if the name
“LoopVar” is one or more characters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As described below, for variable styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{index}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{file},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{universe}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop}, which string is assigned to a variable can be
incremented via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command.  When there are no more
strings to assign, the variable is exhausted and a flag is set that
causes the next {\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}} command encountered in the input
script to be skipped.  This enables the construction of simple loops
in the input script that are iterated over and then exited from.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained above, an exhausted variable can be re\sphinxhyphen{}used in an input
script.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{delete} style also removes the variable, the same as if
it were exhausted, allowing it to be redefined later in the input
script or when the input script is looped over.  This can be useful
when breaking out of a loop via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{if::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{if}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{jump}}}}
commands before the variable would become exhausted.  For example,

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{label       }\PYG{l+s+sc}{loop}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}
\PYG{k}{print}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{A = \PYGZdl{}a}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdl{}a \PYGZgt{} 2}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{jump in.script break}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{next        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}
\PYG{k}{jump        }\PYG{l+s+sc}{in.script}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}
\PYG{k}{label       }\PYG{l+s+sc}{break}
\PYG{k}{variable    }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delete}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The next sections describe in how all the various variable styles are
defined and what they store.  The styles are listed alphabetically,
except for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} styles, which are
explained together after all the others.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many of the styles store one or more strings.  Note that a single
string can contain spaces (multiple words), if it is enclosed in
quotes in the variable command.  When the variable is substituted for
in another input script command, its returned string will then be
interpreted as multiple arguments in the expanded command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile} style, a filename is provided which contains one or
more sets of values, to assign on a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom basis to the variable.
The format of the file is described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When an atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable is defined, the file is opened and the
first set of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values are read and stored with the variable.
This means the variable can then be evaluated as many times as desired
and will return those values.  There are two ways to cause the next
set of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from the file to be read: use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command or the next() function in an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
variable, as discussed below.  Unlike most variable styles, which
remain defined, atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are \sphinxstylestrong{deleted} during a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{clear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{clear}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rules for formatting the file are as follows.  Each time a set of
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values is read, a non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line is searched for in the file.
The file is read line by line but only up to 254 characters are used.
The rest are ignored.  A comment character “\#” can be used anywhere
on a line and all text following and the “\#” character are ignored;
text starting with the comment character is stripped.  Blank lines
are skipped.  The first non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line is expected to contain a single
integer number as the count \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom lines to follow.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} can
be the total number of atoms in the system or less, indicating that data
for a subset is read.  The next N lines must consist of two numbers,
the atom\sphinxhyphen{}ID of the atom for which a value is set followed by a floating
point number with the value.  The atom\sphinxhyphen{}IDs may be listed in any order.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Every time a set of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom lines is read, the value of the atomfile
variable for \sphinxstylestrong{all} atoms is first initialized to 0.0.  Thus values
for atoms whose ID do not appear in the set in the file will remain
at 0.0.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is a small example for the atomfile variable file format:
\begin{quote}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} first set
4
\PYGZsh{} atom\PYGZhy{}ID value
3 1
4 \PYGZhy{}4
1 0.5
2 \PYGZhy{}0.5

\PYGZsh{} second set
2

2  1.0
4 \PYGZhy{}1.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\end{quote}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{file} style, a filename is provided which contains a list of
strings to assign to the variable, one per line.  The strings can be
numeric values if desired.  See the discussion of the next() function
below for equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, which will convert the string of a
file\sphinxhyphen{}style variable into a numeric value in a formula.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When a file\sphinxhyphen{}style variable is defined, the file is opened and the
string on the first line is read and stored with the variable.  This
means the variable can then be evaluated as many times as desired and
will return that string.  There are two ways to cause the next string
from the file to be read: use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command or the
next() function in an equal\sphinxhyphen{} or atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, as discussed
below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rules for formatting the file are as follows.  A comment character
“\#” can be used anywhere on a line; text starting with the comment
character is stripped.  Blank lines are skipped.  The first “word” of
a non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line, delimited by white\sphinxhyphen{}space, is the “string” assigned
to the variable.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{format} style, an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style or compatible variable is
specified along with a C\sphinxhyphen{}style format string, e.g. “\%f” or “\%.10g”,
which must be appropriate for formatting a double\sphinxhyphen{}precision
floating\sphinxhyphen{}point value and may not have extra characters.  The default
format is “\%.15g”.  This variable style allows an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable
to be formatted precisely when it is evaluated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if you simply wish to print a variable value with desired
precision to the screen or logfile via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{print}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} commands, you can also do this by
specifying an “immediate” variable with a trailing colon and format
string, as part of the string argument of those commands.  This is
explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Commands_parse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Commands parse}}}} doc page.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{getenv} style, a single string is assigned to the variable
which should be the name of an environment variable.  When the
variable is evaluated, it returns the value of the environment
variable, or an empty string if it not defined.  This style of
variable can be used to adapt the behavior of LAMMPS input scripts via
environment variable settings, or to retrieve information that has
been previously stored with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{shell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{shell putenv}}}} command.
Note that because environment variable settings are stored by the
operating systems, they persist even if the corresponding \sphinxstyleemphasis{getenv}
style variable is deleted, and also are set for sub\sphinxhyphen{}shells executed
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{shell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{shell}}}} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} style, one or more strings are specified.  Initially,
the first string is assigned to the variable.  Each time a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command is used with the variable name, the next
string is assigned.  All processors assign the same string to the
variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Index\sphinxhyphen{}style variables with a single string value can also be set by
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch \sphinxhyphen{}var}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} style a numeric value is provided.  This value will
be assigned to the variable until a LAMMPS command sets it to a new
value.  There are currently only two LAMMPS commands that require
\sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} variables as inputs, because they reset them:
{\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_controller::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix controller}}}}.  As mentioned above, an internal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can
be used in place of an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable anywhere else in an input
script, e.g. as an argument to another command that allows for
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} style is identical to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} style except that the
strings are the integers from 1 to N inclusive, if only one argument N
is specified.  This allows generation of a long list of runs
(e.g. 1000) without having to list N strings in the input script.
Initially, the string “1” is assigned to the variable.  Each time a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command is used with the variable name, the next
string (“2”, “3”, etc) is assigned.  All processors assign the same
string to the variable.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{loop} style can also be specified with
two arguments N1 and N2.  In this case the loop runs from N1 to N2
inclusive, and the string N1 is initially assigned to the variable.
N1 \textless{}= N2 and N2 \textgreater{}= 0 is required.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} style a Python function name is provided.  This needs
to match a function name specified in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python}}}} command
which returns a value to this variable as defined by its \sphinxstyleemphasis{return}
keyword.  For example these two commands would be self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{foo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myMultiply}
\PYG{k}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myMultiply}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}foo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{funcs.py}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two commands can appear in either order so long as both are
specified before the Python function is invoked for the first time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each time the variable is evaluated, the associated Python function is
invoked, and the value it returns is also returned by the variable.
Since the Python function can use other LAMMPS variables as input, or
query interal LAMMPS quantities to perform its computation, this means
the variable can return a different value each time it is evaluated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The type of value stored in the variable is determined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{format}
keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python}}}} command.  It can be an integer
(i), floating point (f), or string (s) value.  As mentioned above, if
it is a numeric value (integer or floating point), then the
python\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can be used in place of an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable
anywhere in an input script, e.g. as an argument to another command
that allows for equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{string} style, a single string is assigned to the variable.
Two differences between this style and using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} style exist:
a variable with \sphinxstyleemphasis{string} style can be redefined, e.g. by another command later
in the input script, or if the script is read again in a loop. The other
difference is that \sphinxstyleemphasis{string} performs variable substitution even if the
string parameter is quoted.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{uloop} style is identical to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} style except that the
strings are the integers from 1 to N.  This allows generation of long
list of runs (e.g. 1000) without having to list N strings in the input
script.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{universe} style, one or more strings are specified.  There
must be at least as many strings as there are processor partitions or
“worlds”.  LAMMPS can be run with multiple partitions via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}}.  This variable
command initially assigns one string to each world.  When a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command is encountered using this variable, the first
processor partition to encounter it, is assigned the next available
string.  This continues until all the variable strings are consumed.
Thus, this command can be used to run 50 simulations on 8 processor
partitions.  The simulations will be run one after the other on
whatever partition becomes available, until they are all finished.
Universe\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are incremented using the files
“tmp.lammps.variable” and “tmp.lammps.variable.lock” which you will
see in your directory during such a LAMMPS run.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{world} style, one or more strings are specified.  There must
be one string for each processor partition or “world”.  LAMMPS can be
run with multiple partitions via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}partition command\sphinxhyphen{}line
switch}}}}.  This variable command assigns one string to
each world.  All processors in the world are assigned the same string.
The next command cannot be used with equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, since
there is only one value per world.  This style of variable is useful
when you wish to run different simulations on different partitions, or
when performing a parallel tempering simulation (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{temper::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temper}}}} command), to assign different temperatures to different
partitions.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} styles, a single string is
specified which represents a formula that will be evaluated afresh
each time the variable is used.  If you want spaces in the string,
enclose it in double quotes so the parser will treat it as a single
argument.  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables the formula computes a scalar
quantity, which becomes the value of the variable whenever it is
evaluated.  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector}\sphinxhyphen{}style variables the formula must compute a
vector of quantities, which becomes the value of the variable whenever
it is evaluated.  The calculated vector can be of length one, but it
cannot be a simple scalar value like that produced by an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style
compute.  I.e. the formula for a vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable must have at
least one quantity in it that refers to a global vector produced by a
compute, fix, or other vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables the formula computes one quantity for each atom whenever it
is evaluated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} variables can produce
different values at different stages of the input script or at
different times during a run.  For example, if an \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} variable is
used in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} command, different values could
be printed each timestep it was invoked.  If you want a variable to be
evaluated immediately, so that the result is stored by the variable
instead of the string, see the section below on “Immediate Evaluation
of Variables”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The next command cannot be used with \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}
style variables, since there is only one string.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The formula for an \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} variable can contain a
variety of quantities.  The syntax for each kind of quantity is
simple, but multiple quantities can be nested and combined in various
ways to build up formulas of arbitrary complexity.  For example, this
is a valid (though strange) variable formula:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{pe + c\PYGZus{}MyTemp / vol\PYGZca{}(1/3)}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specifically, a formula can contain numbers, constants, thermo
keywords, math operators, math functions, group functions, region
functions, special functions, feature functions, atom values, atom
vectors, custom atom properties, compute references, fix references, and references to other
variables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most of the formula elements produce a scalar value.  Some produce a
global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector of values.  Global vectors can be produced
by computes or fixes or by other vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.  Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
vectors are produced by atom vectors, computes or fixes which output a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array, and variables that are atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.
Math functions that operate on scalar values produce a scalar value;
math function that operate on global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors do so
element\sphinxhyphen{}by\sphinxhyphen{}element and produce a global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A formula for equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables cannot use any formula element
that produces a global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector.  A formula for a
vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can use formula elements that produce either a
scalar value or a global vector value, but cannot use a formula
element that produces a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector.  A formula for an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
variable can use formula elements that produce either a scalar value
or a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, but not one that produces a global vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are evaluated by other commands that define a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}} on which they operate, e.g. a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command.  When they
invoke the atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, only atoms in the group are included
in the formula evaluation.  The variable evaluates to 0.0 for atoms
not in the group.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Numbers, constants, and thermo keywords}
\label{\detokenize{variable:numbers-constants-and-thermo-keywords}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Numbers can contain digits, scientific notation
(3.0e20,3.0e\sphinxhyphen{}20,3.0E20,3.0E\sphinxhyphen{}20), and leading minus signs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Constants are set at compile time and cannot be changed. \sphinxstyleemphasis{PI} will
return the number 3.14159265358979323846; \sphinxstyleemphasis{on}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{true} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} will
return 1.0; \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{false} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} will return 0.0; \sphinxstyleemphasis{version} will
return a numeric version code of the current LAMMPS version (e.g.
version 2 Sep 2015 will return the number 20150902). The corresponding
value for newer versions of LAMMPS will be larger, for older versions
of LAMMPS will be smaller. This can be used to have input scripts
adapt automatically to LAMMPS versions, when non\sphinxhyphen{}backwards compatible
syntax changes are introduced. Here is an illustrative example (which
will not work, since the \sphinxstyleemphasis{version} has been introduced more recently):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{version\PYGZlt{}20140513}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{communicate vel yes}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{else}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{comm\PYGZus{}modify vel yes}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermo keywords allowed in a formula are those defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command.  Thermo keywords
that require a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} to calculate their values such
as “temp” or “press”, use computes stored and invoked by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command.  This means that you can
only use those keywords in a variable if the style you are using with
the thermo\_style command (and the thermo keywords associated with that
style) also define and use the needed compute.  Note that some thermo
keywords use a compute indirectly to calculate their value (e.g. the
enthalpy keyword uses temp, pe, and pressure).  If a variable is
evaluated directly in an input script (not during a run), then the
values accessed by the thermo keyword must be current.  See the
discussion below about “Variable Accuracy”.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Math Operators}
\label{\detokenize{variable:math-operators}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Math operators are written in the usual way, where the “x” and “y” in
the examples can themselves be arbitrarily complex formulas, as in the
examples above.  In this syntax, “x” and “y” can be scalar values or
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors.  For example, “ke/natoms” is the division of two
scalars, where “vy+vz” is the element\sphinxhyphen{}by\sphinxhyphen{}element sum of two per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
vectors of y and z velocities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Operators are evaluated left to right and have the usual C\sphinxhyphen{}style
precedence: unary minus and unary logical NOT operator “!” have the
highest precedence, exponentiation “\textasciicircum{}” is next; multiplication and
division and the modulo operator “\%” are next; addition and
subtraction are next; the 4 relational operators “\textless{}”, “\textless{}=”, “\textgreater{}”, and
“\textgreater{}=” are next; the two remaining relational operators “==” and “!=”
are next; then the logical AND operator “\&\&”; and finally the logical
OR operator “||” and logical XOR (exclusive or) operator “|\textasciicircum{}” have the
lowest precedence.  Parenthesis can be used to group one or more
portions of a formula and/or enforce a different order of evaluation
than what would occur with the default precedence.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Because a unary minus is higher precedence than exponentiation,
the formula “\sphinxhyphen{}2\textasciicircum{}2” will evaluate to 4, not \sphinxhyphen{}4.  This convention is
compatible with some programming languages, but not others.  As
mentioned, this behavior can be easily overridden with parenthesis;
the formula “\sphinxhyphen{}(2\textasciicircum{}2)” will evaluate to \sphinxhyphen{}4.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 6 relational operators return either a 1.0 or 0.0 depending on
whether the relationship between x and y is TRUE or FALSE.  For
example the expression x\textless{}10.0 in an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable formula will
return 1.0 for all atoms whose x\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate is less than 10.0, and 0.0
for the others.  The logical AND operator will return 1.0 if both its
arguments are non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, else it returns 0.0.  The logical OR operator
will return 1.0 if either of its arguments is non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, else it
returns 0.0.  The logical XOR operator will return 1.0 if one of its
arguments is zero and the other non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, else it returns 0.0.  The
logical NOT operator returns 1.0 if its argument is 0.0, else it
returns 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These relational and logical operators can be used as a masking or
selection operation in a formula.  For example, the number of atoms
whose properties satisfy one or more criteria could be calculated by
taking the returned per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector of ones and zeroes and passing it
to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Math Functions}
\label{\detokenize{variable:math-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Math functions are specified as keywords followed by one or more
parenthesized arguments “x”, “y”, “z”, each of which can themselves be
arbitrarily complex formulas.  In this syntax, the arguments can
represent scalar values or global vectors or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors.  In the
latter case, the math operation is performed on each element of the
vector.  For example, “sqrt(natoms)” is the sqrt() of a scalar, where
“sqrt(y*z)” yields a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector with each element being the
sqrt() of the product of one atom’s y and z coordinates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most of the math functions perform obvious operations.  The ln() is
the natural log; log() is the base 10 log.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The random(x,y,z) function takes 3 arguments: x = lo, y = hi, and z =
seed.  It generates a uniform random number between lo and hi.  The
normal(x,y,z) function also takes 3 arguments: x = mu, y = sigma, and
z = seed.  It generates a Gaussian variate centered on mu with
variance sigma\textasciicircum{}2.  In both cases the seed is used the first time the
internal random number generator is invoked, to initialize it.  For
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style and vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, every processor uses the same
seed so that they each generate the same sequence of random numbers.
For atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, a unique seed is created for each processor,
based on the specified seed.  This effectively generates a different
random number for each atom being looped over in the atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
variable.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Internally, there is just one random number generator for all
equal\sphinxhyphen{}style and vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variables and another one for all
atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.  If you define multiple variables (of each
style) which use the random() or normal() math functions, then the
internal random number generators will only be initialized once, which
means only one of the specified seeds will determine the sequence of
generated random numbers.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ceil(), floor(), and round() functions are those in the C math
library.  Ceil() is the smallest integer not less than its argument.
Floor() if the largest integer not greater than its argument.  Round()
is the nearest integer to its argument.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 7Feb2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ternary(x,y,z) function is the equivalent of the ternary operator
(? and :) in C or C++.  It takes 3 arguments.  The first argument is a
conditional.  The result of the function is y if x evaluates to true
(non\sphinxhyphen{}zero).  The result is z if x evaluates to false (zero).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ramp(x,y) function uses the current timestep to generate a value
linearly interpolated between the specified x,y values over the course
of a run, according to this formula:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
value = x + (y\sphinxhyphen{}x) * (timestep\sphinxhyphen{}startstep) / (stopstep\sphinxhyphen{}startstep)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The run begins on startstep and ends on stopstep.  Startstep and
stopstep can span multiple runs, using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keywords
of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command for
details of how to do this.  If called in between runs or during a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run 0}}}} command, the ramp(x,y) function will return the
value of x.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The stagger(x,y) function uses the current timestep to generate a new
timestep.  X,y \textgreater{} 0 and x \textgreater{} y are required.  The generated timesteps
increase in a staggered fashion, as the sequence
x,x+y,2x,2x+y,3x,3x+y,etc.  For any current timestep, the next
timestep in the sequence is returned.  Thus if stagger(1000,100) is
used in a variable by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify every}}}}
command, it will generate the sequence of output timesteps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
100,1000,1100,2000,2100,3000,etc
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The logfreq(x,y,z) function uses the current timestep to generate a
new timestep.  X,y,z \textgreater{} 0 and y \textless{} z are required.  The generated
timesteps are on a base\sphinxhyphen{}z logarithmic scale, starting with x, and the
y value is how many of the z\sphinxhyphen{}1 possible timesteps within one
logarithmic interval are generated.  I.e. the timesteps follow the
sequence
x,2x,3x,…y*x,x*z,2x*z,3x*z,…y*x*z,x*z\textasciicircum{}2,2x*z\textasciicircum{}2,etc.  For
any current timestep, the next timestep in the sequence is returned.
Thus if logfreq(100,4,10) is used in a variable by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify every}}}} command, it will generate this
sequence of output timesteps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
100,200,300,400,1000,2000,3000,4000,10000,20000,etc
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The logfreq2(x,y,z) function is similar to logfreq, except a single
logarithmic interval is divided into y equally\sphinxhyphen{}spaced timesteps and
all of them are output.  Y \textless{} z is not required.  Thus, if
logfreq2(100,18,10) is used in a variable by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify
every}}}} command, then the interval between 100 and 1000
is divided as 900/18 = 50 steps, and it will generate the sequence of
output timesteps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
100,150,200,...950,1000,1500,2000,...9500,10000,15000,etc
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The logfreq3(x,y,z) function generates y points between x and z (inclusive),
that are separated by a multiplicative ratio: (z/x)\textasciicircum{}(1/(y\sphinxhyphen{}1)). Constraints
are: x,z \textgreater{} 0, y \textgreater{} 1, z\sphinxhyphen{}x \textgreater{}= y\sphinxhyphen{}1. For eg., if logfreq3(10,25,1000) is used in
a variable by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_print::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix print}}}} command, then the interval
between 10 and 1000 is divided into 24 parts with a multiplicative
separation of \textasciitilde{}1.21, and it will generate the following sequence of output
timesteps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
10, 13, 15, 18, 22, 27, 32,...384, 465, 563, 682, 826, 1000
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The stride(x,y,z) function uses the current timestep to generate a new
timestep.  X,y \textgreater{}= 0 and z \textgreater{} 0 and x \textless{}= y are required.  The generated
timesteps increase in increments of z, from x to y, i.e. it generates
the sequence x,x+z,x+2z,…,y.  If y\sphinxhyphen{}x is not a multiple of z, then
similar to the way a for loop operates, the last value will be one
that does not exceed y.  For any current timestep, the next timestep
in the sequence is returned.  Thus if stride(1000,2000,100) is used
in a variable by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify every}}}} command, it
will generate the sequence of output timesteps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1000,1100,1200, ... ,1900,2000
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The stride2(x,y,z,a,b,c) function is similar to the stride() function
except it generates two sets of strided timesteps, one at a coarser
level and one at a finer level.  Thus it is useful for debugging,
e.g. to produce output every timestep at the point in simulation when
a problem occurs.  X,y \textgreater{}= 0 and z \textgreater{} 0 and x \textless{}= y are required, as are
a,b \textgreater{}= 0 and c \textgreater{} 0 and a \textless{} b.  Also, a \textgreater{}= x and b \textless{}= y are required so
that the second stride is inside the first.  The generated timesteps
increase in increments of z, starting at x, until a is reached.  At
that point the timestep increases in increments of c, from a to b,
then after b, increments by z are resumed until y is reached.  For any
current timestep, the next timestep in the sequence is returned.  Thus
if stride2(1000,2000,100,1350,1360,1) is used in a variable by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify every}}}} command, it will generate the
sequence of output timesteps:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
1000,1100,1200,1300,1350,1351,1352, ... 1359,1360,1400,1500, ... ,2000
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vdisplace(x,y) function takes 2 arguments: x = value0 and y =
velocity, and uses the elapsed time to change the value by a linear
displacement due to the applied velocity over the course of a run,
according to this formula:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
value = value0 + velocity*(timestep\sphinxhyphen{}startstep)*dt
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where dt = the timestep size.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The run begins on startstep.  Startstep can span multiple runs, using
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command for details of how to do this.  Note that the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} keyword elaplong = timestep\sphinxhyphen{}startstep.
If used between runs this function will return
the value according to the end of the last run or the value of x if
used before \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} runs.  This function assumes the length of the time
step does not change and thus may not be used in combination with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The swiggle(x,y,z) and cwiggle(x,y,z) functions each take 3 arguments:
x = value0, y = amplitude, z = period.  They use the elapsed time to
oscillate the value by a sin() or cos() function over the course of a
run, according to one of these formulas, where omega = 2 PI / period:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
value = value0 + Amplitude * sin(omega*(timestep\sphinxhyphen{}startstep)*dt)
value = value0 + Amplitude * (1 \sphinxhyphen{} cos(omega*(timestep\sphinxhyphen{}startstep)*dt))
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where dt = the timestep size.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The run begins on startstep.  Startstep can span multiple runs, using
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command for details of how to do this.  Note that the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} keyword elaplong = timestep\sphinxhyphen{}startstep.
If used between runs these functions will return
the value according to the end of the last run or the value of x if
used before \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} runs.  These functions assume the length of the time
step does not change and thus may not be used in combination with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Group and Region Functions}
\label{\detokenize{variable:group-and-region-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Group functions are specified as keywords followed by one or two
parenthesized arguments.  The first argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{ID} is the group\sphinxhyphen{}ID.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dim} argument, if it exists, is \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dir}
argument, if it exists, is \sphinxstyleemphasis{xmin}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xmax}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ymin}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ymax}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zmin}, or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{zmax}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dimdim} argument, if it exists, is \sphinxstyleemphasis{xx} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{zz}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The group function count() is the number of atoms in the group.  The
group functions mass() and charge() are the total mass and charge of
the group.  Xcm() and vcm() return components of the position and
velocity of the center of mass of the group.  Fcm() returns a
component of the total force on the group of atoms.  Bound() returns
the min/max of a particular coordinate for all atoms in the group.
Gyration() computes the radius\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}gyration of the group of atoms.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_gyration::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute gyration}}}} command for a definition
of the formula.  Angmom() returns components of the angular momentum
of the group of atoms around its center of mass.  Torque() returns
components of the torque on the group of atoms around its center of
mass, based on current forces on the atoms.  Inertia() returns one of
6 components of the symmetric inertia tensor of the group of atoms
around its center of mass, ordered as Ixx,Iyy,Izz,Ixy,Iyz,Ixz.
Omega() returns components of the angular velocity of the group of
atoms around its center of mass.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Region functions are specified exactly the same way as group functions
except they take an extra final argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{IDR} which is the region ID.
The function is computed for all atoms that are in both the group and
the region.  If the group is “all”, then the only criteria for atom
inclusion is that it be in the region.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Special Functions}
\label{\detokenize{variable:special-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Special functions take specific kinds of arguments, meaning their
arguments cannot be formulas themselves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum(x), min(x), max(x), ave(x), trap(x), slope(x), sort(x), and
rsort(x) functions each take 1 argument which is of the form “c\_ID” or
“c\_ID{[}N{]}” or “f\_ID” or “f\_ID{[}N{]}” or “v\_name”.  The first two are
computes and the second two are fixes; the ID in the reference should be
replaced by the ID of a compute or fix defined elsewhere in the input
script.  The compute or fix must produce either a global vector or
array.  If it produces a global vector, then the notation without “{[}N{]}”
should be used.  If it produces a global array, then the notation with
“{[}N{]}” should be used, where N is an integer, to specify which column of
the global array is being referenced.  The last form of argument
“v\_name” is for a vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable where “name” is replaced by the
name of the variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum(x), min(x), max(x), ave(x), trap(x), and slope(x) functions
operate on a global vector of inputs and reduce it to a single scalar
value.  This is analogous to the operation of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} command, which performs similar operations on per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
and local vectors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sort(x) and rsort(x) functions operate on a global vector of inputs
and return a global vector of the same length.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum() function calculates the sum of all the vector elements.  The
min() and max() functions find the minimum and maximum element
respectively.  The ave() function is the same as sum() except that it
divides the result by the length of the vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The trap() function is the same as sum() except the first and last
elements are multiplied by a weighting factor of 1/2 when performing
the sum.  This effectively implements an integration via the
trapezoidal rule on the global vector of data.  I.e. consider a set of
points, equally spaced by 1 in their x coordinate: (1,V1), (2,V2),
…, (N,VN), where the Vi are the values in the global vector of
length N.  The integral from 1 to N of these points is trap().  When
appropriately normalized by the timestep size, this function is useful
for calculating integrals of time\sphinxhyphen{}series data, like that generated by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_correlate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/correlate}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slope() function uses linear regression to fit a line to the set
of points, equally spaced by 1 in their x coordinate: (1,V1), (2,V2),
…, (N,VN), where the Vi are the values in the global vector of
length N.  The returned value is the slope of the line.  If the line
has a single point or is vertical, it returns 1.0e20.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 27June2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The sort(x) and rsort(x) functions sort the data of the input vector by
their numeric value: sort(x) sorts in ascending order, rsort(x) sorts
in descending order.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The gmask(x) function takes 1 argument which is a group ID.  It
can only be used in atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.  It returns a 1 for
atoms that are in the group, and a 0 for atoms that are not.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rmask(x) function takes 1 argument which is a region ID.  It can
only be used in atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.  It returns a 1 for atoms that
are in the geometric region, and a 0 for atoms that are not.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The grmask(x,y) function takes 2 arguments.  The first is a group ID,
and the second is a region ID.  It can only be used in atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables.  It returns a 1 for atoms that are in both the group and
region, and a 0 for atoms that are not in both.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The next(x) function takes 1 argument which is a variable ID (not
“v\_foo”, just “foo”).  It must be for a file\sphinxhyphen{}style or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style
variable.  Each time the next() function is invoked (i.e. each time
the equal\sphinxhyphen{}style or atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable is evaluated), the following
steps occur.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For file\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, the current string value stored by the
file\sphinxhyphen{}style variable is converted to a numeric value and returned by
the function.  And the next string value in the file is read and
stored.  Note that if the line previously read from the file was not a
numeric string, then it will typically evaluate to 0.0, which is
likely not what you want.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables, the current per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values stored by
the atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable are returned by the function.  And the
next set of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values in the file is read and stored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since file\sphinxhyphen{}style and atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables read and store the first
line of the file or first set of per\sphinxhyphen{}atoms values when they are
defined in the input script, these are the value(s) that will be
returned the first time the next() function is invoked.  If next() is
invoked more times than there are lines or sets of lines in the file,
the variable is deleted, similar to how the {\hyperref[\detokenize{next::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{next}}}} command
operates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The is\_file(name) function is a test whether \sphinxstyleemphasis{name} is a (readable) file
and returns 1 in this case, otherwise it returns 0.  For that \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}
is taken as a literal string and must not have any blanks in it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The is\_os(name) function is a test whether \sphinxstyleemphasis{name} is part of the OS
information that LAMMPS collects and provides in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_platform:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS8platform7os_infoEv}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{platform::os\_info()}}}}} function.
The argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{name} is interpreted as a regular expression as documented
for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Developer_utils:_CPPv4N9LAMMPS_NS5utils8strmatchERKNSt6stringERKNSt6stringE}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utils::strmatch()}}}}}
function. This allows to adapt LAMMPS inputs to the OS it runs on:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{is\PYGZus{}os}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZca{}Windows}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{shell copy \PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}input\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZcb{}\PYGZbs{}some\PYGZus{}file.txt .}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{k}{else}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{shell cp \PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}input\PYGZus{}dir\PYGZcb{}/some\PYGZus{}file.txt .}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The extract\_setting(name) function enables access to basic settings for
the LAMMPS executable and the running simulation via calling the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Library_properties:_CPPv422lammps_extract_settingPvPKc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lammps\_extract\_setting()}}}}} library function.  For example, the
number of processors (MPI ranks) being used by the simulation or the MPI
process ID (for this processor) can be queried, or the number of atom
types, bond types and so on. For the full list of available keywords
\sphinxstyleemphasis{name} and their meaning, see the documentation for extract\_setting()
via the link in this paragraph.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The label2type(kind,label) function converts type labels into numeric
types, using label maps created by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{labelmap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{labelmap}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} commands.  The first argument is the label
map kind (atom, bond, angle, dihedral, or improper) and the second
argument is the label.  The function returns the corresponding numeric
type or triggers an error if the queried label does not exist.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The is\_typelabel(kind,label) function has the same arguments as
label2type(), but returns 1 if the type label has been assigned,
otherwise it returns 0.  This function can be used to check if a
particular type label already exists in the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 29Aug2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The is\_timeout() function returns 1 when the {\hyperref[\detokenize{timer::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timer timeout}}}} has expired otherwise it returns 0.  This function can be used
to check inputs in combination with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{if::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{if command}}}} to
execute commands after the timer has expired. Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{timeout}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{is\PYGZus{}timeout}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{timeout}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0:10:00}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{timeout}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}Timer has expired\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Feature Functions}
\label{\detokenize{variable:feature-functions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Feature functions allow probing of the running LAMMPS executable for
whether specific features are available, active, or defined.  All 3 of
the functions take two arguments, a \sphinxstyleemphasis{category} and a category\sphinxhyphen{}specific
second argument.  Both are strings and thus cannot be formulas
themselves; only \$\sphinxhyphen{}style immediate variable expansion is possible.
The return value of the functions is either 1.0 or 0.0 depending on
whether the function evaluates to true or false, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{is\_available(category,name)} function queries whether a specific
feature is available in the LAMMPS executable that is being run, i.e
whether it was included or enabled at compile time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This supports the following categories: \sphinxstyleemphasis{command}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{feature}.  For all the categories except \sphinxstyleemphasis{feature}
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{name} is a style name, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{nve} for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} category.  Note
that many LAMMPS input script commands such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{create\_atoms} are
actually instances of a command style which LAMMPS defines, as opposed
to built\sphinxhyphen{}in commands.  For all of these styles except \sphinxstyleemphasis{command},
appending of active suffixes is also tried before reporting failure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{feature} category checks the availability of the following
compile\sphinxhyphen{}time enabled features: GZIP support, PNG support, JPEG support,
FFMPEG support, and C++ exceptions for error handling. Corresponding
names are \sphinxstyleemphasis{gzip}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{png}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{jpeg}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ffmpeg} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{exceptions}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example: Only dump in a given format if the compiled binary supports it.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdl{}(is\PYGZus{}available(feature,png))}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}PNG supported\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{else}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{print \PYGZsq{}PNG not supported\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdl{}(is\PYGZus{}available(feature,ffmpeg)}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{dump 3 all movie 25 movie.mp4 type type zoom 1.6 adiam 1.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{is\_active(category,feature)} function queries whether a specific
feature is currently active within LAMMPS.  The features are grouped
by categories.  Supported categories and features are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{package}: features = \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kokkos} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{newton}: features = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{any}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair}: features = \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{manybody} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_style}: features = \sphinxstyleemphasis{brick} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tiled}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{min\_style}: features = a minimizer style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{run\_style}: features = a run style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atom\_style}: features = an atom style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style}: features = a pair style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bond\_style}: features = a bond style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{angle\_style}: features = an angle style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral\_style}: features = a dihedral style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{improper\_style}: features = an improper style name

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace\_style}: features = a kspace style name

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most of the settings are self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{package}
category, a package may have been included in the LAMMPS build, but
not have enabled by any input script command, and hence be inactive.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} feature in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} category checks whether the
currently defined pair style supports a Pair::single() function as
needed by compute group/group and others features or LAMMPS.
Similarly, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} feature checks whether the inner/middle/outer
mode of r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA is supported by the current pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the categories with \sphinxstyleemphasis{style} in their name, only a single instance
of the style is ever active at any time in a LAMMPS simulation.  Thus
the check is whether the currently active style matches the specified
name.  This check is also done using suffix flags, if available and
enabled.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example 1: Disable use of suffix for PPPM when using GPU package
(i.e. run it on the CPU concurrently while running the pair style on
the GPU), but do use the suffix otherwise (e.g. with OPENMP).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{14.0}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{is\PYGZus{}active}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{package,gpu}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{suffix off}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{kspace\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pppm}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example 2: Use r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA with inner/outer cutoff, if supported by the
current pair style, otherwise fall back to using r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA with simply
the pair keyword and reducing the outer time step.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{timestep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{2.0*}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{1.0+2.0*is\PYGZus{}active}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{pair,respa}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{is\PYGZus{}active}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{pair,respa}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{run\PYGZus{}style respa 4 3 2 2 improper 1 inner 2 5.5 7.0 outer 3 kspace 4}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{else}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{run\PYGZus{}style respa 3 3 2 improper 1 pair 2 kspace 3}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{is\_defined(category,id)} function checks whether an instance of a
style or variable with a specific ID or name is currently defined
within LAMMPS.  The supported categories are \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dump},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fix}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{group}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{region}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable}.  Each of these styles (as
well as the variable command) can be specified multiple times within
LAMMPS, each with a unique \sphinxstyleemphasis{id}.  This function checks whether the
specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} exists.  For category \sphinxstyleemphasis{variable”, the *id} is the
variable name.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Atom Values and Vectors}
\label{\detokenize{variable:atom-values-and-vectors}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom values take an integer argument I from 1 to N, where I is the
atom\sphinxhyphen{}ID, e.g. x{[}243{]}, which means use the x coordinate of the atom
with ID = 243.  Or they can take a variable name, specified as v\_name,
where name is the name of the variable, like x{[}v\_myIndex{]}.  The
variable can be of any style except \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atomfile}
variables.  The variable is evaluated and the result is expected to be
numeric and is cast to an integer (i.e. 3.4 becomes 3), to use an
index, which must be a value from 1 to N.  Note that a “formula”
cannot be used as the argument between the brackets, e.g. x{[}243+10{]}
or x{[}v\_myIndex+1{]} are not allowed.  To do this a single variable can
be defined that contains the needed formula.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the 0 \textless{} atom\sphinxhyphen{}ID \textless{}= N, where N is the largest atom ID
in the system.  If an ID is specified for an atom that does not
currently exist, then the generated value is 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom vectors generate one value per atom, so that a reference like
“vx” means the x\sphinxhyphen{}component of each atom’s velocity will be used when
evaluating the variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The meaning of the different atom values and vectors is mostly
self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Mol} refers to the molecule ID of an atom, and is
only defined if an {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} is being used that
defines molecule IDs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that many other atom attributes can be used as inputs to a
variable by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}} command and then referencing that compute.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Custom atom properties}

vectors or arrays that have been added via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command.  When that command is used specific
names are given to each attribute which are the “name” portion of

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Compute References}
\label{\detokenize{variable:compute-references}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute references access quantities calculated by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}.  The ID in the reference should be replaced by the ID of a
compute defined elsewhere in the input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed on the page for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command,
computes can produce global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values.
Only global and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can be used in a variable.  Computes
can also produce scalars (global only), vectors, and arrays.  See the
doc pages for individual computes to see what different kinds of data
they produce.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can only use scalar values, either from global
or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data.  In the case of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data, this would be a value
for a specific atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can use scalar values (same as for equal\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables), or global vectors of values.  The latter can also be a
column of a global array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can use scalar values (same as for equal\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables), or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors of values.  The latter can also be a
column of a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The various allowed compute references in the variable formulas for
equal\sphinxhyphen{}, vector\sphinxhyphen{}, and atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are listed in the following
table:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable formula wishes to access per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
data from a compute, it must use capital “C” as the ID prefix and not
lower\sphinxhyphen{}case “c”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that if a vector\sphinxhyphen{} or atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable formula needs to
access a scalar value from a compute (i.e. the 5 kinds of values in
the first 5 lines of the table), it can not do so directly.  Instead,
it can use a reference to an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable which stores the
scalar value from the compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The I and J indices in these compute references can be integers or can
be a variable name, specified as v\_name, where name is the name of the
variable.  The rules for this syntax are the same as for indices in
the “Atom Values and Vectors” discussion above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a variable containing a compute is evaluated directly in an input
script (not during a run), then the values accessed by the compute
should be current.  See the discussion below about “Variable
Accuracy”.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Fix References}
\label{\detokenize{variable:fix-references}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix references access quantities calculated by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}.
The ID in the reference should be replaced by the ID of a fix defined
elsewhere in the input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed on the page for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command, fixes can
produce global, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom, local, and per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values.  Only global and
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can be used in a variable.  Fixes can also produce
scalars (global only), vectors, and arrays.  See the doc pages for
individual fixes to see what different kinds of data they produce.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can only use scalar values, either from global
or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data.  In the case of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data, this would be a value
for a specific atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can use scalar values (same as for equal\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables), or global vectors of values.  The latter can also be a
column of a global array.

\sphinxAtStartPar

variables), or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors of values.  The latter can also be a
column of a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

access a scalar value from a fix (i.e. the 5 kinds of values in the
first 5 lines of the table), it can not do so directly.  Instead, it
can use a reference to an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable which stores the scalar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Variable References}
\label{\detokenize{variable:variable-references}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Variable references access quantities stored or calculated by other
variables, which will cause those variables to be evaluated.  The name
in the reference should be replaced by the name of a variable defined
elsewhere in the input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed on this doc page, equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables generate a single
global numeric value, vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variables generate a vector of
global numeric values, and atom\sphinxhyphen{}style and atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables
generate a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector of numeric values.  All other variables
store one or more strings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The formula for an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can use any style of variable
including a vector\_style or atom\sphinxhyphen{}style or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style.  For these
3 styles, a subscript must be used to access a single value from
the vector\sphinxhyphen{}, atom\sphinxhyphen{}, or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.  If a string\sphinxhyphen{}storing
variable is used, the string is converted to a numeric value.  Note
that this will typically produce a 0.0 if the string is not a numeric
string, which is likely not what you want.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The formula for a vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can use any style of variable,
including atom\sphinxhyphen{}style or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.  For these 2 styles,
a subscript must be used to access a single value from the atom\sphinxhyphen{}, or
atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The formula for an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can use any style of variable,
including other atom\sphinxhyphen{}style or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variables.  If it uses a
vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, a subscript must be used to access a single
value from the vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.

\sphinxAtStartPar

vector\sphinxhyphen{}, and atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables are listed in the following table.
Note that there is no ambiguity as to what a reference means, since
referenced variables produce only a global scalar or global vector or
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector.
