\section{fix drude/transform/direct command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:fix-drude-transform-direct-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform::doc}}

\section{fix drude/transform/inverse command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:fix-drude-transform-inverse-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{drude/transform/direct} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{drude/transform/inverse}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{direct}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{inverse}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example input scripts available: examples/PACKAGES/drude


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Transform the coordinates of Drude oscillators from real to reduced
and back for thermalizing the Drude oscillators as described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_drude_transform:lamoureux1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Lamoureux)}}}} using a Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat.  This fix is
designed to be used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermalized Drude oscillator model}}}}.  Polarizable models in LAMMPS are described
on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_polarizable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto polarizable}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Drude oscillators are a pair of atoms representing a single
polarizable atom.  Ideally, the mass of Drude particles would vanish
and their positions would be determined self\sphinxhyphen{}consistently by iterative
minimization of the energy, the cores’ positions being fixed.  It is
however more efficient and it yields comparable results, if the Drude
oscillators (the motion of the Drude particle relative to the core)
are thermalized at a low temperature.  In that case, the Drude
particles need a small mass.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermostats act on the reduced degrees of freedom, which are
defined by the following equations.  Note that in these equations
upper case denotes atomic or center of mass values and lower case
denotes Drude particle or dipole values. Primes denote the transformed
(reduced) values, while bare letters denote the original values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Masses:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M' = M + m\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}m' = \frac {M\, m } {M'}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Positions:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}X' = \frac {M\, X + m\, x} {M'}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}x' = x - X\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Velocities:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V' = \frac {M\, V + m\, v} {M'}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}v' = v - V\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Forces:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F' = F + f\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f' = \frac { M\, f - m\, F} {M'}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This transform conserves the total kinetic energy
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \frac 1 2 \, (M\, V^2\ + m\, v^2)
= \frac 1 2 \, (M'\, V'^2\ + m'\, v'^2)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the virial defined with absolute positions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}X\, F + x\, f = X'\, F' + x'\, f'\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix requires each atom know whether it is a Drude particle or
not.  You must therefore use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix drude}}}} command to
specify the Drude status of each atom type.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
only the Drude core atoms need to be in the group specified for
this fix. A Drude electron will be transformed together with its core
even if it is not itself in the group.  It is safe to include Drude
electrons or non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atoms in the group. The non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable
atoms will simply not be transformed.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix does NOT perform time integration. It only transform masses,
coordinates, velocities and forces. Thus you must use separate time
integration fixes, like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} to actually update the velocities and positions of
atoms.  In order to thermalize the reduced degrees of freedom at
different temperatures, two Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostats must be defined,
acting on two distinct groups.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix drude/transform/direct} command must appear before any
Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostatting fixes.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix drude/transform/inverse}
command must appear after any Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostatting fixes.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fDIRECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{direct}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fNVT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{gCORES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fNVT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{gDRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fINVERSE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{inverse}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{TDRUDE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{drude}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cpu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ebond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ecoul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{elong}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}TDRUDE[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}TDRUDE[2]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this example, \sphinxstyleemphasis{gCORES} is the group of the atom cores and \sphinxstyleemphasis{gDRUDES}
is the group of the Drude particles (electrons). The centers of mass
of the Drude oscillators will be thermostatted at 300.0 and the
internal degrees of freedom will be thermostatted at 1.0.  The
temperatures of cores and Drude particles, in center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass and
relative coordinates, are calculated using {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/drude}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition, if you want to use a barostat to simulate a system at
constant pressure, only one of the Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover fixes must be \sphinxstyleemphasis{npt},
the other one should be \sphinxstyleemphasis{nvt}. You must add a \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute temp/com} and a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\_modify} command so that the temperature of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{npt} fix be just
that of its group (the Drude cores) but the pressure be the overall
pressure \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_press}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cTEMP\PYGZus{}CORE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{gCORES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{com}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fDIRECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{direct}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fNPT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{gCORES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{npt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{298.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{298.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fNPT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cTEMP\PYGZus{}CORE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermo\PYGZus{}press}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fNVT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{gDRUDES}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fINVERSE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drude}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{transform}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{inverse}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this example, \sphinxstyleemphasis{gCORES} is the group of the atom cores and \sphinxstyleemphasis{gDRUDES}
is the group of the Drude particles. The centers of mass of the Drude
oscillators will be thermostatted at 298.0 and the internal degrees of
freedom will be thermostatted at 5.0. The whole system will be
barostatted at 1.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to avoid the flying ice cube problem (irreversible transfer
of linear momentum to the center of mass of the system), you may need
to add a \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix momentum} command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fMOMENTUM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{momentum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\section{fix dt/reset command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:fix-dt-reset-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{dt/reset/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{reset}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Tmin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Tmax}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Xmax}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dt/reset = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = re\sphinxhyphen{}compute dt every N timesteps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tmin = minimum dt allowed which can be NULL (time units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tmax = maximum dt allowed which can be NULL (time units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Xmax = maximum distance for an atom to move in one timestep (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{emax} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{units}

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{emax} value = Emax
  Emax = maximum kinetic energy change for an atom in one timestep (energy units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{units} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{box}
  lattice = Xmax is defined in lattice units
  box = Xmax is defined in simulation box units
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{reset}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0e\PYGZhy{}5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{reset}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{reset}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{emax}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{30}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{box}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Reset the timestep size every N steps during a run, so that no atom
moves further than the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{Xmax} distance, based on current
atom velocities and forces.  Optionally an additional criterion is
imposed by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{emax} keyword, so that no atom’s kinetic energy
changes by more than the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{Emax}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be useful when starting from a configuration with overlapping
atoms, where forces will be large.  Or it can be useful when running
an impact simulation where one or more high\sphinxhyphen{}energy atoms collide with
a solid, causing a damage cascade.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix overrides the timestep size setting made by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} command.  The new timestep size \sphinxstyleemphasis{dt} is
computed in the following manner.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For each atom, the timestep is computed that would cause it to
displace \sphinxstyleemphasis{Xmax} on the next integration step, as a function of its
current velocity and force.  Since performing this calculation exactly
would require the solution to a quartic equation, a cheaper estimate
is generated.  The estimate is conservative in that the atom’s
displacement is guaranteed not to exceed \sphinxstyleemphasis{Xmax}, though it may be
smaller.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{emax} keyword is used, the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{Emax} value
is enforced as a limit on how much an atom’s kinetic energy can
change.  If the timestep required is even smaller than for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Xmax}
displacement, then the smaller timestep is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given this putative timestep for each atom, the minimum timestep value
across all atoms is computed.  Then the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tmin} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tmax} bounds are
applied, if specified.  If one (or both) is specified as NULL, it is
not applied.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run style}}}} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa}, this fix resets the
outer loop (largest) timestep, which is the same timestep that the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}} command sets.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the cumulative simulation time (in time units), which
accounts for changes in the timestep size as a simulation proceeds,
can be accessed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style time}}}}
keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify every/time}}}} option
allows dump files to be written at intervals specified by simulation
time, rather than by timesteps.  Simulation time is in time units;
see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} doc page for details.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options are
relevant to this fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix computes a global scalar which can be accessed by various
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The scalar stores the last
timestep on which the timestep was reset to a new value.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this fix is “intensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  This fix is not invoked during
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.

\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{fix_dt_reset:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify every/time}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{fix efield command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:fix-efield-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_efield::doc}}

\section{fix efield/tip4p command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:fix-efield-tip4p-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ex}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ey}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ez}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{efield} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{efield/tip4p}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ex,ey,ez = E\sphinxhyphen{}field component values (electric field units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
any of ex,ey,ez can be a variable (see below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended to args

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{region} value = region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of region atoms must be in to have added force
\sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} value = v\_name
  v\_name = variable with name that calculates the potential energy of each atom in the added E\sphinxhyphen{}field
\sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} value = v\_name
  v\_name = variable with name that calculates the electric potential of each atom in the added E\sphinxhyphen{}field
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{kick}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{external\PYGZhy{}field}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{efield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{kick}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{external\PYGZhy{}field}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{efield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}oscillate}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{kick}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{external\PYGZhy{}field}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{efield}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tip4p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add a force \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\) to each charged atom in the group due to an
external electric field being applied to the system.  If the system
contains point\sphinxhyphen{}dipoles, also add a torque on the dipoles due to the
external electric field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 28Mar2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{efield/tip4p} style is used, the E\sphinxhyphen{}field will be applied to
the position of the virtual charge site M of a TIP4P molecule instead of
the oxygen position as it is defined by a corresponding {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_tip4p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{TIP4P pair
style}}}}.  The forces on the M site due to the
external field are projected on the oxygen and hydrogen atoms of the
TIP4P molecules.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For charges, any of the 3 quantities defining the E\sphinxhyphen{}field components can
be specified as an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style or atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}},
namely \sphinxstyleemphasis{ex}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ey}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ez}.  If the value is a variable, it should be
specified as v\_name, where name is the variable name.  In this case, the
variable will be evaluated each timestep, and its value used to
determine the E\sphinxhyphen{}field component.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For point\sphinxhyphen{}dipoles, equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can be used, but atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables are not currently supported, since they imply a spatial
gradient in the electric field which means additional terms with
gradients of the field are required for the force and torque on dipoles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can specify formulas with various mathematical
functions, and include {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command
keywords for the simulation box parameters and timestep and elapsed
time.  Thus it is easy to specify a time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent E\sphinxhyphen{}field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can specify the same formulas as equal\sphinxhyphen{}style
variables but can also include per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values, such as atom
coordinates.  Thus it is easy to specify a spatially\sphinxhyphen{}dependent E\sphinxhyphen{}field
with optional time\sphinxhyphen{}dependence as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} keyword is used, the atom must also be in the
specified geometric {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}} in order to have force added
to it.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Adding a force or torque to atoms implies a change in their potential
energy as they move or rotate due to the applied E\sphinxhyphen{}field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For dynamics via the “run” command, this energy can be optionally
added to the system’s potential energy for thermodynamic output (see
below).  For energy minimization via the “minimize” command, this
energy must be added to the system’s potential energy to formulate a
self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent minimization problem (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword is not allowed if the added field is a constant
vector (ex,ey,ez), with all components defined as numeric constants
and not as variables.  This is because LAMMPS can compute the energy
for each charged particle directly as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{efield} = -\vec{x} \cdot q\vec{E} = -q (x\cdot E_x + y\cdot E_y + z\cdot Ez),\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that \(-\nabla U_{efield} = \vec{F}\).  Similarly for point\sphinxhyphen{}dipole particles
the energy can be computed as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{efield} = -\vec{\mu} \cdot \vec{E} = -\mu_x\cdot E_x + \mu_y\cdot E_y + \mu_z\cdot E_z\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword is optional if the added force is defined with
one or more variables, and if you are performing dynamics via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  If the keyword is not used, LAMMPS will set
the energy to 0.0, which is typically fine for dynamics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword (or \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} keyword, described below)
is required if the added force is defined with
one or more variables, and you are performing energy minimization via
the “minimize” command for charged particles.  It is not required for
point\sphinxhyphen{}dipoles, but a warning is issued since the minimizer in LAMMPS
does not rotate dipoles, so you should not expect to be able to
minimize the orientation of dipoles in an applied electric field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword specifies the name of an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} which is used to compute the energy of each
atom as function of its position.  Like variables used for \sphinxstyleemphasis{ex},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ey}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ez}, the energy variable is specified as “v\_name”, where “name”
is the variable name.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword is used during an energy
minimization, you must ensure that the formula defined for the
atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} is consistent with the force
variable formulas, i.e. that \sphinxhyphen{}Grad(E) = F.  For example, if the force
due to the electric field were a spring\sphinxhyphen{}like F = kx, then the energy
formula should be E = \sphinxhyphen{}0.5kx\textasciicircum{}2.  If you don’t do this correctly, the
minimization will not converge properly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} keyword can be used as an alternative to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword
to specify the name of an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, which is used to compute the
added electric potential to each atom as a function of its position.  The
variable should have units of electric field multiplied by distance (that is,
in \sphinxtitleref{units real}, the potential should be in volts). As with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy}
keyword, the variable name is specified as “v\_name”. The energy added by this
fix is then calculated as the electric potential multiplied by charge.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} keyword is mainly intended for correct charge
equilibration in simulations with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_qeq_reaxff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix qeq/reaxff}}}},
since with variable charges the electric potential can be known
beforehand but the energy cannot.  A small additional benefit is that
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword requires an additional conversion to energy units
which the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} keyword avoids.  Thus, when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential}
keyword is specified, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} keyword must not be used.  As with
\sphinxstyleemphasis{energy}, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} keyword is not allowed if the added field is a
constant vector.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{potential} keyword is not supported by \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix
efield/tip4p}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_efield:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} option is supported by this
fix to add the potential energy inferred by the added force due to the
electric field to the global potential energy of the system as part of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}}.  The default setting for
this fix is {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify energy no}}}}.  Note that this
energy is a fictitious quantity but is needed so that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command can include the forces added by this fix in a
consistent manner.  I.e. there is a decrease in potential energy when
atoms move in the direction of the added force due to the electric
field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial} option is supported by this
fix to add the contribution due to the added forces on atoms to both the
global pressure and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress of the system via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
pressure}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}} commands.  The former can be accessed by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}}.  The default setting for
this fix is {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify virial no}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} option is supported by this
fix. This allows to set at which level of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA}}}}
integrator the fix adding its forces. Default is the outermost level.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix computes a global scalar and a global 3\sphinxhyphen{}vector of forces,
which can be accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The scalar is the potential energy discussed above.
The vector is the total force added to the group of atoms.  The scalar
and vector values calculated by this fix are “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forces due to this fix are imposed during an energy minimization,
invoked by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.  You should not
specify force components with a variable that has time\sphinxhyphen{}dependence for
use with a minimizer, since the minimizer increments the timestep as
the iteration count during the minimization.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the fictitious potential energy associated with the
added forces to be included in the total potential energy of the
system (the quantity being minimized), you MUST enable the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} option for this fix.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\section{fix ehex command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ehex:fix-ehex-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_ehex:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_ehex::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ehex:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ehex}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nevery}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{F}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ehex  = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
nevery = add/subtract heat every this many timesteps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
F = energy flux into the reservoir (energy/time units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended to args

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{region} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{constrain} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hex}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{region} value = region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of region (reservoir) atoms must be in for added thermostatting force
\sphinxstyleemphasis{constrain} value = none
  apply the constraint algorithm (SHAKE or RATTLE) again at the end of the timestep
\sphinxstyleemphasis{com} value = none
  rescale all sites of a constrained cluster of atom if its COM is in the reservoir
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hex} value = none
  omit the coordinate correction to recover the HEX algorithm
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} SPC/E water, from examples/in.ehex.spce}

\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{frattle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rattle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e\PYGZhy{}10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{400}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ehex:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix implements the asymmetric version of the enhanced heat
exchange algorithm {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ehex:wirnsberger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wirnsberger)}}}}. The eHEX algorithm is
an extension of the heat exchange algorithm {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ehex:ikeshoji}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ikeshoji)}}}} and
adds an additional coordinate integration to account for higher\sphinxhyphen{}order
truncation terms in the operator splitting.  The original HEX
algorithm (implemented as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_heat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix heat}}}}) is known to
exhibit a slight energy drift limiting the accessible simulation times
to a few nanoseconds.  This issue is greatly improved by the new
algorithm decreasing the energy drift by at least a factor of a
hundred (LJ and SPC/E water) with little computational overhead.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In both algorithms (non\sphinxhyphen{}translational) kinetic energy is constantly
swapped between regions (reservoirs) to impose a heat flux onto the
system.  The equations of motion are therefore modified if a particle
\(i\) is located inside a reservoir \(\Gamma_k\) where \(k>0\).  We
use \(\Gamma_0\) to label those parts of the simulation box which
are not thermostatted.)  The input parameter \sphinxstyleemphasis{region\sphinxhyphen{}ID} of this fix
corresponds to \(k\).  The energy swap is modelled by introducing an
additional thermostatting force to the equations of motion, such that
the time evolution of coordinates and momenta of particle \(i\)
becomes {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ehex:wirnsberger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wirnsberger)}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot{\mathbf r}_i &= \mathbf v_i,  \\
\dot{\mathbf v}_i &= \frac{\mathbf f_i}{m_i} + \frac{\mathbf g_i}{m_i}.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermostatting force is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf g_i = \begin{cases}
\frac{m_i}{2}   \frac{ F_{\Gamma_{k(\mathbf r_i)}}}{ K_{\Gamma_{k(\mathbf r_i)}}}
\left(\mathbf v_i -  \mathbf v_{\Gamma_{k(\mathbf r_i)}} \right) &  \mbox{$k(\mathbf r_i)> 0$ (inside a reservoir),} \\
 0                                     &  \mbox{otherwise, }
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(m_i\) is the mass and \(k(\mathbf r_i)\) maps the particle
position to the respective reservoir. The quantity
\(F_{\Gamma_{k(\mathbf r_i)}}\) corresponds to the input parameter
\sphinxstyleemphasis{F}, which is the energy flux into the reservoir. Furthermore,
\(K_{\Gamma_{k(\mathbf r_i)}}\) and \(v_{\Gamma_{k(\mathbf r_i)}}\)
denote the non\sphinxhyphen{}translational kinetic energy and the center of mass
velocity of that reservoir. The thermostatting force does not affect
the center of mass velocities of the individual reservoirs and the
entire simulation box. A derivation of the equations and details on
the numerical implementation with velocity Verlet in LAMMPS can be
found in reference “(Wirnsberger)”\#\_Wirnsberger.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix only integrates the thermostatting force and must be
combined with another integrator, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}, to
solve the full equations of motion.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is different from a thermostat such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}} in that energy is
added/subtracted continually.  Thus if there is not another mechanism
in place to counterbalance this effect, the entire system will heat or
cool continuously.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If heat is subtracted from the system too aggressively so that
the group’s kinetic energy would go to zero, then LAMMPS will halt
with an error message. Increasing the value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{nevery} means that
heat is added/subtracted less frequently but in larger portions.  The
resulting temperature profile will therefore be the same.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix will default to {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_heat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_heat}}}} (HEX algorithm) if
the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{hex} is specified.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Compatibility with SHAKE and RATTLE (rigid molecules)}:

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is compatible with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rattle}}}}. If either of these constraining algorithms is
specified in the input script and the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{constrain} is set, the
bond distances will be corrected a second time at the end of the
integration step.  It is recommended to specify the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} in
addition to the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{constrain}. With this option all sites of a
constrained cluster are rescaled, if its center of mass is located
inside the region. Rescaling all sites of a cluster by the same factor
does not introduce any velocity components along fixed bonds. No
rescaling takes place if the center of mass lies outside the region.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can only use the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} along with \sphinxstyleemphasis{constrain}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To achieve the highest accuracy it is recommended to use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rattle}}}} with the keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{constrain} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} as
shown in the second example. Only if RATTLE is employed, the velocity
constraints will be satisfied.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Even if RATTLE is used and the keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{constrain}
are both set, the coordinate constraints will not necessarily be
satisfied up to the target precision. The velocity constraints are
satisfied as long as all sites of a cluster are rescaled (keyword
\sphinxstyleemphasis{com}) and the cluster does not span adjacent reservoirs. The current
implementation of the eHEX algorithm introduces a small error in the
bond distances, which goes to zero with order three in the
timestep. For example, in a simulation of SPC/E water with a timestep
of 2 fs the maximum relative error in the bond distances was found to
be on the order of \(10^{-7}\) for relatively large
temperature gradients.  A higher precision can be achieved by
decreasing the timestep.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\section{fix electrode/conq command}

\section{fix electrode/thermo command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_electrode:fix-electrode-thermo-command}}

Accelerator Variant: \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/thermo/intel}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_electrode:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/thermo}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = arguments used by a particular style
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conp} args = potential eta
\sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conq} args = charge eta
\sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/thermo} args = potential eta \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} values
     potential = electrode potential
     charge = electrode charge
     eta = reciprocal width of electrode charge smearing (can be NULL if eta keyword is used)
     \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} values = T\_v tau\_v rng\_v
         T\_v = temperature of thermo\sphinxhyphen{}potentiostat
         tau\_v = time constant of thermo\sphinxhyphen{}potentiostat
         rng\_v = integer used to initialize random number generator
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{algo} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{etypes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ffield} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{write\_mat} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{write\_inv} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{read\_mat} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{read\_inv} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{qtotal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eta}

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{algo} values = \sphinxstyleemphasis{mat\_inv} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mat\_cg} tol or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cg} tol
    specify the algorithm used to compute the electrode charges
\sphinxstyleemphasis{symm} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}
    turn on/off charge neutrality constraint for the electrodes
\sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} values = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID val
    group\sphinxhyphen{}ID = group of atoms treated as additional electrode
    val = electric potential or charge on this electrode
\sphinxstyleemphasis{etypes} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}
    turn on/off type\sphinxhyphen{}based optimized neighbor lists (electrode and electrolyte types may not overlap)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ffield} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}
    turn on/off finite\sphinxhyphen{}field implementation
\sphinxstyleemphasis{write\_mat} value = filename
    filename = file to which to write elastance matrix
\sphinxstyleemphasis{write\_inv} value = filename
    filename = file to which to write inverted matrix
\sphinxstyleemphasis{read\_mat} value = filename
    filename = file from which to read elastance matrix
\sphinxstyleemphasis{read\_inv} value = filename
    filename = file from which to read inverted matrix
\sphinxstyleemphasis{qtotal} value = number or \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_} equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable
    add overall potential so that all electrode charges add up to \sphinxstyleemphasis{qtotal}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{eta} value = d\_propname
    d\_propname = a custom double vector defined via fix property/atom
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_electrode:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fxconp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{bot}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{electrode}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{conp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.805}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{couple}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{top}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{couple}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ref}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{write\PYGZus{}inv}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inv.csv}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{symm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{on}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fxconp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{electrodes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{electrode}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{conq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.805}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{algo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e\PYGZhy{}5}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fxconp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{bot}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{electrode}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{thermo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.805}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{298}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{couple}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{top}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_electrode:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode} fixes implement the constant potential method (CPM)
({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:siepmann}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Siepmann}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:reed3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Reed}}}}), and modern variants,
to accurately model electrified, conductive electrodes. This is
primarily useful for studying electrode\sphinxhyphen{}electrolyte interfaces,
especially at high potential differences or ionicities, with non\sphinxhyphen{}planar
electrodes such as nanostructures or nanopores, and to study dynamic
phenomena such as charging or discharging time scales or conductivity or
ionic diffusivities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode} fix allows users to set additional electrostatic
relationships between the specified groups which model useful
electrostatic configurations:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conp} sets potentials or potential differences between electrodes
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
(resulting in changing electrode total charges)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conq} sets the total charge on each electrode
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
(resulting in changing electrode potentials)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/thermo} sets a thermopotentiostat
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:deissenbeck}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Deissenbeck)}}}} between two electrodes
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
(resulting in changing charges and potentials with appropriate
average potential difference and thermal variance)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first group\sphinxhyphen{}ID provided to each fix specifies the first electrode
group, and more group(s) are added using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} keyword for each
additional group.  While \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/thermo} only accepts two groups,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{electrode/conq} accept any number of groups, up to
LAMMPS’s internal restrictions (see Restrictions below). Electrode
groups must not overlap, i.e.  the fix will issue an error if any
particle is detected to belong to at least two electrode groups.

\sphinxAtStartPar
CPM involves updating charges on groups of electrode particles, per time
step, so that the system’s total energy is minimized with respect to
those charges.  From basic electrostatics, this is equivalent to making
each group conductive, or imposing an equal electrostatic potential on
every particle in the same group (hence the name CPM).  The charges are
usually modelled as a Gaussian distribution to make the charge\sphinxhyphen{}charge
interaction matrix invertible ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:gingrich}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Gingrich}}}}).  The keyword
\sphinxstyleemphasis{eta} specifies the distribution’s width in units of inverse length.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Three algorithms are available to minimize the energy, varying in how
matrices are pre\sphinxhyphen{}calculated before a run to provide computational
speedup. These algorithms can be selected using the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{algo}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{algo mat\_inv} pre\sphinxhyphen{}calculates the capacitance matrix and obtains the
charge configuration in one matrix\sphinxhyphen{}vector calculation per time step

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{algo mat\_cg} pre\sphinxhyphen{}calculates the elastance matrix (inverse of
capacitance matrix) and obtains the charge configuration using a
conjugate gradient solver in multiple matrix\sphinxhyphen{}vector calculations per
time step

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{algo cg} does not perform any pre\sphinxhyphen{}calculation and obtains the charge
configuration using a conjugate gradient solver and multiple
calculations of the electric potential per time step.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For both \sphinxstyleemphasis{cg} methods, the command must specify the conjugate gradient
tolerance. \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/thermo} currently only supports the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mat\_inv}
algorithm.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm} can be set \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} (or \sphinxstyleemphasis{off}) to turn on (or turn off)
the capacitance matrix constraint that sets total electrode charge to be
zero.  This has slightly different effects for each \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode}
variant.  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/conp}, with \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm off}, the potentials
specified are absolute potentials, but the charge configurations
satisfying them may add up to an overall non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, varying charge for
the electrodes (and thus the simulation box). With \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm on}, the total
charge over all electrode groups is constrained to zero, and potential
differences rather than absolute potentials are the physically relevant
quantities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/conq}, with \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm off}, overall neutrality is
explicitly obeyed or violated by the user input (which is not
checked!). With \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm on}, overall neutrality is ensured by ignoring the
user\sphinxhyphen{}input charge for the last listed electrode (instead, its charge
will always be minus the total sum of all other electrode charges). For
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/thermo}, overall neutrality is always automatically
imposed for any setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm}, but \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm on} allows finite\sphinxhyphen{}field
mode (\sphinxstyleemphasis{ffield on}, described below) for faster simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all three fixes, any potential (or charge for \sphinxstyleemphasis{conq}) can be
specified as an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable prefixed with “v\_”. For example,
the following code will ramp the potential difference between electrodes
from 0.0V to 2.0V over the course of the simulation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fxconp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{bot}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{electrode}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{conp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.805}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{couple}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{top}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}v}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{symm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{on}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{v}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ramp}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{0.0, 2.0}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that these fixes only parse their supplied variable name when
starting a run, and so these fixes will accept equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables
defined \sphinxstyleemphasis{after} the fix definition, including variables dependent on the
fix’s own output. This is useful, for example, in the fix’s internal
finite\sphinxhyphen{}field commands (see below).  For an advanced example of this see
the in.conq2 input file in the directory
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/PACKAGES/electrode/graph\sphinxhyphen{}il}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix necessitates the use of a long range solver that calculates and
provides the matrix of electrode\sphinxhyphen{}electrode interactions and a vector of
electrode\sphinxhyphen{}electrolyte interactions.  The Kspace styles
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald/electrode}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/electrode} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/electrode/intel} are
created specifically for this task {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:ahrens-iwers}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ahrens\sphinxhyphen{}Iwers)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For systems with non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic boundaries in one or two directions dipole
corrections are available with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}}.
For ewald/electrode a two\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional Ewald summation {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:hu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hu)}}}}
can be used by setting “slab ew2d”:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kspace\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{slab}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{slab\PYGZus{}factor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{k}{kspace\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{wire}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{wire\PYGZus{}factor}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}
\PYG{k}{kspace\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{slab}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ew2d}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two implementations for the calculation of the elastance matrix are
available with pppm and can be selected using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{amat onestep/twostep}
keyword.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{onestep} is the default; \sphinxstyleemphasis{twostep} can be faster for large
electrodes and a moderate mesh size but requires more memory.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{kspace\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{onestep}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{twostep}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all versions of the fix, the keyword\sphinxhyphen{}value \sphinxstyleemphasis{ffield on} enables the
finite\sphinxhyphen{}field mode ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:dufils}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Dufils}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:tee}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Tee}}}}), which uses
an electric field across a periodic cell instead of non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic
boundary conditions to impose a potential difference between the two
electrodes bounding the cell. The fix (with name \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID}) detects which
of the two electrodes is “on top” (has the larger maximum \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate
among all particles).  Assuming the first electrode group is on top, it
then issues the following commands internally:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fix\PYGZhy{}ID\PYGZus{}ffield\PYGZus{}zfield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{f\PYGZus{}fix\PYGZhy{}ID[2]\PYGZhy{}f\PYGZus{}fix\PYGZhy{}ID[1]}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{lz}
\PYG{n}{efield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID\PYGZus{}efield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{efield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}fix}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID\PYGZus{}ffield\PYGZus{}zfield}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which implements the required electric field as the potential difference
divided by cell length.  The internal commands use variable so that the
electric field will correctly vary with changing potentials in the
correct way (for example with equal\sphinxhyphen{}style potential difference or with
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/conq}).  This keyword requires two electrodes and will
issue an error with any other number of electrodes. This keyword
requires electroneutrality to be imposed (\sphinxstyleemphasis{symm on}) and will issue an
error otherwise.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all versions of the fix, the keyword\sphinxhyphen{}value \sphinxstyleemphasis{etypes on} enables
type\sphinxhyphen{}based optimized neighbor lists. With this feature enabled, LAMMPS
provides the fix with an occasional neighbor list restricted to
electrode\sphinxhyphen{}electrode interactions for calculating the electrode matrix,
and a perpetual neighbor list restricted to electrode\sphinxhyphen{}electrolyte
interactions for calculating the electrode potentials, using particle
types to list only desired interactions, and typically resulting in
5\textendash{}10\% less computational time.  Without this feature the fix will
simply use the active pair style’s neighbor list.  This feature cannot
be enabled if any electrode particle has the same type as any
electrolyte particle (which would be unusual in a typical simulation)
and the fix will issue an error in that case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 17Apr2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{qtotal} causes \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/conp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix
electrode/thermo} to add an overall potential to all electrodes so that
the total charge on the electrodes is a specified amount (which may be
an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable).  For example, if a user wanted to simulate a
solution of excess cations such that the total electrolyte charge is +2,
setting \sphinxstyleemphasis{qtotal \sphinxhyphen{}2} would cause the total electrode charge to be \sphinxhyphen{}2, so
that the simulation box remains overall electroneutral. Since \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix
electrode/conq} constrains the total charges of individual electrodes,
and since \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm on} constrains the total charge of all electrodes to be
zero, either option is incompatible with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{qtotal} keyword (even if
\sphinxstyleemphasis{qtotal} is set to zero).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 17Apr2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{eta} takes the name of a custom double vector defined via
fix property/atom.  The values will be used instead of the standard eta
value.  The property/atom fix must be for vector of double values and
use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ghost on} option.


\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_electrode:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix currently does not write any information to restart files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\_modify tf} option enables the Thomas\sphinxhyphen{}Fermi metallicity model
({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:scalfi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Scalfi}}}}) and allows parameters to be set for each atom type.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{length}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If this option is used, these two parameters must be set for
all atom types of the electrode:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{tf} is the Thomas\sphinxhyphen{}Fermi length \(l_{TF}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxtitleref{voronoi} is the Voronoi volume per atom in units of length cubed

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Different types may have different \sphinxtitleref{tf} and \sphinxtitleref{voronoi} values.
The following self\sphinxhyphen{}energy term is then added for all electrode atoms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A_{ii} += \frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \times \frac{4 \pi l_{TF}^2}{\mathrm{Voronoi volume}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\_modify timer} option turns on (off) additional timer outputs in the log
file, for code developers to track optimization.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{timer}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{on}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{off}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes compute a global (extensive) scalar, a global (intensive)
vector, and a global array, which can be accessed by various
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The global scalar outputs the energy added to the system by this fix,
which is the negative of the total charge on each electrode multiplied
by that electrode’s potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The global vector outputs the potential on each electrode (and thus has
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} entries if the fix manages \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} electrode groups), in {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} of electric field multiplied by distance (thus volts for \sphinxstyleemphasis{real}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units).  The electrode groups’ ordering follows the order in
which they were input in the fix command using \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple}. The global
vector output is useful for \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/conq} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix
electrode/thermo}, where potential is dynamically updated based on
electrolyte configuration instead of being directly set.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The global array has \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} rows and \sphinxstyleemphasis{2N+1} columns, where the fix manages
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} electrode groups managed by the fix. For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}\sphinxhyphen{}th row of the
array, the elements are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
array{[}I{]}{[}1{]} = total charge that group \sphinxstyleemphasis{I} would have had \sphinxstyleemphasis{if it were
at 0 V applied potential}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
array{[}I{]}{[}2 to \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} + 1{]} = the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} entries
of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}\sphinxhyphen{}th row of the electrode capacitance matrix (definition
follows)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
array{[}I{]}{[}\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} + 2 to \sphinxstyleemphasis{2N} + 1{]} = the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} entries of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{I}\sphinxhyphen{}th row of the electrode elastance matrix (the inverse of the
electrode capacitance matrix)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(N \times N\) electrode capacitance matrix, denoted \(\mathbf{C}\)
in the following equation, summarizes how the total charge induced on each
electrode (\(\mathbf{Q}\) as an \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}\sphinxhyphen{}vector) is related to the potential on
each electrode, \(\mathbf{V}\), and the charge\sphinxhyphen{}at\sphinxhyphen{}0V \(\mathbf{Q}_{0V}\)
(which is influenced by the local electrolyte structure):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{Q}_{0V} + \mathbf{C} \cdot \mathbf{V}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The charge\sphinxhyphen{}at\sphinxhyphen{}0V, electrode capacitance and elastance matrices are internally
used to calculate the potentials required to induce the specified total
electrode charges in \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/conq} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix electrode/thermo}. With the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{symm on} option, the electrode capacitance matrix would be singular, and thus
its last row is replaced with \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} copies of its top\sphinxhyphen{}left entry
(\(\mathbf{C}_{11}\)) for invertibility.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The global array output is mainly useful for quickly determining the ‘vacuum
capacitance’ of the system (capacitance with only electrodes, no electrolyte),
and can also be used for advanced simulations setting the potential as some
function of the charge\sphinxhyphen{}at\sphinxhyphen{}0V (such as the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{in.conq2}} example mentioned above).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please cite {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:ahrens-iwers2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ahrens\sphinxhyphen{}Iwers2022)}}}} in any publication that
uses this implementation.  Please cite also the publication on the combination
of the CPM with PPPM if you use \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/electrode} {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_electrode:ahrens-iwers}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ahrens\sphinxhyphen{}Iwers)}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_electrode:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For algorithms that use a matrix for the electrode\sphinxhyphen{}electrode
interactions, positions of electrode particles have to be immobilized at
all times.

\sphinxAtStartPar
With \sphinxstyleemphasis{ffield off} (i.e. the default), the box geometry is expected to be
\sphinxstyleemphasis{z}\sphinxhyphen{}non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic (i.e. \sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary p p f}), and this fix will issue an
error if the box is \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}\sphinxhyphen{}periodic. With \sphinxstyleemphasis{ffield on}, the box geometry is
expected to be \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}\sphinxhyphen{}periodic, and this fix will issue an error if the box
is \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}\sphinxhyphen{}non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parallelization for the fix works best if electrode atoms are evenly
distributed across processors. For a system with two electrodes at the bottom
and top of the cell this can be achieved with \sphinxstyleemphasis{processors * * 2}, or with the
line

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdl{}(extract\PYGZus{}setting(world\PYGZus{}size) \PYGZpc{} 2) == 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{then}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{processors * * 2}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
which avoids an error if the script is run on an odd number of
processors (such as on just one processor for testing).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix creates an additional group named \sphinxstyleemphasis{{[}fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID{]}\_group} which is the
union of all electrode groups supplied to LAMMPS. This additional group
counts towards LAMMPS’s limitation on the total number of groups
(currently 32), which may not allow scripts that use that many groups to
run with this fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The matrix\sphinxhyphen{}based algorithms (\sphinxstyleemphasis{algo mat\_inv} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{algo mat\_cg}) currently
store an interaction matrix (either elastance or capacitance) of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} by
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} doubles for each MPI process. This memory requirement may be
prohibitive for large electrode groups.  The fix will issue a warning if
it expects to use more than 0.5 GiB of memory.


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_electrode:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default keyword\sphinxhyphen{}option settings are \sphinxstyleemphasis{algo mat\_inv}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{symm off},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{etypes off} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ffield off}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.
