\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{clump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}bodyid}

\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}bodyid}
\PYG{k}{read\PYGZus{}restart}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{data.rigid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Bodies}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{clump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{small}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i\PYGZus{}bodyid}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Treat one or more sets of atoms as independent rigid bodies.  This
means that each timestep the total force and torque on each rigid body
is computed as the sum of the forces and torques on its constituent
particles.  The coordinates, velocities, and orientations of the atoms
in each body are then updated so that the body moves and rotates as a
single entity.  This is implemented by creating internal data structures
for each rigid body and performing time integration on these data
structures.  Positions, velocities, and orientations of the constituent
particles are regenerated from the rigid body data structures in every
time step. This restricts which operations and fixes can be applied to
rigid bodies. See below for a detailed discussion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples of large rigid bodies are a colloidal particle, or portions
of a biomolecule such as a protein.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example of small rigid bodies are patchy nanoparticles, such as those
modeled in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid:zhang1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{this paper}}}} by Sharon Glotzer’s group,
clumps of granular particles, lipid molecules consisting of one or
more point dipoles connected to other spheroids or ellipsoids,
irregular particles built from line segments (2d) or triangles (3d),
and coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grain models of nano or colloidal particles consisting of a
small number of constituent particles.  Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command can also be used to rigidify small molecules of
2, 3, or 4 atoms, e.g. water molecules.  That fix treats the
constituent atoms as point masses.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes also update the positions and velocities of the atoms in
each rigid body via time integration, in the NVE, NVT, NPT, or NPH
ensemble, as described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two main variants of this fix, fix rigid and fix
rigid/small.  The NVE/NVT/NPT/NHT versions belong to one of the two
variants, as their style names indicate.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Not all of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bodystyle} options and keyword/value options are
available for both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} variants.  See
details below.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} styles are typically the best choice for a system with a
small number of large rigid bodies, each of which can extend across
the domain of many processors.  It operates by creating a single
global list of rigid bodies, which all processors contribute to.
MPI\_Allreduce operations are performed each timestep to sum the
contributions from each processor to the force and torque on all the
bodies.  This operation will not scale well in parallel if large
numbers of rigid bodies are simulated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles are typically best for a system with a large
number of small rigid bodies.  Each body is assigned to the atom
closest to the geometrical center of the body.  The fix operates using
local lists of rigid bodies owned by each processor and information is
exchanged and summed via local communication between neighboring
processors when ghost atom info is accumulated.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles the ghost atom cutoff must be large
enough to span the distance between the atom that owns the body and
every other atom in the body.  This distance value is printed out
when the rigid bodies are defined.  If the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} cutoff plus neighbor skin does not span this
distance, then you should use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify cutoff}}}} command with a setting epsilon larger than the
distance.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Which of the two variants is faster for a particular problem is hard
to predict.  The best way to decide is to perform a short test run.
Both variants should give identical numerical answers for short runs.
Long runs should give statistically similar results, but round\sphinxhyphen{}off
differences may accumulate to produce divergent trajectories.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You should not update the atoms in rigid bodies via other
time\sphinxhyphen{}integration fixes (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
nvt}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_move::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix move}}}}), or you will have conflicting updates to positions and
velocities resulting in unphysical behavior in most cases. When
performing a hybrid simulation with some atoms in rigid bodies, and
some not, a separate time integration fix like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} should be used for the
non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes are overkill if you simply want to hold a collection of
atoms stationary or have them move with a constant velocity.  A
simpler way to hold atoms stationary is to not include those atoms
in your time integration fix.  E.g. use “fix 1 mobile nve” instead
of “fix 1 all nve”, where “mobile” is the group of atoms that you
want to move.  You can move atoms with a constant velocity by
assigning them an initial velocity (via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} command), setting the force on them to 0.0 (via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_setforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix setforce}}}} command), and integrating them
as usual (e.g. via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} command).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The aggregate properties of each rigid body are calculated at the
start of a simulation run and are maintained in internal data
structures. The properties include the position and velocity of the
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the body, its moments of inertia, and its angular
momentum.  This is done using the properties of the constituent
atoms of the body at that point in time (or see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile}
keyword option).  Thereafter, changing these properties of
individual atoms in the body will have no effect on a rigid body’s
dynamics, unless they effect any computation of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom forces or
torques. If the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} (the default), the
rigid body data structures will be recreated at the beginning of
each \sphinxstyleemphasis{run} command; if the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, the
rigid body data structures will be built only at the very first
\sphinxstyleemphasis{run} command and maintained for as long as the rigid fix is
defined. For example, you might think you could displace the atoms
in a body or add a large velocity to each atom in a body to make it
move in a desired direction before a second run is performed, using
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{displace_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{displace\_atoms}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} commands.  But these commands will not
affect the internal attributes of the body unless \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} is set
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}. With \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} (or using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile}
option, which implies \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}) the position and velocity of
individual atoms in the body will be reset when time integration
starts again.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Each rigid body must have two or more atoms.  An atom can belong to at
most one rigid body.  Which atoms are in which bodies can be defined
via several options.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles, which require that \sphinxstyleemphasis{bodystyle} be
specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom}, you can define a system that has
no rigid bodies initially.  This is useful when you are using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keyword in conjunction with another fix that is adding rigid
bodies on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly as molecules, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} the entire fix group of atoms is treated as one
rigid body.  This option is only allowed for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule}, atoms are grouped into rigid bodies by their
respective molecule IDs: each set of atoms in the fix group with the
same molecule ID is treated as a different rigid body.  This option is
allowed for both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles.  Note that
atoms with a molecule ID = 0 will be treated as a single rigid body.
For a system with atomic solvent (typically this is atoms with
molecule ID = 0) surrounding rigid bodies, this may not be what you
want.  Thus you should be careful to use a fix group that only
includes atoms you want to be part of rigid bodies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} is similar to bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} except that it
is more flexible in using other per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties to define the sets
of atoms that form rigid bodies.  A custom per\sphinxhyphen{}atom integer vector
defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command
can be used.  Or an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} can be used; the floating\sphinxhyphen{}point value produced by the
variable is rounded to an integer.  As with bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule},
each set of atoms in the fix groups with the same integer value is
treated as a different rigid body.  Since fix property/atom custom
vectors and atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables produce values for all atoms, you
should be careful to use a fix group that only includes atoms you want
to be part of rigid bodies.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To compute the initial center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position and other properties
of each rigid body, the image flags for each atom in the body are
used to “unwrap” the atom coordinates.  Thus you must ensure that
these image flags are consistent so that the unwrapping creates a
valid rigid body (one where the atoms are close together),
particularly if the atoms in a single rigid body straddle a
periodic boundary.  This means the input data file or restart file
must define the image flags for each atom consistently or that you
have used the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command to specify them correctly.
If a dimension is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic then the image flag of each atom
must be 0 in that dimension, else an error is generated.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords discussed next are only allowed for
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, each rigid body is acted on by other atoms which induce an
external force and torque on its center of mass, causing it to
translate and rotate.  Components of the external center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass force
and torque can be turned off by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords.
This may be useful if you wish a body to rotate but not translate, or
vice versa, or if you wish it to rotate or translate continuously
unaffected by interactions with other particles.  Note that if you
expect a rigid body not to move or rotate by using these keywords, you
must ensure its initial center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass translational or angular
velocity is 0.0.  Otherwise the initial translational or angular
momentum the body has will persist.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An xflag, yflag, or zflag set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} means turn off the component of
force of torque in that dimension.  A setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} means turn on
the component, which is the default.  Which rigid body(s) the settings
apply to is determined by the first argument of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords.  It can be an integer M from 1 to Nbody, where
Nbody is the number of rigid bodies defined.  A wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can
be used in place of, or in conjunction with, the M argument to set the
flags for multiple rigid bodies.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or
“n*” or “m*n”.  If N = the number of rigid bodies, then an asterisk
with no numeric values means all bodies from 1 to N.  A leading
asterisk means all bodies from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all bodies from n to N (inclusive).  A middle asterisk
means all types from m to n (inclusive).  Note that you can use the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords as many times as you like.  If a
particular rigid body has its component flags set multiple times, the
settings from the final keyword are used.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For computational efficiency, you may wish to turn off pairwise and
bond interactions within each rigid body, as they no longer
contribute to the motion.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}} commands are
used to do this.  If the rigid bodies have strongly overlapping
atoms, you may need to turn off these interactions to avoid
numerical problems due to large equal/opposite intra\sphinxhyphen{}body forces
swamping the contribution of small inter\sphinxhyphen{}body forces.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For computational efficiency, you should typically define one fix
rigid or fix rigid/small command which includes all the desired rigid
bodies.  LAMMPS will allow multiple rigid fixes to be defined, but it
is more expensive.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The constituent particles within a rigid body can be point particles
(the default in LAMMPS) or finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles, such as spheres or
ellipsoids or line segments or triangles.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style
sphere and ellipsoid and line and tri}}}} commands for more
details on these kinds of particles.  Finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles contribute
differently to the moment of inertia of a rigid body than do point
particles.  Finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles can also experience torque (e.g. due
to {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{frictional granular interactions}}}}) and have an
orientation.  These contributions are accounted for by these fixes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Forces between particles within a body do not contribute to the
external force or torque on the body.  Thus for computational
efficiency, you may wish to turn off pairwise and bond interactions
between particles within each rigid body.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify
exclude}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}}
commands are used to do this.  For finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles this also
means the particles can be highly overlapped when creating the rigid
body.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nve}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small/nve} styles
perform constant NVE time integration.  They are referred to below as
the 4 NVE rigid styles.  The only difference is that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles use an integration technique based on Richardson
iterations.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nve} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small/nve} styles uses the
methods described in the paper by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid:miller3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Miller}}}}, which are
thought to provide better energy conservation than an iterative
approach.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nvt} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nvt/small} styles performs constant NVT
integration using a Nose/Hoover thermostat with chains as described
originally in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid:hoover}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Hoover)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid:martyna2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Martyna)}}}}, which thermostats both the translational and rotational
degrees of freedom of the rigid bodies.  They are referred to below as
the 2 NVT rigid styles.  The rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body algorithm used by \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nvt}
is described in the paper by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid:kamberaj}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Kamberaj}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/npt}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nph}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/npt/small}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nph/small}
styles perform constant NPT or NPH integration using a Nose/Hoover
barostat with chains.  They are referred to below as the 4 NPT and NPH
rigid styles.  For the NPT case, the same Nose/Hoover thermostat is
also used as with \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nvt} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nvt/small}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The barostat parameters are specified using one or more of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{iso},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{aniso}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} keywords.  These keywords give you
the ability to specify 3 diagonal components of the external stress
tensor, and to couple these components together so that the dimensions
they represent are varied together during a constant\sphinxhyphen{}pressure
simulation.  The effects of these keywords are similar to those
defined in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt/nph}}}}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/npt}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nph}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/npt/small}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nph/small} styles do not support triclinic (non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal)
boxes.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The target pressures for each of the 6 components of the stress tensor
can be specified independently via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} keywords, which
correspond to the 3 simulation box dimensions.  For each component,
the external pressure or tensor component at each timestep is a ramped
value during the run from \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pstart} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pstop}. If a target pressure
is specified for a component, then the corresponding box dimension
will change during a simulation.  For example, if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} keyword is
used, the y\sphinxhyphen{}box length will change.  A box dimension will not change
if that component is not specified, although you have the option to
change that dimension via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all barostat keywords, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pdamp} parameter operates like the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp} parameter, determining the time scale on which pressure is
relaxed.  For example, a value of 10.0 means to relax the pressure in
a timespan of (roughly) 10 time units (e.g. \(\tau\) or fs or ps
\sphinxhyphen{} see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Regardless of what atoms are in the fix group (the only atoms which
are time integrated), a global pressure or stress tensor is computed
for all atoms.  Similarly, when the size of the simulation box is
changed, all atoms are re\sphinxhyphen{}scaled to new positions, unless the keyword
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dilate} is specified with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{dilate\sphinxhyphen{}group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} for a group that
represents a subset of the atoms.  This can be useful, for example, to
leave the coordinates of atoms in a solid substrate unchanged and
controlling the pressure of a surrounding fluid.  Another example is a
system consisting of rigid bodies and point particles where the
barostat is only coupled with the rigid bodies.  This option should be
used with care, since it can be unphysical to dilate some atoms and
not others, because it can introduce large, instantaneous
displacements between a pair of atoms (one dilated, one not) that are
far from the dilation origin.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} keyword allows two or three of the diagonal components of
the pressure tensor to be “coupled” together.  The value specified
with the keyword determines which are coupled.  For example, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}
means the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pxx} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pzz} components of the stress tensor are coupled.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Xyz} means all 3 diagonal components are coupled.  Coupling means two
things: the instantaneous stress will be computed as an average of the
corresponding diagonal components, and the coupled box dimensions will
be changed together in lockstep, meaning coupled dimensions will be
dilated or contracted by the same percentage every timestep.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Pstart}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pstop}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pdamp} parameters for any coupled dimensions must
be identical.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Couple xyz} can be used for a 2d simulation; the \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
dimension is simply ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{iso} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{aniso} keywords are simply shortcuts that are
equivalent to specifying several other keywords together.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{iso} means couple all 3 diagonal components together when
pressure is computed (hydrostatic pressure), and dilate/contract the
dimensions together.  Using “iso Pstart Pstop Pdamp” is the same as
specifying these 4 keywords:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
x Pstart Pstop Pdamp
y Pstart Pstop Pdamp
z Pstart Pstop Pdamp
couple xyz
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{aniso} means \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} dimensions are controlled
independently using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pxx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pyy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Pzz} components of the
stress tensor as the driving forces, and the specified scalar external
pressure.  Using “aniso Pstart Pstop Pdamp” is the same as specifying
these 4 keywords:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
x Pstart Pstop Pdamp
y Pstart Pstop Pdamp
z Pstart Pstop Pdamp
couple none
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword/value option pairs are used in the following ways.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} keyword determines, whether the rigid body properties
are re\sphinxhyphen{}initialized between run commands. With the option \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} (the
default) this is done, with the option \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} this is not done. Turning
off the re\sphinxhyphen{}initialization can be helpful to protect rigid bodies against
unphysical manipulations between runs or when properties cannot be
easily re\sphinxhyphen{}computed (e.g. when read from a file). When using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile}
keyword, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} option is automatically set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{langevin} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tparam} keywords perform thermostatting
of the rigid bodies, altering both their translational and rotational
degrees of freedom.  What is meant by “temperature” of a collection of
rigid bodies and how it can be monitored via the fix output is
discussed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{langevin} keyword applies a Langevin thermostat to the constant
NVE time integration performed by any of the 4 NVE rigid styles:
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nve}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small/nve}.  It cannot
be used with the 2 NVT rigid styles: \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nvt}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small/nvt}.
The desired temperature at each timestep is a ramped value during the
run from \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstart} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstop}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp} parameter is specified in
time units and determines how rapidly the temperature is relaxed.  For
example, a value of 100.0 means to relax the temperature in a timespan
of (roughly) 100 time units (\(\tau\) or fs or ps \sphinxhyphen{} see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command).  The random \# \sphinxstyleemphasis{seed} must be a positive
integer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The way that Langevin thermostatting operates is explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} doc page.  If you wish to simply viscously
damp the rotational motion without thermostatting, you can set
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstart} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstop} to 0.0, which means only the viscous drag term in
the Langevin thermostat will be applied.  See the discussion on the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscous::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscous}}}} page for details.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{langevin} keyword is used with fix rigid versus fix
rigid/small, different dynamics will result for parallel runs.  This
is because of the way random numbers are used in the two cases.  The
dynamics for the two cases should be statistically similar, but will
not be identical, even for a single timestep.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tparam} keywords apply a Nose/Hoover thermostat to the
NVT time integration performed by the 2 NVT rigid styles.  They cannot
be used with the 4 NVE rigid styles.  The desired temperature at each
timestep is a ramped value during the run from \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstart} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstop}.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp} parameter is specified in time units and determines how
rapidly the temperature is relaxed.  For example, a value of 100.0
means to relax the temperature in a timespan of (roughly) 100 time
units (tau or fs or ps \sphinxhyphen{} see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Nose/Hoover chains are used in conjunction with this thermostat.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tparam} keyword can optionally be used to change the chain settings
used.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tchain} is the number of thermostats in the Nose Hoover chain.
This value, along with \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp} can be varied to dampen undesirable
oscillations in temperature that can occur in a simulation.  As a rule
of thumb, increasing the chain length should lead to smaller
oscillations. The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{pchain} specifies the number of thermostats
in the chain thermostatting the barostat degrees of freedom.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are alternate ways to thermostat a system of rigid bodies.
You can use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} to treat the
individual particles in the rigid bodies as effectively immersed in
an implicit solvent, e.g. a Brownian dynamics model.  For hybrid
systems with both rigid bodies and solvent particles, you can
thermostat only the solvent particles that surround one or more
rigid bodies by appropriate choice of groups in the compute and fix
commands for temperature and thermostatting.  The solvent
interactions with the rigid bodies should then effectively
thermostat the rigid body temperature as well without use of the
Langevin or Nose/Hoover options associated with the fix rigid
commands.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keyword can only be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles.  It
must be used when other commands, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}, add rigid bodies
on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly during a simulation.  You specify a \sphinxstyleemphasis{template\sphinxhyphen{}ID}
previously defined using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} command, which
reads a file that defines the molecule.  You must use the same
\sphinxstyleemphasis{template\sphinxhyphen{}ID} that the other fix which is adding rigid bodies uses.
The coordinates, atom types, atom diameters, center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass, and
moments of inertia can be specified in the molecule file.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}} command for details.  The only settings
required to be in this file are the coordinates and types of atoms in
the molecule, in which case the molecule command calculates the other
quantities itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that these other fixes create new rigid bodies, in addition to
those defined initially by this fix via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bodystyle} setting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that when using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keyword, extra restart information
about all rigid bodies is written out whenever a restart file is
written out.  See the NOTE in the next section for details.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword allows a file of rigid body attributes to be read
in from a file, rather then having LAMMPS compute them.  There are 5
such attributes: the total mass of the rigid body, its center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
position, its 6 moments of inertia, its center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity, and
the 3 image flags of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position.  For rigid bodies
consisting of point particles or non\sphinxhyphen{}overlapping finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
particles, LAMMPS can compute these values accurately.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, for rigid bodies consisting of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles which
overlap each other, LAMMPS will ignore the overlaps when computing
these 4 attributes, which means the dynamics of the bodies will be
incorrect.  The amount of error this induces depends on the amount of
overlap.  To avoid this issue, the values can be pre\sphinxhyphen{}computed
(e.g. using Monte Carlo integration).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of the file is as follows.  Note that the file does not
have to list attributes for every rigid body integrated by fix rigid.
Only bodies which the file specifies will have their computed
attributes overridden.  The file can contain initial blank lines or
comment lines starting with “\#” which are ignored.  The first
non\sphinxhyphen{}blank, non\sphinxhyphen{}comment line should list N = the number of lines to
follow.  The N successive lines contain the following information:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ID1 masstotal xcm ycm zcm ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz vxcm vycm vzcm lx ly lz ixcm iycm izcm
ID2 masstotal xcm ycm zcm ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz vxcm vycm vzcm lx ly lz ixcm iycm izcm
...
IDN masstotal xcm ycm zcm ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz vxcm vycm vzcm lx ly lz ixcm iycm izcm
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rigid body IDs are all positive integers.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single}
bodystyle, only an ID of 1 can be used.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} bodystyle,
IDs from 1 to Ng can be used where Ng is the number of specified
groups.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} bodystyle, use the molecule ID for the
atoms in a specific rigid body as the rigid body ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The masstotal and center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass coordinates (xcm,ycm,zcm) are
self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory.  The center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass should be consistent with what
is calculated for the position of the rigid body with all its atoms
unwrapped by their respective image flags.  If this produces a
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass that is outside the simulation box, LAMMPS wraps it
back into the box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 6 moments of inertia (ixx,iyy,izz,ixy,ixz,iyz) should be the
values consistent with the current orientation of the rigid body
around its center of mass.  The values are with respect to the
simulation box XYZ axes, not with respect to the principal axes of the
rigid body itself.  LAMMPS performs the latter calculation internally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The (vxcm,vycm,vzcm) values are the velocity of the center of mass.
The (lx,ly,lz) values are the angular momentum of the body.  The
(vxcm,vycm,vzcm) and (lx,ly,lz) values can simply be set to 0 if you
wish the body to have no initial motion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The (ixcm,iycm,izcm) values are the image flags of the center of mass
of the body.  For periodic dimensions, they specify which image of the
simulation box the body is considered to be in.  An image of 0 means
it is inside the box as defined.  A value of 2 means add 2 box lengths
to get the true value.  A value of \sphinxhyphen{}1 means subtract 1 box length to
get the true value.  LAMMPS updates these flags as the rigid bodies
cross periodic boundaries during the simulation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} keywords and write restart files
during a simulation, then each time a restart file is written, the
fix also write an auxiliary restart file with the name rfile.rigid,
where “rfile” is the name of the restart file,
e.g. tmp.restart.10000 and tmp.restart.10000.rigid.  This auxiliary
file is in the same format described above.  Thus it can be used in
a new input script that restarts the run and re\sphinxhyphen{}specifies a rigid
fix using an \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword and the appropriate filename.  Note
that the auxiliary file will contain one line for every rigid body,
even if the original file only listed a subset of the rigid bodies.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the system has rigid bodies with finite\sphinxhyphen{}size overlapping particles
and the model uses the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gravity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gravity}}}} command to
apply a gravitational force to the rigid bodies, then the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gravity}
keyword should be used in the following manner.

\sphinxAtStartPar
First, the group specified for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gravity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gravity}}}}
command should not include any atoms in rigid bodies which have
overlapping particles.  It can be empty (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group empty}}}} command) or only contain single particles not in rigid
bodies, e.g. background particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Second, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword should be used to specify the total mass
and other properties of the rigid bodies with overlaps, so that their
dynamics will be modeled correctly, as explained above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Third, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gravity} keyword should be used the with the ID of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_gravity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix gravity}}}} command as its argument.  The rigid
fixes will access the gravity fix to extract the current direction of
the gravity vector at each timestep (which can be static or dynamic).
A gravity force will then be applied to each rigid body at its
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position using its total mass.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temperature compute}}}} with a group that
includes particles in rigid bodies, the degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom removed by
each rigid body are accounted for in the temperature (and pressure)
computation, but only if the temperature group includes all the
particles in a particular rigid body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A 3d rigid body has 6 degrees of freedom (3 translational, 3
rotational), except for a collection of point particles lying on a
straight line, which has only 5, e.g a dimer.  A 2d rigid body has 3
degrees of freedom (2 translational, 1 rotational).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You may wish to explicitly subtract additional
degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom if you use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords to
eliminate certain motions of one or more rigid bodies.  LAMMPS does
not do this automatically.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rigid body contribution to the pressure of the system (virial) is
also accounted for by this fix.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If your simulation is a hybrid model with a mixture of rigid bodies
and non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles (e.g. solvent) there are several ways these
rigid fixes can be used in tandem with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nph}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you wish to perform NVE dynamics (no thermostatting or
barostatting), use one of 4 NVE rigid styles to integrate the rigid
bodies, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} to integrate the non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid
particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you wish to perform NVT dynamics (thermostatting, but no
barostatting), you can use one of the 2 NVT rigid styles for the rigid
bodies, and any thermostatting fix for the non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles
({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/berendsen}}}}).  You can also use one
of the 4 NVE rigid styles for the rigid bodies and thermostat them
using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} on the group that contains
all the particles in the rigid bodies.  The net force added by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} to each rigid body effectively
thermostats its translational center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass motion.  Not sure how
well it does at thermostatting its rotational motion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you wish to perform NPT or NPH dynamics (barostatting), you cannot
use both {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} and the NPT or NPH rigid styles.  This
is because there can only be one fix which monitors the global
pressure and changes the simulation box dimensions.  So you have 3
choices:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use one of the 4 NPT or NPH styles for the rigid bodies.  Use the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dilate} all option so that it will dilate the positions of the
non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles as well.  Use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} (or any
other thermostat) for the non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} for the group of non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles.  Use
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dilate} all option so that it will dilate the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
positions of the rigid bodies as well.  Use one of the 4 NVE or 2 NVT
rigid styles for the rigid bodies.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_press_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix press/berendsen}}}} to compute the
pressure and change the box dimensions.  Use one of the 4 NVE or 2 NVT
rigid styles for the rigid bodies.  Use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} (or
any other thermostat) for the non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In all case, the rigid bodies and non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles both contribute
to the global pressure and the box is scaled the same by any of the
barostatting fixes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You could even use the second and third options for a non\sphinxhyphen{}hybrid
simulation consisting of only rigid bodies, assuming you give
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} an empty group, though it’s an odd thing to
do.  The barostatting fixes ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_press_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
press/berensen}}}}) will monitor the pressure and
change the box dimensions, but not time integrate any particles.  The
integration of the rigid bodies will be performed by fix rigid/nvt.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about the 4 NVE rigid styles is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary
restart files}}}}.  The exception is if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol}
keyword is used, in which case an auxiliary file is written out with
rigid body information each time a restart file is written, as
explained above for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword.  For the 2 NVT rigid styles,
the state of the Nose/Hoover thermostat is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary
restart files}}}}.  Ditto for the 4 NPT and NPH rigid styles,
and the state of the Nose/Hoover barostat.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for info on how to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify a fix in an
input script that reads a restart file, so that the operation of the
fix continues in an uninterrupted fashion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{press} options are
supported by the 4 NPT and NPH rigid styles to change the computes
used to calculate the instantaneous pressure tensor.  Note that the 2
NVT rigid fixes do not use any external compute to compute
instantaneous temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{bodyforces} option is supported by
all rigid styles to set whether per\sphinxhyphen{}body forces and torques are
computed early or late in a timestep, i.e. at the post\sphinxhyphen{}force stage or
at the final\sphinxhyphen{}integrate stage or the timestep, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cumulative energy change in the system imposed by the 6 NVT, NPT,
NPH rigid fixes, via either thermostatting and/or barostatting, is
included in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}} keywords
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve}.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}
doc page for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 2 NVE rigid fixes compute a global scalar which can be accessed by
various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The scalar value
calculated by these fixes is “intensive”.  The scalar is the current
temperature of the collection of rigid bodies.  This is averaged over
all rigid bodies and their translational and rotational degrees of
freedom.  The translational energy of a rigid body is 1/2 m v\textasciicircum{}2,
where m = total mass of the body and v = the velocity of its center of
mass.  The rotational energy of a rigid body is 1/2 I w\textasciicircum{}2, where I =
the moment of inertia tensor of the body and w = its angular velocity.
Degrees of freedom constrained by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords
are removed from this calculation, but only for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/nve} fixes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 6 NVT, NPT, NPH rigid fixes compute a global scalar which can be
accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The scalar
is the same cumulative energy change due to these fixes described
above.  The scalar value calculated by this fix is “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial} option is supported by
these fixes to add the contribution due to the added forces on atoms
to both the global pressure and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress of the system via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
stress/atom}}}} commands.  The former can be
accessed by {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}}.  The default
setting for this fix is {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify virial yes}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid} styles (but not the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles) compute a
global array of values which can be accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output
commands}}}}.  Similar information about the bodies
defined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigid/small} styles can be accessed via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_rigid_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute rigid/local}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of rows in the array is equal to the number of rigid
bodies.  The number of columns is 15.  Thus for each rigid body, 15
values are stored: the xyz coords of the center of mass (COM), the xyz
components of the COM velocity, the xyz components of the force acting
on the COM, the xyz components of the torque acting on the COM, and
the xyz image flags of the COM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The center of mass (COM) for each body is similar to unwrapped
coordinates written to a dump file.  It will always be inside (or
slightly outside) the simulation box.  The image flags have the same
meaning as image flags for atom positions (see the “dump” command).
This means you can calculate the unwrapped COM by applying the image
flags to the COM, the same as when unwrapped coordinates are written
to a dump file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The force and torque values in the array are not affected by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords in the fix rigid command; they reflect
values before any changes are made by those keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ordering of the rigid bodies (by row in the array) is as follows.
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} keyword there is just one rigid body.  For the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} keyword, the bodies are ordered by ascending molecule ID.
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} keyword, the list of group IDs determines the ordering
of bodies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values calculated by these fixes are “intensive”, meaning
they are independent of the number of atoms in the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of these fixes can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords
of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  These fixes are not invoked during
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes are all part of the RIGID package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Assigning a temperature via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity create}}}}
command to a system with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rigid bodies}}}} may not have
the desired outcome for two reasons.  First, the velocity command can
be invoked before the rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body fix is invoked or initialized and the
number of adjusted degrees of freedom (DOFs) is known.  Thus it is not
possible to compute the target temperature correctly.  Second, the
assigned velocities may be partially canceled when constraints are
first enforced, leading to a different temperature than desired.  A
workaround for this is to perform a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run 0}}}} command, which
ensures all DOFs are accounted for properly, and then rescale the
temperature to the desired value before performing a simulation.  For
example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{velocity }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12345}
\PYG{k}{run}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{                             }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} temperature may not be 300K}
\PYG{k}{velocity }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} now it should be}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Related commands}

{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}}
exclude, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are force * on on on and torque * on on on,
meaning all rigid bodies are acted on by center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass force and
torque.  Also Tchain = Pchain = 10, Titer = 1, Torder = 3, reinit = yes.

\section{fix rigid/meso command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:fix-rigid-meso-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{meso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bodystyle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rigid/meso = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bodystyle = \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{group}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single} args = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} args = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} args = \sphinxstyleemphasis{i\_propname} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_varname}
  i\_propname = an integer property defined via fix property/atom
  v\_varname  = an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable
\sphinxstyleemphasis{group} args = N groupID1 groupID2 ...
  N = \# of groups
  groupID1, groupID2, ... = list of N group IDs
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} values = M xflag yflag zflag
  M = which rigid body from 1\sphinxhyphen{}Nbody (see asterisk form below)
  xflag,yflag,zflag = off/on if component of center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass force is active
\sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} values = M xflag yflag zflag
  M = which rigid body from 1\sphinxhyphen{}Nbody (see asterisk form below)
  xflag,yflag,zflag = off/on if component of center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass torque is active
\sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} filename
  filename = file with per\sphinxhyphen{}body values of mass, center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass, moments of inertia
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ellipsoid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{meso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{rods}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{meso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{spheres}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{meso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{on}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{particles}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{meso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{on}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{spheres}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{meso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sphere3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{torque}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{off}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Treat one or more sets of mesoscopic SPH/SDPD particles as independent
rigid bodies.  This means that each timestep the total force and torque
on each rigid body is computed as the sum of the forces and torques on
its constituent particles.  The coordinates and velocities of the
particles in each body are then updated so that the body moves and
rotates as a single entity using the methods described in the paper by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:miller}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Miller)}}}}. Density and internal energy of the particles will
also be updated. This is implemented by creating internal data structures
for each rigid body and performing time integration on these data
structures.  Positions and velocities of the constituent particles are
regenerated from the rigid body data structures in every time step. This
restricts which operations and fixes can be applied to rigid bodies. See
below for a detailed discussion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The operation of this fix is exactly like that described by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/nve}}}} command, except that particles’ density,
internal energy and extrapolated velocity are also updated.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You should not update the particles in rigid bodies via other
time\sphinxhyphen{}integration fixes (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_sph::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix sph}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_sph_stationary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
sph/stationary}}}}), or you will have conflicting
updates to positions and velocities resulting in unphysical
behavior in most cases. When performing a hybrid simulation with
some atoms in rigid bodies, and some not, a separate time
integration fix like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_sph::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix sph}}}} should be used for
the non\sphinxhyphen{}rigid particles.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes are overkill if you simply want to hold a collection of
particles stationary or have them move with a constant velocity. To
hold particles stationary use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_sph_stationary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix sph/stationary}}}} instead. If you would like to move particles
with a constant velocity use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_meso_move::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix meso/move}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The aggregate properties of each rigid body are
calculated at the start of a simulation run and are maintained in
internal data structures. The properties include the position and
velocity of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the body, its moments of inertia, and
its angular momentum.  This is done using the properties of the
constituent particles of the body at that point in time (or see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile}
keyword option).  Thereafter, changing these properties of individual
particles in the body will have no effect on a rigid body’s dynamics, unless
they effect any computation of per\sphinxhyphen{}particle forces or torques. If the
keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} (the default), the rigid body data
structures will be recreated at the beginning of each \sphinxstyleemphasis{run} command;
if the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, the rigid body data structures
will be built only at the very first \sphinxstyleemphasis{run} command and maintained for
as long as the rigid fix is defined. For example, you might think you
could displace the particles in a body or add a large velocity to each particle
in a body to make it move in a desired direction before a second run is
performed, using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{displace_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{displace\_atoms}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}}
commands.  But these commands will not affect the internal attributes
of the body unless \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}. With \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
(or using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} option, which implies \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}) the position
and velocity of individual particles in the body will be reset when time
integration starts again.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Each rigid body must have two or more particles.  A particle can belong
to at most one rigid body.  Which particles are in which bodies can be
defined via several options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} the entire fix group of particles is treated as
one rigid body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule}, particles are grouped into rigid bodies by their
respective molecule IDs: each set of particles in the fix group with the
same molecule ID is treated as a different rigid body.  Note that particles
with a molecule ID = 0 will be treated as a single rigid body. For a
system with solvent (typically this is particles with molecule ID = 0)
surrounding rigid bodies, this may not be what you want.  Thus you
should be careful to use a fix group that only includes particles you
want to be part of rigid bodies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{custom} is similar to bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} except that it
is more flexible in using other per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties to define the sets
of particles that form rigid bodies.  An integer vector defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} command can be used.  Or an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style or atomfile\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} can be used; the
floating\sphinxhyphen{}point value produced by the variable is rounded to an
integer.  As with bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule}, each set of particles in the fix
groups with the same integer value is treated as a different rigid
body.  Since fix property/atom vectors and atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables
produce values for all particles, you should be careful to use a fix group
that only includes particles you want to be part of rigid bodies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For bodystyle \sphinxstyleemphasis{group}, each of the listed groups is treated as a
separate rigid body.  Only particles that are also in the fix group are
included in each rigid body.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To compute the initial center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position and other
properties of each rigid body, the image flags for each particle in the
body are used to “unwrap” the particle coordinates.  Thus you must
ensure that these image flags are consistent so that the unwrapping
creates a valid rigid body (one where the particles are close together)
, particularly if the particles in a single rigid body straddle a
periodic boundary.  This means the input data file or restart file must
define the image flags for each particle consistently or that you have
used the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command to specify them correctly.  If a
dimension is non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic then the image flag of each particle must be
0 in that dimension, else an error is generated.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, each rigid body is acted on by other particles which induce
an external force and torque on its center of mass, causing it to
translate and rotate.  Components of the external center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass force
and torque can be turned off by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords.
This may be useful if you wish a body to rotate but not translate, or
vice versa, or if you wish it to rotate or translate continuously
unaffected by interactions with other particles.  Note that if you
expect a rigid body not to move or rotate by using these keywords, you
must ensure its initial center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass translational or angular
velocity is 0.0. Otherwise the initial translational or angular
momentum, the body has, will persist.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An xflag, yflag, or zflag set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} means turn off the component of
force or torque in that dimension.  A setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} means turn on
the component, which is the default.  Which rigid body(s) the settings
apply to is determined by the first argument of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords.  It can be an integer M from 1 to Nbody, where
Nbody is the number of rigid bodies defined.  A wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can
be used in place of, or in conjunction with, the M argument to set the
flags for multiple rigid bodies.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or
“n*” or “m*n”.  If N = the number of rigid bodies, then an asterisk
with no numeric values means all bodies from 1 to N.  A leading
asterisk means all bodies from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all bodies from n to N (inclusive).  A middle asterisk
means all bodies from m to n (inclusive).  Note that you can use the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords as many times as you like.  If a
particular rigid body has its component flags set multiple times, the
settings from the final keyword are used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For computational efficiency, you should typically define one fix
rigid/meso command which includes all the desired rigid bodies. LAMMPS
will allow multiple rigid/meso fixes to be defined, but it is more
expensive.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword/value option pairs are used in the following ways.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} keyword determines, whether the rigid body properties
are re\sphinxhyphen{}initialized between run commands. With the option \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} (the
default) this is done, with the option \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} this is not done. Turning
off the re\sphinxhyphen{}initialization can be helpful to protect rigid bodies against
unphysical manipulations between runs or when properties cannot be
easily re\sphinxhyphen{}computed (e.g. when read from a file). When using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile}
keyword, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{reinit} option is automatically set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword allows a file of rigid body attributes to be read
in from a file, rather then having LAMMPS compute them.  There are 5
such attributes: the total mass of the rigid body, its center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
position, its 6 moments of inertia, its center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity, and
the 3 image flags of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position.  For rigid bodies
consisting of point particles or non\sphinxhyphen{}overlapping finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
particles, LAMMPS can compute these values accurately.  However, for
rigid bodies consisting of finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles which overlap each
other, LAMMPS will ignore the overlaps when computing these 4
attributes.  The amount of error this induces depends on the amount of
overlap.  To avoid this issue, the values can be pre\sphinxhyphen{}computed
(e.g. using Monte Carlo integration).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of the file is as follows.  Note that the file does not
have to list attributes for every rigid body integrated by fix rigid.
Only bodies which the file specifies will have their computed
attributes overridden.  The file can contain initial blank lines or
comment lines starting with “\#” which are ignored.  The first
non\sphinxhyphen{}blank, non\sphinxhyphen{}comment line should list N = the number of lines to
follow.  The N successive lines contain the following information:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ID1 masstotal xcm ycm zcm ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz vxcm vycm vzcm lx ly lz ixcm iycm izcm
ID2 masstotal xcm ycm zcm ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz vxcm vycm vzcm lx ly lz ixcm iycm izcm
...
IDN masstotal xcm ycm zcm ixx iyy izz ixy ixz iyz vxcm vycm vzcm lx ly lz ixcm iycm izcm
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rigid body IDs are all positive integers.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single}
bodystyle, only an ID of 1 can be used.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} bodystyle,
IDs from 1 to Ng can be used where Ng is the number of specified
groups.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} bodystyle, use the molecule ID for the
atoms in a specific rigid body as the rigid body ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The masstotal and center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass coordinates (xcm,ycm,zcm) are
self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory.  The center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass should be consistent with what
is calculated for the position of the rigid body with all its atoms
unwrapped by their respective image flags.  If this produces a
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass that is outside the simulation box, LAMMPS wraps it
back into the box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 6 moments of inertia (ixx,iyy,izz,ixy,ixz,iyz) should be the
values consistent with the current orientation of the rigid body
around its center of mass.  The values are with respect to the
simulation box XYZ axes, not with respect to the principal axes of the
rigid body itself.  LAMMPS performs the latter calculation internally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The (vxcm,vycm,vzcm) values are the velocity of the center of mass.
The (lx,ly,lz) values are the angular momentum of the body.  The
(vxcm,vycm,vzcm) and (lx,ly,lz) values can simply be set to 0 if you
wish the body to have no initial motion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The (ixcm,iycm,izcm) values are the image flags of the center of mass
of the body.  For periodic dimensions, they specify which image of the
simulation box the body is considered to be in.  An image of 0 means
it is inside the box as defined.  A value of 2 means add 2 box lengths
to get the true value.  A value of \sphinxhyphen{}1 means subtract 1 box length to
get the true value.  LAMMPS updates these flags as the rigid bodies
cross periodic boundaries during the simulation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword and write restart
files during a simulation, then each time a restart file is written,
the fix also write an auxiliary restart file with the name
rfile.rigid, where “rfile” is the name of the restart file,
e.g. tmp.restart.10000 and tmp.restart.10000.rigid.  This auxiliary
file is in the same format described above.  Thus it can be used in a
new input script that restarts the run and re\sphinxhyphen{}specifies a rigid fix
using an \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword and the appropriate filename.  Note that the
auxiliary file will contain one line for every rigid body, even if the
original file only listed a subset of the rigid bodies.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword is used, an auxiliary file is written out
with rigid body information each time a restart file is written, as
explained above for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options are relevant to this
fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix computes a global array of values which can be accessed by
various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of rows in the array is equal to the number of rigid
bodies.  The number of columns is 28.  Thus for each rigid body, 28
values are stored: the xyz coords of the center of mass (COM), the xyz
components of the COM velocity, the xyz components of the force acting
on the COM, the components of the 4\sphinxhyphen{}vector quaternion representing the
orientation of the rigid body, the xyz components of the angular velocity
of the body around its COM, the xyz components of the torque acting on the
COM, the 3 principal components of the moment of inertia, the xyz components
of the angular momentum of the body around its COM, and the xyz image
flags of the COM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The center of mass (COM) for each body is similar to unwrapped
coordinates written to a dump file.  It will always be inside (or
slightly outside) the simulation box.  The image flags have the same
meaning as image flags for particle positions (see the “dump” command).
This means you can calculate the unwrapped COM by applying the image
flags to the COM, the same as when unwrapped coordinates are written
to a dump file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The force and torque values in the array are not affected by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{torque} keywords in the fix rigid command; they reflect
values before any changes are made by those keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ordering of the rigid bodies (by row in the array) is as follows.
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} keyword there is just one rigid body.  For the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} keyword, the bodies are ordered by ascending molecule ID.
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} keyword, the list of group IDs determines the ordering
of bodies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values calculated by this fix are “intensive”, meaning they
are independent of the number of particles in the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is not invoked during {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is part of the DPD\sphinxhyphen{}SMOOTH package and also depends on the RIGID
package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS was built with both packages. See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix requires that atoms store density and internal energy as
defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sph}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All particles in the group must be mesoscopic SPH/SDPD particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,changed}{Changed in version 29Aug2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is incompatible with deformation controls that remap velocity,
for instance the \sphinxstyleemphasis{remap v} option of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}}.


\subsection{Related commands}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_meso_move::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix meso/move}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_rigid_meso:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are force * on on on and torque * on on on,
meaning all rigid bodies are acted on by center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass force and
torque. Also reinit = yes.
