\section{fix tfmc command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tfmc:fix-tfmc-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_tfmc:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_tfmc::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tfmc:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tfmc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Delta}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tfmc = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Delta = maximal displacement length (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Temp = imposed temperature of the system

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
seed = random number seed (positive integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/arg pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rot}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{com} args = xflag yflag zflag
  xflag,yflag,zflag = 0/1 to exclude/include each dimension
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rot} args = none
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tfmc:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tfmc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{159345}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tfmc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.05}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{600.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{658943}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tfmc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{750.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{387068}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rot}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tfmc:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform uniform\sphinxhyphen{}acceptance force\sphinxhyphen{}bias Monte Carlo (fbMC) simulations,
using the time\sphinxhyphen{}stamped force\sphinxhyphen{}bias Monte Carlo (tfMC) algorithm
described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tfmc:mees}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mees)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tfmc:bal}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bal)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One successful use case of force\sphinxhyphen{}bias Monte Carlo methods is that they
can be used to extend the time scale of atomistic simulations, in
particular when long time scale relaxation effects must be considered;
some interesting examples are given in the review by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tfmc:neyts}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Neyts)}}}}.
An example of a typical use case would be the modelling of chemical
vapor deposition (CVD) processes on a surface, in which impacts by
gas\sphinxhyphen{}phase species can be performed using MD, but subsequent relaxation
of the surface is too slow to be done using MD only. Using tfMC can
allow for a much faster relaxation of the surface, so that higher
fluxes can be used, effectively extending the time scale of the
simulation. (Such an alternating simulation approach could be set up
using a {\hyperref[\detokenize{jump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{loop}}}}.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
The initial version of tfMC algorithm in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tfmc:mees}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mees)}}}} contained an
estimation of the effective time scale of such a simulation, but it
was later shown that the speed\sphinxhyphen{}up one can gain from a tfMC simulation
is system\sphinxhyphen{} and process\sphinxhyphen{}dependent, ranging from none to several orders
of magnitude. In general, solid\sphinxhyphen{}state processes such as
(re)crystallization or growth can be accelerated by up to two or three
orders of magnitude, whereas diffusion in the liquid phase is not
accelerated at all. The observed pseudodynamics when using the tfMC
method is not the actual dynamics one would obtain using MD, but the
relative importance of processes can match the actual relative
dynamics of the system quite well, provided \sphinxstyleemphasis{Delta} is chosen with
care. Thus, the system’s equilibrium is reached faster than in MD,
along a path that is generally roughly similar to a typical MD
simulation (but not necessarily so). See {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tfmc:bal}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bal)}}}} for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each step, all atoms in the selected group are displaced using the
stochastic tfMC algorithm, which is designed to sample the canonical
(NVT) ensemble at the temperature \sphinxstyleemphasis{Temp}. Although tfMC is a Monte
Carlo algorithm and thus strictly speaking does not perform time
integration, it is similar in the sense that it uses the forces on all
atoms in order to update their positions. Therefore, it is implemented
as a time integration fix, and no other fixes of this type (such as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}}) should be used at the same time. Because
velocities do not play a role in this kind of Monte Carlo simulations,
instantaneous temperatures as calculated by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{temperature computes}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}} have no meaning: the only relevant
temperature is the sampling temperature \sphinxstyleemphasis{Temp}.  Similarly, performing
tfMC simulations does not require setting a {\hyperref[\detokenize{timestep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{timestep}}}}
and the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{simulated time}}}} as calculated by LAMMPS is
meaningless.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The critical parameter determining the success of a tfMC simulation is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Delta}, the maximal displacement length of the lightest element in
the system: the larger it is, the longer the effective time scale of
the simulation will be (there is an approximately quadratic
dependence). However, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Delta} must also be chosen sufficiently small
in order to comply with detailed balance; in general values between 5
and 10 \% of the nearest neighbor distance are found to be a good
choice. For a more extensive discussion with specific examples, please
refer to {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tfmc:bal}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bal)}}}}, which also describes how the code calculates
element\sphinxhyphen{}specific maximal displacements from \sphinxstyleemphasis{Delta}, based on the
fourth root of their mass.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Because of the uncorrelated movements of the atoms, the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
of the fix group will not necessarily be stationary, just like its
orientation. When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} keyword is used, all atom positions will
be shifted (after every tfMC iteration) in order to fix the position
of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass along the included directions, by setting the
corresponding flag to 1. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rot} keyword does the same for the
rotational component of the tfMC displacements after every iteration.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rot} keywords should not be used if an external
force is acting on the specified fix group, along the included
directions. This can be either a true external force (e.g.  through
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall}}}}) or forces due to the interaction with atoms
not included in the fix group. This is because in such cases,
translations or rotations of the fix group could be induced by these
external forces, and removing them will lead to a violation of
detailed balance.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\section{fix tgnpt/drude command}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style\_name = \sphinxstyleemphasis{tgnvt/drude} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tgnpt/drude}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/values pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} \sphinxstyleemphasis{iso} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{aniso} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tri} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tchain} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pchain} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mtk} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tloop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ploop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nreset} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{scaleyz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{flip} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fixedpoint}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} values = Tstart Tstop Tdamp Tdrude Tdamp\_drude
    Tstart, Tstop = external temperature at start/end of run (temperature units)
    Tdamp = temperature damping parameter (time units)
    Tdrude = desired temperature of Drude oscillators (temperature units)
    Tdamp\_drude = temperature damping parameter for Drude oscillators (time units)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{iso} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{aniso} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tri} values = Pstart Pstop Pdamp
    Pstart,Pstop = scalar external pressure at start/end of run (pressure units)
    Pdamp = pressure damping parameter (time units)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz} values = Pstart Pstop Pdamp
    Pstart,Pstop = external stress tensor component at start/end of run (pressure units)
    Pdamp = stress damping parameter (time units)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xyz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{tchain} value = N
    N = length of thermostat chain (1 = single thermostat)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{pchain} value = N
    N length of thermostat chain on barostat (0 = no thermostat)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{mtk} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = add in MTK adjustment term or not
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{tloop} value = M
    M = number of sub\sphinxhyphen{}cycles to perform on thermostat
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{ploop} value = M
    M = number of sub\sphinxhyphen{}cycles to perform on barostat thermostat
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{nreset} value = reset reference cell every this many timesteps
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexy} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = scale xy with ly
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{scaleyz} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = scale yz with lz
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexz} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = scale xz with lz
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{flip} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = allow or disallow box flips when it becomes highly skewed
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{fixedpoint} values = x y z
    x,y,z = perform barostat dilation/contraction around this point (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands are variants of the Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover fix styles {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} for thermalized Drude polarizable
models.  They apply temperature\sphinxhyphen{}grouped Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat (TGNH)
proposed by {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_drude2:tgnh-son}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Son)}}}}.  When there are fast vibrational
modes with frequencies close to Drude oscillators (e.g. double bonds or
out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}plane torsions), this thermostat can provide better kinetic
energy equipartitioning.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The difference between TGNH and the original Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat is that,
TGNH separates the kinetic energy of the group into three contributions:
molecular center of mass (COM) motion,
motion of COM of atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs or non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atoms relative to molecular COM,
and relative motion of atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs.
An independent Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover chain is applied to each type of motion.
The temperatures for these three types of motion are denoted as
molecular translational temperature (\(T_\mathrm{M}\)), real atomic temperature (\(T_\mathrm{R}\)) and Drude temperature (\(T_\mathrm{D}\)),
which are defined in terms of their associated degrees of freedom (DOF):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}T_\mathrm{M}=\frac{\Sigma_{i}^{N_\mathrm{mol}} M_i V_i^2}{3 \left ( N_\mathrm{mol} - \frac{N_\mathrm{mol}}{N_\mathrm{mol,sys}} \right ) k_\mathrm{B}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}T_\mathrm{R}=\frac{\Sigma_{i}^{N_\mathrm{real}} m_i (v_i-v_{M,i})^2}{(N_\mathrm{DOF} - 3 N_\mathrm{mol} + 3 \frac{N_\mathrm{mol}}{N_\mathrm{mol,sys}} - 3 N_\mathrm{drude}) k_\mathrm{B}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}T_\mathrm{D}=\frac{\Sigma_{i}^{N_\mathrm{drude}} m_i^{\prime} v_i^{\prime 2}}{3 N_\mathrm{drude} k_\mathrm{B}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \(N_\mathrm{mol}\) and \(N_\mathrm{mol,sys}\) are the numbers of molecules in the group and in the whole system, respectively.
\(N_\mathrm{real}\) is the number of atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pairs and non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atoms in the group.
\(N_\mathrm{drude}\) is the number of Drude particles in the group.
\(N_\mathrm{DOF}\) is the DOF of the group.
\(M_i\) and \(V_i\) are the mass and the COM velocity of the i\sphinxhyphen{}th molecule.
\(m_i\) is the mass of the i\sphinxhyphen{}th atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pair or non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atom.
\(v_i\) is the velocity of COM of i\sphinxhyphen{}th atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pair or non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atom.
\(v_{M,i}\) is the COM velocity of the molecule the i\sphinxhyphen{}th atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pair or non\sphinxhyphen{}polarizable atom belongs to.
\(m_i^\prime\) and \(v_i^\prime\) are the reduced mass and the relative velocity of the i\sphinxhyphen{}th atom\sphinxhyphen{}Drude pair.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes require that each atom knows whether it is a Drude particle or
not.  You must therefore use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix drude}}}} command to
specify the Drude status of each atom type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Because the TGNH thermostat thermostats the molecular COM motion,
all atoms belonging to the same molecule must be in the same group.
That is, these fixes can not be applied to a subset of a molecule.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For this fix to act correctly, ghost atoms need to know their velocity.
You must use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify}}}} command to enable this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes assume that the translational DOF of the whole system is removed.
It is therefore recommended to invoke {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_momentum::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix momentum}}}} command so that the \(T_\mathrm{M}\) is calculated correctly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermostat parameters are specified using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword.
The thermostat is applied to only the translational DOF
for the particles.  The translational DOF can also have
a bias velocity removed before thermostatting takes place; see the
description below.  The desired temperature for molecular and real atomic motion is a
ramped value during the run from \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstart} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstop}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp}
parameter is specified in time units and determines how rapidly the
temperature is relaxed.  For example, a value of 10.0 means to relax
the temperature in a timespan of (roughly) 10 time units (e.g. \(\tau\)
or fs or ps \sphinxhyphen{} see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command).
The parameter \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdrude} is the desired temperature for Drude motion at each timestep.
Similar to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp}, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp\_drude} parameter determines the relaxation speed for Drude motion.
Fix group are the only ones whose velocities and positions are updated
by the velocity/position update portion of the integration.
Other thermostat\sphinxhyphen{}related keywords are \sphinxstyleemphasis{tchain} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tloop},
which are detailed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat will not work well for arbitrary values
of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp}.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp} is too small, the temperature can fluctuate
wildly; if it is too large, the temperature will take a very long time
to equilibrate.  A good choice for many models is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp} of around
100 timesteps.  A smaller \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tdamp\_drude} value would be required
to maintain Drude motion at low temperature.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{100.0*dt}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nv}{20.0*dt}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The barostat parameters for fix style \sphinxstyleemphasis{tgnpt/drude} is specified
using one or more of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{iso}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{aniso}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tri}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{couple} keywords.  These keywords give you the
ability to specify all 6 components of an external stress tensor, and
to couple various of these components together so that the dimensions
they represent are varied together during a constant\sphinxhyphen{}pressure
simulation. Other barostat\sphinxhyphen{}related keywords are \sphinxstyleemphasis{pchain}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{mtk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ploop},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nreset}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{scaleyz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{flip}and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fixedpoint}.
The meaning of barostat parameters are detailed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Regardless of what atoms are in the fix group (the only atoms which
are time integrated), a global pressure or stress tensor is computed
for all atoms.  Similarly, when the size of the simulation box is
changed, all atoms are re\sphinxhyphen{}scaled to new positions.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/berendsen}}}} command
which performs thermostatting but NO time integration, these fixes
perform thermostatting/barostatting AND time integration.  Thus you
should not use any other time integration fix, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} on atoms to which this fix is applied.
Likewise, these fixes should not be used on atoms that also
have their temperature controlled by another fix \sphinxhyphen{} e.g. by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin/drude}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto thermostat}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_barostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto barostat}}}} doc pages for a discussion of different
ways to compute temperature and perform thermostatting and
barostatting.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Like other fixes that perform thermostatting, this fix can be used
with {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute commands}}}} that remove a “bias” from the
atom velocities.  E.g. to apply the thermostat only to atoms within a
spatial {\hyperref[\detokenize{region::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{region}}}}, or to remove the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
velocity from a group of atoms, or to remove the x\sphinxhyphen{}component of
velocity from the calculation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is not done by default, but only if the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} command is used to assign a temperature compute to this
fix that includes such a bias term.  See the doc pages for individual
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp commands}}}} to determine which ones include
a bias.  In this case, the thermostat works in the following manner:
bias is removed from each atom, thermostatting is performed on the
remaining thermal degrees of freedom, and the bias is added back in.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
However, not all temperature compute commands are valid to be used
with these fixes.  Precisely, only temperature compute that does
not modify the DOF of the group can be used.  E.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_ramp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
temp/ramp}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute viscosity/cos}}}} compute the kinetic energy after remove a
velocity gradient without affecting the DOF of the group, then they
can be invoked in this way.  In contrast, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_partial::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
temp/partial}}}} may remove the DOF at one or
more dimensions, therefore it cannot be used with these fixes.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes writes the state of all the thermostat and barostat
variables to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for info on how to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify
a fix in an input script that reads a restart file, so that the
operation of the fix continues in an uninterrupted fashion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{press} options are
supported by these fixes.  You can use them to assign a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} you have defined to this fix which will be used in its
thermostatting or barostatting procedure, as described above.  If you
do this, note that the kinetic energy derived from the compute
temperature should be consistent with the virial term computed using
all atoms for the pressure.  LAMMPS will warn you if you choose to
compute temperature on a subset of atoms.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If both the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{press} keywords are used in a single
thermo\_modify command (or in two separate commands), then the order
in which the keywords are specified is important.  Note that a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pressure compute}}}} defines its own
temperature compute as an argument when it is specified.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword will override this (for the pressure compute being
used by fix npt), but only if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword comes after the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{press} keyword.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword comes before the \sphinxstyleemphasis{press}
keyword, then the new pressure compute specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{press}
keyword will be unaffected by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} setting.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cumulative energy change in the system imposed by these fixes, due
to thermostatting and/or barostatting, are included in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}} keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecouple} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{econserve}.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} page for
details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes compute a global scalar which can be accessed by various
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The scalar is the same
cumulative energy change due to this fix described in the previous
paragraph.  The scalar value calculated by this fix is “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes also compute a global vector of quantities, which can be
accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The vector
values are “intensive”.  The vector stores the three temperatures
\(T_\mathrm{M}\), \(T_\mathrm{R}\) and \(T_\mathrm{D}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes can ramp their external temperature and pressure over
multiple runs, using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keywords of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command for details of how
to do this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes are not invoked during {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes are only available when LAMMPS was built with the
DRUDE package.  These fixes cannot be used with dynamic groups as
defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}} command.  These fixes cannot be
used in 2D simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{X}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} cannot be barostatted if the associated dimension is not
periodic.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Xy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz} can only be barostatted if the
simulation domain is triclinic and the second dimension in the keyword
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{y} dimension in \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}) is periodic.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read data}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands specify whether the simulation box is orthogonal or
non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal (triclinic) and explain the meaning of the xy,xz,yz
tilt factors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} keyword, the final \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tstop} cannot be 0.0 since it would
make the external T = 0.0 at some timestep during the simulation which
is not allowed in the Nose/Hoover formulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{scaleyz yes}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexz yes}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{scalexy yes} options
can only be used if the second dimension in the keyword is periodic,
and if the tilt factor is not coupled to the barostat via keywords
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tri}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tgnh_drude:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_drude::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix drude}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_npt}}}},

ploop = 1, nreset = 0, couple = none,
flip = yes, scaleyz = scalexz = scalexy = yes if periodic in second
dimension and not coupled to barostat, otherwise no.

\index{fix thermal/conductivity@\spxentry{fix thermal/conductivity}}\ignorespaces 

\section{fix thermal/conductivity command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:fix-thermal-conductivity-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermal}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{conductivity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{edim}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nbin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
thermal/conductivity = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = perform kinetic energy exchange every N steps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
edim = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} = direction of kinetic energy transfer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nbin = \# of layers in edim direction (must be even number)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{swap}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{swap} value = Nswap = number of swaps to perform every N steps
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermal}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{conductivity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermal}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{conductivity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{swap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe algorithm described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:muller-plathe1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{this paper}}}} to exchange kinetic energy between two particles
in different regions of the simulation box every N steps.  This
induces a temperature gradient in the system.  As described below this
enables the thermal conductivity of a material to be calculated.  This
algorithm is sometimes called a reverse non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (reverse
NEMD) approach to computing thermal conductivity.  This is because the
usual NEMD approach is to impose a temperature gradient on the system
and measure the response as the resulting heat flux.  In the
Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe method, the heat flux is imposed, and the temperature
gradient is the system’s response.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute heat/flux}}}} command for details
on how to compute thermal conductivity in an alternate way, via the
Green\sphinxhyphen{}Kubo formalism.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simulation box is divided into \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} layers in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{edim}
direction, where the layer 1 is at the low end of that dimension and
the layer \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} is at the high end.  Every N steps, Nswap pairs of
atoms are chosen in the following manner.  Only atoms in the fix group
are considered.  The hottest Nswap atoms in layer 1 are selected.
Similarly, the coldest Nswap atoms in the “middle” layer (see below)
are selected.  The two sets of Nswap atoms are paired up and their
velocities are exchanged.  This effectively swaps their kinetic
energies, assuming their masses are the same.  If the masses are
different, an exchange of velocities relative to center of mass motion
of the two atoms is performed, to conserve kinetic energy.  Over time,
this induces a temperature gradient in the system which can be
measured using commands such as the following, which writes the
temperature profile (assuming z = edim) to the file tmp.profile:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute   }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{variable  }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}ke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m}{1.5}
\PYG{k}{compute   }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{layers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.05}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduced}
\PYG{k}{fix       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{layers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.profile}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that by default, Nswap = 1, though this can be changed by the
optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{swap} keyword.  Setting this parameter appropriately, in
conjunction with the swap rate N, allows the heat flux to be adjusted
across a wide range of values, and the kinetic energy to be exchanged
in large chunks or more smoothly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “middle” layer for velocity swapping is defined as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin}/2 +
1 layer.  Thus if \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} = 20, the two swapping layers are 1 and 11.
This should lead to a symmetric temperature profile since the two
layers are separated by the same distance in both directions in a
periodic sense.  This is why \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} is restricted to being an even
number.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As described below, the total kinetic energy transferred by these
swaps is computed by the fix and can be output.  Dividing this
quantity by time and the cross\sphinxhyphen{}sectional area of the simulation box
yields a heat flux.  The ratio of heat flux to the slope of the
temperature profile is proportional to the thermal conductivity of the
fluid, in appropriate units.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:muller-plathe1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe paper}}}} for details.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your system is periodic in the direction of the heat flux,
then the flux is going in 2 directions.  This means the effective heat
flux in one direction is reduced by a factor of 2.  You will see this
in the equations for thermal conductivity (kappa) in the Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe
paper.  LAMMPS is simply tallying kinetic energy which does not
account for whether or not your system is periodic; you must use the
value appropriately to yield a kappa for your system.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After equilibration, if the temperature gradient you observe is
not linear, then you are likely swapping energy too frequently and are
not in a regime of linear response.  In this case you cannot
accurately infer a thermal conductivity and should try increasing the
Nevery parameter.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options
are relevant to this fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix computes a global scalar which can be accessed by various
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The scalar is the cumulative
kinetic energy transferred between the bottom and middle of the
simulation box (in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{edim} direction) is stored as a scalar
quantity by this fix.  This quantity is zeroed when the fix is defined
and accumulates thereafter, once every N steps.  The units of the
quantity are energy; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command for details.
The scalar value calculated by this fix is “intensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  This fix is not invoked during {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Swaps conserve both momentum and kinetic energy, even if the masses of
the swapped atoms are not equal.  Thus you should not need to
thermostat the system.  If you do use a thermostat, you may want to
apply it only to the non\sphinxhyphen{}swapped dimensions (other than \sphinxstyleemphasis{vdim}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS does not check, but you should not use this fix to swap the
kinetic energy of atoms that are in constrained molecules, e.g. via
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  This is
because application of the constraints will alter the amount of
transferred momentum.  You should, however, be able to use flexible
molecules.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:zhang2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Zhang paper}}}} for a discussion and results
of this idea.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running a simulation with large, massive particles or molecules
in a background solvent, you may want to only exchange kinetic energy
between solvent particles.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ehex::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ehex}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_heat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix heat}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscosity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix viscosity}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute heat/flux}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are swap = 1.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity:muller-plathe1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe)} Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe, J Chem Phys, 106, 6082 (1997).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Zhang)} Zhang, Lussetti, de Souza, Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe, J Phys Chem B,
109, 15060\sphinxhyphen{}15067 (2005).

\index{fix ti/spring@\spxentry{fix ti/spring}}\ignorespaces 

\section{fix ti/spring command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:fix-ti-spring-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ti}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spring}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{k}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{t\PYGZus{}eq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ti/spring = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
k = spring constant (force/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
t\_eq = number of steps for the equilibration procedure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
t\_s = number of steps for the switching procedure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended to args

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{function}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{function} value = function\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  function\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of the switching function (1 or 2)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Example}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:example}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ti}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spring}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{function}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix allows you to compute the free energy of crystalline solids
by performing a nonequilibrium thermodynamic integration between the
solid of interest and an Einstein crystal. A detailed explanation of
how to use this command and choose its parameters for optimal
performance and accuracy is given in the paper by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:freitas1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Freitas}}}}. The paper also presents a short summary of the
theory of nonequilibrium thermodynamic integration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The thermodynamic integration procedure is performed by rescaling the
force on each atom. Given an atomic configuration the force (F) on
each atom is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F = \left( 1-\lambda \right) F_{\text{solid}} + \lambda F_{\text{harm}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where F\_solid is the force that acts on an atom due to an interatomic
potential (\sphinxstyleemphasis{e.g.} EAM potential), F\_harm is the force due to the
Einstein crystal harmonic spring, and lambda is the coupling parameter
of the thermodynamic integration. An Einstein crystal is a solid where
each atom is attached to its equilibrium position by a harmonic spring
with spring constant \sphinxstyleemphasis{k}. With this fix a spring force is applied
independently to each atom in the group defined by the fix to tether
it to its initial position. The initial position of each atom is its
position at the time the fix command was issued.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix acts as follows: during the first \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_eq} steps after the fix
is defined the value of lambda is zero. This is the period to
equilibrate the system in the lambda = 0 state. After this the value
of lambda changes dynamically during the simulation from 0 to 1
according to the function defined using the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{function}
(described below), this switching from lambda from 0 to 1 is done in
\sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_s} steps. Then comes the second equilibration period of \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_eq} to
equilibrate the system in the lambda = 1 state. After that, the
switching back to the lambda = 0 state is made using \sphinxstyleemphasis{t\_s} timesteps
and following the same switching function. After this period the value
of lambda is kept equal to zero and the fix has no other effect on the
dynamics of the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The processes described above is known as nonequilibrium thermodynamic
integration and is has been shown ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:freitas1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Freitas}}}}) to present a
much superior efficiency when compared to standard equilibrium
methods. The reason why the switching it is made in both directions
(potential to Einstein crystal and back) is to eliminate the
dissipated heat due to the nonequilibrium process. Further details
about nonequilibrium thermodynamic integration and its implementation
in LAMMPS is available in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:freitas1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Freitas}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{function} keyword allows the use of two different lambda
paths. Option \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} results in a constant rate of change of lambda with
time:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda(\tau) = \tau\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\tau\) is the scaled time variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{t/t\_s}. The option \sphinxstyleemphasis{2}
performs the lambda switching at a rate defined by the following
switching function
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda(\tau) = \tau^5 \left( 70 \tau^4 - 315 \tau^3 + 540 \tau^2 -
420 \tau + 126 \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This function has zero slope as lambda approaches its extreme values
(0 and 1), according to {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:dekoning96}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{de Koning}}}} this results in
smaller fluctuations on the integral to be computed on the
thermodynamic integration. The use of option \sphinxstyleemphasis{2} is recommended since
it results in better accuracy and less dissipation without any
increase in computational resources cost.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:freitas1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Freitas}}}}, it is important to keep
the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass fixed during the thermodynamic integration. A
nonzero total velocity will result in divergences during the
integration due to the fact that the atoms are ‘attached’ to their
equilibrium positions by the Einstein crystal. Check the option
\sphinxstyleemphasis{zero} of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}}. The use of the Nose\sphinxhyphen{}Hoover thermostat ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}) is \sphinxstyleemphasis{NOT} recommended due to its well documented issues
with the canonical sampling of harmonic degrees of freedom (notice
that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chain} option will \sphinxstyleemphasis{NOT} solve this problem). The
Langevin thermostat ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}) correctly
thermostats the system and we advise its usage with ti/spring
command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix writes the original coordinates of tethered atoms to
{\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so that the spring effect will
be the same in a restarted simulation. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read restart}}}} command for info on how to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify a fix in an
input script that reads a restart file, so that the operation of the
fix continues in an uninterrupted fashion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} option is supported by
this fix to add the energy stored in the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom springs to the
global potential energy of the system as part of {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic
output}}}}. The default setting for this fix is
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify energy no}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix computes a global scalar and a global vector quantities which
can be accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}. The
scalar is an energy which is the sum of the spring energy for each
atom, where the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy is \(0.5 \cdot k \cdot r^2\).
The vector stores 2 values.  The first value is the coupling parameter lambda.
The second value is the derivative of lambda with respect to the integer
timestep \sphinxstyleemphasis{s}, i.e. \(\frac{d \lambda}{d s}\).  In order to obtain
\(\frac{d \lambda}{d t}\),
where t is simulation time, this 2nd value needs to be divided by the
timestep size (e.g. 0.5 fs).  The scalar and vector values calculated
by this fix are “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forces due to this fix are imposed during an energy minimization,
invoked by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom spring energy to be included in the
total potential energy of the system (the quantity being minimized),
you MUST enable the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} option for
this fix.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_spring::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix spring}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}FIX package. It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package. See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ti_spring:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword default is function = 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar

Science, 112, 333 (2016).

\sphinxAtStartPar

\index{fix tmd@\spxentry{fix tmd}}\ignorespaces 

\section{fix tmd command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd:fix-tmd-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rho\PYGZus{}final}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tmd = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rho\_final = desired value of rho at the end of the run (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file1 = filename to read target structure from

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = dump TMD statistics every this many timesteps, 0 = no dump

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
file2 = filename to write TMD statistics to (only needed if N \textgreater{} 0)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{tmdatoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{target\PYGZus{}file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmd\PYGZus{}dump\PYGZus{}file}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform targeted molecular dynamics (TMD) on a group of atoms.  A
holonomic constraint is used to force the atoms to move towards (or away
from) the target configuration.  The parameter “rho” is monotonically
decreased (or increased) from its initial value to rho\_final at the end
of the run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rho has distance units and is a measure of the root\sphinxhyphen{}mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared
distance (RMSD) between the current configuration of the atoms in the
group and the target coordinates listed in file1.  Thus a value of
rho\_final = 0.0 means move the atoms all the way to the final
structure during the course of the run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The target file1 can be ASCII text or a gzipped text file (detected by
a .gz suffix).  The format of the target file1 is as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
0.0 25.0 xlo xhi
0.0 25.0 ylo yhi
0.0 25.0 zlo zhi
125     24.97311   1.69005     23.46956 0 0 \PYGZhy{}1
126     1.94691    2.79640     1.92799  1 0 0
127     0.15906    3.46099     0.79121  1 0 0
...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 3 lines may or may not be needed, depending on the format of
the atoms to follow.  If image flags are included with the atoms, the
first 3 lo/hi lines \sphinxstylestrong{must} appear in the file.  If image flags are not
included, the first 3 lines \sphinxstylestrong{must not} appear.  The 3 lines contain the
simulation box dimensions for the atom coordinates, in the same format
as in a LAMMPS data file (see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The remaining lines each contain an atom ID and its target x,y,z
coordinates.  The atom lines (all or none of them) can optionally be
followed by 3 integer values: nx,ny,nz.For periodic dimensions, they
specify which image of the box the atom is considered to be in, i.e. a
value of N (positive or negative) means add N times the box length to
the coordinate to get the true value.  Those 3 integers either must
be given for all atoms or none.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom lines can be listed in any order, but every atom in the group
must be listed in the file.  Atoms not in the fix group may also be
listed; they will be ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Comments starting with ‘\#’ and empty lines may be included as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
TMD statistics are written to file2 every N timesteps, unless N is
specified as 0, which means no statistics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The atoms in the fix tmd group should be integrated (via a fix nve,
nvt, npt) along with other atoms in the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Restarts can be used with a fix tmd command.  For example, imagine a
10000 timestep run with a rho\_initial = 11 and a rho\_final = 1.  If a
restart file was written after 2000 time steps, then the configuration
in the file would have a rho value of 9.  A new 8000 time step run
could be performed with the same rho\_final = 1 to complete the
conformational change at the same transition rate.  Note that for
restarted runs, the name of the TMD statistics file should be changed
to prevent it being overwritten.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For more information about TMD, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tmd:schlitter1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Schlitter1)}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_tmd:schlitter2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Schlitter2)}}}}.


\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options
are relevant to this fix.  No global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities are stored
by this fix for access by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix can ramp its rho parameter over multiple runs, using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keywords of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command for details of how to do this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is not invoked during {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tmd:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}FIX package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All TMD fixes must be listed in the input script after all integrator
fixes (nve, nvt, npt) are applied.  This ensures that atoms are moved
before their positions are corrected to comply with the constraint.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atoms that have a TMD fix applied should not be part of a group to
which a SHAKE fix is applied.  This is because LAMMPS assumes there
are not multiple competing holonomic constraints applied to the same
atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To read gzipped target files, you must compile LAMMPS with the
\sphinxhyphen{}DLAMMPS\_GZIP option.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_settings::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build settings}}}}
doc page for details.

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ttm:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ttm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C\PYGZus{}e}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rho\PYGZus{}e}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{kappa\PYGZus{}e}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma\PYGZus{}s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ny}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ttm}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{mod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{init\PYGZus{}file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ny}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/grid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
seed = random number seed to use for white noise (positive integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
remaining arguments for fix ttm or fix ttm/grid
\begin{sphinxalltt}
C\_e  = electronic specific heat (energy/(electron*temperature) units)
rho\_e = electronic density (electrons/volume units)
kappa\_e = electronic thermal conductivity (energy/(time*distance*temperature) units)
gamma\_p = friction coefficient due to electron\sphinxhyphen{}ion interactions (mass/time units)
gamma\_s = friction coefficient due to electronic stopping (mass/time units)
v\_0 = electronic stopping critical velocity (velocity units)
Nx = number of thermal solve grid points in the x\sphinxhyphen{}direction (positive integer)
Ny = number of thermal solve grid points in the y\sphinxhyphen{}direction (positive integer)
Nz = number of thermal solve grid points in the z\sphinxhyphen{}direction (positive integer)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
remaining arguments for fix ttm/mod:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
init\PYGZus{}file = file with the parameters to TTM
Nx = number of thermal solve grid points in the x\PYGZhy{}direction (positive integer)
Ny = number of thermal solve grid points in the y\PYGZhy{}direction (positive integer)
Nz = number of thermal solve grid points in the z\PYGZhy{}direction (positive integer)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value(s) pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{outfile}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{set} value = Tinit
  Tinit = initial electronic temperature at all grid points (temperature units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} value = file.in with grid values for electronic temperatures
\sphinxstyleemphasis{outfile} values = Nout file.out
  Nout = dump grid temperatures every this many timesteps
  file.out = filename to write grid temperatures to
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
