\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ttm:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use a two\sphinxhyphen{}temperature model (TTM) to represent heat transfer through
and between electronic and atomic subsystems.  LAMMPS models the
atomic subsystem as usual with a molecular dynamics model and the
classical force field specified by the user.  The electronic subsystem
is modeled as a continuum, or a background “gas”, on a regular grid
which overlays the simulation domain.  Energy can be transferred
spatially within the grid representing the electrons.  Energy can also
be transferred between the electronic and atomic subsystems.  The
algorithm underlying this fix was derived by D. M.  Duffy
and A. M. Rutherford and is discussed in two J Physics: Condensed
Matter papers: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:duffy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Duffy)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:rutherford}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rutherford)}}}}.  They used this algorithm in cascade simulations where
a primary knock\sphinxhyphen{}on atom (PKA) was initialized with a high velocity to
simulate a radiation event.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The description in this subsection applies to all 3 fix styles:
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/grid}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/grid} distributes the regular grid across processors consistent
with the subdomains of atoms owned by each processor, but is otherwise
identical to fix ttm.  Note that fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm} stores a copy of the grid on
each processor, which is acceptable when the overall grid is reasonably
small.  For larger grids you should use fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/grid} instead.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod} adds options to account for external heat sources (e.g. at
a surface) and for specifying parameters that allow the electronic heat
capacity to depend strongly on electronic temperature.  It is more
expensive computationally than fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm} because it treats the thermal
diffusion equation as non\sphinxhyphen{}linear.  More details on fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod} are
given below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Heat transfer between the electronic and atomic subsystems is carried
out via an inhomogeneous Langevin thermostat.  Only atoms in the fix
group contribute to and are affected by this heat transfer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This thermostatting differs from the regular Langevin thermostat
({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}) in three important ways.  First,
the Langevin thermostat is applied uniformly to all atoms in the
user\sphinxhyphen{}specified group for a single target temperature, whereas the TTM
fixes apply Langevin thermostatting locally to atoms within the
volumes represented by the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified grid points with a target
temperature specific to that grid point.  Second, the Langevin
thermostat couples the temperature of the atoms to an infinite heat
reservoir, whereas the heat reservoir for the TTM fixes is finite and
represents the local electrons.  Third, the TTM fixes allow users to
specify not just one friction coefficient, but rather two independent
friction coefficients: one for the electron\sphinxhyphen{}ion interactions
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{gamma\_p}), and one for electron stopping (\sphinxstyleemphasis{gamma\_s}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the friction coefficient due to electron stopping, \sphinxstyleemphasis{gamma\_s}, is
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, electron stopping effects are included for atoms moving
faster than the electron stopping critical velocity, \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_0}.  For
further details about this algorithm, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:duffy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Duffy)}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:rutherford}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rutherford)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy transport within the electronic subsystem is solved according
to the heat diffusion equation with added source terms for heat
transfer between the subsystems:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}C_e \rho_e \frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t} =
\bigtriangledown (\kappa_e \bigtriangledown T_e) -
g_p (T_e - T_a) + g_s T_a'\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(C_e\) is the specific heat, \(\rho_e\) is the density,
\(\kappa_e\) is the thermal conductivity, \sphinxstyleemphasis{T} is temperature, the
“e” and “a” subscripts represent electronic and atomic subsystems
respectively, \(g_p\) is the coupling constant for the electron\sphinxhyphen{}ion
interaction, and \(g_s\) is the electron stopping coupling
parameter.  \(C_e\), \(\rho_e\), and \(\kappa_e\) are
specified as parameters to the fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/grid}.  The other
quantities are derived.  The form of the heat diffusion equation used
here is almost the same as that in equation 6 of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:duffy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Duffy)}}}},
with the exception that the electronic density is explicitly
represented, rather than being part of the specific heat parameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, the TTM fixes assume that none of the user\sphinxhyphen{}supplied
parameters will vary with temperature. Note that {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:duffy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Duffy)}}}}
used a tanh() functional form for the temperature dependence of the
electronic specific heat, but ignored temperature dependencies of any of
the other parameters.  See more discussion below for fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes do not perform time integration of the atoms in the fix
group, they only rescale their velocities.  Thus a time integration
fix such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve}}}} should be used in conjunction
with these fixes.  These fixes should not normally be used on atoms
that have their temperature controlled by another thermostatting
fix, e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes require use of an orthogonal 3d simulation box with
periodic boundary conditions in all dimensions.  They also require
that the size and shape of the simulation box do not vary
dynamically, e.g. due to use of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}} command.
Likewise, the size/shape of processor subdomains cannot vary due to
dynamic load\sphinxhyphen{}balancing via use of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix balance}}}} command.  It is possible however to load balance
before the simulation starts using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{balance::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{balance}}}}
command, so that each processor has a different size subdomain.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Periodic boundary conditions are also used in the heat equation solve
for the electronic subsystem.  This varies from the approach of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:rutherford}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rutherford)}}}} where the atomic subsystem was
embedded within a larger continuum representation of the electronic
subsystem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keyword specifies a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Tinit} temperature value to initialize
the value stored on all grid points.  By default the temperatures
are all zero when the grid is created.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword specifies an input file of electronic temperatures
for each grid point to be read in to initialize the grid, as an alternative
to using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The input file is a text file which may have comments starting with
the ‘\#’ character.  Each line contains four numeric columns:
ix,iy,iz,Temperature.  Empty or comment\sphinxhyphen{}only lines will be
ignored. The number of lines must be equal to the number of
user\sphinxhyphen{}specified grid points (Nx by Ny by Nz).  The ix,iy,iz are grid
point indices ranging from 1 to Nxyz inclusive in each dimension.  The
lines can appear in any order.  For example, the initial electronic
temperatures on a 1 by 2 by 3 grid could be specified in the file as
follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} UNITS: metal COMMENT: initial electron temperature
1 1 1 1.0
1 1 2 1.0
1 1 3 1.0
1 2 1 2.0
1 2 2 2.0
1 2 3 2.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
where the electronic temperatures along the y=0 plane have been set to
1.0, and the electronic temperatures along the y=1 plane have been set
to 2.0.  If all the grid point values are not specified, LAMMPS will
generate an error. LAMMPS will check if a “UNITS:” tag is in the first
line and stop with an error, if there is a mismatch with the current
units used.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The electronic temperature at each grid point must be a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero
positive value, both initially, and as the temperature evolves over
time.  Thus you must use either the \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} keyword or be
restarting a simulation that used this fix previously.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{outfile} keyword has 2 values.  The first value \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nout} triggers
output of the electronic temperatures for each grid point every Nout
timesteps.  The second value is the filename for output, which will be
suffixed by the timestep.  The format of each output file is exactly
the same as the input temperature file. It will contain a comment in
the first line reporting the date the file was created, the LAMMPS
units setting in use, grid size and the current timestep.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix ttm/grid command does not support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{outfile} keyword.
Instead you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid}}}} command to output
the electronic temperature on the distributed grid to a dump file or
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart}}}} command which creates a file specific
to this fix which the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read restart}}}} command
reads.  The file has the same format as the file the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} option
reads.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the fix ttm and fix ttm/mod commands, the corresponding atomic
temperature for atoms in each grid cell can be computed and output by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command to create a 3d
array of chunks consistent with the grid used by this fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the fix ttm/grid command the same thing can be done using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_grid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/grid}}}} command and its per\sphinxhyphen{}grid values can
be output via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump grid}}}} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Additional details for fix ttm/mod}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod} uses the heat diffusion equation with possible external
heat sources (e.g. laser heating in ablation simulations):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}C_e \rho_e \frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t} =
\bigtriangledown (\kappa_e \bigtriangledown T_e) -
g_p (T_e - T_a) + g_s T_a' + \theta (x-x_{surface})I_0 \exp(-x/l_{skin})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\theta\) is the Heaviside step function, \(I_0\) is the
(absorbed) laser pulse intensity for ablation simulations,
\(l_{skin}\) is the depth of the skin\sphinxhyphen{}layer, and all other
designations have the same meaning as in the former equation. The
duration of the pulse is set by the parameter \sphinxstyleemphasis{tau} in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{init\_file}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod} also allows users to specify the dependencies of
\(C_e\) and \(\kappa_e\) on the electronic temperature. The
specific heat is expressed as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}C_e = C_0 + (a_0 + a_1 X + a_2 X^2 + a_3 X^3 + a_4 X^4) \exp (-(AX)^2)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(X = \frac{T_e}{1000}\), and the thermal conductivity is
defined as \(\kappa_e = D_e \cdot rho_e \cdot C_e\), where
\(D_e\) is the thermal diffusion coefficient.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Electronic pressure effects are included in the TTM model to account for
the blast force acting on ions because of electronic pressure gradient
(see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:chen}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chen)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:norman}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Norman)}}}}).  The total force
acting on an ion is:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{\vec F}_i = - \partial U / \partial {\vec r}_i + {\vec
F}_{langevin} - \nabla P_e/n_{ion}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(F_{langevin}\) is a force from Langevin thermostat
simulating electron\sphinxhyphen{}phonon coupling, and \(\nabla P_e/n_{ion}\) is
the electron blast force.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The electronic pressure is taken to be \(P_e = B \cdot rho_e \cdot
C_e \cdot T_e\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
The current fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod} implementation allows TTM simulations with a
vacuum. The vacuum region is defined as the grid cells with zero
electronic temperature. The numerical scheme does not allow energy
exchange with such cells. Since the material can expand to previously
unoccupied region in some simulations, the vacuum border can be allowed
to move. It is controlled by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface\_movement} parameter in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{init\_file}. If it is set to 1, then “vacuum” cells can be changed to
“electron\sphinxhyphen{}filled” cells with the temperature \sphinxstyleemphasis{T\_e\_min} if atoms move
into them (currently only implemented for the case of 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional
motion of a flat surface normal to the X axis). The initial locations of
the interfaces of the electron density to the vacuum can be set in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{init\_file} via \sphinxstyleemphasis{lsurface} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rsurface} parameters. In this case,
electronic pressure gradient is calculated as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla_x P_e = \left[\frac{C_e{}T_e(x)\lambda}{(x+\lambda)^2} +
\frac{x}{x+\lambda}\frac{(C_e{}T_e)_{x+\Delta
x}-(C_e{}T_e)_{x}}{\Delta x} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\lambda\) is the electron mean free path (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:norman}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Norman)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ttm:pisarev}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Pisarev)}}}})

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix \sphinxstyleemphasis{ttm/mod} parameter file \sphinxstyleemphasis{init\_file} has the following syntax.
Every line with an odd number is considered as a comment and
ignored. The lines with the even numbers are treated as follows:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
a\_0, energy/(temperature*electron) units
a\_1, energy/(temperature\textasciicircum{}2*electron) units
a\_2, energy/(temperature\textasciicircum{}3*electron) units
a\_3, energy/(temperature\textasciicircum{}4*electron) units
a\_4, energy/(temperature\textasciicircum{}5*electron) units
C\_0, energy/(temperature*electron) units
A, 1/temperature units
rho\_e, electrons/volume units
D\_e, length\textasciicircum{}2/time units
gamma\_p, mass/time units
gamma\_s, mass/time units
v\_0, length/time units
I\_0, energy/(time*length\textasciicircum{}2) units
lsurface, electron grid units (positive integer)
rsurface, electron grid units (positive integer)
l\_skin, length units
tau, time units
B, dimensionless
lambda, length units
n\_ion, ions/volume units
surface\_movement: 0 to disable tracking of surface motion, 1 to enable
T\_e\_min, temperature units
\end{sphinxalltt}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ttm:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix ttm and fix ttm/mod commands write the state of the electronic
subsystem and the energy exchange between the subsystems to
{\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  The fix ttm/grid command does
not yet support writing of its distributed grid to a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for info on how to
re\sphinxhyphen{}specify a fix in an input script that reads a restart file, so that
the operation of the fix continues in an uninterrupted fashion.  Note
that the restart script must define the same size grid as the original
script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix ttm/grid command also outputs an auxiliary file each time a
restart file is written, with the electron temperatures for each grid
cell.  The format of this file is the same as that read by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} option explained above.  The filename is the same as the
restart filename with “.ttm” appended.  This auxiliary file can be
read in for a restarted run by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{infile} option for the fix
ttm/grid command, following the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options are relevant to
these fixes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes compute 2 output quantities stored in a vector of length
2, which can be accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The first quantity is the total energy of the
electronic subsystem.  The second quantity is the energy transferred
from the electronic to the atomic subsystem on that timestep. Note
that the velocity verlet integrator applies the fix ttm forces to the
atomic subsystem as two half\sphinxhyphen{}step velocity updates: one on the current
timestep and one on the subsequent timestep.  Consequently, the change
in the atomic subsystem energy is lagged by half a timestep relative
to the change in the electronic subsystem energy. As a result of this,
users may notice slight fluctuations in the sum of the atomic and
electronic subsystem energies reported at the end of the timestep.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values calculated are “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fix ttm/grid command also outputs a per\sphinxhyphen{}grid vector which stores
the electron temperature for each grid cell in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}. which can be accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The length of the vector (distributed across all
processors) is Nx * Ny * Nz.  For access by other commands, the name
of the single grid produced by fix ttm/grid is “grid”.  The name of
its per\sphinxhyphen{}grid data is “data”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of the fixes can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords
of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  The fixes are not invoked during
{\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ttm:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All these fixes are part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}FIX package. They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As mentioned above, these fixes require 3d simulations and orthogonal
simulation boxes periodic in all 3 dimensions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These fixes used a random number generator to Langevin thermostat the
electron temperature.  This means you will not get identical answers
when running on different numbers of processors or when restarting a
simulation (even on the same number of processors).  However, in a
statistical sense, simulations on different processor counts and
restarted simulation should produce results which are statistically
the same.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ttm:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_dt_reset::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix dt/reset}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_ttm:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\index{fix tune/kspace@\spxentry{fix tune/kspace}}\ignorespaces 

\section{fix tune/kspace command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:fix-tune-kspace-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tune}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tune/kspace = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = invoke this fix every N steps

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tune}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix tests each kspace style (Ewald, PPPM, and MSM), and
automatically selects the fastest style to use for the remainder
of the run. If the fastest style is Ewald or PPPM, the fix also
adjusts the Coulombic cutoff towards optimal speed. Future versions
of this fix will automatically select other kspace parameters
to use for maximum simulation speed. The kspace parameters may
include the style, cutoff, grid points in each direction, order,
Ewald parameter, MSM parallelization cut\sphinxhyphen{}point, MPI tasks to use, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rationale for this fix is to provide the user with
as\sphinxhyphen{}fast\sphinxhyphen{}as\sphinxhyphen{}possible simulations that include long\sphinxhyphen{}range electrostatics
(kspace) while meeting the user\sphinxhyphen{}prescribed accuracy requirement. A
simple heuristic could never capture the optimal combination of
parameters for every possible run\sphinxhyphen{}time scenario. But by performing
short tests of various kspace parameter sets, this fix allows
parameters to be tailored specifically to the user’s machine, MPI
ranks, use of threading or accelerators, the simulated system, and the
simulation details. In addition, it is possible that parameters could
be evolved with the simulation on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly, which is useful for systems
that are dynamically evolving (e.g. changes in box size/shape or
number of particles).

\sphinxAtStartPar
When this fix is invoked, LAMMPS will perform short timed tests of
various parameter sets to determine the optimal parameters. Tests are
performed on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly, with a new test initialized every N steps. N should
be chosen large enough so that adequate CPU time lapses between tests,
thereby providing statistically significant timings. But N should not be
chosen to be so large that an unfortunate parameter set test takes an
inordinate amount of wall time to complete. An N of 100 for most problems
seems reasonable. Once an optimal parameter set is found, that set is
used for the remainder of the run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix uses heuristics to guide it’s selection of parameter sets to test,
but the actual timed results will be used to decide which set to use in the
simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is not necessary to discard trajectories produced using sub\sphinxhyphen{}optimal
parameter sets, or a mix of various parameter sets, since the user\sphinxhyphen{}prescribed
accuracy will have been maintained throughout. However, some users may prefer
to use this fix only to discover the optimal parameter set for a given setup
that can then be used on subsequent production runs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix starts with kspace parameters that are set by the user with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}}
commands. The prescribed accuracy will be maintained by this fix throughout
the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options are relevant to this
fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  This fix is not invoked during {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is part of the KSPACE package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not set “neigh\_modify once yes” or else this fix will never be
called.  Reneighboring is required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is not compatible with a hybrid pair style, long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion,
TIP4P water support, or long\sphinxhyphen{}range point dipole support.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{boundary::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{boundary}}}}
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_modify}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/long}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/charmm/coul/long}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_long::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/long}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_long::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/long/coul/long}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_buck::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style buck/coul/long}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{fix_tune_kspace:default}}
\sphinxstepscope

\index{fix vector@\spxentry{fix vector}}\ignorespaces 

\section{fix vector command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_vector:fix-vector-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_vector:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_vector::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_vector:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nevery}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
vector = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nevery = use input values every this many timesteps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more input values can be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
value = c\_ID, c\_ID{[}N{]}, f\_ID, f\_ID{[}N{]}, v\_name

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
c\PYGZus{}ID = global scalar calculated by a compute with ID
c\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith component of global vector calculated by a compute with ID
f\PYGZus{}ID = global scalar calculated by a fix with ID
f\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith component of global vector calculated by a fix with ID
v\PYGZus{}name = value calculated by an equal\PYGZhy{}style variable with name
v\PYGZus{}name[I] = Ith component of vector\PYGZhy{}style variable with name
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/args pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{nmax}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nmax} length = set maximal length of vector to \textless{}length\textgreater{}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_vector:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}integral}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nmax}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_vector:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use one or more global values as inputs every few timesteps, and simply
store them as a sequence.  For a single specified value, the values are
stored as a global vector of growing length.  For multiple specified
values, they are stored as rows in a global array, whose number of rows
is growing.  The resulting vector or array can be used by other
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{nmax} keyword can be used to restrict the length of the
vector to the given \sphinxstyleemphasis{length} value.  Once the restricted vector is
filled, the oldest entry will be discarded when a entry is added.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One way to to use this command is to accumulate a vector that is
numerically integrated using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable trap()}}}}
function. For example, the velocity auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation function (VACF)
can be integrated, to yield a diffusion coefficient, as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vacf}
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[4]}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{diff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{trap}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{f\PYGZus{}5}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}diff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The group specified with this command is ignored.  However, note that
specified values may represent calculations performed by computes and
fixes which store their own “group” definitions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each listed value can be the result of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or the evaluation of an equal\sphinxhyphen{}style or vector\sphinxhyphen{}style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  In each case, the compute, fix, or variable
must produce a global quantity, not a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local quantity.  And
the global quantity must be a scalar, not a vector or array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Computes}}}} that produce global quantities are those which
do not have the word \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} in their style name.  Only a few
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}} produce global quantities.  See the doc pages for
individual fixes for info on which ones produce such values.
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Variables}}}} of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} are the only
ones that can be used with this fix.  Variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} cannot
be used, since they produce per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} argument specifies on what timesteps the input values
will be used in order to be stored.  Only timesteps that are a
multiple of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery}, including timestep 0, will contribute values.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} is a small number and the simulation runs for many
steps, the accumulated vector or array can become very large and
thus consume a lot of memory. The implementation limit is about
2 billion entries. Using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nmax} keyword mentioned above can
avoid that by limiting the size of the vector.
\end{quote}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if you perform multiple runs, using the “pre no” option of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command to avoid initialization on subsequent runs,
then you need to use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keyword with the first {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}
command with a timestep value that encompasses all the runs.  This is
so that the vector or array stored by this fix can be allocated to a
sufficient size.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “c\_”, a compute ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  If no bracketed term is
appended, the global scalar calculated by the compute is used.  If a
bracketed term is appended, the Ith element of the global vector
calculated by the compute is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that there is a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} command
which can sum per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities into a global scalar or vector which
can thus be accessed by fix vector.  Or it can be a compute defined not
in your input script, but by {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermodynamic output}}}}
or other fixes such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}}.  See the doc pages for these commands which give
the IDs of these computes.  Users can also write code for their own
compute styles and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to LAMMPS}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “f\_”, a fix ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  If no bracketed term is
appended, the global scalar calculated by the fix is used.  If a
bracketed term is appended, the Ith element of the global vector
calculated by the fix is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that some fixes only produce their values on certain timesteps,
which must be compatible with \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery}, else an error will result.
Users can also write code for their own fix styles and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to
LAMMPS}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “v\_”, a variable name must follow which has
been previously defined in the input script.  An equal\sphinxhyphen{}style or
vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable can be referenced; the latter requires a
bracketed term to specify the Ith element of the vector calculated by
the variable.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command for details.
Note that variables of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{equal} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vector} define a formula
which can reference individual atom properties or thermodynamic
keywords, or they can invoke other computes, fixes, or variables when
they are evaluated, so this is a very general means of specifying
quantities to be stored by fix vector.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_vector:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options are
relevant to this fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix produces a global vector or global array which can be
accessed by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The values
can only be accessed on timesteps that are multiples of \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector is produced if only a single input value is specified.
An array is produced if multiple input values are specified.
The length of the vector or the number of rows in the array grows
by 1 every \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} timesteps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the fix produces a vector, then the entire vector will be either
“intensive” or “extensive”, depending on whether the values stored in
the vector are “intensive” or “extensive”.  If the fix produces an
array, then all elements in the array must be the same, either
“intensive” or “extensive”.  If a compute or fix provides the value
stored, then the compute or fix determines whether the value is
intensive or extensive; see the page for that compute or fix for further
info.  Values produced by a variable are treated as intensive.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix can allocate storage for stored values accumulated over
multiple runs, using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stop} keywords of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command for details of how to
do this.  If using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run pre no}}}} command option, this is
required to allow the fix to allocate sufficient storage for stored
values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is not invoked during {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.

none

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{fix viscosity command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:fix-viscosity-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscosity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vdim}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pdim}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nbin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
viscosity = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = perform momentum exchange every N steps

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
vdim = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} = which momentum component to exchange

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pdim = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} = direction of momentum transfer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nbin = \# of layers in pdim direction (must be even number)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{swap} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vtarget}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{swap} value = Nswap = number of swaps to perform every N steps
\sphinxstyleemphasis{vtarget} value = V or INF = target velocity of swap partners (velocity units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscosity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscosity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{swap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vtarget}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe algorithm described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscosity:muller-plathe2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{this paper}}}} to exchange momenta between two particles in
different regions of the simulation box every N steps.  This induces a
shear velocity profile in the system.  As described below this enables
a viscosity of the fluid to be calculated.  This algorithm is
sometimes called a reverse non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium MD (reverse NEMD) approach
to computing viscosity.  This is because the usual NEMD approach is to
impose a shear velocity profile on the system and measure the response
via an off\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal component of the stress tensor, which is
proportional to the momentum flux.  In the Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe method, the
momentum flux is imposed, and the shear velocity profile is the
system’s response.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simulation box is divided into \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} layers in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pdim}
direction, where the layer 1 is at the low end of that dimension and
the layer \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} is at the high end.  Every N steps, Nswap pairs of
atoms are chosen in the following manner.  Only atoms in the fix group
are considered.  Nswap atoms in layer 1 with positive velocity
components in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{vdim} direction closest to the target value \sphinxstyleemphasis{V} are
selected.  Similarly, Nswap atoms in the “middle” layer (see below) with
negative velocity components in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{vdim} direction closest to the
negative of the target value \sphinxstyleemphasis{V} are selected.  The two sets of Nswap
atoms are paired up and their \sphinxstyleemphasis{vdim} momenta components are swapped
within each pair.  This resets their velocities, typically in opposite
directions.  Over time, this induces a shear velocity profile in the
system which can be measured using commands such as the following,
which writes the profile to the file tmp.profile:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{layers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.05}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduced}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{f1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{layers}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.profile}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that by default, Nswap = 1 and vtarget = INF, though this can be
changed by the optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{swap} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vtarget} keywords.  When vtarget =
INF, one or more atoms with the most positive and negative velocity
components are selected.  Setting these parameters appropriately, in
conjunction with the swap rate N, allows the momentum flux rate to be
adjusted across a wide range of values, and the momenta to be
exchanged in large chunks or more smoothly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “middle” layer for momenta swapping is defined as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin}/2 + 1
layer.  Thus if \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} = 20, the two swapping layers are 1 and 11.
This should lead to a symmetric velocity profile since the two layers
are separated by the same distance in both directions in a periodic
sense.  This is why \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} is restricted to being an even number.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As described below, the total momentum transferred by these velocity
swaps is computed by the fix and can be output.  Dividing this
quantity by time and the cross\sphinxhyphen{}sectional area of the simulation box
yields a momentum flux.  The ratio of momentum flux to the slope of
the shear velocity profile is proportional to the viscosity of the
fluid, in appropriate units.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscosity:muller-plathe2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe paper}}}} for details.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If your system is periodic in the direction of the momentum
flux, then the flux is going in 2 directions.  This means the
effective momentum flux in one direction is reduced by a factor of 2.
You will see this in the equations for viscosity in the Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe
paper.  LAMMPS is simply tallying momentum which does not account for
whether or not your system is periodic; you must use the value
appropriately to yield a viscosity for your system.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
After equilibration, if the velocity profile you observe is not
linear, then you are likely swapping momentum too frequently and are
not in a regime of linear response.  In this case you cannot
accurately infer a viscosity and should try increasing the Nevery
parameter.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An alternative method for calculating a viscosity is to run a NEMD
simulation, as described on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_nemd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto nemd}}}} doc page.
NEMD simulations deform the simulation box via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some features or combination of settings in LAMMPS do not support
non\sphinxhyphen{}orthogonal boxes.  Using fix viscosity keeps the box orthogonal;
thus it does not suffer from these limitations.


\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options
are relevant to this fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix computes a global scalar which can be accessed by various
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  The scalar is the cumulative
momentum transferred between the bottom and middle of the simulation
box (in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pdim} direction) is stored as a scalar quantity by this
fix.  This quantity is zeroed when the fix is defined and accumulates
thereafter, once every N steps.  The units of the quantity are
momentum = mass*velocity.  The scalar value calculated by this fix is
“intensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.  This fix is not invoked during {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{energy minimization}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}FIX package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Swaps conserve both momentum and kinetic energy, even if the masses of
the swapped atoms are not equal.  Thus you should not need to
thermostat the system.  If you do use a thermostat, you may want to
apply it only to the non\sphinxhyphen{}swapped dimensions (other than \sphinxstyleemphasis{vdim}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS does not check, but you should not use this fix to swap
velocities of atoms that are in constrained molecules, e.g. via {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  This is because
application of the constraints will alter the amount of transferred
momentum.  You should, however, be able to use flexible molecules.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_viscosity:maginn}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Maginn paper}}}} for an example of using this algorithm
in a computation of alcohol molecule properties.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When running a simulation with large, massive particles or molecules
in a background solvent, you may want to only exchange momenta between
solvent particles.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscosity:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix thermal/conductivity}}}}

\section{fix viscous command}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous:fix-viscous-command}}\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{viscous/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscous}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
viscous = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gamma = damping coefficient (force/velocity units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} values = type ratio
    type = atom type (1\sphinxhyphen{}N)
    ratio = factor to scale the damping coefficient by
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{flow}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscous}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{damp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscous}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add a viscous damping force to atoms in the group that is proportional
to the velocity of the atom.  The added force can be thought of as a
frictional interaction with implicit solvent, i.e. the no\sphinxhyphen{}slip Stokes
drag on a spherical particle.  In granular simulations this can be
useful for draining the kinetic energy from the system in a controlled
fashion.  If used without additional thermostatting (to add kinetic
energy to the system), it has the effect of slowly (or rapidly)
freezing the system; hence it can also be used as a simple energy
minimization technique.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The damping force \(F_i\) is given by \(F_i = - \gamma v_i\).
The larger the coefficient, the faster the kinetic energy is reduced.
If the optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} is used, \(\gamma\) can scaled up or
down by the specified factor for atoms of that type.  It can be used
multiple times to adjust \(\gamma\) for several atom types.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You should specify gamma in force/velocity units.  This is not
the same as mass/time units, at least for some of the LAMMPS
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} options like “real” or “metal” that are not
self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a Brownian dynamics context, \(\gamma = \frac{k_B T}{D}\), where
\(k_B =\) Boltzmann’s constant, \(T\) = temperature, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{D} =
particle diffusion coefficient.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{D} can be written as \(\frac{k_B
T}{3 \pi \eta d}\), where \(\eta =\) dynamic viscosity of the
frictional fluid and d = diameter of particle.  This means \(\gamma
= 3 \pi \eta d\), and thus is proportional to the viscosity of the fluid
and the particle diameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the current implementation, rather than have the user specify a
viscosity, \(\gamma\) is specified directly in force/velocity units.
If needed, \(\gamma\) can be adjusted for atoms of different sizes
(i.e. \(\sigma\)) by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that Brownian dynamics models also typically include a randomized
force term to thermostat the system at a chosen temperature.  The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}} command does this.  It has the same
viscous damping term as fix viscous and adds a random force to each
atom.  The random force term is proportional to the square root of the
chosen thermostatting temperature.  Thus if you use fix langevin with a
target \(T = 0\), its random force term is zero, and you are
essentially performing the same operation as fix viscous.  Also note
that the gamma of fix viscous is related to the damping parameter of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}, however the former is specified in
units of force/velocity and the latter in units of time, so that it can
more easily be used as a thermostat.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options are
relevant to this fix.  No global or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities are stored by
this fix for access by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} option is supported by this
fix. This allows to set at which level of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA}}}}
integrator the fix is modifying forces. Default is the outermost level.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forces due to this fix are imposed during an energy minimization,
invoked by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.  This fix should only
be used with damped dynamics minimizers that allow for
non\sphinxhyphen{}conservative forces.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}} command
for details.

\section{fix viscous/sphere command}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous_sphere:syntax}}

ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
viscous/sphere = style name of this fix command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gamma = damping coefficient (torque/angular velocity units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} values = \sphinxstyleemphasis{type ratio} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name}
    type = atom type (1\sphinxhyphen{}N)
    ratio = factor to scale the damping coefficients by
    v\_name = reference to atom style variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous_sphere:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add a viscous damping torque to finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical particles in the group
that is proportional to the angular velocity of the atom.  In granular
simulations this can be useful for draining the rotational kinetic energy from
the system in a controlled fashion.  If used without additional thermostatting
(to add kinetic energy to the system), it has the effect of slowly (or rapidly)
freezing the system; hence it can also be used as a simple energy minimization
technique.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The damping torque \(T_i\) is given by \(T_i = - \gamma \omega_i\).
The larger the coefficient, the faster the rotational kinetic energy is reduced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} is used, \(\gamma\) can be scaled up
or down by the specified factor for atoms.  This factor can be set for
different atom types and thus the \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} keyword used multiple times
followed by the atom type and the associated scale factor.  Alternately
the scaling factor can be computed for each atom (e.g. based on its
radius) by using an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You should specify gamma in torque/angular velocity units.  This is not
the same as mass/time units, at least for some of the LAMMPS
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} options like “real” or “metal” that are not
self\sphinxhyphen{}consistent.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the current implementation, rather than have the user specify a viscosity,
\(\gamma\) is specified directly in torque/angular velocity units.
If needed, \(\gamma\) can be adjusted for atoms of different sizes
(i.e. \(\sigma\)) by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
No information about this fix is written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  None of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} options are

this fix for access by various {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.
No parameter of this fix can be used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{start/stop} keywords of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} \sphinxstyleemphasis{respa} option is supported by this
fix. This allows to set at which level of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA}}}}
integrator the fix is modifying torques. Default is the outermost level.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The torques due to this fix are imposed during an energy minimization,
invoked by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{minimize::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimize}}}} command.  This fix should only
be used with damped dynamics minimizers that allow for
non\sphinxhyphen{}conservative forces.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{min\_style}}}} command
for details.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{fix_viscous_sphere:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}FIX package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix requires that atoms store torque and angular velocity (omega)
and a radius as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All particles in the group must be finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spheres.  They cannot
be point particles.

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{fix_wall:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{[tabstyle]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{[N]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{face}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/lj93} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/lj126} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/lj1043} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/colloid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/harmonic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/lepton} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/morse} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/table}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tabstyle = \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} = method of table interpolation (only applies to \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/table})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = use N values in \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} interpolation (only applies to \sphinxstyleemphasis{wall/table})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more face/arg pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
face = \sphinxstyleemphasis{xlo} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xhi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ylo} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yhi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{zlo} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{zhi}

\end{itemize}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args for styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj93} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj126} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj1043} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{colloid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
args = coord epsilon sigma cutoff
coord = position of wall = EDGE or constant or variable
  EDGE = current lo or hi edge of simulation box
  constant = number like 0.0 or \sphinxhyphen{}30.0 (distance units)
  variable = {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} like v\_x or v\_wiggle
epsilon = strength factor for wall\sphinxhyphen{}particle interaction (energy or energy/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)
  epsilon can be a variable (see below)
sigma = size factor for wall\sphinxhyphen{}particle interaction (distance units)
  sigma can be a variable (see below)
cutoff = distance from wall at which wall\sphinxhyphen{}particle interactions are cut off (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lepton}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
args = coord expression cutoff
coord = position of wall = EDGE or constant or variable
  EDGE = current lo or hi edge of simulation box
  constant = number like 0.0 or \sphinxhyphen{}30.0 (distance units)
  variable = {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} like v\_x or v\_wiggle
expression = Lepton expression for the potential  (energy units)
cutoff = distance from wall at which wall\sphinxhyphen{}particle interactions are cut off (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
args = coord D\_0 alpha r\_0 cutoff
coord = position of wall = EDGE or constant or variable
  EDGE = current lo or hi edge of simulation box
  constant = number like 0.0 or \sphinxhyphen{}30.0 (distance units)
  variable = {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} like v\_x or v\_wiggle
D\_0 = depth of the potential (energy units)
  D\_0 can be a variable (see below)
alpha = width factor for wall\sphinxhyphen{}particle interaction (1/distance units)
  alpha can be a variable (see below)
r\_0 = distance of the potential minimum from the face of region (distance units)
  r\_0 can be a variable (see below)
cutoff = distance from wall at which wall\sphinxhyphen{}particle interactions are cut off (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
args = coord filename keyword cutoff
coord = position of wall = EDGE or constant or variable
  EDGE = current lo or hi edge of simulation box
  constant = number like 0.0 or \sphinxhyphen{}30.0 (distance units)
  variable = {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} like v\_x or v\_wiggle
filename = file containing tabulated energy and force values
keyword = section identifier to select a specific table in table file
cutoff = distance from wall at which wall\sphinxhyphen{}particle interactions are cut off (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{units} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fld} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pbc}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{units} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{box}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{lattice} = the wall position is defined in lattice units
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{box} = the wall position is defined in simulation box units
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fld} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = invoke the wall constraint to be compatible with implicit FLD
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = invoke the wall constraint in the normal way
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pbc} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = allow periodic boundary in a wall dimension
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = require non\sphinxhyphen{}perioidic boundaries in any wall dimension
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}
