\section{compute chunk/spread/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom:compute-chunk-spread-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spread}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunk/spread/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more inputs can be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
input = c\_ID, c\_ID{[}N{]}, f\_ID, f\_ID{[}N{]}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
c\PYGZus{}ID = global vector calculated by a compute with ID
c\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of global array calculated by a compute with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
f\PYGZus{}ID = global vector calculated by a fix with ID
f\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of global array calculated by a fix with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spread}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mychunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}gyration}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a calculation that “spreads” one or more per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values to
each atom in the chunk.  This can be useful in several scenarios:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For creating a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump file}}}} where each atom lists info about
the chunk it is in, e.g. for post\sphinxhyphen{}processing purposes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
To access chunk value in {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}} that
need info about the chunk each atom is in.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
To use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command to spatially
average per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values calculated by a per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk compute.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples are given below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For inputs that are computes, they must be a compute that calculates
per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values.  These are computes whose style names end in
“/chunk”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For inputs that are fixes, they should be a fix that calculates
per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values.  For example, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} (assuming it is time\sphinxhyphen{}averaging
per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk data).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For each atom, this compute accesses its chunk ID from the specified
\sphinxstyleemphasis{chunkID} compute, then accesses the per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk value in each input.
Those values are copied to this compute to become the output for that
atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values generated by this compute will be 0.0 for atoms not in the
specified compute group \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.  They will also be 0.0 if the atom
is not in a chunk, as assigned by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunkID} compute.  They will
also be 0.0 if the current chunk ID for the atom is out\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}bounds with
respect to the number of chunks stored by a particular input compute
or fix.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS does not check that a compute or fix which calculates
per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values uses the same definition of chunks as this compute.
It’s up to you to be consistent.  Likewise, for a fix input, LAMMPS
does not check that it is per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk data.  It only checks that the fix
produces a global vector or array.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Each listed input is operated on independently.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a bracketed index I is used, it can be specified using a wildcard
asterisk with the index to effectively specify multiple values.  This
takes the form “*” or “*n” or “n*” or “m*n”.  If N = the number of
columns in the array, then an asterisk with no numeric values means
all indices from 1 to N.  A leading asterisk means all indices from 1
to n (inclusive).  A trailing asterisk means all indices from n to N
(inclusive).  A middle asterisk means all indices from m to n
(inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a wildcard is the same as if the individual columns of the array
had been listed one by one.  E.g. these 2 compute chunk/spread/atom
commands are equivalent, since the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_com_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute com/chunk}}}} command creates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array
with 3 columns:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mychunk}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spread}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mychunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spread}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mychunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[3]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of writing a dump file the with the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
(COM) for the chunk each atom is in.  The commands below can be added
to the bench/in.chain script.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cmol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cmol}
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{comchunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spread}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cmol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{dump            }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}comchunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{dump\PYGZus{}modify     }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sort}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The same per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk data for each atom could be used to define per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
forces for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_addforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix addforce}}}} command.  In this
example the forces act to pull atoms of an extended polymer chain
towards its COM in an attractive manner.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zu}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{k}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}k}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{c\PYGZus{}comchunk[1]\PYGZhy{}c\PYGZus{}prop[1]}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}k}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{c\PYGZus{}comchunk[2]\PYGZhy{}c\PYGZus{}prop[2]}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}k}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{c\PYGZus{}comchunk[3]\PYGZhy{}c\PYGZus{}prop[3]}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{addforce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}fx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}fy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}fz}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/atom}}}} is used
to generate unwrapped coordinates for use in the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom force
calculation, so that the effect of periodic boundaries is accounted
for properly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Over time this applied force could shrink each polymer chain’s radius
of gyration in a polymer mixture simulation.  Here is output from the
bench/in.chain script.  Thermo output is shown for 1000 steps, where
the last column is the average radius of gyration over all 320 chains
in the 32000 atom system:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
compute         gyr all gyration/chunk cmol
variable        ave equal ave(c\PYGZus{}gyr)
thermo\PYGZus{}style    custom step etotal press v\PYGZus{}ave

       0    22.394765    4.6721833     5.128278
     100    22.445002    4.8166709    5.0348372
     200    22.500128    4.8790392    4.9364875
     300    22.534686    4.9183766    4.8590693
     400    22.557196    4.9492211    4.7937849
     500    22.571017    4.9161853    4.7412008
     600    22.573944    5.0229708    4.6931243
     700    22.581804    5.0541301    4.6440647
     800    22.584683    4.9691734    4.6000016
     900     22.59128    5.0247538    4.5611513
    1000    22.586832      4.94697    4.5238362
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example for using one set of chunks, defined for molecules,
to compute the dipole moment vector for each chunk.  E.g. for water
molecules. Then spreading those values to each atom in each chunk.
Then defining a second set of chunks based on spatial bins.  And
finally, using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command to
calculate an average dipole moment vector per spatial bin.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cmol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dipole}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cmol}
\PYG{k}{compute       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{spread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spread}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cmol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}dipole[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}dipole[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}dipole[3]}
\PYG{k}{compute       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cspatial}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduced}
\PYG{k}{fix           }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ave}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cspatial}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}spread[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}} command requires
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values as input.  That is why the compute chunk/spread/atom
command is used to assign per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values to each atom in the chunk.
If a molecule straddles bin boundaries, each of its atoms contributes
in a weighted manner to the average dipole moment of the spatial bin
it is in.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array, which can be
accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output is a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector if a single input value is specified,
otherwise a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array is output.  The number of columns in the
array is the number of inputs provided.  The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values for the
vector or each column of the array will be in whatever
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} the corresponding input value is in.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector or array values are “intensive”.

\label{\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce/chunk}}}}

\section{compute cluster/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:compute-cluster-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom::doc}}

\section{compute fragment/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:compute-fragment-atom-command}}

\section{compute aggregate/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:compute-aggregate-atom-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cluster}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fragment}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{aggregate}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cluster/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fragment/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{aggregate/atom} = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = distance within which to label atoms as part of same cluster (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended to \sphinxstyleemphasis{fragment/atom}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{single}
\begin{quote}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} to treat single atoms (no bonds) as fragments
\end{sphinxalltt}
\end{quote}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cluster}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fragment}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fragment}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{aggregate}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cluster_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that assigns each atom a cluster, fragment, or
aggregate ID.  Only atoms in the compute group are clustered and
assigned cluster IDs. Atoms not in the compute group are assigned an
ID = 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A cluster is defined as a set of atoms, each of which is within the
cutoff distance from one or more other atoms in the cluster.  If an
atom has no neighbors within the cutoff distance, then it is a 1\sphinxhyphen{}atom
cluster.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A fragment is similarly defined as a set of atoms, each of which has a
bond to another atom in the fragment.  Bonds can be defined initially
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data file}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_bonds}}}} commands, or dynamically by fixes which create or
break bonds like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_create::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
bond/create}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_swap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/swap}}}},
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_break::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/break}}}}.  The cluster ID or fragment
ID of every atom in the cluster will be set to the smallest atom ID of
any atom in the cluster or fragment, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fragment/atom} style, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single} keyword determines whether
single atoms (not bonded to another atom) are treated as one\sphinxhyphen{}atom
fragments or not, based on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} setting.  If the setting
is \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} (the default), their fragment IDs are set to 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An aggregate is defined by combining the rules for clusters and
fragments (i.e., a set of atoms, where each of them is within the cutoff
distance from one or more atoms within a fragment that is part of
the same cluster). This measure can be used to track molecular assemblies
like micelles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For computes \sphinxstyleemphasis{cluster/atom} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{aggregate/atom} a neighbor list
needed to compute cluster IDs is constructed each time the compute is
invoked.  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity too
frequently or to have multiple \sphinxstyleemphasis{cluster/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{aggregate/atom}
style computes.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This
is the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command, and means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the
neighbor list.  Because this fix uses the neighbor list, it also means
those pairs will not be included when computing the clusters. This
does not apply when using long\sphinxhyphen{}range coulomb (\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/msm},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/wolf} or similar.  One way to get around this would be to set
special\_bond scaling factors to very tiny numbers that are not exactly
zero (e.g., \(1.0 \times 10^{-50}\)). Another workaround is to write a
dump file and use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to compute the clusters
for snapshots in the dump file.  The rerun script can use a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command that includes all pairs in
the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the compute fragment/atom style, each fragment is identified
using the current bond topology.  This will not account for bonds
broken by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}} command
because it does not perform a full update of the bond topology data
structures within LAMMPS.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\section{compute cna/atom command}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cna}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cna/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = cutoff distance for nearest neighbors (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cna}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.08}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the CNA (Common Neighbor
Analysis) pattern for each atom in the group.  In solid\sphinxhyphen{}state systems
the CNA pattern is a useful measure of the local crystal structure
around an atom.  The CNA methodology is described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:faken}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Faken)}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:tsuzuki1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tsuzuki)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, there are five kinds of CNA patterns LAMMPS recognizes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fcc = 1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
hcp = 2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bcc = 3

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
icosahedral = 4

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
unknown = 5

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the CNA pattern will be 0 for atoms not in the specified
compute group.  Note that normally a CNA calculation should only be
performed on mono\sphinxhyphen{}component systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The CNA calculation can be sensitive to the specified cutoff value.
You should ensure the appropriate nearest neighbors of an atom are
found within the cutoff distance for the presumed crystal structure
(e.g., 12 nearest neighbor for perfect FCC and HCP crystals, 14 nearest
neighbors for perfect BCC crystals).  These formulas can be used to
obtain a good cutoff distance:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r_{c}^{\mathrm{fcc}} = & \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + 1\right) a
  \approx 0.8536 a \\
r_{c}^{\mathrm{bcc}} = & \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2} + 1) a
  \approx 1.207 a \\
r_{c}^{\mathrm{hcp}} = & \frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{4+2x^{2}}{3}}\right) a\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(a\) is the lattice constant for the crystal structure concerned
and in the HCP case, \(x = (c/a) / 1.633\), where 1.633 is the ideal
\(c/a\) for HCP crystals.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that since the CNA calculation in LAMMPS uses the neighbors
of an owned atom to find the nearest neighbors of a ghost atom, the
following relation should also be satisfied:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r_c + r_s > 2*{\rm cutoff}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(r_c\) is the cutoff distance of the potential, \(r_s\)
is the skin
distance as specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} command, and
cutoff is the argument used with the compute cna/atom command.  LAMMPS
will issue a warning if this is not the case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (e.g. each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently or to have multiple compute/dump commands, each with a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cna/atom} style.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be a number from 0 to 5, as explained
above.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_centro_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centro/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cna_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{compute cnp/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom:compute-cnp-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cnp/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = cutoff distance for nearest neighbors (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cnp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.08}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the Common Neighborhood
Parameter (CNP) for each atom in the group.  In solid\sphinxhyphen{}state systems
the CNP is a useful measure of the local crystal structure
around an atom and can be used to characterize whether the
atom is part of a perfect lattice, a local defect (e.g., a dislocation
or stacking fault), or at a surface.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the CNP parameter will be 0.0 for atoms not in the
specified compute group.  Note that normally a CNP calculation should
only be performed on single component systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This parameter is computed using the following formula from
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom:tsuzuki2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tsuzuki)}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Q_{i} = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j = 1}^{n_i} \left\lVert \sum_{k = 1}^{n_{ij}}  \vec{R}_{ik} + \vec{R}_{jk} \right\rVert^{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} goes over the \(n_i\) nearest neighbors of atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i}, and the index \sphinxstyleemphasis{k} goes over the \(n_{ij}\) common nearest neighbors
between atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}. \(\vec{R}_{ik}\) and
\(\vec{R}_{jk}\) are the vectors connecting atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{k} to atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}.  The quantity in the double sum is computed
for each atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The CNP calculation is sensitive to the specified cutoff value.
You should ensure that the appropriate nearest neighbors of an atom are
found within the cutoff distance for the presumed crystal structure.
E.g. 12 nearest neighbor for perfect FCC and HCP crystals, 14 nearest
neighbors for perfect BCC crystals.  These formulas can be used to
obtain a good cutoff distance:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r_{c}^{\mathrm{fcc}} = & \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + 1\right) a
  \approx 0.8536 a \\
r_{c}^{\mathrm{bcc}} = & \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2} + 1) a
  \approx 1.207 a \\
r_{c}^{\mathrm{hcp}} = & \frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{4+2x^{2}}{3}}\right) a\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(a\) is the lattice constant for the crystal structure concerned
and in the HCP case, \(x = (c/a) / 1.633\), where 1.633 is the ideal
\(c/a\) for HCP crystals.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Also note that since the CNP calculation in LAMMPS uses the neighbors
of an owned atom to find the nearest neighbors of a ghost atom, the
following relation should also be satisfied:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r_c + r_s > 2*{\rm cutoff}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(r_c\) is the cutoff distance of the potential, \(r_s\) is
the skin
distance as specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} command, and
cutoff is the argument used with the compute cnp/atom command.  LAMMPS
will issue a warning if this is not the case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (e.g., each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently or to have multiple compute/dump commands, each with a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cnp/atom} style.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be real positive numbers. Some typical CNP
values:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
FCC lattice = 0.0
BCC lattice = 0.0
HCP lattice = 4.4

FCC (111) surface = 13.0
FCC (100) surface = 26.5
FCC dislocation core = 11
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\label{\detokenize{compute_cnp_atom:restrictions}}

LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_com:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_com:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_com:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the group
of atoms, including all effects due to atoms passing through periodic
boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector of three quantities is calculated by this compute, which
are the \((x,y,z)\) coordinates of the center of mass.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass in
“unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with each atom.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of
“unwrapped” coordinates.  See the Atoms section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags and
how they are set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags
(e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_com:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 3, which can be
accessed by indices 1\textendash{}3 by any command that uses global vector values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values are “intensive”.  The vector values will be in
distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\section{compute com/chunk command}

\subsection{Syntax}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Examples}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_com_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass for multiple
chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates the \((x,y,z)\) coordinates of the center of mass
for each chunk, which includes all effects due to atoms passing through
periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not
in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the
“all” group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero chunk IDs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the chunk’s
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass in “unwrapped” form, by using the image flags
associated with each atom.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command
for a discussion of “unwrapped” coordinates.  See the Atoms section of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags
and how they are set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags
(e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute com/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_com_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array where the number of rows = the
number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  The number of columns is
3 for the \((x,y,z)\) center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass coordinates of each chunk.  These
values can be accessed by any command that uses global array values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\section{compute composition/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:compute-composition-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
composition/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} value = distance cutoff
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{composition}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{composition}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}
\PYG{k}{comm\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 21Nov2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates a local composition vector for each
atom. For a central atom with \(M\) neighbors within the neighbor cutoff sphere,
composition is defined as the number of atoms of a given type
(including the central atom) divided by (\(M+1\)).  For a given central atom,
the sum of all compositions equals one.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute uses the number of atom types, not chemical species, assigned in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.  If an interatomic potential has two
species (i.e., Cu and Ni) assigned to four different atom types in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} (i.e., ‘Cu Cu Ni Ni’), the compute will
output four fractional values.  In those cases, the user may desire an extra
calculation step to consolidate per\sphinxhyphen{}type fractions into per\sphinxhyphen{}species fractions.
This calculation can be conducted within LAMMPS using another compute such as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}}, an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable command}}}}, or as a
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing step.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} defines the distance cutoff used when
searching for neighbors. The default value is the cutoff specified by
the pair style. If no pair style is defined, then a cutoff must be
defined using this keyword. If the specified cutoff is larger than
that of the pair\_style plus neighbor skin (or no pair style is
defined), the \sphinxstyleemphasis{comm\_modify cutoff} option must also be set to match
that of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (i.e. each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.
This is the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command, and means those pairwise interactions do
not appear in the neighbor list.  Because this compute uses the
neighbor list, it also means those pairs will not be included in
the order parameter.  This difficulty can be circumvented by
writing a dump file, and using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to
compute the order parameter for snapshots in the dump file.  The
rerun script can use a {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command
that includes all pairs in the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with \(1 + N\) columns, where \(N\)
is the number of atom types. The first column is a count of the number of atoms
used to calculate composition (including the central atom), and each subsequent
column indicates the fraction of that atom type within the cutoff sphere.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values can be accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}}
doc page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor styles ‘bin’ or ‘nsq’}}}}.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_composition_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} = pair style cutoff.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
contact/atom = style name of this compute command

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_contact_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{contact}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{contact}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mygroup}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_contact_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the number of contacts
for each atom in a group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The contact number is defined for finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical particles as
the number of neighbor atoms which overlap the central particle,
meaning that their distance of separation is less than or equal to the
sum of the radii of the two particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the contact number will be 0.0 for atoms not in the
specified compute group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID} argument allows to specify from which group atoms
contribute to the coordination number. Default setting is group ‘all’.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_contact_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, whose values can be
accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be a number \(\ge 0.0\), as explained
above.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_contact_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the GRANULAR package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires that atoms store a radius as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}} command.

\label{\detokenize{compute_coord_atom:compute-coord-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_coord_atom:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_coord_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_coord_atom::doc}}

Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{coord/atom/kk}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} args = cutoff {[}\sphinxstyleemphasis{group} group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID{]} typeN
  cutoff = distance within which to count coordination neighbors (distance units)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID = select group\sphinxhyphen{}ID to restrict which atoms to consider for coordination number (optional)

\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_coord_atom:examples}}

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coord}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orientorder}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_coord_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute performs calculations between neighboring atoms to
determine a coordination value.  The specific calculation and the
meaning of the resulting value depend on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cstyle} keyword used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} cstyle calculates one or more traditional coordination
numbers for each atom.  A coordination number is defined as the number
of neighbor atoms with specified atom type(s), and optionally within
the specified group, that are within the specified cutoff distance from
the central atom. The compute group selects only the central atoms; all
neighboring atoms, unless selected by type, type range, or group option,
are included in the coordination number tally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{group} keyword allows to specify from which group atoms
contribute to the coordination number. Default setting is group ‘all.’

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{typeN} keywords allow specification of which atom types
contribute to each coordination number.  One coordination number is
computed for each of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{typeN} keywords listed.  If no \sphinxstyleemphasis{typeN}
keywords are listed, a single coordination number is calculated, which
includes atoms of all types (same as the “*” format, see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{typeN} keywords can be specified in one of two ways.  An explicit
numeric value can be used, as in the second example above.  Or a
wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can be used to specify a range of atom types.  This
takes the form “*” or “*n” or “m*” or “m*n”.  If \(N\) is the number of
atom types, then an asterisk with no numeric values means all types
from 1 to \(N\).  A leading asterisk means all types from 1 to n
(inclusive).  A trailing asterisk means all types from m to \(N\)
(inclusive).  A middle asterisk means all types from m to n
(inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{orientorder} cstyle calculates the number of “connected” neighbor
atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} around each central atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}.  For this \sphinxstyleemphasis{cstyle}, connected is
defined by the orientational order parameter calculated by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute orientorder/atom}}}} command.
This \sphinxstyleemphasis{cstyle} thus allows one to apply the ten Wolde’s criterion to
identify crystal\sphinxhyphen{}like atoms in a system, as discussed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_coord_atom:tenwolde1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{ten Wolde}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ID of the previously specified {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute orientorder/atom}}}} command is specified as
\sphinxstyleemphasis{orientorderID}.  The compute must invoke its \sphinxstyleemphasis{components} option to
calculate components of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ybar\_lm} vector for each atoms, as
described in its documentation.  Note that orientorder/atom compute
defines its own criteria for identifying neighboring atoms.  If the
scalar product (\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ybar\_lm(i)}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ybar\_lm(j)}), calculated by the
orientorder/atom compute is larger than the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{threshold},
then \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} are connected, and the coordination value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} is
incremented by one.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all \sphinxstyleemphasis{cstyle} settings, all coordination values will be 0.0 for
atoms not in the specified compute group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (i.e., each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This
is the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command, and means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the
neighbor list.  Because this fix uses the neighbor list, it also means
those pairs will not be included in the coordination count.  One way
to get around this, is to write a dump file, and use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to compute the coordination for snapshots
in the dump file.  The rerun script can use a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command that includes all pairs in
the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array values will be a number \(\ge 0.0\), as
explained above.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_count_type:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that counts the current number of atoms for each
atom type.  Or the number of bonds (angles, dihedrals, impropers) for
each bond (angle, dihedral, improper) type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The former can be useful if atoms are added to or deleted from the
system in random ways, e.g. via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pour::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pour}}}}, or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_evaporate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix evaporate}}}}
commands.  The latter can be useful in reactive simulations where
molecular bonds are broken or created, as well as angles, dihedrals,
impropers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for this command, bonds (angles, etc) are the topological
kind enumerated in a data file, initially read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command or defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{molecule::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{molecule}}}}
command.  They do not refer to implicit bonds defined on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly by
bond\sphinxhyphen{}order or reactive pair styles based on the current conformation
of small clusters of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands can turn off topological bonds (angles, etc) by setting
their bond (angle, etc) types to negative values.  This command
includes the turned\sphinxhyphen{}off bonds (angles, etc) in the count for each
type:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands can create and/or break topological bonds (angles,
etc).  In the case of breaking, they remove the bond (angle, etc) from
the system, so that they no longer exist ({\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{BPM bond styles}}}} are exceptions,
see the discussion below).  Thus they are not included in the counts
for each type:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{delete_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{delete\_bonds remove}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_react::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/react}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_create::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/create}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_bond_break::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix bond/break}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{BPM package}}}} bond styles

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} then the count of atoms for each atom
type is tallied.  Only atoms in the specified group are counted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom count for each type can be normalized by the total number of
atoms like so:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{typevec}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{count}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} number of atoms of each type}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{normtypes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}typevec}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atoms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} divide by total number of atoms}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ntypes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{extract\PYGZus{}setting}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{ntypes}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} number of atom types}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}normtypes[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{ntypes}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} vector variable needs upper limit}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly, bond counts can be normalized by the total number of bonds.
The same goes for angles, dihedrals, and impropers (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} then the count of bonds for each bond
type is tallied.  Only bonds with both atoms in the specified group
are counted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}, broken bonds with a bond type of zero are also
counted.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_quartic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style quartic}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{BPM
bond styles}}}} break bonds by doing this.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_broken_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto broken bonds}}}} doc page for more details.
Note that the group setting is ignored for broken bonds; all broken
bonds in the system are counted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} then the count of angles for each
angle type is tallied.  Only angles with all 3 atoms in the specified
group are counted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} then the count of dihedrals for
each dihedral type is tallied.  Only dihedrals with all 4 atoms in the
specified group are counted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting is \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} then the count of impropers for
each improper type is tallied.  Only impropers with all 4 atoms in the
specified group are counted.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_count_type:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of counts.  If the mode is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper}, then the
vector length is the number of atom types or bond types or angle types
or dihedral types or improper types, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the mode is \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} this compute also calculates a global scalar
which is the number of broken bonds with type = 0, as explained above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values can be used by any command that uses global scalar or
vector values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar and vector values calculated by this compute are both
“intensive”.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_count_type:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_count_type:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_count_type:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute damage/atom@\spxentry{compute damage/atom}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute damage/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:compute-damage-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{damage}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
damage/atom = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{damage}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom damage for each atom
in a group.  This is a quantity relevant for {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Peridynamics models}}}}.  See \sphinxhref{PDF/PDLammps\_overview.pdf}{this document} for an
overview of LAMMPS commands for Peridynamics modeling.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “damage” of a Peridynamics particles is based on the bond breakage
between the particle and its neighbors.  If all the bonds are broken
the particle is considered to be fully damaged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Peridynamics Howto}}}} for a formal definition
of “damage” and more details about Peridynamics as it is implemented in
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can be used with all the Peridynamic pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The damage value will be 0.0 for atoms not in the specified compute
group.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values are unitless numbers (damage) \(\ge 0.0\).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the PERI package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute dilatation/atom}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_plasticity_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute plasticity/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_damage_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\section{compute dihedral command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:compute-dihedral-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dihedral = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that extracts the dihedral energy calculated by
each of the dihedral sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles used in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style hybrid}}}} command.  These values are made
accessible for output or further processing by other commands.  The
group specified for this command is ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is useful when using {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style hybrid}}}} if you want to know the portion of the
total energy contributed by one or more of the hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length \(N\), where \(N\)
is the number of sub\_styles defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style hybrid}}}} command, which can be accessed by
the indices 1 through \(N\).  These values can be used by any command that
uses global scalar or vector values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values are “extensive” and will be in energy
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute dihedral/local@\spxentry{compute dihedral/local}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute dihedral/local command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral_local:compute-dihedral-local-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral_local:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral_local::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral_local:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dihedral/local = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more values may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{phi} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{phi} = tabulate dihedral angles
\sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name} = equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable with name (see below)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/args pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{set}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{set} args = phi name
  phi = only currently allowed arg
  name = name of variable to set with phi
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral_local:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{phi}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{phi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}cos}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{phi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral_local:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates properties of individual dihedral
interactions.  The number of datums generated, aggregated across all
processors, equals the number of dihedral angles in the system, modified
by the group parameter as explained below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{phi} (\(\phi\)) is the dihedral angle, as defined in the diagram
on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name} can be used together with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keyword to compute a
user\sphinxhyphen{}specified function of the dihedral angle \(\phi\).  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{name}
specified for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name} value is the name of an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} which should evaluate a formula based on
a variable which will store the angle \(\phi\).  This other variable must
be an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{internal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} defined in the input
script; its initial numeric value can be anything.  It must be an
internal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable, because this command resets its value
directly.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{set} keyword is used to identify the name of this
other variable associated with \(\phi\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the value of \(\phi\) for each angle which stored in the internal
variable is in radians, not degrees.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, these commands can be added to the bench/in.rhodo
script to compute the \(\cos\phi\) and \(\cos^2\phi\) of every dihedral
angle in the system and output the statistics in various ways:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{internal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cos}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cos}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{v\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cossq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cos}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{v\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{cos}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{v\PYGZus{}p}\PYG{n+nv}{)}

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dtype}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{phi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}cos}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}cossq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{phi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}3[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}

\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{histo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.histo}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}} command will output the angle (\(\phi\)),
\(\cos(\phi)\), and \(\cos^2(\phi)\) for every dihedral in the system.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command will print the average of
those quantities via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} command
with thermo output.  And the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_histo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/histo}}}}
command will histogram the cosine(angle) values and write them to a file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The local data stored by this command is generated by looping over all
the atoms owned on a processor and their dihedrals.  A dihedral will
only be included if all four atoms in the dihedral are in the specified
compute group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that as atoms migrate from processor to processor, there will be
no consistent ordering of the entries within the local vector or array
from one timestep to the next.  The only consistency that is
guaranteed is that the ordering on a particular timestep will be the
same for local vectors or arrays generated by other compute commands.
For example, dihedral output from the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/local}}}} command can be combined
with data from this command and output by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}
command in a consistent way.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of how to do this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dtype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{datom4}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{phi}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[3]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[4]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[5]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[1]}

\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dihedral_local:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a local vector or local array depending on the
number of values.  The length of the vector or number of rows in the
array is the number of dihedrals.  If a single value is specified, a
local vector is produced.  If two or more values are specified, a
local array is produced where the number of columns is equal to the number of
values.  The vector or array can be accessed by any command that uses
local values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output for \sphinxstyleemphasis{phi} will be in degrees.
