\section{compute dilatation/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom:compute-dilatation-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dilatation}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dilatation/atom = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dilatation}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom dilatation for each
atom in a group.  This is a quantity relevant for {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Peridynamics
models}}}}.  See \sphinxhref{PDF/PDLammps\_overview.pdf}{this document}
for an overview of LAMMPS commands for Peridynamics modeling.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For small deformation, dilatation of is the measure of the volumetric
strain.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The dilatation \(\theta\) for each peridynamic particle \(i\) is
calculated as a sum over its neighbors with unbroken bonds, where the
contribution of the \(ij\) pair is a function of the change in bond
length (versus the initial length in the reference state), the volume
fraction of the particles and an influence function.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Peridynamics Howto}}}} for a formal definition of
dilatation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can only be used with a subset of the Peridynamic
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair styles}}}}: \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/lps}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/ves}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{peri/eps}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The dilatation value will be 0.0 for atoms not in the specified
compute group.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values are unitless numbers \((\theta \ge 0.0)\).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dilatation_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the PERI package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\section{compute dipole command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:compute-dipole-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole::doc}}

\section{compute dipole/tip4p command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:compute-dipole-tip4p-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{mass} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometry} = use COM or geometric center for charged chunk correction (optional)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dw}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{water}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{geometry}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dw}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{water}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tip4p}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the dipole vector and total dipole
for a group of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes calculate the x,y,z coordinates of the dipole vector and
the total dipole moment for the atoms in the compute group.  This
includes all effects due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.
For a group with a net charge the resulting dipole is made position
independent by subtracting the position vector of the center of mass or
geometric center times the net charge from the computed dipole
vector.  Both per\sphinxhyphen{}atom charges and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom dipole moments, if present,
contribute to the computed dipole.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 28Mar2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p} includes adjustments for the charge carrying
point M in molecules with TIP4P water geometry.  The corresponding
parameters are extracted from the pair style.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the dipole in “unwrapped”
form, by using the image flags associated with each atom.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of “unwrapped”
coordinates.  See the Atoms section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags and how they are
set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags (e.g., to 0) before
invoking this compute by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes calculate a global scalar containing the magnitude of the
computed dipole moment and a global vector of length 3 with the dipole
vector.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview
of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The computed values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
dipole units (i.e., charge {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} times distance
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p} is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package. It is
only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p} can only be used with tip4p pair styles.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute dipole/chunk}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the center of mass is the default setting for the net charge correction.

\section{compute dipole/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:compute-dipole-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk::doc}}

\section{compute dipole/tip4p/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:compute-dipole-tip4p-chunk-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/chunk} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p/chunk}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{mass} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometry} = use COM or geometric center for charged chunk correction (optional)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dw}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{water}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{geometry}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the dipole vector and total dipole
for multiple chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom to a
single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified as
chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a molecule
or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}} doc pages for
details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how they can be
used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes calculate the \((x,y,z)\) coordinates of the dipole
vector and the total dipole moment for each chunk, which includes all
effects due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.  For chunks
with a net charge the resulting dipole is made position independent by
subtracting the position vector of the center of mass or geometric
center times the net charge from the computed dipole vector.  Both
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom charges and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom dipole moments, if present, contribute to
the computed dipole.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 28Mar2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p/chunk} includes adjustments for the charge
carrying point M in molecules with TIP4P water geometry.  The
corresponding parameters are extracted from the pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not in
that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will thus
also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the “all”
group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with non\sphinxhyphen{}zero
chunk IDs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the chunk’s dipole in
“unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with each atom.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of
“unwrapped” coordinates.  See the Atoms section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags
and how they are set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags
(e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute com/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes calculate a global array where the number of rows = the
number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
chunk/atom}}}} command.  The number of columns is 4
for the \((x,y,z)\) dipole vector components and the total dipole of
each chunk.  These values can be accessed by any command that uses
global array values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
dipole units (i.e., charge {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} times distance
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p/chunk} is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE
package. It is only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dipole/tip4p/chunk} can only be used with tip4p pair
styles.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_com_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute com/chunk}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_dipole::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute dipole}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dipole_chunk:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the center of mass is the default setting for the net charge correction.

\section{compute displace/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_displace_atom:compute-displace-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_displace_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_displace_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_displace_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{displace}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
displace/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/arg pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{refresh}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{refresh} arg = name of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom variable
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_displace_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{displace}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{displace}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{refresh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myVar}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_displace_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the current displacement of each
atom in the group from its original (reference) coordinates, including
all effects due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector of four quantities per atom is calculated by this compute.
The first three elements of the vector are the \((dx,dy,dz)\)
displacements.  The fourth component is the total displacement
(i.e., \(\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The displacement of an atom is from its original position at the time
the compute command was issued.  The value of the displacement will be
0.0 for atoms not in the specified compute group.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initial coordinates are stored in “unwrapped” form, by using the
image flags associated with each atom.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of “unwrapped” coordinates.  See
the Atoms section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a
discussion of image flags and how they are set for each atom.  You
can reset the image flags (e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute
by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the quantities calculated by this compute to be
continuous when running from a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart file}}}}, then
you should use the same ID for this compute, as in the original run.
This is so that the fix this compute creates to store per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities will also have the same ID, and thus be initialized
correctly with time = 0 atom coordinates from the restart file.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{refresh} option can be used in conjunction with the “dump\_modify
refresh” command to generate incremental dump files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The definition and motivation of an incremental dump file is as
follows.  Instead of outputting all atoms at each snapshot (with some
associated values), you may only wish to output the subset of atoms
with a value that has changed in some way compared to the value the
last time that atom was output.  In some scenarios this can result in
a dramatically smaller dump file.  If desired, by post\sphinxhyphen{}processing the
sequence of snapshots, the values for all atoms at all timesteps can
be inferred.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A concrete example using this compute, is a simulation of atom
diffusion in a solid, represented as atoms on a lattice.  Diffusive
hops are rare.  Imagine that when a hop occurs an atom moves more than
a distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{Dhop}.  For any snapshot we only want to output atoms that
have hopped since the last snapshot.  This can be accomplished with
something like the following commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{write\PYGZus{}dump      }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} see comment below}

\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Dhop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.6}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{check}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{c\PYGZus{}dsp[4] \PYGZgt{} v\PYGZus{}Dhop}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dsp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{displace}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{refresh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{check}
\PYG{k}{dump            }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}
\PYG{k}{dump\PYGZus{}modify     }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{append}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thresh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}dsp[4]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{Dhop}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                }\PYG{n}{refresh}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}dsp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify thresh}}}} command will only output
atoms that have displaced more than \(0.6~\AA\) on each
snapshot (assuming metal units).  The dump\_modify \sphinxstyleemphasis{refresh} option triggers a
call to this compute at the end of every dump.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{refresh} argument for this compute is the ID of an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} which calculates a Boolean value (0 or 1)
based on the same criterion used by dump\_modify thresh.  This compute
evaluates the atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable.  For each atom that returns 1 (true),
the original (reference) coordinates of the atom (stored by
this compute) are updated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The effect of these commands is that a particular atom will only be
output in the dump file on the snapshot after it makes a diffusive
hop.  It will not be output again until it makes another hop.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that in the first snapshot of a subsequent run, no atoms will be
typically be output.  That is because the initial displacement for all
atoms is 0.0.  If an initial dump snapshot is desired, containing the
initial reference positions of all atoms, one way to do this is
illustrated above.  An initial write\_dump command can be used before
the first run.  It will contain the positions of all the atoms,
Options in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump\_modify}}}} command above will
append new output to that same file and delay the output until a later
timestep.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{delay} setting avoids a second time = 0 snapshot which
would be empty.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with four columns, which can be

a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page
for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array values will be in distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

incremental dump files.

\section{compute dpd command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd:compute-dpd-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dpd}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dpd = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dpd}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that accumulates the total internal conductive
energy (\(U^{\text{cond}}\)), the total internal mechanical energy
(\(U^{\text{mech}}\)), the total chemical energy (\(U^\text{chem}\))
and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} average of the internal temperature (\(\theta_\text{avg}\))
for the entire system of particles.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_dpd_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute dpd/atom}}}} command if you want
per\sphinxhyphen{}particle internal energies and internal temperatures.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The system internal properties are computed according to the following
relations:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U^\text{cond} = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} u_{i}^\text{cond} \\
U^\text{mech} = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} u_{i}^\text{mech} \\
U^\text{chem} = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} u_{i}^\text{chem} \\
            U = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} (u_{i}^\text{cond}
                  + u_{i}^\text{mech} + u_{i}^\text{chem}) \\
\theta_{avg} = & \biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}
                       \frac{1}{\theta_{i}}\biggr)^{-1} \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(N\) is the number of particles in the system.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 5 (\(U^\text{cond}\),
\(U^\text{mech}\), \(U^\text{chem}\), \(\theta_\text{avg}\),
\(N\)), which can be accessed by indices 1 through 5.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values will be in energy and temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command also requires use of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style dpd}}}}
command.

{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_dpd_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute dpd/atom}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_dpd_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that accesses the per\sphinxhyphen{}particle internal conductive energy
(\(u^\text{cond}\)), internal mechanical energy (\(u^\text{mech}\)),
internal chemical energy (\(u^\text{chem}\)) and internal temperatures
(\(\theta\)) for each particle in a group.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_dpd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute dpd}}}} command if you want the total
internal conductive energy, the total internal mechanical energy, the
total chemical energy and average internal temperature of the entire system or
group of dpd particles.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_edpd_temp_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom temperature
for each eDPD particle in a group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The temperature is a local temperature derived from the internal energy
of each eDPD particle based on the local equilibrium hypothesis.
For more details please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_edpd_temp_atom:espanol1997}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Espanol1997)}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_edpd_temp_atom:li2014a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Li2014)}}}}.

output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the electric field at each atom in a group.
The compute should only enabled with pair and kspace styles that are provided
by the DIELECTRIC package because only these styles compute the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
electric field at every time step.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The electric field is a 3\sphinxhyphen{}component vector.  The value of the electric field
components will be 0.0 for atoms not in the specified compute group.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword/value option pairs are used in the following ways.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} keywords, the real\sphinxhyphen{}space and reciprocal\sphinxhyphen{}space
contributions to the electric field can be turned off and on.

efield/atom/wolf = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
alpha = damping parameter (inverse distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{limit} group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID = limit computing the electric field contributions to a group (default: all)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} value = set cutoff for computing contributions to this value (default: maximum cutoff of pair style)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{efield}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{wolf}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.2}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mols}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{efield}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{wolf}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{limit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{water}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 8Feb2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that approximates the electric field at each atom in a group.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{E}_i = \frac{\vec{F}coul_i}{q_i} = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{q_j}{r_{ij}^2} \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The electric field at the position of the atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} is the coulomb force
on a unit charge at that point, which is equivalent to dividing the
Coulomb force by the charge of the individual atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this compute the electric field is approximated as the derivative of
the potential energy using the Wolf summation method, described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:wolf4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wolf}}}}, given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_i = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j \neq i}
\frac{q_i q_j {\rm erfc}(\alpha r_{ij})}{r_{ij}} +
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j \neq i}
\frac{q_i q_j {\rm erf}(\alpha r_{ij})}{r_{ij}} \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\alpha\) is the damping parameter, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{erf()} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{erfc()}
are error\sphinxhyphen{}function and complementary error\sphinxhyphen{}function terms.  This
potential is essentially a short\sphinxhyphen{}range, spherically\sphinxhyphen{}truncated,
charge\sphinxhyphen{}neutralized, force\sphinxhyphen{}shifted, pairwise \sphinxstyleemphasis{1/r} summation.  With a
manipulation of adding and subtracting a self term (for i = j) to the
first and second term on the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand\sphinxhyphen{}side, respectively, and a small
enough \(\alpha\) damping parameter, the second term shrinks and the
potential becomes a rapidly\sphinxhyphen{}converging real\sphinxhyphen{}space summation.  With a
long enough cutoff and small enough \(\alpha\) parameter, the
electric field calculated by the Wolf summation method approaches that
computed using the Ewald sum.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the electric field components will be 0.0 for atoms not in
the specified compute group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit} keyword is used, only contributions from atoms in the
selected group will be considered, otherwise contributions from all
atoms within the cutoff are included.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword is used, the cutoff used for the electric
field approximation can be set explicitly.  By default it is the largest
cutoff of any pair style force computation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Computational Efficiency}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute will loop over a full neighbor list just like a pair
style does when computing forces, thus it can be quite time\sphinxhyphen{}consuming
and slow down a calculation significantly when its data is used in
every time step.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_efield_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute efield/atom}}}} command of the DIELECTRIC package is more
efficient in comparison, since the electric field data is collected
and stored as part of the force computation at next to no extra
computational cost.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector contains 3 values per atom which are the x\sphinxhyphen{}, y\sphinxhyphen{}, and
z\sphinxhyphen{}direction electric field components in force units.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package. It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor styles ‘bin’ or ‘nsq’}}}}.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style coul/wolf}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_efield_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute efield/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit} = all and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} = largest cutoff
for pair styles.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_efield_wolf_atom:wolf4}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Wolf)} D. Wolf, P. Keblinski, S. R. Phillpot, J. Eggebrecht, J Chem
Phys, 110, 8254 (1999).

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute entropy/atom@\spxentry{compute entropy/atom}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute entropy/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:compute-entropy-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{entropy}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
entropy/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
sigma = width of Gaussians used in the \(g(r)\) smoothing

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = cutoff for the \(g(r)\) calculation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{avg} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{local}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{avg} args = neigh cutoff2
    neigh value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = whether to average the pair entropy over neighbors
    cutoff2 = cutoff for the averaging over neighbors
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{local} arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = use the local density around each atom to normalize the g(r)
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{entropy}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{n}{.}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{entropy}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{n}{.}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{avg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{n}{.}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{entropy}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.125}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{avg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the pair entropy fingerprint for
each atom in the group. The fingerprint is useful to distinguish between
ordered and disordered environments, for instance liquid and solid\sphinxhyphen{}like
environments, or glassy and crystalline\sphinxhyphen{}like environments. Some
applications could be the identification of grain boundaries, a
melt\sphinxhyphen{}solid interface, or a solid cluster emerging from the melt.
The advantage of this parameter over others is that no a priori
information about the solid structure is required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This parameter for atom i is computed using the following formula from
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:piaggi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Piaggi)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:nettleton}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nettleton)}}}} ,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_S^i=-2\pi\rho k_B \int\limits_0^{r_m} \left [ g(r) \ln g(r) - g(r) + 1 \right ] r^2 dr\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(r\) is a distance, \(g(r)\) is the radial distribution function
of atom \(i\), and \(\rho\) is the density of the system.
The \(g(r)\) computed for each atom \(i\) can be noisy and therefore it
is smoothed using
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}g_m^i(r) = \frac{1}{4 \pi \rho r^2} \sum\limits_{j} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} e^{-(r-r_{ij})^2/(2\sigma^2)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the sum over \(j\) goes through the neighbors of atom \(i\) and
\(\sigma\) is a parameter to control the smoothing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The input parameters are \sphinxstyleemphasis{sigma} the smoothing parameter \(\sigma\),
and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} for the calculation of \(g(r)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{avg} has the setting \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then this compute also
averages the parameter over the neighbors  of atom \(i\) according to
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left< s_S^i \right>  = \frac{\sum_j s_S^j + s_S^i}{N + 1},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the sum over \(j\) goes over the neighbors of atom \(i\) and
\(N\) is the number of neighbors. This procedure provides a sharper
distinction between order and disorder environments. In this case the input
parameter \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff2} is the cutoff for the averaging over the neighbors and
must also be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{avg yes} option is used, the effective cutoff of the neighbor
list should be \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}+\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff2} and therefore it might be necessary
to increase the skin of the neighbor list with:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
neighbor \PYGZlt{}skin distance\PYGZgt{} bin
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{local yes} option is used, the \(g(r)\) is normalized by the
local density around each atom, that is to say the density around each
atom  is the number of neighbors within the neighbor list cutoff divided
by the corresponding volume. This option can be useful when dealing with
inhomogeneous systems such as those that have surfaces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are typical input parameters for fcc aluminum (lattice
constant \(4.05~\AA\)),

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
compute 1 all entropy/atom 0.25 5.7 avg yes 3.7
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
and for bcc sodium (lattice constant \(4.23~\AA\)),

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
compute 1 all entropy/atom 0.25 7.3 avg yes 5.1
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, this compute calculates the pair entropy value for each
atom as a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by any command that
uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair entropy values have units of the Boltzmann constant. They are
always negative, and lower values (lower entropy) correspond to more
ordered environments.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_cna_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute cna/atom}}}}
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_centro_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centro/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default values for the optional keywords are avg = no and local = no.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:piaggi}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Piaggi)} Piaggi and Parrinello, J Chem Phys, 147, 114112 (2017).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_entropy_atom:nettleton}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Nettleton)} Nettleton and Green, J Chem Phys, 29, 6 (1958).

\index{compute erotate/asphere@\spxentry{compute erotate/asphere}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute erotate/asphere command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:compute-erotate-asphere-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{erotate}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{asphere}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
erotate/asphere = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{erotate}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{asphere}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the rotational kinetic energy of
a group of aspherical particles.  The aspherical particles can be
ellipsoids, or line segments, or triangles.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} commands
for descriptions of these options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all 3 types of particles, the rotational kinetic energy is
computed as \(\frac12 I \omega^2\), where \(I\) is the inertia tensor
for the aspherical particle and \(\omega\) is its angular velocity, which
is computed from its angular momentum if needed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{2d models}}}}, ellipsoidal particles are
treated as ellipsoids, not ellipses, meaning their moments of inertia
will be the same as in 3d.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the KE).  This value can be
used by any command that uses a global scalar value from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “extensive”.  The
scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires that ellipsoidal particles atoms store a shape
and quaternion orientation and angular momentum as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style ellipsoid}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires that line segment particles atoms store a length
and orientation and angular velocity as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style line}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires that triangular particles atoms store a size and
shape and quaternion orientation and angular momentum as defined by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style tri}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All particles in the group must be of finite size.  They cannot be point
particles.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute erotate/sphere}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_asphere:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_rigid:compute-erotate-rigid-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_rigid:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_rigid::doc}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
erotate/rigid = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of rigid body fix

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_rigid:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{erotate}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myRigid}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_rigid:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the rotational kinetic energy of
a collection of rigid bodies, as defined by one of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command variants.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rotational energy of each rigid body is computed as
\(\frac12 I \omega_\text{body}^2\),
where \(I\) is the inertia tensor for the rigid body and
\(\omega_\text{body}\) is its angular velocity vector.
Both \(I\) and \(\omega_\text{body}\) are in the frame of
reference of the rigid body (i.e., \(I\) is diagonal).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID} should be the ID of one of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}
commands which defines the rigid bodies.  The group specified in the
compute command is ignored.  The rotational energy of all the rigid
bodies defined by the fix rigid command in included in the calculation.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_rigid:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the summed rotational energy
of all the rigid bodies).  This value can be used by any command that
uses a global scalar value from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “extensive”.  The
scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_rigid:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the RIGID package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{compute erotate/sphere command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:compute-erotate-sphere-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{erotate/sphere/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{erotate}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{sphere}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
erotate/sphere = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{erotate}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{sphere}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the rotational kinetic energy of
a group of spherical particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rotational energy is computed as \(\frac12 I \omega^2\),
where \(I\) is the moment of inertia for a sphere and \(\omega\)
is the particle’s angular velocity.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{2d models}}}}, particles are treated as
spheres, not disks, meaning their moment of inertia will be the same
as in 3d.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the KE).  This value can be
used by any command that uses a global scalar value from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “extensive”.  The
scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires that atoms store a radius and angular velocity
(omega) as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All particles in the group must be finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spheres or point
particles.  They cannot be aspherical.  Point particles will not
contribute to the rotational energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_erotate_sphere_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the rotational kinetic energy for
each particle in a group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rotational energy is computed as \(\frac12 I \omega^2\), where
\(I\) is the moment of inertia for a sphere and \(\omega\) is the
particle’s angular velocity.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{2d models}}}}, particles are treated as
spheres, not disks, meaning their moment of inertia will be the same
as in 3d.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the rotational kinetic energy will be 0.0 for atoms not
in the specified compute group or for point particles with a radius of 0.0.

\section{compute event/displace command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace:compute-event-displace-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{event}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{displace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{threshold}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
event/displace = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
threshold = minimum distance any particle must move to trigger an event (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{event}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{displace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that flags an “event” if any particle in the
group has moved a distance greater than the specified threshold
distance when compared to a previously stored reference state
(i.e., the previous event).  This compute is typically used in
conjunction with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{prd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{prd}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{tad::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tad}}}} commands,
to detect if a transition to a new minimum energy basin has occurred.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This value calculated by the compute is equal to 0 if no particle has
moved far enough, and equal to 1 if one or more particles have moved
further than the threshold distance.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the system is undergoing significant center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass motion,
due to thermal motion, an external force, or an initial net momentum,
then this compute will not be able to distinguish that motion from
local atom displacements and may generate “false positives”.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the flag).  This value can be
used by any command that uses a global scalar value from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “intensive”.  The
scalar value will be a 0 or 1 as explained above.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_event_displace:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the REPLICA
package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc
page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{prd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{prd}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{tad::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tad}}}}

\section{compute fabric command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:compute-fabric-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fabric}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{attribute}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fabric = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type} = cutoffs determined based on atom types
\sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} = cutoffs determined based on atom diameters (atom style sphere)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more attributes may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
attribute = \sphinxstyleemphasis{contact} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{branch} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/normal} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/tangential}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{contact} = contact tensor
\sphinxstyleemphasis{branch} = branch tensor
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force/normal} = normal force tensor
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force/tangential} = tangential force tensor
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{type/include}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{type/include} value = arg1 arg2
  arg = separate lists of types (see below)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fabric}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{contact}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{normal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{include}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1},2\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fabric}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{radius}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{normal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tangential}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a compute that calculates various fabric tensors for pairwise
interaction {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fabric:ouadfel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouadfel)}}}}. Fabric tensors are commonly used
to quantify the anisotropy or orientation of granular contacts but can also
be used to characterize the direction of pairwise interactions in general
systems. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} settings are used to select whether interactions
cutoffs are determined by atom types or by the sum of atomic radii (atom
style sphere), respectively. Calling this compute is roughly the cost of a
pair style invocation as it involves a loop over the neighbor list. If the
normal or tangential force tensors are requested, it will be more expensive
than a pair style invocation as it will also recalculate all pair forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Four fabric tensors are available: the contact, branch, normal force, or
tangential force tensor. The contact tensor is calculated as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}C_{ab}  =  \frac{15}{2} (\phi_{ab} - \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{Tr}(\phi) \delta_{ab})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(a\) and \(b\) are the \(x\), \(y\), \(z\)
directions, \(\delta_{ab}\) is the Kronecker delta function, and
the tensor \(\phi\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\phi_{ab}  =  \sum_{n = 1}^{N_p} \frac{r_{a} r_{b}}{r^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(n\) loops over the \(N_p\) pair interactions in the simulation,
\(r_{a}\) is the \(a\) component of the radial vector between the
two pairwise interacting particles, and \(r\) is the magnitude of the
radial vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The branch tensor is calculated as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}B_{ab}  =  \frac{15}{2\, \mathrm{Tr}(D)} (D_{ab} - \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{Tr}(D) \delta_{ab})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the tensor \(D\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D_{ab}  =  \sum_{n = 1}^{N_p}
             \frac{1}{N_c (r^2 + C_{cd} r_c r_d)}
             \frac{r_{a} r_{b}}{r}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(N_c\) is the total number of contacts in the system and the
subscripts \(c\) and \(d\) indices are summed according to Einstein
notation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The normal force fabric tensor is calculated as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F^n_{ab}  =  \frac{15}{2\, \mathrm{Tr}(N)} (N_{ab} - \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{Tr}(N) \delta_{ab})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the tensor \(N\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}N_{ab}  =  \sum_{n = 1}^{N_p}
             \frac{1}{N_c (r^2 + C_{cd} r_c r_d)}
             \frac{r_{a} r_{b}}{r^2} f_n\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and \(f_n\) is the magnitude of the normal, central\sphinxhyphen{}body force between the two atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, the tangential force fabric tensor is only defined for pair styles that
apply tangential forces to particles, namely granular pair styles. It is calculated
as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F^t_{ab}  =  \frac{5}{\mathrm{Tr}(N)} (T_{ab} - \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{Tr}(T) \delta_{ab})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the tensor \(T\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}T_{ab}  =  \sum_{n = 1}^{N_p}
             \frac{1}{N_c (r^2 + C_{cd} r_c r_d)}
             \frac{r_{a} r_{b}}{r^2} f_t\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and \(f_t\) is the magnitude of the tangential force between the two atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{type/include} keyword filters interactions based on the types of the two atoms.
Interactions between two atoms are only included in calculations if the atom types
are in the two lists. Each list consists of a series of type
ranges separated by commas. The range can be specified as a
single numeric value, or a wildcard asterisk can be used to specify a range
of values.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or “m*” or “m*n”.  For
example, if \(M\) is the number of atom types, then an asterisk with no
numeric values means all types from 1 to \(M\).  A leading asterisk means
all types from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing asterisk means all types from
m to \(M\) (inclusive).  A middle asterisk means all types from m to n
(inclusive).  Multiple \sphinxstyleemphasis{type/include} keywords may be added.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of doubles and a global scalar. The
vector stores the unique components of the first requested tensor in the
order \(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\),
\(yz\) followed by the same components for all subsequent tensors.
The length of the vector is therefore six times the number of requested
tensors. The scalar output is the number of pairwise interactions included
in the calculation of the fabric tensor.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This fix is part of the GRANULAR package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}}
doc page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{fabric} does not support pair styles
with many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.  It also does not
support models with long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic or dispersion forces,
i.e. the kspace\_style command in LAMMPS.  It also does not support the
following fixes which add rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body constraints: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rattle}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}}. It does not support
granular pair styles that extend beyond the contact of atomic radii
(e.g., JKR and DMT).


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_fabric:ouadfel}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{compute fep command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep:compute-fep-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_fep:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_fep::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{attribute}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fep = name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp = external temperature (as specified for constant\sphinxhyphen{}temperature run)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more attributes with args may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
attribute = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} args = pstyle pparam I J v\_delta
  pstyle = pair style name (e.g., \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut})
  pparam = parameter to perturb
  I,J = type pair(s) to set parameter for
  v\_delta = variable with perturbation to apply (in the units of the parameter)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} args = aparam I v\_delta
  aparam = \sphinxstyleemphasis{charge} = parameter to perturb
  I = type to set parameter for
  v\_delta = variable with perturbation to apply (in the units of the parameter)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = ignore tail correction to pair energies (usually small in fep)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = include tail correction to pair energies
\sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = ignore volume changes (e.g., in \sphinxstyleemphasis{NVE} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{NVT} trajectories)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = include volume changes (e.g., in \sphinxstyleemphasis{NPT} trajectories)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep:examples}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Example input scripts available: examples/PACKAGES/fep


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Apply a perturbation to parameters of the interaction potential and
recalculate the pair potential energy without changing the atomic
coordinates from those of the reference, unperturbed system. This
compute can be used to calculate free energy differences using several
methods, such as free\sphinxhyphen{}energy perturbation (FEP), finite\sphinxhyphen{}difference
thermodynamic integration (FDTI) or Bennet’s acceptance ratio method
(BAR).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential energy of the system is decomposed in three terms: a
background term corresponding to interaction sites whose parameters
remain constant, a reference term \(U_0\) corresponding to the
initial interactions of the atoms that will undergo perturbation, and
a term \(U_1\) corresponding to the final interactions of
these atoms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U(\lambda) = U_{\mathrm{bg}} + U_1(\lambda) + U_0(\lambda)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A coupling parameter \(\lambda\) varying from 0 to 1 connects the
reference and perturbed systems:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda &= 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad U = U_{\mathrm{bg}} + U_0 \\
\lambda &= 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad U = U_{\mathrm{bg}} + U_1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is possible but not necessary that the coupling parameter (or a
function thereof) appears as a multiplication factor of the potential
energy. Therefore, this compute can apply perturbations to interaction
parameters that are not directly proportional to the potential energy
(e.g., \(\sigma\) in Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potentials).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can be combined with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} to
perform multistage free\sphinxhyphen{}energy perturbation calculations along
stepwise alchemical transformations during a simulation run:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta_0^1 A = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Delta_{\lambda_i}^{\lambda_{i+1}} A = - k_B T
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \ln \left< \exp \left( - \frac{U(\lambda_{i+1}) -
U(\lambda_i)}{k_B T} \right) \right>_{\lambda_i}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is suitable for the finite\sphinxhyphen{}difference thermodynamic
integration (FDTI) method {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep:mezei}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mezei)}}}}, which is based on an
evaluation of the numerical derivative of the free energy by a
perturbation method using a very small \(\delta\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta_0^1 A = \int_{\lambda=0}^{\lambda=1} \left( \frac{\partial
A(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda} \right)_\lambda \mathrm{d}\lambda \approx
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} w_i \frac{A(\lambda_{i} + \delta) - A(\lambda_i)}{\delta}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(w_i\) are weights of a numerical quadrature. The
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} command can be used to define the stages of
\(\lambda\) at which the derivative is calculated and averaged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute fep calculates the exponential Boltzmann term and also the
potential energy difference \(U_1 -U_0\). By
choosing a very small perturbation \(\delta\) the thermodynamic
integration method can be implemented using a numerical evaluation of
the derivative of the potential energy with respect to \(\lambda\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta_0^1 A = \int_{\lambda=0}^{\lambda=1} \left< \frac{\partial
U(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda} \right>_\lambda \mathrm{d}\lambda \approx
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} w_i \left< \frac{U(\lambda_{i} + \delta) -
U(\lambda_i)}{\delta} \right>_{\lambda_i}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Another technique to calculate free energy differences is the
acceptance ratio method {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep:bennet}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bennet)}}}}, which can be implemented
by calculating the potential energy differences with \(\delta = 1.0\) on
both the forward and reverse routes:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left< \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left[\left(U_1 - U_0 - \Delta_0^1A \right) /k_B T
\right]} \right>_0 = \left< \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left[\left(U_0 - U_1 +
\Delta_0^1A \right) /k_B T \right]} \right>_1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the free energy difference is determined by numerical
root finding to establish the equality.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Concerning the choice of how the atomic parameters are perturbed in
order to setup an alchemical transformation route, several strategies
are available, such as single\sphinxhyphen{}topology or double\sphinxhyphen{}topology strategies
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep:pearlman}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Pearlman)}}}}. The latter does not require modification of
bond lengths, angles or other internal coordinates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTES: This compute command does not take kinetic energy into account,
therefore the masses of the particles should not be modified between
the reference and perturbed states, or along the alchemical
transformation route.  This compute command does not change bond
lengths or other internal coordinates {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep:boreschkarplus}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Boresch, Karplus)}}}}.
