\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that it is easy to add new potentials and their parameters to
this list.  All it typically takes is adding an extract() method to
the pair\_*.cpp file associated with the potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command, I and J can be
specified in one of two ways.  Explicit numeric values can be used for
each, as in the first example above.  I \(\le\) J is required.  LAMMPS sets
the coefficients for the symmetric J,I interaction to the same
values. A wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can be used in place of or in conjunction
with the I,J arguments to set the coefficients for multiple pairs of
atom types.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or “m*” or “m*n”.  If
\(N\) is the number of atom types, then an asterisk with no numeric values
means all types from 1 to \(N\).   A leading asterisk means all types from
1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing asterisk means all types from m to N
(inclusive).  A middle asterisk means all types from m to n
(inclusive).  Note that only type pairs with I \(\le\) J are considered; if
asterisks imply type pairs where J \(<\) I, they are ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid or hybrid/overlay}}}} is being
used, then the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pstyle} will be a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style name.  You must specify
I,J arguments that correspond to type pair values defined (via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command) for that sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name} argument for keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} is the name of an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} which will be evaluated each time
this compute is invoked.  It should be specified as v\_name, where name
is the variable name.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{atom} attribute enables atom properties to be changed.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{aparam} argument is the name of the parameter to change.  This is the
current list of atom parameters that can be used with this compute:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
charge = charge on particle

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name} argument for keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} is the name of an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} which will be evaluated each time
this compute is invoked.  It should be specified as v\_name, where name
is the variable name.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} keyword controls the calculation of the tail correction to
“van der Waals” pair energies beyond the cutoff, if this has been
activated via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command. If the
perturbation is small, the tail contribution to the energy difference
between the reference and perturbed systems should be negligible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then the Boltzmann term is multiplied
by the volume so that correct ensemble averaging can be performed over
trajectories during which the volume fluctuates or changes {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep:allentildesley}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Allen and Tildesley)}}}}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta_0^1 A = - k_B T \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \ln \frac{\left< V \exp \left( -
\frac{U(\lambda_{i+1}) - U(\lambda_i)}{k_B T} \right)
\right>_{\lambda_i}}{\left< V \right>_{\lambda_i}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 3 which contains the
energy difference ( \(U_1-U_0\) ) as c\_ID{[}1{]}, the
Boltzmann factor \(\exp(-(U_1-U_0)/k_B T)\), or
\(V \exp(-(U_1-U_0)/k_B T)\), as c\_ID{[}2{]} and the
volume of the simulation box \(V\) as c\_ID{[}3{]}. \(U_1\) is the
pair potential energy obtained with the perturbed parameters and
\(U_0\) is the pair potential energy obtained with the
unperturbed parameters. The energies include kspace terms if these
are used in the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These output results can be used by any command that uses a global
scalar or vector from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options. For example, the computed values can be averaged using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values calculated by this compute are “extensive”.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is distributed as the FEP package.  It is only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_fep_soft::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style …/soft}}}}


\subsection{Default}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{volume} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.

\section{compute fep/ta command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:compute-fep-ta-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fep}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{ta}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{plane}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale\PYGZus{}factor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fep/ta = name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp = external temperature (as specified for constant\sphinxhyphen{}temperature run)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
plane = \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
scale\_factor = multiplicative factor for change in plane area

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = ignore tail correction to pair energies (usually small in fep)
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = include tail correction to pair energies
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fep}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{ta}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{298}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0005}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 4May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the change in the free energy due
to a test\sphinxhyphen{}area (TA) perturbation {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:gloor}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Gloor)}}}}. The test\sphinxhyphen{}area
approach can be used to determine the interfacial tension of the system
in a single simulation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\gamma = \lim_{\Delta \mathcal{A} \to 0} \left( \frac{\Delta A_{0 \to 1 }}{\Delta \mathcal{A}}\right)_{N,V,T}
= - \frac{k_B T}{\Delta \mathcal{A}} \ln \left\langle \exp\left(\frac{-(U_1 - U_0)}{k_B T}\right) \right\rangle_0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
During the perturbation, both axes of \sphinxstyleemphasis{plane} are scaled by multiplying
\(\sqrt{\mathrm{scale\_factor}}\), while the other axis divided by
\(\mathrm{scale\_factor}\) such that the overall volume of the system is
maintained.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} keyword controls the calculation of the tail correction to
“van der Waals” pair energies beyond the cutoff, if this has been
activated via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command. If the
perturbation is small, the tail contribution to the energy difference
between the reference and perturbed systems should be negligible.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 3 which contains the
energy difference \((U_1-U_0)\) as c\_ID{[}1{]}, the Boltzmann factor
\(\exp\bigl(-(U_1-U_0)/k_B T\bigr)\), as c\_ID{[}2{]} and the change in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{plane}
area \(\Delta \mathcal{A}\) as c\_ID{[}3{]}. \(U_1\) is the potential
energy of the perturbed state and \(U_0\) is the potential energy of
the reference state.  The energies include kspace terms if these are
used in the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These output results can be used by any command that uses a global
scalar or vector from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output options. For
example, the computed values can be averaged using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Constraints, like fix shake, may lead to incorrect values for energy difference.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is distributed as the FEP package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fep}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_fep_ta:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Gloor)} Gloor, J Chem Phys, 123, 134703 (2005)

\sphinxstepscope

\section{compute global/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom:compute-global-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
global/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
index = c\_ID, c\_ID{[}N{]}, f\_ID, f\_ID{[}N{]}, v\_name

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
c\PYGZus{}ID = per\PYGZhy{}atom vector calculated by a compute with ID
c\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of per\PYGZhy{}atom array calculated by a compute with ID
f\PYGZus{}ID = per\PYGZhy{}atom vector calculated by a fix with ID
f\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of per\PYGZhy{}atom array calculated by a fix with ID
v\PYGZus{}name = per\PYGZhy{}atom vector calculated by an atom\PYGZhy{}style variable with name
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more inputs can be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
input = c\_ID, c\_ID{[}N{]}, f\_ID, f\_ID{[}N{]}, v\_name

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
c\PYGZus{}ID = global vector calculated by a compute with ID
c\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of global array calculated by a compute with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
f\PYGZus{}ID = global vector calculated by a fix with ID
f\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of global array calculated by a fix with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
v\PYGZus{}name = global vector calculated by a vector\PYGZhy{}style variable with name
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{global}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[3]}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{global}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a calculation that assigns global values to each atom from
vectors or arrays of global values.  The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} parameter
is used to determine which global value is assigned to each atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} parameter must reference a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array from a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or the evaluation of an
atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  Each \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} value must
reference a global vector or array from a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or the evaluation of an vector\sphinxhyphen{}style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.  Details are given below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} value for an atom is used as an index \(I\) (from 1 to
\(N\), where \(N\) is the number of atoms) into the vector
associated with each of the input values.  The \(I\)th value
from the input vector becomes one output value for that atom.  If the
atom is not in the specified group, or the index \(I < 1\) or
\(I > M\), where \(M\) is the actual length of the input vector,
then an output value of 0.0 is assigned to the atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An example of how this command is useful, is in the context of
“chunks” which are static or dynamic subsets of atoms.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command assigns unique chunk IDs
to each atom.  Its output can be used as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} parameter for
this command.  Various other computes with “chunk” in their style
name, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_com_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute com/chunk}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd/chunk}}}}, calculate properties for each
chunk.  The output of these commands are global vectors or arrays,
with one or more values per chunk, and can be used as input values for
this command.  This command will then assign the global chunk value to
each atom in the chunk, producing a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array
as output.  The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values can then be output to a dump file or
used by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input,
as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As a concrete example, these commands will calculate the displacement
of each atom from the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the molecule it is in, and
dump those values to a dump file.  In this case, each molecule is a
chunk.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zu}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{glob}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{global}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop[1]}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}glob[1]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop[2]}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}glob[2]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop[3]}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}glob[3]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{dist}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sqrt}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{v\PYGZus{}dx*v\PYGZus{}dx+v\PYGZus{}dy*v\PYGZus{}dy+v\PYGZus{}dz*v\PYGZus{}dz}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}glob[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}glob[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}glob[3]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dist}
\PYG{k}{dump\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sort}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can add these commands to the bench/in.chain script to see how
they work.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for input values from a compute or fix, the bracketed index
I can be specified using a wildcard asterisk with the index to
effectively specify multiple values.  This takes the form “*” or “*n”
or “m*” or “m*n”.  If \(N\) is the size of the vector
(for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} = scalar)
or the number of columns in the array (for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} = vector), then an
asterisk with no numeric values means all indices from 1 to \(N\).
A leading asterisk means all indices from 1 to n (inclusive).  A
trailing asterisk means all indices from m to \(N\) (inclusive).
A middle asterisk means all indices from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a wildcard is the same as if the individual columns of the array
had been listed one by one. For example, the following two compute global/atom
commands are equivalent, since the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_com_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute com/chunk}}}}
command creates a global array with three columns:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{global}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[3]}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{global}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}com[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This section explains the \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} parameter.  Note that it must
reference per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values, as contrasted with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} values, which
must reference global values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that all of these options generate floating point values.  When
they are used as an index into the specified input vectors, they
simple rounded down to convert the value to integer indices.  The
final values should range from 1 to \(N\) (inclusive), since they are used
to access values from \(N\)\sphinxhyphen{}length vectors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} begins with “c\_”, a compute ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  The compute must generate
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities.  See the individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} doc
page for details.  If no bracketed integer is appended, the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
vector calculated by the compute is used.  If a bracketed integer is
appended, the Ith column of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array calculated by the
compute is used.  Users can also write code for their own compute
styles and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to LAMMPS}}}}.  See the
discussion above for how I can be specified with a wildcard asterisk
to effectively specify multiple values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} begins with “f\_”, a fix ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  The Fix must generate
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities.  See the individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} page for
details.  Note that some fixes only produce their values on certain
timesteps, which must be compatible with when compute global/atom
references the values, else an error results.  If no bracketed integer
is appended, the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector calculated by the fix is used.  If a
bracketed integer is appended, the Ith column of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array
calculated by the fix is used.  Users can also write code for their
own fix style and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to LAMMPS}}}}.  See the
discussion above for how I can be specified with a wildcard asterisk
to effectively specify multiple values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} begins with “v\_”, a variable name must follow which has
been previously defined in the input script.  It must be an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.  Atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can
reference thermodynamic keywords and various per\sphinxhyphen{}atom attributes, or
invoke other computes, fixes, or variables when they are evaluated, so
this is a very general means of generating per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities to use
as \sphinxstyleemphasis{index}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This section explains the kinds of \sphinxstyleemphasis{input} values that can be used.
Note that inputs reference global values, as contrasted with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{index} parameter which must reference per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “c\_”, a compute ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  The compute must generate a
global vector or array.  See the individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} doc
page for details.  If no bracketed integer is appended, the vector
calculated by the compute is used.  If a bracketed integer is
appended, the Ith column of the array calculated by the compute is
used.  Users can also write code for their own compute styles and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to LAMMPS}}}}.  See the discussion above for how
I can be specified with a wildcard asterisk to effectively specify
multiple values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “f\_”, a fix ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  The fix must generate a
global vector or array.  See the individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} doc page
for details.  Note that some fixes only produce their values on
certain timesteps, which must be compatible with when compute
global/atom references the values, else an error results.  If no
bracketed integer is appended, the vector calculated by the fix is
used.  If a bracketed integer is appended, the Ith column of the array
calculated by the fix is used.  Users can also write code for their
own fix style and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to LAMMPS}}}}.  See the
discussion above for how I can be specified with a wildcard asterisk
to effectively specify multiple values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “v\_”, a variable name must follow which has
been previously defined in the input script.  It must be a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.  Vector\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can
reference thermodynamic keywords and various other attributes of
atoms, or invoke other computes, fixes, or variables when they are
evaluated, so this is a very general means of generating a vector of
global quantities which the \sphinxstyleemphasis{index} parameter will reference for
assignment of global values to atoms.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If a single input is specified this compute produces a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
vector.  If multiple inputs are specified, this compute produces a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array values, where the number of columns is equal to the
number of inputs specified.  These values can be used by any command
that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array values from a compute as input.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array values will be in whatever units the
corresponding input values are in.

\label{\detokenize{compute_global_atom:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar

{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}}

\section{compute group/group command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:compute-group-group-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group2\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group/group = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID = group ID of second (or same) group

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{off} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{inter} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intra}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{upper}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{upper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mine}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{wall}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the total energy and force
interaction between two groups of atoms: the compute group and the
specified group2.  The two groups can be the same.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, which is the default, then the
the interaction energy will include a pair component which is defined
as the pairwise energy between all pairs of atoms where one atom in
the pair is in the first group and the other is in the second group.
Likewise, the interaction force calculated by this compute will
include the force on the compute group atoms due to pairwise
interactions with atoms in the specified group2.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The energies computed by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword do not include tail
corrections, even if they are enabled via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{inter} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{intra} than an
additional check is made based on the molecule IDs of the two atoms in
each pair before including their pairwise interaction energy and
force.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inter} setting, the two atoms must be in different
molecules.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{intra} setting, the two atoms must be in the same
molecule.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, which is not the default, and
if a {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} is defined, then the interaction
energy will include a Kspace component which is the long\sphinxhyphen{}range
Coulombic energy between all the atoms in the first group and all the
atoms in the second group.  Likewise, the interaction force calculated by
this compute will include the force on the compute group atoms due to
long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interactions with atoms in the specified group2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Normally the long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic energy converges only when the net
charge of the unit cell is zero.  However, one can assume the net
charge of the system is neutralized by a uniform background plasma,
and a correction to the system energy can be applied to reduce
artifacts. For more information see {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_group_group:bogusz}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bogusz)}}}}.  If the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, which is the default, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace}
contributions are included, then this energy correction term will be
added to the total group\sphinxhyphen{}group energy.  This correction term does not
affect the force calculation and will be zero if one or both of the
groups are charge neutral.  This energy correction term is the same as
that included in the regular Ewald and PPPM routines.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecule} setting only affects the group/group
contributions calculated by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword.  It does not affect
the group/group contributions calculated by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} keyword.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute does not calculate any bond or angle or dihedral or
improper interactions between atoms in the two groups.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The pairwise contributions to the group\sphinxhyphen{}group interactions are
calculated by looping over a neighbor list.  The Kspace contribution
to the group\sphinxhyphen{}group interactions require essentially the same amount of
work (FFTs, Ewald summation) as computing long\sphinxhyphen{}range forces for the
entire system.  Thus it can be costly to invoke this compute too
frequently.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This is
the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command,
and means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the neighbor list.
Because this compute uses a neighbor list, it also means those pairs will
not be included in the group/group interaction.  This does not apply when
using long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulomb interactions
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/msm}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/wolf} or similar).  One way to get
around this would be to set \sphinxstyleemphasis{special\_bond} scaling factors to very tiny
numbers that are not exactly zero (e.g., \(1.0 \times 10^{-50}\)).
Another workaround would be to write a dump file and use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to compute the group/group interactions for
snapshots in the dump file. The rerun script can use a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command that includes all pairs in the
neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you desire a breakdown of the interactions into a pairwise and
Kspace component, simply invoke the compute twice with the appropriate
yes/no settings for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} keywords.  This is no more
costly than using a single compute with both keywords set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}.
The individual contributions can be summed in a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} if desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This \sphinxhref{PDF/kspace.pdf}{document} describes how the long\sphinxhyphen{}range
group\sphinxhyphen{}group calculations are performed.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the energy) and a global
vector of length 3 (force), which can be accessed by indices 1\textendash{}3.
These values can be used by any command that uses global scalar or
vector values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both the scalar and vector values calculated by this compute are
“extensive”.  The scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
The vector values will be in force {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Not all pair styles can be evaluated in a pairwise mode as required by
this compute.  For example, three\sphinxhyphen{}body and other many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials,
such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tersoff}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sw::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber}}}} cannot be used.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{EAM}}}}
potentials will re\sphinxhyphen{}use previously computed embedding term contributions,
so the computed pairwise forces and energies are based on the whole
system and not valid if particles have been moved since.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Not all {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Kspace styles}}}} support the calculation of
group/group interactions. The regular \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} styles do.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_group_group:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are pair = yes, kspace = no, boundary = yes,
molecule = off.

\section{compute gyration command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration:compute-gyration-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gyration}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gyration = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gyration}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the radius of gyration \(R_g\) of the
group of atoms, including all effects due to atoms passing through
periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(R_g\) is a measure of the size of the group of atoms, and is computed as
the square root of the \(R_g^2\) value in this formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_g^2 = \frac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i (r_i - r_{\text{cm}})^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(M\) is the total mass of the group, \(r_{\text{cm}}\) is the
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position of the group, and the sum is over all atoms in
the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A \(R_g^2\) tensor, stored as a 6\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also calculated
by this compute.  The formula for the components of the tensor is the
same as the above formula, except that \((r_i - r_{\text{cm}})^2\) is
replaced by
\((r_{i,x} - r_{\text{cm},x}) \cdot (r_{i,y} - r_{\text{cm},y})\) for the
\(xy\) component, and so on.  The six components of the vector are ordered
\(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\), \(yz\).
Note that unlike the scalar \(R_g\), each of the six values of the tensor
is effectively a “squared” value, since the cross\sphinxhyphen{}terms may be negative
and taking a square root would be invalid.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to \(R_g\) in “unwrapped” form,
by using the image flags associated with each atom.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of “unwrapped” coordinates.
See the Atoms section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a
discussion of image flags and how they are set for each atom.  You can
reset the image flags (e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (\(R_g\)) and a global vector of
length 6 (\(R_g^2\) tensor), which can be accessed by indices 1\textendash{}6.  These
values can be used by any command that uses a global scalar value or
vector values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar and vector values calculated by this compute are
“intensive”.  The scalar and vector values will be in distance and
distance\(^2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, respectively.

\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\section{compute gyration/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_chunk:compute-gyration-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gyration}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{tensor}
\begin{sphinxalltt}

\end{sphinxalltt}

\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gyration}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gyration}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tensor}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the radius of gyration \(R_g\) for
multiple chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates the radius of gyration \(R_g\) for each chunk,
which includes all effects due to atoms passing through periodic
boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(R_g\) is a measure of the size of a chunk, and is computed by the
formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_g^2 = \frac{1}{M} \sum_i m_i (r_i - r_{\text{cm}})^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(M\) is the total mass of the chunk, \(r_{\text{cm}}\) is
the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position of the chunk, and the sum is over all atoms in the
chunk.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not
in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the
“all” group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero chunk IDs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tensor} keyword is specified, then the scalar \(R_g\) value is not
calculated, but an \(R_g\) tensor is instead calculated for each chunk.
The formula for the components of the tensor is the same as the above
formula, except that \((r_i - r_{\text{cm}})^2\) is replaced by
\((r_{i,x} - r_{\text{cm},x}) \cdot (r_{i,y} - r_{\text{cm},y})\) for the
\(xy\) component, and so on.  The six components of the tensor are
ordered \(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\), \(yz\).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to \(R_g\) in “unwrapped” form,
by using the image flags associated with each atom.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}}
command for a discussion of “unwrapped” coordinates.
See the Atoms section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a
discussion of image flags and how they are set for each atom.  You can
reset the image flags (e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute gyration/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gyration}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tensor} keyword is not
specified and a global array if it is.  The length of the vector or
number of rows in the array = the number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as
calculated by the specified {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}}
command.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tensor} keyword is specified, the global array has six
columns.  The vector or array can
be accessed by any command that uses global values from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All the vector or array values calculated by this compute are
“intensive”.  The vector or array values will be in distance
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, since they are the square root of values
represented by the formula above.

\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{molecule}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gyration}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{shape}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor of a
group of atoms and three shape parameters. The computation includes all effects
due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The three computed shape parameters are the asphericity, \(b\),
the acylindricity, \(c\), and the relative shape anisotropy, \(k\),
viz.,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}b &= l_z - \frac12(l_y+l_x) \\
c &= l_y - l_x \\
k &= \frac{3}{2} \frac{l_x^2+l_y^2+l_z^2}{(l_x+l_y+l_z)^2} - \frac{1}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(l_x \le l_y \le l_z\) are the three eigenvalues of the gyration
tensor. A general description of these parameters is provided in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape:mattice1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mattice)}}}} while an application to polymer systems
can be found in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape:theodorou1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Theodorou)}}}}.
The asphericity is always non\sphinxhyphen{}negative and zero only when the three principal
moments are equal. This zero condition is met when the distribution of
particles is spherically symmetric (hence the name asphericity) but also
whenever the particle distribution is symmetric with respect to the three
coordinate axes (e.g., when the particles are distributed uniformly on a cube,
tetrahedron or other Platonic solid). The acylindricity is always non\sphinxhyphen{}negative
and zero only when the two principal moments are equal. This zero condition is
met when the distribution of particles is cylindrically symmetric (hence the
name, acylindricity), but also whenever the particle distribution is symmetric
with respect to the two coordinate axes (e.g., when the
particles are distributed uniformly on a regular prism).
The relative shape anisotropy is bounded between zero (if all points are
spherically symmetric) and one (if all points lie on a line).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the gyration tensor in
“unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with each atom.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of “unwrapped”
coordinates. See the Atoms section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
command for a discussion of image flags and how they are set for each
atom.  You can reset the image flags (e.g., to 0) before invoking this
compute by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 6, which can be accessed by
indices 1\textendash{}6. The first three values are the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor
followed by the asphericity, the acylindricity and the relative shape
anisotropy.  The computed values can be used by any command that uses global
vector values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values calculated by this compute are
“intensive”.  The first five vector values will be in
distance\(2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} while the sixth one is dimensionless.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor and
three shape parameters of multiple chunks of atoms. The computation includes
all effects due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The three computed shape parameters are the asphericity, \(b\),
the acylindricity, \(c\), and the relative shape anisotropy, \(k\),
viz.,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}b &= l_z - \frac12(l_y+l_x) \\
c &= l_y - l_x \\
k &= \frac{3}{2} \frac{l_x^2+l_y^2+l_z^2}{(l_x+l_y+l_z)^2} - \frac{1}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(l_x \le l_y \le l_z\) are the three eigenvalues of the gyration
tensor. A general description of these parameters is provided in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape_chunk:mattice2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mattice)}}}} while an application to polymer systems
can be found in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape_chunk:theodorou2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Theodorou)}}}}. The asphericity is always
non\sphinxhyphen{}negative and zero only when the three principal moments are equal.
This zero condition is met when the distribution of particles is spherically
symmetric (hence the name asphericity) but also whenever the particle
distribution is symmetric with respect to the three coordinate axes (e.g.,
when the particles are distributed uniformly on a cube, tetrahedron, or other
Platonic solid). The acylindricity is always non\sphinxhyphen{}negative and zero only when
the two principal moments are equal. This zero condition is met when the
distribution of particles is cylindrically symmetric (hence the name,
acylindricity), but also whenever the particle distribution is symmetric with
respect to the two coordinate axes (e.g., when the particles are distributed
uniformly on a regular prism). The relative shape anisotropy
is bounded between 0 (if all points are spherically symmetric) and 1
(if all points lie on a line).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tensor keyword must be specified in the compute gyration/chunk command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the gyration tensor in
“unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with each atom.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of “unwrapped”
coordinates. See the Atoms section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
command for a discussion of image flags and how they are set for each
atom.  You can reset the image flags (e.g., to 0) before invoking this
compute by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_gyration_shape_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array with six columns,
which can be accessed by indices 1\textendash{}6. The first three columns are the
eigenvalues of the gyration tensor followed by the asphericity, the
acylindricity and the relative shape anisotropy.  The computed values can be
used by any command that uses global array values from a compute as input.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS
output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array calculated by this compute is
“intensive”.  The first five columns will be in
distance\(^2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} while the sixth one is dimensionless.

\index{compute heat/flux@\spxentry{compute heat/flux}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute heat/flux command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:compute-heat-flux-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{flux}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
heat/flux = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ke\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of a compute that calculates per\sphinxhyphen{}atom kinetic energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pe\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of a compute that calculates per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
stress\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of a compute that calculates per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myFlux}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{flux}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myKE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myPE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myStress}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the heat flux vector based on
contributions from atoms in the specified group.  This can be used by
itself to measure the heat flux through a set of atoms (e.g., a region
between two thermostatted reservoirs held at different temperatures),
or to calculate a thermal conductivity using the equilibrium
Green\sphinxhyphen{}Kubo formalism.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For other non\sphinxhyphen{}equilibrium ways to compute a thermal conductivity, see
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_kappa::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto kappa}}}} doc page.  These include use of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_thermal_conductivity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix thermal/conductivity}}}} command
for the Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Plathe method.  Or the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_heat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix heat}}}} command
which can add or subtract heat from groups of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute takes three arguments which are IDs of other
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}}.  One calculates per\sphinxhyphen{}atom kinetic energy
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{ke\sphinxhyphen{}ID}), one calculates per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy (\sphinxstyleemphasis{pe\sphinxhyphen{}ID)}, and the
third calculates per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress (\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress\sphinxhyphen{}ID}).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These other computes should provide values for all the atoms in
the group this compute specifies.  That means the other computes could
use the same group as this compute, or they can just use group “all”
(or any group whose atoms are superset of the atoms in this compute’s
group).  LAMMPS does not check for this.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In case of two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions, the heat flux \(\mathbf{J}\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{J} &= \frac{1}{V} \left[ \sum_i e_i \mathbf{v}_i - \sum_{i} \mathbf{S}_{i} \mathbf{v}_i \right] \\
&= \frac{1}{V} \left[ \sum_i e_i \mathbf{v}_i + \sum_{i<j} \left( \mathbf{F}_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{v}_j \right) \mathbf{r}_{ij} \right] \\
&= \frac{1}{V} \left[ \sum_i e_i \mathbf{v}_i + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i<j} \bigl( \mathbf{F}_{ij} \cdot \left(\mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{v}_j \right) \bigr) \mathbf{r}_{ij} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(e_i\) in the first term of the equation
is the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy (potential and kinetic).
This is calculated by the computes \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke\sphinxhyphen{}ID}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe\sphinxhyphen{}ID}. \(\mathbf{S}_i\) in the second term is the
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress tensor calculated by the compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centroid/stress/atom}}}}
for possible definitions of atomic stress \(\mathbf{S}_i\)
in the case of bonded and many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.
The tensor multiplies \(\mathbf{v}_i\) by a \(3\times3\) matrix
to yield a vector.
Note that as discussed below, the \(1/V\) scaling factor in the
equation for \(\mathbf{J}\) is \sphinxstylestrong{not} included in the calculation
performed by these computes; you need to add it for a volume appropriate to the
atoms included in the calculation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}}
commands have options for which
terms to include in their calculation (pair, bond, etc).  The heat
flux calculation will thus include exactly the same terms. Normally
you should use {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom virial}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centroid/stress/atom virial}}}}
so as not to include a kinetic energy term in the heat flux.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux} has been reported to produce unphysical
values for angle, dihedral, improper and constraint force contributions
when used with {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}},
as discussed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:surblys3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Surblys2019)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:boone}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Boone)}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:surblys4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Surblys2021)}}}}. You are strongly advised to
use {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centroid/stress/atom}}}},
which has been implemented specifically for such cases.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Due to an implementation detail, the \(y\) and \(z\)
components of heat flux from {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}
contribution when computed via {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}}
are highly unphysical and should not be used.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Green\textendash{}Kubo formulas relate the ensemble average of the
auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation of the heat flux \(\mathbf{J}\)
to the thermal conductivity \(\kappa\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\kappa  = \frac{V}{k_B T^2} \int_0^\infty \langle J_x(0)  J_x(t) \rangle \, \mathrm{d} t = \frac{V}{3 k_B T^2} \int_0^\infty \langle \mathbf{J}(0) \cdot  \mathbf{J}(t)  \rangle \, \mathrm{d}t\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The heat flux can be output every so many timesteps (e.g., via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command).  Then as a
post\sphinxhyphen{}processing operation, an auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation can be performed, its
integral estimated, and the Green\textendash{}Kubo formula above evaluated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_correlate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/correlate}}}} command can calculate
the auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation.  The trap() function in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command can calculate the integral.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An example LAMMPS input script for solid argon is appended below.  The
result should be an average conductivity
\(\approx 0.29~\mathrm{W/m \cdot K}\).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 6.
The first three components are the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\)
components of the full heat flux vector
(i.e., \(J_x\), \(J_y\), and \(J_z\)).
The next three components are the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\)
components of just the convective portion of the flux (i.e., the
first term in the equation for \(\mathbf{J}\)).
Each component can be accessed by indices 1\textendash{}6. These values can be used by any
command that uses global vector values from a compute as input.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} documentation for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values calculated by this compute are “extensive”, meaning
they scale with the number of atoms in the simulation.  They can be
divided by the appropriate volume to get a flux, which would then be an
“intensive” value, meaning independent of the number of atoms in the
simulation.  Note that if the compute group is “all”, then the
appropriate volume to divide by is the simulation box volume.  However,
if a group with a subset of atoms is used, it should be the volume
containing those atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values will be in energy*velocity {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  Once
divided by a volume the units will be that of flux, namely
energy/area/time {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}

\label{\detokenize{compute_heat_flux:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}
