\section{compute hexorder/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:compute-hexorder-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hexorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
hexorder/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{degree} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} value = distance cutoff
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} value = number of nearest neighbors
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{degree} value = degree \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} of order parameter
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hexorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hexorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{degree}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nnn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates \(q_n\) the bond\sphinxhyphen{}orientational
order parameter for each atom in a group. The hexatic (\sphinxstyleemphasis{n} = 6) order
parameter was introduced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:nelson}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Nelson and Halperin}}}} as a way to detect
hexagonal symmetry in two\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional systems. For each atom, \(q_n\)
is a complex number (stored as two real numbers) defined as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}q_n = \frac{1}{nnn}\sum_{j = 1}^{nnn} e^{n i \theta({\bf r}_{ij})}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the sum is over the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} nearest neighbors
of the central atom. The angle \(\theta\)
is formed by the bond vector \(r_{ij}\) and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} axis.
\(\theta\) is calculated only using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} components,
whereas the distance from the
central atom is calculated using all three
\sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} components of the bond vector.
Neighbor atoms not in the group
are included in the order parameter of atoms in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} defines the distance cutoff
used when searching for neighbors. The default value, also
the maximum allowable value, is the cutoff specified
by the pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} defines the number of nearest
neighbors used to calculate \(q_n\). The default value is 6.
If the value is NULL, then all neighbors up to the
distance cutoff are used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{degree} sets the degree \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} of the order parameter.
The default value is 6. For a perfect hexagonal lattice with
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} = 6,
\(q_6 = e^{6 i \phi}\) for all atoms, where the constant \(0 < \phi < \frac{\pi}{3}\)
depends only on the orientation of the lattice relative to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} axis.
In an isotropic liquid, local neighborhoods may still exhibit
weak hexagonal symmetry, but because the orientational correlation
decays quickly with distance, the value of \(\phi\) will be different for
different atoms, and so when \(q_6\) is averaged over all the atoms
in the system, \(| \left< q_6 \right> | << 1\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of \(q_n\) is set to zero for atoms not in the
specified compute group, as well as for atoms that have less than
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} neighbors within the distance cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (i.e. each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This
is the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command, and means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the
neighbor list.  Because this fix uses the neighbor list, it also means
those pairs will not be included in the order parameter.  This
difficulty can be circumvented by writing a dump file, and using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to compute the order parameter for
snapshots in the dump file.  The rerun script can use a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command that includes all pairs in
the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with 2 columns, giving the
real and imaginary parts \(q_n\), a complex number restricted to the
unit disk of the complex plane (i.e., \(\Re(q_n)^2 + \Im(q_n)^2 \le 1\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values can be accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute orientorder/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_coord_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute coord/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_centro_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centro/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} = pair style cutoff, \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} = 6, \sphinxstyleemphasis{degree} = 6


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom:nelson}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Nelson)} Nelson, Halperin, Phys Rev B, 19, 2457 (1979).

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute hma@\spxentry{compute hma}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute hma command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:compute-hma-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_hma::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
hma = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of fix that specifies the set temperature during canonical simulation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keywords or keyword/argument pairs must be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{anharmonic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{u} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{p} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cv}

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{anharmonic} = compute will return anharmonic property values
\sphinxstyleemphasis{u} = compute will return potential energy
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p} value = Pharm = compute will return pressure
   Pharm = difference between the harmonic pressure and lattice pressure
           as described below
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cv} = compute will return the heat capacity
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{u}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{anharmonic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{u}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{u}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cv}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the properties of a solid (potential
energy, pressure or heat capacity), using the harmonically\sphinxhyphen{}mapped averaging
(HMA) method.
This command yields much higher precision than the equivalent compute commands
({\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}}, etc.)
commands during a canonical simulation of an atomic crystal. Specifically,
near melting HMA can yield averages of a given precision an order of magnitude
faster than conventional methods, and this only improves as the temperatures is
lowered.  This is particularly important for evaluating the free energy by
thermodynamic integration, where the low\sphinxhyphen{}temperature contributions are the
greatest source of statistical uncertainty.  Moreover, HMA has other
advantages, including smaller potential\sphinxhyphen{}truncation effects, finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
effects, smaller timestep inaccuracy, faster equilibration and shorter
decorrelation time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
HMA should not be used if atoms are expected to diffuse.  It is also
restricted to simulations in the NVT ensemble.  While this compute may
be used with any potential in LAMMPS, it will provide inaccurate results
for potentials that do not go to 0 at the truncation distance;
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth_linear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/smooth/linear}}}} and Ewald
summation should work fine, while {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut}}}}
will perform poorly unless the potential is shifted (via
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift) or the cutoff is large.
Furthermore, computation of the heat capacity with this compute is
restricted to those that implement the \sphinxstyleemphasis{single\_hessian} method in Pair.
Implementing \sphinxstyleemphasis{single\_hessian} in additional pair styles is simple.
Please contact Andrew Schultz (ajs42 at buffalo.edu) and David Kofke
(kofke at buffalo.edu) if your desired pair style does not have this
method.  This is the list of pair styles that currently implement
\sphinxstyleemphasis{single\_hessian}:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth_linear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/smooth/linear}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this method, the analytically known harmonic behavior of a crystal is removed from the traditional ensemble
averages, which leads to an accurate and precise measurement of the anharmonic contributions without contamination
by noise produced by the already\sphinxhyphen{}known harmonic behavior.
A detailed description of this method can be found in ({\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_hma:hma-moustafa}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Moustafa}}}}). The potential energy is computed by the formula:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left< U\right>_\text{HMA} = \frac{d}{2} (N-1) k_B T  + \left< U + \frac{1}{2} \vec F\cdot\Delta \vec r \right>\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(N\) is the number of atoms in the system, \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s
constant, \(T\) is the temperature, \(d\) is the dimensionality of the
system (2 or 3 for 2d/3d), \(\vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r\) is the sum of dot
products of the atomic force vectors and displacement (from lattice sites)
vectors, and \(U\) is the sum of pair, bond, angle, dihedral, improper,
kspace (long\sphinxhyphen{}range), and fix energies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pressure is computed by the formula:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left< P\right>_{HMA} = \Delta \hat P + \left< P_\text{vir}
+ \frac{\beta \Delta \hat P - \rho}{d(N-1)} \vec F\cdot\Delta \vec r \right>\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\rho\) is the number density of the system, \(\Delta \hat P\)
is the difference between the harmonic and lattice pressure,
\(P_\text{vir}\) is the virial pressure computed as the sum of pair, bond,
angle, dihedral, improper, kspace (long\sphinxhyphen{}range), and fix contributions to the
force on each atom, and \(k_B=1/k_B T\).  Although the method will work for
any value of \(\Delta \hat P\)
specified (use pressure {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}), the precision of the resultant
pressure is sensitive to \(\Delta \hat P\); the precision tends to be
best when \(\Delta \hat P\) is the actual the difference between the
lattice pressure and harmonic pressure.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left<C_V \right>_\text{HMA} = \frac{d}{2} (N-1) k_B
 + \frac{1}{k_B T^2} \left( \left<U_\text{HMA}^2 \right>
                      - \left<U_\text{HMA}\right>^2 \right) + \frac{1}{4 T}
\left<\vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r + \Delta r \cdot\Phi\cdot \Delta\vec r\right>\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\Phi\) is the Hessian matrix. The compute hma command
computes the full expression for \(C_V\) except for the
\(\left<U_\text{HMA}\right>^2\) in the variance term, which can be obtained
by passing the \sphinxstyleemphasis{u} keyword; you must add this extra contribution to the
\(C_V\) value reported by this compute.  The variance term can cause
significant round\sphinxhyphen{}off error when computing \(C_V\).  To address this, the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{anharmonic} keyword can be passed and/or the output format can be specified
with more digits.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{float}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}22.15e}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZsq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{anharmonic} keyword will instruct the compute to return anharmonic
properties rather than the full properties, which include lattice, harmonic
and anharmonic contributions.
When using this keyword, the compute must be first active (it must be included
via a {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command) while the atoms are
still at their lattice sites (before equilibration).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The temp\sphinxhyphen{}ID specified with compute hma command should be same as the fix\sphinxhyphen{}ID of
the Nose\textendash{}Hoover ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}) or
Berendsen ({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/berendsen}}}}) thermostat used for
the simulation. While using this command, the Langevin thermostat
({\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}})
should be avoided as its extra forces interfere with the HMA implementation.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute hma command should be used right after the energy minimization, when the atoms are at their lattice sites.
The simulation should not be started before this command has been used in the input script.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following example illustrates the placement of this command in the input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{min\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cg}
\PYG{k}{minimize}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e\PYGZhy{}35}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e\PYGZhy{}15}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500000}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{thermostatid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{u}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermostatid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{600.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{600.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute hma should be used when the atoms of the solid do not diffuse. Diffusion will reduce the precision in the potential energy computation.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify energy yes}}}} command must also be specified if a fix is to contribute potential energy to this command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An example input script that uses this compute is included in
examples/PACKAGES/hma/ along with corresponding LAMMPS output showing that the HMA
properties fluctuate less than the corresponding conventional properties.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector that includes the n properties
requested as arguments to the command (the potential energy, pressure and/or heat
capacity).  The elements of the vector can be accessed by indices 1\textendash{}n by any
command that uses global vector values as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values calculated by this compute are “extensive”.  The
scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  It is enabled only
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usage restricted to canonical (NVT) ensemble simulation only.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dynamical_matrix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dynamical matrix}}}} provides a finite difference
formulation of the Hessian provided by Pair’s single\_hessian, which is used by
this compute.


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_hma:hma-moustafa}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Moustafa)} Sabry G. Moustafa, Andrew J. Schultz, and David A. Kofke, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Very fast averaging of thermal properties of crystals by molecular simulation},
\sphinxhref{https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.92.043303}{Phys. Rev. E {[}92{]}, 043303 (2015)}

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute improper@\spxentry{compute improper}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute improper command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:compute-improper-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_improper::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{improper}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
improper = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{improper}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that extracts the improper energy calculated by
each of the improper sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles used in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style hybrid}}}} command.  These values are made
accessible for output or further processing by other commands.  The
group specified for this command is ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is useful when using {\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style hybrid}}}} if you want to know the portion of the
total energy contributed by one or more of the hybrid sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length \(N\), where \(N\) is
the number of sub\_styles defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style hybrid}}}} command.
These styles can be accessed by the indices 1 through \(N\).
These values can be used by any command that uses global scalar or vector
values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}}
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values are “extensive” and will be in energy
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute improper/local@\spxentry{compute improper/local}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute improper/local command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:compute-improper-local-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{improper}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
improper/local = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more values may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{chi}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{chi} = tabulate improper angles
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{improper}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chi}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates properties of individual improper
interactions.  The number of datums generated, aggregated across all
processors, equals the number of impropers in the system, modified by
the group parameter as explained below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{chi} is the improper angle, as defined in the doc pages for
the individual improper styles listed on
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The local data stored by this command is generated by looping over all
the atoms owned on a processor and their impropers.  An improper will
only be included if all four atoms in the improper are in the specified
compute group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that as atoms migrate from processor to processor, there will be
no consistent ordering of the entries within the local vector or array
from one timestep to the next.  The only consistency that is
guaranteed is that the ordering on a particular timestep will be the
same for local vectors or arrays generated by other compute commands.
For example, improper output from the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/local}}}} command can be combined
with data from this command and output by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}
command in a consistent way.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of how to do this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iatom1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iatom2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iatom3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{iatom4}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{improper}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chi}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[3]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[4]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[5]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[1]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a local vector or local array depending on the
number of keywords.  The length of the vector or number of rows in the
array is the number of impropers.  If a single keyword is specified, a
local vector is produced.  If two or more keywords are specified, a
local array is produced where the number of columns = the number of
keywords.  The vector or array can be accessed by any command that
uses local values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output for \sphinxstyleemphasis{chi} will be in degrees.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/local}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_improper_local:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute inertia/chunk@\spxentry{compute inertia/chunk}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute inertia/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk:compute-inertia-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inertia}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
inertia/chunk = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inertia}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the inertia tensor for multiple
chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates the six components of the symmetric inertia
tensor for each chunk, ordered
\(I_{xx},I_{yy},I_{zz},I_{xy},I_{yz},I_{xz}\).
The calculation includes all effects due to atoms passing through periodic
boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not
in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the
“all” group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero chunk IDs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the chunk’s inertia
tensor in “unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with
each atom.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion
of “unwrapped” coordinates.  See the Atoms section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags and
how they are set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags
(e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute inertia/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inertia}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_inertia_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array where the number of rows = the
number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.
The number of columns is 6, one for each of the 6 components of the inertia
tensor for each chunk, ordered as listed above.  These values can be accessed
by any command that uses global array values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
mass*distance\(^2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the translational kinetic energy
of a group of particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The kinetic energy of each particle is computed as \(\frac{1}{2} m
v^2\), where \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{v} are the mass and velocity of the particle,
respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is a subtle difference between the quantity calculated by this
compute and the kinetic energy calculated by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{etotal}
keyword used in thermodynamic output, as specified by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command.  For this compute, kinetic
energy is “translational” kinetic energy, calculated by the simple
formula above.  For thermodynamic output, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} keyword infers
kinetic energy from the temperature of the system with
\(\frac{1}{2} k_B T\) of energy for each degree of freedom.  For the
default temperature computation via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}} command, these are the same.
However, different computes that calculate temperature can subtract out
different non\sphinxhyphen{}thermal components of velocity and/or include different degrees
of freedom (translational, rotational, etc.).


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

can be used by any command that uses a global scalar value from a
compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page
for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “extensive”.  The
scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff:compute-ke-atom-eff-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{eff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ke/atom/eff = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{eff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom translational
(nuclei and electrons) and radial kinetic energy (electron only) in a
group.  The particles are assumed to be nuclei and electrons modeled
with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{electronic force field}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The kinetic energy for each nucleus is computed as \(\frac{1}{2} m
v^2\), where \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} corresponds to the corresponding nuclear mass, and the
kinetic energy for each electron is computed as \(\frac{1}{2} (m_e
v^2 + \frac{3}{4} m_e s^2)\), where \(m_e\) and \sphinxstyleemphasis{v} correspond to the mass
and translational velocity of each electron, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{s} to its radial
velocity, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is a subtle difference between the quantity calculated by this
compute and the kinetic energy calculated by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{etotal}
keyword used in thermodynamic output, as specified by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command. For this compute, kinetic
energy is “translational” plus electronic “radial” kinetic energy,
calculated by the simple formula above. For thermodynamic output, the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} keyword infers kinetic energy from the temperature of the system
with \(\frac{1}{2} k_B T\) of energy for each (nuclear\sphinxhyphen{}only) degree
of freedom in eFF.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The temperature in eFF should be monitored via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_eff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/eff}}}} command, which can be printed with
thermodynamic output by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}}
command, as shown in the following example:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{effTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{eff}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{effTemp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the kinetic energy will be 0.0 for atoms (nuclei or
electrons) not in the specified compute group.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a scalar quantity for each atom, which can be
accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom computes as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS
output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_atom_eff:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EFF package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_eff:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the kinetic energy of motion of a
group of eFF particles (nuclei and electrons), as modeled with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{electronic force field}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The kinetic energy for each nucleus is computed as \(\frac{1}{2} m
v^2\) and the kinetic energy for each electron is computed as
\(\frac{1}{2}(m_e v^2 + \frac{3}{4} m_e s^2)\), where \(m\)
corresponds to the nuclear mass, \(m_e\) to the electron mass, \(v\)
to the translational velocity of each particle, and \(s\) to the radial
velocity of the electron, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is a subtle difference between the quantity calculated by this
compute and the kinetic energy calculated by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{etotal}
keyword used in thermodynamic output, as specified by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style}}}} command.  For this compute, kinetic
energy is “translational” and “radial” (only for electrons) kinetic
energy, calculated by the simple formula above.  For thermodynamic
output, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} keyword infers kinetic energy from the temperature of
the system with \(\frac{1}{2} k_B T\) of energy for each degree of
freedom.  For the eFF temperature computation via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_eff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
temp\_eff}}}} command, these are the same.  But
different computes that calculate temperature can subtract out different
non\sphinxhyphen{}thermal components of velocity and/or include other degrees of
freedom.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}

The temperature in eFF models should be monitored via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_eff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/eff}}}} command, which can be
printed with thermodynamic output by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}} command, as shown in the following
example:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{effTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{eff}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{effTemp}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ke_rigid:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the translational kinetic energy
of a collection of rigid bodies, as defined by one of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command variants.

\sphinxAtStartPar

commands which defines the rigid bodies.  The group specified in the
compute command is ignored.  The kinetic energy of all the rigid
bodies defined by the fix rigid command in included in the
calculation.

\section{compute mliap command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:compute-mliap-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mliap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mliap = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
two or more keyword/value pairs must be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{model} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{descriptor} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gradgradflag}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{model} values = style
  style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliappy}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{descriptor} values = style filename
  style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ace}
  filename = name of file containing descriptor definitions
\sphinxstyleemphasis{gradgradflag} value = 0/1
  toggle gradgrad method for force gradient
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mliap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{model}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{descriptor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sna}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta06A.mliap.descriptor}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mliap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{model}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{descriptor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H\PYGZus{}N\PYGZus{}O\PYGZus{}ccs.yace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gradgradflag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute style \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliap} provides a general interface to the gradient
of machine\sphinxhyphen{}learning interatomic potentials with respect to model parameters.
It is used primarily for calculating the gradient of energy, force, and
stress components with respect to model parameters, which is useful when
training {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_mliap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mliap pair\_style}}}} models to match target data.
It provides separate definitions of the interatomic potential functional
form (\sphinxstyleemphasis{model}) and the geometric quantities that characterize the atomic
positions (\sphinxstyleemphasis{descriptor}). By defining \sphinxstyleemphasis{model} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{descriptor} separately,
it is possible to use many different models with a given descriptor,
or many different descriptors with a given model. Currently, the compute
supports \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic} SNAP descriptor computes used in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style snap}}}}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} SO3 descriptor computes, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} ACE descriptor computes used in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style pace}}}},
and it is straightforward to add new descriptor styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliap} command must be followed by two keywords
\sphinxstyleemphasis{model} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{descriptor} in either order.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{model} keyword is followed by the model style (\sphinxstyleemphasis{linear},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliappy}).  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliappy} model is only available if
LAMMPS is built with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliappy} Python module. There are
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_extras:mliap}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{specific installation instructions}}}} for that module.
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliap} compute, specifying a \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} model will compute the
specified descriptors and gradients with respect to linear model parameters
whereas \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic} will do the same, but for the quadratic products of
descriptors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{descriptor} keyword is followed by a descriptor style, and
additional arguments.  The compute currently supports three descriptor
styles: \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{so3}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ace}, but it is is straightforward to add
additional descriptor styles.  The SNAP descriptor style \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna} is the
same as that used by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style snap}}}}, including the
linear, quadratic, and chem variants.  A single additional argument
specifies the descriptor filename containing the parameters and setting used
by the SNAP descriptor.  The descriptor filename usually ends in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{.mliap.descriptor} extension.  The format of this file is identical to
the descriptor file in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_mliap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style mliap}}}}, and is
described in detail there.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ACE descriptor style \sphinxstyleemphasis{ace} is the same as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style pace}}}}.
A single additional argument specifies the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ace} descriptor filename
that contains parameters and settings for the ACE descriptors. This file
format differs from the SNAP or SO3 descriptor files, and has a \sphinxstyleemphasis{.yace} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{.ace} extension. However, as with other mliap descriptor styles, this file
is identical to the ace descriptor file in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_mliap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style mliap}}}},
where it is described in further detail.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of LAMMPS atom types (and the value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelems} in the model)
must match the value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelems} in the descriptor file.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliap} calculates a global array containing gradient information.
The number of columns in the array is \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelems} \(\times\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{nparams} + 1.
The first row of the array contain the derivative of potential energy with
respect to. to each parameter and each element. The last six rows
of the array contain the corresponding derivatives of the
virial stress tensor, listed in Voigt notation: \sphinxstyleemphasis{pxx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pyy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pzz},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pyz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pxz}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pxy}. In between the energy and stress rows are
the \(3N\) rows containing the derivatives of the force components.
See section below on output for a detailed description of how
rows and columns are ordered.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The element in the last column of each row contains
the potential energy, force, or stress, according to the row.
These quantities correspond to the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified reference potential
that must be subtracted from the target data when training a model.
The potential energy calculation uses the built in compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_pe}.
The stress calculation uses a compute called \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliap\_press} that is
automatically created behind the scenes, according to the following
command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mliap\PYGZus{}press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pressure}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{virial}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See section below on output for a detailed explanation of the data
layout in the global array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{gradgradflag} controls how the force
gradient is calculated. A value of 1 requires that the model provide
the matrix of double gradients of energy with respect to both parameters
and descriptors. For the linear and quadratic models this matrix is
sparse and so is easily calculated and stored. For other models, this
matrix may be prohibitively expensive to calculate and store.
A value of 0 requires that the descriptor provide the derivative
of the descriptors with respect to the position of every neighbor atom.
This is not optimal for linear and quadratic models, but may be
a better choice for more complex models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atoms not in the group do not contribute to this compute.
Neighbor atoms not in the group do not contribute to this compute.
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (i.e., each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified reference potentials includes bonded and
non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded pairwise interactions, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This
is the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command, and means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the
neighbor list.  Because this fix uses the neighbor list, it also means
those pairs will not be included in the calculation. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}}
command is not an option here, since the reference potential is required
for the last column of the global array. A work\sphinxhyphen{}around is to prevent
pairwise interactions from being removed by explicitly adding a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tiny} positive value for every pairwise interaction that would otherwise be
set to zero in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliap} evaluates a global array.  The columns are arranged into
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nelems} blocks, listed in order of element \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}. Each block
contains one column for each of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nparams} model parameters.
A final column contains the corresponding energy, force component
on an atom, or virial stress component. The rows of the array appear
in the following order:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1 row: Derivatives of potential energy with respect to each parameter of each element.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(3N\) rows: Derivatives of force components; the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
components of the force on atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} appear in consecutive rows. The atoms are
sorted based on atom ID.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
6 rows: Derivatives of the virial stress tensor with respect to each
parameter of each element. The ordering of the rows follows Voigt notation:
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pxx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pyy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pzz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pyz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pxz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pxy}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values can be accessed by any command that uses a global array
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options. To see how this command
can be used within a Python workflow to train machine\sphinxhyphen{}learning interatomic
potentials, see the examples in \sphinxhref{https://github.com/FitSNAP/FitSNAP}{FitSNAP}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the ML\sphinxhyphen{}IAP package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package. In addition, building LAMMPS with
the ML\sphinxhyphen{}IAP package requires building LAMMPS with the ML\sphinxhyphen{}SNAP package.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mliappy} model also requires building LAMMPS with the PYTHON
package. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ace} descriptor also requires building LAMMPS with the
ML\sphinxhyphen{}PACE package. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for
more info. Note that \sphinxtitleref{kk} (KOKKOS) accelerated variants of SNAP and
ACE descriptors are not compatible with \sphinxtitleref{mliap descriptor}.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_mliap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style mliap}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_mliap:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword defaults are gradgradflag = 1

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute momentum@\spxentry{compute momentum}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute momentum command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:compute-momentum-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{momentum}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
momentum = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{momentum}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the translational momentum \sphinxstyleemphasis{p}
of a group of particles.  It is computed as the sum
\(\vec{p} = \sum_i m_i \cdot \vec{v}_i\)
over all particles in the compute group, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{v} are
the mass and velocity vector of the particle, respectively.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector (the summed momentum) of
length 3. This value can be used by any command that uses a global
vector value from a compute as input. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector value calculated by this compute is “extensive”. The vector
value will be in mass*velocity {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:related-commands}}

\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_momentum:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute msd@\spxentry{compute msd}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute msd command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:compute-msd-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_msd::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msd = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{average}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{com} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{average} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{upper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{average}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement
(MSD) of the group of atoms, including all effects due to atoms
passing through periodic boundaries.  For computation of the non\sphinxhyphen{}Gaussian
parameter of mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement, see the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd/nongauss}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector of four quantities is calculated by this compute.  The first three
elements of the vector are the squared \sphinxstyleemphasis{dx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dz} displacements,
summed and averaged over atoms in the group.  The fourth element is the total
squared displacement (i.e., \(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\)), summed and
averaged over atoms in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slope of the mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement (MSD) versus time is
proportional to the diffusion coefficient of the diffusing atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The displacement of an atom is from its reference position. This is
normally the original position at the time
the compute command was issued, unless the \sphinxstyleemphasis{average} keyword is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}.
The value of the displacement will be
0.0 for atoms not in the specified compute group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} option is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} then the effect of any drift in
the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the group of atoms is subtracted out before the
displacement of each atom is calculated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{average} option is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} then the reference position of
an atom is based on the average position of that atom, corrected for
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass motion if requested.  The average position is a running
average over all previous calls to the compute, including the current
call. So on the first call it is current position, on the second call
it is the arithmetic average of the current position and the position
on the first call, and so on.  Note that when using this option, the
precise value of the mean square displacement will depend on the
number of times the compute is called. So, for example, changing the
frequency of thermo output may change the computed displacement. Also,
the precise values will be changed if a single simulation is broken up
into two parts, using either multiple run commands or a restart
file. It only makes sense to use this option if the atoms are not
diffusing, so that their average positions relative to the center of
mass of the system are stationary. The most common case is crystalline
solids undergoing thermal motion.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initial coordinates are stored in “unwrapped” form, by using the
image flags associated with each atom.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of “unwrapped” coordinates.  See the
Atoms section of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a
discussion of image flags and how they are set for each atom.  You
can reset the image flags (e.g. to 0) before invoking this compute by
using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the quantities calculated by this compute to be
continuous when running from a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart file}}}}, then
you should use the same ID for this compute, as in the original run.
This is so that the fix this compute creates to store per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities will also have the same ID, and thus be initialized
correctly with atom reference positions from the restart file.  When
\sphinxstyleemphasis{average} is set to yes, then the atom reference positions are
restored correctly, but not the number of samples used obtain them. As
a result, the reference positions from the restart file are combined
with subsequent positions as if they were from a single sample,
instead of many, which will change the values of msd somewhat.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 4, which can be
accessed by indices 1\textendash{}4 by any command that uses global vector values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values are “intensive”.  The vector values will be in
distance\(^2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{msd} cannot be used with a dynamic group.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd/nongauss}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_displace_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute displace\_atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_store_state::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix store/state}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd/chunk}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option default are com = no, average = no.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute msd/chunk@\spxentry{compute msd/chunk}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute msd/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk:compute-msd-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msd/chunk = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement
(MSD) for multiple chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Four quantities are calculated by this compute for each chunk.  The
first 3 quantities are the squared \sphinxstyleemphasis{dx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dz} displacements of the
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass.  The fourth component is the total squared displacement
(i.e., \(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\)) of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass.  These calculations
include all effects due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not
in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the
“all” group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero chunk IDs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The slope of the mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement (MSD) versus time is
proportional to the diffusion coefficient of the diffusing chunks.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The displacement of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the chunk is from its
original center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass position, calculated on the timestep this
compute command was first invoked.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} calculated by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command must remain constant
each time this compute is invoked, so that the displacement for each chunk
from its original position can be computed consistently.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk}
does not remain constant, an error will be generated.  If needed, you
can enforce a constant \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} by using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nchunk once} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ids once}
options when specifying the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}}
command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute stores the original position (of the
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass) of each chunk.  When a displacement is calculated on a
later timestep, it is assumed that the same atoms are assigned to the
same chunk ID.  However LAMMPS has no simple way to ensure this is the
case, though you can use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ids once} option when specifying the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  Note that if
this is not the case, the MSD calculation does not have a sensible
meaning.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The initial coordinates of the atoms in each chunk are stored in
“unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with each atom.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of
“unwrapped” coordinates.  See the Atoms section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags and
how they are set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags
(e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the quantities calculated by this compute to be
continuous when running from a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart file}}}}, then
you should use the same ID for this compute, as in the original run.
This is so that the fix this compute creates to store per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk
quantities will also have the same ID, and thus be initialized
correctly with chunk reference positions from the restart file.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute msd/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array where the number of rows = the
number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.
The number of columns = 4 for \sphinxstyleemphasis{dx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dz}, and the total displacement.
These values can be accessed by any command that uses global array values from
a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
distance\(^2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
