\index{compute msd/nongauss@\spxentry{compute msd/nongauss}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute msd/nongauss command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:compute-msd-nongauss-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nongauss}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
msd/nongauss = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{com}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{com} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nongauss}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{upper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{msd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nongauss}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{com}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the mean\sphinxhyphen{}squared displacement
(MSD) and non\sphinxhyphen{}Gaussian parameter (NGP) of the group of atoms,
including all effects due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector of three quantities is calculated by this compute.  The first
element of the vector is the total squared displacement,
\(dr^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2\), of the atoms, and the second is the
fourth power of these displacements, \(dr^4 = (dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)^2\),
summed and averaged over atoms in the group.  The third component is the
non\sphinxhyphen{}Gaussian diffusion parameter NGP,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{NGP}(t) = \frac{3\left\langle(r(t)-r(0))^4\right\rangle}
                     {5\left\langle(r(t)-r(0))^2\right\rangle^2} - 1.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The NGP is a commonly used quantity in studies of dynamical
heterogeneity.  Its minimum theoretical value \((-0.4)\) occurs when all
atoms have the same displacement magnitude.  \(\text{NGP}=0\) for Brownian
diffusion, while \(\text{NGP} > 0\) when some mobile atoms move faster than
others.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} option is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} then the effect of any drift in
the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the group of atoms is subtracted out before the
displacement of each atom is calculated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd}}}} page for further important
NOTEs, which also apply to this compute.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 3, which can be
accessed by indices 1\textendash{}3 by any command that uses global vector values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values are “intensive”.  The first vector value will be in
distance\(^2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, the second is in
distance\(^4\) units, and the third is dimensionless.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{msd/nongauss} cannot be used with a dynamic group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_msd_nongauss:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option default is com = no.

\sphinxstepscope

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_nbond_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 4May2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that computes the number of bonds each atom is
part of.  Bonds which are broken are not counted in the tally.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bpm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto broken bonds}}}} page for more information.
The number of bonds will be zero for atoms not in the specified
compute group. This compute does not depend on Newton bond settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond/type} is specified, only bonds of \sphinxstyleemphasis{btype} are
counted.

\section{compute omega/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:compute-omega-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{omega}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
omega/chunk = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{omega}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the angular velocity (omega) of
multiple chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates the three components of the angular velocity
vector for each chunk via the formula
\(\vec L = \mathrm{I}\cdot \vec\omega\), where \(\vec L\) is the
angular momentum vector of the chunk, \(\mathrm{I}\) is its moment of
inertia tensor, and \(\omega\) is the angular velocity of the chunk.
The calculation includes all effects due to atoms passing through periodic
boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not
in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the
“all” group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero chunk IDs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the chunk’s angular
velocity in “unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with
each atom.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion
of “unwrapped” coordinates.  See the Atoms section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags and
how they are set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags
(e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute omega/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{omega}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array where the number of rows is the
number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  The number of columns is 3 for the three
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}) components of the angular velocity for each chunk.
These values can be accessed by any command that uses global array
values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}}
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
velocity/distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable omega() function}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_omega_chunk:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{compute orientorder/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:compute-orientorder-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{orientorder/atom/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orientorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
orientorder/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs may be appended
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{degrees} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl/hat} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{components} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} value = distance cutoff
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} value = number of nearest neighbors
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{degrees} values = nlvalues, l1, l2,...
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl/hat} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{components} value = ldegree
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} value = number of atoms in each pass
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orientorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orientorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{degrees}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nnn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orientorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{wl}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{hat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{orientorder}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{components}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates a set of bond\sphinxhyphen{}orientational
order parameters \(Q_\ell\) for each atom in a group. These order parameters
were introduced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:steinhardt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Steinhardt et al.}}}} as a way to
characterize the local orientational order in atomic structures.
For each atom, \(Q_\ell\) is a real number defined as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\bar{Y}_{\ell m} = & \frac{1}{nnn}\sum_{j = 1}^{nnn} Y_{\ell m}\bigl( \theta( {\bf r}_{ij} ), \phi( {\bf r}_{ij} ) \bigr) \\
Q_\ell  = & \sqrt{\frac{4 \pi}{2 \ell  + 1} \sum_{m = -\ell }^{m = \ell } \bar{Y}_{\ell m} \bar{Y}^*_{\ell m}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first equation defines the local order parameters as averages
of the spherical harmonics \(Y_{\ell m}\) for each neighbor.
These are complex number components of the 3D analog of the 2D order
parameter \(q_n\), which is implemented as LAMMPS compute
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hexorder/atom}}}}.
The summation is over the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} nearest
neighbors of the central atom.  The angles \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) are
the standard spherical polar angles
defining the direction of the bond vector \(r_{ij}\).
The phase and sign of \(Y_{\ell m}\) follow the standard conventions,
so that \(\mathrm{sign}(Y_{\ell\ell}(0,0)) = (-1)^\ell\).
The second equation defines \(Q_\ell\), which is a
rotationally invariant non\sphinxhyphen{}negative amplitude obtained by summing
over all the components of degree \(\ell\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} defines the distance cutoff
used when searching for neighbors. The default value, also
the maximum allowable value, is the cutoff specified
by the pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} defines the number of nearest
neighbors used to calculate \(Q_\ell\). The default value is 12.
If the value is NULL, then all neighbors up to the
specified distance cutoff are used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{degrees} defines the list of order parameters to
be computed.  The first argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{nlvalues} is the number of order
parameters. This is followed by that number of non\sphinxhyphen{}negative integers giving the
degree of each order parameter. Because \(Q_2\) and all odd\sphinxhyphen{}degree order
parameters are zero for atoms in cubic crystals (see
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:steinhardt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Steinhardt}}}}), the default order parameters are \(Q_4\),
\(Q_6\), \(Q_8\), \(Q_{10}\), and \(Q_{12}\). For the FCC
crystal with \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} =12,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Q_4 = \sqrt{\frac{7}{192}} \approx 0.19094\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The numerical values of all order
parameters up to \(Q_{12}\) for a range of commonly encountered
high\sphinxhyphen{}symmetry structures are given in Table I of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:mickel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Mickel et al.}}}},
and these can be reproduced with this compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl} will output the third\sphinxhyphen{}order invariants \(W_\ell\)
(see Eq. 1.4 in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:steinhardt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Steinhardt}}}}) for the same degrees as
for the \(Q_\ell\) parameters. For the FCC crystal with \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} = 12,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}W_4 = -\sqrt{\frac{14}{143}} \left(\frac{49}{4096}\right) \pi^{-3/2} \approx -0.0006722136\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl/hat} will output the normalized third\sphinxhyphen{}order
invariants \(\hat{W}_\ell\) (see Eq. 2.2 in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:steinhardt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Steinhardt}}}})
for the same degrees as for the \(Q_\ell\) parameters. For the FCC crystal
with \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} =12,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{W}_4 = -\frac{7}{3} \sqrt{\frac{2}{429}} \approx -0.159317\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The numerical values of \(\hat{W}_\ell\) for a range of commonly
encountered high\sphinxhyphen{}symmetry structures are given in Table I of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:steinhardt}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Steinhardt}}}}, and these can be reproduced with this keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{components} will output the components of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{normalized} complex vector
\(\hat{Y}_{\ell m} = \bar{Y}_{\ell m}/|\bar{Y}_{\ell m}|\)
of degree \sphinxstyleemphasis{ldegree}, which must be included in the list of order parameters to
be computed. This option can be used in conjunction with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_coord_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute coord\_atom}}}} to calculate the ten Wolde’s
criterion to identify crystal\sphinxhyphen{}like particles, as discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:tenwolde2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{ten Wolde}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} is only applicable when using the
the KOKKOS package and is ignored otherwise. This keyword controls
the number of atoms in each pass used to compute the bond\sphinxhyphen{}orientational
order parameters and is used to avoid running out of memory. For example
if there are 32768 atoms in the simulation and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize}
is set to 16384, the parameter calculation will be broken up
into two passes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of \(Q_\ell\) is set to zero for atoms not in the
specified compute group, as well as for atoms that have less than
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} neighbors within the distance cutoff, unless \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} is NULL.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (i.e., each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This
is the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command, and means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the
neighbor list.  Because this fix uses the neighbor list, it also means
those pairs will not be included in the order parameter.  This
difficulty can be circumvented by writing a dump file, and using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to compute the order parameter for
snapshots in the dump file.  The rerun script can use a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command that includes all pairs in
the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with \sphinxstyleemphasis{nlvalues} columns,
giving the \(Q_\ell\) values for each atom, which are real numbers in the
range \(0 \le Q_\ell \le 1\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl} is set to yes, then the \(W_\ell\) values for each
atom will be added to the output array, which are real numbers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl/hat} is set to yes, then the \(\hat{W}_\ell\)
values for each atom will be added to the output array, which are real numbers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{components} is set, then the real and imaginary parts
of each component of \sphinxstyleemphasis{normalized} \(\hat{Y}_{\ell m}\) will be added to the
output array in the following order:
\(\Re(\hat{Y}_{-m}),\) \(\Im(\hat{Y}_{-m}),\)
\(\Re(\hat{Y}_{-m+1}),\) \(\Im(\hat{Y}_{-m+1}), \dotsc,\)
\(\Re(\hat{Y}_m),\) \(\Im(\hat{Y}_m).\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
In summary, the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array will contain \sphinxstyleemphasis{nlvalues} columns, followed by
an additional \sphinxstyleemphasis{nlvalues} columns if \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl} is set to yes, followed by
an additional \sphinxstyleemphasis{nlvalues} columns if \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl/hat} is set to yes, followed
by an additional 2*(2* \sphinxstyleemphasis{ldegree}+1) columns if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{components}
keyword is set.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values can be accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_coord_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute coord/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_centro_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute centro/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_hexorder_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute hexorder/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_orientorder_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} = pair style cutoff, \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} = 12,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{degrees} = 5 4 6 8 10 12 (i.e., \(Q_4\), \(Q_6\), \(Q_8\), \(Q_{10}\), and \(Q_{12}\)),
\sphinxstyleemphasis{wl} = no, \sphinxstyleemphasis{wl/hat} = no, \sphinxstyleemphasis{components} off, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} = 16384

\section{compute pace command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pace:compute-pace-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pace:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pace::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pace:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ace\PYGZus{}potential\PYGZus{}filename}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pace = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ace\_potential\_filename = file name (in the .yace or .ace format from {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pace pair\_style}}}}) including ACE hyper\sphinxhyphen{}parameters, bonds, and generalized coupling coefficients

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{1}
   \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} = descriptors are summed over atoms of each type
   \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} = descriptors are listed separately for each atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{1}
   \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} = descriptor gradients are summed over atoms of each type
   \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} = descriptor gradients are listed separately for each atom pair
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pace:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coupling\PYGZus{}coefficients.yace}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coupling\PYGZus{}coefficients.yace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coupling\PYGZus{}coefficients.yace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pace:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 7Feb2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a set of quantities related to the atomic
cluster expansion (ACE) descriptors of the atoms in a group.  ACE
descriptors are highly general atomic descriptors, encoding the radial
and angular distribution of neighbor atoms, up to arbitrary bond order
(rank).  The detailed mathematical definition is given in the paper by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pace:drautz19}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Drautz)}}}}.  These descriptors are used in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pace pair\_style}}}}.  Quantities obtained from \sphinxtitleref{compute
pace} are related to those used in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pace pair\_style}}}} to
evaluate atomic energies, forces, and stresses for linear ACE models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, the energy for a linear ACE model is calculated as:
\(E=\sum_i^{N\_atoms} \sum_{\boldsymbol{\nu}} c_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
B_{i,\boldsymbol{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\).  The ACE descriptors for atom \sphinxtitleref{i}
\(B_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}}\), and \(c_{\nu}\) are linear model
parameters.  The detailed definition and indexing convention for ACE
descriptors is given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pace:drautz19}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Drautz)}}}}.  In short, body
order \(N\), angular character, radial character, and chemical
elements in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N\sphinxhyphen{}body} descriptor are encoded by \(\nu\).  In the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pace pair\_style}}}}, the linear model parameters and the
ACE descriptors are combined for efficient evaluation of energies and
forces.  The details and benefits of this efficient implementation are
given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pace:lysogorskiy21}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Lysogorskiy)}}}}, but the combined
descriptors and linear model parameters for the purposes of \sphinxtitleref{compute
pace} may be expressed in terms of the ACE descriptors mentioned above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(c_{\boldsymbol{\nu}} B_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}}= \sum_{\boldsymbol{\nu}' \in \boldsymbol{\nu} } \big[ c_{\boldsymbol{\nu}} C(\boldsymbol{\nu}') \big] A_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}'}\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
where the bracketed terms on the right\sphinxhyphen{}hand side are the combined functions
with linear model parameters typically provided in the \sphinxtitleref{\textless{}name\textgreater{}.yace} potential
file for \sphinxtitleref{pace pair\_style}. When these bracketed terms are multiplied by the
products of the atomic base from {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pace:drautz19}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Drautz)}}}},
\(A_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu'}}\), the ACE descriptors are recovered but they
are also scaled by linear model parameters. The generalized coupling coefficients,
written in short\sphinxhyphen{}hand here as \(C(\boldsymbol{\nu}')\), are the generalized
Clebsch\sphinxhyphen{}Gordan or generalized Wigner symbols. It may be desirable to reverse the
combination of these descriptors and the linear model parameters so that the
ACE descriptors themselves may be used. The ACE descriptors and their gradients
are often used when training ACE models, performing custom data analysis,
generalizing ACE model forms, and other tasks that involve direct computation of
descriptors. The key utility of \sphinxtitleref{compute pace} is that it can compute the ACE
descriptors and gradients so that these tasks can be performed during a LAMMPS
simulation or so that LAMMPS can be used as a driver for tasks like ACE model
parameterization. To see how this command can be used within a Python workflow
to train ACE potentials, see the examples in
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/FitSNAP/FitSNAP}{FitSNAP}. Examples on using outputs from
this compute to construct general ACE potential forms are demonstrated in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pace:goff23}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Goff)}}}}. The various keywords and inputs to \sphinxtitleref{compute pace}
determine what ACE descriptors and related quantities are returned in a compute
array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficient file, \sphinxtitleref{\textless{}name\textgreater{}.yace}, ultimately defines the number of ACE
descriptors to be computed, their maximum body\sphinxhyphen{}order, the degree of angular
character they have, the degree of radial character they have, the chemical
character (which element\sphinxhyphen{}element interactions are encoded by descriptors),
and other hyper\sphinxhyphen{}parameters defined in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pace:drautz19}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Drautz)}}}}. These may
be modeled after the potential files in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pace pair\_style}}}},
and have the same format. Details on how to generate the coefficient files
to train ACE models may be found in \sphinxhref{https://github.com/FitSNAP/FitSNAP}{FitSNAP}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} determines whether or not to list the descriptors of
each atom separately, or sum them together and list in a single row. If
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} then a single descriptor row is used, which contains
the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom ACE descriptors \(B_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}}\) summed over all
atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} to produce \(B_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\). If \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} is set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{1} this is replaced by a separate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom ACE descriptor row for each atom.
In this case, the entries in the final column for these rows are set to zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} determines whether to sum atom gradients or list
them separately. If \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} is set to 0, the ACE
descriptor gradients w.r.t. atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} are summed over all atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i’}
of, which may be useful when training linear ACE models on atomic forces.
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} is set to 1, gradients are listed separately for each pair of atoms.
Each row corresponds
to a single term \(\frac{\partial {B_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}}}}{\partial {r}^a_j}\)
where \({r}^a_j\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a\sphinxhyphen{}th} position coordinate of the atom with global
index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}. This also changes the number of columns to be equal to the number of
ACE descriptors, with 3 additional columns representing the indices \(i\),
\(j\), and \(a\), as explained more in the Output info section below.
The option \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag=1} requires that \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag=1}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is noted here that in contrast to {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pace::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pace pair\_style}}}},
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{.yace} file for \sphinxtitleref{compute pace} typically should not contain linear
parameters for an ACE potential. If \(c_{\nu}\) are included,
the value of the descriptor will not be returned in the \sphinxtitleref{compute} array,
but instead, the energy contribution from that descriptor will be returned.
Do not do this unless it is the desired behavior.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{In short, you should not plug in a ‘.yace’ for a pace potential into this
compute to evaluate descriptors.}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Generalized Clebsch\sphinxhyphen{}Gordan or Generalized Wigner symbols (with appropriate
factors) must be used to evaluate ACE descriptors with this compute.} There
are multiple ways to define the generalized coupling coefficients. Because
of this, this compute will not revert your potential file to a coupling
coefficient file. Instead this compute allows the user to supply coupling
coefficients that follow any convention.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} = 1 produces a global array with \(N + 3N^2 + 1\) rows
which becomes expensive for systems with more than 1000 atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise interactions between
atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This is the default
setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command, and
means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the neighbor list.
Because this fix uses the neighbor list, it also means those pairs
will not be included in the calculation.  One way to get around this,
is to write a dump file, and use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to
compute the ACE descriptors for snapshots in the dump file.
The rerun script can use a {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command that includes all pairs in the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pace:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pace} evaluates a global array.  The columns are arranged into
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes} blocks, listed in order of atom type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}. Each block contains
one column for each ACE descriptor, the same as for compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute snap}}}}. A final column contains the corresponding energy, force
component on an atom, or virial stress component. The rows of the array
appear in the following order:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1 row: \sphinxstyleemphasis{pace} average descriptor values for all atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
3*\sphinxstyleemphasis{n} force rows: quantities, with derivatives w.r.t. x, y, and z coordinate of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} appearing in consecutive rows. The atoms are sorted based on atom ID and run up to the total number of atoms, \sphinxstyleemphasis{n}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
6 rows: \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial} quantities summed for all atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, if \(\# \; B_{i, \boldsymbol{\nu}}\) =30 and ntypes=1, the number of columns in the
The number of columns in the global array generated by \sphinxstyleemphasis{pace} are 31, and
931, respectively, while the number of rows is 1+3*\sphinxstyleemphasis{n}+6, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{n}
is the total number of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bik} keyword is set to 1, the structure of the pace array is expanded.
The first \(N\) rows of the pace array
correspond to \(\# \; B_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}}\) instead of a single row summed over atoms \(i\).
In this case, the entries in the final column for these rows
are set to zero. Also, each row contains only non\sphinxhyphen{}zero entries for the
columns corresponding to the type of that atom. This is not true in the case
of \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} keyword = 1 (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} keyword is set to 1, this changes the structure of the
global array completely.
Here the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities are replaced with rows corresponding to
descriptor gradient components on single atoms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\partial {B_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}}  }}{\partial {r}^a_j}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \({r}^a_j\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a\sphinxhyphen{}th} position coordinate of the atom with global
index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}. The rows are
organized in chunks, where each chunk corresponds to an atom with global index
\(j\). The rows in an atom \(j\) chunk correspond to
atoms with global index \(i\). The total number of rows for
these descriptor gradients is therefore \(3N^2\).
The number of columns is equal to the number of ACE descriptors,
plus 3 additional left\sphinxhyphen{}most columns representing the global atom indices
\(i\), \(j\),
and Cartesian direction \(a\)  (0, 1, 2, for x, y, z).
The first 3 columns of the first \(N\) rows belong to the reference
potential force components. The remaining K columns contain the
\(B_{i,\boldsymbol{\nu}}\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom descriptors corresponding to the non\sphinxhyphen{}zero entries
obtained when \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} = 1.
The first column of the last row, after the first
\(N + 3N^2\) rows, contains the reference potential
energy. The virial components are not used with this option. The total number of
rows is therefore \(N + 3N^2 + 1\) and the number of columns is \(K + 3\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values can be accessed by any command that uses global values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} = 0

\section{compute pair command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:compute-pair-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pstyle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{[nstyle]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{[evalue]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pair = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pstyle = style name of a pair style that calculates additional values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
nsub = \sphinxstyleemphasis{n}\sphinxhyphen{}instance of a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style, if a pair style is used multiple times in a hybrid style

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{evalue} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul} or blank (optional)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gauss}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ecoul}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epair}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reaxff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that extracts additional values calculated by a
pair style, and makes them accessible for output or further processing
by other commands.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The group specified for this command is \sphinxstylestrong{ignored}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{pstyle} must be a pair style used in your simulation
either by itself or as a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid or hybrid/overlay}}}} command. If the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style is
used more than once, an additional number \sphinxstyleemphasis{nsub} has to be specified
in order to choose which instance of the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style will be used by
the compute. Not specifying the number in this case will cause the
compute to fail.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{evalue} setting is optional.  All
pair styles tally a potential energy \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair} which may be broken into
two parts: \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul} such that \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} + \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul}.
If the pair style calculates Coulombic interactions, their energy will
be tallied in \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul}.  Everything else (whether it is a Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
style van der Waals interaction or not) is tallied in \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl}.  If
\sphinxstyleemphasis{evalue} is blank or specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair}, then \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair} is stored
as a global scalar by this compute.  This is useful when using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}} if you want to know the portion
of the total energy contributed by one sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{evalue} is
specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul}, then just that portion of the energy
is stored as a global scalar.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy returned by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} keyword does not include tail
corrections, even if they are enabled via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some pair styles tally additional quantities, e.g. a breakdown of
potential energy into 14 components is tallied by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_reaxff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style reaxff}}}} command.  These values (1 or more)
are stored as a global vector by this compute.  See the page for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{individual pair styles}}}} for info on these values.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar which is \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul}.  If the pair style supports it, it also calculates a global
vector of length \(\ge\) 1, as determined by the pair style.  These values
can be used by any command that uses global scalar or vector values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar and vector values calculated by this compute are
“extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The vector
values will typically also be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, but see
the page for the pair style for details.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_bond::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute bond}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pair}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{evalue} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{epair}, nsub = 0.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute pair/local@\spxentry{compute pair/local}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute pair/local command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair_local:compute-pair-local-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pair_local:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pair_local::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair_local:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pair/local = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more values may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{dist} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dx} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eng} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fx} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{p1} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{p2} or …
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dist} = pairwise distance
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dx},\sphinxstyleemphasis{dy},\sphinxstyleemphasis{dz} = components of pairwise distance
\sphinxstyleemphasis{eng} = pairwise energy
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} = pairwise force
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fx},\sphinxstyleemphasis{fy},\sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} = components of pairwise force
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{p2}, ... = pair style specific quantities for allowed N values
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/arg pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{type} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius}
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair_local:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eng}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dist}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eng}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dist}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eng}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fz}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dist}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{p3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair_local:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates properties of individual pairwise
interactions.  The number of datums generated, aggregated across all
processors, equals the number of pairwise interactions in the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The local data stored by this command is generated by looping over the
pairwise neighbor list.  Info about an individual pairwise interaction
will only be included if both atoms in the pair are in the specified
compute group, and if the current pairwise distance is less than the
force cutoff distance for that interaction, as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{dist} is the distance between the pair of atoms.
The values \sphinxstyleemphasis{dx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dz} are the \((x,y,z)\) components of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{distance} between the pair of atoms. This value is always the
distance from the atom of higher to the one with the lower atom ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{eng} is the interaction energy for the pair of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{force} is the force acting between the pair of atoms, which
is positive for a repulsive force and negative for an attractive
force.  The values \sphinxstyleemphasis{fx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} are the \((x,y,z)\) components of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force} on atom I. For pair styles that apply non\sphinxhyphen{}central forces,
such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{granular pair styles}}}}, these values only include
the \((x,y,z)\) components of the normal force component.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A pair style may define additional pairwise quantities which can be
accessed as \sphinxstyleemphasis{p1} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{pN}, where \(N\) is defined by the pair style.
Most pair styles do not define any additional quantities, so \(N = 0\).
An example of ones that do are the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{granular pair styles}}}}
which calculate the tangential force between two particles and return
its components and magnitude acting on atom \(I\) for
\(N \in \{1,2,3,4\}\).  See individual pair styles for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using \sphinxstyleemphasis{pN} with pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid}, the output will be the Nth
quantity from the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style that computes the pairwise interaction
(based on atom types).  If that sub\sphinxhyphen{}style does not define a \sphinxstyleemphasis{pN},
the output will be 0.0.  The maximum allowed \(N\) is the maximum number
of quantities provided by any sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using \sphinxstyleemphasis{pN} with pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} the quantities
from all sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles that provide them are concatenated together
into one long list. For example, if there are 3 sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles and
2 of them have additional output (with 3 and 4 quantities,
respectively), then 7 values (\sphinxstyleemphasis{p1} up to \sphinxstyleemphasis{p7}) are defined.
The values \sphinxstyleemphasis{p1} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{p3} refer to quantities defined by the first
of the two sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles.  Values \sphinxstyleemphasis{p4} to \sphinxstyleemphasis{p7} refer to quantities
from the second of the two sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles.  If the referenced \sphinxstyleemphasis{pN}
is not computed for the specific pairwise interaction (based on
atom types), then the output will be 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{dist}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dy} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dz} will be in distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
The value \sphinxstyleemphasis{eng} will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
The values \sphinxstyleemphasis{force}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} will be in force {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
The values \sphinxstyleemphasis{pN} will be in whatever units the pair style defines.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword determines how the force cutoff distance
for an interaction is determined.  For the default setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{type},
the pairwise cutoff defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}}
command for the types of the two atoms is used.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius}
setting, the sum of the radii of the two particles is used as a
cutoff.  For example, this is appropriate for granular particles which
only interact when they are overlapping, as computed by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{granular pair styles}}}}.
Note that if a granular model defines atom
types such that all particles of a specific type are monodisperse
(same diameter), then the two settings are effectively identical.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that as atoms migrate from processor to processor, there will be
no consistent ordering of the entries within the local vector or array
from one timestep to the next.  The only consistency that is
guaranteed is that the ordering on a particular timestep will be the
same for local vectors or arrays generated by other compute commands.
For example, pair output from the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/local}}}} command can be combined
with data from this command and output by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}
command in a consistent way.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of how to do this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{patom1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{patom2}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dist}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eng}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[3]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For pairs, if two atoms I,J are involved in 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, and 1\textendash{}4
interactions within the molecular topology, their pairwise interaction
may be turned off, and thus they may not appear in the neighbor list,
and will not be part of the local data created by this command.  More
specifically, this will be true of I,J pairs with a weighting factor
of 0.0; pairs with a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero weighting factor are included.  The
weighting factors for 1\textendash{}2, 1\textendash{}3, and 1\textendash{}4 pairwise interactions are set
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command.  An exception is if
long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombics are being computed via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command, then atom pairs with
weighting factors of zero are still included in the neighbor list, so
that a portion of the long\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction contribution can be
computed in the pair style.  Hence in that case, those atom pairs will
be part of the local data created by this command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pair_local:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a local vector or local array depending on the
number of keywords.  The length of the vector or number of rows in the
array is the number of pairs.  If a single keyword is specified, a
local vector is produced.  If two or more keywords are specified, a
local array is produced where the number of columns = the number of
keywords.  The vector or array can be accessed by any command that
uses local values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output for \sphinxstyleemphasis{dist} will be in distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The
output for \sphinxstyleemphasis{eng} will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The output for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} will be in force {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
The output for \sphinxstyleemphasis{pN} will be in whatever units the pair style defines.


\subsection{Restrictions}

\section{compute pe command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pe:compute-pe-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pe:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pe:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pe = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pe:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{molPE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{angle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{improper}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pe:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the potential energy of the
entire system of atoms.  The specified group must be “all”.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe/atom}}}} command if you want per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
energies.  These per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values could be summed for a group of atoms
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The energy is calculated by the various pair, bond, etc. potentials
defined for the simulation.  If no extra keywords are listed, then the
potential energy is the sum of pair, bond, angle, dihedral, improper,
\(k\)\sphinxhyphen{}space (long\sphinxhyphen{}range), and fix energy (i.e., it is as though all the
keywords were listed).  If any extra keywords are listed, then only
those components are summed to compute the potential energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(k\)\sphinxhyphen{}space contribution requires 1 extra FFT each timestep the energy
is calculated, if using the PPPM solver via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}} command.  Thus it can increase the cost of the
PPPM calculation if it is needed on a large fraction of the simulation
timesteps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Various fixes can contribute to the total potential energy of the
system if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} contribution is included.  See the doc pages for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{individual fixes}}}} for details of which ones compute a
potential energy.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify energy yes}}}} command must also be
specified if a fix is to contribute potential energy to this command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A compute of this style with the ID of “thermo\_pe” is created when
LAMMPS starts up, as if this command were in the input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the “thermo\_style” command for more details.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pe:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the potential energy).  This
value can be used by any command that uses a global scalar value from
a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page
for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “extensive”.  The
scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\section{compute pe/atom command}

\label{\detokenize{compute_pe_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
pe/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pe_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pe_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that computes the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy for
each atom in a group.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}} command if
you want the potential energy of the entire system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy is calculated by the various pair, bond, etc
potentials defined for the simulation.  If no extra keywords are
listed, then the potential energy is the sum of pair, bond, angle,
dihedral, improper, \(k\)\sphinxhyphen{}space (long\sphinxhyphen{}range), and fix energy (i.e., it is as
though all the keywords were listed).  If any extra keywords are listed,
then only those components are summed to compute the potential energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the energy of each atom is due to its interaction with all
other atoms in the simulation, not just with other atoms in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For an energy contribution produced by a small set of atoms (e.g., 4
atoms in a dihedral or 3 atoms in a Tersoff 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction), that
energy is assigned in equal portions to each atom in the set (e.g., 1/4 of the
dihedral energy to each of the four atoms).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style charmm}}}} style calculates
pairwise interactions between 1\textendash{}4 atoms.  The energy contribution of
these terms is included in the pair energy, not the dihedral energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The KSpace contribution is calculated using the method in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe_atom:heyes1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Heyes)}}}} for the Ewald method and a related method for PPPM,
as specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}} command.
For PPPM, the calculation requires 1 extra FFT each timestep that
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy is calculated.  This \sphinxhref{PDF/kspace.pdf}{document}
describes how the long\sphinxhyphen{}range per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy calculation is performed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Various fixes can contribute to the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy of the
system if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} contribution is included.  See the doc pages for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{individual fixes}}}} for details of which ones compute a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify energy yes}}}} command must also be
specified if a fix is to contribute per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy to this
command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom potential energy compared to total potential
energy, these lines in an input script should yield the same result
in the last 2 columns of thermo output:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{peratom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}peratom}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}pe}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy does not include any Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones tail
corrections to the energy added by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify tail yes}}}} command, since those are
contributions to the global system energy.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_plasticity_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom plasticity for each
atom in a group.  This is a quantity relevant for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Peridynamics models}}}}.
See \sphinxhref{PDF/PDLammps\_overview.pdf}{this document}
for an overview of LAMMPS commands for Peridynamics modeling.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The plasticity for a Peridynamic particle is the so\sphinxhyphen{}called consistency
parameter (\(\lambda\)).  For elastic deformation, \(\lambda = 0\),
otherwise \(\lambda > 0\) for plastic deformation.  For details, see
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_plasticity_atom:mitchell}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mitchell)}}}} and the PDF doc included in the LAMMPS
distribution in \sphinxhref{PDF/PDLammps\_EPS.pdf}{doc/PDF/PDLammps\_EPS.pdf}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command can be invoked for one of the Peridynamic
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_peri::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair styles}}}}: peri/eps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The plasticity value will be 0.0 for atoms not in the specified
compute group.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_plasticity_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values are unitless numbers \(\lambda \ge 0.0\).

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ldd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pod}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}coefficients.pod}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{gdd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{podd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{global}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}coefficients.pod}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pod_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 27June2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates a set of quantities related to the
POD descriptors of the atoms in a group. These computes are used
primarily for calculating the dependence of energy and force components
on the linear coefficients in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pod::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pod pair\_style}}}},
which is useful when training a POD potential to match target data. POD
descriptors of an atom are characterized by the radial and angular
distribution of neighbor atoms. The detailed mathematical definition is
given in the papers by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pod_atom:nguyen20222c}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen and Rohskopf)}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pod_atom:nguyen20232c}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen2023)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pod_atom:nguyen20242c}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen2024)}}}},
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pod_atom:nguyen20243c}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen and Sema)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod/atom} calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom POD descriptors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{podd/atom} calculates derivatives of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom POD
descriptors with respect to atom positions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod/local} calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom POD descriptors and their
derivatives with respect to atom positions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod/global} calculates the global POD descriptors and their
derivatives with respect to atom positions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples how to use Compute POD commands are found in the directory
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/PACKAGES/pod}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All of these compute styles produce \sphinxstyleemphasis{very} large per\sphinxhyphen{}atom output
arrays that scale with the total number of atoms in the system.
This will result in \sphinxstyleemphasis{very} large memory consumption for systems
with a large number of atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_pod_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod/atom} produces an 2D array of size \(N \times M\),
where \(N\) is the number of atoms and \(M\) is the number of
descriptors. Each column corresponds to a particular POD descriptor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{podd/atom} produces an 2D array of size \(N \times (M * 3
N)\). Each column corresponds to a particular derivative of a POD
descriptor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod/local} produces an 2D array of size \((1 + 3N) \times
(M * N)\).  The first row contains the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom descriptors, and the last
3N rows contain the derivatives of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom descriptors with respect
to atom positions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod/global} produces an 2D array of size \((1 + 3N) \times
(M)\).  The first row contains the global descriptors, and the last 3N
rows contain the derivatives of the global descriptors with respect to
atom positions.

\label{\detokenize{compute_pod_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes are part of the ML\sphinxhyphen{}POD package.  They are only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.
