\section{compute rdf command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:compute-rdf-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nbin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{itype1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{jtype1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{itype2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{jtype2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rdf = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nbin = number of RDF bins

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
itypeN = central atom type for Nth RDF histogram (integer, type label, or asterisk form)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
jtypeN = distribution atom type for Nth RDF histogram (integer, type label, or asterisk form)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} value = Rcut
  Rcut = cutoff distance for RDF computation (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the radial distribution function
(RDF), also called \(g(r)\), and the coordination number for a group of
particles.  Both are calculated in histogram form by binning pairwise
distances into \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbin} bins from 0.0 to the maximum force cutoff
defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command or the cutoff
distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rcut} specified via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword.  The bins are of
uniform size in radial distance.  Thus a single bin encompasses a thin
shell of distances in 3d and a thin ring of distances in 2d.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise
interactions between atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This
is the default setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command, and means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the
neighbor list.  Because this fix uses a neighbor list, it also means
those pairs will not be included in the RDF. This does not apply when
using long\sphinxhyphen{}range coulomb interactions (\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/msm},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/wolf} or similar.  One way to get around this would be to set
special\_bond scaling factors to very tiny numbers that are not exactly
zero (e.g., \(1.0 \times 10^{-50}\)).  Another workaround is to write a
dump file, and use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to compute the RDF for
snapshots in the dump file.  The rerun script can use a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command that includes all pairs in
the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default the RDF is computed out to the maximum force cutoff defined
by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword
is used, then the RDF is computed accurately out to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rcut} \(> 0.0\)
distance specified.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Normally, you should only use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword if no pair
style is defined (e.g., the {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command is being used to
post\sphinxhyphen{}process a dump file of snapshots) or if you really want the RDF
for distances beyond the pair\_style force cutoff and cannot easily
post\sphinxhyphen{}process a dump file to calculate it.  This is because using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword incurs extra computation and possibly communication,
which may slow down your simulation.  If you specify \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rcut} \(\le\)
force cutoff, you will force an additional neighbor list to be built at
every timestep this command is invoked (or every reneighboring
timestep, whichever is less frequent), which is inefficient.  LAMMPS
will warn you if this is the case.  If you specify a \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rcut} \textgreater{} force
cutoff, you must ensure ghost atom information out to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rcut} + \sphinxstyleemphasis{skin}
is communicated, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify cutoff}}}}
command, else the RDF computation cannot be performed, and LAMMPS will
give an error message.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{skin} value is what is specified with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}} command.  In this case, you are forcing a
large neighbor list to be built just for the RDF computation, and
extra communication to be performed every timestep.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} arguments are optional.  These arguments
must come in pairs.  If no pairs are listed, then a single histogram
is computed for \(g(r)\) between all atom types.  If one or more pairs are
listed, then a separate histogram is generated for each
\sphinxstyleemphasis{itype},\sphinxstyleemphasis{jtype} pair.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} settings can be specified in one of three
ways.  One or both of the types in the I,J pair can be a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_type_labels::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{type label}}}}.  Or an explicit numeric value can be
used, as in the fourth example above. Or a wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk can be used
to specify a range of atom types.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or
“m*” or “m*n”. If \(N\) is the number of atom types, then an asterisk
with no numeric values means all types from 1 to \(N\). A leading
asterisk means all types from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing asterisk
means all types from m to \(N\) (inclusive).  A middle asterisk means
all types from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If both \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} are single values, as in the fourth example
above, this means that a \(g(r)\) is computed where atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN}
are the central atom, and atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} are the distribution
atom.  If either \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} represent a range of values via
the wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk, as in the fifth example above, this means that a
\(g(r)\) is computed where atoms of any of the range of types represented
by \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} are the central atom, and atoms of any of the range of
types represented by \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} are the distribution atom.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pairwise distances are generated by looping over a pairwise neighbor
list, just as they would be in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}}
computation.  The distance between two atoms \(I\) and \(J\) is
included in a specific histogram if the following criteria are met:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
atoms \(I\) and \(J\) are both in the specified compute group

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the distance between atoms \(I\) and \(J\) is less than the maximum
force cutoff

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the type of the \(I\) atom matches \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} (one or a range of types)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the type of the \(J\) atom matches \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} (one or a range of types)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is OK if a particular pairwise distance is included in more than
one individual histogram, due to the way the \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN}
arguments are specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(g(r)\) value for a bin is calculated from the histogram count by
scaling it by the idealized number of how many counts there would be
if atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} were uniformly distributed.  Thus it
involves the count of \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} atoms, the count of \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} atoms, the
volume of the entire simulation box, and the volume of the bin’s thin
shell in 3d (or the area of the bin’s thin ring in 2d).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A coordination number \(\mathrm{coord}(r)\) is also calculated, which is
the number of atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} within the current bin or closer, averaged
over atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN}.  This is calculated as the area\sphinxhyphen{} or
volume\sphinxhyphen{}weighted sum of \(g(r)\) values over all bins up to and including
the current bin, multiplied by the global average volume density of
atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute rdf calculation
to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} command, for
example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myRDF}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myRDF[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.rdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array in which the number of rows is
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nbins} and the number of columns is \(1 + 2N_\text{pairs}\), where
\(N_\text{pairs}\) is the number of \(I,J\) pairings specified.
The first column has the bin coordinate (center of the bin), and each
successive set of two columns has the \(g(r)\) and \(\text{coord}(r)\)
values for a specific set of \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} versus \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN} interactions,
as described above.  These values can be used
by any command that uses a global values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values calculated by this compute are all “intensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first column of array values will be in distance
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The \(g(r)\) columns of array values are normalized
numbers \(\ge 0.0\).  The coordination number columns of array values are
also numbers \(\ge 0.0\).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, the RDF is not computed for distances longer than the
largest force cutoff, since the neighbor list creation will only contain
pairs up to that distance (plus neighbor list skin).  This distance can
be increased using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword but this keyword is only valid
with {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor styles ‘bin’ and ‘nsq’}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want an RDF for larger distances, you can also use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to post\sphinxhyphen{}process a dump file, use {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_zero::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair
style zero}}}} and set the force cutoff to be longer in the
rerun script.  Note that in the rerun context, the force cutoff is
arbitrary and with pair style zero you are not computing any forces, and
you are not running dynamics you are not changing the model that
generated the trajectory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The definition of \(g(r)\) used by LAMMPS is only appropriate for
characterizing atoms that are uniformly distributed throughout the
simulation cell. In such cases, the coordination number is still correct
and meaningful.  As an example, if a large simulation cell contains only
one atom of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{itypeN} and one of \sphinxstyleemphasis{jtypeN}, then \(g(r)\) will
register an arbitrarily large spike at whatever distance they happen to
be at, and zero everywhere else.  The function \(\text{coord}(r)\)
will show a step change from zero to one at the location of the spike in
\(g(r)\).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
compute rdf can handle dynamic groups and systems where atoms
are added or removed, but this causes that certain normalization
parameters need to be re\sphinxhyphen{}computed in every step and include collective
communication operations. This will reduce performance and limit
parallel efficiency and scaling. For systems, where only the type
of atoms changes (e.g., when using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_atom_swap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix atom/swap}}}}),
you need to explicitly request the dynamic normalization updates
via {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify dynamic/dof yes}}}}
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_adf::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute adf}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rdf:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword defaults are cutoff = 0.0 (use the pairwise force cutoff).

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute reaxff/atom/kk@\spxentry{compute reaxff/atom/kk}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute reaxff/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:compute-reaxff-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{reaxff/atom/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reaxff}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{attribute}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
reaxff/atom = name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
attribute = \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} args = nsub
  nsub = \sphinxstyleemphasis{n}\sphinxhyphen{}instance of a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style, if a pair style is used multiple times in a hybrid style
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bonds}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bonds} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = ignore list of local bonds
  \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} = include list of local bonds
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reaxff}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 7Feb2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that extracts bond information computed by the ReaxFF
potential specified by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_reaxff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style reaxff}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, it produces per\sphinxhyphen{}atom data that includes the following columns:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
abo = atom bond order (sum of all bonds)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
nlp = number of lone pairs

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
nb = number of bonds

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Bonds will only be included if its atoms are in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition, if \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{bonds}} is set to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{yes}}, the compute will also produce a
local array of all bonds on the current processor whose atoms are in the group.
The columns of each entry of this local array are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
id\_i = atom i id of bond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
id\_j = atom j id of bond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bo = bond order of bond

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array and local array depending on the
number of keywords. The number of rows in the local array is the number of
bonds as described above. Both per\sphinxhyphen{}atom and local array have 3 columns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The arrays can be accessed by any command that uses local and per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for
an overview of LAMMPS output options.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute reaxff/atom command requires that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_reaxff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style reaxff}}}} is invoked.  This fix is part of the REAXFF package.  It is only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\label{\detokenize{compute_reaxff_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_reaxff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style reaxff}}}}


\subsection{Default}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{bonds} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}.

\section{compute reduce command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:compute-reduce-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}}

\section{compute reduce/region command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:compute-reduce-region-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{reduce} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{reduce/region}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{reduce} arg = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{reduce/region} arg = region\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  region\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of region to use for choosing atoms
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mode = \sphinxstyleemphasis{sum} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{min} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{minabs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{max} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxabs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ave} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumsq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{avesq} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumabs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{aveabs}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more inputs can be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
input = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vx} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{vz} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fx} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} or c\_ID or c\_ID{[}N{]} or f\_ID or f\_ID{[}N{]} or v\_name
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{x},\sphinxstyleemphasis{y},\sphinxstyleemphasis{z},\sphinxstyleemphasis{vx},\sphinxstyleemphasis{vy},\sphinxstyleemphasis{vz},\sphinxstyleemphasis{fx},\sphinxstyleemphasis{fy},\sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} = atom attribute (position, velocity, force component)
c\_ID = per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local vector calculated by a compute with ID
c\_ID{[}I{]} = Ith column of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local array calculated by a compute with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
f\_ID = per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local vector calculated by a fix with ID
f\_ID{[}I{]} = Ith column of per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local array calculated by a fix with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
v\_name = per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector calculated by an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable with name
\end{sphinxalltt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/args pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{replace} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{inputs}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{replace} args = vec1 vec2
  vec1 = reduced value from this input vector will be replaced
  vec2 = replace it with vec1{[}N{]} where N is index of max/min value from vec2
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inputs} arg = peratom or local
  peratom = all inputs are per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities (default)
  local = all input are local quantities
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}force}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{k}{region }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{subbox}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}force}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}press[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}ave}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}myKE}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}press[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{f\PYGZus{}ave}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}myKE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inputs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{peratom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{max}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}index[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}index[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}dist}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{replace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{replace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{max}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{inputs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a calculation that “reduces” one or more vector inputs into
scalar values, one per listed input.  For the compute reduce command,
the inputs can be either per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local quantities and must all be
of the same kind (per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local); see discussion of the optional
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inputs} keyword below.  The compute reduce/region command can only be
used with per\sphinxhyphen{}atom inputs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom attributes are per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{computes}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}} can generate either per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local quantities,
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}} generate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} command and its
special functions which can perform the same reduction operations as
the compute reduce command on global vectors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The reduction operation is specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sum}
option adds the values in the vector into a global total.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{min}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{max} options find the minimum or maximum value across all vector
values.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{minabs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxabs} options find the minimum or maximum
value across all absolute vector values.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ave} setting adds the
vector values into a global total, then divides by the number of
values in the vector.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumsq} option sums the square of the
values in the vector into a global total.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{avesq} setting does
the same as \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumsq}, then divides the sum of squares by the number of
values.  The last two options can be useful for calculating the
variance of some quantity (e.g., variance = sumsq \(-\) ave\(^2\)).  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumabs} option sums the absolute values in the
vector into a global total.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{aveabs} setting does the same as
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sumabs}, then divides the sum of absolute values by the number of
values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each listed input is operated on independently.  For per\sphinxhyphen{}atom inputs,
the group specified with this command means only atoms within the
group contribute to the result.  Likewise for per\sphinxhyphen{}atom inputs, if the
compute reduce/region command is used, the atoms must also currently
be within the region.  Note that an input that produces per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities may define its own group which affects the quantities it
returns.  For example, if a compute is used as an input which
generates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, it will generate values of 0.0 for atoms
that are not in the group specified for that compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each listed input can be an atom attribute (position, velocity, force
component) or can be the result of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or the evaluation of an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for values from a compute or fix, the bracketed index \(I\) can
be specified using a wildcard asterisk with the index to effectively
specify multiple values.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or “m*” or
“m*n”.  If \(N\) is the size of the vector (for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} = scalar) or the
number of columns in the array (for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} = vector), then an asterisk
with no numeric values means all indices from 1 to \(N\).  A leading
asterisk means all indices from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all indices from m to \(N\) (inclusive).  A middle asterisk
means all indices from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a wildcard is the same as if the individual columns of the array
had been listed one by one. For example, the following two compute reduce
commands are equivalent, since the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}} command creates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
array with six columns:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myPress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myPress[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myPress[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myPress[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myPress[3]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                         }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myPress[4]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myPress[5]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myPress[6]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The atom attribute values (\sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fx},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fz}) are self\sphinxhyphen{}explanatory.  Note that other atom attributes
can be used as inputs to this fix by using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
property/atom}}}} command and then specifying an
input value from that compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “c\_”, a compute ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  Valid computes can generate
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local quantities.  See the individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} page for details.  If no bracketed integer is appended, the
vector calculated by the compute is used.  If a bracketed integer is
appended, the Ith column of the array calculated by the compute is
used.  Users can also write code for their own compute styles and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to LAMMPS}}}}.  See the discussion above for how
\(I\) can be specified with a wildcard asterisk to effectively
specify multiple values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “f\_”, a fix ID must follow which has been
previously defined in the input script.  Valid fixes can generate
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local quantities.  See the individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}
page for details.  Note that some fixes only produce their values on
certain timesteps, which must be compatible with when compute reduce
references the values, else an error results.  If no bracketed integer
is appended, the vector calculated by the fix is used.  If a bracketed
integer is appended, the Ith column of the array calculated by the fix
is used.  Users can also write code for their own fix style and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{add them to LAMMPS}}}}.  See the discussion above for how
\(I\) can be specified with a wildcard asterisk to effectively
specify multiple values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a value begins with “v\_”, a variable name must follow which has
been previously defined in the input script.  It must be an
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}.  Atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variables can
reference thermodynamic keywords and various per\sphinxhyphen{}atom attributes, or
invoke other computes, fixes, or variables when they are evaluated, so
this is a very general means of generating per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities to
reduce.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{replace} keyword is used, two indices \sphinxstyleemphasis{vec1} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{vec2} are
specified, where each index ranges from 1 to the number of input
values.  The replace keyword can only be used if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} is \sphinxstyleemphasis{min}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{max}.  It works as follows.  A min/max is computed as usual on
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{vec2} input vector.  The index \(N\) of that value within
\sphinxstyleemphasis{vec2} is also stored.  Then, instead of performing a min/max on the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{vec1} input vector, the stored index is used to select the \(N\)th element of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{vec1} vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, for example, if you wish to use this compute to find the bond
with maximum stretch, you can do it as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{batom1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{batom2}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dist}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{max}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{replace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{replace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}3[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}3[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}3[3]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first two input values in the compute reduce command are vectors
with the IDs of the two atoms in each bond, using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/local}}}} command.  The last input
value is bond distance, using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_bond_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute bond/local}}}} command.  Instead of taking the
max of the two atom ID vectors, which does not yield useful
information in this context, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{replace} keywords will extract the
atom IDs for the two atoms in the bond of maximum stretch.  These atom
IDs and the bond stretch will be printed with thermodynamic output.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 21Nov2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{inputs} keyword allows selection of whether all the inputs are
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local quantities.  As noted above, all the inputs must be
the same kind (per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local).  Per\sphinxhyphen{}atom is the default setting.
If a compute or fix is specified as an input, it must produce per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
or local data to match this setting.  If it produces both, e.g. for
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute voronoi/atom}}}} command, then
this keyword selects between them.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If a single input is specified this compute produces a global scalar
value.  If multiple inputs are specified, this compute produces a
global vector of values, the length of which is equal to the number of
inputs specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed below, for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sum}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumabs}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumsq} modes, the
value(s) produced by this compute are all “extensive”, meaning their
value scales linearly with the number of atoms involved.  If
normalized values are desired, this compute can be accessed by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_style custom}}}} command with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify norm yes}}}} set as an option.  Or it
can be accessed by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}} that divides by the
appropriate atom count.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar if a single input value is
specified or a global vector of length \(N\), where \(N\) is
the number of inputs, and which can be accessed by indices 1 to
\(N\).  These values can be used by any command that uses global
scalar or vector values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto
output}}}} doc page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All the scalar or vector values calculated by this compute are
“intensive”, except when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sum}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumabs}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sumsq} modes are used on
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom or local vectors, in which case the calculated values are
“extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar or vector values will be in whatever {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}
the quantities being reduced are in.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As noted above, the compute reduce/region command can only be used
with per\sphinxhyphen{}atom inputs.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default value for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inputs} keyword is peratom.

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute reduce/chunk@\spxentry{compute reduce/chunk}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute reduce/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:compute-reduce-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
reduce/chunk = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mode = \sphinxstyleemphasis{sum} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{min} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{max}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more inputs can be listed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
input = c\_ID, c\_ID{[}N{]}, f\_ID, f\_ID{[}N{]}, v\_ID

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
c\PYGZus{}ID = per\PYGZhy{}atom vector calculated by a compute with ID
c\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of per\PYGZhy{}atom array calculated by a compute with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
f\PYGZus{}ID = per\PYGZhy{}atom vector calculated by a fix with ID
f\PYGZus{}ID[I] = Ith column of per\PYGZhy{}atom array calculated by a fix with ID, I can include wildcard (see below)
v\PYGZus{}name = per\PYGZhy{}atom vector calculated by an atom\PYGZhy{}style variable with name
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mychunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cluster}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a calculation that reduces one or more per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vectors into
per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values.  This can be useful for diagnostic output.  Or when
used in conjunction with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/spread/atom}}}} command it can be
used to create per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values that induce a new set of chunks with a
second {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  An
example is given below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For each atom, this compute accesses its chunk ID from the specified
\sphinxstyleemphasis{chunkID} compute.  The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom value from an input contributes
to a per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk value corresponding the the chunk ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The reduction operation is specified by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} setting and is
performed over all the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from the atoms in each chunk.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sum} option adds the pre\sphinxhyphen{}atom values to a per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk total.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{min} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{max} options find the minimum or maximum value of the
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values for each chunk.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
reduction operation.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunkID} compute returns a 0 for the
chunk ID of an atom (i.e., the atom is not in a chunk defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command), that atom will
also not contribute to the reduction operation.  An input that is a
compute or fix may define its own group which affects the quantities
it returns.  For example, a compute with return a zero value for atoms
that are not in the group specified for that compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each listed input is operated on independently.  Each input can be the
result of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix}}}} or the evaluation
of an atom\sphinxhyphen{}style {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for values from a compute or fix, the bracketed index I can
be specified using a wildcard asterisk with the index to effectively
specify multiple values.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or “m*” or
“m*n”.  If \(N\) is the size of the vector (for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} = scalar) or the
number of columns in the array (for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mode} = vector), then an asterisk
with no numeric values means all indices from 1 to \(N\).  A leading
asterisk means all indices from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all indices from n to \(N\) (inclusive).  A middle asterisk
means all indices from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a wildcard is the same as if the individual columns of the array
had been listed one by one.  For example, the following two compute reduce/chunk
commands are equivalent, since the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_property_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute property/chunk}}}} command creates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
array with 3 columns:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vz}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mychunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{max}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mychunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{max}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop[3]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of using this compute, in conjunction with the
compute chunk/spread/atom command to identify self\sphinxhyphen{}assembled micelles.
The commands below can be added to the examples/in.micelle script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Imagine a collection of polymer chains or small molecules with
hydrophobic end groups.  All the hydrophobic (HP) atoms are assigned
to a group called “phobic”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands will assign a unique cluster ID to all HP atoms within
a specified distance of each other.  A cluster will contain all HP
atoms in a single molecule, but also the HP atoms in nearby molecules
(e.g., molecules that have clumped to form a micelle due to the
attraction induced by the hydrophobicity).  The output of the
chunk/reduce command will be a cluster ID per chunk (molecule).
Molecules with the same cluster ID are in the same micelle.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{phobic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} specific to in.micelle model}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cluster}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{phobic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cluster}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cmol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{phobic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cmol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cluster}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk info could be output in at least two ways:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.phobic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}

\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{spread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spread}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cmol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}reduce}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cluster}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}spread}
\PYG{k}{dump\PYGZus{}modify }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sort}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{id}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the first case, each snapshot in the tmp.phobic file will contain
one line per molecule.  Molecules with the same value are in the same
micelle.  In the second case each dump snapshot contains all atoms,
each with a final field with the cluster ID of the micelle that the HP
atoms of that atom’s molecule belong to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The result from compute chunk/spread/atom can be used to define a new
set of chunks, where all the atoms in all the molecules in the same
micelle are assigned to the same chunk (i.e., one chunk per micelle).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{micelle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}spread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{compress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Further analysis on a per\sphinxhyphen{}micelle basis can now be performed using any
of the per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk computes listed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc page (e.g., count the number of atoms in each micelle, calculate
its center or mass, shape/moments of inertia, and radius of gyration).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{micelle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{count}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}prop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.micelle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each snapshot in the tmp.micelle file will have one line per micelle
with its count of atoms, plus a first line for a chunk with all the
solvent atoms.  By the time 50000 steps have elapsed, there are a
handful of large micelles.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector if a single input value is
specified, otherwise a global array is output.  The number of columns
in the array is the number of inputs provided.  The length of the
vector or the number of vector elements or array rows = the number of
chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  The vector or array can
be accessed by any command that uses global values from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values for the vector or each column of the array will be
in whatever {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} the corresponding input value is in.
The vector or array values are “intensive”.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_spread_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/spread/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_reduce_chunk:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{compute rheo/property/atom@\spxentry{compute rheo/property/atom}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute rheo/property/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom:compute-rheo-property-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rheo}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rheo/property/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
input = one or more atom attributes

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
possible attributes = phase, surface, surface/r,
                      surface/divr, surface/n/a, coordination,
                      shift/v/a, energy, temperature, heatflow,
                      conductivity, cv, viscosity, pressure, rho,
                      grad/v/ab, stress/v/ab, stress/t/ab, nbond/shell
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{phase} = atom phase state
\sphinxstyleemphasis{surface} = atom surface status
\sphinxstyleemphasis{surface/r} = atom distance from the surface
\sphinxstyleemphasis{surface/divr} = divergence of position at atom position
\sphinxstyleemphasis{surface/n/a} = a\sphinxhyphen{}component of surface normal vector
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coordination} = coordination number
\sphinxstyleemphasis{shift/v/a} = a\sphinxhyphen{}component of atom shifting velocity
\sphinxstyleemphasis{energy} = atom energy
\sphinxstyleemphasis{temperature} = atom temperature
\sphinxstyleemphasis{heatflow} = atom heat flow
\sphinxstyleemphasis{conductivity} = atom conductivity
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cv} = atom specific heat
\sphinxstyleemphasis{viscosity} = atom viscosity
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure} = atom pressure
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rho} = atom density
\sphinxstyleemphasis{grad/v/ab} = ab\sphinxhyphen{}component of atom velocity gradient tensor
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/v/ab} = ab\sphinxhyphen{}component of atom viscous stress tensor
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/t/ab} = ab\sphinxhyphen{}component of atom total stress tensor (pressure and viscous)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nbond/shell} = number of oxide bonds
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rheo}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{phase}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{surface}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{r}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{surface}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{n}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pressure}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rheo}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{v}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{grad}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{v}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{xx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{v}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{o}{*}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 29Aug2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that stores atom attributes specific to the RHEO
package for each atom in the group.  This is useful so that the values
can be used by other {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}} that take
computes as inputs. See for example, the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/atom}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_histo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/histo}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For vector attributes, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift/v/}\(\alpha\), one must specify
\(\alpha\) as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} component, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift/v/x}.
Alternatively, a wild card * will include all components, \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} in
2D or \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} in 3D.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For tensor attributes, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{grad/v/}\(\alpha \beta\), one must specify
both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) as  \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}, e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{grad/v/xy}.
Alternatively, a wild card * will include all components. In 2D, this
includes \sphinxstyleemphasis{xx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yx}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{yy}. In 3D, this includes \sphinxstyleemphasis{xx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{zz}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many properties require their respective fixes, listed below in related
commands, be defined. For instance, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{viscosity} attribute is the
viscosity of a particle calculated by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo_viscosity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo/viscous}}}}. The meaning of less obvious
properties is described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{phase} property indicates whether the particle is in a fluid state,
a value of 0, or a solid state, a value of 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface} property indicates the surface designation produced by
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{interface/reconstruct} option of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo}}}}. Bulk
particles have a value of 0, surface particles have a value of 1, and
splash particles have a value of 2. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface/r} property is the
distance from the surface, up to the kernel cutoff length. Surface particles
have a value of 0. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface/n/}\(\alpha\) properties are the
components of the surface normal vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift/v/}\(\alpha\) properties are the components of the shifting
velocity produced by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} option of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nbond/shell} property is the number of shell bonds that have been
activated from {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_rheo_shell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond style rheo/shell}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values are stored in a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or array as discussed
below.  Zeroes are stored for atoms not in the specified group or for
quantities that are not defined for a particular particle in the group


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rheo_property_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array depending
on the number of input values.  Generally, if a single input is specified,
a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector is produced.  If two or more inputs are specified, a
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array is produced where the number of columns = the number of
inputs. However, if a wild card * is used for a vector or tensor, then
the number of inputs is considered to be incremented by the dimension or
the dimension squared, respectively. The vector or array can be accessed
by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector or array values will be in whatever {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} the
corresponding attribute is in (e.g., density units for \sphinxstyleemphasis{rho}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rheo_oxidation::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rheo/oxdiation}}}},

\section{compute rigid/local command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:compute-rigid-local-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigidID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{input2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rigid/local = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rigidID = ID of fix rigid/small command or one of its variants

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
input = one or more rigid body attributes

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
possible attributes = id, mol, mass,
                      x, y, z, xu, yu, zu, ix, iy, iz
                      vx, vy, vz, fx, fy, fz,
                      omegax, omegay, omegaz,
                      angmomx, angmomy, angmomz,
                      quatw, quati, quatj, quatk,
                      tqx, tqy, tqz,
                      inertiax, inertiay, inertiaz
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
id = atom ID of atom within body which owns body properties
mol = molecule ID used to define body in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} command
mass = total mass of body
x,y,z = center of mass coords of body
xu,yu,zu = unwrapped center of mass coords of body
ix,iy,iz = box image that the center of mass is in
vx,vy,vz = center of mass velocities
fx,fy,fz = force of center of mass
omegax,omegay,omegaz = angular velocity of body
angmomx,angmomy,angmomz = angular momentum of body
quatw,quati,quatj,quatk = quaternion components for body
tqx,tqy,tqz = torque on body
inertiax,inertiay,inertiaz = diagonalized moments of inertia of body
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myRigid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that simply stores rigid body attributes for
rigid bodies defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} command
or one of its NVE, NVT, NPT, NPH variants.  The data is stored as
local data so it can be accessed by other {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}} that process local data, such as the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this command only works with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} command or its variants, not the fix rigid
command and its variants.  The ID of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} command used to define rigid bodies must
be specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{rigidID}.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} command is
typically used to define a handful of (potentially very large) rigid
bodies.  It outputs similar per\sphinxhyphen{}body information as this command
directly from the fix as global data; see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} page for details

\sphinxAtStartPar
The local data stored by this command is generated by looping over all
the atoms owned on a processor.  If the atom is not in the specified
\sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} or is not part of a rigid body it is skipped.  If it is not
the atom within a body that is assigned to store the body information
it is skipped (only one atom per body is so assigned).  If it is the
assigned atom, then the info for that body is output.  This means that
information for \(N\) bodies is generated.  \(N\) may be less than the
number of bodies defined by the fix rigid command, if the atoms in some bodies
are not in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Which atom in a body owns the body info is determined internal
to LAMMPS; it’s the one nearest the geometric center of the body.
Typically you should avoid this complication, by defining the group
associated with this fix to include/exclude entire bodies.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that as atoms and bodies migrate from processor to processor,
there will be no consistent ordering of the entries within the local
vector or array from one timestep to the next.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example of how to use this compute to dump rigid body info
to a file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rigid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myRigid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mol}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fz}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.dump}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[3]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[4]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[5]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[6]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}1[7]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
This section explains the rigid body attributes that can be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{id} attribute is the atom\sphinxhyphen{}ID of the atom which owns the rigid body, which is
assigned by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mol} attribute is the molecule ID of the rigid body.  It should
be the molecule ID which all of the atoms in the body belong to, since
that is how the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}} command defines its
rigid bodies.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mass} attribute is the total mass of the rigid body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two options for outputting the coordinates of the center of
mass (COM) of the body.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} attributes write the COM
“unscaled”, in the appropriate distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}
(\(\AA\), \(\sigma\), etc).  Use \sphinxstyleemphasis{xu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zu} if you want the COM “unwrapped” by
the image flags for each body.  Unwrapped means that if the body
COM has passed through a periodic boundary one or more times, the value
is generated what the COM coordinate would be if it had not been
wrapped back into the periodic box.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The image flags for the body can be generated directly using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ix},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{iy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{iz} attributes.  For periodic dimensions, they specify which
image of the simulation box the COM is considered to be in.  An image
of 0 means it is inside the box as defined.  A value of 2 means add 2
box lengths to get the true value.  A value of \(-1\) means subtract 1 box
length to get the true value.  LAMMPS updates these flags as the rigid
body COMs cross periodic boundaries during the simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{vx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{vz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{fz} attributes are components of
the COM velocity and force on the COM of the body.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{omegax}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omegay}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{omegaz} attributes are the angular
velocity components of the body in the system frame around its COM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{angmomx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{angmomy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{angmomz} attributes are the angular
momentum components of the body in the system frame around its COM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{quatw}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{quati}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{quatj}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{quatk} attributes are the
components of the 4\sphinxhyphen{}vector quaternion representing the orientation of
the rigid body.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set}}}} command for an explanation of
the quaternion vector.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tqx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tqy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tqz} attributes are components of the torque acting
on the body around its COM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{inertiax}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{inertiay}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{inertiaz} attributes are components of
diagonalized inertia tensor for the body (i.e., the three moments of inertia
for the body around its principal axes), as computed internally by
LAMMPS.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a local vector or local array depending on the
number of keywords.  The length of the vector or number of rows in the
array is the number of rigid bodies.  If a single keyword is
specified, a local vector is produced.  If two or more keywords are
specified, a local array is produced where the number of columns = the
number of keywords.  The vector or array can be accessed by any
command that uses local values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS
output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector or array values will be in whatever {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} the
corresponding attribute is in:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
id,mol = unitless

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mass = mass units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
x,y,z and xy,yu,zu = distance units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
vx,vy,vz = velocity units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fx,fy,fz = force units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
omegax,omegay,omegaz = radians/time units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
angmomx,angmomy,angmomz = mass*distance\(^2\)/time units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
quatw,quati,quatj,quatk = unitless

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
tqx,tqy,tqz = torque units

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
inertiax,inertiay,inertiaz = mass*distance\(^2\) units

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the RIGID package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_rigid_local:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_reduce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute reduce}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\index{compute saed@\spxentry{compute saed}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute saed command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_saed:compute-saed-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_saed:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_saed::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_saed:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{saed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lambda}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{typeN}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
saed = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lambda = wavelength of incident radiation (length units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type1 type2 … typeN = chemical symbol of each atom type (see valid options below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{Kmax} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Zone} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dR\_Ewald} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{c} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{manual} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{echo}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Kmax} value = Maximum distance explored from reciprocal space origin
               (inverse length units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Zone} values = z1 z2 z3
  z1,z2,z3 = Zone axis of incident radiation. If z1=z2=z3=0 all
             reciprocal space will be meshed up to \sphinxstyleemphasis{Kmax}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dR\_Ewald} value = Thickness of Ewald sphere slice intercepting
                   reciprocal space (inverse length units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{c} values = c1 c2 c3
  c1,c2,c3 = parameters to adjust the spacing of the reciprocal
             lattice nodes in the h, k, and l directions respectively
\sphinxstyleemphasis{manual} = flag to use manual spacing of reciprocal lattice points
           based on the values of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{c} parameters
\sphinxstyleemphasis{echo} = flag to provide extra output for debugging purposes
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_saed:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{saed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0251}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Kmax}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.70}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Zone}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dR\PYGZus{}Ewald}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
