\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates a set of quantities related to the
bispectrum components of the atoms in a group. These computes are used
primarily for calculating the dependence of energy, force, and stress
components on the linear coefficients in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{snap pair\_style}}}}, which is useful when training a SNAP potential to match
target data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Bispectrum components of an atom are order parameters characterizing the
radial and angular distribution of neighbor atoms. The detailed
mathematical definition is given in the paper by Thompson et
al. {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:thompson20141}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Thompson)}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The position of a neighbor atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i’} relative to a central atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} is a
point within the 3D ball of radius \(R_{ii'}\) = \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcutfac}
\((R_i + R_i')\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
Bartok et al. {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:bartok20101}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bartok)}}}}, proposed mapping this 3D
ball onto the 3\sphinxhyphen{}sphere, the surface of the unit ball in a
four\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional space.  The radial distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{r} within \sphinxstyleemphasis{R\_ii’} is
mapped on to a third polar angle \(\theta_0\) defined by,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\theta_0 = {\sf rfac0} \frac{r-r_{min0}}{R_{ii'}-r_{min0}} \pi\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In this way, all possible neighbor positions are mapped on to a subset
of the 3\sphinxhyphen{}sphere.  Points south of the latitude \(\theta_0\) =
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rfac0} \(\pi\) are excluded.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The natural basis for functions on the 3\sphinxhyphen{}sphere is formed by the
representatives of \sphinxstyleemphasis{SU(2)}, the matrices \(U^j_{m,m'}(\theta, \phi,
\theta_0)\).  These functions are better known as \(D^j_{m,m'}\), the
elements of the Wigner \sphinxstyleemphasis{D}\sphinxhyphen{}matrices {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:meremianin2006}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Meremianin}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:varshalovich1987}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Varshalovich}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:mason2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Mason)}}}} The density of neighbors on the 3\sphinxhyphen{}sphere can be written as
a sum of Dirac\sphinxhyphen{}delta functions, one for each neighbor, weighted by
species and radial distance. Expanding this density function as a
generalized Fourier series in the basis functions, we can write each
Fourier coefficient as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}u^j_{m,m'} = U^j_{m,m'}(0,0,0) + \sum_{r_{ii'} < R_{ii'}}{f_c(r_{ii'}) w_{\mu_{i'}} U^j_{m,m'}(\theta_0,\theta,\phi)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(w_{\mu_{i'}}\) neighbor weights are dimensionless numbers that
depend on \(\mu_{i'}\), the SNAP element of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i’}, while the
central atom is arbitrarily assigned a unit weight.  The function
\(f_c(r)\) ensures that the contribution of each neighbor atom goes
smoothly to zero at \(R_{ii'}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f_c(r)   = & \frac{1}{2}(\cos(\pi \frac{r-r_{min0}}{R_{ii'}-r_{min0}}) + 1), r \leq R_{ii'} \\
         = & 0,  r > R_{ii'}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The expansion coefficients \(u^j_{m,m'}\) are complex\sphinxhyphen{}valued and
they are not directly useful as descriptors, because they are not
invariant under rotation of the polar coordinate frame. However, the
following scalar triple products of expansion coefficients can be shown
to be real\sphinxhyphen{}valued and invariant under rotation {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:bartok20101}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bartok)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}B_{j_1,j_2,j}  =
\sum_{m_1,m'_1=-j_1}^{j_1}\sum_{m_2,m'_2=-j_2}^{j_2}\sum_{m,m'=-j}^{j} (u^j_{m,m'})^*
H {\scriptscriptstyle \begin{array}{l} {j} {m} {m'} \\
     {j_1} {m_1} {m'_1} \\
     {j_2} {m_2} {m'_2} \end{array}}
     u^{j_1}_{m_1,m'_1} u^{j_2}_{m_2,m'_2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The constants \(H^{jmm'}_{j_1 m_1 m_{1'},j_2 m_ 2m_{2'}}\) are
coupling coefficients, analogous to Clebsch\sphinxhyphen{}Gordan coefficients for
rotations on the 2\sphinxhyphen{}sphere. These invariants are the components of the
bispectrum and these are the quantities calculated by the compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}. They characterize the strength of density correlations at
three points on the 3\sphinxhyphen{}sphere. The j2=0 subset form the power spectrum,
which characterizes the correlations of two points. The lowest\sphinxhyphen{}order
components describe the coarsest features of the density function, while
higher\sphinxhyphen{}order components reflect finer detail. Each bispectrum component
contains terms that depend on the positions of up to 4 atoms (3
neighbors and the central atom).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} calculates the derivative of the bispectrum
components summed separately for each LAMMPS atom type:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\sum_{i' \in I} \frac{\partial {B^{i'}_{j_1,j_2,j}  }}{\partial {\bf r}_i}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sum is over all atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i’} of atom type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}.  For each atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i},
this compute evaluates the above expression for each direction, each
atom type, and each bispectrum component.  See section below on output
for a detailed explanation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom} calculates the virial contribution due to the
derivatives:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-{\bf r}_i \otimes \sum_{i' \in I} \frac{\partial {B^{i'}_{j_1,j_2,j}}}{\partial {\bf r}_i}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Again, the sum is over all atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i’} of atom type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}.  For each atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i}, this compute evaluates the above expression for each of the six
virial components, each atom type, and each bispectrum component.  See
section below on output for a detailed explanation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} calculates a global array containing information related
to all three of the above per\sphinxhyphen{}atom computes \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom}. The first row of the array contains the summation of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom} over all atoms, but broken out by type. The last six rows of
the array contain the summation of \sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom} over all atoms, broken
out by type. In between these are 3*\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} rows containing the same
values computed by \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} (these are already summed over all atoms
and broken out by type). The element in the last column of each row
contains the potential energy, force, or stress, according to the row.
These quantities correspond to the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified reference potential
that must be subtracted from the target data when fitting SNAP.  The
potential energy calculation uses the built in compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{thermo\_pe}.  The
stress calculation uses a compute called \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap\_press} that is
automatically created behind the scenes, according to the following
command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{snap\PYGZus{}press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pressure}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{virial}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See section below on output for a detailed explanation of the data
layout in the global array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 3Aug2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid/local} commands calculate
bispectrum components for a regular grid of points.  These are
calculated from the local density of nearby atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i’} around each grid
point, as if there was a central atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} at the grid point. This is
useful for characterizing fine\sphinxhyphen{}scale structure in a configuration of
atoms, and it is used in the \sphinxhref{https://github.com/casus/mala}{MALA package} to build machine\sphinxhyphen{}learning surrogates
for finite\sphinxhyphen{}temperature Kohn\sphinxhyphen{}Sham density functional theory ({\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:ellis2021}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Ellis
et al.}}}}) Neighbor atoms not in the group do not contribute
to the bispectrum components of the grid points. The distance cutoff
\(R_{ii'}\) assumes that \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} has the same type as the neighbor atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i’}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid} calculates a global array containing bispectrum
components for a regular grid of points.
The grid is aligned with the current box dimensions, with the
first point at the box origin, and forming a regular 3d array with
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{ny}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{nz} points in the x, y, and z directions. For triclinic
boxes, the array is congruent with the periodic lattice vectors
a, b, and c. The array contains one row for each of the
\(nx \times ny \times nz\) grid points, looping over the index for \sphinxstyleemphasis{ix} fastest,
then \sphinxstyleemphasis{iy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{iz} slowest.  Each row of the array contains the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} coordinates of the grid point, followed by the bispectrum
components. See section below on output for a detailed explanation of the data
layout in the global array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid/local} calculates bispectrum components of a regular
grid of points similarly to compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid} described above.
However, because the array is local, it contains only rows for grid points
that are local to the processor subdomain. The global grid
of \(nx \times ny \times nz\) points is still laid out in space the same as for \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid},
but grid points are strictly partitioned, so that every grid point appears in
one and only one local array.  The array contains one row for each of the
local grid points, looping over the global index \sphinxstyleemphasis{ix} fastest,
then \sphinxstyleemphasis{iy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{iz} slowest.  Each row of the array contains
the global indexes \sphinxstyleemphasis{ix}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{iy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{iz} first, followed by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} coordinates of the grid point, followed by the bispectrum
components. See section below on output for a detailed explanation of the data
layout in the global array.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of all bispectrum components will be zero for atoms not in
the group. Neighbor atoms not in the group do not contribute to the
bispectrum of atoms in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The neighbor list needed to compute this quantity is constructed each
time the calculation is performed (i.e. each time a snapshot of atoms
is dumped).  Thus it can be inefficient to compute/dump this quantity
too frequently.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcutfac} is a scale factor that controls the ratio of
atomic radius to radial cutoff distance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{rfac0} and the optional keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmin0} define the
linear mapping from radial distance to polar angle \(theta_0\) on the
3\sphinxhyphen{}sphere, given above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{twojmax} defines which
bispectrum components are generated. See section below on output for a
detailed explanation of the number of bispectrum components and the
ordered in which they are listed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{switchflag} can be used to turn off the switching
function \(f_c(r)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{bzeroflag} determines whether or not \sphinxstyleemphasis{B0}, the bispectrum
components of an atom with no neighbors, are subtracted from the
calculated bispectrum components. This optional keyword normally only
affects compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}. However, when \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadraticflag} is on, it
also affects \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadraticflag} determines whether or not the quadratic
combinations of bispectrum quantities are generated.  These are formed
by taking the outer product of the vector of bispectrum components with
itself.  See section below on output for a detailed explanation of the
number of quadratic terms and the ordered in which they are listed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{chem} activates the explicit multi\sphinxhyphen{}element variant of the
SNAP bispectrum components. The argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelements} specifies the
number of SNAP elements that will be handled.  This is followed by
\sphinxstyleemphasis{elementlist}, a list of integers of length \sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes}, with values in the
range {[}0, \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelements} ), which maps each LAMMPS type to one of the SNAP
elements.  Note that multiple LAMMPS types can be mapped to the same
element, and some elements may be mapped by no LAMMPS type. However, in
typical use cases (training SNAP potentials) the mapping from LAMMPS
types to elements is one\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}one.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The explicit multi\sphinxhyphen{}element variant invoked by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chem} keyword
partitions the density of neighbors into partial densities for each
chemical element.  This is described in detail in the paper by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:cusentino2020}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Cusentino et al.}}}} The bispectrum components are
indexed on ordered triplets of elements:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}B_{j_1,j_2,j}^{\kappa\lambda\mu} =
\sum_{m_1,m'_1=-j_1}^{j_1}\sum_{m_2,m'_2=-j_2}^{j_2}\sum_{m,m'=-j}^{j} (u^{\mu}_{j,m,m'})^*
H {\scriptscriptstyle \begin{array}{l} {j} {m} {m'} \\
     {j_1} {m_1} {m'_1} \\
     {j_2} {m_2} {m'_2} \end{array}}
     u^{\kappa}_{j_1,m_1,m'_1} u^{\lambda}_{j_2,m_2,m'_2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(u^{\mu}_{j,m,m'}\) is an expansion coefficient for the partial density of neighbors
of element \(\mu\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}u^{\mu}_{j,m,m'} =  w^{self}_{\mu_{i}\mu} U^{j,m,m'}(0,0,0) + \sum_{r_{ii'} < R_{ii'}}{\delta_{\mu\mu_{i'}}f_c(r_{ii'}) w_{\mu_{i'}} U^{j,m,m'}(\theta_0,\theta,\phi)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(w^{self}_{\mu_{i}\mu}\) is the self\sphinxhyphen{}contribution, which is
either 1 or 0 (see keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{wselfallflag} below),
\(\delta_{\mu\mu_{i'}}\) indicates that the sum is only over
neighbor atoms of element \(\mu\), and all other quantities are the
same as those appearing in the original equation for \(u^j_{m,m'}\)
given above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{wselfallflag} defines the rule used for the
self\sphinxhyphen{}contribution.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{wselfallflag} is on, then
\(w^{self}_{\mu_{i}\mu}\) = 1. If it is off then
\(w^{self}_{\mu_{i}\mu}\) = 0, except in the case of
\({\mu_{i}=\mu}\), when \(w^{self}_{\mu_{i}\mu}\) = 1.  When the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{chem} keyword is not used, this keyword has no effect.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{bnormflag} determines whether or not the bispectrum
component \(B_{j_1,j_2,j}\) is divided by a factor of \(2j+1\).
This normalization simplifies force calculations because of the
following symmetry relation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{B_{j_1,j_2,j}}{2j+1} = \frac{B_{j,j_2,j_1}}{2j_1+1} = \frac{B_{j_1,j,j_2}}{2j_2+1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This option is typically used in conjunction with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chem} keyword,
and LAMMPS will generate a warning if both \sphinxstyleemphasis{chem} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{bnormflag}
are not both set or not both unset.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{switchinnerflag} with value 1
activates an additional radial switching
function similar to \(f_c(r)\) above, but acting to switch off
smoothly contributions from neighbor atoms at short separation distances.
This is useful when SNAP is used in combination with a simple
repulsive potential. For a neighbor atom at
distance \(r\), its contribution is scaled by a multiplicative
factor \(f_{inner}(r)\) defined as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}             = & 0,  r \leq S_{inner} - D_{inner} \\
f_{inner}(r) = & \frac{1}{2}(1 - \cos(\frac{\pi}{2} (1 + \frac{r-S_{inner}}{D_{inner}})), S_{inner} - D_{inner} < r \leq S_{inner} + D_{inner} \\
             = & 1,  r > S_{inner} + D_{inner}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the switching region is centered at \(S_{inner}\) and it extends a distance \(D_{inner}\)
to the left and to the right of this.
With this option, additional keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{sinner} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dinner} must be used,
each followed by \sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes}
values for \(S_{inner}\) and \(D_{inner}\), respectively.
When the central atom and the neighbor atom have different types,
the values of \(S_{inner}\) and \(D_{inner}\) are
the arithmetic means of the values for both types.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} are only used by compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap}.
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} determines whether or not to list the descriptors
of each atom separately, or sum them together and list in a single row.
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} is set
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{0} then a single bispectrum row is used, which contains the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom bispectrum
descriptors \(B_{i,k}\) summed over all atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} to produce
\(B_k\).  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} is set
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{1} this is replaced by a separate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom bispectrum row for each atom.
In this case, the entries in the final column for these rows
are set to zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} determines whether to sum atom gradients or list
them separately. If \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} is set to 0, the bispectrum
descriptor gradients w.r.t. atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} are summed over all atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i’}
of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I} (similar to \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} above).
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} is set to 1, gradients are listed separately for each pair of atoms.
Each row corresponds
to a single term \(\frac{\partial {B_{i,k}  }}{\partial {r}^a_j}\)
where \({r}^a_j\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a\sphinxhyphen{}th} position coordinate of the atom with global
index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}. This also changes
the number of columns to be equal to the number of bispectrum components, with 3
additional columns representing the indices \(i\), \(j\), and \(a\),
as explained more in the Output info section below. The option \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag=1}
requires that \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag=1}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} = 1 produces a global array with \(N + 3N^2 + 1\) rows
which becomes expensive for systems with more than 1000 atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a bonded system, then the settings of {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command can remove pairwise interactions between
atoms in the same bond, angle, or dihedral.  This is the default
setting for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command, and
means those pairwise interactions do not appear in the neighbor list.
Because this fix uses the neighbor list, it also means those pairs
will not be included in the calculation.  One way to get around this,
is to write a dump file, and use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{rerun::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{rerun}}}} command to
compute the bispectrum components for snapshots in the dump file.
The rerun script can use a {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}}
command that includes all pairs in the neighbor list.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} allows for the calculation of the bispectrum over a
specific target number of neighbors. This option is only implemented for
the compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}.  An optimal cutoff radius for defining the
neighborhood of the central atom is calculated by means of a dichotomy
algorithm.  This iterative process allows to assign weights to
neighboring atoms in order to match the total sum of weights with the
target number of neighbors.  Depending on the radial weight function
used in that process, the cutoff radius can fluctuate a lot in the
presence of thermal noise.  Therefore, in addition to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} keyword,
the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{wmode} allows to choose whether a Heaviside (\sphinxstyleemphasis{wmode} = 0)
function or a Hyperbolic tangent function (\sphinxstyleemphasis{wmode} = 1) should be used.
If the Heaviside function is used, the cutoff radius exactly matches the
distance between the central atom an its \sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn}’th neighbor.  However, in
the case of the hyperbolic tangent function, the dichotomy algorithm
allows to span the weights over a distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta} in order to reduce
fluctuations in the resulting local atomic environment fingerprint.  The
detailed formalism is given in the paper by Lafourcade et
al. {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:lafourcade2023-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Lafourcade)}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom} calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array, each column
corresponding to a particular bispectrum component.  The total number of
columns and the identity of the bispectrum component contained in each
column depend of the value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{twojmax}, as described by the following
piece of python code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
for j1 in range(0,twojmax+1):
    for j2 in range(0,j1+1):
        for j in range(j1\PYGZhy{}j2,min(twojmax,j1+j2)+1,2):
            if (j\PYGZgt{}=j1): print j1/2.,j2/2.,j/2.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are \(m(m+1)/2\) descriptors with last index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j},
where \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} = \(\lfloor j \rfloor + 1\).
Hence, for even \sphinxstyleemphasis{twojmax} = 2(\sphinxstyleemphasis{m}\sphinxhyphen{}1), \(K = m(m+1)(2m+1)/6\), the \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}\sphinxhyphen{}th pyramidal number,
and for odd \sphinxstyleemphasis{twojmax} = 2 \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}\sphinxhyphen{}1, \(K = m(m+1)(m+2)/3\), twice the \sphinxstyleemphasis{m}\sphinxhyphen{}th tetrahedral number.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{diagonal} keyword allowing other possible choices
for the number of bispectrum components was removed in 2019,
since all potentials use the value of 3, corresponding to the
above set of bispectrum components.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} evaluates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array. The columns are arranged
into \sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes} blocks, listed in order of atom type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}.  Each block
contains three sub\sphinxhyphen{}blocks corresponding to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
components of the atom position.  Each of these sub\sphinxhyphen{}blocks contains \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}
columns for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} bispectrum components, the same as for compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom} evaluates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array. The columns are arranged
into \sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes} blocks, listed in order of atom type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}.  Each block
contains six sub\sphinxhyphen{}blocks corresponding to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{xx}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{yy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{zz},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{yz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{xz}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{xy} components of the virial tensor in Voigt
notation.  Each of these sub\sphinxhyphen{}blocks contains \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} columns for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}
bispectrum components, the same as for compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} evaluates a global array.  The columns are arranged into
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes} blocks, listed in order of atom type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}. Each block contains
one column for each bispectrum component, the same as for compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}. A final column contains the corresponding energy, force
component on an atom, or virial stress component. The rows of the array
appear in the following order:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1 row: \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom} quantities summed for all atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
3*\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} rows: \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} quantities, with derivatives w.r.t. x, y, and z coordinate of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} appearing in consecutive rows. The atoms are sorted based on atom ID.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
6 rows: \sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom} quantities summed for all atoms of type \sphinxstyleemphasis{I}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, if \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} =30 and ntypes=1, the number of columns in the
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom arrays generated by \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom} are 30, 90, and 180, respectively. With \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic} value=1,
the numbers of columns are 930, 2790, and 5580, respectively.  The
number of columns in the global array generated by \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} are 31, and
931, respectively, while the number of rows is 1+3*\sphinxstyleemphasis{N}+6, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
is the total number of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid} evaluates a global array.
The array contains one row for each of the
\(nx \times ny \times nz\) grid points, looping over the index for \sphinxstyleemphasis{ix} fastest,
then \sphinxstyleemphasis{iy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{iz} slowest.  Each row of the array contains the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} coordinates of the grid point, followed by the bispectrum
components.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/grid/local} evaluates a local array.
The array contains one row for each of the
local grid points, looping over the global index \sphinxstyleemphasis{ix} fastest,
then \sphinxstyleemphasis{iy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{iz} slowest.  Each row of the array contains
the global indexes \sphinxstyleemphasis{ix}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{iy}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{iz} first, followed by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} coordinates of the grid point, followed by the bispectrum
components.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic} keyword value is set to 1, then additional columns
are generated, corresponding to the products of all distinct pairs of
bispectrum components. If the number of bispectrum components is \sphinxstyleemphasis{K},
then the number of distinct pairs is \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}(\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}+1)/2.  For compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sna/atom} these columns are appended to existing \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} columns.  The
ordering of quadratic terms is upper\sphinxhyphen{}triangular, (1,1),(1,2)…(1,\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}),(2,1)…(\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}1,\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}1),(\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}1,\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}),(\sphinxstyleemphasis{K},\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}).
For computes \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{snav/atom} each set of \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}(\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}+1)/2
additional columns is inserted directly after each of sub\sphinxhyphen{}block of
linear terms i.e. linear and quadratic terms are contiguous.  So the
nesting order from inside to outside is bispectrum component, linear
then quadratic, vector/tensor component, type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chem} keyword is used, then the data is arranged into
\(N_{elem}^3\) sub\sphinxhyphen{}blocks, each sub\sphinxhyphen{}block corresponding to a
particular chemical labeling \(\kappa\lambda\mu\) with the last
label changing fastest.  Each sub\sphinxhyphen{}block contains \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} bispectrum
components. For the purposes of handling contributions to force, virial,
and quadratic combinations, these \(N_{elem}^3\) sub\sphinxhyphen{}blocks are
treated as a single block of \(K N_{elem}^3\) columns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bik} keyword is set to 1, the structure of the snap array is expanded.
The first \(N\) rows of the snap array
correspond to \(B_{i,k}\) instead of a single row summed over atoms \(i\).
In this case, the entries in the final column for these rows
are set to zero. Also, each row contains only non\sphinxhyphen{}zero entries for the
columns corresponding to the type of that atom. This is not true in the case
of \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} keyword = 1 (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dgradflag} keyword is set to 1, this changes the structure of the
global array completely.
Here the \sphinxstyleemphasis{snad/atom} quantities are replaced with rows corresponding to
descriptor gradient components on single atoms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\partial {B_{i,k}  }}{\partial {r}^a_j}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \({r}^a_j\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{a\sphinxhyphen{}th} position coordinate of the atom with global
index \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}. The rows are
organized in chunks, where each chunk corresponds to an atom with global index
\(j\). The rows in an atom \(j\) chunk correspond to
atoms with global index \(i\). The total number of rows for
these descriptor gradients is therefore \(3N^2\).
The number of columns is equal to the number of bispectrum components,
plus 3 additional left\sphinxhyphen{}most columns representing the global atom indices
\(i\), \(j\),
and Cartesian direction \(a\)  (0, 1, 2, for x, y, z).
The first 3 columns of the first \(N\) rows belong to the reference
potential force components. The remaining K columns contain the
\(B_{i,k}\) per\sphinxhyphen{}atom descriptors corresponding to the non\sphinxhyphen{}zero entries
obtained when \sphinxstyleemphasis{bikflag} = 1.
The first column of the last row, after the first
\(N + 3N^2\) rows, contains the reference potential
energy. The virial components are not used with this option. The total number of
rows is therefore \(N + 3N^2 + 1\) and the number of columns is \(K + 3\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
These values can be accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options. To see how this command
can be used within a Python workflow to train SNAP potentials, see the
examples in \sphinxhref{https://github.com/FitSNAP/FitSNAP}{FitSNAP}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes are part of the ML\sphinxhyphen{}SNAP package.  They are only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style snap}}}}
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_slcsa_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute slcsa/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sna_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional keyword defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmin0} = 0,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{switchflag} = 1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bzeroflag} = 1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadraticflag} = 0,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bnormflag} = 0, \sphinxstyleemphasis{wselfallflag} = 0, \sphinxstyleemphasis{switchinnerflag} = 0,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{nnn} = \sphinxhyphen{}1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{wmode} = 0, \sphinxstyleemphasis{delta} = 1.e\sphinxhyphen{}3

\section{compute sph/e/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:compute-sph-e-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sph}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{e}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
sph/e/atom = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sph}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{e}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom internal energy
for each atom in a group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The internal energy is the energy associated with the internal degrees
of freedom of an SPH particle, i.e. a Smooth\sphinxhyphen{}Particle Hydrodynamics
particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See \sphinxhref{PDF/SPH\_LAMMPS\_userguide.pdf}{this PDF guide} to using SPH in
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the internal energy will be 0.0 for atoms not in the
specified compute group.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the SPH package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_e_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

sph/rho/atom = style name of this compute command

\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_rho_atom:examples}}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_rho_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom SPH density for each
atom in a group, i.e. a Smooth\sphinxhyphen{}Particle Hydrodynamics density.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The SPH density is the mass density of an SPH particle, calculated by
kernel function interpolation using “pair style sph/rhosum”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See \sphinxhref{PDF/SPH\_LAMMPS\_userguide.pdf}{this PDF guide} to using SPH in
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the SPH density will be 0.0 for atoms not in the
specified compute group.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_rho_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be in mass/volume {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_t_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sph}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
sph/t/atom = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_t_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sph}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{t}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_t_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom internal temperature
for each atom in a group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The internal temperature is the ratio of internal energy over the heat
capacity associated with the internal degrees of freedom of an SPH
particles, i.e. a Smooth\sphinxhyphen{}Particle Hydrodynamics particle.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}T_{int} = E_{int} / C_{V,int}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See \sphinxhref{PDF/SPH\_LAMMPS\_userguide.pdf}{this PDF guide} to using SPH in
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The value of the internal energy will be 0.0 for atoms not in the
specified compute group.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_t_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input.  See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of
LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_sph_t_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{compute spin command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:compute-spin-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_spin::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
spin = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{out\PYGZus{}mag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates magnetic quantities for a system
of atoms having spins.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates the following 6 magnetic quantities:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the three first quantities are the x,y and z coordinates of the total
magnetization,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the fourth quantity is the norm of the total magnetization,

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The fifth quantity is the magnetic energy (in eV),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sixth one is referred to as the spin temperature, according
to the work of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_spin:nurdin1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nurdin)}}}}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute spin calculation
is to define some of the quantities as variables, and to use the thermo and
thermo\_style commands, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{out\PYGZus{}mag}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}

\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mag\PYGZus{}z}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}out\PYGZus{}mag[3]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mag\PYGZus{}norm}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}out\PYGZus{}mag[4]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{temp\PYGZus{}mag}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}out\PYGZus{}mag[6]}

\PYG{k}{thermo}\PYG{+w}{                  }\PYG{l+m}{10}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}mag\PYGZus{}z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}mag\PYGZus{}norm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}temp\PYGZus{}mag}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This series of commands evaluates the total magnetization along z, the norm of
the total magnetization, and the magnetic temperature. Three variables are
assigned to those quantities. The thermo and thermo\_style commands print them
every 10 timesteps.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
metal units ({\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}).


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin} compute is part of the SPIN package.  This compute is only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with this package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.  The atom\_style
has to be “spin” for this compute to be valid.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Related commands:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_spin:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Nurdin)} Nurdin and Schotte Phys Rev E, 61(4), 3579 (2000)

\section{compute stress/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:compute-stress-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}}

\section{compute centroid/stress/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:compute-centroid-stress-atom-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of compute that calculates temperature, can be NULL if not needed

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{improper} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myRamp}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{centroid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dihedral}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{improper}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that computes per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress tensor for each
atom in a group.  In case of compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom}, the tensor for
each atom is symmetric with 6 components and is stored as a 6\sphinxhyphen{}element
vector in the following order: \(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\),
\(xy\), \(xz\), \(yz\).  In case of compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom}, the tensor for each atom is asymmetric with 9
components and is stored as a 9\sphinxhyphen{}element vector in the following order:
\(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\),
\(yz\), \(yx\), \(zx\), \(zy\).  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
pressure}}}} command if you want the stress tensor
(pressure) of the entire system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The stress tensor for atom \(I\) is given by the following
formula, where \(a\) and \(b\) take on values \(x\),
\(y\), \(z\) to generate the components of the tensor:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S_{ab}  =  - m v_a v_b - W_{ab}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first term is a kinetic energy contribution for atom \(I\).
See details below on how the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp\sphinxhyphen{}ID} can affect the
velocities used in this calculation. The second term is the virial
contribution due to intra and intermolecular interactions, where the
exact computation details are determined by the compute style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In case of compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom}, the virial contribution is:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} W_{ab} & = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_p} (r_{1_a} F_{1_b} + r_{2_a} F_{2_b}) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_b} (r_{1_a} F_{1_b} + r_{2_a} F_{2_b})  \\
& + \frac{1}{3} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_a} (r_{1_a} F_{1_b} + r_{2_a} F_{2_b} + r_{3_a} F_{3_b}) + \frac{1}{4} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_d} (r_{1_a} F_{1_b} + r_{2_a} F_{2_b} + r_{3_a} F_{3_b} + r_{4_a} F_{4_b}) \\
& + \frac{1}{4} \sum_{n = 1}^{N_i} (r_{1_a} F_{1_b} + r_{2_a} F_{2_b} + r_{3_a} F_{3_b} + r_{4_a} F_{4_b}) + {\rm Kspace}(r_{i_a},F_{i_b}) + \sum_{n = 1}^{N_f} r_{i_a} F_{i_b}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first term is a pairwise energy contribution where \(n\) loops
over the \(N_p\) neighbors of atom \(I\), \(\mathbf{r}_1\)
and \(\mathbf{r}_2\) are the positions of the two atoms in the
pairwise interaction, and \(\mathbf{F}_1\) and
\(\mathbf{F}_2\) are the forces on the two atoms resulting from the
pairwise interaction.  The second term is a bond contribution of
similar form for the \(N_b\) bonds which atom \(I\) is part
of.  There are similar terms for the \(N_a\) angle, \(N_d\)
dihedral, and \(N_i\) improper interactions atom \(I\) is part
of.  There is also a term for the KSpace contribution from long\sphinxhyphen{}range
Coulombic interactions, if defined.  Finally, there is a term for the
\(N_f\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fixes}}}} that apply internal constraint forces
to atom \(I\). Currently, only the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} commands contribute to this term.  As
the coefficients in the formula imply, a virial contribution produced
by a small set of atoms (e.g. 4 atoms in a dihedral or 3 atoms in a
Tersoff 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction) is assigned in equal portions to each atom
in the set.  E.g. 1/4 of the dihedral virial to each of the 4 atoms,
or 1/3 of the fix virial due to SHAKE constraints applied to atoms in
a water molecule via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command.
As an exception, the virial contribution from
constraint forces in {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}} on each atom
is computed from the constraint force acting on the corresponding atom
and its position, i.e. the total virial is not equally distributed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In case of compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom}, the virial contribution is:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} W_{ab} & = \sum_{n = 1}^{N_p} r_{I0_a} F_{I_b} + \sum_{n = 1}^{N_b} r_{I0_a} F_{I_b} + \sum_{n = 1}^{N_a} r_{I0_a}  F_{I_b} + \sum_{n = 1}^{N_d} r_{I0_a} F_{I_b} + \sum_{n = 1}^{N_i} r_{I0_a} F_{I_b} \\
& + {\rm Kspace}(r_{i_a},F_{i_b}) + \sum_{n = 1}^{N_f} r_{i_a} F_{i_b}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As with compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom}, the first, second, third, fourth and
fifth terms are pairwise, bond, angle, dihedral and improper
contributions, but instead of assigning the virial contribution
equally to each atom, only the force \(\mathbf{F}_I\) acting on
atom \(I\) due to the interaction and the relative position
\(\mathbf{r}_{I0}\) of the atom \(I\) to the geometric center
of the interacting atoms, i.e. centroid, is used.  As the geometric
center is different for each interaction, the \(\mathbf{r}_{I0}\)
also differs. The sixth term, Kspace contribution,
is computed identically to compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom}.
The seventh term is handed differently depending on
if the constraint forces are due to {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.
In case of SHAKE constraints, each distance constraint is
handed as a pairwise interaction.
E.g. in case of a water molecule, two OH and one HH distance
constraints are treated as three pairwise interactions.
In case of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}},
all constraint forces in the molecule are treated
as a single many\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction with a single centroid position.
In case of water molecule, the formula expression would become
identical to that of the three\sphinxhyphen{}body angle interaction.
Although the total system virial is the same as
compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom}, compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom} is know to
result in more consistent heat flux values for angle, dihedrals,
improper and constraint force contributions
when computed via {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute heat/flux}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If no extra keywords are listed, the kinetic contribution \sphinxstyleemphasis{and} all
of the virial contribution terms are included in the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress
tensor.  If any extra keywords are listed, only those terms are
summed to compute the tensor.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{virial} keyword means include all
terms except the kinetic energy \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the stress for each atom is due to its interaction with all
other atoms in the simulation, not just with other atoms in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Details of how compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom} obtains the virial for individual
atoms for either pairwise or many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials, and including the
effects of periodic boundary conditions is discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:thompson2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Thompson)}}}}.  The basic idea for many\sphinxhyphen{}body
potentials is to treat each component of the force computation between
a small cluster of atoms in the same manner as in the formula above
for bond, angle, dihedral, etc interactions.  Namely the quantity
\(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{F}\) is summed over the atoms in the
interaction, with the \(r\) vectors unwrapped by periodic
boundaries so that the cluster of atoms is close together.  The total
contribution for the cluster interaction is divided evenly among those
atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Details of how compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom} obtains the virial for
individual atoms are given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:surblys1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Surblys2019)}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:surblys2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Surblys2021)}}}}, where the
idea is that the virial of the atom \(I\) is the result of only
the force \(\mathbf{F}_I\) on the atom due to the interaction and
its positional vector \(\mathbf{r}_{I0}\), relative to the
geometric center of the interacting atoms, regardless of the number of
participating atoms.  The periodic boundary treatment is identical to
that of compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom}, and both of them reduce to identical
expressions for two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions, i.e. computed values for
contributions from bonds and two\sphinxhyphen{}body pair styles, such as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones}}}}, will be the same, while contributions
from angles, dihedrals and impropers will be different.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style charmm}}}} style calculates
pairwise interactions between 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 atoms.  The virial contribution of
these terms is included in the pair virial, not the dihedral virial.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The KSpace contribution is calculated using the method in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:heyes2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Heyes)}}}} for the Ewald method and by the methodology
described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:sirk1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sirk)}}}} for PPPM.  The choice of KSpace
solver is specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm}}}}
command.  Note that for PPPM, the calculation requires 6 extra FFTs
each timestep that per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress is calculated.  Thus it can
significantly increase the cost of the PPPM calculation if it is
needed on a large fraction of the simulation timesteps.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp\sphinxhyphen{}ID} argument can be used to affect the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom velocities
used in the kinetic energy contribution to the total stress.  If the
kinetic energy is not included in the stress, than the temperature
compute is not used and can be specified as NULL.  If the kinetic
energy is included and you wish to use atom velocities as\sphinxhyphen{}is, then
\sphinxstyleemphasis{temp\sphinxhyphen{}ID} can also be specified as NULL.  If desired, the specified
temperature compute can be one that subtracts off a bias to leave each
atom with only a thermal velocity to use in the formula above, e.g. by
subtracting a background streaming velocity.  See the doc pages for
individual {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute commands}}}} to determine which ones
include a bias.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that as defined in the formula, per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress is the negative
of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom pressure tensor.  It is also really a stress*volume
formulation, meaning the computed quantity is in units of
pressure*volume.  It would need to be divided by a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom volume to
have units of stress (pressure), but an individual atom’s volume is
not well defined or easy to compute in a deformed solid or a liquid.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute voronoi/atom}}}} command for
one possible way to estimate a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom volume.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, if the diagonal components of the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress tensor are
summed for all atoms in the system and the sum is divided by
\(dV\), where \(d\) = dimension and \(V\) is the volume of
the system, the result should be \(-P\), where \(P\) is the
total pressure of the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These lines in an input script for a 3d system should yield that
result. I.e. the last 2 columns of thermo output will be the same:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{peratom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{compute        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}peratom[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}peratom[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}peratom[3]}
\PYG{k}{variable       }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{c\PYGZus{}p[1]+c\PYGZus{}p[2]+c\PYGZus{}p[3]}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{3*vol}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{etotal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}press}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress does not include any Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones tail
corrections to the pressure added by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify tail yes}}}} command, since those are contributions to the global
system pressure.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute stress/atom can be used in a number of ways.  Here is an
example to compute a 1\sphinxhyphen{}d pressure profile in x\sphinxhyphen{}direction across the
complete simulation box. You will need to adjust the number of bins and the
selections for time averaging to your specific simulation.  This assumes
that the dimensions of the simulation cell does not change.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} set number of bins}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{nbins}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fraction}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}nbins}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} define bins as chunks}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cchunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{d}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{fraction}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduced}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{stress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} apply conversion to pressure early since we have no variable style for processing chunks}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{press}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{c\PYGZus{}stress[1]+c\PYGZus{}stress[2]+c\PYGZus{}stress[3]}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{3.0*vol*\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}fraction\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{binpress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cchunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}press}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{avg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{40}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{400}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}binpress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave\PYGZus{}stress.txt}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom} calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with 6 columns,
which can be accessed by indices 1\sphinxhyphen{}6 by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
values from a compute as input.  Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom}
produces a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with 9 columns, but otherwise can be used in
an identical manner to compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom}.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto
output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output
options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ordering of the 6 columns for \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/atom} is as follows: xx, yy,
zz, xy, xz, yz.  The ordering of the 9 columns for
\sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom} is as follows: xx, yy, zz, xy, xz, yz, yx, zx,
zy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array values will be in pressure*volume {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} as discussed above.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{centroid/stress/atom} does not support pair styles
with many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{EAM}}}} is an exception,
since its computations are performed pairwise), nor granular pair
styles with pairwise forces which are not aligned with the vector
between the pair of particles.  All bond styles are supported.  All
angle, dihedral, improper styles are supported with the exception of
INTEL and KOKKOS variants of specific styles.  It also does not
support models with long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic or dispersion forces,
i.e. the kspace\_style command in LAMMPS.  It also does not implement the
following fixes which add rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body constraints:
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/*}}}} and the OpenMP accelerated version of {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}},
while all other {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/*/small}}}} are implemented.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS will generate an error if one of these options is included in
your model.  Extension of centroid stress calculations to these force
and fix styles is planned for the future.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pe::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pe}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default the compute includes contributions from the keywords:
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ke pair bond angle dihedral improper kspace fix}}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:heyes2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Heyes)} Heyes, Phys Rev B, 49, 755 (1994).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:sirk1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Sirk)} Sirk, Moore, Brown, J Chem Phys, 138, 064505 (2013).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:thompson2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Thompson)} Thompson, Plimpton, Mattson, J Chem Phys, 131, 154107 (2009).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_atom:surblys1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Surblys2019)} Surblys, Matsubara, Kikugawa, Ohara, Phys Rev E, 99, 051301(R) (2019).

\index{compute stress/cartesian@\spxentry{compute stress/cartesian}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute stress/cartesian command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:compute-stress-cartesian-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cartesian}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = argument specific to the compute style

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cartesian} args = dim1 bin\_width1 dim2 bin\_width2 keyword
  dim1 = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}
  bin\_width1 = width of the bin
  dim2 = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL}
  bin\_width2 = width of the bin
  keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond}
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cartesian}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cartesian}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{y}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{z}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cartesian}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cartesian} defines computations that calculate profiles of the
diagonal components of the local stress tensor over one or two Cartesian
dimensions, as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:ikeshoji2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ikeshoji)}}}}. The stress tensor is
split into a kinetic contribution \(P^k\) and a virial contribution
\(P^v\). The sum gives the total stress tensor \(P = P^k+P^v\).
This compute obeys momentum balance through fluid interfaces. They use the
Irving\textendash{}Kirkwood contour, which is the straight line between particle pairs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023: }Added support for bond styles

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute only supports pair and bond (no angle, dihedral, improper,
or kspace) forces. By default, if no extra keywords are specified, all
supported contributions to the stress are included (ke, pair, bond). If any
keywords are specified, then only those components are summed.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The output columns for \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cartesian} are the position of the
center of the local volume in the first and second dimensions, number
density, \(P^k_{xx}\), \(P^k_{yy}\), \(P^k_{zz}\),
\(P^v_{xx}\), \(P^v_{yy}\), and \(P^v_{zz}\). There are 8
columns when one dimension is specified and 9 columns when two
dimensions are specified. The number of bins (rows) is
\((L_1/b_1)(L_2/b_2)\), where \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are the lengths
of the simulation box in the specified dimensions and \(b_1\) and
\(b_2\) are the specified bin widths. When only one dimension is
specified, the number of bins (rows) is \(L_1/b_1\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This array can be output with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}},

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{p}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cartesian}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{x}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}p[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dump\PYGZus{}p.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values calculated by this compute are “intensive”.  The stress
values will be in pressure {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}. The number density
values are in inverse volume {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTE 1: The local stress does not include any Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones tail
corrections to the stress added by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify tail yes}}}}
command, since those are contributions to the global system pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTE 2: The local stress profiles generated by these computes are
similar to those obtained by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_mop::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{method\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}planes (MOP)}}}}.
A key difference is that compute
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_mop::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{stress/mop/profile}}}}
considers particles crossing a set of planes, while
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cartesian} computes averages for a set of small volumes.
Moreover, this compute computes the diagonal components of the stress
tensor \(P_{xx}\), \(P_{yy}\), and \(P_{zz}\), while
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} computes the components
\(P_{ix}\), \(P_{iy}\), and \(P_{iz}\), where \(i\) is the
direction normal to the plane.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More information on the similarities and differences can be found in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:ikeshoji2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ikeshoji)}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes calculate the stress tensor contributions for pair and bond
forces only (no angle, dihedral, improper, or kspace force).
It requires pairwise force calculations not available for most
many\sphinxhyphen{}body pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes are part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} doc page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_mop::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/mop/profile}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/spherical}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/cylinder}}}}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian:ikeshoji2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Ikeshoji)} Ikeshoji, Hafskjold, Furuholt, Mol Sim, 29, 101\sphinxhyphen{}109, (2003).
