\section{compute stress/cylinder command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:compute-stress-cylinder-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear::doc}}

\section{compute stress/spherical command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:compute-stress-spherical-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = stress/spherical or stress/cylinder

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = argument specific to the compute style

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cylinder} args = zlo zh Rmax bin\_width keyword
  zlo = minimum z\sphinxhyphen{}boundary for cylinder
  zhi = maximum z\sphinxhyphen{}boundary for cylinder
  Rmax = maximum radius to perform calculation to
  bin\_width = width of radial bins to use for calculation
  keyword = ke (zero or one can be specified)
    ke = yes or no
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/spherical}
  x0, y0, z0 = origin of the spherical coordinate system
  bin\_width = width of spherical shells
  Rmax = maximum radius of spherical shells
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cylinder}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{15.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cylinder}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{15.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spherical}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cylinder}, and compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/spherical} define computations that calculate profiles of the
diagonal components of the local stress tensor in the specified
coordinate system. The stress tensor is split into a kinetic
contribution \(P^k\) and a virial contribution \(P^v\). The sum
gives the total stress tensor \(P = P^k+P^v\). These computes can
for example be used to calculate the diagonal components of the local
stress tensor of surfaces with cylindrical or spherical
symmetry. These computes obeys momentum balance through fluid
interfaces. They use the Irving\textendash{}Kirkwood contour, which is the straight
line between particle pairs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cylinder} computes the stress profile along the
radial direction in cylindrical coordinates, as described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:addington1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Addington)}}}}. The compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/spherical}
computes the stress profile along the radial direction in spherical
coordinates, as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:ikeshoji4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ikeshoji)}}}}.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default output columns for \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cylinder} are the radius to the
center of the cylindrical shell, number density, \(P^k_{rr}\),
\(P^k_{\phi\phi}\), \(P^k_{zz}\), \(P^v_{rr}\),
\(P^v_{\phi\phi}\), and \(P^v_{zz}\). When the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{ke} is
set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}, the kinetic contributions are not calculated, and
consequently there are only 5 columns: the position of the center of the
cylindrical shell, the number density, \(P^v_{rr}\),
\(P^v_{\phi\phi}\), and \(P^v_{zz}\). The number of bins (rows) is
\(R_\text{max}/b\), where \(b\) is the specified bin width.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The output columns for \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/spherical} are the position of the center
of the spherical shell, the number density, \(P^k_{rr}\),
\(P^k_{\theta\theta}\), \(P^k_{\phi\phi}\), \(P^v_{rr}\),
\(P^v_{\theta\theta}\), and \(P^v_{\phi\phi}\). There are 8
columns and the number of bins (rows) is \(R_\text{max}/b\), where
\(b\) is the specified bin width.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This array can be output with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}},

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spherical}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}p[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dump\PYGZus{}p.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values calculated by this compute are “intensive”.  The stress
values will be in pressure {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}. The number density
values are in inverse volume {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTE 1: The local stress does not include any Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones tail
corrections to the stress added by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify tail yes}}}}
command, since those are contributions to the global system pressure.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes calculate the stress tensor contributions for pair styles
only (i.e., no bond, angle, dihedral, etc. contributions, and in the
presence of bonded interactions, the result may be incorrect due to
exclusions for {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special bonds}}}} excluding pairs of atoms
completely). It requires pairwise force calculations not available for most
many\sphinxhyphen{}body pair styles.  Note that \(k\)\sphinxhyphen{}space calculations are also excluded.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes are part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} doc page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressure}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_mop::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/mop/profile}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/cartesian}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_curvilinear:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword default for ke in style \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cylinder} is yes.

\section{compute stress/mop/profile command}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_mop:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dir}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keywords}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dir = \sphinxstyleemphasis{x} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{z} is the direction normal to the plane

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = argument specific to the compute style

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keywords = \sphinxstyleemphasis{kin} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{conf} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{total} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bond} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{angle} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dihedral} (one or more can be specified)

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop} args = pos
  pos = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lower} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{center} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{upper} or coordinate value (distance units) is the position of the plane
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} args = origin delta
  origin = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lower} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{center} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{upper} or coordinate value (distance units) is the position of the first plane
  delta = value (distance units) is the distance between planes
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_mop:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop} and compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} define
computations that calculate components of the local stress tensor using
the method of planes {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_mop:mop-todd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Todd)}}}}.  Specifically in compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop} calculates 3 components are computed in directions \sphinxstyleemphasis{dir},\sphinxstyleemphasis{x}; \sphinxstyleemphasis{dir},\sphinxstyleemphasis{y}; and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dir},\sphinxstyleemphasis{z}; where \sphinxstyleemphasis{dir} is the direction
normal to the plane, while in compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} the profile
of the stress is computed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Contrary to methods based on histograms of atomic stress (i.e., using
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute stress/atom}}}}), the method of planes
is compatible with mechanical balance in heterogeneous systems and at
interfaces {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_mop:mop-todd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Todd)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The stress tensor is the sum of a kinetic term and a configurational
term, which are given respectively by Eq. (21) and Eq. (16) in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_mop:mop-todd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Todd)}}}}. For the kinetic part, the algorithm considers
that atoms have crossed the plane if their positions at times
\(t-\Delta t\) and \(t\) are one on either side of the plane,
and uses the velocity at time \(t-\Delta t/2\) given by the velocity
Verlet algorithm.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023: }contributions from bond, angle and dihedral potentials

\sphinxAtStartPar
Between one and seven keywords can be used to indicate which contributions
to the stress must be computed: total stress (total), kinetic stress
(kin), configurational stress (conf), stress due to bond stretching
(bond), stress due to angle bending (angle), stress due to dihedral terms (dihedral)
and/or due to pairwise non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions (pair).

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTE 1: The configurational stress is computed considering all pairs of
atoms where at least one atom belongs to group group\sphinxhyphen{}ID.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTE 2: The local stress does not include any Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones tail
corrections to the stress added by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify tail yes}}}} command, since those are contributions to the global
system pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOTE 3: The local stress profile generated by compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} is similar to that obtained by compute
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_stress_cartesian::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{stress/cartesian}}}}.
A key difference is that compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile}
considers particles crossing a set of planes, while
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cartesian} computes averages for a set
of small volumes.
Moreover, \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/cartesian} compute computes the diagonal components of the stress
tensor \(P_{xx}\), \(P_{yy}\), and \(P_{zz}\), while
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} computes the components
\(P_{ix}\), \(P_{iy}\), and \(P_{iz}\), where \(i\) is the
direction normal to the plane.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_mop:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop} calculates a global vector (indices starting at 1),
with 3 values for each declared keyword (in the order the keywords have
been declared). For each keyword, the stress tensor components are
ordered as follows: stress\_dir,x, stress\_dir,y, and stress\_dir,z.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} instead calculates a global array, with 1
column giving the position of the planes where the stress tensor was
computed, and with 3 columns of values for each declared keyword (in the
order the keywords have been declared). For each keyword, the profiles
of stress tensor components are ordered as follows: stress\_dir,x;
stress\_dir,y; and stress\_dir,z.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values are in pressure {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values produced by this compute can be accessed by various
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{output commands}}}}.  For instance, the results can be
written to a file using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command. Please see the example in the examples/PACKAGES/mop folder.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_stress_mop:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These styles are part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package. They are only
enabled if LAMMPS is built with that package. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} doc page on for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The method is implemented for orthogonal simulation boxes whose
size does not change in time, and axis\sphinxhyphen{}aligned planes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The method only works with two\sphinxhyphen{}body pair interactions, because it
requires the class method \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Pair::single()}} to be implemented, which is
not possible for manybody potentials.  In particular, compute
\sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop/profile} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/mop} do not work with more than two\sphinxhyphen{}body
pair interactions, long range (kspace) interactions and
improper intramolecular interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The impact of fixes that affect the stress (e.g. fix langevin) is
also not included in the stress computed here.

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_tally:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group2}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{ID}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/tally} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/tally} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/virial/tally} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe/tally} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe/mol/tally} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/tally}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group2\sphinxhyphen{}ID = group ID of second (or same) group

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_tally:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{upper}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{left}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{right}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{lower}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lower}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{subregion}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{flux}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{liquid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{flux}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{virial}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{solid}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_tally:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates properties between two groups of
atoms by accumulating them from pairwise non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded computations.
Except for \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/virial/tally}, the two groups can be the same.
This is similar to {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_group_group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute group/group}}}}
only that the data is
accumulated directly during the non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded force computation. The
computes \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/tally}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe/tally}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/tally}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/tally} are primarily provided as example how to program
additional, more sophisticated computes using the tally callback
mechanism. Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe/mol/tally} is one such style, that can—through using
this mechanism—separately tally intermolecular
and intramolecular energies. Something that would otherwise be
impossible without integrating this as a core functionality into
the base classes of LAMMPS.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/tally} obtains the heat flux
(strictly speaking, heat flow) inside the first group,
which is the sum of the convective contribution
due to atoms in the first group and the virial contribution
due to interaction between the first and second groups:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{Q}=  \sum_{i \in \text{group 1}} e_i \mathbf{v}_i + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i \in \text{group 1}} \sum_{\substack{j \in \text{group 2} \\ j \neq i } } \left( \mathbf{F}_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{v}_j \right) \mathbf{r}_{ij}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When the second group in \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/tally} is set to “all”,
the resulting values will be identical
to that obtained by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute heat/flux}}}},
provided only pairwise interactions exist.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/virial/tally} obtains the total virial heat flux
(strictly speaking, heat flow) into the first group due to interaction
with the second group, and is defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Q = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i \in \text{group 1}} \sum_{j \in \text{group 2}} \mathbf{F}_{ij} \cdot \left(\mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{v}_j \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Although, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/virial/tally} compute
does not include the convective term,
it can be used to obtain the total heat flux over control surfaces,
when there are no particles crossing over,
such as is often in solid\textendash{}solid and solid\textendash{}liquid interfaces.
This would be identical to the method of planes method.
Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/virial/tally} compute is distinctly different
from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/tally} computes,
that are essentially volume averaging methods.
The following example demonstrates the difference:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} System with only pairwise interactions.}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Non\PYGZhy{}periodic boundaries in the x direction.}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Has LeftLiquid and RightWall groups along x direction.}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Heat flux over the solid\PYGZhy{}liquid interface}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hflow\PYGZus{}hfvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RightWall}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{flux}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{virial}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LeftLiquid}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hflux\PYGZus{}hfvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}hflow\PYGZus{}hfvt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{ly*lz}\PYG{n+nv}{)}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} x component of approximate heat flux vector inside the liquid region,}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} two approaches.}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myKE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myPE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pe}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myStress}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{stress}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{virial}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hflow\PYGZus{}hf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LeftLiquid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{flux}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myKE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myPE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{myStress}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hflux\PYGZus{}hf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}hflow\PYGZus{}hf[1]}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{volLiq}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hflow\PYGZus{}hft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LeftLiquid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{flux}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{all}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hflux\PYGZus{}hft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}hflow\PYGZus{}hft[1]}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{volLiq}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Pressure over the solid\PYGZhy{}liquid interface, three approaches.}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{force\PYGZus{}gg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RightWall}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{k}{group }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LeftLiquid}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{press\PYGZus{}gg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}force\PYGZus{}gg[1]}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{ly*lz}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{force\PYGZus{}ft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RightWall}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{force}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tally}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LeftLiquid}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{rforce\PYGZus{}ft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{RightWall}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}force\PYGZus{}ft[1]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{press\PYGZus{}ft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}rforce\PYGZus{}ft}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{ly*lz}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{rforce\PYGZus{}hfvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{reduce}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}hflow\PYGZus{}hfvt[1]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{press\PYGZus{}hfvt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}rforce\PYGZus{}hfvt}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{ly*lz}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The pairwise contributions are computing via a callback that the
compute registers with the non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded pairwise force computation.
This limits the use to systems that have no bonds, no Kspace, and no
many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. On the other hand, the computation does not
have to compute forces or energies a second time and thus can be much
more efficient. The callback mechanism allows to write more complex
pairwise property computations.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_tally:output-info}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe/tally} calculates a global scalar (the energy) and a per
atom scalar (the contributions of the single atom to the global
scalar).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{pe/mol/tally} calculates a global four\sphinxhyphen{}element vector containing
(in this order): \sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul} for intramolecular pairs and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{evdwl} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecoul} for intermolecular pairs. Since molecules are
identified by their molecule IDs, the partitioning does not have to be
related to molecules, but the energies are tallied into the respective
slots depending on whether the molecule IDs of a pair are the same or
different.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{force/tally} calculates a global scalar (the force magnitude)
and a per atom 3\sphinxhyphen{}element vector (force contribution from each atom).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{stress/tally} calculates a global scalar
(average of the diagonal elements of the stress tensor) and a per atom
vector (the six elements of stress tensor contributions from the
individual atom).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
As in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_heat_flux::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute heat/flux}}}},
compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/tally} calculates a global vector of length 6,
where the first three components are the \(x\), \(y\), \(z\)
components of the full heat flow vector,
and the next three components are the corresponding components
of just the convective portion of the flow (i.e., the
first term in the equation for \(\mathbf{Q}\)).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat/flux/virial/tally} calculates a global scalar (heat flow)
and a per atom three\sphinxhyphen{}element vector
(contribution to the force acting over atoms in the first group
from individual atoms in both groups).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both the scalar and vector values calculated by this compute are
“extensive”.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_tally:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the TALLY package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Not all pair styles can be evaluated in a pairwise mode as required by
this compute.  For example, 3\sphinxhyphen{}body and other many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials, such
as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tersoff}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sw::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber}}}}
cannot be used.  {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{EAM}}}} potentials only include the pair
potential portion of the EAM interaction when used by this compute, not
the embedding term.  Also bonded or Kspace interactions do not
contribute to this compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These computes are not compatible with accelerated pair styles from the
GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS, or OPENMP packages. They will either create an error
or print a warning when required data was not tallied in the required way
and thus the data acquisition functions from these computes not called.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When used with dynamic groups, a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run 0}}}} command needs to
be inserted in order to initialize the dynamic groups before accessing
the computes.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_tdpd_cc_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the per\sphinxhyphen{}atom chemical
concentration of a specified species for each tDPD particle in a
group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The chemical concentration of each species is defined as the number of
molecules carried by a tDPD particle for dilute solution.  For more
details see {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_tdpd_cc_atom:li2015a}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Li2015)}}}}.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_tdpd_cc_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector, which can be accessed by
any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a compute as input. See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS
output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The per\sphinxhyphen{}atom vector values will be in the units of chemical species
per unit mass.

\label{\detokenize{compute_tdpd_cc_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the DPD\sphinxhyphen{}MESO package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\section{compute temp command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp:compute-temp-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the temperature of a group of
atoms.  A compute of this style can be used by any command that
computes a temperature, e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}},
etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The temperature is calculated by the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}T  = \frac{2 E_\mathrm{kin}}{N_\mathrm{DOF} k_B} \quad \mathrm{with} \quad
E_\mathrm{kin} = \sum^{N_\mathrm{atoms}}_{i=1} \frac{1}{2} m_i v^2_i \quad \mathrm{and} \quad
N_\mathrm{DOF} = n_\mathrm{dim} N_\mathrm{atoms} - n_\mathrm{dim} - N_\mathrm{fix DOFs}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(E_\mathrm{kin}\) is the total kinetic energy of the group of
atoms, \(n_\mathrm{dim}\) is the dimensionality of the simulation
(i.e. either 2 or 3), \(N_\mathrm{atoms}\) is the number of atoms in
the group, \(N_\mathrm{fix DOFs}\) is the number of degrees of
freedom removed by fix commands (see below), \(k_B\) is the
Boltzmann constant, and \(T\) is the resulting computed temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A symmetric tensor, stored as a six\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also calculated
by this compute for use in the computation of a pressure tensor by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressue}}}} command.  The formula for
the components of the tensor is the same as the above expression for
\(E_\mathrm{kin}\), except that the 1/2 factor is NOT included and
the \(v_i^2\) is replaced by \(v_{i,x} v_{i,y}\) for the
\(xy\) component, and so on.  Note that because it lacks the 1/2
factor, these tensor components are twice those of the traditional
kinetic energy tensor.  The six components of the vector are ordered
\(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\),
\(yz\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of atoms contributing to the temperature is assumed to be
constant for the duration of the run; use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic} option of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command if this is not the case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute subtracts out degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom due to fixes that
constrain molecular motion, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  This means the temperature of groups of
atoms that include these constraints will be computed correctly.  If
needed, the subtracted degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom can be altered using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra} option of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command.
By default this \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra} component is initialized to
\(n_\mathrm{dim}\) (as shown in the formula above) to represent the
degrees of freedom removed from a system due to its translation
invariance due to periodic boundary conditions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A compute of this style with the ID of “thermo\_temp” is created when
LAMMPS starts up, as if this command were in the input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{thermo\PYGZus{}temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the “thermo\_style” command for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto thermostat}}}} page for a
discussion of different ways to compute temperature and perform
thermostatting.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the temperature) and a global
vector of length six (symmetric tensor), which can be accessed by
indices 1\textendash{}6.  These values can be used by any command that uses
global scalar or vector values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS
output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “intensive”.  The
vector values are “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value is in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The vector
values are in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\section{compute temp/asphere command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere:compute-temp-asphere-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{asphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp/asphere = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dof}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} value = bias\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  bias\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of a temperature compute that removes a velocity bias
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dof} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate}
  all = compute temperature of translational and rotational degrees of freedom
  rotate = compute temperature of just rotational degrees of freedom
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{asphere}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{asphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bias}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tempCOM}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myTemp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{mobile}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{asphere}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dof}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rotate}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the temperature of a group of
aspherical particles, including a contribution from both their
translational and rotational kinetic energy.  This differs from the
usual {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}} command, which assumes point
particles with only translational kinetic energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles (aspherical or spherical) can be included in
the group.  For 3d finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles, each has six degrees of
freedom (three translational, three rotational).  For 2d finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
particles, each has three degrees of freedom (two translational, one
rotational).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This choice for degrees of freedom (DOF) assumes that all finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
aspherical or spherical particles in your model will freely rotate,
sampling all their rotational DOF.  It is possible to use a
combination of interaction potentials and fixes that induce no torque
or otherwise constrain some of all of your particles so that this is
not the case.  Then there are fewer DOF and you should use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify extra/dof}}}} command to adjust
the DOF accordingly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, an aspherical particle with all three of its shape
parameters the same is a sphere.  If it does not rotate, then it should
have 3 DOF instead of 6 in 3d (or two instead of three in 2d).  A
uniaxial aspherical particle has two of its three shape parameters the
same.  If it does not rotate around the axis perpendicular to its
circular cross section, then it should have 5 DOF instead of 6 in 3d.
The latter is the case for uniaxial ellipsoids in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gayberne::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{GayBerne model}}}} since there is no induced torque around the optical
axis.  It will also be the case for biaxial ellipsoids when exactly two
of the semiaxes have the same length and the corresponding relative well
depths are equal.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The translational kinetic energy is computed the same as is described by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}} command.  The rotational kinetic
energy is computed as \(\frac12 I \omega^2\), where \(I\) is the
inertia tensor for the aspherical particle and \(\omega\) is its
angular velocity, which is computed from its angular momentum.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{2d models}}}}, particles are treated as
ellipsoids, not ellipses, meaning their moments of inertia will be
the same as in 3d.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A kinetic energy tensor, stored as a six\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also
calculated by this compute.  The formula for the components of the
tensor is the same as the above formula, except that \(v^2\) and
\(\omega^2\) are replaced by \(v_x v_y\) and \(\omega_x
\omega_y\) for the \(xy\) component, and the appropriate elements of
the moment of inertia tensor are used.  The six components of the vector
are ordered \(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\),
\(yz\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
A symmetric tensor, stored as a six\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also calculated
by this compute for use in the computation of a pressure tensor by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressue}}}} command.  The formula for the
components of the tensor is the same as the above expression for
\(E_\mathrm{kin}\), except that the 1/2 factor is NOT included and
the \(v_i^2\) and \(\omega^2\) are replaced by \(v_x v_y\)
and \(\omega_x \omega_y\) for the \(xy\) component, and so on.
And the appropriate elements of the moment of inertia tensor are used.
Note that because it lacks the 1/2 factor, these tensor components are
twice those of the traditional kinetic energy tensor.  The six
components of the vector are ordered \(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\),
\(xy\), \(xz\), \(yz\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of atoms contributing to the temperature is assumed to be
constant for the duration of the run; use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic/dof} option of
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command if this is not the
case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute subtracts out translational degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom due to fixes
that constrain molecular motion, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  This means the temperature of groups
of atoms that include these constraints will be computed correctly.  If
needed, the subtracted degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom can be altered using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra/dof} option of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto thermostat}}}} page for a
discussion of different ways to compute temperature and perform
thermostatting.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword/value option pairs are used in the following ways.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} keyword, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias\sphinxhyphen{}ID} refers to the ID of a temperature
compute that removes a “bias” velocity from each atom.  This allows
compute temp/sphere to compute its thermal temperature after the
translational kinetic energy components have been altered in a
prescribed way (e.g., to remove a flow velocity profile).  Thermostats
that use this compute will work with this bias term.  See the doc
pages for individual computes that calculate a temperature and the doc
pages for fixes that perform thermostatting for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dof} keyword, a setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} calculates a temperature
that includes both translational and rotational degrees of freedom.
A setting of \sphinxstyleemphasis{rotate} calculates a temperature that includes only
rotational degrees of freedom.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the temperature) and a global
vector of length 6 (symmetric tensor), which can be accessed by indices
1\textendash{}6.  These values can be used by any command that uses global scalar
or vector values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “intensive”.  The vector
values are “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value is in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The vector
values are in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_asphere:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the ASPHERE package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute requires that atoms store angular momentum and a quaternion
as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style ellipsoid}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All particles in the group must be finite\sphinxhyphen{}size.  They cannot be point
particles, but they can be aspherical or spherical as defined by their
shape attribute.

\section{compute temp/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:compute-temp-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp/chunk = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more values can be listed as value1,value2,etc.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kecom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
temp = temperature of each chunk
kecom = kinetic energy of each chunk based on velocity of center of mass
internal = internal kinetic energy of each chunk
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{com} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
  yes = subtract center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity from each chunk before calculating temperature
  no = do not subtract center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} value = bias\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  bias\sphinxhyphen{}ID = ID of a temperature compute that removes a velocity bias
\sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} value = dof\_per\_atom
  dof\_per\_atom = define this many degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom per atom
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} value = dof\_per\_chunk
  dof\_per\_chunk = define this many degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom per chunk
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{internal}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bias}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tpartial}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adof}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the temperature of a group of
atoms that are also in chunks, after optionally subtracting out the
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity of each chunk.  By specifying optional values,
it can also calculate the per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk temperature or energies of the
multiple chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The temperature is calculated by the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{KE} = \frac{\text{DOF}}{2} k_B T,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where KE is the total kinetic energy of all atoms assigned to chunks
(sum of \(\frac12 m v^2\)), DOF is the the total number of degrees of
freedom for those atoms, \(k_B\) is Boltzmann constant, and \(T\) is the
absolute temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The DOF is calculated as \(N\times\)\sphinxstyleemphasis{adof}
+ \(N_\text{chunk}\times\)\sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof},
where \(N\) is the number of atoms contributing to the kinetic energy,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} is the number of degrees of freedom per atom, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} is the number of degrees of freedom per chunk.
By default, \sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} = 2 or 3 = dimensionality of system, as set via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dimension}}}} command, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} = 0.0.
This gives the usual formula for temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A symmetric tensor, stored as a six\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also calculated
by this compute.  The formula for the components of the tensor is the
same as the above expression for \(E_\mathrm{kin}\), except that
the 1/2 factor is NOT included and the \(v_i^2\) is replaced by
\(v_{i,x} v_{i,y}\) for the \(xy\) component, and so on.  Note
that because it lacks the 1/2 factor, these tensor components are
twice those of the traditional kinetic energy tensor.  The six
components of the vector are ordered \(xx\), \(yy\),
\(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\), \(yz\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the number of atoms contributing to the temperature is
calculated each time the temperature is evaluated since it is assumed
the atoms may be dynamically assigned to chunks.  Thus there is no
need to use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic} option of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command for this compute style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If any optional values are specified, then per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk quantities are
also calculated and stored in a global array, as described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} value calculates the temperature for each chunk by the
formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{KE} = \frac{\text{DOF}}{2} k_B T,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where KE is the total kinetic energy of the chunk of atoms (sum of
\(\frac12 m v^2\)), DOF is the total number of degrees of freedom for all
atoms in the chunk, \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant, and \(T\) is the
absolute temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of degrees of freedom (DOF) in this case is calculated as
\(N\times\)\sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} + \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof}, where \(N\) is the number
of atoms in the chunk, \sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} is the number of degrees of freedom
per atom, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} is the number of degrees of freedom per
chunk.  By default, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} = 2 or 3 = dimensionality of system, as set
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dimension::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dimension}}}} command, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} = 0.0.
This gives the usual formula for temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{kecom} value calculates the kinetic energy of each chunk as if
all its atoms were moving with the velocity of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of
the chunk.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} value calculates the internal kinetic energy of each
chunk.  The interal KE is summed over the atoms in the chunk using an
internal “thermal” velocity for each atom, which is its velocity minus
the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity of the chunk.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that currently the global and per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk temperatures calculated
by this compute only include translational degrees of freedom for each
atom.  No rotational degrees of freedom are included for finite\sphinxhyphen{}size
particles.  Also no degrees of freedom are subtracted for any velocity
bias or constraints that are applied, such as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_partial::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/partial}}}}, or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.
This is because those degrees of
freedom (e.g., a constrained bond) could apply to sets of atoms that
are both included and excluded from a specific chunk, and hence the
concept is somewhat ill\sphinxhyphen{}defined.  In some cases, you can use the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} keywords to adjust the calculated degrees of freedom
appropriately, as explained below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk temperature calculated by this compute and the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk temp}}}} command can be different.
This compute calculates the temperature for each chunk for a single
snapshot.  Fix ave/chunk can do that but can also time average those
values over many snapshots, or it can compute a temperature as if the
atoms in the chunk on different timesteps were collected together as
one set of atoms to calculate their temperature.  This compute allows
the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity of each chunk to be subtracted before
calculating the temperature; fix ave/chunk does not.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Only atoms in the specified group contribute to the calculations performed
by this compute.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}}
command defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are
not in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the “all”
group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with non\sphinxhyphen{}zero
chunk IDs.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk results of the compute
temp/chunk calculation to a file is to use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}} command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword/value option pairs are used in the following ways.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} keyword can be used with a value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} to subtract the
velocity of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass for each chunk from the velocity of the
atoms in that chunk, before calculating either the global or per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk
temperature.  This can be useful if the atoms are streaming or
otherwise moving collectively, and you wish to calculate only the
thermal temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} keyword, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias\sphinxhyphen{}ID} refers to the ID of a temperature
compute that removes a “bias” velocity from each atom.  This also
allows calculation of the global or per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk temperature using only
the thermal temperature of atoms in each chunk after the translational
kinetic energy components have been altered in a prescribed way
(e.g., to remove a velocity profile).  It also applies to the calculation
of the other per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk values, such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{kecom} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal}, which
involve the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity of each chunk, which is calculated
after the velocity bias is removed from each atom.  Note that the
temperature compute will apply its bias globally to the entire system,
not on a per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk basis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} keywords define the values used in the degree of
freedom (DOF) formulas used for the global or per\sphinxhyphen{}chunk temperature,
as described above.  They can be used to calculate a more appropriate
temperature for some kinds of chunks.  Here are three examples:

\sphinxAtStartPar
If spatially binned chunks contain some number of water molecules and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} is used to make each molecule rigid, then
you could calculate a temperature with six degrees of freedom (DOF) (three
translational, three rotational) per molecule by setting \sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} to 2.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_partial::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/partial}}}} is used with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} keyword to only allow the x component of velocity to contribute
to the temperature, then \sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} = 1.0 would be appropriate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If each chunk consists of a large molecule, with some number of its
bonds constrained by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} or the entire molecule
by {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid/small}}}}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{adof} = 0.0 and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cdof} could be
set to the remaining degrees of freedom for the entire molecule
(entire chunk in this case; i.e., 6 for 3d, or 3 for 2d, for a rigid
molecule).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the temperature) and a global
vector of length 6 (symmetric tensor), which can be accessed by
indices 1\textendash{}6.  These values can be used by any command that uses
global scalar or vector values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS
output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute also optionally calculates a global array, if one or more
of the optional values are specified.  The number of rows in the array
is the number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  The number of
columns is the number of specified values (1 or more).  These values
can be accessed by any command that uses global array values from a
compute as input.  Again, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “intensive”.  The
vector values are “extensive”.  The array values are “intensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value is in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The vector
values are in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The array values will be
in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp} value, and in
energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kecom} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{internal} values.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{com} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} keywords cannot be used together.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/chunk temp}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option defaults are com no, no bias, adof = dimensionality of the
system (2 or 3), and cdof = 0.0.

\sphinxstepscope

\section{compute temp/com command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_com:compute-temp-com-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_com:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_com::doc}}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_com:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the temperature of a group of
atoms, after subtracting out the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity of the group.
This is useful if the group is expected to have a non\sphinxhyphen{}zero net
velocity for some reason.  A compute of this style can be used by any
command that computes a temperature,
(e.g., {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity has been subtracted from each atom,
the temperature is calculated by the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{KE} = \frac{\text{dim}}{2} N k_B T,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where KE is the total kinetic energy of the group of atoms (sum of
\(\frac12 m v^2\)), dim = 2 or 3 is the dimensionality of the
simulation, \(N\) is number of atoms in the group, \(k_B\) is
the Boltzmann constant, and \(T\) is the absolute temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A symmetric tensor, stored as a six\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also calculated
by this compute for use in the computation of a pressure tensor by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressue}}}} command.  The formula for
the components of the tensor is the same as the above expression for
\(E_\mathrm{kin}\), except that the 1/2 factor is NOT included and
the \(v_i^2\) is replaced by \(v_{i,x} v_{i,y}\) for the
\(xy\) component, and so on.  Note that because it lacks the 1/2
factor, these tensor components are twice those of the traditional
kinetic energy tensor.  The six components of the vector are ordered
\(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\),
\(yz\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of atoms contributing to the temperature is assumed to be
constant for the duration of the run; use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic} option of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command if this is not the case.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The removal of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity by this fix is essentially
computing the temperature after a “bias” has been removed from the
velocity of the atoms.  If this compute is used with a fix command
that performs thermostatting then this bias will be subtracted from
each atom, thermostatting of the remaining thermal velocity will be
performed, and the bias will be added back in.  Thermostatting fixes
that work in this way include {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/berendsen}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute subtracts out degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom due to fixes that
constrain molecular motion, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  This means the temperature of groups of
atoms that include these constraints will be computed correctly.
If needed, the subtracted degrees\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}freedom can be altered using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra} option of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto thermostat}}}} page for a
discussion of different ways to compute temperature and perform
thermostatting.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_com:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the temperature) and a global
vector of length 6 (symmetric tensor), which can be accessed by
indices 1\textendash{}6.  These values can be used by any command that uses
global scalar or vector values from a compute as input.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS
output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “intensive”.  The
vector values are “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value is in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The vector
values is in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{compute temp/cs command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:compute-temp-cs-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{group2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
temp/cs = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group1 = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID of either cores or shells

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
group2 = group\sphinxhyphen{}ID of either shells or cores

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{oxygen\PYGZus{}c\PYGZhy{}s}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O\PYGZus{}core}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O\PYGZus{}shell}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{core\PYGZus{}shells}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cores}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shells}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the temperature of a system based
on the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity of atom pairs that are bonded to each
other.  This compute is designed to be used with the adiabatic
core/shell model of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:mitchellfincham1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mitchell and Fincham)}}}}.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_coreshell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto coreshell}}}} page for an overview of
the model as implemented in LAMMPS.  Specifically, this compute enables
correct temperature calculation and thermostatting of core/shell pairs
where it is desirable for the internal degrees of freedom of the
core/shell pairs to not be influenced by a thermostat.  A compute of
this style can be used by any command that computes a temperature via
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_modify}}}} (e.g., {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this compute does not require all ions to be polarized, hence
defined as core/shell pairs.  One can mix core/shell pairs and ions
without a satellite particle if desired. The compute will consider the
non\sphinxhyphen{}polarized ions according to the physical system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For this compute, core and shell particles are specified by two
respective group IDs, which can be defined using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{group::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{group}}}} command.  The number of atoms in the two groups must be the
same and there should be one bond defined between a pair of atoms in the
two groups.  Non\sphinxhyphen{}polarized ions which might also be included in the
treated system should not be included into either of these groups, they
are taken into account by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{group\sphinxhyphen{}ID} (second argument) of the
compute.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The temperature is calculated by the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{KE} = \frac{\text{dim}}{2} N k_B T,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where KE is the total kinetic energy of the group of atoms (sum of
\(\frac12 m v^2\)), dim = 2 or 3 is the dimensionality of the
simulation, \(N\) is the number of atoms in the group, \(k_B\)
is the Boltzmann constant, and \(T\) is the absolute temperature.
Note that the velocity of each core or shell atom used in the KE
calculation is the velocity of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass (COM) of the
core/shell pair the atom is part of.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A symmetric tensor, stored as a six\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also calculated
by this compute for use in the computation of a pressure tensor by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressue}}}} command.  The formula for the
components of the tensor is the same as the above expression for
\(E_\mathrm{kin}\), except that the 1/2 factor is NOT included and
the \(v_i^2\) is replaced by \(v_{i,x} v_{i,y}\) for the
\(xy\) component, and so on.  Note that because it lacks the 1/2
factor, these tensor components are twice those of the traditional
kinetic energy tensor.  The six components of the vector are ordered
\(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\), \(yz\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The change this fix makes to core/shell atom velocities is essentially
computing the temperature after a “bias” has been removed from the
velocity of the atoms.  This “bias” is the velocity of the atom relative
to the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity of the core/shell pair.  If this compute
is used with a fix command that performs thermostatting then this bias
will be subtracted from each atom, thermostatting of the remaining
center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity will be performed, and the bias will be added
back in.  This means the thermostatting will effectively be performed on
the core/shell pairs, instead of on the individual core and shell atoms.
Thermostatting fixes that work in this way include {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
temp/berendsen}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The internal energy of core/shell pairs can be calculated by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/chunk}}}} command, if chunks are
defined as core/shell pairs.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_coreshell::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto coreshell}}}} doc page for more discussion on how to do this.


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the temperature) and a global
vector of length 6 (symmetric tensor), which can be accessed by indices
1\textendash{}6.  These values can be used by any command that uses global scalar
or vector values from a compute as input.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “intensive”.  The vector
values are “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value is in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The vector
values are in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_cs:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of core/shell pairs contributing to the temperature is
assumed to be constant for the duration of the run.  No fixes should
be used which generate new molecules or atoms during a simulation.

{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_temp_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute temp/chunk}}}}

\section{compute temp/deform command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_deform:compute-temp-deform-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_deform:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_deform:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_deform::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{temp/deform/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_temp_deform:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{deform}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\item {}

\item {}
