\sphinxAtStartPar
ti = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more attribute/arg pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = pair style (lj/cut, gauss, born, etc.) or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
pair style args = atype v\_name1 v\_name2
  atype = atom type (see asterisk form below)
  v\_name1 = variable with name1 that is energy scale factor and function of lambda
  v\_name2 = variable with name2 that is derivative of v\_name1 with respect to lambda
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} args = atype v\_name1 v\_name2
  atype = atom type (see asterisk form below)
  v\_name1 = variable with name1 that is energy tail correction scale factor and function of lambda
  v\_name2 = variable with name2 that is derivative of v\_name1 with respect to lambda
\sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} args = atype v\_name1 v\_name2
  atype = atom type (see asterisk form below)
  v\_name1 = variable with name1 that is K\sphinxhyphen{}Space scale factor and function of lambda
  v\_name2 = variable with name2 that is derivative of v\_name1 with respect to lambda
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ti:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ti}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}lj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dlj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}c}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}ks}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dks}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ti}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}lj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dlj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}c}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{kspace}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}ks}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}dks}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ti:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the derivative of the interaction
potential with respect to \sphinxstyleemphasis{lambda}, the coupling parameter used in a
thermodynamic integration.  This derivative can be used to infer a
free energy difference resulting from an alchemical simulation, as
described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_ti:eike}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Eike}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Typically this compute will be used in conjunction with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} command which can perform alchemical
transformations by adjusting the strength of an interaction potential
as a simulation runs, as defined by one or more
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}}
commands.  This scaling is done via a prefactor on the energy, forces,
virial calculated by the pair or \(k\)\sphinxhyphen{}space style.  The prefactor is
often a function of a \sphinxstyleemphasis{lambda} parameter which may be adjusted from 0 to 1
(or vice versa) over the course of a {\hyperref[\detokenize{run::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run}}}}.
The time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent adjustment is what the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}}
command does.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Assume that the unscaled energy of a pair\_style or kspace\_style is
given by \(U\).  Then the scaled energy is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_s = f(\lambda) U\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(f\) is some function of \(\lambda\).  What this compute
calculates is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{dU_s}{d\lambda} = U \frac{df(\lambda)}{d\lambda}
  = \frac{U_s}{f(\lambda)} \frac{df(\lambda)}{d\lambda},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
which is the derivative of the system’s scaled potential energy \(U_s\)
with respect to \(\lambda\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
To perform this calculation, you provide one or more atom types as
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atype}.  The variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{atype} can be specified in one of two ways.
An explicit numeric value can be used, as in the first example above, or a
wildcard asterisk can be used in place of or in conjunction with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atype} argument to select multiple atom types.  This takes the form
“*” or “*n” or “m*” or “m*n”.  If \(N\) is the number of atom types,
then an asterisk with no numeric values means all types from 1 to \(N\).
A leading asterisk means all types from 1 to n (inclusive).  A trailing
asterisk means all types from m to N (inclusive).  A middle asterisk
means all types from m to n (inclusive).

\sphinxAtStartPar
You also specify two functions, as {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variables}}}}.
The first is specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name1}, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{name1} is the name of the
variable, and is \(f(\lambda)\) in the notation above.  The second is
specified as \sphinxstyleemphasis{v\_name2}, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{name2} is the name of the variable, and is
\(df(\lambda)/d\lambda\) in the notation above (i.e., it is the analytic
derivative of \(f\) with respect to \(\lambda\)).
Note that the \sphinxstyleemphasis{name1} variable is also typically given as an
argument to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An alchemical simulation may use several pair potentials together,
invoked via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid or hybrid/overlay}}}}
command.  The total \(dU_s/d\lambda\) for the overall system is calculated
as the sum of each contributing term as listed by the keywords in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_ti::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute ti}}}} command.  Individual pair potentials can be
listed, which will be sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles in the hybrid case.  You can also include a
\(k\)\sphinxhyphen{}space term via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{kspace} keyword.  You can also include a pairwise
long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail correction to the energy via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tail} keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For each term, you can specify a different (or the same) scale factor
by the two variables that you list.  Again, these will typically
correspond toe the scale factors applied to these various potentials
and the \(k\)\sphinxhyphen{}space contribution via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More details about the exact functional forms for the computation of
\(du/dl\) can be found in the paper by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_ti:eike}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Eike}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ti:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar, namely \(dU_s/d\lambda\).  This
value can be used by any command that uses a global scalar value from
a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page
for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “extensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value will be in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_ti:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}COMPUTE package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\section{compute torque/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk:compute-torque-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{torque}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunkID}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
torque/chunk = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
chunkID = ID of {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{torque}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molchunk}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the torque on multiple chunks of
atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified
as chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a
molecule or atoms in a spatial bin.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}}
doc pages for details of how chunks can be defined and examples of how
they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates the three components of the torque vector for eqch
chunk, due to the forces on the individual atoms in the chunk around
the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass of the chunk.  The calculation includes all effects
due to atoms passing through periodic boundaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not
in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the
“all” group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero chunk IDs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of an atom contribute to the chunk’s torque in
“unwrapped” form, by using the image flags associated with each atom.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}} command for a discussion of
“unwrapped” coordinates.  See the Atoms section of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command for a discussion of image flags and
how they are set for each atom.  You can reset the image flags
(e.g., to 0) before invoking this compute by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{set image}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute torque/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{torque}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array where the number of rows is equal to the
number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  The number of columns
is three for the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) components of the torque
for each chunk.  These values can be accessed by any command that uses global
array values from a compute as input.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page
for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
force\sphinxhyphen{}distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\label{\detokenize{compute_torque_chunk:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\section{compute vacf command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:compute-vacf-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vacf}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
vacf = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vacf}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{upper}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vacf}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the velocity auto\sphinxhyphen{}correlation
function (VACF), averaged over a group of atoms.  Each atom’s
contribution to the VACF is its current velocity vector dotted into
its initial velocity vector at the time the compute was specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A vector of four quantities is calculated by this compute.  The first three
elements of the vector are \(v_x v_{x,0}\) (and similar for the
\(y\) and \(z\) components), summed and averaged over atoms in the
group, where \(v_x\) is the current \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the velocity of
the atom and \(v_{x,0}\) is the initial \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the velocity
of the atom.  The fourth element of the vector is the total VACF
(i.e., \((v_x v_{x,0} + v_y v_{y,0} + v_z v_{z,0})\)),
summed and averaged over atoms in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The integral of the VACF versus time is proportional to the diffusion
coefficient of the diffusing atoms.  This can be computed in the
following manner, using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variable trap()}}}} function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute         }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vacf}
\PYG{k}{fix             }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}2[4]}
\PYG{k}{variable        }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{diff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dt}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{trap}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{f\PYGZus{}5}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}diff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the quantities calculated by this compute to be
continuous when running from a {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{restart file}}}}, then
you should use the same ID for this compute, as in the original run.
This is so that the fix this compute creates to store per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities will also have the same ID, and thus be initialized
correctly with time=0 atom velocities from the restart file.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global vector of length 4, which can be
accessed by indices 1\textendash{}4 by any command that uses global vector values
from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vector values are “intensive”.  The vector values will be in
velocity\(^2\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_msd::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute msd}}}}

\label{\detokenize{compute_vacf:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{compute vcm/chunk command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vcm_chunk:compute-vcm-chunk-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_vcm_chunk:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_vcm_chunk::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}

\subsection{Examples}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_vcm_chunk:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity for
multiple chunks of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In LAMMPS, chunks are collections of atoms defined by a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command, which assigns each atom
to a single chunk (or no chunk).  The ID for this command is specified as
chunkID.  For example, a single chunk could be the atoms in a molecule or atoms
in a spatial bin.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_chunk::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto chunk}}}} doc pages for details of how chunks can be
defined and examples of how they can be used to measure properties of a system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates the \((x,y,z)\) components of the center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass
velocity for each chunk.  This is done by summing mass*velocity for
each atom in the chunk and dividing the sum by the total mass of the
chunk.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that only atoms in the specified group contribute to the
calculation.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command
defines its own group; atoms will have a chunk ID = 0 if they are not
in that group, signifying they are not assigned to a chunk, and will
thus also not contribute to this calculation.  You can specify the
“all” group for this command if you simply want to include atoms with
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero chunk IDs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simplest way to output the results of the compute vcm/chunk
calculation to a file is to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_ave_time::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix ave/time}}}}
command, for example:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cc1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecule}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{myChunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vcm}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{chunk}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cc1}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ave}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}myChunk[}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tmp.out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mode}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{vector}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Output info}

This compute calculates a global array where the number of rows is the
number of chunks \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nchunk} as calculated by the specified
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_chunk_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute chunk/atom}}}} command.  The number of
columns is 3 for the \((x,y,z)\) center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass velocity coordinates of
each chunk. These values can be accessed by any command that uses global array
values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}}
page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array values are “intensive”.  The array values will be in
velocity {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\section{compute viscosity/cos command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:compute-viscosity-cos-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscosity}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cos}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
viscosity/cos = style name of this compute command

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{real}
\PYG{k}{compute  }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{cos}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{viscosity}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cos}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{V}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}cos[7]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.02E\PYGZhy{}5}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} A/fs\PYGZca{}2}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{density}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{density}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{lz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lz}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{reciprocalViscosity}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}V}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{A}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{39.4784}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}lz}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}lz}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} 1/(Pa*s)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the velocity amplitude of a group of atoms
with an cosine\sphinxhyphen{}shaped velocity profile and the temperature of them
after subtracting out the velocity profile before computing the kinetic energy.
A compute of this style can be used by any command that computes a temperature
(e.g., {\hyperref[\detokenize{thermo_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{thermo\_modify}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix npt}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This command together with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_accelerate_cos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_accelerate/cos}}}}
enables viscosity calculation with periodic perturbation method,
as described by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:hess1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Hess}}}}.
An acceleration along the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}direction is applied to the simulation
system by using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_accelerate_cos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix\_accelerate/cos}}}} command.
The acceleration is a periodic function along the \(z\)\sphinxhyphen{}direction:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a_{x}(z) = A \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi z}{l_{z}}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(A\) is the acceleration amplitude, \(l_z\) is the
\(z\)\sphinxhyphen{}length of the simulation box. At steady state, the acceleration
generates a velocity profile:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}v_{x}(z) = V \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi z}{l_{z}}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The generated velocity amplitude \(V\) is related to the
shear viscosity \(\eta\) by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V = \frac{A \rho}{\eta}\left(\frac{l_{z}}{2 \pi}\right)^{2},\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and it can be obtained from ensemble average of the velocity profile via
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V = \frac{\sum\limits_i 2 m_{i} v_{i, x} \cos \left(\frac{2 \pi z_i}{l_{z}}\right)}{\sum\limits_i m_{i}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(m_i\), \(v_{i,x}\) and \(z_i\) are the mass,
\(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component velocity, and \(z\)\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate of a particle,
respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the cosine\sphinxhyphen{}shaped collective velocity in the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}direction has been
subtracted for each atom, the temperature is calculated by the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\text{KE} = \frac{\text{dim}}{2} N k_B T,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where KE is the total kinetic energy of the group of atoms (sum of
\(\frac12 m v^2\)), dim = 2 or 3 is the dimensionality of the simulation,
\(N\) is the number of atoms in the group, \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann
constant, and \(T\) is the absolute temperature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A symmetric tensor, stored as a six\sphinxhyphen{}element vector, is also calculated
by this compute for use in the computation of a pressure tensor by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pressure::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pressue}}}} command.  The formula for
the components of the tensor is the same as the above expression for
\(E_\mathrm{kin}\), except that the 1/2 factor is NOT included and
the \(v_i^2\) is replaced by \(v_{i,x} v_{i,y}\) for the
\(xy\) component, and so on.  Note that because it lacks the 1/2
factor, these tensor components are twice those of the traditional
kinetic energy tensor.  The six components of the vector are ordered
\(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(xy\), \(xz\),
\(yz\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The number of atoms contributing to the temperature is assumed to be
constant for the duration of the run; use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic} option of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command if this is not the case.
However, in order to get meaningful results, the group ID of this compute should
be all.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The removal of the cosine\sphinxhyphen{}shaped velocity component by this command is
essentially computing the temperature after a “bias” has been removed
from the velocity of the atoms.  If this compute is used with a fix
command that performs thermostatting then this bias will be subtracted
from each atom, thermostatting of the remaining thermal velocity will
be performed, and the bias will be added back in.  Thermostatting
fixes that work in this way include {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nh::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nvt}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_rescale::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/rescale}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_temp_berendsen::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix temp/berendsen}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_langevin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix langevin}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute subtracts out degrees of freedom due to fixes that
constrain molecular motion, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}.  This means that the temperature of groups of
atoms that include these constraints will be computed correctly.  If
needed, the subtracted degrees of freedom can be altered using the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{extra} option of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute\_modify}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_thermostat::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto thermostat}}}} page for a discussion of
different ways to compute temperature and perform thermostatting.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global scalar (the temperature) and a global
vector of length 7, which can be accessed by indices 1\textendash{}7.  The first
six elements of the vector are those of the symmetric tensor discussed
above.  The seventh is the cosine\sphinxhyphen{}shaped velocity amplitude \(V\),
which can be used to calculate the reciprocal viscosity, as shown in
the example.  These values can be used by any command that uses global
scalar or vector values from a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto
output}}}} page for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value calculated by this compute is “intensive”.  The
first six elements of vector values are “extensive”,
and the seventh element of vector values is “intensive”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scalar value is in temperature {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The first
six elements of vector values are in energy {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  The
seventh element of vector value us in velocity {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the MISC package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since this compute depends on {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_accelerate_cos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix accelerate/cos}}}}
which can only work for 3d systems, it cannot be used for 2d systems.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_accelerate_cos::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix accelerate/cos}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_viscosity_cos:default}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\index{compute voronoi/atom@\spxentry{compute voronoi/atom}}\ignorespaces 

\section{compute voronoi/atom command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:compute-voronoi-atom-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{arg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
voronoi/atom = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{only\_group} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{occupation} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{edge\_histo} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{edge\_threshold} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{face\_threshold} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neighbors}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{only\_group} = no arg
\sphinxstyleemphasis{occupation} = no arg
\sphinxstyleemphasis{surface} arg = sgroup\sphinxhyphen{}ID
  sgroup\sphinxhyphen{}ID = compute the dividing surface between group\sphinxhyphen{}ID and sgroup\sphinxhyphen{}ID
    this keyword adds a third column to the compute output
\sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} arg = v\_r
  v\_r = radius atom style variable for a poly\sphinxhyphen{}disperse Voronoi tessellation
\sphinxstyleemphasis{edge\_histo} arg = maxedge
  maxedge = maximum number of Voronoi cell edges to be accounted in the histogram
\sphinxstyleemphasis{edge\_threshold} arg = minlength
  minlength = minimum length for an edge to be counted
\sphinxstyleemphasis{face\_threshold} arg = minarea
  minarea = minimum area for a face to be counted
\sphinxstyleemphasis{neighbors} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} = store list of all neighbors or no
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{precipitate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{surface}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{matrix}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{3b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{precipitate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{radius}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}r}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{solute}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{only\PYGZus{}group}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{defects}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{occupation}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{neighbors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates the Voronoi tessellation of the
atoms in the simulation box.  The tessellation is calculated using all
atoms in the simulation, but non\sphinxhyphen{}zero values are only stored for atoms
in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities are calculated by this compute.  The first is
the volume of the Voronoi cell around each atom.  Any point in an
atom’s Voronoi cell is closer to that atom than any other.  The second
is the number of faces of the Voronoi cell. This is equal to the
number of nearest neighbors of the central atom, plus any exterior
faces (see note below).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{only\_group} keyword is specified the tessellation is performed
only with respect to the atoms contained in the compute group. This is
equivalent to deleting all atoms not contained in the group prior to
evaluating the tessellation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface} keyword is specified a third quantity per atom is
computed: the Voronoi cell surface of the given atom. \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface} takes
a group ID as an argument. If a group other than \sphinxstyleemphasis{all} is specified,
only the Voronoi cell facets facing a neighbor atom from the specified
group are counted towards the surface area.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the example above, a precipitate embedded in a matrix, only atoms
at the surface of the precipitate will have non\sphinxhyphen{}zero surface area, and
only the outward facing facets of the Voronoi cells are counted (the
hull of the precipitate). The total surface area of the precipitate
can be obtained by running a “reduce sum” compute on c\_2{[}3{]}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} keyword is specified with an atom style variable as
the argument, a poly\sphinxhyphen{}disperse Voronoi tessellation is
performed. Examples for radius variables are

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{r1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{type==1}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{type==2}\PYG{n+nv}{)}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{0.4}
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{radius}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{property}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{radius}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{r2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}radius}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here v\_r1 specifies a per\sphinxhyphen{}type radius of 0.1 units for type 1 atoms
and 0.4 units for type 2 atoms, and v\_r2 accesses the radius property
present in atom\_style sphere for granular models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{edge\_histo} keyword activates the compilation of a histogram of
number of edges on the faces of the Voronoi cells in the compute
group. The argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxedge} of the this keyword is the largest
number of edges on a single Voronoi cell face expected to occur in the
sample. This keyword generates output of a global vector by this
compute with \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxedge}+1 entries. The last entry in the vector
contains the number of faces with more than \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxedge} edges. Since the
polygon with the smallest amount of edges is a triangle, entries 1 and
2 of the vector will always be zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{edge\_threshold} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{face\_threshold} keywords allow the
suppression of edges below a given minimum length and faces below a
given minimum area. Ultra short edges and ultra small faces can occur
as artifacts of the Voronoi tessellation. These keywords will affect
the neighbor count and edge histogram outputs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{occupation} keyword is specified the tessellation is only
performed for the first invocation of the compute and then stored.
For all following invocations of the compute the number of atoms in
each Voronoi cell in the stored tessellation is counted. In this mode
the compute returns a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with 2 columns. The first column
is the number of atoms currently in the Voronoi volume defined by this
atom at the time of the first invocation of the compute (note that the
atom may have moved significantly). The second column contains the
total number of atoms sharing the Voronoi cell of the stored
tessellation at the location of the current atom. Numbers in column
one can be any positive integer including zero, while column two
values will always be greater than zero. Column one data can be used
to locate vacancies (the coordinates are given by the atom coordinates
at the time step when the compute was first invoked), while column two
data can be used to identify interstitial atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neighbors} value is set to yes, then this compute also creates
a local array with 3 columns. There is one row for each face of each
Voronoi cell. The 3 columns are the atom ID of the atom that owns the
cell, the atom ID of the atom in the neighboring cell (or zero if the
face is external), and the area of the face.  The array can be
accessed by any command that uses local values from a compute as
input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for an
overview of LAMMPS output options. More specifically, the array can be
accessed by a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}} command to write a file
containing all the Voronoi neighbors in a system:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{voronoi}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{neighbors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\PYG{k}{dump }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{d2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dump.neighbors}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{index}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}6[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}6[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}6[3]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{face\_threshold} keyword is used, then only faces with areas
greater than the threshold are stored.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The Voronoi calculation is performed by the freely available
\sphinxhref{https://math.lbl.gov/voro++/}{Voro++ package}, written by Chris Rycroft at UC Berkeley and LBL,
which must be installed on your system when building LAMMPS for use
with this compute.  See instructions on obtaining and installing the
Voro++ software in the src/VORONOI/README file.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The calculation of Voronoi volumes is performed by each processor
for the atoms it owns, and includes the effect of ghost atoms
stored by the processor.  This assumes that the Voronoi cells of
owned atoms are not affected by atoms beyond the ghost atom cut\sphinxhyphen{}off
distance.  This is usually a good assumption for liquid and solid
systems, but may lead to underestimation of Voronoi volumes in low
density systems.  By default, the set of ghost atoms stored by each
processor is determined by the cutoff used for {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} interactions.  The cutoff can be set explicitly via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify cutoff}}}} command.  The Voronoi
cells for atoms adjacent to empty regions will extend into those
regions up to the communication cutoff in \(x\), \(y\), or
\(z\).  In that situation, an exterior face is created at the
cutoff distance normal to the \(x\), \(y\), or \(z\)
direction.  For triclinic systems, the exterior face is parallel to
the corresponding reciprocal lattice vector.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Voro++ package performs its calculation in 3d.  This will still
work for a 2d LAMMPS simulation, provided all the atoms have the
same \(z\)\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate. The Voronoi cell of each atom will be a
columnar polyhedron with constant cross\sphinxhyphen{}sectional area along the
\(z\)\sphinxhyphen{}direction and two exterior faces at the top and bottom of
the simulation box. If the atoms do not all have the same
\(z\)\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate, then the columnar cells will be accordingly
distorted. The cross\sphinxhyphen{}sectional area of each Voronoi cell can be
obtained by dividing its volume by the \(z\) extent of the
simulation box.  Note that you define the \(z\) extent of the
simulation box for 2d simulations when using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_box::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_box}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} commands.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,deprecated}{Deprecated since version 21Nov2023: }The \sphinxstyleemphasis{peratom} keyword was removed as it is no longer required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a per\sphinxhyphen{}atom array with two columns. In regular
dynamic tessellation mode the first column is the Voronoi volume, the
second is the neighbor count, as described above (read above for the
output data in case the \sphinxstyleemphasis{occupation} keyword is specified).  These
values can be accessed by any command that uses per\sphinxhyphen{}atom values from a
compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} page for
an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{edge\_histo} keyword is used, then this compute generates a
global vector of length \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxedge}+1, containing a histogram of the
number of edges per face.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neighbors} value is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}, then this compute calculates a
local array with three columns. There is one row for each face of each
Voronoi cell.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Voronoi cell volume will be in distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} cubed.
The Voronoi face area will be in distance {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} squared.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the VORONOI package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It also requires you have a copy of the Voro++ library built and
installed on your system.  See instructions on obtaining and
installing the Voro++ software in the src/VORONOI/README file.

\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump custom}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump local}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{compute_voronoi_atom:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default for the neighbors keyword is no.

\section{compute xrd command}
\label{\detokenize{compute_xrd:compute-xrd-command}}\label{\detokenize{compute_xrd:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{compute_xrd::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{compute_xrd:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{group\PYGZhy{}ID}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xrd}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lambda}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{typeN}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ID, group\sphinxhyphen{}ID are documented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute}}}} command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
xrd = style name of this compute command

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lambda = wavelength of incident radiation (length units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
type1 type2 … typeN = chemical symbol of each atom type (see valid options below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{2Theta} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{c} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{LP} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{manual} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{echo}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{2Theta} values = Min2Theta Max2Theta
  Min2Theta,Max2Theta = minimum and maximum 2 theta range to explore
  (radians or degrees)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{c} values = c1 c2 c3
  c1,c2,c3 = parameters to adjust the spacing of the reciprocal
             lattice nodes in the h, k, and l directions respectively
\sphinxstyleemphasis{LP} value = switch to apply Lorentz\sphinxhyphen{}polarization factor
  0/1 = off/on
\sphinxstyleemphasis{manual} = flag to use manual spacing of reciprocal lattice points
           based on the values of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{c} parameters
\sphinxstyleemphasis{echo} = flag to provide extra output for debugging purposes
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{compute_xrd:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define a computation that calculates X\sphinxhyphen{}ray diffraction intensity as described
in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_xrd:xrd-coleman}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Coleman)}}}} on a mesh of reciprocal lattice nodes defined
by the entire simulation domain (or manually) using a simulated radiation
of wavelength \sphinxstyleemphasis{lambda}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The X\sphinxhyphen{}ray diffraction intensity, \(I\), at each reciprocal lattice point,
\(k\), is computed from the structure factor, \(F\), using the
equations:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}I &= L_p(\theta)\frac{F^{*}F}{N} \\
F(\mathbf{k}) &= \sum_{j=1}^{N}f_j(\theta)exp(2\pi i \mathbf{k}\cdot \mathbf{r}_j) \\
L_p(\theta) &= \frac{1+\cos^2(2\theta)}{\cos(\theta)\sin^2(\theta)} \\
\frac{\sin(\theta)}{\lambda} &= \frac{\left\lVert\mathbf{k}\right\rVert}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\mathbf{k}\) is the location of the reciprocal lattice node,
\(r_j\) is the position of each atom, \(f_j\) are atomic
scattering factors, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Lp} is the Lorentz\sphinxhyphen{}polarization factor, and
\(\theta\) is the scattering angle of diffraction.  The
Lorentz\sphinxhyphen{}polarization factor can be turned off using the optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{LP}
keyword.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Diffraction intensities are calculated on a three\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional mesh of
reciprocal lattice nodes. The mesh spacing is defined either (a) by the
entire simulation domain or (b) manually using selected values as shown
in the 2D diagram below.

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics[scale=0.75]{{xrd_mesh}.png}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a mesh defined by the simulation domain, a rectilinear grid is
constructed with spacing \(c A^{-1}\) along each reciprocal lattice
axis, where \(A\) is a matrix containing the vectors corresponding
to the edges of the simulation cell. If one or two directions has
non\sphinxhyphen{}periodic boundary conditions, then the spacing in these directions
is defined from the average of the (inversed) box lengths with periodic
boundary conditions.  Meshes defined by the simulation domain must
contain at least one periodic boundary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{manual} flag is included, the mesh of reciprocal lattice nodes
will be defined using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{c} values for the spacing along each
reciprocal lattice axis. Note that manual mapping of the reciprocal
space mesh is good for comparing diffraction results from multiple
simulations; however, it can reduce the likelihood that Bragg
reflections will be satisfied unless small spacing parameters
(\(< 0.05~\AA^{-1}\)) are implemented.
Meshes with manual spacing do not require a periodic boundary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The limits of the reciprocal lattice mesh are determined by range of
scattering angles explored.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{2Theta} parameter allows the user
to reduce the scattering angle range to only the region of interest
which reduces the cost of the computation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The atomic scattering factor, \(f_j\), accounts for the reduction in
diffraction intensity due to Compton scattering.  Compute xrd uses
analytical approximations of the atomic scattering factors that vary
for each atom type (type1 type2 … typeN) and angle of diffraction.
The analytic approximation is computed using the formula
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_xrd:colliex}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Colliex)}}}}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f_j\left ( \frac{\sin(\theta)}{\lambda} \right )=\sum_{i=1}^{4}
a_i \exp\left ( -b_i \frac{\sin^{2}(\theta)}{\lambda^{2}} \right )+c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Coefficients parameterized by {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_xrd:peng}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Peng)}}}} are assigned for each
atom type designating the chemical symbol and charge of each atom
type. Valid chemical symbols for compute xrd are:

\subsection{Output info}
\label{\detokenize{compute_xrd:output-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute calculates a global array.  The number of rows in the
array is the number of reciprocal lattice nodes that are explored
which by the mesh.  The global array has two columns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first column contains the diffraction angle in the units (radians
or degrees) provided with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{2Theta} values. The second column contains
the computed diffraction intensities as described above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The array can be accessed by any command that uses global values from
a compute as input.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_output::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto output}}}} doc page
for an overview of LAMMPS output options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All array values calculated by this compute are “intensive”.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{compute_xrd:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This compute is part of the DIFFRACTION package.  It is only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The compute\_xrd command does not work for triclinic cells.

The option defaults are \sphinxstyleemphasis{2Theta} = 1 179 (degrees), \sphinxstyleemphasis{c} = 1 1 1, \sphinxstyleemphasis{LP} = 1,
no manual flag, no echo flag.

\section{pair\_style adp command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:pair-style-adp-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_adp::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{adp/kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{adp/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adp}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adp}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta.adp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{AlCu.adp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cu}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{adp} computes pairwise interactions for metals and metal alloys
using the angular dependent potential (ADP) of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_adp:mishin}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mishin)}}}},
which is a generalization of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{embedded atom method (EAM) potential}}}}.  The LAMMPS implementation is discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_adp:singh}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Singh)}}}}.  The total energy Ei of an atom I is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_i            & = F_\alpha \left( \sum_{j\neq i} \rho_\beta (r_{ij}) \right) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j\neq i}\phi_{\alpha\beta}(r_{ij})+ \frac{1}{2} \sum_s (\mu_i^s)^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{s,t} (\lambda_i^{st})^2 - \frac{1}{6} \nu_i^2 \\
\mu_i^s        & = \sum_{j\neq i}u_{\alpha\beta}(r_{ij})r_{ij}^s\\
\lambda_i^{st} & = \sum_{j\neq i}w_{\alpha\beta}(r_{ij})r_{ij}^sr_{ij}^t\\
\nu_i          & = \sum_s\lambda_i^{ss}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(F\) is the embedding energy which is a function of the atomic
electron density \(\rho\), \(\phi\) is a pair potential interaction,
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are the element types of atoms \(I\) and
\(J\), and \(s\) and \(t = 1,2,3\) and refer to the cartesian
coordinates.  The \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\) terms represent the dipole
and quadruple distortions of the local atomic environment which extend the
original EAM framework by introducing angular forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that unlike for other potentials, cutoffs for ADP potentials are
not set in the pair\_style or pair\_coeff command; they are specified in
the ADP potential files themselves.  Likewise, the ADP potential files
list atomic masses; thus you do not need to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{mass::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mass}}}}
command to specify them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{ADP potentials are available from:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The NIST WWW site at \sphinxurl{https://www.ctcms.nist.gov/potentials}.
Note that ADP potentials obtained from NIST must be converted
into the extended DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} format discussed below.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The OpenKIM Project at
\sphinxurl{https://openkim.org/browse/models/by-type}
provides ADP potentials that can be used directly in LAMMPS with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim command}}}} interface.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{adp} style which
specifies an extended DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file, which contains information
for \(M\) elements.  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying \(N\)
additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff command,
where \(N\) is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N\) element names = mapping of extended \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways to
specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, the potentials/AlCu.adp file, included in the
potentials directory of the LAMMPS distribution, is an extended \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl}
file which has tabulated ADP values for w elements and their alloy
interactions: Cu and Al.  If your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atoms types
and you want the first 3 to be Al, and the fourth to be Cu, you would use
the following pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{AlCu.adp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cu}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The first three Al arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the Al
element in the extended \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.  The final Cu argument maps
LAMMPS atom type 4 to the Al element in the extended \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.
Note that there is no requirement that your simulation use all the
elements specified by the extended \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a mapping value is specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed.
This can be used when an \sphinxstyleemphasis{adp} potential is used as part of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.  The NULL values are placeholders for atom types
that will be used with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Adp} files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS distribution
have an “.adp” suffix.  A DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file extended for ADP is
formatted as follows.  Basically it is the standard \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} format
with additional tabulated functions u and w added to the file after
the tabulated pair potentials.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_eam}}}}
command for further details on the \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} format.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lines 1,2,3 = comments (ignored)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 4: \(N_{\text{elements}}\) Element1 Element2 … ElementN

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 5: \(N_{\rho}\), \(d_{\rho}\), \(N_r\), \(d_r\), cutoff

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the 5 header lines are \(N_{\text{elements}}\) sections, one for each
element, each with the following format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 1 = atomic number, mass, lattice constant, lattice type (e.g. FCC)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
embedding function \(F(\rho)\) (\(N_{\rho}\) values)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density function \(\rho(r)\) (\(N_r\) values)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the \(N_{\text{elements}}\) sections, \(N_r\) values for each pair potential
\(\phi(r)\) array are listed for all \(i,j\) element pairs in the same format
as other arrays.  Since these interactions are symmetric (\(i,j = j,i\))
only \(\phi\) arrays with \(i \geq j\) are listed, in the following order:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}i,j = (1,1), (2,1), (2,2), (3,1), (3,2), (3,3), (4,1), ..., (N_{\text{elements}},N_{\text{elements}}).\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tabulated values for each \(\phi\) function are listed as
\(r*\phi\) (in units of eV\sphinxhyphen{}Angstroms), since they are for atom pairs, the
same as for {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{other EAM files}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After the \(\phi(r)\) arrays, each of the \(u(r)\) arrays are listed in the
same order with the same assumptions of symmetry.  Directly following
the \(u(r)\), the \(w(r)\) arrays are listed.  Note that \(\phi(r)\) is the only
array tabulated with a scaling by \(r\).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, where types I and J correspond to
two different element types, no special mixing rules are needed, since
the ADP potential files specify alloy interactions explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in tabulated potential files.
Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in
an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the MANYBODY package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_eam}}}}


\subsection{Default}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_adp:singh}}

\section{pair\_style agni command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:pair-style-agni-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_agni::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{agni/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{agni}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{agni}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al.agni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{agni} style computes the many\sphinxhyphen{}body vectorial force components for
an atom as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_i^u                  & = \sum_t^{N_t}\alpha_t \cdot \exp\left[-\frac{\left(d_{i,t}^u\right)^2}{2l^2}\right] \\
d_{i,t}^u              & = \left|\left| V_i^u(\eta) - V_t^u(\eta) \right|\right| \\
V_i^u(\eta)            & = \sum_{j \neq i}\frac{r^u_{ij}}{r_{ij}} \cdot e^{-\left(\frac{r_{ij}}{\eta} \right)^2} \cdot f_d\left(r_{ij}\right) \\
f_d\left(r_{ij}\right) & = \frac{1}{2} \left[\cos\left(\frac{\pi r_{ij}}{R_c}\right) + 1 \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(u\) labels the individual components, i.e. \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\), and \(V\) is the
corresponding atomic fingerprint. \(d\) is the Euclidean distance between
any two atomic fingerprints. A total of \(N_t\) reference atomic
environments are considered to construct the force field file. \(\alpha_t\)
and \(l\) are the weight coefficients and length scale parameter of the
non\sphinxhyphen{}linear regression model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The method implements the recently proposed machine learning access to
atomic forces as discussed extensively in the following publications \sphinxhyphen{}
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_agni:botu2015adaptive}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Botu1)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_agni:botu2015learning}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Botu2)}}}}. The premise
of the method is to map the atomic environment numerically into a
fingerprint, and use machine learning methods to create a mapping to the
vectorial atomic forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{agni} style which
specifies an AGNI potential file containing the parameters of the
force field for the needed elements. These are mapped to LAMMPS atom
types by specifying \(N\) additional arguments after the filename in the
pair\_coeff command, where \(N\) is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N\) element names = mapping of AGNI elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the force field file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
An AGNI force field is fully specified by the filename which contains the
parameters of the force field, i.e., the reference training environments
used to construct the machine learning force field. Example force field
and input files are provided in the examples/PACKAGES/agni directory.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_agni:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, only elemental systems are implemented. Also, the method
only provides access to the forces and not energies or stresses.
The lack of potential energy data makes this pair style incompatible with
several of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{min_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{minimizer algorthms}}}} like \sphinxstyleemphasis{cg} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{sd}.
It should work with damped dynamics based minimizers like \sphinxstyleemphasis{fire} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{quickmin}.  However, one can access the energy via thermodynamic
integration of the forces as discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_agni:botu2016construct}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Botu3)}}}}.  This pair style is part of the
MISC package. It is only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that
package. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more
info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The AGNI force field files provided with LAMMPS (see the
potentials directory) are parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
You can use the AGNI potential with any LAMMPS units, but you would need
to create your own AGNI potential file with coefficients listed in the
appropriate units if your simulation does not use “metal” units.
