\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_aip_water_2dm:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 15Jun2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{aip/water/2dm} style computes the anisotropic interfacial potential
(AIP) potential for interfaces of water with two\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional (2D)
materials as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_aip_water_2dm:feng1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Feng1)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_aip_water_2dm:feng2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Feng2)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E  = & \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} V_{ij} \\
V_{ij}  = & {\rm Tap}(r_{ij})\left \{ e^{-\alpha (r_{ij}/\beta -1)}
             \left [ \epsilon + f(\rho_{ij}) + f(\rho_{ji})\right ] -
              \frac{1}{1+e^{-d\left [ \left ( r_{ij}/\left (s_R \cdot r^{eff} \right ) \right )-1 \right ]}}
              \cdot \frac{C_6}{r^6_{ij}} \right \}\\
\rho_{ij}^2 = & r_{ij}^2 - ({\bf r}_{ij} \cdot {\bf n}_i)^2 \\
\rho_{ji}^2  = & r_{ij}^2 - ({\bf r}_{ij} \cdot {\bf n}_j)^2 \\
f(\rho)  = &  C e^{ -( \rho / \delta )^2 } \\
{\rm Tap}(r_{ij})  = & 20\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^7 -
                        70\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^6 +
                        84\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^5 -
                        35\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^4 + 1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where \(\mathrm{Tap}(r_{ij})\) is the taper function which provides
a continuous cutoff (up to third derivative) for interatomic separations
larger than \(r_c\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style ilp\_graphene\_hbn}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style uses the atomic normal vector definition from
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_aip_water_2dm:feng1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Feng1)}}}}), where the atomic normal vectors of the
hydrogen atoms are assumed to lie along the corresponding
oxygen\sphinxhyphen{}hydrogen bonds and the normal vector of the central oxygen
atom is defined as their average.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The provided parameter file, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CBNOH.aip.water.2dm}}, is intended for use
with \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, with energies in meV.  Two additional
parameters, \sphinxstyleemphasis{S}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcut} are included in the parameter file. \sphinxstyleemphasis{S} is
designed to facilitate scaling of energies; \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcut} is the cutoff for an
internal, short distance neighbor list that is generated for speeding up
the calculation of the normals for all atom pairs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters presented in the provided parameter file,
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CBNOH.aip.water.2dm}}, are fitted with the taper function enabled by
setting the cutoff equal to 16.0 Angstrom.  Using a different cutoff
or taper function setting should be carefully checked as they can
lead to significant errors.  These parameters provide a good
description in both short\sphinxhyphen{} and long\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction regimes. This
is essential for simulations in high pressure regime (i.e., the
interlayer distance is smaller than the equilibrium distance).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential must be used in combination with hybrid/overlay.  Other
interactions can be set to zero using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff settings}}}} with the pair style set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style tallies a breakdown of the total interlayer potential
energy into sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories, which can be accessed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
pair}}}} command as a vector of values of length 2.  The 2
values correspond to the following sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{E\_vdW} = vdW (attractive) energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{E\_Rep} = Repulsive energy

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To print these quantities to the log file (with descriptive column
headings) the following commands could be included in an input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{aip}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{water}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{n}{dm}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Evdw}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[1]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Erep}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[2]}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}Erep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}Evdw}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_aip_water_2dm:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the pair\_modify mix, shift, table, and
tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write their information to binary restart
files, since it is stored in potential files. Thus, you need to
re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_aip_water_2dm:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the INTERLAYER package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the newton setting to be \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} for pair
interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CBNOH.aip.water.2dm}} potential file provided with LAMMPS is
parameterized for \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units.  You can use this pair style with any
LAMMPS units, but you would need to create your own potential file with
parameters in the appropriate units, if your simulation does not use
\sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units.

\label{\detokenize{pair_airebo:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LJ\PYGZus{}flag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{TORSION\PYGZus{}flag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff\PYGZus{}min}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo/morse} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rebo}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = LJ or Morse cutoff (\(\sigma\) scale factor) (AIREBO and AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M only)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LJ\_flag = 0/1 to turn off/on the LJ or Morse term (AIREBO and AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M only, optional)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
TORSION\_flag = 0/1 to turn off/on the torsion term (AIREBO and AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M only, optional)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff\_min = Start of the transition region of cutoff (\(\sigma\) scale factor) (AIREBO and AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M only, optional)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_airebo:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{airebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{airebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{CH.airebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{airebo}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{morse}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{CH.airebo}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{m}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{CH.rebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_airebo:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo} pair style computes the Adaptive Intermolecular Reactive
Empirical Bond Order (AIREBO) Potential of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo:stuart}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Stuart)}}}} for a
system of carbon and/or hydrogen atoms.  Note that this is the initial
formulation of AIREBO from 2000, not the later formulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo/morse} pair style computes the AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M potential, which
is equivalent to AIREBO, but replaces the LJ term with a Morse potential.
The Morse potentials are parameterized by high\sphinxhyphen{}quality quantum chemistry
(MP2) calculations and do not diverge as quickly as particle density
increases. This allows AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M to retain accuracy to much higher pressures
than AIREBO (up to 40 GPa for Polyethylene). Details for this potential
and its parameterization are given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo:oconnor}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(O’Conner)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{rebo} pair style computes the Reactive Empirical Bond Order (REBO)
Potential of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo:brenner}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Brenner)}}}}. Note that this is the so\sphinxhyphen{}called
second generation REBO from 2002, not the original REBO from 1990.
As discussed below, second generation REBO is closely related to the
initial AIREBO; it is just a subset of the potential energy terms
with a few slightly different parameters

\sphinxAtStartPar
The AIREBO potential consists of three terms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i}
\left[ E^{\text{REBO}}_{ij} + E^{\text{LJ}}_{ij} +
 \sum_{k \neq i,j} \sum_{l \neq i,j,k} E^{\text{TORSION}}_{kijl} \right] \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, all three terms are included.  For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo} style, if
the first two optional flag arguments to the pair\_style command are
included, the LJ and torsional terms can be turned off.  Note that
both or neither of the flags must be included.  If both of the LJ an
torsional terms are turned off, it becomes the second\sphinxhyphen{}generation REBO
potential, with a small caveat on the spline fitting procedure
mentioned below.  This can be specified directly as pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{rebo}
with no additional arguments.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The detailed formulas for this potential are given in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo:stuart}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Stuart)}}}}; here we provide only a brief description.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(E^{\text{REBO}}\) term has the same functional form as the hydrocarbon REBO
potential developed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo:brenner}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Brenner)}}}}.  The coefficients for
\(E^{\text{REBO}}\) in AIREBO are essentially the same as Brenner’s potential, but
a few fitted spline values are slightly different.  For most cases the
\(E^{\text{REBO}}\) term in AIREBO will produce the same energies, forces and
statistical averages as the original REBO potential from which it was
derived.  The \(E^{\text{REBO}}\) term in the AIREBO potential gives the model its
reactive capabilities and only describes short\sphinxhyphen{}ranged C\sphinxhyphen{}C, C\sphinxhyphen{}H and H\sphinxhyphen{}H
interactions (\(r < 2 \AA\)). These interactions have strong
coordination\sphinxhyphen{}dependence through a bond order parameter, which adjusts
the attraction between the I,J atoms based on the position of other
nearby atoms and thus has 3\sphinxhyphen{} and 4\sphinxhyphen{}body dependence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(E^{\text{LJ}}\) term adds longer\sphinxhyphen{}ranged interactions (\(2 < r < \text{cutoff}\)) using a
form similar to the standard {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Lennard Jones potential}}}}.
The \(E^{\text{LJ}}\) term in AIREBO contains a series of switching functions so
that the short\sphinxhyphen{}ranged LJ repulsion (\(1/r^{12}\)) does not interfere with
the energetics captured by the \(E^{\text{REBO}}\) term.  The extent of the \(E^{\text{LJ}}\)
interactions is determined by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} argument to the pair\_style
command which is a scale factor.  For each type pair (C\sphinxhyphen{}C, C\sphinxhyphen{}H, H\sphinxhyphen{}H)
the cutoff is obtained by multiplying the scale factor by the sigma
value defined in the potential file for that type pair.  In the
standard AIREBO potential, \(\sigma_{CC} = 3.4 \AA\), so with a scale
factor of 3.0 (the argument in pair\_style), the resulting \(E^{\text{LJ}}\) cutoff
would be \(10.2 \AA\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default, the longer\sphinxhyphen{}ranged interaction is smoothly switched off
between 2.16 and 3.0 \(\sigma\). By specifying \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff\_min} in addition
to \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}, the switching can be configured to take place between
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff\_min} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}. \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff\_min} can only be specified if all
optional arguments are given.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(E^{\text{TORSION}}\) term is an explicit 4\sphinxhyphen{}body potential that describes
various dihedral angle preferences in hydrocarbon configurations.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{rebo} style which specifies an AIREBO, REBO, or AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M potential
file with parameters for C and H.  Note that as of LAMMPS version
15 May 2019 the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rebo} style in LAMMPS uses its own potential
file (CH.rebo).  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying
N additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff command,
where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N\) element names = mapping of AIREBO elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, if your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atom types and you want
the first 3 to be C, and the fourth to be H, you would use the following
pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CH.airebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The first three C arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the C
element in the AIREBO file.  The final H argument maps LAMMPS atom
type 4 to the H element in the AIREBO file.  If a mapping value is
specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed.  This can be used
when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{airebo} potential is used as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.
The NULL values are placeholders for atom types that will be used with
other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters/coefficients for the AIREBO potentials are listed in
the CH.airebo file to agree with the original {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo:stuart}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Stuart)}}}}
paper.  Thus the parameters are specific to this potential and the way
it was fit, so modifying the file should be done cautiously.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly the parameters/coefficients for the AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M potentials are
listed in the CH.airebo\sphinxhyphen{}m file to agree with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo:oconnor}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(O’Connor)}}}}
paper. Thus the parameters are specific to this potential and the way
it was fit, so modifying the file should be done cautiously. The
AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M Morse potentials were parameterized using a cutoff of
3.0 (\(\sigma\)). Modifying this cutoff may impact simulation accuracy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style tallies a breakdown of the total AIREBO potential
energy into sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories, which can be accessed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}} command as a vector of values of length 3.
The 3 values correspond to the following sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(E_{\text{REBO}}\) = REBO energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(E_{\text{LJ}}\) = Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(E_{\text{TORSION}}\) = Torsion energy

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To print these quantities to the log file (with descriptive column
headings) the following commands could be included in an input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{airebo}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{REBO}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[1]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{LJ}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[2]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{TORSION}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[3]}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}REBO}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}LJ}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}TORSION}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_airebo:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
mix, shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_airebo:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles are part of the MANYBODY package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair potentials require the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be
“on” for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The CH.airebo and CH.airebo\sphinxhyphen{}m potential files provided with LAMMPS (see
the potentials directory) are parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  You can use the pair styles with \sphinxstyleemphasis{any} LAMMPS units, but you
would need to create your own AIREBO or AIREBO\sphinxhyphen{}M potential file with
coefficients listed in the appropriate units, if your simulation does
not use “metal” units.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair styles provided here \sphinxstylestrong{only} support potential files parameterized
for the elements carbon and hydrogen (designated with “C” and “H” in the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command.  Using potential files for other elements will trigger
an error.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_amoeba:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{amoeba} style computes the AMOEBA polarizable field formulated
by Jay Ponder’s group at the U Washington at St Louis {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-ren}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ren)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-shi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Shi)}}}}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hippo} style computes
the HIPPO polarizable force field, an extension to AMOEBA, formulated
by Josh Rackers and collaborators in the Ponder group {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-rackers}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rackers)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These force fields can be used when polarization effects are desired
in simulations of water, organic molecules, and biomolecules including
proteins, provided that parameterizations (Tinker PRM force field
files) are available for the systems you are interested in.  Files in
the LAMMPS potentials directory with a “amoeba” or “hippo” suffix can
be used.  The Tinker distribution and website have additional force
field files as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto amoeba}}}} doc page, the
intermolecular (non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded) portion of the AMOEBA force field contains
these terms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{amoeba} = U_{multipole} + U_{polar} + U_{hal}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while the HIPPO force field contains these terms:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{hippo} = U_{multipole} + U_{polar} + U_{qxfer} + U_{repulsion} + U_{dispersion}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Conceptually, these terms compute the following interactions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(U_{hal}\) = buffered 14\sphinxhyphen{}7 van der Waals with offsets applied to hydrogen atoms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(U_{repulsion}\) = Pauli repulsion due to rearrangement of electron density

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(U_{dispersion}\) = dispersion between correlated, instantaneous induced dipole moments

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(U_{multipole}\) = electrostatics between permanent point charges, dipoles, and quadrupoles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(U_{polar}\) = electronic polarization between induced point dipoles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(U_{qxfer}\) = charge transfer effects

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the AMOEBA versus HIPPO force fields typically compute the
same term differently using their own formulas.  The references on
this doc page give full details for both force fields.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The formulas for the AMOEBA energy terms are:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{hal} = & \epsilon_{ij} \left( \frac{1.07}{\rho_{ij} + 0.07} \right)^7 \left( \frac{1.12}{\rho_{ij}^7 + 0.12} - 2 \right) \\
U_{multipole} = & \vec{M}_i\boldsymbol{T_{ij}}\vec{M}_j, \quad \mbox{with} \quad
   \vec{M} = \left(q, \vec{\mu}_{perm}, \boldsymbol{\Theta} \right) \\
U_{polar} = & \frac{1}{2}\vec{\mu}_i^{ind} \vec{E}_i^{perm}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The formulas for the HIPPO energy terms are:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{multipole} = & Z_i \frac{1}{r_{ij}} Z_j + Z_i T_{ij}^{damp} \vec{M}_j + Z_j T_{ji}^{damp} \vec{M}_i + \vec{M}_i T_{ij}^{damp} \vec{M}_j, \quad \mbox{with} \quad
   \vec{M} = \left(q, \vec{\mu}_{perm}, \boldsymbol{\Theta} \right) \\
U_{polar} = & \frac{1}{2}\vec{\mu}_i^{ind} \vec{E}_i^{perm} \\
U_{qxfer} = & \epsilon_i e^{-\eta_j r_{ij}} + \epsilon_j e^{-\eta_i r_{ij}} \\
U_{repulsion} = & \frac{K_i K_j}{r_{ij}} S^2
   S^2 = \left( \int{\phi_i \phi_j} dv \right)^2 = \vec{M}_i\boldsymbol{T_{ij}^{repulsion}}\vec{M}_j \\
U_{dispersion} = & -\frac{C_6^iC_6^j}{r_{ij}^6} \left( f_{damp}^{dispersion} \right)_{ij}^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The AMOEBA and HIPPO force fields compute long\sphinxhyphen{}range charge, dipole,
and quadrupole interactions as well as long\sphinxhyphen{}range dispersion
effects.  However, unlike other models with long\sphinxhyphen{}range interactions
in LAMMPS, this does not require use of a KSpace style via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command.  That is because for
AMOEBA and HIPPO the long\sphinxhyphen{}range computations are intertwined with
the pairwise computations.  So these pair style include both short\sphinxhyphen{}
and long\sphinxhyphen{}range computations.  This means the energy and virial
computed by the pair style as well as the “Pair” timing reported by
LAMMPS will include the long\sphinxhyphen{}range calculations.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The implementation of the AMOEBA and HIPPO force fields in LAMMPS was
done using F90 code provided by the Ponder group from their \sphinxhref{https://dasher.wustl.edu/tinker/}{Tinker MD
code}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The current implementation (July 2022) of AMOEBA in LAMMPS matches the
version discussed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-ponder}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ponder)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-ren}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ren)}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-shi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Shi)}}}}.  Likewise the current
implementation of HIPPO in LAMMPS matches the version discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_amoeba:amoeba-rackers}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rackers)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 8Feb2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator support via the GPU package is available.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with either the \sphinxstyleemphasis{amoeba} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hippo} styles which specifies two Tinker files, a PRM and KEY file.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{protein.prm.amoeba}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{protein.key.amoeba}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{water.prm.hippo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{..}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{water.key.hippo}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples of the PRM files are in the potentials directory with an
*.amoeba or *.hippo suffix.  The examples/amoeba directory has
examples of both PRM and KEY files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A Tinker PRM file is composed of sections, each of which has multiple
lines.  A Tinker KEY file is composed of lines, each of which has a
keyword followed by zero or more parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The list of PRM sections and KEY keywords which LAMMPS recognizes are
listed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto amoeba}}}} doc page.  If not
recognized, the section or keyword is skipped.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if the KEY file is specified as NULL, then no file is
required; default values for various AMOEBA/HIPPO settings are used.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto amoeba}}}} doc page also gives the default
settings.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 3Nov2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{amoeba} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hippo} pair styles support extraction of two per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
quantities by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pair}}}} command.  This allows the
quantities to be output to files by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} or otherwise
processed by other LAMMPS commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The names of the two quantities are “uind” and “uinp” for the induced
dipole moments for each atom.  Neither quantity needs to be triggered by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pair}}}} command in order for these pair styles to
calculate it.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_amoeba:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
mix, shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary
restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.
Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in
an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the GPU accelerated pair styles ‘amoeba/gpu’ or ‘hippo/gpu’
when compiling the GPU package for OpenCL has a few known issues
when running on integrated GPUs and the calculation may crash.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The GPU accelerated pair styles are also not (yet) compatible
with single precision FFTs.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_amoeba:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles are part of the AMOEBA package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} doc page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The AMOEBA and HIPPO potential (PRM) and KEY files provided with
LAMMPS in the potentials and examples/amoeba directories are Tinker
files parameterized for Tinker units.  Their numeric parameters are
converted by LAMMPS to its real units {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  Thus you
can only use these pair styles with real units.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These potentials do not yet calculate per\sphinxhyphen{}atom energy or virial
contributions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As explained on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{AMOEBA and HIPPO howto}}}} page,
use of these pair styles to run a simulation with the AMOEBA or HIPPO
force fields requires several things.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first is a data file generated by the tools/tinker/tinker2lmp.py
conversion script which uses Tinker file force field file input to
create a data file compatible with LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second is use of these commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style amoeba}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds one/five}}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
And third, depending on the model being simulated, these
commands for intramolecular interactions may also be required:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style class2}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style amoeba}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_fourier::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style fourier}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style amoeba}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_pitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix amoeba/pitorsion}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_bitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix amoeba/bitorsion}}}}

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_amoeba:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style amoeba}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_style class2}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style amoeba}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_fourier::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style fourier}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{improper_amoeba::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{improper\_style amoeba}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_pitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix amoeba/pitorsion}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_amoeba_bitorsion::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix amoeba/bitorsion}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds one/five}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}}


\subsection{Default}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\index{pair\_style atm@\spxentry{pair\_style atm}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style atm command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_atm:pair-style-atm-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_atm:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_atm::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_atm:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff\PYGZus{}triple}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = cutoff for each pair in 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff\_triple = additional cutoff applied to product of 3 pairwise distances (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_atm:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.072}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.064}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.080}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.100}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.125}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_atm:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{atm} style computes a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_atm:axilrod}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Axilrod\sphinxhyphen{}Teller\sphinxhyphen{}Muto}}}}
potential for the energy E of a system of atoms as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & = \nu\frac{1+3\cos\gamma_1\cos\gamma_2\cos\gamma_3}{r_{12}^3r_{23}^3r_{31}^3} \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\nu\) is the three\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction strength.  The distances
between pairs of atoms \(r_{12}\), \(r_{23}\), \(r_{31}\) and the angles \(\gamma_1\), \(\gamma_2\),
\(\gamma_3\) are as shown in this diagram:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{pair_atm_dia}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for the interaction between a triplet of atoms \(I,J,K\), there
is no “central” atom.  The interaction is symmetric with respect to
permutation of the three atoms. Thus the \(\nu\) value is
the same for all those permutations of the atom types of \(I,J,K\)
and needs to be specified only once, as discussed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{atm} potential is typically used in combination with a two\sphinxhyphen{}body
potential using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid/overlay}}}}
command as in the example above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential for a triplet of atom is calculated only if all 3 distances
\(r_{12}\), \(r_{23}\), \(r_{31}\) between the three atoms satisfy
\(r_{IJ} < \text{cutoff}\).  In addition, the product of the 3 distances
\(r_{12} r_{23} r_{31}\) \textless{} cutoff\_triple \(^3\) is required, which
excludes from calculation the triplets with small contribution to the
interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K\) = atom type of the third atom (1 to \(N_{\text{types}}\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\nu\) = prefactor (energy/distance\textasciicircum{}9 units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K\) can be specified in one of two ways.  An explicit numeric value
or type label can be used, as in the second example above.   LAMMPS
sets the coefficients for the other 5 symmetric interactions to the same
values.  E.g. if \(I = 1\), \(J = 2\), \(K = 3\), then these 6
values are set to the specified \(\nu\): \(\nu_{123}\),
\(\nu_{132}\), \(\nu_{213}\), \(\nu_{231}\), \(\nu_{312}\),
\(\nu_{321}\).  This enforces the symmetry discussed above.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A wildcard asterisk can be used for K to set the coefficients for
multiple triplets of atom types.  This takes the form “*” or “*n” or
“n*” or “m*n”.  If \(N\) equals the number of atom types, then an asterisk with
no numeric values means all types from 1 to \(N\).  A leading asterisk
means all types from 1 to \(n\) (inclusive).  A trailing asterisk means
all types from \(n\) to \(N\) (inclusive).  A middle asterisk means all types
from \(m\) to \(n\) (inclusive).  Note that only type triplets with \(J \leq K\) are
considered; if asterisks imply type triplets where \(K < J\), they are
ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a pair\_coeff command can override a previous setting for the
same \(I,J,K\) triplet.  For example, these commands set \(\nu\) for all \(I,J.K\)
triplets, then overwrite nu for just the \(I,J,K = 2,3,4\) triplet:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for a simulation with a single atom type, only a single
entry is required, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.25}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a simulation with two atom types, four pair\_coeff commands will
specify all possible nu values:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu2}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu3}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu4}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a simulation with three atom types, ten pair\_coeff commands will
specify all possible nu values:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu2}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu3}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu4}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu6}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu7}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu8}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nu10}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
By default the \(\nu\) value for all triplets is set to 0.0.  Thus it is
not required to provide pair\_coeff commands that enumerate triplet
interactions for all \(K\) types.  If some \(I,J,K\) combination is not
specified, then there will be no 3\sphinxhyphen{}body ATM interactions for that
combination and all its permutations.  However, as with all pair
styles, it is required to specify a pair\_coeff command for all \(I,J\)
combinations, else an error will result.

\section{pair\_style awpmd/cut command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_awpmd:pair-style-awpmd-cut-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_awpmd:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_awpmd::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_awpmd:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{awpmd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rc = global cutoff, \sphinxhyphen{}1 means cutoff of half the shortest box length

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{hartree} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dproduct} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{uhf} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{free} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pbc} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{harm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{ermscale} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{flex\_press}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hartree} value = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dproduct} value = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{uhf} value = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{free} value = none
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pbc} value = Plen
  Plen = periodic width of electron = \sphinxhyphen{}1 or positive value (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} value = Flen
  Flen = fixed width of electron = \sphinxhyphen{}1 or positive value (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{harm} value = width
  width = harmonic width constraint
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ermscale} value = factor
  factor = scaling between electron mass and width variable mass
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flex\_press} value = none
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_awpmd:examples}}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{awpmd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{40.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{uhf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{free}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20.0}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_awpmd:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style contains an implementation of the Antisymmetrized Wave
Packet Molecular Dynamics (AWPMD) method.  Need citation here.  Need
basic formulas here.  Could be links to other documents.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rc is the cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair\_style command allows for several optional keywords
to be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hartree}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dproduct}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{uhf} keywords specify the form of the
initial trial wave function for the system.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hartree} keyword
is used, then a Hartree multielectron trial wave function is used.  If
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dproduct} keyword is used, then a trial function which is a
product of two determinants for each spin type is used.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{uhf}
keyword is used, then an unrestricted Hartree\sphinxhyphen{}Fock trial wave function
is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{free}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{pbc}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} keywords specify a width constraint on
the electron wave packets.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{free} keyword is specified, then there is no
constraint.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pbc} keyword is used and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Plen} is specified as
\sphinxhyphen{}1, then the maximum width is half the shortest box length.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{Plen}
is a positive value, then the value is the maximum width.  If the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fix} keyword is used and \sphinxstyleemphasis{Flen} is specified as \sphinxhyphen{}1, then electrons
have a constant width that is read from the data file.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{Flen} is a
positive value, then the constant width for all electrons is set to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Flen}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{harm} keyword allow oscillations in the width of the
electron wave packets.  More details are needed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ermscale} keyword specifies a unitless scaling factor
between the electron masses and the width variable mass.  More
details needed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{flex\_press} keyword is used, then a contribution from the
electrons is added to the total virial and pressure of the system.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential is designed to be used with {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style wavepacket}}}} definitions, in order to handle the
description of systems with interacting nuclei and explicit electrons.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{awpmd/cut}, the cutoff coefficient is optional.  If it is not
used (as in some of the examples above), the default global value
specified in the pair\_style command is used.

\section{pair\_style beck command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_beck:pair-style-beck-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_beck:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_beck:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_beck:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_beck::doc}}

\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_beck:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{beck}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{399.671876712}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0000867636112694}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.675}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.390}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0003746}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{399.671876712}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0000867636112694}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.675}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.390}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0003746}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_beck:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{beck} computes interactions based on the potential by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_beck:beck}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Beck)}}}}, originally designed for simulation of Helium.  It
includes truncation at a cutoff distance \(r_c\).
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(r) &= A \exp\left[-\alpha r - \beta r^6\right] - \frac{B}{\left(r^2+a^2\right)^3} \left(1+\frac{2.709+3a^2}{r^2+a^2}\right) \qquad r < r_c \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(B\) (energy\sphinxhyphen{}distance\textasciicircum{}6 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\alpha\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\beta\)  (1/distance\textasciicircum{}6 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional.  If not specified, the global cutoff
\(r_c\) is used.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar

\index{pair\_style body/nparticle@\spxentry{pair\_style body/nparticle}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style body/nparticle command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle:pair-style-body-nparticle-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{body}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nparticle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff for interactions (distance units)


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{body}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{nparticle}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_nparticle:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{body/nparticle} is for use with body particles and calculates
pairwise body/body interactions as well as interactions between body
and point\sphinxhyphen{}particles.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} doc page
for more details on using body particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is designed for use with the “nparticle” body style,
which is specified as an argument to the “atom\sphinxhyphen{}style body” command.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} page for more details about
the body styles LAMMPS supports.  The “nparticle” style treats a body
particle as a rigid body composed of N sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coordinates of a body particle are its center\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}mass (COM).  If
the COMs of a pair of body particles are within the cutoff (global or
type\sphinxhyphen{}specific, as specified above), then all interactions between
pairs of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles in the two body particles are computed.
E.g. if the first body particle has 3 sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles, and the second
has 10, then 30 interactions are computed and summed to yield the
total force and torque on each body particle.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the example just described, all 30 interactions are computed
even if the distance between a particular pair of sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles is
greater than the cutoff.  Likewise, no interaction between two body
particles is computed if the two COMs are further apart than the
cutoff, even if the distance between some pairs of their sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles
is within the cutoff.  Thus care should be used in defining the cutoff
distances for body particles, depending on their shape and size.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar rules apply for a body particle interacting with a point
particle.  The distance between the two particles is calculated using
the COM of the body particle and the position of the point particle.
If the distance is within the cutoff and the body particle has N
sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles, then N interactions with the point particle are
computed and summed.  If the distance is not within the cutoff, no
interactions between the body and point particle are computed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interaction between two sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles, or a sub\sphinxhyphen{}particle and point
particle, or between two point particles is computed as a Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
interaction, using the standard formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & = 4 \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
                    \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]
                    \qquad r < R_c \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(R_c\) is the cutoff.  As explained above, an interaction involving
one or two body sub\sphinxhyphen{}particles may be computed even for \(r > R_c\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{body}, the following coefficients must be defined for each
pair of atoms types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in
the examples above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional.  If not specified, the global cutoff
is used.

\index{pair\_style body/rounded/polygon@\spxentry{pair\_style body/rounded/polygon}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style body/rounded/polygon command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:pair-style-body-rounded-polygon-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{body}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rounded}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{polygon}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delta\PYGZus{}ua}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
c\PYGZus{}n = normal damping coefficient
c\PYGZus{}t = tangential damping coefficient
mu = normal friction coefficient during gross sliding
delta\PYGZus{}ua = multiple contact scaling factor
cutoff = global separation cutoff for interactions (distance units), see below for definition
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{body}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rounded}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{polygon}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{body/rounded/polygon} is for use with 2d models of body
particles of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polygon}.  It calculates pairwise
body/body interactions which can include body particles modeled as
1\sphinxhyphen{}vertex circular disks with a specified diameter.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} page for more details on using body
rounded/polygon particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pairwise interaction between rounded polygons is described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:pair-fraige}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Fraige}}}}, where a polygon does not have sharp corners,
but is rounded at its vertices by circles centered on each vertex with
a specified diameter.  The edges of the polygon are defined between
pairs of adjacent vertices.  The circle diameter for each polygon is
specified in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read data}}}}
command.  This is a 2d discrete element model (DEM) which allows for
multiple contact points.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that when two particles interact, the effective surface of each
polygon particle is displaced outward from each of its vertices and
edges by half its circle diameter (as in the diagram below of a gray
and yellow square particle).  The interaction forces and energies
between two particles are defined with respect to the separation of
their respective rounded surfaces, not by the separation of the
vertices and edges themselves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means that the specified cutoff in the pair\_style command is the
cutoff distance, \(r_c\), for the surface separation, \(\delta_n\) (see figure
below).  This is the distance at which two particles no longer
interact.  If \(r_c\) is specified as 0.0, then it is a contact\sphinxhyphen{}only
interaction.  I.e. the two particles must overlap in order to exert a
repulsive force on each other.  If \(r_c > 0.0\), then the force between
two particles will be attractive for surface separations from 0 to
\(r_c\), and repulsive once the particles overlap.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that unlike for other pair styles, the specified cutoff is not
the distance between the centers of two particles at which they stop
interacting.  This center\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}center distance depends on the shape and
size of the two particles and their relative orientation.  LAMMPS
takes that into account when computing the surface separation distance
and applying the \(r_c\) cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forces between vertex\sphinxhyphen{}vertex, vertex\sphinxhyphen{}edge, and edge\sphinxhyphen{}edge overlaps
are given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_n &= \begin{cases}
        k_n \delta_n - c_n v_n     &  \delta_n \le 0 \\
       -k_{na} \delta_n - c_n v_n  &  0 < \delta_n \le r_c \\
       0                           & \delta_n > r_c \\
       \end{cases} \\
F_t &= \begin{cases}
       \mu k_n \delta_n - c_t v_t & \delta_n \le 0 \\
       0                          & \delta_n > 0
       \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{pair_body_rounded}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that \(F_n\) and \(F_t\) are functions of the surface separation
\(\delta_n = d - (R_i + R_j)\).  In this model, when
\((R_i + R_j) < d < (R_i + R_j) + r_c\), that is, \(0 < \delta_n < r_c\),
the cohesive region of the two surfaces overlap and the two surfaces are
attractive to each other.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:pair-fraige}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Fraige}}}}, the tangential friction force between two
particles that are in contact is modeled differently prior to gross
sliding (i.e. static friction) and during gross\sphinxhyphen{}sliding (kinetic
friction).  The latter takes place when the tangential deformation
exceeds the Coulomb frictional limit.  In the current implementation,
however, we do not take into account frictional history, i.e. we do
not keep track of how many time steps the two particles have been in
contact nor calculate the tangential deformation.  Instead, we assume
that gross sliding takes place as soon as two particles are in
contact.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atom types
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples above,
or in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(k_n\) (energy/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(k_{na}\) (energy/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Effectively, \(k_n\) and \(k_{na}\) are the slopes of the red lines in the plot
above for force versus surface separation, for \(\delta_n < 0\) and
\(0 < \delta_n < r_c\) respectively.


\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
mix, shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and
pair\_coeff commands in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles are part of the BODY package.  They are only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polygon:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polyhedron:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{body/rounded/polygon} is for use with 3d models of body
particles of style \sphinxstyleemphasis{rounded/polyhedron}.  It calculates pairwise
body/body interactions which can include body particles modeled as
1\sphinxhyphen{}vertex spheres with a specified diameter.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_body::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto body}}}} page for more details on using body
rounded/polyhedron particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pairwise interaction between the rounded polyhedra is described
in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polyhedron:pair-wang}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wang}}}}, where a polyhedron does not have sharp corners
and edges, but is rounded at its vertices and edges by spheres
centered on each vertex with a specified diameter.  The edges of the
polyhedron are defined between pairs of adjacent vertices.  Its faces
are defined by a loop of edges.  The sphere diameter for each polygon
is specified in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read data}}}}
command.  This is a discrete element model (DEM) which allows for
multiple contact points.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that when two particles interact, the effective surface of each
polyhedron particle is displaced outward from each of its vertices,
edges, and faces by half its sphere diameter.  The interaction forces
and energies between two particles are defined with respect to the
separation of their respective rounded surfaces, not by the separation
of the vertices, edges, and faces themselves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means that the specified cutoff in the pair\_style command is the
cutoff distance, \(r_c\), for the surface separation, \(\delta_n\) (see figure
below).  This is the distance at which two particles no longer
interact.  If \(r_c\) is specified as 0.0, then it is a contact\sphinxhyphen{}only
interaction.  I.e. the two particles must overlap in order to exert a
repulsive force on each other.  If \(r_c > 0.0\), then the force between
two particles will be attractive for surface separations from 0 to
\(r_c\), and repulsive once the particles overlap.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that unlike for other pair styles, the specified cutoff is not
the distance between the centers of two particles at which they stop
interacting.  This center\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}center distance depends on the shape and
size of the two particles and their relative orientation.  LAMMPS
takes that into account when computing the surface separation distance
and applying the \(r_c\) cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forces between vertex\sphinxhyphen{}vertex, vertex\sphinxhyphen{}edge, vertex\sphinxhyphen{}face, edge\sphinxhyphen{}edge,
and edge\sphinxhyphen{}face overlaps are given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_n &= \begin{cases}
       k_n \delta_n - c_n v_n,    & \delta_n \le 0 \\
      -k_{na} \delta_n - c_n v_n  & 0 < \delta_n \le r_c \\
       0                          & \delta_n > r_c \\
       \end{cases} \\
F_t &= \begin{cases}
       \mu k_n \delta_n - c_t v_t & \delta_n \le 0 \\
       0                          & \delta_n > 0
       \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{pair_body_rounded}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_body_rounded_polyhedron:pair-wang}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wang}}}}, the tangential friction force between two
particles that are in contact is modeled differently prior to gross
sliding (i.e. static friction) and during gross\sphinxhyphen{}sliding (kinetic
friction).  The latter takes place when the tangential deformation
exceeds the Coulomb frictional limit.  In the current implementation,
however, we do not take into account frictional history, i.e. we do
not keep track of how many time steps the two particles have been in
contact nor calculate the tangential deformation.  Instead, we assume
that gross sliding takes place as soon as two particles are in
contact.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atom types
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples above,
or in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(k_n\) (energy/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(k_{na}\) (energy/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Effectively, \(k_n\) and \(k_{na}\) are the slopes of the red lines in the plot
above for force versus surface separation, for \(\delta_n\) \textless{} 0 and
\(0 < \delta_n < r_c\) respectively.

\index{pair\_style bop@\spxentry{pair\_style bop}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style bop command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_bop:pair-style-bop-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_bop:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_bop::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_bop:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
