\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dpd_fdt:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} compute the force for dissipative
particle dynamics (DPD) simulations.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt} style is used to
perform DPD simulations under isothermal and isobaric conditions,
while the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} style is used to perform DPD simulations
under isoenergetic and isoenthalpic conditions (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_dpd_fdt:lisal3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Lisal)}}}}).
For DPD simulations in general, the force on atom I due to atom J is
given as a sum of 3 terms
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{f}  = & (F^C + F^D + F^R) \hat{r_{ij}} \qquad \qquad r < r_c \\
F^C      = & A w(r) \\
F^D      = & - \gamma w^2(r) (\hat{r_{ij}} \bullet \vec{v}_{ij}) \\
F^R      = & \sigma w(r) \alpha (\Delta t)^{-1/2} \\
w(r)     = & 1 - \frac{r}{r_c}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(F^C\) is a conservative force, \(F^D\) is a dissipative
force, and \(F^R\) is a random force.  \(\hat{r_{ij}}\) is a
unit vector in the direction \(r_i - r_j\), \(\vec{v}_{ij}\) is
the vector difference in velocities of the two atoms, \(\vec{v}_i -
\vec{v}_j\), \(\alpha\) is a Gaussian random number with zero mean
and unit variance, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dt} is the timestep size, and \(w(r)\) is a
weighting factor that varies between 0 and 1, \(r_c\) is the
pairwise cutoff.  Note that alternative definitions of the weighting
function exist, but would have to be implemented as a separate pair
style command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt}, the fluctuation\sphinxhyphen{}dissipation theorem defines
\(\gamma\) to be set equal to \(\sigma^2/(2 T)\), where \sphinxstyleemphasis{T} is the
set point temperature specified as a pair style parameter in the above
examples.  The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of
atoms types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the
examples above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (force units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (force*time\textasciicircum{}(1/2) units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional.  If not specified, the global DPD
cutoff is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} is used to perform DPD simulations under
isoenergetic and isoenthalpic conditions.  The fluctuation\sphinxhyphen{}dissipation
theorem defines \(\gamma\) to be set equal to \(\sigma^2/(2
\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is the average internal temperature for
the pair. The particle internal temperature is related to the particle
internal energy through a mesoparticle equation of state (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
eos}}}}). The differential internal conductive and mechanical
energies are computed within style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}du_{i}^{cond}  = & \kappa_{ij}(\frac{1}{\theta_{i}}-\frac{1}{\theta_{j}})\omega_{ij}^{2} + \alpha_{ij}\omega_{ij}\zeta_{ij}^{q}(\Delta{t})^{-1/2} \\
du_{i}^{mech}  = & -\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{ij}\omega_{ij}^{2}(\frac{\vec{r}_{ij}}{r_{ij}}\bullet\vec{v}_{ij})^{2} -
\frac{\sigma^{2}_{ij}}{4}(\frac{1}{m_{i}}+\frac{1}{m_{j}})\omega_{ij}^{2} -
\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{ij}\omega_{ij}(\frac{\vec{r}_{ij}}{r_{ij}}\bullet\vec{v}_{ij})\zeta_{ij}(\Delta{t})^{-1/2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\alpha_{ij}^{2}  = & 2k_{B}\kappa_{ij} \\
\sigma^{2}_{ij}  = & 2\gamma_{ij}k_{B}\Theta_{ij} \\
\Theta_{ij}^{-1}  = & \frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{\theta_{i}}+\frac{1}{\theta_{j}})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\zeta_ij^q\) is a second Gaussian random number with zero mean and
unit variance that is used to compute the internal conductive
energy. The fluctuation\sphinxhyphen{}dissipation theorem defines \(alpha^2\) to
be set equal to \(2k_B\kappa\), where \(\kappa\) is the
mesoparticle thermal conductivity parameter.  The following coefficients
must be defined for each pair of atoms types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples above, or in the data file or
restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (force units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (force*time\textasciicircum{}(1/2) units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\kappa\) (energy*temperature/time units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional.  If not specified, the global DPD
cutoff is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pairwise energy associated with styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} is only due to the conservative force term \(F^C\),
and is shifted to be zero at the cutoff distance \(r_c\).  The
pairwise virial is calculated using only the conservative term.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The forces computed through the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} styles
can be integrated with the velocity\sphinxhyphen{}Verlet integration scheme or the
Shardlow splitting integration scheme described by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_dpd_fdt:lisal3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Lisal)}}}}.  In the cases when these pair styles are combined with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shardlow::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shardlow}}}}, these pair styles differ from the
other dpd styles in that the dissipative and random forces are split
from the force calculation and are not computed within the pair style.
Thus, only the conservative force is computed by the pair style, while
the stochastic integration of the dissipative and random forces are
handled through the Shardlow splitting algorithm approach.  The Shardlow
splitting algorithm is advantageous, especially when performing DPD
under isoenergetic conditions, as it allows significantly larger
timesteps to be taken.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dpd_fdt:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands are part of the DPD\sphinxhyphen{}REACT package.  They are only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} require use of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel yes}}}} option so that velocities are
stored by ghost atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dpd/fdt/energy} requires {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style dpd}}}}
to be used in order to properly account for the particle internal
energies and temperatures.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\index{pair\_style drip@\spxentry{pair\_style drip}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style drip command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:pair-style-drip-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_drip::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{[styles}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...]}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
styles = other styles to be overlayed with drip (optional)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{none}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C.drip}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C.drip}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{CH.airebo}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C.drip}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{CH.airebo}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{drip} computes the interlayer interactions of layered materials using
the dihedral\sphinxhyphen{}angle\sphinxhyphen{}corrected registry\sphinxhyphen{}dependent (DRIP) potential as described
in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_drip:wen2018}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wen)}}}}, which is based on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_drip:kolmogorov2005}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kolmogorov)}}}}
potential and provides an improved prediction for forces.
The total potential energy of a system is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = & \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} \sum_{j\notin\text{layer}\,i} \phi_{ij} \\
\phi_{ij} = &f_\text{c}(x_r) \left[ e^{-\lambda(r_{ij} - z_0 )} \left[C+f(\rho_{ij})+  g(\rho_{ij}, \{\alpha_{ij}^{(m)}\}) \right]- A\left (\frac{z_0}{r_{ij}} \right)^6 \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the \(r^{-6}\) term models the attractive London dispersion,
the exponential term is designed to capture the registry effect due to
overlapping \sphinxstyleemphasis{pi} bonds, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{fc} is a cutoff function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential (DRIP) only provides the interlayer interactions between
graphene layers. So, to perform a realistic simulation, it should be used in
combination with an intralayer potential such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{REBO}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tersoff}}}}.
To keep the intralayer interactions unaffected, we should avoid applying DRIP
to contribute energy to intralayer interactions. This can be achieved by
assigning different molecular IDs to atoms in different layers, and DRIP is
implemented such that only atoms with different molecular ID can interact with
each other. For this purpose, {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style}}}} “molecular” or
“full” has to be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On the other way around, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{REBO}}}} ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tersoff}}}}
or any other potential used to provide the intralayer interactions) should not
interfere with the interlayer interactions described by DRIP. This is typically
automatically achieved using the commands provided in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples} section
above, since the cutoff distance for carbon\sphinxhyphen{}carbon interaction in the intralayer
potentials (e.g. 2 Angstrom for {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{REBO}}}}) is much smaller than
the equilibrium layer distance of graphene layers (about 3.4 Angstrom).
If you want, you can enforce this by assigning different atom types to atoms in
different layers, and apply an intralayer potential to one atom type.
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_hybrid}}}} for details.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command for DRIP takes \sphinxstyleemphasis{4+N} arguments, where
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} is the number of LAMMPS atom types. The fist three arguments must be fixed
to be \sphinxstyleemphasis{* * drip}, the fourth argument is the path to the DRIP parameter file,
and the remaining N arguments specifying the mapping between element in the
parameter file and atom types. For example, if your LAMMPS simulation has 3 atom
types and you want all of them to be C, you would use the following pair\_coeff
command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C.drip}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a mapping value is specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed. This
could be useful when DRIP is used to model part of the system where other
element exists. Suppose you have a hydrocarbon system, with C of atom type 1
and H of atom type 2, you can use the following command to inform DRIP not to
model H atoms:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{drip}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C.drip}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{CH.airebo}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential parameters developed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_drip:wen2018}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wen)}}}} are provided with
LAMMPS (see the “potentials” directory). Besides those in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_drip:wen2018}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wen}}}}, an
additional parameter “normal\_cutoff”, specific to the LAMMPS implementation, is
used to find the three nearest neighbors of an atom to construct the normal.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the pair\_modify mix, shift, table,
and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write their information to binary restart files, since
it is stored in potential files. Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and
pair\_coeff commands in an input script that reads a restart file.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the INTERLAYER package. It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on” for
pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{C.drip} parameter file provided with LAMMPS (see the “potentials”
directory) is parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}. You can use
the DRIP potential with any LAMMPS units, but you would need to create
your own custom parameter file with coefficients listed in the
appropriate units, if your simulation does not use “metal” units.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lebedeva_z::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lebedeva\_z}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_kolmogorov_crespi_z::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style kolmogorov/crespi/z}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_kolmogorov_crespi_full::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style kolmogorov/crespi/full}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style ilp/graphene/hbn}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Wen)} M. Wen, S. Carr, S. Fang, E. Kaxiras, and E. B. Tadmor, Phys. Rev. B,
98, 235404 (2018)

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_drip:kolmogorov2005}}

\index{pair\_style dsmc@\spxentry{pair\_style dsmc}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style dsmc command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc:pair-style-dsmc-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dsmc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{max\PYGZus{}cell\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{seed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{weighting}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Tref}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nrecompute}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Nsample}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
max\_cell\_size = global maximum cell size for DSMC interactions (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
seed = random \# seed (positive integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
weighting = macroparticle weighting

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tref = reference temperature (temperature units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nrecompute = re\sphinxhyphen{}compute v*sigma\_max every this many timesteps (timesteps)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nsample = sample this many times in recomputing v*sigma\_max

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dsmc}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{34387}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{dsmc} computes collisions between pairs of particles for a
direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) model following the exposition in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_dsmc:bird}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bird)}}}}.  Each collision resets the velocities of the two
particles involved.  The number of pairwise collisions for each pair
or particle types and the length scale within which they occur are
determined by the parameters of the pair\_style and pair\_coeff
commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Stochastic collisions are performed using the variable hard sphere
(VHS) approach, with the user\sphinxhyphen{}defined \sphinxstyleemphasis{max\_cell\_size} value used as
the maximum DSMC cell size, and reference cross\sphinxhyphen{}sections for
collisions given using the pair\_coeff command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There is no pairwise energy or virial contributions associated with
this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficient must be defined for each pair of atoms types
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples above,
or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
sigma (area units, i.e. distance\sphinxhyphen{}squared)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The global DSMC \sphinxstyleemphasis{max\_cell\_size} determines the maximum cell length
used in the DSMC calculation.  A structured mesh is overlayed on the
simulation box such that an integer number of cells are created in
each direction for each processor’s subdomain.  Cell lengths are
adjusted up to the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified maximum cell size.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
To perform a DSMC simulation with LAMMPS, several additional options
should be set in your input script, though LAMMPS does not check for
these settings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since this pair style does not compute particle forces, you should use
the “fix nve/noforce” time integration fix for the DSMC particles,
e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nve}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{noforce}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style assumes that all particles will communicated to
neighboring processors every timestep as they move.  This makes it
possible to perform all collisions between pairs of particles that are
on the same processor.  To ensure this occurs, you should use
these commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{neighbor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bin}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{every}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{delay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{check}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no}
\PYG{k}{atom\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sort}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{n}{communicate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{single}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands ensure that LAMMPS communicates particles to
neighboring processors every timestep and that no ghost atoms are
created.  The output statistics for a simulation run should indicate
there are no ghost particles or neighbors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to get correct DSMC collision statistics, users should
specify a Gaussian velocity distribution when populating the
simulation domain. Note that the default velocity distribution is
uniform, which will not give good DSMC collision rates. Specify
“dist gaussian” when using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{velocity::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{velocity}}}} command
as in the following:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{velocity }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{create}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{594.6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{87287}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{loop}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{geom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dist}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gaussian}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support mixing.  Thus, coefficients for all
I,J pairs must be specified explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift option for the energy of the pair interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant
for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.  Note
that the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified random number seed is stored in the restart
file, so when a simulation is restarted, each processor will
re\sphinxhyphen{}initialize its random number generator the same way it did
initially.  This means the random forces will be random, but will not
be the same as they would have been if the original simulation had
continued past the restart time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_dsmc:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the MC package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires an {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom style}}}} with per
atom type masses.

{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_noforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/noforce}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{neighbor::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neighbor}}}},

\section{pair\_style e3b command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:pair-style-e3b-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{e3b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Otype}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Otype = atom type (numeric or type label) for oxygen

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
one or more keyword/value pairs must be appended.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ea} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Eb} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ec} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{E2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{K3} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{K2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rc3} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rc2} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bondL} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} keyword is given, no others are needed.
Otherwise, all are mandatory except for \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh}.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} keyword is always optional.

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} arg = \sphinxstyleemphasis{2011} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{2015} = which set of predefined parameters to use
         2011 = use the potential parameters from {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_e3b:tainter2011}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tainter 2011)}}}}
         2015 = use the potential parameters from {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_e3b:tainter2015}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tainter 2015)}}}}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ea} arg = three\sphinxhyphen{}body energy for type A hydrogen bonding interactions (energy units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Eb} arg = three\sphinxhyphen{}body energy for type B hydrogen bonding interactions (energy units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ec} arg = three\sphinxhyphen{}body energy for type C hydrogen bonding interactions (energy units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{E2} arg = two\sphinxhyphen{}body energy correction (energy units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{K3} arg = three\sphinxhyphen{}body exponential constant (inverse distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{K2} arg = two\sphinxhyphen{}body exponential constant (inverse distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Rc3} arg = three\sphinxhyphen{}body cutoff (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Rc2} arg = two\sphinxhyphen{}body cutoff (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Rs} arg = three\sphinxhyphen{}body switching function cutoff (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bondL} arg = intramolecular OH bond length (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} arg = approximate integer number of molecules within Rc3 of an oxygen atom
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{e3b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ea}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{35.85}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Eb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{240.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ec}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{449.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{E2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{108269.9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{K3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.907}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{K2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.872}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rc3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rc2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bondL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9572}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{e3b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tip4p}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.15}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{e3b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{preset}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2011}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{e3b}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{OW}
\PYG{k}{labelmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{atom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{OW}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{HW}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ea}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{35.85}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Eb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{240.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ec}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{449.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{E2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{108269.9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{K3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.907}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{K2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.872}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rc3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rc2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bondL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9572}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Used in example input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
examples/PACKAGES/e3b/in.e3b\PYGZhy{}tip4p2005
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{e3b} style computes an "explicit three\sphinxhyphen{}body" (E3B) potential for water {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_e3b:kumar}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kumar 2008)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E =& E_2 \sum_{i,j}e^{-k_2 r_{ij}} + E_A \sum_{\substack{i,j,k,\ell \\
\in \textrm{type A}}} f(r_{ij})f(r_{k\ell}) + E_B \sum_{\substack{i,j,k,\ell \\
\in \textrm{type B}}} f(r_{ij})f(r_{k\ell}) + E_C \sum_{\substack{i,j,k,\ell \\
\in \textrm{type C}}} f(r_{ij})f(r_{k\ell}) \\
f(r) =& e^{-k_3 r}s(r) \\
s(r) =& \begin{cases}
1 & r<R_s \\
\displaystyle\frac{(R_f-r)^2(R_f-3R_s+2r)}{(R_f-R_s)^3} & R_s\leq r\leq R_f \\
0 & r>R_f\\
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential was developed as a water model that includes the
three\sphinxhyphen{}body cooperativity of hydrogen bonding explicitly.  To use it in
this way, it must be applied in conjunction with a conventional two\sphinxhyphen{}body
water model, through pair style {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid/overlay}}}}.  The
three body interactions are split into three types: A, B, and C.  Type A
corresponds to anti\sphinxhyphen{}cooperative double hydrogen bond donor interactions.
Type B corresponds to the cooperative interaction of molecules that both
donate and accept a hydrogen bond.  Type C corresponds to
anti\sphinxhyphen{}cooperative double hydrogen bond acceptor interactions.  The
three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions are smoothly cutoff by the switching function
s(r) between Rs and Rc3.  The two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions are designed to
correct for the effective many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions implicitly included in
the conventional two\sphinxhyphen{}body potential.  The two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions are cut
off sharply at Rc2, because K3 is typically significantly smaller than
K2.  See {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_e3b:kumar}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kumar 2008)}}}} for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command is used with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{e3b} style and the first two arguments must be * *.  The oxygen atom
type for the pair style is passed as the only argument to the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style} command, not in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command.  The hydrogen
atom type is inferred from the ordering of the atoms.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Every atom of type Otype must be part of a water molecule.
Each water molecule must have consecutive IDs with the oxygen first.
This pair style does not test that this criteria is met.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If using type labels, the type labels must be defined before calling
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command must have at least one keyword/value pair, as
described above.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} keyword sets the potential parameters to
the values used in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_e3b:tainter2011}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tainter 2011)}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_e3b:tainter2015}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tainter 2015)}}}}.  To use the water models defined in
those references, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{e3b} style should always be used in conjunction
with an \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/tip4p/long} style through \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style hybrid/overlay},
as demonstrated in the second example above.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset 2011} option
should be used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip4p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{TIP4P water model}}}}.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{preset 2015} option should be used with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_tip4p::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{TIP4P/2005 water
model}}}}.  If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} keyword is used, no other keyword
is needed.  Changes to the preset parameters can be made by specifying
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} keyword followed by the specific parameter to change, like
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ea}.  Note that the other keywords must come after \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} in the
pair\_style command.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{e3b} style can also be used to implement any
three\sphinxhyphen{}body potential of the same form by specifying all the keywords
except \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh}: \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ea}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Eb}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ec}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{E2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{K3}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{K2}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rc3}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{Rc2},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Rs}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{bondL}.  The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{bondL} specifies the intramolecular
OH bond length of the water model being used.  This is needed to include
H atoms that are within the cutoff even when the attached oxygen atom is
not.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style allocates arrays sized according to the number of
pairwise interactions within Rc3.  To do this it needs an estimate for
the number of water molecules within Rc3 of an oxygen atom.  This
estimate defaults to 10 and can be changed using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} keyword,
which takes an integer as an argument.  If the neigh setting is too
small, the simulation will fail with the error “neigh is too small”.  If
the neigh setting is too large, the pair style will use more memory than
necessary.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style tallies a breakdown of the total E3B potential energy
into sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories, which can be accessed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}} command as a vector of values of length 4.  The 4 values
correspond to the terms in the first equation above: the E2 term, the Ea
term, the Eb term, and the Ec term.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the examples/PACKAGES/e3b directory for a complete example script.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is incompatible with {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{respa}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on”
for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires a fixed number of atoms in the simulation, so it is incompatible with fixes like {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deposit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deposit}}}}.
If the number of atoms changes between runs, this pair style must be re\sphinxhyphen{}initialized by calling the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeffs} commands.
This is not a fundamental limitation of the pair style, but the code currently does not support a variable number of atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{preset} keyword currently only works with real, metal, si, and cgs {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{pair_e3b:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The option default for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{neigh} keyword is 10.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eam:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam} computes pairwise interactions for metals and metal alloys
using embedded\sphinxhyphen{}atom method (EAM) potentials {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam:daw}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Daw)}}}}.  The total
energy Ei of an atom I is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_i = F_\alpha \left(\sum_{j \neq i}\ \rho_\beta (r_{ij})\right) +
      \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j \neq i} \phi_{\alpha\beta} (r_{ij})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where F is the embedding energy which is a function of the atomic
electron density rho, phi is a pair potential interaction, and alpha
and beta are the element types of atoms I and J.  The multi\sphinxhyphen{}body
nature of the EAM potential is a result of the embedding energy term.
Both summations in the formula are over all neighbors J of atom I
within the cutoff distance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cutoff distance and the tabulated values of the functionals F,
rho, and phi are listed in one or more files which are specified by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.  These are ASCII text files
in a DYNAMO\sphinxhyphen{}style format which is described below.  DYNAMO was the
original serial EAM MD code, written by the EAM originators.  Several
DYNAMO potential files for different metals are included in the
“potentials” directory of the LAMMPS distribution.  All of these files
are parameterized in terms of LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{metal units}}}}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam} style reads single\sphinxhyphen{}element EAM potentials in the
DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} format.  Either single element or alloy systems can be
modeled using multiple \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} files and style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam}.  For the alloy
case LAMMPS mixes the single\sphinxhyphen{}element potentials to produce alloy
potentials, the same way that DYNAMO does.  Alternatively, a single
DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file or Finnis/Sinclair EAM file can be used by LAMMPS
to model alloy systems by invoking the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/cd} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/fs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/he} styles as described below.  These files require no
mixing since they specify alloy interactions explicitly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that unlike for other potentials, cutoffs for EAM potentials are not
set in the pair\_style or pair\_coeff command; they are specified in the EAM
potential files themselves.  Likewise, valid EAM potential files usually
contain atomic masses; thus you may not need to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{mass::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mass}}}}
command to specify them, unless the potential file uses a dummy value (e.g.
0.0). LAMMPS will print a warning, if this is the case.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are web sites that distribute and document EAM potentials stored
in DYNAMO or other formats:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxurl{https://www.ctcms.nist.gov/potentials}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxurl{https://openkim.org}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These potentials should be usable with LAMMPS, though the alternate
formats would need to be converted to the DYNAMO format used by LAMMPS
and described on this page.  The NIST site is maintained by Chandler
Becker (cbecker at nist.gov) who is good resource for info on
interatomic potentials and file formats.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The OpenKIM Project at
\sphinxurl{https://openkim.org/browse/models/by-type}
provides EAM potentials that can be used directly in LAMMPS with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kim_commands::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kim command}}}} interface.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The EAM potential files tabulate the embedding energy as a function
of the local electron density \(\rho\).  When atoms get too
close, this electron density may exceed the range for which the
embedding energy was tabulated for.  To avoid crashes, LAMMPS will
assume a linearly increasing embedding energy for electron densities
beyond the maximum tabulated value.  LAMMPS will print a warning when
this happens.  It may be acceptable at the beginning of an
equilibration (e.g. when using randomized coordinates) but would be a
big concern for accuracy if it happens during production runs.  The
EAM potential file triggering the warning during production is thus
not a good choice, and the EAM model in general not likely a good
model for the kind of system under investigation.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam}, potential values are read from a file that is in the
DYNAMO single\sphinxhyphen{}element \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} format.  If the DYNAMO file was created
by a Fortran program, it cannot have “D” values in it for exponents.
C only recognizes “e” or “E” for scientific notation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam} a potential file must be assigned to each I,I pair of
atom types by using one or more pair\_coeff commands, each with a
single argument:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the following command

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cuu3.eam}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
will read the cuu3 potential file and use the tabulated Cu values for
F, phi, rho that it contains for type pairs 1,1 and 2,2 (type pairs
1,2 and 2,1 are ignored).  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} doc
page for alternate ways to specify the path for the potential file.
In effect, this makes atom types 1 and 2 in LAMMPS be Cu atoms.
Different single\sphinxhyphen{}element files can be assigned to different atom types
to model an alloy system.  The mixing to create alloy potentials for
type pairs with I != J is done automatically the same way that the
serial DYNAMO code originally did it; you do not need to specify
coefficients for these type pairs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Funcfl} files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS
distribution have an “.eam” suffix.  A DYNAMO single\sphinxhyphen{}element \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl}
file is formatted as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 1: comment (ignored)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 2: atomic number, mass, lattice constant, lattice type (e.g. FCC)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 3: Nrho, drho, Nr, dr, cutoff

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
On line 2, all values but the mass are ignored by LAMMPS.  The mass is
in mass {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, e.g. mass number or grams/mole for metal
units.  The cubic lattice constant is in Angstroms.  On line 3, Nrho
and Nr are the number of tabulated values in the subsequent arrays,
drho and dr are the spacing in density and distance space for the
values in those arrays, and the specified cutoff becomes the pairwise
cutoff used by LAMMPS for the potential.  The units of dr are
Angstroms; I’m not sure of the units for drho \sphinxhyphen{} some measure of
electron density.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the three header lines are three arrays of tabulated values:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
embedding function F(rho) (Nrho values)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
effective charge function Z(r) (Nr values)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density function rho(r) (Nr values)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The values for each array can be listed as multiple values per line,
so long as each array starts on a new line.  For example, the
individual Z(r) values are for r = 0,dr,2*dr, … (Nr\sphinxhyphen{}1)*dr.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The units for the embedding function F are eV.  The units for the
density function rho are the same as for drho (see above, electron
density).  The units for the effective charge Z are “atomic charge” or
sqrt(Hartree * Bohr\sphinxhyphen{}radii).  For two interacting atoms i,j this is used
by LAMMPS to compute the pair potential term in the EAM energy
expression as r*phi, in units of eV\sphinxhyphen{}Angstroms, via the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r \cdot \phi = 27.2 \cdot 0.529 \cdot Z_i \cdot Z_j\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where 1 Hartree = 27.2 eV and 1 Bohr = 0.529 Angstroms.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy} computes pairwise interactions using the same
formula as style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam}.  However the associated
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command reads a DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file
instead of a \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} file.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Setfl} files can be used to model a
single\sphinxhyphen{}element or alloy system.  In the alloy case, as explained
above, \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} files contain explicit tabulated values for alloy
interactions.  Thus they allow more generality than \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} files for
modeling alloys.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy}, potential values are read from a file that is
in the DYNAMO multi\sphinxhyphen{}element \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} format, except that element names
(Ni, Cu, etc) are added to one of the lines in the file.  If the
DYNAMO file was created by a Fortran program, it cannot have “D”
values in it for exponents.  C only recognizes “e” or “E” for
scientific notation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy} style
which specifies a DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file, which contains information for
M elements.  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying N
additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff command,
where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, the potentials/NiAlH\_jea.eam.alloy file is a \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl}
file which has tabulated EAM values for 3 elements and their alloy
interactions: Ni, Al, and H.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} doc
page for alternate ways to specify the path for the potential file.
If your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atoms types and you want the first 3 to
be Ni, and the fourth to be Al, you would use the following pair\_coeff
command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NiAlH\PYGZus{}jea.eam.alloy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The first three Ni arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the Ni
element in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.  The final Al argument maps LAMMPS atom
type 4 to the Al element in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.  Note that there is no
requirement that your simulation use all the elements specified by the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a mapping value is specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed.
This can be used when an \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy} potential is used as part of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.  The NULL values are placeholders for atom types
that will be used with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Setfl} files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS distribution
have an “.eam.alloy” suffix.  A DYNAMO multi\sphinxhyphen{}element \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file is
formatted as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lines 1,2,3 = comments (ignored)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 4: Nelements Element1 Element2 … ElementN

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 5: Nrho, drho, Nr, dr, cutoff

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file, line 4 only lists Nelements = the \# of
elements in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.  For LAMMPS, the element name (Ni, Cu,
etc) of each element must be added to the line, in the order the
elements appear in the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The meaning and units of the values in line 5 is the same as for the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} file described above.  Note that the cutoff (in Angstroms) is
a global value, valid for all pairwise interactions for all element
pairings.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the 5 header lines are Nelements sections, one for each
element, each with the following format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 1 = atomic number, mass, lattice constant, lattice type (e.g. FCC)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
embedding function F(rho) (Nrho values)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density function rho(r) (Nr values)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} files, only the mass (in mass {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}},
e.g. mass number or grams/mole for metal units) is used by LAMMPS from
the first line.  The cubic lattice constant is in Angstroms.  The F and
rho arrays are unique to a single element and have the same format and
units as in a \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the Nelements sections, Nr values for each pair potential
phi(r) array are listed for all i,j element pairs in the same format
as other arrays.  Since these interactions are symmetric (i,j = j,i)
only phi arrays with i \textgreater{}= j are listed, in the following order: i,j =
(1,1), (2,1), (2,2), (3,1), (3,2), (3,3), (4,1), …, (Nelements,
Nelements).  Unlike the effective charge array Z(r) in \sphinxstyleemphasis{funcfl} files,
the tabulated values for each phi function are listed in \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} files
directly as r*phi (in units of eV\sphinxhyphen{}Angstroms), since they are for atom
pairs.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/cd} is similar to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy} style, except that it
computes alloy pairwise interactions using the concentration\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
embedded\sphinxhyphen{}atom method (CD\sphinxhyphen{}EAM).  This model can reproduce the enthalpy
of mixing of alloys over the full composition range, as described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam:stukowski}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Stukowski)}}}}. Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/cd/old} is an older, slightly
different and slower two\sphinxhyphen{}site formulation of the model {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam:caro}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Caro)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair\_coeff command is specified the same as for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy}
style.  However the DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file must has two
lines added to it, at the end of the file:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 1: Comment line (ignored)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 2: N Coefficient0 Coefficient1 … CoefficientN

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last line begins with the degree \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} of the polynomial function
\sphinxstyleemphasis{h(x)} that modifies the cross interaction between A and B elements.
Then \sphinxstyleemphasis{N+1} coefficients for the terms of the polynomial are then
listed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Modified EAM \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} files used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/cd} style must contain
exactly two elements, i.e. in the current implementation the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/cd}
style only supports binary alloys.  The first and second elements in
the input EAM file are always taken as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{A} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{B} species.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{CD\sphinxhyphen{}EAM} files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS
distribution have a “.cdeam” suffix.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/fs} computes pairwise interactions for metals and metal
alloys using a generalized form of EAM potentials due to Finnis and
Sinclair {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam:finnis1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Finnis)}}}}.  Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/he} is similar to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/fs} except that it allows for negative electron density in
order to capture the behavior of helium in metals {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam:zhou6}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Zhou6)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The total energy Ei of an atom I is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_i = F_\alpha \left(\sum_{j \neq i}\
\rho_{\alpha\beta} (r_{ij})\right) +
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j \neq i} \phi_{\alpha\beta} (r_{ij})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\rho_{\alpha\beta}\) refers to the density contributed
by a neighbor atom J of element \(\beta\) at the site of atom I
of element \(\alpha\).
This has the same form as the EAM formula above, except that rho is
now a functional specific to the elements of both atoms I and J,
so that different elements can contribute differently to the total
electron density at an atomic site depending on the identity of the
element at that atomic site.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The associated {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/fs}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/he} reads a DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file that has been extended to include
additional \(\rho_{\alpha\beta}\) arrays of tabulated values.  A
discussion of how FS EAM differs from conventional EAM alloy potentials is
given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam:ackland1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ackland1)}}}}.  An example of such a potential is the
same author’s Fe\sphinxhyphen{}P FS potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam:ackland2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ackland2)}}}}.  Note that while
FS potentials always specify the embedding energy with a square root
dependence on the total density, the implementation in LAMMPS does not
require that; the user can tabulate any functional form desired in the
FS potential files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/fs} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/he} the form of the pair\_coeff command is exactly
the same as for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy}, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NiAlH\PYGZus{}jea.eam.fs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
with N additional arguments after the filename, where N is
the number of LAMMPS atom types.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}
doc page for alternate ways to specify the path for the potential
file.  The N values determine the mapping of LAMMPS atom types to EAM
elements in the file, as described above for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy}.  As
with \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy}, if a mapping value is NULL, the mapping is not
performed.  This can be used when an \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/fs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/he} potential is
used as part of a \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.  The NULL values are used as
placeholders for atom types that will be used with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
FS EAM and HE EAM files include more information than the DYNAMO \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl}
format files read by \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy}, in that i,j density functionals for
all pairs of elements are included as needed by the Finnis/Sinclair
formulation of the EAM.

\sphinxAtStartPar
FS EAM files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS distribution
have an “.eam.fs” suffix.  They are formatted as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lines 1,2,3 = comments (ignored)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 4: Nelements Element1 Element2 … ElementN

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 5: Nrho, drho, Nr, dr, cutoff

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 5\sphinxhyphen{}line header section is identical to an EAM \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the header are Nelements sections, one for each element \(\beta\),
each with the following format:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 1 = atomic number, mass, lattice constant, lattice type (e.g. FCC)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
embedding function F(rho) (Nrho values)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density function \(\rho_{1\beta} (r)\) for element \(\beta\) at element 1 (Nr values)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density function \(\rho_{2\beta} (r)\) for element \(\beta\) at element 2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
density function \(\rho_{N_{elem}\beta} (r)\) for element \(\beta\) at element \(N_{elem}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The units of these quantities in line 1 are the same as for \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl}
files.  Note that the rho(r) arrays in Finnis/Sinclair can be
asymmetric (\(\rho_{\alpha\beta} (r) \neq \rho_{\beta\alpha} (r)\) )
so there are Nelements\textasciicircum{}2 of them listed in the file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following the Nelements sections, Nr values for each pair potential
phi(r) array are listed in the same manner (r*phi, units of
eV\sphinxhyphen{}Angstroms) as in EAM \sphinxstyleemphasis{setfl} files.  Note that in Finnis/Sinclair,
the phi(r) arrays are still symmetric, so only phi arrays for i \textgreater{}= j
are listed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
HE EAM files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS distribution
have an “.eam.he” suffix.  They are formatted as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
lines 1,2,3 = comments (ignored)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 4: Nelements Element1 Element2 … ElementN

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
line 5: Nrho, drho, Nr, dr, cutoff, rhomax

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The 5\sphinxhyphen{}line header section is identical to an FS EAM file
except that line 5 lists an additional value, rhomax. Unlike in FS EAM
files where embedding energies F(rho) are always defined between rho = 0
and rho = (Nrho \sphinxhyphen{}1)drho, F(rho) in HE EAM files are defined between
rho = rhomin and rho = rhomax.  Since drho = (rhomax \sphinxhyphen{} rhomin)/(Nrho \sphinxhyphen{} 1),
rhomin = rhomax \sphinxhyphen{} (Nrho \sphinxhyphen{} 1)drho.  The embedding energies F(rho) are
listed for rho = rhomin, rhomin + drho, rhomin + 2drho, …, rhomax.
This gives users additional flexibility to define a negative rhomin and
therefore an embedding energy function that works for both positive and
negative electron densities.  The format and units of these sections are
identical to the FS EAM files (see above).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 3Nov2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/fs}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/he} pair styles support
extraction of two per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pair}}}}
command.  This allows the quantities to be output to files by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dump::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dump}}}} or otherwise processed by other LAMMPS commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The names of the two quantities are “rho” and “fp” for the density and
derivative of the embedding energy for each atom.  Neither quantity
needs to be triggered by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix pair}}}} command in order
for these pair styles to calculate it.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eam:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, where types I and J correspond to
two different element types, mixing is performed by LAMMPS as
described above with the individual styles.  You never need to specify
a pair\_coeff command with I != J arguments for the eam styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The eam pair styles do not write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary
restart files}}}}, since it is stored in tabulated potential
files.  Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff
commands in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The eam pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

All of these styles are part of the MANYBODY package.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build
package}}}} page for more info.

\section{pair\_style edip command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:pair-style-edip-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_edip::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip/omp}


\section{pair\_style edip/multi command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:pair-style-edip-multi-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip/multi}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{edip}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si.edip}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip/multi} styles compute a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_edip:edip}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{EDIP}}}}
potential which is popular for modeling silicon materials where
it can have advantages over other models such as the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sw::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tersoff}}}}
potentials. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip} style has been programmed for single element
potentials, while \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip/multi} supports multi\sphinxhyphen{}element EDIP runs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In EDIP, the energy E of a system of atoms is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E  = & \sum_{j \ne i} \phi_{2}(R_{ij}, Z_{i}) + \sum_{j \ne i} \sum_{k \ne i,k > j} \phi_{3}(R_{ij}, R_{ik}, Z_{i}) \\
\phi_{2}(r, Z)  = & A\left[\left(\frac{B}{r}\right)^{\rho} - e^{-\beta Z^2}\right]exp{\left(\frac{\sigma}{r-a}\right)} \\
\phi_{3}(R_{ij}, R_{ik}, Z_i)  = & exp{\left(\frac{\gamma}{R_{ij}-a}\right)}exp{\left(\frac{\gamma}{R_{ik}-a}\right)}h(cos\theta_{ijk},Z_i) \\
Z_i  = & \sum_{m \ne i} f(R_{im}) \qquad
f(r) = \begin{cases}
       1 & \quad r<c \\
       \exp\left(\frac{\alpha}{1-x^{-3}}\right) & \quad c<r<a \\
       0 & \quad r>a
       \end{cases} \\
h(l,Z)  = & \lambda [(1-e^{-Q(Z)(l+\tau(Z))^2}) + \eta Q(Z)(l+\tau(Z))^2 ] \\
Q(Z)  = & Q_0 e^{-\mu Z} \qquad \tau(Z) = u_1 + u_2 (u_3 e^{-u_4 Z} - e^{-2u_4 Z})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\phi_2\) is a two\sphinxhyphen{}body term and \(\phi_3\) is a
three\sphinxhyphen{}body term.  The summations in the formula are over all neighbors J
and K of atom I within a cutoff distance = a.  Both terms depend on the
local environment of atom I through its effective coordination number
defined by Z, which is unity for a cutoff distance \textless{} c and gently goes
to 0 at distance = a.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{edip} style which
specifies a EDIP potential file with parameters for all
needed elements.  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying
N additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff command,
where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of EDIP elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine a file Si.edip has EDIP values for Si.

\sphinxAtStartPar
EDIP files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS
distribution have a “.edip” suffix.  Lines that are not blank or
comments (starting with \#) define parameters for a triplet of
elements.  The parameters in a single entry correspond to the two\sphinxhyphen{}body
and three\sphinxhyphen{}body coefficients in the formula above:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 1 (the center atom in a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 3

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
B (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoffA (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoffC (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\alpha\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\beta\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\eta\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\gamma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(lambda\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mu\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\tau\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Q0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
u1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
u2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
u3

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
u4

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The A, B, beta, sigma parameters are used only for two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.
The eta, gamma, lambda, mu, Q0 and all u1 to u4 parameters are used only
for three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. The alpha and cutoffC parameters are used
for the coordination environment function only.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The EDIP potential file must contain entries for all the
elements listed in the pair\_coeff command.  It can also contain
entries for additional elements not being used in a particular
simulation; LAMMPS ignores those entries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a single\sphinxhyphen{}element simulation, only a single entry is required
(e.g. SiSiSi).  For a two\sphinxhyphen{}element simulation, the file must contain 8
entries (for SiSiSi, SiSiC, SiCSi, SiCC, CSiSi, CSiC, CCSi, CCC), that
specify EDIP parameters for all permutations of the two elements
interacting in three\sphinxhyphen{}body configurations.  Thus for 3 elements, 27
entries would be required, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the moment, only a single element parameterization is
implemented. However, the author is not aware of other
multi\sphinxhyphen{}element EDIP parameterization. If you know any and
you are interest in that, please contact the author of
the EDIP package.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_edip:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
MANYBODY package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc
page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on”
for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The EDIP potential files provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials directory)
are parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
You can use the EDIP potential with any LAMMPS units, but you would need
to create your own EDIP potential file with coefficients listed in the
appropriate units if your simulation does not use “metal” units.

\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eff:examples}}
