\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eff:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style contains a LAMMPS implementation of the electron Force
Field (eFF) potential currently under development at Caltech, as
described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eff:jaramillo-botero}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Jaramillo\sphinxhyphen{}Botero)}}}}.  The eFF for Z\textless{}6
was first introduced by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eff:su}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Su)}}}} in 2007. It has been extended to
higher Zs by using effective core potentials (ECPs) that now cover up
to second and third row p\sphinxhyphen{}block elements of the periodic table.

\sphinxAtStartPar
eFF can be viewed as an approximation to QM wave packet dynamics and
Fermionic molecular dynamics, combining the ability of electronic
structure methods to describe atomic structure, bonding, and chemistry
in materials, and of plasma methods to describe nonequilibrium
dynamics of large systems with a large number of highly excited
electrons.  Yet, eFF relies on a simplification of the electronic
wave function in which electrons are described as floating Gaussian
wave packets whose position and size respond to the various dynamic
forces between interacting classical nuclear particles and spherical
Gaussian electron wave packets.  The wave function is taken to be a
Hartree product of the wave packets.  To compensate for the lack of
explicit antisymmetry in the resulting wave function, a spin\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
Pauli potential is included in the Hamiltonian.  Substituting this
wave function into the time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent Schrodinger equation produces
equations of motion that correspond \sphinxhyphen{} to second order \sphinxhyphen{} to classical
Hamiltonian relations between electron position and size, and their
conjugate momenta.  The N\sphinxhyphen{}electron wave function is described as a
product of one\sphinxhyphen{}electron Gaussian functions, whose size is a dynamical
variable and whose position is not constrained to a nuclear
center. This form allows for straightforward propagation of the
wave function, with time, using a simple formulation from which the
equations of motion are then integrated with conventional MD
algorithms. In addition to this spin\sphinxhyphen{}dependent Pauli repulsion
potential term between Gaussians, eFF includes the electron kinetic
energy from the Gaussians.  These two terms are based on
first\sphinxhyphen{}principles quantum mechanics.  On the other hand, nuclei are
described as point charges, which interact with other nuclei and
electrons through standard electrostatic potential forms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The full Hamiltonian (shown below), contains then a standard
description for electrostatic interactions between a set of
delocalized point and Gaussian charges which include, nuclei\sphinxhyphen{}nuclei
(NN), electron\sphinxhyphen{}electron (ee), and nuclei\sphinxhyphen{}electron (Ne). Thus, eFF is a
mixed QM\sphinxhyphen{}classical mechanics method rather than a conventional force
field method (in which electron motions are averaged out into ground
state nuclear motions, i.e a single electronic state, and particle
interactions are described via empirically parameterized interatomic
potential functions). This makes eFF uniquely suited to simulate
materials over a wide range of temperatures and pressures where
electronically excited and ionized states of matter can occur and
coexist.  Furthermore, the interactions between particles \sphinxhyphen{}nuclei and
electrons\sphinxhyphen{} reduce to the sum of a set of effective pairwise potentials
in the eFF formulation.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{eff/cut} style computes the pairwise
Coulomb interactions between nuclei and electrons (E\_NN,E\_Ne,E\_ee),
and the quantum\sphinxhyphen{}derived Pauli (E\_PR) and Kinetic energy interactions
potentials between electrons (E\_KE) for a total energy expression
given as,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U\left(R,r,s\right) =  E_{NN} \left( R \right) + E_{Ne} \left( {R,r,s} \right) + E_{ee} \left( {r,s} \right) + E_{KE} \left( {r,s} \right) + E_{PR} \left( { \uparrow  \downarrow ,S} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The individual terms are defined as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{KE}  = & \frac{\hbar^2 }{{m_{e} }}\sum\limits_i {\frac{3}{{2s_i^2 }}} \\
E_{NN}  = & \frac{1}{{4\pi \varepsilon _0 }}\sum\limits_{i < j} {\frac{{Z_i Z_j }}{{R_{ij} }}} \\
E_{Ne}  = & - \frac{1}{{4\pi \varepsilon _0 }}\sum\limits_{i,j} {\frac{{Z_i }}{{R_{ij} }}Erf\left( {\frac{{\sqrt 2 R_{ij} }}{{s_j }}} \right)} \\
E_{ee}  = & \frac{1}{{4\pi \varepsilon _0 }}\sum\limits_{i < j} {\frac{1}{{r_{ij} }}Erf\left( {\frac{{\sqrt 2 r_{ij} }}{{\sqrt {s_i^2  + s_j^2 } }}} \right)} \\
E_{Pauli}  = & \sum\limits_{\sigma _i  = \sigma _j } {E\left( { \uparrow  \uparrow } \right)_{ij}}  + \sum\limits_{\sigma _i  \ne \sigma _j } {E\left( { \uparrow  \downarrow } \right)_{ij}} \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where, s\_i correspond to the electron sizes, the sigmas i’s to the
fixed spins of the electrons, Z\_i to the charges on the nuclei, R\_ij
to the distances between the nuclei or the nuclei and electrons, and
r\_ij to the distances between electrons.  For additional details see
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eff:jaramillo-botero}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Jaramillo\sphinxhyphen{}Botero)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The overall electrostatics energy is given in Hartree units of energy
by default and can be modified by an energy\sphinxhyphen{}conversion constant,
according to the units chosen (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{electron\_units}}}}).  The
cutoff Rc, given in Bohrs (by default), truncates the interaction
distance.  The recommended cutoff for this pair style should follow
the minimum image criterion, i.e. half of the minimum unit cell
length.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential is designed to be used with {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style electron}}}} definitions, in order to handle the
description of systems with interacting nuclei and explicit electrons.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{eff/cut}, the cutoff coefficient is optional.  If it is not used
(as in some of the examples above), the default global value specified
in the pair\_style command is used.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit/eradius} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure/evirials} keywords are optional.
Neither or both must be specified.  If not specified they are unset.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit/eradius} keyword is used to restrain electron size from
becoming excessively diffuse at very high temperatures were the
Gaussian wave packet representation breaks down, and from expanding as
free particles to infinite size.  If unset, electron radius is free to
increase without bounds.  If set, a restraining harmonic potential of
the form E = 1/2k\_ss\textasciicircum{}2 for s \textgreater{} L\_box/2, where k\_s = 1 Hartrees/Bohr\textasciicircum{}2,
is applied on the electron radius.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure/evirials} keyword is used to control between two types
of pressure computation: if unset, the computed pressure does not
include the electronic radial virials contributions to the total
pressure (scalar or tensor).  If set, the computed pressure will
include the electronic radial virial contributions to the total
pressure (scalar and tensor).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ecp} keyword is used to associate an ECP representation for a
particular atom type.  The ECP captures the orbital overlap between a
core pseudo particle and valence electrons within the Pauli repulsion.
A list of type:element\sphinxhyphen{}symbol pairs may be provided for all ECP
representations, after the “ecp” keyword.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Default ECP parameters are provided for C, N, O, Al, and Si.
Users can modify these using the pair\_coeff command as exemplified
above.  For this, the User must distinguish between two different
functional forms supported, one that captures the orbital overlap
assuming the s\sphinxhyphen{}type core interacts with an s\sphinxhyphen{}like valence electron
(s\sphinxhyphen{}s) and another that assumes the interaction is s\sphinxhyphen{}p.  For systems
that exhibit significant p\sphinxhyphen{}character (e.g. C, N, O) the s\sphinxhyphen{}p form is
recommended. The “s” ECP form requires 3 parameters and the “p” 5
parameters.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There are two different pressures that can be reported for eFF
when defining this pair\_style, one (default) that considers electrons
do not contribute radial virial components (i.e. electrons treated as
incompressible ‘rigid’ spheres) and one that does.  The radial
electronic contributions to the virials are only tallied if the
flexible pressure option is set, and this will affect both global and
per\sphinxhyphen{}atom quantities.  In principle, the true pressure of a system is
somewhere in between the rigid and the flexible eFF pressures, but,
for most cases, the difference between these two pressures will not be
significant over long\sphinxhyphen{}term averaged runs (i.e. even though the energy
partitioning changes, the total energy remains similar).
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This implementation of eFF gives a reasonably accurate description
for systems containing nuclei from Z = 1\sphinxhyphen{}6 in “all electron”
representations.  For systems with increasingly non\sphinxhyphen{}spherical
electrons, Users should use the ECP representations.  ECPs are now
supported and validated for most of the second and third row elements of
the p\sphinxhyphen{}block.  Predefined parameters are provided for C, N, O, Al, and
Si.  The ECP captures the orbital overlap between the core and valence
electrons (i.e. Pauli repulsion) with one of the functional forms:
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{Pauli(ECP_s)} = & p_1\exp\left(-\frac{p_2r^2}{p_3+s^2} \right) \\
E_{Pauli(ECP_p)} = & p_1\left( \frac{2}{p_2/s+s/p_2} \right)\left( r-p_3s\right)^2\exp \left[ -\frac{p_4\left( r-p_3s \right)^2}{p_5+s^2} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where the first form correspond to core interactions with s\sphinxhyphen{}type valence
electrons and the second to core interactions with p\sphinxhyphen{}type valence
electrons.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The current version adds full support for models with fixed\sphinxhyphen{}core and
ECP definitions.  to enable larger timesteps (i.e. by avoiding the
high frequency vibrational modes \sphinxhyphen{}translational and radial\sphinxhyphen{} of the 2 s
electrons), and in the ECP case to reduce the increased orbital
complexity in higher Z elements (up to Z\textless{}18).  A fixed\sphinxhyphen{}core should be
defined with a mass that includes the corresponding nuclear mass plus
the 2 s electrons in atomic mass units (2x5.4857990943e\sphinxhyphen{}4), and a
radius equivalent to that of minimized 1s electrons (see examples
under /examples/PACKAGES/eff/fixed\sphinxhyphen{}core).  An pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}core should be
described with a mass that includes the corresponding nuclear mass,
plus all the core electrons (i.e no outer shell electrons), and a
radius equivalent to that of a corresponding minimized full\sphinxhyphen{}electron
system.  The charge for a pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}core atom should be given by the
number of outer shell electrons.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In general, eFF excels at computing the properties of materials in
extreme conditions and tracing the system dynamics over multi\sphinxhyphen{}picosecond
timescales; this is particularly relevant where electron excitations
can change significantly the nature of bonding in the system. It can
capture with surprising accuracy the behavior of such systems because
it describes consistently and in an unbiased manner many different
kinds of bonds, including covalent, ionic, multicenter, ionic, and
plasma, and how they interconvert and/or change when they become
excited.  eFF also excels in computing the relative thermochemistry of
isodemic reactions and conformational changes, where the bonds of the
reactants are of the same type as the bonds of the products.  eFF
assumes that kinetic energy differences dominate the overall exchange
energy, which is true when the electrons present are nearly spherical
and nodeless and valid for covalent compounds such as dense hydrogen,
hydrocarbons, and diamond; alkali metals (e.g. lithium), alkali earth
metals (e.g. beryllium) and semimetals such as boron; and various
compounds containing ionic and/or multicenter bonds, such as boron
dihydride.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eff:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the cutoff distance for the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{eff/cut} style can be mixed.  The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.
See the “pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift option is not relevant for
these pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{eff/long} (not yet available) style supports the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option for tabulation of the
short\sphinxhyphen{}range portion of the long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eff:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles will only be enabled if LAMMPS is built with the
EFF package.  It will only be enabled if LAMMPS was built with
that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for
more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles require that particles store electron attributes
such as radius, radial velocity, and radial force, as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}}.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{electron} atom style does all of
this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thes pair styles require you to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel yes}}}} command so that velocities are stored by ghost
atoms.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eff:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_eim:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{eim} computes pairwise interactions for ionic compounds
using embedded\sphinxhyphen{}ion method (EIM) potentials {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eim:zhou2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Zhou)}}}}.  The
energy of the system E is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=i_1}^{i_N} \phi_{ij} \left(r_{ij}\right) + \sum_{i=1}^{N}E_i\left(q_i,\sigma_i\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first term is a double pairwise sum over the J neighbors of all I
atoms, where \(\phi_{ij}\) is a pair potential.  The second term sums over
the embedding energy E\_i of atom I, which is a function of its charge
q\_i and the electrical potential \(\sigma_i\) at its location.  E\_i, q\_i,
and \(sigma_i\) are calculated as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}q_i  = & \sum_{j=i_1}^{i_N} \eta_{ji}\left(r_{ij}\right) \\
\sigma_i  = & \sum_{j=i_1}^{i_N} q_j \cdot \psi_{ij} \left(r_{ij}\right) \\
E_i\left(q_i,\sigma_i\right)  = & \frac{1}{2} \cdot q_i \cdot \sigma_i\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\eta_{ji}\) is a pairwise function describing electron flow from atom
I to atom J, and \(\psi_{ij}\) is another pairwise function.  The multi\sphinxhyphen{}body
nature of the EIM potential is a result of the embedding energy term.
A complete list of all the pair functions used in EIM is summarized
below
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\phi_{ij}\left(r\right) = & \left\{ \begin{array}{lr}
\left[\frac{E_{b,ij}\beta_{ij}}{\beta_{ij}-\alpha_{ij}}\exp\left(-\alpha_{ij} \frac{r-r_{e,ij}}{r_{e,ij}}\right)-\frac{E_{b,ij}\alpha_{ij}}{\beta_{ij}-\alpha_{ij}}\exp\left(-\beta_{ij} \frac{r-r_{e,ij}}{r_{e,ij}}\right)\right]f_c\left(r,r_{e,ij},r_{c,\phi,ij}\right),& p_{ij}=1 \\
\left[\frac{E_{b,ij}\beta_{ij}}{\beta_{ij}-\alpha_{ij}} \left(\frac{r_{e,ij}}{r}\right)^{\alpha_{ij}}  -\frac{E_{b,ij}\alpha_{ij}}{\beta_{ij}-\alpha_{ij}} \left(\frac{r_{e,ij}}{r}\right)^{\beta_{ij}}\right]f_c\left(r,r_{e,ij},r_{c,\phi,ij}\right),& p_{ij}=2
\end{array}
\right.\\
\eta_{ji} = & A_{\eta,ij}\left(\chi_j-\chi_i\right)f_c\left(r,r_{s,\eta,ij},r_{c,\eta,ij}\right) \\
\psi_{ij}\left(r\right) = & A_{\psi,ij}\exp\left(-\zeta_{ij}r\right)f_c\left(r,r_{s,\psi,ij},r_{c,\psi,ij}\right) \\
f_{c}\left(r,r_p,r_c\right) = & 0.510204 \cdot \mathrm{erfc}\left[\frac{1.64498\left(2r-r_p-r_c\right)}{r_c-r_p}\right] - 0.010204\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \(E_b, r_e, r_(c,\phi), \alpha, \beta, A_(\psi), \zeta, r_(s,\psi),
r_(c,\psi), A_(\eta), r_(s,\eta), r_(c,\eta), \chi,\) and pair function type
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p} are parameters, with subscripts \sphinxstyleemphasis{ij} indicating the two species of
atoms in the atomic pair.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Even though the EIM potential is treating atoms as charged ions,
you should not use a LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} that stores a
charge on each atom and thus requires you to assign a charge to each
atom, e.g. the \sphinxstyleemphasis{charge} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{full} atom styles.  This is because the
EIM potential infers the charge on an atom from the equation above for
q\_i; you do not assign charges explicitly.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
All the EIM parameters are listed in a potential file which is
specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.  This is an
ASCII text file in a format described below.  The “ffield.eim” file
included in the “potentials” directory of the LAMMPS distribution
currently includes nine elements Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, F, Cl, Br, and I.
A system with any combination of these elements can be modeled.  This
file is parameterized in terms of LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{metal units}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that unlike other potentials, cutoffs for EIM potentials are not
set in the pair\_style or pair\_coeff command; they are specified in the
EIM potential file itself.  Likewise, the EIM potential file lists
atomic masses; thus you do not need to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{mass::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{mass}}}}
command to specify them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eim} style which
specifies an EIM potential file and the element(s) to extract
information for.  The EIM elements are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by
specifying N additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff
command, where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Elem1, Elem2, …

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
EIM potential file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of EIM elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example like one of those above, suppose you want to model a
system with Na and Cl atoms.  If your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atoms
types and you want the first 3 to be Na, and the fourth to be Cl, you would
use the following pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Na}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ffield.eim}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Na}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Na}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Na}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cl}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The filename is the EIM potential file.  The Na and Cl arguments
(before the file name) are the two elements for which info will be
extracted from the potential file.  The first three trailing Na
arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the EIM Na element.  The
final Cl argument maps LAMMPS atom type 4 to the EIM Cl element.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a mapping value is specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed.
This can be used when an \sphinxstyleemphasis{eim} potential is used as part of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.  The NULL values are placeholders for atom types
that will be used with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ffield.eim file in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS
distribution is formatted as follows:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lines starting with \# are comments and are ignored by LAMMPS.  Lines
starting with “global:” include three global values. The first value
divides the cations from anions, i.e., any elements with
electronegativity above this value are viewed as anions, and any
elements with electronegativity below this value are viewed as
cations. The second and third values are related to the cutoff
function \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. the 0.510204, 1.64498, and 0.010204 shown in the above
equation can be derived from these values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lines starting with “element:” are formatted as follows: name of
element, atomic number, atomic mass, electronic negativity, atomic
radius (LAMMPS ignores it), ionic radius (LAMMPS ignores it), cohesive
energy (LAMMPS ignores it), and q0 (must be 0).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lines starting with “pair:” are entered as: element 1, element 2,
r\_(c,phi), r\_(c,phi) (redundant for historical reasons), E\_b, r\_e,
alpha, beta, r\_(c,eta), A\_(eta), r\_(s,eta), r\_(c,psi), A\_(psi), zeta,
r\_(s,psi), and p.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The lines in the file can be in any order; LAMMPS extracts the info it
needs.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\subsection{Examples}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fractional}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6.params}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{h2o}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{h2o}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exponent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6.params}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{h2o}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exponent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6.params}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exponent}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6.params}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{none}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exp6.params}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{polynomial}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{filename}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_exp6_rx:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{exp6/rx} is used in reaction DPD simulations, where the
coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained (CG) particles are composed of \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} species whose
reaction rate kinetics are determined from a set of \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} reaction rate
equations through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rx::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rx}}}} command.  The species of
one CG particle can interact with a species in a neighboring CG
particle through a site\sphinxhyphen{}site interaction potential model.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{exp6/rx} style computes an exponential\sphinxhyphen{}6 potential given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{ij}(r) = \frac{\epsilon}{\alpha-6}\{6\exp[\alpha(1-\frac{r_{ij}}{R_{m}})]-\alpha(\frac{R_{m}}{r_{ij}})^6\}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the \(\epsilon\) parameter determines the depth of the
potential minimum located at \(R_m\), and \(\alpha\) determines
the softness of the repulsion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficients must be defined for each species in a given particle
type via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, where the first argument is the filename that includes the
exponential\sphinxhyphen{}6 parameters for each species.  The file includes the
species tag followed by the \(\alpha, \epsilon\) and \(R_m\)
parameters. The format of the file is described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second and third arguments specify the site\sphinxhyphen{}site interaction
potential between two species contained within two different
particles.  The species tags must either correspond to the species
defined in the reaction kinetics files specified with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rx::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rx}}}} command or they must correspond to the tag “1fluid”,
signifying interaction with a product species mixture determined
through a one\sphinxhyphen{}fluid approximation.  The interaction potential is
weighted by the geometric average of either the mole fraction concentrations
or the number of molecules associated with the interacting coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained
particles (see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fractional} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecular} weighting pair style options).
The coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained potential is stored before and after the
reaction kinetics solver is applied, where the difference is defined
to be the internal chemical energy (uChem).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fourth argument specifies the type of scaling that will be used
to scale the EXP\sphinxhyphen{}6 parameters as reactions occur.  Currently, there
are three scaling options:  \sphinxstyleemphasis{exponent}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{polynomial} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Exponent scaling requires two additional arguments for scaling
the \(R_m\) and \(\epsilon\) parameters, respectively.  The scaling factor
is computed by phi\textasciicircum{}exponent, where phi is the number of molecules
represented by the coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grain particle and exponent is specified
as a pair coefficient argument for \(R_m\) and \(\epsilon\), respectively.
The \(R_m\) and \(\epsilon\) parameters are multiplied by the scaling
factor to give the scaled interaction parameters for the CG particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Polynomial scaling requires a filename to be specified as a pair
coeff argument.  The file contains the coefficients to a fifth order
polynomial for the \(\alpha\), \(\epsilon\) and \(R_m\) parameters that depend
upon phi (the number of molecules represented by the CG particle).
The format of a polynomial file is provided below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} option to the scaling does not have any additional pair coeff
arguments.  This is equivalent to specifying the \sphinxstyleemphasis{exponent} option with
\(R_m\) and \(\epsilon\) exponents of 0.0 and 0.0, respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The final argument specifies the interaction cutoff (optional).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of a tabulated file is as follows (without the
parenthesized comments):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} exponential\PYGZhy{}6 parameters for various species      (one or more comment or blank lines)

h2o  exp6  11.00 0.02 3.50                          (species, exp6, alpha, Rm, epsilon)
no2  exp6  13.60 0.01 3.70
...
co2  exp6  13.00 0.03 3.20
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of the polynomial scaling file as follows (without the
parenthesized comments):
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\# POLYNOMIAL FILE          (one or more comment or blank lines)

\#  General Functional Form:
\#  A*phi\textasciicircum{}5 + B*phi\textasciicircum{}4 + C*phi\textasciicircum{}3 + D*phi\textasciicircum{}2 + E*phi + F
\#
\#  Parameter  A        B         C        D         E        F
                           (blank)
alpha        0.0000   0.00000   0.00008  0.04955  \sphinxhyphen{}0.73804  13.63201
epsilon      0.0000   0.00478  \sphinxhyphen{}0.06283  0.24486  \sphinxhyphen{}0.33737   2.60097
rm           0.0001  \sphinxhyphen{}0.00118  \sphinxhyphen{}0.00253  0.05812  \sphinxhyphen{}0.00509   1.50106
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A section begins with a non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line whose first character is not a
“\#”; blank lines or lines starting with “\#” can be used as comments
between sections.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following a blank line, the next N lines list the species and their
corresponding parameters.  The first argument is the species tag, the
second argument is the exp6 tag, the third argument is the \(\alpha\)
parameter (energy units), the fourth argument is the \(\epsilon\) parameter
(energy\sphinxhyphen{}distance\textasciicircum{}6 units), and the fifth argument is the \(R_m\) parameter
(distance units).  If a species tag of “1fluid” is listed as a pair
coefficient, a one\sphinxhyphen{}fluid approximation is specified where a
concentration\sphinxhyphen{}dependent combination of the parameters is computed
through the following equations:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_{m}^{3} = & \sum_{a}\sum_{b} x_{a}x_{b}R_{m,ab}^{3} \\
\epsilon  = & \frac{1}{R_{m}^{3}}\sum_{a}\sum_{b} x_{a}x_{b}\epsilon_{ab}R_{m,ab}^{3} \\
\alpha    = & \frac{1}{\epsilon R_{m}^{3}}\sum_{a}\sum_{b} x_{a}x_{b}\alpha_{ab}\epsilon_{ab}R_{m,ab}^{3}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\epsilon_{ab} = & \sqrt{\epsilon_{a}\epsilon_{b}} \\
R_{m,ab}      = & \frac{R_{m,a}+R_{m,b}}{2} \\
\alpha_{ab}   = & \sqrt{\alpha_{a}\alpha_{b}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and \(x_a\) and \(x_b\) are the mole fractions of a and b, respectively, which
comprise the gas mixture.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_exp6_rx:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support mixing.  Thus, coefficients for all
I,J pairs must be specified explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift option
for the energy of the exp() and 1/r\textasciicircum{}6 portion of the pair interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not support the pair\_modify tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range
tail corrections to energy and pressure for the A,C terms in the
pair interaction.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar

They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_fep_soft:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/cut/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/tip4p/long/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/charmm/coul/long/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/coul/cut/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/coul/long/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/cut/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tip4p/long/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse/soft}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = list of arguments for a particular style

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft} args = n alpha\_lj cutoff
  n, alpha\_LJ = parameters of soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones interactions (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/cut/soft} args = n alpha\_LJ alpha\_C cutoff (cutoff2)
  n, alpha\_LJ, alpha\_C = parameters of soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for LJ (and Coulombic if only 1 arg) (distance units)
  cutoff2 = global cutoff for Coulombic (optional) (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long/soft} args = n alpha\_LJ alpha\_C cutoff
  n, alpha\_LJ, alpha\_C = parameters of the soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for LJ (and Coulombic if only 1 arg) (distance units)
  cutoff2 = global cutoff for Coulombic (optional) (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/tip4p/long/soft} args = otype htype btype atype qdist n alpha\_LJ alpha\_C cutoff (cutoff2)
  otype,htype = atom types (numeric or type label) for TIP4P O and H
  btype,atype = bond and angle types (numeric or type label) for TIP4P waters
  qdist = distance from O atom to massless charge (distance units)
  n, alpha\_LJ, alpha\_C = parameters of the soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for LJ (and Coulombic if only 1 arg) (distance units)
  cutoff2 = global cutoff for Coulombic (optional) (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/charmm/coul/long/soft} args = n alpha\_LJ alpha\_C inner outer (cutoff)
  n, alpha\_LJ, alpha\_C = parameters of the soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  inner, outer = global switching cutoffs for LJ (and Coulombic if only 5 args)
  cutoff = global cutoff for Coulombic (optional, outer is Coulombic cutoff if only 5 args)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/soft} args = n alpha\_lj cutoff
  n, alpha\_LJ = parameters of soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones interactions (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/coul/cut/soft} args = n alpha\_LJ alpha\_C cutoff (cutoff2)
  n, alpha\_LJ, alpha\_C = parameters of soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for LJ (and Coulombic if only 1 arg) (distance units)
  cutoff2 = global cutoff for Coulombic (optional) (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/coul/long/soft} args = n alpha\_LJ alpha\_C cutoff (cutoff2)
  n, alpha\_LJ, alpha\_C = parameters of soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for LJ (and Coulombic if only 1 arg) (distance units)
  cutoff2 = global cutoff for Coulombic (optional) (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/cut/soft} args = n alpha\_C cutoff
  n, alpha\_C = parameters of the soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for Coulomb interactions (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long/soft} args = n alpha\_C cutoff
  n, alpha\_C = parameters of the soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for Coulomb interactions (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tip4p/long/soft} args = otype htype btype atype qdist n alpha\_C cutoff
  otype,htype = atom types (numeric or type label) for TIP4P O and H
  btype,atype = bond and angle types (numeric or type label) for TIP4P waters
  qdist = distance from O atom to massless charge (distance units)
  n, alpha\_C = parameters of the soft\sphinxhyphen{}core potential
  cutoff = global cutoff for Coulomb interactions (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{morse/soft} args = n lf cutoff
  n = soft\sphinxhyphen{}core parameter
  lf = transformation range is lf \textless{} lambda \textless{} 1
  cutoff = global cutoff for Morse interactions (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tip4p}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{soft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.15}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.8}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{morse}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{soft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

Example input scripts available: examples/PACKAGES/fep


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_fep_soft:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles have a soft repulsive core, tunable by a parameter lambda,
in order to avoid singularities during free energy calculations when sites are
created or annihilated {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_fep_soft:beutler}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Beutler)}}}}.  When lambda tends to 0 the pair
interaction vanishes with a soft repulsive core.  When lambda tends to 1, the pair
interaction approaches the normal, non\sphinxhyphen{}soft potential. These pair styles
are suited for “alchemical” free energy calculations using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt_fep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt/fep}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fep}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft} style and related sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles compute the 12\sphinxhyphen{}6 Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
and Coulomb potentials modified by a soft core, with the functional form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \lambda^n 4 \epsilon \left\{
\frac{1}{ \left[ \alpha_{\mathrm{LJ}} (1-\lambda)^2 +
\left( \displaystyle\frac{r}{\sigma} \right)^6 \right]^2 } -
\frac{1}{ \alpha_{\mathrm{LJ}} (1-\lambda)^2 +
\left( \displaystyle\frac{r}{\sigma} \right)^6 }
\right\} \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/soft} style is a 9\sphinxhyphen{}6 potential with the exponent of the
denominator of the first term in brackets taking the value 1.5 instead of 2
(other details differ, see the form of the potential in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/class2}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Coulomb interactions can also be damped with a soft core at short distance,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \lambda^n \frac{ C q_i q_j}{\epsilon \left[ \alpha_{\mathrm{C}}
(1-\lambda)^2 + r^2 \right]^{1/2}} \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the Coulomb part \(C\) is an energy\sphinxhyphen{}conversion constant, \(q_i\) and
\(q_j\) are the charges on the two atoms, and epsilon is the dielectric
constant which can be set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dielectric::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dielectric}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficient lambda is an activation parameter. When \(\lambda = 1\) the
pair potential is identical to a Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones term or a Coulomb term or a
combination of both. When \(\lambda = 0\) the interactions are
deactivated. The transition between these two extrema is smoothed by a soft
repulsive core in order to avoid singularities in potential energy and forces
when sites are created or annihilated and can overlap {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_fep_soft:beutler}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Beutler)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters \(n\), \(\alpha_\mathrm{LJ}\) and
\(\alpha_\mathrm{C}\) are set in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command,
before the cutoffs.  Usual choices for the exponent are \(n = 2\) or
\(n = 1\). For the remaining coefficients \(\alpha_\mathrm{LJ} = 0.5\)
and \(\alpha_\mathrm{C} = 10~\text{A}^2\) are appropriate choices. Plots of
the 12\sphinxhyphen{}6 LJ and Coulomb terms are shown below, for lambda ranging from 1 to 0
every 0.1.

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{lj_soft}.jpg}

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{coul_soft}.jpg}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/cut/soft} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long/soft} pair styles, as well
as for the equivalent \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2} versions, the following coefficients must be
defined for each pair of atoms types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}
command as in the examples above, or in the data file or restart files read by
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands,
or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda\) (activation parameter, between 0 and 1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff1 (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff2 (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The latter two coefficients are optional.  If not specified, the global
LJ and Coulombic cutoffs specified in the pair\_style command are used.
If only one cutoff is specified, it is used as the cutoff for both LJ
and Coulombic interactions for this type pair.  If both coefficients
are specified, they are used as the LJ and Coulombic cutoffs for this
type pair.  You cannot specify 2 cutoffs for style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft},
since it has no Coulombic terms. For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/cut/soft} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long/soft} only lambda and the optional cutoff2 are to be
specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/tip4p/long/soft} implements a soft\sphinxhyphen{}core version of the TIP4P water
model. The usage of the TIP4P pair style is documented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_lj}}}} styles. In the soft version the parameters \(n\),
\(\alpha_\mathrm{LJ}\) and \(\alpha_\mathrm {C}\) are set in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command, after the specific parameters of the
TIP4P water model and before the cutoffs. The activation parameter lambda is
supplied as an argument of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command, after
epsilon and sigma and before the optional cutoffs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If using type labels, the type labels must be defined before calling
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/charmm/coul/long/soft} implements a soft\sphinxhyphen{}core version of the modified
12\sphinxhyphen{}6 LJ potential used in CHARMM and documented in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style
lj/charmm/coul/long}}}} style. In the soft version the parameters
\(n\), \(\alpha_\mathrm{LJ}\) and \(\alpha_\mathrm{C}\) are set in
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command, before the global cutoffs. The
activation parameter lambda is introduced as an argument of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command, after \(\epsilon\) and \(\sigma\) and before the
optional eps14 and sigma14.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/soft} implements a soft\sphinxhyphen{}core version of the 9\sphinxhyphen{}6 potential in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_class2::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/class2}}}}. In the soft version the parameters
\(n\), \(\alpha_\mathrm{LJ}\) and \(\alpha_\mathrm{C}\) are set in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command, before the global cutoffs. The
activation parameter lambda is introduced as an argument of the the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command, after \(\epsilon\) and
\(\sigma\) and before the optional cutoffs.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/cut/soft}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long/soft} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tip4p/long/soft} sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles are
designed to be combined with other pair potentials via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style
hybrid/overlay}}}} command.  This is because they have no repulsive
core.  Hence, if used by themselves, there will be no repulsion to keep two
oppositely charged particles from overlapping each other. In this case, if
\(\lambda = 1\), a singularity may occur.  These sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles are suitable to
represent charges embedded in the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones radius of another site (for
example hydrogen atoms in several water models). The \(\lambda\) must
be defined for each pair, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/cut/soft} can accept an optional cutoff as
the second coefficient.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the soft\sphinxhyphen{}core Coulomb potentials with long\sphinxhyphen{}range solvers (\sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long/soft}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long/soft}, etc.)  in a free energy
calculation in which sites holding electrostatic charges are being created or
annihilated (using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt_fep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt/fep}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fep}}}}) it is important to adapt both the \(\lambda\) activation
parameter (from 0 to 1, or the reverse) and the value of the charge (from 0
to its final value, or the reverse). This ensures that long\sphinxhyphen{}range
electrostatic terms (kspace) are correct. It is not necessary to use
soft\sphinxhyphen{}core Coulomb potentials if the van der Waals site is present during the
free\sphinxhyphen{}energy route, thus avoiding overlap of the charges. Examples are
provided in the LAMMPS source directory tree, under examples/PACKAGES/fep.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To avoid division by zero do not set \(\sigma = 0\) in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft}
and related styles; use the lambda parameter instead to activate/deactivate
interactions, or use \(\epsilon = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\).
Alternatively, when sites do not interact though the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones term
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long/soft} or similar sub\sphinxhyphen{}style can be used via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid/overlay}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse/soft} variant modifies the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_morse::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_morse}}}} style at
short range to have a soft core. The functional form differs from that of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/soft} styles, and is instead given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{split}
s(\lambda) =& (1 - \lambda) / (1 - \lambda_f), \qquad B = -2D e^{-2 \alpha
r_0} (e^{\alpha r_0} - 1) / 3 \\
E =& D_0 \left[ e^{- 2 \alpha (r - r_0)} - 2 e^{- \alpha (r - r_0)} \right] +
s(\lambda) B e^{-3\alpha(r-r_0)}, \qquad \hspace{2.85em}\lambda \geq
\lambda_f,\quad r < r_c \\
E =& \left( D_0 \left[ e^{- 2 \alpha (r - r_0)} - 2 e^{- \alpha (r - r_0)}
\right] + B e^{-3\alpha(r-r_0)} \right)(\lambda/\lambda_f)^n, \qquad \lambda
< \lambda_f,\quad r < r_c
\end{split}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse/soft} style requires the following pair coefficients:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(D_0\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\alpha\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_0\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda\) (unitless, between 0.0 and 1.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional. If not specified, the global morse cutoff is
used.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_fep_soft:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The different versions of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft} pair styles support mixing.  For
atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the \(\epsilon\) and \(\sigma\)
coefficients and cutoff distance for these pair styles can be mixed.  The default
mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric} for 12\sphinxhyphen{}6 styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The mixing rule for epsilon and sigma for \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/class2/soft} 9\sphinxhyphen{}6 potentials is to
use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{sixthpower} formulas. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify mix}}}} setting
is thus ignored for class2 potentials for \(\epsilon\) and
\(\sigma\). However it is still followed for mixing the cutoff distance. See
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse/soft} pair style does not support mixing. Thus, coefficients for all
LJ pairs must be specified explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the pair styles with soft core support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift option for the energy of the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones portion of the pair
interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The different versions of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft} pair styles support the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} tail option for adding a long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail
correction to the energy and pressure for the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones portion of the pair
interaction.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The analytical form of the tail corrections for energy and pressure used in
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/soft} potentials are approximate, being identical to that of the
corresponding non\sphinxhyphen{}soft potentials scaled by a factor \(\lambda^n\). The
errors due to this approximation should be negligible. For example, for a
cutoff of \(2.5\sigma\) this approximation leads to maximum relative
errors in tail corrections of the order of 1e\sphinxhyphen{}4 for energy and virial
(\(\alpha_\mathrm{LJ} = 0.5, n = 2\)). The error vanishes when lambda
approaches 0 or 1. Note that these are the errors affecting the long\sphinxhyphen{}range
tail (itself a correction to the interaction energy) which includes other
approximations, namely that the system is homogeneous (local density equal
the average density) beyond the cutoff.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{morse/soft} pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of these pair styles write information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need to be specified
in an input script that reads a restart file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_fep_soft:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The pair styles with soft core are only enabled if LAMMPS was built with the
FEP package. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{long} versions also require the KSPACE package to be
installed. The soft \sphinxstyleemphasis{tip4p} versions also require the MOLECULE package to be
installed. These styles are only enabled if LAMMPS was built with those
packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more
info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_fep_soft:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt_fep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt/fep}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_fep::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute fep}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none

Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss/gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss/omp}


\section{pair\_style gauss/cut command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gauss:pair-style-gauss-cut-command}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss/cut/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gauss:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gauss}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff for Gauss interactions (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gauss:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gauss}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gauss}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.2805}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.45}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.112}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gauss:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss} computes a tethering potential of the form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = - A \exp(-B r^2) \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
between an atom and its corresponding tether site which will typically
be a frozen atom in the simulation.  \(r_c\) is the cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atom types
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples above,
or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
B (1/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional. If not specified, the global cutoff
is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss/cut} computes a generalized Gaussian interaction potential
between pairs of particles:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \frac{H}{\sigma_h\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left[-\frac{(r-r_{mh})^2}{2\sigma_h^2}\right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where H determines together with the standard deviation \(\sigma_h\)
the peak height of the Gaussian function, and \(r_{mh}\) the peak
position.  Examples of the use of the Gaussian potentials include
implicit solvent simulations of salt ions {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gauss:lenart2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Lenart)}}}} and
of surfactants {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gauss:jusufi2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Jusufi)}}}}.  In these instances the
Gaussian potential mimics the hydration barrier between a pair of
particles. The hydration barrier is located at \(r_{mh}\) and has a
width of \(\sigma_h\). The prefactor determines the height of the
potential barrier.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atom types
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above,
or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
H (energy * distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{mh}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma_h\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional. If not specified, the global cutoff
is used.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gauss:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the A, B, H, sigma\_h, r\_mh
parameters, and the cutoff distance for these pair styles can be mixed:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sqrt{\frac{1}{B}}\) (distance units, see below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
H (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{mh}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma_h\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.
Only \sphinxstyleemphasis{arithmetic} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric} mix values are supported.
See the “pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The A and H parameters are mixed using the same rules normally
used to mix the “epsilon” parameter in a Lennard Jones interaction.
The sigma\_h, r\_mh, and the cutoff distance are mixed using the same
rules used to mix the “sigma” parameter in a Lennard Jones interaction.
The B parameter is converted to a distance (sigma), before mixing
(using sigma=B\textasciicircum{}\sphinxhyphen{}0.5), and converted back to a coefficient
afterwards (using B=sigma\textasciicircum{}2).
Negative A values are converted to positive A values (using abs(A))
before mixing, and converted back after mixing
(by multiplying by min(sign(Ai),sign(Aj))).
This way, if either particle is repulsive (if Ai\textless{}0 or Aj\textless{}0),
then the default interaction between both particles will be repulsive.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss} style there is no effect due to the Gaussian well
beyond the cutoff; hence reasonable cutoffs need to be specified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss/cut} style supports the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift
option for the energy of the Gauss\sphinxhyphen{}potential portion of the pair
interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table and tail options are not
relevant for these pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need to be
specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gauss} pair style tallies an “occupancy” count of how many
Gaussian\sphinxhyphen{}well sites have an atom within the distance at which the force
is a maximum = sqrt(0.5/b).  This quantity can be accessed via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}} command as a vector of values of
length 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To print this quantity to the log file (with a descriptive column
heading) the following commands could be included in an input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{gauss}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gauss}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{occ}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}gauss[1]}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}occ}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip
