\section{pair\_style gayberne command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:pair-style-gayberne-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:index-3}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{gayberne/gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{gayberne/intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{gayberne/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gayberne}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{upsilon}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gamma = shift for potential minimum (typically 1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
upsilon = exponent for eta orientation\sphinxhyphen{}dependent energy function

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mu = exponent for chi orientation\sphinxhyphen{}dependent energy function

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff for interactions (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gayberne}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.7}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gayberne} styles compute a Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne anisotropic LJ interaction
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gayberne:berardi}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Berardi)}}}} between pairs of ellipsoidal particles or an
ellipsoidal and spherical particle via the formulas
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U ( \mathbf{A}_1, \mathbf{A}_2, \mathbf{r}_{12} ) = & U_r (
\mathbf{A}_1, \mathbf{A}_2, \mathbf{r}_{12}, \gamma ) \cdot \eta_{12} (
\mathbf{A}_1, \mathbf{A}_2, \upsilon ) \cdot \chi_{12} ( \mathbf{A}_1,
\mathbf{A}_2, \mathbf{r}_{12}, \mu ) \\
U_r = & 4 \epsilon ( \varrho^{12} - \varrho^6) \\
\varrho = & \frac{\sigma}{ h_{12} + \gamma \sigma}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\mathbf{A}_1\) and \(\mathbf{A}_2\) are the
transformation matrices from the simulation box frame to the body frame
and \(r_{12}\) is the center to center vector between the particles.
\(U_r\) controls the shifted distance dependent interaction based on
the distance of closest approach of the two particles (\(h_{12}\))
and the user\sphinxhyphen{}specified shift parameter \(\gamma\).  When both
particles are spherical, the formula reduces to the usual Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
interaction (see details below for when Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne treats a particle as
“spherical”).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For large uniform molecules it has been shown that the energy
parameters are approximately representable in terms of local contact
curvatures {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gayberne:everaers2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Everaers)}}}}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\epsilon_a = \sigma \cdot { \frac{a}{ b \cdot c } }; \epsilon_b =
\sigma \cdot { \frac{b}{ a \cdot c } }; \epsilon_c = \sigma \cdot {
\frac{c}{ a \cdot b } }\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The variable names utilized as potential parameters are for the most
part taken from {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gayberne:everaers2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Everaers)}}}} in order to be consistent with
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_resquared::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{RE\sphinxhyphen{}squared pair potential}}}}.  Details on the
upsilon and mu parameters are given
\sphinxhref{PDF/pair\_resquared\_extra.pdf}{here}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More details of the Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne formulation are given in the references
listed below and in \sphinxhref{PDF/pair\_gayberne\_extra.pdf}{this supplementary document}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use of this pair style requires the NVE, NVT, or NPT fixes with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{asphere} extension (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/asphere}}}}) in
order to integrate particle rotation.  Additionally, {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style
ellipsoid}}}} should be used since it defines the rotational
state and the size and shape of each ellipsoidal particle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) = well depth (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) = minimum effective particle radii (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon_{i,a}\) = relative well depth of type I for side\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}side interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon_{i,b}\) = relative well depth of type I for face\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}face interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon_{i,c}\) = relative well depth of type I for end\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}end interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon_{j,a}\) = relative well depth of type J for side\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}side interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon_{j,b}\) = relative well depth of type J for face\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}face interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon_{j,c}\) = relative well depth of type J for end\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}end interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional.  If not specified, the global
cutoff specified in the pair\_style command is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is typical with the Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne potential to define \(\sigma\) as
the minimum of the 3 shape diameters of the particles involved in an I,I
interaction, though this is not required.  Note that this is a different
meaning for \(\sigma\) than the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_resquared::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style resquared}}}} potential uses.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(\epsilon_i\) and \(\epsilon_j\) coefficients are actually
defined for atom types, not for pairs of atom types.  Thus, in a series
of pair\_coeff commands, they only need to be specified once for each
atom type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Specifically, if any of \(\epsilon_{i,a}\), \(\epsilon_{i,b}\),
\(\epsilon_{i,c}\) are non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, the three values are assigned to
atom type I.  If all the \(\epsilon_i\) values are zero, they are
ignored.  If any of \(\epsilon_{j,a}\), \(\epsilon_{j,b}\),
\(\epsilon_{j,c}\) are non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, the three values are assigned to
atom type J.  If all three epsilon\_j values are zero, they are ignored.
Thus the typical way to define the \(\epsilon_i\) and
\(\epsilon_j\) coefficients is to list their values in “pair\_coeff
I J” commands when I = J, but set them to 0.0 when I != J.  If you do
list them when I != J, you should ensure they are consistent with their
values in other pair\_coeff commands, since only the last setting will
be in effect.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that if this potential is being used as a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}}, and there is no “pair\_coeff I I”
setting made for Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne for a particular type I (because I\sphinxhyphen{}I
interactions are computed by another hybrid pair potential), then you
still need to ensure the \(\epsilon\) a,b,c coefficients are assigned to
that type. e.g. in a “pair\_coeff I J” command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \(\epsilon_{a}\) = \(\epsilon_{b}\) = \(\epsilon_{c}\) for an atom type, and if the shape
of the particle itself is spherical, meaning its 3 shape parameters
are all the same, then the particle is treated as an LJ sphere by the
Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne potential.  This is significant because if two LJ spheres
interact, then the simple Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones formula is used to compute
their interaction energy/force using the specified epsilon and sigma
as the standard LJ parameters.  This is much cheaper to compute than
the full Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne formula.  To treat the particle as a LJ sphere
with sigma = D, you should normally set \(\epsilon_{a}\) = \(\epsilon_{b}\) = \(\epsilon_{c}\) =
1.0, set the pair\_coeff \(\sigma = D\), and also set the 3 shape
parameters for the particle to D.  The one exception is that if the 3
shape parameters are set to 0.0, which is a valid way in LAMMPS to
specify a point particle, then the Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne potential will treat
that as shape parameters of 1.0 (i.e. a LJ particle with
\(\sigma = 1\)), since it requires finite\sphinxhyphen{}size particles.  In
this case you should still set the pair\_coeff \(\sigma\) to 1.0
as well.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the epsilon and sigma coefficients
and cutoff distance for this pair style can be mixed.  The default mix
value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See the “pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style supports the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift
option for the energy of the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones portion of the pair
interaction, but only for sphere\sphinxhyphen{}sphere interactions.  There is no
shifting performed for ellipsoidal interactions due to the anisotropic
dependence of the interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant
for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gayberne:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gayberne} style is part of the ASPHERE package.  It is only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles require that atoms store torque and a quaternion to
represent their orientation, as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}}.  It also require they store a per\sphinxhyphen{}type
{\hyperref[\detokenize{set::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{shape}}}}.  The particles cannot store a per\sphinxhyphen{}particle
diameter.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires that atoms be ellipsoids as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style ellipsoid}}}} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Particles acted on by the potential can be finite\sphinxhyphen{}size aspherical or
spherical particles, or point particles.  Spherical particles have all
3 of their shape parameters equal to each other.  Point particles have
all 3 of their shape parameters equal to 0.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Gay\sphinxhyphen{}Berne potential does not become isotropic as r increases
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gayberne:everaers2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Everaers)}}}}.  The distance\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}closest\sphinxhyphen{}approach
approximation used by LAMMPS becomes less accurate when high\sphinxhyphen{}aspect
ratio ellipsoids are used.

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gran:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Kn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Kt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gamma\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{xmu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dampflag}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{gran/hooke} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gran/hooke/history} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gran/hertz/history}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Kn = elastic constant for normal particle repulsion (force/distance units or pressure units \sphinxhyphen{} see discussion below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Kt = elastic constant for tangential contact (force/distance units or pressure units \sphinxhyphen{} see discussion below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gamma\_n = damping coefficient for collisions in normal direction (1/time units or 1/time\sphinxhyphen{}distance units \sphinxhyphen{} see discussion below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gamma\_t = damping coefficient for collisions in tangential direction (1/time units or 1/time\sphinxhyphen{}distance units \sphinxhyphen{} see discussion below)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
xmu = static yield criterion (unitless value between 0.0 and 1.0e4)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dampflag = 0 or 1 if tangential damping force is excluded or included

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit\_damping}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{limit\_damping} value = none
   limit damping to prevent attractive interaction
\end{sphinxalltt}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Versions of LAMMPS before 9Jan09 had different style names for
granular force fields.  This is to emphasize the fact that the
Hertzian equation has changed to model polydispersity more accurately.
A side effect of the change is that the Kn, Kt, gamma\_n, and gamma\_t
coefficients in the pair\_style command must be specified with
different values in order to reproduce calculations made with earlier
versions of LAMMPS, even for monodisperse systems.  See the NOTE below
for details.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gran:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gran}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{hooke}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{history}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gran}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{hooke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{70000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{30.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gran}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{hooke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{70000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{30.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{limit\PYGZus{}damping}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gran:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gran} styles use the following formulas for the frictional force
between two granular particles, as described in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran:brilliantov}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Brilliantov)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran:silbert}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Silbert)}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran:zhang3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Zhang)}}}}, when the distance r between two particles of radii
Ri and Rj is less than their contact distance d = Ri + Rj.  There is
no force between the particles when r \textgreater{} d.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two Hookean styles use this formula:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_{hk} = (k_n \delta \mathbf{n}_{ij} -
m_{eff} \gamma_n\mathbf{ v}_n) -
(k_t \boldsymbol{\Delta} \mathbf{s}_t +
m_{eff} \gamma_t \mathbf{v}_t)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hertzian style uses this formula:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_{hz} = \sqrt{\delta} \sqrt{\frac{R_i R_j}{R_i + R_j}} F_{hk} =
  \sqrt{\delta} \sqrt{\frac{R_i R_j}{R_i + R_j}}
  \Big[ (k_n \delta \mathbf{n}_{ij} -
    m_{eff} \: \gamma_n \mathbf{ v}_n) -
    (k_t \boldsymbol{\Delta} \mathbf{s}_t +
    m_{eff} \: \gamma_t \mathbf{v}_t) \Big]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In both equations the first parenthesized term is the normal force
between the two particles and the second parenthesized term is the
tangential force.  The normal force has 2 terms, a contact force and a
damping force.  The tangential force also has 2 terms: a shear force
and a damping force.  The shear force is a “history” effect that
accounts for the tangential displacement between the particles for the
duration of the time they are in contact.  This term is included in
pair styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke/history} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/history}, but is not included
in pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke}.  The tangential damping force term is included
in all three pair styles if \sphinxstyleemphasis{dampflag} is set to 1; it is not included
if \sphinxstyleemphasis{dampflag} is set to 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The other quantities in the equations are as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\delta\) = d \sphinxhyphen{} r = overlap distance of 2 particles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_n\) = elastic constant for normal contact

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_t\) = elastic constant for tangential contact

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\gamma_n\) = viscoelastic damping constant for normal contact

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\gamma_t\) = viscoelastic damping constant for tangential contact

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(m_{eff} = M_i M_j / (M_i + M_j) =\) effective mass of 2 particles of mass M\_i and M\_j

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\boldsymbol{\Delta} \mathbf{s}_t =\) tangential displacement vector between 2 particles which is truncated to satisfy a frictional yield criterion

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n_{ij} =\) unit vector along the line connecting the centers of the 2 particles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(V_n =\) normal component of the relative velocity of the 2 particles

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(V_t =\) tangential component of the relative velocity of the 2 particles

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(K_n\), \(K_t\), \(\gamma_n\), and \(\gamma_t\)
coefficients are specified as parameters to the pair\_style command.  If
a NULL is used for \(K_t\), then a default value is used where
\(K_t = 2/7 K_n\).  If a NULL is used for \(\gamma_t\), then a
default value is used where \(\gamma_t = 1/2 \gamma_n\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interpretation and units for these 4 coefficients are different in
the Hookean versus Hertzian equations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hookean model is one where the normal push\sphinxhyphen{}back force for two
overlapping particles is a linear function of the overlap distance.
Thus the specified \(K_n\) is in units of (force/distance).  Note
that this push\sphinxhyphen{}back force is independent of absolute particle size (in
the monodisperse case) and of the relative sizes of the two particles
(in the polydisperse case).  This model also applies to the other terms
in the force equation so that the specified \(\gamma_n\) is in units
of (1/time), \(K_t\) is in units of (force/distance), and
\(\gamma_t\) is in units of (1/time).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Hertzian model is one where the normal push\sphinxhyphen{}back force for two
overlapping particles is proportional to the area of overlap of the
two particles, and is thus a non\sphinxhyphen{}linear function of overlap distance.
Thus Kn has units of force per area and is thus specified in units of
(pressure).  The effects of absolute particle size (monodispersity)
and relative size (polydispersity) are captured in the radii\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
prefactors.  When these prefactors are carried through to the other
terms in the force equation it means that the specified \(\gamma_n\) is in
units of (1/(time*distance)), \(K_t\) is in units of (pressure), and
\(\gamma_t\) is in units of (1/(time*distance)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that in the Hookean case, \(K_n\) can be thought of as a linear
spring constant with units of force/distance.  In the Hertzian case,
\(K_n\) is like a non\sphinxhyphen{}linear spring constant with units of
force/area or pressure, and as shown in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran:zhang3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Zhang)}}}}
paper, \(K_n = 4G / (3(1-\nu))\) where \(\nu =\) the Poisson ratio,
G = shear modulus = \(E / (2(1+\nu))\), and E = Young’s modulus.  Similarly,
\(K_t = 4G / (2-\nu)\).  (NOTE: in an earlier version of the manual, we incorrectly
stated that \(K_t = 8G / (2-\nu)\).)

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus in the Hertzian case \(K_n\) and \(K_t\) can be set to
values that corresponds to properties of the material being modeled.
This is also true in the Hookean case, except that a spring constant
must be chosen that is appropriate for the absolute size of particles in
the model.  Since relative particle sizes are not accounted for, the
Hookean styles may not be a suitable model for polydisperse systems.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In versions of LAMMPS before 9Jan09, the equation for Hertzian
interactions did not include the \(\sqrt{r_i r_j / (r_i + r_j)}\)
term and thus was not as accurate for polydisperse systems.  For
monodisperse systems, \(\sqrt{ r_i r_j /(r_i+r_j)}\) is a
constant factor that effectively scales all 4 coefficients:
\(K_n, K_t, \gamma_n, \gamma_t\).  Thus you can set the values of
these 4 coefficients appropriately in the current code to reproduce
the results of a previous Hertzian monodisperse calculation.  For
example, for the common case of a monodisperse system with particles
of diameter 1, all 4 of these coefficients should now be set 2x
larger than they were previously.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Xmu is also specified in the pair\_style command and is the upper limit
of the tangential force through the Coulomb criterion Ft = xmu*Fn,
where Ft and Fn are the total tangential and normal force components
in the formulas above.  Thus in the Hookean case, the tangential force
between 2 particles grows according to a tangential spring and
dash\sphinxhyphen{}pot model until Ft/Fn = xmu and is then held at Ft = Fn*xmu until
the particles lose contact.  In the Hertzian case, a similar analogy
holds, though the spring is no longer linear.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Normally, xmu should be specified as a fractional value between
0.0 and 1.0, however LAMMPS allows large values (up to 1.0e4) to allow
for modeling of systems which can sustain very large tangential
forces.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The effective mass \sphinxstyleemphasis{m\_eff} is given by the formula above for two
isolated particles.  If either particle is part of a rigid body, its
mass is replaced by the mass of the rigid body in the formula above.
This is determined by searching for a {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rigid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rigid}}}}
command (or its variants).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For granular styles there are no additional coefficients to set for
each pair of atom types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.
All settings are global and are made via the pair\_style command.
However you must still use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} for all
pairs of granular atom types.  For example the command

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
should be used if all atoms in the simulation interact via a granular
potential (i.e. one of the pair styles above is used).  If a granular
potential is used as a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid}}}}, then specific atom types can be used in the
pair\_coeff command to determine which atoms interact via a granular
potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If two particles are moving away from each other while in contact, there
is a possibility that the particles could experience an effective attractive
force due to damping. If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit\_damping} keyword is used, this option
will zero out the normal component of the force if there is an effective
attractive force.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gran:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} mix, shift, table, and tail options
are not relevant for granular pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so a pair\_style command does not need to be
specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The single() function of these pair styles returns 0.0 for the energy
of a pairwise interaction, since energy is not conserved in these
dissipative potentials.  It also returns only the normal component of
the pairwise interaction force.  However, the single() function also
calculates 10 extra pairwise quantities.  The first 3 are the
components of the tangential force between particles I and J, acting
on particle I.  The fourth is the magnitude of this tangential force.
The next 3 (5\sphinxhyphen{}7) are the components of the relative velocity in the
normal direction (along the line joining the 2 sphere centers).  The
last 3 (8\sphinxhyphen{}10) the components of the relative velocity in the
tangential direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These extra quantities can be accessed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair/local}}}} command, as \sphinxstyleemphasis{p1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{p2}, …,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p10}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gran:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All the granular pair styles are part of the GRANULAR package.  It is
only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles require that atoms store torque and angular velocity
(omega) as defined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}}.  They also
require a per\sphinxhyphen{}particle radius is stored.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{sphere} atom style does
all of this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires you to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel yes}}}} command so that velocities are stored by ghost
atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles will not restart exactly when using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command, though they should provide
statistically similar results.  This is because the forces they
compute depend on atom velocities.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Accumulated values for individual contacts are saved to to restart
files but are not saved to data files. Therefore, forces may
differ significantly when a system is reloaded using A
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.

\section{pair\_style granular command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_granular:pair-style-granular-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_granular:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_granular::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_granular:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff (optional).  See discussion below.
