\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_granular:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hooke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear\PYGZus{}nohistory}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{damping}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass\PYGZus{}velocity}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hooke}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear\PYGZus{}history}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{damping}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mass\PYGZus{}velocity}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hertz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mindlin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{limit\PYGZus{}damping}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hertz}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{material}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mindlin\PYGZus{}rescale}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{damping}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tsuji}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{jkr}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mindlin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{800.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{twisting}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{marshall}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hertz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear\PYGZus{}history}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{300.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{twisting}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{marshall}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dmt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mindlin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{twisting}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{marshall}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dmt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mindlin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{twisting}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{marshall}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{granular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hertz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{50.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tangential}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mindlin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{heat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{area}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_granular:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{granular} styles support a variety of options for the normal,
tangential, rolling and twisting forces resulting from contact between
two granular particles. This expands on the options offered by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair gran/*}}}} pair styles. The total computed forces
and torques are the sum of various models selected for the normal,
tangential, rolling and twisting modes of motion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All model choices and parameters are entered in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command, as described below.  Unlike
e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gran::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair gran/hooke}}}}, coefficient values are not
global, but can be set to different values for different combinations
of particle types, as determined by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}
command.  If the contact model choice is the same for two particle
types, the mixing for the cross\sphinxhyphen{}coefficients can be carried out
automatically. This is shown in the last example, where model
choices are the same for type 1 \sphinxhyphen{} type 1 as for type 2 \sphinxhyphen{} type2
interactions, but coefficients are different. In this case, the
mixed coefficients for type 1 \sphinxhyphen{} type 2 interactions can be determined from
mixing rules discussed below.  For additional flexibility,
coefficients as well as model forms can vary between particle types,
as shown in the fourth example: type 1 \sphinxhyphen{} type 1 interactions are based
on a Johnson\sphinxhyphen{}Kendall\sphinxhyphen{}Roberts normal contact model and 2\sphinxhyphen{}2 interactions
are based on a DMT cohesive model (see below).  In that example, 1\sphinxhyphen{}1
and 2\sphinxhyphen{}2 interactions have different model forms, in which case mixing of
coefficients cannot be determined, so 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 interactions must be
explicitly defined via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff 1 *} command, otherwise an
error would result.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The first required keyword for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command is the normal
contact model. Currently supported options for normal contact models
and their required arguments are:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke} : \(k_n\), \(\eta_{n0}\) (or \(e\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz} : \(k_n\), \(\eta_{n0}\) (or \(e\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material} : E, \(\eta_{n0}\) (or \(e\)), \(\nu\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dmt} : E, \(\eta_{n0}\) (or \(e\)), \(\nu\), \(\gamma\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr} : E, \(\eta_{n0}\) (or \(e\)), \(\nu\), \(\gamma\)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(k_n\) is spring stiffness (with units that depend on model
choice, see below); \(\eta_{n0}\) is a damping prefactor (or, in its
place a coefficient of restitution \(e\), depending on the choice of
damping mode, see below); E is Young’s modulus in units of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{length}\textasciicircum{}2, i.e. \sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure}; \(\nu\) is Poisson’s ratio and
\(\gamma\) is a surface energy density, in units of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{energy}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{length}\textasciicircum{}2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke} model, the normal, elastic component of force acting
on particle \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} due to contact with particle \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{ne, Hooke} = k_n \delta_{ij} \mathbf{n}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where \(\delta_{ij} = R_i + R_j - \|\mathbf{r}_{ij}\|\) is the particle
overlap, \(R_i, R_j\) are the particle radii, \(\mathbf{r}_{ij} = \mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\) is the vector separating the two
particle centers (note the i\sphinxhyphen{}j ordering so that \(\mathbf{F}_{ne}\) is
positive for repulsion), and \(\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_{ij}}{\|\mathbf{r}_{ij}\|}\).  Therefore,
for \sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke}, the units of the spring constant \(k_n\) are
\sphinxstyleemphasis{force}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{distance}, or equivalently \sphinxstyleemphasis{mass}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{time\textasciicircum{}2}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz} model, the normal component of force is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{ne, Hertz} = k_n R_{eff}^{1/2}\delta_{ij}^{3/2} \mathbf{n}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(R_{eff} = R = \frac{R_i R_j}{R_i + R_j}\) is the effective
radius, denoted for simplicity as \sphinxstyleemphasis{R} from here on.  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz}, the
units of the spring constant \(k_n\) are \sphinxstyleemphasis{force}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{length}\textasciicircum{}2, or
equivalently \sphinxstyleemphasis{pressure}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material} model, the force is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{ne, Hertz/material} = \frac{4}{3} E_{eff} R^{1/2}\delta_{ij}^{3/2} \mathbf{n}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(E_{eff} = E = \left(\frac{1-\nu_i^2}{E_i} + \frac{1-\nu_j^2}{E_j}\right)^{-1}\)
is the effective Young’s modulus, with \(\nu_i, \nu_j\) the Poisson ratios
of the particles of types \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}. \(E_{eff}\) is denoted as \sphinxstyleemphasis{E} from here on.
Note that if the elastic modulus and the shear modulus of the two particles are the
same, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material} model is equivalent to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz} model with
\(k_n = 4/3 E\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{dmt} model corresponds to the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:dmt1975}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Derjaguin\sphinxhyphen{}Muller\sphinxhyphen{}Toporov)}}}} cohesive model, where the force
is simply Hertz with an additional attractive cohesion term:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{ne, dmt} = \left(\frac{4}{3} E R^{1/2}\delta_{ij}^{3/2} - 4\pi\gamma R\right)\mathbf{n}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr} model is the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:jkr1971}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Johnson\sphinxhyphen{}Kendall\sphinxhyphen{}Roberts)}}}} model,
where the force is computed as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{ne, jkr} = \left(\frac{4Ea^3}{3R} - 2\pi a^2\sqrt{\frac{4\gamma E}{\pi a}}\right)\mathbf{n}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(a\) is the radius of the contact zone, related to the overlap
\(\delta\) according to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\delta = a^2/R - 2\sqrt{\pi \gamma a/E}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS internally inverts the equation above to solve for \sphinxstyleemphasis{a} in terms
of \(\delta\), then solves for the force in the previous
equation. Additionally, note that the JKR model allows for a tensile
force beyond contact (i.e. for \(\delta < 0\)), up to a maximum of
\(3\pi\gamma R\) (also known as the ‘pull\sphinxhyphen{}off’ force).  Note that this
is a hysteretic effect, where particles that are not contacting
initially will not experience force until they come into contact
\(\delta \geq 0\); as they move apart and (\(\delta < 0\)), they
experience a tensile force up to \(3\pi\gamma R\), at which point they
lose contact.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
In addition, the normal force is augmented by a damping term of the
following general form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{n,damp} = -\eta_n \mathbf{v}_{n,rel}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\mathbf{v}_{n,rel} = (\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i) \cdot \mathbf{n}\ \mathbf{n}\) is the component of relative velocity along
\(\mathbf{n}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping} keyword to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command followed by
a keyword determines the model form of the damping factor \(\eta_n\),
and the interpretation of the \(\eta_{n0}\) or \(e\) coefficients
specified as part of the normal contact model settings. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping}
keyword and corresponding model form selection may be appended
anywhere in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair coeff} command.  Note that the choice of damping
model affects both the normal and tangential damping (and depending on
other settings, potentially also the twisting damping).  The options
for the damping model currently supported are:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{velocity}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mass\_velocity}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{viscoelastic}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tsuji}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coeff\_restitution}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping} keyword is not specified, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{viscoelastic} model is
used by default.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping velocity}, the normal damping is simply equal to the
user\sphinxhyphen{}specified damping coefficient in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{normal} model:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_n = \eta_{n0}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\eta_{n0}\) is the damping coefficient specified for the normal
contact model, in units of \sphinxstyleemphasis{mass}/\sphinxstyleemphasis{time}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping mass\_velocity}, the normal damping is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_n = \eta_{n0} m_{eff}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\eta_{n0}\) is the damping coefficient specified for the normal
contact model, in units of 1/\sphinxstyleemphasis{time} and
\(m_{eff} = m_i m_j/(m_i + m_j)\) is the effective mass.
Use \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping mass\_velocity} to reproduce the damping behavior of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair gran/hooke/*}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping viscoelastic} model is based on the viscoelastic
treatment of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:brill1996}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Brilliantov et al)}}}}, where the normal
damping is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_n = \eta_{n0}\ a m_{eff}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \sphinxstyleemphasis{a} is the contact radius, given by \(a =\sqrt{R\delta}\)
for all models except \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr}, for which it is given implicitly according
to \(\delta = a^2/R - 2\sqrt{\pi \gamma a/E}\).  For \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping viscoelastic},
\(\eta_{n0}\) is in units of 1/(\sphinxstyleemphasis{time}*\sphinxstyleemphasis{distance}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tsuji} model is based on the work of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:tsuji1992}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tsuji et al)}}}}.
Here, the damping coefficient specified as part of the normal model is interpreted
as a restitution coefficient \(e\). The damping constant \(\eta_n\) is
given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_n = \alpha (m_{eff}k_n)^{1/2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For normal contact models based on material parameters, \(k_n = 4/3Ea\). This
damping model is not compatible with cohesive normal models such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{JKR} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{DMT}.
The parameter \(\alpha\) is related to the restitution coefficient \sphinxstyleemphasis{e}
according to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\alpha = 1.2728-4.2783e+11.087e^2-22.348e^3+27.467e^4-18.022e^5+4.8218e^6\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The dimensionless coefficient of restitution \(e\) specified as part
of the normal contact model parameters should be between 0 and 1, but
no error check is performed on this.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{coeff\_restitution} model is useful when a specific normal coefficient of
restitution \(e\) is required. In these models, the normal coefficient of
restitution \(e\) is specified as an input. Following the approach of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:brill1996}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Brilliantov et al)}}}}, when using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke} normal model,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coeff\_restitution} calculates the damping coefficient as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_n = \sqrt{\frac{4m_{eff}k_n}{1+\left( \frac{\pi}{\log(e)}\right)^2}} ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For any other normal model, e.g. the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material} models, the damping
coefficient is:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_n = -2\sqrt{\frac{5}{6}}\frac{\log(e)}{\sqrt{\pi^2+(\log(e))^2}}(R_{eff} \delta_{ij})^{\frac{1}{4}}\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}k_n m_{eff}} ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(k_n = \frac{4}{3} E_{eff}\) for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material} model. Since
\sphinxstyleemphasis{coeff\_restitution} accounts for the effective mass, effective radius, and
pairwise overlaps (except when used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke} normal model) when calculating
the damping coefficient, it accurately reproduces the specified coefficient of
restitution for both monodisperse and polydisperse particle pairs.  This damping
model is not compatible with cohesive normal models such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{JKR} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{DMT}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The total normal force is computed as the sum of the elastic and
damping components:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_n = \mathbf{F}_{ne} + \mathbf{F}_{n,damp}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command also requires specification of the tangential
contact model. The required keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{tangential} is expected, followed
by the model choice and associated parameters. Currently supported
tangential model choices and their expected parameters are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{linear\_nohistory} : \(x_{\gamma,t}\), \(\mu_s\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{linear\_history} : \(k_t\), \(x_{\gamma,t}\), \(\mu_s\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin} : \(k_t\) or NULL, \(x_{\gamma,t}\), \(\mu_s\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin/force} : \(k_t\) or NULL, \(x_{\gamma,t}\), \(\mu_s\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale} : \(k_t\) or NULL, \(x_{\gamma,t}\), \(\mu_s\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale/force} : \(k_t\) or NULL, \(x_{\gamma,t}\), \(\mu_s\)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(x_{\gamma,t}\) is a dimensionless multiplier for the normal
damping \(\eta_n\) that determines the magnitude of the tangential
damping, \(\mu_t\) is the tangential (or sliding) friction
coefficient, and \(k_t\) is the tangential stiffness coefficient.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{tangential linear\_nohistory}, a simple velocity\sphinxhyphen{}dependent Coulomb
friction criterion is used, which mimics the behavior of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair
gran/hooke} style. The tangential force \(\mathbf{F}_t\) is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_t =  -\min(\mu_t F_{n0}, \|\mathbf{F}_\mathrm{t,damp}\|) \mathbf{t}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tangential damping force \(\mathbf{F}_\mathrm{t,damp}\) is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_\mathrm{t,damp} = -\eta_t \mathbf{v}_{t,rel}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tangential damping prefactor \(\eta_t\) is calculated by scaling
the normal damping \(\eta_n\) (see above):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_t = -x_{\gamma,t} \eta_n\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The normal damping prefactor \(\eta_n\) is determined by the choice
of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping} keyword, as discussed above.  Thus, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{damping}
keyword also affects the tangential damping.  The parameter
\(x_{\gamma,t}\) is a scaling coefficient. Several works in the
literature use \(x_{\gamma,t} = 1\) ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:marshall2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Marshall}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:tsuji1992}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Tsuji et al}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:silbert2001}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Silbert et al}}}}).  The relative
tangential velocity at the point of contact is given by
\(\mathbf{v}_{t, rel} = \mathbf{v}_{t} - (R_i\boldsymbol{\Omega}_i + R_j\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j) \times \mathbf{n}\), where \(\mathbf{v}_{t} = \mathbf{v}_r - \mathbf{v}_r\cdot\mathbf{n}\ \mathbf{n}\),
\(\mathbf{v}_r = \mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i\) .
The direction of the applied force is \(\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{v_{t,rel}}/\|\mathbf{v_{t,rel}}\|\) .

\sphinxAtStartPar
The normal force value \(F_{n0}\) used to compute the critical force
depends on the form of the contact model. For non\sphinxhyphen{}cohesive models
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hooke}), it is given by the magnitude of
the normal force:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_{n0} = \|\mathbf{F}_n\|\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For cohesive models such as \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dmt}, the critical force is
adjusted so that the critical tangential force approaches \(\mu_t F_{pulloff}\), see {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:marshall2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Marshall}}}}, equation 43, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:thornton1991}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Thornton}}}}.  For both models, \(F_{n0}\) takes the
form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F_{n0} = \|\mathbf{F}_{ne} + 2 F_{pulloff}\|\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where \(F_{pulloff} = 3\pi \gamma R\) for \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr}, and
\(F_{pulloff} = 4\pi \gamma R\) for \sphinxstyleemphasis{dmt}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The remaining tangential options all use accumulated tangential
displacement (i.e. contact history), except for the options
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin/force} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale/force}, that use accumulated
tangential force instead, and are discussed further below.
The accumulated tangential displacement is discussed in details below
in the context of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear\_history} option. The same treatment of
the accumulated displacement applies to the other options as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{tangential linear\_history}, the tangential force is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_t =  -\min(\mu_t F_{n0}, \|-k_t\mathbf{\xi} + \mathbf{F}_\mathrm{t,damp}\|) \mathbf{t}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\mathbf{\xi}\) is the tangential displacement accumulated
during the entire duration of the contact:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\xi} = \int_{t0}^t \mathbf{v}_{t,rel}(\tau) \mathrm{d}\tau\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This accumulated tangential displacement must be adjusted to account
for changes in the frame of reference of the contacting pair of
particles during contact. This occurs due to the overall motion of the
contacting particles in a rigid\sphinxhyphen{}body\sphinxhyphen{}like fashion during the duration
of the contact. There are two modes of motion that are relevant: the
‘tumbling’ rotation of the contacting pair, which changes the
orientation of the plane in which tangential displacement occurs; and
‘spinning’ rotation of the contacting pair about the vector connecting
their centers of mass (\(\mathbf{n}\)).  Corrections due to the
former mode of motion are made by rotating the accumulated
displacement into the plane that is tangential to the contact vector
at each step, or equivalently removing any component of the tangential
displacement that lies along \(\mathbf{n}\), and rescaling to
preserve the magnitude.  This follows the discussion in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:luding2008}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Luding}}}}, see equation 17 and relevant discussion in that
work:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\xi} = \left(\mathbf{\xi'} - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{\xi'})\mathbf{n}\right) \frac{\|\mathbf{\xi'}\|}{\|\mathbf{\xi'} - (\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{\xi'})\mathbf{n}\|}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\mathbf{\xi'}\) is the accumulated displacement prior to the
current time step and \(\mathbf{\xi}\) is the corrected
displacement. Corrections to the displacement due to the second mode
of motion described above (rotations about \(\mathbf{n}\)) are not
currently implemented, but are expected to be minor for most
simulations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Furthermore, when the tangential force exceeds the critical force, the
tangential displacement is re\sphinxhyphen{}scaled to match the value for the
critical force (see {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:luding2008}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Luding}}}}, equation 20 and related
discussion):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\xi} = -\frac{1}{k_t}\left(\mu_t F_{n0}\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{F}_{t,damp}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tangential force is added to the total normal force (elastic plus
damping) to produce the total force on the particle. The tangential
force also acts at the contact point (defined as the center of the
overlap region) to induce a torque on each particle according to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\tau}_i = -(R_i - 0.5 \delta) \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{F}_t\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\tau}_j = -(R_j - 0.5 \delta) \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{F}_t\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{tangential mindlin}, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:mindlin1949}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Mindlin}}}} no\sphinxhyphen{}slip solution
is used which differs from the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear\_history} option by an additional factor
of \(a\), the radius of the contact region. The tangential force is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_t =  -\min(\mu_t F_{n0}, \|-k_t a \mathbf{\xi} + \mathbf{F}_\mathrm{t,damp}\|) \mathbf{t}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(a\) is the radius of the contact region, given by \(a =\sqrt{R\delta}\)
for all normal contact models, except for \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr}, where it is given
implicitly by \(\delta = a^2/R - 2\sqrt{\pi \gamma a/E}\), see
discussion above. To match the Mindlin solution, one should set
\(k_t = 8G_{eff}\), where \(G_{eff}\) is the effective shear modulus given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}G_{eff} = \left(\frac{2-\nu_i}{G_i} + \frac{2-\nu_j}{G_j}\right)^{-1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(G_i\) is the shear modulus of a particle of type \(i\), related to Young’s
modulus \(E_i\) and Poisson’s ratio \(\nu_i\) by \(G_i = E_i/(2(1+\nu_i))\).
This can also be achieved by specifying \sphinxstyleemphasis{NULL} for \(k_t\), in which case a
normal contact model that specifies material parameters \(E_i\) and
\(\nu_i\) is required (e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dmt} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr}). In this
case, mixing of the shear modulus for different particle types \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{j} is done according to the formula above.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The radius of the contact region \(a\) depends on the normal overlap.
As a result, the tangential force for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin} can change due to
a variation in normal overlap, even with no change in tangential displacement.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{tangential mindlin/force}, the accumulated elastic tangential force
characterizes the contact history, instead of the accumulated tangential
displacement. This prevents the dependence of the tangential force on the
normal overlap as noted above. The tangential force is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_t =  -\min(\mu_t F_{n0}, \|\mathbf{F}_{te} + \mathbf{F}_\mathrm{t,damp}\|) \mathbf{t}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The increment of the elastic component of the tangential force
\(\mathbf{F}_{te}\) is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{F}_{te} = -k_t a \mathbf{v}_{t,rel} \mathrm{d}\tau\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The changes in frame of reference of the contacting pair of particles during
contact are accounted for by the same formula as above, replacing the
accumulated tangential displacement \(\xi\), by the accumulated tangential
elastic force \(F_{te}\). When the tangential force exceeds the critical
force, the tangential force is directly re\sphinxhyphen{}scaled to match the value for
the critical force:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{te} = - \mu_t F_{n0}\mathbf{t} + \mathbf{F}_{t,damp}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The same rules as those described for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin} apply regarding the tangential
stiffness and mixing of the shear modulus for different particle types.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale} option uses the same form as \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin}, but the
magnitude of the tangential displacement is re\sphinxhyphen{}scaled as the contact
unloads, i.e. if \(a < a_{t_{n-1}}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\xi} = \mathbf{\xi_{t_{n-1}}} \frac{a}{a_{t_{n-1}}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(t_{n-1}\) indicates the value at the previous time
step. This rescaling accounts for the fact that a decrease in the
contact area upon unloading leads to the contact being unable to
support the previous tangential loading, and spurious energy is
created without the rescaling above ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:waltonpc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Walton}}}} ).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin}, a decrease in the tangential force already occurs as the
contact unloads, due to the dependence of the tangential force on the normal
force described above. By re\sphinxhyphen{}scaling \(\xi\), \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale}
effectively re\sphinxhyphen{}scales the tangential force twice, i.e., proportionally to
\(a^2\). This peculiar behavior results from use of the accumulated
tangential displacement to characterize the contact history. Although
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale} remains available for historic reasons and backward
compatibility purposes, it should be avoided in favor of \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale/force}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale/force} option uses the same form as \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin/force},
but the magnitude of the tangential elastic force is re\sphinxhyphen{}scaled as the contact
unloads, i.e. if \(a < a_{t_{n-1}}\):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{te} = \mathbf{F}_{te, t_{n-1}} \frac{a}{a_{t_{n-1}}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This approach provides a better approximation of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:mindlin1953}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Mindlin\sphinxhyphen{}Deresiewicz}}}}
laws and is more consistent than \sphinxstyleemphasis{mindlin\_rescale}. See discussions in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:thornton2013}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Thornton et al, 2013}}}}, particularly equation 18(b) of that
work and associated discussion, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:agnolinroux2007}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Agnolin and Roux, 2007}}}},
particularly Appendix A.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{rolling} keyword enables rolling friction, which resists
pure rolling motion of particles. The options currently supported are:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{none}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sds} : \(k_{roll}\), \(\gamma_{roll}\), \(\mu_{roll}\)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{rolling} keyword is not specified, the model defaults to \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{rolling sds}, rolling friction is computed via a
spring\sphinxhyphen{}dashpot\sphinxhyphen{}slider, using a ‘pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}force’ formulation, as detailed
by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:luding2008}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Luding}}}}. Unlike the formulation in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:marshall2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Marshall}}}}, this allows for the required adjustment of
rolling displacement due to changes in the frame of reference of the
contacting pair.  The rolling pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}force is computed analogously to
the tangential force:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{roll,0} =  k_{roll} \mathbf{\xi}_{roll}  - \gamma_{roll} \mathbf{v}_{roll}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\mathbf{v}_{roll} = -R(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_i - \boldsymbol{\Omega}_j) \times \mathbf{n}\) is the relative rolling
velocity, as given in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:wang2015}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wang et al}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:luding2008}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Luding}}}}. This differs from the expressions given by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:kuhn2004}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Kuhn and Bagi}}}} and used in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:marshall2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Marshall}}}}; see {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:wang2015}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wang et al}}}} for details. The rolling displacement is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\xi}_{roll} = \int_{t_0}^t \mathbf{v}_{roll} (\tau) \mathrm{d} \tau\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A Coulomb friction criterion truncates the rolling pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}force if it
exceeds a critical value:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{F}_{roll} =  \min(\mu_{roll} F_{n,0}, \|\mathbf{F}_{roll,0}\|)\mathbf{k}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{v}_{roll}/\|\mathbf{v}_{roll}\|\) is the direction of
the pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}force.  As with tangential displacement, the rolling
displacement is rescaled when the critical force is exceeded, so that
the spring length corresponds the critical force. Additionally, the
displacement is adjusted to account for rotations of the frame of
reference of the two contacting particles in a manner analogous to the
tangential displacement.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rolling pseudo\sphinxhyphen{}force does not contribute to the total force on
either particle (hence ‘pseudo’), but acts only to induce an equal and
opposite torque on each particle, according to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\tau_{roll,i} =  R \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{F}_{roll}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\tau_{roll,j} =  -\tau_{roll,i}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{twisting} keyword enables twisting friction, which
resists rotation of two contacting particles about the vector
\(\mathbf{n}\) that connects their centers. The options currently
supported are:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{none}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sds} : \(k_{twist}\), \(\gamma_{twist}\), \(\mu_{twist}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{marshall}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twisting} keyword is not specified, the model defaults to \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For both \sphinxstyleemphasis{twisting sds} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{twisting marshall}, a history\sphinxhyphen{}dependent
spring\sphinxhyphen{}dashpot\sphinxhyphen{}slider is used to compute the twisting torque. Because
twisting displacement is a scalar, there is no need to adjust for
changes in the frame of reference due to rotations of the particle
pair. The formulation in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:marshall2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Marshall}}}} therefore provides
the most straightforward treatment:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\tau_{twist,0} = -k_{twist}\xi_{twist} - \gamma_{twist}\Omega_{twist}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \(\xi_{twist} = \int_{t_0}^t \Omega_{twist} (\tau) \mathrm{d}\tau\) is the twisting angular displacement, and
\(\Omega_{twist} = (\mathbf{\Omega}_i - \mathbf{\Omega}_j) \cdot \mathbf{n}\) is the relative twisting angular velocity. The torque
is then truncated according to:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\tau_{twist} = \min(\mu_{twist} F_{n,0}, \tau_{twist,0})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to the sliding and rolling displacement, the angular
displacement is rescaled so that it corresponds to the critical value
if the twisting torque exceeds this critical value:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\xi_{twist} = \frac{1}{k_{twist}} (\mu_{twist} F_{n,0}sgn(\Omega_{twist}) - \gamma_{twist}\Omega_{twist})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{twisting sds}, the coefficients \(k_{twist}, \gamma_{twist}\)
and \(\mu_{twist}\) are simply the user input parameters that follow
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{twisting sds} keywords in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{twisting\_marshall}, the coefficients are expressed in terms of
sliding friction coefficients, as discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:marshall2009}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Marshall}}}} (see equations 32 and 33 of that work):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}k_{twist} = 0.5k_ta^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_{twist} = 0.5\eta_ta^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mu_{twist} = \frac{2}{3}a\mu_t\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, the twisting torque on each particle is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\tau}_{twist,i} = \tau_{twist}\mathbf{n}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{\tau}_{twist,j} = -\mathbf{\tau}_{twist,i}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
If two particles are moving away from each other while in contact, there
is a possibility that the particles could experience an effective attractive
force due to damping. If the optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{limit\_damping} keyword is used, this option
will zero out the normal component of the force if there is an effective
attractive force. This keyword cannot be used with the JKR or DMT models.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat} keyword enables heat conduction. The options currently
supported are:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{none}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{radius} : \(k_{s}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{area} : \(h_{s}\)

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat} keyword is not specified, the model defaults to \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat} \sphinxstyleemphasis{radius}, the heat
\(Q\) conducted between two particles is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Q = 2 k_{s} a \Delta T\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\Delta T\) is the difference in the two particles’ temperature,
\(k_{s}\) is a non\sphinxhyphen{}negative numeric value for the conductivity (in units
of power/(length*temperature)), and \(a\) is the radius of the contact and
depends on the normal force model. This is the model proposed by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_granular:vargasmccarthy2001}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Vargas and McCarthy}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{heat} \sphinxstyleemphasis{area}, the heat
\(Q\) conducted between two particles is given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Q = h_{s} A \Delta T\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\Delta T\) is the difference in the two particles’ temperature,
\(h_{s}\) is a non\sphinxhyphen{}negative numeric value for the heat transfer
coefficient (in units of power/(area*temperature)), and \(A=\pi a^2\) is
the area of the contact and depends on the normal force model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the option \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} must either be used in all or none of of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} calls. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_heat_flow::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix heat/flow}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_property_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix property/atom}}}} for more information on this
option.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{granular} pair style can reproduce the behavior of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair gran/*} styles with the appropriate settings (some very
minor differences can be expected due to corrections in
displacement history frame\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}reference, and the application
of the torque at the center of the contact rather than
at each particle). The first example above
is equivalent to \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair gran/hooke 1000.0 NULL 50.0 50.0 0.4 1}.
The second example is equivalent to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair gran/hooke/history 1000.0 500.0 50.0 50.0 0.4 1}.
The third example is equivalent to
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair gran/hertz/history 1000.0 500.0 50.0 50.0 0.4 1 limit\_damping}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS automatically sets pairwise cutoff values for \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style
granular} based on particle radii (and in the case of \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr} pull\sphinxhyphen{}off
distances). In the vast majority of situations, this is adequate.
However, a cutoff value can optionally be appended to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style
granular} command to specify a global cutoff (i.e. a cutoff for all
atom types). Additionally, the optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} keyword can be passed
to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command, followed by a cutoff value.  This will
set a pairwise cutoff for the atom types in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command.
These options may be useful in some rare cases where the automatic
cutoff determination is not sufficient, e.g.  if particle diameters
are being modified via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fix adapt} command. In that case, the
global cutoff specified as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style granular} command
is applied to all atom types, unless it is overridden for a given atom
type combination by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} value specified in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair coeff}
command.  If \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} is only specified in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair coeff} command
and no global cutoff is appended to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_style granular} command,
then LAMMPS will use that cutoff for the specified atom type
combination, and automatically set pairwise cutoffs for the remaining
atom types.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_granular:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} mix, shift, table, and tail options
are not relevant for granular pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Mixing of coefficients is carried out using geometric averaging for
most quantities, e.g. if friction coefficient for type 1\sphinxhyphen{}type 1
interactions is set to \(\mu_1\), and friction coefficient for type
2\sphinxhyphen{}type 2 interactions is set to \(\mu_2\), the friction coefficient
for type1\sphinxhyphen{}type2 interactions is computed as \(\sqrt{\mu_1\mu_2}\)
(unless explicitly specified to a different value by a \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff 1 2
…} command). The exception to this is elastic modulus, only
applicable to \sphinxstyleemphasis{hertz/material}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dmt} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{jkr} normal contact
models. In that case, the effective elastic modulus is computed as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{eff,ij} = \left(\frac{1-\nu_i^2}{E_i} + \frac{1-\nu_j^2}{E_j}\right)^{-1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{i\sphinxhyphen{}j} coefficients \(E_{ij}\) and \(\nu_{ij}\) are
explicitly specified, the effective modulus is computed as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{eff,ij} = \left(\frac{1-\nu_{ij}^2}{E_{ij}} + \frac{1-\nu_{ij}^2}{E_{ij}}\right)^{-1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{eff,ij} = \frac{E_{ij}}{2(1-\nu_{ij}^2)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so a pair\_style command does not need to be
specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The single() function of these pair styles returns 0.0 for the energy
of a pairwise interaction, since energy is not conserved in these
dissipative potentials.  It also returns only the normal component of
the pairwise interaction force.  However, the single() function also
calculates 13 extra pairwise quantities.  The first 3 are the
components of the tangential force between particles I and J, acting
on particle I.  The fourth is the magnitude of this tangential force.
The next 3 (5\sphinxhyphen{}7) are the components of the rolling torque acting on
particle I. The next entry (8) is the magnitude of the rolling torque.
The next entry (9) is the magnitude of the twisting torque acting
about the vector connecting the two particle centers.
The next 3 (10\sphinxhyphen{}12) are the components of the vector connecting
the centers of the two particles (x\_I \sphinxhyphen{} x\_J). The last quantity (13)
is the heat flow between the two particles, set to 0 if no heat model
is active.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These extra quantities can be accessed by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair/local}}}} command, as \sphinxstyleemphasis{p1}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{p2}, …,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{p12}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_granular:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the GRANULAR package.  It is
only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires that atoms store per\sphinxhyphen{}particle radius,
torque, and angular velocity (omega) as defined by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires you to use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{comm_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{comm\_modify vel yes}}}}
command so that velocities are stored by ghost atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style will not restart exactly when using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command, though it should provide
statistically similar results.  This is because the forces it
computes depend on atom velocities and the atom velocities have
been propagated half a timestep between the force computation and
when the restart is written, due to using Velocity Verlet time
integration. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command
for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Accumulated values for individual contacts are saved to restart
files but are not saved to data files. Therefore, forces may
differ significantly when a system is reloaded using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.

\section{pair\_style lj/gromacs command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:pair-style-lj-gromacs-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:index-6}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:index-5}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:index-4}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:index-3}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs::doc}}

\section{pair\_style lj/gromacs/coul/gromacs command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:pair-style-lj-gromacs-coul-gromacs-command}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs/coul/gromacs/kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs/coul/gromacs/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs/coul/gromacs}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = list of arguments for a particular style

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs} args = inner outer
  inner, outer = global switching cutoffs for Lennard Jones
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs/coul/gromacs} args = inner outer (inner2) (outer2)
  inner, outer = global switching cutoffs for Lennard Jones (and Coulombic if only 2 args)
  inner2, outer2 = global switching cutoffs for Coulombic (optional)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{gromacs}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{gromacs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{gromacs}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{gromacs}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs} styles compute shifted LJ and Coulombic interactions
with an additional switching function S(r) that ramps the energy and force
smoothly to zero between an inner and outer cutoff.  It is a commonly
used potential in the \sphinxhref{https://www.gromacs.org}{GROMACS} MD code and for
the coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained models of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gromacs:marrink}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Marrink)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{LJ} = & 4 \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
         \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right] + S_{LJ}(r)
                    \qquad r < r_c \\
E_C  = & \frac{C q_i q_j}{\epsilon  r} + S_C(r) \qquad r < r_c \\
S(r) = & C \qquad r < r_1 \\
S(r) = & \frac{A}{3} (r - r_1)^3 + \frac{B}{4} (r - r_1)^4 + C \qquad  r_1 < r < r_c \\
A = & (-3 E'(r_c) + (r_c - r_1) E''(r_c))/(r_c - r_1)^2 \\
B = & (2 E'(r_c) - (r_c - r_1) E''(r_c))/(r_c - r_1)^3 \\
C = & -E(r_c) + \frac{1}{2} (r_c - r_1) E'(r_c) - \frac{1}{12} (r_c - r_1)^2 E''(r_c)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_1\) is the inner cutoff; \(r_c\) is the outer cutoff.  The
coefficients A, B, and C are computed by LAMMPS to perform the shifting
and smoothing.  The function S(r) is actually applied once to each term
of the LJ formula and once to the Coulombic formula, so there are 2 or 3
sets of A,B,C coefficients depending on which pair\_style is used.  The
boundary conditions applied to the smoothing function are as follows:
\(S'(r_1) = S''(r_1) = 0, S(r_c) = -E(r_c), S'(r_c) = -E'(r_c)\),
and \(S''(r_c) = -E''(r_c)\), where E(r) is the corresponding term
in the LJ or Coulombic potential energy function.  Single and double
primes denote first and second derivatives with respect to r,
respectively.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The inner and outer cutoff for the LJ and Coulombic terms can be the
same or different depending on whether 2 or 4 arguments are used in
the pair\_style command.  The inner LJ cutoff must be \textgreater{} 0, but the
inner Coulombic cutoff can be \textgreater{}= 0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
inner (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
outer (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that sigma is defined in the LJ formula as the zero\sphinxhyphen{}crossing
distance for the potential, not as the energy minimum at \(2^{1/6} \sigma\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last 2 coefficients are optional inner and outer cutoffs for style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs}.  If not specified, the global \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} values
are used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last 2 coefficients cannot be used with style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/gromacs/coul/gromacs} because this force field does not allow
varying cutoffs for individual atom pairs; all pairs use the global
cutoff(s) specified in the pair\_style command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gromacs:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the epsilon and sigma coefficients
and cutoff distance for all of the lj/cut pair styles can be mixed.
The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See the “pair\_modify” command
for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the GROMACS pair styles support the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift option, since the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
portion of the pair interaction is already smoothed to 0.0 at the
cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant
for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the GROMACS pair styles support the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail
corrections to energy and pressure, since there are no corrections for
a potential that goes to 0.0 at the cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the GROMACS pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do
not need to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the GROMACS pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair}
keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not
support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\section{pair\_style gw command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:pair-style-gw-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_gw::doc}}

\section{pair\_style gw/zbl command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:pair-style-gw-zbl-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{gw} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{gw/zbl}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gw}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.gw}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gw}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{zbl}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.gw.zbl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{gw} style computes a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_gw:gao}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Gao\sphinxhyphen{}Weber}}}} potential;
similarly \sphinxstyleemphasis{gw/zbl} combines this potential with a modified
repulsive ZBL core function in a similar fashion as implemented
in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tersoff/zbl}}}} pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unfortunately the author of this contributed code has not been
able to submit a suitable documentation explaining the details
of the potentials. The LAMMPS developers thus have finally decided
to release the code anyway with only the technical explanations.
For details of the model and the parameters, please refer to the
linked publication.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{gw} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{gw/zbl}
styles which specifies a Gao\sphinxhyphen{}Weber potential file with parameters
for all needed elements.  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by
specifying N additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff
command, where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of GW elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine a file SiC.gw has Gao\sphinxhyphen{}Weber values for Si and C.
If your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atoms types and you want the first 3 to
be Si, and the fourth to be C, you would use the following pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.gw}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The first three Si arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the Si
element in the GW file.  The final C argument maps LAMMPS atom type 4
to the C element in the GW file.  If a mapping value is specified as
NULL, the mapping is not performed.  This can be used when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gw}
potential is used as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.  The NULL values
are placeholders for atom types that will be used with other
potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Gao\sphinxhyphen{}Weber files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS
distribution have a “.gw” suffix.  Gao\sphinxhyphen{}Weber with ZBL files
have a “.gz.zbl” suffix. The structure of the potential files
is similar to other many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials supported by LAMMPS.
You have to refer to the comments in the files and the literature
to learn more details.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, where types I and J correspond to
two different element types, mixing is performed by LAMMPS as
described above from values in the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the MANYBODY package. It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on”
for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Gao\sphinxhyphen{}Weber potential files provided with LAMMPS (see the
potentials directory) are parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.
You can use the GW potential with any LAMMPS units, but you would need
to create your own GW potential file with coefficients listed in the
appropriate units if your simulation does not use “metal” units.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_gw:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{pair\_style harmonic/cut command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:pair-style-harmonic-cut-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/cut/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/cut}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 17Feb2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/cut} computes pairwise repulsive\sphinxhyphen{}only harmonic interactions with the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = k (r_c - r)^2  \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(r_c\) is the cutoff.  Note that the usual 1/2 factor is
included in \(k\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(k\) (energy/distance\textasciicircum{}2 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_c\) (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the \(k\) and \(r_c\)
coefficients can be mixed. The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.
See the “pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since the potential is zero at and beyond the cutoff parameter by
construction, there is no need to support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift or tail options for the energy and pressure of the
pair interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}},
so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need to be specified in an input script
that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\label{\detokenize{pair_harmonic_cut:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/cut} pair style is only enabled if LAMMPS was
built with the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR package.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.
