\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hbond_dreiding:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hbond/dreiding} styles compute the Acceptor\sphinxhyphen{}Hydrogen\sphinxhyphen{}Donor (AHD)
3\sphinxhyphen{}body hydrogen bond interaction for the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{DREIDING}}}}
force field, given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E  = & \left[LJ(r) | Morse(r) \right] \qquad \qquad \qquad r < r_{\rm in} \\
   = & S(r) * \left[LJ(r) | Morse(r) \right] \qquad \qquad r_{\rm in} < r < r_{\rm out} \\
   = & 0 \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad r > r_{\rm out} \\
LJ(r)  = & AR^{-12}-BR^{-10}cos^n\theta=
      \epsilon\left\lbrace 5\left[ \frac{\sigma}{r}\right]^{12}-
      6\left[ \frac{\sigma}{r}\right]^{10}  \right\rbrace cos^n\theta\\
Morse(r)  = & D_0\left\lbrace \chi^2 - 2\chi\right\rbrace cos^n\theta=
      D_{0}\left\lbrace e^{- 2 \alpha (r - r_0)} - 2 e^{- \alpha (r - r_0)}
      \right\rbrace cos^n\theta \\
S(r)  = & \frac{ \left[r_{\rm out}^2 - r^2\right]^2
\left[r_{\rm out}^2 + 2r^2 - 3{r_{\rm in}^2}\right]}
{ \left[r_{\rm out}^2 - {r_{\rm in}}^2\right]^3 }\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(r_{\rm in}\) is the inner spline distance cutoff,
\(r_{\rm out}\) is the outer distance cutoff, \(\theta_c\) is
the angle cutoff, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} is the cosine periodicity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \sphinxstyleemphasis{r} is the radial distance between the donor (D) and acceptor
(A) atoms and \(\theta\) is the bond angle between the acceptor, the
hydrogen (H) and the donor atoms:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{dreiding_hbond}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions can be defined for pairs of acceptor and
donor atoms, based on atom types.  For each donor/acceptor atom pair,
the third atom in the interaction is a hydrogen permanently bonded to
the donor atom, e.g. in a bond list read in from a data file via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.  The atom types of possible
hydrogen atoms for each donor/acceptor type pair are specified by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command (see below).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hbond/dreiding/lj} is the original DREIDING potential of
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hbond_dreiding:pair-mayo}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mayo)}}}}.  It uses a LJ 12/10 functional for the Donor\sphinxhyphen{}Acceptor
interactions. To match the results in the original paper, use n = 4.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hbond/dreiding/morse} is an improved version using a Morse
potential for the Donor\sphinxhyphen{}Acceptor interactions. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hbond_dreiding:liu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Liu)}}}} showed
that the Morse form gives improved results for Dendrimer simulations,
when n = 2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Howto_bioFF::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Howto bioFF}}}} page for more information
on the DREIDING force field.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Because the Dreiding hydrogen bond potential is only one portion
of an overall force field which typically includes other pairwise
interactions, it is common to use it as a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid/overlay}}}} command, where another pair style
provides the repulsive core interaction between pairs of atoms, e.g. a
1/r\textasciicircum{}12 Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones repulsion.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the hbond/dreiding pair styles with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid/overlay}}}}, you should explicitly define pair
interactions between the donor atom and acceptor atoms, (as well as
between these atoms and ALL other atoms in your system).  Whenever
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style hybrid/overlay}}}} is used, ordinary mixing
rules are not applied to atoms like the donor and acceptor atoms
because they are typically referenced in multiple pair styles.
Neglecting to do this can cause difficult\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}detect physics problems.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the original Dreiding force field paper 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded
interactions ARE allowed.  If this is desired for your model, use the
special\_bonds command (e.g. “special\_bonds lj 0.0 0.0 1.0”) to turn
these interactions on.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for pairs of eligible
donor/acceptor types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as
in the examples above.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike other pair styles and their associated
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} commands, you do not need to specify
pair\_coeff settings for all possible I,J type pairs.  Only I,J type
pairs for atoms which act as joint donors/acceptors need to be
specified; all other type pairs are assumed to be inactive.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command can be specified multiple
times for the same donor/acceptor type pair.  This enables multiple
hydrogen types to be assigned to the same donor/acceptor type pair.
For other pair\_styles, if the pair\_coeff command is re\sphinxhyphen{}used for the
same I.J type pair, the settings for that type pair are overwritten.
For the hydrogen bond potentials this is not the case; the settings
are cumulative.  This means the only way to turn off a previous
setting, is to re\sphinxhyphen{}use the pair\_style command and start over.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hbond/dreiding/lj} style the list of coefficients is as
follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
K = hydrogen atom type = 1 to Ntypes, or type label

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
donor flag = \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{n} = exponent in formula above

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
distance cutoff \(r_{\rm in}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
distance cutoff \(r_{\rm out}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
angle cutoff (degrees)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hbond/dreiding/morse} style the list of coefficients is as
follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
K = hydrogen atom type = 1 to Ntypes, or type label

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
donor flag = \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(D_0\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\alpha\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_0\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{n} = exponent in formula above

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
distance cutoff \(r_{\rm in}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
distance cutoff \(r_{out}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
angle cutoff (degrees)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A single hydrogen atom type K can be specified, or a wild\sphinxhyphen{}card asterisk
can be used in place of or in conjunction with the K arguments to
select multiple types as hydrogen atoms.  This takes the form
“*” or “*n” or “n*” or “m*n”.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}
command page for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the donor flag is \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}, then the atom of type I in the pair\_coeff
command is treated as the donor, and J is the acceptor.  If the donor
flag is \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}, then the atom of type J in the pair\_coeff command is
treated as the donor and I is the donor.  This option is required
because the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command requires that I \textless{}= J.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) and \(\sigma\) are settings for the hydrogen bond
potential based on a Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones functional form.  Note that sigma is
defined as the zero\sphinxhyphen{}crossing distance for the potential, not as the
energy minimum at \(2^{1/6} \sigma\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(D_0\) and \(\alpha\) and \(r_0\) are settings for the
hydrogen bond potential based on a Morse functional form.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last 3 coefficients for both styles are optional.  If not
specified, the global n, distance cutoff, and angle cutoff specified
in the pair\_style command are used.  If you wish to only override the
second or third optional parameter, you must also specify the preceding
optional parameters.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hbond_dreiding:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not support mixing. You must explicitly identify
each donor/acceptor type pair.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift
option for the energy of the interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant for
these pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands need to be
re\sphinxhyphen{}specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles tally a count of how many hydrogen bonding
interactions they calculate each timestep and the hbond energy.  These
quantities can be accessed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}}
command as a vector of values of length 2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To print these quantities to the log file (with a descriptive column
heading) the following commands could be included in an input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{hb}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hbond}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dreiding}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{lj}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{n\PYGZus{}hbond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}hb[1]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}number hbonds}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{E\PYGZus{}hbond}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}hb[2]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}hbond energy}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}E\PYGZus{}hbond}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hbond_dreiding:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
MOLECULE package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc page
for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}


\subsection{Default}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstylestrong{(Mayo)} Mayo, Olfason, Goddard III, J Phys Chem, 94, 8897\sphinxhyphen{}8909
(1990).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_hbond_dreiding:liu}}

\index{pair\_style hdnnp@\spxentry{pair\_style hdnnp}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style hdnnp command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:pair-style-hdnnp-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hdnnp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{value}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = short\sphinxhyphen{}range cutoff of HDNNP (maximum symmetry function cutoff radius)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keyword/value pairs may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{dir} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{showew} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{showewsum} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxew} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{resetew} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cflength} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{cfenergy}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
value depends on the preceding keyword:

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{dir} value = directory
    directory = Path to HDNNP configuration files
\sphinxstyleemphasis{showew} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{showewsum} value = summary
          summary = Write EW summary every this many timesteps (\sphinxstyleemphasis{0} turns summary off)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{maxew} value = threshold
      threshold = Maximum number of EWs allowed
\sphinxstyleemphasis{resetew} value = \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{no}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cflength} value = length
         length = Length unit conversion factor
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cfenergy} value = energy
         energy = Energy unit conversion factor
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hdnnp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.35}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{showew}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{showewsum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{maxew}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{resetew}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cflength}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.8897261328}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cfenergy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0367493254}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hdnnp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dir}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{./}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{showewsum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10000}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{S}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cu}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style adds an interaction based on the high\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional neural network
potential (HDNNP) method as presented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:behler-parrinello-2007}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Behler and Parrinello 2007)}}}}. HDNNPs are machine learning potentials which require
careful training of neural networks prior to application in MD simulations. The
pair style uses an interface to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{n2p2} library {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:singraber-behler-dellago-2019}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Singraber, Behler and
Dellago 2019)}}}} which is available on Github
\sphinxhref{https://github.com/CompPhysVienna/n2p2}{here}. Please see the \sphinxstyleemphasis{n2p2}
\sphinxhref{https://compphysvienna.github.io/n2p2/}{documentation} for further details.
\sphinxstyleemphasis{n2p2} (and hence this pair style) is compatible with neural network potentials
trained with its own tools {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:singraber-et-al-2019}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Singraber et al 2019)}}}}
and with \sphinxhref{https://www.uni-goettingen.de/de/560580.html}{RuNNer}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff} command with two asterisk wild\sphinxhyphen{}cards is used with this
pair style. Its additional arguments define the mapping of LAMMPS atom types to
n2p2 elements.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the above example LAMMPS types 1 and 2 are mapped to the elements “H” and “O”
in n2p2, respectively. Multiple types may map to the same element, or some types
may not be mapped at all. For example, if the LAMMPS simulation has four atom
types, the command

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
maps atom types 1 and 2 to the element “H”, type 3 to “O” and type 4 is not mapped
(indicated by NULL).  Atoms mapped to NULL are ignored by the HDNNP calculation,
i.e. they do not contribute in any way to the evaluation of HDNNP energies and forces.
This may be useful in a setup with {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid pair styles}}}}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The mandatory pair style argument \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} must match the short\sphinxhyphen{}range cutoff radius
of the HDNNP.  This corresponds to the maximum cutoff radius of all symmetry
functions (the atomic environment descriptors of HDNNPs) used.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The cutoff must be given in LAMMPS length units, even if the neural network
potential has been trained using a different unit system (see remarks about the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cflength} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cfenergy} keywords below for details).
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The numeric value may be slightly larger than the actual maximum symmetry
function cutoff radius (to account for rounding errors when converting units),
but must not be smaller.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{dir} keyword to specify the directory containing the HDNNP configuration
files. The directory must contain \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{input.nn}} with neural network and symmetry
function setup, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scaling.data}} with symmetry function scaling data and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{weights.???.data}} with weight parameters for each element.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{showew} can be used to turn on/off the display of extrapolation
warnings (EWs) which are issued whenever a symmetry function value is out of
bounds defined by minimum/maximum values in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scaling.data}}. An extrapolation
warning may look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{} NNP EXTRAPOLATION WARNING \PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{} STRUCTURE:      0 ATOM:       119 ELEMENT: Cu SYMFUNC:   32 TYPE:  3 VALUE:  2.166E\PYGZhy{}02 MIN:  2.003E\PYGZhy{}05 MAX:  1.756E\PYGZhy{}02}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
stating that the value 2.166E\sphinxhyphen{}02 of symmetry function 32 of type 3 (Narrow Angular symmetry function), element Cu (see the log file for a symmetry function listing) was out
of bounds (maximum in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scaling.data}} is 1.756E\sphinxhyphen{}02) for atom 119. Here, the
atom index refers to the LAMMPS tag (global index) and the structure index is
used to print out the MPI rank the atom belongs to.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{showew} keyword should only be set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} for debugging purposes.
Extrapolation warnings may add lots of overhead as they are communicated each
timestep. Also, if the simulation is run in a region where the HDNNP was not
correctly trained, lots of extrapolation warnings may clog log files and the
console. In a production run use \sphinxstyleemphasis{showewsum} instead.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{showewsum} can be used to get an overview of extrapolation warnings
occurring during an MD simulation. The argument specifies the interval at which
extrapolation warning summaries are displayed and logged. An EW summary may look
like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{} NNP EW SUMMARY \PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{}\PYGZsh{} TS:        100 EW         11 EWPERSTEP  1.100E\PYGZhy{}01}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, at timestep 100 the occurrence of 11 extrapolation warnings since the last
summary is reported, which corresponds to an EW rate of 0.11 per timestep.
Setting \sphinxstyleemphasis{showewsum} to 0 deactivates the EW summaries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A maximum number of allowed extrapolation warnings can be specified with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{maxew} keyword. If the number of EWs exceeds the \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxew} argument the
simulation is stopped. Note however that this is merely an approximate threshold
since the check is only performed at the end of each timestep and each MPI
process counts individually to minimize communication overhead.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{resetew} alters the behavior of the above mentioned \sphinxstyleemphasis{maxew}
threshold. If \sphinxstyleemphasis{resetew} is set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes} the threshold is applied on a
per\sphinxhyphen{}timestep basis and the internal EW counters are reset at the beginning of
each timestep. With \sphinxstyleemphasis{resetew} set to \sphinxstyleemphasis{no} the counters accumulate EWs along the
whole trajectory.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the training of a neural network potential has been performed with different
physical units for length and energy than those set in LAMMPS, it is still
possible to use the potential when the unit conversion factors are provided via
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{cflength} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cfenergy} keywords. If for example, the HDNNP was
parameterized with Bohr and Hartree training data and symmetry function
parameters (i.e. distances and energies in “input.nn” are given in Bohr and
Hartree) but LAMMPS is set to use \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units (Angstrom and eV) the correct
conversion factors are:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{cflength}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.8897261328}

\PYG{n}{cfenergy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0367493254}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, arguments of \sphinxstyleemphasis{cflength} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{cfenergy} are the multiplicative factors
required to convert lengths and energies given in LAMMPS units to respective
quantities in native HDNNP units (1 Angstrom = 1.8897261328 Bohr, 1 eV =
0.0367493254 Hartree).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not support mixing. The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command
should only be invoked with asterisk wild cards (see above).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not write information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.
Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer}
keywords.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hdnnp:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the ML\sphinxhyphen{}HDNNP package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hybrid:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{molecular}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{factor1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{factor2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{scaled}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{factor1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{factor2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style1,style2 = list of one or more pair styles and their arguments

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
factor1,factor2 = scale factors for pair styles, may be a variable

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hybrid:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/molecular}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled}
styles enable the use of multiple pair styles in one simulation.  With
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} style, exactly one pair style is assigned to each pair of
atom types.  With the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} styles, one
or more pair styles can be assigned to each pair of atom types.  With
the hybrid/molecular style, pair styles are assigned to either intra\sphinxhyphen{}
or inter\sphinxhyphen{}molecular interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The assignment of pair styles to type pairs is made via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.  The major difference between
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} styles is that the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} adds a scale factor for each sub\sphinxhyphen{}style contribution to
forces, energies and stresses.  Because of the added complexity, the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} style has more overhead and thus may be slower than
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/molecular} pair style accepts \sphinxstyleemphasis{only} two sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles: the
first is assigned to intra\sphinxhyphen{}molecular interactions (i.e. both atoms
have the same molecule ID), the second to inter\sphinxhyphen{}molecular interactions
(i.e. interacting atoms have different molecule IDs).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are two examples of hybrid simulations.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} style could
be used for a simulation of a metal droplet on a LJ surface.  The metal
atoms interact with each other via an \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam} potential, the surface atoms
interact with each other via a \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut} potential, and the metal/surface
interaction is also computed via a \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut} potential.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} style could be used as in the second example above,
where multiple potentials are superimposed in an additive fashion to
compute the interaction between atoms.  In this example, using \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{coul/long} together gives the same result as if the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long} potential were used by itself.  In this case, it
would be more efficient to use the single combined potential, but in
general any combination of pair potentials can be used together in to
produce an interaction that is not encoded in any single pair\_style
file, e.g. adding Coulombic forces between granular particles.  Another
limitation of using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} variant, that it does not generate
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut} parameters for mixed atom types from a mixing rule due to
restrictions discussed below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} style is used instead of \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay},
contributions from sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles are weighted by their scale factors, which
may be fractional or even negative.  Furthermore the scale factors may
be variables that may change during a simulation.  This enables
switching smoothly between two different pair styles or two different
parameter sets during a run in a similar fashion as could be done
with {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_alchemy::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix alchemy}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All pair styles that will be used are listed as “sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles” following
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} keyword, in any order.  In case of the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} pair style, each sub\sphinxhyphen{}style is prefixed with a scale
factor.  The scale factor is either a floating point number or an equal
style (or equivalent) variable.  Each sub\sphinxhyphen{}style’s name is followed by
its usual arguments, as illustrated in the examples above.  See the doc
pages of the individual pair styles for a listing and explanation of the
appropriate arguments for them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that an individual pair style can be used multiple times as a
sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.  For efficiency reasons this should only be done if your
model requires it.  E.g. if you have different regions of Si and C atoms
and wish to use a Tersoff potential for pure Si for one set of atoms,
and a Tersoff potential for pure C for the other set (presumably with
some third potential for Si\sphinxhyphen{}C interactions), then the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff} could be listed twice.  But if you just want to use a
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones or other pairwise potential for several different atom
type pairs in your model, then you should just list the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style once
and use the pair\_coeff command to assign parameters for the different
type pairs.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
There is one exception to this option to list an individual
pair style multiple times: GPU\sphinxhyphen{}enabled pair styles in the GPU package.
This is because the GPU package currently assumes that only one
instance of a pair style is being used.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the pair\_coeff commands, the name of a pair style must be added
after the I,J type specification, with the remaining coefficients
being those appropriate to that style.  If the pair style is used
multiple times in the pair\_style command, then an additional numeric
argument must also be specified which is a number from 1 to M where M
is the number of times the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style was listed in the pair style
command.  The extra number indicates which instance of the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style
these coefficients apply to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, consider a simulation with 3 atom types: types 1 and 2
are Ni atoms, type 3 are LJ atoms with charges.  The following
commands would set up a hybrid simulation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eam}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{alloy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{eam}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{alloy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nialhjea}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ni}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.3}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example of using the same pair style multiple times, consider a
simulation with 2 atom types.  Type 1 is Si, type 2 is C.  The
following commands would model the Si atoms with Tersoff, the C atoms
with Tersoff, and the cross\sphinxhyphen{}interactions with Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is not recommended to read pair coefficients for a hybrid style from a “Pair Coeffs”
or “PairIJ Coeffs” section of a data file via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command,
since those sections expect a fixed number of lines, either one line per atom type or
one line pair pair of atom types, respectively.  When reading from a data file, the
lines of the “Pair Coeffs” and “PairIJ Coeffs” are changed in the same way as the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_coeff}
command, i.e. the name of the pair style to which the parameters apply must follow the
atom type (or atom types), e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Pair Coeffs

1 lj/cut/coul/cut 1.0 1.0
...

PairIJ Coeffs

1 1 lj/cut/coul/cut 1.0 1.0
...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the pair\_coeff command for some potentials such as
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style eam/alloy}}}} includes a mapping specification
of elements to all atom types, which in the hybrid case, can include
atom types not assigned to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{eam/alloy} potential.  The NULL
keyword is used by many such potentials (eam/alloy, Tersoff, AIREBO,
etc), to denote an atom type that will be assigned to a different
sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} style, each atom type pair I,J is assigned to exactly
one sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.  Just as with a simulation using a single pair style,
if you specify the same atom type pair in a second pair\_coeff command,
the previous assignment will be overwritten.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} styles, each atom type pair
I,J can be assigned to one or more sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles.  If you specify the same
atom type pair in a second pair\_coeff command with a new sub\sphinxhyphen{}style, then
the second sub\sphinxhyphen{}style is added to the list of potentials that will be
calculated for two interacting atoms of those types.  If you specify the
same atom type pair in a second pair\_coeff command with a sub\sphinxhyphen{}style that
has already been defined for that pair of atoms, then the new pair
coefficients simply override the previous ones, as in the normal usage
of the pair\_coeff command.  E.g. these two sets of commands are the
same:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.8}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms types via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as described above, or in the
“Pair Coeffs” or “PairIJ Coeffs” section of the data file read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command, or by mixing as described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For all of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} styles,
every atom type pair I,J (where I \textless{}= J) must be assigned to at least one
sub\sphinxhyphen{}style via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the
examples above, or in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}, or by mixing as described below.  Also all sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles
must be used at least once in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With hybrid pair styles the use of mixing to generate pair
coefficients is significantly limited compared to the individual pair
styles.  LAMMPS \sphinxstylestrong{never} performs mixing of parameters from
different sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles, \sphinxstylestrong{even} if they use the same type of
coefficients, e.g. contain a Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential variant.  Those
parameters must be provided explicitly.  Also for \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} mixing is \sphinxstylestrong{only} performed for pairs of atom
types for which only a single pair style is assigned.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus it is strongly recommended to provide all mixed terms
explicitly.  For non\sphinxhyphen{}hybrid styles those could be generated and
written out using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{write_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{write\_coeff command}}}} and
then edited as needed to comply with the requirements for hybrid
styles as explained above.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want there to be no interactions between a particular pair of
atom types, you have 3 choices.  You can assign the pair of atom types
to some sub\sphinxhyphen{}style and use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude type}}}}
command.  You can assign it to some sub\sphinxhyphen{}style and set the coefficients
so that there is effectively no interaction (e.g. epsilon = 0.0 in a LJ
potential).  Or, for \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled}
simulations, you can use this form of the pair\_coeff command in your
input script or the “PairIJ Coeffs” section of your data file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{none}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
or this form in the “Pair Coeffs” section of the data file:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
3  none
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If an assignment to \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} is made in a simulation with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} pair style, it wipes out all
previous assignments of that pair of atom types to sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that you may need to use an {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style}}}} hybrid
command in your input script, if atoms in the simulation will need
attributes from several atom styles, due to using multiple pair
styles with different requirements.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Different force fields (e.g. CHARMM vs. AMBER) may have different rules
for applying exclusions or weights that change the strength of pairwise
non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions between pairs of atoms that are also 1\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3,
and 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 neighbors in the molecular bond topology. This is normally a
global setting defined the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command.
However, different weights can be assigned to different hybrid
sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify special}}}} command.
This allows multiple force fields to be used in a model of a hybrid
system, however, there is no consistent approach to determine parameters
automatically for the interactions \sphinxstylestrong{between} atoms of the two force
fields, thus this approach this is only recommended when particles
described by the different force fields do not mix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example for combining CHARMM and AMBER: The global \sphinxstyleemphasis{amber}
setting sets the 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 interactions to non\sphinxhyphen{}zero scaling factors and
then overrides them with 0.0 only for CHARMM:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{amber}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{charmm}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{charmm}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This input achieves the same effect:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{charmm}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.83333333}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{charmm}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example for combining Tersoff with OPLS/AA based on
a data file that defines bonds for all atoms where \sphinxhyphen{} for the
Tersoff part of the system \sphinxhyphen{} the force constants for the bonded
interactions have been set to 0. Note the global settings are
effectively \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/coul 0.0 0.0 0.5} as required for OPLS/AA:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{special\PYGZus{}bonds}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e\PYGZhy{}20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1e\PYGZhy{}20}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{special}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For use with the various {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_tally::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute */tally}}}}
computes, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify compute/tally}}}}
command can be used to selectively turn off processing of
the compute tally styles, for example, if those pair styles
(e.g. many\sphinxhyphen{}body styles) do not support this feature.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} page for details on
the specific syntax, requirements and restrictions.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential energy contribution to the overall system due to an
individual sub\sphinxhyphen{}style can be accessed and output via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute
pair}}}} command.  Note that in the case of pair style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} this is the \sphinxstylestrong{unscaled} potential energy of the
selected sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Several of the potentials defined via the pair\_style command in
LAMMPS are really many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials, such as Tersoff, AIREBO, MEAM,
ReaxFF, etc.  The way to think about using these potentials in a
hybrid setting is as follows.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A subset of atom types is assigned to the many\sphinxhyphen{}body potential with a
single {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command, using “* *” to include
all types and the NULL keywords described above to exclude specific
types not assigned to that potential.  If types 1,3,4 were assigned in
that way (but not type 2), this means that all many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions
between all atoms of types 1,3,4 will be computed by that potential.
Pair\_style hybrid allows interactions between type pairs 2\sphinxhyphen{}2, 1\sphinxhyphen{}2,
2\sphinxhyphen{}3, 2\sphinxhyphen{}4 to be specified for computation by other pair styles.  You
could even add a second interaction for 1\sphinxhyphen{}1 to be computed by another
pair style, assuming pair\_style hybrid/overlay is used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
But you should not, as a general rule, attempt to exclude the many\sphinxhyphen{}body
interactions for some subset of the type pairs within the set of 1,3,4
interactions, e.g. exclude 1\sphinxhyphen{}1 or 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 interactions.  That is not
conceptually well\sphinxhyphen{}defined for many\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions, since the
potential will typically calculate energies and foces for small groups
of atoms, e.g. 3 or 4 atoms, using the neighbor lists of the atoms to
find the additional atoms in the group.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, you can still use the pair\_coeff none setting or the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{neigh_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{neigh\_modify exclude}}}} command to exclude certain
type pairs from the neighbor list that will be passed to a many\sphinxhyphen{}body
sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.  This will alter the calculations made by a many\sphinxhyphen{}body
potential beyond the specific pairs, since it builds its list of 3\sphinxhyphen{}body,
4\sphinxhyphen{}body, etc interactions from the pair lists.  You will need to think
\sphinxstylestrong{carefully} as to whether excluding such pairs produces a physically
meaningful result for your model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For example, imagine you have two atom types in your model, type 1 for
atoms in one surface, and type 2 for atoms in the other, and you wish
to use a Tersoff potential to compute interactions within each
surface, but not between the surfaces.  Then either of these two command
sequences would implement that model:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{none}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{neigh\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exclude}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{type}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Either way, only neighbor lists with 1\sphinxhyphen{}1 or 2\sphinxhyphen{}2 interactions would be
passed to the Tersoff potential, which means it would compute no
3\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions containing both type 1 and 2 atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is another example to use 2 many\sphinxhyphen{}body potentials together in an
overlapping manner using hybrid/overlay.  Imagine you have CNT (C atoms)
on a Si surface.  You want to use Tersoff for Si/Si and Si/C
interactions, and AIREBO for C/C interactions.  Si atoms are type 1; C
atoms are type 2.  Something like this will work:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{airebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.tersoff.custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{airebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CH.airebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that to prevent the Tersoff potential from computing C/C
interactions, you would need to \sphinxstylestrong{modify} the SiC.tersoff potential
file to turn off C/C interaction, i.e. by setting the appropriate
coefficients to 0.0.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} styles
delegate computation to the individual sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles, the suffix
versions of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} styles are used to
propagate the corresponding suffix to all sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles, if those
versions exist. Otherwise the non\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated version will be used.
The individual accelerated sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles are part of the GPU, KOKKOS,
INTEL, OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only
enabled if LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hybrid:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Any pair potential settings made via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command are passed along to all
sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles of the hybrid potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, if the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style assigned to I,I and
J,J is the same, and if the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style allows for mixing, then the
coefficients for I,J can be mixed.  This means you do not have to
specify a pair\_coeff command for I,J since the I,J type pair will be
assigned automatically to the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style defined for both I,I and J,J and
its coefficients generated by the mixing rule used by that sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} style, there is an
additional requirement that both the I,I and J,J pairs are assigned to a
single sub\sphinxhyphen{}style.  If this requirement is not met, no I,J coeffs will be
generated, even if the sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles support mixing, and I,J pair
coefficients must be explicitly defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} command for
details of mixing rules.  See the See the page for the sub\sphinxhyphen{}style to
see if allows for mixing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The hybrid pair styles supports the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options for an I,J pair interaction, if the
associated sub\sphinxhyphen{}style supports it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the hybrid pair styles, the list of sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles and their respective
settings are written to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}} command does not need to specified in an
input script that reads a restart file.  However, the coefficient
information is not stored in the restart file.  The same is true for
{\hyperref[\detokenize{write_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data files}}}}.  Thus, pair\_coeff commands need to be
re\sphinxhyphen{}specified in the restart input script.  For pair style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} also the names of any variables used as scale factors
are restored, but not the variables themselves, so those may need to be
redefined when continuing from a restart.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles support the use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command, if
their sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles do.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_hybrid:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using a long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic solver (via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command) with a hybrid pair\_style,
one or more sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles will be of the “long” variety,
e.g. \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/cut/coul/long} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{buck/coul/long}.  You must ensure that the
short\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic cutoff used by each of these long pair styles is
the same or else LAMMPS will generate an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/scaled} currently only works for non\sphinxhyphen{}accelerated
pair styles and pair styles from the OPT package.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/molecular} is not compatible with manybody potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When using pair styles from the GPU package they must not be listed
multiple times.  LAMMPS will detect this and abort.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ilp/graphene/hbn} style computes the registry\sphinxhyphen{}dependent interlayer
potential (ILP) potential as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:leven1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Leven1)}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:leven2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Leven2)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:maaravi2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Maaravi)}}}}.
The normals are calculated in the way as described
in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:kolmogorov2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kolmogorov)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E  = & \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} V_{ij} \\
V_{ij}  = & {\rm Tap}(r_{ij})\left \{ e^{-\alpha (r_{ij}/\beta -1)}
             \left [ \epsilon + f(\rho_{ij}) + f(\rho_{ji})\right ] -
              \frac{1}{1+e^{-d\left [ \left ( r_{ij}/\left (s_R \cdot r^{eff} \right ) \right )-1 \right ]}}
              \cdot \frac{C_6}{r^6_{ij}} \right \}\\
\rho_{ij}^2 = & r_{ij}^2 - ({\bf r}_{ij} \cdot {\bf n}_i)^2 \\
\rho_{ji}^2  = & r_{ij}^2 - ({\bf r}_{ij} \cdot {\bf n}_j)^2 \\
f(\rho)  = &  C e^{ -( \rho / \delta )^2 } \\
{\rm Tap}(r_{ij})  = & 20\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^7 -
                        70\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^6 +
                        84\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^5 -
                        35\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^4 + 1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where \(\mathrm{Tap}(r_{ij})\) is the taper function which provides
a continuous cutoff (up to third derivative) for interatomic separations
larger than \(r_c\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:maaravi2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Maaravi)}}}}. The definitions of
each parameter in the above equation can be found in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:leven1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Leven1)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:maaravi2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Maaravi)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is important to include all the pairs to build the neighbor list for
calculating the normals.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential (ILP) is intended for interlayer interactions between two
different layers of graphene, hexagonal boron nitride (h\sphinxhyphen{}BN) and their hetero\sphinxhyphen{}junction.
To perform a realistic simulation, this potential must be used in combination with
intralayer potential, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_airebo::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{AIREBO}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Tersoff}}}} potential.
To keep the intralayer properties unaffected, the interlayer interaction
within the same layers should be avoided. Hence, each atom has to have a layer
identifier such that atoms residing on the same layer interact via the
appropriate intralayer potential and atoms residing on different layers
interact via the ILP. Here, the molecule id is chosen as the layer identifier,
thus a data file with the “full” atom style is required to use this potential.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter file (e.g. BNCH.ILP), is intended for use with \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal}
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, with energies in meV. Two additional parameters,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{S}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcut} are included in the parameter file. \sphinxstyleemphasis{S} is designed to
facilitate scaling of energies. \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcut} is designed to build the neighbor
list for calculating the normals for each atom pair.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters presented in the parameter file (e.g. BNCH.ILP),
are fitted with taper function by setting the cutoff equal to 16.0
Angstrom.  Using different cutoff or taper function should be careful.
The parameters for atoms pairs between Boron and Nitrogen are fitted with
a screened Coulomb interaction {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coul_shield::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{coul/shield}}}}. Therefore,
to simulated the properties of h\sphinxhyphen{}BN correctly, this potential must be used in
combination with the pair style {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coul_shield::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{coul/shield}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Four new sets of parameters of ILP for 2D layered Materials with bilayer and
bulk configurations are presented in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:ouyang1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang1)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:ouyang2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang2)}}}}, respectively.
These parameters provide a good description in both short\sphinxhyphen{} and long\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction regimes.
While the old ILP parameters published in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:leven2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Leven2)}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:maaravi2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Maaravi)}}}} are only suitable for long\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction
regime. This feature is essential for simulations in high pressure
regime (i.e., the interlayer distance is smaller than the equilibrium
distance). The benchmark tests and comparison of these parameters can
be found in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:ouyang1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang1)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:ouyang2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang2)}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential must be used in combination with hybrid/overlay.
Other interactions can be set to zero using pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style tallies a breakdown of the total interlayer potential
energy into sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories, which can be accessed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}} command as a vector of values of length 2.
The 2 values correspond to the following sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{E\_vdW} = vdW (attractive) energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{E\_Rep} = Repulsive energy

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To print these quantities to the log file (with descriptive column
headings) the following commands could be included in an input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ilp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{graphene}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{hbn}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Evdw}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[1]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Erep}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[2]}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}Erep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}Evdw}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the pair\_modify mix, shift, table, and
tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write their information to binary restart
files, since it is stored in potential files. Thus, you need to
re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the INTERLAYER package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the newton setting to be \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} for pair
interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The BNCH.ILP potential file provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials
directory) are parameterized for \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units.  You can use this
potential with any LAMMPS units, but you would need to create your own
custom BNCH.ILP potential file with coefficients listed in the appropriate
units, if your simulation does not use \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_ilp_tmd:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 17Feb2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{ilp/tmd} style computes the registry\sphinxhyphen{}dependent interlayer
potential (ILP) potential for transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD)
as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_tmd:ouyang7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang7)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_tmd:jiang}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Jiang)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E  = & \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} V_{ij} \\
V_{ij}  = & {\rm Tap}(r_{ij})\left \{ e^{-\alpha (r_{ij}/\beta -1)}
             \left [ \epsilon + f(\rho_{ij}) + f(\rho_{ji})\right ] -
              \frac{1}{1+e^{-d\left [ \left ( r_{ij}/\left (s_R \cdot r^{eff} \right ) \right )-1 \right ]}}
              \cdot \frac{C_6}{r^6_{ij}} \right \}\\
\rho_{ij}^2 = & r_{ij}^2 - ({\bf r}_{ij} \cdot {\bf n}_i)^2 \\
\rho_{ji}^2  = & r_{ij}^2 - ({\bf r}_{ij} \cdot {\bf n}_j)^2 \\
f(\rho)  = &  C e^{ -( \rho / \delta )^2 } \\
{\rm Tap}(r_{ij})  = & 20\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^7 -
                        70\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^6 +
                        84\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^5 -
                        35\left ( \frac{r_{ij}}{R_{cut}} \right )^4 + 1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where \(\mathrm{Tap}(r_{ij})\) is the taper function which provides
a continuous cutoff (up to third derivative) for interatomic separations
larger than \(r_c\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_graphene_hbn::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style ilp\_graphene\_hbn}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is important to include all the pairs to build the neighbor list for
calculating the normals.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Since each MX2 (M = Mo, W and X = S, Se Te) layer contains two
sub\sphinxhyphen{}layers of X atoms and one sub\sphinxhyphen{}layer of M atoms, the definition of the
normal vectors used for graphene and h\sphinxhyphen{}BN is no longer valid for TMDs.
In {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_tmd:ouyang7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang7)}}}}, a new definition is proposed, where for
each atom \sphinxtitleref{i}, its six nearest neighboring atoms belonging to the same
sub\sphinxhyphen{}layer are chosen to define the normal vector \sphinxtitleref{\{bf n\}\_i}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter file (e.g. TMD.ILP), is intended for use with \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal}
{\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}, with energies in meV. Two additional parameters,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{S}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcut} are included in the parameter file. \sphinxstyleemphasis{S} is designed to
facilitate scaling of energies. \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcut} is designed to build the neighbor
list for calculating the normals for each atom pair.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters presented in the parameter file (e.g. TMD.ILP),
are fitted with taper function by setting the cutoff equal to 16.0
Angstrom.  Using different cutoff or taper function should be careful.
These parameters provide a good description in both short\sphinxhyphen{} and long\sphinxhyphen{}range
interaction regimes. This feature is essential for simulations in high pressure
regime (i.e., the interlayer distance is smaller than the equilibrium
distance). The benchmark tests and comparison of these parameters can
be found in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_ilp_tmd:ouyang7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang7)}}}}.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential must be used in combination with hybrid/overlay.
Other interactions can be set to zero using pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{none}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style tallies a breakdown of the total interlayer potential
energy into sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories, which can be accessed via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_pair::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute pair}}}} command as a vector of values of length 2.
The 2 values correspond to the following sub\sphinxhyphen{}categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{E\_vdW} = vdW (attractive) energy

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{E\_Rep} = Repulsive energy

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
To print these quantities to the log file (with descriptive column
headings) the following commands could be included in an input script:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{compute }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ilp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tmd}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Evdw}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[1]}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{Erep}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c\PYGZus{}0[2]}
\PYG{k}{thermo\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{custom}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{step}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{temp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}Erep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}Evdw}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_ilp_tmd:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the pair\_modify mix, shift, table, and
tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write their information to binary restart
files, since it is stored in potential files. Thus, you need to
re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_ilp_tmd:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the INTERLAYER package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the newton setting to be \sphinxstyleemphasis{on} for pair
interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The TMD.ILP potential file provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials
directory) are parameterized for \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units.  You can use this
potential with any LAMMPS units, but you would need to create your own
custom TMD.ILP potential file with coefficients listed in the appropriate
units, if your simulation does not use \sphinxstyleemphasis{metal} units.

{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_none::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_none}}}},
