\section{pair\_style lj/relres command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:pair-style-lj-relres-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/relres/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{relres}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rsi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rsi = inner switching cutoff between the fine\sphinxhyphen{}grained and coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained potentials (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rso = outer switching cutoff between the fine\sphinxhyphen{}grained and coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained potentials (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rci = inner cutoff beyond which the force smoothing for all interactions is applied (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rco = outer cutoff for all interactions (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{relres}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{5.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/relres} computes a LJ interaction using the Relative
Resolution (RelRes) framework which applies a fine\sphinxhyphen{}grained (FG)
potential between near neighbors and a coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained (CG) potential
between far neighbors {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:chaimovich1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chaimovich1)}}}}. This approach
can improve the computational efficiency by almost an order of
magnitude, while maintaining the correct static and dynamic behavior of
a reference system {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:chaimovich2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chaimovich2)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \left\{\begin{array}{lr}
     4 \epsilon^{\scriptscriptstyle FG} \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma^{FG}}{r}\right)^{12} - \left(\frac{\sigma^{FG}}{r}\right)^6 \right]-\Gamma_{si}, & \quad\mathrm{if}\quad  r< r_{si}, \\
     \sum_{m=0}^{4} \gamma_{sm}\left(r-r_{si}\right)^m-\Gamma_{so} ,   & \quad\mathrm{if}\quad  r_{si}\leq r< r_{so}, \\
     4 \epsilon^{\scriptscriptstyle CG} \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma^{CG}}{r}\right)^{12} -     \left(\frac{\sigma^{CG}}{r}\right)^6 \right]-\Gamma_c, &  \quad\mathrm{if}\quad  r_{so}\leq r<r_{ci}, \\
     \sum_{m=0}^{4} \gamma_{cm}\left(r-r_{ci}\right)^m -\Gamma_c, & \quad\mathrm{if}\quad  r_{ci}\leq r< r_{co}, \\
     0, & \quad\mathrm{if}\quad  r\geq r_{co}.\end{array}\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The FG parameters of the LJ potential (\(\epsilon^{FG}\) and
\(\sigma^{FG}\)) are applied up to the inner switching cutoff,
\(r_{si}\), while the CG parameters of the LJ potential
(\(\epsilon^{CG}\) and \(\sigma^{CG}\)) are applied beyond the
outer switching cutoff, \(r_{so}\). Between \(r_{si}\) and
\(r_{so}\) a polynomial smoothing function is applied so that the
force and its derivative are continuous between the FG and CG
potentials.  An analogous smoothing function is applied between the
inner and outer cutoffs (\(r_{ci}\) and \(r_{co}\)).
The offsets \(\Gamma_{si}\), \(\Gamma_{so}\) and
\(\Gamma_{c}\) ensure the continuity of the energy over the entire
domain.  The corresponding polynomial coefficients \(\gamma_{sm}\)
and \(\gamma_{cm}\), as well as the offsets are automatically
computed by LAMMPS.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy and force resulting from this methodology can be plotted via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atom types
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples above,
or in the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands, or by
mixing as will be described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon^{FG}\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma^{FG}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon^{CG}\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma^{CG}\) (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Additional parameters can be defined to specify different
\(r_{si}\), \(r_{so}\), \(r_{ci}\), \(r_{co}\) for
a particular set of atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{si}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{so}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{ci}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{co}\) (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These parameters are optional, and they are used to override the global
cutoffs as defined in the pair\_style command.  If not specified, the
global values for \(r_{si}\), \(r_{so}\), \(r_{ci}\), and
\(r_{co}\) are used.  If this override option is employed, all four
arguments must be specified.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are some guidelines for using the pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/relres} command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In general, RelRes focuses on the speedup of pairwise interactions between
all LJ sites. Importantly, it works with any settings and flags (e.g.,
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} settings and {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}}
flags) that can be used in a molecular simulation with the
conventional LJ potential. In particular, all intramolecular topology
with its energetics (i.e., bonds, angles, etc.) remains unaltered.

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the most basic level in the RelRes framework, all sites are mapped into
clusters. Each cluster is just a collection of sites bonded together (the
bonds themselves are not part of the cluster). In general, a molecule may
be comprised of several clusters, and preferably, no two sites in a cluster
are separated by more than two bonds. There are two categories of sites in
RelRes: “hybrid” sites embody both FG and CG models, while “ordinary” sites
embody just FG characteristics with no CG features. A given cluster has
a single hybrid site (typically its central site) and several ordinary sites
(typically its peripheral sites). Notice that while clusters are necessary
for the RelRes parameterization (discussed below), they are not actually
defined in LAMMPS. Besides, the total number of sites in the cluster are
called the “mapping ratio”, and this substantially impacts the computational
efficiency of RelRes: For a mapping ratio of 3, the efficiency factor is
around 4, and for a mapping ratio of 5, the efficiency factor is around 5
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:chaimovich2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chaimovich2)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The flexibility of LAMMPS allows placing any values for the LJ
parameters in the input script. However, here are the optimal
recommendations for the RelRes parameters, which yield the correct
structural and thermal behavior in a system of interest
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:chaimovich1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chaimovich1)}}}}.  One must first assign a complete set of
parameters for the FG interactions that are applicable to all atom types.
Regarding the parameters for the CG interactions, the rules rely on the
site category (if it is a hybrid or an ordinary site). For atom types of
ordinary sites, \(\epsilon^{CG}\) must be set to 0 (zero) while the
specific value of \(\sigma^{CG}\) is irrelevant. For atom types of
hybrid sites, the CG parameters should be generally calculated using the
following equations:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma_I^{CG}=\frac{\left((\sum_{\alpha\in A}\sqrt{\epsilon_\alpha^{FG}\left(\sigma_\alpha^{FG}\right)^{12}}\right)^{1/2}}{\left((\sum_{\alpha\in A}\sqrt{\epsilon_\alpha^{FG}\left(\sigma_\alpha^{FG}\right)^6}\right)^{1/3}}
\quad\mathrm{and}\quad
\epsilon_I^{CG}=\frac{\left((\sum_{\alpha\in A}\sqrt{\epsilon_\alpha^{FG}\left(\sigma_\alpha^{FG}\right)^6}\right)^4}{\left((\sum_{\alpha\in A}\sqrt{\epsilon_\alpha^{FG}\left(\sigma_\alpha^{FG}\right)^{12}}\right)^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(I\) is an atom type of a hybrid site of a particular cluster
\(A\), and corresponding with this cluster, the summation proceeds over
all of its sites \(\alpha\).  These equations are derived from the
monopole term in the underlying Taylor series, and they are indeed relevant
only if geometric mixing is applicable for the FG model; if this is not the
case, Ref. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:chaimovich2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chaimovich2)}}}} discusses the alternative
formula, and in such a situation, the pair\_coeff command should be explicitly
used for all combinations of atom types \(I\;!=J\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The switching distance (the midpoint between inner and outer switching
cutoffs) is another crucial factor in RelRes: decreasing it improves the
computational efficiency, yet if it is too small, the molecular simulations
may not capture the system behavior correctly.  As a rule of thumb,
the switching distance should be approximately \(\,\sim\! 1.5\sigma\)
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:chaimovich1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chaimovich1)}}}}; recommendations can be found in
Ref. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:chaimovich2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Chaimovich2)}}}}.
Regarding the switching smoothing zone, \(\,\sim\!0.1\sigma\) is
recommended; if desired, smoothing can be eliminated by setting
the inner switching cutoff, \(r_{si}\), equal to the outer
switching cutoff, \(r_{so}\) (the same is true for the other cutoffs
\(r_{ci}\) and \(r_{co}\)).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine that in your system, a molecule is comprised just
of one cluster such that one atom type (\#1) is associated with
its hybrid site, and another atom type (\#2) is associated with its ordinary
sites (in total, there are 2 atom types). If geometric mixing is applicable,
the following commands should be used:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{relres}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rsi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}CG1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}CG1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a more complex situation, there may be two distinct clusters in a system
(these two clusters may be on same molecule or on different molecules),
each with its own switching cutoffs.  If there are still two atom types
in each cluster as in the earlier example, the commands should be:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{relres}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rsi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}CG1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}CG1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rsi1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{       }\PYG{n}{Rsi1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}CG3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}CG3}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{         }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this example, the switching cutoffs for the first cluster (atom types 1
and 2) is defined explicitly in the pair\_coeff command which overrides the
global values, while the second cluster (atom types 3 and 4) uses the global
definition from the pair\_style command. The emphasis here is that the atom
types that belong to a specific cluster should have the same switching/cutoff
arguments.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the case that geometric mixing is not applicable, for simulating the
system from the previous example, we recommend using the following commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{relres}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rsi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}CG1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}CG1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Rsi1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Rso1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG12}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG12}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{Rsi1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Rso1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}CG13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}CG13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rsi13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG14}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG14}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{Rsi13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG2}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG2}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{Rsi1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Rso1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG23}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG23}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{Rsi13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG24}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG24}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{Rsi13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rso13}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rci}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rco}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG3}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG3}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}CG3}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}CG3}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG34}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG34}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{epsilon\PYGZus{}FG4}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{sigma\PYGZus{}FG4}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{          }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}modify}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Notice that the CG parameters are mixed only for interactions between atom
types associated with hybrid sites, and that the cutoffs are
mixed on the cluster basis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
More examples can be found in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{examples/relres} folder.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_relres:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs \(I,\:J\) with \(I\;!=J\), the
\(\epsilon^{FG}\), \(\sigma^{FG}\), \(\epsilon^{CG}\),
\(\sigma^{CG}\), \(r_{si}\), \(r_{so}\), \(r_{ci}\),
and \(r_{co}\) parameters for this pair style can be mixed, if
not defined explicitly. All parameters are mixed according to the
pair\_modify mix option.  The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric},
and it is recommended to use with this \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/relres} style.  See the
“pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style supports the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift
option for the energy of the pair interaction. It is recommended to set
this option to \sphinxstyleemphasis{yes}.  Otherwise, the offset \(\Gamma_{c}\)
is set to zero. Constants \(\Gamma_{si}\) and \(\Gamma_{so}\) are
not impacted by this option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant
for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure, since the energy of the pair interaction is smoothed to 0.0
at the cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need to be
specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\section{pair\_style lj/smooth command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:pair-style-lj-smooth-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/smooth/gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/smooth/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{smooth}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rin}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Rc}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rin = inner cutoff beyond which force smoothing will be applied (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rc = outer cutoff for lj/smooth interactions (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{smooth}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/smooth} computes a LJ interaction with a force smoothing
applied between the inner and outer cutoff.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & =  4 \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
                      \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]
                      \qquad r < r_{in} \\
F & =  C_1 + C_2 (r - r_{in}) + C_3 (r - r_{in})^2 + C_4 (r - r_{in})^3
                    \qquad r_{in} < r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The polynomial coefficients C1, C2, C3, C4 are computed by LAMMPS to
cause the force to vary smoothly from the inner cutoff \(r_{in}\) to the
outer cutoff \(r_c\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
At the inner cutoff the force and its first derivative
will match the non\sphinxhyphen{}smoothed LJ formula.  At the outer cutoff the force
and its first derivative will be 0.0.  The inner cutoff cannot be 0.0.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
this force smoothing causes the energy to be discontinuous both
in its values and first derivative.  This can lead to poor energy
conservation and may require the use of a thermostat.  Plot the energy
and force resulting from this formula via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command to see the effect.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{in}\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_c\) (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last 2 coefficients are optional inner and outer cutoffs.  If not
specified, the global values for \(r_{in}\) and \(r_c\) are used.

\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the epsilon, sigma, Rin
coefficients and the cutoff distance for this pair style can be mixed.
Rin is a cutoff value and is mixed like the cutoff.  The other
coefficients are mixed according to the pair\_modify mix option.  The
default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See the “pair\_modify” command for
details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style supports the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift
option for the energy of the pair interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar

for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure, since the energy of the pair interaction is smoothed to 0.0
at the cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth_linear:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/smooth/linear} computes a truncated and force\sphinxhyphen{}shifted LJ
interaction (aka Shifted Force Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones) that combines the
standard 12/6 Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones function and subtracts a linear term based
on the cutoff distance, so that both, the potential and the force, go
continuously to zero at the cutoff \(r_c\) {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_smooth_linear:toxvaerd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Toxvaerd)}}}}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\phi\left(r\right) & =  4 \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
                    \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right] \\
E\left(r\right) & =  \phi\left(r\right)  - \phi\left(r_c\right) - \left(r - r_c\right) \left.\frac{d\phi}{d r} \right|_{r=r_c}       \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional. If not specified, the global
LJ cutoff specified in the pair\_style command is used.

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{0.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_switch3_coulgauss_long:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/switch3/coulgauss} style evaluates the LJ
vdW potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = 4\epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12}-\left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{6} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{mm3/switch3/coulgauss/long} style evaluates the MM3
vdW potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_mm3:mm3-allinger1989}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Allinger)}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & = \epsilon_{ij} \left[ -2.25 \left(\frac{r_{v,ij}}{r_{ij}}\right)^6 + 1.84(10)^5 \exp\left[-12.0 r_{ij}/r_{v,ij}\right] \right] S_3(r_{ij}) \\
r_{v,ij} & =  r_{v,i} + r_{v,j} \\
\epsilon_{ij} & = \sqrt{\epsilon_i \epsilon_j}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Both potentials go smoothly to zero at the cutoff r\_c as defined by the
switching function
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}S_3(r) = \left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll}
                    1 & \quad\mathrm{if}\quad r < r_\mathrm{c} - w \\
                    3x^2 - 2x^3 & \quad\mathrm{if}\quad r < r_\mathrm{c} \quad\mathrm{with\quad} x=\frac{r_\mathrm{c} - r}{w} \\
                    0 & \quad\mathrm{if}\quad r >= r_\mathrm{c}
                \end{array} \right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where w is the width defined in the arguments. This potential
is combined with Coulomb interaction between Gaussian charge densities:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \frac{q_i q_j \mathrm{erf}\left( r/\sqrt{\gamma_1^2+\gamma_2^2} \right) }{\epsilon r_{ij}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(q_i\) and \(q_j\) are the charges on the two atoms,
\(\epsilon\) is the dielectric constant which can be set by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dielectric::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dielectric}}}} command, \(\gamma_i\) and
\(\gamma_j\) are the widths of the Gaussian charge distribution and
erf() is the error\sphinxhyphen{}function.  This style has to be used in conjunction
with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command

\sphinxAtStartPar
If one cutoff is specified it is used for both the vdW and Coulomb
terms.  If two cutoffs are specified, the first is used as the cutoff
for the vdW terms, and the second is the cutoff for the Coulombic term.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\gamma\) (distance)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lj_switch3_coulgauss_long:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the epsilon and sigma coefficients
and cutoff distance for all of the lj/long pair styles can be mixed.
The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See the “pair\_modify” command
for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Shifting the potential energy is not necessary because the switching
function ensures that the potential is zero at the cut\sphinxhyphen{}off.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table and
options since they can tabulate the short\sphinxhyphen{}range portion of the
long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thes pair styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding a long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail correction to the
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones portion of the energy and pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spline}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{500}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{density}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{local}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{density}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{benzene\PYGZus{}water.localdensity.table}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_local_density:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The local density (LD) potential is a mean\sphinxhyphen{}field manybody potential,
and, in some way, a generalization of embedded atom models (EAM).  The
name “local density potential” arises from the fact that it assigns an
energy to an atom depending on the number of neighboring atoms of a
given type around it within a predefined spherical volume (i.e., within
the cutoff).  The bottom\sphinxhyphen{}up coarse\sphinxhyphen{}graining (CG) literature suggests
that such potentials can be widely useful in capturing effective
multibody forces in a computationally efficient manner and thus improve
the quality of CG models of implicit solvation {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_local_density:sanyal1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sanyal1)}}}} and phase\sphinxhyphen{}segregation in liquid mixtures {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_local_density:sanyal2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sanyal2)}}}}, and provide guidelines to determine the extent of manybody
correlations present in a CG model {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_local_density:rosenberger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rosenberger)}}}}.
The LD potential in LAMMPS is primarily intended to be used as a
corrective potential over traditional pair potentials in bottom\sphinxhyphen{}up CG
models via {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_hybrid::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{hybrid/overlay pair style}}}} with other
explicit pair interaction terms (e.g., tabulated, Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones, Morse
etc.).  Because the LD potential is not a pair potential per se, it is
implemented simply as a single auxiliary file with all specifications
that will be read upon initialization.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus when used as the only interaction in the system, there is no
corresponding pair\_coeff command and when used with other pair styles using the
hybrid/overlay option, the corresponding pair\_coeff command must be supplied
*  * as placeholders for the atom types.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{System with a single CG atom type:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A system of a single atom type (e.g., LJ argon) with a single local density (LD)
potential would have an energy given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{LD} = \sum_i F(\rho_i)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\rho_i\) is the LD at atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \(F(\rho)\) is
similar in spirit to the embedding function used in EAM potentials. The
LD at atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} is given by the sum
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \varphi(r_{ij})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\varphi\) is an indicator function that is one at r=0 and
zero beyond a cutoff distance R2. The choice of the functional form of
\(\varphi\) is somewhat arbitrary, but the following piecewise cubic
function has proven sufficiently general: {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_local_density:sanyal1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sanyal1)}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_local_density:sanyal2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sanyal2)}}}} {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_local_density:rosenberger}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rosenberger)}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(r) =
\begin{cases}
1 & r \le R_1 \\
c_0 + c_2r^2 + c_4r^4 + c_6r^6  & r \in (R_1, R_2) \\
0 & r \ge R_2
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The constants \sphinxstyleemphasis{c} are chosen so that the indicator function smoothly
interpolates between 1 and 0 between the distances R1 and R2, which are
called the inner and outer cutoffs, respectively. Thus phi satisfies
phi(R1) = 1, phi(R2) = dphi/dr @ (r=R1) =  dphi/dr @ (r=R2) = 0. The embedding
function F(rho) may or may not have a closed\sphinxhyphen{}form expression. To maintain
generality, it is practically represented with a spline\sphinxhyphen{}interpolated table
over a predetermined range of rho. Outside of that range it simply adopts zero
values at the endpoints.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It can be shown that the total force between two atoms due to the LD potential
takes the form of a pair force, which motivates its designation as a LAMMPS
pair style. Please see {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_local_density:sanyal1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sanyal1)}}}} for details of the derivation.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Systems with arbitrary numbers of atom types:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential is easily generalized to systems involving multiple atom types:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{LD} = \sum_i a_\alpha F(\rho_i)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the LD expressed as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho_i = \sum_{j \neq i} b_\beta \varphi(r_{ij})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\alpha\) gives the type of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}, \(\beta\) the
type of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}, and the coefficients \sphinxstyleemphasis{a} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{b} filter for atom
types as specified by the user. \sphinxstyleemphasis{a} is called the central atom filter as
it determines to which atoms the potential applies; \(a_{\alpha} =
1\) if the LD potential applies to atom type \(\alpha\) else zero. On the
other hand, \sphinxstyleemphasis{b} is called the neighbor atom filter because it specifies
which atom types to use in the calculation of the LD; \(b_{\beta} =
1\) if atom type \(\beta\) contributes to the LD and zero otherwise.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the potentials need not be symmetric with respect to atom
types, which is the reason for two distinct sets of coefficients \sphinxstyleemphasis{a}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{b}. An atom type may contribute to the LD but not the
potential, or to the potential but not the LD. Such decisions are
made by the user and should (ideally) be motivated on physical
grounds for the problem at hand.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{General form for implementation in LAMMPS:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Of course, a system with many atom types may have many different possible LD
potentials, each with their own atom type filters, cutoffs, and embedding
functions. The most general form of this potential as implemented in the
pair\_style local/density is:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{LD} = \sum_k U_{LD}^{(k)} = \sum_i \left[ \sum_k a_\alpha^{(k)} F^{(k)} \left(\rho_i^{(k)}\right) \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where, \sphinxstyleemphasis{k} is an index that spans the (arbitrary) number of applied LD
potentials N\_LD. Each LD is calculated as before with:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho_i^{(k)} = \sum_j b_\beta^{(k)} \varphi^{(k)} (r_{ij})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The superscript on the indicator function phi simply indicates that it is
associated with specific values of the cutoff distances R1(k) and R2(k). In
summary, there may be N\_LD distinct LD potentials. With each potential type (k),
one must specify:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the inner and outer cutoffs as R1 and R2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the central type filter a(k), where k = 1,2,…N\_LD

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the neighbor type filter b(k), where k = 1,2,…N\_LD

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the LD potential function F(k)(rho), typically as a table that is later spline\sphinxhyphen{}interpolated

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Tabulated input file format:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Line 1:             comment or blank (ignored)
Line 2:             comment or blank (ignored)
Line 3:             N\PYGZus{}LD N\PYGZus{}rho (\PYGZsh{} of LD potentials and \PYGZsh{} of tabulated values, single space separated)
Line 4:             blank (ignored)
Line 5:             R1(k) R2(k) (lower and upper cutoffs, single space separated)
Line 6:             central\PYGZhy{}types (central atom types, single space separated)
Line 7:             neighbor\PYGZhy{}types (neighbor atom types single space separated)
Line 8:             rho\PYGZus{}min rho\PYGZus{}max drho (min, max and diff. in tabulated rho values, single space separated)
Line 9:             F(k)(rho\PYGZus{}min + 0.drho)
Line 10:            F(k)(rho\PYGZus{}min + 1.drho)
Line 11:            F(k)(rho\PYGZus{}min + 2.drho)
...
Line 9+N\PYGZus{}rho:       F(k)(rho\PYGZus{}min + N\PYGZus{}rho . drho)
Line 10+N\PYGZus{}rho:      blank (ignored)

Block 2

Block 3

Block N\PYGZus{}LD
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lines 5 to 9+N\_rho constitute the first block. Thus the input file is separated
(by blank lines) into N\_LD blocks each representing a separate LD potential and
each specifying its own upper and lower cutoffs, central and neighbor atoms,
and potential.  In general, blank lines anywhere are ignored.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_local_density:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support automatic mixing. For atom type pairs
\(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) != \(\beta\), even
if LD potentials of type (\(\alpha\), \(\alpha\)) and
(\(\beta\), \(\beta\)) are provided, you will need to explicitly
provide LD potential types (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) and
(\(\beta\), \(\alpha\)) if need be (Here, the notation
(\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) means that \(\alpha\) is the central
atom to which the LD potential is applied and \(\beta\) is the
neighbor atom which contributes to the LD potential on \(\alpha\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The local/density pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in tabulated potential files.
Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in
an input script that reads a restart file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_local_density:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The local/density pair style is a part of the MANYBODY package. It is
only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\section{pair\_style lubricate/poly command}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricate:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flaglog}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flagfld}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutinner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flagHI}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flagVF}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricate} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricate/poly}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mu = dynamic viscosity (dynamic viscosity units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flaglog = 0/1 to exclude/include log terms in the lubrication approximation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flagfld = 0/1 to exclude/include Fast Lubrication Dynamics (FLD) effects

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutinner = inner cutoff distance (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = outer cutoff for interactions (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flagHI (optional) = 0/1 to exclude/include 1/r hydrodynamic interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flagVF (optional) = 0/1 to exclude/include volume fraction corrections in the long\sphinxhyphen{}range isotropic terms

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricate:examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(all assume radius = 1)

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lubricate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.05}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.8}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lubricate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}

\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adapt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lubricate}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}mu}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricate:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricate} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricate/poly} compute hydrodynamic
interactions between mono\sphinxhyphen{}disperse finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical particles in
a pairwise fashion.  The interactions have 2 components.  The first is
Ball\sphinxhyphen{}Melrose lubrication terms via the formulas in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lubricate:ball1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ball and Melrose)}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}W & =  - a_{sq} | (v_1 - v_2) \bullet \mathbf{nn} |^2 -
a_{sh} | (\omega_1 + \omega_2) \bullet
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{nn}) - 2 \Omega_N |^2 - \\
&  a_{pu} | (\omega_1 - \omega_2) \bullet (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{nn}) |^2 -
a_{tw} | (\omega_1 - \omega_2) \bullet \mathbf{nn} |^2  \qquad r < r_c \\
& \\
\Omega_N & = \mathbf{n} \times (v_1 - v_2) / r\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
which represents the dissipation W between two nearby particles due to
their relative velocities in the presence of a background solvent with
viscosity \sphinxstyleemphasis{mu}.  Note that this is dynamic viscosity which has units of
mass/distance/time, not kinematic viscosity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Asq (squeeze) term is the strongest and is included if \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} is
set to 1 (default). It scales as 1/gap where gap is the separation
between the surfaces of the 2 particles. The Ash (shear) and Apu
(pump) terms are only included if \sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog} is set to 1. They are the
next strongest interactions, and the only other singular interaction,
and scale as log(gap). Note that \sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog} = 1 and \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} = 0 is
invalid, and will result in a warning message, after which \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} will
be set to 1. The Atw (twist) term is currently not included. It is
typically a very small contribution to the lubrication forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagVF} settings are optional.  Neither should be
used, or both must be defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cutinner} sets the minimum center\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}center separation that will be
used in calculations irrespective of the actual separation.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Cutoff}
is the maximum center\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}center separation at which an interaction is
computed.  Using a \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} less than 3 radii is recommended if
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog} is set to 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The other component is due to the Fast Lubrication Dynamics (FLD)
approximation, described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lubricate:kumar1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kumar)}}}}, which can be
represented by the following equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F^{H} = -R_{FU}(U-U^{\infty}) + R_{FE}E^{\infty}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where U represents the velocities and angular velocities of the
particles, \(U^{\infty}\) represents the velocity and the angular velocity
of the undisturbed fluid, and \(E^{\infty}\) represents the rate of strain
tensor of the undisturbed fluid with viscosity \sphinxstyleemphasis{mu}. Again, note that
this is dynamic viscosity which has units of mass/distance/time, not
kinematic viscosity. Volume fraction corrections to R\_FU are included
as long as \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagVF} is set to 1 (default).

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using the FLD terms, these pair styles are designed to be used
with explicit time integration and a correspondingly small timestep.
Thus either {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_sphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/sphere}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_asphere::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix
nve/asphere}}}} should be used for time integration.
To perform implicit FLD, see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lubricateU::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lubricateU}}}} command.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricate} requires monodisperse spherical particles; style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricate/poly} allows for polydisperse spherical particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The viscosity \sphinxstyleemphasis{mu} can be varied in a time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent manner over the
course of a simulation, in which case in which case the pair\_style
setting for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mu} will be overridden.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}}
command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the suspension is sheared via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}}
command then the pair style uses the shear rate to adjust the
hydrodynamic interactions accordingly. Volume changes due to fix
deform are accounted for when computing the volume fraction
corrections to R\_FU.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When computing the volume fraction corrections to R\_FU, the presence of
walls (whether moving or stationary) will affect the volume fraction
available to colloidal particles. This is currently accounted for with
the following types of walls: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/lj93}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/lj126}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/colloid}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/harmonic}}}}.  For these wall styles, the correct
volume fraction will be used when walls do not coincide with the box
boundary, as well as when walls move and thereby cause a change in the
volume fraction.  Other wall styles may still work, but they will result
in the volume fraction being computed based on the box boundaries.
Several wall styles are not compatible with these pair styles and using
them will result in an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since lubrication forces are dissipative, it is usually desirable to
thermostat the system at a constant temperature. If Brownian motion
(at a constant temperature) is desired, it can be set using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_brownian::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style brownian}}}} command. These pair styles
and the brownian style should use consistent parameters for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mu},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagfld}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutinner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagVF}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutinner (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two coefficients are optional.  If neither is specified, the two
cutoffs specified in the pair\_style command are used.  Otherwise both
must be specified.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricate:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the two cutoff distances for this
pair style can be mixed.  The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See
the “pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift option for the energy of the pair interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant
for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricate:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These styles are part of the COLLOID package.  They are only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only spherical monodisperse particles are allowed for pair\_style
lubricate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only spherical particles are allowed for pair\_style lubricate/poly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles will not restart exactly when using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command, though they should provide
statistically similar results.  This is because the forces they
compute depend on atom velocities.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} command for more details.

\section{pair\_style lubricateU command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:pair-style-lubricateu-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU::doc}}

\section{pair\_style lubricateU/poly command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:pair-style-lubricateu-poly-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flaglog}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutinner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gdot}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flagHI}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{flagVF}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU/poly}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mu = dynamic viscosity (dynamic viscosity units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flaglog = 0/1 to exclude/include log terms in the lubrication approximation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutinner = inner cut off distance (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = outer cutoff for interactions (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
gdot = shear rate (1/time units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flagHI (optional) = 0/1 to exclude/include 1/r hydrodynamic interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flagVF (optional) = 0/1 to exclude/include volume fraction corrections in the long\sphinxhyphen{}range isotropic terms

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
(all assume radius = 1)

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lubricateU}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.05}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.8}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU/poly} compute velocities and
angular velocities for finite\sphinxhyphen{}size spherical particles such that the
hydrodynamic interaction balances the force and torque due to all
other types of interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interactions have 2 components.  The first is
Ball\sphinxhyphen{}Melrose lubrication terms via the formulas in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:ball2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ball and Melrose)}}}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}W & =  - a_{sq} | (v_1 - v_2) \bullet \mathbf{nn} |^2 -
a_{sh} | (\omega_1 + \omega_2) \bullet
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{nn}) - 2 \Omega_N |^2 - \\
&  a_{pu} | (\omega_1 - \omega_2) \bullet (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{nn}) |^2 -
a_{tw} | (\omega_1 - \omega_2) \bullet \mathbf{nn} |^2  \qquad r < r_c \\
& \\
\Omega_N & = \mathbf{n} \times (v_1 - v_2) / r\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
which represents the dissipation W between two nearby particles due to
their relative velocities in the presence of a background solvent with
viscosity \sphinxstyleemphasis{mu}.  Note that this is dynamic viscosity which has units of
mass/distance/time, not kinematic viscosity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Asq (squeeze) term is the strongest and is included as long as
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} is set to 1 (default). It scales as 1/gap where gap is the
separation between the surfaces of the 2 particles. The Ash (shear)
and Apu (pump) terms are only included if \sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog} is set to 1. They
are the next strongest interactions, and the only other singular
interaction, and scale as log(gap). Note that \sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog} = 1 and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} = 0 is invalid, and will result in a warning message, after
which \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} will be set to 1. The Atw (twist) term is currently not
included. It is typically a very small contribution to the lubrication
forces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagVF} settings are optional.  Neither should be
used, or both must be defined.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cutinner} sets the minimum center\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}center separation that will be
used in calculations irrespective of the actual separation.  \sphinxstyleemphasis{Cutoff}
is the maximum center\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}center separation at which an interaction is
computed.  Using a \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff} less than 3 radii is recommended if
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog} is set to 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The other component is due to the Fast Lubrication Dynamics (FLD)
approximation, described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:kumar2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kumar)}}}}.  The equation being
solved to balance the forces and torques is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-R_{FU}(U-U^{\infty}) = -R_{FE}E^{\infty} - F^{rest}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where U represents the velocities and angular velocities of the
particles, \(U^{\infty}\) represents the velocities and the angular
velocities of the undisturbed fluid, and \(E^{\infty}\) represents
the rate of strain tensor of the undisturbed fluid flow with viscosity
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mu}. Again, note that this is dynamic viscosity which has units of
mass/distance/time, not kinematic viscosity.  Volume fraction
corrections to R\_FU are included if \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagVF} is set to 1 (default).

\sphinxAtStartPar
F\sphinxstyleemphasis{rest} represents the forces and torques due to all other types of
interactions, e.g. Brownian, electrostatic etc.  Note that this
algorithm neglects the inertial terms, thereby removing the restriction
of resolving the small interial time scale, which may not be of interest
for colloidal particles.  These pair styles solve for the velocity such
that the hydrodynamic force balances all other types of forces, thereby
resulting in a net zero force (zero inertia limit).  When defining these
pair styles, they must be defined last so that when these styles are
invoked all other types of forces have already been computed.  For the
same reason, they won’t work if additional non\sphinxhyphen{}pair styles are defined
(such as bond or Kspace forces) as they are calculated in LAMMPS after
the pairwise interactions have been computed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using these styles, the pair styles are designed to be used with
implicit time integration and a correspondingly larger timestep.
Thus either {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_noforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/noforce}}}} should be used
for spherical particles defined via {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style sphere}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_asphere_noforce::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/asphere/noforce}}}} should be used for spherical particles
defined via {\hyperref[\detokenize{atom_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{atom\_style ellipsoid}}}}.  This is
because the velocity and angular momentum of each particle is set by
the pair style, and should not be reset by the time integration fix.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU} requires monodisperse spherical particles; style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU/poly} allows for polydisperse spherical particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the suspension is sheared via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}}
command then the pair style uses the shear rate to adjust the
hydrodynamic interactions accordingly. Volume changes due to fix
deform are accounted for when computing the volume fraction
corrections to R\_FU.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When computing the volume fraction corrections to R\_FU, the presence of
walls (whether moving or stationary) will affect the volume fraction
available to colloidal particles. This is currently accounted for with
the following types of walls: {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/lj93}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/lj126}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/colloid}}}}, and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{wall/harmonic}}}}.  For these wall styles, the correct
volume fraction will be used when walls do not coincide with the box
boundary, as well as when walls move and thereby cause a change in the
volume fraction. To use these wall styles with pair\_style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU}
or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lubricateU/poly}, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{fld yes} option must be specified in the fix
wall command.  Other wall styles may still work, but they will result
in the volume fraction being computed based on the box boundaries.
Several wall styles are not compatible with these pair styles and using
them will result in an error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Since lubrication forces are dissipative, it is usually desirable to
thermostat the system at a constant temperature. If Brownian motion
(at a constant temperature) is desired, it can be set using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_brownian::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style brownian}}}} command. These pair styles
and the brownian style should use consistent parameters for \sphinxstyleemphasis{mu},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{flaglog}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagfld}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutinner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{cutoff}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagHI} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{flagVF}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutinner (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The two coefficients are optional.  If neither is specified, the two
cutoffs specified in the pair\_style command are used.  Otherwise both
must be specified.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the two cutoff distances for this
pair style can be mixed.  The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See
the “pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift option for the energy of the pair interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant
for these pair styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles do not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need to be
specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_lubricateU:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These styles are part of the COLLOID package.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Currently, these pair styles assume that all other types of
forces/torques on the particles have been already been computed when it
is invoked.  This requires this style to be defined as the last of the
pair styles, and that no fixes apply additional constraint forces.  One
exception is the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_wall::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix wall/colloid}}}} commands, which has
an “fld” option to apply their wall forces correctly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only spherical monodisperse particles are allowed for pair\_style
lubricateU.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only spherical particles are allowed for pair\_style lubricateU/poly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For sheared suspensions, it is assumed that the shearing is done in the
xy plane, with x being the velocity direction and y being the
velocity\sphinxhyphen{}gradient direction. In this case, one must use {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_deform::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix deform}}}} with the same rate of shear (erate).

\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles are only compatible with the following wall fixes:
doc:\sphinxtitleref{fix wall/lj93, fix wall/lj126, fix wall/lj1043, fix wall/colloid,
fix wall/harmonic, fix wall/lepton, fix wall/morse, fix wall/table
\textless{}fix\_wall\textgreater{}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lubricate::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lubricate}}}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\subsection{Examples}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.2}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{buck}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{mdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{200.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lennard}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{mdf}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1021760.3664}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2120.317338}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_mdf:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/mdf}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{buck/mdf} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{lennard/mdf} compute the standard 12\sphinxhyphen{}6
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones and Buckingham potential with the addition of a taper
function that ramps the energy and force smoothly to zero between an
inner and outer cutoff.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{smooth}(r) = E(r)*f(r)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The tapering, \sphinxstyleemphasis{f(r)}, is done by using the Mei, Davenport, Fernando
function {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_mdf:mei}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mei)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f(r) & = 1.0  \qquad \qquad \mathrm{for} \qquad r < r_m \\
f(r) & = (1 - x)^3*(1+3x+6x^2) \quad \mathrm{for} \qquad r_m < r < r_{cut} \\
f(r) & = 0.0  \qquad \qquad \mathrm{for} \qquad  r >= r_{cut} \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}x = \frac{(r-r_m)}{(r_{cut}-r_m)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \(r_m\) is the inner cutoff radius and \(r_{cut}\) is the
outer cutoff radius.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/mdf} pair\_style, the potential energy, \sphinxstyleemphasis{E(r)}, is the
standard 12\sphinxhyphen{}6 Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones written in the epsilon/sigma form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(r) = 4 \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
                         \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Either the first two or all of the following coefficients must be
defined for each pair of atoms types via the pair\_coeff command as in
the examples above, or in the data file read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}. The two cutoffs default to the global values and
\(\epsilon\) and \(\sigma\) can also be determined by mixing as
described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\epsilon\) (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\sigma\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_m\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{cut}\) (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{buck/mdf} pair\_style, the potential energy, \sphinxstyleemphasis{E(r)}, is the
standard Buckingham potential with three required coefficients.
The two cutoffs can be omitted and default to the corresponding
global values:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(r) = A e^{(-r/\rho)} -\frac{C}{r^6}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{A} (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\rho\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{C} (energy\sphinxhyphen{}distance\textasciicircum{}6 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_m\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{cut}\) (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lennard/mdf} pair\_style, the potential energy, \sphinxstyleemphasis{E(r)}, is the
standard 12\sphinxhyphen{}6 Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones written in the A/B form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(r) = \frac{A}{r^{12}} - \frac{B}{r^{6}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the pair\_coeff command as in the examples above, or in the
data file read by the read\_data commands, or by mixing as described below.
The two cutoffs default to their global values and must be either both
given or both left out:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{A} (energy\sphinxhyphen{}distance\textasciicircum{}12 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{B} (energy\sphinxhyphen{}distance\textasciicircum{}6 units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_m\) (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_{cut}\) (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_mdf:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the \(\epsilon\) and
\(\sigma\) coefficients and cutoff distances for the lj/mdf pair
style can be mixed.  The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See the
“pair\_modify” command for details. The other two pair styles buck/mdf
and lennard/mdf do not support mixing, so all I,J pairs of coefficients
must be specified explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
None of the lj/mdf, buck/mdf, or lennard/mdf pair styles supports
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift option or long\sphinxhyphen{}range
tail corrections to pressure and energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These styles can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  They do not support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\label{\detokenize{pair_mdf:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These pair styles can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}PAIR package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc
page for more info.
