\section{pair\_style pod command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_pod:pair-style-pod-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_pod:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_pod:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_pod::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_pod:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pod}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_pod:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pod}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta\PYGZus{}coefficients.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_pod:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 22Dec2022.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod} defines the proper orthogonal descriptor (POD)
potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pod:nguyen20222b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen and Rohskopf)}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pod:nguyen20232b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen2023)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pod:nguyen20242b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen2024)}}}},
and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_pod:nguyen20243b}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Nguyen and Sema)}}}}.  The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fitpod}}}} is used to fit the POD potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod} style which
specifies a POD parameter file followed by a coefficient file, a
projection matrix file, and a centroid file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The POD parameter file (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Ta\_param.pod}}) can contain blank and comment
lines (start with \#) anywhere. Each non\sphinxhyphen{}blank non\sphinxhyphen{}comment line must
contain one keyword/value pair. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fitpod}}}} for
the description of all the keywords that can be assigned in the
parameter file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The coefficient file (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Ta\_coefficients.pod}}) contains coefficients for
the POD potential. The top of the coefficient file can contain any
number of blank and comment lines (start with \#), but follows a strict
format after that. The first non\sphinxhyphen{}blank non\sphinxhyphen{}comment line must contain:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
model\_coefficients: \sphinxstyleemphasis{ncoeff} \sphinxstyleemphasis{nproj} \sphinxstyleemphasis{ncentroid}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is followed by \sphinxstyleemphasis{ncoeff} coefficients, \sphinxstyleemphasis{nproj} projection matrix entries,
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{ncentroid} centroid coordinates, one per line. The coefficient
file is generated after training the POD potential using {\hyperref[\detokenize{fitpod_command::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fitpod}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, if a LAMMPS indium phosphide simulation has 4 atoms
types, with the first two being indium and the third and fourth being
phophorous, the pair\_coeff command would look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{InP\PYGZus{}param.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{InP\PYGZus{}coefficients.pod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{In}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{In}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{P}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The two filenames are for the parameter and coefficient files, respectively.
The two trailing ‘In’ arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1 and 2 to the
POD ‘In’ element. The two trailing ‘P’ arguments map LAMMPS atom types
3 and 4 to the POD ‘P’ element.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a POD mapping value is specified as NULL, the mapping is not
performed.  This can be used when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{pod} potential is used as part of
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.  The NULL values are placeholders for atom
types that will be used with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples about training and using POD potentials are found in the
directory lammps/examples/PACKAGES/pod and the Github repo \sphinxurl{https://github.com/cesmix-mit/pod-examples}.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_pod:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, where types I and J correspond to
two different element types, mixing is performed by LAMMPS with
user\sphinxhyphen{}specifiable parameters as described above.  You never need to
specify a pair\_coeff command with I != J arguments for this style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart
files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you need
to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are

They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}

You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\section{pair\_style polymorphic command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:pair-style-polymorphic-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{polymorphic}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{polymorphic}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{polymorphic}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{FeCH\PYGZus{}BOP\PYGZus{}I.poly}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Fe}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{H}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{TlBr\PYGZus{}msw.poly}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Tl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Br}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{CuTa\PYGZus{}eam.poly}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cu}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{GaN\PYGZus{}tersoff.poly}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ga}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{GaN\PYGZus{}sw.poly}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ga}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{polymorphic} pair style computes a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body free\sphinxhyphen{}form potential
({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:zhou3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Zhou3}}}}) for the energy E of a system of atoms as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{i=N}\sum_{j=1}^{j=N}\left[\left(1-\delta_{ij}\right)\cdot U_{IJ}\left(r_{ij}\right)-\left(1-\eta_{ij}\right)\cdot F_{IJ}\left(X_{ij}\right)\cdot V_{IJ}\left(r_{ij}\right)\right] \\
X_{ij} & = \sum_{k=i_1,k\neq j}^{i_N}W_{IK}\left(r_{ik}\right)\cdot G_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta_{jik}\right)\cdot P_{JIK}\left(\Delta r_{jik}\right) \\
\Delta r_{jik} & = r_{ij}-\xi_{IJ}\cdot r_{ik}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where I, J, K represent species of atoms i, j, and k, \(i_1, ...,
i_N\) represents a list of \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}‘s neighbors, \(\delta_{ij}\) is a
Dirac constant (i.e., \(\delta_{ij} = 1\) when \(i = j\), and
\(\delta_{ij} = 0\) otherwise), \(\eta_{ij}\) is similar
constant that can be set either to \(\eta_{ij} = \delta_{ij}\) or
\(\eta_{ij} = 1 - \delta_{ij}\) depending on the potential type,
\(U_{IJ}(r_{ij})\), \(V_{IJ}(r_{ij})\), \(W_{IK}(r_{ik})\)
are pair functions, \(G_{JIK}(\cos\theta_{jik})\) is an angular
function, \(P_{JIK}(\Delta r_{jik})\) is a function of atomic
spacing differential \(\Delta r_{jik} = r_{ij} - \xi_{IJ} \cdot
r_{ik}\) with \(\xi_{IJ}\) being a pair\sphinxhyphen{}dependent parameter, and
\(F_{IJ}(X_{ij})\) is a function of the local environment variable
\(X_{ij}\). This generic potential is fully defined once the
constants \(\eta_{ij}\) and \(\xi_{IJ}\), and the six functions
\(U_{IJ}(r_{ij})\), \(V_{IJ}(r_{ij})\), \(W_{IK}(r_{ik})\),
\(G_{JIK}(\cos\theta_{jik})\), \(P_{JIK}(\Delta r_{jik})\), and
\(F_{IJ}(X_{ij})\) are given. Here LAMMPS uses a global parameter
\(\eta\) to represent \(\eta_{ij}\). When \(\eta = 1\),
\(\eta_{ij} = 1 - \delta_{ij}\), otherwise \(\eta_{ij} =
\delta_{ij}\). Additionally, \(\eta = 3\) indicates that the function
\(P_{JIK}(\Delta r)\) depends on species I, J and K, otherwise
\(P_{JIK}(\Delta r) = P_{IK}(\Delta r)\) only depends on species I
and K. Note that these six functions are all one dimensional, and hence
can be provided in a tabular form. This allows users to design different
potentials solely based on a manipulation of these functions. For
instance, the potential reduces to a Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber potential
({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:sw}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SW}}}}) if we set
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_{ij} & = \delta_{ij} (\eta = 2~or~\eta = 0),\xi_{IJ}=0 \\
U_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = A_{IJ}\cdot\epsilon_{IJ}\cdot \left(\frac{\sigma_{IJ}}{r}\right)^q\cdot \left[B_{IJ}\cdot \left(\frac{\sigma_{IJ}}{r}\right)^{p-q}-1\right]\cdot exp\left(\frac{\sigma_{IJ}}{r-a_{IJ}\cdot \sigma_{IJ}}\right) \\
V_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \sqrt{\lambda_{IJ}\cdot \epsilon_{IJ}}\cdot exp\left(\frac{\gamma_{IJ}\cdot \sigma_{IJ}}{r-a_{IJ}\cdot \sigma_{IJ}}\right) \\
F_{IJ}\left(X\right) & = -X \\
P_{JIK}\left(\Delta r\right) & = P_{IK}\left(\Delta r\right) = 1 \\
W_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \sqrt{\lambda_{IJ}\cdot \epsilon_{IJ}}\cdot exp\left(\frac{\gamma_{IJ}\cdot \sigma_{IJ}}{r-a_{IJ}\cdot \sigma_{IJ}}\right) \\
G_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta\right) & = \left(\cos\theta+\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential reduces to a Tersoff potential ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:tersoff}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Tersoff}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:poly-albe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Albe1}}}}) if we set
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_{ij} & = \delta_{ij} (\eta = 2~or~\eta = 0),\xi_{IJ}=1 \\
U_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \frac{D_{e,IJ}}{S_{IJ}-1}\cdot exp\left[-\beta_{IJ}\sqrt{2S_{IJ}}\left(r-r_{e,IJ}\right)\right]\cdot f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \\
V_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \frac{S_{IJ}\cdot D_{e,IJ}}{S_{IJ}-1}\cdot exp\left[-\beta_{IJ}\sqrt{\frac{2}{S_{IJ}}}\left(r-r_{e,IJ}\right)\right]\cdot f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \\
F_{IJ}\left(X\right) & = \left(1+X\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\
P_{JIK}\left(\Delta r\right) & = P_{IK}\left(\Delta r\right) = exp\left(2\mu_{IK}\cdot \Delta r\right) \\
W_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \\
G_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta\right) & = \gamma_{IK}\left[1+\frac{c_{IK}^2}{d_{IK}^2}-\frac{c_{IK}^2}{d_{IK}^2+\left(h_{IK}+\cos\theta\right)^2}\right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
1, r\leq R_{IJ}-D_{IJ} \\
\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}cos\left[\frac{\pi\left(r+D_{IJ}-R_{IJ}\right)}{2D_{IJ}}\right], R_{IJ}-D_{IJ} < r < R_{IJ}+D_{IJ} \\
0, r \geq R_{IJ}+D_{IJ}
\end{array}\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential reduces to a modified Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber potential
({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:zhou3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Zhou3}}}}) if we set
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_{ij} & = \delta_{ij} (\eta = 2~or~\eta = 0),\xi_{IJ}=0 \\
U_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \varphi_{R,IJ}\left(r\right)-\varphi_{A,IJ}\left(r\right) \\
V_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = u_{IJ}\left(r\right) \\
F_{IJ}\left(X\right) & = -X \\
P_{JIK}\left(\Delta r\right) & = P_{IK}\left(\Delta r\right) = 1 \\
W_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = u_{IJ}\left(r\right) \\
G_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta\right) & = g_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential reduces to a Rockett\sphinxhyphen{}Tersoff potential ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:wang3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wang3}}}}) if we set
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_{ij} & = \delta_{ij} (\eta = 2~or~\eta = 0),\xi_{IJ}=1 \\
U_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = A_{IJ}exp\left(-\lambda_{1,IJ}\cdot r\right)f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right)f_{ca,IJ}\left(r\right) \\
V_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \left\{\begin{array}{l}B_{IJ}exp\left(-\lambda_{2,IJ}\cdot r\right)f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right)+ \\ A_{IJ}exp\left(-\lambda_{1,IJ}\cdot r\right)f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \left[1-f_{ca,IJ}\left(r\right)\right]\end{array} \right\} \\
F_{IJ}\left(X\right) & = \left[1+\left(\beta_{IJ}X\right)^{n_{IJ}}\right]^{-\frac{1}{2n_{IJ}}} \\
P_{JIK}\left(\Delta r\right) & = P_{IK}\left(\Delta r\right) = exp\left(\lambda_{3,IK}\cdot \Delta r^3\right) \\
W_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \\
G_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta\right) & = 1+\frac{c_{IK}^2}{d_{IK}^2}-\frac{c_{IK}^2}{d_{IK}^2+\left(h_{IK}+\cos\theta\right)^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(f_{ca,IJ}(r)\) is similar to the \(f_{c,IJ}(r)\) defined
above:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f_{ca,IJ}\left(r\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}
1, r\leq R_{a,IJ}-D_{a,IJ} \\
\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}cos\left[\frac{\pi\left(r+D_{a,IJ}-R_{a,IJ}\right)}{2D_{a,IJ}}\right], R_{a,IJ}-D_{a,IJ} < r < R_{a,IJ}+D_{a,IJ} \\
0, r \geq R_{a,IJ}+D_{a,IJ}
\end{array}\right.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential becomes the embedded atom method ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:poly-daw}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Daw}}}})
if we set
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_{ij} & = 1-\delta_{ij} (\eta = 1),\xi_{IJ}=0 \\
U_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \phi_{IJ}\left(r\right) \\
V_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = 1 \\
F_{II}\left(X\right) & = -2F_I\left(X\right) \\
P_{JIK}\left(\Delta r\right) & = P_{IK}\left(\Delta r\right) = 1 \\
W_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = f_{J}\left(r\right) \\
G_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta\right) & = 1\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the embedded atom method case, \(\phi_{IJ}(r)\) is the pair
energy, \(F_I(X)\) is the embedding energy, \sphinxstyleemphasis{X} is the local
electron density, and \(f_J(r)\) is the atomic electron density
function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential reduces to another type of Tersoff potential ({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:zhou4}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Zhou4}}}}) if we set
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\eta_{ij} & = \delta_{ij} (\eta = 3),\xi_{IJ}=1 \\
U_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \frac{D_{e,IJ}}{S_{IJ}-1}\cdot exp\left[-\beta_{IJ}\sqrt{2S_{IJ}}\left(r-r_{e,IJ}\right)\right]\cdot f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \cdot T_{IJ}\left(r\right)+V_{ZBL,IJ}\left(r\right)\left[1-T_{IJ}\left(r\right)\right] \\
V_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \frac{S_{IJ}\cdot D_{e,IJ}}{S_{IJ}-1}\cdot exp\left[-\beta_{IJ}\sqrt{\frac{2}{S_{IJ}}}\left(r-r_{e,IJ}\right)\right]\cdot f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \cdot T_{IJ}\left(r\right) \\
F_{IJ}\left(X\right) & = \left(1+X\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\
P_{JIK}\left(\Delta r\right) & = \omega_{JIK} \cdot exp\left(\alpha_{JIK}\cdot \Delta r\right) \\
W_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = f_{c,IJ}\left(r\right) \\
G_{JIK}\left(\cos\theta\right) & = \gamma_{JIK}\left[1+\frac{c_{JIK}^2}{d_{JIK}^2}-\frac{c_{JIK}^2}{d_{JIK}^2+\left(h_{JIK}+\cos\theta\right)^2}\right] \\
T_{IJ}\left(r\right) & = \frac{1}{1+exp\left[-b_{f,IJ}\left(r-r_{f,IJ}\right)\right]} \\
V_{ZBL,IJ}\left(r\right) & = 14.4 \cdot \frac{Z_I \cdot Z_J}{r}\sum_{k=1}^{4}\mu_k \cdot exp\left[-\nu_k \left(Z_I^{0.23}+Z_J^{0.23}\right) r\right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(f_{c,IJ}(r)\) is the same as defined above. This Tersoff
potential differs from the one above because the \(P_{JIK}(\Delta
r)\) function is now dependent on all three species I, J, and K.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the tabulated functions are created using the parameters of
Stillinger\sphinxhyphen{}Weber, Tersoff, and EAM potentials, the polymorphic pair
style will produce the same global properties (energies and stresses)
and the same forces as the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sw::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{sw}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tersoff}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{eam}}}} pair styles. The polymorphic
pair style also produces the same per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties (energies and
stresses) as the corresponding {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{tersoff}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_eam::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{eam}}}} pair styles. However, due to a different
partitioning of global properties to per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties, the
polymorphic pair style will produce different per\sphinxhyphen{}atom properties
(energies and stresses) as the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sw::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{sw}}}} pair style. This does
not mean that polymorphic pair style is different from the sw pair
style. It just means that the definitions of the atom energies and atom
stresses are different.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the polymorphic pair style
which specifies a potential file for all needed elements.  These are
mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying N additional arguments after
the filename in the pair\_coeff command, where N is the number of LAMMPS
atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of polymorphic potential elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the pair\_coeff page for alternate ways to specify the path for
the potential file. Several files for polymorphic potentials are
included in the potentials directory of the LAMMPS distribution. They
have a “poly” suffix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine the GaN\_tersoff.poly file has tabulated functions
for Ga\sphinxhyphen{}N tersoff potential. If your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atom types and
you want the first 3 to be Ga, and the fourth to be N, you would use the
following pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{GaN\PYGZus{}tersoff.poly}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ga}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ga}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ga}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first two arguments must be * * to span all pairs of LAMMPS atom
types. The first three Ga arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the
Ga element in the polymorphic file. The final N argument maps LAMMPS
atom type 4 to the N element in the polymorphic file. If a mapping value
is specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed. This can be used
when an polymorphic potential is used as part of the hybrid pair
style. The NULL values are placeholders for atom types that will be used
with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Potential files in the potentials directory of the LAMMPS distribution
have a “.poly” suffix. At the beginning of the files, an unlimited
number of lines starting with ‘\#’ are used to describe the potential and
are ignored by LAMMPS. The next line lists two numbers:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
ntypes eta
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes} represent total number of species defined in the potential
file, \(\eta = 1\) reduces to embedded atom method, \(\eta = 3\)
assumes a three species dependent \(P_{JIK}(\Delta r)\) function,
and all other values of \(\eta\) assume a two species dependent
\(P_{JK}(\Delta r)\) function. The value of \sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes} must equal the
total number of different species defined in the pair\_coeff command. The
next \sphinxstyleemphasis{ntypes} lines each lists two numbers and a character string
representing atomic number, atomic mass, and name of the species of the
ntypes elements:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atomic\PYGZhy{}number atomic\PYGZhy{}mass element\PYGZhy{}name(1)
atomic\PYGZhy{}number atomic\PYGZhy{}mass element\PYGZhy{}name(2)
...
atomic\PYGZhy{}number atomic\PYGZhy{}mass element\PYGZhy{}name(ntypes)
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The next line contains four numbers:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
nr ntheta nx xmax
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here nr is total number of tabular points for radial functions U, V, W,
P, ntheta is total number of tabular points for the angular function G,
nx is total number of tabular points for the function F, xmax is a
maximum value of the argument of function F. Note that the pair
functions \(U_{IJ}(r)\), \(V_{IJ}(r)\), \(W_{IJ}(r)\) are
uniformly tabulated between 0 and cutoff distance of the IJ pair,
\(G_{JIK}(\cos\theta)\) is uniformly tabulated between \sphinxhyphen{}1 and 1,
\(P_{JIK}(\Delta r)\) is uniformly tabulated between \sphinxhyphen{}rcmax and
rcmax where rcmax is the maximum cutoff distance of all pairs, and
\(F_{IJ}(X)\) is uniformly tabulated between 0 and xmax. Linear
extrapolation is assumed if actual simulations exceed these ranges.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The next ntypes*(ntypes+1)/2 lines contain two numbers:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
cut xi(1)
cut xi(2)
...
cut xi(ntypes*(ntypes+1)/2)
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here cut means the cutoff distance of the pair functions, “xi” is
\(\xi\) as defined in the potential functions above. The
ntypes*(ntypes+1)/2 lines are related to the pairs according to the
sequence of first ii (self) pairs, i = 1, 2, …, ntypes, and then ij
(cross) pairs, i = 1, 2, …, ntypes\sphinxhyphen{}1, and j = i+1, i+2, …, ntypes
(i.e., the sequence of the ij pairs follows 11, 22, …, 12, 13, 14,
…, 23, 24, …).

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the final blocks of the potential file, U, V, W, P, G, and F
functions are listed sequentially. First, U functions are given for each
of the ntypes*(ntypes+1)/2 pairs according to the sequence described
above. For each of the pairs, nr values are listed. Next, similar arrays
are given for V and W functions. If P functions depend only on pair
species, i.e., \(\eta \neq 3\), then P functions are also listed the
same way the next. If P functions depend on three species, i.e.,
\(\eta = 3\), then P functions are listed for all the
ntypes*ntypes*ntypes IJK triplets in a natural sequence I from 1 to
ntypes, J from 1 to ntypes, and K from 1 to ntypes (i.e., IJK = 111,
112, 113, …, 121, 122, 123 …, 211, 212, …). Next, G functions are
listed for all the ntypes*ntypes*ntypes IJK triplets similarly. For each
of the G functions, ntheta values are listed. Finally, F functions are
listed for all the ntypes*(ntypes+1)/2 pairs in the same sequence as
described above.  For each of the F functions, nx values are listed.


\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart
files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files. Thus, you need
to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If using create\_atoms command, atomic masses must be defined in the
input script. If using read\_data, atomic masses must be defined in the
atomic structure data file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the MANYBODY package. It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package. See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair potential requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be
“on” for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential files provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials directory)
are parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}. You can use any LAMMPS
units, but you would need to create your own potential files.

\label{\detokenize{pair_polymorphic:related-commands}}

\index{pair\_style python@\spxentry{pair\_style python}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style python command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:pair-style-python-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_python:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_python::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff for interactions in python potential classes


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{py\PYGZus{}pot.LJCutMelt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{py\PYGZus{}pot.HarmonicCut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{B}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{py\PYGZus{}pot.LJCutSPCE}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{OW}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} pair style provides a way to define pairwise additive
potential functions as python script code that is loaded into LAMMPS
from a python file which must contain specific python class definitions.
This allows to rapidly evaluate different potential functions without
having to modify and re\sphinxhyphen{}compile LAMMPS. Due to python being an
interpreted language, however, the performance of this pair style is
going to be significantly slower (often between 20x and 100x) than
corresponding compiled code. This penalty can be significantly reduced
through generating tabulations from the python code through the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command, which is supported by this style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command is used with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{python} pair style which specifies a python class inside a python module
or a file that LAMMPS will look up in the current directory, a folder
pointed to by the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LAMMPS\_POTENTIALS}} environment variable or somewhere
in your python path.  A single python module can hold multiple python pair
class definitions.  The class definitions itself have to follow specific
rules that are explained below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Atom types in the python class are specified through symbolic
constants, typically strings. These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by
specifying N additional arguments after the class name in the
pair\_coeff command, where N must be the number of currently defined
atom types:

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine a file \sphinxstyleemphasis{py\_pot.py} has a python potential class
names \sphinxstyleemphasis{LJCutMelt} with parameters and potential functions for a two
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones atom types labeled as ‘LJ1’ and ‘LJ2’. In your LAMMPS
input and you would have defined 3 atom types, out of which the first
two are supposed to be using the ‘LJ1’ parameters and the third the
‘LJ2’ parameters, then you would use the following pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{py\PYGZus{}pot.LJCutMelt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LJ1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LJ1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{LJ2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first two arguments \sphinxstylestrong{must} be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom
types.  The first two LJ1 arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1 and 2 to
the LJ1 atom type in the LJCutMelt class of the py\_pot.py file.  The
final LJ2 argument maps LAMMPS atom type 3 to the LJ2 atom type the
python file.  If a mapping value is specified as NULL, the mapping is
not performed, any pair interaction with this atom type will be
skipped. This can be used when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} potential is used as part of
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} pair style. The NULL values are then
placeholders for atom types that will be used with other potentials.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The python potential file has to start with the following code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}future\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{print\PYGZus{}function}

\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{LAMMPSPairPotential}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb}{object}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf+fm}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}init\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n+nb}{dict}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{lj}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}
    \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{map\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{name}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{ltype}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{ltype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{name}
    \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{check\PYGZus{}units}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{units} \PYG{o}{!=} \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
           \PYG{k}{raise} \PYG{n+ne}{Exception}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Conflicting units: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ vs. }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZpc{}s}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}} \PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Any classes with definitions of specific potentials have to be derived
from this class and should be initialize in a similar fashion to the
example given below.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The class constructor has to set up a data structure containing
the potential parameters supported by this class.  It should also
define a variable \sphinxstyleemphasis{self.units} containing a string matching one of the
options of LAMMPS’ {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} command, which is used to
verify, that the potential definition in the python class and in the
LAMMPS input match.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here is an example for a single type Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential class
\sphinxstyleemphasis{LJCutMelt} in reduced units, which defines an atom type \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj} for
which the parameters epsilon and sigma are both 1.0:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{LJCutMelt}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LAMMPSPairPotential}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf+fm}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}init\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n+nb}{super}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LJCutMelt}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n+nf+fm}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}init\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set coeffs: 48*eps*sig**12, 24*eps*sig**6,}
        \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}              4*eps*sig**12,  4*eps*sig**6}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{units} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{lj}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{coeff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{lj}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{lj}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{48.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mf}{24.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mf}{4.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mf}{4.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The class also has to provide two methods for the computation of the
potential energy and forces, which have be named \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute\_force},
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{compute\_energy}, which both take 3 numerical arguments:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rsq   = the square of the distance between a pair of atoms (float)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
itype = the (numerical) type of the first atom

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
jtype = the (numerical) type of the second atom

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This functions need to compute the (scaled) force and the energy,
respectively, and use the result as return value. The functions need
to use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pmap} dictionary to convert the LAMMPS atom type number
to the symbolic value of the internal potential parameter data structure.
Following the \sphinxstyleemphasis{LJCutMelt} example, here are the two functions:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{compute\PYGZus{}force}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
     \PYG{n}{coeff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}
     \PYG{n}{r2inv}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rsq}
     \PYG{n}{r6inv}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{r2inv}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{r2inv}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{r2inv}
     \PYG{n}{lj1} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}
     \PYG{n}{lj2} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}
     \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{r6inv} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lj1}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{r6inv} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}} \PYG{n}{lj2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{r2inv}

 \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{compute\PYGZus{}energy}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
     \PYG{n}{coeff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}
     \PYG{n}{r2inv}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rsq}
     \PYG{n}{r6inv}  \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{r2inv}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{r2inv}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{r2inv}
     \PYG{n}{lj3} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{]}
     \PYG{n}{lj4} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{]}
     \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{r6inv} \PYG{o}{*} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{lj3}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{r6inv} \PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}} \PYG{n}{lj4}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
for consistency with the C++ pair styles in LAMMPS, the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{compute\_force} function follows the conventions of the Pair::single()
methods and does not return the pairwise force directly, but the force
divided by the distance between the two atoms, so this value only needs
to be  multiplied by delta x, delta y, and delta z to conveniently obtain
the three components of the force vector between these two atoms.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below is a more complex example using \sphinxstyleemphasis{real} units and defines an interaction
equivalent to:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{real}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This uses the default geometric mixing.  The equivalent input with pair
style \sphinxstyleemphasis{python} is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{real}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{py\PYGZus{}pot.Harmonic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{A}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{B}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that while for pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic/cut} the cutoff is implicitly
set to the minimum of the harmonic potential, for pair style python a
global cutoff must be set and it must be equal or larger to the implicit
cutoff of the potential in python, which has to explicitly return zero
force and energy beyond the cutoff.  Also, the mixed parameters have to
be explicitly provided.  The corresponding python code is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{Harmonic}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{LAMMPSPairPotential}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf+fm}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}init\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n+nb}{super}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{Harmonic}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n+nf+fm}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}init\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{units} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{real}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}
        \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} set coeffs: K, r0}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{coeff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{A}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{A}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.2}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mf}{9.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
                              \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{B}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{sqrt}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.2}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.4}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mf}{9.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
                      \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{B}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{A}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{sqrt}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.2}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.4}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mf}{9.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
                              \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{B}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}  \PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.4}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{l+m+mf}{9.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

    \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{compute\PYGZus{}force}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{coeff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}
        \PYG{n}{r} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{sqrt}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{n}{delta} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{r}
        \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{r} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{delta}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{r}
        \PYG{k}{else}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}

    \PYG{k}{def}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nf}{compute\PYGZus{}energy}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{coeff} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{itype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pmap}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{jtype}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{]}
        \PYG{n}{r} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{math}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{sqrt}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{p}{)}
        \PYG{n}{delta} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{r}
        \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{r} \PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}} \PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{delta}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{delta}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{coeff}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}
        \PYG{k}{else}\PYG{p}{:}
            \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Performance Impact}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The evaluation of scripted python code will slow down the computation
of pairwise interactions quite significantly. However, this performance
penalty can be worked around through using the python pair style not
for the actual simulation, but to generate tabulated potentials using
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command.  This will also enable
GPU or multi\sphinxhyphen{}thread acceleration through the GPU, KOKKOS, or OPENMP
package versions of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} pair style.  Please see below for a
LAMMPS input example demonstrating how to build a table file:
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{python}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{py\PYGZus{}pot.LJCutMelt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}
\PYG{k}{shell}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{n}{f}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj.table}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}write}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rsq}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.01}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that it is strongly recommended to try to \sphinxstylestrong{delete} the potential
table file before generating it. Since the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair\_write} command will
always \sphinxstylestrong{append} to a table file, while pair style table will use the
\sphinxstylestrong{first match}. Thus when changing the potential function in the python
class, the table pair style will still read the old variant unless the
table file is first deleted.

\sphinxAtStartPar
After switching the pair style to \sphinxstyleemphasis{table}, the potential tables need
to be assigned to the LAMMPS atom types like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2000}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{lj.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This can also be done for more complex systems.  Please see the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{examples/python} folders for a few more examples.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Mixing of potential parameters has to be handled inside the provided
python module. The python pair style simply assumes that force and
energy computation can be correctly performed for all pairs of atom
types as they are mapped to the atom type labels inside the python
potential class.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the PYTHON package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_table::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair style table}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{pair_python:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\index{pair\_style quip@\spxentry{pair\_style quip}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style quip command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:pair-style-quip-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_quip::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{quip}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{n}{quip}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gap\PYGZus{}example.xml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{Potential xml\PYGZus{}label=GAP\PYGZus{}2014\PYGZus{}5\PYGZus{}8\PYGZus{}60\PYGZus{}17\PYGZus{}10\PYGZus{}38\PYGZus{}466}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{14}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sw\PYGZus{}example.xml}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{IP SW}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{14}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{quip} provides an interface for calling potential routines from
the QUIP package. QUIP is built separately, and then linked to
LAMMPS. The most recent version of the QUIP package can be downloaded
from GitHub:
\sphinxurl{https://github.com/libAtoms/QUIP}. The
interface is chiefly intended to be used to run Gaussian Approximation
Potentials (GAP), which are described in the following publications:
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_quip:bartok-2010}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bartok et al)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_quip:bartok-phd}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(PhD thesis of Bartok)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{quip} style that
specifies a QUIP potential file containing the parameters of the
potential for all needed elements in XML format. This is followed by a
QUIP initialization string. Finally, the QUIP elements are mapped to
LAMMPS atom types by specifying N atomic numbers, where N is the
number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
QUIP filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
QUIP initialization string

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N atomic numbers = mapping of QUIP elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A QUIP potential is fully specified by the filename which contains the
parameters of the potential in XML format, the initialization string,
and the map of atomic numbers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
GAP potentials can be obtained from the \sphinxhref{https://libatoms.github.io/GAP/data.html}{GAP models and databases page
on the libAtoms homepage \textasciigrave{}https://libatoms.github.io}, where the appropriate
initialization strings are also advised. The list of atomic numbers must
be matched to the LAMMPS atom types specified in the LAMMPS data file or
elsewhere.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Two examples input scripts are provided in the examples/PACKAGES/quip
directory.


\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
mix, shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the ML\sphinxhyphen{}QUIP package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
QUIP potentials are parameterized in electron\sphinxhyphen{}volts and Angstroms and
therefore should be used with LAMMPS metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
QUIP potentials are generally not designed to work with the scaling
factors set by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} command.  The
recommended setting in molecular systems is to include all
interactions, i.e. to use \sphinxstyleemphasis{special\_bonds lj/coul 1.0 1.0 1.0}. Scaling
factors \textgreater{} 0.0 will be ignored and treated as 1.0. The only exception
to this rule is if you know that your QUIP potential needs to exclude
bonded, 1\sphinxhyphen{}3, or 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 interactions and does not already do this exclusion
within QUIP. Then a factor 0.0 needs to be used which will remove such
pairs from the neighbor list. This needs to be very carefully tested,
because it may remove pairs from the neighbor list that are still
required.

\label{\detokenize{pair_quip:related-commands}}

{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}

\index{pair\_style rann@\spxentry{pair\_style rann}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style rann command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:pair-style-rann-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_rann::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rann}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Type1\PYGZus{}element}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Type2\PYGZus{}element}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Type3\PYGZus{}element...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rann}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Mg.rann}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Mg}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{MgAlalloy.rann}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Mg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Mg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Mg}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{rann} computes pairwise interactions for a variety of
materials using rapid atomistic neural network (RANN) potentials
({\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rann:dickel}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Dickel}}}} , {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rann:nitol}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Nitol}}}}).  Neural network
potentials work by first generating a series of symmetry functions
i.e. structural fingerprints from the neighbor list and then using these
values as the input layer of a neural network.  There is a single output
neuron in the final layer which is the energy.  Atomic forces are found
by analytical derivatives computed via back\sphinxhyphen{}propagation.  For alloy
systems, each element has a unique network.


\subsection{Potential file syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:potential-file-syntax}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The RANN potential is defined by a single text file which contains all
the fitting parameters for the alloy system.  The potential file also
defines the active fingerprints, network architecture, activation
functions, etc.  The potential file is divided into several sections
which are identified by one of the following keywords:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
atomtypes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
mass

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fingerprintsperelement

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fingerprints

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
fingerprintconstants

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
screening (optional)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
networklayers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
layersize

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
weight

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bias

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
activationfunctions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
calibrationparameters (ignored)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ‘\#’ character is treated as a comment marker, similar to LAMMPS
input scripts.  Sections are not required to follow a rigid ordering,
but do require previous definition of prerequisite information.  E.g.,
fingerprintconstants for a particular fingerprint must follow the
fingerprints definition; layersize for a particular layer must follow
the declaration of network layers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{atomtypes} are defined as follows using element keywords separated by spaces.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
atomtypes:
Fe Mg Al etc.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mass} must be specified for each element keyword as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
mass:Mg:
24.305
mass:Fe:
55.847
mass:Al:
26.982
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fingerprintsperelement} specifies how many fingerprints are active for
computing the energy of a given atom.  This number must be specified for
each element keyword.  Active elements for each fingerprint depend upon
the type of the central atom and the neighboring atoms.  Pairwise
fingerprints may be defined for a Mg atom based exclusively on its Al
neighbors, for example.  Bond fingerprints may use two neighbor lists of
different element types.  In computing fingerprintsperelement from all
defined fingerprints, only the fingerprints defined for atoms of a
particular element should be considered, regardless of the elements used
in its neighbor list.  In the following code, for example, some
fingerprints may compute pairwise fingerprints summing contributions
about Fe atoms based on a neighbor list of exclusively Al atoms, but if
there are no fingerprints summing contributions of all neighbors about a
central Al atom, then fingerprintsperelement of Al is zero:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
fingerprintsperelement:Mg:
5
fingerprintsperelement:Fe:
2
fingerprintsperelement:Al:
0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fingerprints} specifies the active fingerprints for a certain element
combination.  Pair fingerprints are specified for two elements, while
bond fingerprints are specified for three elements.  Only one
fingerprints header should be used for an individual combination of
elements.  The ordering of the fingerprints in the network input layer
is determined by the order of element combinations specified by
subsequent \sphinxstyleemphasis{fingerprints} lines, and the order of the fingerprints
defined for each element combination.  Multiple fingerprints of the same
style or different ones may be specified.  If the same style and element
combination is used for multiple fingerprints, they should have
different id numbers.  The first element specifies the atoms for which
this fingerprint is computed while the other(s) specify which atoms to
use in the neighbor lists for the computation.  Switching the second and
third element type in bond fingerprints has no effect on the
computation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
fingerprints:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:
radial\PYGZus{}0 radialscreened\PYGZus{}0 radial\PYGZus{}1
fingerprints:Mg\PYGZus{}Al\PYGZus{}Fe:
bond\PYGZus{}0 bondspin\PYGZus{}0
fingerprints:Mg\PYGZus{}Al:
radial\PYGZus{}0 radialscreened\PYGZus{}0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following fingerprint styles are currently defined.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rann:fingerprints}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{formulation section}}}} below for their definitions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
radial

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
radialscreened

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
radialspin

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
radialscreenedspin

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bond

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bondscreened

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bondspin

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
bondscreenedspin

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fingerprintconstants}  specifies the meta\sphinxhyphen{}parameters for a defined fingerprint.  For all radial styles, re, rc,
alpha, dr, o, and n must be specified.  re should usually be the stable interatomic distance, rc is the cutoff
radius, dr is the cutoff smoothing distance, o is the lowest radial power term (which may be negative), and n
is the highest power term.  The total length of the fingerprint vector is (n\sphinxhyphen{}o+1).  alpha is a list of decay parameters
used for exponential decay of radial contributions.  It may be set proportionally to the bulk modulus similarly
to MEAM potentials, but other values may provided better fitting in special cases.  Bond style fingerprints require
specification of re, rc, alphak, dr, k, and m.  Here m is the power of the bond cosines and k is the number of
decay parameters.  Cosine powers go from 0 to m\sphinxhyphen{}1 and are each computed for all values of alphak.  Thus the total
length of the fingerprint vector is m*k.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
fingerprintconstants:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:radialscreened\PYGZus{}0:re:
3.193592
fingerprintconstants:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:radialscreened\PYGZus{}0:rc:
6.000000
fingerprintconstants:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:radialscreened\PYGZus{}0:alpha:
5.520000 5.520000 5.520000 5.520000 5.520000
fingerprintconstants:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:radialscreened\PYGZus{}0:dr:
2.806408
fingerprintconstants:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:radialscreened\PYGZus{}0:o:
\PYGZhy{}1
fingerprintconstants:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:radialscreened\PYGZus{}0:n:
3
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{screening} specifies the Cmax and Cmin values used in the screening
fingerprints. Contributions form neighbors to the fingerprint are
omitted if they are blocked by a closer neighbor, and reduced if they
are partially blocked.  Larger values of Cmin correspond to neighbors
being blocked more easily.  Cmax cannot be greater than 3, and Cmin
cannot be greater than Cmax or less than zero.  Screening may be omitted
in which case the default values Cmax = 2.8, Cmin = 0.8 are used.  Since
screening is a bond computation, it is specified separately for each
combination of three elements in which the latter two may be
interchanged with no effect.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
screening:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:Cmax:
2.700000
screening:Mg\PYGZus{}Mg\PYGZus{}Mg:Cmin:
0.400000
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{networklayers} species the size of the neural network for each atom.
It counts both the input and output layer and so is 2 + \textless{}hidden layers\textgreater{}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
networklayers:Mg:
3
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{layersize} specifies the length of each layer, including the input
layer and output layer.  The input layer is layer 0.  The size of the
input layer size must match the summed length of all the fingerprints
for that element, and the output layer size must be 1:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
layersize:Mg:0:
14
layersize:Mg:1:
20
layersize:Mg:2:
1
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} specifies the weight for a given element and layer.  Weight
cannot be specified for the output layer.  The weight of layer i is a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{m} x \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} matrix where \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} is the layer size of \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} is the layer size of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i}+1:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
weight:Mg:0:
w11 w12 w13 ...
w21 w22 w23 ...
...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bias} specifies the bias for a given element and layer.  Bias cannot be
specified for the output layer.  The bias of layer i is a nx1 vector
where n is the layer size of i+1:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
bias:Mg:0:
b1
b2
b3
...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{activationfunctions} specifies the activation function for a given
element and layer.  Activation functions cannot be specified for the
output layer:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
activationfunctions:Mg:0:
sigI
activationfunctions:Mg:1:
linear
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following activation styles are currently specified.  See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rann:activations}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{formulation section}}}} below for their definitions.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
sigI

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
linear

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{calibrationparameters} specifies a number of parameters used to calibrate the potential. These are ignored
by LAMMPS.


\subsection{Formulation}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:formulation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In the RANN formulation, the total energy of a system of atoms
is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \sum_{\alpha} E^{\alpha}\\\\
E^{\alpha} = {}^{N}\!A^{\alpha}\\\\
{}^{n+1}\!A_i^{\alpha} = {}^{n}\!F\left({}^{n}\!W_{ij}{\;}^{n}\!A_j^{\alpha}+{}^{n}\!B_i\right)\\\\
{}^{0}\!A_i^{\alpha} = \left[\begin{array}{c} {}^1\!S\!f^\alpha\\ {}^2\!S\!f^\alpha \\...\\\end{array}\right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here \(E^\alpha\) is the energy of atom \(\alpha\),
\({}^n\!F()\), \({}^n\!W_{ij}\) and \({}^n\!B_i\) are the
activation function, weight matrix and bias vector of the n\sphinxhyphen{}th layer
respectively.  The inputs to the first layer are a collection of
structural fingerprints which are collected and reshaped into a single
long vector.  The individual fingerprints may be defined in any order
and have various shapes and sizes.  Multiple fingerprints of the same
type and varying parameters may also be defined in the input layer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Eight types of structural fingerprints are currently defined.  In the
following, \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) span the full neighbor list
of atom \(\alpha\).  \(\delta_i\) are decay meta\sphinxhyphen{}parameters, and
\(r_e\) is a meta\sphinxhyphen{}parameter roughly proportional to the first
neighbor distance.  \(r_c\) and \(dr\) are the neighbor cutoff
distance and cutoff smoothing distance respectively.
\(S^{\alpha\beta}\) is the MEAM screening function {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rann:baskes97}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Baskes)}}}}, \(s_i^\alpha\) and \(s_i^\beta\) are the atom spin
vectors {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rann:tranchida7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tranchida)}}}}.  \(r^{\alpha\beta}\) is the
distance from atom \(\alpha\) to atom \(\beta\), and
\(\theta^{\alpha\beta\gamma}\) is the bond angle:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}cos\left(\theta^{\alpha\beta\gamma}\right)=\frac{\mathbf{r}^{\alpha\beta} \cdot \mathbf{r}^{\alpha\gamma}}{r^{\alpha\beta}r^{\alpha\gamma}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(S^{\alpha\beta}\) is defined as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_rann:baskes97}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Baskes)}}}}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}X^{\gamma\beta} = \left(\frac{r^{\gamma\beta}}{r^{\alpha\beta}}\right)^2\\
\\
X^{\alpha\gamma} = \left(\frac{r^{\alpha\gamma}}{r^{\alpha\beta}}\right)^2\\
\\
C = \frac{2\left(X^{\alpha\gamma}+X^{\gamma\beta}\right)-\left(X^{\alpha\gamma}-X^{\gamma\beta}\right)^2-1}{1-\left(X^{\alpha\gamma}-X^{\gamma\beta}\right)^2}\\
\\
f_c(x) = \left[\begin{array}{l}  1 \; \: x \geq 1\\ \left(1-\left(1-x\right)^4\right)^2 \; \: 0<x<1\\0\; \; x\leq0\end{array}\right.\\
\\
S^{\alpha\beta\gamma} = f_c\left(\frac{C-C_{min}}{C_{max}-C_{min}}\right)\\
\\
S^{\alpha\beta} = \prod_\gamma S^{\alpha\beta\gamma}\\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The structural fingerprints are computed as follows:

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:fingerprints}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{radial}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^r\!S\!f_i^\alpha = \sum_{\beta} \left(\frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}\right)^ie^{-\delta_i \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{bond}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^b\!S\!f_{ij}^\alpha = \sum_{\beta}\sum_{\gamma} \left(cos(\theta_{\alpha\beta\gamma})\right)^ie^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}e^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\gamma}}{r_e}}f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\gamma}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{radialscreened}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^{rsc}\!S\!f_i^\alpha = \sum_{\beta} \left(\frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}\right)^ie^{-\delta_i \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}S^{\alpha\beta}f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{bondscreened}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^{bsc}\!S\!f_{ij}^\alpha = \sum_{\beta}\sum_{\gamma} \left(cos(\theta_{\alpha\beta\gamma})\right)^ie^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}e^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\gamma}}{r_e}}S^{\alpha\beta}S^{\alpha\gamma}f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\gamma}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{radialspin}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^{rsp}\!S\!f_i^\alpha = \sum_{\beta} \left(\frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}\right)^ie^{-\delta_i \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}\left(\mathbf{s^\alpha \cdot s^\beta}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{bondspin}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^{bsp}\!S\!f_{ij}^\alpha = \sum_{\beta}\sum_{\gamma} \left(cos(\theta_{\alpha\beta\gamma})\right)^ie^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}e^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\gamma}}{r_e}}\left(\mathbf{s^\alpha \cdot s^\beta}\right)\left(\mathbf{s^\alpha \cdot s^\gamma}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\gamma}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{radialscreenedspin}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^{rscsp}\!S\!f_i^\alpha = \sum_{\beta} \left(\frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}\right)^ie^{-\delta_i \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}S^{\alpha\beta}\left(\mathbf{s^\alpha \cdot s^\beta}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{bondscreenedspin}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}{}^{bscsp}\!S\!f_{ij}^\alpha = \sum_{\beta}\sum_{\gamma} \left(cos(\theta_{\alpha\beta\gamma})\right)^ie^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\beta}}{r_e}}e^{-\delta_j \frac{r^{\alpha\gamma}}{r_e}}S^{\alpha\beta}S^{\alpha\gamma}\left(\mathbf{s^\alpha \cdot s^\beta}\right)\left(\mathbf{s^\alpha \cdot s^\gamma}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\beta}}{dr}\right)f_c\left(\frac{r_c-r^{\alpha\gamma}}{dr}\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The activation functions are computed as follows:

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:activations}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{sigI}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F^{sigI}(x) = 0.1x+0.9ln\left(e^x+1\right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{linear}

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F^{linear}(x) = x\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{rann} is part of the ML\sphinxhyphen{}RANN package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that
package.  Additionally, if any spin fingerprint styles are used LAMMPS must be built with the SPIN
package as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{rann} does not support computing per\sphinxhyphen{}atom stress or using {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify nofdotr}}}}.


\subsection{Defaults}
\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:defaults}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Cmin = 0.8, Cmax = 2.8.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:baskes97}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Baskes)} Baskes, Materials Chemistry and Physics, 50(2), 152\sphinxhyphen{}158, (1997).

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:dickel}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Dickel)} Dickel, Francis, and Barrett, Computational Materials Science 171 (2020): 109157.

\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{pair_rann:nitol}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Nitol)} Nitol, Dickel, and Barrett, Computational Materials Science 188 (2021): 110207.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{(Tranchida)} Tranchida, Plimpton, Thibaudeau and Thompson, Journal of Computational Physics, 372, 406\sphinxhyphen{}425, (2018).
