\section{pair\_style smd/tri\_surface command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_triangulated_surface:pair-style-smd-tri-surface-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_triangulated_surface:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_triangulated_surface::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_triangulated_surface:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{smd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tri\PYGZus{}surface}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{scale\PYGZus{}factor}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_triangulated_surface:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{smd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{tri\PYGZus{}surface}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{contact\PYGZus{}stiffness}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_triangulated_surface:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{smd/tri\_surface} style calculates contact forces between SPH
particles and a rigid wall boundary defined via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_smd_wall_surface::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{smd/wall\_surface}}}} fix.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The contact forces are calculated using a Hertz potential, which
evaluates the overlap between a particle (whose spatial extents are
defined via its contact radius) and the triangle.  The effect is that
a particle cannot penetrate into the triangular surface.  The
parameter \textless{}contact\_stiffness\textgreater{} has units of pressure and should equal
roughly one half of the Young’s modulus (or bulk modulus in the case
of fluids) of the material model associated with the SPH particle

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale\_factor} can be used to scale the particles’
contact radii. This can be useful to control how close particles can
approach the triangulated surface. Usually, \sphinxstyleemphasis{scale\_factor} =1.0.

\section{pair\_style smd/ulsph command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_ulsph:pair-style-smd-ulsph-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_ulsph:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_ulsph::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
these keywords must be given

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{*DENSITY\_SUMMATION} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{*DENSITY\_CONTINUITY} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{*VELOCITY\_GRADIENT} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{*NO\_VELOCITY\_GRADIENT} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{*GRADIENT\_CORRECTION} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{*NO\_GRADIENT\_CORRECTION}
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smd_ulsph:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{smd/ulsph} style computes particle interactions according to
continuum mechanics constitutive laws and an updated Lagrangian
Smooth\sphinxhyphen{}Particle Hydrodynamics algorithm.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is invoked similar to the following command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{smd}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{ulsph}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{DENSITY\PYGZus{}CONTINUITY}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{VELOCITY\PYGZus{}GRADIENT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{NO\PYGZus{}GRADIENT\PYGZus{}CORRECTION}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{COMMON}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rho0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{c0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Q1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Cp}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hg}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{               }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{END}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} denote the \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAMMPS} particle types for which this
pair style is defined. Note that \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j} can be different, i.e.,
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ulsph} cross interactions between different particle types are
allowed. However, \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}\textendash{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{i} respectively \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}\textendash{}\sphinxstyleemphasis{j} pair\_coeff lines have
to precede a cross interaction.  In contrast to the usual \sphinxstyleemphasis{LAMMPS}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{pair coeff} definitions, which are given solely a number of floats
and integers, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ulsph} \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair coeff} definition is organized using
keywords. These keywords mark the beginning of different sets of
parameters for particle properties, material constitutive models, and
damage models. The \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair coeff} line must be terminated with the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{*END} keyword. The use the line continuation operator \sphinxstyleemphasis{\&} is
recommended. A typical invocation of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ulsph} for a solid body
would consist of an equation of state for computing the pressure (the
diagonal components of the stress tensor), and a material model to
compute shear stresses (the off\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal components of the stress
tensor).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the use of *GRADIENT\_CORRECTION can lead to severe numerical
instabilities. For a general fluid simulation, *NO\_GRADIENT\_CORRECTION
is recommended.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Please see the \sphinxhref{PDF/MACHDYN\_LAMMPS\_userguide.pdf}{SMD user guide} for a
complete listing of the possible keywords and material models.

\index{pair\_style smtbq@\spxentry{pair\_style smtbq}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style smtbq command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq:pair-style-smtbq-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{smtbq}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{smtbq}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ffield.smtbq.Al2O3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Al}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style computes a variable charge SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q (Second\sphinxhyphen{}Moment
tight\sphinxhyphen{}Binding QEq) potential as described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:smtb-q-1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q\_1}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:smtb-q-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q\_2}}}}.
This potential was first proposed in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:smtb-q-0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q\_0}}}}.
Briefly, the energy of metallic\sphinxhyphen{}oxygen systems is given by three contributions:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{tot} & =  E_{ES} + E_{OO} + E_{MO} \\
E_{ES}  & =  \sum_i{\biggl[ \chi_{i}^{0}Q_i + \frac{1}{2}J_{i}^{0}Q_{i}^{2} +
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j\neq i}{ J_{ij}(r_{ij})f_{cut}^{R_{coul}}(r_{ij})Q_i Q_j } \biggr] } \\
E_{OO}  & =  \sum_{i,j}^{i,j = O}{\biggl[Cexp( -\frac{r_{ij}}{\rho} ) - Df_{cut}^{r_1^{OO}r_2^{OO}}(r_{ij}) exp(Br_{ij})\biggr]}  \\
E_{MO}  & =  \sum_i{E_{cov}^{i} + \sum_{j\neq i}{ Af_{cut}^{r_{c1}r_{c2}}(r_{ij})exp\bigl[-p(\frac{r_{ij}}{r_0} -1) \bigr] } }\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(E_{tot}\) is the total potential energy of the system,
\(E_{ES}\) is the electrostatic part of the total energy,
\(E_{OO}\) is the interaction between oxygen atoms and
\(E_{MO}\) is a short\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction between metal and oxygen
atoms. This interactions depend on interatomic distance \(r_{ij}\)
and/or the charge \(Q_{i}\) of atoms \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}. Cut\sphinxhyphen{}off function enables
smooth convergence to zero interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters appearing in the upper expressions are set in the
ffield.SMTBQ.Syst file where Syst corresponds to the selected system
(e.g. field.SMTBQ.Al2O3). Examples for \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\),
\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) are provided.  A single pair\_coeff command
is used with the SMTBQ styles which provides the path to the potential
file with parameters for needed elements. These are mapped to LAMMPS
atom types by specifying additional arguments after the potential
filename in the pair\_coeff command. Note that atom type 1 must always
correspond to oxygen atoms. As an example, to simulate a \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\) system,
atom type 1 has to be oxygen and atom type 2 Ti. The following
pair\_coeff command should then be used:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{PathToLammps}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{potentials}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{ffield.smtbq.TiO2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{O}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ti}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The electrostatic part of the energy consists of two components

\sphinxAtStartPar
self\sphinxhyphen{}energy of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} in the form of a second order charge dependent
polynomial and a long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic electrostatic interaction. The
latter uses the wolf summation method described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:wolf2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Wolf}}}},
spherically truncated at a longer cutoff, \(R_{coul}\). The
charge of each ion is modeled by an orbital Slater which depends on
the principal quantum number (\sphinxstyleemphasis{n}) of the outer orbital shared by the
ion.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Interaction between oxygen, \(E_{OO}\), consists of two parts,
an attractive and a repulsive part. The attractive part is effective
only at short range (\textless{} \(r_2^{OO}\)). The attractive
contribution was optimized to study surfaces reconstruction
(e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:smtb-q-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q\_2}}}} in \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\)) and is not necessary
for oxide bulk modeling. The repulsive part is the Pauli interaction
between the electron clouds of oxygen. The Pauli repulsion and the
coulombic electrostatic interaction have same cut off value. In the
ffield.SMTBQ.Syst, the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{‘buck’} allows to consider only the
repulsive O\sphinxhyphen{}O interactions. The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{‘buckPlusAttr’} allows to
consider the repulsive and the attractive O\sphinxhyphen{}O interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The short\sphinxhyphen{}range interaction between metal\sphinxhyphen{}oxygen, \(E_{MO}\) is
based on the second moment approximation of the density of states with
a N\sphinxhyphen{}body potential for the band energy term,
\(E^i_{cov}\), and a Born\sphinxhyphen{}Mayer type repulsive terms
as indicated by the keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{‘second\_moment’} in the
ffield.SMTBQ.Syst. The energy band term is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E_{cov}^{i(i=M,O)} & = - \biggl\{\eta_i(\mu \xi^{0})^2 f_{cut}^{r_{c1}r_{c2}}(r_{ij})
\biggl( \sum_{j(j=O,M)}{ exp[ -2q(\frac{r_{ij}}{r_0} - 1)] } \biggr)
\delta Q_i \bigl( 2\frac{n_0}{\eta_i} - \delta Q_i \bigr) \biggr\}^{1/2} \\
\delta Q_i & =  | Q_i^{F} | - | Q_i |\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\eta_i\) is the stoichiometry of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i},
\(\delta Q_i\) is the charge delocalization of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i},
compared to its formal charge
\(Q^F_i\). \(n_0\), the number of hybridized
orbitals, is calculated with to the atomic orbitals shared
\(d_i\) and the stoichiometry
\(\eta_i\). \(r_{c1}\) and \(r_{c2}\) are the two
cutoff radius around the fourth neighbors in the cutoff function.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the formalism used here, \(\xi^0\) is the energy
parameter. \(\xi^0\) is in tight\sphinxhyphen{}binding approximation the
hopping integral between the hybridized orbitals of the cation and the
anion. In the literature we find many ways to write the hopping
integral depending on whether one takes the point of view of the anion
or cation. These are equivalent vision. The correspondence between the
two visions is explained in appendix A of the article in the
SrTiO3 {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:smtb-q-3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q\_3}}}} (parameter \(\beta\) shown in
this article is in fact the \(\beta_O\)). To summarize the
relationship between the hopping integral \(\xi^O\)  and the
others, we have in an oxide \(\mathrm{C_n O_m}\) the following
relationship:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\xi^0 & = \frac{\xi_O}{m} = \frac{\xi_C}{n} \\
\frac{\beta_O}{\sqrt{m}} & = \frac{\beta_C}{\sqrt{n}} = \xi^0 \frac{\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}}{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus parameter \(\mu\), indicated above, is given by \(\mu = \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{m})\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential offers the possibility to consider the polarizability of
the electron clouds of oxygen by changing the slater radius of the
charge density around the oxygen atoms through the parameters \sphinxstyleemphasis{rBB, rB and
rS} in the ffield.SMTBQ.Syst. This change in radius is performed
according to the method developed by E. Maras
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:smtb-q-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q\_2}}}}. This method needs to determine the number of
nearest neighbors around the oxygen. This calculation is based on
first (\(r_{1n}\)) and second (\(r_{2n}\)) distances
neighbors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q potential is a variable charge potential. The equilibrium
charge on each atom is calculated by the electronegativity
equalization (QEq) method. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_smtbq:rick3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Rick}}}} for further detail. One
can adjust the frequency, the maximum number of iterative loop and the
convergence of the equilibrium charge calculation. To obtain the
energy conservation in NVE thermodynamic ensemble, we recommend to use
a convergence parameter in the interval 10e\sphinxhyphen{}5 \sphinxhyphen{}
10e\sphinxhyphen{}6 eV.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The ffield.SMTBQ.Syst files are provided for few systems. They consist
of nine parts and the lines beginning with ‘\#’ are comments (note that
the number of comment lines matter). The first sections are on the
potential parameters and others are on the simulation options and
might be modified. Keywords are character type and must be enclosed in
quotation marks (‘’).
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Number of different element in the oxide:

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N\_elem= 2 or 3

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Atomic parameters

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the anion (oxygen)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Name of element (char) and stoichiometry in oxide

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Formal charge and mass of element

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Principal quantum number of outer orbital n), electronegativity (\(\chi^0_i\)) and hardness (\(J^0_i\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ionic radius parameters  : max coordination number (\sphinxstyleemphasis{coordBB} = 6 by default), bulk coordination number \sphinxstyleemphasis{(coordB)}, surface coordination number  \sphinxstyleemphasis{(coordS)} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rBB, rB and rS}  the slater radius for each coordination number. (\sphinxstylestrong{note : If you don’t want to change the slater radius, use three identical radius values})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Number of orbital shared by the element in the oxide (\(d_i\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For each cations (metal):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Name of element (char) and stoichiometry in oxide

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Formal charge and mass of element

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Number of electron in outer orbital \sphinxstyleemphasis{(ne)}, electronegativity (\(\chi^0_i\)), hardness (\(J^0_i\)) and \(r_{Slater}\) the slater radius for the cation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Number of orbitals shared by the elements in the oxide (\(d_i\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Potential parameters:

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keyword for element1, element2 and interaction potential
(‘second\_moment’ or ‘buck’ or ‘buckPlusAttr’) between element 1
and 2.  If the potential is ‘second\_moment’, specify ‘oxide’ or
‘metal’ for metal\sphinxhyphen{}oxygen or metal\sphinxhyphen{}metal interactions respectively.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Potential parameter:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If type of potential is ‘second\_moment’ : A (eV), \sphinxstyleemphasis{p},
\(\zeta^0\) (eV) and \sphinxstyleemphasis{q}, \(r_{c1} (\AA)\), \(r_{c2}
(\AA)\) and \(r_0 (\AA)\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If type of potential is ‘buck’ : \sphinxstyleemphasis{C} (eV) and \(\rho (\AA)\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If type of potential is ‘buckPlusAttr’ : \sphinxstyleemphasis{C} (eV) and \(\rho
(\AA)\) \sphinxstyleemphasis{D} (eV), \sphinxstyleemphasis{B} \((\AA^{-1})\), \(r^{OO}_1 (\AA)\) and
\(r^{OO}_2 (\AA)\)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tables parameters:

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Cutoff radius for the Coulomb interaction (\(R_{coul}\))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Starting radius (\(r_{min} = 1,18845 \AA\)) and increments
(\(dr = 0.001 \AA\)) for creating the potential table.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rick model parameter:

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} : parameter to set the frequency of the charge
resolution. The charges are evaluated each \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nevery} time steps.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Max number of iterative loop (\sphinxstyleemphasis{loopmax}) and convergence criterion
(\sphinxstyleemphasis{prec}) in eV of the charge resolution

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Coordination parameter:

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
First (\(r_{1n}\)) and second (\(r_{2n}\)) neighbor distances
in angstroms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Charge initialization mode:

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keyword (\sphinxstyleemphasis{QInitMode}) and initial oxygen charge
(\(Q_{init}\)). If keyword = ‘true’, all oxygen charges are
initially set equal to \(Q_{init}\). The charges on the cations
are initially set in order to respect the neutrality of the box. If
keyword = ‘false’, all atom charges are initially set equal to 0 if
you use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{create_atoms::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{create\_atoms}}}} command or the charge
specified in the file structure using {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
command.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{7}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Mode for the electronegativity equalization (Qeq)

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keyword (\sphinxstyleemphasis{mode}) followed by:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
QEqAll  (one QEq group) |   no parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
QEqAllParallel (several QEq groups) |   no parameters

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Surface |   zlim   (QEq only for z\textgreater{}zlim)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Parameter if necessary

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Divider line

\end{itemize}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{)}%
\setcounter{enumi}{8}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Verbose

\end{enumerate}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want the code to work in verbose mode or not : ‘true’ or ‘false’

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to print or not in the file ‘Energy\_component.txt’ the
three main contributions to the energy of the system according to the
description presented above : ‘true’ or ‘false’ and
\(N_{Energy}\). This option writes to the file every
\(N_{Energy}\) time steps. If the value is ‘false’ then
\(N_{Energy} = 0\). The file takes into account the possibility to
have several QEq groups \sphinxstyleemphasis{g} then it writes: time step, number of atoms
in group \sphinxstyleemphasis{g}, electrostatic part of energy, \(E_{ES}\), the
interaction between oxygen, \(E_{OO}\), and short range
metal\sphinxhyphen{}oxygen interaction, \(E_{MO}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you want to print to the file ‘Electroneg\_component.txt’ the
electronegativity component (\(\frac{\partial E_{tot}}{\partial
Q_i}\)) or not: ‘true’ or ‘false’ and \(N_{Electroneg}\). This
option writes to the file every \(N_{Electroneg}\) time steps. If
the value is ‘false’ then \(N_{Electroneg} = 0\).  The file
consist of atom number \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}, atom type (1 for oxygen and \# higher
than 1 for metal), atom position: \sphinxstyleemphasis{x}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{y} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{z}, atomic charge
of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}, electrostatic part of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} electronegativity,
covalent part of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} electronegativity, the hopping integral of
atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} \((Z\beta^2)_i\) and box electronegativity.

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This last option slows down the calculation dramatically.  Use
only with a single processor simulation.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
mix, shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
needs to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_smtbq:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the SMTBQ package and is only enabled
if LAMMPS is built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This potential requires using atom type 1 for oxygen and atom type
higher than 1 for metal atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on”
for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The SMTB\sphinxhyphen{}Q potential files provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials
directory) are parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.

\section{pair\_style snap command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:pair-style-snap-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_snap::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap/intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{snap}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{snap}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{InP.snapcoeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{InP.snapparam}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{In}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{In}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{P}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} defines the spectral neighbor analysis potential
(SNAP), a machine\sphinxhyphen{}learning interatomic potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap:thompson20142}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Thompson)}}}}.  Like the GAP framework of Bartok et
al. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap:bartok20102}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bartok2010)}}}}, SNAP uses bispectrum components
to characterize the local neighborhood of each atom in a very general
way. The mathematical definition of the bispectrum calculation and its
derivatives w.r.t. atom positions is identical to that used by
{\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute snap}}}}, which is used to fit SNAP
potentials to \sphinxstyleemphasis{ab initio} energy, force, and stress data.  In SNAP, the
total energy is decomposed into a sum over atom energies. The energy of
atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} is expressed as a weighted sum over bispectrum components.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E^i_{SNAP}(B_1^i,...,B_K^i) = \beta^{\mu_i}_0 + \sum_{k=1}^K \beta_k^{\mu_i} B_k^i\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(B_k^i\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{k}\sphinxhyphen{}th bispectrum component of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i},
and \(\beta_k^{\mu_i}\) is the corresponding linear coefficient that
depends on \(\mu_i\), the SNAP element of atom \sphinxstyleemphasis{i}. The number of
bispectrum components used and their definitions depend on the value of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{twojmax} and other parameters defined in the SNAP parameter file
described below.  The bispectrum calculation is described in more detail
in {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute sna/atom}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that unlike for other potentials, cutoffs for SNAP potentials are
not set in the pair\_style or pair\_coeff command; they are specified in
the SNAP potential files themselves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} style which
specifies a SNAP coefficient file followed by a SNAP parameter file
and then N additional arguments specifying the mapping of SNAP
elements to LAMMPS atom types, where N is the number of
LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SNAP coefficient file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SNAP parameter file

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of SNAP elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, if a LAMMPS indium phosphide simulation has 4 atoms
types, with the first two being indium and the third and fourth being
phophorous, the pair\_coeff command would look like this:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{snap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{InP.snapcoeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{InP.snapparam}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{In}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{In}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{P}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{P}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The two filenames are for the coefficient and parameter files, respectively.
The two trailing ‘In’ arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1 and 2 to the
SNAP ‘In’ element. The two trailing ‘P’ arguments map LAMMPS atom types
3 and 4 to the SNAP ‘P’ element.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a SNAP mapping value is specified as NULL, the mapping is not
performed.  This can be used when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} potential is used as part of
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.  The NULL values are placeholders for atom
types that will be used with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The name of the SNAP coefficient file usually ends in the “.snapcoeff”
extension. It may contain coefficients for many SNAP elements. The only
requirement is that each of the unique element names appearing in the
LAMMPS pair\_coeff command appear exactly once in the SNAP coefficient
file. It is okay if the SNAP coefficient file contains additional
elements not in the pair\_coeff command, except when using \sphinxstyleemphasis{chemflag}
(see below).  The name of the SNAP parameter file usually ends in the
“.snapparam” extension. It contains a small number of parameters that
define the overall form of the SNAP potential.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways to specify the path for these
files.

\sphinxAtStartPar
SNAP potentials are quite commonly combined with one or more other
LAMMPS pair styles using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/overlay} pair style.  As an
example, the SNAP tantalum potential provided in the LAMMPS potentials
directory combines the \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{zbl} pair styles. It is invoked by
the following commands:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{zblcutinner}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{zblcutouter}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.8}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{zblz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{73}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{n}{zbl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{zblcutinner}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{zblcutouter}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{snap}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zbl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zbl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{zblz}\PYG{n+nv}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{snap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta06A.snapcoeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta06A.snapparam}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Ta}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is convenient to keep these commands in a separate file that can be
inserted in any LAMMPS input script using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{include::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{include}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The top of the SNAP coefficient file can contain any number of blank and
comment lines (start with \#), but follows a strict format after
that. The first non\sphinxhyphen{}blank non\sphinxhyphen{}comment line must contain two integers:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
nelem  = Number of elements

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ncoeff = Number of coefficients

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is followed by one block for each of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelem} elements.
The first line of each block contains three entries:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Element name (text string)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
R = Element radius (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
w = Element weight (dimensionless)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This line is followed by \sphinxstyleemphasis{ncoeff} coefficients, one per line.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The SNAP parameter file can contain blank and comment lines (start
with \#) anywhere. Each non\sphinxhyphen{}blank non\sphinxhyphen{}comment line must contain one
keyword/value pair. The required keywords are \sphinxstyleemphasis{rcutfac} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{twojmax}. Optional keywords are \sphinxstyleemphasis{rfac0}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{rmin0},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{switchflag}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{bzeroflag}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadraticflag}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{chemflag},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bnormflag}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{wselfallflag},  \sphinxstyleemphasis{switchinnerflag},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{sinner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{dinner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{parallelthresh}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The default values for these keywords are
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rfac0} = 0.99363

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rmin0} = 0.0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{switchflag} = 1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bzeroflag} = 1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{quadraticflag} = 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{chemflag} = 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bnormflag} = 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{wselfallflag} = 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{switchinnerflag} = 0

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} = 32768

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{parallelthresh} = 8192

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For detailed definitions of all of these keywords,
see the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_sna_atom::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute sna/atom}}}} doc page.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadraticflag} is set to 1, then the SNAP energy expression includes
additional quadratic terms that have been shown to increase the overall
accuracy of the potential without much increase in computational cost
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap:wood20182}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wood)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E^i_{SNAP}(\mathbf{B}^i) = \beta^{\mu_i}_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mu_i} \cdot \mathbf{B}_i + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{B}^t_i \cdot \boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mu_i} \cdot \mathbf{B}_i\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\mathbf{B}_i\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}vector of bispectrum components,
\(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mu_i}\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}vector of linear
coefficients for element \(\mu_i\), and
\(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mu_i}\) is the symmetric \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} by \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} matrix
of quadratic coefficients.  The SNAP coefficient file should contain
\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}(\sphinxstyleemphasis{K}+1)/2 additional coefficients in each element block, the
upper\sphinxhyphen{}triangular elements of \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mu_i}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{chemflag} is set to 1, then the energy expression is written in
terms of explicit multi\sphinxhyphen{}element bispectrum components indexed on ordered
triplets of elements, which has been shown to increase the ability of
the SNAP potential to capture energy differences in chemically complex
systems, at the expense of a significant increase in computational cost
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_snap:cusentino20202}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Cusentino)}}}}.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E^i_{SNAP}(\mathbf{B}^i) = \beta^{\mu_i}_0 + \sum_{\kappa,\lambda,\mu} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\kappa\lambda\mu}_{\mu_i} \cdot \mathbf{B}^{\kappa\lambda\mu}_i\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\mathbf{B}^{\kappa\lambda\mu}_i\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}vector of
bispectrum components for neighbors of elements \(\kappa\),
\(\lambda\), and \(\mu\) and
\(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\kappa\lambda\mu}_{\mu_i}\) is the
corresponding \sphinxstyleemphasis{K}\sphinxhyphen{}vector of linear coefficients for element
\(\mu_i\). The SNAP coefficient file should contain a total of
\(K N_{elem}^3\) coefficients in each element block, where
\(N_{elem}\) is the number of elements in the SNAP coefficient file,
which must equal the number of unique elements appearing in the LAMMPS
pair\_coeff command, to avoid ambiguity in the number of coefficients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keyword \sphinxstyleemphasis{switchinnerflag} activates an additional switching function
that smoothly turns off contributions to the SNAP potential from neighbor
atoms at short separations. If \sphinxstyleemphasis{switchinnerflag} is set to 1 then
the additional keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{sinner} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{dinner} must also be provided.
Each of these is followed by \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelements} values, where \sphinxstyleemphasis{nelements}
is the number of unique elements appearing in appearing in the LAMMPS
pair\_coeff command. The element order should correspond to the order
in which elements first appear in the pair\_coeff command reading from
left to right.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The keywords \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{parallelthresh} are only applicable when
using the pair style \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap} with the KOKKOS package on GPUs and are
ignored otherwise.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} keyword controls the number of atoms
in each pass used to compute the bispectrum components and is used to
avoid running out of memory.  For example if there are 8192 atoms in the
simulation and the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} is set to 4096, the bispectrum
calculation will be broken up into two passes (running on a single GPU).
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{parallelthresh} keyword controls a crossover threshold for
performing extra parallelism.  For small systems, exposing additional
parallelism can be beneficial when there is not enough work to fully
saturate the GPU threads otherwise.  However, the extra parallelism also
leads to more divergence and can hurt performance when the system is
already large enough to saturate the GPU threads.  Extra parallelism
will be performed if the \sphinxstyleemphasis{chunksize} (or total number of atoms per GPU)
is smaller than \sphinxstyleemphasis{parallelthresh}.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The previously used \sphinxstyleemphasis{diagonalstyle} keyword was removed in 2019,
since all known SNAP potentials use the default value of 3.
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, where types I and J correspond to
two different element types, mixing is performed by LAMMPS with
user\sphinxhyphen{}specifiable parameters as described above.  You never need to
specify a pair\_coeff command with I != J arguments for this style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart
files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you need
to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_snap:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This style is part of the ML\sphinxhyphen{}SNAP package.  It is only enabled if LAMMPS
was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap/intel} accelerator variant will \sphinxstyleemphasis{only} be available if LAMMPS
is built with Intel \sphinxstyleemphasis{compilers} and for CPUs with AVX\sphinxhyphen{}512 support.
While the INTEL package in general allows multiple floating point
precision modes to be selected, \sphinxstyleemphasis{snap/intel} will currently always use
full double precision regardless of the precision mode selected.
Additionally, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel} variant of snap will \sphinxstylestrong{NOT} use multiple
threads with OpenMP.

\section{pair\_style soft command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:pair-style-soft-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:index-3}}\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_soft::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{soft/gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{soft/kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{soft/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{soft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff for soft interactions (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{soft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.0}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{soft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prefactor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ramp}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{0,30}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adapt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{soft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}prefactor}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{soft} computes pairwise interactions with the formula
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = A \left[ 1 + \cos\left(\frac{\pi r}{r_c}\right) \right]
\qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
It is useful for pushing apart overlapping atoms, since it does not
blow up as r goes to 0.  A is a prefactor that can be made to vary in
time from the start to the end of the run (see discussion below),
e.g. to start with a very soft potential and slowly harden the
interactions over time.  \(r_c\) is the cutoff.
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_limit::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/limit}}}} command for another way
to push apart overlapping atoms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atom types
via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples above,
or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last coefficient is optional.  If not specified, the global soft
cutoff is used.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The syntax for {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} with a single A
coeff is different in the current version of LAMMPS than in older
versions which took two values, Astart and Astop, to ramp between
them.  This functionality is now available in a more general form
through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} command, as explained below.
Note that if you use an old input script and specify Astart and Astop
without a cutoff, then LAMMPS will interpret that as A and a cutoff,
which is probably not what you want.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_adapt::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix adapt}}}} command can be used to vary A for one
or more pair types over the course of a simulation, in which case
pair\_coeff settings for A must still be specified, but will be
overridden.  For example these commands will vary the prefactor A for
all pairwise interactions from 0.0 at the beginning to 30.0 at the end
of a run:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{prefactor}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ramp}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{0,30}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{fix }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{all}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adapt}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pair}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{soft}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v\PYGZus{}prefactor}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that a formula defined by an {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{equal\sphinxhyphen{}style variable}}}}
can use the current timestep, elapsed time in the current run, elapsed
time since the beginning of a series of runs, as well as access other
variables.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the A coefficient and cutoff
distance for this pair style can be mixed.  A is always mixed via a
\sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric} rule.  The cutoff is mixed according to the pair\_modify
mix value.  The default mix value is \sphinxstyleemphasis{geometric}.  See the
“pair\_modify” command for details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift option, since the pair interaction goes to 0.0 at the cutoff.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table and tail options are not
relevant for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\label{\detokenize{pair_soft:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_heatconduction:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sph/heatconduction style computes heat transport between SPH particles.
The transport model is the diffusion equation for the internal energy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See \sphinxhref{PDF/SPH\_LAMMPS\_userguide.pdf}{this PDF guide} to using SPH in
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
D diffusion coefficient (length\textasciicircum{}2/time units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
h kernel function cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_heatconduction:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not support mixing.  Thus, coefficients for all
I,J pairs must be specified explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style does not write information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}.  Thus, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and
pair\_coeff commands in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\section{pair\_style sph/idealgas command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_idealgas:pair-style-sph-idealgas-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_idealgas:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_idealgas::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_idealgas:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sph}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{idealgas}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_idealgas:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sph}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{idealgas}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.4}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_idealgas:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sph/idealgas style computes pressure forces between particles
according to the ideal gas equation of state:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p = (\gamma - 1) \rho e\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\gamma = 1.4\) is the heat capacity ratio, \(\rho\) is
the local density, and e is the internal energy per unit mass.  This
pair style also computes Monaghan’s artificial viscosity to prevent
particles from interpenetrating {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sph_idealgas:ideal-monoghan}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Monaghan)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_lj:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sph/lj style computes pressure forces between particles according
to the Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones equation of state, which is computed according to
Ree’s 1980 polynomial fit {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sph_lj:ree}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ree)}}}}. The Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones parameters
epsilon and sigma are set to unity.  This pair style also computes
Monaghan’s artificial viscosity to prevent particles from
interpenetrating {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sph_lj:monoghan}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Monaghan)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See \sphinxhref{PDF/SPH\_LAMMPS\_userguide.pdf}{this PDF guide} to using SPH in
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\nu\) artificial viscosity (no units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
h kernel function cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_sph_taitwater:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The sph/taitwater style computes pressure forces between SPH particles
according to Tait’s equation of state:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p = B \biggl[\left(\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}\right)^{\gamma} - 1\biggr]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\gamma = 7\) and \(B = c_0^2 \rho_0 / \gamma\), with
\(\rho_0\) being the reference density and \(c_0\) the reference
speed of sound.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style also computes Monaghan’s artificial viscosity to
prevent particles from interpenetrating {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_sph_taitwater:monaghan}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Monaghan)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See \sphinxhref{PDF/SPH\_LAMMPS\_userguide.pdf}{this PDF guide} to using SPH in
LAMMPS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\rho_0\) reference density (mass/volume units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(c_0\) reference soundspeed (distance/time units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\nu\) artificial viscosity (no units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
h kernel function cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{args}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica/coul/long}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
args = list of arguments for a particular style

\end{itemize}
\begin{sphinxalltt}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica} args = cutoff
  cutoff = global cutoff for Lennard Jones interactions (distance units)
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica/coul/long} args = cutoff (cutoff2)
  cutoff = global cutoff for LJ (and Coulombic if only 1 arg) (distance units)
  cutoff2 = global cutoff for Coulombic (optional) (distance units)
\end{sphinxalltt}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spica:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spica}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.5}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj12\PYGZus{}6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.8}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spica}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spica}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj9\PYGZus{}6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spica}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{msm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{spica}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{msm}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lj9\PYGZus{}6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spica:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica} styles compute a 9/6, 12/4, 12/5, or 12/6 Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones potential,
given by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = & \frac{27}{4} \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{9} -
                      \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]
                      \qquad r < r_c \\
E = & \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
                      \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^4 \right]
                      \qquad r < r_c \\
E = & \frac{12}{7}\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)^{\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)} \epsilon
                      \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
                      \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^5 \right]
                      \qquad r < r_c \\
E = &  4 \epsilon  \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -
                      \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]
                      \qquad r < r_c\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as required for the SPICA (formerly called SDK) and the pSPICA Coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained MD parameterization discussed in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spica:shinoda3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Shinoda)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spica:devane}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(DeVane)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spica:seo}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Seo)}}}}, and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spica:miyazaki}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Miyazaki)}}}}.
\(r_c\) is the cutoff.
Summary information on these force fields can be found at \sphinxurl{https://www.spica-ff.org}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica/coul/long} computes the adds Coulombic interactions
with an additional damping factor applied so it can be used in
conjunction with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command and
its \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm/cg} option.  The Coulombic cutoff
specified for this style means that pairwise interactions within
this distance are computed directly; interactions outside that
distance are computed in reciprocal space.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands, or by mixing as described below:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cg\_type (lj9\_6, lj12\_4, lj12\_5, or lj12\_6)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
epsilon (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
sigma (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff1 (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that sigma is defined in the LJ formula as the zero\sphinxhyphen{}crossing
distance for the potential, not as the energy minimum. The prefactors
are chosen so that the potential minimum is at \sphinxhyphen{}epsilon.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The latter 2 coefficients are optional.  If not specified, the global
LJ and Coulombic cutoffs specified in the pair\_style command are used.
If only one cutoff is specified, it is used as the cutoff for both LJ
and Coulombic interactions for this type pair.  If both coefficients
are specified, they are used as the LJ and Coulombic cutoffs for this
type pair.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica/coul/long} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica/coul/msm} only the LJ cutoff can be
specified since a Coulombic cutoff cannot be specified for an
individual I,J type pair.  All type pairs use the same global
Coulombic cutoff specified in the pair\_style command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original implementation of the above styles are
style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/sdk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/sdk/coul/long}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/sdk/coul/msm},
and available for backward compatibility.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spica:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, the epsilon and sigma coefficients
and cutoff distance for all of the lj/spica pair styles \sphinxstyleemphasis{cannot} be mixed,
since different pairs may have different exponents. So all parameters
for all pairs have to be specified explicitly through the “pair\_coeff”
command. Defining then in a data file is also not supported, due to
limitations of that file format.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the lj/spica pair styles support the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift option for the energy of the
Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones portion of the pair interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica/coul/long} pair styles support the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option since they can tabulate
the short\sphinxhyphen{}range portion of the long\sphinxhyphen{}range Coulombic interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the lj/spica pair styles write their information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do
not need to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The lj/spica and lj/cut/coul/long pair styles do not support
the use of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, and \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spica:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
All of the lj/spica pair styles are part of the CG\sphinxhyphen{}SPICA package.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lj/spica/coul/long} style also requires the KSPACE package to be built
(which is enabled by default).  They are only enabled if LAMMPS was
built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}}
doc page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_spica::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style spica}}}}

\section{pair\_style spin/dipole/cut command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:pair-style-spin-dipole-cut-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole::doc}}

\section{pair\_style spin/dipole/long command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:pair-style-spin-dipole-long-command}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff for magnetic dipole energy and forces
(optional) (distance units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{8.0}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dipole}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{long}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{9.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/dipole/cut} computes a short\sphinxhyphen{}range dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole
interaction between pairs of magnetic particles that each
have a magnetic spin.
The magnetic dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions are computed by the
following formulas for the magnetic energy, magnetic precession
vector omega and mechanical force between particles I and J.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathcal{H}_{\rm long} & =
-\frac{\mu_{0} \left( \mu_B\right)^2}{4\pi}
\sum_{i,j,i\neq j}^{N}
 \frac{g_i g_j}{r_{ij}^3}
 \biggl(3
 \left(\vec{e}_{ij}\cdot \vec{s}_{i}\right)
 \left(\vec{e}_{ij}\cdot \vec{s}_{j}\right)
 -\vec{s}_i\cdot\vec{s}_j \biggr) \\
 \mathbf{\omega}_i & =
 \frac{\mu_0 (\mu_B)^2}{4\pi\hbar}\sum_{j}
 \frac{g_i g_j}{r_{ij}^3}
 \, \biggl(
 3\,(\vec{e}_{ij}\cdot\vec{s}_{j})\vec{e}_{ij}
 -\vec{s}_{j} \biggr) \\
 \mathbf{F}_i & =
 \frac{3\, \mu_0 (\mu_B)^2}{4\pi} \sum_j
 \frac{g_i g_j}{r_{ij}^4}
 \biggl[\bigl( (\vec{s}_i\cdot\vec{s}_j)
 -5(\vec{e}_{ij}\cdot\vec{s}_i)
 (\vec{e}_{ij}\cdot\vec{s}_j)\bigr) \vec{e}_{ij}+
 \bigl(
 (\vec{e}_{ij}\cdot\vec{s}_i)\vec{s}_j+
 (\vec{e}_{ij}\cdot\vec{s}_j)\vec{s}_i
 \bigr)
 \biggr]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\vec{s}_i\) and \(\vec{s}_j\) are the spin on two magnetic
particles, r is their separation distance, and the vector \(\vec{e}_{ij}
= \frac{r_i - r_j}{\left| r_i - r_j \right|}\) is the direction vector
between the two particles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/dipole/long} computes long\sphinxhyphen{}range magnetic dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole
interaction.
A {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} must be defined to
use this pair style.  Currently, {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style ewald/dipole/spin}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style pppm/dipole/spin}}}} support long\sphinxhyphen{}range magnetic
dipole\sphinxhyphen{}dipole interactions.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} table option is not relevant
for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
tail option for adding long\sphinxhyphen{}range tail corrections to energy and
pressure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands do not need
to be specified in an input script that reads a restart file.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dipole:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/dipole/cut} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/dipole/long} styles are part of
the SPIN package.  They are only enabled if LAMMPS was built with that
package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more
info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using dipole/spin pair styles with \sphinxstyleemphasis{electron} {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}} is not
currently supported.

{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_nve_spin::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix nve/spin}}}}

\index{pair\_style spin/dmi@\spxentry{pair\_style spin/dmi}}\ignorespaces 

\section{pair\_style spin/dmi command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:pair-style-spin-dmi-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dmi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{cutoff}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff = global cutoff pair (distance in metal units)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{spin}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{dmi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dmi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2.6}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.001}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dmi}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{4.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00109}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/dmi} computes the Dzyaloshinskii\sphinxhyphen{}Moriya (DM) interaction
between pairs of magnetic spins.
According to the expression reported in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:rohart}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rohart)}}}}, one has
the following DM energy:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{H}_{dm} = \sum_{{ i,j}=1,i\neq j}^{N}
\left( \vec{e}_{ij} \times \vec{D} \right)
\cdot\left(\vec{s}_{i}\times \vec{s}_{j}\right),\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\vec{s}_i\) and \(\vec{s}_j\) are two neighboring magnetic spins of
two particles, \(\vec{e}_ij = \frac{r_i - r_j}{\left| r_i - r_j \right|}\)
is the unit vector between sites \sphinxstyleemphasis{i} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{j}, and \(\vec{D}\) is the
DM vector defining the intensity (in eV) and the direction of the
interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:rohart}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Rohart)}}}}, \(\vec{D}\) is defined as the direction normal to the film oriented
from the high spin\sphinxhyphen{}orbit layer to the magnetic ultra\sphinxhyphen{}thin film.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The application of a spin\sphinxhyphen{}lattice Poisson bracket to this energy (as described
in {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:tranchida5}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tranchida)}}}}) allows to derive a magnetic torque omega, and a
mechanical force F (for spin\sphinxhyphen{}lattice calculations only) for each magnetic
particle i:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\vec{\omega}_i = -\frac{1}{\hbar} \sum_{j}^{Neighb} \vec{s}_{j}\times \left(\vec{e}_{ij}\times \vec{D} \right)
~~{\rm and}~~
\vec{F}_i = -\sum_{j}^{Neighb} \frac{1}{r_{ij}} \vec{D} \times \left( \vec{s}_{i}\times \vec{s}_{j} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
More details about the derivation of these torques/forces are reported in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_spin_dmi:tranchida5}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tranchida)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/dmi} pair style, the following coefficients must be defined for
each pair of atoms types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in
the examples above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands, and
set in the following order:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rc (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
|D| (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dx, Dy, Dz  (direction of D)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that rc is the radius cutoff of the considered DM interaction, |D| is
the norm of the DM vector (in eV), and Dx, Dy and Dz define its direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
None of those coefficients is optional.  If not specified, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spin/dmi}
pair style cannot be used.

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exchange}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.01575}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.965}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{offset}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{yes}
