\section{pair\_style table command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table:pair-style-table-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table:index-3}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap} = method of interpolation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = use N values in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} tables

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = use 2\textasciicircum{}N values in \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap} tables

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dispersion} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tip4p}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pppm}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{bitmap}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{12}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{morse.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ENTRY1}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{morse.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ENTRY1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{7.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} creates interpolation tables from potential energy and
force values listed in a file(s) as a function of distance.  When
performing dynamics or minimization, the interpolation tables are used
to evaluate energy and forces for pairwise interactions between
particles, similar to how analytic formulas are used for other pair
styles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interpolation tables are created as a pre\sphinxhyphen{}computation by fitting
cubic splines to the file values and interpolating energy and force
values at each of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} distances.  During a simulation, the tables are
used to interpolate energy and force values as needed for each pair of
particles separated by a distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{R}.  The interpolation is done in
one of 4 styles: \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup} style, the distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{R} is used to find the nearest
table entry, which is the energy or force.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} style, the distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{R} is used to find the 2
surrounding table values from which an energy or force is computed by
linear interpolation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} style, cubic spline coefficients are computed and
stored for each of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} values in the table, one set of splines for
energy, another for force.  Note that these splines are different than
the ones used to pre\sphinxhyphen{}compute the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} values.  Those splines were fit
to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfile} values in the tabulated file, where often \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfile} \textless{}
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N}.  The distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{R} is used to find the appropriate set of spline
coefficients which are used to evaluate a cubic polynomial which
computes the energy or force.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap} style, the specified \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} is used to create
interpolation tables that are 2\textasciicircum{}N in length.  The distance \sphinxstyleemphasis{R} is used
to index into the table via a fast bit\sphinxhyphen{}mapping technique due to
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_table:wolff2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wolff)}}}}, and a linear interpolation is performed between
adjacent table values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The filename specifies a file containing tabulated energy and force
values.  The keyword specifies a section of the file.  The cutoff is
an optional coefficient.  If not specified, the outer cutoff in the
table itself (see below) will be used to build an interpolation table
that extend to the largest tabulated distance.  If specified, only
file values up to the cutoff are used to create the interpolation
table.  The format of this file is described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If your tabulated potential(s) are designed to be used as the
short\sphinxhyphen{}range part of one of the long\sphinxhyphen{}range solvers specified by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{kspace_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{kspace\_style}}}} command, then you must use one or
more of the optional keywords listed above for the pair\_style command.
These are \sphinxstyleemphasis{ewald} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{pppm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{msm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{dispersion} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tip4p}.  This
is so LAMMPS can ensure the short\sphinxhyphen{}range potential and long\sphinxhyphen{}range
solver are compatible with each other, as it does for other
short\sphinxhyphen{}range pair styles, such as {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lj_cut_coul::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/cut/coul/long}}}}.  Note that it is up to you to ensure
the tabulated values for each pair of atom types has the correct
functional form to be compatible with the matching long\sphinxhyphen{}range solver.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are some guidelines for using the pair\_style table command to
best effect:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Vary the number of table points; you may need to use more than you think
to get good resolution.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Always use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command to produce a plot
of what the final interpolated potential looks like.  This can show up
interpolation “features” you may not like.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Start with the linear style; it’s the style least likely to have problems.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} in the pair\_style command equal to the “N” in the tabulation
file, and use the “RSQ” or “BITMAP” parameter, so additional interpolation
is not needed.  See discussion below.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Make sure that your tabulated forces and tabulated energies are
consistent (dE/dr = \sphinxhyphen{}F) over the entire range of r values.  LAMMPS
will warn if this is not the case.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use as large an inner cutoff as possible.  This avoids fitting splines
to very steep parts of the potential.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Suitable tables in the correct format for use with these pair styles can
be created by LAMMPS itself using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}}
command.  In combination with the pair styles {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_python::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{python}}}},
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_lepton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{lepton, or lepton/coul}}}} this can be a powerful
mechanism to implement and test tables for use with LAMMPS.  Another
option to generate tables is the Python code in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools/tabulate}}
folder of the LAMMPS source code distribution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of a tabulated file has an (optional) header followed by a
series of one or more sections, defined as follows (without the
parenthesized comments). The header must start with a \sphinxtitleref{\#} character
and the DATE: and UNITS: tags will be parsed and used:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} DATE: 2020\PYGZhy{}06\PYGZhy{}10  UNITS: real  CONTRIBUTOR: ... (header line)
\PYGZsh{} Morse potential for Fe   (one or more comment or blank lines)

MORSE\PYGZus{}FE                   (keyword is first text on line)
N 500 R 1.0 10.0           (N, R, RSQ, BITMAP, FPRIME parameters)
                           (blank)
1 1.0 25.5 102.34          (index, r, energy, force)
2 1.02 23.4 98.5
...
500 10.0 0.001 0.003
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A section begins with a non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line whose first character is not a
“\#”; blank lines or lines starting with “\#” can be used as comments
between sections.  The first line begins with a keyword which
identifies the section.  The line can contain additional text, but the
initial text must match the argument specified in the pair\_coeff
command.  The next line lists (in any order) one or more parameters
for the table.  Each parameter is a keyword followed by one or more
numeric values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter “N” is required and its value is the number of table
entries that follow.  Note that this may be different than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
specified in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style table}}}} command.  Let
Ntable = \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} in the pair\_style command, and Nfile = “N” in the
tabulated file.  What LAMMPS does is a preliminary interpolation by
creating splines using the Nfile tabulated values as nodal points.  It
uses these to interpolate energy and force values at Ntable different
points.  The resulting tables of length Ntable are then used as
described above, when computing energy and force for individual pair
distances.  This means that if you want the interpolation tables of
length Ntable to match exactly what is in the tabulated file (with
effectively no preliminary interpolation), you should set Ntable =
Nfile, and use the “RSQ” or “BITMAP” parameter.  This is because the
internal table abscissa is always RSQ (separation distance squared),
for efficient lookup.

\sphinxAtStartPar
All other parameters are optional.  If “R” or “RSQ” or “BITMAP” does
not appear, then the distances in each line of the table are used
as\sphinxhyphen{}is to perform spline interpolation.  In this case, the table values
can be spaced in \sphinxstyleemphasis{r} uniformly or however you wish to position table
values in regions of large gradients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If used, the parameters “R” or “RSQ” are followed by 2 values \sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi}.  If specified, the distance associated with each energy and
force value is computed from these 2 values (at high accuracy), rather
than using the (low\sphinxhyphen{}accuracy) value listed in each line of the table.
The distance values in the table file are ignored in this case.
For “R”, distances uniformly spaced between \sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi} are
computed; for “RSQ”, squared distances uniformly spaced between
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo*rlo} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi*rhi} are computed.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you use “R” or “RSQ”, the tabulated distance values in the
file are effectively ignored, and replaced by new values as described
in the previous paragraph.  If the distance value in the table is not
very close to the new value (i.e. round\sphinxhyphen{}off difference), then you will
be assigning energy/force values to a different distance, which is
probably not what you want.  LAMMPS will warn if this is occurring.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If used, the parameter “BITMAP” is also followed by 2 values \sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi}.  These values, along with the “N” value determine the ordering
of the N lines that follow and what distance is associated with each.
This ordering is complex, so it is not documented here, since this
file is typically produced by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command
with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap} option.  When the table is in BITMAP format, the “N”
parameter in the file must be equal to 2\textasciicircum{}M where M is the value
specified in the pair\_style command.  Also, a cutoff parameter cannot
be used as an optional third argument in the pair\_coeff command; the
entire table extent as specified in the file must be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If used, the parameter “FPRIME” is followed by 2 values \sphinxstyleemphasis{fplo} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fphi} which are the derivative of the force at the innermost and
outermost distances listed in the table.  These values are needed by
the spline construction routines.  If not specified by the “FPRIME”
parameter, they are estimated (less accurately) by the first 2 and
last 2 force values in the table.  This parameter is not used by
BITMAP tables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following a blank line, the next N lines list the tabulated values.
On each line, the first value is the index from 1 to N, the second value is
r (in distance units), the third value is the energy (in energy units),
and the fourth is the force (in force units).  The r values must increase
from one line to the next (unless the BITMAP parameter is specified).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that one file can contain many sections, each with a tabulated
potential.  LAMMPS reads the file section by section until it finds
one that matches the specified keyword.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support mixing.  Thus, coefficients for all
I,J pairs must be specified explicitly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}} shift, table, and tail options are
not relevant for this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style writes the settings for the “pair\_style table” command
to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so a pair\_style command does
not need to specified in an input script that reads a restart file.
However, the coefficient information is not stored in the restart
file, since it is tabulated in the potential files.  Thus, pair\_coeff
commands do need to be specified in the restart input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.

\section{pair\_style table/rx command}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table_rx:pair-style-table-rx-command}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table_rx:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table_rx:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{pair_table_rx::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/rx/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table_rx:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap} = method of interpolation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = use N values in \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} tables

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
weighting = fractional or molecular (optional)

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table_rx:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{fractional}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{rx}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{molecular}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rxn.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ENTRY1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{h2o}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{h2o}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rxn.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ENTRY1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{n}{fluid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rxn.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ENTRY1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{h2o}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{no2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_table_rx:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/rx} is used in reaction DPD simulations,where the
coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained (CG) particles are composed of \sphinxstyleemphasis{m} species whose
reaction rate kinetics are determined from a set of \sphinxstyleemphasis{n} reaction rate
equations through the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rx::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rx}}}} command.  The species of
one CG particle can interact with a species in a neighboring CG
particle through a site\sphinxhyphen{}site interaction potential model. Style
\sphinxstyleemphasis{table/rx} creates interpolation tables of length \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} from pair
potential and force values listed in a file(s) as a function of
distance.  The files are read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interpolation tables are created by fitting cubic splines to the
file values and interpolating energy and force values at each of \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
distances.  During a simulation, these tables are used to interpolate
energy and force values as needed.  The interpolation is done in one
of 4 styles: \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{lookup} style, the distance between two atoms is used to find
the nearest table entry, which is the energy or force.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} style, the pair distance is used to find 2
surrounding table values from which an energy or force is computed by
linear interpolation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} style, a cubic spline coefficients are computed and
stored at each of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} values in the table.  The pair distance is
used to find the appropriate set of coefficients which are used to
evaluate a cubic polynomial which computes the energy or force.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap} style, the N means to create interpolation tables
that are 2\textasciicircum{}N in length.  The pair distance is used to index into the
table via a fast bit\sphinxhyphen{}mapping technique {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_table_rx:wolff}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Wolff)}}}} and a linear
interpolation is performed between adjacent table values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each pair of atoms
types via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command as in the examples
above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
species1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
species2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff (distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The filename specifies a file containing tabulated energy and force
values.  The keyword specifies a section of the file.  The cutoff is
an optional coefficient.  If not specified, the outer cutoff in the
table itself (see below) will be used to build an interpolation table
that extend to the largest tabulated distance.  If specified, only
file values up to the cutoff are used to create the interpolation
table.  The format of this file is described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The species tags define the site\sphinxhyphen{}site interaction potential between
two species contained within two different particles.  The species
tags must either correspond to the species defined in the reaction
kinetics files specified with the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_rx::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix rx}}}} command or they
must correspond to the tag “1fluid”, signifying interaction with a
product species mixture determined through a one\sphinxhyphen{}fluid approximation.
The interaction potential is weighted by the geometric average of
either the mole fraction concentrations or the number of molecules
associated with the interacting coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained particles (see the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fractional} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{molecular} weighting pair style options). The coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grained potential is
stored before and after the reaction kinetics solver is applied, where
the difference is defined to be the internal chemical energy (uChem).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are some guidelines for using the pair\_style table/rx command to
best effect:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Vary the number of table points; you may need to use more than you think
to get good resolution.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Always use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command to produce a plot
of what the final interpolated potential looks like.  This can show up
interpolation “features” you may not like.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Start with the linear style; it’s the style least likely to have problems.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} in the pair\_style command equal to the “N” in the tabulation
file, and use the “RSQ” or “BITMAP” parameter, so additional interpolation
is not needed.  See discussion below.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Make sure that your tabulated forces and tabulated energies are consistent
(dE/dr = \sphinxhyphen{}F) along the entire range of r values.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use as large an inner cutoff as possible.  This avoids fitting splines
to very steep parts of the potential.

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of a tabulated file is a series of one or more sections,
defined as follows (without the parenthesized comments):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} Morse potential for Fe   (one or more comment or blank lines)

MORSE\PYGZus{}FE                   (keyword is first text on line)
N 500 R 1.0 10.0           (N, R, RSQ, BITMAP, FPRIME parameters)
                           (blank)
1 1.0 25.5 102.34          (index, r, energy, force)
2 1.02 23.4 98.5
...
500 10.0 0.001 0.003
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A section begins with a non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line whose first character is not a
“\#”; blank lines or lines starting with “\#” can be used as comments
between sections.  The first line begins with a keyword which
identifies the section.  The line can contain additional text, but the
initial text must match the argument specified in the pair\_coeff
command.  The next line lists (in any order) one or more parameters
for the table.  Each parameter is a keyword followed by one or more
numeric values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter “N” is required and its value is the number of table
entries that follow.  Note that this may be different than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
specified in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style table/rx}}}} command.  Let
Ntable = \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} in the pair\_style command, and Nfile = “N” in the
tabulated file.  What LAMMPS does is a preliminary interpolation by
creating splines using the Nfile tabulated values as nodal points.  It
uses these to interpolate as needed to generate energy and force
values at Ntable different points.  The resulting tables of length
Ntable are then used as described above, when computing energy and
force for individual pair distances.  This means that if you want the
interpolation tables of length Ntable to match exactly what is in the
tabulated file (with effectively no preliminary interpolation), you
should set Ntable = Nfile, and use the “RSQ” or “BITMAP” parameter.
The internal table abscissa is RSQ (separation distance squared).

\sphinxAtStartPar
All other parameters are optional.  If “R” or “RSQ” or “BITMAP” does
not appear, then the distances in each line of the table are used
as\sphinxhyphen{}is to perform spline interpolation.  In this case, the table values
can be spaced in \sphinxstyleemphasis{r} uniformly or however you wish to position table
values in regions of large gradients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If used, the parameters “R” or “RSQ” are followed by 2 values \sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo}
and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi}.  If specified, the distance associated with each energy and
force value is computed from these 2 values (at high accuracy), rather
than using the (low\sphinxhyphen{}accuracy) value listed in each line of the table.
The distance values in the table file are ignored in this case.
For “R”, distances uniformly spaced between \sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi} are
computed; for “RSQ”, squared distances uniformly spaced between
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo*rlo} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi*rhi} are computed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If used, the parameter “BITMAP” is also followed by 2 values \sphinxstyleemphasis{rlo} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{rhi}.  These values, along with the “N” value determine the ordering
of the N lines that follow and what distance is associated with each.
This ordering is complex, so it is not documented here, since this
file is typically produced by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}} command
with its \sphinxstyleemphasis{bitmap} option.  When the table is in BITMAP format, the “N”
parameter in the file must be equal to 2\textasciicircum{}M where M is the value
specified in the pair\_style command.  Also, a cutoff parameter cannot
be used as an optional third argument in the pair\_coeff command; the
entire table extent as specified in the file must be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If used, the parameter “FPRIME” is followed by 2 values \sphinxstyleemphasis{fplo} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{fphi} which are the derivative of the force at the innermost and
outermost distances listed in the table.  These values are needed by
the spline construction routines.  If not specified by the “FPRIME”
parameter, they are estimated (less accurately) by the first 2 and
last 2 force values in the table.  This parameter is not used by
BITMAP tables.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following a blank line, the next N lines list the tabulated values.
On each line, the first value is the index from 1 to N, the second value is
r (in distance units), the third value is the energy (in energy units),
and the fourth is the force (in force units).  The r values must increase
from one line to the next (unless the BITMAP parameter is specified).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that one file can contain many sections, each with a tabulated
potential.  LAMMPS reads the file section by section until it finds
one that matches the specified keyword.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff} style computes a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body Tersoff potential
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:tersoff-11}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_1)}}}} for the energy E of a system of atoms as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} V_{ij} \\
V_{ij} & = f_C(r_{ij} + \delta) \left[ f_R(r_{ij} + \delta) + b_{ij} f_A(r_{ij} + \delta) \right] \\
f_C(r) & = \left\{ \begin{array} {r@{\quad:\quad}l}
  1 & r < R - D \\
  \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \frac{r-R}{D} \right) &
    R-D < r < R + D \\
  0 & r > R + D
  \end{array} \right. \\
f_R(r) & =  A \exp (-\lambda_1 r) \\
f_A(r) & =  -B \exp (-\lambda_2 r) \\
b_{ij} & =  \left( 1 + \beta^n {\zeta_{ij}}^n \right)^{-\frac{1}{2n}} \\
\zeta_{ij} & =  \sum_{k \neq i,j} f_C(r_{ik} + \delta) g \left[ \theta_{ijk}(r_{ij}, r_{ik}) \right]
                 \exp \left[ {\lambda_3}^m (r_{ij} - r_{ik})^m \right] \\
g(\theta) & =  \gamma_{ijk} \left( 1 + \frac{c^2}{d^2} -
                \frac{c^2}{\left[ d^2 + (\cos \theta - \cos \theta_0)^2\right]} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(f_R\) is a two\sphinxhyphen{}body term and \(f_A\) includes three\sphinxhyphen{}body
interactions.  The summations in the formula are over all neighbors
J and K of atom I within a cutoff distance = R + D. \(\delta\) is
an optional negative shift of the equilibrium bond length, as described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/table} style uses tabulated forms for the two\sphinxhyphen{}body,
environment and angular functions. Linear interpolation is performed
between adjacent table entries. The table length is chosen to be
accurate within 10\textasciicircum{}\sphinxhyphen{}6 with respect to the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff} style energy.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/table} should give better performance in terms of speed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff} style
which specifies a Tersoff potential file with parameters for all
needed elements.  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying
N additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff command,
where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of Tersoff elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine the SiC.tersoff file has Tersoff values for Si
and C.  If your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atoms types and you want the
first 3 to be Si, and the fourth to be C, you would use the following
pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The first three Si arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the Si
element in the Tersoff file.  The final C argument maps LAMMPS atom
type 4 to the C element in the Tersoff file.  If a mapping value is
specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed.  This can be used
when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff} potential is used as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style.
The NULL values are placeholders for atom types that will be used with
other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tersoff files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS distribution
have a “.tersoff” suffix.  Lines that are not blank or comments
(starting with \#) define parameters for a triplet of elements.  The
parameters in a single entry correspond to coefficients in the formula
above:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 1 (the center atom in a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 2 (the atom bonded to the center atom)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 3 (the atom influencing the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 bond in a bond\sphinxhyphen{}order sense)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
m

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\gamma\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_3\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
d

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\cos\theta_0\) (can be a value \textless{} \sphinxhyphen{}1 or \textgreater{} 1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
n

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\beta\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_2\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
B (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
R (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
D (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_1\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (energy units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The n, \(\beta\), \(\lambda_2\), B, \(\lambda_1\), and A
parameters are only used for
two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.  The m, \(\gamma\), \(\lambda_3\), c, d,
and \(\cos\theta_0\)
parameters are only used for three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. The R and D
parameters are used for both two\sphinxhyphen{}body and three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. The
non\sphinxhyphen{}annotated parameters are unitless.  The value of m must be 3 or 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Tersoff potential file must contain entries for all the elements
listed in the pair\_coeff command.  It can also contain entries for
additional elements not being used in a particular simulation; LAMMPS
ignores those entries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a single\sphinxhyphen{}element simulation, only a single entry is required
(e.g. SiSiSi).  For a two\sphinxhyphen{}element simulation, the file must contain 8
entries (for SiSiSi, SiSiC, SiCSi, SiCC, CSiSi, CSiC, CCSi, CCC), that
specify Tersoff parameters for all permutations of the two elements
interacting in three\sphinxhyphen{}body configurations.  Thus for 3 elements, 27
entries would be required, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As annotated above, the first element in the entry is the center atom
in a three\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction and it is bonded to the second atom and the
bond is influenced by the third atom.  Thus an entry for SiCC means Si
bonded to a C with another C atom influencing the bond.  Thus
three\sphinxhyphen{}body parameters for SiCSi and SiSiC entries will not, in
general, be the same.  The parameters used for the two\sphinxhyphen{}body
interaction come from the entry where the second element is repeated.
Thus the two\sphinxhyphen{}body parameters for Si interacting with C, comes from the
SiCC entry.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters used for a particular
three\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction come from the entry with the corresponding
three elements.  The parameters used only for two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions
(n, \(\beta\), \(\lambda_2\), B, \(\lambda_1\), and A)
in entries whose second and third
element are different (e.g. SiCSi) are not used for anything and can
be set to 0.0 if desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the twobody parameters in entries such as SiCC and CSiSi
are often the same, due to the common use of symmetric mixing rules,
but this is not always the case. For example, the beta and n parameters in
Tersoff\_2 {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:tersoff-21}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_2)}}}} are not symmetric.
Similarly, the threebody parameters in entries such as SiCSi and SiSiC
are often the same, but this is not always the case, particularly
the value of R, which is sometimes typed on the
first and second elements, sometimes on the first and third elements.
Hence the need to specify R and D explicitly for all element triples.
For example, while Tersoff’s notation
in Tersoff\_2 {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:tersoff-21}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_2)}}}} is ambiguous on this point,
and properties of the zincblende lattice are the same for either choice,
Tersoff’s results for rocksalt are consistent with typing on the first
and third elements. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:albe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Albe et al.}}}} adopts the same convention.
Conversely, the potential for B/N/C from the Cagin group
uses the opposite convention, typing on the first and second elements.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We chose the above form so as to enable users to define all commonly
used variants of the Tersoff potential.  In particular, our form
reduces to the original Tersoff form when m = 3 and gamma = 1, while
it reduces to the form of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:albe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Albe et al.}}}} when beta = 1 and m = 1.
Note that in the current Tersoff implementation in LAMMPS, m must be
specified as either 3 or 1.  Tersoff used a slightly different but
equivalent form for alloys, which we will refer to as Tersoff\_2
potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:tersoff-21}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_2)}}}}.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/table} style implements
Tersoff\_2 parameterization only.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS parameter values for Tersoff\_2 can be obtained as follows:
\(\gamma_{ijk} = \omega_{ik}\), \(\lambda_3 = 0\) and the value of
m has no effect.  The parameters for species i and j can be calculated
using the Tersoff\_2 mixing rules:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda_1^{i,j} & = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_1^i + \lambda_1^j)\\
\lambda_2^{i,j} & = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_2^i + \lambda_2^j)\\
A_{i,j} & = (A_{i}A_{j})^{1/2}\\
B_{i,j} & = \chi_{ij}(B_{i}B_{j})^{1/2}\\
R_{i,j} & = (R_{i}R_{j})^{1/2}\\
S_{i,j} & = (S_{i}S_{j})^{1/2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tersoff\_2 parameters R and S must be converted to the LAMMPS
parameters R and D (R is different in both forms), using the following
relations: R=(R’+S’)/2 and D=(S’\sphinxhyphen{}R’)/2, where the primes indicate the
Tersoff\_2 parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the potentials directory, the file SiCGe.tersoff provides the
LAMMPS parameters for Tersoff’s various versions of Si, as well as his
alloy parameters for Si, C, and Ge. This file can be used for pure Si,
(three different versions), pure C, pure Ge, binary SiC, and binary
SiGe.  LAMMPS will generate an error if this file is used with any
combination involving C and Ge, since there are no entries for the GeC
interactions (Tersoff did not publish parameters for this
cross\sphinxhyphen{}interaction.)  Tersoff files are also provided for the SiC alloy
(SiC.tersoff) and the GaN (GaN.tersoff) alloys.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many thanks to Rutuparna Narulkar, David Farrell, and Xiaowang Zhou
for helping clarify how Tersoff parameters for alloys have been
defined in various papers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword computes the energy E of a system of atoms, whose
formula is the same as the Tersoff potential. The only modification is
that the original equilibrium bond length ( \(r_0\)) of the system
is shifted to \(r_0-\delta\).  The minus sign arises because each
radial distance \(r\) is replaced by \(r+\delta\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword is designed for simulations of closely matched van
der Waals heterostructures.  For instance, consider the case of a system
with few\sphinxhyphen{}layers graphene atop a thick hexagonal boron nitride (h\sphinxhyphen{}BN)
substrate simulated using periodic boundary conditions. The experimental
lattice mismatch of \textasciitilde{}1.8\% between graphene and h\sphinxhyphen{}BN is not well captured
by the equilibrium lattice constants of available potentials, thus a
small in\sphinxhyphen{}plane strain will be introduced in the system when building a
periodic supercell.  To minimize the effect of strain on simulation
results, the \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword allows adjusting the equilibrium bond
length of one of the two materials (e.g., h\sphinxhyphen{}BN). Validation, benchmark
tests, and applications of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword can be found in
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:mandelli1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Mandelli\_1)}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff:ouyang5}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Ouyang\_1)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the specific case discussed above, the force field can be defined as

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{overlay}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m}{0.00407}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ilp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{graphene}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{hbn}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{shield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{16.0}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rebo}\PYG{+w}{              }\PYG{n}{CH.rebo}\PYG{+w}{     }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{NULL}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{tersoff}\PYG{+w}{           }\PYG{n}{BNC.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{B}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{NULL}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ilp}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{graphene}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{hbn}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{BNCH.ILP}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{B}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{N}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{shield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.70}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{shield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.695}
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{coul}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{shield}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.69}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, where types I and J correspond to
two different element types, mixing is performed by LAMMPS as
described above from values in the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart
files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you need
to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the MANYBODY package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on”
for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword is not supported by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/gpu},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/table} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/table/omp}
variants.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/intel} pair style is only available when compiling LAMMPS
with the Intel compilers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Tersoff potential files provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials
directory) are parameterized for {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{“metal” units}}}}.  In addition
the pair style supports converting potential parameters on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly between
“metal” and “real” units. You can use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff} pair style variants
with any LAMMPS units setting, but you would need to
create your own Tersoff potential file with coefficients listed in the
appropriate units if your simulation does not use “metal” or “real” units.

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod/c} styles computes a bond\sphinxhyphen{}order type
interatomic potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:kumagai}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Kumagai)}}}} based on a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body Tersoff
potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:tersoff-12}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_1)}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:tersoff-22}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_2)}}}} with
modified cutoff function and angular\sphinxhyphen{}dependent term, giving the energy
E of a system of atoms as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E & = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} V_{ij} \\
V_{ij} & = f_C(r_{ij} + \delta) \left[ f_R(r_{ij} + \delta) + b_{ij} f_A(r_{ij} + \delta) \right] \\
f_C(r) & = \left\{ \begin{array} {r@{\quad:\quad}l}
  1 & r < R - D \\
  \frac{1}{2} - \frac{9}{16} \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \frac{r-R}{D} \right) - \frac{1}{16} \sin \left( \frac{3\pi}{2} \frac{r-R}{D} \right) &
    R-D < r < R + D \\
  0 & r > R + D
  \end{array} \right. \\
f_R(r) & = A \exp (-\lambda_1 r) \\
f_A(r) & = -B \exp (-\lambda_2 r) \\
b_{ij} & = \left( 1 + {\zeta_{ij}}^\eta \right)^{-\frac{1}{2n}} \\
\zeta_{ij} & = \sum_{k \neq i,j} f_C(r_{ik} + \delta) g(\theta_{ijk})
                 \exp \left[ \alpha (r_{ij} - r_{ik})^\beta \right] \\
g(\theta) & = c_1 + g_o(\theta) g_a(\theta) \\
g_o(\theta) & = \frac{c_2 (h - \cos \theta)^2}{c_3 + (h - \cos \theta)^2} \\
g_a(\theta) & = 1 + c_4 \exp \left[ -c_5 (h - \cos \theta)^2 \right] \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(f_R\) is a two\sphinxhyphen{}body term and \(f_A\) includes three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.
\(\delta\) is an optional negative shift of the
equilibrium bond length, as described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The summations in the formula are over all neighbors J and K of atom I
within a cutoff distance = R + D.
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod/c} style differs from \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod} only in the
formulation of the V\_ij term, where it contains an additional c0 term.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V_{ij} = f_C(r_{ij} + \delta) \left[ f_R(r_{ij} + \delta) + b_{ij} f_A(r_{ij} + \delta) + c_0 \right] \\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The modified cutoff function \(f_C\) proposed by {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:murty}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Murty)}}}} and
having a continuous second\sphinxhyphen{}order differential is employed. The
angular\sphinxhyphen{}dependent term \(g(\theta)\) was modified to increase the
flexibility of the potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod} potential is fitted to both the elastic constants
and melting point by employing the modified Tersoff potential function
form in which the angular\sphinxhyphen{}dependent term is improved. The model
performs extremely well in describing the crystalline, liquid, and
amorphous phases {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:schelling}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Schelling)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod} style
which specifies a Tersoff/MOD potential file with parameters for all
needed elements.  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying
N additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff command,
where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of Tersoff/MOD elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine the Si.tersoff\_mod file has Tersoff values for Si.
If your LAMMPS simulation has 3 Si atoms types, you would use the following
pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si.tersoff\PYGZus{}mod}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The three Si arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the Si element
in the Tersoff/MOD file. If a mapping value is specified as NULL, the
mapping is not performed.  This can be used when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod}
potential is used as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} pair style. The NULL values
are placeholders for atom types that will be used with other
potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tersoff/MOD file in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS
distribution have a “.tersoff.mod” suffix. Potential files for the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod/c} style have the suffix “.tersoff.modc”. Lines that are
not blank or comments (starting with \#) define parameters for a triplet
of elements.  The parameters in a single entry correspond to
coefficients in the formulae above:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 1 (the center atom in a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 2 (the atom bonded to the center atom)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 3 (the atom influencing the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 bond in a bond\sphinxhyphen{}order sense)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\beta\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\alpha\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
h

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\eta\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\beta_{ters}\) = 1 (dummy parameter)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_2\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
B (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
R (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
D (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_1\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
n

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c1

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c2

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c3

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c4

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c5

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c0 (energy units, tersoff/mod/c only)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The n, \(\eta\), \(\lambda_2\), B, \(\lambda_1\), and A parameters are only used for
two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.  The \(\beta\), \(\alpha\), c1, c2, c3, c4, c5, h
parameters are only used for three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. The R and D
parameters are used for both two\sphinxhyphen{}body and three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.
The c0 term applies to \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod/c} only. The non\sphinxhyphen{}annotated
parameters are unitless.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Tersoff/MOD potential file must contain entries for all the elements
listed in the pair\_coeff command.  It can also contain entries for
additional elements not being used in a particular simulation; LAMMPS
ignores those entries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a single\sphinxhyphen{}element simulation, only a single entry is required
(e.g. SiSiSi). As annotated above, the first element in the entry is
the center atom in a three\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction and it is bonded to the
second atom and the bond is influenced by the third atom.  Thus an entry
for SiSiSi means Si bonded to a Si with another Si atom influencing the bond.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword computes the energy E of a system of atoms, whose formula
is the same as the Tersoff potential. The only modification is that the original
equilibrium bond length ( \(r_0\)) of the system is shifted to \(r_0-\delta\).
The minus sign arises because each radial distance \(r\) is replaced by \(r+\delta\).
More information on this option is given on the main {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_tersoff}}}} page.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you
need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input
script that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff_mod:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the MANYBODY package.  It is only enabled
if LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on”
for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword is not supported by the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/gpu},
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/table} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/table/omp}
variants.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod} potential files provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials
directory) are parameterized for metal {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{units}}}}.  You can
use the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/mod} pair style with any LAMMPS units, but you would need to
create your own Tersoff/MOD potential file with coefficients listed in the
appropriate units if your simulation does not use “metal” units.

\subsection{Examples}

\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.tersoff.zbl}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/zbl} style computes a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body Tersoff potential
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:zbl-tersoff-1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_1)}}}} with a close\sphinxhyphen{}separation pairwise modification
based on a Coulomb potential and the Ziegler\sphinxhyphen{}Biersack\sphinxhyphen{}Littmark
universal screening function {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:zbl-zbl}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(ZBL)}}}}, giving the energy E of a
system of atoms as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} E & = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} V_{ij} \\
 V_{ij} & =  (1 - f_F(r_{ij} + \delta)) V^{ZBL}(r_{ij} + \delta)
             + f_F(r_{ij} + \delta) V^{Tersoff}(r_{ij} + \delta) \\
 f_F(r) & =  \frac{1}{1 + e^{-A_F(r - r_C)}}\\
 \\
 \\
 V^{ZBL}(r) & = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{Z_1 Z_2 \,e^2}{r} \phi(r/a) \\
a & = \frac{0.8854\,a_0}{Z_{1}^{0.23} + Z_{2}^{0.23}}\\
\phi(x) & =  0.1818e^{-3.2x} + 0.5099e^{-0.9423x} + 0.2802e^{-0.4029x} + 0.02817e^{-0.2016x}\\
\\
\\
V^{Tersoff}(r) & = f_C(r) \left[ f_R(r) + b_{ij} f_A(r) \right] \\
f_C(r) & = \left\{ \begin{array} {r@{\quad:\quad}l}
  1 & r < R - D \\
  \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \frac{r-R}{D} \right) &
    R-D < r < R + D \\
  0 & r > R + D
  \end{array} \right. \\
f_R(r) & = A \exp (-\lambda_1 r) \\
f_A(r) & = -B \exp (-\lambda_2 r) \\
b_{ij} & = \left( 1 + \beta^n {\zeta_{ij}}^n \right)^{-\frac{1}{2n}} \\
\zeta_{ij} & = \sum_{k \neq i,j} f_C(r_{ik} + \delta) g(\theta_{ijk})
                 \exp \left[ {\lambda_3}^m (r_{ij} - r_{ik})^m \right] \\
g(\theta) & =  \gamma_{ijk} \left( 1 + \frac{c^2}{d^2} -
                \frac{c^2}{\left[ d^2 + (\cos \theta - \cos \theta_0)^2\right]} \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(f_F\) term is a fermi\sphinxhyphen{}like function used to smoothly connect the ZBL
repulsive potential with the Tersoff potential.  There are 2
parameters used to adjust it: \(A_F\) and \(r_C\).  \(A_F\)
controls how “sharp”
the transition is between the two, and \(r_C\) is essentially the cutoff
for the ZBL potential.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the ZBL portion, there are two terms. The first is the Coulomb
repulsive term, with Z1, Z2 as the number of protons in each nucleus,
e as the electron charge (1 for metal and real units) and \(\epsilon_0\)
as the permittivity of vacuum.  The second part is the ZBL universal
screening function, with a0 being the Bohr radius (typically 0.529
Angstroms), and the remainder of the coefficients provided by the
original paper.  This screening function should be applicable to most
systems.  However, it is only accurate for small separations
(i.e. less than 1 Angstrom).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the Tersoff portion, \(f_R\) is a two\sphinxhyphen{}body term and \(f_A\)
includes
three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. The summations in the formula are over all
neighbors J and K of atom I within a cutoff distance = R + D.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\delta\) is an optional negative shift of the
equilibrium bond length, as described below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Only a single pair\_coeff command is used with the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/zbl} style
which specifies a Tersoff/ZBL potential file with parameters for all
needed elements.  These are mapped to LAMMPS atom types by specifying
N additional arguments after the filename in the pair\_coeff command,
where N is the number of LAMMPS atom types:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N element names = mapping of Tersoff/ZBL elements to atom types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} page for alternate ways
to specify the path for the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, imagine the SiC.tersoff.zbl file has Tersoff/ZBL values
for Si and C.  If your LAMMPS simulation has 4 atoms types and you
want the first 3 to be Si, and the fourth to be C, you would use the
following pair\_coeff command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{pair\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{SiC.tersoff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{Si}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{C}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first 2 arguments must be * * so as to span all LAMMPS atom types.
The first three Si arguments map LAMMPS atom types 1,2,3 to the Si
element in the Tersoff/ZBL file.  The final C argument maps LAMMPS
atom type 4 to the C element in the Tersoff/ZBL file.  If a mapping
value is specified as NULL, the mapping is not performed.  This can be
used when a \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/zbl} potential is used as part of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid}
pair style.  The NULL values are placeholders for atom types that will
be used with other potentials.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Tersoff/ZBL files in the \sphinxstyleemphasis{potentials} directory of the LAMMPS
distribution have a “.tersoff.zbl” suffix.  Lines that are not blank
or comments (starting with \#) define parameters for a triplet of
elements.  The parameters in a single entry correspond to coefficients
in the formula above:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 1 (the center atom in a 3\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 2 (the atom bonded to the center atom)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
element 3 (the atom influencing the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 bond in a bond\sphinxhyphen{}order sense)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
m

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\gamma\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_3\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
c

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
d

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\cos\theta_0\) (can be a value \textless{} \sphinxhyphen{}1 or \textgreater{} 1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
n

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\beta\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_2\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
B (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
R (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
D (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\lambda_1\) (1/distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A (energy units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(Z_i\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(Z_j\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ZBLcut (distance units)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ZBLexpscale (1/distance units)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The n, \(\beta\), \(\lambda_2\), B, \(\lambda_1\), and A
parameters are only used for
two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions.  The m, \(\gamma\), \(\lambda_3\), c, d,
and \(\cos\theta_0\)
parameters are only used for three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. The R and D
parameters are used for both two\sphinxhyphen{}body and three\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions. The
\(Z_i\), \(Z_j\), ZBLcut, ZBLexpscale parameters are used in the
ZBL repulsive
portion of the potential and in the Fermi\sphinxhyphen{}like function.  The
non\sphinxhyphen{}annotated parameters are unitless.  The value of m must be 3 or 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Tersoff/ZBL potential file must contain entries for all the
elements listed in the pair\_coeff command.  It can also contain
entries for additional elements not being used in a particular
simulation; LAMMPS ignores those entries.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For a single\sphinxhyphen{}element simulation, only a single entry is required
(e.g. SiSiSi).  For a two\sphinxhyphen{}element simulation, the file must contain 8
entries (for SiSiSi, SiSiC, SiCSi, SiCC, CSiSi, CSiC, CCSi, CCC), that
specify Tersoff parameters for all permutations of the two elements
interacting in three\sphinxhyphen{}body configurations.  Thus for 3 elements, 27
entries would be required, etc.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As annotated above, the first element in the entry is the center atom
in a three\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction and it is bonded to the second atom and the
bond is influenced by the third atom.  Thus an entry for SiCC means Si
bonded to a C with another C atom influencing the bond.  Thus
three\sphinxhyphen{}body parameters for SiCSi and SiSiC entries will not, in
general, be the same.  The parameters used for the two\sphinxhyphen{}body
interaction come from the entry where the second element is repeated.
Thus the two\sphinxhyphen{}body parameters for Si interacting with C, comes from the
SiCC entry.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameters used for a particular
three\sphinxhyphen{}body interaction come from the entry with the corresponding
three elements.  The parameters used only for two\sphinxhyphen{}body interactions
(n, \(\beta\), \(\lambda_2\), B, \(\lambda_1\), and A)
in entries whose second and third
element are different (e.g. SiCSi) are not used for anything and can
be set to 0.0 if desired.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the twobody parameters in entries such as SiCC and CSiSi
are often the same, due to the common use of symmetric mixing rules,
but this is not always the case. For example, the beta and n parameters in
Tersoff\_2 {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:zbl-tersoff-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_2)}}}} are not symmetric.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We chose the above form so as to enable users to define all commonly
used variants of the Tersoff portion of the potential.  In particular,
our form reduces to the original Tersoff form when m = 3 and gamma =
1, while it reduces to the form of {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:zbl-albe}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Albe et al.}}}} when beta = 1
and m = 1.  Note that in the current Tersoff implementation in LAMMPS,
m must be specified as either 3 or 1.  Tersoff used a slightly
different but equivalent form for alloys, which we will refer to as
Tersoff\_2 potential {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:zbl-tersoff-2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Tersoff\_2)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
LAMMPS parameter values for Tersoff\_2 can be obtained as follows:
\(\gamma = \omega_{ijk}\), \(\lambda_3 = 0\) and the value of
m has no effect.  The parameters for species i and j can be calculated
using the Tersoff\_2 mixing rules:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda_1^{i,j} & = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_1^i + \lambda_1^j)\\
\lambda_2^{i,j} & = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_2^i + \lambda_2^j)\\
A_{i,j} & = (A_{i}A_{j})^{1/2}\\
B_{i,j} & = \chi_{ij}(B_{i}B_{j})^{1/2}\\
R_{i,j} & = (R_{i}R_{j})^{1/2}\\
S_{i,j} & = (S_{i}S_{j})^{1/2}\\\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tersoff\_2 parameters R and S must be converted to the LAMMPS
parameters R and D (R is different in both forms), using the following
relations: R=(R’+S’)/2 and D=(S’\sphinxhyphen{}R’)/2, where the primes indicate the
Tersoff\_2 parameters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the potentials directory, the file SiCGe.tersoff provides the
LAMMPS parameters for Tersoff’s various versions of Si, as well as his
alloy parameters for Si, C, and Ge. This file can be used for pure Si,
(three different versions), pure C, pure Ge, binary SiC, and binary
SiGe.  LAMMPS will generate an error if this file is used with any
combination involving C and Ge, since there are no entries for the GeC
interactions (Tersoff did not publish parameters for this
cross\sphinxhyphen{}interaction.)  Tersoff files are also provided for the SiC alloy
(SiC.tersoff) and the GaN (GaN.tersoff) alloys.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Many thanks to Rutuparna Narulkar, David Farrell, and Xiaowang Zhou
for helping clarify how Tersoff parameters for alloys have been
defined in various papers.  Also thanks to Ram Devanathan for
providing the base ZBL implementation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword computes the energy E of a system of atoms, whose
formula is the same as the Tersoff potential. The only modification is
that the original equilibrium bond length ( \(r_0\)) of the system
is shifted to \(r_0-\delta\).  The minus sign arises because each
radial distance \(r\) is replaced by \(r+\delta\).  More
information on this option is given on the main {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_tersoff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_tersoff}}}} page.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Mixing, shift, table, tail correction, restart, rRESPA info}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:mixing-shift-table-tail-correction-restart-rrespa-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For atom type pairs I,J and I != J, where types I and J correspond to
two different element types, mixing is performed by LAMMPS as
described above from values in the potential file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not support the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_modify::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_modify}}}}
shift, table, and tail options.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style does not write its information to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart
files}}}}, since it is stored in potential files.  Thus, you need
to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the pair\_style and pair\_coeff commands in an input script
that reads a restart file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style can only be used via the \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} keyword of the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{run\_style respa}}}} command.  It does not support the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{inner}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{middle}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer} keywords.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{pair_tersoff_zbl:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style is part of the MANYBODY package.  It is only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with that package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pair style requires the {\hyperref[\detokenize{newton::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{newton}}}} setting to be “on”
for pair interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{shift} keyword is currently not supported for the \sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/gpu} and
\sphinxstyleemphasis{tersoff/kk} variants of this pair style.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tersoff/zbl potential files provided with LAMMPS (see the potentials
directory) are parameterized for {\hyperref[\detokenize{units::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{“metal” units}}}}.  Also the
pair style supports converting potential file parameters on\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}fly
between “metal” and “real” units.  You can use the tersoff/zbl pair
style with any LAMMPS units, but you would need to create your own
tersoff/zbl potential file with coefficients listed in the appropriate
units if your simulation does not use “metal” or “real” units.
