\section{angle\_style table command}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:angle-style-table-command}}\label{\detokenize{angle_table:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{angle_table:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{angle_table::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{N}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} = method of interpolation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
N = use N values in table

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ENTRY1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} creates interpolation tables of length \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} from angle
potential and derivative values listed in a file(s) as a function of
angle The files are read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_coeff}}}}
command.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interpolation tables are created by fitting cubic splines to the
file values and interpolating energy and derivative values at each of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{N} angles.  During a simulation, these tables are used to interpolate
energy and force values on individual atoms as needed.  The
interpolation is done in one of 2 styles: \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} style, the angle is used to find 2 surrounding table
values from which an energy or its derivative is computed by linear
interpolation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} style, a cubic spline coefficients are computed and
stored at each of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} values in the table.  The angle is used to
find the appropriate set of coefficients which are used to evaluate a
cubic polynomial which computes the energy or derivative.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each angle type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The filename specifies a file containing tabulated energy and
derivative values.  The keyword specifies a section of the file.  The
format of this file is described below.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Suitable tables for use with this angle style can be created by LAMMPS
itself from existing angle styles using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_write}}}} command.  This can be useful to have a template file for
testing the angle style settings and to build a compatible custom file.
Another option to generate tables is the Python code in the
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools/tabulate}} folder of the LAMMPS source code distribution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of a tabulated file is as follows (without the
parenthesized comments):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} Angle potential for harmonic (one or more comment or blank lines)

HAM                           (keyword is the first text on line)
N 181 FP 0 0 EQ 90.0          (N, FP, EQ parameters)
                              (blank line)
1 0.0 200.5 2.5               (index, angle, energy, derivative)
2 1.0 198.0 2.5
...
181 180.0 0.0 0.0
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A section begins with a non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line whose first character is not a
“\#”; blank lines or lines starting with “\#” can be used as comments
between sections.  The first line begins with a keyword which
identifies the section.  The line can contain additional text, but the
initial text must match the argument specified in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_coeff}}}} command.  The next line lists (in any
order) one or more parameters for the table.  Each parameter is a
keyword followed by one or more numeric values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter “N” is required and its value is the number of table
entries that follow.  Note that this may be different than the \sphinxstyleemphasis{N}
specified in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_style table}}}} command.  Let
Ntable = \sphinxstyleemphasis{N} in the angle\_style command, and Nfile = “N” in the
tabulated file.  What LAMMPS does is a preliminary interpolation by
creating splines using the Nfile tabulated values as nodal points.  It
uses these to interpolate as needed to generate energy and derivative
values at Ntable different points.  The resulting tables of length
Ntable are then used as described above, when computing energy and
force for individual angles and their atoms.  This means that if you
want the interpolation tables of length Ntable to match exactly what
is in the tabulated file (with effectively no preliminary
interpolation), you should set Ntable = Nfile.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “FP” parameter is optional.  If used, it is followed by two values
fplo and fphi, which are the second derivatives at the innermost and
outermost angle settings.  These values are needed by the spline
construction routines.  If not specified by the “FP” parameter, they
are estimated (less accurately) by the first two and last two
derivative values in the table.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The “EQ” parameter is also optional.  If used, it is followed by a the
equilibrium angle value, which is used, for example, by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}} command.  If not used, the equilibrium angle is
set to 180.0.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following a blank line, the next N lines list the tabulated values.
On each line, the first value is the index from 1 to N, the second value is
the angle value (in degrees), the third value is the energy (in energy
units), and the fourth is \sphinxhyphen{}dE/d(theta) (also in energy units).  The third
term is the energy of the 3\sphinxhyphen{}atom configuration for the specified
angle.  The last term is the derivative of the energy with respect to
the angle (in degrees, not radians).  Thus the units of the last term
are still energy, not force.  The angle values must increase from one
line to the next.  The angle values must also begin with 0.0 and end
with 180.0, i.e. span the full range of possible angles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that one file can contain many sections, each with a tabulated
potential.  LAMMPS reads the file section by section until it finds
one that matches the specified keyword.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This angle style writes the settings for the “angle\_style table”
command to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so a angle\_style
command does not need to specified in an input script that reads a
restart file.  However, the coefficient information is not stored in
the restart file, since it is tabulated in the potential files.  Thus,
angle\_coeff commands do need to be specified in the restart input
script.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This angle style can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
MOLECULE package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc page
for more info.


\subsection{Related commands}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_coeff}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_write}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{angle_table:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
none

\sphinxstepscope

\section{angle\_style zero command}
\label{\detokenize{angle_zero:angle-style-zero-command}}\label{\detokenize{angle_zero:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{angle_zero::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{angle_zero:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zero}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keyword}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
zero or more keywords may be appended

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword = \sphinxstyleemphasis{nocoeff}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{angle_zero:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zero}
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{zero}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nocoeff}
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}
\PYG{k}{angle\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{120.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{angle_zero:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using an angle style of zero means angle forces and energies are not
computed, but the geometry of angle triplets is still accessible to
other commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{compute_angle_local::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{compute angle/local}}}}
command can be used to compute the theta values for the list of
triplets of angle atoms listed in the data file read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command.  If no angle style is defined,
this command cannot be used.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional \sphinxstyleemphasis{nocoeff} flag allows to read data files with AngleCoeff
section for any angle style. Similarly, any {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_coeff}}}} commands
will only be checked for the angle type number and the rest ignored.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the {\hyperref[\detokenize{angle_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{angle\_coeff}}}} command must be used for
all angle types. If specified, there can be only one value, which is
going to be used to assign an equilibrium angle, e.g. for use with
{\hyperref[\detokenize{fix_shake::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{fix shake}}}}.

\label{\detokenize{angle_zero:restrictions}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
none
\end{quote}

\index{dihedral\_style charmmfsw@\spxentry{dihedral\_style charmmfsw}}\ignorespaces 
\index{dihedral\_style charmmfsw/kk@\spxentry{dihedral\_style charmmfsw/kk}}\ignorespaces 

\section{dihedral\_style charmm command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:dihedral-style-charmm-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:index-5}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:index-4}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:index-3}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:index-2}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm/intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm/kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm/omp}


\section{dihedral\_style charmmfsw command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:dihedral-style-charmmfsw-command}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style = \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{charmm}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{charmmfsw}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{180}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.8}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{180}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} dihedral styles use the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = K [ 1 + \cos (n \phi - d) ]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:dihedral-mackerell}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(MacKerell)}}}} for a description of the CHARMM
force field.  This dihedral style can also be used for the AMBER force
field (see comment on weighting factors below).  See
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:dihedral-cornell}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Cornell)}}}} for a description of the AMBER force
field.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The newer \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} style was released in March 2017.  We
recommend it be used instead of the older \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} style when running
a simulation with the CHARMM force field, either with long\sphinxhyphen{}range
Coulombics or a Coulombic cutoff, via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/charmmfsw/coul/long}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/charmmfsw/coul/charmmfsh}}}} commands respectively.
Otherwise the older \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} style is fine to use.  See the discussion
below and more details on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style charmm}}}} doc
page.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n\) (integer \textgreater{}= 0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(d\) (integer value of degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
weighting factor (1.0, 0.5, or 0.0)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The weighting factor is required to correct for double counting
pairwise non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones interactions in cyclic systems or
when using the CHARMM dihedral style with non\sphinxhyphen{}CHARMM force fields.
With the CHARMM dihedral style, interactions between the first and fourth
atoms in a dihedral are skipped during the normal non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded force
computation and instead evaluated as part of the dihedral using
special epsilon and sigma values specified with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_coeff}}}} command of pair styles that contain
“lj/charmm” (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/charmm/coul/long}}}})
In 6\sphinxhyphen{}membered rings, the same 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 interaction would be computed twice
(once for the clockwise 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 pair in dihedral 1\sphinxhyphen{}2\sphinxhyphen{}3\sphinxhyphen{}4 and once in the
counterclockwise dihedral 1\sphinxhyphen{}6\sphinxhyphen{}5\sphinxhyphen{}4) and thus the weighting factor has
to be 0.5 in this case.  In 4\sphinxhyphen{}membered or 5\sphinxhyphen{}membered rings, the 1\sphinxhyphen{}4
dihedral also is counted as a 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 or 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 interaction when going around
the ring in the opposite direction and thus the weighting factor is
0.0, as the 1\sphinxhyphen{}2 and 1\sphinxhyphen{}3 exclusions take precedence.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that this dihedral weighting factor is unrelated to the scaling
factor specified by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special bonds}}}} command
which applies to all 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 interactions in the system.  For CHARMM force
fields, the special\_bonds 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 interaction scaling factor should be set
to 0.0. Since the corresponding 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions are
computed with the dihedral.  This means that if any of the weighting
factors defined as dihedral coefficients (fourth coeff above) are
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero, then you must use a pair style with “lj/charmm” and set the
special\_bonds 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 scaling factor to 0.0 (which is the
default). Otherwise 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions in dihedrals will be
computed twice.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For simulations using the CHARMM force field with a Coulombic cutoff,
the difference between the \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} styles is in the
computation of the 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 non\sphinxhyphen{}bond interactions, though only if the
distance between the two atoms is within the switching region of the
pairwise potential defined by the corresponding CHARMM pair style,
i.e. within the outer cutoff specified for the pair style.  The
\sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} style should only be used when using the corresponding
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/charmmfsw/coul/charmmfsw}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style lj/charmmfsw/coul/long}}}} commands.  Use
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} style with the older {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_style}}}}
commands that have just “charmm” in their style name.  See the
discussion on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_charmm::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{CHARMM pair\_style}}}} page for
details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that for AMBER force fields, which use pair styles with “lj/cut”,
the special\_bonds 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 scaling factor should be set to the AMBER
defaults (1/2 and 5/6) and all the dihedral weighting factors (fourth
coeff above) must be set to 0.0. In this case, you can use any pair
style you wish, since the dihedral does not need any Lennard\sphinxhyphen{}Jones
parameter information and will not compute any 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded
interactions.  Likewise the \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmm} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{charmmfsw} styles are
identical in this case since no 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded interactions are
computed.

\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_charmm:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When using run\_style {\hyperref[\detokenize{run_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{respa}}}}, these dihedral styles
must be assigned to the same r\sphinxhyphen{}RESPA level as \sphinxstyleemphasis{pair} or \sphinxstyleemphasis{outer}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When used in combination with CHARMM pair styles, the 1\sphinxhyphen{}4
{\hyperref[\detokenize{special_bonds::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{special\_bonds}}}} scaling factors must be set to 0.0.
Otherwise non\sphinxhyphen{}bonded contributions for these 1\sphinxhyphen{}4 pairs will be
computed multiple times.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These dihedral styles can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
MOLECULE package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc page
for more info.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_class2:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2} dihedral style uses the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E        = & E_d + E_{mbt} + E_{ebt} + E_{at} + E_{aat} + E_{bb13} \\
E_d      = & \sum_{n=1}^{3} K_n [ 1 - \cos (n \phi - \phi_n) ] \\
E_{mbt}  = & (r_{jk} - r_2) [ A_1 \cos (\phi) + A_2 \cos (2\phi) + A_3 \cos (3\phi) ] \\
E_{ebt}  = & (r_{ij} - r_1) [ B_1 \cos (\phi) + B_2 \cos (2\phi) + B_3 \cos (3\phi) ] + \\
           & (r_{kl} - r_3) [ C_1 \cos (\phi) + C_2 \cos (2\phi) + C_3 \cos (3\phi) ] \\
E_{at}   = & (\theta_{ijk} - \theta_1) [ D_1 \cos (\phi) + D_2 \cos (2\phi) + D_3 \cos (3\phi) ] + \\
           & (\theta_{jkl} - \theta_2) [ E_1 \cos (\phi) + E_2 \cos (2\phi) + E_3 \cos (3\phi) ] \\
E_{aat}  = & M (\theta_{ijk} - \theta_1) (\theta_{jkl} - \theta_2) \cos (\phi) \\
E_{bb13} = & N (r_{ij} - r_1) (r_{kl} - r_3)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(E_d\) is the dihedral term, \(E_{mbt}\) is a middle\sphinxhyphen{}bond\sphinxhyphen{}torsion term,
\(E_{ebt}\) is an end\sphinxhyphen{}bond\sphinxhyphen{}torsion term, \(E_{at}\) is an angle\sphinxhyphen{}torsion term, \(E_{aat}\)
is an angle\sphinxhyphen{}angle\sphinxhyphen{}torsion term, and \(E_{bb13}\) is a bond\sphinxhyphen{}bond\sphinxhyphen{}13 term.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) are equilibrium angles and \(r_1\), \(r_2\), and
\(r_3\) are equilibrium bond lengths.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_class2:dihedral-sun}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Sun)}}}} for a description of the COMPASS class2 force field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Coefficients for the \(E_d\), \(E_{mbt}\), \(E_{ebt}\),
\(E_{at}\), \(E_{aat}\), and \(E_{bb13}\) formulas must be
defined for each dihedral type via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}
command as in the example above, or in the data file
or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These are the 6 coefficients for the \(E_d\) formula:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\phi_1\) (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_2\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\phi_2\) (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_3\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(phi_3\) (degrees)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \(E_{mbt}\) formula, each line in a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command in the input script lists
5 coefficients, the first of which is \sphinxstyleemphasis{mbt} to indicate they are
MiddleBondTorsion coefficients.  In a data file, these coefficients
should be listed under a \sphinxstyleemphasis{MiddleBondTorsion Coeffs} heading and you
must leave out the \sphinxstyleemphasis{mbt}, i.e. only list 4 coefficients after the
dihedral type.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{mbt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_1\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_2\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_3\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_2\) (distance)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \(E_{ebt}\) formula, each line in a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command in the input script lists
9 coefficients, the first of which is \sphinxstyleemphasis{ebt} to indicate they are
EndBondTorsion coefficients.  In a data file, these coefficients
should be listed under a \sphinxstyleemphasis{EndBondTorsion Coeffs} heading and you must
leave out the \sphinxstyleemphasis{ebt}, i.e. only list 8 coefficients after the dihedral
type.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{ebt}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(B_1\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(B_2\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(B_3\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_1\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_2\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_3\) (energy/distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_1\) (distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_3\) (distance)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \(E_{at}\) formula, each line in a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command in the input script lists
9 coefficients, the first of which is \sphinxstyleemphasis{at} to indicate they are
AngleTorsion coefficients.  In a data file, these coefficients should
be listed under a \sphinxstyleemphasis{AngleTorsion Coeffs} heading and you must leave out
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{at}, i.e. only list 8 coefficients after the dihedral type.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{at}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(D_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(D_2\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(D_3\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(E_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(E_2\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(E_3\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta_1\) (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta_2\) (degrees)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) are specified in degrees, but
LAMMPS converts them to radians internally; hence the various
\(D\) and \(E\) are effectively energy per radian.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \(E_{aat}\) formula, each line in a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command in the input script lists 4 coefficients,
the first of which is \sphinxstyleemphasis{aat} to indicate they are AngleAngleTorsion
coefficients.  In a data file, these coefficients should be listed
under a \sphinxstyleemphasis{AngleAngleTorsion Coeffs} heading and you must leave out the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{aat}, i.e. only list 3 coefficients after the dihedral type.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{aat}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(M\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta_1\) (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta_2\) (degrees)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) are specified in degrees, but
LAMMPS converts them to radians internally; hence \(M\) is
effectively energy per radian\textasciicircum{}2.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \(E_{bb13}\) formula, each line in a
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command in the input script lists
4 coefficients, the first of which is \sphinxstyleemphasis{bb13} to indicate they are
BondBond13 coefficients.  In a data file, these coefficients should be
listed under a \sphinxstyleemphasis{BondBond13 Coeffs} heading and you must leave out the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bb13}, i.e. only list 3 coefficients after the dihedral type.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{bb13}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N\) (energy/distance\textasciicircum{}2)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(r_1\) (distance)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_cosine_shift_exp:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cosine/shift/exp} dihedral style uses the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = -U_{min}\frac{e^{-a U(\theta,\theta_0)}-1}{e^a-1} \quad\mbox{with}\quad U(\theta,\theta_0)=-0.5 \left(1+\cos(\theta-\theta_0) \right)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(U_{min}\), \(\theta\), and \(a\) are defined for
each dihedral type.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential is bounded between \(\left[-U_{min}:0\right]\) and the minimum is located
at the angle \(\theta_0\). The a parameter can be both positive or negative
and is used to control the spring constant at the equilibrium.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The spring constant is given by \(k=a e^a \frac{U_{min}}{2 \left(e^a-1\right)}\).
For \(a>3\) and  \(\frac{k}{U_{min}} = \frac{a}{2}\) to better than 5\% relative error. For negative
values of the a parameter, the spring constant is essentially zero,
and anharmonic terms takes over. The potential is furthermore well
behaved in the limit \(a \rightarrow 0\), where it has been implemented to linear
order in \(a\) for \(a < 0.001\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(U_{min}\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\theta\) (angle)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a\) (real number)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_cosine_squared_restricted:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 17Apr2024.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{cosine/squared/restricted} dihedral style uses the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = K [\cos(\phi) - \cos(\phi_0)]^2 / \sin^2(\phi)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
, which is commonly used in the MARTINI force field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_cosine_squared_restricted:restricted-bul}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Bulacu)}}}} for a description of the restricted dihedral for the MARTINI force field.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\phi_0\) (degrees)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\phi_0\) is specified in degrees, but LAMMPS converts it to radians internally.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_fourier:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{fourier} dihedral style uses the potential:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \sum_{i=1,m} K_i  [ 1.0 + \cos ( n_i \phi - d_i ) ]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(m\) (integer \textgreater{}=1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n_1\) (integer \textgreater{}= 0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(d_1\) (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{[}…{]}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_m\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n_m\) (integer \textgreater{}= 0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(d_m\) (degrees)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are

They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_harmonic:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} dihedral style uses the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = K [ 1 + d  \cos (n \phi) ]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(d\) (+1 or \sphinxhyphen{}1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n\) (integer \textgreater{}= 0)

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here are important points to take note of when defining LAMMPS
dihedral coefficients for the harmonic style, so that they are
compatible with how harmonic dihedrals are defined by other force
fields:
\end{sphinxadmonition}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The LAMMPS convention is that the trans position = 180 degrees, while
in some force fields trans = 0 degrees.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some force fields reverse the sign convention on \(d\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Some force fields let \(n\) be positive or negative which corresponds to
\(d = 1\) or \(d = -1\) for the harmonic style.

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_helix:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{helix} dihedral style uses the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = A [1 - \cos(\theta)] + B [1 + \cos(3 \theta)] +
    C [1 + \cos(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4})]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This coarse\sphinxhyphen{}grain dihedral potential is described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_helix:guo}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Guo)}}}}.
For dihedral angles in the helical region, the energy function is
represented by a standard potential consisting of three minima, one
corresponding to the trans (t) state and the other to gauche states
(g+ and g\sphinxhyphen{}).  The paper describes how the \(A\), \(B\) and,
\(C\) parameters are chosen so as to balance secondary (largely
driven by local interactions) and
tertiary structure (driven by long\sphinxhyphen{}range interactions).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(B\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C\) (energy)

\end{itemize}

functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}

produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,

You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script

\section{dihedral\_style hybrid command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid:dihedral-style-hybrid-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid/kk}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{style2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style1,style2 = list of one or more dihedral styles

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hybrid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{helix}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{harmonic}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{6.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{helix}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{hybrid} style enables the use of multiple dihedral styles in one
simulation.  An dihedral style is assigned to each dihedral type.  For
example, dihedrals in a polymer flow (of dihedral type 1) could be
computed with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} potential and dihedrals in the wall
boundary (of dihedral type 2) could be computed with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{helix}
potential.  The assignment of dihedral type to style is made via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command or in the data file.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the dihedral\_coeff commands, the name of a dihedral style must be
added after the dihedral type, with the remaining coefficients being
those appropriate to that style.  In the example above, the 2
dihedral\_coeff commands set dihedrals of dihedral type 1 to be
computed with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{harmonic} potential with coefficients 6.0, 1, 3 for
K, d, n.  All other dihedral types (2\sphinxhyphen{}N) are computed with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{helix}
potential with coefficients 10, 10, 10 for A, B, C.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If dihedral coefficients are specified in the data file read via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command, then the same rule applies.
E.g. “harmonic” or “helix”, must be added after the dihedral type, for
each line in the “Dihedral Coeffs” section, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Dihedral Coeffs

1 harmonic 6.0 1 3
2 helix 10 10 10
...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2} is one of the dihedral hybrid styles, the same rule holds
for specifying additional AngleTorsion (and EndBondTorsion, etc)
coefficients either via the input script or in the data file.
I.e. \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2} must be added to each line after the dihedral type.  For
lines in the AngleTorsion (or EndBondTorsion, etc) Coeffs section of the data
file for dihedral types that are not \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2}, you must use an
dihedral style of \sphinxstyleemphasis{skip} as a placeholder, e.g.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
AngleTorsion Coeffs

1 skip
2 class2 1.0 1.0 1.0 3.0 3.0 3.0 30.0 50.0
...
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that it is not necessary to use the dihedral style \sphinxstyleemphasis{skip} in the
input script, since AngleTorsion (or EndBondTorsion, etc) coefficients
need not be specified at all for dihedral types that are not \sphinxstyleemphasis{class2}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A dihedral style of \sphinxstyleemphasis{none} with no additional coefficients can be used
in place of a dihedral style, either in a input script dihedral\_coeff
command or in the data file, if you desire to turn off interactions
for specific dihedral types.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_hybrid:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This dihedral style can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
MOLECULE package.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc page
for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike other dihedral styles, the hybrid dihedral style does not store
dihedral coefficient info for individual sub\sphinxhyphen{}styles in {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary
restart files}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{write_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{data files}}}}.  Thus when
restarting a simulation, you need to re\sphinxhyphen{}specify the dihedral\_coeff
commands.

\section{dihedral\_style lepton command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_lepton:dihedral-style-lepton-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_lepton:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_lepton:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_lepton::doc}}

Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{lepton/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_lepton:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_lepton:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lepton}

\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{k*(1 + d*cos(n*phi)); k=75.0; d=1; n=2}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{45*(1\PYGZhy{}cos(4*phi))}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{k2*cos(phi) + k3*cos(phi)\PYGZca{}2; k2=100.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{k*(phi\PYGZhy{}phi0)\PYGZca{}2; k=85.0; phi0=120.0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_lepton:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{versionmodified,added}{Added in version 8Feb2023.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dihedral style \sphinxstyleemphasis{lepton} computes dihedral interactions between four
atoms forming a dihedral angle with a custom potential function.  The
potential function must be provided as an expression string using “phi”
as the dihedral angle variable.  For example \sphinxtitleref{“200.0*(phi\sphinxhyphen{}120.0)\textasciicircum{}2”}
represents a {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{quadratic dihedral}}}} potential
around a 120 degree dihedral angle with a force constant \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} of 200.0
energy units:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U_{dihedral,i} = K (\phi_i - \phi_0)^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxhref{https://simtk.org/projects/lepton}{Lepton library}, that the
\sphinxstyleemphasis{lepton} dihedral style interfaces with, evaluates this expression
string at run time to compute the pairwise energy.  It also creates an
analytical representation of the first derivative of this expression
with respect to “phi” and then uses that to compute the force between
the dihedral atoms as defined by the topology data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The potential function expression for each dihedral type is provided via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands.  The expression is in energy units.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The Lepton expression must be either enclosed in quotes or must not
contain any whitespace so that LAMMPS recognizes it as a single keyword.
More on valid Lepton expressions below.  Dihedral angles are internally
computed in radians and thus the expression must assume “phi” is in
radians.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\sphinxAtStartPar
Numbers may be given in either decimal or exponential form.  All of the
following are valid numbers: \sphinxtitleref{5}, \sphinxtitleref{\sphinxhyphen{}3.1}, \sphinxtitleref{1e6}, and \sphinxtitleref{3.12e\sphinxhyphen{}2}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an extension to the standard Lepton syntax, it is also possible to
use LAMMPS {\hyperref[\detokenize{variable::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{variables}}}} in the format “v\_name”.  Before
evaluating the expression, “v\_name” will be replaced with the value of
the variable “name”.  This is compatible with all kinds of scalar
variables, but not with vectors, arrays, local, or per\sphinxhyphen{}atom
variables.  If necessary, a custom scalar variable needs to be defined
that can access the desired (single) item from a non\sphinxhyphen{}scalar variable.
As an example, the following lines will instruct LAMMPS to ramp
the force constant for a harmonic bond from 100.0 to 200.0 during the
next run:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{variable }\PYG{n+nv+nvIdentifier}{fconst}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{equal}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ramp}\PYG{n+nv}{(}\PYG{n+nv}{100.0, 200}\PYG{n+nv}{)}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{lepton}
\PYG{k}{bond\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{v\PYGZus{}fconst * (r\PYGZca{}2)}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
An expression may be followed by definitions for intermediate values that appear in the
expression. A semicolon “;” is used as a delimiter between value definitions. For example,
the expression:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{o}{\PYGZca{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{n}{b}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{b}\PYG{o}{\PYGZca{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{a}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{b}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{n}{b1}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{b2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
is exactly equivalent to

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{\PYGZca{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{a1}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{a2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{b1}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{b2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{b1}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{b2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{\PYGZca{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The definition of an intermediate value may itself involve other
intermediate values. Whitespace and quotation characters (’\textquotesingle{}’ and ‘”’)
are ignored.  All uses of a value must appear \sphinxstyleemphasis{before} that value’s
definition.  For efficiency reasons, the expression string is parsed,
optimized, and then stored in an internal, pre\sphinxhyphen{}parsed representation for
evaluation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Evaluating a Lepton expression is typically between 2.5 and 5 times
slower than the corresponding compiled and optimized C++ code.  If
additional speed or GPU acceleration (via GPU or KOKKOS) is required,
the interaction can be represented as a table.  Suitable table files
can be created either internally using the {\hyperref[\detokenize{pair_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{pair\_write}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{bond_write::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{bond\_write}}}} command or through the Python scripts
in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Tools:tabulate}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{tools/tabulate}}}} folder.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script

{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_multi_harmonic:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{multi/harmonic} dihedral style uses the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \sum_{n=1,5} A_n  \cos^{n-1}(\phi)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_2\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_3\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_4\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_5\) (energy)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}

\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{10.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{20.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{30.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_nharmonic:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{nharmonic} dihedral style uses the potential:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \sum_{i=1,n} A_i  \cos^{i-1}(\phi)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n\) (integer \textgreater{}=1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_2\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_n\) (energy)

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_opls:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{opls} dihedral style uses the potential
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = & \frac{1}{2} K_1 [1 + \cos(\phi)] + \frac{1}{2} K_2 [1 - \cos(2 \phi)] + \\
    & \frac{1}{2} K_3 [1 + \cos(3 \phi)] + \frac{1}{2} K_4 [1 - \cos(4 \phi)]\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that the usual 1/2 factor is not included in the K values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This dihedral potential is used in the OPLS force field and is
described in {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_opls:watkins}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(Watkins)}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the data file or restart files read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}} commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_2\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_3\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_4\) (energy)

\end{itemize}

\section{dihedral\_style quadratic command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic:dihedral-style-quadratic-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic:index-1}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Accelerator Variants: \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic/omp}


\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{quadratic}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{quadratic}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{80.0}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_quadratic:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{quadratic} dihedral style uses the potential:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = K (\phi - \phi_0)^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This dihedral potential can be used to keep a dihedral in a predefined
value (cis=zero, right\sphinxhyphen{}hand convention is used).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example
above, or in the data file or restart files read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} or {\hyperref[\detokenize{read_restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_restart}}}}
commands:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\phi_0\) (degrees)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\phi_0\) is specified in degrees, but LAMMPS converts it to
radians internally; hence \(K\) is effectively energy per
radian\textasciicircum{}2.

\section{dihedral\_style spherical command}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_spherical:dihedral-style-spherical-command}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_spherical:index-0}}\label{\detokenize{dihedral_spherical::doc}}

\subsection{Syntax}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_spherical:syntax}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Examples}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_spherical:examples}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{286.1}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{124}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{90.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{90.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{l+m}{69.3}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{93.9}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{90}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{90}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                    }\PYG{l+m}{49.1}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{74.4}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}
\PYG{+w}{                    }\PYG{l+m}{25.2}\PYG{+w}{   }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.00}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0}\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{48.1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_spherical:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{spherical} dihedral style uses the potential:

\noindent{\hspace*{\fill}\sphinxincludegraphics{{dihedral_spherical_angles}.jpg}\hspace*{\fill}}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(\phi,\theta_1,\theta_2) & = \sum_{i=1}^N\nolimits\ C_i\ \Phi_i(\phi)\ \Theta_{1i}(\theta_1)\ \Theta_{2i}(\theta_2) \\
\Phi_{i}(\phi)            & = u_i - \mathrm{cos}((\phi   - a_i)K_i) \\
\Theta_{1i}(\theta_1)     & = v_i - \mathrm{cos}((\theta_1-b_i)L_i) \\
\Theta_{2i}(\theta_2)     & = w_i - \mathrm{cos}((\theta_2-c_i)M_i)\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For this dihedral style, the energy can be any function that combines the
4\sphinxhyphen{}body dihedral\sphinxhyphen{}angle (\(\phi\)) and the two 3\sphinxhyphen{}body bond\sphinxhyphen{}angles
(\(\theta_1\), \(\theta_2\)).
For this reason, there is usually no need to define 3\sphinxhyphen{}body “angle” forces
separately for the atoms participating in these interactions.
It is probably more efficient to incorporate 3\sphinxhyphen{}body angle forces into
the dihedral interaction even if it requires adding additional terms to
the expansion (as was done in the second example).  A careful choice of
parameters can prevent singularities that occur with traditional
force\sphinxhyphen{}fields whenever theta1 or theta2 approach 0 or 180 degrees.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The last example above corresponds to an interaction with a single energy
minima located near \(\phi=93.9\), \(\theta_1=74.4\),
\(\theta_2=48.1\) degrees, and it remains numerically stable at all
angles (\(\phi\), \(\theta_1\), \(\theta_2\)). In this example,
the coefficients 49.1, and 25.2 can be physically interpreted as the
harmonic spring constants for theta1 and theta2 around their minima.
The coefficient 69.3 is the harmonic spring constant for phi after
division by sin(74.4)*sin(48.1) (the minima positions for theta1 and theta2).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The following coefficients must be defined for each dihedral type via the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above, or in
the Dihedral Coeffs section of a data file read by the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{read_data::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{read\_data}}}} command:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n\) (integer \textgreater{}= 1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_1\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_1\) (typically an integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a_1\) (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(u_1\) (typically 0.0 or 1.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(L_1\) (typically an integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(b_1\) (degrees, typically 0.0 or 90.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(v_1\) (typically 0.0 or 1.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(M_1\) (typically an integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(c_1\) (degrees, typically 0.0 or 90.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(w_1\) (typically 0.0 or 1.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{[}…{]}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_n\) (energy)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(K_n\) (typically an integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a_n\) (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(u_n\) (typically 0.0 or 1.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(L_n\) (typically an integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(b_n\) (degrees, typically 0.0 or 90.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(v_n\) (typically 0.0 or 1.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(M_n\) (typically an integer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(c_n\) (degrees, typically 0.0 or 90.0)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(w_n\) (typically 0.0 or 1.0)

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_spherical:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This dihedral style can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the

\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}style}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{n}{cut}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{linear}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1000}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{aat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{1.0}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{177}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{180}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{DIH\PYGZus{}TABLE1}
\PYG{k}{dihedral\PYGZus{}coeff}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{2}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{aat}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{0.5}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{170}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{180}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{file.table}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{DIH\PYGZus{}TABLE2}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsection{Description}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_table:description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} and \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/cut} dihedral styles create interpolation tables
of length \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} from dihedral potential and derivative values listed
in a file(s) as a function of the dihedral angle “phi”.  The files are
read by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command.  For
dihedral style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/cut} additionally an analytic cutoff that is
quadratic in the bond\sphinxhyphen{}angle (theta) is applied in order to regularize
the dihedral interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The interpolation tables are created by fitting cubic splines to the
file values and interpolating energy and derivative values at each of
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} dihedral angles. During a simulation, these tables are used
to interpolate energy and force values on individual atoms as
needed. The interpolation is done in one of 2 styles: \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} or
\sphinxstyleemphasis{spline}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} style, the dihedral angle (phi) is used to find 2
surrounding table values from which an energy or its derivative is
computed by linear interpolation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the \sphinxstyleemphasis{spline} style, cubic spline coefficients are computed and
stored at each of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} evenly\sphinxhyphen{}spaced values in the
interpolated table.  For a given dihedral angle (phi), the appropriate
coefficients are chosen from this list, and a cubic polynomial is used
to compute the energy and the derivative at this angle.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For dihedral style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} the following coefficients must be defined
for each dihedral type via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}
command as in the example above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The filename specifies a file containing tabulated energy and derivative
values. The keyword specifies which section of the file to read.  The
format of this file is the same for both dihedral styles and described
below.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For dihedral style \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/cut} the following coefficients must be
defined for each dihedral type via the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command as in the example above.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
style (= aat)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff prefactor (unitless)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff angle1 (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
cutoff angle2 (degrees)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filename

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
keyword

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cutoff dihedral style uses a tabulated dihedral interaction with a
cutoff function:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f(\theta) & = K \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \theta < \theta_1 \\
f(\theta) & = K \left(1-\frac{(\theta - \theta_1)^2}{(\theta_2 - \theta_1)^2}\right) \qquad \theta_1 < \theta < \theta_2\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The cutoff includes a prefactor \sphinxstyleemphasis{K} to the cutoff function \(f(\theta)\).
While this value would ordinarily be 1, there may be situations where the value
could be different.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cutoff \(\theta_1\) specifies the angle (in degrees) below which
the dihedral interaction is unmodified, i.e. the cutoff function is 1.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The cutoff function is applied between \(\theta_1\) and
\(\theta_2\), which is the angle at which the cutoff function drops
to zero.  The value of zero effectively “turns off” the dihedral
interaction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The filename specifies a file containing tabulated energy and derivative
values. The keyword specifies which section of the file to read.  The
format of this file is the same for both dihedral styles and described
below.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Suitable tables for use with this dihedral style can be created using
the Python code in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tools/tabulate}} folder of the LAMMPS source
code distribution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The format of a tabulated file is as follows (without the
parenthesized comments).  It can begin with one or more comment
or blank lines.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYGZsh{} Table of the potential and its negative derivative

DIH\PYGZus{}TABLE1                   (keyword is the first text on line)
N 30 DEGREES                 (N, NOF, DEGREES, RADIANS, CHECKU/F)
                             (blank line)
1 \PYGZhy{}168.0 \PYGZhy{}1.40351172223 0.0423346818422
2 \PYGZhy{}156.0 \PYGZhy{}1.70447981034 0.00811786522531
3 \PYGZhy{}144.0 \PYGZhy{}1.62956100432 \PYGZhy{}0.0184129719987
...
30 180.0 \PYGZhy{}0.707106781187 0.0719306095245

\PYGZsh{} Example 2: table of the potential. Forces omitted

DIH\PYGZus{}TABLE2
N 30 NOF CHECKU testU.dat CHECKF testF.dat

1 \PYGZhy{}168.0 \PYGZhy{}1.40351172223
2 \PYGZhy{}156.0 \PYGZhy{}1.70447981034
3 \PYGZhy{}144.0 \PYGZhy{}1.62956100432
...
30 180.0 \PYGZhy{}0.707106781187
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A section begins with a non\sphinxhyphen{}blank line whose first character is not a
“\#”; blank lines or lines starting with “\#” can be used as comments
between sections. The first line begins with a keyword which
identifies the section. The line can contain additional text, but the
initial text must match the argument specified in the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}} command. The next line lists (in
any order) one or more parameters for the table. Each parameter is a
keyword followed by one or more numeric values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Following a blank line, the next N lines list the tabulated values. On
each line, the first value is the index from 1 to N, the second value is
the angle value, the third value is the energy (in energy units), and
the fourth is \sphinxhyphen{}dE/d(phi) also in energy units). The third term is the
energy of the 4\sphinxhyphen{}atom configuration for the specified angle.  The fourth
term (when present) is the negative derivative of the energy with
respect to the angle (in degrees, or radians depending on whether the
user selected DEGREES or RADIANS).  Thus the units of the last term
are still energy, not force. The dihedral angle values must increase
from one line to the next.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dihedral table splines are cyclic.  There is no discontinuity at 180
degrees (or at any other angle).  Although in the examples above, the
angles range from \sphinxhyphen{}180 to 180 degrees, in general, the first angle in
the list can have any value (positive, zero, or negative).  However
the \sphinxstyleemphasis{range} of angles represented in the table must be \sphinxstyleemphasis{strictly} less
than 360 degrees (2pi radians) to avoid angle overlap.  (You may not
supply entries in the table for both 180 and \sphinxhyphen{}180, for example.)  If
the user’s table covers only a narrow range of dihedral angles,
strange numerical behavior can occur in the large remaining gap.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Parameters:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parameter “N” is required and its value is the number of table
entries that follow. Note that this may be different than the N
specified in the {\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_style::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_style table}}}} command.
Let \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} is the number of table entries requested dihedral\_style
command, and let \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfile} be the parameter following “N” in the
tabulated file (“30” in the sparse example above).  What LAMMPS does
is a preliminary interpolation by creating splines using the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfile}
tabulated values as nodal points.  It uses these to interpolate as
needed to generate energy and derivative values at \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} different
points (which are evenly spaced over a 360 degree range, even if the
angles in the file are not).  The resulting tables of length \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable}
are then used as described above, when computing energy and force for
individual dihedral angles and their atoms.  This means that if you
want the interpolation tables of length \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} to match exactly what
is in the tabulated file (with effectively nopreliminary
interpolation), you should set \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} = \sphinxstyleemphasis{Nfile}.  To ensure the
nodal points in the user’s file are aligned with the interpolated
table entries, the angles in the table should be integer multiples of
360/\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} degrees, or 2*PI/\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} radians (depending on your
choice of angle units).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional “NOF” keyword allows the user to omit the forces
(negative energy derivatives) from the table file (normally located in
the fourth column).  In their place, forces will be calculated
automatically by differentiating the potential energy function
indicated by the third column of the table (using either linear or
spline interpolation).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional “DEGREES” keyword allows the user to specify angles in
degrees instead of radians (default).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional “RADIANS” keyword allows the user to specify angles in
radians instead of degrees.  (Note: This changes the way the forces
are scaled in the fourth column of the data file.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional “CHECKU” keyword is followed by a filename.  This allows
the user to save all of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} different entries in the
interpolated energy table to a file to make sure that the interpolated
function agrees with the user’s expectations.  (Note: You can
temporarily increase the \sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable} parameter to a high value for this
purpose.  “\sphinxstyleemphasis{Ntable}“ is explained above.)

\sphinxAtStartPar
The optional “CHECKF” keyword is analogous to the “CHECKU” keyword.
It is followed by a filename, and it allows the user to check the
interpolated force table.  This option is available even if the user
selected the “NOF” option.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Note that one file can contain many sections, each with a tabulated
potential. LAMMPS reads the file section by section until it finds one
that matches the specified keyword.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Styles with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{gpu}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{intel}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{kk}, \sphinxstyleemphasis{omp}, or \sphinxstyleemphasis{opt} suffix are
functionally the same as the corresponding style without the suffix.
They have been optimized to run faster, depending on your available
hardware, as discussed on the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}}
page.  The accelerated styles take the same arguments and should
produce the same results, except for round\sphinxhyphen{}off and precision issues.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These accelerated styles are part of the GPU, INTEL, KOKKOS,
OPENMP, and OPT packages, respectively.  They are only enabled if
LAMMPS was built with those packages.  See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} page for more info.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can specify the accelerated styles explicitly in your input script
by including their suffix, or you can use the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Run_options::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{\sphinxhyphen{}suffix command\sphinxhyphen{}line switch}}}} when you invoke LAMMPS, or you can use the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{suffix::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{suffix}}}} command in your input script.

\sphinxAtStartPar
See the {\hyperref[\detokenize{Speed_packages::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Accelerator packages}}}} page for more
instructions on how to use the accelerated styles effectively.


\subsection{Restart, fix\_modify, output, run start/stop, minimize info}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_table:restart-fix-modify-output-run-start-stop-minimize-info}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These dihedral styles write the settings for the “dihedral\_style table”
or “dihedral\_style table/cut” command to {\hyperref[\detokenize{restart::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{binary restart files}}}}, so a dihedral\_style command does not need to specified in an
input script that reads a restart file.  However, the coefficient
information loaded from the table file(s) is not stored in the restart
file, since it is tabulated in the potential files.  Thus, suitable
dihedral\_coeff commands do need to be specified in the restart input
script after reading the restart file.


\subsection{Restrictions}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_table:restrictions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstyleemphasis{table} dihedral style can only be used if LAMMPS was built with the
MOLECULE package.  The \sphinxstyleemphasis{table/cut} dihedral style can only be used if
LAMMPS was built with the EXTRA\sphinxhyphen{}MOLECULE package. See the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{Build_package::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Build package}}}} doc page for more info.

\label{\detokenize{dihedral_table:related-commands}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{dihedral_coeff::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{dihedral\_coeff}}}}


\subsection{Default}
\label{\detokenize{dihedral_table:default}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
